# Christologia Sacra


## 1 First Disputation. On the eternal deity of Christ

Thesis I.

Since in this Article concerning Christ there is nothing to be said beyond what is clear from the sacred utterances, His commendation cannot be greater than that which is taken from the Old and New Testaments themselves. Let us therefore hear that of Jeremiah: Let him who glories glory in this, says JEHOVAH, to know and to know me, etc. Which Paul applies to our Savior, and from thence concludes: I did not judge myself to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ and Him crucified.

II. For he who knows Him has progressed most in Theology, since this is eternal life, as Christ Himself attests: that they may know You, (the Father) the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent. With which that of the Wise Man harmonizes: To know You, O God, is perfect justice, and to know Your justice and power is the root of immortality.

III. Let all things therefore, when compared to Christ, be vile as ζημίαν (loss) and σκύβαλα (refuse). Let our philosophy, as Bernard says, be the more sublime one: to know JESUS and Him crucified. To love Him surpasses all knowledge.

IV. Truly, therefore, χριστογνωσία (knowledge of Christ) is and is called the nucleus of all Theological wisdom, the foundation of religious practice, the sum of eternal salvation, and the metropolis of the Christian faith, which being attacked, the whole of Christianity collapses.

V. As this article concerning Christ is highly fruitful, so it is also most sublime. It is to be wondered at here, not to be pried into, since it is confessedly a great mystery of godliness, into which even the angels desire to παρακύψαι (look). This is that miraculously singular and singularly miraculous thing which Damascenus called the most new of all new things, which is the only new thing under the sun. Closing the eyes of reason to its sublimity, let us submit ourselves with a fisherman's faith, lest we be led astray from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus.

VI. There are indeed two parts of Christology, the former of which treats of the person, the latter of the office of the person: concerning the former we shall be concerned through several Disputations by this method.

VII. It will treat 1. of the true Deity of Christ, 2. of his true Humanity, 3. of the Incarnation of the Word, 4. of the formation of the flesh of Christ, 5. of the assumption of the flesh of Christ, 6. of the union of the two natures in Christ considered generally, 7. of Nestorianism, 8. of Eutychianism, 9. of the true manner of the personal union, 10. of the communication of the hypostasis, 11. of the communication of the natures, 12. of the personal predications, God loved every work and word.

IIX. Believing by the catholic faith that Christ is God-man, they gather that divinity and humanity are joined in Christ, without the prior knowledge of which, the personal union, of which they are the material, cannot be conveniently taught. Therefore, we shall now treat first of the Divinity of Christ, and we shall consider: I. The term Nature. II. The divine nature itself specifically, where 1. the heretics attacking it, 2. the titles attributed to Christ regarding his divinity. III. The demonstration of the Divinity of Christ. IV. We shall briefly review and propose practical meditations.

Latin:

Thesis I.

CUm in hoc Articulo de Christo nihil præterea dicendum, nisi quæ ex sacris eloqviis clarènt, ipsius eommendatio major esse nõ potest, qvàm qvæ ex ipsis V. & N. Instrumentis sumitur. Audiamus ergo illud Jeremiæ: In hoc glorietur qui gloriatur, dicit JEHOVA, scire & nosse me, &c. Qvod Paulus ad Salvatorem nostrum adplicat, indeq́ve concludit; Non judicavi me scire aliqvid inter vos, nisi Jesum Christum & hunc crucifixum.

II. Hunc enim qui novit in Theologia plurimum profecit siqvidem hæc vita æterna est, attestante ipso Christo, ut cognoscant te, (patrem) solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Jesum Christum. Cui concinnat illud Sapientis: Nosse te, Deum, consummata justitia est, & scire justitiam & virtutem tuam radix est immortalitatis.

III. Sordeant ergo omnia ad Christum collata ut ζημίαν & σκύβαλα. Sit nostra, ut ait Bernhardus, sublimior Philosophia scire JESUM & hunc crucifixum. Hunc diligere superat omnem scientiam.

IV. Verè igitur χριστογνωσία est & dicitur omnis sapientiæ Theologicæ nucleus, religiosæ πράξεως fundamentum, æternæ salutis summa, & fidei Christianæ metropolis, qvâ oppugnatâ totus Christianismus labitur.

V. Ut autem summè fructuosus, sic & maximè sublimis est hic de Christo articulus. Mirandum hîc, non rimandum, qvippe ὁμολογουμένως magnum pietatis mysterium, in qvod & angeli gestiunt παρακύψαι. Hoc est illud mirabiliter singulare & singulariter mirabile, qvod Damascenus dixit omnium novorum maximè novum, quod solum novum sub sole. Illius sublimati oculos rationis claudentes piscatoriâ fide nos submittamus, ne excitamur à simplicitate, quæ est in Christo Jesu.

VI. Sunt verò χρηστολογίας duæ partes, qvarum prior de persona, posterior de personæ officio agit: De illa per aliqvot Disputationes hac methodo solliciti erimus.

VII. Aget 1. de vera Christi Deitate. 1. de vera ipsius Humanitate, 3. de Incarnatione ῤ λόγε, 4. de Carnis Christi formatione, 5. de carnis Christi assumptione. 6. de duarum naturarum in Christo unione generatim considerata. 7. de Nestorianismo, 8. de Euticheismo, 9. de vera unionis personalis ratione, 10. de communicatione ὑποςάσεως, 11. de communicatione naturarum, 12. de prædicationibus personalibus, Θεὸς ἡγάπα πάντος ἔργε καὶ λόγε.

IIX. Fide catholicâ credentes Christum homo-deum colligunt, in Christo conjungi divinitatem & humanitatem, qvibus non præcognitis de unione personali, cujus sunt materiale, commodè doceri neqvit. Igitur primò de Divinitate Christi nunc agemus, & considerabimus. I. Vocabulum Naturæ. II. Ipsam divinam naturam in specie, ubi 1. Hæreticos eam oppugnantes, 2. titulos Christo, qvoad divinitatem tributos. III. Divinitatis Christi ἀπόδειξιν. IV. Meditationes practicas breviter recensebimus & proponemus.


### Chapter I. Of the term Nature

CHAPTER I. Of the term Nature.

IX. The word nature, derived from being born, has various meanings both among philosophers and among theologians. We here attend only to that by which, for theologians, nature is the same as a certain complete substance constituted by its own essence, and having in itself the principle of all operations.

X. Four things are to be observed concerning this word: 1. that the Greek fathers, according to Damascene, hold ousia, physis, and morphe as synonyms, which nevertheless are distinguished by others such that the former signifies the bare essence, which is expressed by definition: the latter adds natural and essential properties: the third furthermore includes accidents, following nature, by which as if by colors ousia and physis are depicted.

XI. 2. The name of physis or nature does not apply to the Divinity according to the primary imposition of the words. For that is said as if from phyein or phyesthai, from becoming or being born, and thus physis is the action of the one producing and the passion of the one being produced. This is said of that thing which has been produced by the motion of generation and birth. For verbal nouns in our language signify a thing made by motion. But neither applies to God. Usage, however, has prevailed that we express divinity through the term of divine nature, since it is nature (not passively but) actively.

XII. 5. The Fathers here more willingly used the name of nature than of essence, so that Eutyches might be refuted more strongly, as he was confusing natures and the properties of natures, since nature, beyond οὐσίαν, also hints at the properties themselves.

XIII. The terms (God and man, Divine nature and human nature) indeed signify one thing, yet they differ as concrete and abstract. By the latter, the bare essence which is possessed is noted; by the former, the subject which possesses the essence, and thus one hypostasis is connoted.

XIV. Truly the Devil, a master of craft, in the state of creation wished to make a man a God, and thus he withdrew the created righteousness: On the contrary, in the state of restoration, he attempts to make a true God a mere man by attacking the divinity of Christ, so that he may withdraw eternal salvation from us. This opinion he instills outside the Church into Jews, Turks, and other gentiles. Within the Church, he tends toward the same end through his hosts of heretics.

XV. The Christ-fighters, however, are divided into ancient and recent. See those enumerated historically according to the centuries of years in the Magdeburg Centuries. We, because of the narrow limits of brevity, which both the nature of the theses and the paper dictate, will here present them reduced into certain classes according to the distribution of Chemnitz.

XVI. There are, therefore, three hosts of such heretics. The first of the ἀνυποςάτων, blaspheming that Christ began at his birth and did not exist at all before the incarnation, except in the idea of God. The second of the ἑτερουσίων, who indeed conceded that there was in Christ, besides the human nature, a certain other, the same heavenly and self-subsistent one, but that it was not of the same substance with the Father the Creator. The third of the ἀνομοίων, contending that the Son, although he is equal to the Father in substance, is nevertheless not similar in power and operation,

XVII. We call those recent who, after the reformation instituted by Luther, began to attack the divinity of Christ. Among whom today the Socinians, named after that ill-fated Faustus Socinus, lead the way.

XIIX. Furthermore, that things are not only expressed but also known through names, Theology also proves, since we know hardly anything more about God and his Son besides their names. Whence that well-known saying of the Hebrews שמו יהוה הוא שמו and that of the Christians: The name of Christ is the knowledge of Christ. For which reason our Theology is in large part nominal, and the divine Theologian is called a Grammarian. XIX. We therefore rightly begin from the titles given to Christ regarding his divinity, and they are either ἔγγραφοι or Biblical, or ἄγραφοι or Ecclesiastical, adopted by the orthodox fathers. Among those, God, Son of God, and λόγος are preeminent.

XX. The word GOD is considered either absolutely, concerning the divine essence, and signifies the three persons conjointly; or determinately, as it denotes the divine essence limited by a certain character, and therefore restricted to this or that person: thus we accept the name of GOD here, and by it the Son of GOD is always specifically denoted.

XXI. Furthermore, it is commonly said that God has four sons: 1. begotten from eternity, who is the λόγος. 2. created in time, who is Adam. 3. born of Mary, who is Christ, as man. 4. adopted, who is any Christian whatsoever. Here we speak only of the first. And we call that a Son which, produced from the essence of some intelligent substance, is similar to it in nature. The λόγος, therefore, produced from the essence of God, is similar to God and thus is likewise God. Whence he is expressly called the Son of God, and indeed not made, but begotten, nay, the Only-begotten on account of the lack of fellow-begotten ones.

XXII. Regarding the word λόγος, it is asked: 1. What does it signify? As to its first imposition, it denotes a word, for it is from λέγειν, to speak: because men, angels, and God speak, there is a threefold word: human, angelic, and divine. Otherwise, it is taken: 1. for the reason of man and is called λόγος ἔμφυτος; 2. for the concept of the mind and is called ἐνδιάθετος; 3. for the word whether written or spoken aloud and is called προφορικός. But here it is clearly taken in a heavenly sense for the λόγος ὄυσιώδῃ and ὑφεςῶτι.

XXIII. 2. In what sense and for what reasons is the Son of God called λόγος? There is a twofold reason for the appellation; the former concerns GOD, the latter concerns men: The former concerns eternal generation; the latter manifests his office. With respect to the Deity, he is the internal word and is similar to the λόγος ἐνδιάθετος on account of the mode of generation of the mental concept and the real difference by which it is distinguished from the mind. With respect to his office, he is the external word, and is similar to the λόγος προφορικός on account of certain conveniences with the external word, which see in the Lectures of the President.

XXIV. 2. How should the word λόγος be translated? Some render it by 'sermo' (discourse), others by 'ratio' (reason). For us, that version by which it is rendered as 'verbum' (word), is favored 1. on account of the respect for both, concerning which in the preceding thesis, in this word inclusion. 2. on account of the simplicity of the meaning. 3. on account of the indication of a greater mystery. 4. on account of the agreement of the Chaldean paraphrast and the fathers receiving that word as if into the canon.

XXV. 4. Did John first and alone attribute the title λόγος to the Son of God? This is denied by the clear letter of Ps. 33:6, 2 Sam. 7:20, 2 Sam. 23:2, and by the Chaldean paraphrase very often rendering the word יהוה and אלהים by מימר, to intimate that the discourse in the text is about the Son of God, as in Gen. 24:5, ch. 48:21, Isa. 8:5, Hos. 1:7, and elsewhere. Furthermore, the passage Heb. 4:12 is not inconveniently understood as much of the prophetic word as of the spoken word. Others add Luke 1:2.

XXVI. 5. Does it signify the whole subsistent after the incarnation, or only the simple person? The latter is preferred, for the reason that the word λόγος is found used nowhere for a composite person in either a Biblical or Ecclesiastical sense, since by λόγος is always understood the uniting one who assumes, which is only a simple hypostasis. The same is proven by the mode of speaking, by which we say Christ consists of the incarnate λόγος and the assumed flesh, which shines forth further from personal predications (as the λόγος is man, and conversely) and of the communication of properties (the λόγος has suffered) in which the λόγος is taken not for the whole Christ, but for the assuming person.

XXVII. The remaining names are Jehovah Jer. 23:6, Jehovah of hosts Isa. 47:4, God of Israel Amos 4:12, God the Savior Isa. 12:2, Adonai ch. 4:4, Adonai Jehovah ch. 40:10, Jehovah most high Ps. 47:3, Ruler Mic. 5:2, Sun of Righteousness Mal. 4:2, Wisdom Prov. 8:1, μονογενὴς John 1:18, Power of God 1 Cor. 1:24, image of God (substantial) Col. 1:18, Brightness of the glory of God and the express image of his substance Heb. 1:3, Beginning and end Rev. 1:8, First and last ch. 13:11, Lord of lords ch. 17:14.

XXIIX. Among ecclesiastical titles, they obtain the primacy. 1. αὐτόθεος. It is said so, however, with respect to the divine nature. For it is not from a superior principle, but God from himself, and as the λόγος operates from himself, and through himself, and from no other, so also he is from himself, and through himself, and from no other. Considered personally, however, the λόγος is not said to be so, since in that respect he has his divinity not from himself, but from the Father. In short: αὐτόθεος is with respect to temporal production, he is not αὐτόθεος with respect to personal production. 2. ὁμούσιος, by which word both the unity of essence and the real distinction of persons are significantly hinted at, and that word cannot easily be eluded by adversaries through any crafty interpretation.

XXIX. Furthermore. And if in the Article of the Trinity, as in its proper seat, the eternal existence of the Son of God is demonstrated, and is here presupposed by us as sufficiently proven there, since the Son of God is not considered here absolutely as he is a simple person, but with respect to the incarnation, as he personally united flesh to himself, we shall nevertheless submit four testimonies confirming the Divinity of Christ out of abundance.

XXX. The first exists in Gen. 48, in which is contained a blessing (not of charity, by which we pray well for every neighbor, but) of authority, and indeed Patriarchal, which is an invocation of the devout, by which Jacob prayed that the promises might be fulfilled in his sons.

XXXI. Moreover, there are three objects to be noted in that [passage]: 1. To whom, 2. what, 3. by whom, Jacob prayed. The former were Ephraim and Manasseh, v. 16. The latter are goods both corporal and spiritual, among which the primary one is the assumption into the covenant of grace, and preservation in the same. For in general the Hebrew phrase (to call a name upon someone) expresses the profession or adoption and denomination of a name: But in particular, when there is talk of the name of the Patriarchs, it is to be reckoned in the covenant and to become a participant in all the promises made to the Fathers: This is described by three epithets. 1. He is called GOD, before whom the Fathers walked, 2. GOD who fed Jacob from his youth. 3. The Angel delivering him from all evil.

XXXII. The Orthodox observe here the singular number in the verb 'let him bless,' by which they judge the unity of the divine essence and the trinity of persons to be hinted at, understanding by the God of the Patriarchs, the Father; by the God feeding, the Holy Spirit; by the Angel, the Son of GOD, who is otherwise called the angel of the divine face, and the angel of the Covenant. What the Photinians may except here in the very conflict of the Disputation, we shall see ξυν̓ θεῷ.

XXXIII. The second is from the first three verses of chapter 1 of John. taken, in which such predicates are attributed to the λόγος (whom we presuppose here to denote the Son of God, who is substantially the word of the eternal Father), which firmly establish the divinity of Christ.

XXXIV. And it is taken 1. From the existence ἐν ἀρχῇ. The word ἀρχὴs, however, hints at 1. the beginning of time and creation. 2. any beginning outside of GOD, which can be thought of or posited before creation. 3. eternity itself. For that which was indefinitely ἐν ἀρχῇ, that must certainly be eternal. Hence the phrases ἐν ἀρχῇ or ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς denote eternity, as in 2 Thess. 2:13, and whatever beginning you may assume, it is nevertheless true and remains: In the beginning was the Word.

XXXV. II. It is from the existence πρὸς τὸν θεόν. The word ὁ θεὸς is taken here restrictively for the person of the Father, which the prefixed article also teaches. Next, ἦν is to be noted, by which a perpetual state is signified. Thirdly, it is said πρὸς τὸν θεὸν to indicate a peculiar subsistence.

XXXVI. III. It is taken from the express appellation of God, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. He, therefore, who is called God absolutely, is in reality true and eternal God. For this is what is sought: is Christ true God? John answers, the Word was God, which he declares more expressly in 1 John 5:20.

XXXVII. IV. It is taken from the creation of things, which can be ascribed to nothing but a substance subsisting by itself and indeed a divine one, whose work it is alone, Isa. 41:20, ch. 45:7.

XXXIIX. The third is that of John 8:58. Where, especially against the Photinians, it is to be noted 1. The words γενέσθαι and εἶναι are placed here absolutely and without addition, therefore they cannot be understood otherwise than of existence. 2. I am, is a verb of predication, not of the third but of the second element. 3. Distinct names are not placed in the text; it is not said before Abram becomes Abraham, but absolutely before Abraham came to be, etc. He, therefore, who was before Abraham came to be or existed, did not begin to exist for the first time in the last times of the world. And consequently, Christ, besides the human nature assumed from Mary, consists of another, prior and existing before Abraham, which cannot be other than divine.

XXXIX. The fourth we take from Rom. 9:5. Where Christ is called ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων Θεὸς εὐλόγητος εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας ἀμὴν, which eulogium is the property of the one true God alone, as is evident from Rom. 1:5, 2 Cor. 1:3, Eph. 1:3, 1 Pet. 1:3. Nor can this doxology be referred to God the Father without great dislocation of the text, as the Arians wish, as the very inspection of the text clearly shows, indicating the subject. In what respect, according to which part, it is fitting for Christ to be from the fathers, namely, according to the flesh. What need is there for this limitation, if Christ had no other nature besides the flesh?

XL. Finally. Although it is better to treat moral matters 'επιδημίᾳ (popularly) rather than ἀκαδημαικῶς (academically), yet, since they also pertain to a full treatment of Christology, we do not wish to leave them entirely untouched here, at least by indicating one or two of them.

XLI. We are taught therefore 1. from thesis 15, 16, 17, not to take offense at the multitude of heresies. Satan possesses antiquity; he is always the adversary of God. What wonder is it, therefore, if even in this last old age of the world he strives to attack the Church with mines through so many heretics, since he did the same in the time of Christ and the primitive Church. 2. That we observe the causes both of heresies and of divine permission. Among the former, the primary one is arrogant pride. For unless heretics had first swelled in their hearts, they would not arrive at the contests of perverse assertion, says Gregory; among the latter shine forth I. The notification of the Church. For the more it is hindered, the more conspicuous it is rendered. II. The purgation of the Church. For truly heresies are the purgations of the Church. III. The illustration of the truth. Heretics indeed seem like snuffers, at first obscuring the light of the Church, but afterwards it arises more clearly, etc.

XLII. The enumeration of the divine names in thesis 18 and following serves 1. for doctrine, so that from them we may rightly know Christ and his majesty; 2. for consolation. For what can Satan, the world, and the flesh do against us, when our Christ is GOD, Lord of Lords, the mighty God, etc.; 3. for correction. Let us amend our lives lest we provoke Christ. For if he is offended, God is offended, who is an avenger having fury, being angry with his enemies, Nah. 1:2.

XLIII. Concerning the third member, it is asked, why it was necessary for the redeemer to be true GOD? We know no causes a priori, since here the will of the maker is the entire reason for the deed; a posteriori, however, two causes we gather: the first is the magnitude of the evil. There was upon us the wrath of God, the curse of the law, the tyranny of the Devil, etc., from which evils no one but God could deliver us. The second is the magnitude of the good to be conferred upon us, such as reconciliation with God the Father, the restoration of the divine image, the fulfillment of the law, the revelation of the Gospel, protection from the tyranny of the Devil, etc. All of which can come to us from no one but God alone.

XLIV. Let us therefore acknowledge with a grateful heart such great philanthropy of God. By grace He gave, when we were not, that we might be; by grace He gave, when we were lost, that we might be well. Therefore.

Through ages knowing no limit, to the supreme Father be glory and honor, with the Son, and the Spirit the Paraclete. Amen.

Latin:

CAPUT I. De voce Naturæ.

IX. Naturæ vox à nascendo dicta, varias habet tùm apud Philosophos, tùm apud Theologos significationes. Nos hîc illam saltem attendimur, qvâ Theologis natura idem est, qvod substantia qvædam completa per ὑσίαν suam constituta, & in se habens principium omnium operationum.

X. Observentur circa hanc vocem qvatuor, 1. patres Græcos teste Damasceno, ὐσίαν φύσιν & μόρφην pro synonymis habere, qvæ tamen aliis sic distingvuntur, ut illa significet essentiam nudam, qvæ exprimitur per definitionem: Ista superaddat proprietates naturales & essentiales: Hæc insuper includat accidentia, naturam seqventia, qvibus qvasi coloribus ὐσία & φύσις depinguntur.

XI. 2. Divinitate neqve φύσεως neqve naturæ nomen competere juxta primam vocum impositionem. Illud enim dicitur ὡς εἰ τὸ φύειν vel φύεσθαι, à fiendo vel nascendo, adeoq; φύσις est actio τῦ φύεντος & passio τῦ φυομένε. Hoc de illa re dicitur, qvæ motu generationis ac nativitatis producta est. Verbalia enim in nostra appellatione rem motu factam significant. Utrumqve autem in Deum non cadit. Usus tamen obtinuit, ut divinitatem per terminum naturæ divinæ exprimamus, qvippe (non passivè sed) activè natura est.

XII. 5. Patres hîc libentius nomen naturæ, quàm essentiæ usurpasse, ut eo fortius refutaretur Eutyches, naturas naturarumq; proprietates confundens quum natura præter ὐσίαν ipsas quoque proprietates subinnuat.

XIII. Voces (Deus & homo, Divina natura & humana natura) rem quidem unam dicere, attamen ut concretum & abstractum differre. Per has notatur nuda essentia, quæ habetur: per illas subjectum, quod habet essentiam, adeoque hypostasis una connotatur.

XIV. Verè Diabolus μυελοτεχνὴς in statu confectionis ex homine mero voluit facere Deum, & ita concreatam justitiam subtraxit: Contra in statu refectionis ex vero Deo conatur facere hominem merum impugnando Christi divinitatem, ut nobis æternam salutem subtrahat. Hanc opinionem extra Ecclesiam instillat Judæis, Turcis, gentilibusq; aliis. In Ecclesia ad idem tendit per sua hæreticorum agmina.

XV. Dispescuntur autem χριςόμαχοι in veteres & recentes. Illos juxta annorum secula historicè enumerata, vide in Centuriis Magdeburgensibus. Nos ab angustos brevitatis, quam & natura thesium & charta dictitat, limites, hîc eos in certas classes juxta distributionem Chemnitii redactos exhibebimus.

XVI. Tria ergo sunt talium hæreticorum agmina Primum τῶν ἀνυποςάτων, blasphemantium Christum per nativitatem primùm cepisse & ante incarnationem prorsus non extitisse, nisi in idea Dei.- Alterum τῶν ἑτερουσίων, qui concessêre quidem in Christo præter naturam humanam esse qvandam aliam, eandem cœlestem, & per se subsistentem, verum non esse ejusdem substantiæ cum patre creatore. Tertium τῶν ἀνομοίων, contendentium, Filium, quamvis patri æqvalis sit in substantiâ, tamen non esse simile potentiâ & operatione,

XVII. Recentes dicimus, qui post reformationem à Luthero institutam Christi divinitatem oppugnare cœperunt. Inter quos hodiè Sociniani, ab infausto illo Fausto Socino dicti, familiam ducunt.

XIIX. Porrò per nomina non tantùm res efferri sed & cognosci, etiam Theologia comprobat, cum de Deo, ipsiusq; Filio præter nomina vix plura sciamus. Unde scitum illud hebræorum שמו יהוה הוא שמו & illud Christianorum: Nomen Christi est notitia Christi. Quam ob rem Theologia nostra magna ex parte nominalis, & Theologus divinus Grammaticus dicitur. XIX. A titulis ergò Christo qvoad divinitatem datis, rectè incipimus & sunt illi vel ἔγγραφοι seu Biblici, vel ἄγραφοι seu Ecclesiastici ob Orthodoxis patribus adsumpti. Inter illos eminent Deus Filius Dei, λόγος.

XX. Vox DEI consideratur vel absolutè, de divina essentia, & tres personas conjunctim significat; vel determinatè, prout notat divinam essentiam certo charactere limitatam, ideoq; in hac aut illa persona restrictam: ita nomen DEI hic adcipimus, semperq; per id DEI Filius in specie notatur.

XXI. Deinde qvatuor filios Deum habere, vulgò dicitur 1. genitum ab æterno, qvi λόγος. 2. creatum. in tempore, qvi Adam. 3. natum ex Maria, qvi Christus, qvà homo. 4. cooptatum, qvi est Christianus qvilibet. De primo hîc tantum sermo. Et dicitur nobis Filius id, qvod de essentia alicujus intelligentis substantiæ productum, simile est ei in natura. Λόγος igitur ex essentia Dei productus, Deo similis atqve sic pariter Deus est. Unde expressè dicitur Dei filius, & qvidem non factus, sed genitus, imo Unigenitus ob genituræ sociorum carentiam.

XXII. Circa vocem λόγε qværitur 1. Qvid significet? Qvod ad primam impositionem notat verbum, est enim à λέγειν, dicere: qvia loqvuntur homines, angeli, Deus, triplex est verbum, humanum, angelicum, divinum. Aliàs sumitur 1. pro ratione hominis & dicitur λόγος ἔμφυτος, 2. pro conceptu mentis, & dicitur ἐνδιάθετος, 3. pro verbo sive scripto sive voce prolato, & dicitur προφορικός. Ast hîc planè cœlesti significatione sumitur pro λόγῳ ὄυσιώδῃ & ὑφεςῶτι.

XXIII. 2. Qvo sensu & ob quas causas Filius Dei dicatur λόγος? Duplex appellationis ratio est, prior DEUM, posterior homines concernit: Illa generationem æternam; hæc officium manifestat. Respectu Dietatis est verbum internum & similis est λόγω ἐνδιαθέτῳ ob conceptus mentalis generationis modum & differentiam realem, qva ille à mente distinguitur. Respectu officii externum verbum est, & est similis λόγῳ προφορικῷ ob qvasdam cum externo verbo convenientias, qvas vide in Prælect. Dn. Præsidis.

XXIV. 2. Quî vox λόγος verti debeat? Reddunt alij per sermonem, alii per rationem. Nobis versio illa, qvâ per verbum, Wort/ redditur. adridet 1. ob utriusq; respectus, de qvo thesi præced. in hac voce inclusionem. 2. ob significationis simplicitatem. 3. ob majoris mysterij indigitationem. 4. ob consensum Chaldæi paraphrastis & patrum vocem illam qvasi in canonem recipientium.

XXV. 4. Num Johannes primus & solus titulum λόγꙋ filio DEi attribuerit? Negatur id ex clara litera Psal. 33. v. 6. 2. Sam. 7. v. 20. 2. Sam. 23. v. 2. & ex paraphrasi Chaldæa sæpissimè vocem יהוה & אלהים per מימר reddente, ad innuendum de Filio Dei sermonem in textu fieri, ut Gen. 24. v. 5. c. 48. v. 21. Esa. 8. v. 5. Ose. 1. v. 7. & passim. Deinde locus Heb. 4. v. 12. non incommodè tam de verbo προφατικῷ qvam de προφορικῷ intelligitur. Addunt alii Luc. 1. v. 2.

XXVI. 5. An post incarnationem significet totum ὑφιςάμενον, vel simplicem tantum personam? Placet posterius, eò qvòd vox λόγꙋ neq; Biblico neq; Ecclesiastico sensu, ullibipro persona composita reperiatur usurpata, cum per λόγον semper intelligatur unitum adsumens, qvod est solummodo simplex hypostasis. Idem evincit & modus loqvendi, qvo dicimus Christum constare ex λόγῳ incarnato & carne adsumptâ, qvod elucet ulterius ex prædicationibus personalibus (ut λόγꙋ est homo, & contrá) & ἰδιοποιήσεως (λόγꙋ est passus) in qvibus λόγꙋ non pro toto Christo, sed pro persona adsumente sumitur.

XXVII. Reliqva nomina sunt Jehova Jer. 23, 6. Jehova exercituum Esa. 47, 4. Deus Israel Amos 4, 12. Deus Salvator Esa. 12, 2. Adonai c. 4, 4. Adonai Jehova c. 40, 10. Jehova excelsus Ps. 47, 3. Dominator Mich. 5, 2. Sol Justitiæ Malach. 4, 2. Sapientia Prov. 8, 1. μονογενὴς Joh. 1, 18. Virtus Dei 1. Cor. 1, 24. imago Dei (substantialis) Colos. 1, 18. Splendor gloriæ Dei & character substantiæ ejus Heb. 1, 3. Principium & finis Apoc. 1, 8. Primus & novissimus c. 13, 11. Dominus dominantium cap. 17, 14.

XXIIX. Inter Ecclesiasticos titulos primatum obtinent. 1. αὐτόθεꙋ. Dicitur verô sic respectu naturæ divinæ. Est enim non à superiori principio, sed à seipso Deus, & uti λόγꙋ operatur à se, & per se, & à nullo alio, sic etiam est à se, & per se, & à nullo alio. Personaliter verò consideratus λόγꙋ sic non dicitur, qvippè eo respectu θεότητα non à se, sed à patre habet. Breviter: αὐτόθεꙋ est respectu productionis temporalis, non est αὐτόθεος respectu productionis personalis. 2. ὁμούσιος, quâ voce tùm essentiæ unitas, tùm personarum distinctio realis significanter innuitur, & subdola aliquâ interpretatione vox illa ab adversariis haud facile eludi potest

XXIX. Porrò. Et si in Articulo Trinitatis, tanquam in sede propriâ, Æterna Filii Dei existentia demonstratur, & à nobis hîc præsupponitur tanquam ibi satis probata, siquidem Filius Dei hîc non consideratur absolutè prout persona simplex est, sed respectu incarnationis, prout carnem sibi personaliter univit, quatuor tamen testimonia Divinitatem Christi confirmantia ex abundanti submittemus.

XXX. Primum extat Gen. 48. in quo continetur benedictio (non charitatis quâ benè precamur omni proximo, sed) auctoritatis, & quidem Patriarchalis, quæ est devotæ invocatio, quâ precatus est Jacob, ut promissiones in filiis adimplerentur.

XXXI. Notanda autem in illâ tria sunt Objecta, 1. Cui, 2. quid, 3. à quo, precatus sit Jacobus. Illud fuerunt Ephraim & Manasse v. 16. Istud sunt bona & corporalia & spiritualia, inter quæ primarium est adsumptio in foedus gratiæ, & conservatio in eodem. In genere enim phrasis hebræa (vocari nomen super aliquo) nominis professionem vel adoptionem & denominationem exprimit: Ast in specie cum de Patriarcharum nomine est sermo, est censeri in foedere & participem fieri omnium promissionum Patribus factarum: Hoc tribus epithetis describitur. 1. dicitur DEUS, coram quo ambularunt Patres, 2. DEUS qui pavit Jacobum à juventute. 3. Angelus eripiens eum ab omni malo.

XXXII. Observant hîc Orthodoxi numerum singularem in verbo benedicat, quo innui censent unitatem essentiæ divinæ, & personarum trinitatem, intelligentes per Deum Patriarcharum, Patrem; per Deum pascentem, Spiritum S. per Angelum, Filium DEI, qui aliàs dicitur angelus divinæ faciei, & angelus Foederis. Quid hîc excipiant Photiniani in ipso Disputationis conflictu ξυν̓ θεῷ videbimus.

XXXXIII. Secundum est ex tribus prioribus versic. cap. 1. Johan. desumptum, in qvibus talia attribuuntur λόγῳ (qvem hîc Filium Dei, qvi est verbum æterni patris substantialiter, notare præsupponimus) prædicata, qvæ firmiter divinitatem Christi adstruunt.

XXXIV. Et sumitur 1. Existentia ἐν ἀρχῇ, Innuit autem vox ἀρχὴs 1. principium temporis & creationis. 2. principium qvodvis extra DEUM, qvod ante creationem cogitari, ponivè potest. 3. ipsâm æternitatem. Qvod enim indefinitè fuit ἐν ἀρχῇ, illud utiq́; æternum esse oportet. Hinc phrases ἐν ἀρχῇ vel ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς notant æternitatem ut 2. Thes. 2. v. 13. & qvodcunq; adsumas principium tamen verum est & manet: In principio erat verbum.

XXXV. II. est ab existentia πρὸς τὸν θεόν. Vox ὁ θεὸς hic restricte pro persona patris adcipitur, qvod etiam Articulus præfixus docet. Deinde notandum ἦν, qvo status perpetuus significatur. Tertio dicitur πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ad indicandam peculiarem subsistentiam.

XXXVI. III. Sumitur ab expressa Dei adpellatione καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. Qvi ergo absolutè dicitur Deus, reipsa verus & æternus Deus est. Hoc enim qveritur; an Christus sit verus Deus? respondet Johannes ὁ λόγος ἦν θεὸς, qvod declarat expressiùs 1. Joh. 5, 20.

XXXVII. IV. sumitur à creatione rerum, qvæ non nisi substantiæ per se subsistenti & qvidem divinæ adscribi potest, cujus solummodo opus est Esa. 41, 20. c. 45, 7.

XXXIIX. Tertium sit illud Joh. 8, 58. Ubi adprimè contra Photinianos notandum 1. Verba γενέσθαι & εἶναι absolutè & sine additamento hîc poni, non igitur possunt aliter intelligi, qvàm de existentia. 2. Ego sum, esse prædicationis non tertii sed secundi adjecti, 3. distinctè nomina non poni in textu, non dicitur antequam Abram fiat Abraham, sed absolutè ante fieri Abrahamum &c. Qvi igitur fuit anteqvam fieret vel esset Abraham, is non cœpit primum esse ultimis mundi temporibus. Et per conseqvens, Christus præter naturam humanam ex Maria adsumtam, constat alia priori, & ante Abrahamum existente, qvæ non potest esse alia, qvàm divina.

XXXIX, Qvartum sumimus ex Rom. 9, 5. Ubi Christus dicitur ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων Θεὸς εὐλόγητος εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας ἀμὴν, qvod elogium solius veri Dei proprium est, ut patet ex Rom. 1, 5. 2. Cor. 1, 3. Eph. 1, 3. 1. Pet. 1, 3. neq; δοξολογία hæc sine magna textus luxatione ad Deum patrem ut Arriani volunt, referri potest, ut ipsatextus inspectio clare ostendit, indicant subjectum. Qvo secundum qvamnam partem Christo conveniat esse ex patribus, videlicet, secundum carnem. Qvâ limitatione qvid opus, si præter carnem Christus aliam naturam non haberet?

XL. Tandem. Etsi moralia tractare potius sit 'επιδημίᾳ qvam ἀκαδημαικῶς, ea tamen, qvum ad plenam χριστολογίας tractationem etiam spectent, intacta hîc planè relinqvere nolumus, eorum unum vel alterum saltem indicando.

XLI. Docemur ergo 1. ex thesi 15, 16, 17. ne scandalum adripiamus ob multitudinem hærefeωn. Sathan antiqvam obtinet, semper est Dei adversarius. Qvid igitur mirum si & in hac ultima mundi senecta Ecclesiam cuniculis per tot hæreticos oppugnare satagat, cumidem fecerit tempore Christi & primitivæ Ecclesiæ. 2. ut observemus causas tum hærefeωn, tùm permissionis divinæ. Inter illas primaria est superciliosus fastus. Nisi enim hæretici prius in corde intumuissent, ad pravæ adnertionis certamina non pervenirent, ait Gregorius; Inter has elucent I. Ecclesiæ notificatio. Qvò enim magis impeditur, eò magis conspicua redditur. II. Ecclesiæ purgatio Verè enim hæreses sunt purgamenta Ecclesiæ. III. Veritatis illustratio. Videntur qvidem hæretici instar emunctoriorum primò lumen Ecclesiæ obfuscentes, sed postmodum clarius illud exsurgit &c.

XLII. Enumeratio divinorum nominum th. 18. & seq. facit 1. ad doctrinam, ut ex iis rectè Christum ipsiusq; majestatem cognoscamus 2. ad consolationem. Qvid enim contra nos Sathan, mundus, caro, cum Christus noster sit DEUS, Dominus Dominantium, Deus fortis &c. 3. ad correctionem. Emendemus vitam ne irritemus Christum. Nam hoc offenso, Deus offenditur, qvi ultor est habens furorem, irascens inimicis, Nah. 1, 2.

XLIII. Circa tertium membrum.qværitur, cur redemptorem verum DEum esse oportuerit? A priori causas nullas scimus, cum hic voluntas facientis sit tota facti ratio; à posteriori tamen duas causas colligimus; Prima est magnitudo mali. Erat super nos ira Dei, maledictio legis, Tyrannis Diaboli &c. a quibus malis nemo nisi Deus nos liberare potuit. Secunda est magnitudo boni nobis conferendi, ut reconciliatio cum Deo patre, restitutio imaginis divinae, impletio legis, revelatio Evangelii, custodia a tyrannide Diaboli, &c. Quae omnia a nemine nisi a solo Deo nobis obvenire queunt.

XLIV. Adnoscamus igitur animo grato tantam Dei φιλανθρωπίαν. Ex gratia dedit, cum non essemus, ut essemus; ex gratia dedit, cum perditi essemus, ut bene essemus. Ergo.

Per secula meta nescia Patri supremo gloria Honorg sit cum Filio, Et Spiritu Paracleto. Amen.


## 2 Second Disputation. On the Human Nature of Christ

Thesis I.

It was demonstrated in the previous disputation that the Son of GOD, our Lord Jesus Christ, true God from true God and born from the substance of the Father, is of the same essence, glory, and majesty as He; it follows now that we must prove that the same Son of God, for us men and for our salvation, when the fullness of time came, descended from the heavens and was incarnate and made man,

II. In the beginning, however, it must be seen in what manner the Devil has always endeavored to attack and destroy this article through his instruments.

III. The source and origin of all the heresies that have arisen under the Gospel was that Simon Magus, whom Luke mentions in the Acts, who among other things also taught that Christ neither came nor suffered anything from the Jews.

IV. Following him at the beginning of the second century were the Gnostics, distinguishing Christ as a different person from JESUS, and [saying] that He [Christ] into him [Jesus] already born

and teaching that he descended as a grown man of nearly 30 years. Read of many more and monstrous fables of theirs concerning the Incarnation of Christ in Irenaeus.

V. From these, as the same Irenaeus testifies, the Valentinians began their occasion of error: they thought that the Son of God passed through the virgin Mary as if through a conduit or pipe without any flesh assumed from her. The Anabaptists renewed this error in the memory of the Fathers: and Michael Servetus of Aragon does not depart much from them, when he asserts that the flesh of Christ is divine and begotten from the substance of the Father.

VI. In the reign of Antoninus Pius, Cerdo and his disciple Marcion denied that the Son of God assumed true flesh, but thought that he was held to be a man by men only putatively, and consequently that he performed his actions and sufferings not truly but according to δόκησιν & φαντασιαν (appearance and fantasy). It is certain that this heresy was known in the first century from Ignatius, provided those epistles which are extant are his. The Manichaeans defended the same, whose sect's leader began to be recognized in the 4th year of the Emperor Aurelian.

VII. Under Constantine the Great, Arius arose in A.D. 324, who indeed acknowledged a true body in Christ, but denied that he assumed a soul, feigning that the divinity sustained those actions and parts which are proper to a soul. The Eunomians, who were also called Aetians, were of the same error: as were also Apollinaris the father and the son, of Laodicea, around the times of the Emperor Julian, who nevertheless differ from the Arians in this, that they say CHRIST assumed σάρκα ἐμψυχωμένην (ensouled flesh) indeed, but destitute of a rational soul, and that there was in CHRIST a ψυχὴν φυτικὴν καὶ ἄλογον (vegetative and irrational soul), but not a λογικὴν (rational one), and which we call νοῦν καὶ ἡγεμονικὸν (mind and governing principle). Furthermore, Augustine says that they themselves thought in such a way about the flesh of Christ that they said the flesh and the Word were of the same substance: asserting that the Word was made flesh, i.e., that something of the Word was converted into flesh, but not that the flesh was taken from Mary. Their followers are called διμοιρῖται (dimoirites) by Epiphanius. They are condemned in a certain Council of Constantinople and at Rome by Damasus.

VIII. It is not unlikely that Eutyches the Archimandrite also fell into error on the occasion of this heresy of the Apollinarists. He arose under the Emperor Marcian, teaching that the natures in Christ were not joined, but confused, and that he himself had a divine body. For he thought that Nestorius, who constituted two persons in Christ because of the diversity of natures, could not be refuted otherwise than by establishing only one nature of his after the incarnation: wherefore he did not deny his two natures before the union; but after the union, he used to say, I confess one nature. They are condemned together with Dioscorus, Bishop of Alexandria, in the Council of Chalcedon.

IX. From this Eutychianism many heretics later arose, and first indeed the Monophysites, with Peter the Fuller and Severus as authors, condemned in the fifth Ecumenical Council held at Constantinople. Secondly, the Acephali, who were also called Angelitae, did not deny two natures in CHRIST, provided that their properties were conceded to be confused.

X. Thirdly, the Aphthartodocetae, denying that the body of CHRIST was subject to destruction or a participant in any natural affections. The author or most fierce champion of this dogma was the Emperor Justinian, as Evagrius testifies.

XI. Fourthly, the Monothelites, with Sergius of Constantinople as author, who, not daring to assert the condemned confusion of the two natures, wished to encrust it with a certain covering, and posited only one will and operation in Christ; see Camerarius for the occasion of this heresy. They are condemned in the sixth Ecumenical Council celebrated at Constantinople, under the Emperor Constantine Pogonatus.

XII. And thus far it has been set forth how wonderfully and at the same time miserably the human nature of Christ has always been attacked; it follows that we should defend the same as accurately as possible with arguments sought from Scripture.

XIII. But first there occur words or names in the Holy Scriptures from which the true humanity of Christ can be demonstrated, and they are either abstract or concrete, of which the former express the nature, while the latter express the person, yet denominated from the human nature.

XIV. Among the primary abstracts there are two. 1. The word σαρκός; which, although it is taken in various ways in the Scriptures, yet when it is predicated of Christ, it is taken synecdochically, and declares the whole nature of man, and indeed insofar as it is weak, as in John 1:14, 1 Timothy 3:16, Hebrews 2:14, 1 John 4:2.

XV. The other is the word Seed: hence in Hebrews 2:16 the Word is said to have assumed the seed of Abraham, and in Galatians 3:16 he is called the seed of Abraham, of David in 2 Samuel 7:12, the seed of the woman in Genesis 3:15, the blessed seed in Genesis 22:18.

XVI. Among concrete terms there are three that are principal. First, he is named man, Rom. 5:15, 1 Cor. 15:21, 1 Tim. 2:5. Secondly, he is called Son & 1. indeed of man, Dan. 7, 13. Matt. 8, 20. Mark 2, 10. Luke 5, 24. & passim elsewhere. 2. Of Abraham & David, Matt. 1, 1. ch. 6, 27. ch. 22, 42. Mark 12, 35. Luke 18, 39. ch. 20, 41. 3. Of Mary, Matt. 13, 55. XVII. Thirdly he is called the firstborn 1. of Mary, Matt. 1, 25. 2. firstborn among brothers, Rom. 8, 29. 3. firstborn of every creature, Col. 1, 15. 4. firstborn from the dead, Col. 1, 18. Apoc. 1, 5. VIII. Besides these, other names are also read as attributed to CHRIST on account of his humanity. For he is called the fruit of the womb, the fruit of the sublime earth, the Rod from the root of Jesse, a man surrounded by a woman, the fruit of the womb of Mary, the fruit of the loins of David, the firstfruits of those who sleep, etc.: from all of which the truth of the human nature can be demonstrated quite firmly against any adversaries whatsoever.

XIX. Secondly, those testimonies offer themselves to us which prove that CHRIST had a true body. For he himself, Matt. 14, 25. Mark 6, 49. Luke 24, 39. denies that his body is phantastic or a specter or a spirit. Furthermore, true members are attributed to Christ in the scriptures, such as flesh, blood, bones, head, face, eyes, ears, mouth, tongue, chest, side, hands, feet, &c. This is also evident from the saying of Paul, Heb. 2, 14. as children partake of flesh and blood, so also the son of God: or children have flesh and blood not supposedly but in reality: Therefore, so does Christ.

XX. Thirdly, there are testimonies which assert that Christ was truly conceived and born of the virgin Mary, and not brought down from heaven, as Matt. 1, v. 16. Luke 1, v. 35. Gal. 4, 4. Luke 1, v. 43. he is called the fruit of the womb of Mary, not a guest. Hence the blessed Vigilius, book 3, says: The angel spoke to Mary, that which shall be born of thee, in order to declare more manifestly the truth of the body to be taken from the virgin. For what was the cause for the Word of God to make a passage through the womb of a virgin, if he sought to take nothing from it?

XXI. Fourthly, a true soul is attributed to Christ, and indeed a rational one, Matt. 20, 28. ch. 26, 38. ch. 27, 50. Proper attributes of a soul are attributed to him, such as knowledge and choice, Isa. 7, 15. Wisdom and Prudence, Luke 2, 40. 47. 52. Will and desire, John 5, 30. Luke 22, 15. Effects of a soul are attributed to him, such as love, John 13, 34. Zeal, John 2, 18. Sadness, Matt. 26, 38. Joy, John 11, 15. Fear, Mark 14, 33. &c: From which Fulgentius elegantly demonstrates that there was a true soul in Christ: whence also Epiphanius says that this confession is opposed to AThe Apollinarians held that the Savior had a flesh and body that was not soulless, not insensate, and not unintelligent.

XXII. Nor are two diverse and unconfused wills, namely divine and human, any less found in Christ; for He Himself shows these to us as distinct when He says, 'I do not seek my own will,' that is, the one proper to me by reason of the humanity assumed, 'but the will of the Father who sent me'; with whom, since there is one and the same essence for me, there is also one and the same will, and elsewhere, 'Not as I will, but as you will.'

XXIII. Hence it was concluded thus in the Sixth General Council: Just as it is absurd to assert three wills in the three persons of the Trinity, since there is one nature which is followed by one will; so it is impious to deny two natural wills and two natural operations in the one person of Christ, who has two natures.

XXIV. Sixthly, a not insignificant argument for proving the true humanity of Christ is the fact that it is established that He assumed a body that was truly passible, both from the complaints of the body itself described throughout, and from the testimonies of the Old and New Testament, by which the passion and what happened regarding it are copiously described. For He is called a man of sorrows and one who truly bore our infirmities. Whence Fulgentius: 'Christ had all the infirmities of the flesh, voluntary indeed, but true, because He took up the nature of human flesh not in fantasy, but in truth.'

XXV. Just as therefore He is true and perfect man, so also Christ, insofar as He is true man, has His own properties, both common and proper:

XXVI. Common properties are either perpetual or essential, or temporary or accidental. Essential properties belong either to the whole or to the parts. Those of the whole are, for example, to be a finite creature, to live, to feel, to be moved, etc. The properties of the parts are either those of the soul, such as to be incorporeal, invisible, etc., or those of the body, such as to be extended, circumscribed, etc.: and all these belong to the humanity of Christ, since in all things, that is to say, in all essential things, He was made like unto us. Hence Ignatius elegantly says: Mary brought forth a true body, which was the dwelling-place of the divine nature, such, indeed, as would have in common with us all things that are proper to a human body.

XXVII. Temporary or accidental properties are also either of the whole, and to this pertains the state of emptying, or of the parts, namely of the soul, such as ignorance of certain things, increase of wisdom, sadness, etc., and of the body, such as, besides the assumed infirmities, existing in only one place, being seen in act, being touched, etc.; for these are not perpetual and ἰδιώδες [peculiar] properties.

XXVIII. The attributes proper or individuating to the assumed flesh, by which it is distinguished from other men, are in turn either of the whole or of the parts. Those of the whole are either transitory or perpetual. Among the former, the principal ones are conception by the Holy Spirit, Luke 1, 35; birth from a virgin, Luke 2, 7; descent into hell, Eph. 4, 9; ascension into heaven, Mark 16, 19; return for judgment, Acts 1, 11; John 5, 27.

XXIX. Perpetual attributes of the whole are anhypostasia (because the assumed flesh does not subsist through a peculiar hypostasis), subsistence in the Logos, immunity from sin, communication of idioms, sitting at the right hand of the Father.

XXX. The individuating attributes of the parts are either of the soul, whose perpetual attribute is the fullness of habitual grace, or of the body, whose perpetual attributes are immunity from diseases, incorruptibility, and supreme glorification, which happened to the body after the resurrection; a transitory one, however, is the miraculous and absolute formation in the womb of the virgin.

XXXI. From these it is clear that the difference between the humanity of Christ and our own is only accidental, and does not remove the essential agreement.

XXXII. These things concerning the attributes; there follow the infirmities, which Christ, inasmuch as he was made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man (Phil. 2, 7), assumed by his own most free will, compelled by no necessity, and they are either of the body or of the soul.

XXXIII. Christ assumed those infirmities of the body which are common to all and followed original sin, such as the enduring of cold and heat, painful hunger and thirst, difficult labor, sleep, fatigue, pains, and death itself, which were blameless in Christ, as Damascenus says. But he did not assume personal infirmities, such as diseases of every kind, nor culpable ones, namely concupiscence or inordinate motions.

XXXIV. Likewise, he did not assume personal infirmities of the mind, such as being born dull-witted, etc., or culpable ones, such as original sin, but only common ones, and those blameless.

XXXV. Among these, the first is ignorance of the mind and natural lack of knowledge of things, which was no less in Christ as a boy than in other men, as is evident from the statements in Is. 7:15, Luke 2:40, 52, and Matt. 21:19. However, there was not in Christ the ignorance of a depraved disposition, which is joined with error, but one of pure negation and simple.

XXXVI. Secondly, there are natural affections and appetites, among which joy, sadness, love, hatred, hope, fear, wonder, and zeal or anger are especially attributed to Christ in the Scriptures.

XXXVII. Yet these affections and infirmities are not in Christ in one and the same way as they are in us. For besides the fact that they adhere to us by necessity of nature, but to Christ by most free will, they also differ from one another in their objects, manner of desiring, adjuncts, and effects.

XXXIIX. Moreover, he assumed our defects for the price of our salvation, so that he might be able to shed his blood and thus redeem us, says Bonaventure. And Fulgentius: Whatever infirmity of soul there was, he both took on and endured without sin, so that while he conquered the passions of the human soul in the soul which he received, he might also free our souls from infirmities.

XXXIX. It remains now that we see in a few words why it was necessary for Christ to be true man: 1. This was done on account of the office of mediator: for unless you provide such a one between God and man, who is so much a mediator that he is both from both, i.e., that he is both God on account of his divinity, and the same is man on account of his human nature, he does not show how human things are to be reconciled to divine, says B. Vigilius.

XL. 2. On account of the liberation of human nature: It was, because of the fall of Adam, guilty of divine wrath and subject to eternal damnation: therefore the λόγος assumed the same into his own ὑπόστασιν, so that thus in it and through it, it might be freed from the guilt of all punishments. Whence Damascenus: God did not wish the Tyrant to be conquered by man except through man.

XLI. 3. On account of the necessary passion: for divine justice demanded that, because we had deserved the most grievous punishments, sin should be punished in that very nature which had sinned and through which God had been offended, and that the angry God should be appeased. Whence it is said in the Protevangelium: the seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.

XLII. 4. On account of the shedding of blood and death. Without the shedding of blood there is no remission, Heb. 9, 22, nor is a testament ratified without the death of the testator, v. 16. CHRIST therefore had to become man, so that he might shed his blood and die for us and by his death abolish him who had the power of death.

XLIII. 5. On account of brotherhood and the condition of being head: the Messiah had to be the brother of men according to Ps. 22:23, Heb. 2:11. And at the same time our head, Eph. 4:15, 16. But how could he be either brother or head if he had not assumed our nature?

XLIV. 6. On account of necessary compassion: our redeemer and high priest must be merciful, who can sympathize with our infirmities. But this could not be done so conveniently unless he himself, having been made man, had been tempted in all things, as the Apostle concludes in Heb. 2:17, 18 and ch. 4:15. Therefore, in that he was surrounded by infirmity, in that he sympathized with our ignorance and errors, and in that he felt compassion for our infirmities, says Fulgentius.

XLV. 7. To testify to the highest love of the Son of God. For who hereafter could doubt the love of Christ: no one ever hated his own flesh but nourishes and cherishes it, Eph. 5:29. But Christ is of our flesh and of our bones. Therefore he will sincerely love us, sufficiently nourish us, and powerfully cherish us. The grace of God could not be more weightily commended than that the only Son of God himself, remaining incommunicably in himself, should put on man, and give to men the hope of his love, with man as the mediator, says Augustine.

XLVI. 8. To excite the ardor of charity: for it is fair that we love him in return who loved us so intensely that he assumed not angels but our seed. Let the wicked blush, who repay Christ with evil deeds for benefits, with hatred for love, and with insults for gratitude. We, on the contrary, let us love him who loves us, and for such great compassion let us sing an eternal hymn of glory with thankful hearts. Let others marvel at the wonders of the world; but let us, with Cyprian, marvel at God in the womb of a virgin, the omnipotent in a cradle.

XLVII. And thus, briefly and according to the plan of the institution, let these things be proposed for discussion to establish the human nature in Christ.

To the immortal and only wise God be thanks and glory through Jesus Christ forever.

Latin:

Thesis I.

Demonstratum est priori disputatione, Filium DEI Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum verum Deum de vero Deo & ex substantia Patris natum ejusdem esse cum ipso essentiae, gloriae, & majestatis; consequens nunc est, ut probemus eundem Dei filium, propter nos homines & propter nostram salutem ubi venit plenitudo temporis, descendisse de coelis & incarnatum & hominem factum esse,

II. Principio autem videndum est, quo pacto Diabolus articulum hunc per organa sua oppugnare & destruere molitus semper fuerit.

III. Omnium vero haereseon, quae sub Evangelium ortae sunt fons & origo fuit Simon ille Magus, cujus in actis Lucas meminit, qui inter caetera quoque docuit, Christum nec venisse, nec a Judaeis quicquam pertulisse.

IV. Secuti hunc sunt initio secundi seculi Gnostici Christum ut aliam personam a JESU distinguentes, & illum in hunc jam natum

& grandem pene 30. annorum descendisse docentes. Horum plures ac portentosas de Incarnatione Christi fabulas lege apud Irenæum.

V. Ab his teste eodem Irenæo Valentiniani errandi occasionem cœperunt: putârunt illi, Filium Dei per virginem Mariam tanquam per canalem aut fistulam sine ullâ de illa assumptâ carne transiisse. Renovarunt hunc errorem Patrum memoriâ Anabaptistæ: nec multum ab iis abit Michaël Servetus Arrago, quando carnem Christi divinam esse & genitam asserit ex substantiâ Patris.

VI. Imperante Antonino Pio Cerdon & Marcion ejus discipulus negarunt filium Dei veram assumpsisse carnem, sed putative tantum esse habitum pro homine ab hominibus, ac proinde non verè sed secudum δόκησιν & φαντασιαν actiones & passiones suas peregisse arbitrati sunt. Notam fuisse hanc hæresin primo seculo constat ex Ignatio, dummodo ejus sunt, quæ extant Epistolæ. Propugnarunt eandem Manichæi, quorum sectæ antesignanus agnosci cœpit an 4. Aureliani Imp.

VII. Sub Constantino Magno surrexit Arius A. C. 324. qui in Christo verum quidem corpus agnovit, sed animam ipsum assumsisse negavit, fingendo divinitatem, eas quæ animæ sunt propriæ, actiones & partes sustinuisse. Ejusdem erroris fuêre Eunomiani, qui & Aëtiani dicti: nec non Apollinaris pater & filius, Laodiceni, circa tempora Juliani Imp. qui tamen in hoc ab Arrianis differunt, quod dicant, CHRISTUM assumpsisse σάρκα ἐμψυχωμένην quidem, sed anima rationali destitutam, & fuisse in CHRISTO ψυχὴν φυτικὴν καὶ ἄλογον, non autem λογικὴν, & quam νοῦν καὶ ἡγεμονικὸν appellamus. Præterea Augustinus ait ipsos de carne Christi ita sensisse, ut dicerent carnem & verbum ejusdem substantiæ: asserentes Verbum carnem factum esse, h. e. verbi aliquid in carnem fuisse conversum, non autem carnem de Maria susceptam. Sectatores eorum Epiphanio vocantur διμοιρῖται. Damnantur in Concilio quodam Constantinopolitano & Romæ à Damasco.

IIX. Occasione hujus Appollinaristarum hæreseos Eutychen quoq; Archimandritam in errorem esse prolapsum vero nō est absimile. Exortus is est Imperatore Marciano, docens in Christo non conjunctas, sed confusas esse naturas, ipsumq; divinum habere corpus. Putabat enim non posse aliter refelli Nestorium, ob diversitatem naturarum duas in Christo constituentem personas, nisi statueretur una tantum ejus natura post incarnationem: quare non inficiebatur fuis, se duas naturas πρὸς τῆς ἑνώσεως; μετὰ δὲ τὴν ἕνωσιν, inqviebat, μίαν φύσιν ὁμολογῶ. Damnantur una cum Dioscoro Episcopo Alexandrino in Concilio Chalcedonensi.

IX. Ab hoc Eutychianismo complures postea provenere hæretici, & primo qvidé μονοφυσῖται autoribus Petro Gnapheo & Severo damnati in Concilio qvinto Oecumenico, Constantinopoli habito. Secundo Acephali, qvi & Angelitæ dicti, non negebant illi duas in CHRISTO naturas, modo earum propiëtates confusæ concederentur.

X. Tertiò Ἀφθαρτοδοκήται, negantes corpus CHRISTI internecioni fuisse obnoxium, aut ullarum affectionum naturalium particeps. Hujus dogmatis sive autor sive propugnator fuit acerrimus Justinianos Imperator, teste Evagrio.

XI. Qvartò Μονοθελῆται autore Sergio Constantinopolitano qvi non audientes damnatam confusionem duarum naturarum asserere, tegumento qvodam eam incrustare voluerunt, unamqve tantùm in Christo voluntatem & operationem collocarunt, occasione m hærcseos vide apud Camerar. Damnantur in Concilio sexto Oecumenico Constantinopoli celebrato, Imperatore Constantino Pogonato.

XII. Atq; hactenus expositum est, qvam mirabiliter simul & miserabiliter humana Christi natura impugnata semper fuerit, cóseqvens est, ut eandem argumentis ex scriptura petitis, qvam fieri potest, accuratissimè defendamus.

XIII. Occurrunt autem primò vocabula sive nomina in S. S. ex qvibus vera Christi humanitas potest demonstrari, eaq; sunt vel abstracta vel concreta, qvorum illa naturam, hæc personam â naturâ tamen humanâ denominatam exprimunt.

XIV. Inter abstracta primaria sunt duo. 1. Vocabulum σαρκός; qvod qvamvis diversimodè in scripturis accipiatur, de Christo tamen qvando prædicatur, Synechdochicè sumitur, totamq; hominis naturam declarat, & qvidem qvatenus infirma est, ut Joh. 1, 14. 1. Tim. 3, 16. Hebr. 2, 14. 1. Joh. 4, 2.

XV. Alterũ est vocabulum Seminis: hinc Hebr. 2, 16. λόγος dicitur assumpsisse semen Abrahæ, & Gal. 3, 16. appellatur semẽ Abrahæ, Davidis, 2. Sam. 7, 12. semen mulieris, Gen. 3, 15. semen benedictum, Gen. 22, 18.

XVI. Inter vocabula concreta tria sunt præcipua. Primò nominatur homo, Rom. 5, 15. 1. Cor. 15, 21. 1. Tim. 2. 5. Secundò appellatur Filius & 1. qvidem hominis, Dan. 7, 13. Matth. 8, 20. Marc. 2, 10. Luc. 5, 24. & passim alibi. 2. Abrahæ & Davidis, Matth. 1, 1. cap. 6, 27. cap. 22, 42. Marc. 12, 35. Luc. 18, 39. cap. 20, 41. 3. Mariæ, Matth. 13, 55. XVII. Tertiò vocatur primogenitus 1. Mariæ, Matth. 1, 25. 2. primogenitus inter fratres, Rom. 8, 29. 3. primogenitus omnis creaturæ, Col. 1, 15. 4. primogenitus ex mortuis, Coloss, 1, 18. Apocal. 1, 5. VIII. Præter hæc alia qvoqve CHRISTO nomina propter humanitatem tributa leguntur. Vocatur enim fructus ventris, fructus terræ sublimis, Virga de radice Jesse, vir â fœminâ circumdatus, fructus ventris Mariæ, fructus lumborum Davidis, primitiæ dormientium &c: ex qvibus omnibus humanæ naturæ veritas contra qvosvis adversarios satis firmiter potest demonstrari.

XIX. Secundo ea nobis sese offerunt testimonia, qvæ probant CHRISTUM verum habuisse corpus. Ipse enim Matth. 14, 25. Marc. 6, 49. Luc. 24, 39. negat corpus suum phantasticum aut spectrum seu spiritum esse. Tribuuntur deinde Christo in scripturis vera membra, ut sunt caro, sangvis, ossa, caput, facies, oculi, aures, os, lingva, pectus, latus, manus, pedes, &c. Constat id qvoqve ex dicto Pauli Hebr. 2, 14. ut pueri participant carne & sangvine, sic & filius Dei: aut pueri non putative sed re ipsa carnem habent & sangvinem : E. & Christus.

XX. Tertiò adsunt testimonia, qvæ Christum verè ex Maria virgine conceptum & natum esse asserunt, non verò è cœlo delatum, ut Mat. 1, v. 16. Luc. 1, v. 35. Gal. 4, 4. Luc. 1, v. 43. dicitur fructus ventris Mariæ, non hospes. Hinc B. Virgilius lib. 3. inqvit: Angelus ad Mariam locutus est, qvod nascetur ex te, ut veritatem corporis sumendam ex virgine manifestius declararet. Nam quæ fuit caussa Dei verbo per uterum virginis transuum facere, si nihil inde qværebat adsumere?

XXI. Qvartò tribuitur Christo vera anima & qvidem rationalis, Matth. 20, 28. cap. 26, 38. cap. 27. 50. Tribuuntur ipsi propria animæ attributa, qvalia sunt scientia & electio, Esa. 7, 15. Sapientia & Prudentia, Luc. 2, 40. 47. 52. Voluntas & desiderium, Joh. 5, 30. Luc. 22, 15. Tribuuntur ipsi effectus animæ, ut amor, Joh. 13, 34. Zelus, Joh. 2, 18. Tristitia, Matth. 26, 38. Gaudium, Joh. 11, 15. Timor, Marc. 14, 33. &c: Ex qvibus eleganter demonstrat Fulgentius, veram in Christo fuisse animam: unde & Epiphan. hanc confessionem oppositam esse ait Apollinaristis οὐκ ἄψυχον, οὐκ ἀναίσθητον, οὐκ ἀνόητον σάρκα, καὶ σῶμα εἶχεν σωτήρ.

XXII. Neq; minus in Christo reperiuntur qvintò duæ diversæ ac inconfusæ voluntates, divina videlicet & humana, has enim ipse nobis distinctas ostendit, qvando ait, non quæro voluntatem meam, scilicet mihi ratione assumtæ humanitatis propriam, sed voluntatem ejus, qui misit me patris; cum qvo videlicet qvia mihi una & eadem est essentia, una qvoqve & eadem est voluntas, & alibi Non sicut ego volo sed sicut tu vis.

XXIII. Hinc in Concilio generali sexto ita conclusum est: Sicut in tribus personis Trinitatis tres voluntates asserere absurdum est, quoniam una natura est, qvam conseqvitur una voluntas; ita in una Christi persona, quæ duas naturas habet, duas voluntates & duas operationes naturales negare impium est.

XXIV. Sextò ad probandam veram Christi humanitatē non leve est argumentū, qvod corp⁹ vere passibile assumpsisse constat tum ex qverelis ipsi⁹ passim descriptis, tum ex testimoniis veteris & novi Testamenti, qvibus passio & qvæ circa eam acciderunt, copiosè describuntur. Vocatur enim vir dolorum & qui vere langvores nostros portaverit. Unde Fulgentius: Omnes carnis infirmitates voluntarias qvidem, sed veras Christus habuit, quia carnis humanæ naturam non in phantasia, sed in veritate suscepit.

XXV. Sicut itaqve verus & perfectus homo, sic qvoq; Christus, qvatenus verus homo, suas habet proprietates tùm communes tùm proprias:

XXVI. Communes sunt vel perpetuæ seu essentiales, vel temporariæ seu accidentales. Essentiales sunt vel totius vel partium. Totius, ut esse creatum finitum, vivere, sentire, moveri, &c. Partium proprietates sunt vel animæ, ut esse incorporeum, invisibilem &c. vel corporis, ut esse qvantum, circumscriptum &c: atq; hæ humanitati Christi conveniunt omnes, qvoniam in omnibus nempè essentialibus nobis factus est similis. Hinc eleganter Ignatius: Verum corpus Maria peperit, qvod esset divina naturæ domicilium, tale nimirum; qvod omnia quæ propria sunt humani corporis, nobiscum haberet communia.

XXVII. Proprietates temporariæ seu accidentales, etiam sunt vel totius, atq; huc spectat status exanitionis, vel partium, videlicet animæ, ut ignorantia quarundum rerum, incrementum sapientiæ, tristitia &c. & corporis, qualia sunt præter assumptas infirmitates, in uno tantum loco existere, actu videri, palpari &c. hæc enim non sunt perpetua & ἰδιώδες propria.

XXIIX. Attributa vero carnis assumptæ propria seu individuantia, quibus ab aliis hominibus distinguitur vicissim sunt vel totius vel partium. Totius sunt vel transitoria vel perpetua. Inter illa præcipua sunt conceptio ex Spiritu S. Luc. 1, 35. nativitas ex virgine, Luc. 2, 7. descensus ad inferos. Eph. 4, 9. ascensus in cœlum Marc. 16, 19. reditus ad judicium. Act. 1, 11. Joh. 5, 27.

XXIX. Totius perpetua sunt ἀνυποστασία, (quia caro assumpta non subsistit per peculiarem ὑπόστασιν) subsistentia in λόγῳ immunitas à peccato, communicatio idiomatum, sessio ad dextram Patris.

XXX. Attributa individuantia partium sunt vel animæ, cujus perpetuum est habitualis gratiæ plenissima, vel corporis, cujus perpetua sunt immunitas à morbis, incorruptibilitas, summa glorificatio, quæ contigit corpori post resurrectionem: transitorium autem miraculosa & absoluta in utero virginis formatio.

XXXI. Ex his patet differentia inter humanitatem Christi & nostram, quæ tantum accidentalis est, & convenientiam essentialem non tollit.

XXXII. Hæc de attributis, sequuntur infirmitates, quas Christus utpote, qui in similitudinem hominum factus est, & habitu inventus ut homo Philip. 2, 7. ex liberrima sua voluntate nulla necessitate coactus assumsit, suntq; vel corporis vel animæ.

XXXIII. Infirmitates corporis eas Christus assumsit, quæ sunt communes omnibus & consecutæ peccatum originale, ut sunt frigoris & æstus perpessio, dolorosa fames & sitis, difficilis labor, somnus, fatigatio, dolores, & mors ipsa, quæ in Christo fuere inculpabiles, ut loquitur Damascenus. Non autem assumsit infirmitates personales, quales sunt omnis generis morbi, nec culpabiles, concupiscentiam videlicet aut motus inordinatos.

XXXIV. Sic neq; infirmitates animi personales ut nasci stolidum &c. aut culpabiles, ut est peccatum originale assumsit, sed tantùm communes, easque inculpabiles.

XXXV. Inter has primo est ignorantia mentis & naturalis rerum imperitia, quæ non minus fuit in Christo puero, qvàm aliis hominibus, ut constat ex dictis Es. 7, 15. Luc. 2, 40. 52. Matth. 21, 19. Non autem fuit in Christo ignorantia pravæ dispositionis, quæ cum errore conjuncta est, sed puræ negationis & simplex.

XXXVI. Secundo sunt affectus & appetitus naturales, inter qvos præcipuè in scripturis de Christo prædicantur lætitia, tristitia, amor, odium, spes, timor, admiratio, & zelus seu ira.

XXXVII. Non tamen uno & eodem modo affectus hi & infirmitates Christo in sunt, ut nobis. Præterqvam enim, quòd nobis adhærent ex necessitate naturæ, Christo verò ex liberrimâ voluntate, etiam objectis, modo appetendi, adjunctis, & effectis à se invicé differūt.

XXXIIX. Assumsit autem defectus nostros propter nostræ salutis precium, ut sangvinem fundere, & ita nos redimere posset, inqvit Bonaventura. Et Fulgentius: Quicquid fuit infirmitatis animæ, sine peccato & suscepit & pertulit, ut dum humanæ animæ passiones in anima, quam accepit, vinceret, nostras quoq; animas ab infirmitatibus liberaret.

XXXIX. Restat nunc ut paucis videamus, qvare Christum verum hominem esse oportuerit: 1. factum id est propter officium mediatoris: nisi enim talem dederis inter Deum & hominem, qvi ita sit medius, ut ex utroq; utrumq; sit, i. e. ut & Deus sit propter divinitatis, & idé homo sit propter humanitatis naturam, humana divinis qvomodo reconcilientur, non ostendit, inqvit B. Vigilius.

XL. 2. Ob naturæ humanæ liberationem: Erat illa ob lapsum Adami rea iræ divinæ & subjecta æternæ damnationis: eandem igitur assumsit λόγος in suam ὑπόστασιν, ut sic in illâ & per illam â reatu pœnarum omnium liberaretur. Unde Damascenus: Deus homine victo non nisi per hominem vinci voluit Tyrannum.

XLI. 3. Propter necessariam passionem: postulabat enim justitia divina, ut quia pœnas gravissimas eramus promeriti, in illâ ipsâ naturâ, quæ peccaverat, & per qvam Deus offensus erat, peccatum puniretur, & Deus iratus placaretur. Unde in Protevangelio dicitur semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis.

XLII. 4. Propter sangvinis effusionem & mortem. Sine sangvinis effusione non fit remissio, Hebr. 9, 22. nec sine morte testatoris testamentum ratum est, v. 16. Debuit itaqve CHRISTUS fieri homo, ut sangvinem effundere & mori posset pro nobis & per mortem aboleret eum, qvi habebat imperium mortis.

XLIII. 5. Propter fraternitatem & capitis conditionem: Messias debuit esse frater hominum juxta Psal. 21, 23. Heb. 2, 11. Simulq; caput nostrum. Eph. 4, 15. 16. Qvomodo autem vel frater vel caput esse posset, si nostram non assumsisset naturam?

XLIV. 6. Propter necessariam compassionem: redemptorem & pontificem nostrum oportet esse misericordem, qvi nostris infirmitatibus possit compati. Hoc autem fieri adeo commodè non posset, nisi & ipse homo factus per omnia tentatus fuisset, ut Apostolus concludit Heb. 2, 17. 18. & cap. 4, 15.. in eo ergo, quo circumdatus fuit infirmitate, in eo condoluit ignorantiæ & erroribus nostris, & in eo compassus est infirmitatibus nostris, ait Fulgentius.

XLV. 7. Ad testandum summum filii DEI amorem. Qvis enim imposterum ambigat de Christi dilectione: nemo unqvam carnem suam odio habuit sed nutrit ac fovet eam, Ephes. 5. v. 29. Christus autem est de carne & de ossibus nostris. E. sincerè nos diliget, sufficienter nutriet, potenter fovebit. Gratia Dei non poterat gravius commendari, qvam ut ipse unicus Dei filius in se incommunicabiliter manens, indueret hominem, & spem dilectionis suæ daret hominibus, homine medio, ait Augustinus.

XLVI. 8. Ad ardorem charitatis excitandum: æqvum enim est ut redamemus eum, qvi nos adeo intensè amavit, ut non angelos sed nostrum semen assumeret. Erubescant impii, qvi Christo pro beneficiis malefacta, pro amore odium, pro gratitudine contumelias reponunt. Nos contra diligamus diligentem nos, & pro tantâ miseratione æternum gloriæ hymnum gratis animis canamus. Mirentur alii mirabilia mundi; nos autem cum Cypriano miremur Deum in utero virginis, omnipotentem in cunabulis.

XLVII. Atq; sic breviter & pro ratione instituti ad adstruendam humanam in Christo naturam hæc ad disputandum proposita sunto.

DEO immortali & soli sapienti sit gratia & gloria per JESUM CHRISTUM in secula.


## 3 Third Disputation. On the Incarnation of the Word

Thesis I.

IN that great mystery of godliness, which is God manifest in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3:16, into which the Angels desire to look, 1 Pet. 1:12, three acts as it were concur: 1. the conception of the flesh, 2. the assumption of the conceived, 3. the union of the assumed.

II. Although between these no interval of time at all is to be thought of or imagined (for with the Angel announcing and the Holy Spirit coming, the Word was immediately in the womb, and immediately the flesh of the Word was within the womb, as Blessed Gregory speaks), yet they are deservedly distinguished for the sake of teaching, lest confusion beget obscurity.

III. We shall therefore divide this part into three peculiar sections, making a beginning from the first and including the same in six chapters. 1. will be on the terms, 2. on the sayings for the incarnation, 3. on the incarnate person, 4. on the time of the incarnation, 5. on the true definition, 6. on practical meditations.

IV. Just as the terms which we use in describing sacred matters are either ἔγγραφοι or biblical; or ἄγραφοι or ecclesiastical; so also in the present mystery.

V. The ἔγγραφοι are: descent, Isa. 64:1, John 6:33, manifestation in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3:16, participation of flesh and blood, Heb. 2:14.

VI. The ἄγραφοι are corporatio (corporation), Hilary in the Prologue on the Psalms; Oeconomia of the Word, Damascene, book 3, ch. 6; admirable mixture, Augustine, Ep. 3 to Volusianus, Gregory Nazianzen, Panegyric Oration on the Nativity of Christ; inhumanatio (becoming human), Damascene, book 3, ch. 13.

VII. But the name more used in the Church is Incarnation. Which the good Latin Fathers also used to signify this Mystery, Augustine, book 10 of The City of God, ch. 24 and 29, Jerome on ch. 1 of Mark, Ambrose on ch. 23 of Luke. And in the same signification the term ἐνσάρκωσις is used by the Greek Fathers.

VIII. The word ἐνσαρκώσεως is indeed taken from John 1, verse 14, where the Apostle says, The Word was made flesh, namely, not by the conversion of the Deity into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity εἰς θεότητα into God.

IX. Therefore, to be incarnated is nothing else than to be made flesh; and incar nation denotes that singularly miraculous act in which the λόγος, or the eternal Son of God, in the fullness of time took our nature into the unity of His ὑπόστασις and intimately united it to Himself.

X. This term therefore implies three things: 1. The λόγος who is incarnated. 2. The flesh which is assumed. 3. The personal concurrence of both.

XI. However, incarnation differs from union. For incarnation is proper to the Word, since it can be predicated of Him alone. For neither humanity nor flesh itself is said to be incarnated, but only the Person of the Son of God; but union pertains to both natures, and is spoken of reciprocally.

XII. Furthermore, the incarnation of the λόγος is predicted as future in the Old Testament by the Prophets; in the New it is declared as having occurred by the Apostles. Sayings occur in both places in great number; we shall bring forward some from each instrument.

XIII. 1. We take from chapter 9 of Isaiah, verse 6: 'A child is born to us,' etc. It is to be noted: 1. That the discourse here is about the Messiah, as is evident from Matthew 4:16. 2. That the Prophet speaks of future things in the past tense on account of their absolute certainty. 3. That by the distinct names of 'child' and 'son,' distinct natures are expressed. 4. That that child is the true God, which the titles attributed to Him sufficiently imply.

XIV. We urge two titles in particular, namely, that He is called: 1. God. 2. Everlasting Father. In Hebrew it is אל, which in general denotes the robust and powerful, but when placed absolutely it is the name of the true God, to whom it is attributed κατ̓ ἐξοχὴν in Jeremiah 32:18. It is to be noted, however, that the Messiah is called not only God, but moreover the mighty God, so that He may be esteemed the true and omnipotent God, not some titular one.

XV. Then He is called Everlasting Father, by which name is implied both His eternal duration and the production of the ages. Now, He who is not only eternal, but also the Father of eternity, must surely be God by nature.

XVI. With these things thus declared, we conclude as follows for the incarnation of the λόγος: He who is true God and Everlasting Father, yet at the same time a little child born in time, must have been incarnated or have assumed human flesh. But the Son of God, who is named God and Everlasting Father, is at the same time a little child born in time. Therefore, the Son of God must have been incarnated or have assumed human flesh.

XVIII. 2. From Jeremiah 23:5: 'Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord,' etc. That the Lord is prophesying here about the Messiah, even the Jews themselves do not deny, proving it by the Targum or Chaldean version. Moreover, the twofold nature of the Messiah is described here by two clear titles. 1. He is named the branch of David. 1. By reason of his origin, 2. by reason of his growth, and indeed righteous both by reason of himself and by reason of us: By reason of himself, since the Messiah is a righteous man in habit and act; by reason of us, on account of merit and application. 2. He is called Jehovah our righteousness. In which it follows that the Messiah is true God, because a name proper to God alone is attributed to him.

XVIII. Hence we form such an argument for the incarnation of the λόγος. Whoever is the true Jehovah and is nevertheless called the branch of David raised up in time, he is without doubt incarnate or has assumed human flesh, but the Son of God sent by the Father into the world is the true Jehovah and is nevertheless at the same time called the branch of David. Therefore, without doubt, the Son of God is incarnate.

XIX. The third is supplied by Micah ch. 5, 2. And thou Bethlehem &c. It is certain that the Messiah is treated here only, from Matt. ch. 2, v. 6. Whose country is first expressed, which is called Bethlehem. 2. A singular name of the Messiah is placed while he is called מושׁל. 3. His temporal birth is described by the word of going forth, which is often the same as to be born. Gen. 15, 4. 2 Sam. 7, 12. &c. Finally, 4. his eternal birth and the true Deity of the Messiah are hinted at by the words: his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity.

XX. That eternal going forth is described by two words: 1. from of old, from ancient times. In the source is מקדם, which word, although it is often taken for a certain and definite beginning of time, nevertheless not rarely denotes eternity when it is used of God, as Hab. 1, v. 12. 2. from the days of the age.
