But מימי עולם has 3 meanings. 1. It is taken for long duration, 2. for the duration of the world, 3. for duration lacking beginning and end, as in this place. For the Hebrews, since they do not have a proper name for eternity, use the names Kedem and Olam to signify it.

XXI. These things being thus explained, we conclude most firmly against the Photinians thus: he who existed from eternity, yet at the same time goes forth in time as a man, it is necessary that he be truly incarnate and assume flesh. But the Messiah as God existed from eternity, and at the same time went forth in time from Bethlehem as a man. Therefore, it is necessary that he be truly incarnate and have assumed flesh.

XXII. 4. The principal passage is John 1, 14. The Word was made flesh, &c. Here by the Word is not to be understood some vanishing voice, but that coessential Word of the Father, namely the only-begotten Son of God, as this very thing is also to be seen immediately in the 1st verse of this chapter, where it is clearly held that the Word was God: but through the flesh, not only one part of human essence, nor even affections, but the whole and entire human nature consisting has been made flesh, he is truly incarnate. But the λόγος or Son of God has been made flesh. Therefore, the λόγος is truly incarnate.

XXIII. 5. We take from the Epistle to the Colossians, ch. 2, 9: in him dwells, etc. In this statement, individual words are to be considered: 1. by the pronoun ἐν ἀυτῶ, reference is made not to the doctrine of Christ, as the Photinians wish, but to Christ himself; 2. by the word κατοικῇ, a fixed and continued dwelling is implied; 3. the indwelling itself is expressed, πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος, that is, the most perfect and most full Deity. 4. The mode of indwelling is described by the adverb σωματικῶς, by which three things are implied: 1. it is the same as truly and really; 2. it is the same as personally; 3. the true subject is implied, which is the σῶμα or humanity of Christ.

XXIV. Whence we argue: Whoever dwells in the flesh personally, as in his own temple, him it certainly behooves to be incarnate. The reason is because to inhabit is explained by being made through the flesh, John 1:14. But the λόγος dwells in the flesh personally as in his own temple. Therefore, it behooves the λόγος to be incarnate. What the Photinians may object to these statements, we shall see in the very act of disputation, God willing. We proceed.

XXV. Although the incarnation is said to be the work of the whole Trinity efficiently and inchoatively (for the Father gives his Son, John 3:16, and sends him, Galatians 4:4, and Christ is anointed by the Holy Spirit, John 3:34, Acts 10:38, Hebrews 1:9), yet it is formally and terminatively of the Son alone, John 1:14, Hebrews 2:14.

XXVI. The Scholastics declare that with the simile of three girls who, joined together, weave one garment, but adapt it to only one. Where the action of forming and externally clothing is indeed common to all, yet not all, but only one is clothed, because this action is not terminated in the three, but in one of the three.

XXVII. Hence rightly Augustine: The Word was made flesh, he says, not the Father, not the Holy Spirit, but the whole Trinity made the flesh of the Son. For the works of the Trinity are inseparable. And Serm. 3 de temp. Since the Deity is one, the divinity is one, both the Father and the Holy Spirit indeed filled the flesh of Christ, but by majesty, not by assumption.

XXIIX. It is therefore to be held firmly that in the incarnation the whole Trinity indeed works, but only the person of the Son is incarnated.

XXIX. Some object here: The works of the Trinity ad extra are undivided, and common to all persons. The incarnation is a work of the whole Trinity ad extra. Therefore.

XXX. I answer briefly. There are three kinds of works of the Trinity: 1. ad intra, 2. ad extra, 3. mixed, which are ad intra by reason of the term, ad extra by reason of the beginning. Those are personal, therefore divided. These are essential, therefore undivided: These are personal and essential, therefore both divided and undivided.

XXXI. The incarnation is a mixed work: which belongs to the three persons efficiently and inchoatively on account of the decree and the production of the flesh: But formally and terminatively it belongs to the Son alone on account of the personal assumption of this flesh.

XXXII. But why the second person of the Deity was incarnated, pious and very useful reasons are brought forward by Justin, Athanasius, Augustine, Irenaeus, and others. Irenaeus, from Genesis 1:27 and Colossians 1:15, brings forward this one: Since man was to be restored to the image of God, it had to be done through that person who is the image and character ὑπόστασεως of God, Heb. 1:3. Likewise, he says elsewhere: it was fitting that the ἀνάπλασις should be of the same one whose πλάσις had been, that is, that he should likewise create and recreate us, make and remake us. Akin to this is that of Athanasius to Epictetus: It was fitting that the one who was to ἀνακτίζειν should be the same as the one who had been the κτίζειν. But the sweetest and most full of pious consolation of all is that of Irenaeus, book 3, ch. 20: Therefore it was necessary for the Son to become man, so that we, who were children of wrath, might receive the adoption of the children of GOD.

XXXIII. But when we say that the Son was incarnated, we do not understand his hypostasis alone considered without the Deity or divine nature, but we believe that the divine nature of the Word, hypostatically limited, was united to the human nature. For the person of the Word cannot be so separated from his nature that the former is believed to be hypostatically joined to the human, but the latter not.

XXXIV. It is objected here: The whole divine nature is incarnated, the whole divine nature is the same as the 3 persons of the Trinity. Therefore these all are incarnated.

XXXV. Resp. A distinction must be made between a twofold consideration of the divine nature: for it is either considered absolutely and simply, as it is common to all three persons of the Trinity, and in this respect we say it is in no way incarnate: or relatively, as the divine nature is limited by some certain personal character, and is understood as either the divine nature begetting, or begotten, or proceeding: and thus we rightly say that the begotten divine nature is incarnate, which is nothing other than the very Son of God himself.

XXXVI. Hence Damascene rightly says: The whole divine nature is incarnate in one of its hypostases; and although it is wholly incarnate, it is not however ὁλικῶς, totally, incarnate, because it is incarnate insofar as it is in the Son, not insofar as it is in the Father and the Holy Spirit.

XXXVII. That the Son of God was not incarnate immediately at the beginning of the world is thought to have been done so that men, struggling with longer-lasting evils, might better recognize the infirmity of their nature and cry out to the physician. For the knowledge of sin is the beginning of salvation.

XXXIIX. 2. That they might first be exercised in the faith of the promises concerning the future Messiah, 3. that God might accustom men to his ways, which are for the most part joined with delay. 4. That he might lead them from the imperfection of the law to the perfection of the Gospel: And finally 5. that on account of the long expectation, the arrival of the Messiah and the benefit of redemption might be valued more highly.

XXXIX. Furthermore, that the arrival of the λόγος was not delayed any longer until the end of the world was done partly for the sake of God and partly for our sake.

XL. For the sake of God 1. that he might show his φιλανθρωπίαν. 2. that he might fulfill the promises made concerning the Messiah. For the sake of us men 1. that more might be able to be converted through the preaching of the Gospel concerning the incarnate λόγος. 2. that the faith of men might be increased. 3. that we might conceive a firm hope of future inheritance. 4. that sincere love might be kindled more and more within us.

XLI. The incarnation of the λόγος was therefore accomplished in the middle age of the world, 1 Corinthians 11:11, Hebrews 1:1, 1 John 1:18. Which time was the most convenient of all 1. because of the removal of the Scepter from Judah. 2. because of the extreme malice of the Jews. 3. because of the reformation of doctrine. 4. because of the great number of the elect. 5. because of the abandonment of hope concerning the arrival of the Messiah.

XLII. These things therefore having now been explained, we give such a definition of the incarnation: The Incarnation is a divine and supernatural action, by which the eternal Son of God assumed a human nature, whole and holy, formed from the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary, into the unity of his ὑποστάσεως [hypostasis] without confusion, and thus became true man, so that he now subsists in two natures, divine and human, personally and inseparably joined.

XLIII. In this definition is expressed 1. the genus, which is an action not human but divine on account of the author, God, and indeed supernatural on account of the singular mode. 2. The specific difference, which is described 1. by reason of the one assuming, who is the λόγος [Logos]. 2. Of the nature assumed, which is human, miraculously produced. 3. Of the mode, which is the assumption of humanity to constitute one ὑφιστάμενον [hypostasized being] in an unconfused and inseparable manner.

XLIV. Hence Athanasius declares this whole matter most briefly and most solidly in his creed, saying that the incarnation of the λόγου [Logos] is nothing other than πρόσληψιν ἀνθρωπότητος εἰς θεότητα [the assumption of humanity into divinity], the assumption of humanity into divinity or into God, as the Latin interpreter translates.

XLV. Finally, practical meditation seems to be able to be included in three principal members, if indeed we consider 1. the causes impelling God, 2. the uses redounding to us, 3. the duties owed for so great a benefit.

XLVI. The causes impelling God are numbered as 3 principally: 1. the consideration of human misery, 2. the inexhaustible love of God, 3. the manifestation of divine glory.

XLVII. The uses redounding from the incarnation are so great that they can scarcely be measured, and so many that they can scarcely be numbered. The most illustrious Mr. President distinguishes them into universal, common, and special, which see in the Praesidium concerning the person of Christ.

XLIIX. Our duty therefore will be that we give thanks to God 1. with the heart, by which we acknowledge such great gifts, and never forget them, Psalm 103:4. 2. With the mouth, that we may celebrate the goodness of God with various Psalms and hymns, according to that passage at Colossians 3:16. 3. With our work, that we may conform our life to the divine will, that the light of our piety may shine, and thus our heavenly Father may be glorified. Matthew 5:16. XLIX. And these are those three heads of practical meditation, which the heavenly messengers seem to have hinted at in their three-stanza hymn. Luke 2:14. For while they give glory to God in the highest, they lead us by the hand to consider the impelling causes and the manner of the manifested glory: while they announce peace on earth, they tacitly insinuate the benefits redounding to us: while they pray for εὐδοκίαν for men, by which they may please God, they look toward the duties owed for so great a benefit. L. Let us therefore always exercise ourselves in these meditations, so that daily we shall sing Glory in the highest with the heavenly host.

Latin:

Thesis I.

IN magno illo pietatis mysterio, qvod Deus manifestatus in carne, 1. Tim. 3, 16. in qvod Angeli gestiunt παρακύψαι 1. Petr. 1, 12. tres qvasi actus concurrunt 1. carnis conceptio 2. conceptæ assumptio, 3. assumptæ unitio.

II. Licet autem inter hos nullum omninò temporis intervallum est cogitandum vel fingendum (nam Angelo nunciante & Spiritu Sancto adveniente mox fuit verbum in utero, mox intra uterum verbi caro, ut B. Gregorius loqvitur) meritô tamen docendi causâ distinguntur, ne obscuritatem pariat confusio.

III. Hanc itaq; partem in tres peculiares sectiones dividemus, initium â prima facturi & eandem sex capitibus inclusuri. 1. erit de vocabulis, 2. de dictis pro incarnatione. 3. de persona incarnata. 4. de tempore incarnationis. 5. de vera definitione. 6. de meditationibus practicis.

IV. Qvemadmodum termini, qvibus in rebus sacris de scribendis utimur, sunt vel ἔγγραφοι seu biblici; vel ἄγραφοι seu Ecclesiaftici; ita etiam præsenti in mysterio.

V. Εγγραφοι sunt: descensus Esai. 64, 1. Joh. 6, 33. manifestatio in carne, 1. Tim. 3, 16. κοινωνία carnis & sangvinis. Heb. 2, 14.

VI. Ἄγραφοι sunt corporatio, Hilarius in Prol. super Psalm Oeconomia verbi Damasc. lib. 3. c. 6. mixtura admirabilis, August. Ep. 3. ad Velus. Greg. Nazian. Orat. Panegy. in Christi nativ. inhumanatio Damasc. l. 3. c. 13.

VII. Sed magis usitatum in Ecclesia nomen est Incarnatio. Qvo etiam ad hoc Mysterium significandum Patres bene Latini usi sunt Aug. libr. 10. de civit. Dei c. 24. & 29. Hier. in c. 1. Marc. Ambros. in c. 23. Lucæ. Atq; in eâdem significatione â Græcis Patribus usurpatur vocabulum ἐνσάρκωσις.

VIII. Desumpta verò est vox ἐνσαρκώσεως ex Joh. 1. vers. 14. ubi Ap. ait, Verbum caro factum est, nim. non conversione Deitatis in carnem, sed assumtione humanitatis εἰς θεότητα in Deum.

IX. Incarnari ergò nihil est aliud, qvâm carnem fieri; & incarnatio notat actum illum mirabiliter singularem, in quo λόγος vel æternus Dei Filius in plenitudine temporis nostram naturam in suæ ὑποςάσεως unitatem suscepit sibique intimè univit.

X. Tria ergo vocabulum hoc innuit 1. λόγον qui incarnatur. 2. carnem, quæ assumitur. 3. utrisq; concursum personalem.

XI. Differt autem incarnatio ab unione. Incarnatio enim verbi propria est, qvippe de quo solo prædicari potest. Nec enim humanitas vel caro ipsa sed Persona Filii Dei dicitur tantùm incarnata; unio verò ad utramq; naturam pertinet, atq; reciprocè dicitur.

XII. Porrò, incarnatio λόγε in V. T. futura prædicitur per Prophetas; in N. facta declaratur per Apostolos. Dicta utrobiq; occurrunt plurima; nos ex qvovis instrumento aliqva proferemus.

XIII. 1. Sumimus ex c. 9. Esaiæ v. 6. Parvulus natus est nobis &c. Notandum 1. de Messia hîc sermonem fieri ut ex Matth. 4, 16. patet. 2. Prophetam de futuris loqvi in tempore præterito ob summam certitudinem. 3. distinctis nominibus pueri & filii distinctas naturas exprimi. 4. puerum illum esse verum Deum, id qvod appellationes tributæ satis insinuant.

XIV. Nos duos cum primis titulos urgemus nempe, qvòd vocatur 1. Deus. 2. pater æternitatis. In Hebræo est אל qvod in genere notat robustum & potentem, sed absolutè positum veri Dei nomen est, cui tribuitur κατ̓ ἐξοχὴν Jer. 38, 18. Notandum verò, qvod Messias non tantùm Deus, sed insuper Deus fortis vocetur, ut verus & omnipotens, non aliqvis nuncupativus æstimetur Deus.

XV. Deinde appellatur pater æternitatis, qvo nomine innuitur cum æterna ipsius duratio, tum seculorum productio. Jam qvi non tantùm æternus, sed etiam pater æternitatis est, eum sanè verum naturâ Deum esse oportet.

XVI. Qvibus ita declaratis pro incarnatione λόγε sic concludimus: Qvi verus Deus & Pater æternitatis, simul tamen puerulus est in tempore natus, eum incarnatum esse vel carnem humamam assumpsisse oportet. Sed Dei Filius, qui nominatur Deus, paterq; æternitatis, simul est puerulus in tempore natus. Qvare Filium Dei incarnatum esse vel carnem humanam assumpsisse oportet.

XVIII. 2. Ex Jer. 23, 5. Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, &c. de Messia hîc Dominum vaticinari, ipsi etiam Judæi non negant probantq́ve per Targum sive Chaldaicam versionem. Duplex autem hîc Mesfiæ natura duobus titulis perspicuis describitur. 1. nominatur germen Davidis. 1. ratione ortus, 2. ratione augmenti, & qvidem justum tum ratione sui, tum ratione nostri: Ratione sui, qvoniam justus est Messias homo habitu & actu; ratione nostri propter meritum & applicationem. 2. Appellatur Jehovah justitia nostra. In qvo seqvitur, Messiam esse verum Deum, qvia nomen soli Deo proprium illi attribuitur.

XIIX. Hinc tale pro incarnatione λόγεν formamus argumentum. Qvicunq; est verus Jehovæ & nihilominus dicitur germen Davidis in tempore suscitatum, is procul dubio incarnatus est vel humanam carnem assumpsit, sed filius Dei à patre missus in mundum, est verus Jehovah & nihilominus unâ dicitur germen Davidis. E. procul dubio Filius Dei incarnatus est.

XIX. Tertium suppeditat Mich. c. 5, 2. Et tu Bethlehem &c. De Mesfia hîc tantum agi constat ex c. 2. Matth. v. 6. cujus primò exprimitur patria, qvæ vocatur Bethlehem 2. Ponitur singulare nomen Messiæ dum vocatur מושׁל. 3. Describitur nativitas temporalis per verbum egrediendi, qvod sæpe idem est ac nasci. Gen. 15, 4. 2. Sam. 7, 12. &c. Tandem 4. innuitur æterna nativitas, & vera Deitas Messiæ per verba: egressus ejus ab initio à diebus æternitatis.

XX. Egressus ille æternus duobus vocabulis describitur 1. â qvondam, ab antiqvo. In fonte est מקדם qvod vocabulum, qvamvis pro certo & definito initio temporis sæpe sumitur: Non rarò tamen æternitatem notat, cum de Deo usurpatur, ut Hab. 1. v. 12. 2. à diebus sœculi. מימי עולם verò 3. habet significationes. 1, Sumitur pro duratione longa, 2. pro duratione mundi, 3. pro duratione principio & fine carente, ut hoc in loco. Hebræi n. cum æternitatis nomen propriũ non habeant, nomine Kedẽ & Olam utuntur ad eam significandam.

XXI. His ita explicatis contra Photinianos firmissinẽ sic concludi mus: qvi extitit ab æterno, simul tamen in tẽmpore egreditur ut homo, illum verè incarnari & carnem assumere oportet. Atqvi Messias qvâ DeƊ extitit ab æterno, & simul in tempore ex Bethlehem egressus est ut homo. E. illum verè incarnatum esse, & carnẽ assumpsisse oportet.

XXII. 4. Principalis locus est Joh. 1, 14. Verbum caro factum est, &c. Hic per verbum non intelligenda est vox aliqva evanescens, sed coessentiale illud verbum Patris, scilicet Filius Dei unigenitus, uti hoc ipsum etiam statim in 1. versu hujus cap.: videre est ubi aperce habetur, quod Deus erat verbum: Per carnem verò, non una tantum humanæ essentiæ pars, neq; etiam affectiones, sed tota & integra natura humana constans anima & corpore sine peccato. Hinc tale fluit argumentum. Qvicunq; caro factus est, is verè incarnatus est. Atqvi λόγος seu filius Dei factus est caro. E. λόγος verè incarnatus est.

XXIII. 5. Sumimus ex Epistola ad Col. c. 2. 9. in ipso habitat, &c. In hoc dicto singula verba consideranda 1. pronomine ἐν ἀυτῶ respicitur non ad doctrinam Christi, ut volunt Photiniani, sed ad ipsum Christum 2. per vocabulum κατοικῇ fixa & continuata innuitur mansio; 3. exprimitur ipsa inhabitatio πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος id est perfectissima & plenissima Deitas. 4. modus inhabitationis describitur adverbio σωματικῶς, qvo 3. innuuntur, 1. idem est qvod verè ac realiter. 2. idem qvod personaliter. 3. innuitur verum subjectum qvod est σῶμα vel humanitas Christi.

XXIV. Unde argumentamur: Qvicunq; incarne habitat personaliter, velut in proprio templo, eum certè incarnatum esse oportet. Ratio, qvia τὸ inhabitare per carnem fieri explicatur. Joh. 1, 14. Sed λόγος habitat in carne personaliter velut in proprio templo. E. λόγον incarnatum esse oportet. Qvid ad hæc dicta excipiant Photiniani, in ipso disputationis actu σὺν Θεῷ videbimus. Nos progredimur.

XXV. Qvamvis incarnatio dicatur opus totius Trinitatis efficienter & inchoativè (Pater enim dat Filium suum, Joh. 3, 16. & mittit eum Galat. 4, 4. & Spiritu Sancto ungitur Christus Joh. 3, 34. Actor. 10, 38. Ebr. 1, 9.) solius tamen Flii formaliter est & terminativè Joh. 1, 14. Ebr. 2, 14.

XXVI. Scholastici declarant illud similitudine trium puellarum, qvæ junctæ unam vestem texunt, sed eam tantùm uni adaptant. Ubi actio formandi & exterius induendi est qvidem omnibus communis, non tamen omnes, sed una tantùm induitur qvia hæc actio non in tribus, sed in una ex tribus terminatur.

XXVII. Hinc rectè Augustinus: Verbum caro factum est, inquit, non Pater, non Spiritus Sanctus, sed carnem Filii tota Trinitas fecit. In separabilia enim sunt opera Trinitatis. Et Serm. 3. de temp. Cum una sit Deitas, una sit divinitas, implevit quidem carnem Christi, & Pater & Spiritus Sanctus, sed majestate non susceptione.

XXIIX. Firmiter itaq; tenendum, in incarnatione operari quidem totam Trinitatem, sed solam Filii personam incarnari.

XXIX. Objiciunt hic nonnulli: Opera Trinitatis ad extra sunt indivisa, & omnibus personis communia. Incarnatio est opus totius Trinitatis ad extra. E.

XXX. Resp. breviter. Tria sunt genera operũ Trinitatis, 1. ad intra, 2. ad extra, 3. mixta, qvæ ad intra ratione termini, ad extra ratione initii. Illa sunt personalia, E. divisa. Ista essentialia. E. indivisa: Hæc personalia & essentialia. E. & divisa & indivisa.

XXXI. Mixtum opus est incarnatio: qvæ trium personarum est efficienter & inchoativè ob decretum & carnis perductionem: Sed formaliter & terminativè solius filii ob personalem istius carnis assumptionem.

XXXII. Cur autem secunda Deitatis persona sit incarnata, rationes piæ & perutiles â Justino, Athan. August. Irenæo & aliis adferuntur. Irenæus ex Genes. 1, 27. & Col. 1, 15. hanc affert: Cum homo restituendus esset ad Dei imaginem, debuit id fieri per eam personam, quæ est imago & character ὑπόστασεως Dei Ebr. 1, 3. item alibi inqvit: decebat ut ejusdem esset ἀνάπλασις, cujus fuerat πλάσις, id est, ut item nos crearet & recrearet, faceret & reficeret. Cui affine est illud Athanasii ad Epict. Conveniebat, ut ejusdem esset ἀνακτίζειν, cujus fuerit κτίζειν. Omnium autem dulcissima & pia consolatione plenissima est illa Irenei lib. 3. c. 20. Ideò Filium oportuit hominem fieri, ut nos, qvi eramus filii iræ adoptionem filiorum DEI reciperemus.

XXXIII. Filium autem qvando incarnatum esse dicimus, non intelligimus solam ejus hypōstasin absq; Deitate seu divina natura consideratam, sed naturam verbi divinam hypostaticè limitatam humanæ naturæ unitam esse credimus. Nam persona τῶ λόγω ab ejusdem natura, non ita segregari potest, ut illæ qvidem humanæ credatur hypostaticè juncta, hæc verò non.

XXXIV. Objicitur hic: Tota divina natura est incarnata, tota natura divina idem est, quod 3. personæ Trinitatis. E. hæ omnes sunt incarnatæ.

XXXV. Resp. Distingvendum est inter duplicem considerationem naturæ divinæ : vel enim consideratur ea absolutè & simpliciter prout scilicet omnibus tribus personis Trinitatis est communis, & hoc respectu eam nullo modo incarnatem dicimus : vel relatè prout natura divina certo qvopiam charactere personali limitata, & vel natura divina gigens, vel genita vel procedens intelligitur: & sic rectè dicimus, naturam divinam genitam esse incarnatam, qvæ nihil aliud est, qvam ipsissimus Dei filius.

XXXVI. Hinc rectè Damasc. dicit: Totam divinam naturam in una suarum hypostaseon incarnatam esse; & licet tota sit incarnata; non tamen ὁlikῶs totaliter est incarnata, quia incarnata est, qvatenus in Filio est, non qvatenus, in Patre & Spiritu Sancto.

XXXVII. Qvod non statim in principio Mundi incarnatus est Filius Dei, factum putatur, ut homines cum diuturnioribus malis conflictati magis agnoscerent infirmitatem suæ naturæ, & ad medicum clamarent. Notitia enim peccati est initium salutis.

XXXIIX. 2. Ut prius exercerentur in fide promissionum de futuro Messia, 3. ut Deus homines assuefaceret ad suos mores, qvi cum mora plerunqve conjuncti. 4. ut ab imperfectione legis ad Evangelii perfectionem traduceret: Et tandem 5. ut ob longam expectationem pluris fieret adventus Messiæ & redemptionis beneficium.

XXXIX. Porrò, qvod adventus λόγε non est diutius usqve in Mundi finem dilatus partim, id propter Deum partim propter nos factum est.

XL. Propter Deum 1. ut suam φιλανθρωπίαν ostenderet 2. ut promissiones de Messia factas impleret. Propter nos homines 1. ut plures per concionem Evangelii de λόγω incarnato possent converti. 2. ut fides hominũ augeretur 3. ut firmam futuræ hæreditatis spem conciperemus. 4. ut sincera dilectiomagis magisq; in nobis accenderetur.

XLI. Peracta itaqve est incarnatio λόγε in media Mundi ætate 1. Corinth. 11. v. 11. Hebr. 1. v. 1. 1. Joh. 1. v. 18. Qvod tempus fuit omnium commodissimum 1. propter ablationem Sceptri de Juda. 2. ob summam Judæorum malitiam. 3. ob doctrinæ reformationem. 4. ob magnum Electorum numerum. 5. ob spei de Messiæ adventu abjectionem.

XLII. His itaque jam explicatis talem damus incarnationis definitionem: Incarnatio est divina & supernaturalis actio, qua aternus Dei Filius naturam humanam integram & sanctam ex obumbratione Spiritus Sancti in utero virginis Maria formatam in unitatem suae ὑποστάσεως sine confusione assumpsit, atque ita verus homo factus est, ut jam in duabus naturis, divina & humana personaliter & indivulse copulatis subsistat.

XLIII. In hac definitione exprimitur 1. genus quod est actio non humana sed divina ob autorem Deum & quidem supernaturalis ob modum singularem. 2. Differentia specifica, quae describitur 1. ratione assumentis, qui λόγος. 2. assumptae naturae, quae humana miraculose producta 3. modi, qui est humanitatis ad constituendum unum ὑφιστάμενον inconfusa & indivulsa assumptio.

XLIV. Hinc Athanas. totam hanc rem brevissime & solidissime declaret in suo symbolo dicens, incarnationem λόγου nihil aliud esse, quam πρόσληψιν ἀνθρωπότητος εἰς θεότητα, assumptionem humanitatis in divinitatem vel in Deum ut vertit latinus interpres.

XLV. Tandem Meditatio practica tribus potissimum membris includi posse videtur, si nempe cogitemus 1. causas Deum impellentes, 2. usus ad nos redundantes, 3. officia pro beneficio tanto debita.

XLVI. Causae Deum impellentes 3. praecipue numerantur 1. miseriae humanae consideratio. 2. inexhausta Dei dilectio, 3. divinae gloriae manifestatio.

XLVII. Usus ex incarnatione redundantes tam magni sunt, ut vix mensurari, tam multi, ut vix numerari queant. Clariss. Dn. Praeses distingvit in universalem, communem & specialem, qui vid. in Praes. de pers. Christi.

XLIIX. Nostrum itaque officium erit, ut agamus Deo gratias 1. corde, quo agnoscamus tanta munera, nec eorum obliviscamur unqvam Psalm. 103, 4. 2. ore; ut variis Psalmis hymnisqve bonitatem Dei celebremus, juxta illud ad Col. 3, 16. 3. opere, ut vitam nostram voluntati divinae conformemus, ut lux pietatis nostrae luceat, & sic glorificetur pater noster coelestis. Matth. 5, 16. XLIX. Atqve haec sunt tria illa meditationis practicae capita, qvae hymno suo tristropho innuisse videntur coelestes nuncii. Luc. 2, 14. Dum enim Deo in excelsis dant gloriam, nos ad causas impellentes, & modum manifestatae gloriae considerandum manu ducunt: dum pacem in terris annunciant, usus ad nos redundantes tacite insinuant: dum hominibus εὐδοκίαν, qvâ placeant Deo, precantur, ad officia pro beneficio tanto debita respiciunt. L. In his ergo meditationibus nos semper exerceamus, ita qvotidie Gloria in excelsis cum coelorum exercitu cantabimus.


## 4 Fourth Disputation. On the Conception and Formation of the Flesh of Christ

Just as the λόγος is rightly said to be incarnate in the womb of Mary, so the flesh is said to be assumed into the ὑπόστασιν of the λόγος. And just as through the assumption of flesh, the λόγος is incarnate: so through the Incarnation of the λόγος, the flesh is assumed. Since, therefore, we have spoken thus far concerning the ἐνσαρκώσει of the λόγος; it remains to explain the assumption of the flesh into the ὑπόστασιν of the λόγος, which its formation or conception precedes.

II. Where, however, it is to be noted that those acts are distinguished for the sake of teaching and by the order of nature, but not in time.

III. For first the flesh of CHRIST was formed or conceived in the womb of Mary, then assumed, and thus united; whence the order appears. Yet all things happened simultaneously, because that flesh was assumed in being conceived, conceived in being assumed, and in being conceived and assumed was united to the λόγος. Simultaneously flesh, simultaneously the flesh of the Word of God, says Damascene, and Lombard repeats.

IV. Wherefore we shall treat of both acts in turn. But now we shall discourse at least of the former in this διασκέψει, following the order of nature, and therefore we shall speak of the formation or conception of the flesh of Christ.

V. The Angel describes this briefly ὐρανοπέμπτως but very clearly, that the Son of GOD was conceived of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Blessed Virgin Mary as a perfect man from her own substance and blood, Luke 1:35, and by those words he expresses both the efficient or producing cause and the material cause. VI. The efficient cause is the Holy Spirit, to whom indeed the conception is attributed not σπερματικῶς, that is, materially, as if he had been conceived from the substance of the Holy Spirit, but δημιουργικῶς, that is, effectively, and by an operation κατ' ἐξοχὴν (pre-eminently).

VII. Which things indeed are not to be understood as if the remaining persons of the whole Trinity were excluded.

VIII. For 1. the sacred text expressly mentions the three Persons, Luke 1:35, namely: 1. The Father, by the name of the Most High. 2. The Son, who by antiphrasis is called the Power of the Most High by the Angel, as will be demonstrated below in Thesis 20. 3. The Holy Spirit, αὐτολεξεί (in the very words) according to the interpretation of Damascene.

IX. 2. The formation of the flesh to be assumed was a purely external work; and therefore common to the whole Trinity on account of the identity of essence and mutual relation, according to the old saying of Augustine: The works of the Trinity toward the outside are undivided.

X. But as there are many other external works which pertain to all the persons, yet are attributed to one singularly and κατ' ἐξοχὴν (pre-eminently): so the formation of the flesh of Christ, although it was performed by the whole Trinity, is nonetheless assigned especially to the Holy Spirit, Luke 1:35, Matthew 1:18, 20. Thus in the Apostles' Creed it is said 'conceived', in the Nicene 'incarnate by the Holy Spirit'.

XI. We think this is done for this reason, because the flesh of Christ was not only merely formed, but was also sanctified and created immune from every stain of sin. But the work of sanctification is proper to the Holy Spirit, to whom therefore the very production of the human nature of Christ is singularly ascribed, since he purified the blood of Mary and the mass from which the flesh was to be formed, sanctified it, and by sanctifying it, formed it whole in nature.

XII. Here, however, the words of the Angel in Luke 1:35 are worthy of meditation, in which two propositions lie hidden. 1. The Holy Spirit will come upon you; τὸ ἐπέλθειν or ἐπέρχεσθαι denotes an action not common and ordinary, the plastic power by which God concurs in the generation of any persons whatsoever, Job 10:8, Psalm 139:5, but a singular and extraordinary miracle, separated from the common course of nature, as in Judges 14:6, Acts 1:8, Luke 24:29.

XIII. For the Holy Spirit was already present to the Virgin Mary by both a universal and a gracious presence, and yet he is said to be about to come anew by reason of a singular presence, by which he sanctified the mass destined for the flesh of Christ, and formed the human nature in the womb without male seed with the greatest miracle.

XIV. HowXIV. When therefore the Angel says to Mary, The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, an action is noted. 1. Singular and miraculous, according to which He was not present before. 2. Powerful and joined with virtue, by which He made her a mother beyond the order of things. 3. Swift and sudden, by which the miraculous conception was brought about unexpectedly and beyond opinion. For the grace of the Holy Spirit knows not slow efforts.

XV. 2. The power of the Most High shall overshadow thee. The Syriac has a word which simply signifies to protect: but there is greater emphasis in the word ἐπισκιάζειν, as Chemnitz notes, which is used in both the Old and New Testaments.

XVI. In the Old Testament it is used to denote a singular presence, both gracious (Deut. 33:12) and majestic (Exod. last, v. 35). Moreover, it is accustomed to be taken for defense, Ps. 91:4, 104:8, just as shadow also signifies protection (Judg. 9:15, Ps. 17:8, 57:2, Eccles. 7:13, Isa. 4:6, and elsewhere).

XVII. In the New Testament it is said of the overshadowing of the bright cloud at the transfiguration of Christ (Matt. 17:5, Mark 9:7, Luke 9:34). It is also used of Peter (Acts 5:15).

XVIII. Whence it appears that that word, if it is spoken properly and of created things, denotes the external sprinkling of a shadow: but if metaphorically and of God, it imports a peculiar manifestation, presence, protection, and filling of that thing which is overshadowed by God, not otherwise than as He filled the tabernacle and temple with His glory.

XIX. The predicate having been thus explained, it must likewise be seen what is denoted by the subject.

XX. However, two things can be understood by the power of the Most High. 1. In general, the action and singular presence of the DEITY or the Holy Spirit or even the whole Trinity, according to which He worked in the Virgin Mary, so that she might conceive the flesh of Christ, and her virginity nevertheless be defended and remain unviolated: and thus the word δύναμις would be taken essentially for the divine power exerting itself effectively and singularly. 2. In particular, the Word or Son of GOD, who is the Father's δύναμις or power; not otherwise than as the firstborn is called in the Scriptures the strength and power of his parent (Gen. 49:3, Deut. 21:17). By which manner His descent from heaven and arrival into the womb of Mary to assume flesh is elegantly expressed.

XXI. For as God once descended into the tabernacle and temple, and filled it with His grace, which action is called overshadowing: so the Son of GOD in the fullness of time descended into the womb of Mary, whom He overshadowed or singularly filled, while He assumed human nature from her most chaste blood, always however defending and preserving unharmed the virginity of the mother.

XXII. And thus the word δυναμεως might be taken personally for the Word Himself, who is the Power of the Father, and miraculously overshadowed Mary at the conception. Thus Gregory, Damascene, and Bede explained it.

XXIII. From what has been said thus far, it is clear that the Holy Spirit coming upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowing her wrought three memorable things: 1. θαυμάσιον ἁγιασμὸν, the miraculous sanctification of the fetus in the womb, Luke 1:35, 'that which is born of thee shall be holy.' 2. ἄμεσον ἐνέργειαν, the immediate operation of the Holy Spirit, ibid. 3. ἕνωσιν ὑποστατικὴν, the admirable union and concurrence of humanity and divinity in one person.

XXIV. These are the highest miracles, which our faith reverently believes, but our mind does not perceive. And for this reason the angel is thought to have used the word 'coming upon' and 'overshadowing,' the emphasis of which we do not sufficiently grasp, so that by the very words we might be admonished that we must abstain from scrutinizing the mystery of the incarnation, as noted by Eusebius, Bernard, and Chemnitz.

XXV. Furthermore, the Son of Mary, because of this conception, 1. is not called the Son of the Holy Spirit, since He is said to be conceived of Him (which was therefore difficult for Augustine to explain), as the Eutychians and Schwenkfeldians insanely claim. Because 1. nowhere in all Scripture is He so called. 2. St. Paul teaches that Christ according to His humanity is plainly ἀπάτωρ (without father), just as according to His divinity He is ἀμήτωρ (without mother). 3. There would be two Fathers in the Holy Trinity, and God made man would have had two Fathers, one of His divinity and another of His humanity, which is ἀφύσλογον (contrary to reason), as Alcuin teaches. 4. The particle 'ex' in Matthew 1:18, 20, does not designate matter, as Jerome revealed some formerly opined, but the efficient cause or the power and operation. Rightly Justin Martyr: 'Conceptus est ὀυ διὰ συνουσίας, ἀλλὰ διὰ δυνάμεως τὴν παρθένον ἐγκύμονα κατέστησε'—He was conceived not through intercourse, but through power He rendered the virgin pregnant.

XXVI. Nor, 2, will the Photinians obtain their affirmative, namely that Christ is the Son of God because of the divine conception, from the particle 'διὸ καὶ'; indeed, it rather vanishes into smoke. For 1. it is not only announced by the angel that the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit is the one overshadowing of the power of God, through which we have shown above that the λόγον ὁμούσιον is rightly understood. 2. By the particle 'therefore' reference is made to the fulfillment of the Prophetic Prediction of Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23. Gabriel shows that this prediction is now to be fulfilled, and the sense of the words is as follows: Because you, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, will give birth with virginity unharmed, hence that which is born shall be called the holy Son of God, and thus the prophecy of Isaiah concerning the Son of the Virgin, whose name is God-man, will be fulfilled.

XXVII. But as regards the material cause, it is the Virgin Mary, descended from the house of David, in whose womb he was conceived.

XXVIII. It was necessary for the mother of the Lord to be a pure and intact virgin for these reasons. 1. The reason of the mystery required it. For what is more admirable than that a Virgin conceives a Son, with virginity uncorrupted? 2. The fulfillment of the prophecies. For thus it had been predicted by Isaiah ch. 7:14, and in that primeval promise he was called the seed not of a man, but of a woman, Gen. 3. And this was the name of the Messiah, Gen. 49:10, שִׁילֹה that is, son of the afterbirth, or son of her in the feminine, His Son/or a man's Son/ because he had to be the son of a Virgin. 3. They think this was done, 1. because it befitted the Creator not to use a customary, but a strange and admirable birth, such as that from a Virgin. Ignatius; see also Chrysostom, Leo the Great, and Bernard. 2. To commend an example of chastity to all, according to Nazianzen and Ambrose, which, however, is not to be accepted in the sense of the Papists, as if the Lord had imposed a perpetual law of virginity, who is himself known as the author of holy marriage. 3. That he might be conceived without sin. 4. That the reparation itself might correspond to the fall. This is the almost common reasoning of the Fathers. Thus Tertullian, Augustine, and Chrysologus.

XXIX. These things are to be well noted against the enemies of unbelief, both those established outside the boundaries of the Church, such as the Jews (whom the passage of Isaiah 7 especially offends, where it concerns the word עַלְמָה) and Pagans, of whom Augustine speaks; and those placed within the borders of the Church, such as the Antimariatæ, or Antidicomarianitæ, Cerinthus before the birth, Jovinian at the birth; Helvidius after the birth.

XXX. We do not indeed deny that Mary is called a Virgin in the Scriptures, not free, but betrothed to Joseph, Matt. 1:18, Luke 1:37. The causes of this matter are explained by Basil, Bernard, Jerome, Lyra, and others.

XXXI. For Mary was not joined to flesh, but the divine power also introduced the members of youth through the virginal womb of the inviolate mother, says Augustine.

- XXXII. The Blessed Fathers, Jerome, Augustine, and Irenaeus, wish this to be prefigured as an admirable mystery and a deed by the type of the closed gate (Ezekiel 44:1), the stone cut out without hands (Daniel 2:34), and the structure of Solomon's temple built without iron tools (1 Kings 6:7); Luther, however, illustrates it with the sun penetrating glass without harming it, in his German song: 'As the sun shines through the glass,' etc.

XXXIII. But that Christ is said to be conceived and born of a woman (Jeremiah 31:22; Galatians 4:4) refers: 1. Not to the deprivation of virginity, but only to the difference of sex, as Augustine says. 2. The noun נקבה is a noun of sex, not of status, which is manifest from almost all the places in which it is used. For it is opposed to the noun זכר, that is, 'male'; but 'male' is a noun of sex, as is evident, without regard to marriage.

XXXIV. Whence it is clear that Mary was a pure, holy, and immaculate Virgin, and the mother of our Lord and Savior, from whom the body of Christ was truly formed.

XXXV. Man consists of two parts: soul and body; the Logos assumed both; both were produced in the womb of Mary, the soul without matter, the body from matter.

XXXVI. The matter of the body of Christ was: 1. A spermatic mass, because the ordinary mode of generation requires it. Nor can it be proven that the flesh of Christ was miraculously created or produced out of nothing; and therefore, since Scripture is silent, no miracle should be invented here. However, it was only a virginal and most pure seed, because Mary conceived as a virgin without the knowledge of a man.

XXXVII. 2. That mass was either brought from heaven or formed elsewhere, but elaborated in Mary's womb, whence Christ is called the fruit of Mary's womb (Luke 1:42). Matthew attempted to express this emphatically when he says, ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχει. For she who is pregnant is called ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα (Genesis 38:24; 2 Kings 11:5; and in the New Testament, Matthew 24:19; 1 Thessalonians 5:3; Revelation 12:2).

…XXXIIX. 3. That mass was sanctified and immune from all sin, not by reason of the first conception, as if Mary had been born, but on account of the sanctification of the Spirit coming upon her. No particle of Mary's body was indeed without sin in itself, yet that mass, from which the body of Christ was to be formed and which was contaminated before the angelic announcement, was afterwards purged, so that from it the holy thing might be conceived, Luke 1:35.

XXXIX. Hence the Messiah is called by Jeremiah in the abstract righteousness, ch. 23; by Daniel the Holy of Holies, ch. 9; by Zechariah Just and Savior, ch. 9:9; by the Apostle a High Priest tempted in all things without sin, Heb. 4:15; innocent, undefiled, separate, ch. 7:26; by Peter a lamb without blemish and without spot, 1 Epist. ch. 1:18, 19.

XL. All indeed who are conceived from the seed of a man are in sins, Rom. 5:12, but Christ is ἄσπορος [seedless], and consequently was conceived without sin.

XLI. For otherwise the humanity could neither have been united to the divinity, nor would it have been sufficient for any part of its office, because it could neither teach righteousness, nor expiate sins, nor intercede for sinners, nor safely rule the universal Church, unless it were just and subject to no sins.

XLII. And thus far concerning the matter of the body of Christ: now we shall say something concerning the manner of the formed and conceived humanity, where three things come into consideration, of which we shall treat in order.

XLIII, 1. Concerning the production of the soul. Zanchius affirms that the soul of Christ was created from nothing and immediately by God, because the souls of other men are not propagated by traducianism, but are created, which Martinius follows.

XLIV. But 1. there are reasons by which the immediate creation of the soul of Christ is firmly proven. 2. The hypothesis concerning the creation of all souls is uncertain and false; indeed, we invert it thus: Such as is the ordinary production of souls, such also was that of the soul of Christ. But the souls of the rest are produced mediately by traducianism. Therefore, the same must be established concerning the soul of Christ.

XLV. The major premise is evident from the opinion of the adversaries, who infer the production of the soul of Christ from the common mode of production. 2. It is rash to invent miracles and to invent exceptions, while Scripture is silent. 3. Because Christ is called the son of man, the son of Mary. But it would be absurd if the body were formed from Mary, but the soul were not propagated at the same time.

XLVI. 2. On the formation of the body. The Scholastics, following Thomas, distinguish between the preparation of the matter and the formation of the body, whom

Zanchius, where he defends that successive preparation of matter, from whom Polanus repeats it.

XLVII. 1. But will this very thing be proven from there? 2. Because the mover is hyperphysical, and the conception itself is thought to have occurred ἐν τῷ νῦν (in the now) and suddenly (which Basil, Leo the Great, Fulgentius, and Damascene teach), no necessity compels us to depart from our opinion.

XLVIII. We therefore maintain that all things were perfectly formed at one and the same time. Damascene agrees, who says, The Son of God constructed for himself animated flesh, not through additions, but completed in one context.

XLIX. Keckermann indeed denies this in System of Theology, book 3, chapter 2. But the orthodox Fathers affirm this, because 1. The power of the agent, that is, the Holy Spirit, is infinite, and therefore could perfect it without delay. 2. The λόγος was never the ὑπόστασις (hypostasis) to any embryo, but only to human and animated flesh, John 1:14. In which opinion Athanasius writes ἐν αὐτῇ ὑπάρξῃ ἐνωθεῖσα σὰρξ τῇ λόγῳ ὑπόστασις. In the very moment of conception, the flesh was united to the person of the Word.

L. 3. On the conception of the whole of humanity. It was done, 1. In an instant, as has been shown, and therefore the ancients said that the conception of the flesh was done, not at least δι᾽ ἡμᾶς for us, nor only καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς, according to us, but ὑπὲρ ὑμᾶς above us. 2. Immediately after the annunciation of the Angel, and after the assent of the Blessed Virgin, Luke 1:38; so think Augustine, Theophylact, Damascene, Gregory the Great, whose words Lombard cites here. 3. The conception was so done that the soul was united with the body simultaneously and suddenly.

Latin:

VTI λόγος in utero Mariae incarnatus, sic caro in λόγῳ ὑπόστασιν assumta rectè dicitur. Et vel uti per assumptionem carnis, λόγος est incarnatus: ita per Incarnationem λόγου caro est assumta. Postqvam igitur de ἐνσαρκώσει λόγου hactenus diximus; restat explicanda carnis in λόγῳ ὑπόστασιν assumtio, qvam praecedit ejusdem formatio vel conceptio.

II. Ubi tamen notandum, actus illos docendi qvidem causa & ordine naturae, non tamen tempore distingvi.

III. Nam primum caro CHRISTI in utero Mariae est formata vel concepta, post assumta, & sic unita; unde apparet ordo. Contigerunt tamen omnia simul, qvia caro illa concipiendo assumta, assumendo concepta, concipiendo assumendoq; λόγῳ fuit unita. Simul caro, simul Dei Verbi caro, inqvit Damascenus, & repetit Lombardus.

IV. Qvare de utrisqve actibus deinceps agemus, Nunc verò de priori saltem, in hac διασκέψει differemus, secuturi ordinem naturae, ideoq; dicturi de carnis Christi formatione vel conceptione.

V. Hanc Angelus ὐρανοπέμπτως breviter ἀλλὰ μάλα λιγέως describit, qvod Filius DEI de Spiritu S. in utero B. Virginis Mariae ex ipsius substantia & sangvine perfectus homo conceptus fuerit, Luc. 1, 35. illisq; verbis tum causam efficientem seu producentem, tum materialem exprimit. VI. Efficiens causa est Spiritus S. cui qvidem conceptio non σπερματικῶς id est, materialiter, ac si ex substantia Spiritus Sancti conceptus fuisset, sed δημιουργικῶς id est effective, & per operationem κατ' ἐξοχὴν attribuitur.

VII. Qvæ qvidem ita non sunt intelligenda, ac si reliqvæ τῆς πανταγῆς τριάδος personæ excluderentur.

IIX. Nam 1. disertè sacer textus trium meminit Personarum Luc. 1, 35. veluti 1. Patris nomine Altissimi. 2. Filii qvi per ἀντίφρασιν Virtus Altissimi ab Angelo appellatur, ut inferius Thes. 20. demonstrabitur. 3. Spiritus Sancti αὐτολεξεί juxta Damasceni interpretationem.

IX. 2. Carnis assumendæ formatio fuit opus purè externum; ideoqve toti Trinitati propter essentiæ ταυτότητα identitatem & mutuum respectum commune juxta vetus Augustini dictum, Opera Trinitatis ad extra sunt indivisa.

X. Ut autem aliàs multa sunt externa opera, qvæ omnibus personis competunt, uni tamen singulariter & κατ' ἐξοχὴν tribuuntur: sic formatio Carnis Christi, licet à tota Trinitate sit peracta, nihilominus assignatur præcipuè Spiritui S. Luc: 1, 35. Matth. 1. 18, 20. Sic in Symbolo Apostolico dicitur conceptus, in Nicæno incarnatus de Spiritu Sancto.

XI. Hoc autem ideo putamus fieri, qvia caro Christi non tantum nude formata, sed insuper sanctificata, & ab omni labe peccati condita est immunis. Opus vero sanctificationis proprium est Spiritui S. cui propterea ipsa productio humanæ Christi naturæ singulariter adscribitur, qvoniam sangvinem Mariæ & massam ex qva formanda caro purgavit, sanctificavit & sanctificando naturâ integram formavit.

XII. Hic autem mediatione digna sunt verba Angeli Luc. 1, 35. in qvibus duæ latent propositiones. 1. Spiritus S. superveniet in te τὸ ἐπέλθειν vel ἐπέρχεσθαι notat actionem non communem & ordinariam πλαστυργίαν qva Deus concurrit ad qvorumvis generationem Job. 10. 8. Pf. 139. 5. sed singularem & extraordinariam á communi naturæ cursu segregatam θαυματουργίαν, ut Jud. 14, 6. Act. 1, 8. Luc. 24. 29.

XIII. Nam præsentia tum universali tum gratiosa Mariæ virgini jam ante adfuit Spiritus S. & tamen de novo dicitur adventurus ratione præsentia singularis, qva massam ad carnem Christi deputatam sanctificavit, & humanam naturam in utero sine virili semine maximo cum miraculo efformavit.

XIV. QvanXIV. Qvando ergo Angelus ad Mariam ait, Spiritus S. superveniet in te, notatur actio. 1. Singularis & miraculosa, secundum qvam antea non adfuit. 2. Potens & cum virtute conjuncta, qva ipsam effecit matrem præter rerum seriem. 3. Velox & repentina, qva subitò & præter opinionem conceptio miraculosa facta est. Nescit enim tarda molimina Spiritus Sancti gratia.

XV. 2. Virtus altissimi obumbravit tibi. Syrus habet verbum, qvod simpliciter significat protegere: sed major est emphasis verbi ἐπισκιάζειν, annotante Chemnitio, qvod & in V. & in N. Testam. usurpatur.

XVI. In V. Test. adhibetur ad notandam singularem præsentiam tum gratiosam Deut. 33, 12. tum Majestaticam Exod. ult. v. 35. Solet insuper pro defensione sumi, Psal. 91, 4. 104, 8. sicut & umbra protectionem significat Jud. 9, 15. Psal. 17, 8. 5-2. Eccles. 7, 13. Esa. 4, 6. & alibi.

XVII. In N. Test. dicitur de umbratione nubis lucidæ in transfiguratione Christi Matth. 17, 5. Mar. 9. 7. Luc. 6, 34. De Petro etiam usurpatur, Act. 1, 15.

XVIII. Unde apparet verbum illud si propriè & de rebus creatis dicatur, notare externam umbræ aspersionem: sin metaphoricè & de Deo importare peculiarem manifestationem, præsentiam, protectionem & impletionem ejus rei, qvi à Deo inumbratur, non secus ac tabernaculum & templum sua gloria implevit.

XIX. Exposito ita prædicato, qvid per subjectum notetur similiter videndum.

XX. Duo autem per virtutem altissimi possunt intelligi. 1. In genere DEITATIS aut Spiritus S. vel etiam totius Trinitatis actio & præsentia singularis, secundum qvam operata est in Maria virgine, ut carnem Christi conciperet, ejusqve Virginitas nihilominus defenderetur & illibata maneret: atqve ita vox δύναμεως sumeretur essentialiter pro divina potentia sese efficaciter & singulariter exerente. 2. In specie λόγος vel DEI Filius, qvi est Patris δύναμις vel potentia; non secus atq; primogenitus appellatur in Scripturis sui parentis robur ac virtus Gen. 49, 3. Deut. 21, 7. Qvo pacto ejus descensus de cœlo, & adventus in uterum Mariæ ad assumendam carnem eleganter exprimitur.

XXI. Ut enim olim descendit DEUS in tabernaculum & templum, illudqve sua gratia replevit, qvæ actio vocatur umbratio: sic Filius DEI in plenitudine temporis descendit in Maria uterum, qvem obumbravit seu singulariter replevit, dum ex ejus castissimis sangvinibus humanam naturam affumpsit, semper tamen defendens & illæsam conservans matris virginitatem.

XXII. Atqve ita vox δυναμεως caperetur personaliter pro ipso Λόγῳ, qvi Patris est Potentia, & Mariam conceptionem miraculose inumbravit. Sic exposuit Gregorius, Damascenus & Beda.

XXIII. Ex hactenus dictis patet, qvod Spiritus Sanctus superveniens & virtus altissimi obumbrans tria fuerint operata memorabilia. 1. θαυμάσιον ἁγιασμὸν sanctificationem miraculosam fœtus in utero Luc. 1, 35. qvod ex te nascetur Sanctum. 2. ἄμεσον ἐνέργειαν, immediatam operationem Spiritus S. ibid. 3. ἕνωσιν ὑποστατικὴν admirabilem humanitatis & divinitatis in una persona concursum.

XXIV. Hæc summa sunt miracula, qvæ fides nostra reverenter credit, mens autem nostra non percipit. - Et propter hanc causam angelus putatur adhibuisse verbum superveniendi & obumbrandi, qvorum emphasin non satis asseqvimur, ut ipsis vocabulis admoneremur à scrutatione mysterii incarnationis abstinendum esse, annotante Eusebio, Bernardo & Chemnitio.

XXV. Porrò Filius Mariæ propter hanc conceptionem 1. non dicitur Filius Spiritus Sancti qvoniam ex illo (qvod Augustino ideo explicatu difficile erat) dicitur conceptus, ut Eutychiani & Schwenkfeldiani insaniunt. Qvia 1. in tota Scriptura nullibi ita vocatur. 2. D. Paulus docet qvod Christus secundum humanitatem planè sit ἀπάτωρ, sicuti secundum divinitatem ἀμήτωρ. 3. Duo Patres essent in S. S. Trinitate, & DEUS homo factus duos habuisset Patres, unum divinitatis alterum humanitatis, qvod ἀφύσλογον docente Alcuino. 4. Particula ex Matth. 1, 18.20. non materiam, ut nonnullos qvondam opinatos fuisse prodidit Hieronymus, sed causam efficiente sive vim & operationem defignat. Rectè Justinus Martyr. Conceptus est ὀυ διὰ συνουσίας, ἀλλὰ διὰ δυνάμεως τὴν παρθένον ἐγκύμονα κατέστησε non per concubitum, sed per virtutem virginem reddidit gravidam.

XXVI. Neqve 2. Photiniani suam affirmativam, nempe ob conceptionem divinam Christum esse filium Dei, ex particula διὸ καὶ obtinebunt, imo potius in fumum abit. Nam 1. non tantum nunciatur ab angelo superventus Spiritus S. sed una inumbratio virtutis Dei, per quam λόγον ὁμούσιον recte intelligi supra ostendimus. 2. Per particulam ideog; respicitur ad complementum Prophetici Vaticinii Esai. 7, 14. Matth. 1, 23. Hanc prædictionem esse jam implendam ostendit Gabriel, & sensus verborum talis est. Qvia tu per operationem SpiritusSancti virginitate illæsa paries, hinc τὸ γενώμενον sanctum vocabitur Dei Filius, adeoqve implebitur Vaticinium Esaiæ de Filio Virginis, cui nomen homo Deus.

XXVII. Cæterum materialem causam qvod attinet,est Virgo Maria ex domo Davidis oriunda, in cujus utero conceptus est.

XXVIII. Virginem esse oportuit matrem Domini puram & intactam his de causis. Reqwirebat id. 1. Mysterii ratio. Qvid enim magis admirabile, qvam qvod Virgo Filium concipit, incorrupta Virginitate. 2. Vaticiniis impletio. Ita enim prædictum erat ab Esaia c. 7, 14. & in primæva illa promissione appellabatur semen non viri, sed mulieris Gen. 3. Et hoc nomen erat Messiæ Gen. 49, 10. שִׁילֹה id est, filius secundinæ, vel filius ejus in fœminino, Jhr Sohn/oder eines Menschen Sohn/ qvia Virginis filius esse debuit. 3. Factum id putant 1. qvod decuerit Creatorẽ, non consveto sed peregrino, admirandoq; uti partu, qvalis est ex Virgine. Ignatius; vide etiam Chrysostomum, Leonem Magnum, & Bernhardum. 2.Ut castitatis exemplum commendaret üniversis, juxta Nazianzenum & Ambrosium, qvod tamen non Pontificiorum sensu accipiendum, quasi virginitatis legem perpetuam Dominus tulerit, qvi & ipse sacri conjugii autor cognoscitur. 3. Ut conciperetur absqve peccato. 4. Ut lapsui responderet ipsa reparatio. Hæc Patrum ratio ferè communis est. Sic Tertullianus, Augustinus & Chrysologus.

XXIX. Hæc probè notanda sunt contra hostes ἀπισίας tum extra Ecclesiæ pomœria constitutos, ut sunt Judæi (qvos magnopere ossendit inprimis locus Esai 7, ubi de voce עַלְמָה) & Pagani, de qvibus Augustinus: tùm intra Ecclesiæ fines positos, ut sunt Antimariatæ, seu Antidicomarianitæ, Cerinthus ante partum, Jovianus in partu; Helvidius post partum.

XXX. Non qvidem diffitemur, qvod Maria in Sacris dicatur Virgo non libera, sed desponsata, Josepho Matth. 1, 18. Luc 1, 37. Hujus rei causas exponuut Basilius, Bernhardus, Hieronymus, Lyra & alii.

XXXI. Nam non copulata fuit Maria carni, sed & virtus divina per inviolatæ matris Virginea viscera, membra juventutis introduxit Augustinus.

- XXXII. Id tanquam admirandum mysterium & factum typo portæ clausæ, Ezech. 44, 1. Lapidis absq; manu revulsi Dan. 2, 34. Structuræ templi Salomonis absq; ferramento ædificati 1. Reg. 6, 7. præfiguratum volunt B. Patres, Hieronymus, Augustinus & Irenæus, Lutherus verò simili illustrat à sole penetrante vitrum, id tamen non lædente, in Cantione germanica: Als die Sonn durch scheint das Glaß/ &c.

XXXIII. Quod verò Christus dicitur conceptus & natus ex muliere Jerem. 31, 22. Gal. 4, 4. respicitur 1. non ad privationem virginitatis, sed tantum ad differentiam sexus, ut dicit Augustinus. 2. nomen נקבה est nomen Sexus non status, quod ex omnibus ferè locis, quibus usurpatur, manifestum est. Opponitur enim nomini זכר id est, Masculus, Masculus autem est nomen sexus, ut constat, absq; respectu ad conjugium.

XXXIV. Unde patet, Mariam puram, sanctam & immaculatam Virginem fuisse matremq; Domini ac Salvatoris nostri, ex qua corpus Christi verè formatum.

XXXV. Constat homo duabus partibus anima & corpore: utramque λόγος assumpsit; utraque in utero Mariæ producta est, anima sine materia, corpus ex materia.

XXXVI. Materia vero corporis Christi fuit. 1. Massa σπερματικὴ, quia ordinarius generationis modus eam requirit. Neque probari potest, carnem Christi miraculosè creatam, aut ex nihilo productam esse; ideoque Scriptura silente, nullum hic miraculum fingendum, Fuit autem semen tantum virgineum & purissimum, quia sine viri cognitione Maria virgo concepit.

XXXVII. 2. Massa illa fuit vel de cœlo delata, vel aliunde formata, sed in Mariæ utero elaborata, unde Christus dicitur fructus ventris Mariæ, Luc. 1, 42. Matthæus conatus est emphaticè exprimere, cum inquit, ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχει. Quæ enim gravida est vocatur ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα Genes. 38, 24. 2. Reg. 11. 5. Et in Nov. Testam. Matth. 24, 19. 1. Thess. 5, 3. Apoc. 12, 2.

XXXIIX. 3. Massa illa sanctificata & ab omni peccato immunis, non ratione primæ conceptionis, quasi Maria absq; peccata originis fuisset nata, sed propter sanctificationem Spiritus supervenientis. Nulla quidem particula corporis Mariæ caruit peccato in se, ista tamen massa, ex qua corpus Christi formandum & quæ ante nuncium angelicum contaminata fuit, post modum purgata est, ut ex illa conciperetur sanctum, Luc. 1, 35.

XXXIX. Hinc Messias à Jeremia in abstracto dicitur justitia c. 23. à Daniele Sanctus Sanctorum c. 9. à Zacharia Justus & Salvator. c. 9, 9. ab Apostolo Pontifex per omnia tentatus absq; peccato. Heb. 4, 15. innocens impollutus, segregatus c. 7, 26. à Petro agnus inculpatus & incontaminatus 1. Epist. c. 1, 18, 19.

XL. Omnes quidẽ qui ex semine viri concipiuntur in peccatis Rom. 5, 12, Christus autẽ ἄσπορος, & consequens sine peccato conceptus est.

XLI. Aliàs enim nec divinitati uniri potuisset humanitas, neq; ulli parte muneris sui sufficiens fuisset, quia nec justitiam docere, nec peccata expiare, nec pro peccatoribus intercedere, nec universam Ecclesiam tuto regere posset, nisi justus nullisq; peccatis obnoxius.

XLII. Atq; hactenus de materia corporis Christi: jam de modo formatæ conceptæq; humanitatis aliqvid dicemus, ubi tria in considerationem veniunt, de qvibus ordine agemus.

XLIII, 1. De productione animæ. Zanchius affirmat, Animam Christi à nihilo & immediatè à Deo creatam esse, quia aliorum hominum animas per traducem non propagentur, sed creentur, qve sequitur Martinius

XLIV. At 1. de sunt rationes, qvibus firmiter probetur immediata creatio animæ Christi 2. Incerta est & falsa hypothesis de omnium animarum creatione; imò invertimus ita: Qvalis est productio animarum ordinaria, talis qvoq; fuit animæ Christi. Sed reliqvorum animæ producuntur mediatè per traducem. Idem igitur de anima Christi statuendum.

XLV. Major patet ex adversariorum sententia, qui à modo productionis communi colligunt productionem animæ Christi. 2. Temerarium est miracula fingere & exceptiones fingere, tacente Scriptura, 3. Qvia Christus vocatur filius hominis, filius Mariæ. Absonum autem foret, corpus ex Maria esse formatum, animam vero simul non propagatam.

XLVI. 2. De formatione corporis. Scholastici ex Thomæ distinguunt inter præparationem materiæ & formationem corporis, qvos seqvitur

Zanchius ubi successivam illam materiæ præparationem defendit, ex quo repetit Polanus.

XLVII. 1. Verum inde probabitur hoc ipsum? 2. Quia movens est hyperphysicum, & conceptio ipsa contra communem Naturæ legem ἐν τῷ νῦν & subitò facta putetur (quod docent Basilius, Leo Magnus, Fulgentius & Damascenus) nulla nos cogit necessitas, ut discedamus à nostra sententia.

XLVIII. Statuimus ergo simul & semel omnia perfectè formata esse. Astipulatur Damascenus, qui ait, Filius Dei construxit sibi carnem animatam, non per additamenta, sed uno contextu absolutum.

XLIX. Negat hoc quidem Keckerman. in Syst. Theol. 3. c. 2. Sed affirmant hoc orthodoxi Patres, quia. 1. Virtus agentis id est, Spiritus S. est infinita, & ideo sine mora perficere potuit. 2. λόγος nunquam fuit ὑπόστασις alicui embryoni, sed tantum humanæ & animatæ carni, Joh. 1, 14. Quam in sententiam Athanasius scribit ἐν αὐτῇ ὑπάρξῃ ἐνωθεῖσα σὰρξ τῇ λόγῳ ὑπόστασις. In ipso conceptionis momento, caro unita est verbi personæ.

L. 3. De conceptione totius humanitatis. Facta est, 1. In instanti, ut ostensum, ideoq; dixerunt veteres, conceptionem carnis factam esse, non saltem δι᾽ ἡμᾶς propter nos, nec tantum καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς, secundum nos, sed ὑπὲρ ὑμᾶς supra nos. 2. Statim post annunciationem Angeli, & post assensum S. Virginis Luc. 1, 38. ita censet Augustinus, Theophylactus, Damascenus, Gregorius Magnus, cujus verba hæc citat Lombardus. 3. Ita facta est conceptio, ut simul subitoq; uniretur anima cum corpore.


### Chapter V, On the End

Chapter V, On the End.

LI. These things therefore having been explained, it remains that we speak of the end of the conception of Christ.

LII. As all things were done for our sake, so the conception of Christ was done for us and for our salvation. The Law requires perfect obedience. But indeed this perfection is lacking in us; we are conceived in sins, and we draw vicious matter from our parents.

LIII. In order, therefore, that our impure conception might be covered before God, Christ, conceived without sin, satisfied the Law in our place, because we ought to have been conceived holily and without sin.

LIV. The satisfaction of CHRIST consists indeed in acting and suffering, of which we call the former active, the latter passive obedience; yet for that reason holiness ought not to be excluded entirely

inhering in CHRIST, in whom he is conceived, since in him is not only the necessary quality of the person of the Mediator, but one part of that most perfect obedience which the Law requires of us.

LV. Wherefore, just as Christ was conceived for our sake, so also was he conceived holy and without sin for our sake, so that by this holiness the uncleanness both of the parents begetting and of the children conceived might be covered. The Apostle seems to hint at this end in Heb. 10:5, and Augustine discourses at length concerning it.

LVI. From this end and consideration of the Holy Conception of Christ we can draw both living consolation, which consists in the washing away of filth, accomplished by the holiness of Christ; and serious admonition, which consists in the pursuit of the holiness of our life. 1. By the example of Christ. 2. By the command of God, Levit. 11:45. 3. By our calling, 1 Pet. 1:15.

LVII. If we do this, we shall be vessels of grace here, and one day of glory, where that which is begun here will be consummated, where we shall be rendered perfect men according to the measure of the fullness of Christ, Ephes. 4:15.

Latin:

Caput V, De Fine.

LI. His itaq; explicatis, restat ut de fine conceptionis Christi dicamus.

LII. Ut omnia nostri causa, sic conceptio Christi propter nos & nostram salutem facta est. Lex requirit perfectam obedientiam. At verò hæc perfectio deest nobis, concipimur in peccatis, & materiam vitiosam trahimus ex parentibus.

LIII. Ut igitur impura conceptio tegeretur coram Deo, Christus sine peccato conceptus, nostri loco satisfecit Legi, quia nos sancte & sine peccato concepti debuimus.

LIV. Consistit quidem CHRISTI satisfactio in agendo & patiendo, quorum illud activam, hoc passivam obedientiam nuncupamus; non tamen ob id excludi penitus debet sanctitas

CHRISTO inhærens, in qva est conceptus, qvippe qvo non tantum est necessaria qvalitas personæ Mediatoris, sed una pars illius perfectissimæ obedientiæ, qvam Lex à nobis reqvirit.

LV. Qvare uti Christus propter nos conceptus, ita & propter nos sanctus & sine peccato conceptus, ut ita istius sanctitate immundities tum parentum gignentium, tum liberorum conceptorum tegeretur. Hunc finem innuere videtur Apostolus Hebr. 10. 5. &c. de illo prolixè differit Augustinus.

LVI. Ex hoc fine & consideratione S. Conceptionis Christi haurire possumus, tum vivam consolationem, qvæ consistit in ablutione sordium, sanctitate Christi peracta; cum seriam admonitionem, qvæ consistit in studio sanctitatis vitæ nostræ. 1. Exemplo Christi. 2. Mandato Dei, Levit. 11, 45. 3. Vocatione nostra, 1. Petr. 1, 15.

LVII. hoc si fecerimus, hîc vasa gratiæ, olim gloriæ erimus, ubi consummabitur, qvod hîc inchoatur, ubi reddemur viri perfecti juxta mensuram plenitudinis Christi, Ephes. 4, 15.


## 5 Disputation V. On the Assumption of the Flesh of Christ

Thesis I.

We have recently treated of the conception of the flesh of Christ; now we must treat of its assumption, which is indeed distinct from the Union and Conception in order, but not in time. For from the moment God assumed man, he simultaneously united soul and body to himself, nor was the flesh first conceived and afterwards assumed, but it was assumed in conception and conceived in assumption, as Lombard speaks in book 3, dist. 2, ch.

II. We shall proceed in this order: 1. We shall prove that the assumption took place. 2. We shall reveal who assumed it. 3. What was assumed. 4. Into what it was assumed. 5. How the assumption took place. And finally, 6. How long this assumption lasts. To which we shall lastly append a very brief practical meditation.

III. To prove the first point, therefore, we bring forward chiefly that classic passage Heb. [2]:14, 16, in which two predicates are proposed concerning the Son of God or Jesus, considered according to his divine nature considerated. For that this is the subject of those predicates is clear from the whole context, and especially from verse 9.

IV. The first predicate stands in verse 14. He became a partaker of flesh and blood as the children. Where it is first to be noted that the term flesh and blood is here taken by the Apostle substantially and absolutely for human nature in itself, just as it is taken in Matt. 16, v. 17, Gal. 1, v. 16, etc., not accidentally and limitedly for human nature insofar as it is corrupted and hence subject to many infirmities, in which sense it is used in John 3, v. 6, 1 Cor. 15, v. 50. For the Son of God was holy, and therefore He was not made a partaker of sinful flesh; whence it follows that human nature is noted here, yet so that infirmities are connoted, but without sin.

V. The Apostle illustrates this by a comparison: As the children partake of flesh and blood; so He likewise became a partaker of them; but the children partake of flesh and blood because they have the same human nature in species. And, just as by the flesh and blood of the children not only the body, but also the soul; not a bare phantom, but true humanity is understood. So the Son of God likewise, that is, integrally and truly, became a partaker of humanity, namely by assuming it into the unity of His person. From which it appears that there is another nature in Christ besides flesh and blood. For he who is said to partake is signified to exist beforehand, and not only to consist of that which he partakes, but to add something more to that which he already is.

VI. The second predicate stands in v. 16. He did not take hold of angels, but the seed of Abraham. Here four things are to be considered. 1. The Assumer. Who is the Son of God, that eternal λόγος, of whom it is said in John 1, 14 in the same sense that He was made flesh. 2. The Assumed, which is named the seed of Abraham. The word Seed in this place is not taken collectively for the whole posterity, as in John 8, v. 37, Rom. 9, v. 7, but singularly for one certain individual as in Gen. 3, v. 15, c. 4, v. 25, c. 22, v. 18, Gal. 3, 16, etc. For it is explained in v. 14 how the Son of God was made a partaker of flesh and blood, and thus it treats of the Incarnation of the λόγος, who certainly did not assume all men or the whole posterity of Abraham, but an individual nature from Mary, the daughter of Abraham.

VII. 4. The word for taking hold. In Greek it is the present 'επιλaμ-

Cάνεται is used for the past tense by an Enallage familiar to the Hebrews. For as above in v. 14, so here it retains the sense of the past. The ancient interpreter and many Fathers rendered it 'he apprehended' as if by an extended hand, as it is taken in Matthew 14:31. But it is more correctly translated by 'he assumed,' because this is the native meaning of that word, and the manner in which the Son of God became a participant of flesh is better explained in this way, namely, by assuming it into the Unity of His Person.

IIX. 4. Antithesis: he did not indeed assume Angels but the seed of Abraham. Because by this Antithesis an exceptional privilege of our nature is hinted at, namely that the Son of GOD raised it in Himself above the Angelic nature. For He often indeed employed Angels for ministries, but He by no means assumed them into the ὑπόστασιν (hypostasis). But the Son of GOD contributed this honor and dignity to human nature, that God and man should be one person, as Ambrose writes upon this passage. And this concerning the first Member.

IX. Therefore, secondly, if anyone should ask: Who assumed it? From those things which have been said in the preceding discussions, it can easily be answered. For it has been proven that neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was Incarnate, but only the λόγον (Word) or the Son of God. John 1:14, Galatians 4:4. Whence it follows of its own accord that only the λόγον (Word) assumed flesh, not the Father or the Holy Spirit.

X. The Scholastics indeed differ at length here: Whether person assumed person, or nature nature; or nature person, or person nature, as can be seen in Lombard, book 3, distinction 5, A. But the answer is straightforward, that a person, not a nature, assumed human nature, namely the second Person of the Trinity, the Son of GOD, the splendor and Image of the eternal Father; nor yet without nature, since it is not entirely really distinct from the Person, whence the divine Nature itself also in a certain way assumed the nature of man, namely through the mediation of the person whose nature it is.

XI. From which appears the distinction concerning the ὑποστατικὴν (hypostatic) assumption. For the assumption, taken actively, belongs to the person. But the union is of both natures, since we say that the person assumed, and that the natures are united to one another. Furthermore, the union is reciprocal, because we assert that the λόγον (Word) is united to the flesh, and conversely, the flesh to the λόγον (Word) (yet so that 1. the λόγος (Word) is also called the Uniting [agent], while the human nature is only called the united [object]. 2. the communication of the ὑποστάσεως (hypostasis) remains only with the divine nature), but the assumption is not reciprocal. Because

The λόγος assumed only so much, and only so much was assumed, that which is well to be observed against the calumnies of the Calvinists in the matter of communication.

XII. Furthermore, the Scholastics raise many questions from Thomas, from which we willingly abstain. For as to their origin, they are not sought from the Holy Scriptures, but from the gaps of human reason. As to words and terms, they are plainly obscure and even by their very sound terrifying and absurd. As to the matter, they are 1. idle and vain, which betray the wit of a man abounding in leisure, who treats of things not necessary, and meanwhile neglects necessary things. 2. curious, because they inquire not about the fact but about the possibility, and rashly presume to exhaust all the riches of divine power. 3. fruitless, both because they cannot be decided from the Scriptures and with certainty, but are only ventilated probably on either side, in the manner customary to the Scholastics; and if they should be decided to the greatest degree, no benefit redounds to us from them. Therefore they are to be placed in that class of questions which we are commanded to avoid, 2 Tim. 2:23, Tit. 3:9.

XIII. These things therefore being omitted, we proceed to the third member, where it must be inquired, What has been assumed? Scripture names that flesh in general, John 1:14. The seed of Abraham in particular, Heb. 2:16. The Fathers commonly call it humanity or human nature, which was 1. ἄτομος or individual: 2. ἀνυπόστατος or destitute of its own personality. Concerning both of which affections something must be said here. And first concerning the singularity of the assumed flesh.

XIV. For human nature, as Damascene teaches in book 3, ch. 11, is considered in three ways: 1. ψιλῇ θεωρίᾳ, when according to simple reason it is abstracted from all individuals and weighed in the mind, and thus it is nothing other than a universal in the mind. 2. ἐν τῷ εἶδει, when we contemplate it existing as such in the individuals themselves, which is what philosophers call a universal outside the mind. 3. ἐν τῷ ἀτομῳ, when we consider it existing in individuals and restricted by individuating conditions, just as in Peter, Paul, etc.

XV. We can express these three meanings most briefly thus. Human nature either denotes the idea of ἀνθρωπότητος conceived in the mind; or the whole human species; or one singular man. Now, however, what is denoted by human nature when the λόγος is said to have assumed it is not difficult to explain.

XVI. For He did not assume a mere Idea of the mind, because this would not be an Incarnation, but a fiction and a deception. Nor did He assume nature considered in the species, because He did not assume all persons of men and unite them to Himself. Whence it follows that the Word assumed human nature in the individual or in the individual, which agrees with our nature in all things as regards the species, but differs in number from all others.

XVII. Moreover, when the Word is said to have assumed all human nature, it is to be understood, i.e., according to kinship, according to the affinity and participation of one and the same flesh and blood, of which He Himself was likewise made a partaker, Heb. 2:14, Eph. 2:6, which statement Damascene explains thus, book 3, ch. 8: We say our nature has risen from the dead, has been assumed, and sits at the right hand of the Father, not because all the hypostases of men have risen, but insofar as all our nature is in the person of Christ. So much for singularity: now a few words must be said about anhypostasia.

XVIII. The Son of God indeed assumed an individual humanity, yet not one self-subsistent, but rather anhypostatic, which by assuming He made enhypostatic, so that now there is one and the same person of the Word and of the flesh, and therefore one, not two, Christs, Rom. 5:15; one, not two, Sons, Matt. 16:16; one, not two, Lords; one, not two, Mediators, 1 Tim. 2:5.

XIX. But Christ is one, either by nature or by person. But not by nature, since He is God and man: therefore by person. And consequently, there is one hypostasis for both natures. Whence it further appears that the flesh is destitute of its own personality, since otherwise there would not be one, but a double hypostasis in the one Christ.

XX. In the fourth member it must be considered: into what was it assumed? The Orthodox Fathers answer that humanity was assumed into the unity of the Person of the Son of God. Now a Person is an individual, incommunicable, perfect substance of a rational nature, having no dependence on another.

XXI. It is a substance, because it is not predicated of accidents. 2. It is individual, because it does not belong to universals. 3. It is incommunicable, because it is never communicated with other persons of the same nature. 4. It is of a rational nature, because brutes are indeed called supposita, but not persons. 5. It is a perfect substance, because it consists of all essential parts necessary for that species. 6. It is not sustained in another, but subsists by itself, by which particle the human nature of Christ is excluded from the name of person, which indeed is an individual and perfect substance of a rational nature, but because it does not subsist by itself, hence it cannot be called a person. 7. It does not have a dependency on another, which is added on account of a rational soul separated from the body, which indeed subsists by itself, but because it has a dependency on the body, it is not held to be a person properly so called.

XXII. Furthermore, it is to be noted here that there is some distinction between ὑπόστασιν and ὑφισάμενον, which terms are expressed by the one name of person among the Latins. For by the former is denoted subsistence or personality, by the latter the subsisting thing itself and that which has personality. When, therefore, the flesh is said to be assumed into the person of the λόγος, it is signified not so much the subsisting thing, as the very subsistence of the λόγος, of which the flesh has been made a participant, so that it subsists not by itself, but by that infinite ὑπόστασιν of the λόγος.

XXIII. Now Fifthly, concerning the manner of the assumption: whether the body was assumed by means of the soul must be stated. At the moment of the Incarnation, there occurred simultaneously 1. the singular overshadowing of the Holy Spirit. 2. the bringing of the mass to the place of generation. 3. the sanctification of the same. 4. the assumption of both parts into the ὑπόστασιν of the overshadowing λόγος. Wherefore, it is not a question here of time, whether the soul was assumed before the body, but only of the order of assumption that is spoken of and inquired into.

XXIV. Most Scholastics, however, hold the affirmative, as can be seen from Lombard, book 3, dist. 2, St. Thomas, c. 3, quest. 6, art. 1 & 5, Bonaventure, book 3, dist. 2, art. 3, quest. 1, and others whose opinion is this: that the λόγος was united to the flesh by means of the intellect. For the divine essence, says Lombard, is of such subtlety and simplicity that it was not fitting for it to be united to a body formed from the slime of the earth, except by means of a rational essence. And therefore they call this medium a medium of congruity, not of connection.

XXV. This opinion may seem to have been drawn from certain sayings of the Fathers, such as Augustine, Epist. 3 to Volusianus, and the book De Agone Christi, c. 18, and especially Damascene, book 3, c. 6, in whose footsteps follow Zanchius, book 2, De Incarnatione, c. 3, quest. 7, Perkins, in his explanation of the Creed, p. 599, and Martinius, book 2, De Persona Christi, part 1, Tract 1, c. 11.

XXVI.
