Although indeed this question can safely be set aside, as it is for the most part Scholastic, and which can be disputed on either side without prejudice to the faith, yet because it is repeated here and there in the books of authors, we shall disclose our opinion concerning it. Let this be the thesis: In the assumption of the body and soul there was no order, but they were assumed into the ὑπόςασιν λόγε simultaneously and at once without distinction of time and order.

XXVII. We provide this thesis established by the following reasons. 1. From the silence of the Scriptures. For nowhere does it mention such an order, but in general it describes the assumption without distinction of order in John 1:14, Heb. 2:16. But since Scripture is silent, we also ought to be silent and not rashly affirm anything, much less litigate about uncertain matters.

XXIIX. 2. From the lack of firm reasons. For whatever is brought forward by the Scholastics is mere speculation of reason, which thinks it incongruous that God should assume a fragile body immediately, and the sum of all their reasons is this: Because the mind is the more worthy part of man, and therefore more similar to God, and because the body is for the sake of the soul, nor could it have been united if it had not been animated. But who does not understand the weakness of this discourse? Let this mystery indeed seem incongruous, yet GOD has rendered it most fitting. Whose goodness and humility is the more known, because He willed to be united immediately with an earthly body. Furthermore, we admit that He assumed nothing but an animated body; yet it does not follow from this that it was by means of the soul. For the λόγος also assumed the soul, not outside the body but in the body or united to the body. Therefore, is it for that reason by means of the body?

XXIX. 3. From the absurdity. If it is incongruous for the body to be assumed immediately, and it is united to the λόγῳ only by means of the soul as being closer to God, it certainly seems to follow that the union between the λόγον and the soul is closer than between the λόγον and the flesh. For that which is assumed immediately is closer to the assumer and is more tightly coupled. But the consequent is absurd, since the mode and the degree of the personal union are the same.

XXX. 4. From the constraint of divine power. For the Scholastics argue about this question as if God could not have assumed the body immediately, unless the soul first intervened and mediated. But who does not see that limits are thus placed upon divine power, as if He could not immediately couple things that are extremely distant?

XXXI. 5. On the dissolution of the natural union. If the soul is the medium of union between the λόγος and the flesh, it would follow that when the soul is separated, the union is dissolved, because that medium of union ceases. But indeed this did not happen, because at the time of death, although the soul was separated from the body naturally, the body was not, however, separated from the λόγος personally. Wherefore if the body could then be immediately united to the λόγος without the soul intervening, why could it not also have been assumed in the first place in that way?

XXXII. We arrive therefore at last at the sixth and final member, which is, On the duration of the assumption, concerning which the Orthodox Fathers affirm with one voice: that which is assumed is never laid aside: whence they established such a canon: That which the λόγος has once assumed, he never lays aside; that is, the personal union lasts eternally, and the humanity assumed within the λόγος is never dismissed or subsists outside the λόγος. For of the kingdom of Christ there is no end, Luke 1:33 [v. 11], and he himself is a priest forever, Heb. 6:20 [v. ult.], ch. 7, and following. And therefore it follows that his humanity also always remains, since otherwise it would not be his humanity.

XXXIII. Against this thesis many doubts are raised, especially those drawn from the death of Christ. Which, however, and whatever others there are, we pass over by design, since they partly rest on a false hypothesis, and partly confuse the natural union with the personal. And therefore they are not of such a kind that they can move us from the true opinion. For we know from the analogy of faith: 1. That Christ truly died. 2. That nevertheless the soul and body remained united to the λόγος. 3. That the actual and complete being of a man ceased, but 4. in the resurrection it was immediately restored. 5. And therefore after that it is perpetually true that that which is assumed is in no way laid aside.

XXXIV. These things suffice for a pious and faithful mind, nor is there need that we wrangle over more. Was Christ at the time of death a true and univocally called man? For first, this is for no one's good, for it makes not for edification but only for agitation. 2. The time of death and burial was very short, which being finished, Christ again began to be a true and perfect man; why therefore shall we stir up idle disputes about that moment of time? 3. Scripture has been silent on this question, and therefore to ventilate it too laboriously is neither necessary nor fruitful. 4. A more prolix disputation on this theme leads to the speculations of reason, and brings back the thorns and trifles of the Scholastics.

XXXV. Now therefore let us conclude this disputation, giving thanks with our whole heart to the immortal and only wise God, who through Jesus Christ his only-begotten Son, assuming our flesh, has mercifully delivered us from infinite misery, from the fear of death and the most sorrowful slavery of sin, from the temptations of the Devil, and from various and innumerable dangers which have surrounded us on every side.

XXXVI. To us, therefore, through this our brother, access is open to God with confidence, Eph. 3:12; for through Christ he is also our Father, and we are his beloved children in the Beloved, Eph. 1:6. As he himself taught when he said: I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God, John 20:17. And therefore let us say from a faithful heart with Augustine: Where my portion reigns, there I believe I reign. Where my blood rules, there I trust I rule: Where my flesh is glorified, there I know that I am glorious.

XXXVII. For the Lord is not so much an enemy that he does not love his own flesh, his own members, and his own bowels, but at length he will translate [us] where there is joy without sorrow; rest without labor: dignity without trembling: riches without loss: health without languor: abundance without failure: life without death: perpetuity without corruption: blessedness without calamity. Where continuous day without night knows not how to have time. Where the soldier after labor is heaped with ineffable gifts. The head embracing the mobile [body] with a perpetual crown.

Latin:

Thesis. I.

ACtum est Proximè de carnis Christi conceptione; Jam nobis agendum de ejusdem assumptione, qvæ ab Unione & Conceptione distincta est qvidem ordine, sed non tempore. Ex qvo enim Deus hominem assumpsit, simulq; sibi univit animam & corpus, nec caro prius fuit concepta & postmodum assumpta sed in conceptione assumta & in assumtione concepta, uti loqvitur Lombardus lib. 3. dist. 2. C.

II. Progrediemur autem hoc ordine. 1. Probabimus, qvod facta sit assumptio. 2. aperiemus, qvis assumserit. 3. Qvid assumtum sit. 4. In qvid assumtum sit. 5. qvomodo assumtio facta sit, Et deniqve 6. qvamdiu hæc duret assumtio. Qvibus postremò brevissimam meditatiunculam practicam subnectemus.

III. Ad primum igitur membrum probandum adducimus præcipuè dictum illud Classicum Hebr. v. 14, 16. In qvo proponuntur duo prædicata de Filio Dei vel Jesu qvo ad divinam naturam considerato. Hoc enim esse subjectum illarum prædicationum patet ex toto contextu, & cum primis ex versu 9.

IV. Primum prædicatum exstat versu 14. Particeps factus est carnis & sangvinis ut pueri. Ubi primo notandum, vocem carnis & sangvinis hic accipi ab Apostolo substantialiter & absolutè pro natura humana per se, quemadmodum accipitur Matth. 16. v. 17. Gal. 1. v. 16. &c. non accidentaliter & limitatè, pro natura humana in quantum corrupta & hinc multis infirmitatibus subjecta est, quo sensu usurpatur Joh. 3. v. 6. 1. Corinth. 15. v. 50. Filius enim DEI sanctus fuit, ideoq; carnis peccatricis non est factus particeps; unde seqvitur primò notari hîc naturam humanam sic tamen ut connotentur infirmitates, sed absq; peccato.

V. Illustrat hoc Apostolus comparatione: Ut pueri communicant carni & sangvini; Sic ipse similiter particeps factus est eorum; pueri verò communicant carni & sangvini qvia naturam humanam specie habeat eandem. Et, sicut per carnem & sangvinem puerorum non solum corpus, sed unà anima; non nudum phantasma, sed vera humanitas intelligitur. Sic Filius Dei similiter, hoc est, integre & verè humanitatis factus est particeps, nimirum assumendo eam in unitatem suæ personæ. Ex qvo apparet, aliam præter carnem & sangvinem in Christo naturam esse. Qvi enim participare dicitur prius exstare fignificatur, nec tantum ex eo qvo participat, constare, sed id qvod jam est, aliqvid amplius adjicere.

VI. Secundum prædicatum extat v. 16. Non Angelos assumsit, sed semen Abrahæ. Hic quatuor sunt consideranda. 1. Assumens. Qvi est Dei Filius, λόγος ille æternus, de qvo Joh. 1, 14. eodem sensu dicitur qvod fit caro factus. 2. Assumptum, qvod nominatur semen Abrahæ. Vox autem Seminis hoc in loco non sumitur collectivè pro tota posteritate, ut Joh. 8, v. 37. Rom. 9, v. 7. sed singulariter pro uno certoq; individuo ut Gen. 3. v. 15. c. 4. v. 25. c. 22. v. 18. Gal. 3, 16. &c. Explicatur enim. v. 14. qvo modo filius Dei factus sit particeps carnis & sangvinis, adeoqve agitur de λόγου Incarnatione qvi sanè non omnes homines aut totam Abrahæ posteritatem, sed naturam Individuam ex Mariæ Abrahæ filia assumpsit.

VII. 4. Verbum Assumendi. In Græco est præsens 'επιλaμ-

Cάνεται pro præterito per Enallagen Hebræis familiarem. Ut enim suprav. 14. ita hic sensus pręteriti obtinet. Antiqv⁹ interpres & multi Patres reddiderunt apprehendit veluti extensa manu uti capitur Matth. 14. 31. Sed rectius vertitur per assumpsit, qvia hæc est nativa verbi illius significatio, & melius ita explicatur modus, qvo Dei Filius particeps factus est carnis nimirum assumendo eam in Unitatem Personæ.

IIX. 4. Antithesis: non utiq; Angelos sed semen Abrahę assumpsit. Qvia Antithesi eximium naturæ nostræ privilegium innuitur, qvod eam Filius DEI inseipso supra Angelicam naturam evexit. Nam Angelos sæpe qvidem adhibuit ad ministeria, sed minimè in ὑπόστασιν assumefit, Verùm hunc honorem & dignitatem humanæ naturæ DEI Filius contribuit, ut Deus & homo una persona esset, scribente Ambrosio super hunc locum. Et hæc de primo Membro.

IX. Ideoq; Secundo, si qvis qværat: Quis assumserit? Ex iis qvæ præcedentibus disputationibus dicta sunt, responderi facilè potest. Probatum est enim nec Patrem nec Spiritum S. esse Incarnatum sed solum λόγον vel Dei Filium. Joh. 1, 14. Gal. 4, 4. Unde ultrò seqvitur etiam solum λόγον assumsisse carnem, non Patrem aut Spiritum S.

X. Scholastici qvidem prolixè hic differunt: An persona personam, vel natura naturam; vel natura personam, vel persona naturam assumserit, ut videre est apud Lomb. lib. 3. dist. 5. A. Sed expedita est responsio, qvod persona non natura assumserit humanam naturam, Persona nempe Trinitatis secunda, Filius DEI splendor & Imago æterni Patris; neq; tamen sine natura, qvippe qvæ à Persona non planè realiter distincta est, unde & ipsa Natura divina qvodamodo assumsit naturam hominis, mediante videlicet persona cujus est natura.

XI. Ex qvo apparet discrimen inter assumtionem ὑποστατικὴν. Nam assumtio activè sumta est personæ. Sed unio est utriusq; naturæ, siqvidem personam assumsisse, & naturas invicem unitas esse dicimus. Deinde unio est reciproca, qvia λόγον carni, & contrà, carnem λόγῳ unitam afferimus (ita tamen ut 1. ὁ λόγος etiam Uniens, humana verò natura tantùm unita dicatur. 2. ὑποστάσεως communicatio apud solam naturam divinā maneat) sed assumtio non est reciproca. Qvia

λόγος tantů asumsit, & tantů asumtą est, id qvod probè contra calumnias Calvinianorúm in negotio de communicatione observandů.

XII. Multas præterea qvæstiones movent ex Thoma Scholastici à qvibus libenter abstinemus. Nam qvoad originem non sunt petitę èx sacris literis, sed ex rationis humanæ lacunis. Qvoad verba & terminos sunt planè obscuræ & vel ipso sono terrificæ & absurdæ. Qvoad rem sunt 1. otiosæ & vanæ, qvæ produnt Ingenium hominis otio abundantis, qvi non necessaria tractat, & interim necessaria negligit. 2. curiosę, qvia qværunt non de facto sed de posse, & omnes divinæ potentiæ divitias exhaurire temerè præsumunt. 3. Infructuosæ, tum qvia ex Scripturis & certo decidi neqveunt, sed tantum probabiliter in utramq; partem ventilantur, more Scholasticis usitato; tum si vel maximè decidantur nihil inde commodi ad nos redundat. Ideoqve in eo genere qvæstionum ponendæ, qvas vitare jubemur 2. Tim. 2. v. 23. Tit. 3, v. 9.

XIII. His igitur omissis progredimur ad Tertium membrum, Ubi inqvirendum est, Qvid assumtum sit? Illud Scriptura nominat carnem in genere Joh. 1. v. 14. Semen Abrahæ in specie, Hebr. 2. v. 16. Patres communiter vocant humanitatem vel humanam naturam, qvæ suit 1. ἄτομος vel individua: 2. ἀνυπόsatος vel propria personalitate destituta. De qva utraq; affectione hic aliqvid dicendum. Et prîmo de singularitate asumtæ carnis.

XIV. Natura enim humana docente Damasceno lib. 3. c. 11. consideratur tripliciter: 1. ψιλῇ θεωρίᾳ qvando secundum simplicem rationem ab omnibus Individuis abstracta, ponderatur in animo, atqve sic nihil aliud est, qvam universale in mente. 2. ἐν τῷ εἶδει, qvando eam in ipsis individuis taliter existentem contemplemur, id qvod Philosophi dicunt, universale extra mentem. 3. ἐν τῷ ἀτομῳ, qvāmdo in Individuis existentem & per conditiones Individuantes restrićtam consideramus, veluti in Petro, Paulo &c.

XV. Hasce tres significationes brevissimis ita efferre possumus. Natura humana vel notat Ideam ἀνθρωπότητος in mente conceptam; vel totam speciem humanam; vel unum singularem hominem. Jam verò qvid per naturam humanam denotetur, qvando λόγος eam assumsisse dicitur explicatu non est difficile.

XVI. Nec enim assumsit nudam mentis Ideam, qvia hoc non effet Incarnatio, sed figmentum & deceptio. Nec assumsit naturam in specie consideratam, qvia non omnes personas hominum assumsit sibiq; Univit. Unde seqvitur λόγον assumsisse naturam humanam ἐν ἀτόμῳ vel in Individuo, qvæ cum nostra natura convenit per omnia qvoad speciem, numero autem differt ab omnibus.

XVII. Cæterùm qvando omnem naturam humanam assumsisse λόγον dicitur, intelligendum, i. e. κατα συγγένειαν, juxta cognationem & participationem unius ejusdemq; carnis & sangvinis, cujus ipse similiter factus est particeps Heb. 2. v. 14. Eph. 2. v. 6. qvod dictum ita explicat Damasc. libr. 3. c. 8. Dicimus naturam nostram surrexisse à mortuis, assumtam esse & sedere ad dextram Patris, non, qvòd omnes hominum ὑποστάσεις surrexerint, sed qvantum omnis nostra natura est in Christi persona. Hactenus de singularitate: Paucis jam de ἀνυποστασία dicendum.

XVIII. Assumsit qvidem Filius DEI humanitatem ἄτομον, non tamen ἰδιοσύστατον, sed potius ἀνυπόστατον, qvam assumendo fecit ἐνυπόστατον, ita ut jam una & eadem sit λόγε & carnis persona, ac propterea Unus non duo Christi Rom. 5. v. 15. Unus non duo Filii Matth. 16, 16. Unus non duo Domini, unus non duo Mediatores 1. Tim. 2, 5.

XIX. Christus autem Unus est vel naturâ, vel personâ. Atqvi non naturâ cum sit DEUS & homo: Qva re personâ. Et per conseqvens, utriqve naturæ Una est ὑπόσασις. Unde porrò apparet, carnem propriâ personalitate destitui, cum alias non Una, sed gemina futura sit in Uno Christo ὑπόσασις.

XX. In Quarto membro considerandum venit. In qvid assumtam fuerit? Patres Orthodoxi respondent, assumtam esse humanitatem in unitatem Personæ Filii Dei. Est autem Persona naturæ rationalis, Individua, Incommunicabilis, perfecta ; substantia, ad aliud dependentiam non habens.

XXI. Substantia est, qvia de accidentibus non prædicatur. 2. Individuum est, qvia universalibus non competit. 3. Incommunicabilis est, qvia cum aliis personis ejusdem naturæ nunqvam communicatur. 4. rationalis naturæ est, Qvia bruta qvidem dicuntur supposita, sed non personæ. 5. Perfecta substantia est, qvia constat omnibus partibus essentialibus ad speciem illam necessariis. 6. Non sustentatur in alio, sed per se subsistit, qua particula a nomine personæ excluditur humana natura Christi, quæ quidem est rationalis naturæ, Individua & perfecta substantia, sed quia per se non subsistit, hinc persona appellari nequit. 7. non dependentiam ad aliud habet, id quod additum propter animam rationalem a corpore separatam, quæ per se quidem subsistit, sed quia dependentiam habet ad corpus, pro persona proprie dicta non habetur.

XXII. Porro hic notandum, quod discrimen aliquod sit inter ὑπόστασιν & ὑφισάμενον, quæ vocabula uno personæ nomine apud Latinos efferuntur. Per illam n. notatur subsistentia vel personalitas, per hoc ipsum subsistens & personalitatem habens. Quando igitur caro dicitur assumta in personam λόγου significatur non tam subsistens, quam ipsa λόγου subsistentia, cujus caro particeps facta est, ut non per se ipsam, sed per illam infinitam τοῦ λόγου ὑπόστασιν subsistat.

XXIII. Jam Quinto de modo assumtionis: An corpus mediante anima fuerit assumptum dicendum erit. In Incarnationis momento simul facta est 1. Spiritus S. obumbratio singularis. 2. massæ ad locum generationis deductio. 3. ejusdem sanctificatio. 4. utriusque partis in ὑπόστασιν obumbrantis λόγου assumptio. Qvare hic non de tempore, an prius sit assumta anima quam corpus sed tantum de ordine assumtionis dicitur ac quæritur.

XXIV. Scholastici autem plerique affirmativam tenent, uti videre est ex Lombardo lib. 3. dist. 2. B. Thoma c. 3. quæst. 6. artic. 1. & 5. Bonaventura lib. 3. dist. 2. art. 3. quæst. 1. & aliis quorum hæc sententia: λόγον esse unitum carni mediante intellectu. Tantæ enim, inquit Lomb. subtilitatis ac simplicitatis est divina essentia, ut corpori de limo terræ formato uniri non congruerit, nisi mediante rationali essentia. Ideoque & medium hoc appellant medium congruentiæ, Non colligantiæ.

XXV. Opinio hæc videatur hausta ex quibusdam dictis Patrum. ut August. Eph. 3. ad Volusianum, & libro de Agone Christi c. 18. præcipue Damasc. l. 3. c. 6. quorum vestigia sequitur Zanchius lib. 2. de Incarn. c. 3. quæst. 7. Perkinsius explicatione Symboli p. 599. Martinius lib. 2. de Persona Christi. part. 1. Tract. 1. c. 11.

XXVI. Quanquam vero & hæc quæstio tuto possit seponi, utpote maximam partem Scholastica, & qvæ in utramq; partem, sine periculo fidei possit disputari, attamen qvia passim repetitur in libris auctorum, nostam de illa mentem aperiemus. Thesis hæc esto: In assumtione corporis & animæ nullus fuit ordo, sed simul & semel sine distinctione temporis & ordinis in ὑπόςασιν λόγε assumta sunt

XXVII. Qvam thesin seqventibus rationibus stabilitam damus. 1. Ascrupturæ silentio. Nuspiam enim talis ordinis meminit, sed in genere assumtionem sine distinctione ordinis describit Joh. 1, 14. Heb. 2, 16. Tacente autem Scriptura & nos tacere neq; temere qvid affirmare, multo minus de incertis litigare debemus.

XXIIX. 2. A defectu firmarum rationum. Qvicqvid enim profertur à Scholasticis est mera speculatio rationis, qvæ putat incongruum esse, ut Deus fragile gorpus assumat immediatè, & summa omnium rationum hæc est. Qvia mens sit pars hominis dignior, eoq; Deo similior, & qvia corpus est propter animam, nec uniri potuisset, si animatum non fuisset. Qvis verò infirmitatem hujus discursus non intelligit? Videatur sanè hoc mysterium incongruum, DEUS tamen illud reddidit convenientissimum. Cujus eò magis innotescit bonitas & humilitas, qvod cum corpore terreno ἀμέσως uniri voluit. Deinde fatemur qvod non nisi corpus animatum assumserit, hinc tamen non seqvitur, qvod mediante anima. Nam & λόγος assumsit animam, non extra corpus sed incorpore vel unitam corpori. Ergone propterea mediante corpore?

XXIX. 3. Ab inconvenienti. Si in incongruum est corpus ἀμέσως assumi, & non nisi anima mediante tanqvam Deo viciniore illud unitum est λόγῳ certè seqvi videtur, qvod arctior sit unio inter λόγον & animam, qvam inter λόγον & carnem. Qvod enim immediate assumitur hoc propinqvius sit assumenti & arctius copulatur. Conseqvens verò est absurdum, cum idem modus idemq; gradus sit Unionis personalis.

XXX. 4. A potentiæ divinæ coactione. Ita enim disputant de hac qvæstione Scholastici, qvasi Deus non potuerit corpus immediatè assumere, nisi prius interveniente & mediante anima. Qvis verò non videt ita limites poni potentiæ divinæ, qvasi extremè distantia non posset immediatè copulare?

XXXI. 5. Ab unionis naturalis solutione. Si Anima est medium Unionis inter λόγον & carnem, seqveretur animà separatã solvi Unionem, qvia cessat illud medium Unionis. At verò hoc non factum est, qvia tempore mortis licèt anima fuerit separata à corpore naturaliter, non tamen fuit corpus á λόγῳ separatum personaliter. Qvarè si tum Corpus immediatè potuit Unitum esse λόγῳ non interveniente animâ, cur non & ita primum potuisset assumi?

XXXII. Accedimus igitur tandem ad Sextum & ultimum membrum qvod est, De Duratione assumtionis, De qvo Patres Orthodoxi uno ore affirmant. Assumtum nunqvam deponi: Unde talem constituerunt Canonem: Qvod λόγος semel assumsit, nunqvam deponere, Hoc est, Unio personalis æternum durat, & humanitas intra λόγον assumta nunqvam extra λόγον dimittitur vel subsistit. Regni enim Christi non est finis Luc. 11. v. 11. & ipse Sacerdos est in æternum Hebr. 6. v. ult. c. 7. & seqq. Ideoq; & humanitatem ejus semper manere conseqvitur, cum aliàs non esset ejus humanitas.

XXXIII. Contra hanc thesin multa moventur dubia, præcipuè à morte Christi petita. Qvæ tamen & si qva sunt alia, consulto præterimus, cum partim falsa nitantur hypothesi, partim confundant Unionem naturalem cum personali. Ideoq; non sint ejusmodi, qvæ à vera sententia nos dimovere qveant. Scimus enim ex fidei analogia. 1. Christum verè mortuum esse. 2. nihilominus animam & corpus λόγῳ unita mansisse. 3. τό esse hominis actuale & completum desiifse, Sed 4. in resurrectione statim fuisse restitutum. 5. Ideoqve post illam perpetuo verum est, qvod τό assumtum nullo modo deponatur.

XXXIV. Hæc pio & fideli animo sufficiunt, nec opus est, ut altercemur pluribus. An Christus tempore mortis verus & univocè dictus homo fuerit? Nam primo nulli hoc est bono, nec enim ad ædificationem sed tantum ad exagitationem facit. 2. fuit brevissimũ mortis & sepulturæ tempus, qvo finito Christus iterum cæpit esse verus & perfect⁹ homo, cur igitur de illo temporis momento lites otiosas movebimus. 3. Scriptura de hac qvæstione tacuit, ideoq; nimis operosè illã ventilare nec necessariu, nec fructuosum est. 4. Prolixior concertatio de hoc themate adducit ad speculationes rationis, & reducit spinas & tricas Scholasticas.

XXXV. Jam igitur concludamus hanc disputationem, gratias toto pectore agentes Deo immortali & soli sapienti, qui per Jesum Christum filium suum Unigenitum carnem nostram assumentem ex infinita miseria, ex metu mortis & tristissima peccati servitute, ex tentationibus Diaboli, variis & innumerabilibus periculis, quæ nos undiq; circumvallarunt, clementer nos liberavit.

XXXVI. Nobis igitur per hunc fratrem nostrum accessus patet ad Deum cum fiducia Eph. 3. v. 12. per Christum enim nobis qvoqve est Pater, & nos filii ejus dilecti in dilecto Ephes. 1. v. 6. Ut ipse docuit cum dixit: Ascendo ad Patrem meum, & Patrem vestrum ad Deum meum & Deum vestrum, Joh. 20. v. 17. Ideoq; ex fideli corde cum Augustino dicamus: Ubi portio mea regnat, ibi me regnare credo. Ubi sangvis meus dominatur, ibi dominari me confido: Ubi caro mea glorificatur, ibi me gloriosum esse cognosco.

XXXVII. Non enim tam inimicus est Dominus ut non diligat carnem suam, membra sua & viscera sua, sed tandem transferet, Ubi gaudium sine mœrore; reqvies sine labore: dignitas sine tremore: opes sine amissione: sanitas sine langvore: abundantia sine defectione: vita sine morte: perpetuitas sine corruptione: beatitudo sine calamitate. Ubi continuus sine nocte dies tempus habere nescit. Ubi miles post laborem donis ineffabilibus cumulatur. Mobile perpetuâ caput amplectente Corona.


## 6 Disputation VI. On the Union of the Two Natures in Christ Considered Generally

Thesis I.

Since in the preceding meetings, both the Incarnation of the λόγος and the conception and assumption of the Flesh of Christ have been treated, the reason of order requires that henceforth a discussion be undertaken concerning the hypostatic concurrence and personal union of both.

II. There are, however, four things necessarily to be explained in this matter: 1. The terms. 2. The controversies. 3. The false methods to be removed. 4. The true one to be indicated; concerning the first two chapters, with the general proof of this article annexed, we shall treat in this disputation, deferring the other two to the following one, with the consent of the God-man.

III. Moreover, all the terms occurring in this place, and in need of explanation, can be included in this one Thesis, which is at the same time a description of our Savior: Jesus Christ is a composite person, from two natures united to one another. We must therefore speak concerning the name 1. of Jesus. 2. of Christ. 3. of Person. 4. of Union.

IV. The glorious name Jesus, insinuated in the Old Testament, Gen. 49. 18. Ps. 14. Ps. 14. 7. Ps. 98. 2. Isa. 52. Hab. 3. 18. foretold in the New Testament, Matt. 1. 21. imposed upon Christ, the son of God and Mary, at his circumcision, Luke 2. It is truly a name above every name, concerning which, although there are many things worthy of consideration, out of a desire for brevity we shall choose only two.

V. 1. It is the notation of the word. It is a common but true opinion that the name Jesus is Hebrew in origin and descends from the verb ישׁע, which indeed is not in use in the Kal, but in the Hiphil is הושׁיע, he saved, or he made safe, which etymology itself we strengthen with the following arguments.

VI. 1. It is from the testimony of the Angel, speaking in Hebrew. Matt. 1. For thus he says: and you shall call his name Jesus; adding the reason for the name, for he himself σώσει, shall save his people from their sins. But to save in Hebrew is ישׁע; therefore, by the force of the language and the knowledge of the letters, it is easily apparent to anyone that the name Jesus descends from this root.

VII. 2. It is from the types. Christ was prefigured by Joshua the leader of the people, and Joshua the high priest after the Babylonian captivity, Hag. 1. 1. Zech. 3. 1. And just as they prefigured him by their deeds, so also by their names, for they are derived from ישׁע, as everyone admits, which is especially evident from Sirach 46. 1. And just as the LXX translated the Hebrew name as Ιησῦς, so there is no doubt that the Apostles, in the description of the proper name of Christ, made the Greek Ιησῦν from the Hebrew in imitation of that version.

VIII. 3. From the testimonies of the Jews, which may be seen in Galatinus and Serarius.

IX. Whence we conclude: The name Jesus descends from the Hebrew ישׁוּעה, which signifies to succor the miserable, the terrified, and those destitute of all help, and to aid them by words and deeds.

X. Furthermore, that word generally includes 3 terms. 1. from whom or the danger. Judg. 8, 22. 1 Sam. 9, 16. 1 Kings 23, 2. Ps. 34, 7. 2. through whom or the medium; to whom or the help itself, 1 Kings 19, 17. Ps. 51, 14. Isa. 45, 17. Jer. 17, 14. which terms are in a certain way indicated by the name Jesus. For the term from which are sins, and the wages of these, from which the Angel predicted Christ would save us. The term through whom was his own obedience, both Active, Rom. 5, 18, and Passive, Acts 20, 28. The term to which is eternal salvation and blessedness, Rom. 8, 30.

XI. Jesus therefore signifies the Savior, who delivered the human race from sins and eternal damnation, and by his obedience acquired for it everlasting salvation. The Greeks say Σωτῆρα, from Σώζειν. The Germans, ein Heyland und Seligmacher. The Latins, Servatorem from servando, or better, Salvatorem from salvando, because, as Cicero admits, more is signified by the word Salvator than by the word Servator: for he saves who, by some means, ensures that salvation is not lost: he saves and gives salvation who restores what was lost, which, since Christ has done, we assert with Manutius and Chemnitius that he is more correctly called Salvator than Servator.

XII. The 2nd member is the proper Attribution of the name Jesus, concerning which the learned teach: that the name Jesus properly belongs to Christ alone. Nevertheless, the Canonical Scripture of the O.T. counts three famous men in particular to whom this name was attributed on account of a likeness. 1. Joshua the son of Nun. 2. Hosea the Prophet. 3. Joshua the Priest, who all, like Christ, had the origin of their name from ישׁע, and were types of the threefold office of Christ: the former of the Royal, the second of the Prophetic, the latter of the Priestly.

XIII. But we posit a fourfold difference between these and Christ: 1. from the imposition, theirs was human, but Christ's was Angelic and Divine; 2. from the signification, they were types, but Christ is the true Savior; 3. from the benefits, they were temporal and partial σωτῆρες, he is universal and eternal; and 4. from the authority, they were ministers of good things: but he is the very author and giver of every good, and the Lord from heaven.

XIV. Whence he is called Savior κατ’ ἐξοχὴν [by way of excellence]. 1. because he alone saves, Acts 4. Isa. 63. 2. because he saves from every evil, Matt. 1. 3. because he saves by merit and efficacy, 1 John 2. and 4. because he saves most perfectly, Rom. 4. here Inchoatively, Imputatively, Effectively; there Consummatively.

XV. Furthermore, just as Jesus is a proper name, so Christ is, by ecclesiastical usage, the surname of our Redeemer: and just as the former promises salvation to the Jews in Hebrew, so this latter promises it to the Gentiles in Greek.

XVI. Christ is not called so from χρῆσθαι, which is 'to use'—whence by error Christ was called Chrestus and Christians Chrestiani, as pleased Justin—nor from chrism, as some of the Scholastics would have it, but from the verb χρίομαι, which is 'I am anointed,' from the third person perfect of which the verbal noun χριστὸς, 'anointed,' ein Gesalbter, Hebrew משיח, is derived.

XVII. Scripture indeed makes mention of a fivefold anointing. I. We name the common and physical, which is either of persons or of things. That is either medicinal (Tob. 6:9), or for pleasure (Esth. 2:12; Judith 10:3, 16:10), or civil (Ruth 3:3), or devotional (Luke 7:38), or for burial (Gen. 50:7, 11). II. The official, which is threefold: either priestly (Exod. 30:30, 40:12; Lev. 4:3), or royal (1 Sam. 9:6; 1 Kings 1:34, 19:17; Isa. 45:1), or prophetic (1 Kings 19:17). III. The spiritual, internal, and common to the faithful (Ps. 105:15; 2 Cor. 1:21; 1 John 2:20). IV. The miraculous (Mark 6:13; James 5:14). V. The singular and plainly divine, from which our Redeemer is called χριστὸς or Anointed, because through a singular anointing above his fellows he was, by GOD the Father, with the oil of gladness, i.e. with the Holy Spirit or his most abundant gifts bringing eternal joy, appointed as our Prophet, King, and Priest.

XIX. Although this name is concrete, as Damascene teaches, the anointing itself pertains not to both natures but only to the human. 1. Because the divinity, since it is immutable and most high, can neither be anointed nor exalted through anointing. 2. Because the nature of the Word cannot have fellows in itself, but according to the human nature Christ has brothers, and thus that he was singularly anointed in it above the rest, no one of those who are accustomed to think rightly has ever doubted, says Damascene.

XIX. The anointing of Christ differs from ours in five ways. 1. In the quantity and quality of the gifts: Christ's are infinite and immense; ours, however, are finite and measured. 2. In dependence, ours depends upon the anointing of Christ; not the contrary. John 1:16. 3. In Origin & Time. Christ's occurred in the first moment of conception: ours happens only after birth, or even at an adult age (in those who are born outside the Church). 4. In Duration: ours is mutable, and can be lost through mortal sins and ordinarily through the Word and Sacraments; but Christ's is ἀμέσως [immediately] and altogether extraordinarily.

XX. The term 3. h. in l. most used, is Person, which the Hebrews call פנים, which word properly signifies face from פנה [he looked], for the reason that we are accustomed to judge concerning persons from the face, and perhaps, because there are as many faces as there are persons. The Rabbis more often use the name גוף which properly denotes body, but synecdochically the whole man or person, whence also for the Greeks sometimes σῶμα is the same as person, Tob. 10:10, and σωματικῶς is the same as personally, Col. 2:8.

XXI. The Greeks call it ὑπόστασιν [hypostasis] or ὑφιστάμενον [subsistent] from the word ὑφίστασθαι which is to establish, to place, and therefore ὑπόστασις signifies that which can exist by itself; by another name they call it πρόσωπον [prosopon].

XXII. The Latins use the word Person, where 1. its derivation is sought. Alsted, bk. 2, lexic. Theolog. p. 39, thinks it is called person, as if 'per se una' [one by itself]; A. Gellius derives it from 'personando' [sounding through], but Scaliger judges it to be called as if 'εἰσόωμα'; We think either that it is not derivative; or that the true reason for its etymology still lies hidden and has not yet been discovered.

XXIII. 3 Its signification, and various acceptance. Valla contends that 'person' signifies only a quality, for the reason that one and the same substance is said to bear several persons. But Valla is mistaken and is deceived, and everyone who follows him. For there is no lack of examples, both of profane and sacred authors, by which 'person' is the same as an individual intelligent substance, and especially a man; thus Cicero, Pliny the Younger, Quintilian, Valerius Maximus write; and the jurists also direct all law either to persons, or to things, or to actions. Thus 2 Cor. 1:11, 'many persons' [is used] for many individuals of men, and Heb. 1:3, the Son is called the character of the person of the Father.

XXIV. Furthermore, there are three principal significations of this word: 1. it is taken Politically for the attributes of a man, whether external or internal, of mind or body, and therefore dignities, wealth, and lineage, fatherland, etc. Thus 2 Cor. 5. n. Comically, when in theaters persons are spoken of, whoever represents certain persons, in which sense Cicero said: I alone sustain three persons, my own, my adversary's, the judge's. 3. Philosophically, which is twofold. 1. Abstractive and Formal, and it denotes the very ὕπαρξιν [existence], subsistence, or personality. 2. Concretive and Material, in which sense a person is an individual, incommunicable, perfect substance of a rational nature, which is not sustained in another, but subsists by itself, and does not have a dependency on another. The Greeks succinctly say that ὑπόστασιν [hypostasis] is ὑφιστάμενον νοερόν [an intelligent subsistent]. An independent and intelligent being.

XXV. But just as philosophers, so theologians accept the word person, and indeed it denotes three things primarily for them: 1. ὕπαρξιν [existence] or subsistence, which although in divine matters it does not differ in reality from ὐσίᾳ [essence]; yet by reason it is distinguished thus, so that the λόγος [Word] is said to have taken flesh into his own ὕπαρξιν [existence], where a certain distinction is placed between the assuming λόγος [Word] and his subsistence, which is the term of the assumption. 2. Simple ὑπόστασιν [hypostasis], consisting of only one nature. 3. Composite ὑπόστασιν [hypostasis], subsisting in two natures.

XXVI. There remains the 4th word accustomed to be used in this book, which is Union. But to be united is nothing other than to be joined, and therefore Union is the joining of several things, by which they are or become one.

XXVII. In which conjunction 5 things are always to be observed. 1. The thing or things to be united. 2. The action of the one uniting. 3. The state following the union. 4. The unity of the thing. 5. The mode of union, and since various modes are reported by others, we, serving this subject, will look at a very few.

XXVIII. Therefore every Union is either extraordinary and supernatural, or ordinary and common. The former is either of persons, or of natures, or of things.

XXIX. Supernatural Union of Persons is fourfold. 1. Principal, by which the Persons of the Trinity are one. 2. Social, by which Angels and the Blessed conspire. 3. Spiritual, by which God and the faithful are united to one another. 4. Ecclesiastical, by which the faithful are one in Christ by the unity of the Spirit and mind.

XXX. The supernatural [ὑπερφυσικὴ] Union of natures is that singular concurrence of the divine and human nature in Christ.

XXXI. Supernatural Union of things is the joining of two things by a singular divine ordination, called Sacramental.

XXX. Ordinary and natural Union is either Substantial or

Accidental [matters], which since they are treated abundantly in compendious books, we prefer to refer the benevolent reader there, rather than to do what has already been done: we shall rather subjoin the heretics who impugn the truth of this doctrine.

XXXIII. Of whom we produce two armies into the field of the Church; the one comprising the Ancients, the other the Moderns.

XXXIV. Of the former kind are: 1. The Ebionites and Cerinthians and all those who denied the divinity of Christ, of which flour are also the Phantastici, who stripped Christ of his true humanity, and therefore, through the negation of one nature, destroyed the union itself. 2. The Samosatenians, who taught that the two natures in Christ exist separately. 3. The Apollinarists, who said that the union of the λόγῳ [Word] and the flesh was made in such a way that something of the λόγος [Word] was converted into flesh, and thus they judged that the Word did not assume flesh from the Virgin Mary, but put on another nature, which came into existence through that conversion. 4. The Nestorians, who, dividing the natures, made two persons and two Christs. 5. The Eutychians, who taught that after the union, the human nature was absorbed by the divine and as it were changed into it. 6. The Μονοφυσῖται [Monophysites], who indeed believed that Christ consisted of two natures, yet contended that he subsisted in them [only as one]. 7. 7. The Ἀκέφαλοι [Acephali], who indeed conceded that the natures in Christ were preserved, but contended that their properties were entirely confused. 8. The Μονοθελῖται [Monothelites], who also allowed two natures in Christ after the union, but acknowledged only one will in him, and that not other than divine. 9. The Accidentarii, who established that the λόγος [Word] assumed the human nature no differently than if someone were to simply put on a garment. 10. The Scholastics, who judged that the personal union was made through some accident really distinct from the human nature and from the Word, which resides in the human nature, and is as it were a bond connecting both extremes.

XXXV. We constitute 4 classes of the Moderns: in the 1st are the Calvinists, who define the personal union through the sustentation of the human nature in the λόγῳ [Word], and thus only through some ̓Αξίωσιν [dignification], as did Nestorius. In the 2nd are the Jesuits, who, while they defend the errors of the Calvinists, fulfill the prophecy made by Luther concerning them: that it would eventually come to pass in the Papacy that Nestorianism would prevail. In the 3rd are the modern Photinians, who call this union a pure and simple figment and an old wives' tale. In the 4th are the Vorstians, who understand by this ἕνωσιν [union] only some influx or infusion of divinity into the humanity.

XXXVI. To all these things we oppose the truth and the orthodox confession: that our Lord Jesus Christ, although He is God and Man, is nevertheless not two, but one Christ only, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person. Establishing this faith by 1. the sayings of Scripture. 2. the symbols of the Church. 3. the votes of the Councils, and 4. the testimonies of the Fathers.

XXXVII. 1. By sayings. 1. either describing the Incarnation of the Λόγος, such as are read in Isa. 9, 6. Jer. 23, 6. Mic. 5, 1. John 1, 14. Phil. 2, 6. 1 Tim. 3, 16. which we explained in disputation 3, section 1, and from which we now conclude thus. He who is incarnate, He truly assumed flesh, and consequently, is truly united with the flesh. But He who is the Λόγος or Son of God is truly incarnate, therefore He truly assumed flesh, and consequently is truly united with the flesh. The consequence of the major premise is firm, because to be incarnate or to be made flesh according to Scripture is not to be changed into flesh, but rather to assume flesh, according to Heb. 2, 14. 16, to which passage some also refer Heb. 10, v. 5.

XXXVIII. Or 2. by sayings in which Christ is called both GOD and Man; for of whatever person different natures are predicated, in that person those natures must be united, if such predications are not to be accused of falsehood. But different natures are predicated of the one Christ, because He is said to be GOD and Man, the Son of GOD and the Son of Man, and is indeed so spoken of that that man, who is Christ, is truly and properly GOD, and conversely that GOD is truly and properly man, according to Jer. 23, 6. Matt. 16, 13. 16. Luke 1, 36. John 9, 35. 1 Cor. 15, 48. Wherefore both those natures must most truly be united in the one person of Christ.

XXXIX. Or 3. By sayings in which it is asserted that there is only one Christ and Redeemer; such are read in Eccles. 12, 13. Ezek. 34, 23. Matt. 23, 8. Rom. 5, 15. 1 Cor. 8, 6. Gal. 3, 16. Eph. 4, 5. 1 Tim. 2, 5. From this, however, we argue thus: Christ is one or is called one either because of one nature, or because of one person; but not because of one nature, because we proved above that He consists of a twofold nature, and is true God and true man. Wherefore He is one because of one ὑπόστασις, and consequently the two natures are personally united in Christ.

XL. Or 4. By the sayings in which opposite attributes are predicated of the one Christ. For he is called eternal, Mic. 5:2, and Creator of the world, John 8:58, and nevertheless in time he is said to be conceived, Luke 1:31, born, ch. 2:7, made of a woman, Gal. 4:4; such predications, as that he is immortal and mortal, infinite and finite, omnipotent and weak, invisible and visible, having all things and possessing nothing, etc., are found many times throughout the Scriptures, from which we conclude thus: To whomever truly divine and truly human properties are attributed in reality, in him there must be two natures, divine and human, most closely united, since divine properties are predicated only of the true God, and human only of the true man. But to the one person, Christ, truly divine and human properties are attributed in reality. Therefore, in the one person of Christ there must be two natures.

XLI. Or 5. By the sayings indicating the communication of idioms, for often divine things are attributed to the Son of Man, such as descending from heaven and being in heaven, John 3:13, and likewise human things are attributed to the Son of God, such as being killed, Acts 3:14, being crucified, 1 Cor. 2:8, etc. All these predications would be false and absurd unless two natures were personally united in Christ. For how could divine things be truly enunciated of a man, and human things of God, if God and man were not one and the same person at the same time.

XLII. 2. By the Ecclesiastical Symbols. For the Apostles in their Symbol profess the only Son of the Father. The Nicene Fathers believe in one Lord Jesus Christ. Athanasius expressly teaches that there are not two, but one Christ, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person.

XLIII. 3. By the votes of the Councils, see Ephesus, Can. 2; Chalcedon, act 5; general, ch. 5.

XLIV. 4. By the testimonies of the Fathers, see Tertullian, against Praxeas; Irenaeus, bk. 3, ch. 17; Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. 11; Nazianzen, epist. 1 to Cledonius; Hilary, bk. 9, on the divinity; Ambrose, book on the Incarnation, ch. 7; Damascene, bk. 3, ch. 3; Chrysostom, on ch. 1 of John, hom. 10; Augustine, bk. 13, on the Trinity, ch. 17; Gregory, bk. 28, moral, ch. 36; but enough of this. To Jesus Christ, who is what he was, and was not what he is now, yet is both, be praise, honor, and glory for ever and ever, Amen.

Latin:

Thesis I.

CVum in præcedentibus congressibus, tàm de λόγꙋ Incarnatione, quam de Carnis Christi conceptione & Assumtione actum sit, ordinis ratio exigit, ut deinceps de utriusqve concursu hypostatico & unione personali tractatio suscipiatur.

II. Qvatuor autem sunt, hâc in materiâ necessariò explicanda, 1. Vocabula. 2. Certamina, 3. Removendi modi falsi, 4. indicandus verus; de primis duobus capitib. annexâ hujus articuli generali probatione hâc disputatione agemus, cætera duo ad seqventem annuente θεανθρώπῳ differentes.

III. Omnes autem termini hoc in loco occurrentes, & explicationis indigi, huic uni Thesi, qvæ simul Salvatoris nostri descriptio est, includi possunt: Jesus Christus est persona composita, ex duabus naturis invicem unitis. Dicendum igitur de nomine 1. Jesu. 2. Christi. 3. Personæ. 4. Unionis.

IV. Nomen Jesus gloriosum, in Vet. Test. insinuatum, Gen. 49. 18. Psal. 14. Psal. 14. 7. Psal. 98. 2. Esa. 52. Habac. 3. 18. in N. Test. prædictum Matth. 1. 21. in circumcisione Christo, Dei & Mariæ filio impositum Luc. 2. Verè nomen est supra omne nomen circa qvod cũ multa consideratu digna sint nos brevitatis studio duo tantum eligem9.

V. 1. Est notatio vocis. Communis est sed vera opinio, nomen Jesu origine Hebræum esse & descendere à verbo ישׁע, qvod in Kal. qvidem non est in usu, sed in Hiphil est הושׁיע salvavit, vel salvum fecit, qvam ipsam Etymologiam seqq. argumentis roboramus.

VI. 1. Est à Testimonio Angeli, hebraicè loqventis. Matth. 1. Sic enim ille ait: & vocabis nomen ejus Jesum; addens rationem nominis, ipse enim σώσει salvum faciet populum suum à peccatis. Salvare autẽ Hebraicè est ישׁע vi ergo lingvæ, & cognitionis literarum ab hac radice nomen Jesus descendere, cuivis facilè apparet.

VII. 2. Est ex typis. Christum præfigurarunt Josua dux populi, & Josua sacerdos magnus post captivitatem Babylonicã, Hag. 1. 1. Zach. 3, 1. ut autem præfigurarunt rebus sic & nominibus, eadem enim à ישׁע derivantur, omnibus fatentibus, qvod præcipuè patet ex Sirac. 46, 1. sicuti verò. LXX. nomen Hebræum verterunt Ιησῦς: ita nullum est dubium, qvin Apostoli in descriptione nominis proprii Christi, ad imitationem illius versionis fecerint Ιησῦν græcum ex Hebræo.

VIII. 3. A testimoniis Judæorum, qvæ videantur apud Gal. & Serariũ.

IX. Undè concludimus: Nomen Jesus, ab Hebræo ישׁוּעה de-scendere, qvod notat miseris, territis, omniq; ope destitutis succurrere, verbisq; & factis illos juvare.

X. Porrò verbum istud plerunŅ; 3. terminos includit. 1. â quo vel periculum. Iudic. 8, 22. 1. Sam. 9, 16. 1. Reg. 23, 2. Psal. 34, 7. 2. per quem vel medium; ad quem vel ipsum auxilium, 1. Reg. 19. 17. Psal. 51, 14. Esa. 45, 17. Ier. 17, 14. qui termini nomine Jesu quodammodo innuuntur. Terminus namŅ; à quo sunt peccata, & horum stipendia, â quibus Christum nos salvos facturum Angelus prædixit. Termin⁹ per quem, fuit ipsius obedientia, tum Activa, Rom. 5, 18. tùm Passiva Actor. 20, 28, Terminus ad quem est æterna salus & beatitudo, Rom. 8. 30.

XI. Jesus ergo significat Salvatorem, qui genus humanum à peccatis, æternaŅ; damnatione liberavit, & sua obedientia illi salutem sempitērnam acquisivit. Græci dicunt Σωτῆρα, à Σώζειν. Germani ein Heyland und Seligmacher. Latini Servatorem à servando, vel melius Salvatorem â salvando, quia fatente Cicerone vocabulo Salvatoris plus significatur, quâm voce Servatoris: Servat enim is, qui ne salus amittatur, aliquâ ratione præstat: Salvat & salutem dat, qui amissam restituit, quod cum Christus fecerit, rectius Salvatorem quâm Servatorem dici cum Manutio & Chemnitio asserimus.

XII. Membrum 2. est propria nominis Jesu Attributio, de qua tradunt Eruditi: nomen Jesus soli Christo propriè convenire. Tres tamen cum primis Scriptura Canonica V. T. numerat viros celebres, quibus hoc nomen ob similitudinem fuerit attributum. 1. Josua filius Nun. 2. Hoseas Propheta. 3. Josua Sacerdos est qui omnes ut Christus à ישׁע nominis originem habuerunt, typiq́ue fuerunt triplicis officii Christi iste Regii, ille Prophetici, hic Sacerdotalis.

XIII. Qvadruplicem verò differentiam inter hos & Christum ponimus 1. ab impositione, illorum fuit humana, Christi verò Angelica & Divina, 2. â significatione, illi fuerunt typi, Christus verò verus Salvator. 3. à beneficiis, illi fuerunt σωτῆρες temporales ac partiales, hic est universalis & æternus, & 4. ab autoritate, illi fuerunt ministri bonorum: hic verò ipse autor & dator omnis boni, DominusŅve de cœlo.

XIV. Unde κατ’ ἐξοχὴν Salvator dicitur. 1. quia solus salvat Actor. 4. Esa. 63, 2. quia ab omni malo salvat. Matth. 1, 3. quia merito & efficacia salvat. 1. Johan. 2, & 4. quia perfectissimè salvat, Rom. 4. hic Inchoativè, Imputativè, Effectivè, illic Consumativè.

XV. Porrò sicuti Jesus nomen Proprium, ita Christus usu Ecclesiastico cognomen est Redemptoris nostri: & sicut illud Hebraicum Judæis; ita & hoc Græcum Gentib. salutem promittit.

XVI. Dicitur autem Christus non ἀπὸ τῦ χρῆσθαι qvod est uti, ex errore Christus Chrestus, & Christiani Chrestiani vocati sunt, sicuti Justino placuit; nec à Chrismate ut qvidam ex Scholasticis volunt, sed à verbo χρίομαι, qvod est ungor, à cujus præteriti tertia persona nomen verbale χριστὸς unctus, ein Gesalbter/ hebr. משיח pervenit.

XVII. Meminit verò scriptura qvintuplicis unctionis. I. Nominamus Vulgarem & Physicam, estqve vel Personarum vel rerum. Illa est vel Medica Tob. 6, 9. vel delitiosa Esth. 2, 12. Judith. 10. 3. c. 16. 10. vel Civilis Ruth. 3, 3. vel devota, Luc. 7, 38. vel exeqvialis, Gen. 50, 7. 11. Officialem, qvæ triplex vel Sacerdotalis Exod. 30, 30. c. 40. 12, Levit. 4, 3. vel Regia 1. Sam. 9, 6. 1. Reg. 1, 34. c. 19, 17. Esai. 45, 1. vel Prophetica 1. Reg. 19, 17. III. Spiritualem internam & fidelibus communem Psalm. 105, 15. 2. Corinth. 1. 21. 1. Johan. 2, 20. IV. Miraculosam Mar. 6, 13. Jacob. 5, 14. V. Singularem & planè divinam, à qva Redemptor noster, χριστὸς vel Unctus dicitur, qvia per singularem unctionem præ consortibus suis à DEO Patre oleo exultationis h. e. Spiritu Sancto vel largissimis ejus donis æternam lætitiam afferentibus in Prophetam, Regem ac Sacerdotem nostrum constitutus fuit.

XIX. Etsi verò nomen hoc Concretum est docente Damasceno, unctio tamen ipsa non utramqve sed tantum humanam naturam attinet. 1. qvia divinitas cum immutabilis sit, & altissima, nec ungi, nec per unctionem exaltari potest. 2. qvia verbi natura consortes secundum se habere neqvit, secundum verò humanam naturam Christum fratres habere atq; sic singulariter præ reliqvis in ea unctum esse neqvaqvam, qvispiam dubitavit eorum, qvi recte sapere sunt consveti, inqvit Damascenus.

XIX. Differt autem unctio Christi à nostra qvintupliciter. 1. Donorum χρία qvantitate & qvalitate: Christi sunt infinita, & immensa; nostra autem finita & dimensa. 2. Dependentiâ, nostra dependet ab unctione Christi; non contra. Joh. 1, 16. 3. Origine & Tempore. Christi facta est in primo conceptionis momento: nostra sit demùm post nativitatem, vel etiam adulta ætate(in iis qui extra Ecclesiam nascuntur.) 4. Duratione: nostra mutabilis est, & per peccata mortalia amitti potest; sed Christi est perpetua, & durabit in æternum. 5. Modo, nostra sit mediate & ordinarie per Verbum & Sacramenta; Christi verò ἀμέσως & prorsus extraordinariè.

XX. Vocabulum 3. h. in l. usitatissimum, est Persona, quod Hebræi vocant פנים, quæ vox propriè significat facies à פנה respexit, eo quod ex facie de personis solemus judicare, & forsitan, quòd sint tot facies, quot personæ. Rabini sæpius utuntur nomine גוף quod propriè notat corpus, synecdochicè verò totum hominem vel personam, unde & Græcis quandoq; σῶμα idem est, quod persona Tob. 10, 10. & σωματικῶς idem quod personaliter. Col. 2, 8.

XXI. Græci vocant ὑπόστασιν vel ὑφιστάμενον ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑφίστασθαι quod est statuere, collocare, ideoq; ὑπόστασις significat id, quod per se constare potest, alio nomine vocant πρόσωπον.

XXII. Latini utuntur voce Personæ, ubi 1. quæritur ejus Derivatio. Alsted. l. 2. lexic. Theolog. p. 39. personam dictam putat, quasi per se unam; A. Gellius à personando deducit, Scaliger verò quasi εἰσόωμα dictam censet; Nos vel non derivativam esse; vel ejus Etymologiæ rationem veram adhuc latere nondumq; inventam esse arbitramur.

XXIII. 3 Ejus significatio, variaque acceptio. Valla contendit, personam duntaxat significare qualitatem, eò quòd una eademq; substantia plures dicatur gerere personas. At fallit & fallitur Valla, omneq; qui eum sequuntur. Nec n. desunt exempla, tam profanorum, quàm sacrorum autorum, quibus persona, idem est quod substantia singularis intelligens, & præsertim homo; ita Cicero. Plinius junior Qvintilianus, Valerius Maximus scribunt; Ictiqvoq; omne jus, vel ad personas, vel ad res, vel ad actiones dirigunt. Sic 2. Cor. 1, 11. multæ personæ, pro multis hominum individuis & Heb. 1, 3. filius character personæ Patris dicitur.

XXIV. Porrò vocabuli hujus significationes præcipuæ sunt tres 1. accipitur Politice pro attributis hominis sive externis sine internis, animi vel corporis, ideoq; huc referuntur dignitates, opes, genus, patria, &c. Sic 2. Cor. 5. n. Comicê, qvando in Theatris personæ dicuntur, qvicunq; personas certas repræsentat, qvo sensu Cicero dixit: sustineo unus tres personas, meam, adversarii, judicis. 3. Philosophicà qvæ duplex. 1. Abstractiva & Formalis notatq; ipsam ὕπαρξιν subsistentiam vel personalitatem. 2. Concretiva & Materialis, qvò sensu persona est naturæ rationalis individua, incommunicabilis perfecta substantia, qvæ non in alio sustentatur, sed per se subsistit, ad aliud etiam dependentiam non habet. Græci dicunt succinctê ὑπόστασιν esse ὑφιστάμενον νοερόν. Ein selbständiges un verständiges Wese.

XXV. Prout verò Philosophi sic Theologi vocem personæ accipiunt, & qvidem iis tria potissimùm denotat: 1. ὕπαρξιν vel subsistentiam, qvæ licet in divinis ab ὐσίᾳ re non differat; ratione tamen sic distingvitur, ut λόγος in suam ὕπαρξιν suscepisse dicatur carnem, ubi qvædum ponitur distinctio inter assumentem λόγον, & ejus subsistentiam, qvæ assumtionis terminus est. 2. Simplicem ὑπόστασιν, unicâ tantum naturâ constantem. 3. ὑπόστασιν compositam, in duabus naturis subsistentem.

XXVI. Superest 4. vocabulum h. in l. usurpari solitum, qvod est Unio. Uniri verò nihil aliud est qvám copulari ideoq; Unio est plurium rerum copulatio, qvâ issa sunt aut fiunt unum.

XXVII. In qvâ Conjunctione semper 5. spectanda. 1. Res vel re unienda. 2. Actio Unientis. 3. Status unitionem conseqvens. 4. Unitas rei. 5. Unionis Modus, qvales cum varii ab aliis referantur, nos materiæ huic servientes paucissimis videbimus.

XXVIII. Omnis ergò Unio est vel extraordinaria & supernaturalis, vel Ordinaria & communis. Illa est vel personarum, vel naturarum vel rerum.

XXIX. Unio Personarum supernaturalis est qvadruplex. 1. Principalis, qvâ Personæ Trinitatis unum sunt. 2. Socialis, qvâ Angeli & Beati conspirant. 3. Spiritualis, qvâ Deus & fideles invicem uniuntur. 4. Ecclesiastica, qva fideles unitate Spirit⁷ & mentis iu Christo unũ sunt.

XXX. Unio ὑπερφυσικὴ naturarum est, singularis ille concursus, divinæ & humanæ naturæ in Christo.

XXXI. Unio supernaturalis rerum, est duarum rerum singulari ordinatione divina copulatio, dicta Sacramentalis.

XXX. Unio ordinaria & naturalis, est vel Substantialis vel

Accidentalis,qvæ cum abundè in libris compendiariis tractentur, eò lectorem benev. remittere, qvâm actum agere malumus: subnectemus potius, hæreticos doctrinæ hujus veritatem impugnantes.

XXXIII. Qvorum duos exercitus in Ecclesiæ campum produci mus; alterum Veteres complectentem alterum Recentes.

XXXIV. Prioris generis sunt. 1. Ebionitæ & Cerinthiani omnesq́; ii, qvi divinitatem Christi negarunt, cujus farinæ sunt & Phantastici,qvi veram humanitatem Christo detraxerunt, ideoq́; per unius naturæ negationem, ipsam unionem sustulerunt. 2. Samosateniani qvi duas naturas in Christo divisim se habere docuerunt. 3. Apollinaristæ qvi Unionem λόγῳ &'carnis ita factam esse dixerunt, ut aliqvid λόγου conversum fuerit in carnem, atq́; sic Verbum non ex Maria virgine assumfsisse carnem, sed aliam induisse naturam, qvæ per illam conversionem extiterit, censuerunt. 4. Nestoriani qvi naturas dividentes, duas personas, duosq́; Christos fecerunt. 5. Eutychiani, qvi post unionem, naturam humanam à divina absorptam & in divinam qvasi mutatam docuerunt. 6. Μονοφυσῖται qviChristum ex duabus naturis constare qvidem crediderunt, in iis tamen subsistere certarunt. 7. Ἀκέφαλοι, qvi naturas in Christo salvas qvidem concesserunt, sed proprietates earundem omninò confusas esse contenderunt. 8. Moνοθελῖται, qvi duas etiam inChristo naturas passi sunt post unionem, sed unam tantum in illo voluntatem, eamq́; non nisi divinam agnoverunt. 9. Accidentarii, qvi statuerunt: λόγον humanam uaturam, non aliter ac si qvis vestem simpliciter induet suscepisse. 10. Scholastici qvi censuerunt: unionem personalem factam esse per aliqvod accidens realiter distinctum à natura humana, & à verbo qvod insit in humana natura, sitq́; qvasi vinculum nectens utrumq́; extremum.

XXXV. Recentiorum classes 4. constituimus, in 1. sunt Calviniani, qvi unionem personalem per sustentationem humanæ naturæ in λόγῳ adeoq́; per ̓Αξίωσιν tantùm aliqvam cum Nestorio definiunt. In 2. Jesuitæ, qvi eosdem dum Calvinistarum errores tuentur, vaticinium Lutheri de ipsis positum implent: futurum tandem in Papatu, ut Nestorianismus invalesceret. In 3. Photiniani moderni, qvi unionem hanc purum putum figmentum & fabulam anilem vocitant. in 4. Vorstiani qvi per ἕνωσιν hanc tantum divinitatis aliqvem influxum vel illapsum in humanitatem intelligunt.

XXXVI. Hisce omnibus verum opponimus & orthodoxam confessionem: Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, licet Deus & Homo sit, non duos tamen, sed unum tantum Christum esse, non confusione substantiae, sed unitate personae. Fidem hanc 1. Scripturae dictis. 2. Ecclesiae symbolis. 3. Conciliorum suffragiis, & 4. Patrum testimoniis stabilientes.

XXXVII. 1. Dictis. 1. vel Incarnationem Λόγου describentibus, qualia leguntur Esa. 9, 6. Jerem. 23, 6. Mich. 5, 1. Johan. 1, 14. Cph. 2, 6. 1. Tim. 3, 16. quae disput. 3. Membr. 1. explicuimus, & ex quibus jam ita colligimus. Qui est incarnatus, ille carnem vere assumsit, & consequenter, cum carne vere est unitus. At qui Λόγος vel filius Dei vere est incarnatus, carnem igitur vere assumsit, & consequenter cum carne vere est unitus. Majoris consequentia firma est, quia incarnari vel carnem fieri juxta Scripturam, non est in carnem mutari, sed carnem potius assumere, juxta Hebr. 2. 14. 16, quo etiam a nonnullis refertur locus, Hebr. 10, v. 5.

XXXVIII. Vel 2. dictis quibus Christus & DEUS & Homo dicitur, de quacunque enim persona praedicantur diversae naturae, in illa istas unitas esse oportet, si tales praedicationes falsitatis argui non debeant. Sed de Christo uno praedicantur diversae naturae, quia dicitur esse DEUS & Homo, filius DEI & filius Hominis, atque ita quidem dicitur ut homo ille, qui Christus est vere & proprie sit DEUS, & vicissim DEUS ille vere & proprie sit homo, juxta Jerem. 23, 6. Matth. 16, 13. 16. Luc. 1, 36. Johan. 9, 35. 1. Cor. 15, 48. quare utramque illam naturam in una Christi persona verissime unitam esse oportet.

XXXIX. Vel 3. Dictis, quibus unum duntaxat esse Christum & Redemptorem asseritur, talia leguntur Eccles. 12, 13. Ezech. 34, 23. Matth. 23, 8. Rom. 5, 15. 1. Cor. 8. 6. Gal. 3. 16. Ephes. 4, 5. 1. Timoth. 2, 5. hinc vero sic argumentamur: Christus unus est aut dicitur propter naturam unam, aut propter unam personam; sed non propter naturam unam quia ipsum constare gemina, & esse verum Deum, verumque hominem supra probavimus. Qvare unus est propter unam ὑπόστασιν, & per consequens duae natura in Christo personaliter sunt unitae.

XL. Vel 4. Dictis,qvibus oppofita attributa de uno Christo prædicantur. Nam dicitur æternus Mich. 5, 2. & Creator mundi Joh. 8, 58. & nihilominus in tempore dicitur conceptus Luc. 1, 31. natus c. 2, 7. factus ex muliere Gal. 4, 4. hujusmodi prædicationes, ut qvod fit immortalis & mortalis, infinitus & finitus, omnipotens & infirmus, invisibilis & visibilis, omnia habens, & nihil possidens &c. multa reperiuntur passim in Scripturis ex qvibus ita concludimus : Cuicunqve vere divina & vere humana propria tribuuntur reipfa; in illo duas naturas divinam & humanam arctissimè unitas esse oportet, cum divina non nisi de Deo vero, & humana non nisi de homine vero prædicentur. Sed uni personæ Christo, vere divina & humana propria tribuuntur reipsa. E. in una persona Christi duas naturas esse oportet.

XLI. Vel 5. Dictis,communicationem Idiomatum indicantibus, sæpè enim filio hominis tribuuntur divina, ut descendere de cœlo, & in cœlo esse, Joh. 3, 13. itemqve Filio Dei tribuuntur humana,ut interfici, Actor. 3, 14. Crucifigi, 1. Corinth. 2, 8. &c. Hæ prædicationes omnes forent falsæ & absurdæ,nisi duæ naturæ in Christo essent personaliter unitæ. Qvomodo enim de homine divina, & de Deo humana verè possent enunciari,si Deus & homo non una eademqve simul esset persona.

XLII. 2. Symbolis Ecclesiasticis. Apostoli enim in suoSymbolo profitentur, filium Patris unicum. Patres Niceni credunt in unum Dominum Jesum Christum. Athanasius expressà docet, non duos sed unum esseChristum non confusione substantiæ,sed unitate personæ.

XLIII. 3. Conciliorum suffragiis, vide Ephesin: Can. 2. Calcedonens. act. 5. generali c. 5.

XLIV. 4. Patrum testimoniis vide Tertull. adversus Praxean.Iren. l. 3. c. 17. Cyrill. Hierofol. Catech. 11. Nazian. epist.1. ad Cledov.Hilar. l. 9. de divin. Ambros. lib. de Incarn. c.7. Damasc. l.3. c.3. Chrysost. in c. 1. Joh. hom. 10. Augustin. l. 13. de Trinit. c.17. Gregor.l.28. moral.c. 36. sed manum de tabula. Jesu Christo, qvi est qvod erat, neq; erat qvod est nunc tamen utrumǻ, sit laus honor & gloria in sempiterna sœcula, Amen.


## 7 Seventh Disputation. On Nestorianism

Thesis I.

As light with darkness; white with black, so truth compared with falsehood becomes more conspicuous and more illustrious. For opposites placed next to each other shine forth more clearly.

II. Since, therefore, in the preceding disputation a general σκέψις (inquiry) from the mind of the Orthodox concerning the union of two natures in Christ was proposed, by which it was shown θεόθεν (from God) that two natures are so united in Christ that, with them and their ἰδιώμασι (properties) preserved and ὐσιωδῶς (essentially) distinct, there is only one person: and since we are subsequently about to explain our opinion on this very matter at greater length: we judge it not only pleasant, but also fruitful, if the antitheses and struggles of our adversaries on this subject are also considered.

III. But among those who formerly attacked the present Article concerning the hypostatic union, and who strive to attack it today, we now challenge the Nestorian with his phalanx, about to descend into the arena of disputation with him.

IV. In order that this may be done skillfully, I establish four chapters of this our συζητήσεως (discussion): of which I. will propose the history of the Nestorian struggle itself: II. the refutation of the Nestorian error: III. will demonstrate that the Calvinists Nestorianize; IV. and finally, that the Lutherans are wrongly and undeservedly accused of Nestorianism.

V. Regarding the first chapter, two things especially come to be noted; 1. The dogma of Nestorius. 2. The state of the controversy.

VI. Concerning the first, it must be known that Nestorius, having been called from Antioch to the Archbishopric of Constantinople by the Emperor Theodosius, did not teach in clear and set words that there are two Christs, two Sons, or two persons in Christ distinct from one another and subsisting separately, of which one is God and the other Man, just as I and you are two in number and distinct persons or ὐφιςάμενα (subsistences). But he used rather words that carried the appearance of ὀρθοδοξίαν (orthodoxy) and implied the unity and identity of the ὑποστάσεως (hypostasis).

VII. For in his Confession he professes that there is one Christ. Take away, he says, every suspicion of a duality of Sons and Lords. And: That there is only one Son of God and man, Christ Jesus: just as there is a single sonship in Christ. He also wished that Mary be called neither ανθρωποτόκον nor θεοτόκον, but χριστοτόκον, to express the unity and identity of the person.

VIII. Whence it appears that Nestorius, if you attend only to the sound of the words, did nothing less than dissolve the person, and by doubling it, constitute two Christs, as is commonly imputed to him: and therefore, not directly, but indirectly and consequently, just as he orthodoxly established a dual nature in Christ, so he heretically established a dual person in the same, on account of his total denial of the κοινωνίας ἰδιωμάτων and of the official ἀποτελεσμάτων.

IX. For, to repeat the matter from the beginning, Nestorius taught: 1. That the ἕνωσις ὑποστατικὴ of the two natures is to be defined, 1. by an inseparable παρουσία or συνέλευσιν and indwelling of the λόγος in the assumed nature, or by the carrying of the human nature. For that he described it solely by the word 'carrying': these words of his show. 'On account of him who carries, I honor him who is carried.' 2. By a communion of name, whereby the Son of Mary can rightly be called the Son of God, on account of him who is united to him. 3. By a communion of operation, inasmuch as the λόγος worked all things in the Son of Mary, as in an animated organ. 4. By a communion of honor. 5. By a communion of affection, inasmuch as the will of the man Christ was always equal to the λόγος.

X. Hence Theodorus the Nestorian issues such a confession concerning the Union: 'We are ignorant in every way of a union according to subsistence. For thus is introduced a tempering of flesh and Divinity, which is nothing other than a confusion, taking away the property of each one.' And Nestorius opposes the third Anathema of the Council of Ephesus with this: 'If anyone does not say that Christ is one according to conjunction, and confesses both subsistences in one communion of the Son: let him be anathema.'

XI. II. That those expressions which are contained in the Apostolic writings, or which are said of Christ by the Saints, or by himself, are to be divided between two persons, and some of these are to be applied as if to a man, who is understood specifically apart from the Word of God, but those others, as worthy of GOD, are to be assigned solely to the Word of GOD the Father.

XII. Hence he asserted that not God, but the man Christ slept in the little boat; And on the contrary, that it was not a man, but Christ God who rebuked the winds and the sea. That Mary is not the Mother of God, but gave birth to a ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον [mere man]. Because Mary was a human, but it is impossible for God to be born of a human. That Emmanuel, or Christ, is not truly God, but rather a θεοφόρον [God-bearer], Deiferum [God-bearer] or θεόδοχον [God-receiver], and that the Son of Mary is carried and sustained by the Son of God: And, that Christ is one, and the Word of God is another: that the λόγον [Word] is the God and Lord of Christ: that God did not suffer, was not crucified, did not die, was not made the firstborn from the dead. Whence he always had in his mouth: Do not boast, Jew, you did not crucify God but a man. And what other blasphemies the heretic uttered besides.

XIII. That each nature of Christ exercises its actions by and for itself without the communication of the other, since there is one in Christ who performs divine things, and another who performs human things.

XIV. IV. That the man Christ received from the Spirit, who glorified him, the power of performing miracles, by which alien power he subsequently used in performing prodigies.

XV. V. That the flesh of Christ is not, as preached, δυνάμει ζωοποιητι- κῇ [by life-giving power], but that this belongs to the Word of God alone.

XVI. VI. That the man Christ is to be co-worshipped and co-glorified with the Word of God.

XVII. VII. That Christ as λόγος [Word] is not the High Priest and Apostle of our confession, but only as a man, and therefore our ψίλος ἄν- θρωπος [mere man] Mediator.

XVIII. VIII. Finally, that Jesus the Son of Mary also offered a sacrifice to God the Father for himself.

XIX. From these things the Fathers concluded that Nestorius 1. confesses ἕνωσιν ὑποστατικὴν only in word, but in reality denies and overturns it. 2. divides Christ into two persons, and thus separates the natures. 3. fashions for the human nature its own subsistence distinct from the λόγῳ. 4. takes away from the same the ἐνέργειαν of giving life. 5. is an idolater and ἀνθρωπολάτρην, adoring him who is not God, assigning Divine operations to a creature subsisting outside the λόγε ὑπόσασιν. 7. Finally, he overturns from the foundation the sacrifice of Christ and the work of redemption.

XX. Briefly, therefore, two things were primarily in controversy between Cyril and Nestorius: 1. The very definition of the union of the two natures in Christ: namely, whether it is σχετικὴ [relative] and κατὰ παράστασιν [by way of presence/juxtaposition], as Nestorius [contends], or indeed ὑποστατικὴ [hypostatic], as Cyril contends? 2. The very consequence or effect of the union; namely, whether a true and real communication of natural properties and official operations is given in Christ? Which is what Nestorius clearly denied against Cyril. Concerning these two, we must now proceed to discourse briefly against Nestorius.

XXI. 1. That the union of the two natures in Christ is not σχετικὴν [relative] or παραστατικὴν [by way of presence], the following arguments prove against Nestorius.

XXII. 1. Because it makes the flesh of Christ ἰδιοπόστατον [having its own hypostasis], αὐθυπόστατον [self-subsistent], καὶ ἰδιοσύστατον [and having its own constitution], and thus introduces a duality of person. For he who is united to another only κατὰ παράστασιν ἢ σχέσιν [by way of presence or relation] stands by him not by the benefit of the ὑποστάσεως [hypostasis] of him to whom he is united κατὰ παράστασιν, but by the benefit of his own ὑποστάσεως, and thus does not constitute one ὑφιστάμενον [subsistent being] with him, since to stand by or stand near imports and presupposes the own ὕπαρξιν [existence] or being of a thing.

XXIII. 2. It admits of separation; since it is σχετικὴ [relative] or respectiva; and therefore accidental. Now, however, it is the nature of accidents that they can be separated from their subjects with little effort. But to even think of such a separable and rather trivial union of the two natures, would it not be blasphemous? Is it not contrary to the Fathers? For according to them, what the Λόγος [Word] has once assumed, He never lays aside. Whence the Ephesine Fathers assert that the union was made ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως καὶ ἀδιασπάστως [indivisibly, inseparably, and indissolubly].

XXIV. 3. It is common to the λόγῳ [Word] with the remaining creatures, since all these are sustained by the λόγῳ at the same time, and have their dependence from Him as creator, as the Apostle testifies, Acts 17:28, Hebrews 1:3. If, therefore, the union of the assumed flesh with the λόγῳ consists in mere παραστάσει [presence], gestation, or sustentation (for these three walk in equal step), what prevents all creatures from being able to be called personally united to the λόγῳ? Why, moreover, did Justin call this mode of union μονότροπον καὶ ἐξαίρετον [unique and exceptional]?

XXV. 4. It pertains to the reborn Saints. For the λόγος is united even with these, as John testifies, ch. 14:23, Peter, 2 Epist. ch. 1:4. But shall we affirm that the saints are personally united with the λόγῳ on account of that gracious κατοίκησιν? Far be it.

XXVI. 5. Carrying and sustaining merely shows, not what the λόγος is by personal and primary act, but what he does by secondary act, since carrying and sustaining is a secondary act. How, therefore, could that mere carrying and sustaining express the union of two natures and a personal act? Whence B. Luther most correctly: This philosophy is most heretical because it denies that the Son of God is man by primary act, but imagines that he sustains the human nature as if by secondary act.

XXVII. 6. Nor is there any reason for Nestorius to retort that he also confesses one person in Christ, one Son, etc. For a bare naming of one person, one Son, one Lord does not suffice for the constitution of a personal union; just as neither the communion of titles, operations, dignities, honor, and affection, nor the consensus of the human will with the divine in Christ, constitute the unity of the person, since all those things pertain not to the unity of the hypostasis but to the secondary act of the subsisting person.

Latin:

Thesis I.

VTilux cum tenebris; album cum nigro, sic veritas cum falsitate collata magis conspicua & illustrior evadit. Contraria enim juxta se posita magis elucescunt.

II. Cùm igitur præcedente disputatione generalis ex mente Orthodoxorum de duarum naturarum in Christo Unione σκέψις proposita fuerit, qvâ θεόθεν ostensum, duas naturas in Christo ita esse unitas, ut iis earundemq́; ἰδιώμασι salvis ac ὐσιωδῶς distinctis, una tantum sit persona: cumq́; deinceps de hac ipsa materia sententiam prolixiùs explicaturi simus: non jucundum modo, sed & fructuosum esse judicamus, si Adversariorum etiam hac de re anthitheses ac certamina considerentur.

III. Ex illis verò qui præsentem Articulum de Unione hypostatica olim impugnârunt, hodieq́; impugnare satagunt, in præsentia Nestorianum suâ cum phalange provocamus, cum eodem in arenam disputationis descensuri.

IV. Quod ut dextrè fiat, quatuor hujus nostræ συζητήσεως capita constituto: quorum I. Ipsam Nestoriani certaminis historiā: II. Nestoriani erroris refutationē proponet: III. Calvinianos Nestorianizare; IV. Deniq; Lutheranos Nestorianismi perperā ac citra meritū insimulari demonstrabit

V. Circa I. Caput duo potissimûm notanda veniunt; 1. Dogma Nestorii. 2. Statas Controversiæ.

VI. De primo sciendum, quôd Nestorius ex Antiochia ad Archiepiscopatum Constantinopolitanum ab Imperatore Theodosio evocatus disertis & conceptis verbis non docuerit, duos esse Christos, duos Filios, aut duas in Christo personas à se invicem distinctas ac se orsim subsistentes, quarum una sit Deus, altera Homo, quemadmodum ego ac tu duæ numero, distinctæq; personæ seu ὐφιςάμενα sumus. Verùm usus est potius verbis ὀρθοδοξίαν præ se ferentibus ac ὑποστάσεως ἑνότητα κὶ ταυτότητα importantibus.

VII. In sua enim Confessione profitetur, Unum esse Christum. Aufer, inquit, omnem suspicionē dualitatis Filiorum & Dominorum. Et: Unum duntaxat esse Filium Dei & hominis Christum Jesum: sicut & unicam in Christo filiationem. Mariam qvoq; nec ανθρωποτόκον nec θεοτόκον sed χριστοτόκον dici voluit, ad exprimendum personæ unitatem ac identitatem.

VIII. Unde apparet, Nestorium, si sonum duntaxat verborum attendas, nihil minus fecisse, qvàm qvòd personam solverit, eamqve duplicando duos Christos constituerit, qvemadmodum ipsi communiter imputatur: ideoq; non directè, verum indirectè & consequenter, ut geminam in Christo naturam orthodoxè; sic geminam in eodem personam hæreticissimè statuit ob omnimodam abnegationé κοινωνίας ἰδιωμάτων κ᾿ ἀποτελεσμάτων officialium.

IX. Nam, ut ab ovo rem repetam, docuit Nestorius 1. qvòd ἕνωσις ὑποστατικὴ duarum naturarum definienda sit, 1. per inseparabilem παρουσίαν vel συνέλευσιν & inhabitationem τῇ λόγῳ in natura assumta, seu per gestationem humanæ naturæ. Nam qvòd eam solâ gestandi voce descripserit: hæc ejus ostendunt verba. Propter eum, qvi gestat, aporo eum, qvi gestatur. 2. Per communionem nominis, qvo Filius Mariæ rectè appellari potest Filius Dei, propter eum, qvi ei unitus est. 3. per communionem operationis, siqvidem λόγος in Mariæ Filio, tanqvam in animato organo cuncta operatus sit. 4. per communioné honoris, 5. per communionem affectus, siqvidem voluntas hominis Christi semper eo æqvalis fuerit τῷ λόγῳ.

X. Hinc Theodor. Nestorianus de Unione talem edit confessionē: Secundum subsistentiam unionem modis omnibus ignoramus. Ita " n. introducitur temperamentum carnis & Divinitatis, qvæ nihil a- " liud est, qvàm confusio, auferens uniuscujusqve proprietatem. Et " Nestorius tertio Anathematismo Ephesini Concilii talem opponit: " Si qvis non secundum conjunctionem unum dixerit Christum, & u- " tramque etiam subsistentiam in una Filii communione confitetur: Ana- " thema sit.

XI. II. Qvòd eæ voces, qvæ in Apostolicis scriptis continentur, vel qvæ de Christo dicuntur à Sanctis, vel ab ipso, dividendæ sint duabus personis, & aliæ qvidem ex his velut homini, qvi præter Dei " verbum specialiter intelligatur, aptandæ, illæ verò tanqvam dignæ " DEO, soli DEI Patris Verbo deputandæ.

" XII. Hinc asseruit, non Deum, sed Christum hominem dormivisse in navicula; Et contrà, non hominem; sed Christum Deum increpâsse ventos ac mare. Mariam non esse Dei genitricem, sed ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον peperisse. Qvia Maria fuerit homo, Deum autem ab homine nasci impossibile sit. Emanuelem, vel Christum non esse veraciter Deum, sed potius θεοφόρον, Deiferum vel θεόδοχον, & Filium Mariæ gestari ac sustentari à Filio Dei: Et, Alium esse Christum, alium Dei Verbum: λόγον esse Deum ac Dominum Christi: Deum non esse passum, non crucifixum, non mortuum, non factum primogenitum ex mortuis. Unde semper in ore habuit: Noli gloriari, Judæe, non Deum sed hominem crucifixisti. Et qvas præterea hæreticus blasphemias effutiit.

XIII. Qvod unaqvæqve natura Christi per ac pro se suas exerceat actiones sinè communicatione alterius, siqvidem alius sit in Christo, qvi divina, & alius, qvi humana peragat.

XIV. IV. Qvod homo Christus acceperit à Spiritu, qvi eum glorificârit, virtutem edendi miracula qvâ etiam alienâ virtute postmodum in edendis prodigiis usus fuerit.

XV. V. Qvòd caro Christi non sit, prædicata δυνάμει ζωοποιητικῇ, sed qvòd illa soli Dei Verbo competat.

XVI. VI. Qvòd homo Christus coadorandus & conglorificandus sit cum Dei Verbo.

XVII. VII. Qvòd Christus ut λόγος non sit Pontifex & Apostolus Confessionis nostræ, sed tantùm ut homo, ideoq; ψίλος ἄνθρωπος noster Mediator.

XVIII. VIII. Deniq; qvòd Jesus Mariæ Filius etiam pro seipso sacrificium Deo Patri obtulerit.

XIX. Ex his Patres concluserunt, Nestorium 1. ἕνωσιν ὑποστατικὴν verbotenus qvidem fateri, revera tamen eam negare ac evertere. 2. Christum in induas personas dividere, atqve sic naturas solvere. 3. Humanæ naturæ propriam subsistentiam à λόγῳ distinctam effingere. 4. Eidem vivificandi ἐνέργειαν adimere. Idololatram & ἀνθρωπολάτρην esse, adorantem eum, qvi non est Deus, Divinas operationes creaturæ extra λόγε ὑπόσασιν subsistenti assignare. 7. Deniqve sacrificium Christi ac opus redemptionis funditus evertere.
