XX. Breviter Ergo duo potissimum inter Cyrillum & Nestorium controversa fuere: 1. Ipsa duarum & in Christo naturarum Unionis definitio: Utrum videlicet Illa sit σχετικὴ & κατὰ παράστασιν, prout Nestorius, an verò ὑποστατικὴ prout Cyrillus contendit? 2. Ipsum conseqvens vel effectus Unionis; Num scilicet vera & realis naturalium idiomatum ac officialium operationum in Christo detur communicatio? Id qvod contra Cyrillum Nestorius planè inficiatus est. De qvibus duobus nunc porrò contra Nestoriū breviter differendū.

XXI. 1. Unionem autem duarum in Christo naturarum non esse σχετικὴν seu παραστατικὴν, contra Nestorium seqventia evincunt argumenta.

XXII. 1. Qvia facit carnem Christi ἰδιοπόστατον, αὐθυπόστατον καὶ ἰδιοσύστατον, adeoq; personæ διπλότητα introducit. Nam qvi alteri unitus est tantum κατὰ παράστασιν ἢ σχέσιν is utiq; non beneficio ὑποστάσεως ejus, cui κατὰ παράστασιν unitus est, sed beneficio propriæ suæ ὑποστάσεως ipsi adsistit, adeoq; non unum cum ipso constituit ὑφιστάμενον, cùm τὸ adsistere seu adstare propriam importet ac præsupponat ὕπαρξιν seu existentiam rei.

XXIII. 2. Separationem admittit; cùm sit σχετικὴ seu respectiva; ideoq; accidentalis. Jam verò Accidentium ea est Natura, ut facili negotio à suis subjectis qveant separari. Talem autem separabilem ac leviusculam duarum naturarum unionem vel saltem cogitare, annon blasphemum foret? Annon Patribus contrarium? Nam juxtà hos, qvod Λόγος semel adsumsit, nunqvam deponit. Unde Patres Ephesini asserunt Unionem factam esse ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως καὶ ἀδιασπάστως.

XXIV. 3. Communis est λόγῳ cum reliqvis creaturis, siqvidem hæ omnes à λόγῳ simul sustentantur, suamq; ab ipso tanqvam creatore depententiam habent, teste Apostolo, Act. 17. v. 28. Hebr. 1. v. 3. Si E. Unio assumtæ carnis cum λόγῳ in nuda duntaxat παραστάσει gestatione aut sustentatione (nam hæc tria pari passu ambulant) consistit, qvid obstat, qvò minus omnes creaturæ τῷ λόγῳ personaliter unitæ dici qveant? Cur autem Justinus hunc unionis modum appellavit μονότροπον καὶ ἐξαίρετον?

XXV. 4. Competit Sanctis renatis. Nam etiam cum his λόγος unitus est, teste Johanne cap. 14. v. 23. Petro, Epist. 2. c. 1. v. 4. Num autem ob gratiosam istam κατοίκησιν sanctos cum λόγῳ personaliter unitos esse affirmabimus? Absit.

XXVI. 5. Gestatio ac sustentatio duntaxat ostendit, non quid ὁ λόγος actu personali ac primo sit, sed quid ille actu secundo agat, siquidem τὸ gestare ac sustentare est actus secundus. Qui E. sola illa gestatio ac sustentatio duarum naturarum unionem, & actum personalem exprimere poterit? Unde B. Lutherus rectissime: Hæc Philosophia est hæreticissima quia negat Filium Dei esse hominem actu primo, sed fingit, eum substentare humana naturam velut actu secundo.

XXVII. 6. Neq; est, quod regerat Nestorius, se qvoqve fateri unam in Christo personam, unum Filium &c. Nam non sufficit ad personalis unionis constitutionem nuda appellatio unius personæ unius Filii, unius Domini: quemadmodum etiam neq; titulorum, operationum, dignitatum, honoris & affectus communio aut consensus voluntatis humanæ cum divina in Christo, unitatem personæ constituunt, siquidem illa omnia non ad unitatem hypostaseos sed ad secundum actum personæ subsistentis pertinent.


### XXIIX. II. Having now proven that the true nature of personal union is not…

XXIIX. II. Having now proven that the true nature of personal union is not properly explained by παράστασιν καὶ παράθεσιν, and therefore that in reality there is only one person of the two natures in Christ; it is further evident that a true and real κοινωνίαν of idioms and operations has necessarily followed that personal union, since these two stand in relation as cause and effect. And therefore it follows infallibly that those things which were noted above in ch. 1, th. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 are most heretically asserted by Nestorius. For all actions and passions properly belong to supposita and persons, as B. Luther speaks with the sounder philosophers.

XXIX. Add that Nestorius contradicts Christ to his face, denying that his flesh is endowed with δυνάμει ζωοποιητικῇ: which doubles the person of Christ, ascribing divine actions only to God the λόγῳ, but human ones only to Christ the man, since according to B. Luther, a division of the person necessarily follows from a division of the works: or as the Scholastics speak: There is one principle of the 'What' [principium Quod], namely one Christ, and one person doing all things: there is a double principle of the 'By Which' [principium Qvo], namely two natures, as two forms: because the form gives the cause of acting.

XXX. And why, I ask, by reason of the crime of ἀνθρωπολατρείας (man-worship), will you be able to clear yourself, Nestorius, by constituting Jesus, the Son of Mary, together with the λόγῳ (Word) as the object of adoration, whom, however, you otherwise most fiercely contend to be a mere man? For does he not in this way, contrary to that passage in Jer. 17:5, place his trust, which is presupposed in one who adores, in a man, and thus with wicked daring steal away the honor owed to GOD, contrary to the express prohibition in Isa. 42:8?

XXXI. What? If only a ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος [mere man] suffered and died for us, as you indeed contend, Nestorius, our redemption is certainly nothing, since a mere man is by no means able to sustain the infinite burden of divine wrath and eternal punishments; therefore it was necessary for the Author of life to be killed, Acts 3:15, and the Lord of glory to be crucified, 1 Cor. 2:8.

XXXII. Finally, is it not clearly insane to assert that the Most Holy ἀναμάρτητον, in whose mouth no guile was found, etc., offered a victim to God the Father for himself? For what need is there of an ἱλαστήριῳ sacrifice, if no offense preceded it?

XXXIII. Thus far we have repressed Nestorius, and have utterly proscribed him and his blasphemies from the precincts of the Church. But would that, oh would that he had not in turn broken into the Church in this our age! For behold! In this last old age of the world, Neo-Nestorians have emerged from the Nestorian ashes, not indeed at the first onset and directly doubling the person: yet consequently, just like the ancient Nestorians, because of the denied true and real communication of idioms, tearing and separating the natures from one another.

XXXIV. But who are they? The Calvinists. For an egg is not so like an egg as these are like the Nestorians. They bear it very ill, and protest with full cheeks, if anyone accuses them of this heresy, and therefore they wish every guilt and suspicion of it to be utterly removed from themselves. 'Who,' writes Danaeus, 'could ever persuade you that we tear apart the natures of our Lord Jesus Christ? Since we pronounce anathema, and indeed with our whole heart, upon anyone who either constitutes two persons in Christ, or tears apart his person.' Therefore, we also believe with our heart and confess with our mouth that when the body of Christ was in the sepulcher during those three days, and his soul in heaven, that hypostatic union of the two natures of Christ nevertheless remained, and was by no means dissolved.

XXXV. Thus, therefore, the Calvinists indeed confess, or at least seem to confess, that there are two natures in Christ, which are so personally united that there is only one Christ, only one person: they confess that, on account of this most intimate union, the natures remain undivided, unsevered, and inseparable: they confess that, on account of this same ἕνωσιν (union) of the natures, the properties are rightly predicated in the concrete of the whole person, and furthermore that the most excellent gifts have been given to the human nature, by which it has been exalted above all creatures.

XXXVI. But that they cast a cataract upon us, and thus rehash Nestorian cabbage, we prove by the following argumentation.

XXXVII. Whoever I. deny one hypostasis of the two natures in Christ. II. Imagine their union to have been made κατὰ παράστασιν (by juxtaposition). III. Imagine that the Λόγον (Word) dwells in the assumed nature in exactly the same way as He dwells in the saints: IV. Deny that the flesh of Christ is to be adored in the unity of the person with the λόγῳ (Word) with one adoration, and finally V. deny that the same is life-giving by that δυνάμει ζωοποιητικῇ (life-giving power) which is proper to the λόγυ (Word) by nature, but is really communicated to the flesh through union with the λόγῳ (Word), they Nestorianize. The reason for the consequence is manifest, since Nestorius also partly denied and partly invented all the things posited in the antecedent.

XXXIIX. But that the Calvinists 1. deny one hypostasis of the two natures in Christ. This is what the following proves.

XXXIX. I. Because they deny that the ἰδιώματα (properties) of the λόγυ (Word) are truly and really communicated to the assumed flesh. Therefore, they deny the ὑποστάσεως κοινωνίαν (communion of the hypostasis) and consequently, there will not be only one hypostasis of the two natures in Christ, but two distinct ones, the one of the λόγυ (Word), the other of the assumed flesh, which is openly Nestorian.

XL. The reason for this consequence is this, because the ὑπόσασις (hypostasis) of the λόγυ (Word) does not differ from the properties in essence, but only in concept, and therefore, with one of the divine properties communicated, the other, indeed all, are necessarily communicated; and conversely: since they are ἀδιαιρέτως (indivisibly) one. For the human nature is either ἐνυπόσατος (in-hypostatic) or ἀνυπόσατος (non-hypostatic), it subsists, or it does not subsist. The latter is false. Therefore, the former is true. If, therefore, the human nature is ἐνυπόσατος (in-hypostatic), it follows that it is either ἀνθυπόσατος (self-hypostatic), subsisting in or through itself, or ἑτερυπόσατος (hetero-hypostatic), subsisting in another. Not the former. For thus there would be two persons in Christ. For, as of one person, there is one subsistence: so

For, as there is one subsistence of one person: so two subsistences presuppose two persons. Therefore the human nature of Christ is ἑτεροϋπόςατος, and consequently has truly had the ὑπόςασιν of the Word communicated to itself, and on account of this it will likewise have been made a partaker of the remaining divine attributes: or if these are ἀκοινώνητα, that will necessarily also be such, since they are most simply one and the same. Because therefore the Calvinists deny the κοινωνίαν ἰδιωμάτων, they consequently deny with Nestorius the κοινωνίαν ὑποςάσεως, and therefore they make the Lord's flesh either ἀνυπόςατον, which is Mahometan, or ἀνθυπόςατον, which is Nestorian.

XLI. 2. Because ἰδιώματα and ὑπόςασις relate to each other as effect and cause, by the positing of which the other is also posited, and vice versa. 3. Because they deny the omnipresence of the human nature of Christ. 4. Because they do not concede that the finite is capable of the infinite. 5. Because they teach that the whole Word is outside the assumed flesh. For a more lengthy demonstration of this first member of the syllogism, see Schroeder on Nestorianism, Argument 7 and following.

XLII. II. They imagine the union of the two natures to have been made κατὰ παράςασιν. For 1. they deny a true communion between the united things and the attributes of the united things, which is otherwise a necessary consequence of a real union per se and ὑποςατικῆς,

XLIII. For that real and per se union is that by which things that are united to some one thing per se, really communicate among themselves. Which indeed happens when one of the united things has the nature of δυνάμεις, and the other of ἐντελέχειας, so that the former may receive, and the latter be received: that it may be communicated to the former, and this may communicate, and that really, whence through such communication it becomes one real thing,

XLIV. Which the philosophers also hint at, teaching that one thing is made by nature out of matter and form, while matter is perfected, form perfects, matter receives, form is received. Just as therefore in one real thing by nature: so the matter stands in one real thing above nature, namely in the God-man. For Christ is one per se, one namely ὑφισάμενον or a 'this something' and one not simple, but composite, namely one person in and from two natures. For the union was made between the human nature and primarily between the person of the Son: but secondarily through the intervention of the person between the nature of the Son also, otherwise than in natural things, where primarily the ἐντελέχεια gives the act of being to the δύναμις, secondarily truly the act of existing. But here the person is first communicated to another nature, whence it exists as one in person: yet in the person [there is] the person's own nature.

XLV. Just as, therefore, between united things, a true and real κοινωνία (communion) intervenes by a union in itself; for by potentiality the ἐντελέχεια (actuality) is communicated: so in this mystery the human nature of Christ, because it behaves like a δύναμις (potentiality), and the Word like an ἐντελέχεια (actuality), it happens thence that the Word truly and really communicates Himself to the flesh.

XLVI. 2. Because they illustrate the union of the two natures in Christ with such similarities, which imply nothing but a certain παράστασιν καὶ συνάφειαν (juxtaposition and connection). Such are those which are taken from Antwerp adjacent to the Ocean; from a planet fixed to its orbit; from a gem adhering to a ring, etc.

XLVII. III. That the Word inhabits the assumed nature in the very same way in which He inhabits the saints. This is clearly evident from the definition of Personal Union handed down by them, which they say is the sustaining and bearing of the assumed flesh by the Word.

XLVIII. Finally, that the last two members of the minor premise are defended by the Calvinists is as certain as it is certain that the sun shines at noon. We conclude, therefore, infallibly, that the Calvinists Nestorianize, ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι (which was to be demonstrated).

XLIX. For the 4th and last chapter, the negative. Thus: I argue. Whoever, with the Ephesian Fathers against Nestorius, assert a true and real κοινωνία (communion) of both the ὑπόστασις (hypostasis) and the ἰδιώματα καὶ ἀποτελέσματα (properties and effects), to them Nestorianism is wrongly objected. The Lutherans do this. Therefore.

L. The consequence of the major premise radiates with its own light. The minor could be most firmly and fully demonstrated from the writings of all the orthodox, if the nature of the institution and the custom of the College allowed this. To Thee, O Jesus, Son of Nun, be praise and honor.

Latin:

XXIIX. II. Evicto nunc, veram unionis personalis rationem per παράστασιν καὶ παράθεσιν non proprie exponi, adeóq; revera unam duntaxat esse duarum in Christo naturarum personam; ultro patet, veram ac realem indiomatum ac operationum κοινωνίαν, necessario istam unionem personalem esse insecutam, siquidem duo ista sese habent, ut causa & effectus. Ideoq; porro infallibiliter sequitur, hæreticissime a Nestorio asseri ea, quæ supra c. 1. th. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18. sunt annotata. Omnes enim actiones & passiones proprie sunt suppositorum ac personaru, uti loquitur cum sanioribus Philosophis B. Luther.

XXIX. Adde quod Nestorius ipsi Christo in faciem contradicat, carnem ejus δυνάμει ζωοποιητικῇ præditam esse, negans: quod personam Christi duplicet, divinas actiones soli Deo λόγῳ: humanas vero soli Christo homini adscribens, siquidem juxta B. Lutherum, ad divisionem operum necessario sequitur divisio personæ: seu ut Scholastici loquuntur: Unum est principium Quod, videlicet unus Christus, & una persona agens omnia: duplex est principium Qvo, videlicet duæ naturæ, tanquam formæ duæ: quia forma dat causam agendi.

XXX. Et quia quæso ratione ab ἀνθρωπολατρείας crimine se purgare poteris Nestorius. Jesum Mariæ Filium, una cum λόγῳ adorationis objectum constituens: qvem tamen alias purum putum hominem esse accerrimè contendit? Annon enim hoc modo contra illud Jer. 17. v. 5. fiduciam suam, qvæ in adorante præsupponitur, collocat in hominem, atq; sic DEO debitum honorem nefario ausu suffuratur contra expressum interdictum, Esa. 42. v. 8.

XXXI. Qvid? qvod si ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος duntaxat pro nobis passus ac mortuus est, uti tu qvidem contendis Nestori, nulla utiq; est nostra redemtio, si qvidem nudus homo infinitum onus iræ divinæ ac æternas pœnas sustinere minimè potest, ideoq; necessum fuit Authorẽ vitæ interfici, Actor. 3. v. 15. ac Dominũ gloriæ crucifigi 1. Cor. 2. v. 8.

XXXII. Deniq; annon planè furiosum est, asserere, Sanctissimum ἀναμάρτητον, in cujus ore non fuit inventus dolus, &c. pro semetipso victimam Deo Patri obtulisse? Nam qvid opus est ἱλαστήριῳ sacrificio, si nulla præcessit offensio?

XXXIII. Hactenus E. Nestorium repressimus, eumq; cum suis blasphemiis penitus ex pomeriis Ecclesiæ proscripsimus. Utinam verò atq; utinam Ille hoc nostro seculo vicissim in Ecclesiam non irrupisset! Nam ecce! Hac postremâ mundi senectâ è cineribus Nestorianis prodiere Neonestoriani, non qvidem primò statim agressu & per directum personam duplicantes: conseqventer tamen, sicut & Veteres Nestoriani, ob negatam veram ac realem idiomatum communicationem, naturas à se invicem divellentes ac separantes.

XXXIV. Qvinam verò sunt illi? Calviniani. Non. n. tam ovum ovo simile, qvam hi Nestorianis. Ægerrimè qvidem ferunt, plenisq; reclamant buccis, si qvis eos hujus hærefeos peragat reos, adeoq; omnem ejusdem reatum ac suspicionem penitus à se remotam volunt. Naturas Domini nostri Jesu Christi, scribit Danæus, nos dilcerpere, ecqvis vobis unqvam persuadere potuit? cùm illi ipsi anathema pronunciemus, & qvidem toto pectore, qvi vel duas in Christo personas constituit, vel ipsius personam divellit. Ergo etiam cum Christi corpus esset per illud triduum in sepulchro, & anima in cœlo, hypostaticam tamen illam duarum Christi naturarum Unionem permansisse, & minimè dissolutam esse, corde credimus & ore confitemur,

XXXV. Sic ergò Calviniani qvidem fatentur, vel certè fateri videntur, in Christo duas esse naturas, qvæ ita sint personaliter unitæs ut unus tantùm Christus, una tantùm sit persona: fatentur ob unionem hanc arctissimam, naturas indivisas, indivulsas & inseparatas manere: fatentur, ob eandem ἕνωσιν naturarum propria rectè in concreto prædicari de tota persona, qvin & humanæ naturæ data esse dona excellentissima, qvibus supra omnes creaturas evecta sit.

XXXVI. Verùm ipsos glaucoma nobis objicere, adeòq; Nestorianam crambem recoqvere, seqventi evincimus argumentatione.

XXXVII. Qvicunq; I. negant unam duarum naturarum in Christo hypostasin. II. Earum unionem κατὰ παράστασιν factam fingunt. III. Λόγον eodem planè modo in assumtâ natura inhabitare, qvo in sanctis habitat: IV. Carnem Christi in unitate personæ cum λόγῳ una adoratione adorandum esse, ac deniq; V. eandem esse vivificam δυνάμει ζωοποιητικῇ illâ, quæ τῦ λόγυ per naturam propria, carni verò per unionem cum λόγῳ realiter est communicata inficiantur, illi Nestorianizant. Ratio Conseqventiæ manifesta est, siqvidem Nestorius etiam omnia in Antecedente posita, partim negavit, partim finxit.

XXXIIX. At qvi Calviniani 1. unam duarum naturarum in Christo hypostasin inficiantur. Id qvod seqventia probant.

XXXIX. I. Qvia negant ἰδιώματα τῦ λόγυ assumtæ Carni verè ac realiter esse communicata. E. negant ὑποστάσεως κοινωνίαν & per conseqvens, non erit una tantùm duarum naturarum in Christo hypostasis, verùm duæ distinctæ, altera τῦ λόγυ, altera carnis assumtæ, qvod apertè Nestorianum.

XL. Ratio hujus conseqventiæ est hæc, qvia ὑπόσασις τῦ λόγυ ab idiomatibus non differt τῷ εἶναι, sed saltem τῷ λογῳ, ac proptera communicato idiomatum divinorum uno, necessario communicatum & alterum, imò omnia; & contra: cum ἀδιαιρέτως unum sint. Humana enim natura aut est ἐνυπόσατος aut ἀνυπόσατος, subsistit, aut non subsistit. Hoc falsum. E. illud verum. Si E. humana natura est ἐνυπόσατος, seqvitur, qvod sit aut ἀνθυπόσατος, in vel per se subsistens, aut ἑτερυπόσατος in alio subsistens. Non illud. Sic enim in Christo duæ forent personæ. Nam, ut unius personæ, una est subsistentia: ita

Nam, ut unius personæ, una est subsistentia: ita duæ subsistentiæ duas præsupponunt personas. E. humana Christi natura est ἑτεροϋπόςατος, adeoq; ὑπόςασιν λογꙋ verè sibi habet communicatam, & propter hanc itidem erit κοινωνὸς facta reliqvorum divinorum idiomatum: aut si hæc sunt ἀκοινώνητα, necessariò etiam illa talis erit, cum sint simplicissimè unum ταυτὸ. Qvia igitur Calviniani negant κοινωνίαν ἰδιωμάτων, conseqventer negant cum Nestorio κοινωνίαν ὑποςάσεως, ac proinde carnem Dominicam faciunt, aut ἀνυπόςατον, qvod Mahumeticum, ἀνθυπόςατον, qvod Nestorianum.

XLI. 2. Qvia ἰδιώματα & ὑπόςασις habent se ut effectus & causa, qvâ positâ ponitur & ille, & vicissim. 3. Qvia omnipræsentiam humanæ Christi naturæ inficiantur. 4. Qvia non concedunt finitum esse capax infiniti. 5. Qvia docent, totum λογον extra carnem assumtam esse. Primum hoc syllogismi membrum prolixiùs demonstrantem vide Schrœderum de Nestorian, Argt. 7. & seqq.

XLII. II. Duarum Naturarum unionem κατὰ παράςασιν factam fingunt. Nam 1. negant veram inter unita & unitorum idiomata communionem, qvæ aliàs Unionis realis per se & ὑποςατικῆς necessarium est conseqvens,

XLIII. Nam 'Inio realis ac per se illa est, qvâ, qvæ ad unum aliqvod per se uniuntur, realiter inter se communicat. Qvod qvidem fit, qvando unitorum alterum habet rationem δυνάμεως, alterum ἐντελέχειας, ut illud recipiat, hoc recipiatur: illi commuicetur, hoc communicet, idq; realiter, unde per communicationem talem fit unum reale,

XLIV. Id qvod & Philosophi innuunt, docentes, unum per naturam fieri ex materia & forma, dum materia perficitur, forma perficit, materia recipit, forma recipitur. Qvemadmodum ergo in uno reali per naturam: ita se res habet in uno reali supra naturam, θεανθρώπῳ nimirum. Est n. Christus unum per se, unum scilicet ὑφιςάμενον seu τόδε τι atq; unum non simplex, sed compositum, personæ nimirum una in & è duabus naturis. Facta n. est unio inter humanam naturam & primò inter personam Filii: secundariô vero interventu personæ inter naturam etiam Filii, secùs qvàm in naturalibus, ubi primò ἐντελέχεια δυνάμει dat actum essendi, secundò vero actum existendi. At hic persona primùm communicatur alteri naturæ, unde existit unum personâ: tamen in persona personæ propria natura.

XLV. Sicut E. inter unita, unione per se intercedit vera & realis κοινωνία; δυνάμει enim communicatur ἐντελέχεια: ita in hoc mysterio humana Christi natura, quia se habet instar δυνάμεως, λογῷ instar ἐντελέχειας, sit inde ut λογῷ verè & realiter carni sese communicet.

XLVI. 2. Qvia unionem duarum in Christo naturarum illustrant ejusmodi similibus, quæ non nisi παράστασιν καὶ συνάφειαν quandam inferunt. Talia sunt, quæ desumuntur ab Antuerpia Oceano adjacente; a Planeta orbi suo affixo: a gemma annulo adhærente &c.

XLVII. III. Λογον eodem planè modo in assumta natura inhabitare, quo in sanctis habitat. Id quod ex Personalis Unionis definitione ab ipsis tradita luculenter patet, quam dicunt esse sustentationem ac gestationem assumtæ carnis a λογῳ.

XLVIII. Postrema deniq; duo Minoris membra 'defendi a Calvinianis tam certum est, quam certum solem lucere in meridie. Concludim9 igitur infallibiliter, Calvinianos Nestorianizare, ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι.

XLIX. Pro 4. & ultimi Cap. negativa. Sic: argumentor. Qvicunque cum Patribus Ephesinis contra Nestorium tum ὑποστάσεως tum ἰδιωμάτων καὶ ἀποτελεσμάτων veram ac realem κοινωνίαν asserunt, illis Nestorianismus malè objicitur. Lutherani hoc faciunt. E.

L. ConseqventiaMajoris suâ luce radiat. Minor ex omnium orthodoxorum scriptis firmissimè & fufissimè demonstrari posset, si ratio instituti & mos Collegii hoc admitteret. Tibi E. Jesu Binuni laus & honor.


## 8 Eighth Disputation. On Eutycheism

The heresy of Nestorius, having been recently exposed and examined, is rightly followed by that of Eutyches, who, denying the division of the natures in Christ, introduced a horrible confusion and per mixture; he exploded the duality of Persons, he feigned a Unity of Nature; he rejected Nestorius, who was attentive to the Property of the Natures and was departing from the Union of the Person; but he himself, by looking at one Person, departing from the properties of the Natures, overturned their Personal Union; Thus, therefore, the former was cast into the abyss of division, the latter is tossed in the sea of confusion; The former refused to confess the Unity of the Person in the duality of Nature, the latter was unwilling to confess the duality of the Natures in one Person. Wherefore, since this undivided Union of the two Natures in Christ has been shown against Nestorius; so the same must be demonstrated as unconfused against Eutyches, which, with Christ the One helping us, we shall perform in this διασκέψει [examination], and shall provide it included in the following chapters: in [the first] we shall treat of the origin, progress, and outcome of Eutychianism in general: in 2. we shall examine the arguments and evasions of Eutyches in particular: in 3. we shall indicate the difference from Nestorianism: in 4. we shall show that the same is falsely attributed to our Churches by our adversaries through the greatest calumny.

Thesis I.

Just as those who embrace the Evangelical Truth, called Christians with Christ as their leader, so those who have departed from it and made themselves unworthy of this name, deservedly bear the names of their heresy, so that the precious may be the better distinguished from the vile: Jer. 15. v. 19.

II. In which matter we have not only the sacrosanct Scripture in agreement with us, approving this difference and observing the distinction, Apoc. 2. v. 6. & 15. and in many other places: but also the whole Catholic and holy Church, which, as Athanasius testifies, exploded the inventors of heresy and segregated them far from itself, so that not even a fellowship of name might be granted to those who have departed from the fellowship of the Evangelical Truth.

III. Hence those who followed Marcion were called Marcionites, Valentinus, Valentinians, Manichaeus, Manichaeans, Arius, Arians, Pelagius, Pelagians, Nestorius, Nestorians, and thus those who followed Eutyches were called Eutychians.

VI. Regarding Eutyches and his origin, authors report this. c Eutyches, an Archimandrite or Abbot of Constantinople under Theodosius the Second in the year 442, while he knew that Nestorius had been condemned for the dissolution of the Person, having slipped into the contrary opinion, asserted the Unity of the Person in such a way that he introduced not a Union of Natures, but a Unity. V. He explained himself more clearly in the Council of Chalcedon, where, being questioned about his doctrine, he replied thus: I, Eutyches, profess that before the Union our Lord Jesus Christ was begotten of two Natures; but after the Union, that there is one Nature of Him, and that His Body is divine; nor do I preach that it was substantial to us, nor subject to the same sufferings as we are.

VI. We include the sum of the heretical assertion in the following members: 1, That the Nature of the Word was changed into flesh, and thus before the Union there were two Natures, after which the Flesh was then absorbed into the b divinity: Chem: de duab Nat.

VII. Some express it thus: that after the coupling of the Divine and Human Nature, a certain third thing, as it were, emerged from both, the human nevertheless being absorbed, as Flavianus reports. c

IIX. Hence he contends that Christ subsists from two Natures indeed, but not in two Natures, as Zanchius reports. d

IX. 2. That the flesh of Christ was not true but apparent and phantastical, and far different from ours; whence 3. that in the sufferings of the Lord one must look not to the flesh but to the divine Nature of the Word, which he said suffered and died, and therefore that all these things are to be ascribed to it.

X. For just as the Word was made flesh, i.e., as he himself explains: Just as the divinity was converted into humanity, so after the Union the humanity was converted into the divinity, so that not the humanity but the deity is said to have suffered and died; see Vigil. lib. 2. contra Eutychetem.

XI. Furthermore, concerning the entry of this heresy, we note also this: that this Eutyches was not so much the inventor of it as its primary defender and champion, because it is gathered from Athanasius a, Cyril b, Epiphanius c, Augustine d, Justin e, and especially Dionysius the Areopagite, who is far older than Eutyches f, and many others, that he drew not a few things from the delirium of the Manichaeans as well as from the dreams of Apollinaris.

XII. The true cause of this error in Eutyches is assigned to this: because he concluded that it could not be obtained against Nestorius that there is one, not two, Persons of Christ, unless the number of the natures corresponded to the Person.

XIII. We come to the progress, in which the first offspring of the Eutychians were the Monophysites, or according to Damascenus, the Schematici, who were also named Theopaschites, and from their location, Egyptians; in which error History records that Philoponus the Grammarian also existed. Following these were the Acephali, who were also called Severites and Julianists; after these, the Agnoetae, Jacobites, Armenians, Monothelites, etc.

XIV. Although some of these dissented from Eutyches in certain matters, and some even added many things to his impiety or errors, nevertheless they are rightly referred here, since they all flowed from the source of this delusion: see more in the Rev. D. Pappus. g.

XV. This same heresy, born under a clearly ill-omened star, was as if recalled from hell in our times, namely in the year of Christ 1529, by the foul-smelling Caspar Schwenckfeld, and with him the whole crowd of Anabaptists, a group if not entirely similar to Eutyches in all things, yet most agreeable in the principal errors.

XVI. Finally, Nicephorus explains the outcome, and indeed that of Eutyches, at the Ecumenical Synod of Chalcedon, the greatest of all synods, the fourth, convened by the Emperor Marcian in the year of Christ 451, in these words: when that confession of Eutyches had been recited in the first session, it was exclaimed by the Fathers, Anathema to those who said these things, Anathema to him who said these things. A.

XVII. We hold the authority of the decree of this Council in such high regard that we consider not only Eutyches himself, but all subsequent followers embracing this delusion, to have been struck by the same thunderbolt of anathema, and that those who follow must be struck as well. See more concerning the great authority of this Council in Polydore Vergil. h.

XIIX. By way of a conclusion, we marvel at the craftiness of Bucanus regarding this chapter, who asserts that the human nature was endowed with divine properties and that Eutyches was condemned because of this assertion: he who does not suffer from a head cold easily smells what this bald offspring intends.

XIX. We proposed the sum of Eutychianism, contained in three principal members, in the preceding chapter; now furthermore the foundations of each are to be considered, and let us do that now in order,

XX. Although, as was said a little while ago, the first member of the Eutychian heresy is not always expressed in the same words, if the matter is weighed accurately, no discrepancy occurs.

XXI. For although, as historians relate, he expressed this dogma of his in various and sufficiently ambiguous ways quite often. Yet from the open confession cited above, it is gathered that he affirmed nothing other than the unity of Nature in the Person of Christ, and indeed not a human, but a divine one.

XXII. The arguments which he is thought to have used are these; 1. It is taken from the passage John 1:14, 'The Word was made flesh.' If the Word was made flesh, certainly the Word did not remain what it was. True, the former, therefore the latter. The consequence of the major premise is this: that which is made, is not made that which it is, but is made some other thing which it is not, just as water is made wine by the nature of the water passing away: The assumption is evident from the Greek ἐγένετο, for γίνεσθαι is to be changed but to become something else; therefore the nature of the Word was converted into flesh.

XXIII. 2. If there are two Natures in Christ, certainly there will be two Persons, the latter being Nestorian, therefore the former. The consequence of the major premise could be shown thus: the individual of a Nature is a Person; Christ assumed an individual Nature. Therefore.

XXIV. 3. If there are two inseparable Natures in Christ, it follows that when one is invoked, the other is also invoked: the latter is against God's Commandment, because God alone is to be worshipped, therefore the former.

XXV. 4. The authority of Cyril is brought forward, which, as Gregor de Valent proves in book 1 from the Council of Chalcedon, Act 5, he is said to have stated that two Natures should not be understood in Christ, but one.

XXVI. We shall omit the rest due to the scarcity of pages, and reserve them for the conflict. But against these we oppose this theorem of ours: θεώρημα.

XXVII. No transmutation falls upon the divine Nature (Mal. 3:6). Whence by union nothing is added to it or taken away, but as it is most simple, so it remains; for what it was, it remained, and what it was not, it assumed; it assumed not a person, but a Nature into the Person by a hypostatic, supernatural union, incomprehensible to all creatures; on account of which we worship and piously venerate the whole Christ in two natures.

XXIIX. We respond therefore to 1. 'The Word was made flesh,' not by the conversion of divinity, which is immutable, into flesh, but by the assumption of Humanity into God, which is proved by the most evident testimonies of Scripture, where this mode of assumption signifies not conversion but association, or as the Scholastics more correctly speak, the denotation of assumption. 1. He notes Phil. 2. v. 7, Heb. 2. v. 16. 2. The little word γίνεσθαι does not always signify a physical transmutation but a coupling and connection, Gen. 2. v. 7, Gal. 2. v. 14, Luke 2. v. 24. 3. It is contrary to the opinion of Eutyches himself, for if the divinity was changed into flesh, it certainly ceased to be what it was, and therefore it is not only Divine Nature, but also Human.

XXX. To 2. By denying the major premise: for it does not follow that where there are two natures there are two persons, and therefore we limit it thus: Where there are two natures subsisting by themselves, so that one subsists outside the other, there are two persons. But the latter is false in Christ; for although he assumed an individual human substance, he did not assume it as subsisting by itself, but in the person of the λόγος: 2. Innumerable scriptural passages testify that that nature is not a distinct person of the λόγος, Rom. 5. v. 15, 1 Cor. 8. v. 6, 1 Tim. 2. v. 5, and yet they assert the duality of natures at the same time, as shown above.

XXXI. To 3. By conceding the antecedent and defending the affirmative, that the whole Christ is to be adored and thus also in the flesh, not indeed in and of itself by reason of the flesh, but by reason of the hypostatic union of the eternal Son of God, Heb. 1. v. 17, Phil. 2. v. 10, wherefore the divine command which is held in Deut. 6. v. 13 is not contrary to us; for it is opposed to idols, 2. because we maintain that not the creature by itself, but the person of the λόγος and thus the eternal Son of God in two natures is to be adored.

XXXII. To 4. Wishing to show that Cyril did not understand the word nature abstractly, but concretely, and thus for the whole person, not that there are two persons but one person in two natures, as Thomas proves.

XXIII. The arguments of the second member follow, of which these are the most principal.

XXXIV. 1. It seems absurd that we should say the Creator assumed a creature, which is subject to all kinds of evils and therefore to sin. Therefore it should rather be judged that it was not such flesh as this of ours is, but far different from it.

XXXV. 2. If he assumed the same flesh that we have, it follows that, because divinity is one thing and humanity is another, God is composed of humanity and deity: the latter is absurd. Therefore the former. Let all other arguments directed against the truth of the flesh of Christ in previous discussions be referred here and discussed.

XXXVI. To these we oppose this thesis of ours from Epist. Phil. 2. v. 6, 7.

Who, when he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, made himself of no reputation, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in fashion as a man.

XXXVII. I answer therefore to 1. that it is a sophism of human reason, for in these matters one must attend not to what reason thinks, but to what God has revealed in his word: 2. We deny that the flesh of Christ was subject to sin, since it is not said that he assumed sin, but man, Heb. 2. v. 14.

XXXVIII. To 2. I say: We do not deny that the Person of Christ consists of divinity and humanity, and that thus there is a certain composition in Christ, yet not a physical one; for if it were such, the Natures would be confounded among themselves, and a mixture of them would occur, but rather a metaphysical one, which does not hinder the simplicity of God; for just as by the absence of the flesh nothing was lost, so by the assumption of the same nothing was added to them.

XXXIX. Finally, the most principal argument of the third member is this: if the divinity did not suffer, Nestorius rightly thought that a mere man suffered and died. The latter is absurd, therefore the former.

XL. To this we oppose the saying in Acts 20. v. 28: God purchased the Church with his own blood; if God, not the Deity, whence—We answer that the major proposition is poorly formed, since actions are of the Person, not of the Natures, according to the rule: To act belongs to the suppositum, etc. Actions and passions are of the Person. Hence each Nature in Christ acts with the communication of the other, yet preserving that which is proper to each Nature, according to the rule of the Council of Chalcedon. Whence, although I cannot say in the abstract, 'The Deity has suffered,' I rightly say, 'God has suffered,' on account of the personal union, namely, of the Deity and Humanity, and the real communication of idioms following from it.

XLI. It remains now to show the difference between Nestorianism and Eutychianism; and just as the whole Nestorian heresy arose from the perversion of the doctrine of the communication of idioms, so also the matter stands with the Eutychian heresy, which authors report to have been expressly opposed to the Nestorian.

XLIII. Just as therefore Nestorius 1. feigned a double Person in Christ along with a double Nature, and that from the fact that he denied that the properties of those diverse Natures could be truly and really attributed to the whole Person, hence he established one Person as having suffered, and another as not having suffered or as impassible.

XLIII. Thus, on the other hand, Eutyches defends the unity of nature on account of the unity of the person, and he does so from this, because he dreamed that unless the properties of both natures are referred to one nature, the Nestorian duality would arise.

XLIV. Hence Vigilius rightly says: You see how dangerous a thing it is either not to believe in one person in Christ or to be unwilling to confess two natures in Him; while I defend the one person of Christ against Nestorius, I am thought to deny the human nature according to Eutyches; while I assert two natures against Eutyches, I am thought to profess two persons according to Eutyches.

XLV. Hence 2. just as Nestorius did not deny but asserted the true humanity of Christ, so on the contrary Eutyches was unwilling to confess the same.

XLVI. Nestorius [held that] divine idioms are not to be attributed to the flesh. Eutyches, on the contrary, established that all idioms are to be ascribed indiscriminately to one nature.

XLVII. Nestorius [held that] a mere man suffered, was crucified, and died; Eutyches [held that] God, not man, and the deity, not the humanity, suffered, died, and was crucified.

XLVIII. These things having been thus demonstrated, we marvel at the remarkable impudence and malice of our adversaries, both of the bald race and of the brotherhood of Esau, by which, without any truth, they strive to ascribe the charge of Nestorianism to our churches, to accuse them of Eutychianism, and thus to traduce the associates of the genuine Augsburg Confession most shamefully before the whole world.

XLIX. What commerce our churches have with Nestorius was seen in the preceding disputation; on the contrary, it has been shown how closely both heretics approach that [position], and therefore for this turn we only thrust upon them this firm and immovable rule of the Council of Ephesus: Whoever denies the real communication of idioms, he denies the unity of the person in Christ; let them untie this knot, if they are men.

L. Furthermore, what else is it to wish to ascribe both the Nestorian and Eutychian dogma to one person than to be insane with reason, to affirm that light and darkness exist at the same time, to establish that white and black can exist at the same time? Since it is known that these heresies differ so greatly from one another and are so contrary to each other that when one is affirmed, the other is completely removed and denied.

LI. What then, the devil, is it that they clamor is Eutychianism?

LII. Is it Eutychian to confess the union of two natures in Christ, not physical but supernatural and therefore personal in the one person of Christ? To dissolve this is Nestorian.

LIII. Is it Eutychian that, on account of this most intimate union of natures, properties are really communicated to one another, and therefore can be rightly predicated in the concrete of the person? To deny it is Nestorian.

LIV. Is it Eutychian to say that the divinity did not suffer, die, or was buried, but that God suffered and died? It is Nestorian to say that a man suffered.

LV. Is it Eutychian to teach that properties are so communicated that they are not mixed nor confused, but that the properties remain safe for the nature to which they belong? The contrary is Nestorian.

LVI. By way of a finishing touch, we tax the impudent lie of the Esauvites, by which, through their signal and innate Esauvitic malice, they do not blush to foist Eutychianism upon blessed Luther and call him a Eutychian, because in book 3 de Concil. he wrote that the divinity suffered; in which matter both betray a more than nefarious crime, for that which Luther refutes there, he is most falsely said to have affirmed.

LVII. Let not the Esauvite race think us so dull that we would attribute any change to the Deity; rather, if they do not openly flee the light, let them say what they think; perhaps what they attribute to us and our churches through the greatest injury, we shall be able with the best right and indeed with truth as our guide to retort upon them, especially since, when I say, Christ is man, just as David is King, Aaron is Priest, let either side defend that there is no other predication and no other union, and let them make the union accidental, so that just as royal majesty can be laid aside while David remains, and the priesthood can be taken away from Aaron while Aaron himself nevertheless remains; so I assume that humanity can be taken away from Christ while the person nevertheless remains safe.

LVIII. Let him see what can be closer to Eutychianism? Therefore we now conclude thus with Augustine: Christ did not die for him who denies that Christ is man, because he died according to his humanity.

Latin:

PRoximè expositam examinatamq; hæresin Nestorii, rectè subseqvitur Eutychis, ut, qvi divusionem Naturarum in Christo negans, horribilem earundem Confusionem & Permixtionem introduxit; dualitatem Personarum explosit, Unitatem Naturæ finxit; Proprietatem Naturarum attendentem & è Personæ Unione excedentem Nestorium rejecit; ipse vero unam Personam intuendo à Naturarum proprietatibus decedens, earundem Personalem Unionem evertit; Ita ergo ille in divisionis voraginem dejectus, hic in confusionis Pelago jactatur; Ille Unitatem Personæ in duplicitate Naturæ confiteri recusabat, hic in Una Persona dualitatem Naturarum confiteri nolebat. Qvocirca cum Unio hæc duarum in Christo Naturarum indivisa contra Nestorium ostensa; ita eadem contra Eutychetem inconfusa demonstranda, qvod Christo Bi Uno adjuvante hac διασκέψει præstabimus, seqventibusq́; capitibus inclusam dabimus: in de Eutycheismi ortu progressu & Egressu in genere acturi: in 2. Argumenta & effugia Eutychis in specie examinaturi: in 3. differentiam à Nestorianismo indicaturi in 4. falso nostris Ecclesiis per q; summam calumniam eandem ab adversariis affingi, ostensuri.

Thesis I.

SIcut illi qvi Veritatem Evangelicam amplectuntur, à Christo duce Christiani appellati, ita qvi ab ea discessum seq́; ipsos hoc nomine indignos fecere, merito sua hæreseos nomina præ se ferunt, qvo pretiosum à vili eo melius distinguatur: Jer. 15. v. 19.

II. Qva in re non tantum nobis consentaneam habemus sacrosanctam Scripturam, hanc differentiam approbantem, distinctionemq́; observantem Apoc. 2. v. 6. & 15. aliisq; in locis plur: sed & totam Catholicam & sanctam Ecclesiam qvæ teste à Athanasio inventores hæresews explosit, proculq́; à se segregavit, ut ne nominis qvidem societas indulgeretur his, qvi à societate Veritatis Evangelicæ discesserunt.

III. Hinc illi qui Marcionem secuti Martionitæ, Valentinum Valentiniani, Manichæum Manichæi, Arrium Arriani, Pelagium Pelagiani, Nestorium Nestoriani, sic qui Eutychetem Eutychiani appellati sunt.

VI. De Eutyche ejusq́; Origine hoc referunt Autores. c Eutyches, Archimandrita seu c Abbas Constantinopolitanus sub Theodosio secundo Anno 442. dum damnatum sciret Nestorium ob Personæ solutionem delapsus ad contrarium sententiam, sic Personæ Unitatatem asseruit, ut non Unionem Naturarum sed Unitatem introduceret. V. Manifestius Temetipsum explicavit in Concilio Chalcedonensi a ubi de sua doctrina interrogatus sic respondit: Ego Eutyches ante Unionem ex duabus Naturis profiteor Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum esse genitum; Post Unionem autem unam ejus esse Naturam, & divinum ejus Corpus; neq; nobis substantiale neq; iisdem nobiscum perpessionibus fuisse obnoxium prædico.

VI. Summam autem hæreticæ assertionis sequentibus includimus membris: 1, Verbi Naturam esse mutatam in carnem, & ita ante Unionem duas esse Naturas, post qvam deinde Caro in b divinitatem absumpta: Chem: de duab Nat.

VII. Qvidam sic efferunt post copulationem Divinæ & Humanæ Naturæ, ex utraq; velut tertiam qvandam extitisse, humana nihilominus absumpta ut refert Flavianus. c

IIX. Hinc ex duabus qvide Naturis sed non in duabus Christum subsistere contendit referente Zanchio. d

IX. 2. Non veram sed apparentem & Phantasticam Christi carnem fuisse longe q; à nostra diversam; unde 3. in Passionibus Domini non ad carnem sed ad divinam verbi Naturam qvam Passam & mortuam dixit respiciendam, adeoq; omnes huic adscribendas esse.

X. Sicut enim Verbum caro factum est, h. e. ut ipse explicat; Sicut divinitas conversa est in humanitatem, ita postqvam propter Unionem Humanitas conversa est in divinitatem non Humanitatem sed Deitatem passam & mortuam dici; vide Vigil. lib. 2. contra Eutychetem.

XI. Circa ingressum porro hujus Hæreseos notamus & hoc, hunc Eutychetem non tam fuisse Inventorem hujus, qvam primarium defenforem & propugnatorem, qvia non pauca cum ex Manichæorum delirio, tum Appollinaris somniis hausisse colligitur ex Athanasio a Cyrillo b Epiphanio c Augustino d Justino e & præcipue Dionysio Areopagita longe antiqviore Eutychete f aliisq; plurimis.

XII. Causa vero erroris hujus in Eutychete hæc assignatur, qvia non aliter contra Nestorium obtineri posse, unam non duas esse Christi Personas, colligebat, nisi numerus Naturarum Personæ responderet.

XIII. Ad progressum devenimus, in qvo Eutychianorum prima propago fuerunt, Monophysitæ, seu juxta Damascenum Schematici, qui & Theopaschitæ, & à loco Aegyptii nominati fuerunt; in quo errore fuisse & Philoponum Grammaticum tradit Historia. Hos secuti Acephali, qui & Severitæ & Julianistæ dicti; hos Agnoëtæ, Jacobitæ, Armenii, Monotheletæ &c.

XIV. Qvorum licet qvidam ab Eutychete in qvibusdam dissenserint, qvidam etiam hujus impietati seu erroribus plures addiderint, nihilominus tamen huc rectè referuntur, cum ex hujus delirii scaturigine omnes promanarint: vid. plu. apud Rev. D. Pappum. g.

XV. Eandem hanc hæresin infausto plane sidere natus ex orco qvasi revocavit nostris temporibus Anno scl. Christi 1529. male olens Casparus Stenckfeld, cum eoq; tota Anabaptistarum caterva, Eutychis si non plane per omnia similem in principalioribus tamen Erroribus convenientissimam.

XVI. Tandem Egressum & qvidem Eutychis in Synodo Chalcedonenfi OEcumenica omnium Synodorum maxima IV. convocatis 630. Episcopis à Martiano Imperatore Anno Christi 451. explicat Nicephorus his verbis: à cum in prima Actione Confessio illa Eutychetis fuisset recitata, exclamatum fuit à Patribus, Anathema eis qui ista dixerant, Anathema huic qui dixit ista. A.

XVII. Cujus Concilii Decreti Authoritatem tantam facimus, ut non tantùm ipsum Eutychetem, sed omnes subsequentes sectatores delirium hoc amplectentes, eodem Anathematis fulmine percussos subseqventesq; percutiendos esse existimemus. Vide plura de maxima hujus Concilii auctoritate apud Polydorum Virgilium. h.

XIIX. Coronidis loco miramur circa hoc caput versutiam Bucani qvic Naturam Humanam proprietatibus divinis fuisse donatam obq; hanc assertionem, Eutychetem damnatum asserit: qvid calva proles velit, facilè qvi Catarro non laborat, olfacit.

XIX. Summam Eutychianismi tribus membris principalioribus inclusam præcedente capite proposuimus jam porro singulorum fundamenta sunt consideranda, idq; jam faciamus ordine,

XX. Etsi ut paulo ante dictum Primum Eutychianæ hæreseos membrum non iisdem verbis semper exprimitur si tamen accurate res pensitetur, nulla discrepantia occurrit.

XXI. Nam etsi variè ut Historici tradunt satisq́; ambigue hoc suum dogma sàpius expresserit. Ex aperta tamen confessione supra citata nihil aliud qvam unitatem Naturæ in Persona Christi & qvidem non Humanæ sed divinæ affirmasse colligitur.

XXII. Argumenta, qvibus usus putatur, hæc sunt; 1. desumptum est ex Loco Joh. 1. v. 14. Verbum caro factum est. Si Verbum est factum Caro, utiq; Verbum non mansit id qvod fuit. Verum Prius E. Posterius. Majoris conseq. hæc est; qvod fit, non fit illud qvod est, sed fit aliud qvid, qvod non est, sicut aqva fit vinum transeunte natura aqvæ: Assumptio patet ex Græco ἐγένετο, γίνεσθαι enim est immutari sed aliud fieri; E• λόγου Natura conversa est in carnem.

XXIII. 2. Si in Christo duæ sunt Naturæ, utiq; erunt duæ Personæ, Posterius Nestorianum, E. Prius Majoris conseqventia sic posset ostendi individualis Naturæ est Persona; Christus assumsit individualem Naturam. E.

XXIV. 3. Si duæ inseparabiles Naturæ sunt in Christo, seqvitur invocata una & alteram invocari: Posterius est contra Dei Mandatum, qvia Solus Deus adorandus E. prius.

XXV. 4. Auctoritas Cyrilli adducitur, qvod ut probat Gregor de Valent l. d. ex Concil. Chalced. Act. 5. dixisse fertur, non oportere in Christo intelligi duas Naturas, sed unam.

XXVI. Reliqva studio ob paucitatem paginarum emittemus, conflictuić; reservamus. Hisce verò opponim⁹ hoc nostrū θεώρημα.

XXVII. In divinam Naturam nulla cadit transmutatio Mal. 3. v. 6. Unde per unionem nihil ei accedit vel decedit, sed uti simplicissima est, ita manet; Nam qvod erat permansit & qvod non erat assumpsit, assumpsit à non personam, sed Naturam in Personam unione hypostatica supernaturali omnibusq́; creaturis incomprehensibili; ob qvam totum Christum in duabus naturis adoramus & piè veneramur.

XXIIX. Respondemus ergò ad 1. Verbum caro factum est, non conversione divinitatis, qvæ est immutabilis, in carnem sed assumptione Humanitatis in Deum, qvod probatur evidentissimis Scripturæ testimoniis, ubi hic assumtionis modus non conversionem sed associationem ut Scholastici loqvuntur rectius assumtionem denotat Phil. 2. v. 7. Hebr. 2. v. 16. 2. vocula γίνεσθαι non semper significat transmutationē Physicam sed copulationē & connexionem Gen. 2. v. 7. Galat. 2. v. 14. Luc. 2. v. 24. 3. Contrariatur sententiæ ipsius Eutychetis, nam si divinitas mutata est in carnem, utiq; desiit esse qvod fuit, adeoq; non tantum Divina est Natura, sed etiam Humana.

XXX. Ad 2. Negando Majorem: non enim seqvitur ubi duæ Naturæ ibi duæ Personæ, ideoq; sic limitamus: Ubi dantur duæ Naturæ per se subsistentes, ita ut una extra alteram subsistat, ibi dantur duæ Personæ. At qvi Posterius in Christo falsum; nam licet individualem assumserit substantiam humanam, non tamen per se; sed in Persona τοῦ λόγου subsistentem assumsit: 2. Naturam verò illam non esse distinctam Personam τοῦ λόγου testantur innumeræ Scripturæ dicta Rom. 5. v. 15. 1. Cor. 8. v. 6. 1. Tim. 2. v. 5. & tamen simul dualitatem Naturam asserunt, ut supra ostensum.

XXXI. Ad 3. Antecedens concedendo, & Affirmativam defendendo, omninò totum Christum adorandum esse & ita etiam in carne, non qvidem in & per se ratione carnis, sed ratione hypostaticæ Unionis æterni Filii Dei Heb. 1. v. 17. Phil. 2. v. 10. qvare mandatum divinum nobis non contrariatur qvod habetur Deut. 6. v. 13. opponitur enim illud. . idolis, 2. qvia non creatura per se sed Personam τοῦ λόγου & ita æternū Dei filium in duabus Naturis adorandū esse statuimus.

XXXII. Ad 4. Cyrillum vocabulū Naturæ non abstractè intellexisse, sed concretè adeò pro tota Persona, ostendere volens non duas Personas sed unam Personam in duabus Naturis esse, ut Thomas probat.

XXIII. Seqvuntur Argumenta secundi Membri qvorum principalissima hæc sunt.

XXXIV. 1. Absonum videtur ut dicamus creaturam Creatorem assumsisse, qvæ omnis generis malis adeoq; peccato obnoxia est. Ergò censendum potius non fuisse ejusmodi carnem qvalis hæc nostra est, sed ab ea longè diversam.

XXXV. 2. Si eandem carnem assumsit qvam nos habemus, seqvitur qvòd, qvia alia est Divinitas, alia Humanitas sit Deus compositus ex humanitate & Deitate: Posterius absurdum. E. Prius Referantur huc omnia alia Argumenta superioribus disputationibus contra veritatem carnis Christi directa discussa.

XXXVI. Hisce opponimus hanc nostram thesin ex Epist. Phil. 2. v. 6, 7.

Qui cum esset in forma Dei, non rapinam arbitratus est, se esse æqualem Deo sed semetipsum ἐκένωσέ exinanivit, evacuavit, formam servi accipiens in similitudine hominum factus καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος, & habitu inventus ut homo.

XXXVII. Respondeo ergo ad 1. esse rationis humanæ sophisma, non enim in his quid ratio sentiat, sed quid Deus in verbo revelaverit attendendum esse: 2. Negamus carnem Christi peccato fuisse obnoxia cum non dicatur peccatu sed homine assumpsisse, Heb. 2. v. 24.

XXXVIII. Ad 2. dico: Non negare nos Personam Christi ex divinitate & humanitate constare, & ita compositionem, qvandam in Christo esse, non tamen illamPhysicam; talis enim si esset confunderentur inter se Naturæ, fieretq; earum permixtio, sed potius Metaphysicam qvæ simplicitati Dei non obest, sicut enim per absentiam carnis nihil decessit, ita per ejusdem assumtione nihil eisdem accessit.

XXXIX. Tandem tertii membriArgumentum principalissimum hoc est, si divinitas non est passa, rectè utiq; sensit Nestorius nudum Hominem passum & mortuum. Posterius absurdum, Prius Ergo.

XL. Huic opponimus dictum Act. 20. v. 28. Deus proprio sanguine acquisivit Ecclesiam; si Deus non Deitas, UndeRespondemus malè Majorem Propositionem formari cum actiones Personæ, non sint Naturarum juxta Regulam: Agere est suppositi, &c. Actiones & Passiones sunt Personæ. Hinc utraq; Natura in Christo agit cum communicatione alterius, servato tamen eo qvod cujusq; Naturæ proprium est, juxtaReg. Concil. Chalced. Unde licet in abstracto dicere non possim, Deitas est passa, rectè tamen dico, Deus est passus ob Personalem scil. Deitatis & HumanitatisUnionem & ex ea realem seqventem idiomatu communicationem.

XLI. Differentia jam porrò Nestorianismi & Eutycheismi ostendenda restat; sicut autem tota hæresis Nestoriana ex perversione doctrinæ de Communicatione idiomatum orta est; ita qvoq; sese res habet cum hæresi Eutychiana quam ex professo Nestorianæ oppositam fuisse tradunt Autores.

XLIII. Sicuti ergoNestorius 1. inChristo cum duplici Natura duplicem Personam finxit idq; inde, qvod diversarum istarumNaturarum proprietates toti Personæ verè ac realiter tribui posse negabat, hinc aliam Personam passam, alia non passam seu impassibile statuit.

XLIII. Sic contra Eutyches ob Unitatem Personæ Unitatem Naturæ defendit, idq́; inde, quia nisi proprietates ambarum Naturarum ad unam referantur Naturam duplicitatem Nestorianam oriri somniavit.

XLIV. Hinc rectè Vigilius: Vides quam periculosa res sit aut unam in Christo non credere Personam aut duas in ipso confiteri nolle Naturas; dum unam contra Nestorium Christi defendo Personam, existimor secundum Eutychetem humanam negare Naturam; dum contra Eutychetem, duas assero Naturas existimor secundum Eutychetem duas profiteri Personas.

XLV. Hinc 2. sicut Nestorius veram Humanitatem Christi non negavit sed asseruit, Ita contrà eandem Eutyches confiteri noluit.

XLVI. Nestorius divina idiomata carni non esse tribuenda. Eutyches contra omnia idiomata uni Naturæ ascribenda indiscrete statuit,

XLVII. Nestorius nudum hominem passum crucifixum mortuum; Eutyches Deum non hominem Deitatem non Humanitatem passam mortuam crucifixam,

XLVIII. His igitur sic demonstratis insignem miramur adversariorum nostorum tum Calvæ Gentis, tum Esavi fraternitatis impudentiam & malitiam quâ citra omnem veritatem nostris Ecclesiis dicam Nestorianismi scribere, Eutycheismi accusare & ita Genuinæ Augustanæ Confessionis Socios coram toto mundo pessime traducere satagunt.

XLIX. Qvid nostris Ecclesiis cum Nestorio commercii sit visum est præcedente disputatione; Contrà verò quam prope utriq; Hæretici eò accedant monstratum est, ideoq; hac vice tantum firmam hanc & immotam Concilii Ephesini Regulam obtrudimus ipsis; Quisquis realem communicationem idiomatum negat, is unitatem Persone in Christo negat, solvant hunc nodum, si viri sunt.

L. Deinde quid aliud est uni utrumq; dogma Nestorianum vel Eutychianum velle asseribere, quam cum ratione insanire, lucem & tenebras simul existere affirmare, album & nigrum simul posse existere statuere? cum notum sit hasce hæreses tantopere â se invicem dissentire, sibiq; ita contrariari ut una adfirmata altera penitus tollatur & negetur.

LI. Qvid igitur, malum, est, qvod Eutycheismum clamitant.

LII. Unionem duarum in Christo Naturarum confiteri, non Physicam sed supernaturalem adeóq; Personalem in una Christi Persona, Eutychianum est? Hanc solvere Nestorianum.

LIII. Propter arctissimam hanc Naturarum Unionem propria invicem realiter communicari, adeóq; in concreto de Persona rectè prædicari posse, Eutychianum est? Negare est Nestorianum.

LIV. Non divinitatem esse passam, mortuam, sepultam; sed Deum esse passum, mortuum, dicere Eutychianum? Hominem passum esse Nestorianum est.

LV. Proprietates ita communicari ut non permisceantur neqt confundantur sed ejus Naturæ cujus sunt proprietates salvæ maneant docere Eutychianum est? contrarium Nestorianum.

LVI. Colophonis loco impudens mendacium Esavvitarum taxamus, a qvo per insignem & innatam Esavviticam malitiam B. Luthero Eutychianismum obtrudere, eumq; Eutychianistam appellare non erubescunt, eo qvod lib. 3. de Concil. scripserit, Divinitatem esse passam; qva in re uterq; plus qvàm nefarium scelus prodit, id enim qvod ibi refutat Lutherus, idem affirmasse falsissimè dicitur.

LVII. Non adeò bardos nos Gens Esavvitica putet, ut qvandam mutationem Deitati tribueremus, qvin potius si lucem non fugiunt apertè, qvod sentiunt dicant, fortasse qvod per summam nobis injuriam nostrisq; Ecclesiis affingunt ipsi, optimo jure & qvidem veritate duce in ipsos retorqvere poterimus, præsertim cum non aliam esse prædicationem & aliam Unionem, cum dico, Christus est homo, qvàm David est Rex, Aaron est Sacerdos, uterq; defendat, unionemq; accidentalem faciat, ut sicut Regia Majestas manente Davide deponi, & Sacerdotium ab Aarone auferri salvo nihilominus ipso manente Aarone possit; Sic assumo; à Christo Humanitatem auferri nihilominus salva manente Persona posse.

LVIII. Videat qvid Eutycheismo propius esse possit? proinde jam sic cum Augustino concludimus: Pro illo Christus non est mortuus, qui Christum Hominem negat, quia mortuus est secundum Hominem.


## 9 Ninth Disputation, On the True Nature of Personal Union

Personal Union considered in general was treated above in disputation 6: but since a distinct knowledge of a thing is far nobler than a confused one: the highest utility and greatest necessity of this mystery require that we speak briefly about the true nature of this same ἑνώσεως (union). So that this may be understood more correctly, 1. We will review the false modes of union. 2. We will indicate the formal aspect of the union itself. 3. We will add a definition, to which 4. corollaries, 5. Attributes, 6. Similitudes, and 7. finally, practical meditations on this union will be subjoined.

Thesis. I.

Here, therefore, we order to be excluded 1. Every substantial and the accidental union of the scholastics, who think that the λόγος (Word) and the flesh are joined by some accident really distinct from both. Which monstrous opinion is refuted by Greg. de Valen. himself.

II. 1. The Nestorian διαίρεσιν (division), about which in disputation 7. And 3. The Eutychian σύγχυσιν (confusion), about which in disputation 8. The former is chastised by Damas. b. 3. on the orthodox faith c. 7. Rung. dif. 3. pub. c. 2. th. 60. The latter, however, by Rung. in the place cited. Bellarm. b. 3. on Christ c. 3. Greg. de Valen. d. 1. q. 2. pun. 1. vol. 4. Zanch. b. 2. on the incarnation of the word c. 3. Polan. b. 6. syntag. c. 16. col. 2435.

III. 4. The Monothelite κεράσιν (mixture), the refutation of which see in Damas. b. 3. c. 13. Chemn. on the two natures c. 18. Zanch. in the place cited.

IV. 5. The Vorstian influx or indwelling, which is open Nestorianism, and therefore can be most strongly repelled by the same reasons.

V. 6. The Calvinistic and Jesuitical sustentation, while many establish that personal union is nothing other than the singular sustentation of the human nature in the λόγῳ (Word).

VI. But this description of the ἑνώσεως ὑποστατικῆς (hypostatic union) is too broad and cold. 1. All creatures are sustained by the λόγῳ (Word), yet not all are personally united with the λόγῳ (Word). 2. To sustain is a secondary act, therefore it does not fully express the personal act. 3. Conser vation, because it is an external work, is common to all persons of the divinity, nor yet on account of this sustentation can the Father be said to be personally united to the flesh.

VII. Therefore we argue thus: If the singular sustentation of human nature is the form of personal union, then it will be either as sustentation, or as singular. If the former, all creatures τῷ λόγῳ (since they are sustained by him and in him) will be personally united: if the latter, why do they not express this singularity, and use only the common term of sustentation, which nevertheless neither declares this mystery correctly, nor distinguishes it fully.

IIX. Finally 7. we expressly confess that personal union does not properly consist in the communication of idioms, since this is a consequence rather than the form of the union. And therefore the Papists and others slander us, who falsely attribute to us that we maintain that the whole and entire essence of the hypostatic union consists in the very κοινωνίᾳ of idioms.

IX. This indeed is taught by us, that that mystery, because it is difficult to know a priori, is conveniently described through the communication of gifts as if by an effect, since effects raise us to the knowledge of causes. But that the very quiddity and form of the union in itself, not considered as it relates to us, is solely and uniquely situated in that κοινωνίᾳ, this has never entered our minds. When therefore the former is declared by the latter, then it is not an accurate definition a priori, but only some description a posteriori,

X. And thus we have hitherto removed all foreign modes of union, which can either be imagined, or have already been invented, or are accustomed to be falsely attributed to us.

XI. But before we come to the union itself, two things must be well observed by us. 1. The material, or what things are united. We have, however, two things which constitute the material: 1. is the fullness of the divinity, or the most true divinity of the λόγος. 2. The assumed flesh.

XII. 2. The unifying principle or the term in which each nature concurs, which is one and the same ὑπόστασις or subsistence of the λόγος, which is infinite. Where it is to be noted, that the nature to be united to the λόγος is not one thing, and the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος, which is called the bond and term of the union, another; but these two are one in reality: they differ, however, in reason; and in the manner of conceiving; whence they are also distinguished in the manner of speaking.

XIII. These things having been thus premised, we betake ourselves to the very form of the Union; which, although it is unique, can nevertheless scarcely be conveniently expressed by a single word.

XIV. Hence we teach that it consists chiefly in three things. 1. In the most intimate presence of the natures. For as every union, so especially the personal one, implies the mutual presence of each of the united things. It is evident from this that the thesis of the Calvinists is impious, by which they pronounce the λόγον to be so entirely in the flesh that he is at the same time entirely outside the flesh. Moved by this wretched argument: The finite is not capable of the infinite.

XV. For 1. the speculation of reason is opposed to the article of faith. 2. If the finite is not capable of the infinite, why is the whole fullness of the Deity said to dwell in Christ? And how has the flesh become a participant of the infinite ὑποστάσεως of the λόγου? Is not the infinite God contained by finite saints, in whom he is said to dwell? Wherefore 3. the equivocation which lies hidden in the word 'containing' must be explained. For it is either taken for local inclusion. And thus the finite will not be capable of the infinite; or for mere μετοχῇ or possession; and thus the finite is capable of the infinite.

XVI. 2. In the most profound περιχωρήσει or immanence of the natures. For those two natures of Christ are not only present to one another, but the λόγος also, like an ἐντελεχείας, permeates, pervades, and penetrates the flesh, which behaves like a δυνάμεως, so that it becomes entirely λογωθεῖσα, verbified, or θεαθεῖσα, deified, not otherwise than as fire penetrates iron, and the soul the body, so that the former becomes ignited, and the latter animated throughout.

XVII. For περιχώρησις is nothing other than the most full and unmixed union of the whole in the whole, in which individuals are in individuals and all things in individuals and individuals in all things and all things in all things, and one is all things.

XVIII. Which is certainly not of one mode, but as the united things vary, it is necessary that it also varies. Therefore a twofold περιχώρησις arises: 1. It is either natural, which is again divided into essential, as between matter and form, body and soul; and into accidental, as between iron and fire. Or 2. supernatural, which is likewise twofold: 1. Essential, such as we say exists between the divine essence and the three persons of the Deity. 2. Hypostatic or Personal, which is in the divine and human natures, concurring into one ὑφισάμενον [subsistent] God-man.

XIX. The reason for this permeation is that the λόγος [Word], as the purest act, penetrates the entire assumed flesh as if it were a δύναμις [power], so that there is nothing in that flesh which is not filled by the λόγος. Whence, by touching the man, God is most truly touched, and by the man being crucified, the Lord of glory himself is rightly said to have been crucified and the Prince of life to have been killed.

XX. 3. In the mutual constitution of one ὑφισταμένε [subsistent]. For the natures of Christ are not only present to one another, nor has one merely migrated into the other, but both together concur to constitute one ὑφισάμενον [subsistent], because the flesh, being ἀνυπόστατος [non-subsistent] in itself, is received into the unity of the λόγος: which very unity of subsistence causes the two natures to be personally united and to constitute one composite ὑφισάμενον [subsistent].

XXI. And from what has been said thus far, we gather such a definition of this union: The personal union is the most intimate coupling of two natures—true humanity formed in the womb of Mary, and true divinity—by the λόγος, and joined by both an intimate περιχωρήσει [interpenetration] and a communion of one ὑποστάσεως [hypostasis], yet without any confusion, to constitute one ὑφισάμενον [subsistent] God-man.

XXII. It is called personal, not because it is of persons, but 1. on account of the term in which, because the two natures coalesce in one ὑποστάσει [hypostasis] in which they participate. 2. On account of the term to which, because they themselves concur into one composite ὑφισάμενον [subsistent]. 3. On account of the singular mode, because they are united neither essentially nor accidentally, but in a plainly peculiar mode, namely so that from them one person is made, one Christ and redeemer of the human race.

XXIII. Whence double consequences flow as if of their own accord: 1. Affirmative, such as: 1. Reception into the college of the Trinity. Hence Augustine, tract. 90 on John: The form of a servant, he says, is joined to the Son in the Trinity for the unity of the person, so that a quaternity is not preached, but a Trinity.

XXIV. That the flesh, however, pertains to the Trinity is proved 1. because not only the λόγος, but also the assumed flesh constitutes the ὑφισάμενον [subsistent] of the second person of the Trinity; for the second person of the Trinity is that very God-man. 2. Because we are baptized not only in the name of the λόγος, but also of the assumed flesh.

XXV. 2. The composition of the Person of Christ. Where we do not understand a physical composition, by which a certain whole emerges from the melting together of many parts: just as from the conjunction of body and soul a certain third nature arises, which is called man.

XXVI. For the person of Christ is not a certain whole distinct from the natures, but nothing else than two natures personally united.

XXVII. However, the manner of speaking has prevailed such that we call the person of Christ composite, and the natures the parts of that person, all of which are to be understood κατ’ ἀναλογίαν (by way of analogy) and in a broad sense. For the person is named σύνθετος (composite) only because it consists of two natures, and these are called parts, since they constitute one ὑφισάμενον (subsistent entity).

XXVIII. Composition, therefore, is taken here under the most common notion, for which it suffices if several things are placed in one. This observation is useful for refuting the objections of the Calvinists, when they clamor that the communication was made to the person, not to the natures, and that all power was given to the person.

XXIX. For since the person is not a certain third thing distinct from the natures, it follows spontaneously that everything which is said of the person is said either of both or of one or the other nature. Now, since it is read that all majesty and power was given to the person in time, one must not stop here, but proceed further: whether it was given to the person according to both, or according to one or the other nature. And because it could not be given according to both natures (for the most high Divinity cannot be exalted), we conclude most firmly that all that was given according to the human nature.

XXX. 3. Mutual presence, so that the λόγος (Word) is not outside the flesh. Where it is to be seen what is to be thought of that dictum of the Calvinists; who indeed concede that the flesh is not outside the λόγος, but strenuously deny that the λόγος is not outside the flesh: by distinguishing between the person and the nature of the λόγος: they concede that the former is not outside the flesh; but because of the infinity of the latter, they say that the λόγος is somewhere where the assumed nature is not.

XXXI. But 1. The person and the divine nature of the λόγος do not differ really, for the λόγος is not composed of two things that are really distinct. 2. If the person of the λόγος were not equally infinite as the nature of the λόγος; certainly such a distinction would intervene between them as there is between the finite

& infinite, that is, real. 3. There will be no difference between the gracious indwelling of the λόγος in the saints, and the ἐνοίκησιν in the flesh of the person, if the λόγος were so entirely in the flesh, that nevertheless, on account of his infinity, he were imagined to be entirely outside the flesh: 4. The most intimate περιχώρησις of the natures in Christ is destroyed.

XXXII. 2. Negative [propositions], such as: 1. The union is not twofold: mediate and immediate, as Sohnius dreams; calling the former the union of the person, the latter the union of the nature of the λόγος with the human nature. For thus, beyond necessity, unions are multiplied, and at the same time assumption and union are confused, which, although they do not differ really, yet differ formally.

XXXIII. Whence that which he calls an immediate union is not, strictly speaking, a union, because a personal union is not between a person and a nature, but turns upon two natures: for which reason it is frequently called by theologians the union of two natures in one person, but not the union of a person and a nature.

XXXIV. 2. Nor are the two natures united only in one place. 1. Because the basis of the subsistence of the man Christ is not place, but the infinite ὑπόστασις of the λόγος. 2. Just as the subsistence of the λόγος is illocal, so also the subsistence of that which is assumed into the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος will be illocal. For this subsistence is the very ὑπόστασις of the λόγος, in which the ἀνυπόστατος flesh subsists personally. 3. Because locality pertains neither to the efficient cause, nor the matter, nor the form, nor the end, nor finally the proper affection of the union. 4. The λόγος would be ἄσαρκος and ἔνσαρκος! An absurdity.

XXXV. Whence it is clear 3. That the person of the λόγος cannot be said to be simultaneously created and uncreated. For human flesh, being ἀνυπόστατος and having become ὑποστᾶσα (the Scholastics render this 'personated'), is said to be not καθ' ἑαυτὴν, but by the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος itself.

XXXVI. From which corollaries follow these two attributes. 1. That this union (if we depart from that which is essential between the three persons of the Trinity) is the greatest of all. For nothing can be said or thought in the whole nature of things that is closer to the λόγος than his own flesh. Wherefore, nowhere and by no reason can any creature be closer to the λόγος than the humanity personally united to him.

…XXXVII. 2. That it is itself both natural and gracious to the man Christ. It is noted here: that 'natural' is not taken as something constituting the nature of a thing, or following upon it once constituted, but insofar as it is the same as that which is inherent in a thing from its birth and beginning. Thus the union was natural to the man Christ, because before the union Christ was never Christ.

XXXVIII. That it was gratuitous is proven from the fact that it was not by the merit of any man, whether of condignity or of congruity, but by the most free and gratuitous will of God, that flesh was assumed into the unity of the person of the λόγος. Whence Augustine elegantly says: In things that have arisen through time, he says, that is the highest grace, that man is joined with God in the unity of the person,

XXXIX. Since, however, this mystery, as Paul testifies, is ὁμολογουμένως great, therefore pious antiquity, for the sake of a better declaration, used some similitudes; and we, intending to imitate this example, will propose them to that end, so that from them, as things more known to us, we may more correctly, more easily, and more clearly perceive those things which are read in the Scriptures to have been handed down concerning this mystery.

XL. The first similitude, therefore, is taken from the sun and primordial light. 2. From body and soul. 3. From iron and fire. Where, however, it must be considered: ἁρμόδιον τὸ παράδειγμα ὀυ κατὰ πάντα, κατὰ τὶ γᾶν: And it is not necessary for paradigms to be similar to the things themselves in every way and without defect, but to have something similar, and indeed something dissimilar.

XLI. These similitudes, therefore, in some way agree and differ; they agree 1. In respect to the union. For as in the sun there is φῶς ἀρχέγονον and the solar body: as in iron there is fire and iron: as in man there is soul and body: so in Christ the divine nature of the λόγος and the human are truly united.

XLII. 2. In respect to one ὑπόστασις. As in the sun, ignited iron, and man, there are indeed two natures or essences; namely, light and the solar body; fire and iron; soul and body; nevertheless, however, there is one Sun, one ignited iron, one man: So in Christ there are two natures essentially distinct; but yet there is one ὑφισάμενον, one Christ, one person,

XLIII. 3. In respect to non-confusion. As in one sun, light with the solar body: in ignited iron, fire with the iron: in man, soul with the body, and their natural and essential actions are not confounded, but truly distinguished: Thus in the one person of Christ, the natures and their natural properties are not confounded, but truly are and remain distinct even in the union itself.

XLIV. 4. With respect to the communication of natures. In the sun, the primordial light, existing as ἀσώματος (incorporeal) before it is united to the solar body, becomes ἐνσώματος (corporeal): Iron is ignited and glows through the intimate permeation of fire: In man, when the rational soul is ἐνσωματᾶται (embodied) and the body is ψυχᾶται (ensouled), man is called man: Thus when the divine nature of the λόγος (Word) is incarnated, the human nature is assumed into the person of the λόγος (Word), then he is called Christ, because then the eternal λόγος (Word) assumed what he was not.

XLV. They differ: 1. The soul and body are imperfect natures. 2. They make a third subsistence. 3. Neither communicates its subsistence to the other, but both depend on a third, which is that of the whole composite. 4. Separation. II. In iron and the sun, heat is sustained by the iron, the primordial light by the solar body. 2. They are separable.

XLVI. But that we may at last make an approach to the final member: that mystical union of the two natures in Christ is a memorial of sin, a sign of divine love, a key of true consolation, and a fire of due thanksgiving.

XLVII. 1.
