It is a memorial of sin, because this very thing drew the λόγος (Word) down from heaven, that he might be united with our flesh, so that in it he might suffer and thus by suffering might redeem the human race. Sin is an abominable thing, nor could the humanity of Christ have made satisfaction for a single sin, however small of all, unless it had been coupled with the deity of the Son, which added strength to overcome the wrath of GOD and to endure it. Let us see, therefore, that our spiritual union with God is kept intact: let evil be fled, lest we be separated again, and let good be chosen, that we may be joined more and more with God, until we all meet in the unity of the faith of the knowledge of the Son of God.

XLVIII. 2. It is a sign of divine love, because although after the fall of Adam we had become most wicked, most base, most miserable: yet God so loved us, us, I say, sinners, that he sent his Son, and betrothed him with human flesh. O infinite love, O most fervent bowels of mercy, by which the dawn from on high has visited us! Truly God is good, nay, He is goodness and love itself, because He has intimately communicated both His grace and His nature with us.

XLIX. 3. It is the key of true consolation. For do you wish to flee with Adam because of the sense of sin? Behold, Christ calls you back, and because of the hypostatic union of our nature with His flesh, He promises a gracious union with GOD. You, therefore, who are in the dust, awaken and give praise: Behold! The Lord comes with salvation, with ointments, with glory. For the Son of God does not come without salvation, nor without anointing as Christ, nor without glory: since He Himself is salvation, He Himself is glory, writes Bernard.

L. 4. It is a fire of due gratitude. For every benefit requires a duty, and for grace, thanks must be rendered. Did He Himself descend from heaven to earth, where we lay miserable? Let us ascend to Him in the heavens, where He reigns glorious. As He is united to our nature personally, so let us be united to Him spiritually. The personal union was made ἀσυγχύτως (without confusion): so let us not mix earthly and heavenly things, the world and Christ, but let us adhere to Him alone. O happy joy and joyful happiness, to be Christ's, to be with Christ, to be in Christ! But he who keeps His commandments remains in Christ and Christ in him. Let us therefore keep them with all our strength by believing and loving: thus He will keep His promise, and will render the reward of eternal life, where we shall be united with Christ in a new way, where we shall always remain joined to Him, where we shall see, love, and praise Him face to face; saying with the Church from Canticles 2:4. Now my king has brought me into the wine cellar, and his banner over me is brightness: to Him be glory and thanksgiving forever, Amen.

Latin:

DE Unione Personali generatim consideratâ supra disput. 6. actum fuit: cùm verò cognitio rei distincta longè sit nobilior confusâ: requirit hujus mysterii summa utilitas, & maxima necessitas, ut de vera ejusdem ἑνώσεως ratione paucis dicamus. Quod ut eò rectius intelligatur, 1. Modos falsos unionis recensebimus. 2. ipsum unionis formale indicabimus. 3. definitionem addemus, cui 4. πορίσματα, 5. Attributa, 6. Similitudines, & 7. deniq; hujus unionis meditationes practicas subjungemus.

Thesis. I.

Hîc ergò exesse jubemus 1. Omnem substantialem & scholasticorum accidentalem unionem, putantium λόγον & carnem conjungi per aliqvod accidens ab utroq; realiter distinctum. Quæ monstrosa opinio ab ipso Gregor. de Valen. refutatur.

II. 1. Nestorianam διαίρεσιν, de quâ disput. 7. Et 3. Eutychianam σύγχυσιν, quâ de disput. 8. Illam castigat Damas. l. 3. de ortho. fid. c. 7. Rung. dif. 3. pub. c. 2. th. 60. Hanc verò Rung. loco d. Bellarm. l. 3. de Christo c. 3. Greg. de Valen. d. 1. q. 2. pun. 1. tom. 4. Zanch. l. 2. de incarn. verb. c. 3. Polan. l. 6. syntag. c. 16. col. 2435.

III. 4. Monotheleticam κεράσιν, cujus refutationem vide in Damas. l. 3. c. 13. Chemn. de duabus naturis c. 18. Zanch. loco d.

IV. 5. Vorstianum influxum vel illapsum, qui est apertus Nestorianismus, ideoq́; iisdem rationibus retundi potest fortissimè.

V. 6. Calvinisticam & Jesuiticam sustentationem, 'dum pleriq; statuunt, unionem personalem nihil esse aliud, quàm singularem humanæ naturæ in λόγῳ sustentationem.

VI. Verùm nimis lata & frigida est hæc ἑνώσεως ὑποστατικῆς descriptio. 1. Omnes Creaturæ sustentantur â λόγῳ, neqve tamen omnes sunt cum λόγῳ personaliter unitæ. 2. Subsistentare est actus secundus, non igitur plenè exprimit actum personalem. 3. Conservatio, quia est opus ad extra, omnibus personis divinitatis est communis, neq; tamen ob hanc sustentationem Pater dici potest personaliter carni unitus.

VII. Proinde sic argumentamur: Si singularis sustentatio humanæ naturæ est forma unionis personalis, tum erit vel quà sustentatio, vel quà singularis. Si illud, omnes creaturæ τῷ λόγῳ (quippe ab illo & in illo sustentantur) erunt personaliter unitæ: sin hoc, cur istam singularitatem non exprimunt, & solo communi sustentationis vocabulo, quod tamen hoc mysterium nec declarat rectè, nec distinguit plenè, utuntur.

IIX. Tandem 7. expressè fatemur, quòd unio personalis propriè non consistat in communicatione Idiomatum, cùm hoc potiùs consequens sit, quàm unionis forma. Ideoq; calumniantur Papicolæ & alii, qui nobis affingunt, quòd in ipsâ Idiomatum κοινωνίᾳ, omnem & totam unionis hypostaticæ essentiam consistere statuamus.

IX. Hoc quidem à nobis traditur, quòd mysterium illud, quia difficulter cognoscitur à priori, per communicationem donorum veluti per effectum commodè describatur, siquidem effectus nos evehunt in notitiam causarum. Quòd autem ipsa quidditas & forma unionis in se, non quo ad nos consideratæ, solùm & unicè in istâ κοινωνίᾳ sita sit, hoc nunquam nobis in mentem venit. Quando igitur illa per hanc declaratur, tunc non est accurata definitio à priori, sed tantùm aliqva descriptio à posteriori,

X. Atqve ita hactenus removimus omnes peregrinos unionis modos, qvi vel fingi possunt, vel jam conficti sunt, vel nobis affingi solent.

XI. Priusqvàm autem ad ipsam unionem veniamus, duo à nobis probè observari debent. 1. Materiale, vel quænam sint unita. Habemus autem duo, quæ constituunt materiale: 1. est plenitudo divinitatis, vel verissima τοῦ λόγου divinitas. 2. Caro assumta.

XII. 2. Τὸ ἑνοποιοῦν vel terminus in quo utraque natura concurrit, qvi est una eademqve ὑπόστασις vel subsistentia τοῦ λόγου infinita. Ubi notandum, qvod non alia res sit natura λόγῳ unienda, & alia ὑπόστασις λόγου, quæ vocatur vinculum & terminus unionis; sed hæc duo sunt re unum : differunt tamen ratione; & modo concipiendi; unde & distingvuntur modo loqvendi.

XIII. His ita prælibatis, ad ipsam formam Unionis nos conferimus; cujus licet unica sit, uno tamen vocabulo exprimi commodè vix potest.

XIV. Hinc in tribus potissimùm eam consistere docemus. 1. In arctissimâ naturarum præsentiâ. Ut enim omnis unio; ita vel maximè personalis, mutuam utriusq; uniti præsentiam importat. Patet hinc, impiam esse θέσιν Calvinianorum, quâ λόγον ita totum in carne esse pronunciant, ut simul totus sit extra carnem. Misero hoc argumento permoti : Finitum non est capax infiniti.

XV. Nam 1. rationis speculatio opponitur fidei articulo. 2. si finitum non est capax infiniti, cur in Christo dicitur habitare tota plenitudo Deitatis? & quomodo caro facta est particeps infinitæ ὑποστάσεως τẽ λόγꭓ? Annon infinitus Deus â finitis sanctis capitur, in qvibus ipse habitare dicitur? Qvare 3. explicanda est æqvivocatio, qvæ latet in vocabulo capiendi. Aut enim sumitur pro locali inclusione. Et sic finitum non erit capax infiniti; aut pro solâ μετοχῇ vel possessione; & sic finitum est capax infiniti.

XVI. 2. In profundissimâ naturarum περιχωρήσει vel immanentiâ. Nec enim duæ illæ Christi naturæ sibi invicem præsentes tantùm sunt, sed λόγꚙ etiam instar ἐντελεχείας permeat, pervadit, penetratq; carnem, qvæ se habet instar δυνάμεως, ut tota fiat λογωθεῖσα verbificata vel θεαθεῖσα deificata, non secus atq; ignis ferrum, & anima corpus penetrat, ut illud ignitum, hoc animatum fiat undiq;.

XVII. Est enim περιχώρησις nihil aliud, quàm totius in totum plenissima & impermixta unio, in qva singula sunt in singulis & omnia in singulis & singula in omnibus & omnia in omnibus, & unum omnia.

XVIII. Qvæ sanè non est unius modi, sed variantibus unitis, illam qvoq; variare necesse est. Duplex ergò oritur περιχώρησις : 1. est vel naturalis, qvæ rursus tum in Essentialem, ut inter materiam & formam, corpus & animam; tum in accidentalem, ut inter ferrum & ignem dispescitur. Vel 2. supernaturalis, qvæ similiter duplex est : 1. Essentialis, qvalem esse dicimus inter divinam essentiam & tres personas Deitatis. 2. Hypostatica vel Personalis, quæ est in divinam & humanam naturas, ad unum ὑφισάμενον θεάνθρωπον concurrentes.

XIX. Cujus permeationis ea est ratio, quòd λόγος tanquam purissimus actus totam carnem assumtam veluti δύναμιν penetrat, adeò ut nihil in carne illa sit, quod λόγῳ non sit repletum. Unde contrectato homine verissimè Deus contrectatur, & crucifixo homine ipse domin⁹ gloriæ crucifixus & dux vitæ interfect⁹ rectè dicitur.

XX. 3. In unius ὑφισταμένε constitutione mutuâ. Non enim naturæ Christi tantùm præsentes sibi sunt invicem, neq; solùm una immigravit in alteram, sed simul utraq; concurrit ad unum ὑφισάμενον constituendum, quia caro in se ἀνυπόστατος in unitatem τῶ λόγꙋ recipitur: quæ ipsa subsistentiæ unitas facit, ut duæ naturæ personaliter uniantur, & unum ὑφισάμενον συνθετον constituant.

XXI. Atq; ex hactenus dictis talem hujus unionis colligimus definitionem: Unio personalis est duarum naturarum, veræ humanitatis in Mariæ utero formatæ, & veræ divinitatis λόγꙋ arctissima, & tum intima περιχωρήσει ac unius ὑποστάσεως communione conjuncta, sine omni tamen confusione, ad unum ὑφισάμενον θεάνθρωπον constituendum copulatio.

XXII. Personalis vocatur, non quia sit personarum, sed 1. ob terminum in quo, quia duæ naturæ in una ὑποστάσει, quâ participant, coalescunt. 2. ob terminum ad quem, quia illæ ipsæ ad unum compositum ὑφισάμενον concurrunt. 3. ob modum singularem, quia nec essentialiter, nec accidentaliter, sed modo planè peculiari uniuntur, ita nempe ut ex iis una fiat persona, unus Christus & redemtor generis humani.

XXIII. Unde duplicia suâ quasi sponte promanant consequentia: 1. Affirmativa, qualia sunt: 1. Receptio in collegium Trinitatis. Hinc August. tract. 90. in Joh. Forma servi, inquit, filio in Trinitate ad unitatem personæ coaptata est, he quaternitas, sed Trinitas prædicetur.

XXIV. Carnem autem ad Trinitatem pertinere, probatur 1. quia non solus λόγος, sed etiam caro assumta constituit ὑφισάμενον secundæ Trinitatis personæ; Est enim secunda persona Trinitatis ille ipse θεάνθρωπος. 2. quia non in solius λόγꙋ; sed etiam carnis assumtæ nomine baptizamur.

XXV. 2. Personæ Christi compositio. Ubi non intelligimus compositionem Physicam, quâ emergit totum qvid ex conflatjone multarum partium: sicut ex conjunctione corporis & animæ tertia qvædam oritur natura, qvæ homo dicitur.

XXVI. Nam Christi persona non est totum qvid â naturis distinctum, sed nihil aliud, qvàm duæ naturæ personaliter unitæ.

XXVII. Modus tamen loqvendi sic obtinuit, ut Christi personam compositam, & naturas dicamus partes illius personæ, qvæ omnia κατ’ ἀναλογίαν qvandam & lato sensu sunt intelligenda. Persona enim nominatur σύνθετος tantùm, qvia duabus constat naturis, & hæ dicuntur partes, qvoniam unum ὑφισάμενον constituunt.

XXVIII. Compositio E. hîc sumitur sub notione communissimâ, ad qvam sufficit, si plura in uno ponantur. Qvæ observatio utilis est ad diluendas Calvinianorum exceptiones, qvando personæ, non naturis, factam esse communicationem, & personæ datam esse omnem potestatem clamitant.

XXIX. Cum enim persona non sit qviddam tertium â naturis distinctum; ultrò seqvitur, omne qvod de persona dicitur, vel de utraq; vel de alterutra natura dici. Jam cùm personæ in tempore data legatur omnis majestas & potestas: hîc non subsistendum est, sed ulteriùs pergendum, an data sit personæ secundùm utramqve, an secundùm alterutram naturam. Et qvia secundùm utramq; naturam dari non potuit, (Divinitas enim altissima exaltari neqvit) secundùm humanam naturam id omne datum esse firmissimè concludimus.

XXX. 3. Mutua præsentia, ut ὁ λόγος non sit extra carnem. Ubi videre est, qvid de illo Calvinianorum effato sentiendum sit; carnem qvidem non extra λόγον esse concedentium, sed λόγον non esse extra carnem strenuè negantium: distinguendo inter personam & naturam λόγε: Illam non esse extra carnem concedunt; propter hujus verò infinitatem λόγον esse alicubi ajunt, ubi non sit natura assumta.

XXXI. Verùm 1. Persona & natura divina τῦ λόγε non differunt realiter, neq; enim λόγος ex duobus realiter distinctis est compositus. 2. Si persona λόγε non esset æqvè infinita ac natura λόγε; utiqve tale inter illas intercederet discrimen, qvale est inter finitum

& infinitum, hoc est, reale. 3. Nulla erit differentia inter inhabitationem τοῦ λόγου in sanctis gratiosam, & inter ἐνοίκησιν in carne personaelm, si λόγος totus ita in carne esset, ut tamen propter infinitatem extra carnem totus esse fingeretur: 4. Arctissima naturarum in Christo περιχώρησις tollitur.

XXXII. 2. Negativa, ut sunt: 1. Unio non est duplex: Mediata & Immediata, ut Sohnius somniat; illam vocans unionem personæ, hanc naturæ λόγου cum humana natura. Ita enim præter necessitatem multiplicantur unita, & simul confunditur assumptio unioq́;, quæ licet non realiter, differunt tamen formaliter.

XXXIII. Unde quam ille unionem immediatam vocat, unio propriè loquendo non est, quia unio personalis non est inter personam & naturam, sed inter duas naturas vertitur: Quâ de causa passim â Theologis appellatur unio duarum naturarum in una persona, non autem unio personæ & naturæ.

XXXIV. 2. Nec unita sunt duæ naturæ tantùm uno in loco. 1. Quia subsistentiæ hominis Christi basis non est locus, sed infinita τῆς λόγου ὑπόστασις. 2. Sicut subsistentia τοῦ λόγου est illocalis: ita & subsistentia ejus, quod in λόγου ὑπόστασιν assumtum, erit illocalis. Est enim subsistentia hæc ipsa τοῦ λόγου ὑπόστασις, in quâ caro ἀνυπόστατος subsistit personaliter. 3. Quia localitas ad unionis neq; efficientem, neq; materiam, neq; formam, neq; finem, nec deniq; propriam affectionem pertinet. 4. λόγος esset ἄσαρκος καὶ ἔνσαρκος! ἄτοπον.

XXXV. Unde patet 3. Personam τοῦ λόγου non posse dici simul creatam & increatam. Nam caro humana ἀνυπόστατος ὑποστᾶσα (Scholastici reddunt personata) dicitur ὐ καθ' ἑαυτὴν, sed ipsius λόγου ὑποστάσει.

XXXVI. Ex quibus πορίσμασι sequuntur hæc duo attributa. 1. Unionem hanc (si ab illâ, quæ est inter tres personas Trinitatis, essentiali discesserimus) esse omnium maximam. Nihil enim dici cogitarivé potest in totâ rerum naturâ, quod sit τῷ λόγῳ suâ carne proximius. Quare nullibi quacunque ratione, ulla creatura vicinior esse potest τῷ λόγῳ suâ personaliter sibi unitâ humanitate.

XXXVII. 2. Illâ ipsam esse homini Christo naturalem & gratuitā. Observetur autem hîc : τὸ naturale non sumi, ut est quiddam naturam rei constituens, vel constitutam conseqvens, sed qvatenus idem est, ac illud qvod à nativitate & primordio rei alicui inest. Sic unio fuit homini Christo naturalis, qvia ante unionem Christus non fuit Christus unqvam.

XXXVIII. Gratuitam autem fuisse probatur ex eo, qvia nullius hominis merito, sive ex condigno sive ex congruo, sed liberrimâ & gratuitâ Dei voluntate, caro in unitatem personæ τοῦ λόγου assumpta est. Unde eleganter Augustinus : In rebus, inqvit, per tempus ortis illa summa gratia est, qvòd homo in unitate personæ conjunctus est cum Deo,

XXXIX. Cùm verò hoc mysterium, teste Paulo, sit ὁμολογουμένως magnum, ideò pia antiqvitas melioris declarationis ergò aliqvot similitudinibus usa est, qvod exemplum & nos imitaturi, istas eo fine proponemus, ut ex iis tanqvam nobis notioribus, rectiùs, faciliùs, planiùs percipiamus ea, qvæ in Scripturis de hoc mysterio tradita leguntur.

XL. Primum igitur simile est â sole & luce primigenia. 2. â corpore & anima. 3. â ferro & igne desumtum. Ubi tamen cogitandum; ἁρμόδιον τὸ παράδειγμα ὀυ κατὰ πάντα, κατὰ τὶ γᾶν: Et non necesse est paradigmata omni modo & absq; defectu similia esse rebus ipsis, sed aliqvid habere simile, aliqvid verò dissimile.

XLI. Istæ ergò similitudines aliqvo modo conveniunt & differunt; Conveniunt 1. Respectu unionis. Ut enim in sole φῶς ἀρχέγονον & corpus solare : ut in ferro ignis & ferrum : ut in homine anima & corpus: Sic in Christo natura divina τοῦ λόγου & humana verè uniuntur.

XLII. 2. Respectu unius ὑποστάσεως, Ut in sole, ferro ignito & homine duæ naturæ qvidem sive essentiæ sunt; lux nimirum & corpus solare; ignis & ferrum; anima & corpus; nihilominus tamen unus est Sol, unum ferrum ignitum, unus homo: Ita in Christo duæ sunt naturæ essentialiter distinctæ; sed tamen unum est ὑφισάμενον, unus Christus, una persona,

XLIII. 3. Respectu inconfusionis. Ut in uno sole lux cum solari corpore : In ferro ignito ignis cum ferro: in homine anima cum corpore, eorumq́; naturales & essentiales actiones non confunduntur, sed verè distingvuntur : Sic in unâ personâ Christi naturæ earumq́; proprietates naturales non confunduntur, sed verè sunt & manent in ipsâ etiam unione distinctæ.

XLIV. 4. Respectu naturarum Communicationis. In sole lux primigenia ἀσώματος existens priùs, qvàm corpori solari unitur, sit ἐνσώματος: Ferrum per intimam ignis pervasionem ignitur & candescit : In homine qvando anima rationalis ἐνσωματᾶται & corpus ψυχᾶται, homo dicitur homo: Sic qvando divina τοῦ λόγου natura incarnatur, humana natura in personam τοῦ λόγου assumitur, tunc dicitur Christus, qvia tunc λόγος æternus, qvòd non erat, assumsit.

XLV. Differunt: 1. Anima & corpus sunt naturæ imperfectæ. 2. Faciunt tertiam subsistentiam. 3. Neutra alteri suam subsistentiam communicat, sed utraq; pendet à tertiâ, qvæ est totius compositi. 4. Separatio. II. In ferro & sole sustentatur calor à ferro, lux primigenia à corpore solari. 2. sunt separabilia.

XLVI. Verùm ut ad ultimum tandem membrum accessum faciamus: mystica illa duarum naturarum in Christo unio est Memoriale peccati, signum amoris divini, Clavis veri solatii, & incendium debitæ gratitudinis.

XLVII. 1. Memoriale peccati est, qvia hoc ipsum cœlo detraxit λόγον, ut cum carne nostrâ uniretur, qvò in illâ pati & sic patiendo genus humanum redimere posset. Abominanda res peccatum est, nec pro unico, qvantumvis omnium minimo, satisfacere potuisset Christi humanitas, nisi copulata fuisset cum deitate filii, qvæ vires addidit ad superandam iram DEI, eamq́; perferendam. Videamus ergò ut sarta conservetur nostra spiritualis cum Deo unio: fugiatur malum, ne denuò separemur, & eligatur bonum, ut cum Deo magis magisq́; conjungamur, donec occurramus omnes in unitatem fidei agnitionis filii Dei.

XLVIII. 2. Signum amoris divini est, qvia licèt post Adami lapsum facti essemus flagitiosissimi, turpissimi, miserrimi: Deus tamen nos, nos, inqvam, peccatores, adeò dilexit, ut filium mitteret, illumq́; cum carne humanâ desponsaret. O infinitum amorem, ô calidissima misericordiæ viscera, quibus nos visitavit oriens ex alto! Verè Deus bonus est, imò ipsa bonitas & caritas est, quia intimè suam nobiscum communicavit & gratiam & naturam.

XLIX. 3. Clavis veri solatii est. Vis enim fugere cum Adamo ob sensum peccati? Ecce Christus te revocat, & propter conjunctionem nostrâ cum carne hypostaticam, spondet conjunctionem cum DEO gratiosam. Vos igitur qui in pulvere estis, expergiscimini & laudate: Ecce! Dominus cum salute, cum unguentis, cum gloria. Neq; enim sine salute Jesus, neq; sine unctione Christus, neq; sine gloriâ venit DEI filius: siquidem ipse salus, ipse gloria, scribit Bernhardus.

L. 4. Incendium debitæ gratitudinis est. Omne enim beneficium requirit officium, & pro gratiâ grates persolvendæ sunt. Descendit ipse de cœlis in terram, ubi jacebamus miseri? adscendamus nos ad ipsum in cœlos, ubi regant gloriosus. Ut ille unitus est naturæ nostræ personaliter: ita nos uniamur ipsi spiritualiter. Unio personalis facta est ἀσυγχύτως: ita non misceamus terrena & cœlestia, mundum & Christum, sed huic soli adhæreamus. O felix jucunditas & jucunda felicitas, esse Christi, esse cum Christo, esse in Christo! Qui autem servat mandata ejus, hic manet in Christo & Christus in illo. Servemus ergò pro viribus credendo & diligendo: Sic ipse servabit promissum, & reddet æternæ vitæ præmium, ubi novâ cum Christo uniemur ratione, ubi semper ipsi manebimus conjuncti, ubi à facie ad faciem videbimus, amabimus, laudabimus; dicentes cum Ecclesiâ ex Cant. 2, 4. Nunc introduxit me rex meus in cellam vinariam, & vexillum ejus super me est claritas: ipsi sit gloria & gratiarum actio in æternum, Amen.


## 10 Tenth Disputation, On the Communication of the Hypostasis

Thesis I.

That CHRIST JESUS is neither ἀδιαςάτως (undivided) in the Nestorian manner, nor συγχύτως (confused) in the Eutychian manner, has been proven above; what the true nature of the personal union is, has been taught just now: But that it does not exist without communication, must now be shown. For as a shadow follows a body, so does communication follow union; as even nature can teach those who, out of excessive wisdom, are accustomed to measure mysteries by nature.

II. For when essential parts are joined, does not something follow, which they call an essential consequent? But what audacity would deny a consequent communication to natures united in Christ?

III. We do not mean this as if we were making the properties that sprout from the essences of natural things the norm for those things that follow from Christ's union; yet by analogy from the former, we are in some way led to the sublimity of the latter; just as in natural things, where essential parts are truly constituted and united, something follows which is called an essential consequent, from which we are led to the knowledge of the thing due to the weakness of the mind: so it must be said that something follows the united natures in Christ, the knowledge of which may teach us the later aspects of this mystery.

IV. Communication follows union, and indeed 1. ὑποστάσεως (of the hypostasis). 2. of the natures. 3. of the idioms. Concerning the former we shall set forth our opinion at this time, concerning the second others will speak, and concerning the latter we shall be taught elsewhere and specifically σὺν θεῷ (with God) we shall be informed.

CHAPTER I.

V. We must delineate, as in a sketch, what we are about to do. Therefore 1. we shall explain the term communication. 2. We shall propose the state of the controversy between us and the Calvinists. 3. We shall append a proof of the true opinion, and at the same time dissolve the objections of the adversaries. 4. We shall elicit some corollaries. 5. We shall add certain questions, and 6. finally we shall conclude with a practical meditation.

VI. Κοινωνία (Koinonia) is from κοινῷ (koinō); communication is from communis. That is common in a general sense which many share. It is not said from 'one' (uno), but from 'munus' (duty/gift), so that it is common which is of the same duty. Now 'munus', according to modern and recent philologists, is from 'mœnibus' (walls) or 'muris' (walls), with the 'r' changed into 'n'. For 'munus' was the burden of repairing the walls, where first they had gathered into one place from the villages to found a town: hence 'monumenta' (monuments). If it was remitted, it was called a 'donum' (gift). Hence 'munio', that is, I make walls, and 'munis', which denotes one who is dutiful; 'immunis', one who is exempt from a burden; 'communis', which word implies a gathering in the same duty. Therefore, 'commune' (common) is properly that which pertains to the repair of the same walls.

VII. Afterwards, 'commune' began to be used for any office which many perform: and finally for that one thing which might belong to many. Moreover, there is no science which does not delight in the word 'commune'. Grammarians have a common gender: Rhetoricians rejoice in commonplaces: Logicians differ concerning a common accident: in Economics, family property comes under the designation of 'commune': Jurists designate public law in this way.

IIX. In the scriptures, it denotes 1. in the Levitical sense, 'unclean', by a Hebrew phrase, to which 'holy' is opposed. 2. generally, the participation of a thing which belongs to many. b In this sense, in the present matter, we say that the ὑπόστασις of the Word is common to both natures, so that both have one and the same subsistence.

IX. But just as 'commune' is used first specially, and afterwards generally, so also is 'communio'. For in its first imposition, it denotes what is fortified on all sides: but in its second, it denotes every participation of one thing, which others call 'Communication'.

X. Commonly, 'communio' and 'communicatio' are grammatical synonyms; strictly, however, they differ as 'unitio' and 'unio'; of which the former denotes the act by which many things are coupled into one, while the latter signifies the state of union following the act. Thus also 'communicatio' designates the act, and 'communio' the state, so that it would be more correct to speak of the 'communio' of the ὑπόστασις. Nevertheless, because of the usage received in the Church, we shall retain the word 'communication', so that it may denote the act and the state at the same time.

XI. There are, however, various modes of communication. In general, communication is either nominal or real. The former occurs 1. by a trope, as when I say, Herod is a fox. 2. for the sake of honor, as when a Doctor's wife is called a doctress. 3. by fiction, as when the Pope is named the head of the Church. This communication has only a community of name.

XII. Real (which also bestows the thing itself in addition) is either natural or supernatural. The former is threefold. 1. There is given a communication between accident and accident, as when I say, The Theologian is a philosopher. 2. between substance and accident, when that which belongs to an accident is attributed to a substance. Thus air is said to be fluid on account of its humidity. 3. there is given a communication between substance and substance, which, however, differs either by reason or in reality. XIII. But if the distinction between subjects is merely mental, there arises 1. communication κατὰ μέθεξιν (by participation), 2. κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν (by synecdoche), 3. κατὰ σύγχυσιν (by confusion). But if the difference is real, then the subjects are either separated or συνδυασμένα (combined) and united. Among separated subjects there is communication α. κατὰ μετάβασιν (by transition), β. κατ' ἀλλοποίωσιν (by alteration), γ. κατὰ χρῆσιν (by use). XIV. But if the subjects are united, there arises communication κατὰ συνδύασιν (by combination), by which, on account of the union, that which is proper to one is really conferred upon the other, without either multiplication or transfusion of itself, for common possession, usurpation, and denomination; for this communication makes so many degrees. XV. Supernatural communication is fourfold: 1. essential, such as that between the persons of the Trinity; 2. spiritual; 3. sacramental. 4. personal, concerning which we must treat further here: and although this has many things in common with the natural (φυ- σικῇ), yet because it has many additional unique features, and similar examples cannot be given, it remains unique and is called by the special name hypostatic (ὑποστατικὴ), partly to denote the cause of the communication, which is personal union, and partly the mode, because it is between those things which are united into one subsistent (ὑφισάμενον).

XVI. But in order that it might be clear what we and what the Calvinists maintain, we must first be certain about the state of the controversy, especially because our adversaries so strenuously babble (βατταλογοῦσι). For at one moment they deny the communication of the hypostasis, at another they affirm it, at another they wrap it in distinctions. They deny it, because they claim that no property can be communicated, as appears from Beza (a), Sadeel (b), and Keckermann (c).

XVII. Beza (d) and Polanus (e) affirm, or seem to affirm, while they both assert and do not deny that an infinite subsistence can be communicated, where indeed they profess orthodoxy in open words, but would that they did so not only in words but also in heart! For I ask, what do the distinctions they use mean, while they contend that communication is taken either for union or for things subsequent to union, of which they concede the former but deny the latter, as is clear from Saxius (a) in his disquisition, Beza's thesis (b), and the response (c) in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, Danaeus' examination of Chemnitz (d), and Polanus' System of Theology (e), where he responds to the Samosatene argument, by which it is denied that an infinite subsistence is communicated: that the word communication is taken either for becoming common to a finite nature:

(but who does not see the trick that union is understood here) or for real transfusion: To which latter, indeed, they falsely attribute to us by calumny a confusion, so very often rejected and refuted by us.

XVIII. But it is manifest that the same thing happens to the Calvinists as Irenaeus says of certain people, they speak similar things, but think dissimilar things; indeed, like a shrew-mouse, they finally betray themselves and their own craftiness. For the question is about true participation, they respond about union, garlic instead of onions, a new method of evading the light of truth.

XIX. Therefore, so that they may be clearer to us: We deny 1. their distinction. But if this seems intolerable to them, we ask that they prove it. 2. We say there is an ἀκυρολογία (improper use of terms) in it. For union is a conjunction, but communication is a giving and bestowing. 3. We urge the Canon of the Fathers: Such as the union, such is the communication, which the new subtlety of the adversaries makes tautological. 4. We object with the confession of Polanus, when he writes that union consists in the communication of the subsistence of the Word with the flesh, unless they wish to say that he is ἀδολεσχεῖν (babbling), i.e., to assert that union consists in union; they will see even from this follower of theirs the distinction of union from communication. 5. We do not admit the instances which they bring forward, and those of people speaking popularly, not attending to ἀκρίβειαν (precision), since we are now disputing, not differing. 6. We leave it to them to weigh that we have long since explained communication, not through union, not through transfusion, but as real participation. Here therefore is Rhodes, here let them dance.

XX. If they wish the matter to be proposed more plainly, this is sought: Whether the λόγος (Word) made His own ὑπόστασις (subsistence), which is proper to Him alone, also common to the assumed flesh, so that through it the flesh might subsist? We hold the affirmative, the adversaries play, as we have shown, with little words, and foist upon us a bare sustenance, just as Martinius and Beza do.

Latin:

Thesis. I.

CHRISTUM JESUM, neq; ἀδιαςάτως Nestoriana, neq; συγχύτως Eutychiana Christum esse, superiùs evictum; quæ sit ratio unionis personalis vera, proximè edoctum: at sine communicatione non esse, ostendendum jam est. Ut enim umbra corpus, sic unita communicatio inseqvitur; ut vel natura docere potest eos; qvi præ nimiâ sapientiâ ex naturâ aliàs mysteria métiri solent.

II. Annon enim partibus essentialibus junctis, aliqvid seqvitur, qvod essentiale conseqvens vocant? At qvæ audacia naturis in Christo unitis, inseqventem communicationem denegaret?

III. Non autem hoc volumus, qvasi propria ex essentiis naturalium rerum propullulantia; normam faciamus earum, qvæ Christi unionem conseqvuntur, ex analogia tamen ab illis, ad horum sublimitatem aliqvo modo devehimur; ita sicut revera constitutas & unitas partes essentiales in naturalibis aliqvid, qvod essentiale conseqvens vocatur, seqvitur, ex qvo ad rei cognitionem ob imbecillitatem mentis deducimur: ita unitas naturas in Christo aliqvid conseqvi, cujus notitia posteriora hujus mysterii nos edoceat, dicendú sit.

IV. Communicatio autem unionem seqvitur & qvidem 1. ὑποστάσεως. 2. naturarum. 3. idiomatum. De illa hac vice nostram sententiam ponemus, de ista alii dicent, de hac alibi docebimur & peculiariter σὺν θεῷ informabimur.

CAPUT. I.

V. Ὡς ἐν τύπῳ, qvid acturi simus, delineandum est. Ergo 1. vocem communicationis expediemus. 2. Statum controversiæ inter nos & Calvinianos proponemus. 3. ἀπόδειξιν veræ sententiæ annectemus, simul objectiones adversariorum diluemus. 4. πορίσματα nonnulla eliciemus. 5. qvæstiones qvasdam adjiciemus, & 6. tandem meditatiunculâ practicâ finiemus.

VI. Κοινωνία à κοινῷ est: communicatio à communi. Commune generatim illud est, qvod multa participant. Non dicitur ab uno, sed à munere, ut commune sit, qvod ejusdem muneris. Munus autem juxta philologos modernos & recentiores est à mœnibus vel muris, r. in n. mutato. Fuit enim munus, onus muris reficiendis, ubi primum unum in locum convenissent è vicis ad condendum oppidum: inde monumenta. Si remittebatur, donum dicebatur. Hinc munio h. e. mœnia facio, & munis qvod officiosum notat; immunis, qvi ab onere exemtus; communis, qvæ vox concursum in eodem munere innuit. Commune ergo propriè est id, qvod ad eorundem murorum refectionem pertinet.

VII. Cœpit postea commune usurpari, pro qvovis officio qvo plures funguntur: & tandem pro eo uno qvod multis competeret. Nulla autem scientia est, qvæ communis voce non delectetur. Grammatici genus commune habent: Rhetores locis communibus gaudent: Logici de communi accidente differunt: in OEconomia res familiaris communis appellatione venit: JCTI publicum jus sic indigitant.

IIX. In scripturis notat 1. sensu Levitico a immundum, phrasi hebræâ, cui opponitur sanctum. 2. generaliter participationem rei, qvæ multis competit. b Hoc sensu in præsenti negocio dicimus ὑπόστασιν λόγου utriq; naturæ communem esse, ita ut utraq; unam & eandem habeat subsistentiam.

IX. Ut autem commune primò specialiter, pòst generaliter usurpatur, sic & communio. Primâ enim impositione notat, qvod undiq; munitio: secundâ verò omnem unius rei participationem, qvam alii vocant Communicationem.

X. Vulgò communio & communicatio synonyma sunt grammatica; ἀκριβῶς tamen differunt ut unitio & unio; qvarum illa notat actum, qvo plura in unum copulantur, hæc autem statum unitionis actum inseqventem fignificat. Ita etiam communicatio actum, communio statum designat, ut ita rectiùs communio ὑποστάσεως diceretur. Ob receptum tamen in Ecclesiâ usum vocem communicationis retinebimus, ita ut actum & statum simul denotet.

XI. Sunt autem communicationis modi varii. In genere communicatio est vel ὀνοματώδης vel πραγματώδης. Illa fit 1. per tropum, ut cùm dico, Herodes est vulpes. 2. ob honorem, ut cùm Doctoris uxor doctorissa vocatur. 3. per fictionem, ut cùm papa caput Ecclesiæ nominatur. Hæc communicatio tantùm nominis communitatem habet.

XII. Realis (qvæ etiam rem insuper largitur) est vel naturalis, vel supernaturalis. Illa triplex est. 1. n. datur communicatio inter accidens & accidens, ut cùm dico, Theologus est philosophus. 2. inter substantiam & accidens, qvando qvod accidenti competit, substantiæ tribuitur. Sic aër dicitur fluidus propter humiditatem. 3. datur communicatio inter substantiam & substantiam, qvæ tamen, vel ratione, vel realiter differt. XIII. Qvod si discrimen inter subjecta mentale tantùm, exoritur 1. communicatio κατὰ μέθεξιν 2. κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν. 3. κατὰ σύγχυσιν. Qvod si verò sit differentia realis, tunc subjecta vel sunt separata vel συνδυασμένα & unita. Inter separata est communicatio α. κατὰ μετάβασιν, β. κατ' ἀλλοποίωσιν, γ. κατὰ χρῆσιν. XIV. Si verò subjecta sint unita, oritur communicatio κατὰ συνδύασιν, quâ propter unionem id qvod unius est proprium, alteri sine sui vel multiplicatione vel transfusione, realiter confertur, ad communem possessionem, usurpationem & denominationem; tot enim gradus hæc communicatio facit. XV. Supernaturalis communicatio quadruplex est. 1. essentialis, qualis inter personas Trinitatis. 2. spiritualis. 3. sacramentalis. 4. personalis, de qua hîc ulterius agendum: & quamvis hæc cum φυσικῇ multa habeat communia, tamen quia singularia insuper multa habet, & similia exempla dari neqveant, singularis etiam manet & peculiari nomine ὑποστατικὴ vocatur, partim ad denotandam causam communicationis, quæ est unio personalis, partim modum, quòd sit inter ea quæ ad unum ὑφισάμενον uniuntur.

XVI. Ut autem constaret, quid nos, & quid Calviniani statuant, omninò priùs de statu controversiæ debemus esse certi, præsertim quia adversarii tam strenuè βατταλογοῦσι. Modò enim negant communicationem ὑποστάσεως, modò affirmant, modò distinctiunculis involvunt. Negant, quia nullum proprium communicari posse perhibent, ut ex Beza a, Sadeele b, Keckermanno c, apparet.

XVII. Affirmant aut affirmare videntur Beza d & Polanus, e dum infinitam subsistentiam communicari posse & afferunt & non negant, ubi sanè apertis verbis orthodoxiam profitentur, sed utinam non modò verbis sed etiam corde! Nam quæso quid volunt sibi distinctiones quibus utuntur, dum communicationem sumi vel pro unione contendunt, aut pro subsequentibus unionem, quarum illam concedunt, hanc verò negant, ut liqvet ex Saxii a disqvis. Bezæ thesi b, & responsione c in Coll. Mompelg. Danæi exam. Chemnit. d, Polani syst. Theol. e, ubi ad argumentum Samosatenicum, quo negatur subsistentiam infinitam communicari, respondet; communicationis vocem sumi vel pro commune fieri naturæ finitæ:

(sed quis fucum non videt unionem hîc intelligi) aut pro transfusione reali: Quo sanè posteriori nobis per calumniam confusionem, sæpissime adeò â nobis rejectam & confutatam, affingit.

XVIII. Manifestum autem est, Calvinianis contingere quod Irenæus de quibusdam dicit, ὅμοια λαλῦσιν, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονῦσιν; imò instar soricis tandem se & versutiam suam produnt. Quæstio enim est de verâ participatione, illi respondent de unione, allium pro cepis, novâ ratione veritatis lucem subterfugiendi.

XIX. Ut ergò nobis apertiores fiant: Negamus 1. distinctionem eorum. Quod si intolerabile illis hoc videtur, probent rogamus. 2. dicimus esse ἀκυρολογίαν in illâ. Nam unio conjunctio est, communicatio autem datio & elargitio. 3. urgemus Canonem Patrum: Qualis unio, talis communicatio, quem tautologicum nova subtilitas adversariorum facit. 4. objicimus confessionem Polani, quando scribit unionem consistere in communicatione subsistentiæ verbi cum carne, nisi ἀδολεσχεῖν ipsum dicere velint, h. e. asserere unionem consistere in unione, videbunt vel ex hoc suo asseclâ distinctionem unionis à communicatione. 5. Instantias, quas adferunt, ac populariter loqventium, ἀκρίβειαν non attendentium, non admittimus, qvippè jam disputamus, non differimus. 6. perpendendum ipsis relinquimus, quòd jamdudum explicaverimus communicationem, non per unionem, non per transfusionem, sed realem participationem. Hic ergo Rhodus, hîc saltent.

XX. Si planiùs rem velint proponi, hoc qværitur: An λόγος ὑπόστασιν suam, qua ipsi soli propria est, etiam communem fecerit carni assumtæ, ita ut per eam caro subsistat? Nos affirmàtivam tenemus, adversariiludunt, ut ostendimus, voculis, & nobis nudam sustentationem obtrudunt, qvemadmodum Martinius & Beza faciunt.


### Chap. III. XXI. But lest we seem to urge our thesis by bare assertion, we will strengthen…

CHAP. III.

XXI. But lest we seem to urge our thesis by bare assertion, we will strengthen our opinion with the most firm of the arguments that could be brought forward, which are very many.

XXII. 1. Therefore it is taken from the unity of the ὑποστάσεως (subsistence) of Christ. For it is read everywhere that Christ is one. Now that is not a unity of nature, since we proved its duality b above; it will therefore be of the ὑποστάσεως (subsistence), which is not proper to human nature, unless we wish to say, λόthe infinite Word to subsist in a finite subsistence. Nor yet is it conflated from the concurrence of both, because thus it would be composite, which is contrary to the nature of subsistence, which is simple. Therefore, it will be the subsistence of the Word alone. Hence we infer: Wherever there is one thing truly and really belonging to many, there is without doubt a true and real communication. For of those things of which it can be said that one thing is of both, those things really participate in that one thing. Now subsume concerning the subsistence of the Word, and the matter will be evident.

XXIII. 2. We urge the subsistence of the flesh itself. For the flesh of Christ is either ἀνυπόστατος (without subsistence) or ἐνυπόστατος (in-subsistent): not the former, because thus it would not exist. Further. It is either αὐθυπόστατος (self-subsistent) or ἑτερυπόστατος (subsistent in another): not the former, for thus Christ would have assumed a person, which is Nestorian. Therefore the latter, but that subsistence is none other than the Word's, because the flesh was assumed by the Word. But how does it subsist? Not by transfusion, for thus the Word himself would no longer subsist: Not by the creation of a new subsistence, for thus a dissolution and duality of person would follow. Therefore by communion. Hence it is inferred: That which subsists in another's subsistence, to that one, that subsistence is truly communicated. For the second act always presupposes the first, but to subsist is a second act, and participation in subsistence presupposes the first act. Now subsume concerning the subsistence of Christ in this manner.

XXIV. 3. This is evident from the definition of communication. For true communion is nothing other than the distribution of one thing among many and the participation in the same. Hence: Where two participate in one thing, there a true communication of this one thing has been made. But in Christ two natures participate in one subsistence of the Word. Therefore. We illustrate the major premise from the confession of our adversaries, Martini l. 2. de persona Christi a and Zanchius b.

XXV. 4. We conclude from the absurd. For unless a true and real participation of one subsistence is granted, Nestorianism cannot be avoided and the union cannot be fully described. For if you say the flesh is sustained by the Word, that also happens to creatures. If you say it is drawn to the subsistence of the Word, you either understand it as a bare concurrence without communion, but Nestorius does not deny even this: or you explain it by subsisting in the Word. I ask however, has a communication of the ὑπόστασις taken place? If you say so, we say so; if you deny it, Nestorianism will follow. Wherefore it is notable that that external sustenance of the flesh is an action of the whole Trinity, since the union of the λόγος with the flesh is an internal work, because only the λόγος is incarnate.

XXVI. 5. We prove our thesis from the denomination by which the humanity of Christ is called ὑπόστασις, a term which the Greek fathers use, by which it is implied that the flesh is personified by the λόγος. Hence: Whatever is personified, to that a person is truly communicated.

XXVII. 6. We cite the testimonies of Damascene, who says the word itself became an ὑπόστασις to the flesh. 7. We are confirmed by the fact that firm arguments fail our adversaries. They indeed stubbornly deny the κοινωνίαν, but with broken little arguments, some of which we shall touch upon.

XXIIX. 1. They urge the definition of a person, in which it is said that a person is incommunicable. Now because the subsistence of the λόγος is a person, it will certainly be incommunicable. But that proposition: Every person is incommunicable, and therefore the major premise of the adversaries, must be limited in three ways. 1. Every person is incommunicable to another person, but not to a nature. 2. It is incommunicable κατὰ μέθεξιν, but not κατ’ ἕνωσιν. 3. It is incommunicable concretely as it is an ὑφιστάμενον, but not abstractly as a subsistence. Now let them prove that we say a person is communicated to a person, κατὰ μέθεξιν and in the concrete.

XXIX. 3. They infer: If the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος is communicated, the Deity will also be communicated, because these do not really differ. But we deny the consequence, which rests on a false ὑπόθεσις, as if the Deity and the person were the same even abstractly. Nor 2. does it follow: The Deity is communicated to the flesh, therefore the flesh is GOD; but this follows: therefore it is deified, because for something to be God, communication is not sufficient, but the independence of the essence is required.

XXX. 4. They place the defense of their cause in this, that they think communication is nothing other than union and the sustenance of the flesh: For they say, there are only two natures in Christ, and besides these there is nothing distinct given, since the person and the nature of the λόγος do not really differ. Hence, although the λόγος has communicated his ὑπόστασις to the flesh, nothing else is noted than that close coalition of both natures, & personal sustenance. Therefore, just as the λόγος itself is communicated to the flesh, so also is the λόγε ὑπόσασις, on account of real identity. But now, the λόγος has been communicated to the flesh through union; why, therefore, not the ὑπόσασις? So that it may appear that communication is nothing other than union.

XXXI. But in this discourse, there are errors in many ways. 1. Union and κοινωνία are confused, which nevertheless must be entirely distinguished. 2. Our superior arguments prove that the flesh of Christ has been made a participant of the divine subsistence in the most proper sense. For although our weakness cannot accurately discern this union and κοινωνία, it ought not to prejudice the truth of the matter.

XXXII. Two things are difficult here. 1. If the true communication of the ὑπόσασις is denied, a personal union cannot be defended against Nestorius. 2. If it is affirmed, we can scarcely show the distinction. There is the truth which we defend; here is the sublimity and weakness which we acknowledge.

XXXIII. The adversaries play with the word 'person,' which is taken either for the subsistent concretely, or for the subsistence abstractly: in the former way, person and nature do not differ, but in the latter, they do in a certain way. But what kind and how great that distinction is, we willingly confess is not entirely clear, and the scruple here concerns the mystery of the Trinity itself, which we can admire, but not pry into.

XXXIV. With this distinction, such as it is, presupposed, we deny that union and communication are the same, because the former denotes only conjunction, while the latter denotes, in addition, a bestowing. From this, however, it is clear at the same time that the major premise of the final argument must be denied, where it is said that just as the λόγος communicated itself (note the insolence of the phrase), so also did the ὑπόσασις. For a false ὑπόθεσις lies hidden here, as if the λόγος and its ὑπόσασις were one and the same, when nevertheless they differ at the very least as a thing and the mode of a thing.

XXXV. Therefore, the communication of the subsistence having been proven, it follows: I. That the flesh of Christ truly has and in reality possesses an infinite ὑπόσασις, proper to the λόγος himself. II. That the flesh of Christ usurps the subsistence of the λόγος, if you take this word in a more general sense.

III. That the flesh of Christ is truly denominated from the communicated ὑπόστασις. IV. That the flesh of Christ has adopted a non-local mode of subsisting through this κοινωνία. V. That many things are predicated of the flesh of Christ personally on account of the communicated ὑπόστασις. VI. That the finite in a certain respect is capable of the infinite. VII. That something proper is truly and really communicated. VIII. That all things proper to the Λόγος are truly and participatively communicated to the assumed flesh.

XXXVI. We defer the exceptions of the Calvinists to the collation, and we shall resolve two doubts concerning this matter. I. It may be asked, whether, if the whole person of the Λόγος is communicated to the flesh, the flesh can rightly be called a part of the person of Christ? II. Whether the κοινωνία of subsistence is more correctly called the form or the effect of the personal union?

XXXVII. As regards the former, the answer is straightforward, if one distinguishes the term person, which is taken either abstractly for subsistence, or concretely for the subsistent. In the former way, the whole ὑπόστασις is rightly said to be communicated, because it is impartible, but his humanity cannot be called a part of it, because it does not actuate it, but is actuated by it. In the latter way, however, it is called a part, but an analogical one.

XXXIIX. In the latter question, the Jesuits wish the κοινωνία of the ὑπόστασις to be referred to the form of the union: most of our own people, however, hold it to be an effect. We think that a distinction must be made between communication and communion: the former is the δόσις of subsistence and pertains to the form of the union; the latter is the possession of the ὑπόστασις and follows the act of communication, whence it is clear that it can be called both the form and the effect of the union, though in a different respect.

XXXIX. This doctrine teaches us, 1. the nature of faith, in which the articles cohere like links in a chain. 2. the infinite wisdom of GOD. 3. the φιλανθρωπίαν. 4. that it is our duty to adhere to GOD, just as the flesh subsists in the subsistence of the Λόγος, so that we may always say with Asaph: It is good for me to adhere to GOD.

Latin:

CAP. III.

XXI. Ne autem nudâ assertione videamur thesin urgere, ex argumentis, qvæ adduci possent, benè multis, nostram sententiam firmissimis roborabimus.

XXII. 1. Ergò desumtum est ab unitate ὑποστάσεως Christi. Nam legitur passim, quòd unus sit Christus. Jam illa unitas naturæ non est, qvippe dualitatem b ejus suprâ probavimus; Erit ergò ὑποστάσεως, qvæ humanæ naturæ propria non est, nisi dicere velimus, λόγον infinitum in finita subsistentia subsistere. Neq; tamen est ex utriusq; concursu conflata, quia sic foret composita, quod contra naturam subsistentiæ, quæ simplex est. E. erit Solius λόγᢏ ὑπόστασις. Hinc inferimus: Ubicunq; est res una pluribus verè ac realiter competens, ibi sine dubio est vera ac realis communicatio. De quibus enim dici potest, quòd unum sit utriusq;, illa realiter de uno illo participant. Jam subsume de ὑποστάσει λόγᢏ, & res evidens erit.

XXIII. 2. Urgemus subsistentiam carnis ipsam. Caro enim Christi, aut est ἀνυπόστατος, aut ἐνυπόστατος: non illud, quia sic non esset. Ulterius. Aut est αὐθυπόστατος aut ἑτερυπόστατος: non illud, sic enim Christus assumsisset personam, quod Nestorianum. E. hoc, at illa subsistentia non nisi λόγᢏ est, quia caro à λόγῳ assumta. At quomodo subsistit? Non transfusione, sic enim λόγος ipse non subsisteret amplius: Non novæ subsistentiæ creatione, sic enim λύσις & dualitas personæ sequeretur. E. κοινωνίᾳ. Hinc infertur: Quod subsistit in aliena ὑποστάσει, illi ὑπόστασις illa verè est communicata. Actus enim secundus semper præsupponit primum, subsistere autem actus secundus, participationem subsistentiæ actum primum præsupponit. Jam de ὑποστάσει Christi h. n. subsume.

XXIV. 3. Patet hoc ex definitione communicationis. Vera enim κοινωνία nil est aliud quàm unius inter plura distributio & de eodem participatio. Hinc: Ubi duo participant de uno, ibi facta est vera hujus unius communicatio. Sed in Christo duæ naturæ participant de una λόγᢏ ὑποστάσει. E. Majorem illustramus à confessione adversariorum, Martinii. l. 2. de persona Christi a & Zanchii b.

XXV. 4. Ab absurdo concludimus. Nisi enim concedatur vera & realis participatio unius ὑποστάσεως, Nestorianismus evitari & unio plenè describi non potest. Si enim dicas carnem sustentari à λόγῳ, etiam illud creaturis fit. Si dicas esse tractam ad verbi subsistentiam, aut intelligis de nudo concursu sine κοινωνίᾳ, at neque hunc Nestorius negat: aut explicas per subsistere in λόγῳ. Quæro autem, factane ὑποστάσεως communicatio? Si dicis; dicimus; si negas, Nestorianismus sequetur. Quocirca notabile est, sustentationem illam carnis externam actionem esse totius Trinitatis, cùm unio λόγυ cum carne sit opus internum, quia solus λόγ est incarnatus.

XXVI. 5. Probamus θέσιν nostram à denominatione, qua humanitas Christi dicitur ὑποστάσα, quo termino utuntur patres græci, quo innuitur carnem à λόγῳ personari. Hinc: Quicquid personatur, illi persona verè communicatur.

XXVII. 6. Citamus testimonia Damasceni, qui dicit ipsum verbum factum est carni ὑπόστασις. 7. Confirmamur ex eo, quòd firmæ rationes adversarios deficiant. Κοινωνίαν quidem negant præfractè, sed ratiunculis infractis, quarum quasdam perstringemus.

XXIIX. 1. E. urgent definitionem personæ, in qua dicitur, quòd persona sit incommunicabilis. Jam quia subsistentia λόγε est persona, utiq; incommunicabilis erit. Verùm illa propositio: Omnis persona est incommunicabilis, adeóq; Major adversariorum limitari debet tripliciter. 1. Omnis persona est incommunicabilis, alteri personæ, non autem naturæ. 2. incommunicabilis est κατα μέτεξιν, non autem κατ’ ἕνωσιν. 3. est incommunicabilis concretè quà est ὑφισάμενον, non verò abstractè, quà subsistentia. Jam autem probent, nos dicere personam communicari personæ, κατὰ μέθεξιν & in concreto.

XXIX. 3. Inferunt. Si ὑπόστασις λόγε est communicata, etiam Deitas erit communicata, quia hæc realiter non differunt. Verùm nos negamus consequentiam, quæ falsa nititur ὑποθέσει, quasi Deitas & persona etiam abstractè essent eadem. Neq; 2. sequitur, carni Deitas est communicata. E. caro DEUS est, sed hoc sequitur, E. deificata est, quia ut aliquid sit Deus, non sufficit communicatio, sed requiritur essentiæ independentia.

XXX. 4. In eo causæ suæ præsidium ponunt, quòd putant communicationem nihil esse aliud quàm unionem & carnis sustentationem: Nam dicunt, sunt tantùm duæ in Christo naturæ, & præter has distinctum quid non datur, cùm persona & natura λόγε realiter nón differant. Hinc licet λόγος communicaverit carni suam ὑπόσασιν, nihil tamen aliud notatur quàm illa arcta coalitio utriusq; naturæ, & personalis sustentatio. Iccirco ut ipse λόγος est communicatus carni, ita etiam λόγε ὑπόσασις, ob realem identitatem. Jam verò λόγος carni communicatus est per unionem, qvidni ergò ὑπόσασις? Ut ita appareat, communicationem nihil esse aliud qvàm unionem.

XXXI. Verùm in hoc discursu multifarià peccatur. 1. unio & κοινωνία confunduntur, qvæ tamen distinguenda omninò sunt. 2. superiora nostra argumenta evincunt, carnem Christi in propriissimo sensu factam esse participem divinæ subsistentiæ. Licet enim accuratè imbecillitas nostra unionem & κοινωνίαν hanc discernere neqveat, rei tamen veritati nihil præjudicare debet.

XXXII. Duo hîc difficilia sunt. 1. Si negatur vera ὑποςάσεως communicatio, non poterit contra Nestorium defendi personalis unio. 2. si affirmatur, discrimen ostendere vix possumus. Ibi veritas, qvam defendamus; hîc sublimitas & imbecillitas, qvam agnoscamus.

XXXIII. Ludunt 3. adversarii voce personæ, qvæ sumitur vel pro subsistente concretè, vel pro subsistentia abstractè: illo modo persona & natura non differunt, hoc autem qvodammodo. Verùm qvale & qvantum discrimen illud sit, lubenter fatemur non omninò liqvēre, & scrupulus hîc Trinitatis mysterium ipsum concernit, qvod mirari, non rimari, possumus.

XXXIV. Præsupposito hoc qvali qvali discrimine, negamus unionem & communicationem esse eadem, qvia illa conjunctionem tantùm, hæc elargitionem insuper notat. Inde verò simul patet, ultimi argumenti majorem negandam esse, qva dicitur, uti se communicavit λόγος (nota phraseos insolentiam) ita & ὑπόσασις. Nam falsa ὑπόθεσις hic latet, qvasi λόγος & ὑπόσασις ejus essent unum & idem, cùm tamen ad minimum differant ut res & modus rei.

XXXV. Comprobatâ ergo communicatione subsistentiæ, seqvitur I. Quòd caro Christi infinitam, ipsiq́; λόγῳ propriam ὑπόσασιν verè habeat & reipsa possideat. II. Quòd caro Christi subsistentiam λόγε usurpet, si vocem hanc generaliori sensu sumas.

III. Quòd caro Christi à communicatâ ὑποστάσει verè denominetur. IV. Quòd caro Christi per hanc κοινωνίαν illocalem subsistendi modum adopta sit. V. Quòd de carne Christi multa prædicentur personaliter ob communicatam ὑπόστασιν. VI. Quòd finitum certo respectu sit capax infiniti. VII. Quod aliquod proprium verè & realiter communicetur. VIII. Quod omnia Λόγου propria, verè ac participativè sint communicata assumtæ carni.

XXXVI. Exceptiones Calvinianorum differimus ad collationem, & duo dubia circa hoc negotium expediemus. I. n. quæri potest, An, si tota persona Λόγου carni est communicata, caro rectè dici possit pars personæ Christi? II. an κοινωνία subsistentiæ rectiùs dicatur formale an effectum unionis personalis?

XXXVII. Quod prius attinet, expedita est responsio, si distinguatur vocabulum personæ, quod sumitur vel abstractè pro subsistentia, vel concretè pro subsistente. Illo modo tota ὑπόστασις rectè dicitur communicata, quia est impartibilis, at humanitas ejus pars dici nequit, quia eam non actuat, sed ab eâ actuatur. Hoc verò modo dicitur pars, verùm analogica.

XXXIIX. Posteriori in quæstione volunt Esavitæ, κοινωνίαν ὑποστάσεως referri debere ad unionis formam: nostratium autem pleriq; habent pro effectu. Nos putamus, distingui debere inter communicationem & inter communionem: illa est δόσις subsistentiæ & pertinet ad formam unitionis; hæc est possessio ὑποστάσεως & seqvitur actum communicationis, unde & formam & effectum dici posse unionis liqvet, pro diverso tamen respectu.

XXXIX. Docet autem hæc doctrina nos, 1. naturam fidei, in qua articuli cohærent, ut annuli in catenâ. 2. infinitam DEI sapientiam. 3. φιλανθρωπίαν. 4. nostrum esse adhærere DEO, ut caro subsistit in Λόγου subsistentiâ, ut semper dicamus cum Asapho; Mihi adhærere DEO bonum est.


## 11 Eleventh Disputation, On the True and Real Communion of the Two Natures in Christ

Thesis I,

That there are two natures in Christ, namely divine and human, and that they are personally united in the same, has been demonstrated briefly and clearly thus far from Holy Theology, the Analogy of faith, and the harmony of Antiquity; now, with a more accessible method of elegant order, as obscure indications so demand, let us traverse in our minds the true and real communion of these natures.

II. Scarcely any part of Christian doctrine is more hateful to the Sacramentarians and the Romanists alike than this very one: And as the little foxes of Samson were indeed diverse in their heads, yet most closely joined by their tails, so today the Sacramentarians join their minds as allies with the Papists in attacking the salutary doctrine concerning the hypostatic communion of natures in Christ, however much they are otherwise most divided,

III. For with unanimous consent they deny the true and real communion of natures; indeed, some proceed to such a degree of moroseness that they are unwilling to concede even a verbal one, dreaming in their own brains of such a union of the two natures in Christ as exists without communion; which is the same as if they were to imagine a sun without splendor, fire without heat, or water without moisture,

IV. By which, truly, both the shaven and the bald clearly betray their signal malice, while in the manner of Eutyches they establish that κοινωνία is nothing but the conversion and mutation of one nature into the other, and they most wickedly confuse union and communication, which are nevertheless distinct and ought not to be thoroughly mixed,

V. Furthermore, so that our opinion may be so much the more certain, and so that nothing different may be imputed to our Churches by the heterodox, I would wish them to weigh accurately what the Formula of Concord establishes concerning our affirmative position, article 8, page 606.

VI. For from that it will be most clearly evident to anyone what the mind of the F.C. and of all who think rightly is; namely, that the two natures in Christ in reality communicate, in such a way that the Deity is in the humanity and the humanity in the Deity, the one in the other, neither outside the other, nor yet is the one the other.

VII. Although this opinion ought to have been placed beyond all hazard of doubt, yet that ill-disposed zeal of the Romanists and Sacramentarians for destroying it makes it necessary that what is indeed sufficiently manifest by itself, and inscribed upon the hearts of all the faithful as if by a ray of the sun, should be affirmed by the most evident arguments, which we shall divide into three classes, of which that infallible measure of faith, censor of errors, and cynosure of the heavens, namely, Holy Scripture, deservedly holds the first place, which confirms our proposition most strongly by the most perspicuous and firm sayings, the chief of which we shall touch upon in the briefest lines.

VIII. Therefore, all those sayings pertain here which corroborate the incarnation of the λόγος and the assumption of flesh into the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος, such as are found in John 1:14, 1 Tim. 3:16, Heb. 2:14.

IX. To these is added that classic oracle of the Holy Spirit, to be stored in the deepest senses, Col. 2:9: In him (Christ) dwells all the fullness of the Deity bodily: which most strongly stabilizes our affirmative. For is not the nature which is inhabited by another a participant of that which inhabits? Since such indwelling is nothing other than mutual interpenetration and participation. Because the θεότης, nay the πλήρωμα θεότητος, and what is greatest, πᾶν πλήρωμα θεότητος, dwells in the assumed humanity of Christ; it follows of its own accord that the human nature of Christ has truly and really been made a participant of the indwelling divine.

X. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews receives this with his assent, while in ch. 2:14 he testifies that human nature has been communicated to the λόγος, or what is the same thing, that the λόγος has truly been made a participant of humanity, as of children.

XI. We assign the second place to that rule for judging all controversies, namely, the analogy of faith, which also confirms our opinion with the firmest foundations.

XII. The Son of God was made man, that he might bring us men back into the grace of God through an ἀποτέλεσμα common to both natures. But how, with the communion of natures denied, could either nature have worked our salvation with the κοινωνία of the other? What, what, I say, in the incarnation was necessary, if one nature has not been made a participant of the other. Let those Cyclopean opponents of κοινωνία see, therefore, how, with this denied or at least called into doubt, they wish to preserve the most sacred mystery of the incarnation intact!

XIII. To whom the infinite ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου has been truly and participatively communicated, to the same has his divine nature been communicated. Because, as the antagonists themselves do not dissent, the ὑπόστασις and the nature of the λόγος are one in reality. Now, however, the ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου has been communicated to the flesh of Christ, as was demonstrated to the eye above. Therefore.

XIV. Between which natures there is a true περιχώρησις, between them there is also a true κοινωνία. Between the divine nature of the λόγος and the human nature of Christ there is a true περιχώρησις. Therefore, between them there is also a true κοινωνία. The major premise is most certain: for περιχώρησις involves the closest presence of natures. The minor premise will be called into doubt by no one who admits a personal union. Hence the Blessed Fathers establish with unanimous consent that the λόγος has intimately immigrated into the flesh and pervaded it entirely, so that it is called by some λο- γωθεῖσα or 'word-ified' no less truly than elegantly. Consequently, the adversaries strive to tear apart the communion of natures with vain and absurd attempts.

XV. Whatever things are united by an intimate and closest mode of union, in such a way indeed that from them one incommunicable ὑφιστάμενον is constituted, between them a true and real communion has arisen. The divine nature of the λόγος and the human nature of Christ, etc. Therefore. The major premise is higher than all ambiguity. The minor premise will be denied neither by Calvinists nor by Mass-priests. Therefore, that which follows is true.

XVI. Human nature is called Deified by Athanasius, anointed with divinity by Nazianzen, divine humanity by Augustine, divine body by Cyril. Because, therefore, the flesh is truly deified, it has also truly been made a participant of the divine nature, since deification is nothing other than participation in the Deity. Conversely, because GOD has in reality been made man, hence he has been truly and really made a participant of the flesh, and thus there is given in Christ a mutual, true, and real κοινωνία of natures.

XVII. Because the properties of the λόγος and the flesh are common, as will be demonstrated in the following meetings, certainly there will also be a certain mutual κοινωνία between the natures, since both because nature and properties always cohere, and because the communion of idioms necessarily presupposes the communion of natures, as the antagonists themselves confess.

XVIII. The whole orthodox and venerable antiquity sings in harmony with the analogy of faith, whose opinion, for the sake of repelling the importunity of heretics, I shall bring forth at least a few testimonies, all of which can be conveniently distributed into six distinct orders.

XIX. 1. The Blessed Fathers expressly testify that the Deity was communicated to the flesh by the Word. For thus the Great Basil: The human flesh of the Lord itself was made a participant of the Deity; and likewise the Blessed Damascene: The soul of the incarnate Son became a participant of the divine nature according to ὑπόsασιν. The same, The Creator lowered Himself so that He might honor my nature, and make it a participant of the divine nature.

XX. 2. The Fathers similarly confess that the Deity was truly made a participant of the flesh. For thus Chapter 5 of the Council of Ephesus argues: The Word communicated similarly as we do to flesh and blood. Nyssen: What is more humble in the King of the whole universe than to have come into communion with our beggarly nature.

XXI. 3. The Fathers with unanimous consent establish that the flesh of Christ is truly deified. Athanasius testifies to this explicitly: when He was God, He assumed flesh and, existing in the flesh, He deifies it. Gregory Nazianzen agrees, who reports thus: Christ consists of two contraries, flesh and spirit, of which the one deifies, the other is deified.

XXII. 4. Not a few Fathers testify that the assumed flesh is God Himself. Athanasius: That very God was made flesh, so that His flesh might be made God, the Word. Augustine: Such was that assumption, that it made God Man and man God.

XXIII. 5. The Fathers call the assumed flesh an organ of the Word, through which and in which He operates effectively. Athanasius: The human nature, having been deified, was made an organ of wisdom, so that He might exercise His energy through it. Cyril: Little by little our nature was manifested, so that it was an instrument of the Deity, which dwelt in it.

XXIV. 6. Certain Fathers, in order to teach a real communication of natures, used the very word 'mixture'. Nazianzen: What could fall more into the humility of man than to be coupled to God and from the mixture to become God. Hilary: GOD is said to be incarnate and mixed, nor is it to be thought that his essence is diminished.

XXV. With these things thus established, it appears clearer than the midday sun that all the adversaries barking at and tearing apart the true and real κοινωνίαν [communion] most shamefully destroy the principles of the Most Holy Faith, overturn the foundations of salvation, and contradict venerable antiquity with full cheeks.

XXVI. Thus far we have set forth the true and orthodox opinion of our Church; it remains that we investigate how it may be able to sustain and overcome the force and hammers of those attacking it.

XXVII. In this place the Esavites, especially Busaeus, are in an uproar, primarily with 4 arguments. 1. If the divine nature is really communicated to the flesh, it clearly follows that the 3 persons of the Trinity are also communicated to the same and therefore incarnated. Because the divine nature is one in number and singular, not proper to the Word of GOD, but common to the three persons.

XXIIX. But if the Esavite tries to thrust his horns here to gore, he overturns by the same impetus, in the Nestorian manner, the hypostatic union itself. For by a like argument I conclude: Either the divine nature of Christ is united, or it is not. If the former, it follows according to the Esavite deduction that all three persons are united, which, since it is prodigiously absurd, impious, and blasphemous, we return his own horrendous blasphemy to the author as a gift. And to the point. The Esavite confuses in one word the divine nature ἁπλῶς [simply] or absolutely as it is common to all persons in the Trinity, and σχετικῶς [relatively] or relatively and determinately accepted insofar as it is restricted to this or that person by a hypostatic character. Here, however, Deity is taken not in common, but in the person; namely, the Deity begotten and communicated to the flesh. Hence there are 4 terms in the Argument.

Latin:

Thesis I,

DUas in Christo naturas, divinam videlicet & humanam, easq; personaliter in eodem unitas esse, hactenus ex SS. Theologia, fidei Analogia & Antiquitatis harmonia breviter & perspicuè demonstratum est; jam faciliori elegantioris ordinis ratione inobscuris inditiis sic exigente harum naturarum veram ac realem communionem percurramus animo.

II. Vix autem ulla doctrinæ Christianæ pars genti cum Sacramentariæ tum Romanensi magis est exosa quam hæc ipsa: Et ut Simsonis vulpeculæ, capitibus quidem diversæ erant, caudis tamen junctissimæ, sic hodie sacramentarii socias jungunt mentes Papicolis in oppugnanda salutari de naturarum in Christo hypostatica communione doctrina, qvantumvis aliàs distractissimi,

III. Unanimi quippe consensu inficiantur veram ac realem naturarum communionem; imò nonnulli eò usq; morositatis progrediuntur, ut ne verbalem quidem velint concedere, talem in cerebello suo somniantes unionem duarum in Christo naturarum, quæ sit sine communione; quod idem, ac si solem absq; splendore, ignem absq; calore, aquam absq; humore fingerent,

IV. Quibus sanè utriq; cùm rasi tùm calvi insignem planè produnt malitiam, dum p. Eutichiano penitus more κοινωνίαν nil nisi unius naturæ in alteram conversionem mutationemq; esse statuunt, p. unionem & communicationem pessimè confundunt, quæ tamen distincta sunt, nec penitus permisceri debent,

V. Cæterùm ut de nostra sententia tantò constet certius, neq; diversum nostris Ecclesiis imputari queat ab heterodoxis, perpendant velim accuratè, quid Formula Concordiæ de nostra statuat affirmativa, art. 8. p. 606.

VI. Exinde enim cuivis liquidissimè constabit quæ F. C. & omnium dextrè sentientium mens sit; duas nimirum in Christo naturas reipsâ communicare, ita ut Deitas sit in humanitate & humanitas in Deitate, altera in altera, neutra extra alteram, neq; tamen altera sit altera.

VII. Etsi autem hæc sententia extra omnem dubitationis aleam debebat esse posita, facit tamen malè feriatum illud Romanensium & Sacramentariorum pro ea destruenda studium, ut quod per se quidem satis est manifestum & ipso quasi Solis radio, omnium fidelium cordibus inscriptum, id evidentissimis argumentis affirmari necesse sit, quod in tres dispescamus classes, quarum merito primas tenet infallibilis illa Fidei mensura, errorum censura, cælorum cynosura, Sacrosancta videlicet Scriptura, quæ dictis maximè perspicuis & firmis nostrum vel maximè confirmat propositum, quarum præcipua brevifsimis tangemus lineolis.

VIII. Pertinent ergò huc Dicta illa omnia, quæ incarnationem λόγε & carnis in ὑπόςασιν λόγε assumtionem corroborant, qualia habentur Joh. 1. 14. 1. Tim. 3. 16. Hebr. 2, 14.

IX. Qvibus suffragatur classicum illud imisq; sensibus reponendum Spiritus Sancti oraculum, Col. 2. 9. In ipso (Christo) inhabitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter: quod vel maximè nostram stabilit affirmativam. Annon enim natura quæ ab altera inhabitatur, sit particeps illius quæ inhabitat? cùm talis inhabitatio nihil aliud sit, quàm mutua immeatio & participatio. Qvia θεότης imò πλήρωμα θεότητος, & quod maximum, πᾶν πλήρωμα θεότητος in assumtâ Christi habitat humanitate; ultrò consequitur, humanam Christi naturam divinæ inhabitantis verè ac realiter factam esse participem.

X. Assensu hæc excipit suo autor Epistolæ ad Hebr. dum c. 2. 14. contestatur, τῷ λόγῳ naturam humanam esse communicatam, vel quod idem est, λόγον humanitatis verè, ut pueros, factū esse participē.

XI. Secundas tribuimus, illi omnium controversiarum dijudicandarum regulæ, Fidei videlicet analogiæ, quæ nostram quoq; sententiam firmissimis confirmat fundaminibus.

XII. Filius DEI factus est homo, ut nos homines per ἀποτέλεσμα utriq; naturæ commune in gratiam DEI reduceret. At quomodo negatâ naturarum communione natura utraq; cum κοινωνίᾳ alterius salutem nostram operari potuisset? Qvid, qvid, inquam, incarnatione opus fuit, si una natura alterius non est facta particeps. Videant ergò cyclopici isti κοινωνίας oppugnatores, quomodo hâc negatâ vel saltem in dubium vocatâ sacratissimum incarnationis mysterium sartum tectum conservare velint!

XIII. Cui verè ac participativè communicata est infinita ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου, eidem communicata est divina ejusdem natura. Quia non dissentientibus ipsis antagonistis ὑπόστασις & natura λόγου re unum sunt. Jam verò carni Christi communicata est ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου, uti superiùs ad oculum demonstratum fuit. Ergo.

XIV. Inter quas naturas est vera περιχώρησις, inter eas etiam est vera κοινωνία. Inter divinam τοῦ λόγου & humanam Christi naturam est vera περιχώρησις. Ergo inter illas etiam est vera κοινωνία. Major certissima: περιχώρησις quippe involvit arctissimam naturarum præsentiam. Minor à nemine unionem personalem admittente in dubium vocabitur. Hinc B. Patres unanimi statuunt consensu, λόγον intimè in carnem immigrasse totamq́; pervasisse, ut λογωθεῖσα vel verbificata à quibusdam non minus verè quâm concinnè appelletur. Irritis proinde & absurdis conatibus communionem naturarum divellere student adversarii.

XV. Quæcunq; intimo & arctissimo unionis modo unita sunt, ita quidem ut ex iis unum sit constitutum incommunicabile ὑφιστάμενον, inter illa vera & realis orta est communio. Divina τοῦ λόγου & humana Christi natura &c. E. Major omni ambiguitate sublimior. Minor nec à Calvinicolis nec Sacrificulis inficiabitur. Verum ergo quod consequitur.

XVI. Humana natura dicitur Deificata ab Athanasio, uncta divinitate à Naz. humanitas divina ab Aug. corpus divinum à Cyrillo. Quia ergo caro verè est deificata, verè quoq; particeps facta est divinæ naturæ, cum deificatio nihil sit aliud quàm Deitatis participatio. Vicissim quia DEUS reipsa factus est homo, hinc verè ac realiter factus est carnis particeps, adeoq; datur in Christo naturarum mutua, vera ac realis κοινωνία.

XVII. Quia propria λόγου & carnis sunt communia, ut in subsecuturis demonstrabitur congressibus, utiq; & inter naturas erit quædam κοινωνία mutua, cùm quia natura & propria semper cohærent, tum quia idiomatum communio necessariò præsupponit communionem naturarum, ipsis antagonistis confitentibus.

XVIII. Succinit Fidei analogiæ tota orthodoxa & veneranda antiqvitas, cujus quæ fuerit sententia ad retundendam hæreticorum importunitatem, paucula saltem illius testimonia promam, quæ omnia commodè in sex distinctos distribui possunt ordines.

XIX. 1. B. Patres testantur expressè Deitatem τῶ λόγῳ esse communicatam carni. Ita enim Magnus Basil. Humana domini caro ipsa facta est particeps Deitatis; nec non B. Damascenus: Incarnati filii anima naturæ divinæ secundùm ὑπόsασιν κοινωνὸς ἐγένετο particeps facta est. Idem, Creator sese demisit ut naturam meam cohonestaret, & divinæ naturæ κοινωγὸν faceret.

XX. 2. Patres similiter fatentur Deitatem τῶ λόγῳ verè factam esse participem carnis Sic enim Capitulum 5. Concilii Ephesini disserit; Verbum communicavit similiter ut nos carni & sanguini. Nissenus: Qvid humilius in rege totius universitatis, quàm venisse in communionem mendicæ nostræ naturæ.

XXI. 3. Patres unanimi statuunt consensu carnem Christi verè esse Deificatam. Disertè id testatur Athanasius; cùm Deus erat, assumsit carnem & in carne existens deificat eam. Consonat Gregorius Naz. qvi ita refert; Christus ex duobus contrariis constat, carne & spiritu, qvorum alterum deificat, alterum deificatum est.

XXII. 4. Patres non pauci testificantur carnem assumtam esse ipsum Deum. Athan. Ille ipse Deus factus est caro, ut ipsius caro efficeretur Deus, verbum. August. Talis erat illa susceptio, quòd Deum Hominem faceret & hominem Deum.

XXIII. 5. Patres assumtam carnem vocant organon λόγῳ, per qvod & in qvo efficaciter operatur, Athanas. Humana natura Deificata est facta organon sapientiæ, ut illa per eam suam energian exerceret. Cyrill. Paulatim natura nostra manifestabatur, sic ut instrumentum esset Deitatis, qvod habitavit in ipsa.

XXIV. 6. Patres qvidam ut realem naturarum communicationem docerent, ipsam mixtionis vocabulum adhibuerunt. Nazian. Qvid cadere majus in humilitatem hominis posset, quàm ut Deo copuletur & ex mixtione Deus fiat. Hilar. DEUS incarnatus esse dicitur & mixtus, nec diminutam esse ejus essentiam existimandũ est.

XXV. Qvibus ita constitu[tis] probare meridiano clarius apparet, omnes in unũ adversarios verã ac realẽ κοινωνίαν allatrantes & lacerantes turpissimè Sacrosanctæ Fidei principia destruere, salutis fundamina evertere & venerandæ antiqvitati plenis buccis cõtradicere.

XXVI. Hactenus veram & orthodoxam Ecclesiæ nostræ posuimus sententiam, restat ut indagemus, qvomodo ea vim & malleos oppugnantium sustinire & superare potis sit.

XXVII. Tumultuantur hoc loco 1. Esavite, Busæus præcipuè, 4. cumprimis rationibus. 1. Si natura divina realiter communicata est carni, planè sequitur, & 3. personas Trinitatis eidem communicatas ac proinde incarnatas esse. Qvia natura divina est una numero & singularis, non verbi DEI propria, sed communis tribus personis.

XXIIX. Sed si Esavita cornua ad ventilandum conatur hîc immittere, evertit eodem impetu more Nestoriano ipsam unionem hypostaticam. Ratione enim parili colligo: Aut divina natura Christi unita est, aut non. Si illud, seqvitur omnes tres personas juxta collectionem Esaviticam esse unitas, qvod cùm prodigiosè absurdum, impium & blasphemum sit, autori strenæ loco blasphemiam suam horrendam remittimus. Et ad rem. Confundit uno verbo Esavita divinam naturam ἁπλῶς vel absolutè prout communis est omnibus personis in Trinitate, & σχετικῶς vel relatè & determinatè acceptam qvatenus ad hanc, illam personam per characterem hypostaticam restricta est. Hic autem sumitur Deitas non in communi, sed in persona; Deitas videlicet genita & carni communicata. Hinc 4. termini in Argumento.


### XXIX. 2. Christ the man (which word in the concrete indicates a person) is…

XXIX. 2. Christ the man (which word in the concrete indicates a person) is truly and really called the Son of God, because the Son of GOD truly and really communicated his person to the man Christ.
