If therefore he also truly and really communicated his Deity to the humanity in the abstract, why should the humanity not also be called divinity? Or if they do not want that, a god or a certain goddess. In Apol. f. 4.

XXX. But whither do you rush with your blasphemies, Venerable (if it pleases your goddesses) Father Busaeus? Away, away with these execrable insults of yours from this great mystery of godliness. Away, and take your Theastros with the infernal goddesses of yours. Certainly if the λόγος, because he was made flesh, is truly flesh, why should not conversely the flesh, because it was made GOD, be truly called God, not however, as you wish, through a Eutychian σύγχυσιν, but through a ὑποστατικὴν ἕνωσιν: not by essential predication, but by an unusual and personal one. Cease furthermore to confuse synonymous predications with paronymous ones, and the matter will be easy. Iron is not fire but ignited, a body is not a soul but animated. Thus the flesh of Christ is not called ὑπόστασις or omnipotence, but ὑπόστασις and omnipotent: in like manner the same flesh is more commonly named not so much God as deified.

XXXI. If the humanity of Christ by reason of personal union or communion of natures is rightly called omnipotent, omniscient God, why not also omnipotence and Deity, since these also in the abstract have been really communicated to the humanity: Ibid. p. 66.

XXXII. The Esavite confuses most wretchedly the attribution of Deity, which indeed belongs to the flesh and to the λόγος, but in different ways; for to the λόγος by nature, to the flesh by the grace of union: and so this collection too is more worthless than fig-leaf trifles.

XXXIII. If divinity could have been communicated to the humanity, it would have been communicated to it either essentially, or formally, or habitually, or subjectively, or extrinsically, or virtually, or μεταφορικῶς. For no other mode of predicating seems to remain. But none of these communications can apply to the Deity. Therefore it could not have been really communicated. Ibid. p. 67.

XXXIV. But Father Busæus deceives and is deceived by the sophism of an insufficient enumeration of modes. For if it is granted that a similar example of communion is not found in nature or elsewhere, must it therefore be denied? It is a μυστήριον, it is a great μυστήριον, it is confessedly a great μυστήριον of godliness, as the Apostle says. If therefore you seek an example, it will not be unique. Therefore the mind is not to be sent here to inquire curiously, but to be brought down to venerate studiously. For human wisdom, trusting in itself, can sooner stumble by inquiring than by leaning [on faith] can uproot this rock, as Anselm discourses no less skillfully than truly.

XXXV. Furthermore, the curiosity of the Sacramentarians also opposes orthodoxy. For so says Sadeel. The term κοινωνίας is clearly unscriptural, and drawn from the pits of the Scholastics. Therefore, one must abstain from it.

XXXVI. But the Calvinist shamefully begs the question. Let him prove it is clearly unscriptural, both as to the letter and as to the sense. For although the term κοινωνίας does not exist, it is sufficient that the thing and the meaning are found. For many things, as Nazianzen testifies, are in the Scriptures which are not stated. Furthermore, it is false that the term κοινωνίας was taken from the pits of the Scholastics. For it is Ecclesiastical, not Scholastic, as is evident from the preceding testimonies of antiquity. Finally, it is false that all things of the Scholastics are to be rejected.

XXXVII. We defer other little arguments which lie hidden under the curious and furious hood of the Calvinistic head to the course of the exercise itself. For the narrowness of the paper calls us to other things.

XXXIIX. From the arguments of the adversaries therefore it is clear that they approach very closely to the Samosatenian heresy because of their identity with the error of the sermonists. For just as the Samosatenians, so they expressly say that natures are incommunicable: and as the Samosatenians openly denied the union of two natures in Christ, so they weaken the same by the denial of a true κοινωνία and render it doubtful. Therefore, let them either finally acknowledge with us a true communion of subsistence and natures, or let them confess that the Samosatenian error concerning the denied hypostatic union is deservedly objected to them, since the one follows firmly from the other.

XXXIX. But here it must be well observed, 1. that personal union and communion of natures are not simply one and the same, but differ in certain respects and ways. For they differ 1. in order, by which union precedes communion. 2. in the habit of the natures. For in union the natures behave more passively, in communion more actively. For there we say two natures are united, here they are said to communicate with each other.

XL. 2. It is to be noted that the communion of natures is and is not the form of personal union, in a different respect: not indeed a logical one, since the natures are not united or constitute one person insofar as they participate; but a metaphysical one, insofar as it is necessarily referred to the perfect description of the manner in which that union was made.

XLI. 3. It must be noted, that the communion of natures is diverso with respect to the personal union it is a consequence and it is not. It is a consequence, if the union is taken formally and precisely for the mere concurrence of the natures into one ὑφισάμενον [subsistence], because that concurrence is by nature prior to the very participation of the natures. For they could not participate in one another, unless they first concurred in one ὑπόστασις [hypostasis]. It is not a consequence, if the union is taken for the whole quiddity and all the requirements pertaining to its full description. For thus communion enters into the constitution of the union, because it refers to the explanation of the mode. And therefore, just as the mode of a thing cannot conveniently be called its effect, so also must it be determined concerning that κοινωνία [communion] of the natures with respect to the union.

XLII. A question arises from what has been said: whether some concord might not at last be entered into between us and our adversaries regarding this controversy of κοινωνία [communion]? Where there are found very many who simply maintain the negative, and some who defend the affirmative.

XLIII. I cannot deny here that the adversaries of both factions expressly profess that they agree with us in all things. See the Heidelbergers in the ausführlichen Bericht [detailed report] c. 1. p. 10. p. 150. 151. Trelcatius the younger l. 2. Instit. loco 4. p. 73. & p. 78. Greg. de Valentia tom. 4. disp. 1. qvæst. 2. Bus. in Apol. c. 4. p. 44. p. 52. 69. 78. 80. 82. & 83.

XLIV. But would that they did not have one thing ready on their tongue and another hidden in their mind! For if they subscribe to our opinion, why do they construct and defend hypotheses that abolish communion? Why do they describe the union not by περιχώρησιν [interpenetration], but only by παρέκφασιν λόγε [manifestation of the Word] and the sustentation of the flesh? Why do not a few of them deny the true communication of the divine ὑπόστασις [hypostasis]? Why do they for the most part confuse the union? Why do they simply deny true communion? Why do many of them explain communion as mere and naked concomitance? Why do they utterly pervert personal predications with their glosses? Why do they enervate the ἰδιοποιΐαν [appropriation] which flows immediately from κοινωνία [communion] by means of ἀλλοίωσιν [alteration]? Why, finally, do they not blush to accuse us of Eutychianism against right and justice, when we ourselves reject and despise such confusion?

XLV. Let our antagonists therefore correct their tongue and their mind, and send a message to the absurdities they have signed. If they do that candidly, clearly, without deceit and pretense, then a Christian and stable consensus in this controversy at least can be entered into with them. Otherwise if it is done, and if they are unwilling to bid farewell to those most absurd hypotheses, let that masked consensus of theirs be gone, let such a concord be gone, by which consciences are constrained and articles of faith are destroyed. For far better, as Bernard testifies, is that discord which joins us to God than the peace which separates us from Him.

XLVI. And let this suffice to have delineated, as in a sketch, the true κοινωνίᾳ of the two natures in Christ, for the sake of brevity, which we ought to observe uniquely like a Cynosura. Finally, in place of a conclusion, let us withdraw our minds from discourse, and examine a little more deeply the use of the communion of natures.

XLVII. Here the most profound abyss of divine love opens itself. For behold, O Man, how the eternal λόγος, true God, out of mere grace humbles Himself into the human race? How He communicates Himself entirely with all fullness to our flesh? What are you, O man? Before birth a foul seed, after it a sack of excrement, at your end food for worms, indeed by nature a child of wrath through sin; yet God, through His ineffable goodness, returns to grace with your lost and depressed nature, and makes it a participant of His own nature. O thing more sublime than any preaching! O inexhaustible bowels of divine mercy! Exult therefore and rejoice, pious Christian. Let this κοινωνία be your firmest tower in adversities, your most solid anchor in temptations, your most certain rock even in the agonies of death. For thus, although you may have been torn away from your God by sin, you are nevertheless rendered most closely joined to Him, and in its own way a κοινωνὸς of the divine nature. O thrice and four times blessed are those who are raised into this glorious fellowship of divine communion!

XLIIX. It places before our eyes, 2, the most evident sign of our honor. For what greater dignity could have happened to us than that which has happened to our nature through true communion with the Deity? It is indeed a sublime honor, I confess, to be placed among Princes: great, that Pharaoh shared his ring with Joseph; greater, that King Ahasuerus received the despised servant Esther into the royal bedchamber. For the eternal King of Kings, the Son of God, receives our flesh, earthly and mortal flesh, into the innermost fellowship of His nature, and has made all divine majesty equally common to it. O incomparable dignity, O ineffable glory! Rejoice in these things, lift yourself up with these things, O generous Microcosm, even if by the world you be mocked, afflicted by evil, and troubled by Satan, yet triumph in this, that your flesh is a partaker of divinity and raised far above angelic glory.

XLIX. Finally, this meditation suggests to us a true example of heretical character, which, as Irenaeus testifies, consists among other things in this, that ὅμοια μὲν λαλῶσι, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονῶσι. And just as a hunter, in order to be able to deceive wild beasts more conveniently, puts on a wild beast's skin, so heretics, especially the Sacramentarians and Romanists (as is clear from the above), wrap themselves in sheep's clothing, so that they may more easily drive simple little sheep into deception. For in their mouth is honey, in their heart is gall; in their words is praise, in their deeds is fraud; they seek friendships, they fabricate snares. O therefore extremely crafty and most wicked men! Always ponder these things, O little flock of Christ, watch and beware of their craftiness, flee their smooth-talking company as worse than a dog or a snake, groaning that Johannine prayer from the depths and with devotion: Preserve me, O Lord, in the truth; thy word is truth.

L. And thus it has pleased us to discourse soberly and piously for this time concerning the true communion of the two natures in Christ; and so we have reached the desired harbor with a firm ship. To the newborn little Jesus, in the ocean of our love, be praise, and may his glory live and flourish among us eternally, Amen.

Latin:

XXIX. 2. Christus homo (qvæ vox in concreto indicat personam) verè & realiter dicitur filius Dei, qvia Filius DEI verè & realiter homini Christo suam personam communicavit. Si igitur & humanitati in abstracto verè & realiter suam communicavit Deitatem, cur non humanitas qvoq; dicatur divinitas? vel si id nolint, Deus aut Dea qvædam. In Apol. f. 4.

XXX. Verùm qvò blasphemiarum proripetis Venerabilis (si Deabus tuis placet) Pater Busæe? Absis, absis hisce execrandis tuis conviciis, à magno hoc pietatis mysterio. Absis, & Theastros cum infernalibus Deabus tuis tibi remissas habeto. Certè si λόγος, quia factus est caro, verè est caro, cur non vice versâ caro quia facta est DEUS verè diceretur Deus, non tamen, ut tu vis, per Eutychianam σύγχυσιν, sed per ὑποστατικὴν ἕνωσιν: non prædicatione essentiali, sed inusitata & personali. Cesses præterea prædicationes synonymicas cum paronymicis confundere, & res in proclivi erit. Ferrum non ignis sed ignitum, corpus non anima sed animatum, Sic Christi caro non dicitur ὑπόστασις vel omnipotentia, sed ὑποστά- σα & omnipotens: pari modo eadem caro non tam Deus quàm deificata nominatur usitatiùs.

XXXI. Si humanitas Christi ratione personalis unionis vel communionis naturarum rectè dicitur omnipotens, omnisciens Deus, cur non & omnipotentia & Deitas, cùm hæc quoq; in abstracto humanitati sint realiter communicata: Ibid. p. 66.

XXXII. Confundit Esavita pessimè attributionem Deitatis, quæ quidem eadem carni & λόγῳ competit, sed diversimodè; Τῷ λόγῳ enim per naturam, carni per unionis gratiam: adeóq; hæc quoq; collectio gerris vanior est ficulis.

XXXIII. Si divinitas humanitati communicari potuisset, aut communicata ei esset essentialiter, aut formaliter, aut habitualiter, aut subjectivè, aut extrinsecus, aut virtualiter aut μεταφορικῶς. Nullus enim alius videtur superesse prædicandi modus. At nulla harum communicationum in Deitatem cadere potest. Non igitur realiter potuit communicari. Ibid. p. 67.

XXXIV. Verùm fallit & fallitur Pater Busæus sophismate insufficientis modorum enumerationis. Concesso enim in natura & alibi non inveniri simile communionis exemplum, an propterea illa neganda? μυστήριον est, μέγα μυστήριον est, ὁμολογυμένως μέγα τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον est, dicente Apostolo. Si ergò exemplum qværis, non erit singulare. Non ergo hîc immittendus animus ad curiosè inqvirendum, sed demittendus ad studiosè venerandum. Citiùs qvippe potest in se confidens humana sapientia inqvirendo impingere, quàm innitendo petram hanc evellere, uti Anshelmus non minùs scitè quàm verè disserit.

XXXV. Porrò curiositas quoq; Sacramentaria orthodoxiæ obstrepit. Ita enim Sadeel. Vocabulum κοινωνίας planè ἄγραφον, & ex lacunis Scholasticorum haustum. Ergò ab illo abstinendum.

XXXVI. Verùm turpiter principium petit Calvinicola. Probet planè esse ἄγραφον, cùm quoad literam, tùm quoad sensum. Etsi enim vocabulum κοινωνίας non extet, sufficit tamen rem & διάνοιαν reperiri. Multa enim, teste Nazianzeno, sunt in Scripturis, quæ non dicuntur. Falsum deinde est, ex scholasticorum lacunis terminum κοινωνίας esse desumptum. Ecclesiasticus enim est, non Scholasticus, uti ex superioribus antiquitatis patescit testimoniis. Falsum deniq; est, omnia scholasticorum esse rejicienda.

XXXVII. Alias ratiunculas quæ sub curioso & furioso capitis Calvinistici latitant liripipio, ad ipsum exercitationis cursum rejicimus. Chartæ enim angustia ad alia nos provocat.

XXXIIX. Ex dictis igitur adversantium argutiis liqvet, eos ob identitatem cum sermonistum erroris ad Samosatenianam hæresin quàm proximè accedere. Ut enim Samosateniani, sic ipsi naturas expressè dicunt incommunicabiles: & ut Samosateniani duarum in Christo naturarum unionem apertè negarunt, sic ipsi eandem per negationem veræ κοινωνίας enervant dubiamq; reddunt. Aut ergò agnoscant tandem nobiscum veram subsistentiæ & naturarum κοινωνίαν, aut fateantur sibi meritò errorem Samosatenicum de negatâ unione hypostaticâ objici, cùm unum firmiter conseqvatur ex alio.

XXXIX. Cæterùm hîc probè observandum, 1. unionem personalem & communionem naturarum simpliciter unum idemq; non esse, sed certis respectibus modisq; differre. Differunt n. 1. ordine, qvo unio antecedit communionem. 2. naturarum habitudine. In unione qvippe habent se naturæ magis passivè, in communione magis activè. Ibi n. dicimus duas naturas uniri, hîc dicuntur invicem communicare.

XL. 2. Notandum communionem naturarum unionis personalis formam esse & non esse, diverso respectu: non qvidem logicam, qvoniam naturæ non uniuntur vel personam unam constituunt qvatenus participant; sed metaphysicam, qvatenus ad perfectam descriptionem modi, qvo unio illa facta est, necessariò refertur.

XLI. 3. Animadvertendum, Communionem naturarum diverso respectu unionis personalis consequens esse & non esse. Esse, si unio sumatur formaliter & præcisè pro solo naturarum concursu ad unum ὑφισάμενον, quia iste concursus naturâ prior est ipso naturarum μετοχῇ. Participare n. invicem non possent, nisi prius in unâ ὑποστάσει concurrerent. Conseq. non est, si unio sumatur pro tota qvidditate & omnibus reqvisitis ad plenam ejus descriptionem pertinentibus. Sic n. communio ingreditur unionis constitutionem, qvia refertur ad modi explicationem. Ideoq́; sicuti modus rei effectum ejus commodè dici neqvit, ita & de κοινωνίᾳ illa naturarum respectu unionis statuendum est.

XLII. Enafcitur ex dictis qvæstio, an non tandem aliqva inter nos & adversarios concordia quoad hanc κοινωνίας controversiam iniri possit? Ubi reperiuntur benè multi, qvi simpliciter negativam tutantur, aliqvi qvi affirmativam defensitant.

XLIII. Diffiteri hîc non possum, utriusq; factionis adversarios exprefsè fateri, se nobiscum consentire per omnia. Videantur Heidelbergenses im ausführlichen Bericht c. 1. p. 10. p. 150. 151. Trelcatius junior l. 2. Instit. loco 4. p. 73. & p. 78. Greg. de Valentia tom. 4. disp. 1. qvæst. 2. Bus. in Apol. c. 4. p. 44. p. 52. 69. 78. 80. 82. & 83.

XLIV. Verùm utinam non aliud lingva promtum, aliud animo gererent reconditum! Si n. nostræ subscribunt sententiæ, cur hypotheses communionem tollentes astruunt & defendunt? cur unionem non per περιχώρησιν, sed per solam παρέκφασιν λόγε & sustentationem carnis describunt? cur non pauci illorum veram communicationem ὑποστάσεως divinæ inficiantur? cur unionem plerumq; confundunt? cur communionem veram simpliciter negant? cur multi illorum communionem exponunt de sola nudaq; concomitantia? cur prædicationes personales suis glossematibus penitùs pervertunt? cur ἰδιοποιΐαν qvæ immediatè fluit ex κοινωνίᾳ per ἀλλοίωσιν enervant? cur deniq; Eutychianismi nos præter jus & fas accusare non erubescunt? cùm talem confusionem ipsimet respumus & aspernemur.

XLV. Corrigant proinde lingvam & mentem Antagonistæ nostri, & nuncium consignatis mittant absurditatibus. Id si fecerint candidè, perspicuè, sine dolo & fuco, tum Christianus & stabilis in hac qvidem controversia consensus cum iis poterit iniri. Secus sifiat, & absurdissimis istis hypothes. valedicere si nolint, valeat illorum personatus consensus, valeat talis concordia, qvâ conscientiæ constringuntur, fideiq; articuli destruuntur. Longè etenim melior, teste Bernhardo, ea est discordia, qvæ nos Deo jungit, qvàm pax qvæ nos ab eodem separat.

XLVI. Et hæc brevitatis gratiâ, qvam Cynosuræ ad instar unicè observare debemus, de verâ duarum in Christo naturarum κοινωνίᾳ ὡς ἐν τύπῳ delineasse sufficiat. Coronidis tandem loco abducamus animos â discursu, & communionis naturarum usum paulò rimemur altiùs.

XLVII. Aperit se hîc abyssus divini amoris profundissima. Ecce enim, ô Homo, ut se æternus λόγος verus Deus ex merâ gratiâ in genus hominum humiliat? ut se totum cum omni plenitudine carni nostræ communicat? Qvid es ô homo? Ante ortum sperma fœtidum, post eum saccus stercorum, in occasu cibus vermium, imò naturâ filius iræ per peccatum; Deus tamen per ineffabilem suam bonitatem in gratiam redit cum perdita & depressa natura tuâ, & suæ illam naturæ facit participem. O rem omni prædicatione sublimiorem! O inexhausta misericordiæ divinæ viscera! Exulta ob id & jubila, pie Christicola. Hæc κοινωνία tua sit turris firmissima in adversitatibus, ancora solidissima in tentationibus, petra certissima in mortis etiam agonibus. Ita enim licet peccato â Deo tuo divulsus fueris; redderis tamen illi conjunctissimus, & suo etiam modo divinæ κοινωνὸς naturæ. O terq; qvaterq; beatos, qvi in gloriosum hocce divinæ communionis evehuntur consortium!

XLIIX. Ob oculos 2. nobis ponit signumHonoris nostri evidentissimum. Ecqvi n. dignitas nobis major potuisset contingere, qvàm qvæ per veram Deitatis communionem nostræ contigit naturæ? Sublimis qvidem honor est, fateor, collocari apud Principes: magnus, qvòd Pharao suum Josepho communicavit annulum; major, qvòd Rex Ahasverus comtemtam Famulam Estheram in regium recepit thalamum. Rex enimRegum æternus DEI filius carnem nostram, carnem terream & mortalem in intimum suæ naturæ recipit consortium, omnemq; divinam majestatem illi pariter communem fecit. O dignitatẽ incomparabilem, ô gloriam ineffabilem! Hisce lætare, hisce te erige, ô generose Mikrokosme, licet â mundo ridearis, à malo affligaris, â Satana tribuleris, tamen in hoc triumpha, qvòd caro tua sit consors divinitatis & longè super angelicam elata gloriam.

XLIX. Suggerit tandem hæc meditatio nobis verum moris hæretici exemplum, qvi teste Irenæo inter cætera in hoc consistit, ut ὅμοια μὲν λαλῶσι, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονῶσι. Et perinde ut venator, qvò feras commodiùs valeat decipere, pellam induit ferinam, sic Hæretici, cumprimis Sacramentarii & Romanenses (uti liqvet ex superiorib.) ovinæ se involvunt, ut ita faciliùs simplices oviculas in fraudem qveant impellere. In illorum enim ore mel, in corde fel; in dictis laus, in factis fraus; amicitias expetunt, insidias fabricant. O igitur extremè versutos pessimósq; Homines! Hæc nunqvam non perpende, ô grex Christi pusillule, vigila & cave ab illorum versutiâ, fuge ceu cane pejus & angve blandiloqva illorum consortia, imis & devotis illud Johanniticum ingemiscens suspiriis, Conserva me Domine in veritate, verbum tuum est Veritas.

L. Atq; hæc hâc vice de verâ naturarum in Christo duarum κοινωνίᾳ sobriè & piè placuit differere; sicq; optatum portum firmâ rate attigimus. Amoris nostri oceano recens nato Jesulo sit laus, & gloria ejus inter nos vivat & vigeat æviterna, Amen.


## 12 Twelfth Disputation, On Personal Predications

From the Communication of Natures flow the Predications, in which one nature is predicated of the other, the divine of the human, and vice versa: some such are read in Scripture a; to which these ecclesiastical ones are equivalent: GOD is man; Man is GOD. Those are called mystical, on account of the huge mystery which they involve: unusual, because they fit no mode of predicating: personal, because they result from the Personal Union. Much has been disputed about these. The whole matter can be resolved in nine distinct questions.

1. Who ought to pass judgment on those matters, the Philosopher or the Theologian? We attribute the judicial role to the Theologian. 2. Are those predications merely verbal? They are most real. 3. What is predicated in Personal [predications], whether Person of Person, or Nature of Person, or indeed Nature of Nature? We affirm the latter. 4. Is a disparate [term] predicated of a disparate [term] in Personal Predications? We affirm it. 5. Are Personal Predications and ought they to be called Paronymous? 6. Can they be reduced analogously to Paronymous [predications]? 7. In what sense are they called Unusual? 8. Can I say in the abstract, Humanity is the DEUS λόγος; and again, the λόγος is Humanity. 9. Can CHRIST be called man and, according to his human Nature, the natural Son of GOD?

Concerning the four prior questions, because they have been dealt with abundantly in the Sober Philosophy by the Mr. President, I propose nothing now; however, I add my vote to his definitive opinion in all of them. But we shall now deal with the five later chapters. Do thou, gracious GOD, favor our endeavors.

Thesis I.

The term Paronymous Predication, because it is ambiguous; it must be known that it is taken by some generally and improperly for every predication in which the predicate is not of the essence but outside the essence of the subject; by others specifically and properly, for a Proper and Usual predication, in which, on account of a union that is especially accidental, a Denominative [term] is contingently enunciated of a subject, which nevertheless is really distinct from the Denominator. II. With this presupposed, we respond to the question in two ways. I. Personal predications can be called Denominative in the former sense. It is better, however, to abstain from that phrase than to use it. III. For who would be so insane as to call such predications Synonymous, or, which is the same thing, to say that the assumed man is of the essence of the assuming λόγος? But since the Predicate is not of the essence of the subject, this Predication could indeed be called Paronymous in an abusive sense: if, namely, Nature is predicated of Nature; but not if in the subject the whole suppositum or Person is posited; because there in reality another Nature, which is predicated, enters into the constitution of the whole suppositum, nor is it outside its essence.

IV. But however they may be said in this way, it is nevertheless better to abstain from that formula of speaking, for these reasons. 1. because that formula of speaking is clearly new, unknown to orthodox Theologians and the Formula of Concord.

V. Nor is there any reason for anyone to object with Scheckius and the Württemberg Theologians, who call these predications accidental personal ones. For the Württemberg Theologians themselves call Scheckius perplexed and obscure, a Gerlachius rejects the authority of Scheckius in particular: nor do they call them personal in that way, but propositions in the third kind of Communication, when a divine idiom is predicated of the human nature, as The human nature of Christ is everywhere; for what purpose, however, they call them accidentally personal, they indicate a little later c, nay, they argue that these are Unusual d, how therefore will they call them Paronymical?

VI. 2. because it is Inconvenient, for if received (1) it will accuse us of inconstancy, who have hitherto fought for the Unusual as if for hearth and home, and now we ourselves wish to reduce Personal ones to ordinary modes. (2) It will provide hiding places for adversaries: Both for the Calvinists, who will say they never disputed otherwise against the unusual; especially Beza, with his Relative Predication, which he brings against Hoffmann a and which Goclenius afterwards also defends b; And Keckermann, who brings forward certain Improper External Analogical Predications, c and indeed expressly designates personal ones as Paronymical d. And for the Papists, to whom we will no longer be able to object Personal ones, and therefore they will more easily obtain their Transubstantiation with this argument: That disparate things cannot be predicated of each other otherwise, unless it happens either Figuratively or by Transubstantiation.

VII. 3. It opens a wide gate to Reason: While those will no longer be thought Mystical, nor simply Unusual, but proper, congruent with Logical modes of Predicating and Usual.

VIII. 4. It is not necessary: Because we have hitherto fought quite successfully against adversaries; although this term was clearly unknown, to say nothing of how by its reception the state of the controversy is changed, and new contentious questions and λογομαχίαι (word-battles) are stirred up. Therefore our conclusion previously posited stands.

IX. Now follows thesis 11. Personal Predications in the second, special, and proper sense are not, nor ought they to be called, Paronymous. Before this thesis is established, it must be known beforehand: 1. Denominatives are sometimes called by some 'Denominated', sometimes 'Denominating', but with a different respect. Denominated passively with respect to the denominating word or abstract (which nevertheless ought to differ really from the Denominative) from which they have the name, as 'strong' from 'strength'. Denominating actively with respect to the denominated subject, of which the denominative is predicated, and to which it attributes its denomination; thus 'strong' is denominating, because it denominates its subject, Samson. It is better, however, for the abstract or accidental form to be called the Denominating, and the subject itself the Denominated; but the Denominative is the Concrete [formed] from the accidental form and the subject.

X. Next, it must be observed that we here understand the Denominative by word and signification at the same time, and consider no Predication to be Paronymous unless the Denominative is in the predicate.

XI. These things having been premised for the sake of clarity, we shall confirm our thesis, partly from Theological principles, partly from Philosophical.

XII. 1. Let these be the Theological hypotheses. 1. Paronymous predications are Logical, Proper, or Usual, and therefore can be reduced to the ordinary mode of predicating: Personal [predications] are not such, by the consent of all the orthodox. Therefore, Personal [predications] are not Paronymous.

XIII. They object, indeed, that Paronymous [predications] are a genus of Proper [predications], not a species, and that they themselves are divided into Proper, Figurative, and Unusual. Resp. This is unheard of in the schools of the philosophers, and no one can be brought forward who has even made mention of Figurative Paronymous [predications]. Furthermore, Theologians understand as 'Proper' all those which are divided into Univocal and Denominative.

XIV. They continue: Affirmative [predications] are divided into Proper, Figurative, and Unusual. Therefore, Paronymous [predications] can also be divided in this way. For just as an Affirmative proposition is so called because of the formal reason of the predication, so it is called Denominative because of the same [reason]. R. The reason is disparate; the division of Predication into Negative and Affirmative is merely formal without respect to the things. this, however, into Synonymical and Paronymical, is not purely formal, but rather material, founded not on the formal disposition of subject and predicate, but on the mode of being.

XV. They reply thirdly, that Personal [propositions] are called unusual, not by reason of the formal mode, but by reason of Material Modes, because they are neither Necessary nor Contingent. Resp. There is error here in many ways. 1. For we deny that that distinction of predications into Synonymical and Paronymical is made only by reason of the Formal mode. For if this were posited, it could be expressed by letters, as is done in the prior books of Aristotle's Analytics. 2. By the appellation of Unusual, all formal and material modes are excluded. 3. Thus would be introduced the scholastic reduction of all Propositions to regular modes, which is vain and impossible

XVI. 2. All Denominative [predications] are accidental: No Personal predication is accidental, nor can it be reduced to it. Therefore, Mystical [predications] are not Denominative.

XVII. 3. In Mystical Predications, disparate things are predicated. In Paronymical ones, however, not disparate but agreeing things. b.

XVIII. 4. Man and GOD, Bread and Body in Mystical predications are Synonymical terms. Therefore, with those placed in the position of predicate, a Paronymical predication cannot be made.

XIX. 2. We prove our thesis from Philosophical principles. 1. Paronyms are those which indeed attribute a name to a subject, but not a definition, nay, not even the name in the nominative case. Personal predicates attribute to their subjects both the name and the definition and in the nominative case. Therefore, they are not Paronyms: Nor are personal predications Paronymical.

XX. 2. The Denominative and the Denominating always differ really and essentially. Man and Humanity, GOD and Deity do not really differ. Therefore, they are not Denominative.

XXI. 3. No predicate of a Denominative Predication is a substantial and absolute term. The predicates of Personal predications are substantial absolute terms. Therefore.

XXII. 4. Every Denominative predication is made into a quality; In Mystical Predications it is not asked what kind of thing GOD is man, or what kind of thing man is GOD. Therefore.

XXIII. 5. No Denominative predication is reciprocated while remaining in the same kind of predication. In Personal [propositions] let there be such a reciprocity. For it is the same kind of predicating when I say, GOD is man: and Man is GOD. E.

XXIV. 6. Every mode of paronymous predication is founded upon an accidental mode of being. But Personal [predications] are not founded upon an accidental mode of being, because a Personal union is not accidental. E.

XXV. 7. Hence the predicate of every Denominative Predication is a Predicable accident, whether it be a Property or a Common [attribute]. But in Personal [predications] such a predicate is not [the case]. E.

XXVI. 8. If for a paronymous predicate some kind of union is required, and the constitution of the predicate outside the essence of the subject. Why could I not also say of ignited iron, Fire is iron, and of an animated body, Body is soul, paronymously? Truly there is no paronymy here, E. nor there.

XXVII. Some object here. (1) If Personal predications fit no mode and are not Logical; it would follow that they are ἀλόγους and absurd. Resp. 1. Although those modes of predicating are not strictly Logical, they nevertheless have the general attributes of Logical predication; they consist of a Subject and a Predicate, and they are Affirmative. 2. There is no consequence; they are unusual and not Logical E. [therefore] Absurd. For besides the habitual Logic in our mind, there is given a divine λόγος, and the Logic of the Holy Spirit, in which these are most logical.

XXVIII. (2). When I say, A certain animal is Man, or a certain white thing is man. The predication is Paronymous. And nevertheless in the former no term is Paronymous; in the latter the predicate is Synonymous. Resp. 1. Distinguish between Regular, Ordered, and natural Predications, and Irregular, Disordered, and preternatural ones, such as these are. The former are partly Synonymous and partly Paronymous. The latter are neither Synonymous nor Paronymous. 2. None of the propositions brought forward is Paronymous; indeed, they can rather be considered as Synonymous. 3. It has not yet been defined by the Scholastics themselves what kind they are.

XXIX. (3). If a Paronym can be predicated Univocally. E. and a Synonym can be predicated Denominatively. But the former is true, as is evident, if a difference is predicated. E. and the latter. Resp. There is a contradiction in the adjective, for something to be predicated not paronymously, and yet to be a Paronym. The predication remains Paronymous when I say, man is rational, because I do not say, man is reason. They press and bring forward predications in which the essential idioms of divinity are predicated of GOD, as when I say, GOD is omnipotent. Resp. Those predications are extraordinary, not synonymous, but identical.

XXX. (4). They say GOD and man are predicated in the concrete, not divinity and humanity in the abstract. Therefore, they are predicated denominatively. Resp. The consequence is not valid. For both genera and species are predicated in the concrete and by concrete terms, and yet they are predicated univocally. Furthermore, some concretes are substantial, as man; others are accidental, as strong. The latter make a paronymous predication, not the former.

Latin:

EX Communicatione Naturarum fluunt Prædicationes, in qvibus una Natura prædicatur de alterâ, divina de humanâ, & contra: tales leguntur in scriptura aliqvot a; qvibus Ecclesiasticæ istæ æqvipollent, DEUS est homo; Homo est DEUS. Dicuntur illæ Mysticæ, ob ingens mysterium, qvod involvunt: Inusitatæ, qvòd ad nullum prædicandi modum qvadrent: Personales, qvia ex Unione Personali resultant. De his multa disputata sunt. Res tota distinctis qvæstionibus novem absolvi potest.

1. Qujnam de illis ferre debeat judicium, an Philosophus, an Theologus? Theologo partes judiciarias nos attribuimus. 2. Num prædicationes illæ tantùm verbales sint? sunt realissimæ. 3. Quid prædicetur in Personalibus, an Persona de Persona, an Natura de Persona, an verò Natura de Natura? Posterius affirmamus. 4. Num in Prædicationibus Personalibus disparatum de disparato prædicetur? Affirmamus. 5. An Prædicationes Personales sint & vocari debeant Paronymicæ? 6. An ἀναλόγως reduci possint ad Paronymicas? 7. Quo sensu dicantur Inusitatæ? 8. An possum in abstracto dicere, Humanitas est DEUS λόγ©; & rursum λόγos est Humanitas. 9. An CHRISTUS homo & secundum humanam Naturam Naturalis DEI filius dici possit?

De qvatuor qvæstionibus prioribus, qvia in Philosophia sobria abunde actum â Dn. Præside, jam nihil propono, sententiæ tamen ipsius definitivæ in omnibus calculum adjicio. De qvinq; vero posterioribus capitibus jam agemus. Tu precor alme DEUS conatibus annue nostris.

Thesis I.

Terminus Prædicationis Paronymicæ, qvia ambiguus; sciendum, â qvibusdam sumi illum γενικῶς & καταχρησικῶς, pro omni Prædicatione, in qva prædicatum non est de essentia scd extra essentiam subjecti: â qvibusdam ἐιδικῶς & Propriè, pro prædicatione Propria & Usitata, in qvâ ob unionem præsertim accidentalem contingenter de subjecto enunciatur Denominativum, qvod tamen â Denominante distinctum est realiter. II. Hoc præsupposito ād qvæstionem dupliciter respondemus. I. Prædicationes Personales priori sensu appellari possunt Denominativæ. Meliùs tamen ab ea phrasi abstinere, quàm ea uti. III. Qvis enim tam amens sit, ut talés prædicationes Synonymicas, vel qvod idem est, hominem assumtum de essentiâ λόγʊ assumentis esse dicat? Qvoniam verò Prædicatum non est de essentia subjecti, dici sanè posset sensu abusivo Paronymica hæc Prædicatio: si videlicet Natura de Natura prædicetur; non verò si in subjecto totum suppositum sive Persona ponatur; quia ibi revera altera Natura, quæ prædicatur, ingreditur constitutionem totius suppositi, neq; extra ipsius est essentiam.

IV. Verùm utut sic dici possint, melius tamen est, ab ista loqvendi formula abstinere, has ob causas. 1. quia ista loqvendi formula planè est nova, Theologis orthodoxis & Formulæ Concordiæ incognita.

V. Nec est ut qvis objiciat Scheckium & Theologos Würtenpergenses, qvi prædicationes has per accidens personales vocant. Ipsi enim Theologi Würtenpergenses Scheckium perplexum & obscurum dicunt, a Gerlachius b Scheckii autoritatem in specie rejicit: nec personales ita vocant, sed propositiones in tertio genere Communicationis, qvando de humana natura prædicatur divinum idioma, ut Humana Christi natura est ubiq;; qvo fine autem per accidens personales vocent, indicant paulo post c, imò disputant has esse Inusitatas d, qvomodo ergò Paranymicas vocabunt?

VI. 2. quia est Incommoda, recepta enim (1) accusabit nos inconstantiæ, qvi pro Inusitatis hactenus tanqvam pro aris & focis dimicavimus, jam ipsi Personales ad modos ordinarios reducere volumus. (2) Adversariis latibula suppeditabit: Tum Calvinianis, qvi contra inusitatas nunqvam aliter se disputâsse dicent; præsertim Bezæ, cum suâ Prædicatione Relativa, qvam contra Hoffmannum a affert & postea etiam Goclenius defendit b; Et Keckermanno afferenti Prædicationes qvasdam Improprias Externas Analogicas, c imo personales expressè Paronymicas indigitanti d. Tum Pontificiis, qvibus Personales oggerere non poterimus amplius ideoq; suam Transsubstantiationem facilius obtinebunt hoc argumento: Qvod disparata aliter de se non possint prædicari, nisi fiat vel Figuratè vel per Transsubstantiationem.

VII. 3. Rationi latam portam pandit: Dum illæ non amplius Mysticæ, nec simpliciter Inusitatæ, sed propriæ, modis Prædicandi Logicis congruæ & Usitatæ, putabuntur.

VIII. 4. Non est necessaria: Qvia sat feliciter hactenus contra adversarios pugnavimus; licet hic terminus planè ignotus fuerit, Ut nihil dicam, qvomodo receptione ejus status controversiæ antiqvus mutetur, novæq; qvæstiones rixosæ & λογομαχίαι excitentur. Stat ergo conclusio nostra antea posita.

IX. Seqvitur jam thesis 11. Personales Prædicationes sensu secundo speciali & proprio non sunt nec appellari debent Paronymicæ. Anteqvam hæc thesis stabiliatur, prænoscendum, 1. Denominativa â qvibusdam dici nonnunqvam Denominata, nonnunqvam Denominantia, verum diverso respectu. Denominata Passivè respectu vocis denominantis sive abstracti (qvod tamen â Denominativo debet differre realiter) â qvo nomen habent, ut fortis â fortitudine. Denominantia Activè respectu subjecti denominati, de qvo prædicatur denominativum, & cui suam denominationem tribuit, sic forte est denominans, qvia denominat suum subjectum Simsonem. Melius tamen est Denominans dici abstractum sive formam accidentalem, Denominatum ipsum subjectum: Denominativum verò Concretum ex forma accidentali & subjecto.

X. Deinde observandum, nos hic Denominativum voce & significatione simul intelligere & Prædicationem Paronymicam putare nullam nisi in prædicato sit Denominativum.

XI. His perspicuitatis gratiâ præmissis, thesin nostram confirmabimus, ex principiis partim Theologicis, partim Philosophicis.

XII. 1. Theologicæ hypotheses hæ sint. 1. Prædicationes paronymicæ sunt Logicæ, Propriæ aut Usitatæ, adeóq; ad prædicandi modum ordinarium reduci qveunt: Personales non sunt tales, consensu omnium orthodoxorum. E. Personales non sunt Paronymicæ.

XIII. Objiciunt qvidem, Paronymicas esse genus Propriarum, non speciem, dividíq; ipsas in Proprias, Figuratas & Inusitatas. Resp. Inauditum hoc in scholis Philosophorum, & nullus adduci poterit, qvi Paronymicarum Figuratarum mentionem saltem fecerit. Deinde Theologi Proprias intelligunt omnes illas, qvæ dividuntur in Univocas & Denominativas.

XIV. Pergunt: Affirmativæ dividuntur in Proprias, Figuratas & Inusitatas. E. & Paronymicæ sic possunt dividi. Nam ut propositio Affirmativa dicitur propter formalem rationē prædicationis, ita propter eandē appellatur Denominativa. R. Dispar est ratio, Divisio Prædicationis in Negativā & Affirmativā merè est formalis sine respectu ad res: hæc verò in Synonymicam & Paronymicam, non purè formalis est, sed potius materialis, fundata non in formali subjecti & prædicati dispositione, sed in modo essendi.

XV. Regerunt tertiò, Personales dici inusitatas, non ratione modi formalis, sed ratione Modorum Materialium, quia nec sint Necessariæ nec Contingentes. Resp. peccari hic multipliciter. 1. enim negamus distinctionem illam prædicationum in Synonymicas & Paronymicas fieri tantum ratione modi Formalis. Hoc enim posito, posset literis exprimi, ut fit in priorum Analyticorū libris Aristotelis. 2. Excluduntur appellatione Inusitatarum modi omnes formales & materiales. 3. Introduceretur sic scholastica omnium Propositionum ad modos regulares reductio, quæ vana & impossibilis

XVI. 2. Omnes Denominativæ sunt accidentales: Nulla prædicatio Personalis est accidentalis, nec ad eam reduci a potest. E. Mysticæ non sunt Denominativæ.

XVII. 3. In Prædicationibus Mysticis disparata prædicantur. In Paronymicis verò non disparata sed consentanea. b.

XVIII. 4. Homo & DEUS, Panis & Corpus in prædicationibus Mysticis sunt termini Synonymici. E. Illis prædicati loco positis Prædicatio paronymica fieri nequit.

XIX. 2. Ex Philosophicis principiis thesin nostram evincimus. 1. Paronyma sunt quæ subjecto quidem tribuunt nomen, sed non definitionem, imo nec nomen in casu recto. Prædicata personalia subjectis suis tribuunt & nomen & definitionem & in casu recto. E. Nec sunt Paronyma: Nec prædicationes personales Paronymicæ.

XX. 2. Denominativum & Denominans semper realiter & essentialiter differunt. Homo & Humanitas, DEUS & Deitas realiter non differunt. E. Non sunt Denominativa.

XXI. 3. Nullum prædicatum Denominativæ Prædicationis est terminus substantialis & absolutus. Personalium prædicationum prædicata sunt termini substantiales absoluti. E.

XXII. 4. Omnis Denominativa prædicatio fit in quale; In Mysticis Prædicationibus non quæritur qualis sit DEUS homo, aut qualis homo DEUS. E.

XXIII. 5. Nulla Denominativa prædicatio reciprocatur manente eodem genere prædicationis. In Personalibus talis sit reciprocatio. Idem enim est genus prædicandi, cum dico, DEUS est homo: & Homo est DEUS. E.

XXIV. 6. Omnis modus prædicandi Paronymus fundatur in modo essendi accidentali. Personales verò non fundantur in modo essendi accidentali, quia unio Personalis non est accidentalis. E.

XXV. 7. Hinc omnis Denominativæ Prædicationis prædicatum est accidens Prædicabile, sive Proprium sive Commune. Sed in Personalibus prædicatum tale non est. E.

XXVI. 8. Siad prædicatum Paronymum reqviritur qvaliscunq; unio, & Prædicati extra essentiam subjecti constitutio. Cur non possem etiam dicere de ferro ignito, Ignis est ferrum, & corpore animato, Corpus est anima, Paronymicè. Verum hic nulla paronymia, E. nec ibi.

XXVII. Objiciunt hic aliqvi. (1) Si prædicationes Personales ad nullum modum qvadrant & Logicæ non sunt; seqveretur, illas esse ἀλόγυς & absurdas. Resp. 1. Licèt illi prædicandi modi propriè Logici non sint, generalia tamen habent prædicationis Logicæ attributa, constant Subjecto, Prædicato, sunt Affirmativæ. 2. Nulla est conseqventia, sunt Inusitatæ & non Logicæ E. Absurdæ. Nam præter Logicam habitualem in mente nostra, datur λόγος divinus, & Logica Spiritus S. in qvâ istæ sunt λογικώταται.

XXVIII. (2). Cum dico, Quoddam animal est Homo, vel quoddam album est homo. Prædicatio est Paronymica. Et nihilominus in priori nullus terminus est Paronymus; in posteriori prædicatum est Synonym. Resp. 1. Dist. inter Prædicationes Regulares, Ordinatas & secundum Naturam, & Irregulares, Inordinatas & præter naturam, qvales hæ sunt. Priores partim sunt Synonymicæ partim Paronymicæ. Posteriores nec Synonymicæ nec Paronymicæ. 2. Nulla allatarum propositionum est Paronymica, imò potius pro Synonymicis haberi possunt. 3. ab ipsis Scholasticis nondũ est definitum, qvales sint.

XXIX. (3). Si Paronymum potest prædicari Univocè. E. & Synonymum potest prædicari Denominativè. Sed verum prius, ut patet, si prædicatur differentia. E. & posterius. Resp. Contradictio est in adjecto, aliqvid prædicari non παρωνύμως, & tamen Paronymum esse. Paronymica manet prædicatio, cum dico, homo est rationalis, quia non dico, homo est ratio. Instant & afferunt praedicationes in quibus Idiomata essentialia divinitatis de DEO praedicantur, ut cum dico, DEUS est omnipotens. Resp. Illas praedicationes esse Extraordinarias, non Synonymicas, sed Identicas.

XXX. (4). Dicunt DEUM & hominem praedicari in concreto, non divinitatem & humanitatem in abstracto. E. Praedicantur Denominative. Resp. Non valet consequentia. Nam & genera & species praedicantur in Concreto & per vocabula concreta, & tamen Univoce praedicantur. Deinde concreta alia sunt substantialia, ut homo; alia accidentalia; ut fortis. Haec faciunt Praedicationem Paronymicam, non ista.


### This regarding the first question, now follows the second

This regarding the first question, now follows the second.

XXXI. There are therefore those who, overcome by the truth, are forced to admit that mystical predications are not denominative: meanwhile, they think they can nevertheless be reduced in some way and ἀναλόγως to paronymous ones.

XXXII. But we hold rather to the negative, moved by these reasons: 1. because all orthodox theologians seriously urge that we should rather think about the removal of mystical [predications] from all customary modes of predicating than about their reduction: and they do not only urge this, but they expressly deny that they can be reduced.

XXXIII. 2. Because if the opposite can neither be nor ought to be reduced to the opposite species, then certainly unusual ones cannot be reduced to any species of the customary opposites.

XXXIV. 3. Because in every reduction a certain agreement is required of that which is reduced with that to which it is reduced, especially in the principal requirement. But personal [predications] have no agreement with denominative ones, since in them there is no paronymous term, which is the principal requirement of denominative ones. They press that there is this agreement between personal and paronymous predications, that the predicate of both is outside the essence of the subject. But this alone does not suffice for paronymous ones; but furthermore, it is required that the other term be paronymous.

XXXV. 4. Because thus we would imitate the Jesuits and Calvinists, some of whom wished them to be reduced to synonymous ones; others to paronymous ones, which, however, has always been contradicted by our theologians, especially by Chemnitz and Hoffmann part. 1. on the use of logical notions q. 7. p. 85. 115.

XXXVI. 5. Because if any kind of similarity and agreement were the cause of reduction, Personal Predications could no less be reduced to Univocal ones, because the terms in them are synonymous. But it is absurd that one Predication can be reduced to two contrary species. Indeed, they would rather be reduced to Synonymical ones, because they have more of the requirements of Synonymical ones; therefore, Personal ones cannot even be reduced ἀναλόγως (analogically) to Paronymous ones.

XXXVII. As regards the third question, we answer very briefly. They are called unusual not only by reason of the Union, such as is not given in the whole of nature, nor only by reason of the special Material Modes, but also of the general Material Modes, Univocal and Paronymous. For they are not Logical, not Proper or Usual, unknown to all Philosophers as to the mode of predicating, not reducible especially to accidental ones, in which mere disparates are predicated, expressed by synonymous words, nor yet either συνωνύμως (synonymously) or παρωνύμως (paronymously).

XXXIIX. As regards the fourth question, the Württemberg Theologians and especially Gerlach hold the affirmative for the following reasons. 1. Because to those words of John ch. 1 v. 14, The Word was made flesh, these are equivalent, the λόγος (Word) is Flesh. Now Flesh here is not a Concrete, but an abstract, and the same as humanity. Which is proved thus, because the word Flesh cannot be resolved into any abstract: nor could I otherwise argue from the word Flesh in John 6 v. 55 for abstractives, which our Theologians nevertheless do; finally, Flesh is never put in the Nominative case with Christ; for I do not say flesh Christ, but flesh of Christ, which denotes an abstractive.

XXXIX. 2. The words Humanity and Man are synonyms here, and by humanity is signified the concrete, namely man with accidents and properties. a.

XL. 3. Because the Fathers speak thus b. Thus our more recent Theologians, Creator is Creature, c. and conversely: Flesh is GOD the Word. Flesh is the second Person of the Trinity. d. Flesh is GOD the Word, and conversely: The human nature of Christ is the Son of GOD. e. Thus the adversaries themselves speak, Flesh is God on account of the Word, f.

XLI. Busæus objects, g. GOD is one at the same time, and three, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But the Humanity is GOD. Therefore. Resp. 1. By insisting, GOD is One and three, the λόγος is GOD. Therefore. 2. The term GOD is taken either Essentially or Personally; in the former way it is taken in the major premise, in the latter in the minor.

XLII. He continues. If the Humanity is GOD, therefore it is one of the persons of the holy Trinity, equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit. But how could the created be equal to the Uncreated? Resp. No equalization of Natures follows, because the human nature by reason of itself remains a creature, not at all equal to GOD: yet Personally and unusually it is rightly said that the λόγος is he who is equal to the Father. This Predication therefore is false: The Humanity is equal to the Father; but that one is true, The Humanity is the λόγος, who is equal to the Father: because equality is an attribute of the λόγος, not truly of the flesh.

XLIII. He proceeds: a If the Humanity is rightly called GOD, it follows that conversely the Deity could be called man. Resp. It is granted, but to those who defend abstractive [terms]. For just as the Union is reciprocal, so also is the Personal Predication. Furthermore, God the λόγος and the Deity of the λόγος are clearly the same thing: and if it is rightly said that the divinity is incarnate, why would it not be said that the flesh is?

XLIV. Meanwhile, however, it is more advisable to use these abstractive locutions sparingly, or rather to abstain from them entirely; since Scripture does not use them, since they are scandalous and easily exposed to the cavils of adversaries, and indeed are not necessary: as Hutterus advises. b.

Latin:

Haec de quaestione prima, sequitur jam secunda.

XXXI. Sunt igitur qui veritate victi fateri coguntur, Praedicationes Mysticas non esse Denominativas: Interim putant eas aliquo tamen modo & ἀναλόγως ad Paronymicas reduci posse.

XXXII. Verum Negativam potius tenemus, moti his rationibus: 1. quia omnes Theologi orthodoxi serio suadent, a ut potius cogitemus de Mysticarum abductione ab omnibus praedicandi modis Usitatis, quam de earum reductione: nec suadent hoc solum, verum reduci posse expresse negant.

XXXIII. 2. Quia si oppositum nec potest nec debet ad speciem oppositam reduci, utiq; nec Inusitatae ad ullam Usitatarum oppositarum speciem reduci poterunt.

XXXIV. 3. Quia in omni reductione reqviritur quaedam convenientia illius quod reducitur cum illo ad quod reducitur, praesertim in reqvisito principali. Sed Personales nullam convenientiam habent cum Denominativis, cum in illis nullus sit terminus Paronymus, quod principale reqvisitum Denominativarum. Instant, illam esse convenientiam Personalium Praedicationum & Paronymicarum, quod utriusq; praedicatum sit extra essentiam subjecti. At non sufficit hoc tantum ad Paronymicas; sed insuper istud reqviritur, ut terminus alter sit Paronymus.

XXXV. 4. Quia sic imitaremur Jesuitas & Calvinianos, qvarum alii a eas reduci voluerunt ad Synonymicas; alii ad Paronymicas, quibus tamen a nostratibus Theologis semper contradictum, præsertim Chemnitio & Hoffmanno part. 1. de usu notit. Logic. q. 7. p. 85. 115.

XXXVI. 5. Qvia si qvaliscunq; similitudo & convenientia causa esset reductionis, Prædicationes Personales non minus ad Univocas possent reduci, qvia termini in ipsis sunt Synonymi. Sed absurdum, unam Prædicationem ad duas contrarias species reduci posse. Imo potius ad Synonymicas reducerentur, qvia plura Synonymicarum reqvisita habent, Personales ergò nec ἀναλόγως reduci possunt ad Paronymicas.

XXXVII. Tertiam qvæstionem qvod attinet, respondemus brevissimè. Inusitatæ dicuntur non tantũ ratione Unionis, qvalis in tota naturâ non datur, nec tantum ratione Modorum Materialium specialium sed & modorum Materialium generalium Univoci & Paronymici. Sunt enim non Logicæ, non Propriæ vel Usitatæ, omnibus Philosophis qvoad modum prædicandi ignotæ, non reducibiles præsertim ad accidentales, inqvibus prædicantur mera disparata vocabulis Synonymicis expressa, neq; tamen vel συνωνύμως vel παρωνύμως.

XXXIIX. Qvartam qvæstionem qvod respectat, Theologi Würtenbergenses & præsertim Gerlachius affirmativam tenet ob seqventes rationes. 1. Qvia illi Johanneæ c. 1. v. 14. Verbum caro factum est, æqvivalent ista, λόγος est Caro. Jam Caro hic non estConcretum, sed abstractum, idemqve qvod humanitas. Qvod ita probatur, qvia vox Carnis in nullum abstractum resolvi potest: nec aliâs ex vocabulo Carnis argumentari possem Joh. 6. vers. 55. pro abstractivis, qvod tamen nostri Theologi faciunt; deniq; Caro nunqvam in casu Recto ponitur cum Christo; non enim dico caro Christus, sed caro Christi, qvod abstractivum notat.

XXXIX. 2. Vox Humanitas & Homo hic sunt Synonyma, significaturq; per humanitatem concretum, qvippe homo cum accidentibus & proprietatibus. a.

XL. 3. Qvia sic Patres loqvuntur b. Sic recentiores nostri Theologi, Creator est Creatura, c. & contra: Caro est DEUS Verbum. Caro est secunda Persona Trinitatis. d. Caro est DEUS Verbum, & contra: Humana Christi natura est Filius DEI. e. Sic ipsi adversarii loqvuntur, Caro propter Verbum Deus est, f.

XLI. Objicit Busæus, g. DEUS est unus simul, & trinus, Pater Filius & S. S. Ast Humanitas est DEUS. E. Resp. 1. Instando, DEUS est Unus & trinus, λόγος est DEUS E. 2. Vocabulum DEI sumitur vel Essentialiter vel Personaliter, priori modo sumitur in majore, posteriori in minore.

XLII. Pergit. Si Humanitas est DEUS, E. Est una ex personis sanctæ Trinitatis, æqualis Patri & Spiritui Sancto. Sed quomodo creata æqualis esse poterit Increatæ? Resp. Nulla seqvitur Naturarum exæqvatio, qvia humana natura ratione sui esse manet creatura, DEO minimè æqvalis: Personaliter tamen & inusitatè rectè dicitur λόγος esse qui est æqualis Patri. Hæc igitur Prædicatio falsa est. Humanitas æqualis Patri; vera autem illa, Humanitas est λόγος, qui est æqualis Patri: quia æqualitas est attributum λόγου, non verè carnis.

XLIII. Progreditur: a Si Humanitas rectè dicitur DEUS, seqvitur qvod vicissim Deitas dici possit homo. Resp. Conceditur, at iis, qvi abstractivas defendunt. Ut enim Unio est reciproca, ita etiam Personalis Prædicatio. Deinde Deus λόγος & Deitas λόγου planè idem sut: & si recte dicitur divinitas est incarnata, cur ea non diceretur caro?

XLIV. Interim tamen consultius est, hisce abstractivis locutionibus parcè uti, vel potius planè ab iis abstinere; cum nec scriptura illis utatur, cum scandalosæ & cavillis adversariorum facile oppositæ, imo non necessariæ: ut monet Hutterus. b.


### Chapter V. Whether it is rightly said that Christ as man and according to human nature is the natural Son of God

CHAPTER V. Whether it is rightly said that Christ as man and according to human nature is the natural Son of GOD.

XLV. Finally, most of our theologians affirm the fifth question. 1. Because the angel calls the human nature, or the holy thing which shall be born of the virgin, [Son of God] in Luke 1:36, not by essence, but by mere grace and the κοινωνίαν (communion) of natures.

XLVI. 2. Because in Hebrews 1:4-5, Christ is said to have inherited a more excellent name than the angels: what indeed is that? Thou art my Son. And 1 Corinthians 15:45, the second man is called the Lord from heaven, which predicate denotes him as the Son of GOD. 3. Because Christ is one and a unique person, if therefore he were not the Son of GOD according to the flesh, he would not be a unique person but one and another, the Son of GOD and not the Son of GOD. 4. Because Christ according to his humanity sometimes calls GOD Father in Scripture: by virtue of the relation according to the same, therefore, he will be the Son of GOD. For where there is fatherhood, there is Sonship. 5. Finally, not only do the Fathers speak thus, but also the adversaries. XLVII. Let this, however, be noted: the second word here is not taken διαζευκτικῶς (disjunctively), as it is a disjunctive particle, but ἐξηγητικῶς (explanatorily) or δει- κτικῶς (demonstratively), as it is an indicative particle.

XLVIII. Furthermore, because these locutions are dangerous, because they are unnecessary, because they can be expressed more significantly, because they are ἄγραφοι (unscriptural) and ambiguous, we ought not to contend much about them.

XLIX. And thus we have finished the consideration of that ineffable Mystery concerning the two Natures in Christ personally united, giving thanks to GOD for the assistance of the Holy Spirit and venerating the same as suppliants, that He may cause us to progress after the example of Christ in wisdom and grace, to His own glory and our eternal salvation, Amen.

Latin:

CAP. V. An rectè dicatur, Christus qua homo & secundum humana naturā est Naturalis DEI Filius.

XLV. Qvintam deniq; qvæstionem affirmant pleriq; nostratium Theologorum. 1. quia sic humanam naturam sive sanctum quod nascetur ex virgine appellat angelus Luc. 1. 36. non per essentiam, sed meram gratiam & naturarum κοινωνίαν.

XLVI. 2. Qvia Hebr. 1. v. 4, 5. Christus dicitur hæreditasse excellentius nomen angelis: qvod verô illud? Filius meus es tu. Et 1. Cor. 15, 45. Secundus homo dicitur Dominus de cœlo, qvod prædicatum notat ipsum DEI filium. 3. Qvia Christus est unus & unica persona, si igitur non esset secundum carnem DEI filius, non esset unica persona sed alius & alius, DEI filius & non DEI Filius. 4. Qvia Christus secundum humanitatem DEUM in scriptura aliqvoties vocat Patrem: vi igitur relationis secundum eandem erit Filius DEI. Ubi enim paternitas, ibi Filiatio. 5. Deniq; sic non solum loqvuntur Patres, sed & adversarii. XLVII. Hoc tamen notetur, vocabulum secundum hic non sumi διαζευκτικῶς, prout est particula Disjunctiva, sed ἐξηγητικῶς vel δεικτικῶς, prout est particula Indicativa.

XLVIII. Deinde qvia hæ locutiones periculosæ, qvia non necessariæ, qvia significantius exprimi possunt, qvia ἄγραφοι & ambiguæ, de iis dimicare multum non debemus.

XLIX. Atq; sic finivimus considerationem ineffabilis istius Mysterii de duabus in Christo Naturis personaliter unitis, gratias agentes DEO pro assistentia Spiritus S. & eundem venerati supplices, ut nos ad exemplum Christi proficere faciat sapientiâ & gratiâ, in ipsius gloriam nostramq; salutem sempiternam, Amen.


## 13 Thirteenth Disputation, On the Communication of Idioms Considered Generally

In several disputations, the doctrine concerning the two natures in Christ, and their union, and hypostatic communication has been treated thus far; it remains now that the effects of that union be declared, which flow from the union of the natures and the most intimate περιχωρήσει (interpenetration).

II. For after the Union has been effected, the denominations of the natures in the Person of Christ, as well as those of the properties and actions, are enunciated about that one ὑφισταμένῳ (subsistent) in a far different way than if either the λόγος ἀσύνθετος (uncompounded Word) were considered, or the human nature were weighed as subsisting by itself in its own personality.

III. And since we must speak in the Church according to a prescription, as Augustine testifies, not freely like philosophers who use free words; in order that we may express the matter, not wrap it up, and that we may declare and distinctly reveal all things: for that reason it pleases us on this occasion to inquire briefly about those things which will recur more often in the following Disputations. 1. Concerning the word Communication, whether it is to be retained, since it is ἄγραφος (unscriptural). 2. Concerning the terms Abstract and Concrete. 3. What the word Communication denotes. 4. How many kinds of Communication of Idioms there are, whether three or four. 5. What order among these kinds. And finally 6. A Practical Meditation, that also three κοινωνίας or degrees flow from our Mystical Union with Christ, will be added.

IV. OF 1. In the Holy Scriptures this phrase (Communication of Idioms) is not found αὐτολεξεὶ, or literally expressed in so many syllables, yet it is not therefore to be immediately banished from the circle or field of Theological Controversies; because in that case many phrases and forms of speech in Theological Controversies would have to be avoided, even by the adversaries themselves, such as Free will, Sacrament, Trinity, etc.

V. And certainly pious antiquity retained this phrase with serious intent, namely to uncover the ἑτεροδοξίαν of Nestorius concerning the unity of the Person of Christ, for which he substituted duality through the denial of the Communication of Idioms: and the confusion of the Natures and their properties by Eutyches. Here, therefore, the Fathers had to fight against the poison of these men, and separate the precious from the vile: that they might therefore perform this with happier labor, and declare more deeply a matter founded in the Scriptures, they employed this phrase, and thus by this means strove strenuously for the truth.

VI. But because for almost an entire century now, the Calvinist race has waged a sufficiently deadly or ἄσπονδον war with the most beloved Church of Christ, and has sufficiently exercised it both regarding other dogmas and this present one, most experienced Theologians could not but retain this phrase, as handed down from hand to hand; they were brought to this, however, not by any petulant affection for novelty, but as Augustine speaks elegantly and gravely, by the necessity of speaking, on account of the deceits and snares of the Calvinists.

VII. We therefore also judge that this should be used, moved by the following foundations. 1. Because the dogma expressed by this word or phrase has the clearest testimonies of the Scriptures. For as often as the Holy Scriptures assign to the Flesh of Christ actions and works which are proper to the Divine Omnipotence, they always imply by the inference of a good consequence that a κοινωνία of omnipotence has been made to the Flesh of Christ: which if you deny, you then deny the very truth of Scripture. This is evident from all those Divine oracles which to those three classes of the communication of Idioms are recalled: V. C. Phil. 2. v. 9. & 10. The cult of adoration is ascribed to the exalted nature, which we know to be a Divine idiom. But how does this happen? In no other way than through the Communication of this idiom having been made, and thus the Communication of Idioms is tacitly insinuated.

VIII. 2. Because the deception of the Calvinists can be best detected by this customary formula of speaking of the Church. For sometimes they speak with the Church, and yet they think differently, and through plausible expressions, as Nazianzen says, they secretly scatter poisons among the unskilled. They themselves also concede the Communication, if you understand the term, as pleases them, concerning the Union: but they extremely detest it, if you take it with us as a consequence of the Union. But just as the Union, so also the Communication of Idioms is founded in the scriptures: thus therefore the former ought to be believed, lest the latter be undermined: the former is to be used, but the latter is not to be suppressed. This phrase must therefore be used, lest the Calvinian virus creep in: which would happen, if the Church did not suppress this poisoned dart through distinct expressions.

IX. 3. Because no necessity compels us to beware of this form of speaking: which if it were given, then this would happen, either because this phrase does not sufficiently express the thing contained in the Holy Scriptures; or because it involves it in more difficulties. But nothing of these sprouts from it: therefore it is to be retained.

X. Finally, there occurs the 4. συμφωνία (agreement) of the Fathers, who never abhorred this form of speaking: I set forth two for many.

Cyril in the book on the incarnation of the Only-Begotten: The λόγος (Word) makes the operations of His Divine Majesty common with His flesh, so that He may also be able to quicken the dead, to heal the infirm.

Damascene, book 2, on the orthodox faith, ch. 15. The Divinity communicates its own glorifications to the body.

XI. ON THE II. TERMS. Philosophers use the terms Abstract and Concrete in one way, and Theologians use them in another. It is not relevant to speak of the former at this time. See the first part of Sob. Phil. p. 179. & seq. of the most excellent and most famous Lord President, my eternally venerable Preceptor. In the School of Theologians, because the greatest snares are laid by adversaries through the abuse of these terms, they must be properly understood.

XII. A Concrete term for Theologians denotes the whole Person of Christ, subsisting in two natures. An Abstract term, however, denotes one nature, not indeed outside the union, but considered distinctly within the union.

XIII. Where, however, it must be well observed that twofold Concretes and Abstracts are established by theologians. For there are given both Concretes of Persons and Natures, and also Abstracts of Persons and Natures. Concerning the former acceptance of the Concrete, it has already been said, to which I refer biblical terms which are attributed to Christ, such as Immanuel, Lord, Mediator, Advocate: sometimes also the term of GOD and of Man implies this signification, as in the sayings, Acts 20:28, John 3:19.

XIV. The Concretes of Natures distinctly denote the Natures themselves, yet not separately, but with the connotation of Personality or Hypostasis, in which both of Christ's natures subsist; and thus, not only is the essence of the natures denoted, but at the same time their hypostasis is also connoted. This acceptance, indeed, the Calvinists deny with full cheeks; but they cannot give sufficient reasons for their denial.

XV. For our opinion, it pleases us to append one Argument here.

If a concretive nature is given in the Person of Christ concerning the predication of nature, a concretive acceptance of natures will also be given. But the former is true. Therefore, I prove the antecedent.

These predications: Man is GOD, and GOD is man, not even the adversaries themselves entirely reject, although they affix and stitch onto them an alien explanation. In these, however, neither is an Abstract predicated of an Abstract, nor a Person of a Person; but a Concrete of Nature of a Concrete of Nature. For the words of GOD and of Man are Concretes, denoting both the essence of the Natures, and at the same time connoting their hypostasis, or personality. And yet, what is this other than to demonstrate the concretive acceptance of Natures? which was to be demonstrated.

XVI. The Abstracts of the Person coincide with the Concretes of Nature, by which only one nature is connoted with its Hypostasis.

The Abstract of Nature, however, connotes the naked essence or quiddity, without the signification of subsistence, such as Humanity, Divinity, etc.

XVII. Furthermore, there flows from this acceptance of Concrete and Abstract that formula of speaking of theologians: The assumed Nature, insofar as it is united with the Son of GOD, is to be considered in the Concrete: But when in itself and through itself by reason of natural properties, then in the abstract. The use of which is the greatest, partly so that nature may be distinguished from nature, partly so that a distinct account of properties may be held; and consequently, what things are by essence, and likewise what things have been bestowed upon which nature by grace, may be declared.

XVIII. OF III. The Communication of Idioms, hitherto employed by Orthodox Theologians with serious intent, is nothing other than a mode of speaking about Christ through distinct formulas of Scripture: or, it is a Class of Predications, containing those testimonies of the Scriptures by which it is declared what the appropriation of human idioms in Christ is, what the operation of the whole Person through both Natures is, and likewise what the glorification of the Assumed Nature is.

XIX. And if this mode of speaking were proposed either indistinctly, or were plainly eliminated from the field of Theological Controversies, then by that very fact an indistinct confusion, and a confusion of indistinctness, and thus mere darkness in speaking about Christ, would be introduced. But what would be the end of these? And who among the learned would be found who could perceive such a vast series of Biblical Predications proposed confusedly, or even distinctly when involved in intricate Disputations; or who could propose them to others with his own faithfulness.

XX. Dr. Chemnitz certainly left us a serious counsel regarding this matter in his book on the two Natures in Christ, p. 61. But I, he says, confess concerning my own simplicity, that I cannot extricate myself from the intricate disputations about this, unless by applying some distinction which the matter itself points out and provides. Therefore, this mode of speaking is highly necessary, and for that reason to be retained in the Schools of Theologians, and is apt for distinctly proposing those things which are enunciated about Christ, and consequently is to be learned with the greatest diligence, and to be applied when necessity requires.

XXI. OF IV. Those who have treated this doctrine of the Communication of Idioms more accurately have hitherto discovered in the scriptures such formulas of speaking about Christ, from which it can be certainly gathered that there are different modes of the Communication of Idioms. For in the beginning there occur such Propositions in which the Idioms of either Nature are enunciated about the whole Person, according to one or the other Nature, such as are found in John 8:56, 1 Cor. 10:9, Matt. 22:42.

XXII. Then there are also found those of this kind, which demonstrate that the Son of GOD, by assuming humanity, to Himself actually appropriated: Hence it happens that those things are predicated of the Son of GOD which are proper to the Humanity, as Acts 20:28, Gal. 2:20, Rom. 8:3, 1 John 1:1.

XXIII. Thirdly, there are also given such propositions of Scripture which affirm that CHRIST, in the work of Redemption, produced one Ἀποτέλεσμα not according to one, but according to both Natures, in which one Nature operates with the communication of the other: with which the Biblical codex is filled, as Gen. 3:15, Luke 9:56, 1 Tim. 2:5, etc.

XXIV. Finally, fourthly, there also occur such [propositions] which show that the properties of the Divine Nature in the Person of CHRIST have been communicated to the Humanity on account of the most intimate Union.

XXV. Moved by all these things, some of the Orthodox Theologians, concerning whom one may see D. Gerlach in his Disputations on the communication of Idioms in the year 1595 and the year 1602, established four classes of Idioms, or four genera; which is not undeservedly to be commended for their diligence.

XXVI. But because the predications of the second Class can be best explained and delivered in the first genus of the communication of Idioms, therefore Theologians have reduced these two Classes into one Genus. And since the Book of Concord has retained that τριχοτομίαν of Idioms, which delivers to us both the matter and the manner of speaking, and the order in these things, it is a matter of conscience for us to depart from that ternary received in the Churches.

XXVII. We therefore constantly count three genera of the communication of Idioms, against the Zwinglio-Calvinist crowd, which τριχοτομίαν I prove thus: There is given a triple Class of propositions in the Holy Scriptures, speaking of CHRIST and his properties after the Union has been made: Therefore also a triple Genus of the communication of Idioms, which flows from this Union. The antecedent has already been proven. The consequent, therefore, will not be denied.

XXVIII. Furthermore, these genera of the communication of Idioms are distinguished from one another; by which it is shown that not one, nor two, but three, or more than two, genera of Idioms are given. For in the first genus, the properties of the Natures are considered distinctly in themselves, and are predicated of the whole Person according to that Nature to which the property primarily belongs, which predication is made in the concrete: and here sometimes is applied distinctive particles, which are διακριτικαὶ & διοριστικαὶ [discriminative and definitive], showing to which nature an idiom, which is predicated of the whole person, belongs by essence, as in the cited passages, 1 Pet. 4 v. 1, Rom. 1 v. 3, c. 9 v. 5, 1 Pet. 5 v. 18. And to this distinction can be referred that rule of Vigilius: The properties of the natures become common to the person.

XXIX. In the second genus, however, is considered the concurrence of operations toward one ἀποτέλεσμα [result] of both natures; where the final cause of the Incarnation shines forth most especially: for the union of the two natures was made for this reason, that the work of redemption and salvation might be perfected in each, with each, and through each nature of CHRIST. To which pertains that rule of the theologians: The names of the office belong to the person according to both natures.

XXX. In the third genus, finally, it is shown which nature, on account of the hypostatic union into whose participation it has come, is adorned with glory, power, and majesty, and other innumerable, singular, and divine heavenly prerogatives; that the human nature is endowed with all these will be shown in its proper place: because the advancement is of the assumed, not of the assuming, as Leo speaks in Epistle 11. All of which are a manifest indication that, because neither can the predications of the first genus be referred to the second, nor those of the second to the third, or vice versa, but they come to be considered and treated distinctly, there are more genera of the communication of idioms than the adversaries wish.

XXXI. ON THE FIFTH. Hitherto in the schools of the theologians these genera have for the most part been enumerated in such a way that ἰδιοποιΐα [appropriation] is referred to the first genus, κοινωνοποιΐα [communication] to the second, and μετακοιΐα [transference] to the third: which order both the Book of Concord and very many orthodox theologians use and have used, as being most apt and easy for teaching.

XXXII. There are, however, some who invert this ancient order and place the third genus before the second, moved by this reasoning: Its cause always precedes its effect. But the communication of the office for performing the work of redemption in the person of Christ, with respect to the communicated majesty, behaves as an effect. Therefore, etc.

XXXIII. Nor, however, do those do badly who retain that received ancient series of enumerating and place the communication of the office before the communication of majesty, because thus also they follow the tracks, and observe the order of doctrine. For we have a most intricate struggle with our Calvinist adversaries concerning the κοινωνίᾳ of Majesty, and therefore we rightly proceed from the easier and less controversial matters to the more difficult and intricate ones.

XXXIV. Meanwhile, this dispute, as the adversaries perhaps think, is not like that of the Cadmean brothers; nor is it one of πραγμάτων or things, but of τάξεως or order, which can be resolved by applying a single distinction.

XXXV. For a distinction must be made between the order of Nature and of Doctrine. The former is followed by those who place the Communication of Majesty before the Communication of Office; the latter by those who place it after; whom we ourselves will gladly follow in what follows, and we will tread in their footsteps.

XXXVI. ON THE POWER. The union of the natures in Christ, and the most real communication of the same and of their properties, entails both our spiritual union with Christ and a most real communication of properties: which are declared at greater length in the book of D. Philip Nicolai on the Mystery of Omnipresence, chapters 4 and 6, from which it is pleasing to append certain things here.

XXXVII.
