Just as the Son of God, by assuming human nature, appropriated all its properties to Himself through ἰδιοποίησιν; so after our Savior Jesus Christ redeemed us (a) with His precious blood, dwelling in us spiritually, He claims for Himself the afflictions of the pious, attributes their dangers to Himself, and imputes to Himself all those things which befall us who adhere to Him through faith; this is evident from the words of Scripture, Zech. 2, v. 8; Matt. 10, v. 40; Luke 10, v. 16; Matt. 25, v. 35, and following.

XXXIIX. But it is most relevant to this place that Christ transfers our sins to Himself, and in turn bestows, imputes, and communicates His righteousness, innocence, and holiness to us through faith. For as the blessed Luther speaks skillfully and gravely: When our sins, death, and curse are transferred to God, then these evils of ours become His own, and His goods become our goods.

XXXIX. Κοινοποιΐα consists in the common operation of God and man joined πνευματικῶς. For in those in whom Christ dwells through faith, He makes them kings and priests, Rev. 5, v. 10, (a) He puts His Spirit in the midst of them, and causes them to walk in His commandments: (e) hence they become a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, etc. (i) judges of the world and of angels: (o) and who offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable, which is their rational worship. These works are not of mere man, or of mere God: but God works, the faithful Christian cooperates Rom. 4:14.

XL. Repentance finally, from our union with Christ, brings about hyperphysical, divine, or heavenly gifts: for this bond of ours with Christ is such that after (a) we have become partakers of the divine nature, God does not leave us in merely natural things, but by his divine efficacy works in us many heavenly, supernatural, gratuitous, and spiritual things; hence (e) our faith is rendered saving: (i) we overcome the world: (o) we put to flight or drive away Satan by resisting: we move the mountains of temptations: we demolish the counsels of demons, etc., all of which are so constituted that, although these things are proper to God alone, yet God does not do these things separately, but in man, with man, and through man. To whom be honor, power, and glory, to the Father, to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, through all ages, Amen.

Latin:

DIsputationibus aliqvot doctrina de duabus naturis in Christo, earundemq; unione, & hypostatica communicatione hactenùs pertractata fuit, superest jam, ut effectus istius unionis declarentur, qvi ex naturarum unione & arctissima περιχωρήσει fluunt.

II. Nam post factam Unionem jam longè aliter, cùm naturarum in Persona Christi, tùm simul idiomatum & actionum denominationes, de uno illo ὑφισταμένῳ enunciantur, qvàm si vel λόγος ἀσύνθετος consideraretur, vel humana natura per sese subsistens in propriâ personalitate pensitaretur.

III. Et qvoniam nobis in Ecclesiâ ex præscripto loqvendum est, teste Augustino, non liberè velut Philosophis, qvi liberis utuntur verbis; ut rem exprimamus, non involvamus, declaremus, ac omnia distinctè patefaciamus: ea propter placet hâc vice de illis, qvæ in subseqventibus Disputationibus sæpius recurrent, βραχέως disqvirere. 1. De voce Communicationis, an retinenda, cùm sit ἄγραφος. 2. De terminis Abstracti & Concreti. 3. Qvid notet Communicationis vox. 4. Quot sint Communicationis Idiomatum genera, num tria, vel quatuor. 5. Quis ordo inter hæc genera. Et tandem 6. Meditatio Practica, quòd etiam tres κοινωνίας seu gradus ex Mysticâ nostri cum Christo Unione fluant, adjicietur.

IV. DE 1. Sacris quidem in literis phrasis isthæc (Communicatio Idiomatum) αὐτολεξεὶ, sive quoad literam totidem syllabis expressa non reperitur, non tamen propterea statim ex circo sive agro Theologicarum Controversiarum releganda; quia sic à multis phrasibus, & loquendi formulis in Controversiis Theologicis, ipsis quoq; adversariis foret abstinendum, ut Liberi arbitrii, Sacramenti, Trinitatis, &c.

V. Et certè gravi consilio retinuit hanc phrasin pia antiqvitas, nimirum ad retegendam Nestorii ἑτεροδοξίαν, circa Personæ Christi unitatem, pro quâ per negationem Communicationis Idiomatum substituebat dualitatem: & Eutychetis Naturarum proprietatumq; confusionem. Hîc igitur contra horum virus pugnandum fuerat Patribus, & pretiosum à vili separandum: Ut igitur labore feliciori hoc præstarent, & rem in Scripturis fundatam penitiùs declararent, phrasin hanc adhibuerunt, adeoq́; hoc medio pro veritate strenuè decertarunt.

VI. Quia vero hactenùs per integrum ferè seculum, cum dilectissimâ Christi Ecclesiâ satis funestum sive ἄσπονδον gens Calviniana duxit bellum, ipsamq́; cùm de aliis, tum de hoc præsenti dogmate satis exercuit, non potuerunt non phrasin hanc, ceu per manus traditam, Theologi exercitatissimi retinere; isthuc autem sunt adducti non aliquâ petulanti novitatis affectione, sed ut eleganter ac graviter loquitur Augustinus, loqvendi necessitate, propter dolos & insidias Calvinianorum.

VII. Usurpandam itaq; hanc & nos censemus, seqventibus moti fundamentis. 1. Quia dogma hac voce, sive phrasi expressum, clarissima habet scripturarum testimonia. Qvotics enim cunq; Sacræ literæ, actiones & opera, quæ Divinæ Omnipotentiæ sunt propria, Carni Christi assignant, semper innuunt per illationem conseqventiæ bonæ, Carni Christi omnipotentiæ κοινωνίαν factam esse: qvam si negas, jam ipsam Scripturæ veritatem inficiaris. Patet hoc ex omnibus illis Divinis oraculis, quæ ad tres illas classes communicationis Idiomatum revocantur: V. C. Phil. 2. v. 9. & 10. Cultus adorationis naturæ exaltatæ adscribitur, qvod Divinum esse idioma scimus. Qvomodo autem hoc fit? Non aliter nisi per factam hujus idiomatis Communicationem, adeoq́; tacitè Communicatio Idiomatum insinuatur.

IIX. 2. Qvia fucus Calvinianorum optimè potest hâc loqvendi Ecclesiæ usitatâ formulâ deprehendi. Qvandoq; enim loqvuntur cum Ecclesiâ, & tamen diversum sentiunt, & per verisimiles locutiones, ut inqvit Nazianzenus, venena clanculùm spargunt apud imperitos. Concedunt & ipsi Communicationem, si intelligas vocem, ut ipsis placet, de Unione: extremè verò detestantur, si pro Unionis conseqvente nobiscum sumas. Ast sicut Unio, sic & Idiomatum Communicatio in scripturis est fundata: ita igitur illa credi debet, ne hæc labefactetur: Illa usurpanda, sed neq; hæc supprimenda. Utendum itaq; hac phrasi, ne serpat virus Calvinianum: qvod fieret, ni per distinctas locutiones spiculum hoc venenatum Ecclesia supprimeret.

IX. 3. Qvia nulla cogit nos necessitas, ut ab hac loqvendi forma nobis caveamus: qvæ si daretur, tum accideret hoc, vel qvia hæc phrasis rem Sacris literis contentam non sufficienter exprimit; vel qvia illam pluribus difficultatibus involvit. Ast horum inde nihil pullulat: retinenda igitur.

X. Accidit tandem 4. Patrum συμφωνία, qvi ab hâc loqvendi formâ nunqvam abhorruerunt: duos pro multis appono.

Cyrillus in lib. de incarn: Unigen: Communes facit λόγος cum carne suâ Divinæ suæ Majestatis operationes, ut possit etiam vivificare mortuos, sanare infirmos.

Damascenus lib. 2. ortho: fid: c. 15. Proprias glorificationes Divinitas corpori communicat.

XI. DE II. Terminis Abstracti & Concreti aliter Philosophi, aliter item utuntur Theologi. De illis hac vice dicere nil attinet. Videatur prima pars Sob. Phil. p. 179. & seq. Excellentiss. & clariffimi Dn. Præsidis, Præceptoris æternùm venerandi. In Scholâ Theologorum, qvia ab Adversariis per abusum horum terminorum insidiæ struntur maximæ, probè veniunt cognoscendi.

XII. Concretum Theologis notat totam Personam Christi, subsistentem in duabus naturis. Abstractum autem alteram naturam, non qvidem extra unionem, sed in unione distinctè consideratam.

XIII. Ubi tamen probè observandum venit, quòd â Theologis duplicia statuantur & Concreta & Abstracta. Dantur enim cùm Personæ & Naturarum Concreta, tùm etiam Personæ & Naturarum Abstracta. De priori acceptione Concreti jam dictum, qvo refer voces Biblicas, qvæ Christo tribuuntur, ut sunt, Immanuel, Dominus, Mediator, Advocatus: qvandoq; etiam terminus DEI & Hominis hanc imimplicant significationem, ut in dictis, Actor. 20. v. 28. Joh. 3.v.19.

XIV. Concreta Naturarum distinctè notant ipsas Naturas, non tamen seorsim, sed cum connotatione Personalitatis sive Hypostaseos, in qvâ utraq; Christi natura subsistit; adeoq; non tantum naturarum notatur essentia, sed simul ipsarum qvoq; connotatur hypostasis. Quam qvidem acceptionem plenis buccis Calviniani pernegant; ast negationis sufficientes neqveunt dare rationes.

XV. Pro nostra sententia unicum placet huc apponere Argumentum.

Si datur Concretiva natura in Persona Christi de natura Prædicatio, dabitur quoq; Concretiva naturarum acceptio. Sed verum prius. E. Antecedens probo.

Prædicationes has: Homo est DEUS, & DEUS est homo, nec ipsi adversarii penitus rejiciunt, licet illis explicationem alienam affingunt & assuunt. In his autem nec Abstractum enunciatur de Abstracto, nec Persona de Persona; sed Concretum Naturæ de Concreto Naturæ. Nam vocabula DEI & Hominis sunt Concreta, notantia & Naturarum essentiam, & simul connotantia earundem hypostasin, sive personalitatem. Atqvi hoc, qvid aliud est, qvàm Naturarum Concretivam acceptionem commonstrare? id qvod demonstrandum erat.

XVI. Abstracta Personæ coincidunt cum Concretis Naturæ, qvibus una tantum connotatur natura cum Hypostasi sua.

Abstractum autem Naturæ nudam essentiam sive qvidditatem, absq; subsistentiæ significatione connotat, ut Humanitas, Divinitas, &c.

XVII. Fluit insuper ex hac Concreti & Abstracti acceptione, illa Theologorum loqvendi formula: Assumpta Natura, quatenus cum Filio DEI est unita, in Concreto consideranda: Quando verò in se & per se ratione proprietatum naturalium, tum in abstracto. Qvorum usus est maximus, partim ut natura discernatur à naturâ, partim ut ratio proprietatum habeatur distincta; adeoq́; quæ per essentiam, quæ item cui naturæ donata sint per gratiam, declaretur.

XIIX. DE III. Communicatio Idiomatum hactenus gravì consilio ab Orthodoxis Theologis usurpata; nil aliud est, qvàm modus dicendi propria per distinctas scripturæ formulas de Christo: sive, est Classis Prædicationum, continens ea scripturarum testimonia, qvibus declaratur, qvalis sit in Christo Idiomatum humanorum appropriatio, qvæ sit totius Personæ per utramq; Naturam operatio, & qvæ item Assumptæ Naturæ glorificatio.

XIX. Et hic modus loqvendi, si vel indistinctè proponeretur, vel planè ex agro Theologicarum Controversiarum eliminaretur, tum eo ipso indistincta confusio, & confusionis indistinctio, atq; sic mera caligo loqvendi de Christo introduceretur. Qvis vero horum foret finis? Et qvis daretur eruditorum, tam ingentem Prædicationum Biblicarum seriem confusè propositam, qvi vel distinctè, intricatis Disputationibus involutam, perciperet; vel aliis suâ fidelitate proponere posset.

XX. Grave certè consilium hac de re nobis reliqvit D. Chemnit: in lib. de duabus Nat: in Christ. m. p. 61. Sed ego, inqvit, de meâ simplicitate fateor, quòd non possim me, ex intricatis de hâc disputationibus, evolvere, nisi adhibitâ aliquâ, quam res ipsa monstrat & præbet, distinctione. Modus igitur hic loqvendi, & summè est necessarius, ideoq́; in Scholis Theologorum retinendus, & ad ea, quæ de Christo enunciantur, distinctè propónenda aptus, adeoq́; summâ diligentiâ addiscendus, & necessitate reqvirente adhibendus.

XXI. DE IV. Qvi accuratius hanc doctrinam de Communicatione Idiomatum tractarunt, deprehenderunt hactenus in scripturis ejusmodi loqvendi formulas de Christo, ex qvibus diversos modos dari Communicationis Idiomatum, certò colligi potest. Nam initio occurrunt ejusmodi Propositiones, in qvibus utriusq; Naturæ Idiomata enunciantur de totâ Personâ, secundum alterutram Naturam, qvales habentur Joh. 8. v. 56. 1. Cor. 10. v. 9. Matth. 22. v. 42.

XXII. Deinde inveniuntur & hujusmodi, qvæ commonstrant, Filium DEI omnia Idiomata Humanitatis, assumendo illam, sibi reapse appropriasse: Hinc fit, ut de Filio DEI ea enuncientur, quæ Humanitatis sunt propria, ut Act. 20. v. 28. Gal. 2. v. 20. Rom. 8. v. 3. 1. Joh. 1. v. 1.

XXIII. Tertio dantur & hujusmodi scripturæ Propositiones, quæ affirmant CHRISTUM in opere Redemptionis, non secundùm unam, sed utramqve Naturam unum produxisse Ἀποτέλεσμα, in qva una Natura operatur cum Communicatione alterius: qvalibus completus est codex Biblicus, ut Gen. 3. v. 15. Luc. 9. v. 56. 1. Tim. 2. v. 5. &c.

XXIV. Deniq; quartò occurrunt & hujusmodi, quæ ostendunt Divinæ Naturæ proprietates in Personâ CHRISTI, Humanitati propter arctissimam Unionem esse communicatas.

XXV. Qvibus omnibus moti nonnulli ex Orthodoxis Theologis, de qvibus videri potest D. Gerlach. in Disput. de commun. Idiom. Anno 1595. & anno 1602. qvatuor classes Idiomatum, sive qvart tuor genera constituerunt; qvæ ipsorum diligentia non immeritò commendanda.

XXVI. Verùm qvia Classis secundæ Prædicationes optimè possunt explicari & tradi in primo genere Communicationis Idiomatum, propterea Theologi has duas Classes in unum Genus retulerunt. Et qvoniam liber Concordiæ τριχοτομίαν illam Idiomatum retinuit, qvi nobis & res & modum loqvendi, & ordinem in his tradit, à ternario illo in Ecclesiis recepto, nobis recedere est religio.

XXVII. Constanter igitur tria Communicationis Idiomatum genera numeramus, contra turbam Zvvinglio-Calvin. qvam τριχοτομίαν ita probo: Datur triplex Classis propositionum in Sacris literis, loqvendi de CHRISTO, ejusqve proprietatibus post factam Unionem: Igitur & triplex Genus communicationis Idiomatum, qvod ex hac Unione profluit. Antecedens probatum jam est. Conseqvens igitur non negabitur.

XXVIII. Porrò isthæc genera Communicationis Idiomatum â se invicem distingvuntur; qvo ostenditur non unum, nec duo, sed tria, sive duobus plura dari Idiomatum genera. In primo enim genere Naturarum proprietates in sese distinctè considerantur, & de totâ Persona enunciantur secundùm eam Naturam, cui proprietas primò competit, qvæ Prædicatio fit in Concreto: & hį̂c qvandoq; adhibentur particulæ Distinctivæ, quæ sunt διακριτικαὶ & διοριστικαὶ, ostendentes, cuinam Naturæ Idioma, quod de tota Persona enunciatur, sit per essentiam competens, ut in dictis, 1. Pet. 4. v. 1. Rom. 1. v. 3. c. 9. v. 5. 1. Pet. 5. v. 18. Et ad hanc Distinctionem referri potest illa Vigilii Regula: Propria Naturarum fiunt communia Personæ.

XXIX. In secundo autem genere consideratur concursus operationum ad unum ἀποτέλεσμα utriusque Naturæ; ubi Incarnationis causa finalis potissimum elucescit : Ideò enim duarum Naturarum Unio est facta, ut opus Redemptionis & Salvationis in utrâq;; cum utrâq; ; & per utramq; CHRISTI Naturam perficeretur. Quò pertinet illa Theologorum Regula: Nomina officii competunt Personæ secundùm utramq; Naturam.

XXX. In tertio deniq; genere ostenditur, quæ Natura propter Unionem Hypostaticam, in cujus participationem devenit, sit ornata gloriâ, potentiâ, & majestate, aliisq; Cœlestibus inenumerabibus, singularibus, & Divinis prærogativis; quibus omnibus dotatam esse Humanam Naturam suo loco ostendetur : quia Assumpti, non Assumentis, est provectio, uti loquitur Leo Epist. 11. Quæ omnia manifesto sunt indicio, quòd quia nec primi generis Prædicationes referri possunt ad secundum, nec secundi ad tertium, aut viceversâ, sed distinctè veniunt considerandæ & tractandæ, dari plura Communicationis Idiomatum genera, quàm Adversarii volunt.

XXXI. DE V. Hactenus in Scholis Theologorum maximâ ex parte genera ista sic enumerata sunt, ut Ιδιοποιΐα ad primum genus, κοινωνοποιΐα ad secundum; μετακοιΐα ad tertium sit relata: quem ordinem cùm liber Concordiæ, tùm permulti Orthodoxi Theologi usurpant & usurparunt, velut ad docendum maximè aptum & facilem.

XXXII. Sunt tamen nonnulli qui priscum hunc ordinem invertunt, & tertiũ genus secundo præponunt, hac moti ratione: Effectum sua semper antecedit causa. Ast Communicatio officii ad opus Redemptionis peragendum in Personâ Christi, respectu communicatæ Majestatis, habet sese ad modum effectus. Ergo. &c.

XXXIII. Neq; tamen illi malè faciunt, qui receptam illam numerandi seriem antiqvam retinent, & communicationem Officii præponunt Communicationi Majestatis, quia sic & Concordiæ vestigia seqvuntur, & doctrinæ ordinem observant. Nam de κοινωνίᾳ Majestatis intricatissima nobis est cum Calvinianis Adversariis pugna, ideoq́; à facilioribus & minùs controversis, ad difficiliora & magis intricata rectè progredimur.

XXXIV. Interim lis hæc, ut fortè opinantur Adversarii, non est ad instar fratrum Cadmæorum; neq; est πραγμάτων sive rerum, sed τάξεως sive ordinis, qvæ unicâ adhibitâ distinctione salvari potest.

XXXV. Distinguendum enim est inter ordinem Naturæ, & Doctrinæ. Illam seqvuntur ij, qvi Communicationem Majestatis præponunt Communicationi Officii: hunc isti, qvi postponunt; qvos in subseqventibus & ipsi lubentes seqvemur, ipsorumq́; semitæ insistemus.

XXXVI. DE VI. Naturarum in Christo Unio, earundemq́; ac proprietatum realissima Communicatio, & nostri cum Christo spiritualem Unionem, & realissimam proprietatum communicationem importat: qvæ prolixius declarantur apud D. Philip. Nicolai in l. de Mysterio Omnipr. cap. 4. & 6. è qvibus qvædam huc apponere placet.

XXXVII. Sicuti Filius DEI Humanam Naturam assumendo, omnes ejusdem proprietates per ἰδιοποίησιν sibi appropriavit: ita postqvam nos (a) sangvine pretioso redemit Servator noster Jesus Christus, in nobis spiritualiter habitans, piorum afflictiones sibi vendicat, ipsorum pericula sibi tribuit, & omnia ilja, qvæ nobis illi per Fidem adhærescentibus obveniunt, imputat; patet hoc ex dictis Scripturæ Zach. 2. v. 8. Matth. 10. v. 40. Luc. 10. v. 16. Matth. 25. v. 35. & seq.

XXXIIX. Maximè autem hujus loci est, qvòd Christus peccata nostra ad se transfert, & vicissim suam justitiam, innocentiam & sanctitatem mediante Fide nobis donat, imputat, & communicat. Nam uti scitè & graviter loqvitur B. Lutherus: Cum peccata, mors & maledictio nostra in DEUM transferuntur, tum hæc nostra mala ipsius fiunt propria, & sua bona, fiunt nostra bona.

XXXIX. Κοινοποιΐα consistit in DEI & Hominis πνευματικῶς copulatorum operatione communi. In qvibus enim Christus per fidem habitat, illos Reges & Sacerdotes facit, Apoc. 5. v. 10. (a) ponit Spiritum suum in medio ipsorum, facitq́; ut in præceptis suis ambulent: (e) hinc fiunt genus electum, Regale Sacerdotium, gens sancta, &c. (i) Judices mundi & Angelorum: (o) qviq́; præbent corpora sua hostiam viventem, sanctam, acceptam, hoc est, rationalem cultum suum. Qvæ opera non sunt meri Hominis, aut meri DEI: sed operatur DEUS, cooperatur fidelis Christianus; gubernat Spiritus Sanctus, & gubernantis ductum Homo seqvitur. Rom. 4. v. 14.

XL. Metatnoia tandem ex Unione nostri cum CHRISTO importat dona hyperphysica, Divina sive Cœlestia: tale enim hoc nostri cum CHRISTO est vinculum, ut postqvam (a) Divinæ Naturæ facti sumus consortes, Deus nos non relinqvat in merè naturalibus, sed Divinâ sua efficacitate operatur in nobis multa cœlestia, & supernaturalia, gratuita & spiritualia; hinc (e) Fides nostra redditur salvifica: (i) vincimus mundum: (o) profligamus sive abigimus resistendo Satanam: transponimus montes tentationum: Demolimur consilia Dæmonum &c. qvæ omnia ita se habent, ut licet sint DEI solius hæc propria; Non tamen separatim Deus hæc facit, sed in homine, cum homine, & per hominem. Cui sit honor, virtus & gloria, Patri, Filio & Spiritui Sancto, per cuncta secula, Amen.


## 14 Fourteenth Disputation, On the First Kind of Communication of Properties

Thesis I.

It is truly said: Those who do not wish to understand one thing correctly, must necessarily interpret many things wrongly; the Church of God experiences this abundantly today among the Sacramentarian people.

II. For after that [people], having been taught to violently twist the first article concerning the Supper, and afterwards with more than giant-like daring, as a ninety-year-old enemy of Christ, began to interpret the remaining articles of faith not only wrongly but also impiously: as this has been proven for the present in the article concerning the person of Christ through several Christological disputations, and will still have to be proven in the doctrine concerning the communication of idioms.

III. Since this was treated generally in the recent disputation, now we descend to its more specific points, in the correct order; and indeed on this occasion we shall treat rather briefly of the FIRST, as they call it, KIND OF COMMUNICATION, worshipping God the Father through his own Son in his Holy and good Spirit, that he may deign to bring the truth to light.

IV. This First kind of Communication is called, to begin with the name, in various ways by the ancients, such as: Ἀλλοίωσις, Ἀντίδοσις, (alternate attribution) ἐναλλαγὴ καὶ κοινωνία ὀνομάτων, i.e., exchange and communication, or what is a more suitable term, communion of names: Ἐπίζευξις ὀνομάτων, i.e., sub- or adjunction of names: οἰκείωσις or familiarity.

V. Today we are accustomed to call it the Communication of Idioms; a term indeed conflated from the diverse opinions of the ancients and primarily from the canon of the Council of Chalcedon: One nature acts with the communication of the other, that which is proper to each; yet it is by no means orthodoxly [conflated], as Piscator of Herborn defends in Disp. 6, thesis 24, Vol. Disp. 2.

VI. For one must distinguish between the common and the communicated; between κοινὸν and κοινωνὸν or κοινωνητόν. The former exists in many things from a common cause, and can even exist between separated things. The latter has only one cause; on account of which it exists in one thing, and is at least between united things. We say that Idioms are communicated, not common things.

VII. And why should a proper thing be called common, if it is communicated? The scent of musk certainly remains proper to itself, even if it becomes common to other things as well. Thus, therefore, a proper thing can be called common, in that it belongs to one primarily, and to another secondarily.

VIII. This first kind of Communication is described as being: When the properties of the natures are predicated of the Person in the concrete; briefly indeed, but most correctly.

IX. Examples of this kind are, CHRIST is before Abraham, John 8:58. The Son of GOD was crucified, Heb. 6:6. The Son of man is in heaven, John 3:13. CHRIST is from the fathers according to the flesh, Rom. 9:5, and similar ones.

X. Moreover, two modes of this First kind are enumerated: The first, from the subject, which is the whole ὑφιστάμενον and therefore συναμφότερον, is called by the peculiar name Συναμφοτερισμὸς: but from the predicate, which is either divine or human, it is called Ἑκατέρασις, Alternation, and is:

Latin:

Thesis I.

VErè dici: Qui unum non rectè intelligere volunt, eos multa malè interpretari oportet; Ecclesia DEI hodie in gente Sacramentaria ubertim experitur.

II. Postqvam enim illa primum Articulum de Cœnâ violenter torqvere edocta, post ausu plusqvam Giganteo, ut nonagenaria CHRISTI inimica, reliqvos Fidei Articulos non tantùm malè sed & impiè interpretari cæpit: uti hoc inpræsentiarum in Articulo de Personâ CHRISTI per aliqvot Disputationes Christologicas probatum, & adhuc in doctrina de Communic. Idiomatum probandum erit.

III. Qvâ de cum in nuperâ Disput. generaliter actum sit, nunc ad ejus specialiora, recto ordine, descendimus; & quidem hac vice de PRIMO, ut vocant, COMMUNICATIONIS GENERE breviuscule agemus, DEUM Patrem per ipsius Filium in Spiritu suo S. & bono venerati simplices, ut veritatem ad lucem redigere dignetur.

IV. Dicitur hoc Primum Communicationis genus, ut a nomine inchoemus, a veteribus varie, ut: Ἀλλοίωσις, Ἀντίδοσις, (alternata attributio) ἐναλλαγὴ καὶ κοινωνία ὀνομάτων, h. e. commutatio & communicatio, sive quod aptius est vocabulum, communio nominum: Ἐπίζευξις ὀνομάτων q. d. sub-vel adjunctionem nominum: οἰκείωσις vel familiaritas.

V. Hodie vocare consuevimus Communicationem Idiomatum; voce quidem ex diversis veterum sententiis & inprimis ex Chalcedonensis Concilii canone: Una natura agit cum communicatione alterius, quod cujusque proprium est; conflata, minime tamen ὀρθοδόξως, ut defendit Piscator Herbornensis Disp. 6. th. 24. Vol. Disp. 2.

VI. Siquidem distinguendum inter commune & communicatum; inter κοινὸν & κοινωνὸν sive κοινωνητόν. Illud ex communi causa multis inest, & potest etiam esse inter separata. Hoc tantum unam habet causam; propter quam uni inest, & est saltem inter unita. Communicari dicimus Idiomata, non communia.

VII. Et cur ὀρθοδόξως proprium dicatur commune, si communicetur? Odor Mosci certe ipsi manet proprius, etiamsi & aliis rebus communis evadat. Sic igitur proprium potest dici commune, ut uni primario, alteri secundario conveniat.

VIII. Describitur hoc primum Communicationis Genus, quod sit: Quando propria naturarum de Persona in Concreto predicantur; breviter quidem, sed rectissime.

IX. Exempla hujus Generis sunt, CHRISTUS est ante Abraham, Joh. 8, 58. Filius DEI crucifixus est, Hebr. 6, 6. Filius hominis est in cœlo, Joh. 3, 13. CHRISTUS est ex patribus secundum carnem, Rom. 9, 5. & similia.

X. Enumerantur autem hujus Primi Generis duo Modi: Primus, a subjecto, quod est totum ὑφιστάμενον adeoq; συναμφότερον, peculiari nomine dicitur Συναμφοτερισμὸς: a predicato vero, quod vel divinum vel humanum, Ἑκατέρασις, Alternatio, vocatur, & est:


### When the property of one nature is truly and really predicated of the whole person, not of one nature separately

When the property of one nature is truly and really predicated of the whole person, not of one nature separately.

XI. Where again, regarding the description of the subject, distinct modes arise; for either it is described by both natures, when, namely, divine or human things are predicated of the θεανθρώπῳ [God-man], as: Christ is before Abraham, John 8. Jesus Christ yesterday, today, and forever, that is, eternal, Heb. 13, 8. Christ is to be born of the seed of David, born, suffered, etc.

XII. Or it is described by the human nature, as the Son of man, while existing in heaven, speaks with Nicodemus on earth, John 3, 13.

XIII. Here, of necessity, room must be left for the common distinction between the subject 'Quod' [that which] and the subject 'Quo' [that by which], in order to avoid the error of Eutyches, which he committed in confounding the natures.

XIV. Scripture, and the Orthodox who follow it, are accustomed to apply a determination by adding particles, as they call them, Distinctive (which, if they are not expressed, are nevertheless tacitly understood), so that it may be known what is attributed to the natures essentially or by property of nature, but to the person appropriatively or by the communication of idioms.

XV. Those three common species of limitation—namely: I. Reduplicative, where the subject is subjected to the predicate primarily and of itself, and it is valid with its determination only in universals: II. Etiological or specificative, where by that ἀναδιπλώσεῖ [reduplication] not the subject but the cause (which two here differ from each other) is expressed, on account of which the predicate belongs to the subject: III. Synecdochical, where for the sake of a part (which cannot be predicated of the subject) the predicate is said to be in the whole, which nevertheless cannot be predicated of it absolutely—cannot be adapted to this business in all respects.

XVI. But these particles here have this use, that they distinguish the natures and show the cause on account of which a natural property is attributed to the whole person.

XVII. Another mode comes under the name of ἰδιοποιΐας [appropriation] or ἰδιοποιήσεως [making one's own], when, namely, human things are predicated of GOD or the λόγῳ [Word], as: The Author of life was killed, Acts 3, 15. The Lord of Glory was crucified, 1 Cor. 2, 8. The Word of life was handled with hands, 1 John 1, 1. The Son of GOD was made of a woman, Gal. 4, 4, etc.

XVIII. Which latter mode differs from the former: I. on the part of the Subject, which there involves both natures, but here is nothing but the λόγος alone assuming. II. on the part of the Predicate, which there is proper to either nature: but here is nothing but proper to the humanity, which by assuming the human Nature the λόγος at the same time appropriated to himself.

XIX. It is evident from what has been said that this First Genus is more correctly called ἰδιοπόιησιν or ἰδιοποιίαν, appropriation or communion, than Communication. For speaking accurately, a person cannot be said to communicate anything to himself, but only appropriates to himself the properties of a nature on account of the ὑποςατικὴν union having taken place, and indeed so closely that nothing of passion can be affirmed of the Human nature which does not redound to the very Son of GOD himself.

XX. For just as truly, that is, not verbally or nominally, but really and truly the λόγος, remaining impassible in his own nature, died in his own flesh (namely, personally), as truly and really it was his (the λόγος's) own flesh.

XXI. Away, therefore, from the Church be Nestorius (whom Greg. de Valen. most mendaciously writes that Luther strove to excuse, as if he had good zeal and right faith), who tears apart the person on account of his denial of the Communication of Idioms, as if each nature acted by itself alone and separately.

XXII. And although he wished to seem to hold orthodoxy regarding the unity of the Person, saying: 'Remove all suspicion of Duality and of Sons'; yet by dividing the terms which are predicated of CHRIST, as if some things belonged to the Man CHRIST and some things to the Man GOD, and thus by denying the communication of Idioms, the Council of Ephesus rightly concludes that he dissolved the person.

XXIII. For actions and passions are not of natures but of the person; how, therefore, can it be rightly said according to Nestorius: 'This the Divine nature of CHRIST does, this his human nature does'? Hence Luther piously: 'To the division of works succeeds the division of the person.'

XXIV. Let there likewise depart from the school of all soberly pious men, as a plague to living consolations, Zwingli's Ἀλλοίωσις, which he taught to be such an exchange of names (τῶν ὀνομάτων ἀντίδοσιν) by which one nature is taken and understood for the other. Thus this proposition, 'The Son of GOD is crucified,' Heb. 6:6, Zwingli o means the same as, Human nature united to the Son of God is crucified. By which very thing certainly both the Communication and the Union are despoiled of all reality and truth, and our salvation of a solid foundation.

XXV. For to die for the life of the world is certainly not only the work of human nature, but also of the Son of God himself, otherwise he would not have needed to be incarnated here. Whence the Apostolic Creed declares one and the same subject of the Passion and object of our Faith, namely Jesus Christ. Therefore, let us not suffer the other nature to be entirely excluded from the passion.

XXVI. Which very thing Dr. Luther long ago invincibly obtained by this argument: This person (pointing to Christ) suffers, dies. But this person is true God. Therefore, true God suffers.

XXVII. Which conclusion clearly shows that it is ἀδύνατον [impossible] that τὸ Deus [God] or the Son of God can be placed for the whole Christ in propositions of this kind. For unless you understand only one of Christ's natures in the Conclusion as well as in the Minor premise, the Minor premise, with the Calvinistic absurdity (by which it is written by the Heidelbergers that Christ and the Son of God are equivalent), will be this: Christ is Christ.

XXVIII. I add also this: That God suffers, who was made flesh. But the λόγος [Word], God, not flesh united to God, was made flesh. Therefore, etc.

XXIX. Nor will certain Calvinists among candidates of more solid literature excuse this Ἀλλοίωσιν [alteration] by their Synecdoche, by which they assert that in propositions of this kind a part is spoken for a part: since I would believe that he who connects at once the subject 'What' and the subject 'By which' speaks not synecdochically or tropically but quite properly, as 'Man writes with his hand,' 'God suffers in the flesh,' etc.

XXX. It is furthermore known that in a synecdochical restriction the restricting part cannot be predicated in the nominative case of that thing which is restricted, for I do not say, 'man is a hand,' etc., which nevertheless is manifest to be done in this example. How then will it be a Synecdoche? I pass over the fact that in synecdochical propositions a part is said for the whole, not a part for a part.

XXXI. Others see Zwingli in this his ἀλλοιώσει [alteration] and Nestorius as not differing, as it is said, in all camps, and therefore they clamor that Luther did not correctly perceive Zwingli's mind here, but attributed something to him.

mitant. For thus the Heidelbergers against the Württembergers: That (namely, where Luther treats of the cursed ἀλλοιώσει of Zwingli) Dr. Luther did not rightly understand Zwingli. Item: God knows it, and every man can also know it, who only wants to read Zwingli's writings, that Dr. Luther has done violence and injustice to the good, honest man in these (namely, Communic. Idiom.) as well as in many other things. And that Dr. Luther once reproached Zwingli, as if he had taught blasphemously concerning the properties of both natures in Christ, etc. But the reader should know that not Dr. Luther himself, but only Dr. Luther's anger has done such a thing.

XXXII. And that they may remove every suspicion from themselves, they write thus: If the Calvinists taught that the suffering and death of Christ were the suffering and death of a mere man, one should tear their tongues out of their throats. And after a few words: It is a very different thing to say that only a man died for us; another, that Christ died for us only according to his human nature. The former they reject, the latter they defend here and there in their German writings.

XXXIII. But they write all these things craftily; so that one may wonder how they dare to weaken such an open truth? Thus Zwingli himself on the Confession of Luther: John 3:13, 14. The Son of Man is named twice, yet nowhere does it signify both natures at once in this way, but in the first place it denotes the divine, in the second place only the human. And elsewhere: If at any time these properties (of the two natures in CHRIST) seem to be interchanged, as when the Lord of glory is said to have been crucified: and the Son of Man to have been in heaven when he was with Nicodemus on earth, it is a trope of ἀλλοιώσεως consisting within the words. And again: I acknowledge the true Divinity of CHRIST, and I acknowledge it in such a way that I judge that nothing should by any means be attributed to it which can less befit it. Similarly, I also acknowledge the true humanity of CHRIST, so that I would in no way wish to be attributed to it that which cannot belong to it.

XXXIV. And Luther expressed this opinion of Zwingli thus: This, says Luther, Zwingli calls Allæosis, when something is said about the Divinity of CHRIST which is nevertheless proper to his humanity: e.g., where it is said: Ought not CHRIST to have suffered these things, and so to enter into his glo ry; there Zwingli trifles, because the word (Christ) in this passage is taken for the human nature.

XXXV. Let them go now, and tell that good man (namely Zwingli, whom they wish to be the only son of a white hen) that an injury was done by Luther, and that his mind was not correctly known to Luther.

XXXVI. And what, I ask, have the Lutherans hitherto attacked in the Zwinglians, other than this same phrase: only the human nature has suffered? Let them explain candidly what differs between man and human nature in Christ, for the question between us and them is not about an ordinary and mere man, but about a Deified man. Therefore, what they write goes up in smoke: When one says that only a man has died for us, when Christ has died for us, then the meaning is that Christ, who has died for us, is only a mere man, and not at the same time God and man. But when one says that Christ has died for us only according to the human nature, it does not have the meaning as if Christ, who has died for us, were only a mere man: But it has the meaning that Christ, although He is at the same time God and man in a single inseparable person, nevertheless did not die according to both the divinity and also the humanity, but only according to the humanity, when He died for us.

XXXVII. To which it pleases me to oppose this one thing: That whose subject truly suffers, it itself also suffers. But the subject of the Word truly suffers. Therefore.

XXXVIII. You ask: The Deity cannot die, therefore only the humanity of CHRIST has died. I respond by denying the consequence from that much-discussed principle: Actions and passions belong to the subject: God dies not in His nature but in His own flesh.

XXXIX. The question here is about enunciations in the abstract, whether, as I say in the concrete, God has suffered, so also correctly, the Deity has suffered, the key has been affixed, has died? I respond: Even though both the ancients and theologians of great name have used them, we nevertheless abstain from them, because 1. Scripture does not know them. 2. The most holy Symbol of our Church, namely the Book of Christian Concord; which is not only written ration of things, on account of the Articles of Faith, but also on account of Phrases, so that a certain norm of speaking might be held in the Church; he preferred to use predications in the concrete; And 3. so that we might the more avoid the calumnies of adversaries, and flee as far as possible from the suspicion of the errors of Eutyches and the Theopaschites.

XL. Nor, however, do we think that those theologians who maintain that it is possible to preach in the abstract in this way should be marked with a censor's rod on that account; for they themselves affirmed this for the reason that they might the better be able to expose the Calvinists and Jesuits who are Nestorianizing and Samosatenizing: nor do they wish to admit such locutions without determination, or to litigate with anyone about them.

XLI. It is also asked, whether in those propositions where human things are predicated of man, there is a Communication of Idioms, and whether these: The Son of man eats, drinks, etc., belong here?

XLII. Resp. Why not? Because the subject here does not stand for the concrete of the nature formally signifying only the assumed human nature, but for the Concrete of the person, so that it signifies the whole composite. For where a property suitable to one nature is attributed to the person in the concrete, there is a communication of Idioms of the first kind.

XLIII. Furthermore, as this: The Son of man was crucified, suffered, etc., is explained by the Communication of Idioms, and is rightly placed in the first kind; so also this: The Son of man eats, drinks, etc. For what is valid in an equal matter, is also valid in a comparable matter.

XLIV. But so that this diligence in speaking may not seem to lack all fruit and consolation, we shall conclude with one or two practical meditations.

XLV. And therefore let this doctrine be for us 1. a key of Christian consolation. The pious mind is certainly struck with amazement at such bowels of mercy, considering that the Son of GOD himself was willing to endure the ignominies and sufferings of his flesh through an ineffable mode of appropriation, for our sake, and therefore it cannot doubt that he himself, who deemed it worthy to endure in the flesh slaps, chains, spittle, mockeries, etc., and to receive them into himself, will at some time associate us, who are of the same substance with him, to himself.

XLVI. Let this doctrine then also cause in us a severe hatred of sin. For that we might become closer to GOD, the Son of GOD himself on account of our sins assumed flesh, and in it he bore all ignominies. Why therefore do we suffer that which would separate us from God? Our sins divide us from God; let us therefore flee and detest them, lest we deviate from God. He who adheres to God is one Spirit with him. Grant therefore, O most high God, that we may adhere solely to you through Jesus Christ in your Holy Spirit. Amen.

Latin:

Cum de totâ personâ, non de alterâ naturâ seorsim, verè & realiter alterius naturæ proprium prædicatur.

XI. Ubi rursus quoad subjecti descriptionem distincti oriuntur modi; Vel enim illud describitur ab utraque natura, quando nimirum de θεανθρώπῳ divina vel humana prædicantur, ut: Christus est ante Abrahamum, Joh. 8. Jesus Christus heri hodie & in secula, hoc est, æternus, Hebr. 13, 8. Christus est ex semine David oriundus, natus, passus, &c.

XII. Vel describitur ab humana natura, ut Filius hominis existens in cœlo loquitur cum Nicodemo in terris, Joh. 3, 13.

XIII. Necessariò hîc vulgari Distinctiunculæ inter subjectum Quod, & subjectum Quo, ad Eutychetis errorem, quem ille in confundendis naturis admisit, vitandum, locus reliquendus venit.

XIV. Scriptura & hanc sequuti Orthodoxi determinationem adhibere solent, addendo particulas, ut vocant, Distinctivas (quæ semper, si non exprimuntur, tacitè tamen subintelliguntur) ut sciri possit, quidnam Naturis essentialiter seu per naturæ proprietatem; personæ vero appropriativè seu per communicationem Idiomatum tribuatur.

XV. Vulgaris illæ tres limitationis species; ut sunt I. Reduplicativa, ubi subjectum primò & per se subjicitur prædicato, valetq; cum determinatione sua tantum in Universalibus: II. Ætiologica seu specificativa, ubi ἀναδιπλώσεῖ illâ non subjectum sed causa (quæ duo hîc à se invicem differunt) exprimitur, propter quam Prædicatum infit subjecto. III. Synecdochica, ubi partis (quæ de subjecto prædicari nequit) gratiâ dicitur prædicatum inesse toti, quod tamen absolutè de illo prædicari nequit; huic negotio per omnia adcommodari non possunt.

XVI. Sed hunc particulæ istæ hîc obtinent usum, ut distinguant naturas, & ostendant causam propter quam proprietas naturalis, toti Personæ tribuatur.

XVII. Alter modus nomine ἰδιοποιΐας vel ἰδιοποιήσεως venit, quando videlicet de DEO vel λόγῳ prædicantur humana, ut Auctor vitæ est interfectus Act. 3, 15. Dominus Gloriæ est crucifixus, 1. Cor. 2, 8, Verbum vitæ manibus contrectatum est, 1. Joh, 1, 1. Filius DEI factus est ex muliere, Gal. 4, 4. &c.

XVIII. Qui posterior modus à priori differt I. ex parte Subjecti, qvod ibi utramqve involvit naturam, hîc vero non est nisi solus λόγός adsumens. II. ex parte Prædicati, qvod ibi est alterutrius naturæ proprium: hîc verò non nisi humanitatis proprium est, qvod adsumendo Naturam humanam λόγός sibi simul adpropria vit.

XIX. Patet ex dictis, rectiùs hoc Primum Genus dici ἰδιοπόιησιν seu ἰδιοποιίαν, adpropriationem sive communionem, qvàm Communicationem. Adcuratè enim loqvendo persona sibi ipsi aliqvid communicare dici haud potest, sed tantùm sibi naturæ propria ob factam unionem ὑποςατικὴν adpropriat & qvidem tàm arctè, ut nihil passionis de Humana natura adfirmari possit, qvod non in ipsissimum DEI Filium redundet.

XX. Qvippe tàm ὄντως, hoc est, non verbaliter, nominetenus, sed realiter & verè λόγός, suâ naturâ manens impassibilis, in suâ carne est mortuus (scilicet personaliter), qvàm verè & realiter ipsius (λόγός) caro propria fuit.

XXI. Apage proinde sit ab Ecclesiâ Nestorius (qvem Lutherum excusare adniti, qvasi bonum Zelum & fidem rectam habuerit, Greg. de Valen. mendacissimè scribit) personam ob Idiomatum Communicationis negationem divellens, qvasi qvævis natura per se sola seorsim sua ageret.

XXII. Et qvamvis ὀρθοδοξίαν qvoad Personæ unitatem tenere videri voluit; dicens: Aufer omnem suspicionem Dualitatis & Filiorum: dividendo tamen voces, qvæ de CHRISTO prædicantur, ac si qvædam convenirent Homini CHRISTO, qvædam Homini DEO, atqve sic Idiomatum communicationem negando, personam solvisse rectè Concilium Ephesinum concludit.

XXIII. Etenim actiones & passiones non naturarum sed personæ sunt, qvî igitur rectè juxta Nestorium dici poterit: Hæc agit Divina CHRISTI natura, hæc agit natura ipsius humana? Hinc piè Lutherus: ad divisionem operum succedit divisio personæ.

XXIV. Facessat similiter à schola omnium sobriè piorum ceu pestis vivarum consolationum Zvvinglii Ἀλλοίωσις, qvam talem τῶν ὀνομάτων ἀντίδοσιν esse docuit, qua una natura sumitur & intelligitur pro alterâ. Sic hæc Propositio Filius DEI crucifigitur, Hebr. 6, 6. Zvvinglio idem sonat, qvod, Humana natura Filio Dei unita crucifigitur. Qvo ipso certè & Communicatio & Unio omni realitate ac veritate, salusq; nostra solido fundamento spoliatur.

XXV. Nam pro mundi vitâ mori certè non est tantùm naturæ humanæ, sed & ipsius Filii Dei opus, alioqvin incarnari hic non necesse habuisset. Unde unum idemq; & Passionis subjectum & Fidei nostræ objectum dicit Symbolum Apostolicum, nempe Jesum Christum. Non igitur & nos alteram naturam penitus à passione excludi patiamur.

XXVI. Qvod ipsum invictè D. Lutherus hoc argumento jamdudum obtinuit: Hæc persona (monstrato Christo) patitur, moritur. Hæc autem persona est verus Deus. Ergo verus Deus patitur.

XXVII. Qvæ Conclusio clarè ostendit, ἀδύνατον esse, ut τὸ Deus vel Dei Filius in ejusmodi propositionibus pro toto Christo poni possit. Nisi enim tàm in Conclusione, qvàm in Minore alteram duntaxat Christi naturam intelliges, Minor Calvinistico absurdo, (qvo Christum & Filium Dei æqvivalere, ab Heidelbergicis scribitur) hæc erit: Christus est Christus.

XXVIII. Addo & hoc: Ille Deus patitur, qvi factus est caro. Atqvi λόγος, Deus, non caro Deo unita, factus est caro. Ergo &c.

XXIX. Neq; apud solidioris literaturæ Candidatos hanc Ἀλλοίωσιν qvidam Calvinicolæ excusabunt suâ Synecdoche, quâ in ejusmodi propositionibus partem pro parte dici adserunt: Siqvidem crediderim ego, non Synecdochicè aut tropicè sed satis propriè ipsum loqvi qvi simul subjectum Quod & subjectum Quo connectit, ut Homo scribit Manu, Deus patitur carne &c.

XXX. Notum præterea est in restrictione Synecdochicâ partem restringentem rem non posse in casu recto de illa re qvæ restringitur enunciari, non enim dico, homo est manus &c. qvod tamen in hoc exemplo fieri manifestum est. Qvomodo ergo Synecdoche erit? Taceo qvòd in Synecdochicis propositionibus pars pro toto, non pars pro parte dicatur.

XXXI. Alii vident Zvvinglium hâc suâ ἀλλοιώσει & Nestorium non totis, qvod dicitur, castris dissidere, itaqve Lutherum Zvvinglii mentem non rectè hîc percepisse, sed ipsi aliqvid adfinxisse, clamitant.

mitant. Sic enim Heidelbergenses contra Würtembergicos: Die (sc. ubi Lutherus de maledictâ Zvvinglii ἀλλοιώσει agit) hat D. Luther den Zwinglium nicht recht verstanden. Item: GOtt weißes/ und es kans auch ein jeder Mensch wissen/der nur des Zwinglii Schrifften lesen wil/daß D. Luther so wohl in diesen (sc. Communic. Idiom.) als in vielen andern Dingen dem guten ehrlichen Mann gewalt und unrecht gethan hat. Und daß D. Luther etwa dem Zwinglio hat fürgeworffen/ als solte er von der Eigenschafften beyder Naturen in Christo/ ꝛc. Gotteslästerlich gelehrt haben. Aber der Leser sol wissen/daß nicht D. Luther selbst/ sondern nur D. Luthers Zorn solches gethan hat.

XXXII. Et ut omnem suspicionem à se removeant, sic scribunt: Wenn die Calvinisten das lehreten / daß das leyden und Sterben Christi eines blossen Menschen Leyden und Sterben wäre / so solte man ihnen die Zunge zum Halse heraus reissen. Et post pauca: Es ist viel ein anders sagen: / das nur ein Mensch für uns gestorben sey; ein anders / daß Christus nur nach der menschlichen Natur für uns gestorben sey. Prius rejiciunt, posterius in suis scriptis Germanicis hinc inde defendunt.

XXXIII. Sed veteratoriè hæc omnia scribunt; ut qvis mirari possit, qvî tam apertam veritatem infirmare audeant? Sic Zvvinglius ipse ad Confessionem Lutheri: Joh. 3, 13. 14. Filius hominis bis nominatus est, nullibi tamen sic utramqve naturam simul significat, sed primo loco divinam, secundo humanam duntaxat denotat. Et alibi: Si qvando proprietates istæ (duarum naturarum in CHRISTO) videntur permutari, ut cum Deus gloriæ dicitur crucifixus: & filius hominis fuisse in cœlo cùm esset cum Nicodemo in terris, tropus est ἀλλοιώσεως intra verba consistens. Et rursus: Veram CHRISTI Divinitatem agnosco, eamqve sic agnosco, ut ipsi neqvàqvam tribuendum censeam, qvod illi minus convenire potest. Similiter veram qvoqve humanitatem CHRISTI agnosco, ut huic etiam, qvod in illam non potest competere, nullo modo velim tribui.

XXXIV. Et hanc Zvvinglii sententiam Lutherus sic expressit: Hoc Zvvinglius, inqvit Luth. vocat Allæosin, cùm aliqvid de Divinitate CHRISTI dicitur, quod tamen humanitatis proprium est: v. g. Ubi dicitur: Nonne hæc oportuit pati CHRISTUM, & ita intrare in gloriam suam; ibi nugatur Zvvinglius, qvod vocabulum (Christus) hoc loco pro humana natura sumatur.

XXXV. Eant nunc, & dicant bono illi viro (videlicet Zvvinglio, qvem solum gallinæ albæ filium volunt) â Luthero factam injuriam, ipsius mentem Luthero non rectè innotuisse.

XXXVI. Et qvid qvæso aliud hactenus Lutherani oppugnarunt in Cinglianis, qvam hanc eandem phrasin: sola natura humana est passa? Edisserant candidè, qvid in Christo differant homo & humana natura, nam non de vulgari & nudo homine sed de homine Deificato, inter nos & illos est qvæstio. In fumum igitur abeunt, qvæ scribunt: Wenn man sagt/ daß nur ein Mensch für uns gestorben sey/ da Christus für uns gestorben ist/ so ist das die Meynung/ daß Christus/ der für uns gestorben ist/ nur ein blosser Mensch/ und nicht zugleich GOtt und Mensch sey. Wenn man aber sagt/ daß Christus nur nach der menschlichen Natur für uns gestorben sey/ so hats nicht die Meynung/ als wenn Christus/ der für uns gestorben ist/ nur ein blosser Mensch sey: Sondern die Meynung hat es/ daß Christus/ ob Er schon zugleich GOtt und Mensch ist in einer einzigen unzertrennten Person/ dennoch nicht beydes nach der Gottheit und auch nach der Menschheit/ sondern allein nach der Menschheit gestorben sey/ da Er für uns gestorben ist.

XXXVII. Qvibus hoc unicum opponere placet: Cujus suppositum verè patitur, idipsum etiam patitur. Atqvi λόγε suppositum verè patitur. E.

XXXVIII. Inqvis: Deitas non potest mori, proinde sola mortua est CHRISTI humanitas. Resp. negando conseqventiam ex illo πολυθρυλλήτῳ, Actiones & passiones sunt suppositi: Moritur Deus non in suâ naturâ sed in suâ propriâ carne.

XXXIX. Qværitur hîc de enunciationibus in abstracto, an, ut in Concreto dico, Deus est passus, sic etiam rectè, Deitas est passa, clavis adfixa, mortua? Resp. Etiamsi & veteres & magni nominis Theologi iis usi fuerint, nos tamen ab istis abstinemus, qvia 1. Scriptura eas nescit. 2. Sacrosanctum Ecclesiæ nostræ Symbolum, videlicet Liber Christianæ Concordiæ; qvi non tantùm est scriptus ratione rerum, ob Fidei Articulos, sed & propter Phrases, ut certa haberetur norma loqvendi in Ecclesia; Praedicationibus in concreto uti maluit; Et 3. ut eò magis adversariorum calumnias declinemus, errorumq́; Eutychetis & Theopaschitarum suspicionem qvàm longissimè fugemus.

XL. Neqve tamen ob id virgulâ censoriâ Theologos illos, qvi sic in abstracto praedicari posse statuunt, notandos censemus; Nam illi ipsi ideò hoc adfirmavere, ut eò melius Calvinicolos & Jesuitas Nestorianizantes & Samosatenizantes producere possent: Neqve sine determinatione ejusmodi locutiones admittere, aut cum aliqvo de illis litigare volunt.

XLI. Qværitur etiam, an in illis propositionibus, ubi de homine humana prædicantur, sit Communicatio Idiomatum, & an illæ: Filius homo edit, bibit &c. huc pertineant?

XLII. Resp. Qvidni? Qvia non subjectum hîc supponit pro naturæ concreto significante formaliter solam naturam humanam adsumptam, sed pro Concreto personæ, ut significet totum compositum. Ubi enim proprietas uni naturæ conveniens tribuitur personæ in concreto, ibi est communicatio Idiomatum primi generis.

XLIII. Insuper, ut hæc: Filius hominis crucifixus, passus est &c. exponitur per Idiomatum Communicationem, & rectè in primo genere locatur; sic & hæc: Filius hominis edit, bibit &c. Quod enim valet in re pari, valet etiam in re compari.

XLIV. Ne autem omni fructu & solatio hæc ita in loqvendo diligentia carere videatur, unâ vel alterâ Meditatione practicâ concludemus.

XLV. Ac proinde sit nobis hæc doctrina 1. clavis solatii Christiani. Obstupescit certè animus pius ob tanta misericordiæ viscera, considerans, qvòd ipse DEI Filius carnis suæ ignominias & passiones per innenarrabilem adpropriationis modũ, nostrûm causâ perferre voluit, ac proinde non dubitare potest, qvin is ipse, qvi dignum duxit in carne alapas, vincula, sputa, irrisiones &c. perferre, ac in se recipere, nos qvi sumus ejusdem cum ipso substantiæ, sibi aliqvando sit adassociaturus.

XLVI. Causet deinde & hæc doctrina in nobis severum peccati odium. Nam ut nos DEO viciniores fieremus, ipse DEI Filius propternostra peccata carnem adsumpsit, & in eâ omnes ignominias portavit. Cur ergo & nos id patremus, qvod nos à Deo sejungeret? Peccata nostra nos à Deo dividunt, fugiamus ergò & detestamur eas, ne à Deo deviemus. Deo qvi adhæret, unus cum eo est Spiritus. Fac ergò summe Deus, ut tibi unicè adhæreamus per Jesum Christum in Spiritu tuo sancto, Amen.


## 15 Fifteenth Disputation, On the Second Kind of Communication of Properties

Thesis I.

We have spoken above in the disputation concerning ἐνανθρωπήσει καὶ ἰδιοποιίᾳ [incarnation and appropriation]; now in the second place, we shall treat of κοινωνοποιίᾳ [communication of operations], following not the order of nature, but the authority of the Formula of Concord.

II. But lest we do this in a disorderly manner, we shall very briefly treat the following parts: 1. The names and appellations of this second kind. 2. The distinctions by which it is distinguished from the first and third kind. 3. The definition. Hence 4. the sense of the Chalcedonian Canon, 'Each nature acts, etc.,' must be investigated. And 5. the struggles of the Monothelites must be considered. 6. It must be explained: Whether to die for the life of the world is an ἀποτέλεσμα [effect/result]? 7. A practical meditation is to be subjoined.

III. I. Part. Various names are imposed by various people upon this second kind of Communication, differing in sound but not in sense: for by Cyril it is called κοινωνοποίησις [communication of operations]; commonly κοινωνοποιία; ἐνεργειῶν κοινωνία and Communication of operations: but by Damascenus it is called συνδρομὴ [concurrence]: both because there is a real communion of the natural operations of both natures, and because those operations are expressed by one locution.

IV. I shall say here that the Calvinists write to us, denying that this second degree is rightly called a kind of Communication, Joh. Combach in Orth. Confes. on the perfection and office of Christ, thesis 59. But I respond: 1. That we are dealing here with the concurrence of natural actions in the person of Christ, with respect to one effect, which, as they flow from the properties of the natures, so they can not inconveniently be referred to the same. 2. That the ancient Church expressly called it a Communication of Attributes, when it defined through the Council of Chalcedon: That each nature in Christ acts μετὰ κοινωνίας [with communion], that which is proper to each.

Whence what else follows but κοινωνία ἰδίων? not to mention the testimonies of Cyril, Epist. 10, 29, and Nazianzen, 4, de Theol.

V. II. As this second kind agrees with the others in the foundation, which is the Personal Union, so it differs from them: 1. In name. 2. In the consideration of the subject. 3. In definition.

VI. 1. The names exist in θ. 3, which belong neither to the first nor to the third degree. 2. In the first degree, the subject is considered as it is the whole person, of whom the properties of both natures are predicated reciprocally: in the third degree, the subject is the assumed Human nature, of which divine things are said, yet not reciprocally: in the second, the whole person is considered, of whom the ἀποτέλεσμα is enunciated in some way reciprocally.

VII. This is what the particles 'according to', 'insofar as', 'in that', etc., denote, which are used in this second and the other kinds of Communication, the function of which is not the same everywhere. For in the first degree they are etiological and specificative: in the third they are specificative only, denominating the Human nature of Christ: in the second degree they are copulative and reduplicative, joining both natures with respect to the same ἀποτέλεσμα.

VIII. And hence arises the definition or description by which the 3rd is distinguished from the other kinds: for it is defined as a true and real communion of the natural and proper ἐνεργειῶν of both Natures in Christ, for the producing of the ἀποτελέσματα of the office of Redemption.

IX. This definition implies that Christ, in his Mediatorial office, does not act in, with, or through one nature, but the person of Christ acts according to both natures, or in both forms, etc., as explained by Damascene, lib. 3, de O. F. c. 15, 19.

X. This can be proved: 1. By the truth of Scripture. 2. By the weight of reasons. 3. By the testimony of the ancient Church.

XI. 1. As the three principal offices of the Mediator are commonly listed—Prophetic, Priestly, Kingly—so the administration of all is ascribed not to nature and nature, but to the person (θεανθρώπῳ), whether denominated by both or by either one, and that either by the divine or the human nature.

XII. Concerning the Prophetic office, there testify, besides others, the oracles of Is. 40, 10, 11; Zech. 13, 7; John 10, 11; John 1, 9, 28; Matt. 11, 27; Matt. 17, 5; 1 John 5, 20; Ezek. 34, 15; Deut. 10, 18; Is. 61, 1, 2.

XIII. Concerning the priestly office, let the sayings 1 Cor. 15, 3; Gal. 1, 4; C. 3, 13 be noted. Eph. 5, 2. Heb. 2, 9. Ef. 35, 4. Jer. 23, 6. c. 33, 16. Os. 1, 7. Act. 20, 28. Rom. 5, 10. c. 8, 3. 32. Gal. 4, 4. 1. Joh. 1, 7. c. 3, 8. Heb. 4, 14. Gen. 3, 15. Matth. 9, 6. Luc. 9, 56. Rom. 5, 15. 1. Tim. 2, 5.

XIV. Christ likewise executes the whole Kingly Office, Luc. 2, 11. 1. Cor. 15, 25. Zach. 9, 9. Pf. 110, 2. who according to his Deity is the Lord of glory himself (essentially) 1. Cor. 2, 8. the author of life (life itself Joh. 1, 4. c. 14, 6.) Act. 3, 13. whose power the righteous branch Jer. 23, 5. received personally Matth. 28, 19. Eph. 1, 22.

XV. 2. We give these few reasons out of many, of which 1. from the end of the incarnation of the λόγος: if the bare λόγος wished to be mediator, or a bare man could be, what need for the λόγος to be incarnated? 2. from the variety of the Mediator's works: for the works of mediation are such that neither bare God could do them, such as shedding blood, dying; nor could a bare man do them savingly, such as shedding blood and dying for the life of the world. 3. from the condition of the Mediator, who had to be a middle party between the dissenting parties, which were God and man: Therefore, both between divinity alone and Humanity alone, the Human-Deity and the Divine-Humanity is the mediatrix, as Aug. speaks beautifully, which Vigilius shows in more detail in lib. 5. c. 4.

XVI. 3. The blessed Chemnitz brings forward quite a few testimonies of orthodox Antiquity in lib. de Duab. Nat. c. 17. p. 270. Mr. Laurentius Lælius in Exeg. art. de perf. Ch. c. 14. th. 13. p. 159. which, with what good faith Bellarmine explains them as only concerning substantial mediation with the Calvinists, the inspection itself shows.

XVII. I pass over the infinite absurdities which emerge in swarms from the opinion of the adversaries, who exclude at will either the divinity or the humanity of Christ from this or that work of the mediator, some of which the blessed Hutter reviews in Expl. l. Conc. p. 277.

XIIX. Moved by these arguments, we believe and confess with heart and mouth from scripture, the Apostolic, Nicene, and Athanasian Creeds, that not a bare nature, but the son of GOD incarnate suffered for our salvation etc. and thus that Christ performs the works of the Mediator according to both natures.

XIX. Let it therefore shame the Photinian Enjedinus to attribute to us that we maintain that Christ is our Mediator only according to the Human Nature, Coroll. 1. in Expl. v. 4. Ps. 110. XX. Nay, rather we detest and execrate this damnable error among the Scholastics, its authors, Lombard. lib. 3. dist. 9. Bonav. ibid. art. 2. qvæst. ult. Thom. part. 3. qvæst. 26. art. 2. XXI. In Stancarus and the Stancarists, the interpolators; and the Jesuits, the propagators: Bell. lib. 5. de Ch. c. 1. seq. Joh. Busæus in Disp. de persona Christi ejusq́; Apologet. θ. 79. XXII. And at the same time in the Calvinists, who indeed refute this error in words, Zanch. Tom. 2. Miscell. c. 9. p. 143. Keker. lib. 3. syst. Theol. p. 329. but in deeds manfully propagate it, as long as they continue to defend their θέσεις & ὑποθέσεις. XXIII. For they deny every real Communication in Christ; therefore also the Communication of the works of Mediation. They say: only the Human nature has suffered, the Anhaltines in Apolog. p. 247. Martyr. in dial. de duab. Nat. in Ch. p. 28. See the Würtemberg Theological Closing-Speech page 171. seq. Item Victory and Triumph / p. 231. seq. Therefore, a naked human nature is the mediator. Martinius of Bremen says that the Lord is indeed mediator according to both natures, yet not all mediatorial acts are performed by both natures, in Exam. qverel. & admo. Balth. Menz. p. 142. 143. Therefore, a mediator is imagined without the function of Mediation, i.e., a dream is seen without sleep and bread is kneaded without flour, as Scaliger has it in Exerc. 359. f. 11. XXIV. Neither the Jesuits will purge themselves of this error by a poorly understood and applied distinction of the Principle which and by which: nor the Calvinists, by their fictitious and masked ἀλλοιώσει, concerning which see θ. 40. For Stancarus also used these pigments and figments, as is clear from his writing against the Tigurines θ. 6. 7. 8. and concerning the exclusive (only), where he candidly confesses that by the exclusive (Only) he does not exclude the divine Nature from the person of Christ, but from the office of Mediation. XXV. Doubtless the Nestorian Stancarus did not want to believe: that both natures in Christ, according to the Canon of the Council of Chalcedon, act with Communication, that which is proper to each: the sense of which is further to be investigated. XXVI. However, the adversaries inflict a double injury upon this Canon: Some, through the crime of forgery, omit the words (with Communication), as the Crypto-Calvinists of Wittenberg in the theses of A.C. 1570 written by M. Majo θ. 32. All, through malice, attach a foreign sense to it, when the words (with

Regarding the communication of the bare presence of the λόγος or union with the suffering flesh, Martinius interprets in the cited work, pp. 102, 103, and Bellarmine in the cited work, ch. 7.

XXVII. But clear words too strongly strike down and evade this remarkable ςρεβλότητα [distortion], which do not urge a bare Jesuit-Zwinglian-Nestorian διαίρεσιν [division], but define a real κοινωνίαν [communion] of natural actions.

XXIIX. This, however, by no means removes the distinction of natural actions (for each nature does what is its own), but only condemns the Nestorian separation. For since after the incarnation Christ as θεάνθρωπος [God-man] acts and suffers, such a distraction of actions and passions cannot be imagined, so that it could properly be said: The divinity alone does this; the humanity of Christ alone suffers that: for a Nestorian rending of the natures follows this separation, which the blessed Luther piously and rightly warns against.

XXIX. And that we may propose our opinion a little more clearly, we distinguish with Damascenus, lib. 3, ch. 15, between ἐνεργoῦν [acting], ἐνεργητικὸν [active], ἐνέργειαν [energy/operation], ἐνέργημα [act], and ἀποτέλεσμα [result]: the first denotes the acting person; the second, the principle of action; the third, the efficacious motion of nature; the fourth, the proper effect of each nature; the fifth, the saving action, flowing from the natural operation of each nature out of both, which is neither purely human nor purely divine, but human-divine and divine-human, and therefore called θεανδρικὴ [theandric] by Damascenus, ch. 19, after Dionysius.

XXX. Damascenus explains this with a beautiful similitude in lib. 3, ch. 15, taken from red-hot iron, which can be briefly formulated thus: Just as in a red-hot sword two natures, fire and iron (for the iron has the cutting property, and the fire the burning property), are observed, which are so intimately united in action that neither acts without the other, nor are they confused, because their difference is preserved in the burning cut and the cutting burn: so in Christ the divine and omnipotent action is of the divinity itself, but the human action is of the humanity and like our own; although in the action of God and man simultaneously they cannot be separated: for the θεάνθρωπος [God-man] works the human things divinely, and the divine things humanly.

XXXI. From what has been said, it appears both how gravely the Eutychians, Monophysites, and Monothelites erred, by confusing partly the natures, partly the essential properties, wills, and actions of the natures; see the acts of the 6th universal Synod around A.D. 680 and Damascenus in the cited work, ch. 14; and also how impudently the Calvinists act by accusing us of this error, Pareus p. 269 of the Irenicum, which, however, we detest, execrate, and overthrow with heart, mouth, and pen.

XXXII. For just as we confess two natures in Christ unconfusedly united, so we believe in the real distinction of the natural wills and operations.

XXXIII. Knowing that those things which are of diverse natures are also of diverse properties and actions, which Damascene, lib. 3 de O. F. c. 15 and in his book on the two wills in Christ, rightly urges and demonstrates, along with the Roman Council c. 9, 12; and this is according to Scripture, which in Matthew 26:39, Mark 14:35-36, and Luke 22:42 shows a human will distinct from the divine, yet not contrary to the divine, as Piscator argues in Herb. obs. 24 from c. 23 of Matthew, where the most holy will indeed shuddered at natural death, yet did not decline the salutary one; but it complained because of the infirmity assumed, which could perpetually rejoice through the glory granted; which Augustine learnedly explains in Ps. 30, Conc. 1.

XXXIV. It now remains to explain VI: Whether to die for the life of the world is proper to the human nature, or indeed an effect and duty of the God-man? The orthodox Lutherans affirm the latter; the heterodox Calvinists, to whom add the Jesuits, the former.

XXXV. And although what was lightly touched upon in thesis 23 and explained more fully in the cited passages might suffice to grasp the opinion of the adversaries, it is nevertheless pleasing to add to these the confession of Dr. Sturm, Theologian of Marburg, in his Apologetic Disputation against Dr. Mentzer, saying: That the flesh of Christ alone trod the winepress of our sins (thesis 19). To the flesh of Christ alone, and to no other besides it, was granted the price and privilege by which the death of the flesh of Christ was held worthy to be accepted by the eternal Father as a sufficient price.

XXXVI. As this confession is clear, so it is impious, pernicious, and absurd; which we demonstrate in a few words as follows.

XXXVII. 1. Whatever work Scripture ascribes to the God-man, that cannot be attributed to the flesh alone without impiety. Scripture ascribes the liberation of the world from the fear of death to the God-man (Hebrews 2:14-15; 1 John 3:5, 8; compare Acts 3:15, 20:28; 1 Corinthians 2:8). Therefore.

XXXVIII. 2. Whatever presupposes infinite power cannot, without an open denial of the Scriptures, be attributed to the flesh alone. To die for the life of the world presupposes infinite power, as the Heidelberg theologians admit im Beschluß p. 113; Keckermann lib. 3. syst. Theol. p. 330. E.; and therefore an infinite price was either not paid or not demanded, as the Photinians urge, Socinus de Chr. serv. part. 3. c. 4. Ostorod. part. 3. Inst. pag. 214. Catech. Racov. p. 261. 262.

XXXIX. 3. Whatever is proper to the human nature of Christ alone, and indeed formally, as Bellarmine explains in lib. 5. c. 1. de Chr., that can be attributed to all men: To die for the life of the world is formally proper to the human nature of Christ alone. Therefore, the conclusion is absurd. Therefore, one of the premises: There is no major premise that relies on this foundation: that what is formally in one individual can be in all individuals of the same species. Therefore, the minor premise.

XL. I hear here the Calvinists and Jesuits clamoring quite importunately: That they by no means maintain that the flesh suffering and dying was alone, but believe it was united with the Λόγος, and for this reason the passion and death are attributed to the Λόγος himself through ἀλλοίωσιν. Paraeus in der Biblischen Rettung p. 95. One would have to distinguish between the principle which acts and that by which it acts, Bell. lib. 5. de Ch. c. 1. §. Est autem. But this clamor is truly empty, which fills the ears, but provides no defense for a desperate cause: We ask: did God really die in his flesh for the world? They answer: The Λόγος was present to the suffering and dying flesh. What does this have to do with the matter? The Λόγος was present to Stephen suffering and dying. Therefore, Stephen's death is a sufficient ransom for sins. An argument worthy of the adversaries: which follows necessarily by connection from Zwingli's ἀλλοίωσιν and Bellarmine's depraved distinction: for whether you resolve Zwingli's ἀλλοίωσιν or the Jesuit's distinction into its own principle, this will finally emerge: that the passion and death are attributed to the Λόγος only verbally, as Beza explains, vol. 1. p. 624. Therefore, Christ is a verbal redeemer. Rejoice, Photinians, you have more companions!

XLI. But keep your verbal mediator for yourselves! We piously believe the God-man really died for us: not only man, but also GOD: for that reason the impassible Λόγος He assumed Human Nature, that He might suffer in the unity of person, who could not suffer in the purity of Nature. XLII. Which Epiphanius beautifully explains, lib. 3. tom. 2. against the Dimaritae, heresy 77. Passion does not fall upon the Deity, but was made in the Human Nature. It was not, however, referred to the Human nature alone, (so that that saying might not be fulfilled in the dispensation of salvation: Cursed is everyone who has hope in man) but it was reckoned to the Deity, since the deity did not suffer, &c.

XLIII. This, this at last is the consideration that raises up a certain hope of salvation for the suffering and trembling soul: Behold! for, O pious soul, the θεάνθρωπος comes to save you, He comes to preserve you through mercy, you who have destroyed yourself through malice. Your Mediator is not a mere man, who might wish and not be able; not a mere God, who might be able and not wish: but GOD and man: Therefore He both wishes, because He is merciful, and is able, because He is omnipotent. a He suffered all things here, that He might free you from all things: He died, that death might be extinguished: He feared, that you might be freed from fear: He grieved, that sorrows might be absent from you. b He took upon Himself your sadness, that He might bestow upon you His joy. c The Lord grieved not for His own wounds but yours, not for His own death but yours. d Take heart therefore, O sinful soul, take heart! do not despair! hope in Him whom you fear, flee to Him from whom you have fled, call upon Him importunately, whom you have proudly provoked, say to Him: Jesus, for the sake of Your sweet name, do unto me according to Your name: e Hear, O Creator, I am Your creature, Your hands have fashioned me, those hands, I say, which were fixed with nails for me. Do not despise, O Lord, the work of Your hands, I pray that You look upon the wounds of Your hands. Behold! in Your hands, O Lord GOD, You have inscribed me, read that very writing and save me. Lo, I sigh to You, Your creature. You are the Creator, recreate me! Lo, I cry to You, Your handiwork! You are Life, vivify me! Lo, I look to You, Your psalm. You are the Psalmist, restore me. And spare me as I speak to You. Necessity has no law, pain compels me to speak: The calamity which I suffer forces me to exclaim. I am sick, I cry to the physician: I am blind, I hasten to the light: I am dead, I sigh for life. You are the physician, You are the light, You are the life, JESUS of Nazareth! Have mercy on me, O son of David, have mercy on me without mercy!

Latin:

Thesis I.

DIctum sup. disputatione de ἐνανθρωπήσει καὶ ἰδιοποιίᾳ; nunc secundo loco, de κοινωνοποιίᾳ agemus, seqventes non naturæ ordinem, sed Formulæ Concordiæ authoritatem.

II. Ne autem ἀτάκτως hoc faciamus, seqq. brevissimè pertractabimus membra: 1. Nomina & Appellationes hujus secundi generis. 2. Discrimina, quibus à primo & tertio genere distingvitur. 3. Definitionem. Hinc 4. indagandum erit sensus Cano. Chalced. Utrąq; Natura agit &c. Et 5. consideranda Certamina Monothelitarum. 6. Explicandum: Num mori pro mundi vitâ sit ἀποτέλεσμα? 7. Meditatio practica subjungenda.

III. I. Memb. Secundo huic Communicationis Generi à variis varia imponuntur nomina, sono non sensu discrepantia: à Cyrillo enim dicitur κοινωνοποίησις: vulgò κοινωνοποιία; ἐνεργειῶν κοινωνία & operationum Communicatio: à Damasceno verò appellatur συνδρομὴ: tum qvòd utriusq; naturæ operationum naturalium realis est communio, tum qvòd operationes illæ unâ locutione exprimuntur.

IV. Dicam hîc nobis scribunt Calviniani, negantes, hunc secundum gradum rectè Communicationis genus appellari, Joh. Combach. in orth. Confes. de perf. & off. Ch. θ. 59. Sed Resp. 1. agi hic de concursu actionum naturalium in personâ Christi, respectu unius Apotelesmatis, qvæ ut à naturarum proprietatibus fluunt, ita ad easdem non incommodè referri possunt. 2. Veterem Ecclesiam expressè Communicationem Idiomatum appellasse, cum per Conc. Chalced. definivit: Utramque naturam in Christo agere μετὰ κοινωνίας, quod cujusq; est ἴδιον.

Unde qvid aliud qvam κοινωνία ἰδίων conseqvitur? ut taceam testimonia Cyrilli Epist. 10. 29. Naz. 4. de Theol.

V. II. Ut hoc secundum genus cum cæteris in fundamento, qvod est Unio personalis, convenit: ita ab iisdem differt. 1. Nomine. 2. Consideratione subjecti. 3. Definitione.

VI. 1. Nomina extant θ. 3. qvæ neq; primo neq; tertio gradui competunt. 2. Subjectum in primo gradu consideratur, ut est tota persona, de qvâ utriusq; naturæ propria prædicantur reciprocè: in tertio gradu subjectum est natura Humana assumpta, de qva divina dicuntur, non tamen reciprocè: in secundo tota persona consideratur, de qva ἀποτέλεσμα enunciatur aliqvaliter reciprocè.

VII. Id qvod notant particulæ; secundùm,qvatenus,qvâ &c. in hoc secundo & cæteris Communicationis generibus usitatæ, qvarum non ubiq; idem est officium. In primo enim gradu sunt ætiologicæ & specificativæ: in tertio sunt specificativæ tantùm, Humanam Christi naturam denominantes: in secundo gradu sunt copulativæ & reduplicativæ, utramq; naturam respectu ejusdé ἀποτελέσματος conjungentes.

VIII. Et hinc definitio vel descriptio, per qvam 3. ab aliis distingvitur generibus, exurgit: Definitur enim vera & realis naturalium & propriarum utriusq; Naturæ in Christo ἐνεργειῶν κοινωνία, ad officii Redemptionis ἀποτελέσματα producendum.

IX. Innuit hæc definitio, Christum in Mediatorio officio, non agere, in, cum, aut per unam naturam, sed personam Christi agere secundùm utramq; naturam, seu in utrâq; formâ &c. explicante Damasc. lib. 3. de O. F. c. 15. 19.

X. Id qvod probari potest: 1. Scripturæ veritate. 2. Rationum gravitate. 3. Ecclesiæ antiqvæ testimonio.

XI. 1. Ut vulgò tria principalia Mediatoris officia recensentur, Propheticum, Sacerdotale, Regium, ita omnium administratio non naturæ & naturæ, sed personæ, (θεανθρώπῳ) adscribitur vel ab utrâq; vel alterutrâ, eâq; vel divinâ vel humanâ naturâ denominatæ.

XII. De Prophetico testantur præter cætera, oracula Es. 40, 10. 11. Zach. 13, 7. Joh. 10, 11. Joh. 1, 9. 28. Matth. 11, 27. Matth. 17, 5. 1. Joh. 5, 20. Ez. 34, 15. Deut. 10, 18. Es. 61, 1. 2.

XIII. De sacerdotali notentur dicta 1. Cor. 15, 3. Gal. 1, 4. C. 3, 13. Eph. 5, 2. Heb. 2, 9. Ef. 35, 4. Jer. 23, 6. c. 33, 16. Os. 1, 7. Act. 20, 28. Rom. 5, 10. c. 8, 3. 32. Gal. 4, 4. 1. Joh. 1, 7. c. 3, 8. Heb. 4, 14. Gen. 3, 15. Matth. 9, 6. Luc. 9, 56. Rom. 5, 15. 1. Tim. 2, 5.

XIV. Regium Officium similiter totus exeqvitur Christus, Luc. 2, 11. 1. Cor. 15, 25. Zach. 9, 9. Pf. 110, 2. qvi secundum Deitatem est ipse Dominus gloriæ (essentialiter) 1. Cor. 2, 8. auctor vitæ (ipsa vita Joh. 1, 4. c. 14, 6.) Act. 3, 13. cujus potestatem germen justum Jer. 23, 5. accepit personaliter Matth. 28, 19. Eph. 1, 22.

XV. 2. Rationes è multis has damus paucas, qvarum 1. à fine incarnationis τοῦ λόγου : si nudus λόγος mediator esse voluit, vel nudus homo esse potuit, qvid opus λόγον incarnari? 2. ab operum Mediatoris varietate: sunt enim opera mediationis talia, qvæ neq; nudus Deus potuit facere, ut fundere sangvinem, mori; neq; nudus homo salutariter facere, ut sangvinem fundere & mori pro mundi vita. 3. à Mediatoris conditione, qvi medius esse debebat inter partes dissidentes, qvæ erant Deus & homo: Igitur & inter divinitatem solam & Humanitatem solam, mediatrix est Humana-Deitas, & Divina-Humanitas, ut Aug. pulchrè loqvitur, qvod pluribus ostendit Vigilius lib. 5. c. 4.

XVI. 3. Testimonia Antiqvitatis orthodoxæ benè multa adducit B. Chem. lib. de Duab. Nat. c. 17. p. 270. Dn. Laurent. Lælius in Exeg. art. de perf. Ch. c. 14. th. 13. p. 159. qvæ qvâ fide Bellarm. cum Calvinianis tantùm de mediatione substantiali exponant, ipsa inspectio monstrat.

XVII. Taceo infinita absurda, qvæ ex sententiâ adversariorum, Christi vel divinitatem vel humanitatem ab hoc vel illo mediatoris opere pro lubitu excludentium, turmatim prodeunt, qvorum nonnulla recenset B. Hutterus in Expl. l. Conc. p. 277.

XIIX. His moti argumentis credimus nos & confitemur corde & ore ex scriptura, Symbolo Apostolico, Niceno, Athanasiano, non nudam naturam, sed DEI filium incarnatum pro salute nostrâ passum &c. & ita Mediatoris opera Christum secundum utramqve naturam peragere.

XIX. Pudeat igitur Enjedinum Photinianum nobis affingere, qvod statuamus, Christum Mediatorem nostrum esse tantùm secundùm Humanam Naturam, Coroll. 1. in Expl. v. 4. Pf. 110. XX. Qvin potius detestamur & execramur damnabilem hunc errorem in Scholasticis, ejus autoribus, Lombard. lib. 3. dist. 9. Bonav. ibid. art. 2. qvæst. ult. Thom. part. 3. qvæst. 26. art. 2. XXI. In Stancaro & Stancariftis interpolatoribus; & Jesuitis propagatoribus: Bell. lib. 5. de Ch. c. 1. seq. Joh. Busæo in Disp. de persona Christi ejusq́; Apologet. θ. 79. XXII. Et simul in Calvinianis, qui errorem hunc verbis quidem refutant, Zanch. Tom. 2. Miscell. c. 9. p. 143. Keker. lib. 3. syst. Theol. p. 329. factis autem viriliter propagant, qvamdiu θέσεις & ὑποθέσεις suas defendere pergunt. XXIII. Negant enim omnem realem Communicationem in Christo; E. etiam Communicationem operum Mediationis. Dicunt: solam Humanam naturam esse passam, Anhaltini in Apolog. p. 247. Martyr. in dial. de duab. Nat. in Ch. p. 28. Vide der Würtembergischen Theol. Schluß-Rede pag. 171. seq. Item Sieg und Triumph / p. 231. seq. E, nuda humana natura est mediatrix. Dicit Martinius Bremens.
