Dominum mediatorem quidem esse secundùm utramq; naturam, non tamen omnia mediatoria gesta utrâq; naturâ absolvi, in Exam. qverel. & admo. Balth. Menz. p. 142. 143. E. mediator fingitur sine Mediationis functione i. e. insomnium cernitur sine somno & panis sine farina pinsitur, ut Scalig. habet Exerc. 359. f. 11. XXIV. Non se purgabunt ab hoc errore vel Jesuitæ malè intellecta & applicata distinctione Principii quod & qvo: vel Calviniani, fictitia & larvata sua ἀλλοιώσει, de quibus θ. 40. Istis enim pigmentis & figmentis etiamStancarus utebatur, ut claret ex scripto contra Tigurinos θ. 6.7.8. & de exclusiva, (tantùm) ubi candidè fatetur, se exclusivâ (Tantùm) non excludere divinam Naturam à personâ Christi, sed ab officio Mediationis. XXV. Nimirum credere noluit Stancarus Nestorianns: utramq; naturam in Christo, juxta Canon. Concilii Chalced. agere cum Communicatione, qvod cujusq; est proprium: cujus sensus porrò est indagandus. XXVI. Inferunt autem huic Canoni adversarii duplicem injuriam: Qvidam per crimen falsi verba(cum Communicatione) omittunt, ut Crypto-Calv. Witteberg. in thesib. A. C. 1570. M. Majo conscriptis θ. 32. Omnes per malitiam alienum affingunt sensum, cum verba(cum

Communicatione) de nudâ λόγου præsentiâ vel unione cum carne patiente interpretantur Martinius l. d. p. 102. 103. & Bell. l. d. c. 7.

XXVII. Sed insignem hanc ςρεβλότητα verba clara nimis fortiter elidunt & eludunt, quæ non nudam Jesuitico-Zvvinglio-Nestorianam urgent διαίρεσιν, sed realem naturalium actionum definiunt κοινωνίαν.

XXIIX. Hæc tamen minimè tollit naturalium actionum distinctionem (utraq; enim natura agit, quod suum est) sed tantum Nestorianam damnat separationem. Cum enim post incarnationem Christus θεάνθρωπος agat & patiatur, actionum & passionem non potest talis fingi distractio, ut propriè dici possit: Hæc agit sola divinitas: illa patitur sola humanitas Christi: separationem enim hanc Nestoriana inseqvitur Naturarum divulsio, quod piè & rectè B. monet Luth.

XXIX. Et ut sententiam nostram paulò clariùs proponamus, distinguimus cum Damasc. lib. 3. c. 15. inter ἐνεργoῦν, ἐνεργητικὸν, ἐνέργειαν, ἐνέργημα, & ἀποτέλεσμα : primum notat personam agentem. 2. actionis principium. 3. efficacem naturæ motum. 4. proprium cujusq; naturæ effectum. 5. actionem salutarem, ex utraq; utriusq; naturæ naturali operatione, promanantem, quæ neq; purè humana, nec purè divina; sed humani-divina, & divini-humana, ideoq́ve à Damasc. c. 19. θεανδρικὴ appellata ex Dionysio.

XXX. Pulchrâ hoc explicat similitudine Damasc. lib. 3. c. 15. à ferro ignito desumptâ, quæ breviter ita formari potest: Sicut in gladio ignito duæ naturæ, ignis & ferri (ἔχει μὲν γὰρ ὁ μὲν σίδηρος τὸ τμητικὸν, τὸ δὲ πῦρ τὸ καυστικὸν) conspiciuntur, quæ in actione ita in timè uniuntur, ut neq; altera absq; alterâ agat, neqve etiam confundantur, qvia differentia earum salvatur in urente sectione & in secante ustione: ita in Christo divinitatis ipsius divina & omnipotens actio est, humanitatis autem humana & nostræ instar; licet in Dei simul & hominis actione disjungi neqveant: operatur enim θεάνθρωπος τὰ ἀνθρώπινα θείκῶς, καὶ θεϊκὰ ἀνθρωπίνως.

XXXI. Ex dictis apparet tum quàm graviter errarint Eutychiani, Monophysitæ & Monothelitæ, partim naturas, partim essentiales naturarum proprietates, voluntates & actiones confundendo; vide acta Synod. VI. univers. circa A. C. 680. & Damasc. d. l. c. 14. tum quàm impudenter agant Calvinistæ, hujus erroris nos accusando, Pareus p. 269. Irenici, qvem tamen corde, ore & calamo, detestamur, execramur, profligamus.

XXXII. Nos enim sicut in Christo duas naturas ἀσυγχύτως confitemur unitas: ita realem Naturalium voluntatum & operationum credimus distinctionem.

XXXIII. Scientes: quæ diversæ sunt naturæ, diversæ etiam esse proprietatis & actionis, id qvod Damasc. lib. 3. de O. F. c. 15. & in lib. de duabus volunt. in Christo recte urget & demonstrat, cum Conc. Roman. c. 9. 12. idq; juxta scripturam, quæ Matth. 26, 39. Mar. 14, 35. 36. Luc. 22, 42. distinctam humanam voluntatem à divina ostendit, non tamen divinæ contrariam, ut Pisc. Herb. arguit obs. 24. ex c. 23. Matth. ubi horrebat quidem sanctissima voluntas mortem naturalem, non detrectabat tamen salutarem: sed qverulabatur ob infirmitatem assumptam; qvæ perpetuò gaudere poterat per gloriam concessam: qvod eruditè explicat August. in Ps. 30. Conc. 1.

XXXIV. Explicandum nunc VI. restat: An mori pro mundi vitâ sit Humanæ naturæ proprium, an verò θεανθρώπꙋ ἀποτέλεσμα & officium? Posterius orthodoxi affirmant Lutherani; prius Cacodoxi Calviniani, qvibus adde Jesuitas.

XXXV. Et qvanqvam ad percipiendam sententiam adversariorum sufficere possent, qvæ th. 23. leviter sunt tacta & locis citatis fusiùs explicata; lubet tamen istis addere Confessionem D. Sturmii Theol. Marp. in Disp. Apolog. contra D. Menz. dicentis: Solam carnem Christi torcular peccatorum nostrorum calcasse th. 19. Soli carni Christi, ac præter eam nulli alii concessum pretium atq; prævilegium, qvo digna habita fuerit mors carnis Christi, ut ab æterno Patre pro pretio sufficiente acceptaretur.

XXXVI. Ut clara hæc est confessio, ita impia, pernitiosa, absurda: qvod paucis ita demonstramus.

XXXVII. 1 Qvodcunq; opus scriptura θεανθρώπῳ adscribit, id soli carni sine impietate tribui non potest. Liberationem mundi à metu mortis scriptura θεανθρώπῳ adscribit Hebr. 2, 14. 15. 1. Joh. 3, 5. 8. confer Act. 3, 15. c. 20, 28. 1. Cor. 2, 8. E.

XXXVIII. 2. Qvod infinitam præsupponit virtutem, id absq; saturis pacta negatione soli carni attribui neqvit. Mori pro mundi vitâ in finitam præsupponit virtutem, fatentibus Theol. Heidelb. im Beschluß p. 113. Kekerm. lib. 3. syst. Theol. p. 330. E. & proinde pretium infinitum vel non est solutum, vel non postulatum, qvod urgent Photiniani, Socinus de Chr. serv. part. 3. c. 4. Ostorod. part. 3. Inst. pag. 214. Catech. Rocov. p. 261. 262.

XXXIX. 3. Qvicqvid est proprium solius Humanæ naturæ Christi & qvidem formaliter, ut Bell. lib. 5. c. 1. de Chr. explicat, id omnibus hominibus poterit attribui: Mori pro mundi vita formaliter solius Hum. Christi est proprium. E. Conclusio absurda. E. aliqva præmissarum: Non major qvæ hoc nititur fundamento: qvod formaliter uni individuo inest, id omnibus ejusdem speciei individuis inesse potest. E. Minor.

XL. Audio hîc importunè admodum Calvinianos & Jesuitas acclamantes: Se neqvaqvam statuere; Carnem patientem & morientem fuisse solam, sed credere fuisse cum Λόγῳ unitam, & hanc ob causam passionem & mortem per ἀλλοίωσιν ipsi Λόγῳ attribui. Paræus in der Biblischen Rettung p. 95. distinguendum esset inter principium qvod agit & qvo agit Bell. lib. 5. de Ch. c. 1. §. Est autem. Sed verè inanis hic est clamor, qvi aures replet, rei desperatæ nullum facit patrocinium: Qværimus nos: an Deus realiter in sua carne pro mundo sit mortuus? Respondent illi: Λόγον carni patienti & morienti fuisse præsentem. Qvid hoc ad rhombum? Λόγος Stephano patienti & morienti fuit præsens. E. Stephani mors est sufficiens pro peccatis λύτρον. Digna adversariis argutatio: qvæ ex Zuvinglii ἀλλοιώσει & Bell. depravatâ distinctione necessario seqvitur nexu: sive enim Zuvinglii ἀλλοίωσιν sive Jesuitæ distinctionem in suum resolvas principium, hoc tandem emerget: passionem & mortem Λόγῳ verbaliter tantum tribui, ut explicat. Bez. vol. 1. p. 624. E. Christus verbalis est redemptor. Gaudete Photiniani, plures habetis socios!

XLI. Sed habete vobis mediatorem vestrum verbalem! Nos piè credimus θεάνθρωπον realiter pro nobis mortuum: non solum hominem, sed etiam DEUM: ideò enim λόγος ἀπαθὴς affumpsit Humanam Naturam, ut pateretur in unitate personæ, qui pati non posset in puritate Naturæ. XLII. Qvod pulchre explicat Epiphan. lib. 3. tom. 2. cont. Dimaritas hæres. 77. Passio in Deitatem non incidit, sed in Humana Natura facta est. Non relata est autem ad Humanam naturam solam, (ut ne impleretur in salutis dispensatione illud dictum: Maledictus omnis, qui spem habet in homine) sed reputata est ad Deitatem, cùm deitas non sit passa, &c.

XLIII. Hæc, hæc demum consideratio animæ patienti & paventi spem certam erigit salutis: Ecce! enim, pia anima, θεάνθρωπος venit ad salvandum te, venit ad servandum te per clementiam, quæ teipsam perdidisti per malitiam. Mediator tuus non nudus homo, qui velit & non possit; non nudus Deus, qui possit & non velit: sed DEUS & homo: Ergò & vult, quia misericors, & potest, quia omnipotens. a Hic omnia perpessus, ut ab omnibus te liberaret: mortuus est, ut mors extingueretur: timuit, ut à timore libereris: doluit, ut dolores ù te abessent. b Suscepit tristitiam tuam, ut tibi largiretur suam lætitiam. c Doluit Dominus non sua vulnera sed tua, non suam mortem sed tuam. d. Respira ergo, ô anima peccatrix, respira! ne desperes! spera in eum quem times, fuge ad eum à quo aufugisti, invoca importunè, quem superbè provocasti, dic ei: Jesu propter nomen tuum dulce, fac mihi secundum nomen tuum: e Audi, ô Creator, creatura tua sum, manus tuæ blasphemaverunt me, manus inquam illæ, quæ affixæ clavis sunt pro me. Opus manuum tuarum, domine, ne despicias, vulnera manuum tuarum precor ut inspicias. Ecce! in manibus tuis Domine DEUS descripsisti me, lege ipsam scripturam & salva me. En ad te suspiro, creatura tua. Creator es, recrea me! En ad te clamo factura tua! Vita es, vivifica me! En ad te respicio, tuum psalma. Psalmator es, restaura me. Es parce mihi colloqventi tibi. Legem non habet necessitas, dolor me compellit dicere: Calamitas, quam patior, cogit me exclamare. Ægrota sum, ad medicum clamo: Cæca sum, ad lucem propero: mortua sum, ad lucem suspiro. Tu es medicus, tu lux, tu vita, JESU Nazarene! Miserere mei, fili David, miserere mei sans misericordia!


## 16 Sixteenth Disputation, On the Third Kind of Communication of Attributes, constructive

Thesis I.

It is truly a thing to be wondered at, what Dr. John, chapter 1, verse 14 of his Gospel, declares concerning the incarnate Word. For although God is this by His own nature, v. 1, in the beginning with God, v. 2, the light, v. 7, and although God cannot be seen, and is light inaccessible, yet he says and professes that we have seen God.

II. But how? The Word became flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father.

III. Therefore, the humility of the Word assuming [flesh] causes His majesty to appear in vile flesh! But that wonder will either suffer some pause, or will be more excited, when we proceed further from the union, of which John speaks, to the communication.

IV. For this teaches that that union was effected by such an efficacious περιχωρήσει [interpenetration], that all power in heaven and on earth, the virtue of vivifying, the cult of adoration, the power of executing judgment, and the majesty of filling all things were delivered to Christ the man.

V. But because these and similar sayings teach the supreme exaltation of the human nature, and because Scripture inculcates this exaltation quite copiously, it seemed good to the doctors of the Church to gather it into a certain order, and to call it the third kind of communication, concerning which we shall discourse at present; for the communication of idioms in general, and the two prior classes in particular, were treated in recent disputations.

VI. But that we may not play out of tune, the principal heads of this construction will be these: 1. An enumeration of the appellations by which this kind is designated. 2. The statement of the definition. 3. A demonstration of the distinction from the remaining kinds. 4. The proof. 5. A declaration of the modes of this communication. 6. An illustration of the same by similar things. 7. A practical meditation.

VII. Therefore, as regards the appellations of this kind, it is most customarily called the communication of majesty. Basil calls it metadosis (communication), Gregory of Nyssa calls it metapoiēsis (transformation): Hilary, Ambrose, Justin, Athanasius, Nazianzen, Epiphanius, Eusebius, and Damascenus call it apotheōsis (deification), theopoiēsis (making divine), logōsis (becoming Word), and theologōsis (becoming divine).

VIII. By others it is called axiōsis (dignification), perispoiēsis (acquisition), plērōsis (fulfillment), theōsis (deification), metalēpsis (participation), prosthēkē (addition), endynamōsis (strengthening), hyperypsōsis sarkos (supreme exaltation of the flesh), epaktos doxa kai dynamis (acquired glory and power), plēthos sarki ex henōseōs prosginomenos (fullness accruing to the flesh from the union), pantokratōria (almightiness), metochē dynameōs theias (participation in divine power).

IX. Some of these nomenclatures, however, must be taken with a grain of salt, lest they pass into Schwenkfeldian rot or Eutychian decay. For they do not intend or understand any equalization, but only exalt the excellence of the flesh, which without any doubt, even in the time of the fathers, was trampled underfoot by the enemies of the Church, and not left in the sublimity of the right hand of the eternal Father.

X. Moreover, most of these names confirm the rule of Athanasius, frequent in the Church at that time, in which he says: ὅσα ἔλαβεν ὁ χριςὸς, κατὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα ἔλαβεν (whatever Christ received, he received according to his humanity).

XI. It is of great importance, in any given genus, to correctly recognize the πρῶτον διαγνωσὸν (first thing to be known), by which that which is to be investigated here must also be examined.

XII. We say it is the human nature of Christ, which receives from the divine [nature] eternal gifts, and even the name which is above every name, Phil. 2, 5.

XIII. Since, however, we say the work of the Father is the Son's, and that which the Son works is the work of the Father, as Cyril advises, let it move no one that Scripture says the Father gave to the Son, because this bestowal most greatly includes the Son.

XIV. For according to Chrysologus: The Son of God bestowed upon the Son of the Virgin, God upon man, divinity upon flesh, what he always possessed with the Father and the Spirit. Hence Athanasius: ἐκ ἄν ἀμφιβάλοι τὶς, ὅτι ἃ δίδωσιν ὁ πατὴρ διὰ τῆ υἱᾶ δίδωσι (no one would doubt that what the Father gives, he gives through the Son).

XV. Indeed, because this giving is an external work, it will be common to the three persons; therefore, it is rightly taught with antiquity: The Father gives to the Son originally; the Son to the assumed flesh personally; the Holy Spirit virtually, and that not verbally, but really.

XVI. Therefore, human nature receives, it does not give; the Logos, however, gives and does not receive. Wherefore the Calvinists fall from Charybdis into Scylla, intending to detract from the flesh, contending that the Logos has received, and thus sinning wickedly against both natures, they take away from both: from the former its excellence, from the latter its ἀυτάρκειαν (self-sufficiency).

XVII. For these men, in other matters quite lynx-eyed, ought to have seen that the Logos is God, and thus to have weighed what is said in Mal. ch. 3, v. 6: Therefore I am the Lord and I do not change.

XVIII. What? That the proper name of God, by which He is called ἀυταρκὴς, and self-sufficient, also pertains to Christ, as Galatinus demonstrates in book 3, chapter 15, of De veritate arcanae Catholicae religionis.

XIX. They ought to have remembered that in the Athanasian Creed the equality of the persons is taught, which would cease if one had some addition, while the other remained ἀυταρκὴς.

XX. But since human nature is capable of this exaltation, and therefore has been subject to changes, as is clear from Phil. 2:7, 9, Isa. 53:13, and Acts 2:13, it must be established that it is primarily intended here, and it must be believed that what is predicated in this category is to be understood of the man Christ.

XXI. Hence the rule placed above in thesis 10 is confirmed, and it is found to be true what Damascenus has in book 3 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 15: τῶν οἱκείων ἀυχημάτων ἡ θεότης τῷ σώματι μεταδίδωσιν, αὐτή τε τῶν τῆς σαρκὸς παθῶν διαμένει ἀμέτοχος.

XXII. These things had to be set forth more fully, lest in establishing the definition regarding the subject that receives the predicates of this class, we should err and thus stumble immediately at the threshold.

XXIII. We think, however, that these things also must be distinguished, namely, the communication which occurs in this category, and then the class which contains and explains the predicates of this communication. The former is called a true and real μετάδοσις, by which the λόγος, the Son of God, communicates Himself and all the glory and majesty of His divine loftiness to His flesh, assumed into the unity of His person, in such a way that whatever the λόγος is and has by essence, the assumed flesh has by the grace of personal union and communication. Mr. Dr. Haffen, p. 311.

XXIV. This class, therefore, or this kind of communication, contains those testimonies of Scripture which clearly testify that the human nature in CHRIST, because it is personally united with the divine nature, has received, besides and above the natural, essential, and permanent prerogatives proper to humanity itself, also singular, most excellent, greatest, supernatural, unsearchable, ineffable, and heavenly prerogatives of majesty and glory, of divine virtue and power, above everything that is named not only in this age, but also in the future.

XXV. It is evident from this why the humanity of CHRIST has such prerogatives, namely on account of the union, which if it is changed into λύσιν [dissolution], all that which is said in Scripture concerning the man Christ will be false.

XXVI. Mention of the gifts is so copious and such a pregnant description is added, both so that the error of those who denied that the man CHRIST, besides his properties befitting his humanity, had received divine ones might be exposed, and so that it might appear that there is another reason for these gifts and for the saints.

XXVII. How, therefore, this genus differs from the others will be easily judged. For the first is of properties, the second of operations, the third of majesty or gifts. In the first, the properties of the natures are distinguished; in the second, the common things are shown; in the third, χαρίσματα or gifts are explained. The first degree is ἰδιοποιΐα [appropriation], the second κοινοποιΐα [communication], the third μετοποιΐα [participation].

XXVIII. By what foundations it can be demonstrated that such a true and real communication, eminence, and exaltation has accrued to the flesh, must now be shown.

XXIX. We presuppose, however, these two things: namely, that the subject receiving is only the flesh, and that which is received is the divinity. 2. That the λόγος and his properties are not distinguished, except as regards our mode of conceiving, formally, concerning which, however, there can be no discussion here (unless we wish to ἑτεροζητεῖν [seek other things]).

XXX. I. The foundation, therefore, is taken from Colossians 2, v. 9, where it is held in express words that in Christ dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. Hence I conclude thus: In whomever the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, so that what is inhabited is the proper flesh of the inhabitant, to him Majesty is truly communicated. But in Christ the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Therefore, to Christ majesty is truly communicated.

XXXI. The consequence of the major premise is evident from this, because, namely, it cannot be conceived what difference there is between πλήρωμα [fullness] and Majesty, since where there is the fullness of the Godhead, there is the Majesty, and vice versa.

XXXII. A more accurate inspection of the text teaches that the minor premise speaks of the flesh of Christ, or it will show this to be absurd, that the matter is so, namely, that the fullness of the Godhead is to dwell in God, God in the divine nature.

XXXIII. II. We take our foundation from those sayings which describe the Majesty of the flesh as if with an outstretched finger, such as Dan. 7. v. 13. & 14. Matth. 11, 26. Philip. 2. v. 5. Ephes. 1. v. 10. Apoc. 5, 12. For from this we weave such an argument: Whoever has received eternal power, which has all things subject to itself, so that from it he receives a name above every name, and who is established above every principality and power, and virtue and dominion and every name that is named in this and the future age, receives power, riches, etc., to him has the divine Majesty of the divine λόγος been truly and really communicated. The former is true of Christ, and the latter.

XXXIV. The major premise does not seem to need proof, since even a blind man could feel that such attributes can belong to no creature, unless it is joined to some person by an intimate union of divinity.

XXXV. We observe how liberally Scripture assists us, while it confirms us by the enumeration of certain prerogatives in what it previously denoted by fullness, so that we may certainly believe that there is nothing in the λόγος, provided it is participative, which ought not to be said of the flesh of the λόγος.

XXXVI. Indeed, it is evident from the frequent repetition of this ὑπερυψώσεως (exaltation), which it adorns with various words, that the Holy Spirit delights in this very article. It is not the least thing that it explains it through the sitting at the right hand of majesty, Hebr. 2. v. 3.

XXXVII. Hence we conclude: Whoever sits at the right hand of the Majesty of God, to him has Majesty been truly and really communicated: But the flesh of Christ sits at the right hand of the Majesty of God: Therefore.

XXXVIII. What it is to sit at the right hand of God, our theologians explain elsewhere; the narrowness of this place does not allow us to explain those things here: but that this sitting is true concerning the human nature of Christ, the blessed Gesner proves in his disputation on the Formula of Concord, p. 322.

XXXIX. That thesis of ours could be strengthened by an enumeration of attributes, such as omniscience, omnipotence, etc., all of which are manifest in the sacred writings and most of them confirmed κατὰ τὸ ρητὸν (according to the letter), but that must be left to subsequent disputations. Yet it is to be wondered at that the Calvinist race, otherwise most logical as it seems to itself, cannot perceive this induction.

XL. I ask that they weigh only this: To whom the ὑπόστασις of the Word is truly communicated, to him also the majesty of the ὑπόστασις. And concerning the flesh of Christ, that is true, and this.

XLI. What if the already mentioned sayings of the fathers could be brought forward to demonstrate this consensus? Whoever wishes may consult Chemnitz’s passages in his booklet on the person of Christ, and he will discover that antiquity agrees with us in a long series.

XLII. It is not, however, the case that the adversaries should be too fearful here, as if there were to be an equalization, abolition, absorption, or any other of these monsters of the natures. For that happens only when both things subjected to equalization have identity of essence, and what is attributed to both is done by way of being per se. But we do not say that the flesh has that Majesty from its essence and per se, but from the personal union.

XLIII. But that happens when things are communicated ἀντιφυ- σικὰ and not per ὑπερφυσικὰ: Since, however, things that are above a nature do not destroy but perfect it, the fear concerning abolition is vain. We wish the same to be understood concerning absorption, and indeed all the more so, as we have often protested that we hold the Eutychian confusion in hatred worse than a snake.

XLIV. Otherwise, concerning the mode of this communication, they respond that it is not verbal but real, not essential and accidental, but personal, so that the Son of God, while retaining the properties of his divine nature within himself and not pouring them out into another subject, truly and really communicates the same to the human nature, so that what he has by essence, this [nature] may possess by the grace of personal union.

XLV. Although an example of such a union and personal communication is not given in nature, it, as well as Holy Scripture, provides similarities which teach not only the communication of properties but also their κοινωνίαν without confusion, equalization, etc.

XLVI. Known are the similarities of Cyril concerning fermentation, of the same concerning the sweetening of honey: of Origen concerning πυρώσει, of others concerning primordial light communicating itself to a natural body. But what need is there for that digression to other things, when we have in ourselves a manifest example of this matter?

XLVII. For does not our soul communicate life, sense, and the remaining properties to the body, or is the soul a body, or is the body destroyed by the soul? Certainly not. As therefore I rightly say, the body is sensible, living, so also I rightly say of the flesh of Christ, by which it becomes full of majesty, omniscient, omnipotent. But if you say, the body is not of itself living? It is well, provided only that you believe it lives, nor do we say that the human nature of Christ is

XLVIII. Athanasius confirms this simile of ours with his vote against the Apollinarists: just as the soul, he says, is in the body, so God the λόγος united to man produces miracles, not separated from the assumed nature, but it pleased him in it, with it, and through it to exert his divine power. But why am I wordy here, when the Reverend and Most Excellent Lord President, my preceptor to be honored for all time, has shown this communication quite prolixly also to the Calvinists, part 1, Sob. p. 84.

XLIX. That flesh is therefore of tremendous Majesty, which was assumed into the unity of the λόγος, because its majesty is the Majesty of God. Worship, O pious ones, fear, O impious ones, tremble, O tyrants, and thus let us all acknowledge the excellence of Christ.

L. But since he is above every principality, who has taken the lead from our blood and flesh, let this be for our confidence. For there is in Jesus Christ himself our Lord, a portion of each one of us, flesh and blood. Where therefore my portion reigns, let us say with Augustine, there I believe I reign; where my flesh is glorified, there I know myself to be glorious. Let us therefore congratulate ourselves on the eminence, but let us subject ourselves to Christ with most humble obedience: to Christ Jesus exalted be glory.

Latin:

Thesis I.

ADmirandum planè est, qvod D. Johannes c. 1, 14. Evangelii sui de incarnato verbo pronunciat. Hoc enim cum naturâ suâ DEus sit, v. 1. in principio apud Deum, v. 2. lux, v. 7. Deus autem videri neqveat, sitq; lux inaccessa, Deum tamen nos vidisse dicit & profitetur.

II. Verùm qvomodo ? ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν, καὶ ἐθεασάμεθα τὴν δόξαν ἀυτῶ, δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρός.

III. Facit ergò assumentis λόγου humilitas, ut in vili carne ejus appareret majestas ! Verùm illa admiratio vel pausam aliqvam patietur, vel magis excitabitur, qvando ulterius ex unione, de qvâ Joannes, procedimus ad communicationem.

IV. Hæc enim docet, ἕνωσιν illam tam efficaci περιχωρήσει factam esse, ut Christo homini tradita sit omnis potestas in cælo & in terra, vis vivificandi, cultus adorationis, potestas judicium faciendi, majestas omnia implendi.

V. Qvia autem hæc & similia dicta humanæ naturæ ὑπερύψωσιν maximè docent, & qvia satis copiosè scriptura hanc exaltationem inculcat, visum fuit doctoribus Ecclesiæ, in certum ordinem cogere, & 3. communicationis genus appellare, de qvo in præsentiarum disseremus; qvippe de communicatione Idiomatum in genere, de duabus classibus prioribus in specie, nuperis disputationibus actum est.

VI. Ne verò extra lyram saltemus, præcipua κατασκευῆς hujus capita ista erunt : 1. Enumeratio appellationum, qvibus hoc genus insignitur. 2. positio definitionis. 3. ostensio discriminis à reliqvis generibus. 4. demonstratio. 5. modi communicationis hujus declaratio, 6. ejusdem per similia illustratio. 7. practica meditatio.

VII. Appellationes itaq; hujus generis qvod attinet, vocatur usitatissimè Majestatis communicatio. Basilius μετάδοσιν vocat, Gregorius Nyssenus μεταποίησιν: Hilarius, Ambrosius, Justinus, Athanasius, Nazianzenus, Epiphanius, Eusebius, Damascenus, ἀποθέωσιν, θεοποίησιν, λόγωσιν, θεολόγωσιν.

VIII. Aliis dicitur ἀξίωσις, περισποίησις, πλήρωσις, θέωσις, μετάληψις, προσθήκη, ἐνδυνάμωσις, ὑπερύψωσις σαρκὸς, ἐπακτητος δόξα καὶ δύναμις, πλῆτος σαρκὶ ἐξ ἑνώσεως προσγινόμενος, παντοκρατορία, μετοχὴ δυνάμεως θείας.

IX. Harum nomenclationum tamen nonnullæ cum grano salis sumendæ, ne in Scvvenkfeldianam putredinem, vel Eutychianum marcorēm transeant. Non enim volunt aut intelligunt exæquationem aliqvam, sed tantùm carnis excellentiam evehunt, qvæ sine omni dubio, patrum qvoqve tempore, ab hostibus Ecclesiæ fuit pedibus conculcata, & in sublimitate dexteræ patris æterni non relicta.

X. Pleraq; autem nomina hæc Athanasii regulam, Ecclesiæ tum freqventem confirmant, qvâ dicit : ὅσα ἔλαβεν ὁ χριςὸς, κατὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα ἔλαβεν.

XI. Multum autem refert, in unoqvolibet genere πρῶτον διαγνωσὸν rectè cognoscere, qvo circa in hîc qvoqve illud investigandum est.

XII. Nos dicimus esse, Humanam Christi naturam, qvæ à divinâ, æterna dona, nomen etiam qvod supra omne nomen est, Philip. 2, 5. accipit.

XIII. Qvoniam autem patris opus, filii dicimus, & id qvod filius operatur, sit opus patris, qvemadmodum Cyrillus monet, neminem moveat qvod scriptura dicit, patrem dedisse filio, qvia hæc largitio filium maximè includit.

XIV. Nam juxta Chrysologum: Filius Dei virginis Filio, Deus homini, divinitas carni contulit, qvod semper cum patre & spiritu possedit. Hinc Athanasius : ἐκ ἄν ἀμφιβάλοι τὶς, ὅτι ἃ δίδωσιν ὁ πατὴρ διὰ τῆ υἱᾶ δίδωσι.

XV. Imò qvia hæc datio opus ad extra est, communis erit tribus personis, iccirtò cum antiqvitate rectè docetur: Dat pater filio originaliter. Filius assumptæ carni personaliter; Spiritus Sanctus virtualiter, & id non verbaliter, verùm realiter.

XVI. Accipit ergò humana natura, non dat, Λόγος autem dat & non accipit. Qvocirca ex Charybdi in Scyllam incidunt Calviniani, carni detracturi, λόγον accepisse contendentes, & ita in utramq; naturam sceleratè peccantes, utriq; adimunt, illi excellentiam, huic ἀυτάρκειαν.

XVII. Debuissent enim isti homines, in cæteris admodum lyncei, videre, λόγον Deum esse, & ita perpendere, qvod Mal. c. 3. v. 9. dicitur : Ergo dominus & non mutor.

XVIII. Qvid? qvòd nomen Dei proprium, qvo ἀυταρκὴς dicitur, sibiq; sufficiens, Christo qvoqve competat, prout Galatinus l. 3. c. 15. de verit. arc. Cath. relig. demonstrat.

XIX. Meminisse debuissent, qvòd in Athanasiano Symbolo æqvalitas personarum doceatur, qvæ cessaret, qvando una aliqvid accessionis haberet, altera ἀυταρκὴς maneret.

XX. Verùm cum humana natura hujus exaltationis capax sit, adeóqve mutationibus obnoxia fuerit, ut ex Phil. 2. v. 7. 9. Esa. 53, 13. Act. 2, 13. liqvet, eam hîc maximè intendi statuendum est, & qvæ in hoc genere prædicantur, de homine Christo accipienda esse, credendum.

XXI. Hinc regula supra th. 10. posita confirmatur, & verum esse deprehenditur, qvod Damascenus l. 3. orthod. fid. c. 15. habet: τῶν οἱκείων ἀυχημάτων ἡ θεότης τῷ σώματι μεταδίδωσιν, αὐτή τε τῶν τῆς σαρκὸς παθῶν διαμένει ἀμέτοχος.

XXII. Fusiùs hæc erant proponenda, ne in ponenda diffinitione, circa subjectum, accipiens prædicata hujus classis, aberraremus, & ita statim in limine impingeremus.

XXIII. Discernenda autem hæc qvoqve esse putamus, communicationem sc. qvæ fit in hoc genere, & deinde classem eam qvæ dicta hujus communicationis continet & explicat. Illa dicitur vera & realis μετάδοσις, qvâ λόγος Filius Dei carni suæ in personæ unitatem assumtæ, seipsum & omnem divinæ suæ celsitudinis gloriam & majestatem ita communicat, ut qvæcunqve λόγος est & habet per essentiam, assumpta caro habeat per unionis & communicationis personalis gratiam. Dn. D. Haffen. p. 311.

XXIV. Classis ergo hæc sive genus hoc communicationis continet ea scripturæ testimonia, qvæ præclarè testantur, qvòd humana natura in CHRISTO, ideò, qvòd cum divinâ naturâ personaliter unita est, præter & supra naturales, essentiales atqve in ipsâ permanentes humanitati proprias, etiam singulares, excellentissimas, maximas, supernaturales, impervestigabiles, ineffabiles atqve cœlestes prærogativas majestatis & gloriæ, virtutis & potentiæ divinæ, super omne qvod nominatur nõ solùm in hoc seculo, sed etiam futuro, acceperit.

XXV. Patescit hinc, cur CHRISTI humanitas, tantas prærogativas habeat, scil. propter unionem, qvæ si in λύσιν commutetur, falsum omne illud erit, qvod de homine Christo in scriptura dicitur.

XXVI. Donorum tam copiosa sit mentio & tam prægnans adjicitur descriptio, tum ut error eorum patefieret, qvi negabant hominem CHRISTUM, præter suas proprietates humanitati convenientes, accepisse divinas, tum ut aliam rationem horum donorum & sanctorum esse, appareret.

XXVII. Qvid ergò hoc genus à cæteris differat, facilè dijudicabitur. Primum enim est proprietatum,alterum operationum,tertium majestatis seu donorum. In primo propria naturarum discernuntur,in altero communia ostenduntur, in tertio χαρίσματα vel dona explicantur. Primus gradus est ἰδιοποιΐα, alter κοινοποιΐα,tertius μετοποιΐα.

XXIIX. Qvibus autem fundamentis demonstrari possit,obtigisse carni veram & realem ejusmodi communicationem, eminentiam & exaltationem, jam ostendendum est.

XXIX. Præsupponimus autem duo ista; sc. subjectum accipiens esse tantùm carnem, receptum divinitatem. 2.Esse λόγθ,& ejus proprietates non distigui,nisi qvoad nostrum concipiendi modum,formaliter, de qvo tamen hîc (nisi velimus ἑτεροζητεῖν) sermo esse non potest.

XXX. I. ergò fundamentum, desumitur ex Colos.2,v.9.ubi conceptis verbis habetur,qvòd in Christo habitet omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Hinc ita concludo: In qvocunqve habitat divinitatis plenitudo corporaliter, ita ut qvod inhabitatur sit inhabitantis propria caro, illi verè Majestas est communicata. Atqvi in Christo habitat divinitatis plenitudo corporaliter. E. Christo verè majestas est communicata.

XXXI. Majoris conseqventia inde patet, qvia scil. cogitari non potest, qvid discriminis sit inter πλήρωμα & inter Majestatem, qvoniam ubi divinitatis plenitudo, ibi Majestatis, & vice versâ.

XXXII. Minorem loqvi de carne Christi, textûs accuratior inspectio docet, aut absurdum hoc monstrabit rem ita se habere, qvod scil. divinitatis plenitudo sit habitatura in Deo, Deus in divina natura.

XXXIII. II. Fundamentum desumimus ex dictis illis quæ extento quasi digito Majestatem carnis describunt, qualia sunt Dan. 7. v. 13. & 14. Matth. 11, 26. Philip. 2. v. 5. Ephes. 1. v. 10. Apoc. 5, 12. Hinc enim tale nectimus argumentum: Quicunq; accepit potestatem æternam, quæ omnia sibi habet subjecta, ita ut inde nomen supra omne nomen accipiat, qviq; constitutus est super omnem principatum & potestatem, & virtutem & dominationem & omne nomen qvod in hoc & futuro seculo nominatur, accipit virtutem, divitias &c. illi verè & realiter communicata est Majestas divina divinî λόγꙋ. De Christo prius est verũ E. & posterius.

XXXIV. Major non videtur probatione egere, cum vel cæcus palpare possit, ejusmodi attributa nulli creaturæ, nisi sit intimâ unione divinitatis alicui personæ conjuncta, posse competere.

XXXV. Animadvertimus qvàm liberaliter nobis scriptura succurrat, dum qvod ante per plenitudinem denotarit, nunc per enumerationem qvarundam prærogativarum nos confirmet, ut certò credamus, nihil esse in λόγῳ, modo illud sit participativum, qvod non dici debeat de carne λόγꙋ.

XXXVI. Imò Spiritum S. hoc ipso articulo delectari, ex crebrâ repetitione hujus ὑπερυψώσεως patet, qvam variis verbis exornat. Non minimum est, qvod illam per sessionem ad dextram majestatis explicat Hebr. 2. v. 3.

XXXVII. Hinc concludimus: Quicunq; sedet ad dextram Majestatis Dei, illi verè & realiter est Majestas communicata: Atqvi caro Christi sedet ad dextram Majestatis Dei: E.

XXXVIII. Qvid sit sedere ad dexteram Dei, Theologi nostri explicant alibi; angustia non patitur hoc in loco ista explicare: de hum: verò Christi natura hanc sessionem veram esse, B. Gesnerus in disp. super Concord, Form. p. 322. probat.

XXXIX. Posset thesis illa nostra enumeratione attributorum, ut omniscientia, omnipotentiæ &c. quæ omnia in sacris manifesta sunt & pleraq; κατὰ τὸ ρητὸν confirmata, roborari, sed illud relinqvendum subseqventibus disputationibus. Hoc tamen mirandum, Calvin. gentem aliàs λογικωτάτην, ut sibi videtur; hanc inductionem non posse percipere.

XL. Unum hoc quæso perpendant: Cui ὑπόστασις λόγου verè est communicata, illi & ὑποστάσεως majestas. Atqvi de carne Christi illud verum E. & hoc.

XLI. Qvod jam dicta patrum possent ad consensum hunc demonstrandum adduci? cui volupe est Chemnitii locos in libello de pers. Christi consulat, & longâ serie antiqvitatem nobis consentire deprehendet.

XLII. Non est tamen ut hîc adversarii nimis meticulosi sint, quasi sic naturarum sit futuræ exæqvatio, abolitio, absorptio vel aliud qvidpiam horum monstrorum. Nam illa tum demum fit, qvãdo utrumq; qvod exeqvationi subjicitur habet identitatem essentiæ, & qvod utriqve attribuitur, fiat per modum per se. Jam autem nos non dicimus qvod caro habeat ex essentiâ & per se istam Majestatem, sed ex unione personali.

XLIII. Ista verò tum contingit qvando communicata sunt ἀντιφυσικὰ & non per ὑπερφυσικὰ: Qvia autem quæ sunt supra naturam aliqvam, non destruunt sed perficiunt, vanus metus de abolitione est. Qvod item de absorptione volumus intellectum & qvidem eò magis, qvo sæpiùs protestati sumus confusionem Eutychianam à nobis sane pejus & angue haberi odio.

XLIV. Aliàs de modo hujus communicationis respondent, qvod non sit verbalis sed realis, non essentialis & accidentalis, sed personalis, ita ut filius Dei divinæ naturæ suæ proprietates intra se retinendo, non in aliud subjectum effundendo easdem hum. naturæ verè ac realiter communicat, ita ut qvod ille habet per essentiam, hæc ista possideat per personalis unionis gratiam.

XLV. Ejusmodi unionis & communicationis personalis exemplum licet in natura non detur, illa tamen, ut & sancta scriptura, suppeditat similia, quæ propriorum non modò communicationem, sed & κοινωνίαν sine confusione, exæqvatione &c. docent.

XLVI. Notæ sunt similitudines Cyrilli de fermendatione, ejusdem de dulcoratione mellis: Origenis de πυρώσει, aliorũ de luce primigeniâ comunicante se corpori naturali. At qvid digressione illâ ad alia opus est, cum in nobis ipsis habeam9 hujus rei manifestum exemplũ.

XLVII. Anima enim nostra annon communicat corpori vitam, sensum & reliqvas proprietates, an tamen anima sit corpus, aut corpus per animam aboletur ? Non sanè. Ut ergo rectè dico, Corpus est sensibile, vivum, ita quoq; de Christi carne rectè dico, qvo fit majestatis plena, omniscia, omnipotens. Qvod si dicas, corpus non est per se vivum ? Benè est, si modo credas vivere, neq; nos dicimus humanam Christi naturam esse per se omnisciam, omnipotentem.

XLVIII. Hoc simile nostrum Athanasius calculo contra Apollinaristas comprobat: sicut anima, inqvit, in corpore, sic Deus λόγος unitus homini edit prodigia, non separatus à naturâ assumptâ, sed placuit ei in eâ, cum eâ & per eam potentiam suam divinam exerere. Verùm qvid ego hîc multus sum, cum satis prolixè hanc communicationem & Calvinianis ostenderit Reverendus & Excellentiss. Dn. Præses, Præceptor meus ætatem honorandus part. 1. Sob. p. 84.

XLIX. Tremendæ ergò Majestatis est caro illa, qvæ in unitatem λόγε assumpta, qvia ejus majestas est Dei Majestas. Veneramini ô pii, metuite ô impii, contremiscite tyranni, & ita omnes agnoscamus Christi excellentiam.

L. Verùm cum is sit super omnem principatum, qvi principavit de sangvine & carne nostrâ, fiduciæ hoc nobis sit. Est enim in ipso Jesu Christo domino nostro, uniuscujusqve nostrûm portio, caro & sangvis. Ubi ergo portio mea regnat, dicamus cum Augustino, ibi me regnare credo; ubi caro mea glorificatur, ibi me gloriosum esse cognosco. Gratulemur ergo nobis de eminentiâ, sed subjiciam⁹ nos Christo humillimâ obedientiâ: Christo Jesu exaltato sit gloria.


## 17 Seventeenth Disputation, On the Third Genus of the Communication of Idioms, ἀνασκευασική (Refutatory)

Thesis I.

Since in the preceding Disputation a beginning was made of that controversy, agitated for many centuries past quite bitterly in the forum of the Church, concerning the Communication of Attributes and divine properties really made to the flesh of Christ, which according to the thread of the Formula of Concord constitutes the third kind of communication, it must now be continued, and we must proceed to its refutation.

II. But in order that the whole business may be the better understood, we shall include and propose the individual points, comprised in a certain order in the following members.

III. 1. Our assertion and opinion must be vindicated and freed from the calumnies, insults, and fabricated imputations of many most foul absurdities, by which our adversaries attempt to render it hateful to all. 2. Certain more common distinctions of the theologians, between the natural and personal act, καθ' αὑτὸ καὶ κατ' ἄλλο, τὸ εἶναι καὶ ἔχειν, must be explained. 3. Certain arguments of the adversaries must be examined and solved. 4. Finally, a certain practical meditation concerning the endeavor of Satan and the manners of heretics must be instituted by us.

IV. CONCERNING I. Neither can impudence be satisfied, nor folly be filled: but it expands its thought and gaping mouth to all things, says Epiphanius concerning the heresy of the Messalians, book 3, heresy 80. Which can be said quite fittingly of the Calvinists in this very controversy, who betray and show at once both their ignorance in defending their own opinion and their impudence in attacking ours.

V. For they tear our opinion apart with the most atrocious calumnies, they very often fraudulently change the state of the controversy so that they may be able to fight against us quite strenuously, and they openly proclaim us in the whole theater of the Church to be Eutychians, Nestorians, Marcionites, Monothelites, Monophysites, and what not? From which heretics, however, our theologians dissent with their whole camp, as they say.

VI. And although our theologians have many times protested, both by tongue and pen, both by voice and writings, both publicly and privately, that they have no commerce with the aforementioned heretics, but rather that they execrate the dogmas of those men from their heart, and have most sharply attacked them in excellent writings published to the world, with the highest applause and fruit of the Church, yet, neglecting all these things, they do not fear to dwell upon such calumnies, having taken pains against their own conscience.

VII. Hence they attribute to us all those absurdities once defended by those heretics, and with great clamor they shout that we equalize the natures, remove their difference, confound and abolish their essential properties, convert one into the other, and include the infinite Λόγον in the finite little body of flesh, when nevertheless the contrary we establish, believe, teach, and defend with greater fruit than they themselves do against these heretics.

VIII. These men are so forgetful of all shame that they do not cease to do us the greatest injury and to accuse our Churches of the most foul heresies, to such an extent that not even Paraeus himself in his Irenicum, in which he nevertheless amicably solicits us for pacification, could abstain from calumnies of this kind, c. 28. art. 13. p. 266. 'Confusion is created if that which is proper to one were also made common to another,' cries Zanchius, l. 2. de Incarn. p. 340. 'The third kind of predication (of the communication of idioms), new and hitherto unheard of, is nothing other than a monster forged partly from the delirium of the Eutychians, partly from the blasphemy of Nestorius, and from the dreams of the Monophysites and Monothelites,' slander the Authors of the Admon. Neost. p. 14. That a real effusion of the essential properties of the Deity into the flesh of Christ, which was the other blasphemy of Eutyches, is introduced by us and brought into the Church, Beza loudly rails, vol. 3. p. 104. 'This very dogma of ours, I contended and contend, does not differ from the blasphemy of Nestorius in the separation of natures, nor from the blasphemy of Eutyches in the confusion of essential properties,' the same man audaciously accuses, p. 101.

IX. But let them continue to shout, to rave, to rail, and to inveigh against our opinion; yet in the writings of our people nothing of this kind will be found, nor will it be constructed by good consequence. 'But if it were enough to have accused, who would be innocent?' says Tertullian somewhere.

X. Some adversary might indeed object that, although we deny the ὁμοφνορίαν [homophronian] in words, we nevertheless think the same as they do in reality, since, given our hypotheses, such absurdities arise and follow from them. To this we respond by denying that any of these things follow from our doctrine concerning the real communication of idioms. For if the person of the Word was really communicated to the human nature of Christ without any change, or multiplication, or transfusion, or even conversion of itself—which the adversaries themselves must necessarily admit, unless they wish to abolish and deny the union itself—what then will be repugnant and the cause why these same things, while the natures and their properties remain safe, should not also be given and communicated to the flesh of Christ essentially without conversion, abolition, etc.?

XI. DEII. As confusion is the mother of errors, so on the contrary distinction is the parent of truth, according to that saying: He who distinguishes well, teaches well; for this reason also theologians, in order to explain more correctly the doctrine of the communication of idioms, have employed several distinctions, as to what is the cause of such communication, and how the communicated properties relate to the human nature,

XII. The first distinction, which is also common and occurs most frequently, is that by which they distinguish between a natural and a personal act. The former, the flesh of Christ, because it is natural flesh and consubstantial with us, possesses in itself and through itself in common with us: but the latter, on account of the hypostatic union, which is flesh hypostatically united to the Deity of the λόγος, it obtains. For the flesh of Christ is not only common flesh, but the flesh of the Son of God himself, from which prerogative it cannot but acquire a higher and more sublime condition.

XIII. It must be noted, however, that the foundation of the personal act is not the whole composite person consisting of both natures, as the adversaries contend, so that they may more easily hide under these shelters and deceive us, but a simple person involving one nature, yet with its own subsistence and personality, which is proposed thus: From whom the union of the human nature with the λόγος depends, from him also depends the communication of the idioms of the λόγος made to the human nature; but that union depends not on the composite person, which involves at the same time the human nature, which cannot unite itself, but on the simple person of the λόγος assuming it. Therefore, as the union, so also the communication depends on that simple person.

XIII. For just as the union of the divine natures of the λόγος and the human is not a natural act but a personal one, so also the communication of divine idioms is a personal act; furthermore, since the flesh is said to be personally united to the λόγος, it must also be said to be personally omnipotent, life-giving, etc.

XIV. Wherefore, although the flesh of Christ is not the whole composite person, it is nevertheless ὑποσᾶσα ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, subsisting in the Word himself, and ἐνυπόσα- τθ, personated, that is, endowed with the subsistence of the λόγος, and thence it has attained a personal act.

XV. Unless, therefore, they wish impiously to establish two persons in Christ, it is necessary that they embrace and assume a personal act. The reason: For the human nature of Christ subsists. It subsists, therefore, either by its own act naturally as other men, or by a personal act of the λόγος from a personal union. But if the Adversaries deny this, then let them bring forward the former. Behold, therefore, two natural acts of subsisting, of the Word and of the Flesh, which is most openly Nestorian.

XVI. Therefore, whatever is said of the humanity of Christ through and on account of the human nature, that is natural to it, and is said of it naturally. But whatever is said of the humanity of Christ through and on account of the hypostatic union, that is personal to it, and is said of it personally, where the term 'personally' designates not only the cause, but also the mode and reason of the attribution.

XVII. Another distinction used in the schools of the Theologians is that by which they distinguish between that which belongs to the human nature καθ' αὑτὸ (of itself) and κατ' ἄλλο (according to another), which indeed differs in words from the former, but in reality coincides with it. Therefore, καθ' αὑτὸ is the same as essential, natural, and whatever pertains to the essence and constitution of the human nature of Christ; but κατ' ἄλλο is that which is from elsewhere, namely, from the hypostatic union.

XIX. Therefore, divine idioms are attributed to the flesh of Christ, and it is rightly called life-giving, not καθ' αὑτὸ but κατ' ἄλλο, not because it is human flesh or such by its own essence or qualities, but because it is the very flesh of the λόγος himself, who is life itself, which is hypostatically united to it, which hypostatic union causes it to be able to give life; wherefore it is said of the flesh of Christ κατ' ἄλλο, just as also subsisting in the ὑπόστασις of the Son of God belongs to the humanity of Christ not καθ' αὑτὸ, but κατ' ἄλλο, namely on account of the λόγος assuming it. For in the same way that the human nature of Christ is said to subsist ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, so also it is said to be omnipresent, etc., since the communication of these attributes is a consequence of that subsistence; but the flesh of Christ κατ' ἄλλο or personally subsists ἐν τῷ λόγῳ. Therefore, it is also κατ' ἄλλο omnipotent, life-giving, and thus also one must judge concerning the rest.

XIX. Thirdly, they are accustomed to distinguish between τὸ εἶναι and ἔχειν, to be and to have. In the former way, divine attributes remain to that nature whose own they are. For the divine nature of the Son is life itself, essential life itself, and essential omnipotence itself. Therefore, the Son of God is life-giving and omnipotent by way of being, in which manner the flesh of Christ is not life-giving, so that it would be life itself, and total and essential life.

XX. But in the latter way, things that are proper are common to the other nature... conjoined to common possession and real, if I may so speak, habitation. Which nevertheless ἔχειν and to have squares with no physical mode of having, but altogether in this place puts on a peculiar and clearly singular rationale, on account of which the flesh of Christ is said ἔχειν to have and to possess, as the hypostasis, so also the idioms of the λόγꙋ.

XXI. Therefore it is not permitted to infer, the flesh of Christ is not omnipotence itself, therefore it neither has omnipotence, nor is it omnipotent. For even the flesh of Christ is not personality itself, just as the λόγꙋ is its own subsistence; if therefore this discourse were valid, by the same reasoning one could infer that the flesh of the λόγꙋ is neither ἐνυπόστατον or personated, nor through union has personality in the λόγῳ, since it is not the ὑπόστασις itself, which is nevertheless most absurd.

XXII. CONCERNING III. It follows now that we should bring forward certain arguments by which our adversaries strive to tear down generally the whole and entire communication of idioms.

XXIII. 1. No property can be communicated to another nature. For thus it would cease to be a property. For that which is and remains a property is not common to another nature; and that which is common is no longer a property, nor can it be so called, Sohn collects, vol. 2, art. 3, p. 502, C. A. Now divine attributes are proper to the divine nature. Therefore they cannot be communicated to the flesh of Christ.

XXIV. We respond: 1. The proposition is most false if it is understood generally, as is evident from those modes which are confessed and beyond controversy on both sides, since the property of a genus is common to the species, the property of a part is common to the whole, and the property of an accident is common to the subject.

XXV. 2. Property and common in this present business of ours ought not to be opposed to one another, since there is not the same respect on both sides, and it is not done according to the same and to the same, which is nevertheless supremely necessary in every legitimate opposition. We distinguish therefore between a subject καθ' ὕπαρξιν and a subject κατὰ συνδύασιν. In the former mode, one idiom in number cannot be in two subjects in number, according to inherence and πρώτοις δεκτικοῖς: for here that canon is valid: Of one property there is only one πρῶτον δεκτικόν. But in the latter mode, the same property is not repugnant to being in two subjects, in one indeed primarily, from whose nature it results; but in the other secondarily, by way of conjunction to common possession, usurpation, and denomination.

XXVI. If properties are really communicated: Therefore all of them; because the properties of the Godhead are really indivisible and inseparable, concludes Sadeel in Vol. oper. Theol. p. 154. fac. b. But eternity, infinity, cannot be said to have been communicated to the flesh of Christ. Therefore neither omnipotence, the power of vivifying, etc., because these attributes have a perpetual co-existence.

XXVII. We answer: 1. The connection is denied, because from the communication of one idiom, the communication of any other whatsoever, or even of all idioms, is not immediately to be inferred: For that co-existence which the adversaries urge has a place in the participation of a subject by participation, in which one subject is receptive of the definition of another, thus to man, that is, to the species, all properties pertaining precisely to the definition of an animal, namely of the genus, are communicated; but it does not have a place in that which exists through the union of subject with subject, which is in our present matter.

XXVIII. 2. The reason for this diversity is partly situated in the properties themselves to be communicated; partly in the other subject, which is not equally receptive or suitable and capable of receiving and usurping all, as is evident from the analogy of ignited iron. Moreover, some idioms are active toward creatures, such as the vivifying power, omnipotence, etc., the traces of which are found in created things: But some are inactive, such as eternity, which are predicated of God alone. The former are assigned to the flesh of Christ, and it is rightly said to be vivifying, omnipotent, because the Word executes such activities in the assumed nature, with it, and through it. But the latter are not said of it immediately, because they produce no activities through the flesh of themselves immediately. Since, however, that omnipotence which has been communicated to the flesh of Christ is eternal and infinite, hence eternity, infinity, can be mediately attributed to the same.

XXIX. 3. If this discourse were valid, in almost the same way a certain Photinian could collect, and could overturn the whole mystery of the Trinity. For if this axiom of the Calvinists is always and universally true: Whatever things do not really differ, but are one certain thing

ἀδιαιρέτως, by the communication of one of them, the other is also communicated, a certain Photinian could easily assume: But the hypostasis and essence of God the Father do not really differ: Therefore both are communicated to the Son, and thus the Son will be the Father, and not the Son, which is absurd.

XXX. CONCERNING THE FOURTH. The last member now follows. A practical meditation on the preceding treatment.

XXXI. Moreover, we have here an excellent specimen of the craftiness and snares which Satan and his members, heretics and false brethren, lay for us, whose efforts, while they strive solely to lead the Church away from Christ, and the manners by which they conduct themselves in this controversy, while they transform themselves into various forms, are here proposed for us to behold as in a most clear mirror.

XXXII. Moreover, those implacable enemies of ours attack the Church in a twofold manner. 1. By craftiness. 2. By violence. While they use the former kind of weapon, they simulate friendship, they rattle off many scriptures, having employed little arguments of human reason that are sufficiently plausible: for the Devil knows how to transform himself into an Angel of light, so that he may thus lead the simpler ones away from the straight path of truth, and circumvent them with deceits and frauds.

XXXIII. But when this way is closed to them by diligent examination of the Scriptures, by the solid solution of sophisms, and by the stripping away of the sheep's clothing, attacking the matter now by another way, he assumes a lupine nature, declares most open hostilities, slanders and accuses, and whatever he could not obtain by craftiness, he attempts to claim for himself with a violent hand and a raging spirit; any sensible person easily sees how he has observed these methods of expanding his kingdom here as well, from whose arts and illusions, since we cannot extricate and save ourselves by our own powers, we humbly ask the God-man himself that he may deign to assist us with his Holy Spirit and protect us from the insults of our enemies, for the glory of his blessed name, which they attack, to whom be praise and thanksgiving forever without end.

Latin:

Thesis I.

CUmin præcedente Disputatione initium factum, sit controversiæ illius multis adhinc seculis satis acerbè in foro Ecclesiæ agitatæ, de Communicatione Idiomatum ac proprietatum divinarum realiter facta carni Christi, qvæ juxta filum formulæ Concordiæ tertium communicationis genus constituit, ea jam est continuanda, & ad ejus ἀνασκευὴν progrediendum.

II. Ut autem totum negocium eò meliùs percipiatur, singula certo ordine subsequentibus membris comprehensa includemus & proponemus.

III. 1. Assertio ac sententia nostra à calumniis, convitiis & consictis imputationibus multarum, foedissimarum absurditatum, quibus Adversarii eam omnibus exosam reddere conantur, est vindicanda & liberanda. 2. Distinctiones quædam usitatiores Theologorum, inter actum naturalem & personalem, καθ' αὑτὸ καὶ κατ' ἄλλο, τὸ εἶναι καὶ ἔχειν sunt explicandæ. 3. Argumenta quædam Adversariorum sunt examinanda & solvenda. 4. deniq; Meditatio quædam practica de conatu Satanæ, ac moribus hæreticorum nobis erit instituenda.

IV. DE I. Neq; satiari impudentia, neq; repleri potest insipientia: sed ad omnia expandit cogitationem & hians os, inquit Epiphanius de hæresi Messalianorum lib. 3. hær. 80. Qvid satis congruè de Calvinianis in hac ipsa controversia dici potest, qui suam simul & inscitiam in propria sententia tuenda, impudentiam verò in nostra impugnanda produnt & ostendunt.

V. Sententiam enim nostram calumniis atrocissimis proscindunt, statum controversiæ sæpissimè fraudulenter immutant, ut sic satis strenuè contra nos pugnare possint, & nos Eutychianos, Nestorianos, Marcionitas, Monotheletas, Monophysitas & quid non? palàm in universo theatro Ecclesiæ proclamant, à quibus tamen hæreticis nostrates Theologi totis quod ajunt castris dissident.

VI. Et licet Theologi nostri tàm linguâ quàm calamo, tàm voce quàm scriptis, tàm publicè quàm privatim, sibi cum antea dictis hæreticis nil commercii esse, sed potiùs sese istorum dogmata ex animo execrari, multòties protestati sint, egregiisq; in lucem editis scriptis acerrimè, summo cum Ecclesiæ plausu ac fructu, ea impugnarint, attamen hisce omnibus neglectis, contra conscientiam datâ operâ in istiusmodi calumniis immorari non verentur.

VII. Hinc omnes illas absurditates ab istis hæreticis olim propugnatas nobis affingunt, magnoq; clamore vociferantur, nos exæqvare naturas, tollere earum differentiam, confundere ac abolere earum proprietates essentiales, unum in alterum convertere, & infinitum Λόγον includere finito carnis corpusculo, cum tamen contrarium statuamus, credamus, doceamus, ac majori cum fructu quàm ipsi contra istos hæreticos propugnemus.

IIX. Ita omnis verecundiæ isti homines sunt obliti, ut nobis summam injuriam facere, Ecclesias nostras teterrimarum hæresewn accusare impudenter non desistant, adeò, ut nec ipse Paræus in suo Irenico, in quo tamen nos ad pacificationem amicè solicitat, ab istiusmodi calumniis abstinere potuerit, c. 28. art. 13. p. 266. Fieri confusionem, si quod unius est proprium, alteri quoque fieret commune, clamitat Zanch. l. 2. de Incarn. p. 340. Tertium prædicationis (communicationis Idiomatum) genus novum & antehac inauditum nil aliud est, quàm monstrũ partim ex Eutychætis delirio partim ex Nestorii blasphemia, Monophysitarum & Monothelitarum somniis, conflatum, calumniantur Auth. Admon. Neost. p. 14. Essentialium Deitatis proprietatum realem in carnem Christi effusionem, quæ fuit altera Eutychætis blasphemia, à nobis introduci ac in Ecclesiam invehi, splendidè conviciatur Beza vol. 3. p. 104. Hoc ipsum dogma, intelligens nostrum, neq; à Nestorii in naturarum separatione, neq; in essentialium proprietatum confusione ab Eutychætis blasphemia discrepare contendi atq; contendo, audacter criminatur idem p. 101.

IX. Verùm pergant illi vociferari, debacchari, convitiari ac in sententiam nostram invehi, in scriptis tamen nostratium nil istiusmodi reperietur, neq; per bonam conseqventiam extruetur. Accusafse autem si sufficiet, quis innocens erit, inqvit alicubi Tertullianus.

X. Posset quidem adversarius aliqvis ita excipere, quòd licèt verbis diffiteamur ὁμοφνορίαν, re tamen idem cum illis sentiamus, cùm stantibus hypotefibus nostris talia absurda ex iis oriantur ac seqvantur. Huic respondemus inficiando, nihil horum ex nostra doctrinâ de reali idiomatum communicatione seqvi. Si enim persona τοῦ Λόγου absq; ulla sui mutatione, vel multiplicatione vel transfusione vel etiam conversione humanæ naturæ Christi realiter fuit communicata, qvod ipsi adversarii fateri necessum habent, nisi ipsissimam unionem tollere ac negare velint, qvid igitur repugnabit & in causa erit, cur non & eâdem ratione salvis manentibus & naturis earumq́; proprietatibus hæ ipsæ carni Christi essentialiter absq; conversione, abolitione &c, sint datæ ac communicatæ.

XI. DEII. Confusio ut est errorum mater, ita econtra distinctio veritatis est genitix, juxta illud: Qui bene distinguit, bene docet, propterea etiam Theologi ad rectiùs explicandam communicationis idiomatum doctrinam aliqvot distinctiones adhibuerunt, qvænam sit causa talis communicationis, & qvomodo proprietates communicatæ sese habeant ad naturã humanã, cui facta est illa communicatiò.

XII. Prima distinctio, qvæ & communis ac freqventissimè occurrit, est, qvâ distinguunt inter actum naturalem & personalem. Illum caro Christi, qvia naturalis caro, nobisq́; consubstantialis, ex se & per se communem nobiscum obtinet: Hunc verò propter unionem hypostaticam, qvi caro hypostaticè unita est Deitati τῦ λόγθ, fortitur. Caro enim Christi non est tantùm communis caro, sed ipsius Filii DEI caro, ex qva prærogativa non potest non altiorum ac sublimiorem conditionem acqvirere.

XIII. Notandum tamen, qvòd fundamentum actus personalis, non sit tota persona composita constans ex ambabus naturis,uti contendunt adversarii, qvò faciliùs sub hisce latibulis latitare, nobisq́; fucum facere possint, sed persona simplex involvens unam naturam, cum sua tamen subsistentia & personalitate, qvod ita propo: A qvo dependet unio humanæ naturæ cum λόγῳ, ab eo etiam dependet communicatio Idiomatum τῦ λόγθ facta humanæ naturæ; Atqvi unio illa dependet non à persona composita, qvæ involvit simul naturam humanam, qva seipsam unire non potest, sed à persona simplici τῦ λόγθ assumentis eam. Ergò ut unio, ita etiam communicatio ab illa persona simplici dependet.

XIII. Sicut enim unio naturarum divinæ τῦ λόγθ & humanæ non est actus naturalis sed personalis, ita etiam communicatio idiomatum divinorum est actus personalis; porrò cùm caro dicatur personaliter unita τῷ λόγῳ etiam personaliter omnipotens, vivificat &c. dicenda erit.

XIV. Qvare licet caro Christi non sit persona tota composita, est tamen ὑποσᾶσα ἐν τῷ λόγῳ in ipso Verbo subsistens, & ἐνυπόσατθ personata, id est, donata subsistentia τῦ λόγθ, indeq́; adepta est actum personalem.

XV. Nisi igitur duas personas in Christo impiè statuere velint, actum personalem ut amplectantur & assumant necessum est. Ratio: Nam humana natura Christi subsistit. Subsistit ergò vel actu proprionaturali ut alii homines, vel actu personali τοῦ λόγου ex unione personali. Sin hoc negant Adversarii. Ergò prius afferent. En igitur duos actus subsistendi naturales, Verbi & Carnis, qvod apertissimè Nestorianum.

XVI. Idcircò qvicqvid per & propter naturam humanam dicitur de humanitate Christi, id naturale ei est, & naturaliter de ea dicitur. Qvicqvid verò per & propter unionem hypostaticam dicitur de humanitate Christi, id personale ei est, & personaliter de ea dicitur, ubi τὸ personaliter non tantùm causam, verùm etiam modum & rationem attributionis designat.

XVII. Altera distinctio in scholis Theologorum usitata est, quâ didistinguunt inter id, qvod naturæ humanæ καθ' αὑτὸ per se, & κατ' ἄλλο secundum aliud competit, quæ qvidem verbis à priore differt, re autem cum illa coincidit. Est igitur καθ' αὑτὸ idem qvod essentiale, naturale, & qvicqvid ad naturæ humanæ Christi essentiam & constitutionem pertinet; κατ' ἄλλο verò qvod aliunde est, nimirum ex unione hypostatica.

XIX. Attribuuntur ergò idiomata divina carni Christi eaq́; rectè dicitur vivifica, non καθ' αὑτὸ sed κατ' ἄλλο, non quia est humana caro vel suâ essentiâ aut qvalitatibus talis, sed quia est propria caro ipsius τοῦ λόγου, qvi est ipsissima vita, quæ illi hypostaticè est unita, quæ unio hypostatica efficit, ut vivificare possit, qvare dicitur de carne Christi κατ' ἄλλο, sicuti etiam subsistere in ὑποστάσει Filii Dei competit humanitati Christi non καθ' αὑτὸ, sed κατ' ἄλλο, scilicet propter τὸν λόγον eam assumentẽ. Nam qvo modo humana natura Christi dicitur subsistere ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, eo etiã dicitur esse omnipræsens &c cùm communicatio horum attributorum sit conseqvens illius subsistentiæ; Atqvi caro Christi κατ' ἄλλο seu personaliter subsistit ἐν τῷ λόγῳ. Ergo & κατ' ἄλλο est omnipotens, vivifica & sic quoq; de cæteris judicandum.

XIX. Tertiò solent distinguere inter τὸ εἶναι καὶ ἔχειν, esse & habere. Illo modo attributa divina manẽt ei naturæ, cujus sunt proprià. Divina n. natura filii est ipsa vita, ipsa ὐσιώδης vita & ipsa ὐσιώδης omnipotentia. Ergo Filius Dei est vivificus & omnipotens τὸ εἶναι, quo pacto caro Christi nõ est vivifica, ita ut ipsissima sit vita, ac tota & essentialis vita.

XX. Posteriori verò modo propria sũt comunia alteri naturæ συνεδυασμένη ad communem possessionem ac realem, ut ita loqvar, habitionem. Qvod tamen ἔχειν & habere ad nullum qvadrat modum habendi physicum, sed omninò in hoc loco peculiarem ac planè singularem induit rationem, propter qvam caro Christi dicitur ἔχειν habere & possidere, ut hypostasin, ita etiam idiomata τῦ λόγꙋ.

XXI Non itaq; licet inferre, caro Christi non est ipsa omnipotentia, ergo neq; omnipotentiam habet, neq; omnipotens est. Nam etiam caro Christi, non est ipsa personalitas, sicuti λόγꙋ est sua ipsa subsistentia; Si igitur discursus iste valeret, eâdem ratione inferre qvis posset, carnem ꙋ λόγꙋ neq; esse ἐνυπόστατον seu personatam, neq; per unionem personalitatem in λόγῳ habere, cùm non sit ipsa ὑπόστασις, id qvod tamen longè absurdissimum.

XXII. DE III. Seqvitur jam, ut qvædam argumenta, qvibus generaliter totam ac omnem idiomatum communicationem adversarii convellere satagunt, in medium producamus.

XXIII. 1. Nullum proprium potest communicari alteri naturæ. Nam sic proprium esse desineret. Qvod enim proprium est & manet, non est commune alteri naturæ; & quod commune est, non jam est proprium, nec dici potest, colligit Sohn. tom. 2. art. 3. p. 502. C. A. Jam attributa divina sunt propria naturæ divinæ. E. carni Christi communicari neqveunt.

XXIV. Respondemus: 1. Propositio est falsissima, si generaliter intelligatur, uti patet ex illis modis, qvi ab utraq; parte sunt in confesso & extra controversiam, cum proprium generis commune sit speciei, proprium partis commune sit toti, & proprium accidentis commune sit subjecto.

XXV. 2. Proprium & commune in præsenti hoc nostro negocio non debent sibi opponi, cùm non sit utrinq; idem respectus, & non fiat secundùm idem & ad idem, qvod tamen in omni legitima oppositione summè est necessarium. Distingvimus igitur inter subjectum καθ' ὕπαρξιν & subjectum κατὰ συνδύασιν. Priori modo unum numero idioma non potest esse in duobus numero subjectis secundùm scilicet inhæsionem & πρώτοις δεκτικοῖς: Hic enim valet ille Canon: Unius proprii non nisi unum πρῶτον δεκτικόν est. Posterioriverò modo idem proprium non repugnat esse in duobus subjectis, in uno quidem per se πρώτως, ex cujus natura resultat; in altero verò δευτέρως, κατὰ συνδύασιν ad communem possessionem, usurpationem & denominationem.

XXVI. Si realiter communicantur proprietates: Ergò omnes; quia Deitatis proprietates sunt realiter indivisibiles & inseparabiles, concludit Sadeel in Vol. oper. Theol. p. 154. fac. b. Atqvi æternitatem, infinitatem, carni Christi communicatam esse dici neqvit. Ergò neq; omnipotentia, vis vivificandi &c. qvia attributa hæc perpetuam habent συνυπαρξίαν.

XXVII. Respondemus: 1. Negatur connexum, qvia non ad unius idiomatis communicationem, statim inferenda est alterius cujuscunq;, vel etiam omnium idiomatum communicatio: Ista enim συνυπαρξία qvam urgent Adversarii, locum habet in participatione subjecti κατὰ μέθεξιν, in qva subjectum unum δεκτικὸν definitionis alterius est, sic homini nimirum speciei communicatæ sunt omnes proprietates ad rationem animalis, nempe generis præcisè spectantes; Non autem locum habet in isto, qvod inest per unionem subjecti cum subjecto, qvod sit in præsenti nostra materia.

XXVIII. 2. Ratio hujus diversitatis partim sita est in ipsis proprietatibus communicandis; partim in subjecto altero, qvod non pariter est δεκτικὸν seu idoneum ac receptibile, ad recipiendum & usurpandum omnes, uti constat ex simili de ferro ignito. Idiomatum autem qvædam sunt ἐνεργητικὰ in creaturas, ut vis vivificatrix, omnipotentia &c. qvorum vestigia in rebus creatis reperiuntur: Qvædam verò sunt ἀνέργητα, ut æternitas, qvæ de solo Deo prædicantur. Illa carni Christi assignantur, & rectè dicitur vivifica, omnipotens, qvia ejusmodi ἐνεργείας in assumpta natura, cum ea & per eam ὁ λόγος exeqvitur. Hæc autem de ea immediatè non dicuntur, qvia nullas ἐνεργείας per carnem de se immediatè edunt. Cùm autem omnipotentia illa, qvæ carni Christi communicata est, æterna & infinita sit, hinc æternitas, infinitas, mediatè eidem attribui potest.

XXIX. 3. Si iste discursus valeret, eodem fermè modo Photinianus qvidam colligere, ac totum mysterium Trinitatis evertere posset. Si enim hoc axioma Calvinianorum semper & universaliter verum est: Qvacunq; realiter non differunt, sed unum sunt qvoddam

ἀδιαιρέτως, illorum communicato uno communicatur etiam alterum, facilè Photinianus qvidam subsumere posset: Atqvi hypostasis & essentia Dei Patris realiter non differunt: Ergò ambo Filio sunt communicata, & sic filius erit Pater, & non Filius, qvod absurdum.

XXX. DE IV. Seqvitur jam ultimum membrum. Meditatio antegressæ tractationis practica.

XXXI. Egregium autem hîc habemus specimen astutiæ ac infidiarum, qvas nobis struunt Satanas ejusqve membra hæretici falsiqve fratres, qvorum conatus, dum Ecclesiam à Christo abducere unicè nituntur, ac mores, qvibus se gerunt in hac controversia, dum in varias formas se transmutant, hîc nobis tanqvam in clarissimo speculo conspiciendi proponuntur.

XXXII. Duplici autem modo hostes illi nostri ἀσπονδοι Ecclesiam aggrediuntur. 1. Astutia. 2. Violentia. Priori dum utuntur armorum genere, simulant amicitiam, multas scripturas crepant, adhibitis ratiunculis humanæ rationis satis plausibilibus: novit etenim Diabolus sese transformare in Angelum lucis, ut ita simpliciores à recto veritatis tramite abducere, dolis ac fraudibus circumvenire possit.

XXXIII. Cùm verò ipsi hæc via diligenti scrutatione Scripturarum, solida Sophismatum solutione ac pellis ovinæ detractione, præcluditur, alia jam via rem aggrediens, lupinam assumit naturam, apertissimas indicit inimicitias, calumniatur & criminatur, & qvicqvid astutia obtinere non potuit, illud violentâ manu, fremente animo sibi vindicare tentat, qvos modos regnum suum ampliandi qvomodo hîc qvoqve observaverit, qvilibet cordatus facilè videt, à qvibus artibus ac præstigiis illius μειοτεχνίτης ejusqve sqvamarum cùm nos ex propriis viribus extricare & salvare non possimus, ipsum θεάνθρωπον supplices rogamus, ut Spiritu suo sancto nobis assistere ac nos ab insultibus hostium protegere dignetur, ob nominis sui benedicti, qvam impugnant, gloriam, cui sit laus & gratiarum actio in secula nunqvam terminanda.


## 18 Eighteenth Disputation, On the Omnipotence communicated to the assumed flesh

Thesis I.

That it is true, which Cyril (a) says: The body of life is glorified with a glory most worthy of God, was proved in general in the previous disputation: We therefore, with good right and good method, descend to more specific matters, intending to set forth in this disputation: 1. An enumeration of the communicated properties. 2. The state of the controversy of this disputation. 3. A proof of the communicated παντοκρατορίας (omnipotence) in general. 4. Specifically, of the δυνάμεως ζωοποιητικῆς (life-giving power), θαυματυργικῆς (miracle-working power), the removal of sins, and the power of judgment. 5. A refutation of some arguments of the opposing party. 6. A practical conclusion.

II. Although, therefore, the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells in Christ (Col. 2:9) and the whole Word was made flesh (John 1:14), not all attributes of the Word are said of the assumed flesh in the same way, but only those which are required for fulfilling the office of Redemption. For to the same end for which the Word assumed flesh, to that same end He communicated His own excellencies to it, namely, that He might accomplish the work of Redemption by such ἀποτελέσμασι (effects).

III. Moreover, these attributes are ascribed to Christ the Redeemer in Scripture: 1. Omnipotence, and specifically indeed, the power of vivifying, of performing miracles, of remitting sins, and of exercising judgment. II. Omniscience. III. Omnipresence, and its various modes and degrees. IV. The worship of adoration, etc. And in these, the remaining attributes, such as infinity, etc., so converge that these δυνάμεις (powers) are called, are, and remain not finite and created, etc., but infinite, uncreated, etc.

IV. Someone might here doubt concerning eternity, whether it also is immediately communicated, since mention is made in Scripture of an eternal priest. (b) But we respond: Christ is called an eternal priest by reason of an eternal office, as appears from the context and especially from the comparison of Aaron and Melchizedek. And therefore, in this place also, that distinction must be observed between the ἐνεργητικὰ (active) and ἀνενεργητικὰ (inactive) attributes of God; Christ can be denominated immediately from the former, but not likewise from the latter.

V. But as regards omnipotence, we believe and confess that not merely some finite and created power, but a truly infinite power, and one proper to the Word himself, has been communicated to Christ according to the flesh; and we acknowledge this as one, not double, by which the whole CHRIST, or both natures personally united, govern the world, and especially the Church, quicken believers, and forgive them their sins, etc.

VI. We have as our chief opponents the Calvinists, who, although they themselves hold diverse opinions, while some seem to acknowledge a scarcely verbal omnipotence of the flesh of Christ. (For thus that godless Simonius says that the human nature is called omnipotent, just as if one were to say that a pen is intelligent, because the man who uses the pen as an instrument is intelligent.) Others indeed concede a supreme power, yet a created one. Oecolampadius absolutely denies it altogether. Some invent a double one. Jacobus ad Portum (and those who follow him) establishes a middle one, which is neither divine nor created. Nevertheless, like the foxes of Samson, they all conspire in this, that they derogate from the uncreated power of the flesh of Christ.

VII. Let the state of the controversy therefore be such: Whether divine and proper power of the Word has been truly and really communicated to Christ according to the flesh, by which he governs all things and quickens believers, etc.? We affirm it, the Calvinists deny it. We shall prove our opinion in order, and first of all generally.

VIII. And this 1. from the sayings of Scripture, which we comprise in a syllogistic form in this manner: To whomsoever is given 1. eternal power. 2. power in heaven and on earth. 3. power over all flesh. 4. every creature which is under the earth, upon the earth, in the sea, and in heaven. 5. to whom all things have been delivered into his hands. 6. and subjected to his feet, nothing excepted; his power is infinite and divine. But such power is given to Christ as man or according to the flesh. Therefore. Since, however, they deny not only the Minor premise, but in certain sayings even the Major, we shall prove both in order where it shall seem necessary.

IX. 1. To the Son of man is given eternal power, Dan. 7:14. The adversaries scarcely find what they may oppose to this testimony, since the human nature of Christ is expressly named, to which divine power is given (for whatever is eternal, that is divine) by the Ancient of days. Nor can they fashion any power without potency; for in Hebrew there is שִׁלְטוֹן from the root שָׁלַט, which word signifies not only to have power, but also to exercise dominion: See Eccl. 2, 19. c. 8, 9. Neh. 5, 15. Esth. 9, 1. etc.

X. 2. All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth, Matt. 28, 18. That this statement also must be understood of the human nature, these arguments taken from the text prove. 1. The circumstance of time after the resurrection. 2. Christ bids farewell to the disciples as he is about to depart from them. 3. He consoles the same with the promise of his presence, and thus of his will, to which he lays down all power as a foundation, so that the faculty may be established. 4. He commends to them the ministry of the Gospel. All these things are either referred directly to the human nature, or denote an office from which humanity cannot be excluded.

XI. But we pay no heed to the trifles of the Calvinists, nor to those who include this power within the bounds of heaven and earth. For why do we not in the same way, with Vorstius, deny the infinite essence of God, which is wont to be described in Scripture by a similar paraphrase? Is. 66, 1. Jer. 23, 24. see Ps. 126, 6.
