Moreover, Jehovah himself also enjoys this title, Gen. 14, 22. c. 24, 3. 7. Ezra 5, 11. Luke 10, 21. Matt. 11, 25. Rev. 17, 24. Then also of others who seek cavils in the word ἐξουσίας. 1. For δύναμις itself is said to be given to Christ, as we shall hear. 2. ἐξουσία is more than δύναμις, for the latter can exist without the former, but the former can in no way exist without the latter (in divine matters). 3. It would be a mere mockery if some power were given without force. 4. Let 1 Chron. 29, 11 and Ps. 103, 19 be compared. Seek more prolix accounts from the most illustrious Mr. President (a) as also from Chemnitz (b), Mentzer (c), Hutter (d), and others.

XII. 3. Power over all flesh, John 17, 2, was given to that nature which had need of clarification. But the λόγος did not have need of it, for he always works, John 5, 17, and exerts himself. Nor can this passage be understood of manifestation, which will only be full on the last day, see Heb. 2, 8, compare 1 Pet. 4, 13; it is necessary, therefore, that we interpret it as a real donation.

XIII. 4. Rev. 5, 12. That this δύναμιν καὶ ἰσχὺν is truly divine is proved 1. by the clear description, by which whatever is created is subjected to this Lamb. 2. By the celebration of the angels and the 24 Elders, who, if they were celebrating some created power so greatly, would have done too much could be seen. And human nature is indicated quite expressly, both because the Lamb is read to have received this power, and because such a Lamb is celebrated, who was slain. But God cannot die. XIV. 5. All things have been delivered into his hands Joh. 3, 25. We see no necessity why the word all should be restricted, nor is the restriction itself added, therefore we do not doubt that it indicates divine power. But they were delivered to that nature, 1. which had need to be endowed with the Holy Spirit without measure. 2. in whom he who believes has eternal life, and he who does not believe shall not see life, etc. XV. 6. All things are subjected to him Ps. 8, 8. and indeed in such a way that nothing can be excepted Heb. 2, 8. except him who subjected all things to him 1. Cor. 15, 26. But all things are subjected to Christ according to that nature, 1. which was made a little lower than the angels. 2. Which deserved to be crowned with glory and honor on account of suffering Hebr. 2, 9. But for the theologian to affirm such things concerning God or the Word Mal. 3, 6. the conclusion therefore stands, Therefore infinite omnipotence, and thus truly divine, is communicated to Christ as man or according to his human nature. The same could be proved from Ps. 110. Matth. 11. Joh. 13. 1. Cor. 15. Eph. 1. Phil. 1. etc. but regard must be had for brevity.

XVI. 2. We add these reasons. 1. He who has been made a partaker of the whole fullness of the Godhead. 2. He who sits at the right hand of the power of God. 3. whose works are truly infinite. 4. He who works effectively in his ministers; his power must necessarily be truly infinite. But Christ according to his human nature is 1. a partaker of the whole fullness of the Godhead Col. 2, 9. 2. sits at the right hand of God (because 1. the session was given to him in time. 2. the order of the Articles in the Apostles' Creed demands it. 3. it is a consequence of the passion of Christ Phil. 2, 8. & 9. Ps. 110. last. 4. the clear letter testifies Matth. 26, 64. 5. it was given by grace Phil. 2, 9.) 3. his works are infinite Act. 4, 7. & 10. 1. Tim. 1, 12. 2. Tim. 4, 17. 4. he works effectively in his ministers. Marc. 16, 20. Therefore.

XVII. We subjoin 3. certain testimonies of the Fathers. Thus therefore Damascene: (a) The human will of CHRIST was not naturally omnipotent: but as it has become truly and according to nature the will of the Word of GOD, so it is also omnipotent. Theophylact:

(b) He gave all things into the hand of the Son according to his humanity. Nicephorus

(c): CHRIST is seen by the Disciples on the mountain in Galilee and confirms that supreme power over heaven and earth was delivered to him by the Father, according to his human nature, of course. Vigilius: (d) The divine nature does not need to be exalted by honors, to be increased by perfections of dignity, to receive the power of heaven and earth by merit of obedience. Therefore, according to the nature of the flesh, he was exalted, honored, crowned, and obtained the dignity of a better name; he who according to the nature of the Word lacked none of these at any time, so that, for instance, he would receive the power of heaven and earth, the inheritance of the nations, and the subjection of all things in time. For did the Creator not have power and dominion over his creature, so that in the last times he might possess these by the grace of a gift? So much for omnipotence; hereafter we shall be briefer.

Latin:

Thesis I.

VErum esse, quod Cyrillus (a) ait: Vitæ corpus est glorificatum claritate Deo dignissima, Superiori disputatione in genere probatum est: Nos igitur bono jure bonaq́; methodo ad specialiora descendimus, hac disputatione proposituri. 1. Idiomatum communicatorum enumerationem. 2. Statum controversiæ hujus disputationis. 3. Probationem communicatæ παντοκρατορίας in genere. 4. In specie δυνάμεως ζωοποιητικῆς, θαυματυργικῆς, ἀφαιρέσεως ἁμαρτημάτων, κριτικῆς. 5. Nonnullorum adversæ partis argumentorum dilutionem. 6. Practicam conclusionem.

II. Licet igitur tota Deitatis plenitudo in Christo inhabitet Col. 2, 9. totumqve verbum caro sit factum Joh. 1, 14. Non omnia tamen λόγε attributa de carne assumta perinde dicuntur, sed ea tantum, qvæ ad obeundum Redemtionis munus reqviruntur. Quo enim fine λόγos carnem assumsit, eo etiam suas excellentias proprias eidem communicavit, nimirum, ut opus Redemtionis ejusmodi ἀποτελέσμασι perageret.

III. Attribuuntur autem Christo Redemtori in scriptura hæc attributa. 1. Omnipotentia, & nominatim qvidem, vis vivificandi, miracula edendi, remittendi peccata, & judicium exercendi. II. Omniscientia. III. Omnipræsentia, ejusq; modi & gradus diversi. IV. Cultus adorationis &c. Et in his attributa reliqva, ut infinitas &c. ita confluunt, ut hæ δυνάμεις non finitæ & creatæ &c. sed infinitæ, increatæ &c. dicantur, sint & maneant.

IV. De æternitate hîc aliqvis dubitare posset, an & illa immediate sit communicata, cum æterni sacerdotis in scriptura fiat mentio. (b) Sed nos respondemus: Sacerdotem æternum dici Christum ratione æterni officii, ut ex contextu, & maximè ex collatione Aaronis & Melchisedechi apparet. Ideoq; & hoc in loco distinctio illa observanda est inter attributa Dei ἐνεργητικὰ, & ἀνενεργητικὰ; ab illis denominari potest Christus immediatè, ab his vero non item,

V. Ad omnipotentiam autem quod attinet, credimus & confitemur, non finitam tantum aliqvam & creatam, sed verè infinitam, ipsiusqve λόγε propriam potentiam Christo secundum carnem esse communicatam; eamqve unam agnoscimus, non duplicem, qva totius CHRISTUS, seu ambæ naturæ personaliter unitæ orbem terrarum, præcipuè vero Ecclesiam gubernant, credentes vivificant, eisqve peccata remittunt &c.

VI. Contradicentes habemus maximè Calvinianos, qvi licet ipsi diversas abeant in sententias, dum alii vix verbalem carnis Christi omnipotentiam agnoscere videntur. (Sic enim ἄθεος ille Simonius, (c) Humanam naturam dicit omnipotentem vocari, perinde ut siqvis calamum intelligentem esse dicat, qvia homo, qvi calamo, ut instrumento utitur, sit intelligens) Alii summam qvidem concedunt, creatam tamen. Oecolampadius ὑποτόμως omnem omninò negat. Qvidam duplicem fingunt. Jacobus ad Portum (& qvi eum seqvuntur) mediam constituit, qvæ neq; divina, neq; creata sit. Tamen vulpecularum instar Samsonis, in hoc conspirant omnes, ut increatam potentiam carni Christi derogent.

VII. Sit igitur status controversiæ talis: An Christo secundum carnem verè & realiter communicata sit divina & λόγε propria omnipotentia, qva omnia gubernet, & credentes vivificet &c? Affirmamus nos, Calviniani negant. Nostram sententiam ordine probabimus, & primò qvidem generaliter.

VIII. Idq; 1. dictis Scripturæ, qvæ forma Syllogistica comprehendimushoc modo: Cuicunq; data est. 1. potestas æterna. 2. potestas in cælo & in terra. 3. potestas omnis carnis. 4. omnis creatura, qvæ sub terra, super terram, in mari & in cælo est. 5. cui omnia tradita sunt in manus. 6. & subjecta pedibus, nihilo excepto; illius potestas est infinita & divina. Talis autem potestas data est Christo homini seu secundum carnem. Ergo. Cum autem non tantum Minorem, verùm in qvibusdam dictis etiam Majorem negent, utramq; ubi opus videbitur ordine probabimus.

IX. 1. Filio hominis data est potestas æterna, Dan. 7, 14. Huic testimonio qvod opponant vix inveniunt adversarii, cum expressê nominetur humana Christi natura, cui divina potestas data est (qvicqvid enim æternum, id divinum) ab antiqvo dierum. Nec potestatem aliqvam absqve potentia fingere possunt ; in Hebræo enim est שִׁלְטוֹן a radice שָׁלַט, qvod vocabulum non tantum potestatem habere, sed & dominium exercere significat : Vide Eccl. 2, 19. c. 8, 9. Neh. 5, 15. Esth. 9, 1. &c.

X. 2. Data est ei potestas in cælo & in terra Matth. 28, 18. Hoc qvoqve dictum de humana natura intelligendum esse, probant hæc ex textu desumta argumenta. 1. Circumstantia temporis post resurrectionem. 2. Valedicit Christus discipulis ab eis recessurus. 3. Eosdem consolatur promissione suæ præsentiæ, adeoqve voluntatis, cui substernit omnem potestatem tanqvam fundamentum, ut constet de facultate. 4. Commendat eis ministerium Evangelii. Hæc omnia vel directè referuntur ad humanam naturam, vel notant officium, â qvo excludi humanitas non potest.

XI. φλυαρίας autem Calvinianorum nihil moramur, tum eorum, qvi potestatem hanc terminis cæli & terræ includunt. Cur enim non eodem modo cum Vorstio infinitam Dei essentiam negamus, qvæ simili paraphrasi in scriptura describi solet ? Es. 66, 1. Jer. 23, 24. vide Ps. 126, 6. tum ipse etiam Jehova hoc titulo gaudet, Gen. 14, 22. c. 24, 3. 7. Esd. 5, 11. Luc. 10. 21. Matth. 11, 25. Apoc. 17, 24. Tum aliorum, qvi in voce ἐξουσίας cavillationes qværunt. 1. ipsa enim δύναμις Christo data dicitur, ut audiemus. 2. ἐξουσία plus est qvàm δύναμις, hæc enim esse potest absqve illa, at illa absqve hac (in rebus divinis) nullo modo. 3. merum esset ludibrium si potestas aliqva daretur absq; vi. 4. Conferantur, 1. Par. 29, 11. Ps. 103, 19. Prolixiora qvære apud clariss. Dn. Præsidem (a) ut & Chemnitium (b) Mentzerum (c) Hutterum (d) & alios

XII. 3. Potestas omnis carnis Joh. 17, 2. illi naturæ data est, qvæ opus habebat clarificatione. λόγος autem non habebat eâ opus, semper enim operatur Joh. 5, 17. & se exerit. Neqve de manifestatione in telligi hic locus potest, qvæ demum plena erit in novissimo die, vide Hebr. 2, 8. confer. 1. Petr. 4, 13. necesse est igitur, ut de reali donatione eum interpretemur.

XIII. 4. Apoc. 5, 12. hanc δύναμιν καὶ ἰσχὺν verè divinam esse, probat 1. luculenta descriptio, qva qvicqvid creatum est huic agno subjicitur. 2. angelorum & 24. Seniorum celebratio, qvi si creatam aliqvam potestatem tantopere celebrarent, nimium fecisse videri possent. Et humana natura satis expresse innuitur, tum qvia Agnus potestatem hanc accepisse legitur, tum qvia talis Agnus celebratur, qvi occisus est. Deus autem mori non possit. XIV. 5. Omnia ei tradita sunt in manus Joh. 3, 25. Nullam videmus necessitatem cur vocabulum omnia sit restringendum, nec ipsa restrictio additur, ideo divinam potentiam innuere non dubitamus. Naturae autem illi tradita sunt, 1. qvae Spiritu S. absqve mensura donari opus habuit. 2. cui qvi credit vitam habet aeternam, & qvi non credit non videbit vitam &c. XV. 6. Omnia ei sunt subjecta Ps. 8, 8. & ita qvidem ut nihil possit excipi Heb. 2, 8. praeterqvam is qvi subjecit ei omnia 1. Cor. 15, 26. Sunt autem Christo omnia subjecta secundum eam naturam, 1. qvae minorata est paulo ab Angelis. 2. Qvae ob passionem gloria & honore coronari meruit Hebr. 2, 9. Aθεολογον autem de Deo seu λογῳ talia affirmare Mal. 3, 6. stat igitur conclusio, Ergo Christo homini seu secundum humanam naturam communicata omnipotentia infinita, adeoqve vere divina. Idem probari posset ex Psal. 110. Matth. 11. Joh. 13. 1. Cor. 15. Eph. 1. Phil. 1. &c. sed brevitatis ratio habenda.

XVI. 2. Addimus has rationes. 1. Qvi factus est κοινωνὸς totius plenitudinis Deitatis. 2. Qvi sedet ad dextram virtutis Dei. 3. cujus opera sunt vere infinita. 4. Qvi efficaciter in ministris suis operatur; illius potestas necesse est ut vere sit infinita. Atqvi Christus secundum humanam naturam est 1. κοινωνὸς totius plenitudinis Deitatis Col. 2, 9. 2. sedet ad dextram Dei (qvia 1. sessio ei data est tempore. 2. ordo Articulorum in symb. Ap. id postulat. 3. est conseqvens passionis Christi Phil. 2, 8. & 9. Ps. 110. ult. 4. clara litera testatur Matth. 26, 64. 5. donata est ex gratia Phil. 2, 9.) 3. opera ejus sunt infinita Act. 4, 7. & 10. 1. Tim. 1, 12. 2. Tim. 4, 17. 4. efficaciter operatur in ministris. Marc. 16, 20. Ergo.

XVII. Subjicimus 3. qvaedam Patrum testimonia. Sic igitur Damascenus: (a) Humana CHRISTI voluntas naturaliter qvidem omnipotens non erat: ut autem vere & secundum naturam DEI verbi voluntas est facta, ita & omnipotens est. Theophylactus:

(b) Omnia dedit in manum Filii juxta humanitatem. Nicephorus

(c): CHRISTUS a Discipulis in Galileae monte conspicitur & sibi â Patre summam potestatem cœli & terræ, juxta humanam scilicet naturam traditam esse confirmat. Vigilius: (d) Divina natura non indiget honoribus sublimari, dignitatis perfectionibus augeri, potestatem cœli & terræ obedientiæ merito accipere. Secundum carnis igitur naturam exaltatus est, honoratus, coronatus, melioris nominis dignitatem adeptus; Qvi secundum naturam verbi nihil horum eguit aliqvando, ut sc. potestatem cœli & terræ, hæreditatem gentium, & subjectionem universorum ex tempore acciperet. Num qvid enim potestatem & dominium creaturæ suæ conditor non habebat, ut novissimis temporibus muneris gratia his potiretur? Hactenus de omnipotentia, posthac breviores erimus.


### XVIII. Let us approach the life-giving power, which, as it is one and the same…

XVIII. Let us approach the life-giving power, which, as it is one and the same person, in whom both the divine nature of the Word and his human nature subsist, so it is itself one and the same, by which both the divine nature of the Word is said to give life, and his human nature. The mode of attribution, however, is different, because it is attributed to the divine nature in itself, κυρίως (properly), πρώτως (primarily), originally. To the human nature of the Word, it is not so attributed, neither subjectively, nor as a property or quality of the flesh, but κατ’ ἄλλο (by another), δευτέρως (secondarily), personally; not verbally, but really; not as it is life itself, but as a participant in life through union, not by essence but on account of the Word, not φυσικῶς (naturally) but ὑπερφυσικῶς (supernaturally); and so when we say: The flesh of Christ is life-giving, it is the same as if we were to say: Christ (who according to his Deity is life itself) is life-giving according to the flesh, insofar as he has that personally united to himself, and has in reality communicated the power of giving life.

XIX. We prove this opinion 1. by sayings, in this way: Whoever 1. feeds and gives us drink unto eternal life. 2. gives the water of life. 3. is the head of the Church, from whom all members grow, etc., he truly possesses the power of giving life. Christ according to his human nature, etc. Therefore, we shall prove the minor premise in order.

XX. 1. He feeds us unto, etc. John 6. I prove that Christ understands his own flesh thus: 1. The bread of The flesh of Christ is the bread of life, v. 51. Therefore. 2. That which makes us live eternally, i.e., is life-giving, the flesh of Christ makes us live eternally, v. 54. Therefore. 3. That which is opposed to Manna, which could not ward off death from the Fathers, that is life-giving, v. 58. The flesh of Christ is opposed to Manna. Therefore. But Christ in this text does not by positing the rite remove the efficacy, but from the merit he argues for the efficacy. Then he commands to eat the flesh, so that we may thus have life. He who does not see the application here, and the ἐνέργειαν of vivifying, is blind like an owl in bright light.

XXI. 2. He gives the water of life, John 4:14. If we compare this passage with Acts 2:33, we see that this benefit pertains to the human nature: for according to the nature by which Christ was exalted, according to that he promised the streams of life. But he was exalted according to his human nature. Therefore.

XXII. 3. He is the head, from whom the members grow, Eph. 1:22, ch. 4:15, ch. 5:23, Col. 1:18, ch. 2:10. That Christ is the head of the Church according to his human nature cannot be denied with any plausible appearance. For being the head pertains to the office, from which those who wish to exclude the human nature act too rashly.

XXIII. 2. We give these reasons. 1. If the flesh of Christ is united to the vivifying λόγῳ in one person, 2. and he united the flesh to himself to that end, that he might bring men back from death to life, it follows that the flesh is vivifying. But the former is true. Therefore. We omit more for the sake of brevity.

XXIV. 3. Let these be the sayings of the Fathers. Damascene: (a) The flesh of the Lord was mortal by itself, and vivifying on account of the union to the λόγον according to person. Cyril: (b) Although the nature of the flesh as flesh is unable to vivify, it nevertheless does this because it has received the whole operation of the Word. Council of Ephesus: (c) εἴ τις ὀυκ ὁμολογεῖ τὴν τῦ κυρίυ σάρκα ζωοποιὸν, ὅτι γέγονεν ἰδία τ̃ λόγυ, τ̃ τὰ παντὰ ζωοποιεῖν ἰσχύοντὸς, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω. Again Cyril: (a) It would be altogether indecent if fire could indeed impart its quality to matter joined to it, and in the same way transform the matter into itself: but the Word of God could not infuse his own and natural good, that is, life, into the flesh joined to him, etc.

XXV. There follows now the miraculous power, which can be understood in large part from the preceding. We say, however, that this power is not natural to the flesh nor does it inhere in it subjectively, nor do we acknowledge a double power, but we firmly maintain that he performs miracles by one and the same power of the λόγου in the assumed flesh, so that the flesh acts as an instrument, not ἄεργον but συνέργον.

XXVI. We produce 1. the following sayings. 1. Acts 10:38, and thus we argue according to which nature 1. God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power 2: and God was with him, according to that nature also Christ bestowed benefits and healed the oppressed, etc. But those things pertain to Christ according to his human nature. Therefore. 2. Peter's sermon, Acts 3, the cause of which was the healed lame man. We did not do this by our own power so that he might walk, but by the power of Jesus whom you crucified. Hence the first argument is twofold, 1. He who gave others the power of healing, and 2. is himself the author of life, he possesses that power: Christ according to his human nature, which could be crucified, gave it to others, and is the author of life. Therefore.

XXVII. This very thing 2. is proven by examples of miracles, in which mention is made, either expressly or implicitly, of the members of the body. Hand, Matt. 8, 3. and 15. Mark 5, 41. ch. 8, 23. Luke 8, 54. ch. 13, 13. Fingers, Mark 7, 33. Spittle, Mark 8, 23. John 9, 6. Voice, Luke 7, 14. ch. 13, 12. Matt. 8, 3. John 11, 43. Touch, Matt. 9, 29. ch. 20, 34. Luke 22, 51. etc.

XXVIII. 3. Thus the Fathers. Eusebius: (b) He mingled divine operation with the Incarnation, exhibiting miracles above man. Cyril: (c) Why did he not rather, as with Lazarus he was content with a word to raise the girl, but also held her hand? Surely, to show his life-giving body: For the body is life.

XXIX. Briefly now concerning the power of forgiving sins. 1. We prove it from Isa. 43, 25. He who 1. bore labors. 2. was not invoked by the Jews, nor honored with offerings, etc. he has the power of forgiving or blotting out iniquities: Christ according to his human nature bore, etc. Therefore. 2. Matt. 9, 6. Here 1. he is expressly named the Son of man. 2. Christ opposes these words to the Scribes who ascribe this work to God alone, compare Mark 2, 3. Luke 5, 21. 3. the crowd therefore glorified God, because he had given that power to men, especially to Christ. For the sake of brevity we omit the remaining passages pertaining to this, such as Dan. 9. Matt. 1. John 1. Also Acts 20. Heb. 9. etc.

XXX. 2. From reasons. 1. Because it pertains to the office of Christ. 2. his blood was shed for the remission of sins Matt. 26, 28. 3. and through his blood we have redemption Col. 1, 20. 1 Pet. 1, 19. justification Rom. 5, 9. etc. Therefore.

…XXXI. Hence Ambrose: (d) The death of Christ is the justification of sinners. And Chrysostom: (e) The cross of Christ is the cause. This has freed us from blindness, restored us from darkness to light, associated those defeated with peace, joined those alienated to God, and made citizens of those who were wandering. This is the firmament of peace, the amputation of discord, and the abundant bestowal of all good things.

XXXII. It remains... we shall conclude in very few words. We prove it 1. from John 5:27, where it is to be noted that Luke 6:22, 69 warns that it was given in time. 2. The particle δι' αὐτὸν ὅτι denotes the human nature itself. 2. Acts 1:11. Such as the ascension, such is the return and the judgment. That was visible and appropriate to human nature. Therefore. 3. Acts 10:24, the one constituted Judge is called anointed, crucified, etc. 4. Acts 17:31, he is called a Man. 5. Dan. 7:13 & 14, it is read that this power was given to the Son of man. 6. Rev. 5:19, to the Lamb that was slain, 7. to him whom every eye shall see. Rev. 1:7.

XXXIII. Hence Cyril: (a) Christ set forth the cause why he said that life and the power of judgment were given to him by the Father, saying, Because he is the son, so that we may understand that all things were given to him as a man. For the only-begotten son is not a participant of life, but is life by nature.

XXXIV. The objections of the adversaries should now be examined, but the nature of our undertaking does not allow us to deal with them at length; we shall submit only one or two. Thus they are accustomed to argue against Omnipotence: He who is omnipotent does not implore the help of another. But Christ, according to his human nature, implored the help of the Father. Therefore. Response 1. Distinguish between that which is done simply, and that which is done by economy. There were other reasons why Christ implored the help of the Father. 1. For he had been sent by him into the world. 2. Because he had to be made like his brothers in all things, so that he might be a faithful High Priest when tempted. Heb. 2:17, ch. 4:15, Phil. 2:7. 2. The states are to be distinguished. For in the time of his Humiliation he did indeed truly have Omnipotence communicated to him; but only in possession, not in use, for the office of the redeemer did not allow that. Now, however, he possesses it both in possession and in use, so that access to him may be open to us with confidence. Heb. 4:16.

XXXV. Against the power of giving life they bring forward such an argument: If the power of giving life was communicated to the flesh of Christ from John 6, it follows that the flesh descended from heaven. The latter is absurd. Therefore the former is also. Response 1. The consequence is denied. For both are in the text, both that the flesh gives life, and that the Person (I) descended from heaven. 2. The word of descending here does not denote local motion, but describes the incarnation, which is predicated neither of the λόγῳ alone, nor of the flesh alone, but of the λόγῳ assuming flesh, and of the flesh assumed by the λόγῳ etc.

XXXVI. They attempt to refute the miraculous power by such an argument: If the fringe of Christ cannot be called miracle-working, although it healed the woman, Luke 8:44, neither can such power be ascribed to the flesh of Christ. Resp. 1. It is blasphemous to compare the flesh of Christ with the fringe, for why do they not say in the same way that the fringe is life-giving? Is the fringe also personally united to the λόγῳ? 2. In the text, Luke says that that power went out (not from the fringe, but) from the flesh of Christ. Therefore, it is to be ascribed to it, not to the fringe.

XXXVII. Against the judicial power, the sayings of Mark 13:32 and Luke 2:52 are usually objected. Since these are used rather to impugn omniscience, we have therefore left them for the following disputation. And thus we have established the truth of our opinion.

XXXVIII. Do not fear, therefore, you worm Jacob and you who are dead of Israel: I am your helper, says the Lord, and your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel. For although you are poor and drunk, not with wine: yet your Lord, who fights for his people, will take from your hand the cup of stupor, the dregs of the bottom, the cup of the Lord's indignation, and you shall not drink it again. Who shall separate you from the love of Christ? Who shall accuse or condemn? It is God who justifies. Christ Jesus is he who died, nay, rather who rose again and sits at the right hand of GOD.

XXXIX. But you who work iniquity, who devour the people of the Lord like bread; do you not know this? How long will you rage and stand against the Lord and against his Christ? Who has been established King over the holy mountain of Zion. He himself will crush you with a rod of iron and break you like a potter's vessel. Kiss the Son, therefore, lest he be angry and you perish in the way, when his wrath has kindled even a little. But blessed will be those who take refuge in him. To him be praise, honor, and glory, for ever and ever.

Latin:

XVIII. Accessum faciamus ad vim vivificatricem, qvæ, ut est una eademq́; persona, in qva & natura divina ꝰ͂ λόγꝣ & natura ejus humana subsistit, sic & ipsa una est & eadem, qva & divina ꝰ͂ λόγꝣ natura dicitur vivificare, & natura ejus humana. Modus autem attributionis diversus, qvia divinæ naturæ tribuitur per se, κυρίως, πρώτως, originaliter. Naturæ verbo humanæ non ita, nec subjectivè, nec ut proprietas aut qvalitas carnis, sed κατ’ ἄλλο, δευτέρως, personaliter; non verbaliter, sed realiter; non ut est vita ipsa, sed ut vitæ per unionem particeps, non per essentiam sed propter λόγον, non φυσικῶς sed ὑπερφυσικῶς, adeoqve cum dicimus: Caro Christi est vivifica, idem est ac si diceremus; Christus (qvi secundum Deitatem ipsa vita est) est vivificus secundum carnem qvatenus illam personaliter sibi habet unitam, & vim vivificandi reipsâ communicavit.

XIX. Hanc sententiam probamus 1. dictis, hoc modo: Qvicunq; 1. nos cibat & potat ad vitam æternam. 2. dat aqvam vitæ. 3. est Ecclesiæ caput, ex qvo omnia membra augescunt &c. ille verè pollet virtute vivificandi. Christus secundum humanam naturam &c. E. Minorem probabimus ordine.

XX. 1.Cibat nos ad &c. Joh. 6. Carnem suam Christum intelligere, ita probo. 1. Panis vitæ est vivificus. Caro Christi est panis vitæ, v. 51. E. 2. Qvod facit nos æternum vivere, i. e. vivificum, caro Christi facit nos æternum vivere v. 54. E. 3. Qvod opponitur Mannæ, qvæ mortem â Patribus arcere non potuit, id est vivificum, v. 58. Caro Christi opponitur Mannæ. E. Non autem Christus in hoc textu meritum ponendo tollit efficaciam, sed ex merito arguit efficaciam. Deinde jubet edere carnem, ut ita vitam habeamus. Qui hic applicationem, & vivificandi ἐνέργειαν non videt, is noctuarum instar in clara luce cæcutit.

XXI. 2. Dat aqvam vitæ Joh. 4, 14. Si conferamus hunc locum cum Act. 2, 33. humanæ naturæ hoc beneficium competere videmus: Nam secundùm quam naturam Christus exaltatus est, secundùm eam promisit fluenta vitæ. Jam verò secundùm humanam naturam exaltatus est. Ergo.

XXII. 3. Est caput, ex qvo membra angescunt Eph. 1, 22. c. 4, 15. c. 5, 23. Col. 1, 18. c. 2, 10. Secundum à humanam naturam Christum esse caput Ecclesiæ, nulla specie verisimili negari potest. Nam caput esse pertinet ad officium, â qvo qvi naturam humanam excludere volunt, nimis agunt temerariè.

XXIII. 2. Rationes has damus. 1. Si caro Christi vivificanti λόγῳ unita est in unam personam 2. & λόγῳ eum in finem carnem sibi univit, ut homines â morte ad vitam reduceret, seqvitur carnem esse vivificam. Verum prius. E. Plures brevitatis ergo omittimus.

XXIV. 3. Dicta Patrum hæc sunto. Damas. (a) Caro Domini erat mortalis per se, & vivificans propter unionem ad λόγον secundùm personam. Cyrillus: (b) Qvamvis natura carnis ut caro est vivificare neqveat, facit tamen hoc qvia totam verbi operationem suscepit. Conc. Eph. (c) εἴ τις ὀυκ ὁμολογεῖ τὴν τῦ κυρίυ σάρκα ζωοποιὸν, ὅτι γέγονεν ἰδία τ̃ λόγυ, τ̃ τὰ παντὰ ζωοποιεῖν ἰσχύοντὸς, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω. Iterum Cyrillus: (a) Indecens omnino esset, si ignis qvidem qvalitatem suam conjunctæ sibi materiæ possit immittere, ac eodem modo materiam in se transmutare: λόγῳ autem Dei proprium & naturale bonum, id est, vitâ conjunctæ sibi carni non posset infundere &c.

XXV. Seqvitur jam virtus θαυματεργικὴ, qvæ magnâ ex parte ex superioribus intelligi potest. Dicimus autem hanc vim carni non esse naturalem nec eidem subjective inhærere, neq; duplicem agnoscimus, sed unâ eademq; vi λόγου in assumptâ carne miracula edere, ut caro se habeat ut instrumentum, non ἄεργον sed συνέργον, firmiter statuimus.

XXVI. Producimus 1. seqventia dicta. 1. Act. 10, 38. & sic argumentamur. Secundùm quam naturam 1. Jesum unxit Deus spiritu sancto, & potentia 2: & Deus cum eo erat, secundùm eam etiam naturam Christus beneficia dedit & sanavit oppressos &c. Atqui illa competunt Christo secundùm humanam naturam. E. 2. concionem Petri, Act. 3. cujus causa erat claudus sanatus. Non nostrâ virtute fecimus ut hic ambularet, sed virtute Jesu quem vos crucifixistis. Hinc duplex est primus argumentum, 1. Qui dedit aliis potestatem sanandi, & 2. est ipse autor vitæ, is pollet eâ virtute: Christus secundum humanam naturam, quæ crucifigi potuit, dedit aliis, & est autor vitæ. E.

XXVII. Hoc ipsum 2. probant exempla miraculorum, in quibus membrorum corporis vel expressè vel implicitè fit mentio. Manûs Matth. 8, 3. & 15. Marc. 5, 41. c. 8, 23. Luc. 8, 54. c. 13, 13. Digitorum, Marc. 7, 33. Sputi, Marc. 8, 23. Joh. 9, 6. Vocis, Luc. 7, 14. c. 13, 12. Matth. 8, 3. Joh. 11, 43. Tactus, Matth. 9, 29. c. 20, 34. Luc. 22, 51. &c.

XXVIII. 3. Sic Patres. Eusebius: (b) Divinam operationem miscuit Incarnationi supra hominem exhibens miracula. Cyrillus: (c) Quare non potius, sicut apud Lazarum contentus fuit sermone ad resuscitandam puellam, sed & tenuit manum illius? nimirum, ut ostenderet, vivificum ejus corpus: Corpus enim est vita.

XXIX. Breviter jam de potestate remittendi peccata. 1. Probamus eam ex Ef. 43, 25. Qui 1. pertulit labores. 2. non est invocatus à Judæis, nec oblationibus honoratus &c. is potestatem habet remittendi seu delendi iniquitates: Christus secundum humanam naturam pertulit &c. Ergo. 2. Matth. 9,6. Hic 1. disertè nominatur Filius hominis. 2. Christus opponit hæc verba Scribis soli Deo id opus adscribentibus, confer Marc. 2, 3. Luc. 5, 21. 3. turba ideò Deum glorificavit, quod eam potestatem dederit hominibus, maximè Christo. Brevitatis gratia omittimus reliqva loca huc facientia, ut Dan. 9. Matth. 1. Joh. 1. Item Act. 20. Hebr. 9. &c.

XXX. 2. Ex rationibus. 1. Qvia pertinet ad officium Christi. 2. sangvis ejus effusus est in remissionem peccatorum Matth. 26, 28. 3. & per sangvinem habemus redemtionem Col. 1, 20. 1. Pet. 1, 19. justificationem Rom. 5, 9. &c. Ergo.

XXXI. Hinc Ambrosius: (d) Mors Christi justificatio est peccatorum. Et Chrysostomus: (e) Crux Christi totius beatitudinis nobiscausa est. Hæc nos à cæcitate liberavit, è tenebris reddidit luci, debellatos qvieti sociavit, alienatos Deo conjunxit, peregrinantes fecit cives. Hæc firmamentum pacis, discordiæ amputatio, bonorum omnium abunda largitio.

XXXII. Restat ... ... paucissimis absolvemus. Probamus eam 1. ex Joh. 5. 27. ubi notandum, qvod 1. eam in tempore datum esse moneat Lucas 6. 22, 69. 2. particula διαυτὸν ὅτι ipsam notet humanam naturam. 2. Act. 1, 11. Qvalis ascensus, talis reditus & judicium. Ille fuit visibilis & humanæ naturæ competens. E. 3. Actor. 10, 24. constitutus Judex dicitur unctus, crucifixus &c. 4. Act. 17, 31. dicitur Vir. 5. Dan. 7, 13. & 14. legitur potestas hæc data Filio hominis. 6. Ap. 5, 19. Agno occiso, 7. ei qvem videbit omnis oculus. Apoc. 1, 7.

XXXIII. Hinc Cyrillus: (a) Christus causam subjecit, qvare vitam & potestatem Judicii sibi à Patre datam dixerit, dicens, Qvia filius est, ut intelligamus, omnia sibi data esse ut homini. Unigenitus enim filius non vitæ particeps sed vita naturaliter est.

XXXIV. Examinandæ jam essent Adversariorum objectiones, sed instituti nostri ratio non patitur fusius de eis agere; unam tantùm alteramve subjiciemus. Sic solent contra Omnipotentiam argutari: Qvi est omnipotens, is alterius opem non implorat. At Christus secundùm humanam naturam Patris opem imploravit. E. Resp. 1. Dist. inter id qvod fit ἁπλῶς, & qvod fit per οἰκονομίαν. Causæ fuerunt aliæ cur Christus opem Patris imploravit. 1. missus enim erat ab ipso in mundum. 2. qvia fratribus suis per omnia fieri debebat ὅμοιος, ut tentatus fidelis esset Pontifex. Hebr. 2, 17. c. 4, 15. Phil. 2, 7. 2. Status sunt discernendi. Tempore enim Exinanitionis habuit qvidem reverâ Omnipotentiam sibi communicatam; sed κτήσει tantùm, non verò χρήσει, id enim officium redemtoris non patiebatur. Jam verò & κτήσει & χρήσει eam possidet, ut cum fiducia nobis ad ipsum pateat accessus. Hebr. 4, 16.

XXXV. Contra vim vivificandi tale afferunt argumentum: Si carni Christi communicata est vis vivificandi ex Joh. 6. seqvitur carnem descendisse de cœlo. Posterius absurdum. Ergo & prius. Resp. 1. Negatur Con. Utrumqve enim est in textu, & carnem vivificare, & Personam (Ego) descendisse de cœlo, 2. Vox descendendi hîc non notat localem motum, sed describit incarnationem, quæ neqve de λόγῳ tantùm, neqve de carne tantùm prædicatur, sed de λόγῳ carnem assumente, & carne à λόγῳ assumtâ &c.

XXXVI. Vim θαυματουργικὴν tali argumento elidere conantur, Si fimbria Christi non potest dici θαυματοποιὴ, licet sanaverit Mulierem, Luc. 8, 44. neqve carni Christi talis vis adscribi potest. Resp. 1. Blasphemum esse carnem Christi cum fimbria conferre, cur enim eodem modo non dicunt fimbriam esse vivificam? An fimbria etiam τῷ λόγῳ personaliter unita est? 2. In textu dicit Lucas vim illam (non â fimbria, sed) â Christi carne exivisse. Illi igitur, non fimbriæ, est adscribenda.

XXXVII. Contra potestatem judiciariam objici solent dicta Marc. 13, 32. & Luc. 2, 53. Quæ ad omniscientiam potius impugnandam adhibentur, reliqvimus igitur illa seqventi disputationi. Et sic nostræ sententiæ veritatem stabilivimus.

XXXVIII. Noli igitur timere vermis Jacob & qvi mortui estis ex Israël: Ego auxiliator sum tibi, inqvit Dominus & redemtor tuus Sanctus Israël. Licet enim pauper sis & ebrius non â vino: Dominator tamen tuus, qvi pugnat pro populo suo, tollet de manu tua calicem soporis, crassamentum fundi, calicem indignationis Domini, nec adjiciet, ut bibas ultra. Qvis separabit te â dilectione Christi? Qvis accusabit aut condemnabit? Deus est qvi justificat. Christus Jesus est qvi mortuus est, imò qvi resurrexit & sedet ad dextram DEI.

XXXIX. Vos verò qvi operamini iniqvitatem, qvi devoratis plebem Domini sicut escam panis; nonne hoc cognoscitis? Qvousqve fremetis & assistetis adversus Dominum & adversus Christum ejus? Qvi constitutus est Rex super montem sanctum Sion. Ipse vos conteret in virga ferrea & tanqvam vas figuli confringet. Osculamini igitur Filium ut non irascatur & pereatis in via, cum exarserit vel minimum ira ejus. Beati autem erunt, qvi ad eum se recipient, Ipsi laus honor & gloria, in seculorum secula.


## 19 Nineteenth Disputation, On the Omniscience Communicated to the Assumed Flesh

Continuation.

Blessed Luther not undeservedly called the Zwinglian exclusive (distinctive, usurped in the Church around the year of Christ 730) ἀλλοίωσιν [alteration] and the resulting Calvinistic verbal communication a mask of the Devil. (a) On account of which he also advised that no credence should be given to the Sacramentarians, although they boast that they believe the article concerning the person of Christ incorruptly and prattle much about it. (b) For this truly verbal and logical communication is a swamp and a sink of all Calvinian errors, a workshop of blasphemy, (c) by which our every remedy, which results from the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and session of Christ at the right hand of the Father against sin and all our enemies, (d) is emptied, and the sense of Scripture is perversely corrupted. For what, I ask, overturns almost the entire doctrine concerning the person of Christ? The Zwinglian ἀλλοίωσις [alteration], which dissolves the personal union, rendered personal predications synecdochical and plainly tropical, and converted the doctrine of the communication of idioms into a mere and pure λογομαχίαν [war of words], as was sufficiently seen in the preceding. And although by this diabolical torch the propositions of the first and second kind of the communication of idioms began to be obscured, nevertheless with no less effort that deadly Calvinian plague attempted to obliterate the third kind also, when it resolves these propositions: The flesh of Christ is life-giving, understand through the real communication of the life of the Son of God: Christ is omnipresent, omnipotent, to be adored with divine worship, omniscient; [it resolves them as:] The flesh of Christ effects life by reason of merit through the work of redemption; Christ's divine nature is to be adored, omniscient, omnipresent, etc. Thus, therefore, what Prosper of Aquitaine writes concerning Vincent the Pelagian, we could deservedly repeat here concerning our adversaries, who, while they accomplish nothing by attacking in general the doctrine concerning the majestic communication of infinite idioms made to the flesh of Christ, attempt to see whether they can obtain anything by attacking individual idioms in a special battle, by increasing the number of accusations against us, and by varying our sense; but how unsuccessfully, has also been seen thus far. Wherefore, since in the preceding exercises the general weapons of the adversaries against the majestic communication of infinite gifts, as well as the special ones objected against omnipotence and the life-giving power, have been repelled, this time [we address] infinite omniscience we shall refute the opposing arguments, and we shall confirm the immovable assertion of orthodox truth. That this may be done εὐτάκτως [orderly], we shall present our treatise contained in these five chapters, of which the first will propose the distinctions of manifold Science: the second will form the state of the controversy: the third will exhibit the demonstrations of our opinion: the fourth will solve the objections of the adversaries: the fifth will conclude the συζήτησιν [disputation] with a practical meditation.

Latin:

Continuatio.

ZVvinglianam ἀλλοίωσιν exclusivam (distinctivam circa annum Christi 730. in Ecclesia usurpatam admittimus) & inde resultantem communicationem verbalem Calvinisticam larvam Diaboli non immeritò appellavit B. Lutherus. (a) Ob quam etiam Sacramentariis, licet se articulum de persona Christi incorruptè credere gloriantibus & multa de eo blaterantibus, nullam fidem adhibendam suasit. (b) Nam verè verbalis hæc & Logica Communicatio lerna & sentina est omnium Calvinianorum errorum, officina blasphemiæ, (c) quâ omne remedium nostrum, quod ex incarnatione, passione, resurrectione & sessione Christi ad patris dexteram adversùs peccatum & omnes inimicos nostros resultat, (d) evacuatur, & scripturæ sensus perversè corrumpitur. Qvid enim quæso totam ferè doctrinam de persona Christi evertit? Zvvingliana ἀλλοίωσις, quæ unionem personalem solvit, prædicationes personales Synecdochicas & planè tropicas effecit, communicationis idiomatum doctrinam in meram & puram λογομαχίαν convertit, uti satis in præcedentibus visum. Etsi verò face hâc Diabolica primi & secundi Generis Communicationis idiomatum propositiones obfusari cœptæ, non minori tamen conamine eâdem tertium qvoqve Genus obliterare tentavit Sontica illa lues Calviniana, qvando propositiones has: Caro Christi est vivifica, intellige per realem vitæ filii Dei Communicationem: Christus est omnipræsens, omnipotens, divino cultu adorandus, omnisciens, resolvit; Caro Christi efficit vitam ratione meriti per opus redemptionis; Christi divina natura est adoranda, omniscía, omnipræsens &c. ita ergò qvod de Vincentio Pelagiano Prosper Aqvitanius scribit, meritò hîc de adversariis repetere possemus, qvi dum in genere doctrinam de majestatica idiomatum infinitorum Communicatione carni Christi facta, aggrediendo, nil efficiunt, Speciali pugnâ singula idiomata impugnando, numerum criminationum in nos augendo, sensumq́; nostrum variando, an aliqvid obtinere possint, tentant; quàm verò infeliciter, visum etiam hactenus; Qvare cum præcedentibus exercitiis generalia adversariorum contra majestaticam infinitorum donorum Communicationem tela, ut & specialia contra omnipotentiam, vim vivificatricem objecta, propulsata sint, hâc vice infinitam omniscientiam impugnantia diluemus, veritatisque; orthodoxæ immotam assertionem confirmabimus. Quod ut εὐτάκτως fiat, tractationem nostram hisce qvinqve capitibus inclusam dabimus, qvorum primum multiplicis Scientiæ distinctiones proponet: Secundum statum controversiæ formabit: tertium demonstrationes nostræ sententiæ exhibebit: qvartum objectiones adversariorum solvet: qvintum practicâ meditatione συζήτησιν concludet.


### Thesis I. Chap. I

Thesis I. CHAP. I.

Although the use of the little word Science is indeed so various, that if we wished to collect all its meanings, the paper would scarcely hold anything else; yet, so that our purpose may be made clearer, we shall note a few, though the principal ones, so that every handle for calumniating may be snatched away from the adversaries.

II. Philosophers and theologians from Scripture indeed use this word. Philosophers use it either accurately or less accurately; taken accurately, it is nothing other than a demonstrative habit, by which conclusions are known from necessary causes, as the Philosopher says. (a) Less accurately, it is nothing other than any knowledge whatsoever about a knowable thing; whence others have divided it into created and uncreated science, in which sense Polanus (b) says that by the former, God knows Himself wholly and totally, but by the latter, Christ knows God indeed wholly, but not totally. It is not the place here to expound how various the distinctions of this less accurate meaning of the word science are. See Tolos. (c)

III. Therefore, theologians also use the word Science from Scripture in various ways. It is used 1. absolutely, and then it denotes: 1. some bare knowledge of a thing, whether good or bad; whence Adam is rightly said to have known that disobedience toward the Creator was bad, and conversely that obedience was good. 2. A thing joined with experience: whence Gideon is said to have made the men of Succoth know their detriment, Judg. 8. v. 16. Thus Gen. 3. v. 22, the evil that followed the disobedience of the transgressed law is called Science. 3. True acknowledgment of God and right doctrine, Isaiah 11. v. 9, Jer. 3. v. 15. To which the Apostle opposes ignorance, 1 Cor. 15. v. 34, Eph. 4. v. 18, that is, a false opinion about God. 4. Knowledge of the divine law, 2 Pet. 1. v. 5, according to which life is to be prudently instituted. 5. Saving faith in Christ, which Scripture describes by fiduciary knowledge, Is. 53. v. 11.

IV. 2. It is attributed to certain things; 1. to God, and it denotes essential knowledge, by which God knows through his own essence, 1. Himself, 1. to the Corinthians 2. v. 11. (d) 2. All things in heaven and on earth 2. Chron. 16. v. 9. Job 28. v. 24. Job 11. v. 7. & 42. v. 2. 3. Present, past, and future, Heb. 4. v. 13. (e) 4. By which he knowingly and prudently governs and disposes all things, Job 15. v. 8. Ps. 35. v. 11. Isa. 40. v. 14. chap. 46. 10. (f)

V. From which it is gathered that knowledge in God is not a power, as a first act, with the second excluded, nor does it exist in God by way of a habit, but by way of a most simple and ultimate act, and therefore that divine knowledge is nothing other than his own divine essence.

VI. 2. To Angels. Which knowledge does not simply agree with the Angelic essence itself, but rather exists in it as an accident; the little word of knowledge attributed to Angels therefore denotes nothing other than that most excellent gift with which Angels are adorned by God, namely, understanding God their creator, and knowing how to judge divine works, 2. Sam. 14. v. 20. (g)

VII. 3. To Men, and it denotes nothing other than the cognition of those things which pertain both to the right use of bodily life and to eternal happiness, granted to men by God. Thus Exod. 31. v. 1. Bezalel is said to be endowed with wisdom and knowledge. Exod. 35. v. 31.

VIII. 4. It is also attributed to brute things, Isa. 1. v. 3. and to inanimate things, Gen. 2. v. 9. & 17. To which we do not add further meanings. (h)

IX. These things being thus foreknown and as it were removed from our scope, we must now arrive at that meaning of the word Knowledge which we make proper to this place. Where, in the beginning, the deception of Gregory of Valencia must be uncovered, who discourses at length about the communicated knowledge of Christ, and does not even touch upon the scope of our orthodox opinion. (i)

X. For when we inquire about the knowledge communicated to the human nature of Christ, by Knowledge in this place we intend the very wisdom of God, uncreated, infinite, and knowing all things, by which God perfectly knows and has explored, in one intuition, both himself and all other creatures in heaven, earth, sea, and hell, past, present, and future things.

XI. Whence it is easy to gather what the state of the controversy is here, and therefore about what matter we are disputing in this place against our adversaries; therefore let it be duly and rightly established and set forth here.

Latin:

Thesis I. CAP. I.

ETsi verò tàm varius sit voculæ Scientia usus, ita ut si omnes ejus significationes colligere vellemus, præter eas vix aliqvid charta caperet; ut propositum nostrum tamen eò fiat clarius, paucas, præcipuas tamen, ut omnis ansa calumniandi eripiatur adversariis, annotabimus.

II. Utuntur verò voce hac & Philosophi & ex Scripturâ Theologi. Philosophi vel accuratè vel minùs accuratè; Accuratè sumpta nihil aliud est, qvàm habitus demonstrativus, qvo cognoscuntur conclusiones ex necessariis causis, dicente Philosopho. (a) Minùs accuratè nihil aliud est qvàm notitia qvævis de re scibili; Unde alii in creatam & increatam scientiam divisêre, qvo sensu Polanus (b) illâ, Se totum & totaliter Deum agnoscere, hâc Christum cognoscere qvidem Deum totum, sed non totaliter, ait. Minùs accuratæ hujus significationis vocabuli scientiæ qvàm variæ sint distinctiones hujus loci non est exponere. Vide Tolos. (c)

III. Scientiæ vocabulo ergò utuntur etiam Theologi ex scriptura variè. Usurpatur 1. absolutè, & tùm denotat: 1. nudam aliqvam notitiam rei sive bonæ sive malæ; unde Adam rectè dicitur scivisse inobedientiam erga creatorem esse malam, obedientiam contrà bonam. 2. Rem cum experimento conjunctam: unde Gedeon viros Suchoth scire fecisse dicitur detrimentum eorum Judic. 8. v. 16. Sic Gen. 3. v. 22. malum inobedientiam transgressæ legis secutum, Scientia dicitur. 3. Veram Dei agnitionem & doctrinam rectam Esaie 11. v. 9. Jer 3. v. 15. Cui opponit Apostolus ignorantiam 1. ad Cor. 15. v. 24. ad Eph. 4. v. 18. id est, falsam de Deo opinionem. 4. Legis divinæ cognitionem. 2. Pet. 1. v. 5. juxta qvam vita prudenter instituenda. 5. Salvificam in Christum fidem, qvam notitiâ fiduciali scriptura describit Es. 53. v. 11.

IV. 2. Certis attribuitur rebus; 1. Deo, notatqve scientiam essentialem, quâ Deus per effentiam suam scit, 1. Seipsum, 1. ad Corinth. 2. v. 11. (d) 2. Omnia in cælo & in terra 2. Par. 16. v. 9. Job. 28. v. 24. Job. 11. v. 7. & 42. v. 2. 3. Præsentia præterita & futura, Hebr. 4. v. 13. (e) 4. Quâ omnia scienter & prudenter gubernat & disponit, Jobi 15. v. 8. Ps. 35. v. 11. Esa. 40. v. 14. cap. 46. 10. (f)

V. Unde colligitur, scientiam in Deo esse non potentiam, tanquam actum primum, secundo excluso, nec inesse Deo per modum habitus, sed per modum actus simplicissimi & ultimi, adeóq; scientiam divinam nil aliud esse, quàm essentiam ipsius divinam.

VI. 2. Angelis. Quæ scientia non simpliciter convenit cum ipsâ essentia Angelica, sed potius inest ei ut accidens; notat igitur vocula scientiæ Angelis attributa, nil aliud, quàm donum illud præstantissimum, quo Angeli sunt ornati à Deo, intelligentes scilicet Deum creatorem suum, & scientes opera divina dijudicare, 2. Sam. 14. v. 20. (g)

VII. 3. Hominibus, notatq; nihil aliud quàm cognitionem earum rerum, quæ tum ad rectum vitæ corporalis usum, tùm ad æternam felicitatem pertinent, hominibus â Deo concessam. Sic Exod. 31. v. 1. Besaleel sapientiâ & scientiâ præditus dicitur. Exod. 35. v. 31.

VIII. 4. Rebus brutis quoq; tribuitur Esa. 1. v. 3. & inanimatis, Gen. 2. v. 9. & 17. Quibus plures fignificationes non addimus. (h)

IX. Hisce ita præcognitis & quasi â scopo nostro remotis, deveniendum jam est ad eam vocis Scientiæ significationem, quam hujus loci propriam facimus. Ubi principiò detegendus fucus Gregorii de Valentia prolixè de communicata scientia Christi disputantis, & ne scopum quidem nostræ sententiæ orthodoxæ attingentis. (i)

X. Qvando enim de communicata humanæ Christi naturæ Scientiæ quærimus, per Scientiam hoc loco ipsam sapientiam Dei increatam, infinitam & omnia cognoscentem, quâ Deus tam se quàm omnes alias creaturas in cælo, terra, mari & inferno, præteritas, præsentes & futuras res, uno intuitu perfectè cognoscit & exploratas habet, intellectam volumus.

XI. Unde facilè colligere licet, hîc quis status controversiæ sit, adeoq; quâ de re loco hoc contra adversarios disputemus; is ergò ritè & rectè constitutus & informatus hic esto.


### XII. Which-

XII. WhichXII. The question is: Whether uncreated and infinite omniscience is really communicated to the human nature of Christ along with the remaining divine attributes, and whether, on account of this communication having been made in the closest union of the two natures in Christ, the human nature of Christ is to be called, and in reality also is, omniscient? This state of the question being thus duly and correctly informed, it is plain to anyone at a glance: 1. that we are not here speaking of any innate and concreated knowledge; such as, since it is given in all men, we cannot deny the same to Christ also. 2. Nor of habitual knowledge, inherent in Christ as an adjunct, by which we concede that Christ surpassed even all the angels, and urge this against those who deny it. 3. Nor of infused knowledge, by which we believe Christ was adorned even above all the prophets and saints; but of knowledge, as has been said, uncreated, immense, and proper to God alone.

XIII. How fraudulently Paraeus deals with us is clear from this, when against his own conscience he corrupts this state of the question by asking: Whether the personal union makes a real communication of infinite idioms in the abstract or in the natures, or indeed only in the concrete? The former of which he says the Lutherans defend: Therefore, that we may have regard for the reason of our present undertaking, who, I ask, of our side ever taught that the flesh of CHRIST is omniscience, or omnipresence, or omnipotence in the abstract? Or are the phrases of Paraeus the same when I say, the flesh of CHRIST is omniscient, and the flesh of CHRIST is omniscience? We therefore reject the abstractive mode of speech, yet in such a way:

XIV. 1. That we add that not every respect of the abstract is simply excluded from these propositions; for as our theologians rightly warn, in this enunciation: The flesh of CHRIST is omniscient, some respect of the abstract is altogether held, since the notation of the subject denotes the nature in CHRIST, namely the human, but not the whole ὑφιςάμενον. 2. That we also warn of this, that this predicate of omniscience is by no means attributed to the subject in the Calvinistic sense abstractively, and thus is not predicated of the human nature alone and subsisting separately, sequestered and divided from the person; for if that were done, omniscience would not have been communicated to the flesh, but would be the omniscience of the flesh by nature. Whence we conclude, since abstraction denotes essential possession, it excludes the mode of abstractive predication. And finally 3. also, that we may plainly reject this mode of speaking, which Schonfeldius uses, asking: Whether omniscience with the remaining infinite mighty works is communicated to Christ as man in himself or into himself? shows that a μετάβασιν and a physical transfusion of properties of the divine nature into the human as a subject of inherence is introduced.

XV. We therefore proceed to demonstrate our thesis thus: I. Whoever has received the Spirit of wisdom, of fortitude, of knowledge, and of understanding, 1. Without any measure. 2. Above all men and Angels, he is endowed with infinite knowledge. Christ as man received the Spirit of wisdom, of fortitude, of knowledge, and of understanding, Is. 11. v. 1. & 2. without measure, John 3. v. 34. above all men and Angels, Ps. 45, 8. Heb. 1. 10. (a) Therefore. The consequence and firmness of the major premise rests upon these foundations: 1. Because where every measure is excluded, there is mere infinity; for the opposition ought to be made according to the same, whence it is gathered that the negation of measure, by which it is said, not according to measure, is opposed to the affirmation concerning measure; as therefore the measurable is finite, so the immeasurable is infinite. (l) 2. Because a manifest distinction proves it. for as the remaining saints and Angels are indeed anointed with the Holy Spirit, but with measure, so this one above the rest without measure: As therefore that communication presupposes finite gifts, so this one presupposes infinite ones.

XVI. 2. He in whom all the treasures of wisdom, knowledge, and cognition of the whole Deity are hidden, he infinitely knows and understands all things: But in the human nature of Christ the treasures of the whole Deity of cognition and knowledge are hidden, Coloss. 2. v. 3. Therefore. The major premise is evident from this: 1. because the knowledge of the Deity is infinite, for God knows all things infinitely. As therefore God knows all things through His infinite knowledge, so Christ as man knows all things through the same communicated knowledge. 2. Because the particle of universality includes all knowledge. Therefore also infinite knowledge. The minor premise is made manifest from the text, for it is evident from there that the discourse is concerning Christ as man: 1. For concerning whom he says v. 9. ἐν αὐτῷ κατοικεῖ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος σωματικῶς; concerning the same he said v. 3. ἐν ᾧ εἰσι πάντες οἱ θησαυροὶ τῆς σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως ἀπόκρυφοι. But he spoke first concerning Christ as man. Therefore also the latter. 2. Because the Apostle expressly distinguishes between that which is hidden, and that in which it is hidden. Now just as that which is hidden is the Deity, so that in which the Deity is hidden is the humanity. Whence Epiphanius in the Ancoratus calls the same σκεῦος δοχεῖον of divine fullness. These foundations overturn all the φλυαρίας of Beza (m) as well as of Sohnius, (n) who responds to the Major of the Argument: 1. since Paul affirms of the whole person that the fullness of the Deity dwells in it. 2. That the Apostle is speaking of human Wisdom: for besides the fact that the latter pretext is manifestly false and implies a manifest contradiction, the former also stands in no way against our argument, since it is not denied that the discourse here is about the person, but it is asked, according to which nature is the statement of the Apostle attributed to the person? Which, since it is not done according to the divine, as has been shown, it remains that it is according to the human.

XVII. 3. Whoever is a καρδιογνώστης, knows all things by his own αὐτοψίᾳ, predicts future things by his own power, and has the state of all creatures known, he is endowed with infinite knowledge: But Christ is a καρδιογνώστης, (o) knows all things, (p) predicts future things, (q) has the state of all creatures known, as is clear from the alleged passages. Therefore. Here again vanishes the petulance of Sohnius in the aforementioned place, denying that the Major is simply true, since there is a universality of things, which although they may be infinite with respect to us, yet their finiteness with respect to God can in no way be denied; for besides the fact that he confuses cognizable things in this instance, which although we may grant them to be finite, with the knowing Science, which we establish as infinite in every way, he also begs the question, while he attributes to God the finiteness of all things as their knowledge falls into God, which is denied, since God knows all things just as He possesses them, infinitely. Then also of him denying the Minor, and contending that the discourse in these places is not about nature, but about the person, to whom let it suffice to have responded with what was said above.

XVIII. 4. He to whom judgment over all men has been committed, in which he ought to hear the prayers of the faithful, to help them, and to render to each one according to his works, is omniscient and endowed with infinite knowledge: To Christ as man has been committed judgment over all men, (r) that in it he might hear the prayers of the faithful, (s) and help them (t) and sympathize with them (u) nay, render to each one according to his works; (x) Therefore. (x) Therefore. The major premise is evident: for it is necessary that he who ought to judge all, should hear prayers, so that he may have all the most profound and hidden things known and perceived, since A. 1. Cor. 4. v. 5. testifies that in this judgment even the hidden things of darkness are to be judged. The things which Shonius barks against this argument are not worthy to be set down, since they can most easily be judged from what has been said. Thus far, therefore, the foundations of the scriptures.

XIX. To these now succeeds, secondly, the orthodox consensus of pious Antiquity, of which we shall recite only the principal testimonies, among which not undeservedly. 1. We cite the words of Theophylact: (y) We all others have received the operation of the Spirit by measure, but to Christ himself the Father did not give the Spirit by measure, one or two mighty works; but he has the Spirit himself entire, therefore God also gave his Spirit to the Prophets, i.e., the operation of the Spirit, yet by measure. Damascene: (z) Human nature does not substantially possess the knowledge of future things, but the soul of the Lord, because of its union with the Word of God, has become rich or enriched, with the remaining signs, so also with the knowledge of future things; we say therefore that our Lord Jesus, God and man, knows all things, since in him are all the treasures of wisdom and divinity. (a) XX. Finally, we demonstrate our opinion with reasons, of which; 1. To whomever the person of the Son of God has been communicated, to him the properties have been communicated: But the Person of the Son of God himself has been communicated to human nature by personal union. Therefore, and consequently, omniscience also. The premises are established from the preceding exercises. 2. Whatever gift has been communicated to Christ in time, that has been communicated either to the divine or to the human nature: not to the divine, since it possesses all things from eternity through eternal generation from the Father. (b) He who thinks otherwise, let him see by what reasoning he wishes to extricate himself from the nets of the Photinians, since they contend that the Word received the Spirit of fortitude and wisdom from the Father: Therefore according to the human. Where certainly this trustworthy rule is observed: Whatever things have been given to Christ in time, they are referred not to the divine but to the human nature. XXI. 3. According to which nature Christ was anointed with the Holy Spirit, according to that he was also made omniscient: But Christ was anointed with the Holy Spirit according to his human nature. Therefore. The major premise is established from the preceding. The minor depends on the orthodox rule of Antiquity: Anointing pertains to humanity. See Damascenus, who discourses learnedly against the ravings of Origen, following Gregory and Cyril. (c)

XXII. 4. If omniscience is not really communicated to the flesh of Christ, it follows: 1. That the divine nature can be communicated without its ἰδιώμασι (idioms/properties). The latter is absurd, therefore the former. 2. That at the time of the final judgment, it cannot undergo the universal judgment of all flesh; for judgment presupposes knowledge of the same. The latter is false; therefore the former is also. 3. That it does not fulfill the office of Mediator in the assumed flesh: the reason is that, according to it, it is ignorant of our infirmities and miseries; if this is so, it cannot intercede for them before the Father, nor carry our prayers to the Father. But indeed all these things are absurd; therefore.

XXIII. Therefore, with these immovable and irrefutable testimonies of both Holy Scripture and the orthodox Fathers, and with firm consequences, the invincible divine truth stands, by which it is asserted that the human nature of CHRIST has truly and really arrived at the κοινωνίαν (communion) of the infinite omniscience of the Λόγος (Word), and just as the Λόγος is omniscient essentially and by nature; so the human nature is omniscient, not indeed naturally, but personally from the union with the omniscient Λόγος; we do not, therefore, make the flesh omniscient considered ἰδικῶς (specifically) and separately. (d)

Latin:

XII. QuæXII. Quæritur: An omniscientia increata & infinita cum reliquis attributis divinis realiter humanæ Christi naturæ sit communicata, & an ob factam communicationem hanc in unione arctissima duarum in Christo naturarum, humana Christi natura dicenda, & reverà etiam sit omniscia? Quo statu sic ritè & rectè informato, cuilibet ad oculum patet: 1. non nobis hîc sermonem esse de scientia aliqva innata & concreata; qualis cùm in omnibus detur hominibus, Christo quoq; eandem demere non possumus. 2. Nec de scientia habituali, Christo tanquam adjunctum inhærente, qvâ Christum etiam omnes Angelos superasse concedimus & contra negantes urgemus. 3. Nec de scientia infusa, qvâ etiam præ omnibus Prophetis & sanctis ornatum fuisse Christum omninò sentimus; Sed de Scientia, ut dictum, increatâ, immensa & soli Deo propria.

XIII. Quam fraudulenter nobiscum agat Paræus, (k) hinc liquet, qvando contra propriam conscientiam ita statum hunc corrumpit, qværendo: An unio personalis faciat idiomatum infinitorum communicationem realem in abstracto seu in naturis, an verò tantum in concreto? qvorum prius Lutheranos defendere ait: Ut ergò præsentis instituti nostri rationem habeamus, qvis qvæso unqvam nostratium docuit, Carnem CHRISTI esse omniscientiam, vel omnipræsentiam, vel omnipotentiam in abstracto? anne verò phrases Paræi sunt eædem, qvando dico, Caro CHRISTI est omniscia, & Caro CHRISTI est omniscientia? Abstractivam ergò locutionem rejicimus, ita tamen:

XIV. 1. Ut addamus, non omnem simpliciter abstracti respectum hisce propositionibus excludi; nam ut rectè nostrates Theologi monent, in hac Enunciatione: Caro CHRISTI est omniscia, omninò aliqvem abstracti respectum haberi, cum subjecti notatio denotet naturam in CHRISTO, humanam scilicet, non verò totum ὑφιςάμενον. 2. Ut & hoc moneamus, prædicatum hoc Omniscientiæ, neqvaqvam sensu Calvinistico attribui subjecto abstractivè, adeoqve de humana natura sola & seorsim subsistente, á persona seqvestrata & divisa prædicari; id enim si fieret, Omniscientia carni non esset communicata, sed esset omniscientia carnis ex natura. Unde concludimus, cùm abstractio possessionem essentialem denotet, communicationem prædicationis abstractivæ modum excludere. Et tandem 3. ctiam, ut planè rejiciamus hunc loqvendi modum, qvo utitur Schonfeldius, qværens; An omniscientia cum reliqvis infinitis virtutibus Christo quà homini in sese vel in ipsemet sit communicata? qvâ formulâ μετάβασιν & Physicam proprietatum transfusionem naturæ divinæ in humanam ceu subjectum inhæsionis introduci, ostendit eruditè Clariss. Winckelmannus, disp. 3. Tom. 2. Giss. th. 25. 26.

XV. Thesin ergò nostram ita demonstrare pergimus: I. Quicunq; accepit Spiritum sapientiæ, fortitudinis, scientiæ & intellectus, 1. Sine omni mensura. 2. Præ omnibus hominibus & Angelis, ille præditus est scientiâ infinitâ. Christus homo accepit Spiritum sapientiæ, fortitudinis, scientiæ & intellectus Es. 11. v. 1. & 2. sine mensura, Joh. 3. v. 34. præ omnibus hominibus & Angelis, Ps. 45, 8. Hebr. 1. 10. (a) Ergo. Majoris consecutio & firmitas nititur hisce fundamentis: 1. Qvia ubi omnis excluditur mensura, ibi mera est infinitas, Oppositio enim fieri debet secundùm idem, unde colligitur, negationem mensuræ, qvâ dicitur, non juxta mensuram, opponi affirmationi de mensura; Ut ergò mensurabile est finitum, ita immensurabile est infinitum. (l) 2. Qvia manifesta distinctio eam comprobat. ut enim reliqvi sancti & Angeli spiritu qvidem sancto uncti, sed cum mensura, ita hic præ reliqvis sine mensura: Sicut ergò Communicatio illa præsupponit dona finita, ita hæc infinita.

XVI. 2. In quo omnes thesauri sapientiæ, scientiæ & cognitionis totius Deitatis absconditi, ille infinitè scit novitq; omnia: Atqui in humana natura totius Deitatis thesauri cognitionis & scientiæ sunt absconditi, Coloss. 2. v. 3. Ergò. Major inde patet: 1. qvia Deitatis Scientia est infinita, infinitè enim Deus omnia novit. Sicut ergò Deus per infinitam suam scientiam omnia novit, ita homo Christus per eandem communicatam omnia novit. 2. Qvia universalitatis particula omnem scientiam includit. Ergò & infinitam. Minor fit manifesta ex textu, ibi enim de Christo homine sermonem esse inde constat: 1. De qvo enim dicit v. 9. ἐν αὐτῷ κατοικεῖ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος σωματικῶς; De eodem dixit v. 3. ἐν ᾧ εἰσι πάντες οἱ θησαυροὶ τῆς σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως ἀπόκρυφοι. Atqvi prius dixit de homine Christo. E. & posterius. 2. Qvia expressè Apostolus discernit inter id qvod absconditum est, & id, in quo absconditum est. Jam sicut id, quod absconditum, Deitas; ita id in quo abscondita Deitas, est humanitas. Unde eandem divinæ plenitudinis σκεῦος δοχεῖον Epiphanius in Ancorato nominat. Quæ fundamenta evertunt omnes φλυαρίας Bezæ (m) ut & Sohnii, (n) ad Argumenti Majorem respondentis: 1. Malè in ea transitum fieri à persona ad naturam, cum Paulus de tota persona affirmet, in ea plenitudinem Deitatis habitare. 2. Apostolum de Sapientia humana loqui: præterquam enim quod posterior prætextus manifesto falsus contradictionem manifestam implicet, prior etiam nostro argumento nil obstat, cum non negetur de persona sermonem hic esse, sed quæratur, secundùm quam naturam effatum Apostoli personæ attribuatur? quod cum non fiat secundùm divinam, ut ostensum est; relinquitur, quod secundùm humanam.

XVII. 3. Quicunque est καρδιογνώστης, propriâ αὐτοψίᾳ omnia pernoscit, propriâ virtute futura prædicit, omnium creaturarum statum cognitum habet, is infinitâ scientiâ præditus est: Atqui Christus est καρδιογνώστης, (o) Omnia pernoscit, (p) futura prædicit, (q) omnium creaturarum statum cognitum habet, ut ex allegatis locis patet. Ergò. Evanescit hic iterum petulantia Sohnii d. l. Majorem simpliciter veram esse negantis, cum universalitas sit rerum, quæ licet nostri respectu infinitæ sint, finitatem tamen ipsis respectu Dei nullâ ratione derogari posse; Præterquam enim quod confundat res cognoscibiles hâc instantiâ, quas licet finitas concedamus, cum Scientia cognoscente, quam omnimodò infinitam statuimus, principium quoq; petit, dum omnium rerum, prout earum notitia in Deum cadit, finitatem Deo attribuit, quod negatur, cum Deus ut infinitè omnia habet, ita cognoscat. Deinde & Minorem negantis, & non de natura, sed persona hisce in locis sermonem esse contendentis, cui quod superius dictum, respondisse sufficiat.

XVIII. 4. Cui traditum est judicium in omnes homines, in quo fidelium preces audire, ipsis opitulari, & unicuique secundùm opera sua reddere debet, is est omniscius, & infinitâ scientiâ præditus: Christo ut homini traditum est judicium in omnes homines, (r) ut in eo fidelium preces audiret, (s) ipsisq; opitularetur (t) & compateretur (u) imò unicuique secundùm opera retribueret; (x) Ergò. (x) Ergo. Major patet : omnes enim qui judicare debet, preces exaudire ei necesse est, ut profundissima & abditissima quæque cognita & perspecta habeat, cùm A. 1. Cor. 4. v. 5. testatur, in hoc judicio etiam tenebrarum occulta sint dijudicanda. Quæ contra hoc argumentum obgannit Shonius, digna non sunt ut apponantur, cum facilimè ex dictis dijudicari queant. Hactenus ergò scripturæ fundamenta.

XIX. Qvibus jam succedit secundò orthodoxus piæ Antiqvitatis consensus, cujus præcipua tantùm recitabimus testimonia, inter quæ non immeritò. 1. Citamus verba Theophylacti : (y) Nos alii omnes ad mensuram accepimus operationem Spiritus, ipsi autem Christo Pater Spiritum non ad mensuram dedit, unam vel duas virtutes; sed ipsum Spiritum integrum habet, igitur & Prophetis Deus dedit suum Spiritum, h. e. operationem Spiritus, tamen ad mensuram. Damascenus : (z) Humana natura substantialiter non obtinet futurarum cognitionem, Domini autem anima propter ipsius ad Dei verbum unionem dives facta sive locuplet a est, cum reliquis signis, ita et iam futurorum cognitione, dicimus igitur Dominum nostrum Jesum, Deum & hominem omnia scire, cum in ipso omnes sint thesauri sapientiæ & divinitatis. (a) XX. Tandem rationibus nostram sententiam demonstramus, quarum ; 1. Cuicunq; communicata est persona filii Dei, ei idiomata sunt communicata : Atqui humanæ naturæ communicata est personali unione ipsa Persona Filii Dei. E. & per consequens etiam omniscentia. Præmissæ ex superioribus constant exercitiis. 2. Quodcunq; donum Christo est communicatum in tempore, id communicatum est vel naturæ divinæ vel humanæ: non divinæ, cùm ea ab æterno per æternam generationem à patre omnia possideat. (b) Secus qui sentit, videat quâ ratione se à retibus Photinianorum extricare velit, cum ipsi contendant λόγον Spiritum fortitudinis & sapientiæ à Patre accepisse: Ergò secundum humanam. Ubi certè observatur regula hæc ἀξιόπιστος: Quæcunqve Christo in tempore data sunt, non ad divinam sed humanam naturam referuntur. XXI. 3. Secundùm quam naturam Christus unctus est Spiritu sancto, secundùm eam quoq; factus est omnisciens: Atqui Christus secundùm humanam naturam unctus est S. S. Ergò. Major ex præcedentibus constat. Minor ex Antiqvitatis regula orthodoxa dependet : Unctio pertinet adhumanitatem. Vide contra deliramenta Origenis ex Gregorio & Cyrillo eruditè differentem Damascenum. (c)

XXII. 4. Si cari Christi realiter non est communicata omniscientia, sequitur: 1. naturam divinam posse communicari absque suis ἰδιώμασι. Absurdum posterius, ergo prius. 2. Tempore novissimi judicii non posse eandem judicium universale omnis carnis obire; Causa enim dijudicatio præsupponit ejusdem notitiam. Falsum posterius; Ergo & prius. 3. Non perficere in assumpta carne officium Mediatoris: ratio, quia juxta eam nostras ignorat infirmitates & miserias; Si hoc, pro iisdem apud Patrem intercedere non potest, nec preces nostras ad Patrem deferre. At vero absurda hæc omnia; Ergò.

XXIII. Hisce ergò immotis & irrefutabilibus, tùm sacræ scripturæ tùm orthodoxorum Patrum testimoniis firmisq́; consequentiis, invicta divina perstat veritas, quâ asseritur naturam CHRISTI humanam verè ac realiter in κοινωνίαν infinitæ omniscientiæ τοῦ λόγου pervenisse, & sicut Λόγον omniscium essentialiter & per naturam; ita humanam naturam omniscientiam non quidem naturaliter, sed personaliter ex unione cum Λόγῳ omniscio esse; non ergò carnem ἰδικῶς & seorsim consideratam omnisciam facimus. (d)


### Chapter IV. XXIV. And although this evident demonstration could suffice for all,…

CHAPTER IV.

XXIV. And although this evident demonstration could suffice for all, nevertheless this attribute, no less than the others communicated to the flesh of Christ, is forced to suffer the hostile incursion of adversaries; I will say nothing now of Vorstius, who attributes discursive knowledge to God, (e) or the Photinians, who take away from God the foreknowledge of future evils, (f) but who steal this divine attribute even from Christ, along with his entire eternal Deity; my mind is set only to weigh the dispute which the sworn associates of Calvin and the adjuncts of the Melanchthonian school stir up against us. For they, reviving the error of the Agnoëtae (whose leader and chief was Themistius, otherwise an acute paraphrast of Aristotle) (g) which was long ago condemned in the Church, indeed acknowledge that God the Word knows all things, but strenuously deny that the assumed humanity does the same; whose words, if the narrowness of the page allowed, we could cite. See Sadeel (h), Sohnius (i), Danaeus (k), Polanus (l), Zanchius (m). But indeed let us subjoin their principal arguments.

XXV. They object to the passage in Mark 13, verse 32, with which chapter 24 of Matthew, verse 36, agrees. The argument would be such: Whoever is ignorant of the day of judgment, he is not omniscient. But. Therefore. Resp. Setting aside those things by which the Fathers variously respond to the Objection of the Arians; (n) some of whom wrote that the later words (as neither the Son of man) were inserted by the Arians, so that the divinity of the Son of God might be more easily destroyed: Others kept saying that the Son was indeed ignorant, because he had not yet experienced that day: Others interpreted these words: neither does the Son of man know, unless the Father knows, but now the Father knows, Therefore also the Son of man. But setting aside, as has been said, these things, I respond 1. A fallacy secundum quid is committed in the argument, for Christ says he is ignorant of the day of judgment, not that he is ignorant absolutely, but as man, that is, by natural act, whence arises this sense: The Son of man is ignorant of the day of judgment as he is man; but the Son of man was not a mere man, therefore he did not say that he was ignorant of the day of judgment simply, but by this reason and by this title, namely of man, he truly said he did not know it.

XXVI. Nor does it stand in the way that in Matthew 24, v. 32, only the Father is said to know; for the particle Only in this place is not opposed to the persons of the divinity, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit remaining within the indivisible ὐσίαν [essence] of the Deity, but to angels and men constituted outside of it; just as the Father is often said to be the only one to be invoked, with the remaining persons included. How Zanchius agrees with us in this explanation, see book 3 de tribus Elohim ch. 9, p. 474, vol. 1 of his works.

XXVII. 2. The States are confused: whence arises the fallacy of many questions: we concede that Christ in the state of humiliation was ignorant of many things which he knows most perfectly in the state of majesty; nor is the communication of idioms made from the very beginning of the union taken away by this agreement in any way; for although through it he always possessed divine omniscience, he did not wish to use it, having hidden it for a time: he possessed it therefore not by reason of χρήσεως [use] but of κτήσεως [possession], in which way we concede that Christ was truly ignorant of many things. Whence 3. it is clear that the first and second act are confused in the argument. 4. It is evident that the adversaries are contrary to themselves in this argument, since Trelcatius, Shonius, Junius, Aretius, etc., admit our explanation of this saying. 5. Let them see what Athanasius, (o) Ambrose, (p) Vigilius, (q) and other Orthodox Fathers of all antiquity answer them.

…XXVIII. 2. Arg. (r) Opposites cannot consist together; Omniscience and ignorance are opposites, Therefore. R. They cannot consist together in the same way, for opposites are considered according to the same respect. 2. The same time: Now, indeed, both by time and by different respect, ignorance and knowledge belong to Christ. Ignorance: 1. in respect of the natural act. 2. in respect of the state of humiliation. Knowledge, in respect of the personal act. 2. Of majesty.

XXIX. 3. To grow in wisdom and knowledge is not to be omniscient: Christ grew in wisdom and knowledge, Luke 2, v. 40. Therefore. R. 1. Subordinate things do not conflict, nor do they mutually cancel each other out: for habitual and infinite or divine wisdom are subordinate: Therefore. That they are subordinate, however, is evident from the fact that Christ was endowed with a perfect rational soul, which is never without this natural knowledge; for just as all natural things in Christ were whole and perfect, indeed far more perfect than in Adam himself, so no imperfection can be attributed to the mind or soul of Christ. Furthermore, that the same [soul] was truly made a partaker of the whole divinity of the Son of God, and therefore of all his attributes; now, unless you wish to posit two contrary acts in Christ at the same time, you are compelled to concede that they are subordinate to one another; see what Damascenus wrote on this opinion.

(t) Therefore, with the Reverend, most illustrious, and excellent Lord Hutter, our teacher of pious memory, to be honored eternally, we say that Christ grew in wisdom in a twofold way: 1. by reason of habitual wisdom. 2. By reason of communicated knowledge, not that the former can be varied, but that the child Jesus grew in that wisdom and λόγῳ by reason of the second act and its exercise.

XXX. 4. Argument. To whom a property is attributed, to the same the essence is attributed: Omniscience is attributed to the flesh, therefore also the essence, and consequently the flesh will be God. R. The consequence is fallacious: 1. Because the properties of united and separated subjects are confused. Thus, therefore, the true major premise is: Of different subjects, whose properties are the same, the substance or essence will also be the same; now I deny the minor premise: for they are not two separated subjects, but united by a most intimate union between themselves, from which that communication arises; just as, therefore, I would conclude ridiculously: To whom a property belongs, to him also the essence belongs: the property of fire belongs to iron. Therefore iron is fire. So I would not conclude any better here. 2. If the communication of the property were to happen quidditatively and essentially, I would concede it: but this does not happen, for the flesh does not become an omniscient God, or omniscience, but it becomes omniscient. Therefore there is no force in the argument.

XXXI.
