We could add more arguments of the adversaries here, were it not that the narrowness of the pages prevents it; we therefore wish them reserved for the conflict, and with Epiphanius we thus finish this fourth chapter, saying: (u) The humanity is united to the divinity, and in it most perfectly knows all things, inasmuch as it is united to God. XXXII. Therefore let this meditation excite devotion in us: Behold, for Christ is omniscient, let us therefore venerate him; he knows our afflictions, and our misery is not hidden before him, wherefore he will not leave prayers in vain, but will hear them at an opportune time: Therefore, faithful soul, trust in him, and do not despair; although he may delay, coming he will come, he will deliver you, and will answer your vows. So be it, so be it.

Latin:

CAP. IV.

XXIV. Etsi verò evidens hæc demonstratio omnibus sufficere posset, non minus tamen & hoc attributum quàm cætera carni Christi communicata hostilem adversariorum incursum pati cogitur; nil jam de Vorstio dicam, scientiam discursivam Deo affingente, (e) vel Photinianis, præscientiã futurorum malorum Deo adimentibus, (f) Christo verò cum æterna tota Deitate, hoc etiam divinum attributum furantibus; litem tantùm quam Calvi Socii jurati & Scholæ Melanchtonianæ Adjuncti nobis movent, perpendere, fert animus. Illi enim Agnoëtarum (quorum Dux & Coryphæus Themistius, acutus alioqvi Aristotelis paraphrastes) (g) reducentes errorem jam olim in Ecclesia damnatum, Deum quidem verbum omnia nosse, assumtam verò humanitatem item strenuè negant; quorum verba, si angustia chartæ pateretur, adducere possemus. Videatur Sadeel (h) Sohnius (i) Danæus (k) Polanus (l) Zanchius (m). At verò argumenta eorum præcipua subnectamus.

XXV. Objiciunt locum Marc. 13. vers. 32. cum qvo concordat cap. 24. Matth. v. 36. Argumentum esset tale: Quicunque ignorat diem diem judicii, is non est omnisciens. Atqui. Ergò. Resp. Missis his quibus ad Objectionem Arrianorum variè respondere Patres; (n) quorum quidam verba posteriora (ut nec Filius hominis) ab Arrianis inserta, quò facilius divinitas filii Dei destrueretur, scripserunt: Alii, ignorasse quidem filium, quod diem eum nondum expertum haberet, dictitarunt: Alii, nec filius hominis scit, nisi pater sciat, jam verò pater scit, Ergò & filius hominis; hæc verba interpretati sunt. Verùm missis, ut dictum, his, resp. 1. Committi in argumento fallaciam secundùm quid, Christus n. dicit se ignorare diem judicii, non quod planè, sed quà homo ignoret, hoc est, actu naturali, unde oritur hic sensus: Filius hominis ignorat diem judicii quà homo est; at filius hominis nudus homo non erat, igitur non simpliciter se diem judicii ignorare, sed hâc ratione & hoc titulo, hominis scilicet, verè eundem nescire dixit.

XXVI. Nec obstat quod Matth. 24. v. 32. Solus Pater dicatur scire; est enim particula Solus hoc loco non opposita personis divinitatis Filii scilicet & S. S. intra indivisibilem ὐσίαν Deitatis permanentibus, sed Angelis & hominibus extra eam constitutis; quomodo Solus Pater dicitur sæpius invocandus, personis reliquis inclusis. Quomodo nobiscum in hac explicatione consentiat Zanchius, vide lib. 3. de tribus Elohim c. 9. p. 474. tom. 1. op.

XXVII. 2. Confundi Status: unde plurium quæst. oritur fallacia: multa Christum in statu exanitionis ignorasse concedimus, quæ in statu majestatis perfectissimè cognoscit; neque communicatio idiomatum ab ipso unionis principio facta hoc pacto ullâ ratione tollitur; etsi enim per eam divinam omniscientiam semper possedit, occultatam tamen ad tempus usurpare noluit: possedit ergò non ratione χρήσεως sed κτήσεως, quomodo multa verè ignorasse Christum concedimus. Unde 3. patet, confundi in argumento actum primum & secundum 4. Constat, sibi ipsis hoc argumento adversarios esse contrarios, cum nostram hujus dicti explicationem admittant, Trelcatius, Shonius, Junius, Aretius &c. 5. Videant, quid respondeat ipsis Athanasius, (o) Ambrosius, (p) Vigilius, (q) & alii Patres Orthodoxi totius antiquitatis.

XXVIII. 2. Arg. (r) Opposita consistere nequeunt; Omniscientia & ignorantia sunt opposita, Ergo. R. non possunt consistere eodem modo, considerantur enim opposita secundùm eundem respectum. 2. Idem tempus: Jam verò & tempore & respectu diverso competit Christo ignorantia & scientia. Ignorantia: 1. respectu actus naturalis. 2. respectu status exinanitionis. Scientia, respectu actus personalis. 2. Majestatis.

XXIX. 3. Sapientiâ & scientiâ crescere non est omniscientem esse: Christus crevit sapientiâ & scientiâ, Luc. 2. v. 40. Ergò. R. 1. Subordinata non pugnant, nec se invicem tollunt: Sapientia n. habitualis & infinita seu divina sunt subordinata: Ergo. Subordinata autem esse, inde patet, quod Christus perfectâ fuerit præditus animâ rationali, quæ absque hac naturali scientia nunquam est; ut enim omnia naturalia in Christo fuerunt integra & perfecta, longè etiam perfectiora quàm in ipso Adamo, ita nulla imperfectio menti vel animæ Christi tribui potest. Deinde, quod idem reverâ particeps factus fuerit totius divinitatis filii Dei, Ergò & omnium attributorum; jam nisi Contrarios duos actus in Christo simul statuere velis, subordinatos eos invicem esse, ut concedas, cogeris; vide quæ in hanc sententiam scripsit Damasc.

(t) Cum Reverendo ergò, Clariss. & Excell. Domino Huttero, præceptore nostro p. m. æternum colendo, duplici modo crevisse Christum Sapientiâ dicimus: 1. ratione sapientiæ habitualis. 2. Ratione scientiæ communicatæ, non quod illa variari possit, sed quod puerulus Jesus ratione actus secundi & usurpationis in illa sapientia & λόγῳ creverit.

XXX. 4. Arg. Cui tribuitur proprium eidem essentia tribuitur: Omniscientia tribuitur carni, Ergò quoq; essentia, & per conseq. caro erit Deus. R. Fallere consequentiam: 1. Qvia confunduntur propria subjectorum unitorum & Separatorum. Ita ergò vera Major est: Diversorum subjectorum, qvorum propria eadem sunt, substantia quoq; seu essentia erit eadem; Jam Minorem nego: non enim duo separata sunt subjecta, sed Unita arctissimâ inter se unione, ex quâ ista communicatio; uti ergò ridiculè concluderem: Cui competit proprium, ei etiam essentia: proprium ignis competit ferro. Ergò ferrū est ignis. Ita non melius hic colligerem. 2. Cómunicatio proprii fieret Quidditativè & Essentialiter, concederem: atqvi hoc non fit, non enim caro fit omnisciens Deus, seu omniscentia, sed fit omniscia. Ergò nulla Argumenti vis est.

XXXI. Plura hic argumenta adversariorum addere possemus, nisi pagellarum obstaret angustia, ea idcirco conflictui reservata volumus, cumque Epiphanio qvartum hoc caput sic finimus, dicentes: (u) Humanitas est unita divinitati, & in ipsa perfectissime novit omnia, utpote quod Deo unita sit. XXXII. Hæc ergò meditatio excitet in nobis devotionem: Ecce enim omnisciens est Christus, veneremur ergò eum; novit afflictiones nostras, & miseria nostra coram ipso abscondita non est, quare non irritas relinqvet preces, sed exaudiet eas tempore opportuno: Fide ergò ipsi anima fidelis, nec despera, licet tardet, veniens tamen veniet, te liberabit, & votis tuis respondebit. Fiat, Fiat.


## 20 Twentieth Disputation, On the Gracious Presence of the Whole Christ

After the examination in the previous disputations was instituted both generally concerning the majesty communicated to the Flesh of Christ by the Word, and specifically concerning Omnipotence and Omniscience: there follows now the question concerning the gracious Presence, in the resolving and explaining of which we shall be engaged in such a way that we may briefly set forth: 1. What it is. 2. The state of the question. 3. The proof. 4. The objections of adversaries, and 5. The practical meditation.

Thesis I.

Augustine derives presence from being at hand (præstò esse). Which etymology agrees most beautifully with the phrase of Scripture: I am with you: Behold I am here: I will not leave you. Zanchius derives it from being before (præesse), which word signifies the same as to be present (adesse), that is, to be at or with someone. That which its opposite, namely to be absent (abesse), i.e., to be far from someone, confirms. II. Therefore the word presence is from the category of relation (ἐκ τῶν πρός τι) and cannot be understood without a relation between the object, which is said to be present, and the subject or thing to which it is present. III. Moreover, the gracious presence of Jesus Christ the God-man is nothing other than the efficacious operation of the present Christ, by which he calls, converts, regenerates, vivifies, and confirms men through the word of the Gospel and the dispensation of the Sacraments. IV. We do not deny that the presence of some thing, taken abstractly and precisely in the school of philosophers, does not consist formally in operation. 1. Because such an operation is supposed to be transient, therefore it requires some external thing to which it may pass: however, that is not required for the very being somewhere. 2. Operation is not a necessary companion of beings. For a thing can exist, even if it does not operate at all. 3. Presence is a relation, but operation is an action. 4. One ubiety can exist where, nevertheless, there is a multiplicity of operation, none the less with the unity of existence preserved regarding the τὸ ubi. 5. This presence is only of an undistanced being, and it belongs to the whole composite according to all its parts. Operation, however, can be even of a distanced being and not according to all its parts. Thus a man understands, but not according to all his parts.

V. But in the school of the holy [fathers], presence is always and everywhere understood either ῥητῶς or διανοητικῶς as κατὰ συμπλοκὴν καὶ περιχώρησιν, and it coheres with operation in such a way that effective governance definitively pertains to presence, and neither can this exist without that, nor that without this.

VI. There are therefore two requirements, as in any, so also in this degree of presence. 1. The substantial nearness of God. 2. The effective operation of God. That is not ὑσιωδῶς this, nor is this θελητικῶς that: although that and this plainly and fully complete the very presence of Christ among creatures taken ὁλικῶς.

VII. It is evident from this 1. that a naked and idle presence of God cannot be shown. Neither can God be found without operation, nor divine operation without God.

VIII. Which orthodoxy even Zanchius himself acknowledged: God, he says, is certainly not (as many think) absent from us, that is, he is not far removed from us, but truly present and near us, nay, in us, and so near us that we also live in him, nay, and are moved, nay, and exist.

IX. The cause, however, of this presence is twofold: of which 1. as regards the Body of Christ itself, it is the personal union, and the exaltation to the right hand of God the Father which followed this. 2. As regards us, the promise of Christ itself. For this presence is of grace; but grace relies solely on the promise.

X. Which promise we confirm with words most sweet and full of living consolation. Matt. 18:20. Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them: And Matt. 28:20. Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the age.

XI. Where two things especially deserve observation. 1. The subject, which Christ says, I: 2. The predicate, I am with you, by which word the presence of Christ is most certainly signified. XII. But let it be noted most studiously that we are speaking neither of angelic presence, nor human, nor any other, however and in whatever way conceived by man, but only of the divine presence of the incarnate λόγος. For there is not one presence of Christ as He is God, and another as He is man, but one and the same, although in a different manner. For it belongs to the λόγος by the immensity of the divine nature: but to the flesh of the λόγος by the hypostatic union, and by the exaltation to the right hand of God. To the former it belongs primarily, of itself and immediately: to the latter secondarily and mediately.

XIII. Which foundations do not oppose and overturn one another (as D. Francus, Professor of the Viadrine Academy, foolishly asserts without foundation) but the one presupposes the other.

XIV. Whence arises the controversy: Whether Christ is present with His faithful according to His deity alone? which the Calvinists hold: Or also according to His human nature? which the Orthodox affirm.

XV. The opinion of these is confirmed 1. By the description of the person of Christ: I, namely, crucified by the Jews, dead, resurrected, and now about to ascend into heaven, am with you. The word, I, by the confession of our adversaries, is the name of a person. But the person was σύνθετος, subsisting in and from two natures. Therefore, it ought not to be changed into the name of the divine nature alone, before that is proven by certain and immovable reasons.

XVI. 2. In the name of Christ the congregation. But we gather in the name of Christ, not of the divine λόγος alone, but of the whole Christ, God and man, according to both natures, our Lord and Savior.

XVII. 3. The express mention of human nature Rev. 1, 13. & seq. 4. The communication of the body and blood of Christ in the supper. 5. The efficacious operation in the whole ministry. Mark 16, 20. Acts 14, 3. Heb. 2, 4. 6. The reason of the office, which is executed not in one nature only, but in both. For the names of the office belong to Christ according to both natures. 7. The confirmation of the disciples. He opposes the promise of presence to the doubting of the disciples, who were not doubting concerning the presence of the divinity, but of the assumed man. 8. The adduction of examples. Of Christ. 1. Addressing Saul on the Damascus road. 2. Standing by him in the Lysian camp. 3. Confirming the same at Rome.

XIIX. But here the Calvinist spirit begins to grow tumultuous, and attempts to enervate these reasons in more than one way, while they seek evasions in the subject and the predicate.

XIX. Regarding the subject, indeed, thinking that there is a synecdochical expression here, while Christ, by naming the person, understands for them a part.

XX. To which in a few words I reply: Wherever Christ names himself, such as he is after the incarnation, he understands the whole person consisting of both natures, and the subject ought to be referred to both, unless the evidence of the text shows otherwise.

XXI. In place of an instance they bring forward the saying in John 8:58, and from it they conclude thus: The word, 'I', does not here signify the whole person, unless someone wishes to argue ignorantly that the human nature also existed before Abraham.

XXII. Reply: That the adversaries err in their allegation of an impertinent testimony, primarily because of a double diversity which occurs in this place. 1. With respect to the person of Christ himself: Christ speaks of his most simple person, such as it was before the incarnation; in Matt. 18 and 28, [he speaks] of the composite person, such as it was after the incarnation. 2. With respect to time: There, the discourse is about the past, and about that eternity in which the Logos was with the Father before all ages. Here, [it is] about the present and future. There, about the Logos not yet incarnate: here, about the Logos already incarnate: Before Abraham, Christ was not what he now is, even though he now is what he then was. For as he then was the Logos, so he also now is, and always will be; but what he now is as man, he was not then. Our assertion is proven by 1. the particle of time, 'Before'. 2. The objection of the Jews, and 3. Christ's response to the objection, as can be seen from a comparison of verses 56, 57, and 58. Therefore our most firm rule established in thesis 20 remains.

XXIII. Chemnitius: That [phrase], 'I am', he says, properly looks to the eternal divinity of the Son. Where, however, we do not wish the office of Mediator to be excluded. For he himself is that Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world. Therefore Job also, who lived a little after Abraham, saw his day; and testified that he was his גֹאֵל [Redeemer], because he was about to free him from sins and resurrect him on the last day. And he openly testified that this his redeemer was even then living, chapter 19, 25.

XXIV. Regarding the predicate, however, while they deny with unanimous consent the presence of the assumed flesh. For thus Calvin: The context, he says, proves that Christ is speaking of nothing less than his flesh, but is promising invincible aid to the disciples, whom against all the [machinations] of Satan and the world may protect and sustain the assaults. Polanus: These words of Christ contain a promise, by which Christ, about to ascend into heaven and to take his body away from them, consoles his disciples, so that they might not think they were deserted if he departed from them in body, but might know that, although he departed in body, he nevertheless remained with them in deity, spirit, power, efficacy, and majesty.

Martinius: Christ is not now ordinarily in his body, except in heaven. Meanwhile, he is present to us by his deity and spirit. That which he can do fully, although he is in his body in the heavens. Thus Piscator, Buseus, Gregorius de Fallentia.

XXV. Resp. 1. It is ἀπαίδευτον [unlearned] to wish to deny the presence of the person, or even of the nature acting graciously, while affirming the presence of grace. For there is one and the same definition of this presence: not one for the deity, another for the humanity. Therefore, either the whole must be affirmed concerning Christ according to his humanity, or the whole must be denied. Therefore, those who deny that Christ is present to the Church according to his humanity, also deny that the same is present by his grace and Spirit; since these always and everywhere cohere in a definitive bond. Therefore, the defined being denied, the definition itself is also denied, and vice versa.

XXVI. 2. The adversaries have hitherto taught with unanimous consent that one must speak of the presence of Christ not in the abstract but in the concrete. We also accept this, saying that Christ, the person in the concrete, not one nature only, but both together: not the nature of the Son separately, not the human nature separately, but God and man in the unity of the person is truly present to the Church, all days even unto the consummation of the age.

XXVII. 3. Martinius himself approves our opinion; saying, He certainly must be everywhere who is present in all places in which men are gathered in his name. But unless he is present in essence, he will not be everywhere by grace, nor will he understand our necessities, nor will he be able to succor them. But the Lord is speaking of a governing and helping presence.

XXVIII. Whence we argue thus: Unless someone is present in essence, he will not be everywhere by grace, nor will he understand our necessities, nor will he be able to succor them. But Christ according to his human nature is not present to us in essence, as is evident from thesis 24. Therefore, he will not be able to be present by grace, nor to understand our necessities, nor to succor them.

Or thus: Christ, in the cited statements of thesis 10, as he is man, promises only his operation, Spirit, power, and efficacy, as the Calvinist thesis holds. Therefore, Christ as man does not promise in those [statements] his presence on earth. Are these not, Calvinist men, contradictions: a governing and helping presence cannot exist without grace and help: And can grace or operation exist without presence?

XXIX. But this is not yet the end; 4. I ask you to weigh the absurdities which follow from your assertion. 1. The definition of Union, which is described by the indwelling of the whole fullness of the Deity in the λόγῳ, would apply only to the λόγῳ in heaven, but not on earth. 2. The whole λόγος would to that extent not be incarnate, but only a certain particle of him, and that a very small one, to which the Humanity might adhere: but all the rest of the part of the λόγῳ would not be incarnate. 3. The λόγῳ, existing on earth, would have men, dwelling in the same place, much more present to himself than his own assumed humanity: as that which would exist only in the heavens, but not on earth with other men, who nevertheless are present to the λόγῳ, so much so that he exists in all, and dwells in the Elect. 4. The υπόςασις would be somewhere, where that which subsists in his ὑποςάσει would not be. 5. Every true union of the λόγῳ and humanity would be taken away, for if the λόγῳ is where the Humanity is not, then he is outside the humanity. Insofar, however, as he is outside it, to that extent he is not within it. Insofar as he is not in it, to that extent he is separated; and therefore not joined, much less united. 6. God would to that extent not be manifested in the flesh, insofar as he is said to be outside the flesh. 7. The ἀδιάςατος union of natures would be torn apart by the διασήματα of places. And why say more? 8. With the λόγῳ existing outside the flesh, it is certain that two Christs are constituted. For where the λόγος alone exists, there are not two natures: not the incarnate λόγῳ; not the συνθετὸς; not man; not Christ, but only the λόγῳ: Christ, however (that is, God and man), is only in the heavens: because he is united only there.

XXX. Thus, indeed, τὸ ψεῦδος πολυσχιδὲς καὶ πολύμορφον is. To err is indeed human, but to persevere in error is extreme madness.

XXXI. Therefore, lest the οἱ ἀντιλέγοντες seem to have deserted the defense of a bad cause, they take refuge in the Ascension into the heavens, the departure from this world, etc.

XXXII. Whence they rise up thus: He who, having left the world, ascended into the heavens, thence to return for judgment, is no longer with us on earth. I assume: The Son of God having been made flesh, having left the world, ascended into heaven, thence to return for judgment. Therefore, the Son of God having been made flesh is no longer conversant with us on earth. The conclusion is absurd, inasmuch as it diametrically conflicts with divine promises 1:13 and following. The fault, therefore, will be in the premises. But there is none in the assumption, which is the Holy Spirit's in the proposition. That, therefore, must be limited thus: He who, having left the world, ascended into heaven (with visible conversation removed from men), thence (visibly) to return for judgment: he is no longer conversant with us on earth (according to that visible mode of conversation). See the foundation of this limitation in the stated Acts 1:11. Thus Christ is to return, ὃν τρόπον you saw him going into heaven.

XXXIII. The consequence, therefore, is most false: Christ ascended visibly into heaven, thence to return for judgment. Therefore, Christ is absent from the militant Church. For departure from this world and divine presence are not contrary.

XXXIV. To this they say: The human nature according to the true mode of a body is in heaven. Therefore, according to the true mode of a body it is not on earth. I concede it. For the presence of Christ in the militant Church does not depend on the natural mode of a body, or on human property or faculty, but is entirely divine, and is referred to the divine person of the Son of God, in whom deity and humanity subsist personally united.

XXXV. Thus, therefore, we conclude: The office of Christ pertains to him according to both natures. It is certain, however, that it pertains to the office of Christ as mediator, high priest, king, and our head, that he be present to his Church, and presentially hear, help, and govern. Therefore, to be present to the Church and presentially to hear, help, and govern, pertains to Christ according to both natures.

XXXVI. Here let it be noted in passing that, while we refer presence to the office, we distinguish between the very power and faculty of being present, which is the divine immensity itself and an essential property; and between actual or operative assistance proceeding from free will.

XXXVII. Most vain, therefore, is the exception of the Calvinists, clamoring that we pass from person to nature; of which crime they themselves are guilty, substituting only the deity for the whole person of the God-man.

XXXVIII. Finally, against the opposing party we produce such an argument: According to that nature Christ promised us his presence, according to which power in heaven and on earth has been given to him. And this was given according to his human nature. Therefore, according to his human nature also he promised us his presence.

XXXIX. O therefore the happy, O the blessed condition of the pious! For behold, is there not for us a struggle against principalities and powers? Does not your adversary the devil go about like a roaring lion? Take heart; Christ is present to you: who is stronger than he? He is in the midst of you, who is more present than he? Nay, he is also our head. 1. By reason of communication. For does not the head give life, sense, and motion to the body? Thus Christ, by the power of his Spirit, communicates spiritual life, vigor, sense, and motion to his members. 2. By reason of conjunction. The head adheres to its members with an inseparable bond: Christ alone thus effects the καταρτισμὸν, the bond and structure of the members with the head and among themselves. Are you therefore clinging, O man, in miseries? Run to the head, and you will obtain help, by the example of the Canaanite woman, Matt. 15, 25. Does a pause of life threaten? Christ will transfer you into a better one, so that through death you may begin to live, and remain immune from eternal death. With the head torn away, a man dies. But what is more miserable than a dead corpse? It is cold, it is stiff, it stinks. Thus the impious are cold, because of the lack of a heavenly head: they are stiff toward any good works: they stink, because of the perpetual evaporations of their crimes. Adhere therefore, O Christian, to your head, and it will adhere to you, and will communicate life, where there is no death, no sadness, no pain, to whom be praise, honor, and blessing forever.

Latin:

POsteaqvam in superioribus disputationib9 examen tum γενικῶς de majestate Carni Christi à λόγῳ communicata, tum εἰδικῶς de Omnipotentia & Omniscientia fuit institutum: seqvitur nunc qvæstio de gratiosa Præsentia, in qvâ enodandâ & explicandâ ita versabimur, ut 1. Qvid ea sit. 2. Statum quæstionis. 3. Probationem. 4. Adversariorum objectiones, & 5. Practicam meditationem breviter exponamus.

Thesis I.

PRæsentiam deducit Augustinus â præstò esse. Qvæ notatio pulcherrimè congruit phrasi scripturæ: Sum vobiscum: Ecce adsum: non relinqvam vos. Zanchius â præesse derivat, qvod verbum significat idem ac adesse, id est, esse ad seu apud aliqvem. Id qvod ipsius contrarium nempe abesse, i. e. procul ab aliqvo esse, confirmat. II. Præsentiæ igitur vocabulum ἐκ τῶν πρός τι est & absq; σχέσει & relatione inter objectum, qvod dicitur esse præsens, & subjectum sive rem, cui illud est præsens, intelligi neqvit. III. Est autem præsentia gratiosa Jesu Christi θεανθρώπου nihil aliud, qvam efficax Christi præsentis operatio, qvâ per verbum Evangelii & Sacramentorum dispensationem homines vocat, convertit, regenerat, vivificat, confirmat. IV. Non negamus, præsentiam alicujus rei abstractè & præcisè in schola Philosophorū sumtā, non consistere formaliter in operatione. 1. quia talis operatio supponitur esse transiens, ideò requirit aliquod externum, ad quod transeat : Illud autem non requiritur ad ipsum esse alicubi. 2. Operatio non est necessarius comes Entium. Potest enim res esse, si maximè non operetur. 3. Præsentia est relatio, operatio verò actio. 4. Ubietas una potest esse, ubi tamen operationis multiplicitas est, nihilominus salvâ existentiæ unitate ad τὸ ubi. 5. Præsentia hæc tantùm entis indistantis est, & competit toti composito juxta omnes partes. Operatio verò etiam entis distantis & non secundum omnes partes esse potest. Sic homo intelligit, sed non secundũ omnes partes.

V. Verùm in Scholâ S. sancti semper & ubiq; vel ῥητῶς vel διανοητικῶς præsentia κατὰ συμπλοκὴν καὶ περιχώρησιν intelligitur, & cum operatione ita cohæret, ut efficax gubernatio definitivè ad præsentiă pertineat, & neq; hæc sine illâ, neq; illa sine hâc esse possit.

VI. Duo igitur requisita sunt, ut in quovis, ita & in hoc præsentiæ gradu. 1. Substantialis Dei propinquitas. 2. Efficax Dei operatio. Illa ὑσιωδῶς non est hæc, nec hæc θελητικῶς est illa: tametsi illa & hæc planè & plenè absolvant ipsam Christi apud creaturas præsentiam ὁλικῶς acceptam.

VII. Patet hinc 1. Dei præsentiam nudam & otiosam ostendi non posse. Nec sine operatione Deum, nec divinam operationem sine Deo inveniri.

VIII. Qvam orthodoxiam vel ipse Zanchius agnovit : Deus, inquit ens, non est certè (ut multi putant) absens â nobis, id est, non est â nobis procul remotus, sed verè præsens & propè nos, imo in nobis atq; ita propè nos, ut nos qvoqve in ipso vivamus, imò & moveamur, imò & simus.

IX. Causa autē hujus præsentiæ duplex est: qvarum 1. qvantum ad ipsum Corpus Christi est personalis unio, & quæ hanc subsequuta est, ad dextram Dei Patris exaltatio. 2. qvantum ad nos, ipsa Christi promissio. Hæc n. præsentia est gratiæ; gratiâ autē nititur sola promissio.

X. Qvam promissionē confirmamus dictis dulcissimâ & vivâ consolatione plenissimis. Matth. 18, 20. Ubi duo aut tres congregati sunt in nomine meo, ibi ego in medio eorum sum : Et Matth. 28, 20. Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usq; ad consummationem seculi.

XI. Ubi duo imprimis observationem merentur. 1. Subjectum, qvod Christus dicit, Ego : 2. Prædicatum, vobiscum sum, qvâ voce præsentia Christi certissimè significatur. XII. Perqvam autem studiosè notètur, nos neqve de præsentiâ angelicâ, neqve humanâ, neqve ullâ aliâ, qvomodocunq; & qvalitercunq; etiam ab homine conceptâ, sed tantùm de præsentiâ τοῦ λόγου incarnati divinâ, loqvi. Non enim est alia Christi, qvâ Deus, alia qvâ homo est, præsentia, sed una eademqve, licet modo diverso. Nam λόγῳ competit ex naturæ divinæ immensitate : carni verò λόγου ex hypostaticâ unione, & ad dextram Dei exaltatione. Illi competit primò, per se & immediatè : Huic secundariò & mediatè.

XIII. Qvæ fundamenta non se mutuo oppugnant & evertunt (ut D. Francus Profess. Academ. Viadrinæ sine fundamento infrunnitus asserit) sed unum præsupponit alterum.

XIV. Unde oritur Controversia: An Christus suis fidelibus adsit secundùm solam deitatem ? qvod Calviniani: An etiam secundùm humanam naturam? qvod Orthodoxi affirmant.

XV. Horum sententiam confirmat 1. Personæ Christi descriptio: Ego, nempè â Judæis crucifixus, mortuus, resuscitatus, & jam jam cælum ascensurus, vobiscum sum. Vox, Ego, adversarior. confessione personæ nomen est. Persona autem σύνθετος erat, in & ex duabus naturis subsistens. Non igitur debet mutari in nomen solius naturæ divinæ, priusqvam certis immotisq́ve rationibus illud evincatur.

XVI. 2. In nomine Christi congregatio. Convenimus autem in nomine Christi, non solius Dei λόγου, sed totius Christi, Dei & hominis, secundum utramq; naturam, Domini & salvatoris nostri.

XVII. 3. Naturæ humanæ expressa mentio Apoc. 1, 13. & seq. 4. Corporis & sangvinis Christi in cæna communicatio. 5. Efficax in toto ministerio operatio. Marc. 16, 20. Act. 14, 3. Hebr. 2, 4. 6. Officii ratio, qvod exeqvitur non in unâ naturâ tantum, sed in utrâqve. Nomina enim officii competunt Christo secundùm utramqve naturam. 7. Discipulor. confirmatio. Promissionem præsentiæ, dubitationi discipulorum, non de divinitatis, sed hominis assumti præsentiâ ambigentium, opponit. 8. Exemplor. adductio. Christi. 1. Saulum in viâ Damascenâ compellantis. 2. ei in Castris Lysianis adstantis. 3. eundem Romæ confirmantis.

XIIX. Verùm hîc tumultuari incipit Spiritus Calvinianus, hasq́; rationes non uno modo enervare conatur, dum in subjecto & prædicato effugia qværunt.

XIX. In Subjecto quidem, putantes synecdochicam hîc esse locutionem, dum Christus nominando personam, partem illis intelligat.

XX. Quibus paucis Resp. Ubicunq; seipsum Christus nominat, qualis est post incarnationem, totam personam utrâq; naturâ constantem intelligit, & subjectum ad utramq; referri debet, nisi aliud ostendat textus evidentia.

XXI. Instantiæ loco adducunt dictum Joh. 8. 58. indeq; sic colligunt: Vocabulum, Ego, hîc non significat totam personam, nisi quis humanam quoq; naturam ante Abrahamum fuisse, imperitè arguere velit.

XXII. R. Adversarios peccare allegatione impertinentis testimonii, ob duplicem inprimis, quæ hoc loco occurrit, diversitatem. 1. Respectu ipsius personæ Christi: loquitur Christus de simplicissimâ suâ personâ, qualis ante ἐνσάρκωσιν; Matt. 18. & 28. de personâ compositâ, qualis erat post incarnationem. 2. Respectu temporis: Ibi sermo est de præterito, & de illa æternitate, quâ λόγος apud Patrem ante omnia secula fuit. Hîc de præsenti & futuro. Ibi de λόγῳ nondum incarnato: hîc de λόγῳ jam incarnato: Ante Abrahamum Christus non erat, quod nunc est, etsi nunc sit, quod tum erat. Ut n. tum fuit λόγος, ita etiam nunc est, & semper erit; quod autem nunc homo est, tunc non erat. Probat nostram assertationem 1. particula temporis, Anteqvam. 2. Judæorum objectio, & 3. Christi ad objectionem respõsio, uti ex collatione vers. 56. 57. & 58. videre est. Manet igitur firmissima nostra regula th. 20. posita.

XXIII. Chemnitius: Illud, Ego sum, inquit, propriè ad æternam filii divinitatem respicit. Ubi tamen Mediatoris officium non exclusum volumus. Ipse enim est agnus ille qui occisus est ab origine mundi. Ideò Job etiam, qui paulò post Abrahamum vixit, ejus diem vidit; eumq; usum גֹאֵל esse testatus est, quod ipsum â peccatis liberaturus & in novissimo die resuscitaturus sit. Et hunc redemtorem suum jam tum vivere apertè testatus est, cap. 19, 25.

XXIV. In prædicato verò, dum unanimi consensu carnis assumtæ præsentiam negant. Sic enim Calvinus: Contextus, inquit, evincit, Christum nihil minus, quam de carne suâ loqvi, sed invictum auxilium promittere discipulis, qvos adversùs omnes Satanæ mundiq; insultus tueatur & sustineat. Polanus: Verba Christi hæc continent promissionem, qvâ consolatur Christus discipulos suos in cœlum asscensurus & corpus suum ab illis ablaturus, ne putarent se deseri, si corpore ab illis abiret, sed scirent; licet corpore discederet: manere tamen ipsum cum illis deitate, spiritu, virtute, efficacia & majestate.

Martinius: Christus corpore suo ordinariè nunc non est, nisi in cœlo. Interim adest nobis deitate suâ & spiritu. Illud qvod facere potest plenè, qvamvis corpore suo sit in cœlis. Ita Piscator, Busæus, Gregorius de Fallentiâ.

XXV. Resp. 1. ἀπαίδευτον esse, affirmatâ gratiæ præsentiâ negare velle præsentiam personæ, vel etiam naturæ gratiosè agentis. Una enim eademq́; præsentiæ hujus definitio est: non alia deitatis, alia humanitatis: Qvare aut tota affirmanda est deChristo juxta humanitatem, aut tota neganda. Qvi E. negant Christum juxta humanitatem adesse Ecclesiæ, negant etiam eundem adesse gratiâ suâ & Spiritu; qvippe qvæ nexu definitivosemper & ubiq; cohærent. Negato igitur definito, ipsa qvoq; definitio negatur, & contra.

XXVI. 2. De præsentiâ Christi non in abstracto sed in concreto loqvendum esse, unanimi hactenus consensu docuerunt adversarii. Acceptamus & nos, dicentes Christum, personam in concreto, non unam naturam tantum, sed utramq; simul: non naturam filii seorsum, non naturam humanam seorsum, sed Deum & hominem in unitate personæ verè adesse Ecclesiæ, omnibus diebus usq; ad consummationem seculi.

XXVII. 3. Ipse Martinius nostram sententiam approbat; Eum certè, inqvens, ubiq; esse oportet, qvi in omnibus locis præsens sit, in qvibus homines in ipsius nomine cōgregantur.Nisi autem essentiâ præsens sit: gratiâ non erit ubivis, nec intelliget necessitates nostras, nec iis succurrere poterit. De præsentia autem gubernatrice & auxiliatrice dominus verba facit.

XXVIII. Unde sic argumentamur: Nisi qvis essentiâ præsens sit, gratiâ non erit ubivis, nec intelliget necessitates nostras, nec iis succurrere poterit. Atqvi Christus secundum humanam naturam nobis præsens non est essentiâ, uti patet ex th. 24. E. nec gratiâ adesse, nec intelligere nostras necessitates, nec iis succurrere poterit.

Vel ita: Christus in allegatis dictis thes. 10. ut homo est, promittit suam operationem, Spiritum, virtutem & efficaciam duntaxat, uti Calviniana thesis habet. E. Christus quà homo non promittit in illis suam in terris præsentiam. Annon viri Calviniani, hæc sunt contraria: præsentia gubernatrix & auxiliatrix non potest esse sine gratia & auxilio: Et gratia vel operatio potest esse sine præsentia?

XXIX. Sed nondum finis est; 4. Absurda, quæ ex vestra assertione sequuntur, quæso ponderate. 1. λόγῳ tantum in cælo, non autem interris conveniet definitio Unionis, quæ describitur inhabitatione totius plenitudinis Deitatis ỡ λόγꙋ. 2. totus λόγος eatenus non esset incarnatus, sed tantùm ejus particula quædam, eaq; valdè exigua, cui Humanitas adhæreat: reliqua verò omnis ỡ λόγꙋ pars, incarnata non esset. 3. λόγꚙ in terris existens haberet homines, ibidem habitantes, sibi longè præsentiores, quam suam propriam humanitatem assumptam: ut quæ in cœlis tantùm existeret, non autem in terris cum alijs hominibus, qui tamen λόγῳ sunt præsentes, adeò ut existat in omnibus, & habitet in Electis. 4. υπόςασις esset alicubi, ubi non esset id, quod in ejus ὑποςάσει subsistit. 5. Tolleretur omnis λόγꙋ & humanitatis vera unio, Nam si λόγꚙ est, ubi Humanitas non est, tum extra humanitatem est. Qvatenus autem extra eam, eatenus non intra eam. Qvatenus non in eâ, eatenus sejunctus: ideoq́; non conjunctus nedum unitus. 6. Deus eatenus non esset manifestatus in carne, qvatenus dicitur extra carnem. 7. ἀδιάςατος naturarum unio, per διασήματα locorum distraheretur. Et qvid multis? 8. λόγῳ extra carnem existente, duos constitui Christos certum est. Nam ubi solus λόγος existit, ibi non sunt duæ naturæ: non λόγꚙ incarnatus; non συνθετὸς: non homo: non Christus sed tantum λόγꚙ: Christus autem (Deus scilicet & homo) tantùm in cœlis: quia ibi tantùm unitus.

XXX. Ita nimirum τὸ ψεῦδος πολυσχιδὲς καὶ πολύμορφον est. Errare quidem humanum, at in errore perseverare, extremæ dementiæ est.

XXXI. Ideoqve ne οἱ ἀντιλέγοντες malæ causæ patrocinium deseruisse videantur, confugiunt ad Ascensionem in cœlos, abitum ex hoc mundo, &c.

XXXII. Unde sic insurgunt: Qvi relicto mundo adscendit in cœlos, inde rediturus ad judicium, is nobiscum in terris amplius non est. Assumo ego: Filius Dei factus caro, relicto mundo, afcendit in cœlos inde ad judicium rediturus. E. Filius Dei factus caro nobiscum in terris amplius non versatur. Conclusio est absurda, qvippe qvæ ê diametro cum divinis promissionibus & exemplis & visione Apoc. 1, 13. & seqq. pugnat. Vitium igitur erit in præmissis. At nullum est in assumtione, qvæ est Spiritus S. E. in propositione. Illa igitur sic limitanda erit : Qvi relicto mundo adscendit in cœlos (subtractâ hominibus visibili conversatione) inde (visibiliter) rediturus ad judicium : is nobiscum in terris (juxta visibilem illum conversationis modum) amplius non versatur. Cujus limitationis fundamentum vide in dicto Actor. 1, 11. Sic rediturus est Christus, ὃν τρόπον vidistis euntem in cœlum.

XXXIII. Conseqventia igitur falsima est: Christus adscendit visibiliter in cœlum, inde rediturus ad judicium. E. Christus abest ab Ecclesia militante. Abitus enim ex hoc mundo, & præsentia divina non sunt contraria.

XXXIV. Ad inqviunt: Humana natura secundum veri corporis modum est in Cœlo. E. secundum verum corporis modum non est in terris. Concedo. Nam præsentia Christi in Ecclesia militante non dependet ex naturali modo corporis, sive ex proprietate vel facultate humana, sed tota divina est, & refertur ad Filii Dei personam divinam, in qvâ deitas & humanitas personaliter unitæ subsistunt.

XXXV. Ita ergo concludimus : Officium Christi competit ei secundùm utramq; naturam. Certum autem est, ad officium Christi mediatoris, pontificis, regis, ac capitis nostri pertinere, ut Ecclesiæ suæ adsit, ac præsens exaudiat, juvet, gubernet. E. adesse Ecclesiæ ac præsenter exaudire, juvare, gubernare, competit Christo secundùm utramq; naturam.

XXXVI. Hic obiter notetur, qvod, dum præsentiam ad officium referimus, distinguamus inter ipsam adessendi virtutem & facultatem, qvæ est ipsa divina immensitas & proprietas essentialis; Et inter actualem sive operosam assistentiam ex liberâ voluntate profectam.

XXXVII. Vanissima proinde est exceptio Calvinistarum, clamitantium nos transire â persona ad naturam; cujus criminis ipsi rei funt, pro tota perfona τῆς θεανθρώπης substituentes solam deitatem.

XXXVIII. Tandem contra adversam partem tale producimus argumentum: Secundùm illam naturam Christus nobis suam promisit præsentiam, secundùm qvam ei potestas in cœlo & terra est data. Atq; hæc data est secundùm humanam. E. secundùm humanam qvoq; naturam nobis suam promisit præsentiam.

XXXIX. O ergò felicem, ô beatam piorum conditionem! Ecce enim estnè nobis colluctatio adversus principes & potestates? Circuitne adversarius vester diabolus tanqvam leo rugiens? Confidite; Christus vobis præsens est: qvo qvis fortior? In medio vestrûm est, qvo qvis præsentior? Imò & caput nostrum est. 1. Ratione communicationis. Annon enim caput corpori dat vitam, sensum & motum? Sic Christus virtute sui Spiritus vitam, vigorum, sensum ac motum spiritualem communicat membris suis. 2. Ratione conjunctionis. Caput nexu indivulso adhæret suis membris: solus ita Christus καταρτισμὸν nexum compagemq; membror. cum capite & inter se efficit. Hæres igitur, ô homo, in miseriis? Ad caput curre, & auxilium conseqvêris, exemplo Cananææ Matth. 15, 25. Imminet pausa vitæ? Christus te in meliorem transferet, ut per mortem vivere incipias, & ab æternâ morte immunis maneas. Avulso capite, homo moritur. Qvid autem mortuo cadavere miserius? Friget, riget, fœtet. Sic impii frigent, ob carentiam cœlestis capitis: rigent ad qvævis bona opera: fœtent, ob perpetuas scelerum evaporationes. Adhæresce E. tuo, ô Christiane, capiti, & illud tibi adhærebit, vitamq;, ubi nulla mors, nulla tristitia, nullus dolor, communicabit, cui sit laus, honor, benedictio in æternum.


## 21 Twenty-first Disputation, On the Universal Omnipresence of Christ

What the long-lived and devout Simeon, with a clearly prophetic Spirit, predicted concerning Christ, the restorer of fallen things and the sole defender of mortals, Luke 2, 34, from that noble Prophet Isaiah ch. 8, 13. 14, that he would be a σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον [sign to be spoken against], that is all too true. For this prophecy of the pious old man is fulfilled at any time, while his person and office are filled with contradictions from every side, and all the shafts of τῶν ἀντιλογιῶν καὶ βλασφημιῶν [contradictions and blasphemies] are aimed at him alone with a laborious effort indeed, but with an entirely futile attempt. This very thing has been done by the heretics of all ages, who, weighing these highest mysteries of the faith concerning the person and office of Christ by the balance of their own reason and corrupted human philosophy—which, as Tertullian testifies, is the origin of all heresies—have stumbled and still stumble, to the eternal loss of souls. I shall say nothing now of the ancient heretics, who attacked the person of the Son by bringing up all sorts of engines, sometimes by assailing one or the other of his natures, sometimes by tearing apart their personal union (which Theodore the Rhetor, presbyter, is the author and witness that Paul of Samosata did), since something has already been treated concerning these above; but I shall speak of those who today make the greatest assault upon the Majesty of Christ, especially his Omnipresence, which the Sacramentarians, and the ill-disposed Jesuits who are acting as their reinforcements in this matter as well, blasphemously agitate under the hateful name of Ubiquity. For piety commands us to fight for the glory of him who, by his own ignominy, procured eternal glory for us: necessity demands that we stand for the truth of that article from which great benefit redounds to us: the glory and majesty of Christ require us to defend him from the insults and blasphemies of his enemies with a pious, true, and sincere spirit. Therefore, the fiercer the προνόμαχοι [champions/fore-fighters] are in attacking, the more eager it becomes for us Christians to be in defending. I shall, however, divide this whole πραγματείαν [treatise], σαφηνείας καὶ εὐπαρακολοθησίας ἕνεκα [for the sake of clarity and ease of following], into six chapters, of which 1. will be, What we understand by the Omnipresence of Christ, where the calumnies of the adversaries are to be noted. 2. The true state [of the question]. 3. The proof. 4. The mode of Omnipresence. 5. The objections of the Calvinists and Hoffmannists. 6. A practical meditation.

Thesis I.

But before we approach the matter itself, we must examine the legitimate state of the controversy, especially since our adversaries attempt to attribute anything they wish in this contest, and fight so strenuously against a figment of their own brain. Which sin is not light against the principal rule of disputation, concerning the correct forming of the state of the controversy.

II. Therefore we must state what we understand by the Omnipresence of GOD, which according to the Holy Code, Jerem. 23, 23. 24. Isaiah 66, 1. 40, 11. 12. Psalm 139, 8. is nothing else than not being δεκτικὴν [receptive/capable of being contained] such that it is grasped and enclosed by any thing, but being δεκτικὴν [receptive/capable of containing] such that it grasps and touches all things with its embrace. Which I think everyone now concedes, since even that impious apostate Porphyry wrote not absurdly about this matter, whom Mr. Dr. Gesner cites.

III. We shall now demonstrate that this πανταπαρουσίαν [omnipresence] has been communicated to the human nature of CHRIST, if I first remove the impious calumnies of the Adversaries in a few words. For they think too crudely about the mode of divine πανταπαρουσίας [omnipresence].

IV. The first calumny, therefore, is when they odiously thrust upon us a most prodigious, local, coextensive [omnipresence], by which the human nature of CHRIST is diffused and prolonged everywhere in places, and infinitely extended, and then direct their arguments against it as if it were the state of the controversy. For Luther several times, as also our own theologians, have quite often taught the exact opposite publicly.

V. We do indeed abhor that delirium of the Adversaries, when they say that we teach that the humanity of CHRIST is omnipresent by reason of its essence and reigns everywhere. For we teach and confess that the humanity of CHRIST by reason of its essence is finite for all eternity, and remains limited by its own dimensions, and retains its own measured quantity no less than other saints perpetually, yet is nowhere separated from the infinite λόγῳ [Word].

VI. Nor thirdly do we concede that the human nature of CHRIST is inclusively omnipresent, or that it is included and contained in created things, in all woods, stones, herbs, leaves of trees, beer barrels, and other impure places of that kind. For our people abhor this local inclusion, readily conceding that it is heretical if anyone says with Schwenkfeld that the body of CHRIST is everywhere in all creatures κατ' ἐσίαν [essentially]: which is certainly against the analogy of faith.

VII. All of which things by the ματαιολόγοις καὶ φρεναπάτοις [vain talkers and deceivers], as Dr.

Paul calls [them] in Tit. 1, [they] are brought forward to this end, that they may deceive the simpler sort, and strive with an altogether impious and fraudulent mouth and heart to seduce [them] from the saving doctrine of our Churches, founded in the Holy Scriptures. VIII. For these opinions, which the Adversaries have ἀπαιδεύτως [unlearnedly] fashioned out of their own wit outside the word of GOD, have never entered the minds of our Theologians. Wherefore we exterminate that dogma as ἑτερόδοξον [heterodox] from the Church.

IX. But omitting their trifles and blasphemies, we propose the genuine state of the controversy thus: Whether Christ, sitting at the right hand of the Father κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον [according to the human], as Basil speaks, κατὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα [according to the humanity], as Theodoret and Athanasius [say], according to his humanity, as we speak, in the unity of his person with τῷ λόγῳ [the Word], is present with all creatures, or rules in the whole world? Which we affirm, the Calvinists deny.

X. To confirm our opinion, we bring forward arguments. I. The express letter. 1. From the O.T. Ps. 110, 1. and that in two ways. 1. From the form of reigning. Whoever rules in the midst of his enemies, he is not absent, but omnipresent. For 1. such dominion requires presence, since no one is in the midst, unless he who can perform the office while present. Beza is therefore impudent when he brings forward that simile of the King of Spain. For there is a very great difference between the kingdoms of this world and the kingdom of Christ. 2. Sitting at the right hand of GOD is nothing else than to reign, as the Lord Paul teaches in 1 Cor. 15, 25, which he explains by τὸ βασιλεύειν [to reign]. But Christ according to his human nature rules in the midst of his enemies, which the συνέπεια [connection] of the text teaches. Indeed he is κύριος πάντων [Lord of all], Acts 10, 35. Therefore. 2. From the seat of his reign and empire. He whose throne and seat is included in no place, but is above all places and present everywhere, he himself, included in no place, will be present everywhere by a most perfect action. But the throne which Christ occupied according to his human nature is such, Isa. 40, 12. 48, 13. Therefore. XI. 2. From the N.T. Eph. 1, 20. 21. & ch. 4, 10. where it is permitted to argue thus: 1. According to which nature Christ died, was resurrected, and was taken up to heaven, according to that he promises his presence: which the συνέπεια [connection] of the whole text places before our eyes. But Christ according to his human nature is, etc., which is clear from the coherence of the text, especially v. 23, indeed even Martinius himself is forced to admit it. Therefore.

XII. 2. He who for this purpose ascended ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὀυρανῶν, ἵνα πλη- ρώσῃ τὰ πάντα [far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things], he is truly present to all things, and powerfully governs them. But Christ according to his human nature, Ephes. 4. 10. Therefore.

XIII. 3. He who fills all things in all, he is also present in proximity according to his substance, and as most present works all things in all. For τὸ implere omnia [to fill all things] denotes the whole dominion of Christ sitting at the right hand of the Father, because it is of infinite virtue and divine power, which is true by the confession and testimony of the Adversaries. But Christ according to his human nature. Therefore.

XIV. 4. The universal word 'All' says it. Therefore it excludes nothing that pertains to this dominion. Where the Pauline phrase τὸ πληρώσῃ τὰ πάν- τα [that he might fill all things] is to be noted, which is read only twice in the New Testament in this sense, and certainly leaves nothing empty, because those things which we fill are certainly by no means destitute of our presence. Therefore it nowhere signifies the dominion of someone absent, but always and everywhere denotes the most present operation of one present over individual and universal creatures in heaven and on earth. See the truth of this phrase in Jeremiah 23:23-24, where it is attributed to God.

XV. Pierius indeed criticizes the most illustrious Lord Doctor Menzer, my teacher to be honored forever, as if he were departing from Luther's explanation. But he demonstrates quite learnedly that this is by no means the case.

XVI. Some take the word πληρώσεως [of filling] concerning the fulfillment of the Scriptures, as a Bucanus and b Martyr, or concerning that which pertains to the completion of an office, as c Beza. But they conclude it ἀπροσδιονύσως [irrelevant/inappropriately], because 1. The universal word is placed indeterminately. 2. The connection of the text protests, since it is a matter of the glory and majesty of the dominion of Christ, and mention is made of the filling of higher and lower places, namely heaven and earth. 3. The customary mode of speaking, and a comparison of the passage Ephesians 1:21-23, contradicts it, where the Holy Spirit, as often as he deals with the fulfillment of the Scriptures, always speaks expressly and determinately, as Matthew 1:22, John 19:36, Acts 1:16, John 13:18.

XVII. Some take it concerning the successive filling of certain places, by reason of which the flesh of Christ fills now these places, now those. But this gloss is ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως [of private interpretation], fighting against the analogy of faith, because 1. The distortion of the text is greatest. 2. Such a fulfillment has never happened nor will it ever happen.

XIIX. Finally, there are those who interpret this concerning the fulfillment of gifts, such as Martinius, Sadeel, and Ursinus. But 1. The universal word 'all', placed without qualification, contradicts this. 2. To fill all things and to fill the Church with gifts are not the same, but they differ as the whole and the part. However, it is concluded unskillfully from the affirmation of one part to the negation of the remaining parts. 3. Paul himself separates them, as the very construction of the text shows, as the Reverend and Illustrious Lord Doctor Menz. etc., learnedly points out. Therefore, he speaks of such a fulfillment, by which Christ, even according to his assumed nature, works and fills all things in all by his present efficacy, which he makes manifest by the most generous outpouring of gifts.

Latin:

QVod de Christo rerum lapsarum restauratore & mortalium assertore unico Luc. 2, 34. ex nobili illo Phopheta Esaia c. 8, 13. 14, vatidico planè Spiritu μακρόβιος καὶ εὐλαβὴς Simeon prædixit, prædixit, fore illum σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον, illud nimis verum est. Prophetia enim hæc pii Senis qvovis tempore adimpletur, dum persona ejus & officium ex omni latere contradictionibus impletur, & tela qvævis τῶν ἀντιλογιῶν καὶ βλασφημιῶν unicè in ipsum operoso qvidem conatu emittunt, sed frustraneo prorsus ausu. Factum id ipsum ab omnium ætatum hæreticis, qvi summa hæc fidei mysteria, de persona & officio Christi,ad rationis suæ, & Philosophiæ humanæ corruptæ, qvæ omnium hæresium, Tertulliano teste, origo est, trutinam exigentes impegerunt,& etiamnum impingunt, cum æternâ animarum jacturâ: De veteribus hæreticis, qvi personam Filii prolatis omnibus machinis impugnarunt, nunc alterutram ejus petendo naturam, nunc illarum unionem personalem distrahendo (qvòd Paulum Samosatenum fecisse, Theodorus Rhetensis presbyter autor ac testis est) jam nihil dicam, siqvidem superiùs de his aliqvid actum, sed de illis, qvi hodiè in Majestatem Christi, præsertim ejus Omnipræsentiam, impetum faciunt maximum, qvam etiam sub exoso Ubiqvitatis nomine Sacramentarii, hâc etiam in parte succenturiantes malè feriati Jesuitæ, blasphemè exagitant. Jubet enim pietas pro ejus pugnare gloriâ, qvi suâ ignominiâ æternam nobis gloriam comparavit: flagitat necessitas, stare pro illius articuli veritate, ex qvo magnum ad nos redundat commodum: postulat Christi gloria & majestas illum ab hostium contumeliis & blasphemiis animo pio, vero & sincero vindicare. Proinde qvo acriores in oppugnando sunt προνόμαχοι, eò alacriores in propugnando nos Christianos decet. Dispescam autem totam hanc πραγματείαν, σαφηνείας καὶ εὐπαρακολοθησίας ἕνεκα in sex capita, qvorum 1. erit, Qvid per Omnipræsentiam Christi intelligamus, ubi calumniæ adversariorum notandæ. 2. Verus status. 3. Probatio. 4. Modus Omnipræsentiæ. 5. Objectiones Calvinistarum & Hoffmannistarum. 6. Meditatio practica.

Thesis I.

PRiusqvam verò rem ipsam accedamus, dispiciendum nobis est de statu controversiæ legitimo, præsertim cùm adversarii nostri qvidvis affingere in hoc certamine attentent, & ita strenuè contra proprii cerebri figmentum pugnent. Qvod peccatum non leve est contra præcipuam disputationis legem, de statu controversiæ rectè formando.

II. Proinde dicendum nobis erit, quid per Omnipræsentiam DEI intelligamus, quæ juxta S. Codicem Jerem. 23, 23. 24. Jesai. 66, 1. 40, 11. 12. Psal. 139, 8. nihil aliud est, quàm non esse δεκτικὴν quæ capiatur & ullâ re concludatur, sed esse δεκτικὴν quæ capiat, & & omnes res complexu suo contingat. Quod jam concedere omnes existimo, siquidem impius etiam ille Apostata Porphyrius hac de re non absurdè scripsit, quem citat Dn. D. Gesnerus.

III. Hanc autem πανταπαρουσίαν τῆς humanæ CHRISTI naturæ communicatam esse jam demonstrabimus, si priùs impias Adversariorum calumnias paucis removero. Nimis enim crassè de modo πανταπαρουσίας divinæ sentiunt.

IV. Prima ergò calumnia est, dum prodigiosissimam, localem, coëxtensam, quâ humana CHRISTI natura ubique locorum diffusa & prolongata, & infinitum diducta sit, odiosè nobis obtrudunt, & contra eam ceu statum controversiæ sua deinde argumenta dirigunt. Nam Lutherus aliqvoties, ut & nostrates Theologi prorsus contrarium sæpiùs docuerunt publicè.

V. Aversamur verò & illud Adversariorum delirium, qvando dicunt, nos docere, humanitatem CHRISTI ratione essentiæ esse omnipræsentem & ubique regnare. Docemus, enim & confitemur, humanitatem CHRISTI ratione essentiæ in omnem æternitatem verò finitam esse, suisqve dimensionibus terminatam permanere, & qvantitatem suam dimensam non minùs qvàm alii sancti perpetuò retinere, ab infinito tamen λόγῳ nuspiam esse segregatam.

VI. Neqve tertiò illud concedimus, humanam CHRISTI naturam inclusivè esse omnipræsentem, aut in rebus creatis, in omnibus lignis, lapidibus, herbis, arborum foliis, cantharis cerevisiariis, & id genus locis aliis impuris inclusum esse & contineri. Abhorrent enim Nostrates ab hac inclusione locali, ultrò concedentes, hereticum esse, si qvis cum Schvenckfeldio dicat, corpus CHRISTI esse ubique in omnibus creaturis κατ' ἐσίαν essentialiter: id quod certè contra analogiam fidei est.

VII. Quæ omnia à ματαιολόγοις καὶ φρεναπάτοις, ut D.

Paulus Tit. 1. vocat, eum in finem adducuntur, ut simpliciores decipere, à salutari Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctrinâ, in sacris literis fundatâ, seducere, impio prorsus & fraudulento ore & corde annituntur. VIII. Nunquam enim in mentem venerunt Nostratibus Theologis hæ opiniones, qvas Adversarii ἀπαιδεύτως extra DEI verbum ex proprio ingenio confinxerunt. Qvare dogma illud ut ἑτερόδοξον ab Ecclesiâ exterminamus.

IX. Verùm omissis ipsorum nugis & blasphemiis statum controversiæ genuinum sic proponimus; An Christus sedens ad dextram Patris κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον, ut Basilius loquitur, κατὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα, ut Theodoretus, Athanasius, secundùm humanitatem, ut nos loqvimur, in unitate personæ cum τῷ λόγῳ omnibus creaturis præsenter adsit, vel in toto mundo dominetur? Qvod affirmamus Nos, Calvinistæ negant.

X. Pro confirmanda nostra sententia, argumenta proferimus. I. Expressam literam. 1. Ex V. T. Psal. 110, 1. idq; dupliciter. 1. A forma regnandi. Qvicunq; dominatur in medio inimicorum, ille non est absens, sed omnipræsens. Nam 1. dominatio talis præreqvirit præsentiam, cùm nemo in medio, nisi qvi præsens officium facere possit. Impudens ergò Beza est, dum simile illud à rege Hispaniarum adducit. Maxima n. est differentia regnorum hujus mundi, & regni Christi. 2. Sessio ad dexteram DEI nihil aliud est, qvàm regnare, docente D. Paulo 1. Cor. 15, 25. qvi per τὸ βασιλεύειν explicat. Atqvi Christus secundùm humanam naturam dominatur in medio inimicorum, id qvod συνέπεια textus docet. Imò est κύριος πάντων, Act. 10, 35. E. 2. A sede regni & imperii. Cujus thronus & sedes nullo loco est inclusa, sed omnibus locis superior & ubiq; præsens est, ille ipse nullo loco inclusus, sed ubiq; perfectissimâ actione præsens erit. At thronus, qvem Christus secundum naturam humanam occupavit, est talis, Esa. 40, 12. 48, 13. Ergo. XI. 2. Ex N. T. Ephes. 1, 20. 21. & c. 4, 10. ubi ita licet argumentari: 1. Secundùm qvam naturam Christus est mortuus, resuscitatus, ad cœlum evectus, secundum eam promittit suam præsentiam: id qvod totius textus συνέπεια nobis ob oculos ponit. Atqvi Christus secundum humanam naturam est &c. id qvod ex cohærentia textus, præsertim v. 23. patet, imò ipse Martinius fateri cogitur. E.

XII. 2. Qvi eo fine ascendit ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὀυρανῶν, ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα, is verè præsens est rebus omnibus, eas potenter gubernat. Atqvi Christus secundùm humanam naturam, Ephes. 4. 10. Ergo.

XIII. 3. Qvi omnia implet in omnibus, is qvoqve in propinqvo adest secundùm substantiam, & præsentissimus omnia in omnibus operatur. Nam τὸ implere omnia totum notat dominium Christi ad dextram Patris sedentis, qvia est infinitæ virtutis & potestatis divinæ, id qvod verum ex Adversariorum confessione & testimonio. Atqvi Christus secundùm humanam naturam. Ergo.

XIV. 4. Vox universalis Omnia dicit. Ergò nihil excludit, qvod ad hoc dominium spectat. Ubi 5. phrasis Paulina τὸ πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα notanda, qvæ bis tantùm in N. T. hoc sensu legitur, & certè nihil relinqvit vacuum, qvia qvæ implemus, ea certè præsentiâ nostrâ haud qvaqvam destituuntur. Ergo nuspiam significat absentem alicujus dominationem, sed semper ubiqve notat præsentissimam præsentis operationem supra singulas & universas creaturas in cælo & in terra. Cujus phraseos veritatem vide Jerem. 23, 23. 24. ubi Deo tribuitur.

XV. Pierius qvidem perstringit Clariss. Dn. D. Menzerum præceptorem meum æternùm honorandum, qvasi à Lutheri discederet explicatione. Verùm eruditè planè demonstrat, minimè id fieri.

XVI. Qvidam vocem πληρώσεως de Scripturarum impletione, ut a Bucanus & b Martyr, aut de eâ, quæ ad consummationem officii pertinet, ut c Beza, accipiunt. Ast ἀπροσδιονύσως colligunt, qvia 1. Vox universalis indeterminatè ponitur. 2. Connexio textûs reclamat, siqvidem de gloriâ & majestate dominii Christi agitur, & impletionis superiorum & inferiorum locorum, nempe cæli & terræ fit mentio. 3. Usitatus loqvendi modus, & collatio dicti Ephes. 1, 21. 22. 23. contrariatur, ubi Spiritus Sanctus, qvoties de Scripturarum impletione agit, semper expressè loqvitur & determinatè, ut Matth. 1, 22. Joh. 19, 36. Act. 1, 16. Joh. 13, 18.

XVII. Qvidam de successivâ aliqvorum locorum impletione accipiunt, ratione cujus nunc hæc, nunc illa loca caro Christi impleat. Sed glossa est ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως pugnans cum analogiâ fidei, qvia 1. maxima est detorsio textus. 2. Impletio talis nunquam facta neque futura est.

XIIX. Sunt denique qui de donorum impletione interpretantur, ut Martinius, Sadeel, Ursinus. Verum 1. Universalis vox Omnia, ἀνεπικῶς posita, contradicit. 2. Non idem sunt, omnia implere & donis implere Ecclesiam, sed differunt ut totum & pars. Ab affirmatione autem unius partis ad negationem reliquarum partium ἀπαιδεύτως concluditur. 3. Paulus ipse disjungit, ut vel ipsa textus constructio ostendit, ut eruditè monstrat Rever. & Cl. Dn. D. Menz. &c. Ergo de tali impletione loquitur, ex qua Christus etiam secundum assumtam naturam omnia in omnibus operatur & implet præsenti efficaciâ, quam largissimâ donorum effusione testatam facit.


### XIX. II. Reasons consistent with the analogy of faith

XIX. II. Reasons consistent with the analogy of faith. 1. From the personal union. If the flesh of Christ is inseparably united to the Word, it will nowhere be absent, but everywhere present, both outside and inside the Church, most present to it. But the former is true, because the hypostatic union 1. Does not consist in the mere sustenance of the human nature, as Keckermann maintains. 2. Nor in the mere presence of the Word to the flesh, as the Nestorians maintain. 3. Nor in a presence or gracious indwelling, which is called a spiritual union. 4. Nor in the infusion of habitual graces; but in the most present interpenetration of the natures and the most present presence of the natures. Wherefore the statement of the Calvinists is impious, when they say that the Word is so entirely in the flesh and within the flesh that he is at the same time outside the flesh, Zanchius, Martinius, and others.

XX. 2. From the communication of the hypostasis of the Word. If the Word communicated himself entirely, and his divinity, to the assumed flesh, it is necessary that he also communicated omnipresence. The former is true, because the Calvinists themselves affirm that the human nature of Christ never had its own hypostasis. Therefore.

XXI. From the exaltation of the human nature to the right hand of God. That which sits totally at the right hand of God the Father, which is total, is present with it everywhere, because Holy Scripture describes the right hand of God in such a way that it is not bound to any place, but rather fills all things. The humanity of Christ sits totally at the whole right hand of God. Psalm 110, 1. & Hebrews 1, 3. Keckermann indeed denies the consequence, which even a blind man could see.

Because the right hand of GOD is not a place or any local difference, but is the omnipresent and infinite seat of GOD. Ps. 139, 10.

XXII. III. The consensus both of orthodox antiquity, such as Cyril in book 12 on John, ch. 32, Theophylact on ch. 4 of Ephesians, Oecumenius on the same chapter, Paschasius in his book on the Holy Eucharist, and also of our adversaries, such as Johannes Stapulensis on ch. 14 of John, and the same author on ch. 12 of 1 Corinthians. Indeed, Zanchius himself, driven by the power of heavenly truth, concedes that according to his humanity Christ is personally everywhere.

XXIII. From all of which it is clearly evident, according to the tenor of Scripture, according to reasons consonant with the analogy of faith, and according to the consensus of the Fathers and our adversaries, that Christ according to his humanity is everywhere, even outside the Church.

XXIV. Thus far we have heard that Christ is present to all creatures: now we must move on to the manner of how the flesh of Christ can be present to all things, while preserving the truth, finitude, and circumscription of his body and soul. Which manner indeed must be defined not from the inventions of philosophers, but from the divine Scriptures.

XXV. For what some slanderously claim regarding the infinity and immensity of the essence of Christ's flesh, describing omnipresence through the extension of Christ's body and its multiplication, etc., is a pure and unadulterated dream, born in the brains of those who think wrongly.

XXVI. But away with the invention of a locally expanded nature: Christ is omnipresent according to his human nature in such a way that, nevertheless, that humanity is not removed from the bounds of its essential properties, but remains finite, remains unconfused, remains whole, safe, and inviolate.

XXVII. For the humanity of Christ has a twofold εἶναι (being), both natural and hypostatic: because he is not only man, but at the same time also God in the unity of his person: therefore, according to the distinction of these acts, the human nature of Christ is circumscribed by the limits of its essence, that is, according to the condition and property of its natural act. However, it is not circumscribed by place according to its hypostatic εἶναι (being), or the personal act proper to the Son of GOD, which is really communicated to his humanity.

XXVIII. Just as, therefore, the two acts of the humanity of Christ are not ἀντιδιῃρημένοι (divided against each other) and contradivided, but through an ineffable περι-

χώρησιν are ὑπάλληλοι: thus to be circumscribed by the limits of essence, and not to be circumscribed by an external place, insofar as εἶναι ὑποστατικὸν they do not introduce conditions κατ' ἀλήθειαν opposed.

XXIX. Which is to be noted against Keckermann, who rashly shouts that the opposite of circumscription, namely ἀπεριγραφίαν, is in no way and by no limitation attributed to the body of Christ.

XXX. They agree, therefore, with each other most excellently, nor does any dissension arise from that.

XXXI. When, therefore, the humanity of Christ is said to be omnipresent to all creatures, it happens personally: yet in such a way that a manifold omnipresence is not established. For there is one omnipresence of Christ, and there are not many, in that, according to different respects, it can be considered in one way or another, namely, in one way with respect to the divine nature, in another with respect to the assumed humanity, and in this very humanity it is again considered differently with respect to the state of humiliation, and differently with respect to the state of glory and exaltation.

XXXII. And thus far indeed concerning the true opinion: it remains that we make a transition to the ἀνασκευήν of the impious and erroneous opinion of the χριστομάχων.

XXXIII. Where two hosts offer themselves for the double difference of those who deny omnipresence. For some deny the same ὁλικῶς, as the Jesuits and Calvinists; some deny the same μερικῶς.

XXXIV. The former use these arguments: 1. From the denial of Holy Scripture. Scripture denies the presence of the humanity of Christ in all places. Therefore it is wrongly affirmed. The antecedent is proved from the birth of Christ, and from both states of humiliation and exaltation, Bellarmine, Martinius, Ursinus.

XXXV. Resp. 1. We have demonstrated the contrary above. 2. The consequence is denied, because it is not appropriate to wish to argue from the denial of the second act to the denial of the first. 3. The arguments of the Calvinists drawn from the state of humiliation do not proceed. For κτῆσις is one thing, χρῆσις is another: according to κτῆσις the humanity of Christ did not lack that excellence in the state of humiliation; but according to χρῆσις, after the ascension into heaven, it obtained that plenary usage.

XXXVI. Those words of the Angel in Mark 16, 6. 7. are urged by Nahum, Zanchius, Sohnius, Martyr, Martinius and others, where they have an ὁμόψηφον in this matter

Costerus: From the words of the angel, 'He is not here,' we learn the falsity of the Lutheran heresy, which posits a communication of idioms between the two natures of Christ: as if his humanity were omnipresent, when the angel openly says of it, 'He is not here.'

XXXVII. To which I reply: 1. There are four terms in this inference. The antecedent speaks of the mode of natural and local presence, the consequent of the mode of supernatural and personal presence. 2. The angel correctly concludes from the hypothesis of the women. Therefore, it is a fallacy of 'secundum quid.' For one mode of absence ought not to be opposed to presence in itself and in general: otherwise, the omnipresence of the Son of God would also have to be denied, who was not present by way of conception before the angelic announcement.

XXXVIII. 2. From the condition of human nature. The body of Christ is truly a human body. Therefore, human idioms are predicated of it. Martinius.

XXXIX. Reply: Not only. For it is not merely a human body in the Union itself, as Martinius maintains, but those things are also attributed to it which can by no means be attributed to a body that is otherwise human: such as subsisting in the person of the Son; being one hyphistamenon with the Son of God, etc. It is therefore a fallacy of the consequent.

XL. He does indeed add the reason, 'Because one true human body cannot be in more than one place.' To which I say: 1. This is a philosophical argument opposed to Scripture. For Scripture allows that it is possible for one body to be present in two or more places. 2. Christ, according to his human nature, is said to have ascended above all places, and thus to have transcended all places. Therefore, by this reasoning, he cannot be bound to one single and definite place.

XLI. 3. From Reason. What is simply impossible is possible in no respect. But for human nature to be omnipresent is ἁπλῶς ἀδύνατον (simply impossible). Therefore, Keckermann argues thus.

XLII. Reply: 1. The major premise must be taken with a limitation: Whatever is simply and φυσικῶς (naturally) and ὑπερφυσικῶς (supernaturally), or not only before men but also before God, is impossible, that is δυνατόν (possible) in no respect. And thus the minor premise is denied. 2. By this reasoning, the personal Union would also be impossible for Keckermann. 3. It would also follow that the human nature of Christ is ἰδιοσύστα- (self-subsistent).

τοι, which certain Calvinists deny. 4. And thus it also removes the session of the man Christ at the right hand of God. 6. Indeed, very many absurdities would follow from that, which, on account of the narrowness of the page, it is not permitted to note.

XLIII. 4. From the testimonies of the Fathers, Bellarmine, Lampadius, and others conclude: That this doctrine contradicts all antiquity. Therefore, it is to be rejected. To which I reply briefly: 1. We have shown the contrary above, and because the prince of theologians, Mr. Dr. Chemnitz, in his golden little book on the two natures, chapter 30, has sufficiently dealt with this matter, I do not wish to do what has already been done.

XLIV. I betake myself to the other rank, who have denied the universal presence of Christ, not (as they themselves write and say) because it is impossible, but because it is neither promised in the Scriptures, nor joined with any evident utility.

XLV. But 1. by that very fact, while they concede it to be possible, they posit it. 2. We are forbidden by conscience to assert that it is not held expressed in Scripture. We have brought forward manifest, firm, and immovable sayings above. Ps. 110:1, 2; Eph. 1:2, 3, and ch. 4:10. 3. We produce the Book of Concord, pages 767, 768, and its Apology, page 159. See Mr. Dr. Hutter in F. C., p. 893, etc. 4. We say it is ἀθεόλογον to wish to determine the presence of the θεάνθρωπος by the boundaries of the Christian world.

XLVI. I would add more arguments, if the narrowness of the pages did not stand in the way; therefore, we wish them reserved for the conflict.

XLVII. This meditation, therefore, on universal presence both renders us cautious, so that we may speak and live piously not only concerning Him and the mysteries, lest we fall into sins; and courageous, while we are reminded that Christ is present with us in all miseries and dangers. Which is our greatest dignity, which, rightly weighing, we shall exclaim with Bernard in a Sermon: Whence is this to us, most pious Lord, that we, little worms creeping upon the face of the earth, we, I say, who are dust and ashes, should deserve to have Thee present before our hands, before our eyes, Thou who, whole and entire, sittest at the right hand of the Father, who also in the moment of one hour, from the rising of the sun even to its setting, from the north even to the south, art present to all, one in many, the same in diverse places. To Thee, Christ the θεάνθρωπος, who truly art made τῷ θεῷ σύνθρονος according to Greg. Theol. as referenced by Damasc. l. 3. c. 17, be praise, honor, and thanksgiving, εἰς ἀϊδιον.

Latin:

XIX. II. Rationes analogiæ fidei consonas. 1. Ab unione personali. Si caro Christi ἀδιαςάτως est unita τῷ λόγῳ, nusquam erit absens, sed ubique locorum tam extra quam intra Ecclesiam ei præsentissima. Sed prius est, quia Unio hypostatica 1. Non consistit in nuda sustentatione humanæ naturæ, ut vult Keckermannus. 2. Neque in nuda præsentia λόγου ad carnem, ut volunt Nestoriani. 3. Neque in præsentia, vel inhabitatione gratiosa, quæ unio spiritualis vocatur. 4. Neq; in infusione gratiarum habitualium; sed in præsentissima naturarum περιχωρήσει & præsentissima naturarum præsentia. Quare impium est effatum Calvinianorum, quando dicunt, λόγον ita totus est in carne & intra carnem, ut simul sit extra carnem, Zanchius, Martinius & alii.

XX. 2. Ab ὑποτάσεως τοῦ λόγου communicatione. Si Λόγος seipsum totum, suamque divinitatem assumtæ carni communicavit, necesse est, ut omnipræsentiam quoque communicaverit. Prius est, quia ipsi Calviniani affirmant, humanam Christi naturam nunquam habuisse propriam ὑπόςασιν. Ergo.

XXI. Ab humanæ naturæ ad dextram Dei evectione. Quod totaliter sedet ad dextram Dei Patris totam, illud cum ea ubivis præstò adest, quia S. Scriptura ita describit dextram Dei, quod nulli loco sit alligata, verùm omnia impleat. Humanitas Christi totaliter ad totam DEI dextram sedet. Psal. 110, 1. & Hebr. 1, 3. Conseqventiam quidem negat Keckermannus, quam tamen vel cæcus videre posset.

Qvia dextra DEI non est locus aut ulla localis differentia, sed est omnipræsens & infinita sedes DEI. Psal. 139, 10.

XXII. III. Consensum tum orthodoxæ antiquitatis, ut Cyrilli in l. 12. Joh. c. 32. Theophylacti in c. 4. Eph. Oecumenii in idem cap. Paschasii l. de S. Euchar. tum Adversariorum, ut Johan. Stapulensis in c. 14. Johan. Idem in c. 12. 1. Cor. Imò ipse Zanchius vi veritatis cœlestis adactus, concedit, secundùm humanitatem Christum personaliter ubiqve esse.

XXIII. Ex qvibus omnibus liqvidò patet, secundum Scripturæ tenorem, secundum rationes analogiæ fidei consonas, secundum consensum Patrum & Adversariorum, Christum secundum humanitatem etiam extra Ecclesiam ubiqve esse.

XXIV. Hactenus audivimus, Christum esse omnibus creaturis præsentem: jam transeundum ad modum, qvomodo caro Christi universis præsens esse qveat, salvis corporis animæqve suæ veritate, finitate & circumscriptione. Qvi qvidem modus non ex commentis philosophantium, sed ex divinis Scripturis definiendus est.

XXV. Nam qvod qvidam de infinitate & immensitate essentiæ carnis Christi calumniantur, describentes omnipræsentiam per extensionem corporis Christi & multiplicationem &c. purum putum somnium est, in cerebro malè sentientium natum.

XXVI. Sed facessat localiter expansæ naturæ commentum: Christus ita omnipræsens est secundum humanam naturam, ut nihilominus humanitas illa finibus essentialium proprietatum suarum non removeatur, sed maneat finita, maneat inconfusa, maneat integra, salva & illibata.

XXVII. Humanitas enim Christi duplex εἶναι habet, & naturale & hypostaticum: qvia homo non tantùm homo est, sed simul qvoqve Deus in personæ unitate: idcircò secundum horum actuum distinctionem humana Christi natura sit circumscripta terminis suæ essentiæ, id est, secundum conditionem & proprietatem actus naturalis. Non autem circumscribitur loco secundum εἶναι hypostaticum, vel actum personalem Filii DEI proprium, humanitati realiter communicatum.

XXVIII. Qvemadmodum igitur duo actus humanitatis Christi non sunt ἀντιδιῃρημένοι & contradivisi, sed per ineffabilem περι-

χώρησιν sunt ὑπάλληλοι: ita circumscriptum esse terminis essentiæ, & non circumscribi loco externo, qvoad εἶναι ὑποστατικὸν non subinferunt conditiones κατ' ἀλήθειαν oppositas.

XXIX. Qvod notandum contra Keckermannum, qvi temerè vociferatur, oppositum circumscriptionis, ἀπεριγραφίαν scilicet, nullo modo & limitatione tribui corpori Christi.

XXX. Conveniunt igitur inter se optimè, neqve ulla inde emergit dissensio.

XXXI. Qvando ergo humanitas Christi omnipræsens dicitur omnibus creaturis, fit illud personaliter: ita tamen ut non multiplex statuatur omnipræsentia. Una n. est Christi omnipræsentia, & non plures sunt, eô, qvòd secundum diversos respectus aliter atq; aliter considerari possit, nempe aliter respectu divinæ naturæ, aliter respectu humanitatis assumtæ, & in hâc ipsâ humanitate illam rursum aliter in respectu status exinanitionis, aliter respectu status gloriæ & exaltationis.

XXXII. Et hactenus qvidem de vera sententia: restat ut ad ἀνασκευήν opinionis impiæ & erroneæ χριστομάχων transitum faciamus.
