XXXIII. Ubi duo sese offerunt agmina pro duplici differentiâ eorum, qvi omnipræsentiam negant. Qvidam n. ὁλικῶς eandem negant, ut Jesuitæ & Calviniani; Qvidam eandem μερικῶς.

XXXIV. Priores his utuntur argumentis: 1. A negatione S. Scripturæ. Scriptura negat humanitatis Christi præsentiam in omnibus locis. Ergo ea perperam affirmatur. Antecedens probatur ex nativitate Christi, & utroq; statu exinanitionis & exaltationis, Bellarm. Martinius, Ursinus.

XXXV. Resp. 1. Contrarium superius demonstravimus. 2. Negatur conseqventia, qvia ab actus secundi negatione ad negationem primi argumentari velle, non est congruum. 3. Argumenta Calvinianorum ducta à statu exinanitionis non procedunt. Aliud enim est κτῆσις, aliud χρῆσις: Secundum κτῆσιν humanitas Christi excellentiâ illâ in statu exinationis non caruit; secundum χρῆσιν verò post ascensionem in cælum plenariam illam usurpationem adepta est.

XXXVI. Illa Angeli verba Marci 16, 6. 7. urget Nahum, Zanchius, Sohnius, Martyr, Martinius & alii, ubi hac in re habent ὁμόψηφον

Costerum: Ex verbis angeli, Non est hic, discimus falsitatem Lutheranæ hæresis, quæ idiomatum communicationem ponit inter duas naturas Christi: quasi humanitas omnipræsens sit, cùm apertè angelus de ea dicat, Non est hic.

XXXVII. Qvibus Resp. 1. Qvatuor sunt termini in hac illatione. Antecedens de modo præsentiæ naturali atqve locali, conseqvens de modo præsentiæ supernaturali & personali loqvitur. 2. Rectè concludit angelus ex hypothesi mulierum. Fallacia igitur à dicto secundum qvid. Unus enim modus absentiæ, præsentiæ per se & in genere opponi non debet: aliás etiam omnipræsentia Filii DEI esset abneganda, qvi ante nuncium angelicum per modum conceptionis non adfuit.

XXXVIII. 2. A conditione humanæ naturæ. Corpus Christi verè est humanum corpus. Ergò Idiomata humana de illo prædicantur. Martinius.

XXXIX. Resp. Non tantùm. Nam non merè humanum corpus est in ipsâ Unione, ut vult Martinius, verùm ea etiam attribuuntur, qvæ minimè corpori aliàs humano tribui possunt: ut subsistere in persona Filii; Cum Filio DEI unum esse hyphistamenon, &c. Est igitur fallacia conseqventis.

XL. Addit qvidem rationem, Qvia unum corpus verum humanum non possit esse nisi uno in loco. Ad qvam dico, 1. Esse argumentum philosophicum Scripturæ oppositum. Nam Scriptura permittit, posse fieri, ut unum corpus possit esse præsens in duobus pluribusve locis. 2. Christus secundùm humanam naturam dicitur scandisse super omnes locos, & sic omnia loca transcendisse. Ergo hac ratione uni semper & definito loco astringi neqvit.

XLI. 3. Ex Ratione. Qvod simpliciter est impossibile, illud nullo respectu sit possibile. Atqvi humanam naturam esse omnipræsentem, est ἁπλῶς ἀδύνατον. E. Ita Keckermannus argumentatur.

XLII. Resp. 1. Limitatè major sumenda est: Qvicqvid simpliciter & φυσικῶς & ὑπερφυσικῶς; vel non tantùm coram hominibus, sed etiam coram DEO etiam est impossibile, illud nullo respectu sit δυνατόν. Atqve ita negatur minor. 2. Hac ratione etiam Keckermanno Unio personalis esset impossibilis. 3. Seqveretur etiam, humanam CHRISTI naturam esse ἰδιοσύστα-

τοι, qvod Calviniani qvidam negant. 4. Et sic qvoqve tollit sessionem Christi hominis ad dextram Dei. 6. Imò qvam plurima seqverentur inde absurda, qvæ propter chartę angustiã annotare non licet.

XLIII. 4. Ex testimoniis Patrum Bellarminus, Lampadius & alii concludunt: Doctrinam hanc toti antiquitati contradicere. Ergo esse rejiciendam. Cui breviter Resp. 1. Contrarium suprà monstravimus, & qvia princeps Theologorum Dn. D. Chemnitius de duab. nat. cap. 30. in aureo libello sufficienter egit hac de re, actum agere nolò.

XLIV. Ad alterum agmen me confero, qvi universalem Christi præsentiam negarunt, non(ut ipsi scribunt & dicunt) qvòd ea impossibilis sit, sed qvòd ea neqve in Scripturis promissa: neq; etiam cum evidenti aliqva utilitate conjuncta sit.

XLV. Verùm 1. eo ipso dum possibilem esse concedunt, illam ponunt. 2. In Scriptura expressam non haberi, conscientia prohibemur, ut nos asseramus. Manifesta, firma & immota suprà protulimus dicta. Ps. 110. 1. 2. Eph. 1, 2. 3. & c. 4, 10. 3. Producimus Librum Concordiæ, pag. 767. 768. & ejus Apologiam, pag. 159. Videatur Dn. D. Hutterus in F. C. p. 893. &c. 4. Α᾿θεόλογον, esse dicimus, præsentiam θεανθρώπου orbis Christiani pomeriis determinare velle.

XLVI. Plura adderem argumenta, nisi pagellarum obstaret angustia, ea idcircò cnnflictui reservata volumus.

XLVII. Hæc ergo meditatio præsentiæ universalis, & cautos nos reddit, ut non tantùm de ipso, deqve mysteriis piè loqvamur, & vivamus, ne in peccata prolabamur; & animosos, dum Christum nobiscum in omnibus miseriis & periculis præstò esse monemur. Qvæ maxima est nostra dignitas, qvam rectè expendentes exclamabimus cum Bernhardo in Serm: Unde hoc nobis, piissime Domine, ut nos vermiculi reptantes super faciem terræ, nos, inqvam, qvi pulvis & cinis sumus, te præsentem habere mereamur præ manibus, præ oculis, qvi totus & integer sedes ad dextram Patris, qvi etiam unius horæ momento ab ortu Solis usqve ad occasum, ab aqvilone usqve ad austrum, præsto es omnibus, unus in multis, idem in diversis locis. Tibi Christo θεανθρώπῳ, qvi verè es τῷ θεῷ σύνθρονος secundùm Greg. Theol. referente Damasc. l. 3. c. 17. factus, sit laus, honor & gratiarum actio, εἰς ἀϊδιον.


## 22 Twenty-second Disputation, On the Religious Adoration of the Flesh of Christ

We have already discussed the three idioms or majestic gifts communicated to the flesh of Christ by the Logos: Omnipotence, Omniscience, and Omnipresence. The order requires that we now deal with the fourth, namely, the Religious Cult of Adoration; which is an axiom necessarily following the real communication of divine majesty(a): and as an effect of the first three idioms(b). Since, therefore, this matter is arduous and of great importance, it must be handled σοφῶς καὶ σαφῶς (wisely and clearly). That this may be done, we shall direct our course toward this cynosure. I. We shall explain what this cult of adoration comprises. II. We shall form the state of the controversy. III. We shall prove the orthodox opinion κατασκευαστικῶς (constructively). IV. We shall reject the ἑτεροδοξίαν & φλυαρίας (heterodoxy and babblings) of the adversaries ἀνασκευαστικῶς (destructively). And finally, V. We shall append a Practical Meditation. May God, kind to our beginnings, descend upon our efforts.

Thesis I.

CHAPTER I.

L. Valla derives 'adorare' (to adore) from 'ad' and 'orare' (to pray). To pray, however, is to entreat with the mouth; just as to supplicate is to seek something by folding the head to the knee. In this manner, therefore, adoration is nothing other than the invocation of another and the imploring of aid.

II. Moreover, the word 'adoration' is ἐκ τῶν πολλαχῶς λεγομένων (one of those things said in many ways), and it is accepted in various ways in Scripture. 1. Broadly, for any political cult and external action of the body, exhibited for the sake of reverence even to creatures: thus it is used in Gen. 19:11, ch. 23:7, 12, ch. 33:3, ch. 42:6, ch. 43:26. Hence for the Hebrews, שׁחה (shachah) is to depress oneself, to bow down; for the Greeks, προσκυνεῖν (proskynein) is to prostrate oneself like a humble little dog at the feet of a master(a).

III. 2. Strictly; for religious cult: and this is either improperly, for the external cult of the body, which is done by act and gesture; in this sense it is used in Psalm 95:6, Matthew 2:11. Or properly, for the internal cult of the mind, by which the intellect acknowledges its own unworthiness and the majesty of GOD: but the will thoroughly subjects and submits itself to GOD, by suppliantly seeking necessary goods, and by giving thanks for those received.

IV. So many, therefore, are the meanings of the word Adoration that occur in the Holy Scriptures: and consequently the distinction of the Papists, (b) of divine worship into λατρείαν, which is divine excellence, and δουλείαν, which is intermediate between divine and human, is frivolous.

V. For Scripture itself, the Fathers, (c) profane writers, (d) use these words indiscriminately: Latria is attributed to men in Deut. 28, 28; Lev. 23, 8; δουλεία to God in Rom. 12, 11; 16, 18; Acts 20, 19. But the distinction was only invented and accepted in later centuries, which not even Bellarmine himself can deny (e).

VI. That impious and idolatrous [distinction] into δουλείαν properly so called, and ὑπερδουλείαν; of which the former is attributed to all other saints, the latter to the humanity of Christ and his mother, concerning which [we shall speak] a little later in the antithesis itself.

VII. A synonym for Religious Adoration is Invocation. Therefore, the Papists are wrong to wish to separate it from Adoration on the grounds that the latter pertains to God alone, while the former is common to God and creatures. For Scripture holds both of these as one and the same, even if in another respect some distinction between them may be admitted. For what is said in Deut. 6, 13, "Worship your one God," is expressed in Ps. 50, 15, "Call upon me": what is stated in Ps. 72, 11, "All kings worshipped him," is enunciated in Rom. 10, 13, "whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord."

VIII. This being established, there also falls that excessive ἀκρίβεια of Schmalz (a), by which he maintains that the adoration of Christ is indeed commanded, but not likewise the invocation, yet that it can be performed by a Christian man because it includes the invocation of the Father. Unless perhaps by Adoration he understands only external worship, which the Calvinist Perkins does (b).

IX. When, therefore, it is asked, is the flesh of Christ to be worshipped? On the part of the predicate, we understand by adoration divine worship, due to God alone, including invocation or the petition of necessary goods, and thanksgiving: not civil or external reverence; or the Papal ὑπερδουλείαν, intermediate between divine and civil; or some Calvinist adoration, which is in any way inferior to that which is due to God.

Latin:

TRia Idiomata sive dona Majestatica carni Christi à λόγω communicata habuimus, Omnipotentiam, Omniscientiam, & Omnipræsentiam. Reqvisit ordo, ut de qvarto jamnunc agamus, nimirum de Cultu Adorationis Religioso; qvi est axioma realem majestatis divinæ communicationem necessario conseqvens(a): & tanqvam effectus priorum trium idiomatum (b). Cùm igitur ardua & magni momenti hæc res sit, σοφῶς καὶ σαφῶς agendum. Qvod ut fiat, ad hanc cynosuram cursum nostrum dirigemus. I. Qvid complectatur iste Adorationis cultus explicabimus. II. Statum Controversiæ formabimus. III. Orthodoxam sententiam κατασκευαστικῶς probabimus. IV. Adversariorum ἑτεροδοξίαν & φλυαρίας ἀνασκευαστικῶς rejiciemus. Et tandem V. Meditationem Practicam subjiciemus. Almæ Deus nostris clemens allabere cœptis.

Thesis I.

CAPUT I.

ADorare deducit L. Valla ab ad & orare. Orare autem est ore precari; sicut supplicare est plicando caput ad genu aliqvid petere. Hoc igitur pacto adoratio nihil est aliud, qvàm alterius invocatio & auxilii imploratio.

II. Est autem vocabulum adorationis ἐκ τῶν πολλαχῶς λεγομένων, & diversimodè in scriptura accipitur. 1. Latè, pro qvovis cultu Politico & externâ corporis actione, reverentiæ causâ etiam creaturis exhibitâ: ita usurpatur, Gen. 19, 11. c. 23, 7. 12. c. 33, 3. C. 42, 6. c. 43, 26. Hinc Hebræis שׁחה sese deprimere, incurvare: Græcis προσκυνεῖν, sese instar humilis catelli ad pedes domini provolvere (a).

III. 2. Strictè; pro cultu religioso: idq; vel impropriè, pro cultu corporis externo, qvi fit actu & gestu; In hoc sensu usurpatur Psalm. 95, 6. Matth. 2, 11. vel propriè, pro cultu animi interno, qvo intellectus suam indignitatem, DEI majestatem agnoscit: voluntas verò sese DEO penitùs subjicit & submittit, suppliciter bona necessaria petendo, & pro acceptis gratias agendo.

IV. Tot igitur significationes vocabuli Adorationis in sacro codice occurrunt: ac proinde frivola est Pontificiorum, (b) cultus divini in λατρείαν, quæ sit excellentia divina, & δουλείαν, quæ media sit inter divinam & humanam, distinctio.

V. Ipsa enim Scriptura, Patres, (c) profani scriptores, (d) his vocabulis indistinctè utuntur: Latria hominibus tribuitur Deut. 28, 28. Lev. 23, 8. δουλεία Deo Rom. 12, 11. c. 16, 18. Act. 20, 19. Discrimen verò posterioribus demum seculis inventum & receptum, quod nec ipse Bellarminus diffiteri potest (e).

VI. Impia illa & Idololatrica, in δουλείαν propriè dictam, & ὑπερδουλείαν; quarum illa tribuatur omnibus sanctis cæteris, ista humanitati Christi & matri ejus, de qua paulò pòst in ipsâ ἀντιθέσει.

VII. Synonymum Religiosæ Adorationis est Invocatio. Malè igitur Papicolæ ipsam discretam volunt ab Adoratione in eo, quod illa soli Deo competat; hæc Deo & creaturis sit communis. Scriptura enim ambo hæc pro uno & eodé habet, utut alio respectu quædam distinctio inter ea admitti possit. Quod enim Deut. 6, 13. dicitur; Unum Deum tuum adora, id Ps. 50, 15. effertur, Invoca me: quod Ps. 72, 11. Adoraverunt eum omnes reges, enunciatur Rom. 10, 13. qui invocaverit nomen Domini.

VIII. Qvo posito cadit & illa Schmalzii (a) nimia ἀκρίβεια, quâ statuit adorationem qvidem Christi esse præceptam: sed non item invocationem, eam tamen è Christiano homine fieri posse, qvia Patris invocationem includat. Nisi fortè per Adorationem tantùm intelligit cultum externum, qvod facit Perkinsius Calvinianus (b).

IX. Qvando igitur qværitur, num caro Christi sit adoranda? Ex parte prædicati intelligimus per adorationem cultum divinum, soli Deo debitum, invocationem sive petitionem bonorum necessariorum, & gratiarum actionem includentem: non civilem aut externam reverentiam; vel Pontificiam ὑπερδουλείαν inter divinam & civilem mediam; aut Calvinianam aliqvam adorationem, qvæ sit illi, qvæ Deo debetur, qvocunque modo inferior.


### Chapter II. X. Therefore, so that the state of the controversy may be correctly formed, it…

CHAPTER II.

X. Therefore, so that the state of the controversy may be correctly formed, it must be investigated on the part of the subject, what is the genuine Object of the adoration of Christ. Is it the sole Deity of the Word to whom the flesh is united? Or is it at the same time the Flesh or Human Nature assumed into the Unity of the Person of the Word? Concerning the former there is no controversy: for who would reach such a point of absurdity as to deny that the λόγον Assumentem [the assuming Word] is adorable? And hence it is that not only the Orthodox, but also the Papists and Calvinists, derive very frequent and most solid arguments from the cult of adoration to prove and demonstrate the Deity of Christ against the Photinians.

XI. The latter comes into controversy. For the Lutherans maintain that the Humanity or Flesh of Christ is to be adored with the λόγῳ [Word] by one and the same adoration. But the adversaries partly deny it outright, and partly contend that it is to be adored by another, slightly inferior, manner.

XII. Where, however, it must be known beforehand that the Lutherans do not here understand the Flesh or Human Nature of Christ by itself, in itself, and according to itself, considered in the abstract outside the Union: but always argue for it in the concrete, insofar as it has been assumed by the Son of GOD into the Unity of Person. They do not maintain that it is by itself, by its own nature, by the property of its nature, naturally, essentially, and πρώτως [primarily] adorable: but only κατ' ἄλλο [by another], δευτέρως [secondarily], personally, through and because of the Union, as Cyril and Damascenus have spoken.

XIII. The state of the controversy is therefore this: Whether Christ is to be invoked with religious worship of adoration not only as GOD, but also as Man, or according to his Human Nature, yet considered in the Union, and thus whole according to both Natures?

XIV. We lay down these foundations for the affirmative and Orthodox opinion: I. The prophecies which predicted that Christ the man was to be adored not only by men, but also by angels: Ps. 22:30, Ps. 72:11, Is. 45:23, ch. 49:7, ch. 60:6, Dan. 7:14. The Apostle applies these prophecies to the flesh of Christ in Phil. 2:10. For he says that this name, so that all things above, on earth, and below may adore him, was given, and indeed out of grace, which the word χαρίζεσθαι [to grant as a favor] shows: that it is a consequence of the Passion and Death: that Christ was exalted through it, and made more excellent than the angels: all of which can in no way be understood of the divine nature of Christ.

XV. II. The commands by which the Church is moved to adore Christ the Lord according to both natures, and is enticed by the promise of being heard and of help, by GOD in Ps. 45:12, by Christ himself in John 14:13, 14, John 16:23, 24, by the Prophets and Apostles in Ps. 97:7, Acts 22:16, Rom. 10:13, Heb. 4:15, 16.

XVI. III. Examples of the pious, who in the New Testament directed the worship of adoration to the whole Christ, such as the Magi Matt. 2, 11. the leper & the centurion Matt. 8, 2. 5. Luke 17, 15. 16. 19. The Canaanite woman Matt. 15, 25. The father of the lunatic Matt. 17, 14. Jairus Mark 5, 23. The blind man Luke 18, 37. Of the Apostles, Matt. 14, 33. chap. 28, 17. & of the Martyrs, Thomas, John 20, 26. Paul, Rom. 1, 7. 1. Corinthians 1, 3. 2. Thessalonians 3, 16. 18. & elsewhere, John, Apoc. 1, 5. Stephen, Acts 7, 59. Of the Church Triumphant & the heavenly host Apoc. 5, 12. 13. nay, even of the demons themselves, Mark 3, 11. chap. 5, 6.

XVII. Reasons: because Christ never rejected this honor; but rather accepted and approved it, and helped those imploring his aid: because in the lowest state of Humiliation he was adored, therefore much more shall he be adored now in the state of Exaltation: because according to both natures he is Redeemer, Mediator, Lord: because Christ as man, about to celebrate the judgment of the whole world, possesses supreme majesty, John 5, 27. Phil. 2, 10. supreme power Matt. 28, 18. because according to his human nature he is to bless us, Genesis 22, 18. Acts 3, 26. because finally according to the nature in which he was tempted, according to that he will help, Heb. 2, 18. All of which things evidently prove that the Flesh of Christ, together with the λόγῳ, ought to be worshipped with one and the same adoration and invocation.

XVIII. V. Testimony of antiquity. For the ancient Church has always professed and embraced this opinion. Thus the Council of Ephesus decreed (a). Thus Athanasius (b) taught, thus Cyril, (c) Chrysostom, (d) Damascene (e) Augustine, (f) & others, as cited by D. Sigwart in his admonition on Irenaeus Part page 628. & following. Gesner in disputation 13. on the F. C. p. 335.

XIX. Our opinion having been confirmed, we must see what the adversaries maintain, who in this controversy are threefold: Papists, Calvinists, & Photinians: for we do not care for the others who wander outside the boundaries of the Church.

XX. The Scholastics therefore and the more recent Papists think that both Natures in Christ are indeed to be adored; but with a double worship: one of which is directed to the divinity and is called λατρεία: the other to the humanity alone and the mother of Christ, and is designated as ὑπερδυλεία. For thus Bellarmine (a), Bede (b), and P. Lombard (c) think.

XXI. But a most absurd tearing apart of the Person of Christ follows from this opinion. For if in that worship there is one respect for his divinity and another for his humanity, a double object of adoration is given: and no longer is one person left; but two are made, which require different worships and different trust (a). For as Christ is one, so faith is one. And because adoration arises from faith, there will be one and the same religious and Christian adoration. Conversely, where there is double adoration, there is double faith, there is a double person.

XXII. Nor can the evasion help them: that the adoration is indeed one in number, but different in degree and respect toward the two natures. For adoration is not founded in each nature, nor is it attributed to each by itself: but it has its foundation in the Deity alone: it is attributed to the Humanity κατ' ἄλλο on account of the Personal Union. With which Thomas agrees (b).

XXIII. And just as on account of the Trinity of Persons a triple worship and adoration is not attributed to the one divine Essence, because the foundation of that worship is the Deity itself, not the distinction of the Persons; so in CHRIST, on account of the duality of Natures, adoration is not doubled, but remains one, on account of the unity of the Person, who is truly GOD, and in whom the Deity and Humanity subsist.

XXIV. The Calvinist Martinius emulates this Jesuitical madness. Hence in the defense of Sadeel against Menzer (from whom, however, he and his other associates make a divorce), these choice flowers are found: 'The honor and reverence which ought to be exhibited to CHRIST is twofold: one appropriate to the λόγῳ, the other to his flesh or Humanity.' p. 86 and following. Because humanity is not Deity. Therefore it is not to be adored as the latter is. See Menzer most learnedly disputing about this controversy against Martinius (a).

XXV. One thing against the Jesuit still deserves admonition. For he shamefully contradicts himself: while here he denies λατρείαν to the flesh of Christ; but to his body in his own feigned and bread-transubstantiated Sacrament, for the sake of establishing his own ἀρτολατρείαν, he attributes the same: (b) nay, even to the Council of Trent itself, which attributes λατρείαν [worship] to the Sacrament (c).

XXVI. The Calvinists next present themselves: of these likewise, as of every many-sided lie, there is not one order. Some act openly, and take away all adoration from the flesh of Christ entirely. L. Danaeus acts as the leader and primary defender. Hence he pronounces all those to be cursed Nestorian idolaters who adore Christ according to the flesh, even while it remains in personal union (d); nay, he holds the adoration of the flesh of Christ in the very same place as the idolatrous invocation of Mary and the rest of the saints (a).

XXVII. He posits the blasphemous reasons for his opinion. I. From Jeremiah 17:5: Cursed is that man who has trust in man, and makes flesh his arm. The flesh of Christ is true flesh. Therefore, cursed is he who directs adoration to the flesh of Christ. Response 1. There are four terms in this syllogism: for the major premise speaks of such a man as Jeremiah describes in verse 9; the minor premise speaks of the man Christ, not naked or fallacious, but who is God, and of whom it is written: Whoever trusts in you shall not be confounded, Rom. 9, last verse. 2. He commits the fallacy of composition and division. For he omits the words which were to be added from the Prophet, and leaves God in his heart. Now, he who pursues and adores the human nature, subsisting and considered in the very person of the Word with religious worship, has not left God, with whom the flesh is one person. 3. Finally, we retort against the adversary himself verse 6 and following. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and whose trust is the Lord. Therefore, blessed is he whose trust is Christ, as God and man.

XXVIII. II. He draws from the statement in Galatians 4:8: Those who serve those who by nature are not gods are idolaters. Those who adore the flesh of Christ do this. Therefore. Response: Again there are four terms. The major premise speaks of fictitious gods and idols; the minor premise speaks of the flesh of Christ in its God-manhood, which to count among the number of idols is of the highest and extreme blasphemy.

XXIX. III. Those who adore fellow servants, and those who are of the brethren, are rebuked by an Angel, Apoc. 19:10 and 22:8. But Christ is our fellow servant and brother. Therefore. Response: The major premise speaks of a naked creature, namely an angel: the minor premise of Christ, who is not only our fellow servant, but also Lord, even in the lowest state of his humiliation, Luke 2:11, John 13:13, Phil. 2:6 and following.

XXX. IV. God alone is to be adored. The flesh of Christ is not God. Resp. The consequence is invalid, because religious adoration is attributed to the humanity not καθ' αὑτὸ [in itself] but κατ' ἄλλο [in another] & by donation: not because it has been made God, but because it is personally united to God & received into the ταυτότητα [identity] of the Person, for which reason Damascenus calls it ὁμόθεον [co-divine].

XXXI. V. He who invokes a creature is blasphemous against God. Deut. 4, 6. 10. Matth. 4, 10. The flesh of Christ, even glorified and remaining in the union of the person, is a creature. E. R. There is an ambiguity in the word Creature: in the Proposition it is taken as an absolute and naked creature; in the Assumption, of such a creature which, having been made one person with the creator himself, is indeed the creator himself. This is what Polanus (a) and Bucanus (b), fellow countrymen of Danaeus himself, confess.

XXXII. VI. Rom. 9, 5. Paul explains by reason of which nature the honor of Christ is to be attributed, namely insofar as he is God blessed above all. Resp. 1. It is ignorance of the refutation. For Paul does not even mention adoration there by a syllable, but treats only incidentally of the person of Christ. Then 2. there is no consequence: Christ is God blessed forever. Therefore Christ born of the Fathers according to the flesh is not blessed.

XXXIII. VII. Isa. 42, 8. I will not give my glory to another. The flesh of Christ is another. E. Resp. briefly, in Christ there is not ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος [another and another], but ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο [one thing and another]. Therefore, when God communicates the glory of adoration to the human nature personally united through the Union, he does not give it to another, but to his own humanity.

XXXIV. VIII. He says it is the error of Nestorius to adore Christ as he is man together with the Word. Resp. Nestorius does not say that the Human Nature of Christ subsisting in the Person of the Word is to be adored with one λατρείᾳ [worship] with the Word: but that the man Christ is to be adored together with the Word as one with another. Of which error certain Papists and Calvinists could be accused without injustice.

XXXV. Finally, Rungius in private college disputation 3, disputation 5, Gefnerus in disputation 13 on the F. C., and Siguvartus in his admonition against the Irenicon of Pareus, who [is] living, examine the Testimonies of the Fathers which he cites and strives to distort to his own sense.

XXXVI. Thus far, therefore, we have had the first order of the Calvinist flock, who simply deny Adoration to the flesh of Christ. To whom not without reason are those numbered who withhold from Christ even the external reverence of genuflection and uncovering the head, as Calvin (a) and many others do in daily practice.

XXXVII. Another order, having learned to cover the wolf with a sheep's skin and to deceive the simpler folk, pretends that adoration was never denied to the flesh of Christ by its accomplices. Hence some (a) grant it to the Humanity of Christ not because of a real communication of divine majesty, but because of the grace of the Union. Others (b) say that the worship of adoration pertains to duty, and thus they think the whole Christ is to be adored according to both natures. Others (c) grant that the flesh of Christ is to be adored with one adoration together with the Deity, but lest they be forced to affirm that the remaining ἀξιώματα (axioms/prerogatives) of divinity have been communicated to it, they deny that adoration is an essential property of God; which, as it can be granted in its own way, so if it is urged for this purpose, for which the adversaries bring it forward, we do not simply admit it. Finally, others (d) determine that the decision of this question is to be reserved for a Council, in this nicely conspiring with the Papists. The narrowness of the paper does not allow us to refute them all in detail.

XXXVIII. The Photinians are also divided in two. Franciscus Davidis denied adoration to Christ plainly and fully, with his fellow tribesmen Blandrata (e) and Socinus (f) contradicting him. The moderns grant it to Christ the man, lest they be forced to confess his Deity: yet in such a way that a pious person may adore Christ with God the Father; meanwhile, he is not bound to do so: nay rather, the adoration is equally good, whether Christ is co-adored or not.

XXXIX. Then they determine that Scripture gives a reminder for the adoration of Christ, meanwhile that it was never commanded, nor could it ever have been commanded, as if indeed the reminders of Scripture, of Christ, and of the Apostles, which Schmalzius (a) concedes, were not praetorian edicts for all true Christians. Since these fabrications rest upon a false hypothesis, as if anything could be religiously adored which is not God, and since they were invented for the sake of overturning the deity of Christ, I judge them unworthy of correction, and deservedly, because of the pages filled, we remit them to the course of the disputation.

XL. In place of a conclusion, this discussion can bring us the sweetest consolation in all calamities: If you suffer, pious soul, approach with firm confidence not to a severe judge, but to a sincere brother, and implore help: you will not suffer a refusal, he is flesh of our flesh, one of our brothers. When the brothers had worshipped Joseph, his compassion for his brothers grew warm, and he sought to weep. Much more will Christ, our most loving brother, open the bowels of mercy to us as we supplicate, and will assist us with his help. A brother cannot deny any duty to a brother: and our heavenly brother Amen.

Latin:

CAP. II.

X. Proinde ut status controversiæ rectè formetur, ex parte subjeEti investigandum, qvodnam sit genuinum adorationis Christi Objectum. An sola Deitas Λόγου cui caro unita? An simul Caro sive Humana Natura in Unitatem Personæ τοῦ Λόγου assumta? De priori nulla est controversia: qvis enim eo absurditatis perveniret, ut λόγον Assumentem adorabilem esse inficias iret? Atq; hinc est, qvod non solùm Orthodoxi, verùm etiam Pontificii & Calviniani ad probandam & demonstrandam contra Photinianos Deitatem Christi argumenta ex adorationis cultu deducunt creberrima & solidissima.

XI. Posterius in controversiam venit. Statuunt enim Lutherani Humanitatem seu Carnem Christi cum λόγῳ esse adorandam unâ eâdemq; adoratione. Adversarii verò partim planè negant, partim aliâ ratione paulò inferiori adorandam contendunt.

XII. Ubi tamen præcognoscendum, Lutheranos Carnem sive Humanam Naturam Christi hîc non intelligere per se, in se, & secundùm se extra Unionem in abstracto consideratam: sed semper disputare pro eâ in Concreto, quatenus à Filio DEI in Unitatem Personæ assumpta est. Non statuere eam per se, ex sua natura, proprietate suæ naturæ, naturaliter, essentialiter & πρώτως esse adorabilem: verùm duntaxat κατ' ἄλλο, δευτέρως, Personaliter, per & propter Unionem, ut Cyrillus & Damascenus locuti sunt.

XIII. Est ergo status controversiæ iste. An Christus non tantùm ut DEUS, verùm etiam ut Homo, seu secundum Humanam Naturam, in Unione tamen consideratam, & sic totus secundùm utramqve Naturam, cultu adorationis Religioso sit invocandus?

XIV. Affirmativæ & Orthodoxæ sententiæ fundamenta ponimus ista: I. Vaticinia, qvæ Christum hominem adorandum prædixerunt non tantùm ab hominibus, sed & ab angelis: Ps. 22, 30. Ps. 72, 11. Es. 45, 23. c. 49, 7. c. 60, 6. Dan. 7, 14. Qvæ vaticinia ad carnem Christi accommodat Apostolus Phil 2, 10. Dicit enim nomen istud, ut adorent eum omnia supera, terrestria & infera, datum esse, & qvidem ex gratia, qvod vocabulum χαρίζεσθαι ostendit: esse conseqvens Passionis & Mortis: Christum per id exaltatum esse, & præstantiorem factum angelis: qvæ omnia de divinâ Christi naturâ minimè intelligi possunt.

XV. II. Mandata, qvibus Ecclesia ad Christum Dominum secundùm utramq; naturam adorandum commovetur, & promissione exauditionis & auxilii allicitur, à DEO Psal. 45, 12. ab ipso Christo, Johan. 14, 13. 14. Joh. 16, 23. 24. à Prophetis & Apostolis Psal. 97, 7. Act. 22, 16. Rom. 10, 13. Hebr. 4, 15. 16.

XVI. III. Exempla piorum, qui in Novo Testamento cultum adorationis direxerunt ad totum Christum, ut Magi Matth. 2, 11. leprosus & centurio Matth. 8, 2. 5. Luc. 17, 15. 16. 19. Mulier Cananæa Matt. 15, 25. Pater Lunatici Matth. 17, 14. Jairus Marc. 5, 23. Cœcus Luc. 18, 37. Apostolorum, Matth. 14, 33. cap. 28, 17. & Martyrum, Thomæ, Johan. 20, 26. Pauli, Rom. 1, 7. 1. Corinth. 1, 3. 2. Thessal. 3, 16. 18. & alibi, Johannis, Apoc. 1, 5. Stephani, Actor. 7, 59. Ecclesiæ Triumphantis & cœlestis militiæ Apoc. 5, 12. 13. imò ipsorum dæmoniorum, Marc. 3, 11. cap. 5, 6.

XVII. Rationes: quia Christus hunc honorem nunquam repudiavit; quin potiùs acceptavit, & approbavit, auxilioķ; implorantibus subvenit: quia in statu Exinanitionis infimo adoratus est, ideò multò magis jam in statu Exaltationis adorabitur: quia secundùm utramq; naturam est Redemtor, Mediator, Dominus: quia Christus homo judicium totius orbis celebraturus summam habet majestatem, Johan. 5, 27. Phil. 2, 10. supremam potentiam Matth. 28, 18. quia secundùm humanam naturam nobis benedicturus est, Genes. 22, 18. Actor. 3, 26. quia deniq; secundùm quam naturam tentatus est, secundùm eam opitulabitur, Hebr. 2, 18. Quæ omnia evidenter probant, Carnem Christi simul cum λόγῳ unâ eademque adoratione ac invocatione coli debere.

XVIII. V. Testimonium antiquitatis. Hanc enim sententiam prisca Ecclesia semper professa & exosculata est. Ita Concilium Ephesinum sancivit (a). Ita Athanasius (b) docuit, ita Cyrillus, (c) Chrysostomus, (d) Damascenus (e) Augustinus, (f) & alii, citante D. Sigvvarto in admon. de Iren. Par. pag. 628. & seq. Gesnero disput. 13. in F. C. p. 335.

XIX. Confirmatâ nostrâ sententiâ videndum quid adversarii statuant, qui in hac controversia triplices, Pontificii, Calviniani & Photiniani: cæteros enim extra pomœria Ecclesiæ vagabundos non curamus.

XX. Scholastici igitur & recentiores Papicolæ, utramq; Naturam in Christo adorandam quidem putant; sed cultu duplici: quorum unus dirigitur ad divinitatem & λατρεία dicitur: alter ad humanitatem solam & matrem Christi, & ὑπερδυλεία indigitatur. Ita enim sentit Bellarminus (a), Beda (b), P. Lombardus. (c)

XXI. Verùm absurdissima ex hac opinione sequitur Personæ Christi divulsio. Nam si in isto cultu alius est respectus ad divinitaté ipsius, ali⁹ ad humanitatem, geminum dàtur objectum adorationis: nec ampliùs una relinquitur persona; sed duæ fiunt, quæ diversos requirunt cultus & diversam fiduciam (a). Nam ut unus est Christus, ita una fides. & qvia adoratio ex fide oritur, erit una eademq; religiosa & Christiana adoratio. Contrà ubi duplex adoratio, ibi duplex fides, ibi duplex persona.

XXII. Nec ipsos juvare potest effugium: quòd adoratio una qvidem sit numero, verùm diversa gradu & respectu ad duas naturas. Adoratio enim non in utraq; natura fundatur, nec utriq; per se tribuitur: sed in solâ Deitate fundamentum habet: Humanitati verò tribuitur κατ' ἄλλο propter Unionem Personalem. Cum qvo consentit Thomas (b).

XXIII. Et quemadmodum propter Personarum Trinitatem uni divinæ Essentiæ non tribuitur triplex cultus & adoratio, qvia fundamentum istius cultus est ipsa Deitas, non Personarum discrimen; ita in CHRISTO propter Naturarum dualitatem, non geminatur adoratio, sed una manet, propter Personæ unitatem, qvæ verè est DEUS, & in qvâ Deitas subsistit & Humanitas.

XXIV. Hanc Jesuiticam vesaniam æmulatur Martinius Calvinista. Hinc in defensione Sadeelis contra Menzerum, (à qvo tamen & reliqvis sociis divortium facit) hi flosculi reperiuntur, 'Honor & reverentia, quæ exhiberi debet CHRISTO, duplex est: a- 'lius λόγῳ conveniens, alius ipsius carni sive Humanitati. pag. 86. & seq. Qvia humanitas non est Deitas. Ergo non adoranda illa ut hæc. Videatur de hac controversia Menzerus eruditissimè disputans contra Martinium (a).

XXV. Unum contra Jesuitam adhuc meretur admonitionem. Turpiter enim sibiipsi contradicit: dum hic carni Christi λατρείαν denegat; corpori verò ipsius in Sacramento suo ficto & pane transsubstantiato propter stabiliendam suam ἀρτολατρείαν, eandem tribuit: (b) imò ipsi Concilio Trident. λατρείαν Sacramento tribuenti (c).

XXVI. Calviniani pòst se offerunt: horum itidem, ut omnemendacium πολυσχιδές, non unus est ordo. Qvidam apertè agunt, & adorationem omnem carni Christi in totum adimunt. Coryphæum & hyperaspisten primarium agit L. Danæus. Hinc Idololatras maledictos Nestorianos pronunciat omnes, qui Christum secundùm carnem adorant etiam in unione personali permanentem (d), imò adorationem carnis Christi eo planè loco habet, quo invocationem Mariæ & reliqvorum sanctorum idololatricam (a).

XXVII. Rationes blasphemæ suæ opinionis hæc ponit. I. Ex Jerem. 17, 5. Maledictus vir ille, qui fiduciam habet in homine, & ponit carnem brachium suum. Caro Christi est vera caro. E. Maledictus qui in carnem Christi adorationem dirigit. Resp. 1. Qvatuor esse terminos in hoc Syllogismo: Major enim loquitur de tali homine, qualem describit Jer. v. 9. Minor de homine Christo non nudo aut fallaci, sed qui Deus est, & de quo scriptum: Qvisquis confidit in te, non confundetur. Rom. 9. v. ult. 2. Committit fallaciam Compos. & Divis. Omittit enim verba, quæ ex Propheta addenda erant, & corde suo relinquit Deum. Jam qui Humanam Naturam in ipsa Persona τοῦ λόγου subsistentem & consideratam cultu religioso proseqvitur & adorat, non reliquit Deum, cum quo caro est una Persona. 3. Tandem retorqvemus in ipsum adversarium v. 6. seq. Benedictus vir, qui confidit in Domino, & cujus fiducia Dominus. E. Benedictus cujus Christus, quà Deus & homo, est fiducia.

XXIIX. II. Depromit ex dicto Gal. 4, 8. Qui serviunt iis, qui naturâ non sunt Dii, Idololatræ sunt. Hoc faciunt, qui carnem Christi adorant. E. Resp. Iterum sunt quatuor termini. Major loquitur de diis fictitiis & idolis; Minor de carne Christi θεανθείᾳ, quam in numerum Idolorum recensere, summæ & extremæ est blasphemiæ.

XXIX. III. Qui conservos, & qui sunt ex fratribus, adorant, ab Angelo reprehenduntur, Apoc. 19, 10. & 22, 8. At Christus est conservus & frater noster. E. Resp. Major loquitur de nuda creatura, videlicet angelo: minor de Christo, qui non tantùm noster conservus, verùm etiam Dominus, in infimo etiam Exinanitionis statu, Luc. 2, 11. Joh. 13, 13. Phil. 2. v. 6. & seqq.

XXX. IV. Solus Deus est adorandus. Caro Christi non est Deus. Resp. Consequentia non valet, quia humanitati religiosa adoratio tribuitur non καθ' αὑτὸ sed κατ' ἄλλο & ex donatione: non quia sit facta Deus, sed quia Deo est personaliter unita & in ταυτότητα Personæ recepta, quâ de causâ Damascenus ipsam dicit ὁμόθεον.

XXXI. V. Qui creaturam invocat, in Deum est blasphemus. Deut. 4, 6. 10. Matth. 4, 10. Caro Christi etiam glorificata & in unione personæ manens est creatura. E. R. Homonymia est in vocabulo Creaturæ: in Propositione sumitur de absolutâ & nudâ creatura; in Assumtione de tali creatura, quæ cum ipso creatore una persona facta, imò ipse creator est. Id quod ipsi Danæi contribules Polanus (a) & Bucanus (b) confitentur.

XXXII. VI. Rom. 9, 5. Paulus explicat, cujus naturæ ratione honor Christi sit tribuendus, nempe quatenus est Deus supra omnia benedictus. Resp. 1. ἄγνοια est τῦ ἐλέγχυ. Paulus enim ibi ne syllabâ quidem adorationis meminit, verùm incidenter tantùm de persona Christi agit. Deinde 2. nulla est conseqvétia: Christus Deus est benedictus in secula. Ergo Christus natus ex Patribus secundùm carnem non est benedictus.

XXXIII. VII. Esa. 42, 8. Gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Caro Christi est alter. E. Resp. breviter, in Christo non est ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος, verùm ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο. Quando ergo Deus adorationis gloriam communicat humanæ naturæ per Unionem personaliter unitæ, non dat illam alteri, sed propriæ suæ humanitati.

XXXIV. VIII. Nestorii dicit esse errorem, Christum quâ homo est unà cum Verbo adorare. Resp. Non ait Nestorius, Humanam Christi Naturam in Persona τῦ λόγυ subsistentem unâ λατρείᾳ cum λόγῳ esse adorandam: sed hominem Christum unà cum λόγῳ tanquam alterum cum altero coadorandum esse. Cujus erroris Pontificii quidam & Calviniani sine injuriâ insimulari possent.

XXXV. Tandem Testimonia Patrum quæ citat, & ad suum sensum detorqvere satagit, examinant Rungius disp. priv. colleg. 3. disp. 5. Gefnerus disp. 13. in F. C. Siguvartus in admonit. contr. Irenic. Parei, qui vivendi.

XXXVI. Hactenus ergò habuimus primum ordinem de grege calvâ, qui Adorationem carni Christi simpliciter denegant. Cui non abs re illi annumerantur, qui Christo externam etiam reverentiam genuflexionis & apertionis capitis detrahunt, ut Calvinus (a) & multi alii in qvotidiana praxi.

XXXVII. Alter ordo lupum pelle ovina tegere & simplicioribus fucum facere doctus prætendit: adorationem carni Christi nunqvam negatam a suis complicibus. Hinc alii (a) eam concedunt Humanitati Christi non propter realem divinæ majestatis communicationem, sed propter Unionis gratiam. Alii (b) cultum adorationis pertinere ad officium ajunt, atq; ita totum Christum secundum utramqve naturam adorandum putant. Alii (c) carnem Christi concedunt adorandam una adoratione cum Deitate, sed ne reliqva ἀξιώματα divinitatis ei communicata esse affirmare cogantur, adorationem proprietatem Dei essentialem negant, qvod ut suo modo concedi potest, ita sic hoc fine, qvo adversarii adferunt, urgeatur, simpliciter non admittimus. Alii (d) deniq; decisionem hujus qvæstionis ad Concilium, in eo belle cum Pontificiis conspirantes, reservandam statuunt. Qvos omnes in specie refutare chartæ angustia non patitur.

XXXVIII. Photiniani etiam διχᾶ διῃρημένοι sunt. Franciscus Davidis adorationem Christo plane & plene denegavit, contradicentibus Blandrata (e) & Socino (f) contribulibus. Moderni eam Christo homini concedunt, ne Deitatem ipsius fateri cogantur: ita tamen ut possit pius Christum cum Deo Patre adorare; interim ad id faciendum non teneatur: qvin potius æqve bona sit adoratio, sive Christus coadoretur sive non.

XXXIX. Deinde statuunt scripturam ad Christi adorationem commonefacere, interim eam nunqvam esse mandatam, nec unqvam madari potuisse, qvasi vero commonitiones scripturæ Christi & Apostolorum, qvas concedit Schmalzius, (a) non sint edicta prætoria omnibus vere Christianis. Qvæ commenta cum falsa hypothesi nitantur, qvasi aliqvid adorari religiose posset, qvòd non sit Deus, cuq; propter evertendam Christi deitate sint efficta, ἐπανόρθωσιν indigna judicam, & merito ob pagellas impletas ad cursum disputationis remittimus.

XL. Colophonis loco dulcissimam nobis consolationem afferre potest hæc διάσκεψις in omnibus calamitatibus: Si pateris, pia anima, accede firma fiducia non ad judicem severum, sed fratrem sincerum, opemq; implora: non feres repulsam, caro est de carne nostra, unus ex fratribus nostris. Cum Josphum adorassent fratres, incalescebant miserationes ejus erga fratres, & qværebat flere. Multò magis Christus frater noster amantissimus nobis supplicibus viscera misericordiæ aperiet,auxilioq; subveniet. Frater fratri officium ullum denegare neqvit: & cœlestis noster frater preces nostras sinet inexauditas? Ipsi sit laus & gloria in secula seculorum, Amen.


## 23 Twenty-third Disputation, On the Genealogy of Christ

Continuation.

Just as the body lives because of the soul, so the soul lives because of Christ, the Holy Fathers once said; and just as the body dies when the soul departs, so when Christ departs from the soul, it perishes; for Christ produces the life of the soul: therefore, such as Christ is as the producer of life, such also is that life which he produces. A righteous man lives a life similar to Christ because of Christ, who dwells in him, so that it is not so much he who lives, as Christ in him, Gal. 2, v. 20. Therefore, it is not the smallest part of Christian knowledge to have known what life Christ lived and what he did in it, so that we may compose our morals and affairs according to it, as a living model of living. Since, therefore, the first chapter of our Christology, namely concerning the Person of Christ, has been given and dispatched; with Christ himself as leader and patron, the second member of it, concerning his Life, will be begun, and will be deduced in several disputations hereafter. We, on this occasion, God willing, will make a happy beginning, intending to speak of the Genealogy of our Lord, and to comprise it in three chapters which will seem necessary to be known. The first of which will prove that the Messiah or Christ necessarily had to arise from the tribe of Judah and the house of David. The second will show that Jesus Christ, with respect to both parents, as much the reputed as the true, arose from that tribe and house, and that there is no disagreement of opinion among the Evangelists describing his genealogy: Finally, the last will end the whole disputation with a brief practical Meditation.

CHAPTER I.

I. That there have been and are various opinions concerning the origin of Christ cannot be unknown. Faustus the Manichaean, as he is in Augustine, asserted that Christ was from the tribe of Levi, and he wished to gather that from Luke, chapter 1, verses 5 and 36, compared.

compared. Augustine himself (who is nevertheless inconsistent in this matter) somewhere wishes him to have sprung from the tribe of Levi and Judah both at once. He wished to give the reason for this opinion with this narrative: that the house of David had been divided into two families, of which one was royal, the other priestly; that Luke described the latter, Matthew the former. Beda adds moreover: Since Christ was both King and Priest at once, it is therefore fitting that he should draw his origin from both tribes. Many other Fathers and many of the Papists of a previous age were of the same opinion.

II. But we, following the guidance of Scripture, derive the origin of Christ from the tribe of Judah alone, and we confirm that orthodox opinion with the following statements. The first of which exists in Gen. 49:8 and following. In which the Patriarch Jacob, about to die, blessing his sons in the Spirit, prophesies that Shiloh or the Messiah would arise from the progeny of Judah. It seems to some, not without reason, that both his person and his office and worship are graphically described in that very place. Worship indeed in v. 8: 'Your brothers shall praise you,' etc., and 'shall bow down,' etc. For the greatest worship that can be shown to Christ by Christian brothers is praise and adoration. Victory: 'Your hand shall be on the necks,' etc. The Cross: 'You have ascended,' etc., v. 9. Burial: 'Resting,' etc. Powerful resurrection: 'Who shall rouse him?' Time of advent: 'It shall not be taken away,' etc., v. 10. Redemption and passion: 'He shall wash,' etc., v. 11. Philanthropia: 'His eyes are more beautiful,' etc., v. 12. The sweetness of his doctrine: 'His teeth,' etc.

III. I cannot but recite here the pious, though perhaps too allegorical, thoughts of the Fathers. For some of them consider the name Jehudah, because since it has a great affinity with the Tetragrammaton, the name of GOD, and preserves all its letters, with the addition moreover of the letter ד, which denotes a door; and since mention is made of a certain door placed toward the East and not to be opened, through which it was not lawful for a man to pass, because the Lord God of Israel passed through it, Ezek. 44:2. Hence they deduce that in this name Jehudah is contained the mystery concerning the Messiah about to enter into this world through a virgin from the tribe of Judah (which was accustomed to pitch its camp toward the East, Num. 2:3) as through a door. Others, however, from this cited passage v. 10 and these words יבא שלה זל, by Cabalistic art with a success certainly happier than reason, gather the name Jesu.

Latin:

Continuatio.

QVemadmodum corpus vivit propter animam, sic anima propter Christum, dixerunt qvondam S. Patres; & sicuti discedente animâ moritur corpus, ita Christo ex anima discedente, ipsa perit; Vitam enim animæ Christus efficit: Qvalis igitur Christus est vitæ effector, talis est etiam illa, qvam efficit, vita. Vir justus propterChristum, qvi in illo habitat,vitam vivit Christo similẽ, ut non tam ipse vivat, qvàm in ipsoChristus, Gal. 2, v. 20. Non ergò minima Christianæ scientiæ pars est, novisse, qvàm vitam & qvid in illa egerit Christus, ut juxta eam, veluti vivum vivendi exemplar, mores & negotia nostra componere possimus. Qvoniam igitur primum Christologias nostræ, nimirum de Personâ Christi, caput expeditum datum est; Ipso Christo duce & auspice, secundum ejus membrum, de Vita ejus inchoabitur, & disputationibus aliqvot imposterum deducetur. Nos hac vice, Deo dante, feliciter initium faciemus, dicturi de Genealogiâ Domini nostri, tribusqve capitibus, qvæ scitu videbuntur necessaria, comprehenseri. Qvorum primum probabit, Messiam sive Christum necessariò ex tribu Juda, domoq; David oriri debuisse. Alterum ostendet, Jesum Christum respectu utriusq; parentis, tàm putatitii qvàm veri, ex eâ tribu domoq; ortum esse, nec ullum esse inter Evangelistas Genealogiâ ejus describentes sententiarum dissidium: Deniq; ultimum brevi Meditatione practicâ totam disputationem finiet.

CAPUT I.

I. Varias fuisse & esse sententias de origine Christi, ignotum esse non potest. Faustus Manichæus, ut est apud Augustinum, asseruit, Christum fuisse ex tribu Levi, idq; colligere voluit ex Luc, cap. 1. v. 5. & 36. collatis.

collatis. Augustinus ipse (qui tamen hac in re varius est) alicubi vult eum ex tribu Levi & Juda utraq; simul ortum. Cujus sententiæ rationem hac narratione reddere voluit. Domum Davidis in duas fuisse divisam familias. Qvarum altera Regia fuerit, Sacerdotalis altera: hanc descripsisseLucam,Matthæum illam. Addit insuper Beda: Qvoniam Christus Rex simul & Sacerdos fuerit, ideò congruum esse, ut ex utraq; tribu ortum suum trahat. In eadem opinione fuerunt & alii Patres multiq; Pontificiorum superioris ævi.

II. Verùm nos Scripturæ ductum seqventes originem Christi ex tribu Juda sola deducimus, eamq; orthodoxam sententiam seqventibus dictis firmamus. Qvorum primum exstat Gen. 49, 8. & seq. In qvo Patriarcha Jacob moriturus, in Spiritu filiis benedicens, vaticinatur ex Judæ progenie oriturum Siloh sive Messiam. Cujus tum personam tum officium & cultum eo ipso in loco graphicè descriptum esse, non absq; ratione nonnullis videtur. Cultum qvidem v. 8. Laudabunt te fratres &c. & adorabunt &c. Maximus enim, qvi Christo à fratribus Christianis exhiberi potest cultus, Laus est & Adoratio. Victoriam: manus tua in cervicibus &c. Crucem: Ascendisti &c. v. 9. Sepulturam: Reqviscens &c. potentem resurrectionem: Qvis suscitabit eum? Tempus adventus: Non auferetur &c. v. 10. Redemtionem & passionem: Lavabit &c. v. 11. Φιλανθρωπίαν: Pulchriores sunt oculi &c. v. 12. Doctrinæ suavitatem: Dentes ejus &c.

III. Non possum qvin hîc recitem Patrum pias, licet nimis fortassis allegoricas, cogitationes. Qvidam enim eorum nomen Jehudah considerant, qvod cùm affinitatem magnam habeat cum Tetragrammate nomine DEI, ejusq; literas omnes, inserto insuper ד, qvod ostium notat, servet; Fiat autem mentio ostii cujusdam versus Orientem positi & non aperiendi, per qvod neqve fas erat virum transire, qvoniam Dominus Deus Israël pertransiit per illam, Ezech. 44, 2. Hinc deducunt, nomine hoc Jehudah contineri illud de Messia per virginem ex tribu Juda (qvæ versus Orientem castra metari solebat, Num. 2, 3.) tanqvam per ostium in hunc mundum ingressuro mysterium: Alii verò ex hoc allegato loco v. 10. hisqve verbis יבא שלה זל arte Cabalisticâ feliciori sanè successu qvàm ratione nomen ישו Jesu colligunt.


### IV. To this

IV. To this

IV. To this most famous saying, it is pleasing to add two others from the New Testament. 1. Apoc. 5, 5, where he is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah, pointing as it were with the finger to the words of the previous prophecy (a lion's whelp). 2. Hebr. 7, 14. Which passage not only indicates the true origin, but also furthermore rejects the false one; It is manifest, he says, that our Lord sprang out of Judah; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood. Therefore, all those who contend that the Messiah was born from another, and specifically from the tribe of Levi, fight against the author of this Epistle, whether he be Paul or some disciple of the Apostles.

V. Whose arguments are not of such moment that they can deter us from this true opinion. For as far as the passage in Luke 1, 5 and 36 is concerned, it could certainly have happened that someone from the tribe of Levi took a wife from the tribe of Judah, or that some Levite gave his daughter in marriage to a Jew. For the examples of Scripture teach that this can happen, such as those of Saul, David, and others; see these passages Exod. 6, 23; 1 Sam. 18, 27; 1 Kings 3, 1; 2 Chron. 22, 11, etc. Nor are those who urge the law of Num. 36, 7-8 so rigid that they admit no exception; indeed, they expressly maintain that the Levitical tribe and the Royal lineage were immune from the observance of that law, but the others were not. For the posterity of Levi is not numbered among the twelve political tribes, for there would be thirteen, since the offspring of Joseph is divided into two tribes. Nor can the Royal family come into their census, since it is public and above all tribes, and has no private property; for we nowhere read that David or Saul, when raised to the kingdom, entered upon their paternal inheritance together with their brothers.

VI. There are also those who consider the word συγγενὴς more strictly, which does not always imply such a close kinship. Because 1. if not all who are called brothers and sisters are from the same tribe, as is evident in Lev. 19, 17; Acts 13, 26; ch. 22, 1, and as can be seen throughout the Pauline Epistles. Therefore, neither are those who are called kinsmen. 2. This word is homonymous, and sometimes denotes the whole nation and all those born from it, Rom. 9, 3, as also the abstract word συγγένεια, Acts 7, 3. Likewise, colleagues in office and religion, Rom. 16, 7, 21, as the opinion of some is probable; although it is more often taken strictly for the family alone, in which sense it is taken in Luke 1, 58, yet that does not prevent it from being taken here in a broader signification.

VII. In the opinion of Augustine there seems to be hardly any probability. I. For the reason which he brings forward openly conflicts with the opinion itself. For 1. if Mary was from the priestly Davidic family, how will she be from the family or tribe of Levi? 2. It would follow that the maternal lineage of Christ cannot be established from the genealogies of the Evangelists, since both, as he himself says, described not the descendants of Levi but of David. II. This reason conflicts with the history of the Kings of Judah, & III. with the passage to the Hebrews Epistle cited above. Moreover, that the descendants of David did not observe that Mosaic law, as the Priests did, can be proven by no probable reason. Indeed, when King Uzziah wished to offer incense, he is rebuffed with these words: It is not your office, but that of the Priests the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to such a ministry, 2 Chron. 26, 18. Nor does anything solid conclude in agreement with Bede: For Christ ought not to have been an earthly Priest, offering incense, but a heavenly and perpetual one, who would offer himself to God as an immaculate lamb. Therefore, regarding the earthly Priesthood, he has nothing in common with the Levites.

VIII. We have proven that Christ had to come from the tribe of Judah; it must now be seen from which family. We have sufficiently clear Scripture, which says that this promise was made to David, 2 Sam. 7, 12. & following, where it is to be noted that some things are to be understood of Solomon alone, but some of Christ, as we are warned in Heb. 1, 5. The same is also proven from the sayings in which mention is made of the shoot of Jesse flourishing again, see Ps. 89, 4, 5. &c. Ps. 132, 11. Ps. 110, 1. Jer. 23, 5. Ezek. 34, 23, 24. Amos 9, 11. &c.

I. In order that we may present this chapter better explained, the genealogies of Christ described by the Evangelists Matthew and Luke will have to be examined. For the admonition of Paul concerning genealogies, which exists in 1 Tim. 1, 4. Tit. 3, 9, does not strike us. For before the coming of the Messiah, the diligent preservation of genealogies was necessary, chiefly for three reasons. I. Political, so that goods might not be confused, which were equally distributed among the tribes in the land of Canaan. II. Ecclesiastical, so that those who assisted at the altar performing divine worship might not be found to be from another tribe than Levi. Hence it is that we read in Nehemiah 7, 63, that some were removed from the Priesthood because they could not exhibit their writing or genealogy after the return from Babylon. III. Spiritual, so that it could be certainly established from which tribe the promised Messiah had arisen. After he had come, and the destruction of both the political and ecclesiastical state was already impending, no use of the Genealogies remained. Hence it happened by divine providence that Herod burned those same ones, which had been set aside in a public place, of which, however, some people retained copied examples privately, and from them raised futile questions, which the Apostle censures.

II. It must, however, necessarily be presupposed that the genealogy of each Evangelist is not one and the same, but different. It is asked, however, in what that diversity consists. There are indeed various opinions, and they have always been, not slightly differing among themselves, which render this dispute most intricate. For many have suffered much human error in reconciling these genealogies, who, after they obtained persistent followers, became, albeit unwillingly and thinking of no such thing, the authors of many disturbances and thorny questions. Hence, concerning Joas, concerning Zorobabel and his parents, concerning Jechonias, concerning Matthat, whom they wish to name Mathan by slightly changing the letters of one of the Evangelists, so many altercations have arisen, of which we shall only touch upon some, since paper would hardly suffice for enumerating them all.

III. Since, however, no opinion has yet been found more congruent with the Holy Scriptures and beloved by the most famous theologians of this century than that of Dr. Chemnitz, we shall follow it in the main points. We posit these differences of the genealogies, from which the true opinion will then shine forth. I. That Matthew began from Abraham, Luke traced his series as far as Adam. II. That they observed a contrary order. III. That Matthew expressed the lineage and family of Solomon and thus of Joseph, but Luke that of Nathan and Mary, which all the circumstances of things and histories, as well as of persons, teach, nor will any reason be able to prove the contrary. IV. That Matthew, otherwise than Luke did, also wished to set down the legal successions of adopted sons; which is proved 1. because he did not consider it important to omit certain entire generations. 2. because he wished to recount the lineage of Joseph, who nevertheless was not the natural, but only the guardian father of Christ. 3. because he makes Zorobabel the son of Salathiel, of whom a little later. 4. because he makes Hezekiah the son of Ahaz, when nevertheless it is evident from the sacred histories that at the time of the birth of Hezekiah, Ahaz was a boy of eleven years. For all the years of Ahaz were 36, 2 Kings 16:2, 2 Chronicles 27:1, who died in the 3rd year of Hoshea, King of Israel; compare verse 1 of chapter 17 of 2 Kings with verse 2 of chapter 16; but in the same year Hezekiah was 25 years old, 2 Kings 18:1, from which, when 36 years of Ahaz are subtracted, eleven remain.

IV. The true opinion, therefore, is that of those who say that Matthew described the lineage of Joseph, but Luke that of Mary, and they place the beginning of the diversity in Solomon and Nathan, after the naming of whom, although they may seem to agree at times in the names, they affirm that they can never agree in the persons. In order that this may appear more clearly, let us explain more lucidly those things which seem to be observed in the genealogy of Matthew.

V. He makes his beginning from David and Abraham, of whom he makes mention first of all in the vestibule, because just as the latter is the source and origin of the whole Jewish nation, so the former is of the family of Christ, and also because to these two Christ had been singularly promised. He distributes their progeny into three groups of fourteen, each of which terminates a period of some illustrious change in the Israelite government. For just as the first was for the most part under the rule of the Judges, so the second enumerates the Kings themselves, and the third takes its beginning together with the princes of the people.

VI. In the first, let us again see the sweet and pious thoughts conceived by the ancients concerning the name of Abraham. To him, when he was previously called Abram, they say that God, not without mystery, added the letter ה. For in the name יהוה, the י, according to Jerome, signifies the beginning and denotes the father; the ו, however, as a conjunction, represents the Holy Spirit, who is called the love and bond that joins; but the ה, which signifies being, points to the son, since all things that have being were made through him, John 1:3, and this is doubled on account of the twofold nature of the son. Hence they think that God inserted this very letter ה into the name of Abraham (as he did for Sarah) to indicate that from his own progeny the Son of God would assume flesh.

VII. The beginning of the second group of fourteen is also the beginning of the disagreement between the Evangelists. For one begins to recount the family of Joseph from Solomon, the other that of Mary from Nathan, the sons of David, and therefore they do not agree in the persons until the very end. Matthew, however, omitted Joram the son of Jehoshaphat, three kings: Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah, and even Athaliah herself; for the reason for this action, see Chemnitz.

IIX. However, one must observe here the wonderful distortion of Scripture by those who wish that both holy writers described one and the same genealogy. For from the summary of times by Philo, they affirm that the descendants of Solomon held the kingdom up to Athaliah, upon whose extinction, along with her sons, it was transferred to the family of Nathan. Furthermore, Joash (the first of that family) and all the kings in succession were binominal, some of whom that Philo enumerates: Joas Heli Simeon (this one indeed trinominal) Her Manasses: Ezechias Jesus. They think, therefore, that that Simeon, whom Luke says was the son of Judah, is the same as Joas, and thus consequently, up to Jechonias Neri, that is, my lamp, because when he was led out of prison by Evil-Merodach, the lamp of David, which seemed extinguished, shone again.

IX. But, while we do not deny that some Kings were binominal. For Ochozias is called Joachaz, 2 Chron. 21:17; Ozias, Azarias, 2 Kings 15:1; we cannot accept this opinion. For besides the fact that this Philo is deservedly judged spurious, although Annius, Lucidus, and Beauxames and others accept him as genuine, this opinion openly conflicts with Scripture. For 2 Kings 11:2 and 4:1, 1 Chron. 3:11, Joas is expressly called the son, and indeed the youngest by birth, of Ochozias, who without doubt was of the posterity of Solomon. Furthermore, this conjecture about the double name of the Kings 1. has no precedent in Scripture. 2. It inflicts force and injury upon the Genealogy. For from Simeon, whom they make Joas, to Neri, whom they wish to be Jechonias, inclusively, 12 names are found, but in the catalogue of the Kings only eleven generations are numbered. Nor can it help them that they say Addi was Joachaz and Melchi was Joachin or Eliachin: for it would follow that Addi and Melchi were brothers, as are Joachaz and Joachin, 2 Chron. 36:4, which is contrary to Luke, who makes one the son of the other.

X. There remains the greatest controversy, which being rightly decided, whatever can be disputed in this matter can be decided with easy effort. Is the same Salathiel, who is in Matthew, the one whom Luke says was the son of Neri? We hold the negative and confirm it with these reasons: 1. Those whose natural parents Scripture names as different cannot be one and the same. But Scripture posits different parents for Salathiel, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved: Because the natural father of Salathiel in Luke is Neri, for Luke does not attend to legal succession. In Matthew, the natural father of Salathiel is Jechonias the last king, which is furthermore proved 1 Chron. 3:17, where the conjecture of F. Junius about a legal father is hardly probable, for it conflicts with the scope of the whole book and all the circumstances. Nor was Jechonias entirely childless, for mention is made of his seed being cast out, Jer. 22:28. XI. II. Those to whom far different sons are assigned in Scripture cannot be one and the same. But etc. Therefore. The minor premise is proven. Because Salathiel, who is in Luke, is the son of Zorobabel, Hag. 1, 1. & 12. c. 2, 3. & 24. Neh. 12, 1. But that other Zorobabel in Matthew, who is the son of Jechoniah, is not a son, but a grandson through a brother, 1 Chron. 3, 19. For the suspicion of those who wish him to be a grandson through a son seems very slight: however that may be, the matter comes to the same thing. III. He whose seed sat upon the throne and ruled is not the same as he whom God himself utterly forbade from the throne and dominion. But the seed of Salathiel, who is in Luke, sat etc., but he whom Matthew makes the son of Jechoniah, him etc. Therefore. We prove the minor premise, because the Zorobabel who was the son of Salathiel was Prince of the people or Leader of Judah, Hag. 1, 1. of whom that phrase, to rule upon the throne and to sit etc., is used, Zech. 6, 13. But the other Salathiel and his sons were not permitted to sit upon the throne, for God had forbidden that, Jer. 22, 30. c. 36, 30. Futile, however, is the exception of those who wish 'seed' to be understood only as sons, not grandsons, since 'seed' when placed so absolutely denotes the whole progeny of posterity, 2 Samuel 7, 12. and that even unto infinite generations, see 2 Cor. 11, 22.

XII. Thus we have seen Matthew derive the family of Joseph from Solomon; now let us see Luke counting the lineage of Mary from Nathan; we have already solved most of the difficulties before, only one or two remain. For concerning Cainan the son of Arphaxad, it is asked whether he is genuine. We have determined that, through the fault of scribes, or even of others who read this name in the Septuagint, it has crept into Luke. Whoever wishes to read a solid confirmation of this opinion will be able to do so in Pareus in his Commentary on Genesis.

XIII. How long the Principate lasted in the family of Nathan is not for us to inquire. It suffices for us to know from Ezekiel c. 22, 26. 27. that the miter, into which the crown was changed, and which was the badge of leaders, must be laid aside before he comes whose the judgment is. But why does Luke call the father of Mary Heli, who nevertheless is commonly called Joachim? Most say that Luke wrote Heli by apheresis for Heliachim. Now, indeed, Heliachim and Joachim seem to be the same name, because: 1. they designate exactly the same thing: God shall raise up: 2. the High Priest, who in Judith 4, 5 was called Eliachim, is in c. 15, 9 Joachim; and Pharaoh in 2 Kings 23, 34 changed the name Heliachim into Joachin. It is therefore the same whether he is named Heli, or Heliachim, or Joachim, since they are one and the same name.

XIV. But the reasons why he substituted Joseph in the place of Mary, they are accustomed to give as the chief ones. 1. Because it is the custom neither among the Hebrews nor in Scripture that the lineage of women should be recorded, but only that of men as the more excellent part. It may be objected, chapter 8 of Judith, where the lineage of Judith is recorded. But the answer is usually given that in that chapter the genealogy of a lone widow is described and the whole series ends in her. However, the genealogy of men is not found described through the lineage of a woman, 2. so that in the state of humiliation Christ might be considered the son of Joseph the carpenter. Let everyone have their own judgment. We, because of the narrowness of the paper, hasten to the end.

These descriptions of the genealogies of Christ could indeed remind us of many things worthy of memory. Some Fathers compare this genealogy to a fishing line. For when it is said: Abraham begat Isaac, etc., a certain line as it were is twisted, at the end of which the Son of God, covered by the flesh of his humanity, is hung like a hook and cast into the deep sea of this world. By this hook the Devil was caught, because in our Redeemer, while he bit the bait of the body, the sting of divinity pierced him, etc. We learn from them that divine promises, although delayed for a time, as it seems to us, are at length fulfilled. To David indeed the blessed seed had been promised, yet the root of Jesse had almost withered, and, cast down from the royal throne, it looked upon the carpenter's tools, when behold, the promises made so many years before suddenly found fulfillment, so that we may truly say that God abundantly compensates for slowness in the threatening of punishments with gravity, and in the promises of benefits with fruitfulness. To Him be honor and glory forever.

Latin:

IV. Huic

IV. Huic dicto clarissimo, alia duo ex Novo Testamento adjungere placet. 1. Apoc. 5, 5. ubi vocatur Leo de tribu Juda, digitum q. ad superioris vaticinii verba (catulus leonis) intendens. 2. Hebr. 7, 14. Qvi locus non tantùm originem veram indicat, verùm etiam falsam insuper rejicit, Manifestum est, inqvit, quòd ex Juda ortus sit Dominus noster, in qua tribu nihil de Sacerdotibus Moses locutus est. Pugnant igitur cum hujus Epistolæ autore, sive is Paulus sit, sive Apostolorum aliqvis discipulus, omnes illi, qvi Messiam ex alia & qvidem nominatim ex tribu Levi ortum esses contendunt.

V. Qvorum argumenta tanti non sunt momenti, ut nos ab hâc verâ sententiâ deterrere possint. Nam qvod ad locum Luc. 1, 5. & 36. attinet, fieri sanè potuit, ut aliqvis de tribu Levi duxerit uxorem de tribu Juda, aut Levitarum aliqvis filiam suam Judæo in matrimonium dederit. Id enim fieri posse exempla Scripturæ docent, ut Saulis, Davidis, aliorum, vide hæc loca Exod. 6, 23. 1. Sam. 18, 27. 1. Reg. 3, 1. 2. Chron. 22, 11. &c. Neq; etiam illi, qvi legem Num. 36, 7. 8. urgent, adeò sunt rigidi, ut nullam admittant exceptionem:qvinimò, id disertè volunt, tribum Leviticam & Regiam stirpem ab legis illius observatione fuisse immunes, cæteras non item. Nec enim Levi posteritas, inter duodecim Politicas tribus numeratur, forent enim tredecim, cum Josephi soboles in duas sit tributa tribus. Nec Regia familia in earum censum venire potest, cùm sit publica, supraq; omnes tribus, & nihil habeat peculii; Nusqvam enim legimus Davidem aut Saulem ad regnum evectos unà cum fratribus paternam adiisse hæreditatem.

VI. Sunt etiam qvi vocabulum συγγενὴς pressius considerant, qvod non semper adeò arctam importat cognationem. Qvia 1. si non omnes, qvi fratres & sorores dicuntur, sunt ex eadem tribu, ut patet Lev. 19, 17. Act. 13, 26. c. 22, 1. & passim in Epistolis Paulinis videre est. Ergo neq;, qvi dicuntur cognati. 2. Vocabulum hoc ὁμώνυμον est, & interdum totam gentem & omnes ex illa ortos notat, Rom. 9, 3. ut & vocabulum abstractum συγγένεια, Act. 7, 3. Item collegas in officio & religione, Rom. 16, 7. 21. ut nonnullorum probabilis est sententia; licet sæpiùs strictè pro sola familia ponatur, qvo sensu capitur Luc. 1, 58. id tamẽ non obstat, qvò min9 hic in latiori significatione sumi possit.

VII. In Augustini sententia vix videtur aliqva inesse probabilitas. I. enim ratio, qvam adducit, apertè pugnat cum ipsâ sententia. Nam 1. si Maria fuit ex sacerdotali familia Davidica, qvomodo erit ex familia seu tribu Levi. 2. Seqveretur, ex Genealogiis Evangelistarum maternum Christi genus constare non posse, cùm uterq;, ut ipse ait, non Levi sed Davidis posteros descripserit. II. Pugnat hæc ratio cum historia Regum Judaicorum, & III. cum loco ad Hebr. Epist. suprâ adducto. Posteros autem Davidis legem illam Mosaicam non observasse, ut & Sacerdotes, nullâ verisimili ratione probari potest. Imò cùm Urias rex adolere vellet, his verbis retunditur: Non est tui officii, sed Sacerdotum filiorum Aaron, qvi consecrati sunt ad hujusmodi ministerium, 2. Par. 26, 18. Neq; Bedæ congruum solidi qvid concludit: Non enim Christus debuit esse Sacerdos terrenus, offerens thymiama, sed cœlestis & perpetuus, qvi seipsum Deo offerret agnum immaculatum. Nihil igitur qvoad Sacerdotium terrenum commune habet cum Levitis.

VIII. Probavimus debuisse Christum venire de tribu Juda; videndum jam, ex qva familiâ. Scripturam habemus satis dilucidam, qvæ Davidi hanc promissionem factam dicit, 2. Sam. 7, 12. & seq. ubi notandum qvædam de solo Solomone, qvædam verò de Christo esse intelligenda, ut monemur Hebr. 1, 5. Idem etiam probatur ex dictis, in qvibus surculi Jesse revirentis fit mentio, vide Ps. 89. 4, 5. &c. Ps. 132, 11. Ps. 110, 1. Jer. 23, 5. Ezech. 34, 23. 24. Amos 9, 11. &c.

I. Id caput ut eò melius demus expeditum, Genealogiæ Christi ab Evangelistis Matthæo & Luca descriptæ erunt expendendæ. Non enim nos ferit admonitio Pauli de genealogiis, qvæ extat 1. Tim. 1, 4. Tit. 3, 9. Nam antè adventum Messiæ necessaria erat Genealogiarum diligens asservatio, tres potissimùm ob causas. I. Politicam, ne bona confunderentur, qvæ æqvaliter in terra Canaan tribubus erant distributa. II. Ecclesiasticam, ne qvi assisterent altari divinum peragentes cultum, ex alia invenirentur tribu qvàm Levi. Inde est, qvod Nehem. 7, 63. legimus, qvosdam fuisse Sacerdotio motos, qvia non potuerint post reditum ex Babylone Scripturam seu Genealogiam suam exhibere. III. Spiritualem, ut certò constare posset, ex qva tribu promissus Messias ortus esset. Qvi postqvam venisset, & excidium tam politici qvàm Ecclesiastici status jamjam impenderet, nullus supererat Genealogiarum usus. Hinc divinitùs factum, ut Herodes easdem in loco publico sepositas combureret, qvarum tamen descripta exemplaria nonnulli privatim retinuerunt, & ex iis qvæstiones futiles movebant, id qvod Apostolus reprehendit.

II. Præsupponendum autem est necessariò, non esse unam & eandem utriusq; Evangelistæ Genealogiam, sed diversas. Qværitur autem, in qvo diversitas ista consistat. Variæ sanè sunt semperq; fuerunt inter se non leviter dissidentes opiniones, qvæ hanc desceptationem reddunt intricatissimam. Multi enim in conciliandis hisce genealogiis multum humani passi sunt, qvi postqvam pertinaces nacti sunt sectatores multarum turbarum& spinosarũ qvæstionum autores inviti licet & nihil tale cogitantes evaserunt. Hinc de Joas, de Zorobabele ejusq; parentibus, de Jechonia, de Matthat, qvem altetum Evangelistarum leviter inflexis literis Mathan nominasse volunt, tot natæ sunt altercationes, qvarum aliqvas tantùm perstringemus, cum omnibus enumerandis vix charta sufficeret.

III. Cùm autem adhuc dum nulla inventa fuerit sententia sacris literis magis congrua & celeberrimis hujus seculi Theologis adamata, qvàm D. Chemnitii, eam nos in principalioribus seqvemur. Has autem ponimus Genealogiarum differentias, ex qvibus deinde vera sententia elucescet. I. Qvòd Matthæus ab Abrahamo initium sumserit, Lucas ad Adamum usq; seriem suam deduxerit. II. Qvod ordine contrariũ servaverint. III. Qvòd Matthæus Salomonis adeóq; Josephi, Lucas verò Nathanis & Marię genus & familiam expresserint, id qvod omnes docent tàm rerum & historiarum, qvàm personarum circũstantiæ, nec ulla ratio contrariũ evincere poterit. IV. Qvòd Matthæus, aliter ac Lucas fecit, legales etiam adoptivorum filiorum successiones apponere voluit; Id qvod probatur 1. qvia pensi non habuit generationes qvasdam integras omittere. 2. qvia Josephi genus recensere voluit, qvi tamen non naturalis; sed tutelaris tantùm pater Christi fuit. 3. qvia Zorobabelem facit filium Salathielis, de qvo paulò pòst. 4. qvia Jehiskiam facit filium Ahas, cùm tamen ex historiis sacris pateat tempore nativitatis Jehiskia, puerum fuisse Ahas annorum undecim, Omnes enim anni Ahas fuerunt 36. 2. Reg. 16, 2. 2. Par. 27, 1. qvi anno 3. Oseæ Regis Israël mortuus est; confer. v. 1. c. 17. 2. Reg. cum v. 2. c. 16. eodem autem anno Jehiskias annorum erat 25. 2. Reg. 18, 1. qvibus à 36. annis Ahas detractis remanent XI.

IV. Vera igitur sententia eorum est, qvi Matthæum dicunt Josephi, Lucam verò Mariæ discripsisse originem, primordium diversitatis in Salomone & Nathane ponunt, post qvorum nominationem licet in nominibus interdum convenire videantur, in personis tamen nunqvam consentire posse affirmant. Qvod ut eò meliùs appareat, ea, qvæ in Matthæi Genealogia videntur observanda, dilucidiùs explicemus.

V. Initium is facit à Davide & Abrahamo, qvorum in vestibulo imprimis mentionem facit, qvia sicut hic totius Judaicæ gentis, ita ille familiæ Christi fons est & origo, tum etiam, qvoniam his duobus singulariter Christus fuerat promissus. Eorum progeniem in tres distribuit tesseradecades, qvarum qvælibet aliqvam illustrium mutationum regiminis Israëlitici terminat periodum. Ut enim prima majori ex parte sub Judicum fuit imperio, ita secunda Reges ipsa enumerat, & tertia unà cum Populi principibus suum sumit principium.

VI. In prima nos iterum svàves & pias Veterum de nomine Abrahami conceptas cogitationes videamus. Huic, cùm anteà vocaretur Abraham, non sine mysterio, dicunt, Deum literam ה addidisse. In nomine enim יהוה, י, teste Hieronymo, principium significat, patremq́; notat: ו verò copulativa Spiritum sanctum repræsentat, qvi amor & nexus copulans dicitur; At ה qvod esse significat, filium indigitat, cùm omnia, qvæ esse habent, per illum facta sint, Joh. 1, 3. idq́ve geminetur ob duplicem filii naturam. Inde putant, Deum hanc ipsam literam ה nomini Abrahami (ut Saræ) inseruisse, ut indicaret ex ipsius progenie filium Dei carnem assumturum.

VII. Secundæ Thesseradecados initium, dissensionis etiam inter Evangelistas est initium, Alter enim incipit Josephi ex Salomone, alter Mariæ ex Nathane Davidis filiis familiam recensere, ideoq́ve ad finem usqve in personis non concordant. Omisit autem Matthæus Joranum filium Josaphat tres Reges Ochoziam, Joas & Amasian, ipsamq́; adeò Atholiam, cujus facti rationem vide apud Chemnitium.

IIX. Observanda autem hîc eorum, qvi unam Genealogiam utrumqve S. scriptorem descripsisse volunt, Scripturæ mirabilis detorsio. Ex Philonis enim breviario temporum affirmant posteros Salomonis usq; ad Athalian tenuisse regnum, qvâ deinde cum filiis exstinctâ translatum illud sit ad familiam Nathan. Præterea Joas (primum scilicet ex ea familia)& omnes deinceps Reges fuisse binomines, qvorū aliqvos enumerat ille Philo: Joas Heli Simeon (hic qvidem trinominis) Her Manasses: Ezechias Jesus. Putant igitur Simeonem illum, qvem Lucas Judæ filium fuisse dicit, eundem esse cum Joas, & sic conseqventer, usq; ad Jechoniam, qvem ut verisimilior sit hæc conjectura, ideò Neri, id est, lucernam meam vocatum ait Philo, qvia cum ab Evilmerodacho ex carcere ductus fuerit, lucerna David, quæ extincta videbatur, iterum illuxerit.
