IX. Verùm, ut non inficias imus, nonnullos Reges fuisse binomines. Nam Ochozias vocatur Joachaz, 2. Par. 21, 17. Ozias Azarias, 2. Reg. 15, 1. ita hanc sententiam recipere non possumus. Præterqvam enim, qvòd hic Philo merito spurius judicatur, licet eum Annius, Lucidus & Beauxames aliiq́; recipiant ut genuinum, apertè hæc opinio pugnant cum Scriptura. Nam 2. Reg. 11, 2. & 4. 1. Par. 3, 11. Joas disertè vocatur filius & qvidem minimus natu Ochoziæ, qvi absq; dubio ex posteritate Salomonis fuit. Deinde hæc conjectura de duplici Regum nomine 1. Scripturam non habet præviam. 2. vim & injuriam Genealogiæ infert. Nam à Simeone, qvem illi Joas faciunt, ad Neri, qvem Jechoniam volunt, inclusivè 12. inveniuntur tur nomina, sed in catalogo Regum undecim tantùm generationes numerantur. Nec juvare illos potest, qvod dicunt Addi fuisse Joachaz & Melchi Joachin seu Eliachin: seqveretur n. Addi & Melchi fuisse fratres, ut sunt Joachaz & Joachin, 2. Par. 36, 4. id qvod contra Lucam est, qvi alterum alterius facit filium.

X. Restat controversia maxima, qvâ ritè dicisâ, qvicqvid in hac re controverti potest, facili negotio decidi potest. An idem Salathiel, qvi est apud Matthæum, cum eo sit, qvem Lucas dicit fuisse filium Neri? Nos negativam tenemus eamq; his rationibus firmamus: 1. Qvorum Scriptura diversos nominat naturales parentes, illi unus & idem esse neqveunt. Atqvi scriptura Salathielis diversos ponit &c. E. Minor probatur; Qvia Salathielis apud Lucam naturalis pater est Neri, legalem n. successionem non attendit Lucas. Apud Matthæum Salathielis pater naturalis est Jechonias rex ultimus, id qvod insuper probatur 1. Par. 3, 17. ubi vix probabilis est conjectura F. Junii, de legali patre, pugnat enim cum scopo totius libri omnibusq́ve circumstantiis. Nec Jechonias in universum fuit orbus, seminis enim ejus mentio fit projecti, Jer. 22, 28. XI. II. Qvibus in Scriptura longè diversi assignantur filii, illi un⁹ & idem esse neqveüt. Atqvi &c. Ergo. Minor probatur. Qvia Salathielis, qvi est apud Lucam, fili⁹ est Zorobabel, Hag. 1, 1. & 12. c. 2, 3. & 24. Neh. 12, 1. Illius verò, qvi Jechoniæ filius est, alter ille Zorobabel apud Matthæum non filius, sed ex fratre nepos est, 1. Par. 3, 19. Tenus enim valdè videtur suspicio eorum, qvi illius ex filio nepotem volunt: qvicqvid autem sit, eodem res recidit. III. Is, cujus semen sedit super thronum, & dominatus est, non est idem cum eo, qvem Deus ipse solio & dominio penitùs interdixit. Atq; Salathielis, qvi est apud Lucam, semen sedit &c. qvem verò Matthæus facit filium Jechoniæ; illum &c. Ergo. Minorem probamus, qvia Salathielis filius Zorobabel fuit Princeps populi seu Dux Juda, Agg. 1, 1. de qvibus phrasis illa, dominari super solio & sedere &c. usurpatur, Zach. 6, 13. Alter verò Salathiel, ejusq́; filii non debuerunt sedere super solium, id enim Deus interdixerat Jerem. 22, 30. c. 36, 30. Futilis autem est eorum exceptio, qvi per semen filios tantùm intelligi volunt, non nepotes, cùm semen ita absolutè positum totam progeniem posteritatis notet, 2. Samuel. 7, 12. idq́; in infinitas usq; generationes, vide 2. Cor. 11, 22.

XII. Sic vidimus Matthæum ex Salomone familiam Josephi deduxisse, jam videamus Lucam Mariæ genus ex Nathane numerantem; plerasq; difficultates jam antè solvim⁹, una tantùm atq; altera restat. Nam de Cainan filio Arphaxad qværitur, an is sit genuinus. Nos statuimus, culpa librariorum, vel aliorum etiam, qvi hoc nomen apud 70. legerunt, in Lucam irrepsisse. Cujus sententiæ confirmationem solidam, qvi volet, legere poterit apud Pareũ in Comm. supr. Genesin.

XIII. Qvousq; duraverit Principatus in familia Nathanis nostrũ non est qværere. Sufficit nobis ex Ezechiele c. 22, 26. 27. scire, qvòd Cidaris, in qvam mutata est corona, & qvæ ducum fuit insigne, anteqvā veniat is, cujus est judicium, obliqva sit ponenda. Cur autem Lucas patrem Mariæ vocat Heli, qvi tamen vulgo Joachin audit? Dicunt pleriq; scripsisse Lucam Heli per ἀφαίρεσιν pro Heliachim. Jam verò Heliachim & Joachim idem videntur esse nœmen, qvia 1. idem omninò designant: Deus suscitabit: 2. Pontifex, qvi Judith 4, 5. vocabatur Eliachim, is c. 15, 9. sit Joachim; & Pharao 2. Reg. 23, 34. nomen Heliachin vertit in Joachin. Perinde igitur est sive Heli nominatur sive Heliachim, sive Joachim, cum unum & idem nomen sint.

XIV. Causas autem, cur loco Mariæ substituerit Josephum, præcipuas dare solent eas. 1. Qvia nec apud Hebræos nec in Scriptura moris sit, ut mulierum genus recenseatur, sed tantùm viri tanqvam præstantioris partis. Objici potest, cap. 8. Judith. ubi genus Judith recensetur. Sed Resp. solet, in eo capite describi genealogiam solius fœminæ viduæ & in ea totam terminari seriem. Viri autem genealogiam per fæminæ genus non inveniri descriptam, 2. ut in statu humiliationis Christus haberetur Josephi fabri filius. Cuilibet suum esto judicium. Nos ab chartæ angustiam properamus ad finem.

Multarum sanè memoriâ dignarum rerum admonere nos possent hæ Genealogiarum Christi descriptiones. Patres nonnulli Genealogiam hanc conferunt cum linea piscatoria. Nam cum dicitur: Abraham genuit Isaac &c. qvædam qvasi linea torqvetur, cujus extremo Filius Dei carne humanitatis suæ tectus hami instar appenditur, & in profundum hujus seculi mittitur pelagus. Hoc hamo Diabolus captus est, qvia in redemtore nostro dum escam corporis momordit, divinitatis illum aculeus perforavit &c. Nos ex eis discimus, promissiones divinas, licet ad tempus, ut nobis videtur, nimium dilatas, tandem impleri. Davidi qvidem promissum erat semen benedictum, penè tamen exaruerat radix Jesse, & de regio solio deturbata fabrilia instrumenta respiciebat, cû ecce promissis ante tot annis factis repentè fides exstitit, ut verè dicere possimus, Tarditatem ut in comminationibus pœnarum gravitate, sic in promissionibus beneficiorû ubertate largiter recompensare Deum. Ipsi sit honor & gloria in secula.


## 24 Twenty-fourth Disputation, On the Virgin Mary, Mother of Christ

Continuation.

Concerning the genealogy and ancestors of our Savior Jesus Christ, we have dealt in the preceding disputation: order demands that we now discuss his Mother, whom he had according to the flesh, the Virgin Mary. But that we may not wander ἀτάκτως & ἀμεθόδως (disorderly and without method), we shall aim at these three heads. I. κατασκευαστικῶς (constructively) we shall propose sound doctrine concerning the glorious Mother of the Messiah. II. ἀνασκευαστικῶς (destructively) we shall reject the blasphemies and ἑτεροδοξίαν (heterodoxy) of our adversaries: and finally III. after a Practical Meditation, we shall sound the retreat.

Christ, bring aid, born of a chaste Virgin.

Thesis I.

Although it is cast beyond all hazard of doubt that the Messiah had a mother; yet at the beginning one may ask: How could Christ have a mother, when he was prefigured by Melchizedek, who is said to be not only ἀπάτωρ but also ἀμήτωρ, Heb. 7, 3.

II. Where the answer is at hand: 1. That Melchizedek is said to have been without father and mother, not indeed in the sense as if he had no parents, and had either fallen from heaven or existed from eternity, as the Melchizedekians raved (a); since the ancients thought that he was Shem, the son of Noah (b): but for the reason that in Gen. 4, where mention is made of him, his parents are not expressly named or recorded.

III. Furthermore 2. since in Christ two births and two natures are to be acknowledged, we learn both from the antitype, who bore the type of Christ, the one divine, the other human; he is ἀπάτωρ according to his humanity, which he received in time not from Joseph, his putative father, but from his mother alone, a virgin, by the power of the Holy Spirit: he is ἀμήτωρ according to his divinity, which he has not from a mother, but from God the Father alone from eternity; yet so that the mother is also rightly called θεοτόκος in personal locutions (a).

IV. This delay being removed, we proceed rightly to the matter itself, where two things will principally have to be attended to: The name of the Mother of the Messiah, and the Person of the Blessed Virgin herself.

V. The name of the Mother of the Lord was Mary. In Hebrew מִרְיָם, in Syriac מַרְיָם, by which name also the sister of Moses is read to be distinguished in Exod. 15, 20, which Schindler (b) explains as 'Exalted', and derives from the root רוּם, 'to be high, elevated'. Some derive it from מָרַר, 'to be bitter, harsh', so that Mary is said to be as it were 'bitter', on account of the bitterness of the sorrows which she endured. Chytreus (c) reports that some ancients interpreted it as 'teacher of the people' from יוֹרֶה and עַם; Jerome wishes it to sound 'Lady' in the Syriac language from the Syriac root מָרָא, 'Lord'. Whence he thinks that 1 Cor. 16, 22, μαρὰν ἀθὰ, is derived, as if it were 'the Lord comes', i.e., to judgment. Some derive it from מַר, which is 'a drop', and יָם, which is 'sea', as if she were called 'a drop of the sea' (d).

VI. Whether the ancient Jews, who preceded Mary, foresaw this name, we leave to its own place. Galatinus attempts to prove by the authority of Rabbi Haccados, who wrote the Revelation of secrets; where he argues from the Cabala that the name of the Father of Mary was also known to them (a).

VII. These things concerning the Name of the Mother of Christ: regarding the Person herself, four things must be observed: Status, Family, Titles, and Dignity.

VIII. 1. Her status was that of a Virgin, and indeed a betrothed one. For the Savior was born of a virgin without male seed, so that the wisdom of God and the unique reason for this mystery might become known: nor was any other than a new mode of conceiving and being born fitting for a new man. The first man, Adam, was born from no other man, but was created immediately by God: the second, Eve, was formed not from a woman, but from a man alone: the third and all remaining men are naturally procreated from man and woman. A fourth mode remained, from a woman without a man, which is Christ's alone, the new mode of a new man, the fourth and final mode revealed in the fourth and final age (b).

IX. Furthermore, he was born from a woman alone without a man, so that from this we might believe him to be something other than a mere man.

X. 3. So that the prophecies of Jeremiah 31:22, Isaiah 7:14, and Ezekiel 44:1 might be fulfilled, as the doctors of the Church and Rabbi Haccados have not without reason expounded regarding this mystery. For this reason also, the future Messiah is designated as the seed of the woman, Genesis 3:15, not of the man.

XI. 4. So that the birth of the eternal λόγος might be more noble on account of the miracle. 5. So that the future Messiah, as a holy and perfect victim for the sins of the world, might be conceived and born without sin, Hebrews 7:26, in which all those procreated from the union of man and woman after the first sin are conceived, Psalm 51:7, Romans 5:12, John 3:6.

XII. 6. So that the restoration might correspond to the fall: the beginning of sin was made through a woman, and indeed a virgin, 1 Timothy 2:14; therefore, the remedy for sins also had to come through a virgin.

XIII. 7. Because it was not fitting that one and the same son should have two Fathers, one in heaven and one on earth; but it was fitting that, just as he received the essence of the Deity from the Father alone, so also he should receive the essence of humanity from the mother alone on earth. (a)

XIV. 8. So that there might be a certain analogy between the birth of Christ and the regeneration of the faithful. For the generation of Christ from a virgin is a sign of our spiritual regeneration, which is not of blood, nor of the desire of the flesh, nor of the desire of man, but is of God. (b)

XV. The Fathers (c) add this reason, 9. that chastity might be commended to us by this example; which we readily accept, if it is not understood in the Papal sense concerning the vow of continence and virginity.

XVI. Hence we not only confess in our Creed that Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit, but also born of the Virgin Mary, because of the words of the angel in Matthew 1:20 and of Isaiah cited in the same place, verse 23.

XVII. Moreover, she retained her virginity safe and incorrupt not only in the conception and birth of Christ, but also after the birth. There can be no doubt about the former: although the latter is not supported by manifest testimonies of Scripture, it is nevertheless pious to believe it, since it is in no way repugnant to the sacred writings: Perkins (a) brings forward another probable reason.

XVIII. But as to the question, was Christ born with Mary's womb opened or closed? Was it with the pain of childbirth or without pain? We answer that it seems more probable that it was done by a closed way, and consequently without pain: which seems to be able to be gathered from the fact that the mother was immediately able to care for the newborn infant: that pain is the punishment of corruption, which was none in Mary: that finally, for the same reason Christ is rightly considered to have been born as he was conceived, namely that he did not break the barriers of virginity, but just as he entered impassibly, so he exited ineffably, as Chemnitz cites from Gregory of Nyssa (b).

XIX. Furthermore, this is also worthy of note, that he was brought into the light not from a free virgin, but one already betrothed, Luke 1:27. The Fathers (c) assert that this was done for the sake of himself, of his mother, and of us.

XX. For his own sake, 1. lest he be proclaimed a bastard and illegitimately born by infidels. 2. so that his genealogy from the lineage of his putative father might be better known. 3. so that he might have a foster-father, guardian, and defender in his infant years. Finally 4. so that the birth of the virgin might be hidden from the Devil, a reason which not a few Fathers use (d), though most reject it (e).

XXI. With respect to the mother, 1. so that her reputation and safety might be provided for, lest she be taken for an adulteress and dragged to punishment. 2. so that she might have a guardian in flight (a), and a witness, by whose association her own chastity might be proven.

XXII. For our sake, 1. that our faith concerning the birth of Christ might be established. For Joseph would have left her far beyond all doubt, if he had doubted her virginity. 2. that it might be shown, that the state of virginity was then by God as well as that of marriage pleasing 3. that the manner of reparation might correspond to the manner of the fall, which drew its origin from a married virgin. 4. For Christ a mother is sought as a spouse, that the Church may be signified as the spouse of Christ (b).

XXIII. II. The Family of Mary. Christ willed to be born not from just any woman, but from her who was sprung from the tribe of Judah and from the house of David. The reason is ready at hand in the Holy Scriptures, namely that the oracles of the Prophets and the decrees of God, Gen. 49:10, 2 Sam. 7:12, might be fulfilled by the very work. Nor would I say it was done ineptly, that the royal lineage might add greater dignity to the Messiah and shadow forth his royal office.

XXIV. III. We acknowledge three titles of Mary in an orthodox manner: two Biblical and one Ecclesiastical. By the angel, Luke 1:28, she is called 1. κεχαριτωμένη, as if beloved freely or affected by grace. 2. by the same and by her kinswoman Elizabeth v. 42, εὐλογημένη, Blessed: not actively as if she were the source of grace and blessing; but passively, since she received singular grace and blessing from God, while she was chosen before all women for the conception and birth of the eternal λόγος.

XXV. By the Church she is commonly called the holy Virgin, or holy Mary. 1. On account of Election and Consecration to this preternatural act, in which sense it is used in Lev. 20:23. 2. On account of Imputation, by which, as to all believers, the holiness of Christ is imputed to her, 1 Cor. 1:30. 3. On account of Renovation, insofar as she was partly sanctified by the Holy Spirit in a peculiar way, lest the Holy of Holies about to be born of her should contract anything unclean from her, of which the angel testifies in Luke 1:35, and partly she was purged through the Word and Sacraments, and thus was holy in an inchoative sense, as all the pious are, Phil. 1:1. 4. On account of Consummation, which she put on in heaven with all the saints, as it is used in 1 Thess. 3:13, 2 Thess. 1:10.

XXVI. The monks add yet one more kind or manner of holiness, namely Sanctification in the womb, where they claim she was preserved from the stain of origin; and they lie, citing the Gospel of Andrew, that she was conceived not ordinarily, but miraculously, through a kiss which her father Joachim planted upon her mother Anna, as Osiander reports.

XXVII. But we, taught by a better source, deny that Mary was ever immune from original stain, moved by reasons not probable, but necessary and drawn from the very fountains of Holy Scripture. I. From the universal statements by which all men are declared to be sinners and conceived in

Latin:

Continuatio.

DE Genealogia & Proavis Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi in præcedenti disputatione actum: ordo postulat, ut de ipsius Genetrice, qvam secundùm carnem habuit, Virgine Maria, jam nunc dispiciamus. Ne verò ἀτάκτως & ἀμεθόδως divagemur, ad tria hæc collimabimus capita. I. κατασκευαστικῶς sanam doctrinam de gloriosa Messiæ Matre proponemus. II. ἀνασκευαστικῶς blasphemias & ἑτεροδοξίαν adversariorum rejiciemus: & tandem III. post Meditationem Practicam receptui canemus.

Christe, fer auxilium, castâ de Virgine nate.

Thesis I.

Licet extra omnem dubitationis aleam jactum sit, MessiamMatrem habuisse; Qværi tamen sub initium potest: Quomodo matrem habere potuerit Christus, cùm præfiguratus fuerit per Melchisedecum, qui non solùm ἀπάτωρ sed & ἀμήτωρ dicitur, Hebr. 7, 3.

II. Ubi responsio in promtu est: 1. Quòd nempè Melchisedecus sine patre & matre fuisse dicatur, non quidem eo sensu, ac si nullos habuerit parentes, & vel cœlitùs delapsus vel ab æterno extiterit, ut Melchisedeciani delirarunt (a); qvoniam veteres arbitrati sunt, ipsum fuisse Semum filium Noachi (b): sed ideò qvod Gen. 4. ubi ipsius mentio, non expressè nominentur nec memorentur ipsius parentes.

III. Deinde 2. cum in Christo agnoscendæ sint duæ nativitates duæqve naturæ, Utramqve ex antitypo, qvi typum Christi gessit, discimus, alteram divinam, alteram humanam; ἀπάτωρ est juxta humanitatem, qvam non ex Josepho patre putatitio, sed ex sola matre virgine Spiritus Sancti virtute in tempore accepit: ἀμήτωρ juxta divinitatem, qvam non ex matre, sed ex solo Patre Deo ab æterno habet; ita tamen ut & mater in Personalibus locutionibus θεοτόκος rectè appelletur (a).

IV. Remorâ hac remotâ rectè ad rem ipsam accedimus, ubi duo principaliter attendenda erunt: Nomen Matris Messiæ, & ipsa Persona B. Virginis.

V. Nomen Matris Domini fuit Maria. Hebræis מִרְיָם, Syris מַרְיָם, qvo nomine & soror Mosis insignita legitur Exod. 15, 20. qvod Excelsam exponit Schindlerus, (b) & deducit ex radice רוּם Altus, elevatus fuit. Qvidam à מָרַר derivant, amarus, acerbus fuit, ita ut Maria dicta sit qvasi amara, ob dolorum acerbitatem, qvos pertulit. Chytreus (c) refert, qvosdam veteres doctricem populi interpretasse à יוֹרֶה & עַם, Hieronymus sermone Syro Dominam sonare vult à radice Syriaca מָרָא Dominus. Unde illud 1. Cor. 16, 22. deductum putat μαρὰν ἀθὰ, qvasi Dominus venit, sc. ad judicium. Nonnulli derivant à מַר qvod est stilla sive gutta, & יָם, qvod mare, qvasi dicta sit stilla Maris (d).

VI. An hoc nomen veteres Judæorum, qvi Mariam antecesserant, præsciverint, suo loco relinqvimus. Galatinus probare conatur autoritate Rabbi Haccados, qvi Revelationem arcanorum scripsit; ubi ipfis nomen qvoq; Patris Mariæ notum fuisse ex Cabala argutatur (a).

VII. Hæc de Nomine Matris Christi: de Persona ipsa qvatuor observanda veniunt: Status, Familia, Tituli & Dignitas.

VIII. 1. Status fuit Virgo & qvidem desponsata. Ex virgine enim sine virili semine natus est Salvator, ut Dei sapientia & singularis hujus mysterii ratio innotescerit: nec novo homini alius nisi novus concipiendi & nascendi modus conveniebat. Primus homo Adam ex nullo alio homine natus, sed à Deo immediatè creatus est: secundus, Eva non ex fœminâ, sed solo viro formata est: Tertii & reliqvi homines omnes ex viro & fœmina naturaliter progenerantur. Qvartus restabat modus ex fœmina sine viro, qvi solius est Christi, novus modus novi hominis, qvartus & ultim⁹ mod⁹ in qvarta & ultima ætate patefactus (b).

IX. Deinde natus est ex fœminâ solâ sine viro, ut hinc illum etiam aliud qvid esse qvàm hominem crederemus.

X. 3. Ut implerentur vaticinia Jerem. 31, 22. Esa. 7, 14. Ezech. 44, 1. ut non abs re de hoc mysterio doctores Ecclesiæ & Rabbi Haccados exposuerunt. Propterea etiam futurus Messias semen mulieris indigitatur, Gen. 3, 15. non viri.

XI. 4. Ut nativitas æterni λόγε propter miraculum esset nobilior. 5. Ut Messias futurus sancta & perfecta victima pro mundi peccatis conciperetur & nasceretur sine peccato, Hebr. 7, 26. in qvo concipiuntur omnes ex viri & fœminæ congressu post primum peccatum progeniti, Pf. 51, 7. Rom. 5, 12. Joh. 3, 6.

XII. 6. Ut lapsui responderet reparatio: Per mulierem & qvidem virginem, peccandi factum est exordium, 1. Tim. 2, 14. per virginem igitur peccatorum qvoq; venire debebat remedium.

XIII. 7. Qvia non decuit, ut unus & idem filius duos haberet Patres, alterum in cœlo, alterum in terra; sed decuit, ut sicut essentiam Deitatis à solo accepit Patre, sic etiam essentiam humanitatis à solâ accipiat matre in terris. (a)

XIV. 8. Ut qvædam sit analogia inter Christi nativitatem & fidelium regenerationem. Generatio enim Christi ex virgine est signum spiritualis nostræ regenerationis, qvæ non ex sangvine neq; ex libidine carnis aut libidine viri, sed ex Deo est. (b)

XV. Patres (c) addunt hanc rationem, 9. ut castitas hoc exemplo nobis commendaretur; qvod facilè recipimus, si non sensu Pontificio de voto continentiæ & virginitatis intelligatur.

XVI. Hinc non solùm confitemur in Symbolo nostro Christum conceptum à Spiritu Sancto, sed & natum ex Maria virgine, propter verba angeli Matth. 1, 20. & Esaiæ ibidem v. 23. citata.

XVII. Virginitatem autem salvam & incorruptam retinuit non tantùm in conceptione & partu Christi, verùm etiam post partum. De priori ambigi non potest: Posterius licet manifestis Scripturæ testimoniis non fulciatur, pium tamen est credere, cum sacris literis minimè repugnet: aliam rationem verisimilem affert Perkinsius (a).

XVIII. Cæterùm ad qvæstionem, an Christus natus sit aperto Mariæ utero, an clauso? an cum dolore partus, an sine dolore? Respondemus, Verisimilius videri, factum id esse viâ clausâ, & per consequens sine dolore: id qvod inde colligi posse videtur, qvòd mater statim potuit infantem natum curare: qvòd dolor pœna sit corruptionis, qvæ in Maria fuit nulla: qvòd deniqve eâdem ratione Christus natus rectè censeatur, qvâ conceptus, ut scilicet non fregerit virginitatis claustra, sed sicut impassibiliter introiit, ita ineffabiliter exivit, ut Chemnitius ex Gregorio Nisseno citat (b).

XIX. Præterea & hoc notatu dignum, qvòd non ex virgine libera, sed jam desponsata, in lucem est editus, Luc. 1, 27. Factum id asserunt Patres (c) tum Sui, tum Matris, tum nostri causâ.

XX. Sui, 1. ne nothus & illegitimè prognatus ab infidelibus proclamaretur. 2. ut ejus genealogia ex putaticii patris genere meliùs innotesceret. 3. ut nutricium, curatorem & defensorem haberet in ætate infantili. Tandem 4. ut partus virginis lateret Diabolum, qvâ ratione Patres non pauci utuntur (d), eam tamen pleriq; rejiciunt (e).

XXI. Matris respectu 1. ut ipsi⁹ famæ & saluti consuleretur, ne pro adulterâ habita ad supplicium traheretur. 2. ut haberet curatorem in fuga, (a) & testem, cujus conversatione ipsius pudicitia comprobaretur.

XXII. Nostri causâ, 1. ut fides nostra de nativitate Christi stabiliretur. Joseph enim procul omne dubium eam reliqvisset, si de ejus virginitate dubitasset. 2. ut ostenderetur, Deo tum statum virginitatis tum conjugii placere 3. ut modus reparationis responderet modo lapsûs,qui originem ex virgine conjugata traxit. 4. Christo mater sponsa qværitur,ut Ecclesia Christi sponsa signetur(b).

XXIII. II. Familia Mariæ. Nasci voluit Christus non ex qvâvis, sed ex eâ, qvæ de tribu Juda,& è domo Davidis orta fuit. Ratio in promtu est in sacris literis, ut nimirum oracula Prophetarum, & decreta Dei, Gen. 49,10. 2. Sam. 7,12. ipso opere complerentur. Nec ineptè factum dixerim,ut regia stirps Messiæ majorem dignitatem adderet, ejusq́ve officium regium adumbraret.

XXIV. III. Titulos Mariæ orthodoxè tres agnoscimus : duos Biblicos & unum Ecclesiasticum. Ab angelo, Luc. 1, 28. dicitur 1. κεχαριτωμένη, qvasi gratis dilecta vel gratiâ affecta. 2. ab eodem & cognatâ Elisabethâ v. 42. εὐλογημένη Benedicta: non activè qvasi fons esset gratiæ & benedictionis; sed passivè, qvoniam à Deo singularem gratiam & benedictionem accepit, dum præ omnibus mulieribus ad conceptionem & partum æterni λόγε electa fuit.

XXV. Ab Ecclesiâ nuncupatur vulgariter Virgo sancta, sive sancta Maria. 1. Propter Electionem & Consecrationem ad actum hunc præternaturalem, qvo sensu usurpatur Lev. 20, 23. 2. Propter Imputationem, qvâ & ipsi,ut omnibus fidelibus, sanctitas Christi imputatur, 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. 3. Propter Renovationem,qvatenus partim peculiari ratione à Spiritu sancto est sanctificata, ne sanctus sanctorum ex eâ nasciturus ex ipsa aliqvid immundum contraheret, de qvo testatur angelus Luc. 1, 35.partim per Verbum &Sacramēta fuit purgata, atq; adeò inchoativè sancta,ut omnes pii Phil. 1.v. 1. 4. Propter Consummationem,qvam in cœlis cum omnibus sanctis induit, ut usurpatur 1.Thess. 3, 13. 2.Thess. 1, v. 10.

XXVI. Monachi sanctitatis speciem seu modum adhuc addunt unicum, Sanctificationem nimirum in utero, ubi à labe originis præservatam dictitant; & exEvangelio Andreæ mentiuntur, ipsam non ordinariè, sed miraculosè, per osculum, qvod Pater Joachimns matri Annæ fixerit,conceptam, referente Osiandro.

XXVII. Verùm nos melioris edocti pernegamus,Mariam unqvā ab originali labe immunē fuisse, moti rationibus non probabilibus, sed necessariis & ex ipsis S.Scripturę fontibus haustis. I. Ex dictis universalibus,qvibus omnes homines peccatores & in peccatis cōcepti enuncia-


### sins, Job 14:4. John 3:6

sins, Job 14:4. John 3:6. Rom. 5:10. II. By exclusive statements, by which Christ alone is exempted from the census of sinners, Luke 1:35. Heb. 4:15, 7:26. III. By statements testifying to the redemption and sanctification of Mary, Luke 1:35, 47, for which there would have been no need if she had existed devoid of sin. IV. By places where the ἀγνοήματα (ignorances/errors) of Mary are recounted, Luke 2:43, 45. John 2:5.

XXVIII. V. From calamities and death, from which she would have been free if she had lacked all sin. VI. Because in Holy Scripture there is deep silence concerning this privilege of Mary, but nothing of a record. VII. From the testimony of antiquity, which up to the times of Lombard, to the year 1150, opined that the Blessed Virgin Mary was conceived in original sin; they attributed ambition and rashness, indeed infidelity, to her, as cited by Perkins (a).

XXIX. Lastly, from the variety of opinions among the Papists themselves. Lombard (b) confesses that Mary was conceived in sin, but that she was purified from it at the conception of Christ. Scotus (c) speaks doubtfully and says it seems probable. Thomas (d) and others think otherwise. Bellarmine (e) confesses that this dogma has not been approved by the Apostolic See, nor is it held by Catholics as an article of faith. We conclude, therefore, that Mary is most rightly called holy; yet that she did not lack every fault and stain of sin, but rather that she was, like us, defiled by hereditary disease and subject to certain παραπτώμασι (transgressions).

XXX. IV. The dignity of Mary is such that we rightly attribute to her the highest veneration and honor. Which is owed to her as a prophetess on earth, Isaiah 8:3, and a saint in heaven, Luke 1:48, ch. 11:27. And it consists in these parts: 1. That we give thanks to God for her. 2. That we pursue her with love. 3. That we celebrate her mighty works, and 4. That we imitate her as much as we are able.

XXXI. However, we judge that she should in no way be treated with divine honor or religiously invoked: 1. Because she is not omniscient so as to hear, nor omnipotent so as to be able to answer our sighs. 2. Because we have neither command, nor example, nor promise for this worship: deprived of which conditions, invocation is condemned as ἐθελοθρησκείας (will-worship), Matt. 15:9, and is convicted of sin, Rom. 14:23; for the measure of faith is the word of God, Rom. 10:17. (a) And thus we teach and think orthodoxly concerning Mary.

XXXII. It remains now that we note the heterodoxy in individual parts and mark it with an obelisk. First, therefore, concerning the name of the Blessed Virgin Most of the Papists are very foolish. Marinus Brixianus without reason derives it from the root מָרַר, he was a rebel. (b) Some boast that Mary is so called as if she were the star of the sea, an error derived from Jerome (who handed down that it means a drop of the sea) either not read correctly or poorly understood, as Drusius notes. (c) And therefore Barradius is ridiculous, (d) who seizes upon this interpretation and thinks Mary is called the star of the sea because she illuminates the world, which is compared to the sea. More foolish are those who derive it either from the Latin word Mare, or think Mary is so called as if it were a bitter sea, as Bonaventura (e) does. Mary, he says, is a sea of grace by flowing, bitter by sympathizing with her son, and a bitter sea by submerging the Devil.

XXXIII. They are too superstitious who teach that this name was destined for the Virgin Mother of God by God from eternity, and that it alone was inscribed with the name of Jesus in the book of life, and they attempt to prove this with many enticements of words, as Barradius does in the cited passage.

XXXIV. Concerning the Person of Mary and indeed I. The state, there were blasphemers 1. Ebion and Cerinthus, who established Mary as the wife of Joseph, and slandered that Christ was born from the intercourse of Joseph and Mary, so that they might make him a ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον [mere man]: Moved by no other reason than that Mary is called the γυνὴ [wife] of Joseph, Matt. 1, 20. and conversely Joseph the ἀνὴρ [husband] of Mary, v. 16. 19. and the father of Christ, Luke 2, 48.

XXXV. But the answer is easy: Regarding the former, consent makes a marriage, not conjugal habit. Joseph and Mary were betrothed, therefore they are called spouses, according to the custom of the Scriptures, Deut. 20, 7. c. 28, 30. This is manifest from c. 1, Matt. v. 18. 19. where Joseph, discovering her pregnant even before intercourse, wished to leave her. Furthermore, it is expressly said that she was the γυνὴ [wife] of Joseph, μεμνηστευμένη, a wife only betrothed, not yet brought home.

XXXVI. Regarding the latter, we say that Joseph is called Father not of Nature, but of Care. Hence Luke speaks significantly and explains himself in c. 3, 23, saying of Christ: He was the son, as was supposed, ὡς ἐνομίζετο, of Joseph.

XXXVII. 2. More impious are the Jews, who even today in their synagogues hawk the glorious mother of Christ as a harlot and concubine, and proclaim it with a virulent mouth. And so that they may maintain this stubborn error of theirs, and not be forced to yield to the clear testimony of Isaiah 7, 14; they shout that the word עַלְמָה does not perpetually signify a virgin, but sometimes than a young woman known by a man, so that it is a name of age rather than of status. And this is against Scripture, in which this word is found in no other meaning: against Etymology itself, since this word signifies a hidden or untouched virgin, descending indeed from the root עלם, He hid: and finally against several Rabbis.

XXXVIII. In order to seek a defense for their bad cause, they wish to prove their opinion from this passage, which is nevertheless controversial: and from another, Proverbs 30:19. Where they pretend that Alma is added to a man, and therefore cannot be taken for a virgin, but for an adulteress and a harlot, and they strive to obtain this from the following verse.

XXXIX. But these are rotten inventions. For in the former passage Isaiah speaks of an unusual work of GOD, which surpasses nature. And yet it is no wonder for a young woman who has known a man to conceive. But they insist that the Prophet here does not speak of the mother of the Messiah, but of his own wife, and they wish to deduce this from chapter 8, 3.

XL. But these are trifles. The woman of whom the Prophet speaks is a young woman. The wife of Isaiah is not such a one, since she has an adult son, as is evident from chapter 7, verse 3. Next, the son of the Alma is the Lord of the land, Isaiah 8:8 and following. 3. The eighth chapter coheres with the ninth, as the context proves, and the Targum and other ancient Hebrews attest. Now, of whom the ninth chapter speaks, of him also the eighth speaks. But the ninth is not to be understood of a ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ (mere man), but of the Messiah. Therefore, the eighth is also. 4. Finally, the son of the Alma is Immanuel; the son of Isaiah is not Immanuel. Therefore. 5. Finally, Rabbi Haccados interprets this passage concerning the Messiah. (a)

XLI. The Jews continue to trifle, arguing thus: The son of the Alma is called Immanuel. The son of Mary is not called Immanuel, but Jesus. Therefore. We see these absurdities and futilities, having learned that Scripture attributes not one name to the Messiah, but several, of which some are of Nature, such as Immanuel; others of Imposition, such as Jesus; others of Office, such as Christ: which, however, do not conflict, but wonderfully agree and correspond.

XLII. As far as the latter passage, Prov. 30:16, is concerned, they can extract nothing from it. For both the manner and the various counsels of the nobles who seek the marriage of a virgin are wonderful. Nor does it move us that mention is made of an adulteress in the following verse; for the sentences of that chapter do not cohere, but are various and entirely diverse and disparate. Furthermore, granted,

That Solomon in the text speaks of an adulteress, the Jews would nevertheless gain nothing, unless this, that the discourse is about a young woman who sold herself as a virgin, although she was a virgin. But the abusive meaning of a word cannot prescribe against its genuine and proper meaning. (a)

XLIII. 3. Furthermore, Helvidius did not deny the virginity of Mary in its entirety, but doubted it in part, namely after the birth of the Messiah. Moved by Matt. 1, v. last, from which he proposed two arguments. 1. Christ is called the firstborn of Mary, hence it follows that she bore more children after Christ. 2. Matthew says, he did not know her until she had given birth. Therefore, Joseph knew her afterwards.

XLIV. We reply in a few words that this dogma is not an article of faith. Meanwhile, this passage of Matthew concludes nothing. For the word 'firstborn' is not always said with respect to a relation to brothers born afterwards. For as he is called the last after whom there is no other, so he is called the firstborn before whom there was no other. Furthermore, the particle 'until' is ambiguous; for sometimes it signifies the limit of the thing to which it is attached, sometimes its continuation. (b)

XLV. Nor does it move us that he is said to have had brothers in Mark 6:3. For brothers are spoken of in four ways: by nature, by nation, by kinship, by affection; it is in the third way that it is stated here concerning Christ.

XLVI. Finally, 4. The Scholastics and Jesuits (c) do not seem to be endowed with a sound mind, while they wish to elicit from Luke 1:34 that Mary made a vow of virginity: as if she had said, I do not know a man, that is, I do not wish to know one: for I have vowed my virginity to God. For those words are not those of one doubting, but of one asking about the manner; which is manifestly clear from the context; and if one looks a little more attentively, the contrary shines forth, so that no place is left for the Papistic conjecture. Add that in the Old Testament such a vow was clearly unknown. (a) The fable, which they bring forward from the Protevangelium of James, we value as a straw, as is right.

XLVII. II. Schmalcius, certainly driven by furies, denies the family of the Blessed Virgin, (b) while he asserts that Christ is said to be born from the lineage of David, not because his mother was from that family, but because she was betrothed to a man who was descended from that family. Since he establishes this opinion with no argument, and since it is extremely diabolical, and subverts the foundation of our whole religion concerning CHRIST the Messiah, we refute it with pious detestation only. But if anyone should wish to press the genealogies of the Evangelists, we refer the adversary to the preceding disputation.

XLVIII. III. Concerning the titles of Mary, the Papists cherish a gross error: while from the fact that Mary is called holy, they affirm that she herself was conceived without original sin, and passed her life without actual sin. But since they have arguments of no value, and deduce them chiefly from that passage in Canticles 4:7, which speaks not of Mary but of the Church of Christ, and have drawn this opinion from the Pseudo-Gospel of Andrew, we return that opinion to its authors.

XLIX. IV. Finally, the Papists extol the dignity of Mary too much. While they judge that she is to be venerated and adored with the religious worship of hyperdulia, they establish feasts for her, and decree that she is to be pursued with honor plainly equal to Christ. It is not permitted to treat of this idolatry at length now, and it is usually disputed elsewhere in the place concerning the invocation of Saints.

L. We now shorten sail. And because Christ is the son of man, and true man born of the virgin Mary alone without a man; thence we evidently conclude against certain fanatical woman-haters: that women are equally human beings as males. For just as life departed into perdition through a woman, so salvation was introduced into the world through a female. Let women seize this sweet consolation in all calamities and in the agony of death. But let us live together, as it befits those who are knowledgeable, with the female vessel as with the weaker one, granting them honor as co-heirs of the grace of life, 1 Peter 3:7. To Christ the God-man be praise and glory.

Latin:

tur, Job. 14, 4. Joh. 3, 6. Rom. 5, 10. II. Dictis Exclusivis, qvibus solus Christus e censu peccatorum exautoratur, Luc. 1, 35. Hebr. 4, 15. 7, 26. III. Dictis de redemtione & sanctificatione Mariæ testantibus Luc. 1, 35. 47. qvo utiqve opus non fuisset, si exors peccati extitisset. IV. Locis, qvibus ἀγνοήματα Mariæ recensentur, Luc. 2, 43. 45. Joh. 2, 5.

XXIIX. V. Ex calamitatibus, & morte, a qvib⁹ libera fuisset, si omni caruisset peccato. VI. Qvia in sacra Scriptura de hoc Mariæ privilegio altum silentium, ὀυδὲν verò ἀπογραφῆς. VII. A Testimonio antiqvitatis, qvæ usqve ad Lombardi tempora ad annum 1150. B. virginem Mariam in originali peccato conceptam fuisse autumavit, ambitionem & temeritatem, imò infidelitatem ipsi attribuerunt, citante Perkinsio (a).

XXIX. Ultimò a varietate sententiarum inter ipsos Papicolas. Lombardus (b) Mariam in peccato conceptam fatetur, sed in conceptione Christi purgatam fuisse ab ipso. Scotus (c) dubitanter loqvitur & probabile videri ait. Thomas (d) & alii aliter sentiunt. Bellarminus (e) fatetur, dogma hoc non esse comprobatum ab Apostolicâ sede, nec pro articulo fidei a Catholicis haberi. Concludimus ergò Mariam sanctam rectissimè appellari; non tamen omni culpâ & peccatorum maculâ caruisse, verùm etiam ut nos morbo hæreditario inqvinatam & qvibusdam παραπτώμασι subjectam fuisse.

XXX. IV. Dignitas Mariæ tanta est, ut ei meritò summam venerationem & honorem tribuamus. Qvi ipsi debetur tanqvam Prophetissæ in terra, Esai 8, 3. & sanctæ in cælis, Luc. 1, 48. c. 11, 27. Et consistit in his membris 1. Ut gratias agamus Deo de eâ. 2. ipsam amore proseqvamur. 3. virtutes ejus celebremus, & 4. pro virili imitemur.

XXXI. Nullo autem modo divino ipsam honore afficiendam aut religiosè invocandam censemus: 1. qvia non est omníscia ut audire, nec omnipotens ut exaudire possit nostra suspiria. 2. qvia hujus cultus nec habemus præceptum, nec exemplum, nec promissum: qvibus conditionibus destituta invocatio ἐθελοθρησκείας damnatur Matth. 15, 9. & peccati arguitur Rom. 14, 23. fidei enim mensura est verbum Dei, Rom. 10, 17. (a) Et sic qvid de Maria orthodoxè docemus & sentimus.

XXXII. Restat nunc ut ἑτεροδοξίαν in singulis membris annotemus ac obelisco signemus. Primò igitur circa Nomen Beatæ virginis valdè ineptiunt pleriq; Pontificiorum. Marinus Brixianus sine ratione à radice מָרַר Rebellis fuit, deducit. (b) Qvidam Mariam dictam qvasi stellam Maris jactitant, errore ducto ex Hieronymo (qvi stillam Maris sonare tradidit) vel non rectè lecto vel malè intellecto, ut notat Drusius. (c) Ac proinderidiculus est Barradius, (d) qvi hanc interpretationem arripit, Mariamqve stellam maris dici putat, qvòd illuminet mundum, qvi comparatur mari. Ineptiores sunt, qvi vel à Mari vocabulo Latino derivant, vel qvasi Mare amarum dictam Mariam putant, ut Bonaventura (e). Maria, inqviens, mare est gratiæ affluendo, amara filio compatiendo, & amarum mare Diabolum submergendo.

XXXIII. Nimium superstitiosi sunt, qvi hoc nomen virgini Deiparæ ab æterno à Deo destinatum, idqve solùm cum nomine Jesu in libro vitæ inscriptum docent, idq; multis verborum lenociniis probare conantur, ut Barradius loco citato.

XXXIV. Circa Personam Mariæ & qvidẽI. Statum, blasphemi fuerunt 1. Ebion & Cerinthus, qvi Mariam conjugem Josephi statuerunt, & Christum ex concubitu Josephi & Mariæ natum esse calumniati sunt, ut eum ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον facerent: Moti nullâ aliâ ratione, qvàm qvòd Maria γυνὴ Josephi dicitur, Matth. 1, 20. & contrà Joseph ἀνὴρ Mariæ, v. 16. 19. & pater Christi, Luc. 2, 48.

XXXV. Verùm responsio est facilis: Ad prius, Consensus facit matrimonium, non consvetudo conjugalis. Desponsati fuerunt Joseph & Maria, ideò conjuges appellantur, more Scripturis consveto, Deut. 20, 7. c. 28, 30. Manifestum hoc est ex c. 1, Matth. v. 18. 19. ubi Joseph jam ante concubitum gravidam deprehendens voluit relinqvere. Deindè expresse dicitur γυνὴ Josephi μεμνηστευμένη, uxor tantummodò desponsata, nondum domum deducta.

XXXVI. Ad posterius dicimus Josephum Patrem dici non Naturæ, sed Curæ. Hinc significanter loqvitur, & sese explicat Lucas c. 3, 3. de Christo inqviens; Erat filius, ut putabatur, ὡς ἐνομίζετο Josephi.

XXXVII. 2. Magis impii sunt Judei, qvi gloriosam Christi matrem adhuc hodiè in suis Synagogis pro scorto & pellice venditant, ac virulento ore proclamant. Et ut obstinatum hunc suum errorem obtineant, nec claro testimonio Esai 7, 14. cedere cogantur; Vocem עַלְמָה non perpetuò virginem significare clamant, sed nonnunquam juvenculam à viro cognitam, ita ut potiùs sit nomen ætatis, quam statûs. Idq́; contra Scripturam, in qua hoc verbum in nullo alio significatu invenitur: contra ipsam Etymologiam, cùm hoc vocabulum absconditam sive illibatam signet virginem, qvippe à radice עלם Abscondidit, descendens: contra aliqvot deniq; Rabbinos.

XXXVIII. Malæ suæ causæ ut patrocinium qværant, opinionem suam probare volunt ex hoc loco, qvi tamen controversus: & altero, Proverb. 30, 19. Ubi Alma viro addi prætendunt, ac proinde pro virgine sumi non posse, verùm pro adultera & scorto, idq́; ex seq. vers. obtinere satagunt.

XXXIX. Verùm putida sunt commenta. Priori enim loco de inusitato DEI opere loqvitur Esaias, qvod superet naturam. Atqvi mirum non est concipere juvenculam, qvæ virum cognovit. Sed instant, Prophetam hîc non loqvi de matre Messiæ, sed de uxore suâ, idq́; ex c. 8, 3. deducere volunt.

XL. Nugæ autem sunt. Fœmina, de qvâ Propheta loqvitur, est juvencula. Uxor Esaiæ talis non est, qvippe filium adultum habens, ut patet ex c. 7. v. 3. Deinde Alma filius est Dominus terræ, Es. 8, 8.& seqq. 3. Caput octavum cum nono cohæret, ut contextus evincit, & Targum & alii veteres Hebræi attestantur. Jam de qvo loqvitur caput nonum, de eo & octavum. Sed nonum non de ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, verùm de Messia intelligendum. Ergo & octavum. 4. Deniq; filius Almæ est Immanuel; filius Esaiæ non est Immanuel. Ergo. 5. Deniq; Rabbi Haccados de Messia interpretatur hunc locum. (a)

XLI. Adhuc nugari pergunt Judæi, ita argumentantes: Filius Almæ dicitur Immanuel. Filius Mariæ non dicitur Immanuel, sed Jesus. E. Nos videmus has ineptias & futilitates, docti Scripturam Messiæ non unum nomen tribuere, sed plura, qvorum alia sunt Naturæ, ut Immanuel; alia Impositionis, ut Jesus; alia Officii, ut Christus: qvæ tamen non pugnant, sed mirè consentiunt & congruunt.

XLII. Posteriorem locum Prov. 30, 16. qvod attinet, ex eo nihil eruere possunt. Nam & mirabilis est ratio, & consilia varia procerum, qvi virginis nuptias ambiunt. Nec movet nos, qvod in seq. vers. adulteræ fiat mentio; sententiæ enim illius capitis non cohærent, sed sunt variæ ac prorsus diversæ & disparatæ. Adhæc, posito,

Salomonem in textu de adulterâ loqvi, nihil tamen lucrarentur Judæi, nisi hoc, sermonem esse de juvenculâ, qvæ se pro virgine venditet, licet virgo fuerit. Abusiva verò significatio vocabuli genuino & proprio non potest præscribere. (a)

XLIII. 3. Porrò Helvidius virginitatem Mariæ in totum non negavit, sed ex parte de ea dubitavit, nempe post partum Messiæ. Motus Matt. 1. v. ult. ex qvo duo proposuit argumenta. 1. Christus dicitur primogenitus Mariæ, hinc seqvitur, qvòd plures post Christum natos peperit. 2. Matthæus dicit, non cognovit eam, donec peperit. Ergo postea cognovit eam Josephus.

XLIV. Nos paucis Resp. hoc dogma non esse articulum fidei. Interim hunc locum Matthæi nihil concludere. Vocabulum enim Primogeniti non semper dicitur respectu relationis ad fratres postea natos. Nam ut novissimus appellatur is, post qvem nullus est alius: ita primogenitus vocatur is, ante qvem non fuit alius. Deinde particula Donec est ambigua; nonnunqvam enim significat terminum rei, cui apponitur, nonnunqvam continuationem. (b)

XLV. Nec nos movet, qvòd fratres habuisse dicitur Marc. 6, 3. Fratres enim qvatuor modis dicuntur: Naturâ, Gente, Cognatione, Affectu; modo tertio hîc de Christo enunciatur.

XLVI. Tandem 4. Scholastici & Jesuitæ (c) non sanâ mente videntur præditi, dum ex Luc. 1, 34. elicere volunt, Mariam votum virginitatis fecisse: ac si dixisset, virum non cognosco, hoc est, cognoscere nolo: Deo enim virginitatem vovi. Nam verba ista non sunt dubitantis, sed modum qværentis: qvod manifestè ex contextu patet; & si paulò attentiùs introspicitur, contrarium enitet, ita ut nullus conjecturæ Papisticæ relinqvatur locus. Adde qvod in Veteri Testamento tale votum planè ignotum erat. (a) Fabulam, qvam ex Protevangelio Jacobi afferunt, ut fas, flocci facimus.

XLVII. II. Familiam B. Virginis negat, furiis certè agitatus Schmalcius, (b) dum asseverat Christum ideò dici natum ex stirpe Davidis, non qvòd mater ejus ex illa familia fuerit, sed qvòd viro ex illa familia oriundo fuerit desponsata. Qvam sententiam cum nullo argumento stabiliat, cumqve ipsa extremè sit diabolica, & fundamentum totius nostræ religionis de CHRISTO Messia subvertat, piâ tantùm detestatione refutamus. Qvod sigenealogias Evangelistarum urgere voluerit, adversarium ad disputationem præcedentem remittimus.

XLVIII. III. De Titulis Mariæ crassum fovent errorem Pontificii: dum ex eo, qvod sancta dicitur Maria, ipsam sine Peccato originali conceptam, vitamq́ve sine actuali traduxisse affirmant. Sed cùm argumenta nihili habeant, potissimùm ex illo Cant. 4, 7. deducant, qvod non de Maria, sed de Ecclesia Christi loqvitur, & ex Pseudevangelio Andreæ hanc opinionem hauserint, opinionem istam suis autoribus remittimus.

XLIX. IV. Dignitatem deniqve Mariæ nimium extollunt Papicolæ. Dum ipsam cultu religioso ὑπερδουλέιας venerandam ac adorandam censent, ipsi festa sanciunt, & planè æqvali cum Christo honore proseqvendam statuunt. De qvâ idololatria jam multis agere non licet, & aliàs in loco de invocatione Sanctorum disputari solet.

L. Nos jam vela contrahimus. Et qvia Christus filius hominis, verusq́ve homo ex solâ virgine Mariâ sine viro natus; Inde contra fanaticos qvosdam μισογυναίκες evidenter concludimus: Mulieres æqvè esse homines ac Masculos. Qvemadmodum enim vita per mulierem abiit in perditionem, ita per fœminam introducta est in mundum salvatio. Arripiant hoc dulce solamen in omnibus calamitatibus & agone mortis fœmellæ. Nos verò cohabitemus, ut scientes decet, vasi muliebri ut infirmiori, tribuentes eis honorem tanqvam cohæredibus gratiæ vitæ, 1. Petr. 3, 7. Christo θεανθρώπῳ laus & gloria.


## 25 Twenty-fifth Disputation, On the Nativity of Christ from the Virgin

Continuation.

AS there are two natures in the God-man, so Scripture indicates a double Nativity of these: one of the natures is divine, begotten through eternal generation; the other is human, produced through temporal birth: The former was made by the Father, without a Mother;

This one from a Mother without a Father: Through the former, the true God and חָסִין [Mighty One] exists; through the latter, the true man and our brother exists: By the former, born before every day, who created every day; by the latter, born in a day, who consecrated every day: Through the former, God is hidden; through the latter, man is manifest: both are wonderful, both are ineffable; in both, 'great is the mystery of godliness' (1 Tim. 3:16), into which even the angels desire 'to look' (1 Pet. 1:12). And while we defend both, we do not abolish either by the affirmation of the other; for we do not condemn the temporal by the perpetuity of the former, nor do we conclude the eternal by the brevity of this temporal one, knowing the Word of God is an inseparable offspring, and the truest flesh of this true offspring; and just as through the former He is truly made אֵל [God], so through the latter He is truly עִמָּנוּאֵל [Immanuel]: We weighed the former in the preceding [sections], and we shall contemplate the latter in the present examination, enclosed within four distinct chapters according to the plan of our undertaking: 1. treating of the Circumstances: 2. the Nativity itself: 3. its Purpose: and finally concluding with a practical meditation.

Thesis I.

As the knowledge of the life of Christ is salutary—inasmuch as it shows the way, if we seek it; the provision for the soul, if we desire it; the truth, if we covet it; the bread which descends from heaven and gives life to the world, if we are hungry; and points out the fountain springing up into eternal life, if we are thirsty—so the contemplation of His Nativity is useful: for this is the greatest declaration of divine love toward us, this is the final fulfillment of all promises, this is the beginning of all salutary knowledge, and the foundation of all Christianity, that we know that God was born a Man.

II. Luke, however, recorded this manifestation of the Word in the flesh with the most accurate description among all the Evangelists, whence Ambrose not undeservedly says of him: 'Luke believed he would be rich enough if he had claimed the Lord's manger out of all things.' For what he observed in the previous chapter, omitting nothing that seemed to contribute to an accurate knowledge of the birth of the precursor of Christ, the same he wished to observe diligently here: following his lead, therefore, and avoiding all the errors of others, lest, intoxicated by the pure wine of falsehoods, we be led away into the drunkenness of human traditions, we shall weigh each thing worthy of note, beginning with the circumstances; of which there are two primarily: Time and Place.

III. We investigate the time, not by the rashness of astrologers who divine this birth from a singular observation of the stars, but by the firmness of historical reasons, of which the Evangelist indicates not a few: therefore we must speak 1. of the remote [time], that is, the year: 2. of the nearer, the day: 3. of the closest, the hour. The year is noted, 1. Generally, by the words of v. 5, ch. 1, which compare with Matt. 2, v. 8, 'In the times of Herod the king.' 2. Specifically, by the words of ch. 2, v. 1 ff., which express the description or census of the whole world made by the edict of Augustus Caesar, while Cyrenius was governor of Syria. I called the first notation general, because the specific year of Herod's reign is expressed neither here nor by Matthew; yet this notation contributes not a little to the certainty of the history, especially since by mentioning this, the Evangelists wished to indicate the time destined by God for this birth, and determined by the words of the prophecy of Jacob, Gen. 49, v. 9, 10, whence not without cause he writes notably in ch. 5, v. 1. Luke: Ἡρώδυ τῦ βασιλέως: with the addition of the article τῦ, the distinguishing force of which accurately 1. indicates a certain person, namely Herod the Great, so called from his deeds, the son of Hyrcanus or Antipater, otherwise called the Ascalonite Idumean, the first foreign king of the Jewish nation, (a) who took away the ordinary rule of the tribe of Judah, though not royal, yet priestly, called the Sanhedrin, (b) and by the wicked slaughter of the judges gathered from the house of David, he avenged the punishment once inflicted upon himself, because, having been condemned for murder, he had been forced to go into exile to escape the death penalty, and thus he fulfilled the prophecy of Jacob, Olympiad 185. (c) 2. It distinguishes this Herod from others called by the same name; of whom the first is Antipas, otherwise the Tetrarch, son of Herod the Great: the other is Herod Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, son of Herod the Great, that is, his grandson: the former is mentioned in Matt. 14, Luke 3, Acts 13, Luke 23, whose history see in Josephus. (d) Of this one, Acts 12, v. 2.

IV. And although there is great controversy among authors concerning the calculation, namely in what year of Herod's reign Christ was born, since some (e) maintain it was the 30th year of Herod, others (f) the 33rd year, yet the opinions of them can be easily reconciled, if the year of the appeal or proclamation is distinguished, in which, namely, Herod was named King of Judea, in the 9th year of the reign of Augustus, at the end of the 184th Olympiad; (g) from the year of his rule, in which he began [to rule] Jerusalem, and in the act itself attained Royal Majesty, in the 12th year of Augustus, and the fourth of the 186th Olympiad: (b) from this [latter] point, those who defend 30 [years] make the beginning of their counting; but those who defend 33 [years] make it from the former; others determine it otherwise, whose reasons let Chronologists weigh.

V. In the special notation, three things come to be observed. 1. Augustus Caesar, by whose edict the census was made: 2. the census itself. Regarding Augustus, two things are raised: 1. what year of the world was current at the time of this census? 2. in what year of his reign was it made? Regarding both, there is great controversy, although greater regarding the former; since there are almost as many opinions and judgments about it as there are heads, as can be seen from Lucas Gauricus, who notes not a few, as does Mr. Dr. Chemnitz. (a) We think the matter is settled in the former doubt, if we follow the method of calculation which Mr. Chemnitz shows in the aforementioned work, along with Dr. Luther and Philipp [Melanchthon], who show the year 3962 from the creation of the world to the year of the reign of Augustus in which Christ was born: and we are moved to retain this [year] by: 1. the certainty of the Holy Scriptures proving this method: 2. the multitude of Orthodox [writers]: Luther, Philipp, Chemnitz, Urspergensis, Funccius (who seems to decline slightly to the year 64) and others, etc. 3. The inconstancy of the other Chronologists: 4. The weakness of the reasons opposed to us, which you will find refuted here and there by Thomas Lydiat. (b)

VI. In removing the other [doubt], we follow the common opinion, namely, that the 42nd year of the reign of Augustus was the time of the birth of Christ; and Epiphanius (c), Orosius (d), and Eusebius (e) follow this, to whom Tertullian (f), Jerome (g), and Irenaeus (h) seem contrary, defending the forty-first year; yet they can be easily reconciled if it is said that either the former looked immediately to the death of Caesar, but the latter to the subsequent year; or that the former, according to the Roman Calendar, referred the time of the birth, which occurred toward the end of the year, to the following year, but the latter counted it in the preceding year not yet elapsed: which reconciliation is necessary, unless we wish to say that the later Fathers clearly erred, is apparent.

: VII. There follows the Description, concerning which the Evangelist says in these words: that the whole world should be described; or as the Vulgate and Erasmus have it: that it should be assessed. What is understood by description in this place, authors also vary. Some wish it to be nothing other than a declaration of names, when everyone was compelled to declare his own name to the supreme Monarch Augustus: † But the opinion of those seems more probable who maintain that in this description a certain tax was imposed upon each and every subject of the Roman Empire, and that therefore all were compelled to declare not only their names, but the entire possession of all their goods; which the word ἀπογράφεσθαι seems not obscurely to hint at, used more often in this meaning in Scripture, especially by the 70. See Esther 10:1, Hebrews 12:23.

VIII And lest this description, by which the whole world (πα̃σα ἡ οἰκυμένη literally: the whole habitable [earth]; understand γη̃) hyperbolically and synecdochically, according to the most common custom of the Romans who arrogantly claimed for themselves a general and universal Empire, and thence snatched the title by which they were called Lords of the World, for that part of the world subject to the Roman Empire, as the Syriac rightly expressed the preceding words ܦܪܝܦܪܐܣܬܝܐܬ: All the people of his dominion; is said to be described; should be confused with that which followed this after some years, when Archelaus was relegated after a reign of 9 years, of whom Josephus makes mention. (a) For that one was universal and of the whole empire; this one was particular and of Judea alone, as Mr. Chemnitz proves in the aforementioned place and Beza in his notes upon this passage. It is not without cause that it is added, 1. that it was the First πρώτη: Although others explain this word thus, that it is called first because its beginning was first made in Syria, since Syria was situated as it were in the middle Zone of the habitable world; others that it is called first in respect to Cyrenius, although others had preceded it; but we believe it more correct to say that it is called first for this reason, 1. because no such [description] had preceded it: 2. nor did any follow in such a manner. 2. That it was done while Cyrenius was President of Syria: which words the Vulgate translates badly as 'by Cyrenius presiding,' against manifest reason and truth, since the Evangelist does not indicate by these words by whom, but when this description was made. And indeed the word Κυρηνίυ is consistently read in all the copies, although among Justin, [b] Josephus, [c] Tacitus, [d] it is called Quirinus; but among Onuphrius and the Syriac Interpreter it is called Quirinius; yet the reconciliation is easy here also, since it is established that names of this kind among the Romans were variously read and written by the Greeks: which answer we think will satisfy not so much the poorly informed Aristarchus, as the severe and harsh Phalaris of Luther, Emser.

IX. Many litigate about the day, especially those who claim it is praiseworthy for themselves to inquire curiously into everything, as do most Papists, especially when they have the authorities of some ancient Fathers. Epiphanius [a] establishes the 6th day of January: Clement of Alexandria [b] reports diverse opinions, of which some counted the 25th of φαρμυθὶ, for us April, some the 25th of πάχων, March: We, in an uncertain matter, destitute of firm reasons, prefer to determine nothing rather than to affirm what is false, and we choose to follow the opinion commonly received by the Fathers, Nicephorus [c], and Augustine [d], retaining the 25th day of December: Whether it was the day of the Sun, as Bellarmine [e] thinks; or of Saturn, as Antonio de Gislan [f] thinks; or of Venus, as Surius thinks; we do not doubt: nor do we defend the opinion of Osiander, who rejects the winter season because of a weak argument.

X. Therefore, just as the day is uncertain, so the hour is more uncertain; the fabrications with which they please themselves, and those who think it better to establish something without Scripture than to be silent with Scripture, whatever they may invent, will not be opposed by us.

XI. And it is clear that this consideration of the time of the Lord's nativity is not an idle thing: because it overthrows, first, the impiety of the Jews, who deny that the true Messiah has come, and it shows the fulfillment of all the prophecies predicting the time of the Messiah's birth, and attributing to him the removal of the scepter from Judah, which happened when Caesar Augustus was a foreigner and Herod was an alien king. Therefore, two passages describing this time can be noted here above all, Gen. 49:10, Dan. 2:44, by which, although the Jews are so manifestly convicted and constrained, yet by diabolical fraud they do not cease to invent all sorts of absurdities, so as to deprave the evidence of the text. For what, I ask, does this malice mean, by which they contend that the saying in Gen. 49 is not to be interpreted in the way we explain it? Hence others understand the little word שֵׁבֶט as a rod of calamities, the vanity of whom is easily refuted: For if the little word שֵׁבֶט denotes calamity, it will be either private or public: If the latter? It follows that from the times of this prophecy there was never a tranquil state in the tribe of Judah until the times of the Messiah, the falsity of which assertion is shown by not a few examples: in particular, the well-known one of David & of Solomon: if they object that this peace did not last long nor was it firm; Resp. 1. that such a political peace is nowhere promised in the Messiah: 2. nor is such to be expected, since this promise made to Judah cannot (according to their own opinion) be fulfilled in such great confusion of all the tribes; The things they prattle about the distinction of tribes to be found in the future through the Messiah are not worthy of refutation, since all that has been brought forward is contrary to divine Scripture. If about that? how does this Prophecy pertain to the tribe of Judah alone? since the others are no less subject to daily miseries and also have promises of paternal hearing and benign relief if they are to show obedience to GOD and seek Him in their pressures; others say the little word שֵׁבֶט denotes a tribe, the vanity of which is easily broken, as will become manifest in the conflict.

XII. Others have invented other dreams. Hence some have transferred the little word שִׁילֹה to David; others have wished to denote by it a city called by this name; some have turned the final ה into ח, against the Chaldean Interpreter and the 70, who manifestly retain the ה, whence not without cause we derive the little word שִׁילֹה from שׁלֹה, following the Chaldean and the Greeks reading thus ᾧ τὰ ἀποκείμενα ἀυτῷ, to whom are those things which are laid up, that is, to whom the Kingdom is laid up, and all most happy things: which reading we also confirm with the calculation of pious Antiquity, see Cyprian. (a) Augustine. (b) and others. You will find the rotten figments which they object sufficiently refuted in the most illustrious Mr. Helv. (c) Mr. Dr. Jacob Martin. (d) and the textual Mercer. (e)

XIII. 2. The impudence of the Anabaptists, who under the pretext of Evangelical liberty abolish all Polity, against whom this accurate notation of the time of the Lord's nativity does not a little, showing that Polity is by no means to be abolished by the Gospel, but rather He wished it to be established by His own nativity, and its laws founded and fortified by His own example Matth. 17. v. 27. nay confirmed Matth. 22. v. 21. which example the Apostles also followed: 1. Petr. 2. v. 13. 18. Rom. 13. v. 1.

XIV. 3. The malignity of the Esavvites, who overturn the state of Life under the perverse pretext of Ecclesiastical power.

XV. As he was accurate in time, so the Evangelist was no less diligent in expressing the place; it is called Bethlehem (for the distinction of the other one in the tribe of Zebulun, of which Jos. 19. v. 15. Jud. 12. v. 8.) called Judah or Judea, even its sworn enemies, Matth. 2. v. 5. Joh. 7. v. 24. compelled by the evidence of the Prophecy of Mich. chap. 5. v. 2. And in this, the Royal house and court does not receive the Savior, and King of Kings and Lord of lords, but a most vile and squalid stable, a manger, in which he could restsent.

XVI. And so nothing is lacking that seems to contribute to establishing the birth of the Messiah, so that the enemies of Christ and of all the faithful (called by them by the contemptuous name of Messilians) render themselves inexcusable by their affected and, against their conscience, malicious blindness, since they know not only that all the oracles have been fulfilled, but also that the place destined for this birth has long since been overturned and utterly destroyed; whence from the agreement and certainty of all the circumstances we conclude further: He whose birth corresponds to all the circumstances determined by the Prophets is the true Messiah, and his birth is already past; But [it is so]. Therefore. 1. For the fullness of time, in which the Messiah ought to be born, Gal. 4. v. 5. is accurately evident from the above, corresponding namely to the prophecies of Gen. 49, 10. Dan. 2. v. 9. to which add, Dan. 9. v. 24. Hagg. 2. v. 7. Mal. 3. v. 1. c. 5. v. 2. nor does the determination of the place fail. 3. and nothing by reasons or appearances is contrary to this birth.

Latin:

Continuatio.

VT duæ sunt θεανθρώπῳ naturæ, ita harum duplicem Nativitatem indicat Scriptura: Naturarum altera est divina per æternam generationem genita; altera humana per temporalem nativitatem producta: Illa facta est à Patre, sine Matre;

Hæc à Matre sine Patre: Per illam verus Deus & חָסִין; per hanc verus homo & frater noster existit: Illâ natus ante omnem diem, qui omnem creavit diem; hâc natus in die, qui omnem consecravit (a) diem: Per illam Deus occultus; Per hanc homo manifestus: (b) utraque mirabilis, utraque inenarrabilis; In utraque ἔστι ὁμολογουμένως μέγα τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον, 1. Tim. 3, v. 5. in quod & Angeli gestiunt παρακύψαι, 1. Petr. 1. v. 12. Et dum utramque defendimus, neutram alterius affirmatione tollimus; Nam nec temporalem primæ istius perpetuitate damnamus; nec æternam hujus temporalis brevitate concludimus, scientes Verbum Dei inseparabilem prolem, & hujus veræ prolis verissimam carnem; (c) Et sicut per illam revera factus est אֵל; ita per hanc verus est עִמָּנוּאֵל: Illam in superioribus perpendimus, hanc pro instituti ratione (d) distinctis qvatuor capitibus inclusam in Præsenti διασκέψει contemplabimur: 1. acturi de Circumstantiis: 2. Nativitate ipsa: 3. Ejus fine: & tandem practicâ meditatione conclusuri.

Thesis I.

Qvàm salutaris vitæ Christi cognitio, utpote qvæ viam, si qværim9, qvæ animæ viaticum, si desideramus, qvæ veritatem, si cupimus, qvæ panem, qvi de cœlo descendit, & dat vitam mundo, si esurimus, ostē- dit, qvæ fontem salientem in vitam æternam, si sitimus, monstrat; Tam utilis est ejusdem Nativitatis contemplatio: Hæc enim maxima amoris divini erga nos declaratio est, hæc ultimum omnium promissionum complementum, hæc omnis salutaris notitiæ principium, & totius Christianismi fundamentum, qvòd sciamus, Deum Hominem efse natum.

II. Hanc verò τοῦ λόγου in carne ἐπιφάνειαν accuratissimâ descriptione inter omnes Evangelistas Lucas consignavit, unde non immeritò de eo Ambrosius (a) inqvit: Lucas se satis divitem fore credidit, si Domini præsepe ex omnibus vindicasset: Qvod enim superiore capite observavit, nihil omittens, qvod ad accuratam præcursoris Christi nativitatis cognitionem facere videbatur, idem hîc diligenter observare voluit: Hujus igitur ductum seqventes, & devitantes omnes aliorum errores, ne sicerâ falsitatum inebriati in temulentiam humanarum traditionum abducamur, singula notatu digna perpendemus, initium facturi à Circumstantiis; qvarum duæ potissimùm: Temporis & Loci.

III. Tempus investigamus non temeritate Genethliacorum, ex singulari astrorum observatione nativitatem hanc divinantium, sed firmitate rationum Historicarum, qvarum non paucas indicat Evangelista: dicendum ergo 1. de remoto, hoc est, anno: 2. propriore, die: 3. proximo, hora. Annus notatur, 1. Generaliter, verbis v. 5. cap. 1. qvæ confer cum Matth. 2. v. 8. Temporibus Herodis regis. 2. Specialiter verbis cap. 2. v. 1. seq. descriptionem seu censum universi orbis factum edicto Augusti Cæsaris præsidente Syriæ Cyrenio, exprimentibus. Generalem primam notationem dixi, eò qvòd certus Regni Herodis annus nec hîc nec à Matthæo sit expressus; non parum tamen notatio hæc facit ad Historiæ certitudinem, præsertim cùm hujus mentione Evangelista indicare voluerint tempus huic nativitati à Deo destinatum, & verbis Prophetiæ Jacobi, Gen. 49. v. 9. 10. determinatum, unde non sine causa notanter scribit cap. 5. v. 1. Lucas: Ἡρώδυ τῦ βασιλέως: addito articulo τῦ, cujus vis διακριτικὴ accuratè 1. indicat Personam certam Herodem nempe Magnum è rebus gestis sic dictum, Hyrcani seu Antipatri Filium, aliàs Ascalonitæ Idumæi dictum, primum Judaicæ gentis Regem peregrinum, (a) qvi ordinarium tribus Judæ imperium licet non Regale, at Sacerdotale, συνέδριον dictum, sustulit, (b) & nefandâ judicum cæde è domo Davidis collectorum pœnam sibi olim inflictam ultus est, qvòd cædis damnatus in exilium migrare coactus fuerat, ut supplicium capitis effugeret, atqve sic Prophetiam Jacobi implevit, Olymp 185. (c) 2. distinguit ab aliis hunc Herodem eodem nomine dictis; qvorum primus Antipas, aliàs Tertarcha filius Herodis Magni: alter verò Herodes Agrippa, filius Aristobuli filii Herodis Magni, hujus scil. nepos: Illius fit mentio, Matth. 14. Luc. 3. Act. 13. Luc. 23. cujus Historiam vide apud Joseph. (d) Hujus Act. 12. v. 2.

IV. Etsi verò de Supputatione, qvoto scil. anno regni Herodis Christus natus sit, magna inter Auctores sit controversia, cùm alii (e) velint fuisse annum Herodis 30. alii (f) annum 33. opiniones tamen eorum facilè componi possunt, si distinguatur annus appellationis seu proclamationis, quo scil. Herodes Rex Judææ appellatus est, anno scil. 9. Imperii Augusti, Olympiadis 184. desinente; (g) ab anno regiminis, quo Hierosolymam cœpit, & ipso actu Regiam Majestatem adeptus est, anno scil. 12. Augusti, & Olympiadis centesimæ octogesimæ sextæ quarto: (b) ab hoc, numerandi initium faciunt, qui 30. ab illo verò, qui 33. defendunt; alii aliter statuunt, quorum rationes Chronologi expendant.

V. In speciali notatione tria observanda veniunt. 1. Augustus Cæsar, cujus edicto facta est descriptio: 2. descriptio ipsa. De Augusto duo moventur: 1. quis Mundi annus actus, tempore hujus descriptionis? 2. quo anno imperii facta? De utroque magna est controversia, licet de priore major; cum tot ferè de eo sint opiniones & sententiæ quot capita, ut videre est ex Luca Gaurico. non paucas notante, ut & Dn. D. Chemnitio. (a) Nos rem expeditam esse in priore dubio putamus, si supputandi modum, quem ostendit Dn. Chemnitius l. d. cum D. Lutheri & Philippo sequamur, qui annum 3962. à condito mundo ad imperii Augusti annum, quo natus est Christus, ostendit: huncq́; ut retineamus, movemur: 1. certitudine sacrarum literarum hunc modum probantium: 2. multitudine Orthodoxorum: Lutheri, Philippi, Chemnitii, Urspergensis, Funccii (qui leviter ad annum 64. declinare videtur) & aliorum &c. 3. Inconstantia cæterorum Chronologorum: 4. Infirmitate rationum nobis oppositarum, quas hinc inde petitas refutatas reperies à Thoma Lydiat. (b)

VI. In altero tollendo sequimur opinionem vulgatam, actum scil. tempore nativitatis Christi annum imperii Augusti 42; Et hanc sequuntur Epiphan. (c) Orosius, (d) Eusebius, (e) quibus contrarii licet videantur Tertull: (f) Hieronym: (g) Irenæus, (h) annum quadragesimum primum defendentes; facilè tamen conciliari possunt, si dicatur, vel illos immediatè respexisse ad obitum Cæsaris, hos verò ad annum subsequentem; vel illos juxta Calendarium Romanum nativitatis Tempus sub finem anni factum ad sequentem annum retulisse, hos verò præcedenti anno nondum elapso adnumerasse: quam conciliationem esse necessariam, nisi manifestò Patres posteriores errasse dicere velimus, apparet.

: VII. Succedit Descriptio, de qva his verbis Evangelista: ut describeretur totus orbis; seu ut Vulg. & Eraf. ut censeretur. Qvid per descriptionem hoc loco intelligatur, etiam Auctores variant. Qvidam nil aliud esse volunt qvàm nominum professionem, qvùm qvisq; nomen proprium summo Monarche Augusto profiteri coactus est: † At probabilior eorum videtur sententia, qvi statuunt, in hâc descriptione omnibus & singulis Imperii Romani subditis certum vectigal impositum esse, adeóq; omnes coactos fuisse non tantùm nomina, sed totam possessionem omnium bonorum profiteri; qvod non obscurè innuere videtur verbum ἀπογράφεσθαι, in hâc significatione sæpiùs in Scriptura usurpatum, præcipuè à 70. Vide Esth. 10. v. 1. Hebr. 12. v. 23.

VIII Et ne confunderetur hæc descriptio, qvâ universus orbis (πα̃σα ἡ οἰκυμένη ad verbum: tota inhabitabilis; subintellige γη̃) ὑπερβολικω̃ς καὶ συνεκδοχικω̃ς more Romanorum usitatissimo per arrogantiam generale & universale Imperium sibi vendicantium, indeq; titulum, qvo Rerum Domini dicerentur, rapientium, pro orbis parte Romanó Imperio subjecta, ut rectè superiora verba Syrus ܦܪܝܦܪܐܣܬܝܐܬ his expressit: Omnis populus ditionis ipsius; descriptus dicitur; cum ea, qvæ hanc post aliqvot annos seqvuta est, Archelao vid. relegato post imperium 9. annorum, cujus meminit Josephus. (a) Illa siqvidem universalis erat & totius imperii; hæc particularis & solius Judææ, ut ex Dion: lib. 56. probat Dn. Chemn. d. l. & Beza in notis super hunc locum. Non sine causa additur, qvòd 1. fuerit Prima πρώτη: Hoc vocabulum licet alii sic explicent, primam nempe idèo dici, qvod initium ejus primò factum fuerit in Syria, cùm Syria sita esset in medio quasi Zona habitabilis; alii qvòd prima respectu Cyrenii dicatur, licet præcesserint aliæ; at rectiùs nos dicere credimus, si primam idèo appellatam putemus, 1. qvod nulla talis præcesserit: 2. nec ulla tali modo seqvuta. 2. Qvòd fuerit facta Præsideute Syriæ Cyrenio: qvæ verba malè vertit vulg. à Cyrenio Præfidente contra manifestam rationem & veritatem, cùm non indicet his verbis Evangelista, à qvo, sed qvando hæc descriptio facta fuerit. Et constanter qvidem vocabulum Κυρηνίυ in omnibus Exemplaribus legitur, qvanqvam apud Justinum, [b] Josephum, [c] Tacitum, [d] Quirinus appelletur; apud Onufrinum verò & Interpretem Syrum Quirinius; facilis tamen & hîc est conciliatio, cùm constet, hujus generis nomina Romanorum à Græcis variè & lecta & scripta fuisse: quam responsionem satisfacturam putamus non tam malè informato Aristarcho, quàm severo & duro Phalari Lutheri, Emsero.

IX. De die multi litigant, ii præsertim, qui omnia curiosè inqvirere sibi laudidicunt, ut pleriq; Pontificii, præsertim cum aliqvot antiqvorum Patrum habent auctoritates. Epiphanius [a] statuit diem 6. Januarii: Clemens Alexandrinus [b] diversas refert sententias, qvorum qvidam diem 25. φαρμυθὶ, nobis Aprilis, qvidam 25. πάχων Martii numerarunt: Nos in re incerta rationibus destituti firmis nil determinare qvàm falsum affirmare malumus, & sententiam vulgò à Patribus receptam, Nicephoro [c] Augustino, [d] 25. Decembris diem retinentes, seqvi: Qvi an fuerit Solis? ut Bellarmino; [e] an Saturni? ut Antonio de Gislan: [f] an Veneris? ut Surio; non ambigimus: nec Osiandri opinionem, ob infirmam rationem tempus Brumale rejicientis, defendimus.

X. Ut ergò dies incertus, ita incertior hora; figmenta qvibus placent, qviq; satiùs sine Scriptura aliqvid statuere qvàm cum Scripturâ tacere putant, qvamcunq; fingant, nobis non adversabuntur.

XI. Atq; hanc Dominicæ nativitatis temporis considerationem nõ otiosum qvid esse patet: qvod evertat 1. Judæorum impietatem, verum Messiam venisse negantium, & ostendat omnium Prophetiarum vaticinantium de tempore nativitatis Messiæ, eiqve ablationem sceptri de Juda adscribentium, complementum, qvòd Cæsare peregrino Augusto, & Rege alienigena Herode factum. Duo ergo loca tempus hoc describentia hîc notari potissimùm possunt, Gen. 49. v. 10. Dan. 2. v. 44. qvibus licet tam manifestè convicti constringantur Judæi, fraude tamen diabolicâ non desinunt absurdissima qvæq; fingere, textûs ut evidentiam depravent. Qvid enim qvæso hæc sibi vult malignitas, qvâ contendunt, dictum Gen. 49. non eo, qvo nos id explicamus modo interpretandum esse? Hinc alii voculam שֵׁבֶט de virgâ calamitatum intelligunt, qvorum vanitas redarguitur facilè: Nam si vocula שֵׁבֶט calamitatem denotat, erit illa vel privata vel publica: Si hæc? Seqvitur, à temporibus hujus Prophetiæ nunqvam in tribu Judæ tranqvillum fuisse usq; ad tempora Messiæ statum, cujus assertionis falsitatem exempla non pauca ostendunt: in specie nota Davidis & Salomonis: si excipiant, pacem hanc non diu durasse nec firmam fuisse; Resp. 1. ejusmodi Politicam pacem in Messia nullibi promissam: 2. nec esse talem expectandam, cum haec tribui Juda promissio facta impleri (juxta ipsorum mentem) in confusione tanta omnium tribuum non possit; Quae de futura per Messiam invenienda distinctione tribuum garriunt, refutatione digna non sunt, cùm prolata omnia divinae Scripturae sint contraria. Si de illa? quomodo haec Prophetia ad solam tribum Juda pertinet? cùm aliae non minus & quotidianis aerumnis subjectae & promissiones quoq; si obedientiam DEO praestiturae, in pressurisq; ipsum quaesiturae sint, de exauditione paterna & benigna sublevatione habeant; alii voculam שֵׁבֶט tribum denotare ajunt, quorum vanitas facilè infringitur, ut in conflictu fiet manifestum.

XII. Alia somnia alii fixerunt. Hinc quidam voculam שִׁילֹה ad Davidem transtulerunt; aliae per eam civitatem hoc nomine dictam denotari voluerunt; quidam ה finale in ח verterunt, contra Chaldaeum Interpretem & 70. manifestè ה retinentes, unde non sine causa voculam שִׁילֹה à שׁלֹה derivamus, sequuti Chaldaeum & Graecos ita legentes ᾧ τὰ ἀποκείμενα ἀυτῷ, cui sunt ea, quae sunt reposita, id est, cui Regnum repositum, & felicissima quaeque: quam lectionem etiam calculo piae Antiquitatis firmamus, vide Cypria. (a) August. (b) & aliorum. Quae putida objiciunt figmenta, satis refutata invenies apud Clariss. Dn. Helv. (c) Dn. D. Jacob. Martin. (d) & textualem Mercerum. (e)

XIII. 2.
