Anabaptistarum impudentiam, omnem praetextu Evangelicae libertatis Politiam tollentium, contra quos non parum facit haec accurata nativitatis Dominicae temporis notatio, ostendens nullâ ratione Politiam Evangelio tollendam, quin potiùs illam sua voluit nativitate stabilitam, suo exemplo ejusdem leges fundatas & munitas Matth. 17. v. 27. imò confirmatas Matth. 22. v. 21. quod exemplum sunt etiam Apostoli sequuti: 1. Petr. 2. v. 13. 18. Rom. 13. v. 1.

XIV. 3. Esavvitarum malignitatem, status Vitae perverso praetextu potestatis Ecclesiasticae evertentium.

XV. Ut accuratus in tempore, ita non minus diligens in loco exprimendo fuit Evangelista; vocatur is Bethlehem (ad distinctionem alterius in tribu Zabulon, de quâ Jos. 19. v. 15. Jud. 12. v. 8.) Juda seu Judæa dictum, etiam abjurati ejus hostes, Matth. 2. v. 5. Joh. 7. v. 24. coacti evidentiæ Prophetiæ Mich. cap. 5. v. 2. Atque in hâc Servatorem, Regemq́ve Regum & Dominum dominantium non excipit Regia domus & aula, sed vilissimum & sqvalidum stabulum, præsepe, in qvo qviescere posset præsens.

XVI. Adeoq; nihil deest, qvod ad stabiliendam Messiæ nativitatem facere videtur, ut inexcusabiles etiam affectatâ sua, & præter conscientiam malitiosâ cæcitate sese reddant hostes Christi omniumq́ve fidelium (Messilianorum nomine per contemtum ab ipsis denominatorum) cum sciant non tantùm omnia oracula impleta, sed & locum huic nativitati destinatum jam olim eversum & funditùs dirutum efse; unde ex circumstantiarum omnium convenientiâ & certitudine ita jam porrò concludimus: Cujus nativitati omnes correspondent circumstantiæ à Prophetis determinatæ, is verus Messias, ejusq́; jam præteriti nativitas; Atqui. E. 1. Plenitudo enim temporis, in qva nasci debeat Messias, Gal. 4. v. 5. ex superioribus accuratè patet, correspondens scil. vaticiniis Gen. 49, 10. Dan. 2. v. 9. qvibus adde, Dan. 9. v. 24. Hagg. 2. v. 7. Mal. 3. v. 1. c. 5. 5. 2. nec loci determinatio fallit. 3. nihilq́ve rationibus vel apparentibus huic nativitati contrariatur.


### Chap. II. XVII. After the circumstances have been weighed, with as much brevity as…

CHAP. II.

XVII. After the circumstances have been weighed, with as much brevity as possible, let us contemplate the Nativity itself, in which there occur for consideration 1. The Mother, of whom we disputed above. 2. The Person being born; And this is not a mere man, although he is man; nor mere flesh, although he is flesh; nor subsisting by itself, although it is subsisting; but God-man: God not without humanity, nor humanity without Deity, as Leo I elegantly [a] says, whence Augustine rightly [b]: Mary conceived the Son of God himself by the reception of his flesh, the Word not subsisting separately and the flesh subsisting separately ἰδικῶς καὶ ἀναμέρως, as Cyril speaks. But with the flesh lacking its own ὑφισαμένῳ and subsisting in the ὑποστάσει of the Son of God: concerning which matter Damascene says thus: The virgin did not bring forth a ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον, [c] but a man θεώθεντα: Thus therefore Mary is rightly called θεοτόκος and God is called incarnate. And although the Person is born, he is nevertheless born according to the flesh: This is that which is wonderfully singular, and singularly wonderful: [d] a work more powerful than the creation of the world itself, of which if a reason is sought, it will not be wonderful; if an example is demanded, it ceases to be singular.

[e] And not only the humanity of this Person, but also the divinity, is proven by 1. Angels: 2. acknowledged by Shepherds: 3. confirmed by the Magi.

XVIII. 3. The mode, which is twofold; Interior, and the other Exterior. Concerning the first, many thorny and superfluous questions are raised, especially by those to whom fabulous traditions are more pleasing than the Scriptures: by others many miracles are fabricated, with which that trifling Proto-Evangelium of James is filled. The primary question usually raised here is that which asks: Did Mary give birth with a closed womb, or indeed an open one? We hold the affirmative, knowing that Mary always remained ἀειπάρθενος, from ἀνδρόθεν: whence, as Jerome once responded to Helvidius, a rustic and stupid man, a disciple of Auxentius, who denied the perpetual virginity of Mary along with his followers, the Antidicomarianites. We believe that God was born through the genitals of a virgin, because we read it: but we do not believe that Mary had intercourse with Joseph after the birth or bore children by him, because we do not read it; Thus we respond in this place to those speaking against us: We acknowledge that Christ was born from the womb, because we read it, but the mode, how? we cannot determine, because we do not read it.

XIX. The exterior mode of the nativity is indicated, not by royal majesty and splendid dignity, but by spontaneous and voluntary poverty. For he entered the world naked: miserably taken up by it, and finding little, or rather nothing beyond misery and poverty; For thus he had to be tempted in all things, and be made like his brothers, and fulfill the prophecies prophesying about this mode of birth: Isa. 29, 14. Zech: 9, 9. By which spontaneous poverty of his he wished to overturn: 1. every vain persuasion concerning a worldly Kingdom, which was attributed to the Messiah, and to show that his kingdom is not of this world, as he himself testifies John 18, v. 36. 2. by his form, as the Bridegroom elegant before the sons of men Cant. 1, he wished to declare to the Bride what kind of face he required from her, not painted and puffed up with pompous pride, but humble and abject, and in no way corresponding to a sumptuous, as it were, Esau-like appearance. 3. To indicate the highest φιλανθρωπίαν and love towards men; that although he was rich, he was willing to be born poor, yet without any uncleanness and filth (since poverty by no means rejects cleanliness, as Erasmus says on this passage), and although he was in the highest majesty by virtue of the Personal union, with the Angels attesting to it, while they call the child of most abject form the Lord v. 11, though the perfidious Naum Calvinist impiously denies it, *he was, yet he did not wish to exert the same.

XX. We proceed, intending to add a few words concerning the purpose of this birth. A host of angels indicates this, v. 10. Μὴ φοβεῖσθε, ἰδὺ γὰρ ἐυαγγε- λίζομαι ὑμῖν χαρὰν μεγάλην ἥ τις ἔςαι παντὶ τῷ λαῷ. Behold, those who are invisible spirits appear visibly; not men proclaim these new tidings to us, but the angels of the almighty God, whose commands they execute as ministers; we have their testimonies, they explain the true purpose of the birth, by them we refute and most powerfully rebuke all blasphemers and those sinning against the most holy birth of the Lord: 1. indeed, overturning the delirium of the most polluted Sadducees, who deny that there are angels, by this angelic apparition; 2. opposing the infatuated persuasion of the Jewish Synagogue, which attributes a pompous Kingdom to the Messiah and arrogates it to itself alone, while the spiritual office of Christ consists in liberation from sin, death, and hell, and assists the corrupt birth of all: 3. opposing the particularity of the desperate bald [Gentile] nation by setting forth the most universal words of the Angel; Which shall be to all the people. 4. thrusting confidently against the doubt of the hesitating Anti-Christian society and the Babylonian metric sect the word more solid than adamant and firmer than all Satanic temptations: Unto you is born; 5. against the impiety of the blasphemous Photinian sect and certain of their like-minded Papist Scholastics, as also Andreas Osiander (in the year 1581), pretending that even if man had not sinned, the incarnation of the Son of God would nevertheless have been necessary, since 1. without the vision of Christ in the flesh, man would not have been perfectly happy; 2. It is unworthy to say that Christ was incarnate by accident, and that he was made sin by accident: Urging the little word Savior, and establishing for certain that, with evil removed, there would have been no need for a Savior, and finally saying: 1. by denying that man could not have been perfectly blessed without sin without the vision of Christ in the flesh, since consequently this aspect of the flesh of Christ, because the flesh was overturned by sin, makes for the happiness of man not without sin, but polluted by sin. 2. By distinguishing, responding that this incarnation of God was not accidental, since God foreknew the fall of man; but with respect to men, it can be called accidental. But we are forced to conclude.

XXI. We include a practical meditation on this angelic psalmody: Δόξα ἐν ὑψίςοις θεῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἐυδοκία.

Latin:

CAP. II.

XVII. Post Circumstantias expensas, qva fieri potuit brevitate, Nativitatem ipsam contemplemur, in qvâ consideranda occurrunt 1. Mater de qva disp. sup. 2. Persona nascens; Et hæc non est nudus homo, licet homo; nec nuda caro, licet sit caro; nec per se subsistens, licet subsistens; sed homo DEUS: DEUS non sine humanitate, nec humanitas sine Deitate, ut eleganter Leo 1. [a] unde rectè Augustinus: [b] Ipsum DEI Filium Maria concepit carnis suæ acceptione, non seorsim subsistente verbo & seorsim subsistente carne ἰδικῶς καὶ ἀναμέρως, ut loqvitur Cyrillus. Sed carne ὑφισαμένῳ proprio carente in ὑποστάσει Filii DEI subsistente: qva de re ita Damasc. Non peperit virgo ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον, [c] sed hominem θεώθεντα : Sic ergo Maria rectè θεοτόκος & Deus incarnatus dicitur. Et licet nascatur Persona, nascitur tamen secundùm carnem: Hoc est illud mirabiliter singulare, & singulariter mirabile: [d] opus potentiùs quàm ipsa mundi creatio, cujus si ratio qværitur, non erit mirabile; si exemplum poscitur, desint esse singulare.

[e] Et hujus Personae non tantùm humanitatem, sed & divinitatem, probant 1. Angeli: 2. agnoscunt Pastores: 3. comprobant Magi.

XVIII. 3. Modus, qvi duplex; Interior, & Exterior alter. Circa primum multae spinosae & supervacanae moventur qvaestiones, ab iis praefertim, qvibus prae Scripturis fabulosae traditiones placent: ab aliis multa confinguntur miracula, qvibus repletur nugatorium illud Prot-Evangelium Jacobi. Primarium hîc qvod moveri solet, id est, qvo qvaeritur: An Maria pepererit alvo clausâ, an verò apertâ? Nos affirmativam tenemus, scientes, qvòd Maria semper manserit ἀειπάρθενος, ex ἀνδρόθεν: unde ut olim Helvidio homini rustico & stupido Auxentii discipulo, perpetuam virginitatem Mariae neganti cum assectis, AntidicoMarianitis, respondit Hieron. Natum esse Deum per virginis genitalia credimus, qvia legimus: Mariam autèm post partum cum Joseph concubuisse aut filios ex ipso sustulisse, non credimus, qvia non legimus; Sic nos hoc loco obloqventibus respondemus: Ex alvo natum esse Christum agnoscimus, quia legimus, modum autem, qvomodo? determinare non possumus, quia non legimus.

XIX. Exteriorem nativitatis modum indicat, non regia majestas & splendida dignitas, sed spontanea & voluntaria paupertas. Nudus enim intravit in mundum: miserè ab eodem assumtus, & parum imò praeter miseriam & paupertatem inveniens nihil; Ita enim per omnia tentari debuit, & fratribus assimilari, & explere Prophetias de hoc nativitatis modo vaticinantes: Esa. 29, 14. Zach: 9, 9. Qvâ suâ spontaneâ paupertate evertere voluit: 1. omnem vanam persuasionem de mundano Regno, qvod affingebatur Messiae, & ostendere regnum suum de hoc mundo non esse, ut testatur ipse Joh. 18, v. 36. 2. formâ suâ Sponsus praefiliis hominum elegans Cant. 1. declarare voluit Sponsae qualem ab ea reqvireret faciem, non fucatam & pomposa superbia elatam, sed humilem & abjectam, minimeqve faustuoso veluti Esauvitico correspondentem. 3. Indicare summam φιλανθρωπίαν & amorem erga homines; qvod cum dives esset, pauper nasci, absq; omni tamen immundiciâ & sorde (cum & paupertas mundiciem minimè respuat, dicente Erasmo super hunc locum) vellet, & cum in summâ majestate vi unionis Personalis, attestantibus id Angelis, dum adjectissimae formae puerum Dominum vocant v. 11. impiè verò negante Naum Calviniano perfido, *fuerit, eandem tamen exerere noluerit.

XX. Progredimur, paucula de fine hujus nativitatis subjecturi. Indicat hunc Angelorum caterva, v. 10. Μὴ φοβεῖσθε, ἰδὺ γὰρ ἐυαγγελίζομαι ὑμῖν χαρὰν μεγάλην ἥ τις ἔςαι παντὶ τῷ λαῷ. Ecce qui sunt Spiritus invisibiles visibiliter apparent; Non homines nobis hæc nova nuncia prædicant, sed angeli Dei omnipotentis, cujus mãdata exesequvntur ministri; horum testimonia habemus, hi verum nativitatis finem explicant, his omnes blasphemos & in sanctissimam nativitatem Domini peccantes refutamus & validissimè perstringimus: 1. qvidem pollutissimorum Saducæorum delirium, Angelos esse negantium, hâc Angelicâ apparitione evertentes; 2. Persvasioni infatuatæ Judaicæ Synagogæ pomposum Regnum Messiæ affingenti, idq́ve sibi soli arroganti, spirituali Christi officio in liberatione à peccato, morte & inferno consistente omniumq́ve nativitati corruptæ subvenienti occurrentes: 3. Desperatæ calvæ Gentis particularitati verba Angeli universalissima reponentes; Quod erit toti populo. 4. dubitationi hæsitantis Anti-Christi societatis Babylonicæq́, metricis sectæ verbum adamante solidius, omnibusq́; Satanicis tentationibus firmius fiducialiter obtrudentes: Vobis natus est; 5. contra impietatem blasphemæ Photinianæ sectæ hujusq́; ὁμοψήφων quorundam Papicolarum Scholasticorum, ut & Andreæ Osiandri, (Anno 1581.) prætendentem, etiam si homo non peccasset, nihilominus incarnationem Filii Dei fuisse necessariam, cùm 1. absq́, visione Christi in carne homo perfectè felix non fuerit; 2. Indignum sit dicere Christum per accidens incarnatum, eum peccatum per accidens factum: Voculam Salvatoris urgentes, certoq́ve statuentes, Sublato malo salvatore haud opus fuisse, & tandem dicentes: 1. negando, absq́; visione Christi in carne hominem sine peccato perfectè beatum esse non potuisse, cum conseqventer tantùm hic aspectus carnis Christi, ob carnem vid. per peccatum eversum, ad hominis non sine peccato, sed peccato polluti felicitatem faciat. 2. Distingvendo, resp. Dei hanc incarnationem non fuisse accidentariam, cùm Deus hominis lapsum præsciverit; respectu verò hominum accidentariam dici posse. Sed concludere cogimur.

XXI. Practicam meditationem huic Psalmodiæ Angelicæ includimur: Δόξα ἐν ὑψίςοις θεῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἐυδοκία.


## 26 Twenty-sixth Disputation, On Circumcision and the Sweetest Name of Jesus

Luke most clearly, above other Evangelists, has left behind a woven history of the infancy and boyhood age of Christ, as he himself testifies in the beginning of his Gospel, v. 3, that he had investigated all things ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς (from the beginning accurately). For when he had described the birth of the forerunner of our Savior, and had reported the conception and birth of our Immanuel JESUS CHRIST at the announcement of the Angel, he immediately sets forth for us the subsequent life: how he was circumcised and named, how he was presented in the temple, how he was received into the arms of Simeon and commended, to whom also the Prophetess Anna approached, and how he disputed in the temple at Jerusalem with the Masters and Doctors, up to his 12th year. We, having already dealt with the rest partly long ago and partly to be dealt with in later sections, will now treat in two sections of the Circumcision, which Christ underwent in his blessed flesh, and of the sweetest name of JESUS given to him at his circumcision. But lest we seem to proceed in a disorderly manner, we will treat three chapters in the former, and four in the latter. In the former, I. will be, why was Christ circumcised? II. whether circumcision ought to be used even today? III. A Practical Meditation. In the latter we will treat I. of the imposition of the name JESUS, its derivation, and likewise its meaning. II. of its novelty. III. of its despisers, and IV. finally we will append a Practical Meditation.

SECTION I. Thesis I.

Christ willed to be circumcised 1. for the fulfillment of the law. Christ the God-man can be considered in two ways, absolutely and relatively. Absolutely and in respect to himself, he did not need circumcision, for circumcision was instituted to apply and seal the covenant of GOD concerning the free remission of sins, but Christ did not need this covenant; for in respect to his divinity he was Lord of the law, and in respect to his humanity he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, Matt. 1:18, he was holy, Luke 1:35, he had committed no iniquity, so that neither was guile found in his mouth, Is. 53:9, he was innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, Heb. 7:26, and thus in every way perfect, in whom there was nothing superfluous either in the flesh or in the mind, which was to be cut off through circumcision. II. Relatively and with respect to us, insofar as for our sake he was made a curse, Gal. 3, 13. and sin, 2 Cor. 5, 21. (not subjectively or infusively, but imputatively and relatively) and in this way he willed to be circumcised, lest that threat of Jehovah Col. 2, 11. and while he suffered himself to be circumcised, he made himself a debtor of the whole law, Gal. 5, 3. so that he might fulfill the law in this manner, Matt. 5, 17. and might redeem us who were under the law and we might be received into the adoption of sons, Gal. 4, 4. etc. and thus by his obedience we might be righteous, Rom. 5, 19. and truly free, John 8, 36. III. Just as therefore he is said to be born not for himself but for us, given not for himself but for us; so also he willed to be circumcised solely for our sake, and to shed the firstfruits of his innocent blood (since without the shedding of blood there is no remission, Heb. 9, 22.). Whence Bernard: He was circumcised for that for which he was born; none of these things for himself, but all for you. And Damascene: The Lord was circumcised, and kept the whole law, that he might fulfill and establish it.

IV. II. As a proof of his humanity; that he might prove in reality that he had not assumed an imaginary or phantastical body, at least such in appearance, as the Docetae and Manichaeans raved, nor brought down from heaven to earth, as the Valentinians once feigned, nor even ἀπαθὲς, as Hilary, who indeed conceded the ὁμογσίαν of Christ's body with ours, yet contended that it never perceived any bodily pains, but received all stripes and blows like the air receiving the stroke of a javelin without feeling it; but that it was truly human as to substance and various affections, such as to thirst, to hunger, to be sorrowful, to be wearied, etc., and that he was in all things (sin excepted, however) like unto us. Cf. Is. 53, 4. Heb. 2, 17. 18. ch. 4, 15. V. III. As a document of his origin. For he willed to show that he was born according to the promise of Gen. 12, 13. from the family and lineage of Abraham, which was distinguished from other nations by circumcision, Gen. 17. For this By the sacrament as a manifest symbol, lest the Jews should have any pretext to despise him on account of his foreskin, he willed to demonstrate that he was truly born of the seed of Abraham; whence also the Apostle teaches that Christ took not hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham, Heb. 2, 16. VI. IV. In contempt of worldly wisdom. Christ willed by his own example not to despise the rite of circumcision as a sign of grace, but to use it as an ordinance of God the heavenly Father at that time as useful and necessary, against every judgment of human wisdom, to which nothing in this rite seems more foolish and contemptible.

VII. There were without any doubt supercilious and sneering men who laughed at this mystery of circumcision, and despised it as an inept and foolish ceremony, saying: what good is that removal of the foreskin? What good is the shedding of the blood of a tender infant? What good is the wound of a bodily member to the soul? Let us see at least the wisest of the heathens, how falsely they speak about the Jews, how they harass and deride them on account of circumcision. Horace calls them Apellae, Martial the circumcised, Catullus the verpi. Cicero calls the religion of the Jews a barbaric superstition. The Manichaeans accused circumcision as a useless thing, an evil and obscene mark.

VIII. But let them laugh as much as they want: What is foolishness to men is wisdom to GOD; for GOD has made foolish the wisdom of this world, 1 Cor. 1:20, and GOD has chosen the things that are foolish according to the world, that He might put to shame the wise, v. 27. Let us therefore be admonished not to loosen the bridle of our reason, but to restrain it, and bring it into captivity to the obedience of Christ, 2 Cor. 10:5. For the natural man οὐ δεχεται τα του πνευματος, 1 Cor. 2:14.

Latin:

LUculentissimè Lucas præ aliis Evangelistis historiam infantiæ & puerilis Christi ætatis pertextam reliqvit, ut ipsemet in Evangelii sui exordio v. 3. testatur, se ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς pervestigasse. Nà cùm præcursoris Salvatoris nostri nativitatem descripsisset, & ad Angeli annunciationem Immanuelis nostri JESU CHRISTI conceptionem partumq; retulisset, statim etiam subseqventem vitam, qvî circumcisus & vocatus, qvî in templo præsentatus, qvî à Simeone in ulnas receptus & commendatus fuerit, cui etiam Anna Prophetissa accesserit, qvî Hierosolymis in templo cum Magistris & Doctoribus disputaverit, ad 12. usq; annum, nobis exponit. Nos cæteris partim jampridem actis, partim in posterioribus agendis, jam de Circumcisione, qvam Christus in benedictâ suâ carne suscepit, & dulcissimo nomine JESU ipsi in circumcisione indito duabus sectionibus agemus. Ne autem ἀτάκτως progredi videamur in priori tria, in posteriori verò qvatuor pertractabimus capita. In priori I. erit, qvare Christus circumcisus? II. num etiam hodiè circumcisio adhiberi debeat? III. Meditatio Practica. In posteriori agemus I. de nominis JESU impositione, derivatione itemq́; significatione. II. de hujus novitate. III. de ejusdem contemptoribus, & IV. tandem Meditationem Practicam subjungemus.

SECTIO I. Thesis I.

CIrcumcidi Christus voluit 1. in legis complementum. Potest Christus θεάνθρωπος dupliciter considerari, absolutè & relatè. Absolutè & ratione sui circumcisione non indiguit, circumcisio enim instituta erat ad applicandum & obsignandum fœdus DEI de gratuita remissione peccatorum, jam verò Christus fœdere hoc non indigebat, respectu qvippe divinitatis legis erat Dominus, respectu verò humanitatis conceptus erat de Spiritu sancto, Matt. 1, 18. erat sanctus, Luc. 1, 35. non fecerat iniqvitatem, ut nec in ejus ore inventus sit dolus Es. 53, 9. innocens erat, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, Hebr, 7,26. & sic undiqvaq; perfectus, in qvo nihil superfluum vel in carne vel in mente, qvod per circumcisionẽ amputandũ esset. II. Relatè & respectu nostri, qvatenus pro nobis fuit factus maledi- &um, Gal. 3, 13. & peccatum, 2. Cor. 5, 21. (non subjectivè vel infusivè, sed imputativè & relativè) & hoc modo circumcidi voluit, ne nos interminatio ista Jehovæ Gen. 17, 14. feriret, ejus n. circumcisio nostra est circumcisio, Col. 2, 11. & dum circumcidi se passus est, totius legis debitorem se fecit, Gal. 5, 3. ut legem hac ratione impleret, Matt. 5, 17. & nos qvi sub lege eramus, redimeret & in adoptionem filiorum reciperemur, Gal. 4, 4. &c. sicq́; ipsius obedientia justi essemus, Rom. 5, 19. & verè liberi, Joh. 8, 36. III. Qvemadmodum igitur non sibi sed nobis natus, non sibi sed nobis datus dicitur; sic etiam nostri duntaxat causâ circumcidi, & innocentis sangvinis sui primitias (cum sine sangvinis effusione nulla fiat remissio, Hebr. 9, 22.) effundere voluit. Unde Bernhard. Circumcisus est propter quod nat⁹ est nihil horũ propter se,sed omnia propter te. Et Damasc. Dominus circumcisus est, omnemq; legem servavit, ut impleret & sisteret.

IV. II. In humanitatis suæ argumentum; Ut reipsâ comprobaret, se non adsumsisse corpus imaginarium sive phantasticum, ad apparentiam saltem tale, ut Docetæ & Manichæi delirarunt, neq; cœlitùs in terram delatum, ut Valentiniani qvondam finxerunt, neq; etiam ἀπαθὲς, ut Hilarius, qvi Christi corporis cum nostris ὁμογσίαν qvidem concessit, nullos tamen unqvam corporis dolores percepifse, verùm omnia verbera & ictus instar aëris jaculi ictum haud sentientis recepisse contendit; sed verè humanum qvoad substantiam & affect⁹ varios, ut sitire, esurire, contristari, defatigari &c. nobis per omnia (excepto tamen peccato) similem fuisse. Conf. Es. 53, 4. Hebr. 2, 17. 18. c. 4, 15. V. III. In ortus sui documentum. Etenim ostendere voluit se juxta promissionem Gen. 12, 13. ex familiâ & prosapiâ Abrahami, qvæ circumcisione ab aliis gentib⁹ discernebatur, Gen. 17. prognatum esse. Hoc n. Sacramento ceu manifesto symbolo, ne Judæi ullum prætextum haberent, illum ob præputium spernendi, demonstrare voluit, se verè è semine Abrahami natum esse; unde etiam Apostolus Christum non angelos, sed semen Abrahæ afsumsisse docet Hebr. 2, 16. VI. IV. In mundanæ sapientiæ contemtum. Voluit Christus suo exemplo circumcisionis ritum tanqvam signum gratiæ non contemnere, sed tanqvam ordinationem Dei Patris cœlestis isto tempore utilem & necessariam confirmare, contra omne humanæ sapientiæ judicium, cui hoc ritu nihil videtur stultius & contemtius.

VII. Fuerunt abq; omni dubio superciliosi & nasutuli, qvi hoc mysterium circumcisionis riserunt, & ceu ceremoniam ineptam atq; stultam contempserunt, dicentes: qvid prosit illa præputii ablatio? qvid profusio sangvinis tenelli infantis? qvid membri corporei vulnus animæ? Videamus saltem sapientissimos Ethnicorum, qvàm falsè loqvantur de Judæis, qvî exagitent & derideant illos propter circumcisionem. Horatius nominat eos Apellas, Martialis recutitos, Catullus verpos. Cicero religionem Judæorum barbaram superstitionem appellat. Manichæi circumcisionem tanqvam rem inutilem, malam & obscænum characterem criminati sunt.

VIII. Sed rideant qvousq; velint: Qvod hominibus stultitia, DEO est sapientia; infatuavit qvippe DEUS sapientiam hujus mundi, 1. Cor. 1, 20. & qvæ stulta sunt secundùm mundum, delegit DEUS, ut pudefaceret sapientes, v. 27. Admoneamur igitur, ne frenum rationis nostræ laxemús, sed illud cohibeamus, & sub obseqvium Christi captivemus, 2. Corinth. 10, 5. Animalis enim homo 8 δεχεται τα του πνευματος, 1. Cor. 2, 14.


### Chap. II. IX. The Jews, the implacable enemies of Immanuel and our Savior, do not receive…

CHAP. II.

IX. The Jews, the implacable enemies of Immanuel and our Savior, do not receive the New Testament and its Sacraments, but tenaciously retain the law and the Sacraments of the O.T., and therefore even today they circumcise their children, and imagine that this circumcision is necessary for them to obtain eternal salvation.

X. But this hinders their salvation. For whoever, whether Jews or Greeks, are still circumcised, are debtors to the whole law, Gal. 5:3, and Christ profits them nothing, v. 2 and 6. For it was only to remain until the time of reformation, Heb. 9:10, in the generations of Abraham, Gen. 17, until the fullness of time, when GOD sent His son, etc., Gal. 4:4, who is the end or perfection of the law, Rom. 10:4. As long, therefore, as it was necessary for the Israelites to be separated from the nations by a peculiar mark on account of the Messiah who was to be born from their lineage and seed, so long the symbol of circumcision was valid; but after the middle wall of partition, which was between them, was broken down, Eph. 2:14, the nations of all peoples were led into the one fold of Christ, this peculiar sign has expired. 2. Because circumcision was a type of Christ, at whose presence it vanished like a shadow. For just as a shadow perishes at the splendor of the Sun; so, with Christ Jesus, the Sun of righteousness, irradiating this world, every shadow of external ceremonies was at once removed among the Jewish people and converted into the splendor of the New Testament. 3. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails in the N. T., but faith working through love, Gal. 5, 6. 4. Because it was abrogated by the unanimous decree of the Apostolic Synod, Act. 15, 24. 25. And 5. Baptism was substituted in its place, Col. 2, 11. 12.

XI. They object that it is called an eternal covenant. But I reply: 1. That the word עוֹלָם is equivocal, and sometimes signifies infinite perpetuity, and sometimes signifies a restricted perpetuity that will last for a certain time, as in this place and elsewhere: for otherwise it would follow that all the sacrifices, concerning which this word is used, also remained for eternity, which nevertheless David predicted would have an end, Dan. 9:27, Jer. 3:16, and which were in fact abrogated about 600 years later. 2. A distinction is made between the covenant itself and the sign of the covenant: the covenant is perpetual, but not circumcision, which is the sign of the covenant; the latter was removed, the former remains for eternity; just as the covenant entered into in Baptism is a truly eternal covenant that will endure even in the other blessed age, although Baptism itself will have its end, when the entire ministry of the word and sacraments is removed on the last day.

XII. The Apostles, however, retained it 1. not as necessary for salvation, but as a free ceremony and, for the time being, adiaphoron. 2. On account of the infirmity of the Jews, Acts 16:3, so that on this occasion they might win them over, 1 Cor. 9:19, 20. But when the circumcised urged it as a seal of faith necessary for salvation, the Apostles plainly abrogated it, Gal. 2:3 & 4, Acts 15:24 & seq., which abrogation rightly continues even today. And from these it is clear that a threefold respect of circumcision is rightly given by orthodox theologians: 1. that of necessity, 2. of liberty, 3. of abrogation. The former was in the Old Testament; the latter in the beginning of the New; this one obtains even today.

XIII. Furthermore, since the circumcision of Christ was as it were a type of another new and spiritual circumcision to be performed by the same in the hearts of the faithful, and indeed the Devil tempts us, of whatever sex we may be, whether men or women, in youth, in manhood, and in old age, in youth with luxury, in with manly pride, in senile avarice, let us circumcise also during the whole time of our life, the Heart, lest evil thoughts, adulteries, murders, theft, etc., boil up from it, Matth. 15, 19. the flesh, lest it burn with the flames of lusts, Eph. 4, 12. Gal. 5, 24. Tit. 2, 12. The ears, lest they be stopped in hearing the word of God, Ps. 95, 8. or be imbued with false opinions, or delight to hear futile things, but the word of God and whatever is pleasing to God and useful to one's neighbor, The eyes, lest they be full of adultery, Matth. 5, 28. 2. Petr. 2, 14. or look upon vanity, Ps. 119, 37. but look to Jehovah our God until He has shown us grace, Ps. 123, 2. The mouth and tongue, lest they speak blasphemy and lying, Ps. 12, 5. Rom. 2, 24. and let them blurt out nothing rashly either about God and His works or about one's neighbor, but let them speak pious and modest things, which may contribute to the praise of God, Ps. 51, 16. and to edification, Eph. 4, 29. The hands, lest they steal any more, but rather labor, that they may be able to distribute alms, Ephes. 4, 28. or even harm the body of one's neighbor, and shed innocent blood, Deut. 27, 25. The feet, lest they go to illicit things, and hasten to evil, Prov. 6, 18. or persist in the way of sinners, Ps. 1, 1.

Latin:

CAP. II.

IX. Judæi ἄσπονδοι Immanuelis & Salvatoris nostri hostes novum Testamentum ejusq; Sacramenta non recipiunt, sed legem & Sacramenta V. T. mordicus retinent, ideoq; etiamnum hodiè liberos suos circumcidunt, hancq; circumcisionem ad salutem æternam conseqvendam necessariam esse sibi imaginantur.

X. Sed impedit hoc ipsorum salutem. 1 Qvicunq; enim sive Judæi sive Græci adhuc circumciduntur, totius legis debitores sunt, Galat. 5, 3. nihilq; Christus ipsis prodest, v. 2. & 6. Permanere qvippe tantum debuit usq; ad tempus correctionis, Hebr. 9, 10. in generationibus Abrahami, Gen. 17. usq; ad plenitudinem temporis, qvo DEUS misit filium suum, &c. Gal. 4, 4. qvi est finis seu perfectio legis, Rom. 10, 4. Qvamdiu igitur Israëlitas propter Messiam ex prosapiâ & semine illorum nasciturum à gentibus peculiari notâ separatos esse oportuit, tamdiu etiam circumcisionis symbolum valuit; postqvam autem interstitium maceriæ, qvod inter illos erat, dirutum fuit, Ephes. 2, 14. omnium gentium nationes in unum Christi ovile ducti sunt, peculiare hoc signum expiravit. 2. Qvia circumcisio fuit typus Christi, qvo præsente veluti umbra evanuit. Qvemadmodum enim ad splendorem Solis umbra perit; sic Sole justitiæ Christo Jesu mundum hunc irradiante, omnis simul umbra externarum ceremoniarum, in populo Judaico sublata, estq; in Novi Testamenti splendorem conversa. 3. Neq; circumcisio, neq; præputium in N. T. valet, sed fides per dilectionem operans, Gal. 5, 6. 4. Qvia unanimi Synodi Apostolicæ decreto abrogata, Act. 15, 24. 25. Et 5. in ejusdem locum Baptismus substitutus, Col. 2, 11. 12.

XI. Objiciunt, dici fœdus æternum. Sed Resp. 1. qvòd vocabulum עוֹלָם sit æqvivocum, & aliqvando significet perpetuitatem infinitam, aliqvando significet perpetuitatem restrictam & certo tempore duraturam, ut hoc loco & alibi: aliàs enim omnia sacrificia, de qvibus vocabulum hoc usurpatur, in æternum qvoq; permansisse seqveretur, qvæ tamen finem habitura David prædixit C. 9, 27. Jer. 3, 16. ipso facto etiam circiter 600. annos abrogata fuerunt. 2. distingvitur inter fœdus ipsum & signum fœderis: fœdus est perpetuum, sed non circumcisio, qvæ est signum fœderis, illud sublatum, hoc manet in æternum; sicut fœdus in Baptismo initum est verè æternum fœdus in altero etiam beato seculo duraturum, licet Baptismus ipse suum habiturus sit finem, sublato toto ministerio verbi & sacramentorum in novissimo die.

XII. Apostoli verò eam retinuerunt 1. non tanqvam ad salutem necessariam, sed tanqvam ceremoniam liberam & ad tempus adiaphoram. 2. propter infirmitatem Judæorum, Act. 16, 3. ut hac occasione eos lucrifacerent, 1. Cor. 9, 19. 20. Qvando verò eam ut signaculum fidei ad salutem necessariam circumcisi urgebant, Apostoli plane eam abrogarunt, Gal. 2. v. 3. & 4. Act. 15. v. 24. & seq. qvæ abrogatio adhuc hodiè rectè perdurat. Et qvibus patet, circumcisionis à Theologis orthodoxis rectè dari triplicem respectum: 1. est necessitatis. 2. libertatis. 3. abrogationis. Ille fuit in veteri Testamento; Iste in principio Novi; Hic hodieq; obtinet.

XIII. Cæterum cum circumcisio Christi velut typus fuerit alterius circumcisionis novæ & spiritualis per eundem in fidelium cordibus faciendæ, & verò Diabolus nos cujuscunq; simus sexûs sive viri sive fœminæ, in juvenili, virili & senili ætate tentet, in juvenili luxuriâ, in virili superbiâ, in senili avaritiâ, circumcidamus etiã toto vitæ nostræ tempore, Cor, ne ex eo ebulliant cogitationes pravæ, adulteria, cædes, furtum &c. Matth. 15,19. carnem, ne ardeat flammis libidinum, Eph. 4. 12. Gal.5,24.Tit. 2,12. Aures, ne obturentur in audiendo verbo Dei Pf.95, 8. neve imbuantur falsis opinionibus, vel gestiant audire res futiles, sed verbum Dei & qvicqvid Deo gratum & proximo utile, Oculos ne sint pleni adulterii, Matth.5,28. 2. Petr.2,14. neve respiciant vanum, Pf. 119.37. sed spectent ad Jehovam Deum nostrum donec gratiam fecerit nobis, Pf.123,2. Os & linguam, ne loqvantur blasphemiam & mendacium, Pf.12,5. Rom. 2,24. nilq; temerè vel de Deo & ejus operibus vel de proximo effutiant, sed pia & pudica loqvantur, qvæ faciant ad laudem Dei, Pfal. 51, 16. & ad ædificationem, Eph.4, 29. Manus, ne ampliùs furentur, sed potiùs laborent, ut possint eleemosynas distribuere, Ephes. 4, 28. neve etiam corpus proximi lædant, & innocentem sangvinam effundant, Deut. 27,25. Pedes, ne vadant ad illicita, & properent ad malum, Prov. 6,18. neve viæ peccatorum insistant, Pf.1,1.


### Section II. Concerning the name Jesus

SECTION II. Concerning the name JESUS.

XIV. Just as in the institution of the Sacrament of circumcision, Gen. 17. God Himself increased the name אַבְרָם which signified 'exalted father', from אב 'father' and רום 'to be exalted, to be high', with the letter ה, to אַבְרָהָם which denotes 'father of a multitude' or of very many nations, from the root הָמָה 'to be multiplied', which etymology God Himself provides; so also among the people of God this custom (which we Christians today also retain as praiseworthy in Baptism) of imposing names upon children at circumcision became established.

XV. Since, therefore, Christ wished to receive the Sacrament of Circumcision in the flesh, He received a name from the thing itself (just as Adam from the red earth, from the root אָדָם 'he was red', and Jacob from עָקַב 'he supplanted', Gen. 25. v. 26. and 33. Noah from 'consolation', Gen. 5, 29. Nabal from 'folly', 1. Sam. 25, 25. Solomon from 'peace', Rehoboam from 'a scourge', John the Baptist from 'grace', etc.), namely from the work of salvation, יְשׁוּעָה Ἰησῦς, JESUS, which also, both before and after the conception, had been commanded to Mary and Joseph by the angel, Luc. 1, 31. Matth. 1, 21.

XVI. Some, however, among whom is Basil, have sought the origin of this name in the Greek language from the future ἰάσω, from which, if α is turned into η, it easily makes the name ἰησῦς, which among them signifies ἰατρὸν, a physician. Others wish it to be a compound of יְהֹוָה, which might express the divine nature of Christ and denote the Lord, and אִ֚ישׁ, which might hint at his human nature and signify a hero or man; and since before Christ the tetragrammaton יְהוָה was ineffable, by the interposition of שׁ in the name Jesu or Jehoschua it was made effable, which was the opinion of Osiander, as cited by Flacius and Chemnitius.

XVII. Although these derivations were invented with good intention, and even if the Son of God is called a physician, Exod. 15, last verse, and our Savior is truly θεάνθρωπος and עִמָּנוּאֵל, in German Gottmann or GOtt und Mensch; yet this most sweet name Jesus is in its origin Hebrew, and is written יְהוֹשׁוּעַ or what seems to be contracted from it, יֵשׁוּעַ (as יוסף for יהוסף Ps. 81, 6); just as also that son of Josedec, who among Haggai and Zechariah is called יְהוֹשׁוּעַ, Ezra 2, 2 and c. 3, 2, Neh. 7, 7, יֵשׁוּעַ (with .. changed because of the rejected letters), as also the son of Nun יְהוֹשׁוּעַ, Neh. 8, 17, יֵשׁוּעַ (Acts 7, 45, ἰησῦς), contrary to the assertion of Galatinus, who denies entirely that they were called יֵשׁוּעַ. Compare also 2 Par. 31, 15 and Col. 4, 11, where this name is also attributed to others.

XIIX. But it descends from the root יָשַׁע in hiphil (for יָשַׁע is not in use in kal), which is the same as he saved, he rescued, he made safe, he helped; from which, by prefixing the letter י Jod, or from the future with the Jod changed in the penultimate to the Heemantic ו vaf, יָשׁוּעַ can easily be formed. And although the third person of the future is regularly יוֹשִׁיעַ, yet sometimes the ה is read as interposed, as 1 Sam. 17, 47, Ps. 116, 6.

XIX. The heavenly messenger, however, retains the Greek writing and pronunciation most used among the people of God at that time, and translates יְהוֹשׁוּעַ or יֵשׁוּעַ as ἰησῦν. But lest a scruple be cast upon anyone because of that variety of writing and pronunciation, he himself provides the root, saying in Matt. 1, 21: You shall call his name JESUS; for he himself shall save his people from their sins. Compare Acts 14, 12 and Heb. 2, 10. The Greeks [use] σωτῆρα from σώζειν. The Latins [use] servatorem from servando, or rather salvatorem from salvando, because, as Cicero himself admits, the word σωτῆρος and σώζειν signifies more than servatoris. The Germans [use] Heyland, either from heilen, from healing our lethal wounds, or from heiligen, or des Landes Heil. It is clear from these that it is written quite incorrectly as IHesus, or by abbreabbreviation with the cross JHS superimposed, which writing is familiar to Papists and Jesuits.

XX. Moreover, it denotes not only the proper name יֵשׁוּעַ, but also salvation itself יְשׁוּעָה, as is clear even from the single 12th chapter of Isaiah, where the word יְשׁוּעָה is repeated three times, v. 2 & 3. Which word the LXX interpreters conveniently rendered by σωτηρίαν or σωτήριον, which Simeon also wished to retain in his famous testimony concerning the Messiah, Luke 2, v. 30.

XXI. It matters not, however, that others were also designated by this sweetest name of Jesus, such as the son of Nun, Jos. 1, Acts 7:45, Heb. 4:8; the son of Josedech, Hagg. 1:1, c. 2 v. 2 & 4, Zach. 3:3, Eccl. 49:14; the son of Sirach, Sir. 50:28. For they shadowed forth not only the name, but also the things of this our Jesus: power, as Joshua the son of Nun, who was a most valiant hero; holiness, as Jehosua the son of Josedech, who was a most holy priest; wisdom, as Jesus the son of Sirach, who was a most learned teacher: and thus this name is attributed to them only δευτέρως (secondarily), as the illustrious Jacobus Martini, my honorable preceptor and promoter, speaks, either because they are types of this our true Savior—for Joshua the leader shadowed forth the kingly office, Josedech the priestly, Jesus Sirach the doctoral or prophetic—or so that that name may be a remembrance of the salvation acquired or to be acquired for us through Christ.

XXII. For He is truly the most powerful leader, Acts 3:14, Mich. 5:2, Dan. 9:25; a faithful high priest, Heb. 2:17, eternal, Heb. 6:20, Ps. 110:4; a most learned teacher, Isa. 50:4.

XXIII. But just as the verb יָשַׁע is used in such a way that it simultaneously embraces the term of salvation from which and to which, concerning which let Chemnitius be consulted. * So also Christ is our Savior not only by reason of the term from which, because He frees us from the curse of the law, from the wrath of God, from the power of death and the Devil, but also by reason of the term to which, because He confers upon us illumination, sanctification, adoption, righteousness, salvation, and other innumerable spiritual gifts.

XXIV. But that the Father is also called Savior; this happens because salvation is a work ad extra and thus of the whole Trinity. Rightly, therefore, it is also ascribed to God the Father, with respect, namely, to His mercy and our misery; but to the Son with respect to acquisition and merit.

XXV. These things having been thus discussed, it is asked, is the name of Jesus new? The handle of this question was provided by that passage in Isaiah 62:4, "And a new name shall be called for you, which the mouth of Jehovah has declared." But we reply that that statement primarily speaks of the beloved bride of Christ, the Church, to whom He promises grace, help, praise, and most ample glory.

XXVI. But if anyone should wish to refer that to the most holy name of Jesus as the head of the Church, we reply that it is new by reason of 1. imposition, because it was imposed upon Him by the angel in a new and wonderful way. And it was called, says the venerable Bede, His glorious name, and most worthy of all worship, the name which is above every name; it was not fitting that it should first be called by men, nor brought into the world by them. 2. plenary manifestation in the N. T. through the preaching of the Gospel, Luke 24, 47. Acts 10, 43. Otherwise, even in the O. T., this name was manifested not only to the Prophets and Jews, as from the sighs of Jacob, Gen. 49, 18. Cf. Is. 53, 4. and Matt. 11, 5. Also Is. 62, 11. Heb. 3, 18. Luke 2, 30. as also from the names of Joshua the leader, Joshua the Priest, and Jesus Sirach, but also to many of the Gentiles in the midst of Gentilism, as is clear from the testimonies of the Sibyls, which the most ancient fathers often cite: 3. signification, for it does not denote an earthly Savior but a heavenly one, not a corporal and common one, but a spiritual one, not a temporary one but a perpetual one. 4. innovation, Is. 43, 19. Ezek. 36, 26. 2 Cor. 5, 17. Rev. 21, 19.

XXVII. The Angel says expressly and roundly in Matt. 1, 21 that the Messiah ought to be called Jesus because He saves His people from their sins. The Photinians contradict this angelic assertion simply; although they concede that Christ is the instrumental cause of our salvation, they nevertheless deny its source and primary or meritorious cause, against the clearest oracles of Scripture, in which He is called ἀρχηγὸς, prince or author of life, Acts 3, 15, of salvation, Heb. 2, 10, in whom and in no other is salvation, Acts 4, 12. Hence He also gives the fountain of water springing up into eternal life, John 4, 14, He is the foundation, besides which no other can be laid, 1 Cor. 3, 11, and through His name all receive remission of sins, Acts 10, 43. Cf. 1 John 1, 7, ch. 2, 2, Rom. 3, 25, Heb. 9, 12.

XXIIX. Akin to these contemners of the name of Jesus (which is a delightful name, a comforting name, than which nothing is sung more sweetly, nothing heard more pleasantly, nothing thought of more sweetly, by the pronunciation of which the whole mouth is filled with wonderful sweetness) are the Calvinists, who, with a certain manly gravity, blush to either bend the knees or uncover their heads at the hearing of it; what is more, they do not hesitate to falsely mock others who do so and proclaim them superstitious.

29. But

XXIX. But by this reasoning, Abraham Gen. 17, 3, Moses & Aaron Num. 16, 4, C. 22, 45, David 2. Sam. 12, 16, c. 6, 10, Solomon 2. Chron. 6, 13, the Magi from the east, Matth. 2, 11, Peter Act. 9, 40, Christ himself & others, who all worshipped by falling upon their faces and knees, must be called superstitious. For the external ceremony of genuflection, as also of uncovering the head, is accustomed to be an index of internal devotion and piety of the heart, that in our heart we love Christ, honor him, and internally and from the heart humble ourselves before him. For his prayer, as Cassiodorus says, is perfect, whose cause cries out, and tongue and act, and speech and life, and thought. And therefore also the Royal Prophet David joins both, Ps. 22, 30, all the fat ones in the earth shall eat and worship, all shall bow their knees before him etc. Conf. Ps. 95, 6. 1. Cor. 11, 4. Phil. 2, 10.

XXX. You ask, why however do we bow our knees only when the name of Jesus is heard, and uncover our heads, but not when he is called Son of God, Son of Mary, Christ etc.? Resp. 1. Son of God, of Mary etc. are his surnames, but this is his proper name. 2. Because this name, as Galatinus (l. 3. de arc. Cath. ver. c. 20.) advises, sufficiently contains the whole process of our salvation, the beginning, middle, and end, wherefore all other things are included. 3. And indeed especially, on account of the practice of our ancestors, which the Calvinists, without probable reason and not without the greatest scandal to the weak, condemn and traduce as an idolatrous ceremony.

XXXI. But the horrible blasphemy of the Jews is to be abominated and detested, who have extracted the radical letter ע from the name of Jesus, so that the name might not have its origin from the office of saving, and they proclaim him with impure mouth not as ישוע but according to their abbreviations as ישו, a liar and impostor, whose name ought to be blotted out, and they spit three times at his name, as also at the name of any Christian. God will spit them out again from his mouth etc. Zach. 12, 10. Apoc. 1, 7.

XXXII. Most basely also do the creatures of Ignatius Loyola abuse this name, who pride themselves on the glorious title of Switzers—I meant Jesuits—as if they alone were the brothers and companions of Jesus, whom nevertheless they impudently contradict in word and deed, while they strive to be not the saved, but the saviors. To these may be added poisoners and enchanters, who begin their actions in the name of Jesus; the superstitious, who hang it written on paper from their necks against infirmities; and the blasphemers, who invoke the Sacraments and wounds of Jesus for the destruction of others.

XXXIII. If you write, it does not taste right to me, unless I read Jesus there: if you dispute or confer, it does not taste right to me, unless Jesus has sounded there. Sing to his name, for it is sweet, the Psalmist exhorts, Ps. 135, 3. In truth, the sweetest name of Jesus is sweet, for it delights the taste, as honey in the mouth; it delights the hearing, as a melody in the ear, so that the bride may rightly say, Cant. 2, 14, let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face is comely; it delights every inner affection, because it is a jubilation in the heart. In short, Jesus is everything to us; if we desire to be cured, he is the physician, Exod. 15, 26; if we burn with fevers, he is the fountain, Ps. 36, 10, Jer. 2, 13, Joh. 4, 14; if we are burdened by iniquity, he is righteousness, Jer. 23, 6; if we are in need of help, he is power, Ps. 24, 8, Ps. 29, 11. Ps. 41, 2. If we desire to go, he is the way, Joh. 15, 5; if we flee from darkness, he is the light, Joh. 8, 12; if we seek food, he is nourishment and the bread of life, Joh. 6, 25. Taste therefore and see how sweet the Lord is. It is not permitted to add more because of the scarcity of paper. Therefore, most sweet Christ JESUS.

Be thou our joy, let our glory be in thee. Who art to be our reward; through all ages forever.

Latin:

SECTIO II. De nomine JESU.

XIV. Qvemadmodum in institutione Sacramenti circumcisionis, Gen. 17. Deus ipse nomen אַבְרָם qvod partem excelsum significabat, ab אב pater & רום exaltari, excelsum esse, auxit litera ה, אַבְרָהָם qvod denotat patrem multitudinis seu plurimarum gentium, à rad. הָמָה multiplicari, qvam Etymologiam Deus ipse tradit; sic etiam in populo Dei mos iste (qvem etiam nos Christiani hodiè ut laudabilem in Baptismo retinemus) imponendi liberis in circumcisione nomina inolevit.

XV. Cùm igitur Christus Circumcisionis Sacramentum in carne recipere vellet, nomen à reipsa, (qvemadmodum Adam à rubrâ terrâ, à rad. אָדָם rubuit, & Jacob ab עָקַב supplantavit, Gen. 25. v. 26. & 33. Noah à consolatione, Gen.5,29. Nabal à stultitia, 1. Sam. 25,25. Salomon à pace, Rehabeam à flagello, Joannes Baptista à gratia &c.) salvationis scilicet opere, יְשׁוּעָה Ἰησῦς, JESUS, qvod etiam cùm ante tum post conceptionem, Mariæ & Josepho ab angelo mandatum erat, Luc. 1, 31. Matth. 1,21. accepit.

XVI. Qvidam verò, inter qvos Basilius, qvæsiverant hujus nominis originem in linguâ Græcâ à Fut. ἰάσω, ex qvo si α in η vertatur, facilè oriatur nomen ἰησῦς, quod apud eos ἰατρὸν medicum fignificat. Alii volunt esse compositum ex יְהֹוָה! quod exprimat divinam Christi naturam denôtetq́; Dominum,& אִ֚ישׁ quod innuat humanam ejus naturam,& significet herôa seu virum,& cùm anteChristum vocabulũ τετραγάμματον יְהוָה! fuerit ineffabile,interposito שׁ in nomine Jesu sive Jehoschua effabile factum esse, quæ opinio fuit Osiandri, citantibus Flacio & Chemnitio.

XVII. Hæ derivationes licet bonâ intentione inventæ, & etiam Filius Dei medicus appelletur, Exod.15.v.ult. Salvatorq́; noster revera sit θεάνθρωπος & עִמָּנוּאֵל, Germanicè Gottmann vel GOtt und Mensch/tamen dulcissimam hoc nomen Jesu origine suâ Hebræum est,& יְהוֹשׁוּעַ! vel quod ex eo contractum videtur יֵשׁוּעַ! (ut יוסף pro יהוסף Ps.81,6.)scribitur; sicuti etiam filius ille Josedec,qvi apudHaggæum & Zachariam יְהוֹשׁוּעַ! Hitzræ 2,2.& c.3,2.Neh.7,7. יֵשׁוּעַ )mutata in .. propter literas rejectas)ut & filius Nun יְהוֹשׁוּעַ! Neh.8,17. יֵשׁוּעַ (Act.7,45. ἰησῦς) contra assertionemGalatini,qvi eos יֵשׁוּעַ vocatos esse omninò negat,vocatur. Conf. etiam 2.Par. 31, 15. & Col.4, 11. ubi hoc nomen etiam aliis tribuitur.

XIIX. Descendit verò à Rad. יָשַׁעַ! in hiphil (יָשַׁע enim in kal non est in usu )qvod idem est ac servavit, salvavit,salvum fecit,opitulatus est; A qvo præposita litera י Jod, vel à Fut. mutato י Jod in penultima in ו vaf Heemanticum facilè formari potest יָשׁוּעַ! Et licet tertia futuri regulariter sit יוֹשִׁיעַ! aliqvoties tamen interposita ה legitur, ut 1. Sam. 17. 47. Ps. 116, 6.

XIX. Retinet autem cœlestis nuntius scriptionem & pronunciationemGræcam tum temporis in populo Dei usitatissimam & יְהוֹשׁוּעַ! vel יֵשׁוּעַ! vértit per ἰησῦν. Ne autem scrupulus alicui injiceretur propter istam scriptionis & pronunciationis varietatem,ipse radicẽ subjicit, inqviens Mat. 1, 21. Vocabis nomen ejus JESUS; ipse enim salvum faciet populum à peccatis ipsorum. Confer. Actor.14, 12.& Hebr.2,10. Græci σωτῆρα à σώζειν. Latini servatorem à servando,vel potiùs salvatorem à salvando,qvia fatente ipso Cicerone vocabulum σωτῆρὸς καὶ τοῦ σώζειν plus significat qvàm servatoris. Germani Heyland /vel ab heilen/ à sanandis vulneribus nostris lethalibus, vel ab heiligen / vel des Landes Heil.Liqvet ex his,parum rectè scribi IHesus,vel per abbreviationem cum superimpositâ cruce JHS, quæ scriptio Pontificiis & Jesuitis familiaris.

XX. Denotat autem non solùm nomen proprium יֵשׁוּעַ, sed ipsam qvoq; salutem יְשׁוּעָה, ut vel ex unico 12. cap. Esaiæ liqvet, ubi ter vocabulum יְשׁוּעָה repetitur, v. 2. & 3. Qvod vocabulum LXX. Interpretes per σωτηρίαν vel σωτήριον commodè reddiderunt, qvod etiam Simeon in præclaro suo de Messiæ testimonio retinere voluit, Luc. 2. v. 30.

XXI. Nihil autem refert, qvòd dulcissimo hoc nomine Jesu etiam alii indigitati fuerint, ut filius Nun, Jos. 1. Act. 7, 45. Hebr. 4, 8. Filius Josedec, Hagg. 1, 1. C. 2. v. 2. & 4. Zach. 3, 3. Eccl. 49, 14. Filius Sirach. Sir. 50, 28. Adumbrarunt enim hujus nostri Jesu, ut nomen, ita & res, potentiam, ut Josua filius Nun, qvi erat heros fortissimus; sanctimoniam, ut Jehosua filius Josedec, qvi sacerdos sanctissimus; sapientiam, ut Jesus filius Sirach, qvi doctor eruditissimus: & sic tantum δευτέρως, ut loqvitur Cl. Jacobus Martini † Præceptor & Promotor meus honorandus, illis hoc nomen tribuitur, vel qvia sunt typi veri hujus nostri Salvatoris, Josua enim dux adumbravit officium Regium, Josedech sacerdotale, Jesus Sirach doctorale seu propheticum; vel ut nomen istud sit recordatio salutis nobis per Christum acqvisitæ vel acqvirendæ.

XXII. Hic enim verè est dux potentissimus Act. 3, 14. Mich. 5, 2. Dan. 9, 25. Pontifex fidelis Hebr. 2, 17. æternus Hebr. 6, 20. Ps. 110, 4. doctor eruditissimus Esa. 50, 4.

XXIII. Qvemadmodū autem verbum יָשַׁע ita usurpatur, ut simul complectatur terminum salvationis à qvo & ad qvem, de qvib⁹ videatur Chemnitius. * Sic etiam Christus est noster Salvator non tantum ratione termini à qvo, qvod nos à maledictione legis, ab irâ Dei, à mortis & Diaboli potestate liberet, sed etiam ratione termini ad qvē, qvod conferat nobis illuminationem, sanctificationem, adoptionem, justitiam, salutem, aliaq; innumerabilia dona spiritualia.

XXIV. Qvod verò etiam Pater Salvator vocetur; Fit hoc ideò, qvia salvatio est opus ad extra & sic totius Trinitatis. Rectè igitur etiam Deo Patri asscribitur, respectu scilicet suæ misericordiæ & nostræ miseriæ; Filio autem respectu acqvisitionis & meriti.

XXV. His ita disputatis, quæritur, an nomen Jesu sit novum? Ansamhujus quæstionis dedit illud Ef. 62, 4. Et vocabitur tibi nomen novum, quod os Jehovah declaravit. Sed Refp. quod dictum illud πρώτως loquatur de dilectâ Christi sponsâ, Ecclesiâ, cui pollicetur gratiam, auxilium, laudem & gloriam amplissimam.

XXVI. Sin autem quis illud ad sanctissimum nomen Jesu tanquàm caput Ecclesiæ referre velit, regerimus, novum illud esse ratione 1. impositionis, quia novo & mirabili modo ab angelo ei est impositum. Et vocatum est, inquit venerabilis Beda, nomen ejus gloriosum, omniq; cultu dignissimum, nomen quod est supra omne nomē, non decuit primum ab hominibus appellari, neque ab eis inferri in mundum. 2. plenariæ manifestationis in N. T. per prædicationem Evangelii Luc. 24, 47. Act. 10. 43. Aliàs etiam in V. T. nomen hoc non solum Prophetis & Judæis, ut ex suspiriis Jacobi Gen. 49, 18. Conf. Ef. 53, 4. & Matth. 11, 5. Item Ef. 62, 11. Hebr 3, 18. Luc. 2, 30. ut & ex nominibus Jehosua ducis, Jehosua Sacerdotis & Jesus Sirach, sed etiam multis Ethnicorum in medio Ethnicismo manifestatum fuisse, ex Sybillarum testimoniis, quæ vetustissimi patres sæpiùs citant, liqvet: 3. significationis, non enim notat Salvatorem terrestrem sed cœlestem, non corporalem & vulgarem, sed spiritualem, non temporarium sed perpetuū. 4. innovationis, Ef. 43, 19. Ezech. 36, 26. 2. Cor. 5, 17. Apoc. 21, 19.

XXVII. Disertè & rotundè dicit Angelus Matth. 1, 21. Messiam ideò Jesum vocari debere, quia salvū facit populum à peccatis ipsorū. Angelicę huic assertioni ἁπλῶς contradicit Photiniani, qui licet Christum causam nostræ salutis instrumentalem concedant, ejus tamen fontem & causam primam sive meritoriam pernegant, contra clarissima Scripturæ oracula, in quibus dicitur ἀρχηγὸς princeps sive autor τῆς ζωῆς, Act. 3, 15. τῆς σωτηρίας, Hebr. 2, 10. in quo & in nullo alio salus, Act. 4, 12. Hinc etiam dat fontem aqvæ salientis in vitam æternam, Joh. 4, 14. est fundamentū, præter quod aliud poni non potest. 1. Cor 3, 11. & per ejus nomen omnes accipiunt remissionem peccatorum, Act. 10, 43. Conf. 1. Joh. 1, 7. c. 2, 2. Rom 3, 25. Hebr. 9, 12.

XXIIX. Hilce nominis Jesu (quod est nomen delectabile, nomen confortans, qve nil canitur svavius, nil auditur jucundi9, nil cogitatur dulcius cujusq; pronunciatione totū os mirâ suavitate repletur) contemtoribus affines sunt Calviniani, qvi gravitate qvâdam virili ad auditū ipsius vel genua flectere vel capita nudare erubescunt, qvid? qvod alios facientes falsè irridere superstitiososqve proclamare non dubitent.

29. Verùm

XXIX. Verum hac ratione & Abraham Gen. 17, 3. Moses & Aaron Num. 16, 4. C. 22, 45. David 2. Sam. 12, 16. c. 6, 10. Salomon 2, Chron. 6, 13. Magi ab oriente, Matth. 2, 11. Petrus Act. 9, 40. Christus ipse & alii, qui omnes in facies & genua procidendo adorarunt, superstitiosi dicendi sunt. Externa enim ceremonia genuflexionis ut & capitis nudationis, solet esse index internae cordis devotionis & pietatis, quod in corde Christum amemus, honoremus, interne & ex corde coram eo nos humaliemus. Ipsius qvippe oratio, ut loquitur Cassiodorus, est perfecta, cujus & causa clamat, & lingva & actus, & sermo & vita, & cogitatio. Ideoq; etiam Regius Propheta David utrumq; conjungit, Pf. 22, 30. omnes pingues in terra edent & adorabunt, coram eo genua flectent omnes &c. Conf. Pf. 95, 6. 1. Cor. 11, 4. Phil. 2, 10.

XXX. Inqvis, cur autem duntaxat audito nomine Jesu genua flectim? & capita nudamus, no vero qvando vocatur filius Dei, fili? Mariae, Christus &c. Resp. 1. Filius Dei, Mariae &c. sunt ejus cognomina, hoc vero ejus nomen proprium. 2. qvia hoc nomen, ut Galatinus (l. 3. de arc. Cath. ver. c. 20.) monet, totum nostrae salutis processum, principium, medium ac finem sufficienter continet, qvare & caetera omnia includuntur. 3. & qvidem praecipue, ob praxin majorum nostrorum, qvam Calviniani sine probabili ratione non absqve summo infirmorum scandalo damnant & tanqva ceremoniam idolatricam traducunt.

XXXI. Abominanda vero & detestanda horribilis Judaeorum blasphemia est, qui lit. radicalem ע ex nomine Jesu extriverunt, ne a salvandi officio nomen habeat, eumqve non ישוע! sed secundum suas abbreviaturas ישו mendacem & impostorem, cujus nomen deleri debeat, impuro ore proclamitant, & ad ejus, ut & alicujus Christiani nomen terna vice expuunt. Expuet eos Deus interum ex ore suo &c. Zach. 12, 10. Apoc. 1, 7.

XXXII. Turpissime etiam hoc nomine abutuntur Ignatii Lojolae creaturae, qvi glorioso Suitarum, Jesuitarum volebam, titulo superbiunt, qvasi ipsi soli fratres sociiqve Jesus sint, cui tamen ore & opere impudenter contradicunt, dum non salvati, sed salvatores esse satagunt. Addantur his venefica & incantatores, qvi suas actiones in nomine Jesu ordiuntur; superstitiosi, qvi illud a collo incharta scriptum contra infirmitates suspendunt; blasphemi, qvi Sacramenta & vulnera Jesu aliis in perniciem imprecantur.

XXXIII. Si scribis, non sapit mihi, nisi legero ibi Jesum: si disputes aut conferas, non sapit mihi, nisi sonuerit ibi Jesus. Psalite nomini ejus, quia svave est, hortatur Psaltes, Ps. 135, 3. Revera dulcissimum nomen Jesu svave est, delectat enim gustum, quia mel in ore; delectat auditum, quia melos in aure, ut merito dicat sponsa, Cant. 2, 14. sonet vox tua in auribus meis, vox enim tua dulcis & facies tua decora; delectat omnem interiorem affectum, quia jubilus in corde. Breviter, omnia Jesus nobis est, si curari desideramus, medicus est, Exod. 15, 26. si febribus æstuamus, fons est, Ps. 36, 10. Jer. 2, 13. Joh. 4, 14. si gravamur iniquitate, justitia est, Jer. 23, 6. si auxilio indigemus, virtus est, Ps. 24, 8. Ps. 29, 11. Ps. 41, 2. si ire desideramus, via est, Joh. 15. 5. si tenebras fugimus, lux est, Joh. 8, 12. si cibum apetimus, alimentum est & panis vitæ, Joh. 6. 25. Gustate igitur & videte, quàm svavis est Dominus. Plura propter chartæ angustiam addere non licet. Ergo dulcissime Christe JESU.

Tu esto nostrum gaudium Sit nostra in te gloria. Qui es futurus præmium; Per cuncta semper secula.


## 27 Twenty-seventh Disputation, On the Advent of the Magi and the Worship Rendered by Them

Our Lord and Savior was indeed born for all, he was born for the sake of all, but he was not received by all, not understood by all: he was understood by the Gentiles, he was not understood by the Jews; he was acknowledged by the Church, he was not acknowledged by the Synagogue, says Blessed Chrysostom. In what manner he was both born and circumcised for all has been sufficiently declared in the preceding disputations: but in what manner he was not received and understood by all, the present history gives us assurance, in which he is honored and adored as GOD by the Magi, and is neglected and despised by Herod and the Jews: the illumination of the Magi stood as a great testimony of the blindness of the Jews: in their land these men sought him whom they did not acknowledge in their own; among them these men found the infant whom they denied among themselves.

II. In memory of these, the Church today not undeservedly follows the feast of the Epiphany with solemn remembrance, which indeed was unknown in the first infancy of the Church, but gradually its name was introduced from the rites of the pagans into Ecclesiastical observance for a pious purpose, as Casaubon proves against Baronius, and observes from Diodorus Siculus and others, that any appearances of a divine deity were called ἐπιφάνειαν by them, and that they often celebrated feast days in memory of these, which they called τὰ ἐπιφάνια from the thing itself, neuter in gender, not feminine.

III. In imitation of this, the ancient Greek Church called not the day of the arrival of the Magi, as is believed today and as Baronius tries to prove, but the birth of the Lord, τὰ ἐπιφάνια, without doubt because Paul calls the birth itself ἐπιφάνειαν; for which solemnity the sixth day of January was appointed, to which many Churches formerly referred the birthday of the Lord, as Chrysostom is the author. Afterwards, however, taught by the Roman Church, they decided to celebrate the day sacred to the birth of Christ together on December 25th.

IV. And although they retained the name, they substituted the cause of its memory as the baptism of Christ, and also the arrival of the Magi. Augustine, however, in sermon 1 on the Epiphany, ascribes four miracles to this feast: the arrival of the Magi, the baptism of Christ, the conversion of water into wine, and the miracle of the five loaves.

V. These things having been tasted beforehand, we make an approach to the history itself, in which the Magi first come to be considered by us: for the words of the Evangelist describing it are as follows: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem.

VI. I find, however, that the Magi are called by a threefold method. 1. Those are called Magi who, taught by demons, were occupied with incantations and wicked arts, and in that sense that Simon in Acts 8:9 and Elymas in Acts 13:8 are called Magi, and there is no doubt that many Fathers took the opportunity from this to designate even these, whom Matthew mentions, as enchanters and sorcerers. 2. Among Herodotus, the name of the Magi is not of an art or profession, but of a nation, and one which formerly inhabited Media. 3. The Magi among the Persians were wise men, or Priests, whose chief duty was to take care of their sacred rites, and to profess wisdom, such as the Gymnosophists are among the Indians, and the philosophers among the Greeks: And the word itself indicates that they were so properly called, which those most skilled in that language have observed to be Persian. And therefore they are not unjustly criticized who, in order to prove that they were Arabs by nation, invent that they came from a certain region of Arabia, which Epiphanius calls Magodia, and that the origin of this name was derived from here. Nor are those less mistaken who contend that it is a Greek word, and wish it to be derived from the verb μάττω, that is, to knead: Casaubon, Exerc. 2. §. 10, demonstrates that it was clearly unknown to Homer and other Greeks of an older age.

VII. Since it is therefore evident from these things that the name Magi is equivocal, it must be seen of what kind of men the Evangelist speaks. He says the Magi came from the East, not as if they had arrived from the furthest borders of the East, but from such a region as was Eastern in comparison to the Jews: but that Arabia is to the south of Judea is clear from Matt. 12, 24, where the queen of Sheba is called the queen of the South. Therefore, Chrysostom rightly thinks that they came from Persia, a region to the east of Judea.

VIII. Whether they were kings, as the Papists contend, cannot be affirmed with certainty by any reason. We do indeed concede this, that no one could be a king of the Persians who had not first received the discipline of the Magi: yet nothing is concluded from that, rather we rightly deny that they were kings, because the Monarchy of the Persians had long since ceased for over three hundred years, for their last king is named in the sacred writings as Darius, otherwise called Codomannus, from whom the kingdom was transferred to Alexander the Great and his successors. It is probable, however, that they were not obscure men or of vile condition, as Mr. Chemnitz gathers from their gifts, but either petty kings or toparchs of the Persian domain, who at that time obeyed the king of the Parthians, as Strabo says somewhere.

IX. As this can be asserted probably, so to affirm that it is so is very rash, certainly no less than to insist that there were only three Magi, no more, nor fewer. For since Scripture reveals nothing about these things, we prefer to withhold our opinion rather than to put forward uncertain things rashly: for, as Theophylact says, ἅ ἡ γραφὴ ἀπεσιώπησεν, ὀυ δεῖ ἐξετάζειν: and the impiety of certain men given to superstitious things is to be detested, who have been accustomed to abuse the names of the Magi and the Shepherds against the bites of serpents, just as Casaubon cites this from a certain Greek author, Exerc. 2. §. 10.

X. Regarding the time also, when the Magi came to Bethlehem, the opinion of the Fathers is not the same. Epiphanius thinks that they came to adore Christ only after two years had passed, and Beza agrees with him. The author of the imperfect work on Matthew seems to hold the same view, who recounts a tradition, or rather a fable, about this matter from an author who, as he himself confesses, is apocryphal. The principal foundation of this opinion is that Herod ordered the infants to be killed from two years old and under according to the time which he had inquired from the Magi: Mr. Chemnitz answers this in various ways; we, with Chrysostom, say in general that the fear and fury of Herod, for the sake of an abundance of caution and the license of persecution, allowed for an even greater time, so that no one of that age, or especially the one for whom the others were to be killed, might escape.

XI. Nor does the conjecture of those seem entirely absurd who, with Chrysostom, Augustine, Theophylact, and others, maintain that that star, which showed the Magi the way into Judea, preceded the birth of Christ by a long interval: for since it was a sign of the birth of Christ, it ought not to have existed for the first time together with it, or after it; for a sign is not of a present thing, but of an imminent one. And they could perhaps gather from the configuration of the star that it was portended by that omen that the King of the Jews was about to be born, and that his birth would fall into the time of its arrival: therefore they asked πoῦ εστιν ὁ τεχθεὶς βασιλεὺς, which those skilled in the Greek language indicate signifies one recently born. However, Herod inquired from the Magi the thing which they knew, namely the time of the star, not that which they were seeking, that is, where he was born, which the Evangelist clearly indicates, v. 7. But since nothing certain could be fished out from them concerning the birth, according to the time of the star which he had explored from them, v. 16, he orders the boys from two years old and under to be killed, not according to the time of the birth of Christ, which Herod did not know. See Scaliger.

XII This observation, as it is not unlike the truth, so this is certain and undoubted, that the Magi came before the purification of Mary. For first they adored the child Jesus in Bethlehem, to which Joseph and Mary had come, so that with other families of the lineage of David they might register their names. But the Law commands the woman who has given birth to remain in her blood for forty days, and to abstain from public view; therefore it was a sin for her to depart from here before she had completed the just days, and it is evident from Luke that, when they had performed everything according to the law of God, they returned into Galilee, and they are never read to have returned to Bethlehem. 13. next, the text confirms this which we have said. For the words τ̃ Ἰησῦ γεννηθέντ̃ imply that they did not come a long time afterwards, but immediately from the birth, and Casaubon notes that this is the force of the aorist participle in the Greek language, so as to denote at the same time the speed of the time, and therefore the Evangelist says γεννηθέντ̃, not γεγεννημένε, of which the latter is used for an action already perfected before, the former for one just perfected and still as it were pending.

XIV. And these things concerning the Magi: but by what guide they came into Bethlehem, they themselves indicate in v. 2: we have seen his star in the East. This magnificent star was the tongue of heaven, which declared the glory of the world, which proclaimed the unusual birth of the virgin with unusual brightness, to which, not appearing afterwards, the Gospel would succeed in the whole world, says Augustine, Ser. 3 de Epiph.

XV. Whether it was natural, and one of those which were created by God from the beginning, or whether it was supernatural, is also usually asked. That it was not natural is indicated by its place, duration, and motion: for it was not in the ethereal region like other stars, but in the air near the earth; otherwise, it could not have so accurately designated the way and the house in which Christ was born to those traveling; nor did it appear before or after, nor was it moved about by the usual motion of stars, but it accommodated itself to the journey of those traveling.

XVI. We do not indeed deny that God the Best and Greatest could easily have removed a real star from its station and delegated it to perform these supernatural duties, but since miracles are not to be multiplied from our own brains without necessity, we maintain rather that it was not a real star, but was so called by similarity, because it appeared in the form of a star, just as we are also accustomed to call a comet a star, and unknown and bright visions are often called stars in Scripture because of their appearance and semblance.

XVII. But concerning its matter and condition, no one will easily determine anything certain. Chrysostom contends that it was not a star at all, but a certain invisible power, full of reason, fashioned in the form of a star, with which Euthymius and Theophylact agree. The author of the work on the miracles of Holy Scripture (a), falsely attributed to Augustine, writes that either an angel or the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a star; truly, the opinion of those who maintain that an angel of God shone before the Magi in the form of a star, just as the pillar of fire was once a guide to the people of Israel, is the most simple, says Mr. Chemnitz, since angels are often said to appear like little flames of fire; it is more probable, however, that it was some unusual meteor, formed not by natural but by divine power from subcelestial and aerial matter in a low place in the air, which was carried not by its own force, but by the governance of either some angel or of God the Best and Greatest.

XIX. Chrysostom is pleased with the idea that this star went before the Magi during their entire journey: for he thinks it appeared constantly as a sort of guide for the journey as far as Palestine, and hid itself near Jerusalem, and in turn shone before them again when they left there for Bethlehem. The author of the work on the miracles of Holy Scripture, however, suggests the contrary, and it seems it can also be gathered from the text.

XIX. God willed the Magi to come to Christ with this star as their guide: for since they were most studious of astrological matters, He passed over all other remedies and called them through those things which custom made familiar to them, condescending to the salvation of men by a certain wonderful dispensation of piety, as Chrysostom says.

XX. It is indeed difficult to say how they could have gathered from the appearance of this star that the King of the Jews was born, and indeed so firmly that, preparing themselves for the journey and coming to Jerusalem, they did not first investigate whether he was born, but immediately where he was, without any hesitation. Certainly, no consequence deduced from the light of nature alone or from principles of reason could have persuaded them of this: for it does not follow that a preternatural star, not seen before, has appeared, therefore the Messiah is born. Nor, however, do we lean to the contrary in such a way as to make their error our own, who think that the Magi knew nothing about Christ being the future Messiah, but imagined for themselves some political king from the appearance of the star, whose benevolence and favor they wished to win for themselves in time with external adoration and gifts, when rather the disturbance of Herod and the people, the power of the tyrant still living, and also the lowly birth in a lowly inn could have provided an occasion for doubting about the king? Everything was externally bare and needy; nothing royal met the eyes of the body there, and yet whom they saw in such poverty, they acknowledged as king. Clearly, aided by an extraordinary and immediate divine revelation, they perceived with other, more penetrating eyes of faith within, by which they beheld royal and divine majesty in the poor equipment and small body, like a light hidden inside a lantern or the Sun inside a cloud.

XXI. Nor are the Magi believed to have been entirely ignorant of the promises concerning the future Messiah. For it is the almost unanimous consensus of the Fathers that they derived their origin from the posterity of Balaam, and held his prophecy, preserved by tradition, which is read in Numbers 24:17: A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a rod shall arise out of Israel, etc.; and when they saw the new and unusual star that had risen, mindful of that oracle, they understood it to be the indicator of the Messiah already born. But since the star rising out of Jacob demonstrates not so much that one which presented itself as conspicuous to the Magi, as Christ himself (inasmuch as he is called the Dayspring from on high, Luke 1:78, and the Morning Star, Rev. 22:16, is called), it is much more likely to say that the writings of Daniel and other Prophets were faithfully preserved among the Persians from the Babylonian captivity, and that from reading them the Magi were instructed about the Messiah when they noticed the new star had risen; for it is an argument that the Bible existed and was accustomed to be read not only among the Jewish people but also among other nations, as shown by the eunuch of Queen Candace. And we do not doubt that Daniel proposed the doctrine concerning the Messiah to the Magi, in whose school he was educated, and left behind among them seeds of it that were not common. Therefore, three things could have concurred for the conversion of the Magi: 1. the light of nature, 2. the supernatural illumination of God from on high, and 3. the instruction of Daniel derived to them by the tradition of the fathers, with the added reading of the Prophets, if any came into their hands.

XXII. Impelled by these things, they come to Jerusalem, seeking that which they thought was not unknown to the Jews: where that King (as the article indicates) of the Jews was born, so long promised and expected; hearing which, Herod trembled as a rival, for he feared that by the born King he himself might be driven from the kingdom, or his sons deprived of the succession. Nor was the King only, but all Jerusalem with him was troubled, either perhaps by fear of the Romans, or because they feared that Herod, if angered, might harass the Jewish race on account of the King. For just as the sea is shaken by contending winds, so when kings oppose one another, the people of the kingdom are harassed, says the author of the Opus Imperfectum in Matthew. Nevertheless, the King thought it would be more prudent for himself and his affairs to inquire into the place predetermined for the birth of this King; therefore, calling a council, he proposes the question to the Chief Priests and Scribes, where Christ was to be born, who, although they are enemies of the truth, for the sake of the truth are compelled to read the letters, and to interpret the prophecy concerning Christ to those who do not know it; they answer, therefore, that the place will be the city of Bethlehem: God willed, says Augustine, that this be inquired of by the Jews, so that while they point out Him in whom they do not believe, they may be condemned by their very own demonstration.monstration.

XXIII. Let the form of the Councils in the Israelite Church be noted here in passing: Herod, as the supreme magistrate, following the example of Hezekiah and Josiah, summons the Chief Priests and Scribes, as the heads of the ecclesiastical ministry, and proposes to them a question, which they define not by magisterial authority, nor from his own brain, but from the word of God, and indeed by pointing out its place. If only councils had always been instituted in the Church according to the example of this one, there would be less litigation between us and the Papists, who attribute absolute authority and jurisdiction to the Pope alone, and a greater accession to the truth would be made daily.

Latin:

DOminus & Salvator noster omnibus quidem natus est, unus propter omnes natus est, sed non ab omnibus susceptus est, non ab omnibus intellectus: intellectus est à gentibus, non intellectus est à Judæis, agnitus est ab Ecclesia, non est agnitus à Synagogâ, inquit B. Chrysostomus.
