Quo pacto pro omnibus & natus & circumcisus, præcedentibus disputationibus satis declaratum est: quo pacto verò non ab omnibus susceptus & intellectus sit, præsens historia, fidem nobis facit, in quâ à Magis ut DEUS honoratur & adoratur, ab Herode & Judæis negligitur & despicitur: Magorum illuminatio magnum testimonium exstitit cæcitatis Judæorum: in terra eorum isti requirebant, quem illi in suâ non agnoscebant; apud eos isti infantem invenerunt quem illi apud se negarunt.

II. In horum memoriam hodierna Ecclesia festum Epiphanias solenni recordatione non immeritò proseqvitur, qvod qvidem in prima Ecclesiæ infantia incognitum fuit, paulatim verò ejus appellatio ex ritibus paganorum pio proposito in Ecclesiasticam observationem est introducta, ut multis probat contra Baronium Casanbonus, & ex Diodoro Siculo atq; aliis observat, ἐπιφάνειαν ipsis dictas qvaslibet numinis divini apparitiones, inq; harum memoriam festos sæpè dies coluisse, qvos à re dixerint τὰ ἐπιφάνια genere neutros non fœminino.

III Ad hujus imitationem vetus Ecclesia Græca non diem adventûs Magorum, ut hodiè creditur, & probare conatur Baronius, sed nativitatis dominicæ τὰ ἐπιφάνια vocavit, sine dubio exinde qvod Paulus ipsam nativitatem ἐπιφάνειαν appellet; cui solennitati sextus dies Januarii est dictus, in qvem etiam multæ Ecclesiæ natalem Domini olim retulerunt, ut autor est Chrysost. Postea tamen à Romanâ edoctæ 25. Decembr. nativitati Christi sacrum unà celebrare constituerunt.

IV. Et qvamvis appellationem retinuerunt, causam tamen ejus memoriam baptismi Christi substituerunt, nec non adventus Magorum. August. verò ser. 1. in Epiph. qvatuor huic festo adscribit miracula, adventus Magorum, baptismi Christi, conversionis aqvæ in vinum, & miraculum qvinq; panum.

V. His itaq; prælibatis ad ipsam historiam accessum facimus, in qvâ primùm Magi nobis considerandi veniunt: verba enim Evangelistæ eam describentis sic habent: Cùm autem natus esset Jesus in Bethlehem civitate Judæ, temporibus Herodis regis, Ecce Magi ab Oriente accesserunt Hierosolymam.

VI. Triplici autem modo Magos appellatos invenio. 1. Iidicti sunt Magi, qvi incantationibus artibusq; nefariis à dæmonibus edocti vacabant, atq; eo sensu Simon ille Act. 8, 9. & Elymas, Act. 13, 8. Magi vocantur, & dubium non est, qvin multi Patres hinc occasionem cœperint, etiam hos, qvorum meminit Matthæus, incantatores & maleficos indigitare. 2. Apud Herodotum & Magorum nomen non artis aut professionis, verùm nationis est, & qvæ Mediam olim inhabitaverit. 3. Magi apud Persas sapientes fuêre, seu Sacerdotes, qvorum præcipuum officium erat, sacra eorum curare, & sapientiamprofiteri, qvales apud Indos sunt Gymnosophistæ, & Græcos Philosophi: Atq; hos sic propriè appellatos indicat vocabulum, qvod Persicum esse observarunt linguæ ejus peritissimi. Ac proinde non injuriâ carpuntur, qvi, ut probent eos fuisse natione Arabes, fingunt ex Arabiæ qvâdam regione venisse, qvam Magodiam vocat Ephiphanius, atq; hinc nominis hujus originem ductam esse. Neq; minus illi errant, qvi Græcam esse vocem contendunt, & à verbo μάττω, id est, pinso, derivari volunt: sanè Homero & aliis Græcis antiqvioris seculi planè fuisse incognitam, demonstrat Casaubonus Exerc. 2. §. 10.

VII. Ex his ergò cùm constet, nomen Magi esse æqvivocum, videndum erit, de qvorum hominum genere loqvatur Evangelista. Dicit venisse Magos ab Oriente, non qvasi ab ultimis Orientis finibus advenerint, verùm ex tali regione, qvæ Judæorum comparatione erat Orientalis: Arabiam verò Judææ meridionalem esse, patet ex Matth. 12, 24. ubi regina Sabæ vocatur regina Austri. Ex Persiâ itaq; regione Judææ orientali venisse rectè existimat Chrysost.

VIII. Reges an fuerint, prout contendunt Pontificii, nullâ ratione certò potest affirmari. Hoc qvidem concedimus, non potuisse regem esse Persarum, qvi non antè Magorum disciplinam percepisset: nil tamen inde concluditur, qvin potiùs rectè negamus eos fuisse reges, qvòd Monarchia Persarum jam dudum desiisset annos ultra trecentos, ultimus enim eorum rex in sacris nominatur Darius, Codomannus aliàs dictus, à qvo regnum ad Alexandrum Magnum ejusq; successores translatum est. Probabile tamen est, eos non fuisse obscuros aut vilis conditionis homines, qvemadmodùm ex muneribus colligit Dn. Chemnitius, sed aut regulos aut toparchas ditionis Persicæ, qvi tunc temporis Parthorum regi parebant, ut ait alicubi Strabo.

IX. Hoc ut probabiliter potest asseri, sic affirmare ita esse, temerarium valdè est, non minùs sanè, qvàm pertendere, tres tantùm fuisse Magos, nó plures, nec pauciores. Cùm enim de his nihil prodat Scriptura, malumus sententiã nostram ἐπέχειν, qvàm ἀκροβαλήτες incerta proferre: nam, ut inqvit Theophyl. ἅ ἡ γραφὴ ἀπεσιώπησεν, ὀυ δεῖ ἐξετάζειν: & detestanda est impietas hominum qvorundam superstitiosibus deditorum, qvi Magorum & Pastorum nominibus contra morsus serpentum abuti consveverũt, qvemadmodum id ex autore qvodam Græco citat Casaubonus, Exerc. 2. §. 10.

X. De tempore quoq; , qvo Magi Bethlehem venerint, non eadem est Patrum opinio. Epiphanius putat exacto demum biennio eos ad adorandum Christum venisse, & cum eo consentit Beza. Idem etiam videtur sentire Autor oper. imp. in Matth. qvi traditionem seu potius fabulam hac de re ex autore, ut ipse fatetur apocrypho multis recenset. Hujus opinionis præcipuum est fundamentum, qvod Herodes infantes occidi jusserit a bimatu & infra juxta tempus, qvod exqvisiverat a Magis : ad hoc varie respondet Dn. Chemnitius ; nos cum Chrysostomo in genere dicimus, pavorem ac furorem Herodis pro abundantia cautionis & licentia persecutionis majus etiam tempus indulsisse, ne quis ejus ætatis, aut is potissimum, propter quem alii essent interimendi, effugeret.

XI. Neq; etiam omnino absurda videtur illorum conjectura, qvi cum Chrysost. August. Theophyl. & aliis statuunt, stellam illam, qvæ Magis viam in Judæam præmonstravit, longo intervallo Christi natalem præcessisse : cùm enim signum fuerit natalis Christi, non debuit simul cum ea, aut post eam primùm existere; qvippe signum non præsentis, sed rei imminentis est. Et potuerunt ex constitutione stellæ fortassis colligere, ostento illo portendi, regem Judæorum nasciturum, & natalem ejus in tempus adventus sui incursurum : proinde interrogabant πoῦ εστιν ὁ τεχθεὶς βασιλεὺς, qvod recens natum significare indicant Græcæ lingvæ periti. Exqvisivit autem Herodes a Magis eam rem, qvam sciebant, nempe tempus stellæ, non eam, qvam qværebant, id est, ubi natus esset, qvod disertè indicat Evangelista, v. 7. De nativitate verò cùm nihil certi ex illis potuerit expiscari, juxta tempus stellæ, qvod ab illis exploraverat, v. 16. pueros a bimatu & infrà occidi jubet, non juxta tempus natalis Christi, qvod ignorabat Herodes. Vide Scaligerum.

XII Hæc observatio ut est vero non absimilis, sic hoc certum est & indubitatum, magos ante purificationem Mariæ venisse. Primò enim puerum Jesum in Bethlehem adorarunt, qvo Joseph & Maria venerant, ut cum aliis gentibus stirpis Davidicæ nomina profiterentur. Lex verò præcipit puerperam manere in sangvine suo qvadraginta diebus, & publico abstinere, proinde nefas ipsi fuit hinc prius discedere, qvàm justos dies obierit, & ex Luca constat, qvod, cùm perfecissent omnia secundùm legem Dei, reversi sint in Galilæam, neq; unqvam leguntur rediisse in Bethlehem. 13. DeinXIII. Deinde hoc, qvod diximus, confirmat textus. Nam verba τ̃ Ἰησῦ γεννηθέντ̃ innuunt, non longo pòst tempore eos venisse, sed statim à nativitate, & hanc esse vim aoristi participii in Græco sermone annotat Causaub. ut simul denotet celeritatem temporis, atq; ideò Evagelista dicit γεννηθέντ̃, non γεγεννημένε, qvorum hoc de perfectâ jam ante actione, illud de modò perfectâ & adhuc qvasi dependente usurpatur.

XIV. Atq; hæc de Magis: qvo verò duce in Bethlehem venerint, ipsi indicant v. 2. vidimus stellam ejus in Oriente. Stella hæc magnifica fuit cœli lingua, quæ narrarat gloriam mundi, quæ inusitatum virginis partum inusitato fulgore clamaret, cui non postea apparenti Evangelium toto orbe succederet, inqvit August. Ser. 3. de Epiph.

XV. An naturalis fuerit, & una ex iis, qvæ ab initio à Deo creatæ sunt, an verò supernaturalis, qværi qvoqve solet. Naturalem non fuiffe indicant locus, duratio, & motus: neq; enim in æthereá regione ut cæteræ stellæ, fuit, sed in aëre terris vicino, aliàs proficiscentibus viam ac domum, in qvâ Christus esset natus, tàm accuratè designare non potuisset: neqve etiam ante vel pòst apparuit, nec solito stellarũ motu circumacta est, sed accommodavit se itineri proficiscentiũ.

XVI. Non qvidem diffitemur Deum Opt. Max. facili negotio veram stellam è statione suâ removere, & ad officia hæc supernaturalia præstanda delegare potuisse, cùm autem miracula ex nostro cerebro citra necessitatem non sint multiplicanda, statuimus potiùs non veram fuisse stellam, sed per similitudinem ita vocatam, qvoniam stellæ specie apparuit, qvemadmodum etiam Cometam stellam appellare solemus, & visiones ignotæ & lucidæ propter speciem & adparentiam in Scripturâ sæpè stellæ vocantur.

XVII. De materia autem & conditione ejus nihil certi facilè qvis determinabit. Chrysost. contendit stellam omninò non fuisse, sed qvãdam invisibilem virtutem, plenam rationis, in specie syderis figuratam, cum qvo consentiunt Euthymius & Theoph. Auctor oper. de mirab. S. S. (a) falsò Augustino attributi, vel angelum, vel Spiritum S. stellæ specie apparuisse scribit, sanè illorum sententiam, qvæ angelum Dei specie stellæ præluxisse Magis statuit, sicut olim columna ignis populi Israëliti ci dux fuit simplicissimam esse, ait Dn. Chemnitius, cùm sæpiùs angeli tanqvam flammulæ ignis apparere dicantur; Probabilius tamen est, fuisse eam meteoron aliqvod insolitum, non naturali sed divinâ virtute ex materiâ subcœlesti & aëreâ in loco aëris humili conflatum, qvod non suâ vi, sed vel angeli alicujus, vel Dei Opt. Max. regimine ferebatur.

XI X. Stellam verò hanc toto itinere Magos præivisse, placet Chrysostomo: putat enim usqve ad Palestinam qvasi itineris ducem semper apparuisse, & prope Hierosolymam sese abscondisse, ac vicissim inde egreffis ad Bethlehem præluxisse. Contrarium autem svadet, Autor operis de mirab. sacræ Scripturæ, atq; ex textu qvoq; colligi posse videtur.

XIX. Hac stellâ duce voluit Deus Magos ad Christum venire: cùm enim rerum Astrologicarum essent studiosissimi, reliqva omnia præteriit remedia, & per ea illos vocat, qvæ familiaria ipsis consvetudo fecebat, mirâ qvâdam dispensatione pietatis ad hominum condescendens salutem, ut inqvit Chrysost.

XX. Difficile verò dictu est, qvomodo ex apparitione hujus stellæ colligere potuerint regem Judæorum esse natum, & qvidem adeò firmiter, ut itineri sese accingentes & Hierosolymam venientes, non primùm an esset natus, sed statim ubi esset, absq; ullâ hæsitatione investigarent. Sanè nulla ex solo lumine naturæ aut principiis ex ratione deductis conseqventia hoc ipsis potuit suadere: neq; enim seqvitur, Stella præternaturalis & antehac non visa apparuit, Ergo Messias natus est. Neqve tamen in contrarium ita deflectimus, ut errorem eorum nostrum faciamus, qvi opinantur nihil Magis constitisse de Christo futuro Messiâ, sed ex apparitione stellæ regem qvendam politicum sibi imaginatos fuisse, cujus benevolentiam & favorem externâ adoratione & muneribus in tempore voluerint sibi conciliare, cùm potiùs perturbatio Herodis ac populi, potestas viventis adhuc tyranni, nec non vilis in vili diversorio nativitas dubitandi de rege occasionem præbere potuissent? Extrinseca nuda erant omnia & egena, nihil ibi regium corporeis oculis occurrit, & qvem tamen in tantâ paupertate viderunt, regem agnoverunt. Videlicet alios perspicaciores fidei oculos extraordinariâ & immediatâ divinitùs adjuti revelatione, intus deprehenderunt, qvibus in paupere apparatu & parvo corpusculo regiam divinamq; majestatem, qvasi lucem intra laternam aut Solem intra nubem latentem, conspexerunt.

XXI. Neq; etiam prorsus promissionum de futuro Messiâ Magi creduntur fuisse ignari. Unanimis enim ferè Patrum est consensus, eos ex posteritate Balaami originem duxisse, & vaticinium ejus traditione conservatum tenuisse, quod legitur Numer. 24, 17. Orietur stella ex Jacob, & consurget virga de Israël &c. atq; ubi exortam novam & insolidam viderint stellam, memores istius oraculi intellexisse, eam esse indicem jam nati Messiâ. Verùm cùm stella ex Jacob oriunda nõ tàm illam, quæ Magis conspicuam se præbuit, quàm ipsum Christum, (quippe qui Oriens ex alto, Luc. 1, 78. & Stella matutina, Apoc. 22, 7. appellatur) demonstret, multò est vero similius dicere, scripta Danielis aliorumq́; Prophetarum, à captivitate Babylonicâ apud Persas fideliter fuisse asservata, & ex eorum lectione Magos de Messiâ edoctos, ubi novam stellam exortam animadverterint: non enim tantùm in populo Judaico, sed apud alias quoq; gentes extitisse biblia & legi solita, argumento est Eunuchus reginæ Candaces. Et de Daniele non dubitamus, quin Magis, in quorum schola educatus est, doctrinam de Messiâ proposuerit, atq; ejus seminaria inter ipsos non vulgaria post se reliquerit. Tria igitur ad conversionem Magorum potuerunt concurrissse, 1. lumen naturæ, 2. supernaturalis Dei ex alto illuminatio, & 3. institutio Danielis traditione patrum ad ipsos derivata, cum adjunctâ Prophetarum lectione, si quis ad eorum manus pervenerint.

XXII. His impulsi Hierosolymam veniunt, quærentes id, quod Judæis putabant non incognitum, ubi natus esset rex ille (ut articulus indicat) Judæorum, tamdiu promissus & exspectatus, quod audiens Herodes tanquam æmulus contremuit, timebat enim ne à nato rege vel ipse regno pelleretur, vel filii successione privarentur. Neqve tantùm rex, sed & tota Hierosolyma cum eo turbata est, aut timore forsitan Romanorum, aut quod metuerent, ne fortè Herodes iratus Judaico regi genus ejus vexaret. Nam quemadmodum certantibus ventis mare concutitur, sic regibus adversantibus sibi, populus regni vexatur, inquit Autor Oper. Imp. in Matth. Nihilo tamen minus sibi ac rebus sui consultius fore putabat rex, exqvirere locum nativitati hujus regis prædefinitum: convocans itaqve concilium qvæstionem proponit Pontificibus ac Scribis, ubi Christus esset nasciturus, qui licet veritatis inimici, pro veritate coguntur legere literas, & Prophetiam de Christo nescientibus interpretari, respondent itaq; locum fore civitatem Bethlehem: voluit Deus, inquit Augustinus, hoc à Judæis inquiri, ut dum ostendunt in quem non credunt, ipsâ suâ demonstratione damnentur.

XXIII. Obiter hic notetur forma Conciliorum in Ecclesia Israëlitica: Herodes utpote magistratus supremus exemplo Ezechiæ & Josuæ convocat Pontifices & Scribas, tanquam capita ministerii Ecclesiastici, iisq́; proponit quæstionem, quam non autoritate pretoriâ, neq; ex suo cerebro, sed ex verbo Dei definiunt, & quidem monstrato ejus loco. Utinam semper in Ecclesia ad exemplum hujus instituta fuissent concilia, minus litigii foret inter nos & Pontificios, soli Papæ omnimodam attribuentes autoritatem & jurisdictionem, majorq́ve qvotidiè veritati fieret accessio.


### On Adoration

ON ADORATION.

XXIV. The council having been concluded, Herod orders the Magi to be called to him, and points out the place to them, upon which news they came to Bethlehem joyful and eager, and entering the house they found the child with Mary his mother, and prostrating themselves they worshipped him. This adoration was not merely political, as his followers maintain with Calvin, but religious at the same time: for it was no longer hidden from the Magi that this child was not only man, but also God by nature; therefore they supplicated him not as man only, but also as God, the author of all good things. Let Lambert Daneau therefore see how he wished to defend himself from this impiety, when he says that the flesh of Christ is not simply the object of true adoration, nay, he pronounces him accursed who adores the flesh of Christ, however much it is considered in union. To us the authority of holy Scripture is more sacred, Phil. 2, 9, and the unanimous consensus of the Fathers: Cyril, and the Ephesian Synod in this manner. If anyone dares to say that the assumed man is to be worshipped together with the Word of God, and does not rather venerate Immanuel with one adoration, and pay one glorification to him, according to the fact that the Word was made flesh, let him be anathema. See similar things in Athanasius (a), Chrysostom (b), Augustine (c), Damascene (d), and others.

XXV. Also according to the custom of their country, the Magi offered gifts, not common ones, but those which were in the highest esteem among them, namely gold, frankincense, and myrrh: for no one could greet the Parthian kings without a gift, says Seneca, Ep. 17. In these, however, the Fathers show a certain mystical interpretation no less piously than elegantly, which the Christian poet Juvencus expressed in this verse:

Thus, they bring gifts, gold, myrrh, to the king, to the man, and to God.

XXVI. These things which we have treated thus far offer us a notable practical meditation. 1. We are taught that God is the God not only of the Jews, but also of the Gentiles: for although He had chosen the Jewish people for His own possession, and had not done so for any other nation, yet He did not simply reject the Gentiles, but always called some from among them to the bosom of the Church, such as Job from the Edomites (a), Jethro from the Midianites (b), Ruth from the Moabites, Rahab from the Canaanites, the Ninevites from the Assyrians. In the New Testament, however, infinite examples of this exist, so that not undeservedly Christ is called the Expectation of the Gentiles, Gen. 49, 10, and the light of the Gentiles, Luke 2, 32.

XVII. 2. By the example of these Magi, let us shake off all sluggishness from our souls, let us rise early and seek the Lord, and just as they could by no means have seen Christ unless they had left their own region far behind, so let us also withdraw from earthly business and cares, and let us run a long journey so that we may be able to see Him: and just as the star was a guide to the Magi to Christ, so let the word of God be a lamp to us, and let it carry a torch before us on the way leading to truth and eternal life: and let us not appear empty-handed in the sight of the Lord, but let us offer Him 1. ourselves in holy obedience, by crucifying our flesh, by cutting off all the desires of the soul with the sword of divine love, and by elevating our intellect and will to heavenly and eternal things, 2. our prayers as sweet-smelling offerings, 3. our resources, by distributing from them to the poor as much as can be done.

XXIIX. 3. The confession of the Jews themselves is an invincible argument for us that the Messiah has long since come. For it is certain that the city of Bethlehem, in which they show from Micah that Christ was to be born, has long since been utterly destroyed and reduced to ashes, and consequently, it is impossible that He can be expected from there any longer. A shortage of paper forbids adding more.

Latin:

DE ADORATIONE.

XXIV. Peracto concilio Magos ad se vocari jubet Herodes, & locum ipsis indicat, qvo nuncio læti ac alacres in Bethlehem venerunt, & intrantes domum invenerunt puerum cum Maria matre ejus, prostratíq; adoraverunt eum. Adoratio hæc non fuit merè politica, ut cum Calvino statuunt ejus asseclæ, sed simul religiosa: nondum enim ampliùs latebat Magos, puerum hunc non hominem solum, sed & naturâ Deum esse, proinde non quasi homini tantùm, sed etiam Deo authori omnium supplicarunt bonorum. Videat itaq; Lambert. Danæus, qvo pacto sese ab hac impietate voluerit vindicare, qvando inqvit, carnem Christi simpliciter non esse objectum veræ adorationis, imò maledictum pronunciat, qui carnem Christi quantamvis in unione consideratam, adoret. Nobis sanctior est sacræ Scripturæ autoritas, Phil. 2, 9. & unanimis Patrum consensus: Cyrillus, Synodusq́; Ephesina in h. m. Siquis audet dicere, assume tum hominem coadorandum Deo verbo, ac non potius unâ adoratione veneratur Immanuelem, unamq́; glorificationem ei dependit, secundum quod verbum caro factum est, anathema sit. Similia vide apud Athanasium (a), Chrysostomum (b), Augustinum (c), Damascenum (d), & alios.

XXV. Ex more qvoq; patriæ suæ obtulerunt Magi munera non vulgaria, sed quæ in summâ apud ipsos erant existimatione, aurũ videlicet, thus & myrrham: nam non poterat quisquam reges Parthos salutare sine munere, inquit Seneca Ep. 17. In his autem mysticam qvandam interpretationem non minus piè quàm eleganter ostendunt Patres, quam Poëta Christianus Juvencus hoc versu expressit:

Thus, aurum, myrrham regią, hominią, Deoą, Dona ferunt.

XXVI. Infignem nobis hæc, qvæ hucusq; tractavimus, præbent meditationem practicam. 1. Docemur, Deum non tantùm Judæorum, sed & gentium esse Deum: quamvis enim in peculium sibi elegerat populum Judaicum, nulli etiam nationi taliter fecerit, simpliciter tamen gentes non rejecerit, sed semper ex iis quosdam ad Ecclesiæ gremium vocavit, utpote ex Edomitis Job (a), ex Medianitis Jethro (b), ex Moabitis Ruth, Cananæis Rahab, Assyriis Ninivitas, In N. T. verò infinita hujus extant exempla, ut ita non immeritò Christus vocetur Expectatio gentium, Gen. 49, 10. & lux gentium, Luc. 2, 32.

XVII. 2. Exemplo horum Magorum omnem ex animis nostris excutiamus torporem, surgamus manè & qværamus Dominum, & quemadmodum illi, nisi procul propriam regionem reliqvissent, neqvaqvam Christum videre potuissent, sic nos qvoq; à terrenis negotiis & curis recedamus, longo itinere curramus, ut ipsum videre possimus: & sicut illis stella dux fuit ad Christum, sic nobis verbum Dei lucerna sit, & facem præferat viæ ad veritatem & vitam ducentis æternam: neq; appareamus in conspectu Domini vacui, sed offeramus ipsi 1. nos ipsos in obseqvia sancta, carnem nostram crucifigendo, omnes animæ cupiditates divini amoris gladio abscindendo, & intellectum ac voluntatem ad res cœlestes & æternas elevando, 2. preces nostras adoramenta svavitatis, 3. facultates nostras, elargiendo ex iis pauperibus, qvantum fieri poterit.

XXIIX. 3. Invictum nobis argumentum est propria Judæorum confessio, Messiam dudum venisse. Certum enim est, civitatem Bethlehem, in qva ex Michea nasciturum Christum ostendunt, jam pridem funditùs eversam & in cineres redactam, ac per conseqvens, impossibile esse, ut inde ampliùs expectari possit. Plura addere chartæ penuria vetat.


## 28 Twenty-eighth Disputation, On the Presentation of Christ, and the Purification of the B. Virgin Mary

Continuation.

Esau being so inflamed with anger against his brother that, with four hundred armed men, he panted for the slaughter of his own brother, Jacob, the Patriarch wished to meet him with three companies, by the gift of the first two of which he might be swayed, and by the compassion of the last, which contained the sweetest Rachel and the honeyed Joseph, he might be moved, refraining himself from violence. God the Greatest, hostile to us on account of the sin of our first parents—for by nature we are indeed children of wrath—seemed to be swayed by gifts before the law and moved by burnt offerings under the law; yet neither of these by itself was sufficiently pleasing, until in the third age of the world after the law, the most blessed Virgin offered the only-begotten Son of the only Parent in the temple. Therefore, just as Esau was not reconciled to his brother until he had embraced his neck in a friendly manner, offering him everything, even giving him his own children: so God would neither have looked upon Abel, nor would He have accepted the labors and victims of the High Priests, unless in the last times all these things had been confirmed by the presentation of the Son. Therefore, the things which the Holy Spirit wished to record concerning her are not trifles, nor does the completion of Mary's childbirth contain anything of dirges or old wives' tales, but things which deserve keen and pious meditation, which, having now discussed those things which preceded this oblation and purification, we shall, with Christ's favor, arrange in such a way that 1. we may desire to be present at the presentation of Christ, 2. we shall weigh the purification of the mother, following the thread of the most holy Luke, and conclude both themes with a practical meditation.

Thesis I.

The Egyptians, who afflicted the people of God—as His firstborn, whom He alone had chosen out of all—with various calamities, lost their own firstborn, perishing by the sword of the angel going about, who killed him who was to sit on the royal throne after Pharaoh, and the firstborn in every house. The Jews, liberated by this reason from misery endured for several centuries, and having also saved their firstborn in this brilliant slaughter, were thereafter bound by the law to consecrate their firstborn to God in memory of so great an event.

II. Christ, the Πρωτότοκος (firstborn) of all creation, who is of the seed of David, Rom. 1:3, wished with wondrous humility to take upon Himself and sustain this condition also, partly so that He might free us from the destroying angel, and partly that He might provide for us an example of obedience.

III. Moreover, the firstborn had to be offered to the Lord: Christ also performed the same, whose presentation the Evangelist, intending to describe, dispatches the matter in two parts, in the former of which the infant is led to the temple, in the latter he is received by Simeon.

IV. Regarding that, mention is made 1. of those bringing him. Concerning Mary the matter is certain, but Joseph was present with her, since he was appointed guardian of Christ, for which reason it is entirely credible that he was also necessary on this journey. 2. Of the place, which is Jerusalem, the metropolis of Judea, chosen as the dwelling place of GOD, 1 Kings 8:13, the city of the great King, Matt. 5:35, built for this purpose, that the tribes might go up there, the tribes of Jah, to celebrate the name of Jehovah, Ps. 122:4.

V. 3. The final cause is added, they brought Christ το παραστησαι τω κυριω, which word Erasmus translates as 'to commend,' in which meaning, however, Beza doubts whether it is read. It is more conveniently rendered by 'to set' [sistere], as also pleases the blessed Chemnitz, book 1, Harmony, p. 230.

VI. Moreover, the foundation of this action was the law promulgated in Exod. 13:2 & 15, which the Evangelist also alleges. Thus, however, the supreme legislator decreed: Sanctify unto me all the firstborn, whatsoever openeth the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and of beast: for it is mine.

VII. Moreover, the firstborn, who are called the beginning of strength and the excellency of power, Gen. 49:3, could not have been sanctified unless the firstborn of all creatures, namely Christ, had sanctified this offering. For he is said to sanctify himself for us, John 17:19, and to give his soul as a λυτρον for many, Matt. 20:28.

VIII. For since every law is a figure of him who was to satisfy the law, this offering and presentation of the firstborn also had to be fulfilled in Christ. It had been signified, however, in Exod. 12:12, that all the firstborn, even the most excellent, ought to be destroyed by the destroying angel, unless some one firstborn, prefigured by the Levitical priesthood, should sanctify himself to the Lord and redeem them. Num. 18:15.

IX. Furthermore, since in addition the other brothers depended upon the firstborn as upon the Lord, and had their fortunes from him, as can easily be deduced from Gen. 27:36, whence he is called πρωτότοκος, the excellency of dignity, Gen. 49:3. Christ, the true firstborn both of Mary and of all creatures, signified by the figure of the Israelites, causes that we his brothers might be made heirs of GOD, and joint-heirs of Christ, Rom. 8. v. 29. whence also the Blessed Chemnitius teaches, l. 5. c. that the title of firstborn is attributed to the Messiah not only typically, but also expressly, Ps. 89. v. 28. Heb. 1, 6.

X. Although therefore Christ is Lord of the law, and conceived by the Holy Spirit, the beloved son of God the Father, he did not need this holy offering, nevertheless from these things which have been set forth, the reasons for this presentation can easily be given and many others added to them: for the present let the following suffice.

XI. Christ was therefore presented to the Lord, 1. because he was the firstborn. But the law commands the firstborn to be consecrated to GOD. 2. because he was of the seed of David, Rom. 1. v. 3. hence because he did not disdain our flesh, and it pleased him to be born from the Fathers, what happened to those who came from the same, he himself also wished to perform. 3. to fulfill the type, to testify that he is that firstborn who was signified by the figures of the O. T., who namely wishes to sanctify himself to the Lord by the victim of his body, that we might be redeemed. 4. because he is the firstborn, to whom the father gave the inheritance of the ends of the earth, Ps. 2. v. 8. he therefore demands here the nations as his inheritance, so that through him the power might be given to us to become children of GOD, John 1. v. 12.

XII. Because also 5. when he was truly the high priest, yet from the tribe of Judah, so that he might thereafter relieve the Levites of that labor, he was about to make the beginning of his priestly office, so that redemption might be made for all, and he might put an end by his own offering, later to be completed on the cross, to the sacrifices performed in the blood of goats.

XIII. But if anyone asserts that this offering was also performed for the sake of his parents, whom he wished to admonish to present their children as a gift of GOD, Ps. 128. to their Lord by his example, he is so far from erring that he rather increases the reasons for the offering of Christ.

XIV. Should anyone here desire those five shekels, of which there is no mention, which were counted for the firstborn priests, and thus estimate that another presentation could be inferred on account of this, concerning which Numbers 18. v. 16., we answer him that since Christ was offered with a certain obligation, namely that he would give his soul as a λύτρον for many.

XV. But the Levites suffered no loss in that, while they remitted those five shekels, which he was abundantly compensating for with the blood of the Son of GOD through his five wounds, nor was it fitting that money be exacted from him who was about to deliver himself up, since the excellence of the latter easily repairs the insignificance of the former.

XVI. Nor is anything obtained against us from Luke 2:27, because they were about to do those things for his sake according to the law, which they had been accustomed to do; for he, being most holy, already performed what belongs to the law, for he was offered and presented that he might sanctify us, intending to compensate for the lack of shekels by a wise plan on the cross.

XVII. But he was received not without a certain remarkable joy, having been expected and desired for so many centuries, just as he was not lacking in an excellent testimony; for the most pious men themselves in the temple, namely Simeon and Anna, provided this, whose dancing and religious embrace acquired for that day, on which the memory of the purification is celebrated, the title of the feast of the reception of Christ, as Emperor Justinian designates it.

XVIII. We shall, however, weigh this reception more deeply. The Evangelist indicates that no light matter is being transacted here by the solemn particle 'Behold' among solemn things. Behold, he says, there was in Jerusalem a man whose name was Simeon, and this man was just and religious, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him, etc.

XIX. Who this Simeon was, whether, as Lyra wishes, someone from the college of priests, because he is said to have blessed the child and his parents, which belonged to the office of the sons of Aaron, Num. 6:23, or the high priest; or whether he was one of the 70 Interpreters, could be doubted.

XX. The first opinion is certainly nothing, for it does not follow: He who blesses is a priest. For in 1 Kings 8:14, King Solomon is said to have blessed, yet it is abundantly clear that he was not a priest. Moreover, what happened here was done by a special impulse of the Holy Spirit, as can be learned from the Gospel history. Indeed, how does it happen that he does not retain the customary formula of blessing in Num. 6:23?

XXI. Those people are mistaken, having neglected the calculation, since Simeon, surnamed the Just, was high priest more than two hundred years before Christ. Wherefore Theophylact's observation is not without weight, from which he gathers from the words of Luke, 'There was a certain man,' that Simeon was not the high priest.

XXII. As regards these, they say that Simeon was one of the college of the seventy-two Interpreters, who, about to interpret the passage of Isaiah ch. 7, 'A virgin shall bear a son,' was doubting, and much about the possibility of that birth he was in doubt. There they say that the Holy Spirit himself promised him that he would not die until he had seen the fulfillment of this prophecy; hence, they narrate that up to the time of the offering, he awaited the saving consolation of Israel with the greatest desire.

XXIII. But that these things are more pleasantly said than easily proven is manifest. We retain the opinion of Petrus Galatinus, who judges that this Simeon was the son of Jonathan (who is the author of the Chaldean paraphrase, which is called the Targum of Jonathan, and who was also a student of Hillel), the teacher of Gamaliel, who was one of the chief members of the Sanhedrin, as is evident from Acts 5:34. The calculation of time makes us believe this, which establishes the Simeon whom Luke describes as the teacher of Gamaliel.

XXIV. But if anyone says that the Rabbis contradict us, it will not deter us, since it is clearer than daylight what confusion is in their books; and if he wishes to continue to doubt regarding this part of this controversy, we ask that he clearly show us the contrary.

XXV. Nor should it seem strange that God wished for testimony to be given about his Son by such an illustrious man, since He had previously become known to the shepherds and the Magi as the more humble among the Jews, from whom the divine Majesty usually makes a beginning, although the eminence of rank does not exclude Simeon from the number of the little ones to whom the inner sanctuaries of the Gospel are revealed.

XXVI. God is certainly no respecter of persons; He does not attend to the shepherd nor the priest; the just man lives by his faith, whether he be from the magnates, or of the middle sort, or from the least. There are many examples which teach that the kingdom of heaven was opened even to men from the Sanhedrin. See John ch. 3:1, ch. 19:39, Acts 5:34, Mark 5:22, Acts 18:17.

XXVII. Our Simeon is described by a triple adjunct: 1. of justice, 2. of religiousness, 3. of hope; by which faith in religion, charity in justice, and hope in expectation are depicted; and so, whether we explain those attributes in this way or another, we estimate that an excellent system of virtues is proposed to us here, not without probability.

XXIIX. If, however, anyone understands the justice of faith to be noted here, by which Simeon apprehends the present Messiah, who is our justice (Jeremiah 23:6, 33:16), he will think the same of him as the most holy Apostle says in Romans 4:3 concerning Abraham, the father of believers, namely that he believ ed it, and that this was imputed to him for righteousness, and thus the power of faith from justification, by this illustrious example, shines forth.

XXIX. He is called 2. εὐλαβὴς, by which some say is understood 'fearful,' others 'religious.' But those inquiring more accurately into the force of the word say that εὐλάβεια denotes a solicitude joined with reverence, lest by acting wrongly we offend him whom we revere, just as Mr. Dr. Winckelmann explains from B. Chemnitius, vol. 4, Giessen disp. 20, thesis 6, and proves from the Greeks.

XXX. And indeed faith is not without fruit, since it strives to offer reverence to him in whom trust is placed, esteeming him most highly, namely, in whom one can be at rest in any storm, whereas he who lacks faith is accustomed to resist and be tossed hither and thither on account of the inconstancy of his mind and the waves of his soul.

XXXI. Hence, fear of this kind is gathered to be necessary for the pious from Rom. 11:20, and is commanded in the same place, as also in Ps. 2:11; from its utility, Phil. 2:12, Heb. 4:1, and it is commended elsewhere throughout.

XXXII. Moreover, our most pious old man is said to have been protected by the helmet of salvation, while he anxiously hoped for the salvation of Israel. O Christ, this is an excellent harmony of virtues, where faith in GOD is given; reverence toward GOD, and hope in GOD. The former teaches the blessedness of the soul, the latter the readiness of the will, the third the desire of the pious appetite. The former looks to GOD as Father, the latter as Lord, the third desires GOD as a Gift.

XXXIII. These virtues were common to Simeon with other pious people; it is peculiar that it is said the Holy Spirit was ἐπ’ αὐτόν, not 'in him' as the Vulgate has it, although if this is retained, it will be a figure of speech: if the former, it teaches the peculiar and extraordinary gifts and holy motions of the Holy Spirit, as appears from Is. 61:1, Num. 11:26, Judg. 11:29, 1 Sam. 10:10, and ch. 19, v. 23.

XXXIV. If anyone asks how the Holy Spirit is in the soul of a just man, since He insinuates Himself through all parts of the world and fills the whole orb with His power and presence, Paulus Granatensis will answer him in his second sermon on the feast of the Purification, p. 159: through gifts and the communion of Himself.

XXXV. But if you do not pour in the leaven of Popery concerning infused righteousness, it is certain that it is truly said from that, that we are called temples of the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. 6, and that such an indwelling is promised to those who holily believe, John 14.

XXXVI. Moreover, the Holy Spirit had promised Simeon that he would live until he had seen the Messiah. Therefore, under His guidance, into the temple he ascends, and with pious devotion receives the desired Shiloh into his arms, filled with such joy that after such great blessedness he did not wish to survive, but humbly and thankfully asks to be dismissed, as a servant of the Lord, thinking himself happy enough that he had seen that which had been granted to Prophets and Patriarchs and Kings in that manner.

XXXVII. While he calls this Christ of his σωτήριον, he esteems him of a greater condition, and we who believe Jesus to be the true God consider ourselves not a little confirmed in our faith from this, which from this attribute also convinces itself of the divinity of Christ against Photinianism.

XXXIIX. While he says this salvation is prepared before the face of all peoples, he looks to Is. ch. 52, v. 10 and 11, v. 10 and 49, 16. While he repeats the light from Is. 42, 16, 49, v. 6, 60, v. 1. Moreover, it is light 1. by reason of doctrine, Ps. 119, v. 105. 2. by reason of application, Luke 1, 79. 3. by reason of renewal, 2 Cor. 3, 18. and finally in the last judgment it will be light, Rev. 22, 5.

XXXIX. But let us dismiss Simeon, let us return to Mary, who is said to have endured the days of purification, again by force of the law, then is narrated to have offered a pair of turtledoves, as the law willed.

XL. That which is held in ancient codices deserves observation, ὅτε ἐπλήσθησαν αἱ ἡμέραι τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ ἀυτῶν, whence some say that what is done here also pertains to Christ, and I remember hearing that this opinion also did not displease the Reverend and Excellent Lord President and my Preceptor in a sermon held on the feast day of this day in the year 1616.

XLI. But it is not to be thought that either Mary or Christ needed this purification: for she conceived by the Holy Spirit, and he is most firmly believed to have been without sin, for who had ever dared to convict him of sin?

XLII. But the blessed virgin did not wish to withdraw herself from the law proposed in Lev. 12, v. 2, lest she should provide a stumbling block: indeed many things are lawful, 1 Cor. 6, 10, but not all things are profitable and edifying. But Christ [did so] for this reason, that he might show the remnants of the foulest Original sin remaining in us at all times, and thus teach that it is not an indifferent matter.

XLIII. No woman in childbirth is indeed impure on account of the birth, but God shows by this law that even works granted to us are not without impurity, and thus are always stained by sin.

XLIV. Those who count only 33 days of purification ought to have added 7 more, as the text advises, for we calculate 40 days.

XLV. The offering of turtledoves was not made for the human race, as some wish, yet it is not without mystery. For turtledoves were offered by Mary on account of humility, who although she was of a poor condition, nevertheless received so much from the Magi that she could have given a lamb for a sacrifice, yet she believed that she was bringing the true Lamb, the Son of God, and so that she might not have begun to submit herself to the Law in vain, she performs what the Law requires elsewhere.

XLVI. Whether this offering was made for her offspring, Augustine inquires in q. 40 in Leviticus, and confirms his affirmative [answer] from a poor distinction, whence we determine that we can dissent from him in this part without prejudice to the authority of so great a man.

XLVII. Whether the purification of Mary was a cleansing from a flow of blood, it does not seem possible to affirm. Polanus indeed, in book 6 of his Syntagma, chapter 17, page 38, column E, argues for the affirmative, but from a false hypothesis, as if the most blessed ever-virgin gave birth with an open womb. We reserve for the conflict those things which could be deduced from that for his side,

XLIIX. But the Roman Pontiff has abused the memory of this holy work worst of all, who defiles the day of purification with an idolatrous bilge-water, and stains it contrary to the institution and mind of the author. For Justinian did not intend for wax candles to be blessed on this day, which are placed in the hands of the dying, as if they were to pass into eternal life by this light, while they are addressed: Take the light into your hand, and walk forth into the Fatherland.

XLIX. Nor is faith to be placed here in Durandus, who desires that Mary should be invoked on this day and honored with candles, so that just as Februa, the mother of Mars, was once celebrated with burning torches, so that she might obtain happiness for the Romans in war from her son, so Mary might intercede for us with Christ. For although we praise the changing of ethnic superstitions into true religion, yet the transition ought not to be made into a worse idolatry, which holy Scripture detests. But this is said to be the invention of Sergius, who was called 'mouth of a pig,' who indeed dug up this dung of superstition with a swinish snout, of which piety toward God and the purity of religion forbid us to be participants.

L. But you, my soul, in the Father our Lord, in Christ presented and receiving us, ponder the mercy, in Jesus the obedience, in Simeon the alatruth unto death, in the Virgin humility. Let us celebrate the former with a hymn, we shall remember the latter while we exist, with Simeon as our teacher we rejoice, we shall prepare ourselves for the humility of a pure heart. May Simeon and Mary be in eternal blessing, to the Father and the Son eternal praise and thanksgiving, which together with the Holy Spirit, O most holy Trinity, receive from us.

Latin:

Continuatio.

ESau fratri irâ ita accenso, ut qvadringentis armatis, internecionem Germani sui, Jacobi anhelaret, Patriarcha tribus occurrere voluit turmis, qvarum duarum priorum dono flecteretur, ultimæ verò, qvæ suavissimam Rachelem, mellitumqs Josephum contineret, commiseratione, â violentiâ sese abstinens, commoveretur. DEus Maximus, ob protoplastarum peccatum nobis infensus, naturâ qvippe iræ filii sumus, muneribus videbatur ante legem flecti & in lege per holocausta moveri, neutrum tamen hotum per se satis arridebat, donec tertiâ mundi ætate post legem, beatissima virgo, unigenitum filium unici parentis, in templo offerret. Ut igitur Esavus non reconciliabatur fratri, usq; dum amicè ejus collum invasisset, omnia ei offerentis, etiam liberos suos donantis: ita DEus nec Abelem respexiffet, nec Pontificum labores victimasq; acceptasset, nisi ultimis temporibus hæc omnia, præsentatione filii confirmata fuissent. Non itaq; crepundia sunt, qvæ Spiritus sanctus de ea annotare voluit, neq; puerperii Mariæ complementum, næniarum qvid habet aut anile, sed qvæ meditationem merentur acrem & piam, qvam disputatis jam eis, qvæ antecesserant oblationem & purificationem hanc, Christo favente ita disponemus, ut 1. præsentationi Christi interesse cupiamus, 2. purificationem matris pensitaturi, filum sanctissimi Lucæ seqventes, meditatiunculâ practicâ, utrumq; thema conclusuri.

Thesis I.

AEgyptiis, qvi populum Dei tanqvam primogenitum ejus, qvem solum ex omnibus elegerat, variis afficiebant calamitatibus, suos primogenitos amisere, gladio circumeuntis angeli pereunte, qvi post Pharaonem sedere debebat in throno regio, & in qvalibet domo primùm edito, necato. Judæi hac ratione liberati â miseriâ aliqvot secula exantlatâ, servatis qvoq; primogenitis in hac luculentâ clade, in rei tantæ memoriam, primogenitos pòst suos ex lege DEo consecrare tenebantur.

II. Πρωτότοκος omnium creaturarum Christus, qvi est ex semine Davidis, Rom. 1. v. 3. hanc conditionem qvoq;, partim ut ab angelo interfectore nos liberaret, partim verò exemplum obedientiæ nobis præberet, suscipere in se & sustinere mirandâ humilitate voluit.

III. Offerri autem Domino primogeniti debebant: Christus qvoqve idem præstitit, cujus præsentationem Evangelista descripturus, duobus membris rem expedit, qvorum priori infans ad templum deducitur, posteriori à Simeone excipitur.

IV. Illud attinet, mentio fit 1. adducentium. De Maria res certa est, at cum ea Josephus aderat, qvippe tutor Christi constitutus, qvo etiam in itinere hoc opus fuisse omninò credibile est. 2. Loci, qvi est Hierosolyma, metropolis Judææ, electa in habitaculum DEI, 1. Reg. 8. v. 13. civitas Regis magni, Matth. 5. v. 35. ad hoc ædificata, ut illuc ascenderent tribus, tribus Jah,ad celebrandum nomen Jehoval, Ps. 122, v. 4.

V. 3. Adjicitur causa finalis, adduxerunt Christum to παραστησαι τω κυριω, qvod verbum Erasmus vertit commendare, in qvo tamen significatu an legatur, Beza ambigit. Convenientius per to sistere redditur, prout etiam B. Chemnitio placet, l. 1. harm. p. 230.

VI. Hujus actionis autem fundamentum lex erat Exod. 13. v. 2. & 15. promulgata, qvam etiam Evangelista allegat. Ita autem decrevit supremus legislator: Sanctifica mihi omne primogenitum, quicquid aperit vulvam in filiis Israël,tam in hominibus quàm in jumentis, meum enim est.

VII. Primogeniti autem, qvi roboris principium & fortitudo, Gen. 49. v. 3. dicuntur, sanctificari non potuissent, nisi omnium creaturarum primogenitus, Christus sc. hanc oblationem sanctificasset. Is enim sanctificare se pro nobis dicitur, Joh.16,19. & λυτρον dare pro multis animam suam, Matth. 20. v. 28.

VIII. Omnis enim lex cum figura sit illius, qvi legi satisfacturus erat, hæc qvoqve primogenitorum oblatio & præsentatio in Christo complenda erat. Significatum autem fuerat Exod. 12. v. 12. omnes primogenitos, etiam præstantissimos, ab angelo vastatore debere interimi, nisi unus aliqvis primogenitus figuratus per sacerdotium Leviticum, se Domino sanctificet, eosq; redimeret. Num. 18. v. 15.

IX. Cæterùm cùm insuper à primogenito cæteri fratres tanqvam Domino pendebant, fortunas suas ab eo habebant, ut ex Gen. 27, 36. deduci facilè potest, unde πρωτότοκος, excellentia dignitatis, Gen. 49. v. 3. dicitur. Christus, verus & Mariæ & creaturarum primogenitus, per figuram Israëlitarum significatus, facit, ut nos fratres ejus, hæredes efficeremur DEI, & cohæredes Christi, Rom, 8. v. 29. unde qvoq; B. Chemnitius docet, l. 5. c. qvòd primogeniti appellatio Mesfiæ non typicè modò, sed etiam expressè tribuatur, Pf. 89. v. 28. Ebr. 1, 6.

X. Licet ergò Christus Dominus legis, & Spiritu sancto conceptus, Patris DEI dilect9 filius, hac sanctificâ oblatione nõ indigebat, nihilominùs ex his, qvę posita sunt, rationes hujus præsentationis facilè reddi possunt & illis aliæ plures addi: impræsentiarũ seqventes sufficiãt.

XI. Sistebatur itaq; Christus Domino, 1. qvia primogenitus. Lex autem jubet primogenitum DEO consecrare. 2. qvia ex semine Davidis, Rom. 1. v. 3. hinc qvia non dedignatus est carnem nostram, & ipsi placuerit ex Patribus nasci, qvod illis, qvi ex iisdem provenirent, obtigit, ipse qvoq; præstare voluit. 3. ut typum compleret, contestaturus se esse illum primogenitum, qvi figuris V. T. significabatur, qvi scil. se velit sanctificare Domino victima corporis sui, ut nos redimamur. 4. qvia ille est primogenitus, cui pater dedit hæreditatem terminos terræ, Pf. 2. v. 8. postulat ergò hîc gentes hæreditatem suam, ut propter illum nobis detur potestas filios DEI fieri, Joan. 1. v. 12.

XII. Qvia & 5. cùm erat sacerdos verè summus, ex tribu tamen Judæ, qvò Levitas labore posthac illo sublevaret, sacerdotalis officii sui initium facturus erat, ut fieret redemptio pro omnibus, finemq; oblatione suâ, pòst in cruce complendâ, sacrificiorum in sangvine hircorum præstitorum faceret.

XIII. Qvod si qvis 6. parentum qvoq; causâ hanc oblationem peractam fuisse, asserat, qvos monere voluerit, ut suos liberos donum DEI, Pf. 128. Domino suo exemplo sisterent, tantum abest ut aberret, ut potiùs rationes oblationis Christi adaugeat.

XIV. Desideret hîc qvispiam, qvinq; illos siclos, qvorum mentio non sit, qvi pro primogenitis sacerdotibus numerabantur, & ita ob hoc aliam præsentationem inferri posse æstimet, de qvibus Numer. 18. v. 16. illi respondemus, qvod cùm certâ obligatione Christus oblatus sit, scil. daturum animam suam λύτρον pro multis.

XV. Nullam autem passi sunt Levitæ jacturam in eo, dum remittebant qvinq; illi siclos, qvi sangvine Filii DEI per vulnera qvinq; largiter hoc compensabat, neq; conveniens erat ab eo exigi pecuniam, qvi semetipsum traditurus esset, cum hujus præstantia illius tenuitatem facilè resarciat.

XVI. Neq; ex cap. 2. Luc. v. 27. contra nos aliqvid obtinetur, qvod ejus causa facturi essent ea ex lege, qvæ consveverant, qvippe qvæ legis sunt, jam præstitit, oblatus enim est & sanctissimus, ut nos sanctificaret præsentatus, defectum siclorum, sapienti consilio in cruce remuneraturus.

XVII. Verùm non sine insigni qvodam gaudio excipiebatur, jam per tot secula expectatus & desideratus, qvemadmodum neq; egregio testimonio destituebatur, hoc enim piissimi ipsi in templo homines Simeon sicilicet & Hanna præbebant, qvorum illius tripudium & religiosus amplexus, festo illi diei, qvo purificationis memoria celebratur, titulum festi exceptionis Christi, sic Justiniano Imperatore indigitante, acqvifivit.

XVIII. Altiùs autem hanc exceptionem pensitabimus. Rem levem hic non peragi Evangelista solenni in solennibus particulâ Ecce indicat. Ecce, inqvit, erat in Hierusalem, cui nomen Simeon, eratq́; homo iste justus ac religiosus, expectans consolationem Israël, & Spiritus sanctus erat super eum, &c.

XIX. Qvis hic Simeon fuerit, an, ut Lira vult, aliqvis ex collegio sacerdotum, qvia benedixisse puero & parentibus dicitur, qvod ad officium filiorum Aaron pertinebat, Num. 6, 23. aut sacerdos summus; an aliqvis ex 70. Interpp. dubitari posset.

XX. Prima sanè sententia nulla est, qvippe non seqvitur: Qvi benedicit, ille sacerdos est. Nam 1. Reg. 8. v. 14. Salomon Rex benedixifse dicitur, qvem tamen Sacerdotem non fuisse abundè constat. Insusuper qvod hic contigit, peculiari Spiritus sancti impulsu factum est, prout ex historiâ Evangelicâ doceri potest. Imò qvî fit, qvòd usitatam formulam benedictionis Num. 6, v. 23. non retineat?

XXI. Isti supputatione neglectâ falsi sunt, cùm Simeon cognomento Justus, summus Pontifex ante Christum annis ampliùs ducentis fuerit. Qvare Theophylacti observatio momento non caret, qvam ex Lucæ verbis, Erat homo qvidam, summum Pontificem Simeonem non fuisse colligit.

XXII. Hos qvod attinet, ferunt, fuisse Simeonem unum ex collegio septuaginta duorum Interpretum, qvi Esaiæ locum c. 7. Virgo pariet filium, interpretaturus, dubitabat, multumq́ve de possibilitate illius partûs ambigebat. Ibi dicunt Spiritum sanctum ipsum pollicitum esse, se moriturum non esse, nisi priùs hujus prophetiæ complementum viderit, hinc usqve ad tempus oblationis maximo cum desiderio, salutarem consolationem Israëlis expectasse, narrant.

XXIII. Verùm svaviùs hæc dici, probari non ita facilè posse, in propatulo est. Nos Petri Galatini sententiam retinemus,qvi censet, hunc Simeonem fuisse filium Jonathæ (qvi author Chaldaicæ paraphraseos, qvæ Thargum Jonathæ dicitur,qvi & auditor Hillelis)præceptorem Gamalielis qvi unus fuit ex præcipuis Synedrii,ut ex Act.5. v.34. constat. Supputatio temporis hoc ut credamus facit,qvæ Simeonem, qvem Lucas describit præceptorem Gamalielis constituit.

XXIV. Qvòd si qvis Rabinos nobis contradicere dicat, non absterrebit nos, qvippe qvanta confusio in eorum libris sit, luce diurnâ clarius est, & si de parte hac controversiæ hujus porrò ambigere velit, ut evidenter nobis contrarium ostendat,qvæsumus.

XXV. Nec mirum videri debet,voluisse Deum à tam illustri viro, de filio suo testimonium dici, cùm Pastoribus & Magis ante innotuerit tanqvam tenuioribus apud Judæos, à qvibus plerumq; initium sapiens Majestas divina facit, qvamvis ordinis eminentia non excludat Simeonem à numero parvulorum, qvibus Evangelii adyta reseruntur.

XXVI. Deus certè προσωπολήπτης non est, non attendit pastorem neq; sacerdotem, justus suâ fide vivit, sive ex magnatibus, sive medioxumus sive minimis sit. Exempla plura sunt, qvæ docent etiam ex synedrio viris regnum cœlorum fuisse reclusum. Videatur Joan. c.3,1. c.19,39. Act.5,34. Marc.5,v.22. Actor.18,17.

XXVII. Describitur autem à triplici adjuncto Simeon noster: 1. justitiæ, 2. religiositatis, 3. spei; qvibus fides in religione,charitas in justitia, spes in expectatione depingitur,adeoq; sive sic sive aliter attributa illa explicemus, non sine probabilitate,virtutum egregium systema hic nobis proponi, æstimamus.

XXIIX. Si qvis autem 1. justitiam fidei hîc intelligat notari, qvâ apprehenditSimeonMessiam præsentem,qvi nostra justitia est,Jerem. 23. v. 6. c. 33, 16. idem de eo sentiet, qvod sanctissimus Apostolus Rom. 4. v.3. dicit de patre credentium Abrahamo, nempe qvòd crediderit, & hoc imputatum ei fuisse ad justitiam, adeoq; fidei vis à justificatione, illustri hoc exemplo elucescat.

XXIX. Dicitur 2. εὐλαβὴς, quo alii timoratum, alii religiosum intelligi dicunt. Verùm accuratiùs inqvirentes in vim vocis dicunt, εὐλάβειαν notare sollicitudinem timori conjunctam cum reverentiâ, ne pravè agendo, illum, qvem reveremur, offendamus, qvemadmodum ex B: Chemnitio Dn. D. Winckelmannus t. 4. Giess. disp. 20. th. 6. explicat & ex Græcis probat.

XXX. Et sanè fides sine fructu non est, qvippe reverentiam annititur præstare illi, in qvo fiducia posita est, eum maximi æstimans, scilicet in qvo qvieta esse in qvovis turbine esse potest, cum, qvi fide caret, ob inconstantiam mentis & fluctus animi refragari, & hinc inde agitari soleat.

XXXI. Hinc timor ejusmodi piis necessarius colligitur ex Rom. 11, 20. & ibidem imperatur, ut & Ps. 2, 11: ab utilitate, Phil. 2, 12. Ebr. 4, 1. & passim alibi commendatur.

XXXII. Galeâ insuper salutis pientissimus noster senex communitus dicitur fuisse, dum anxilè salutare Israëlissperabat. Egregia me Christe hæc virtutum harmonia est, ubi datur fides in DEUM; reverentia erga DEUM & spes de DEO. Docet illa animi beatitatem, ista voluntatis promptitudinem, hæc pii appetitus desiderium. Illa DEUM ut Patrem, ista ut Dominum respicit, hæc ut Donum DEUM appetit.

XXXIII. Hæ virtutes Simeoni cum aliis piis fuêre communes, peculiare est, qvod dicitur, Spiritum sanctum, fuisse ἐπ’ αὐτόν, non ut Vulgata in illo, qvamvis si hoc retineatur, figura dictionis erit: si illud, peculiaria & extraordinaria dona & motus sanctos sancti Spiritus docet, ut ex Es. 61, 1. Num. 11, 26. Jud. 11, 29. 1. Sam. 10, 10. & c. 19. v. 23. apparet.

XXXIV. Si qvis qværat, qvomodo Spiritus sanctus in animâ justi sit, cùm seipsum per omnes partes mundi insinuet, & virtute præsentiâq; suâ orbem totum repleat, illi respondebit Paulus Granatensis cont. 2. de festo purific. p. 159. per dona & communione sui.

XXXV. Qvòd si fermentú Pontificií de infusâ justitiâ non infundas, verè dici illud inde, qvòd templa Spiritus S. 1. Cor. 6. dicamur, constat, & Joh. 14. ejusmodi inhabitatio sanctè credentibus promittatur.

XXXVI. Promiserat autem Spiritus sanctus Simeoni, se tàm diu victurum, usq; dum viderit Messiam. Hujus ergò ductu in templum ascendit, & piâ devotione desideratum Siloh in ulnas suas accipit, tanto gaudio repletus, ut post tantam beatitudinem superesse noluerit, sed dimitti, ut servus Domini, humiliter & gratè petat, satis felicem se esse ratus, quòd illud viderit, quod Prophetis & Patriarchis & Regibus eo modo concessum non fuerat.

XXXVII. Christum hunc suum dum σωτήριον vocat, majoris eum conditionis æstimat, & nos qui Jesum verum Deum credimus, non parum hinc in fide nostra confirmari arbitramur, quæ ex hoc quoq; attributo divinitatem Christi sibi contra Photinifmum persuadet.

XXXIIX. Hoc salutare dum paratum ait, ante faciem populorum omnium, respicit ad Es. c. 52. v. 10. & 11, v. 10. & 49. 16. Dum lumen, ex Esa. 42, 16. 49. v. 6, 60. v. 1. repetit. Est autem lumen 1. ratione doctrinæ, Pf. 119. v. 105. 2. ratione applicationis, Luc. 1, 79. 3. ratione renovationis, 2. Cor. 3, 18. & tandem in extremo judicio lumen erit, Apoc. 22, 5.

XXXIX. Sed dimittamusSimeonem, revertamur ad Mariam, quæ purificationis dies, iterum vi legis, sustinuisse dicitur, deinde obtulifse par turturum, lege ita volente, narratur.

XL. Observationem meretur illud, quod in antiqvis codd. habeatur, ὅτε ἐπλήσθησαν αἱ ἡμέραι τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ ἀυτῶν, unde quæ hîc fiunt, etiam Christum attinere nonnulli dicunt, & eam quoq; sententiam Reverendo & Excell. Dn. Præsidi & Præceptori meo non displicere in concione festi huj⁹ diei anno 1616. habita, me audire memini.

XLI. Non autem putandum, vel Mariam vel Christum hac purificatione eguisse: illa enim à Spiritu sancto concipit, hic sine peccato fuisse creditur firmissimè, qvis enim ipsum de peccato arguere unqvam ausus erat?

XLII. Noluit autem beata virgo legi Lev. 12. v. 2. propositæ se subducere, ne offendiculum præberet: multa qvidem licent 1. Cor. 6, 10. non autem omnia prosunt & ædificant. Christus autem iccircò, ut fœdissimi peccati Originalis purgandi omni tempore in nobis reliqvias ostenderet, adeoq; non esse rem indifferentem doceret.

XLIII. Nulla qvidem puerpera propter partum impura est, sed Deus lege hac oftendit, etiam concessa nobis opera impuritate non carere, adeoq; peccato semper commaculari.

XLIV. Qvi 33. tantùm dies purificationis numerant, addere debebant adhuc 7. textu ita monente, nos enim 40. dies supputamus.

XLV. Oblatio turturum non facta est pro genere humano, ut quidam volunt, interim mysterio non caret. Turtures enim offerebantur à Maria ob humilitatem, quæ paupertinæ conditionis licet fuerit, tamen à Magis tantum accepit, ut agnum pro hostia daret, quæ tamen verum agnum Filium Dei se adducere credidit, & ne frustrà incepisset legi se submittere, quod Lex alibi exigit, præstat.

XLVI. An autem oblatio hæc facta fuerit pro sobole, Augustinus disquirit q. 40. in Levit. & affirmativam suam ex malâ distinctione confirmat, unde hâc in parte ab eo dissentire nos posse salvâ tanti viri authoritate statuimus.

XLVII. An autem purificatio Mariæ purgatio à profluvio sangvinis fuerit, non videtur posse affirmari. Polanus qvidem l. 6. synt. c. 17. f. 38. col. E. pro affirmante pugnat, at ex falsâ hypothesi, qvasi aperto utero pepererit semper-virgo beatissima. Nos quæ pro eo inde deduci possent, conflictui reservamus,

XLIIX. Omnium pessimè autem abusus est. memoriâ hujus sancti operis, Pontifex Romanus, qui idololatricâ sentinâ purificationis diem deturpat, & contra institutum & mentem autoris commaculat. Non enim Justinianus voluit cereas candelas lustrari hoc die, quæ moriturorum manibus inseruntur, quasi lûce hac transituri essent in æternam vitam, dum ipsos affantur: Nim das Liecht in deine Hand/ Und wandel hin ins Vater-Land.

XLIX. Durando neq; hîc fides habenda, qui cupit hâc die Mariam invocandam esse, & candelis honorandam, ut quemadmodum Februa olim Martis mater ardentib' celebrabatur facib', qvo à filio Romanis impetraret in bello felicitatem, ita Maria apud Christum pro nobis intercederet. Qvamvis enim ethnicas superstitiones laudemus mutari in veram religionem, non tamen in deteriorem idololatriam, quam sacra Scriptura detestatur, transitus fieri debet. Verùm Sergii, qui os porci dicebatur, hoc inventum dicitur esse, qui sanè suillo rostro hoc superstitionis stercus effodit, cujus nos participes esse pietas in Deum & religionis puritas vetat.

L. Tu verò anima mea in Patre Domino nostro, in Christo nos præsentato accipiente, perpende misericordiam, in Jesu lo obedientiam, in Simeone alaeritatem ad mortem, in Virgine humilitatem. Illam hymno celebremus, istius recordabimur dum erimus, Simeone præceptore gaudemus, ad puri cordis humilitatem nos præparabimus. Sit Simeon & Maria in æterna benedictione, Patri & Filio æterna laus & gratiarum actio, quam unà cum Spiritu sancto, ô sanctissima Trinitas, à nobis accipe.


## 29 Twenty-ninth Disputation, On the Flight of Christ into Egypt

Continuation.

We saw in the previous disputation the Majesty of Christ shining forth from the solemn adoration of the Magi: in the present one we shall contemplate his supreme humility from the tyrannical persecution of Herod. For behold, the author and giver of light had scarcely looked upon the light of the world, and he is oppressed by feigned goodwill; he had scarcely come into his own, and the Lord of the lands is forced to depart from the land. O thing to be wondered at and stupendous! (a) If the refuge flees, if virtue fears, if the protection migrates: what life? what hope? what security? what defense? Hope for the best! Nor does salvation flee in the flight: nor is the Savior weak because of the flight. For our little boy does not flee the man of truculent slaughter out of fear, but willingly: he flees (b) not by human dread, but by divine dispensation, not by necessity, but by power: (c) so that he might yield to the time, not to Herod. That this may be more clearly revealed, we undertake to consider the FLIGHT of the Savior into Egypt: of which 1. We shall weigh the circumstances. 2. We shall submit controversial questions, if any occur. 3. We shall annex a practical meditation. Do thou, O Christ, guide my mind and my pen!

Thesis I.

The Evangelist, St. Matthew, in verses 13, 14, and 15 of chapter 2 of his Gospel history, notes various circumstances of the flight of our Savior Jesus Christ into Egypt, which we reduce to two principal classes, if we call some circumstances of persons, others of things.

II. The persons are named for us in the Gospel text as threefold: I. Angel s persuading flight: ἰδὲ ἄγγελος κυρίου, where it ought to be observed, 1. The description of the angelic person: Angel of the Lord: for the first name describes the office, the latter the dignity of the legate. Who this Angel was? is asked by some. We pronounce nothing certain about uncertain things, yet it is probable, as Origen opines, that it was Gabriel, who was the faithful interpreter of the mysteries of Christ. 2. The angelic apparition to be observed: φαίνεται κατ᾽ ὄναρ. The Angel does not appear to Joseph while awake, as (a) to Manoah & (b) to Zacharias, but while sleeping, which we ascribe not to the perfection of Joseph, as (c) Eccius does; but to the free dispensation of God. 3. The angelic command: ἐγερθεὶς, & παράλαβε &c. The Angel does not leave the flight to the judgment of Joseph, but commands severely: Arise, he says, take, &c.

III. It may be asked here: Does GOD still deal with us through dreams today? The Legends and practice of the Papists affirm this simply, who have fabricated articles of faith from dreams, and have ineptly founded their absurdities concerning purgatory and indulgences upon nocturnal apparitions, as can be seen in B. (d) Chemnitz. We distinguish between matters of life and matters of faith: we concede with Holy Scripture that men are warned through dreams about the former, not about the latter. And we warn: The revealed word is always to be looked to: if any dream leads us away from it, it is diabolical; if it leads us to it, it is divine.

II. It is asked: Whether, just as in the Old and the beginning of the New Testament, the address of Angels is to be expected and boasted of today? Some Fanatics do this. We answer 1. Although we cannot prescribe any mode of revelation to GOD, we know nevertheless from (a) Scripture: That the varied mode of revelation ceased after the Canon of the New Testament was completed. Whence 2. we are bound to Scripture alone, Luke 16. v. 29. John 5. v. 39. which were written for our salvation: John 20. v. 31. Rom. 15. v. 4. and indeed perfectly, because it can make men perfect, 2. Tim. 3. v. 16. 17. And 3. the extraordinary mission of spirits is denied to men in express words, Luke 16. v. 31. Because 4. this matter is joined with the greatest inconvenience: Satan can transfigure himself into an Angel of light, 2. Cor. 11. v. 14. and in the very act he does transfigure himself, when he sells diabolical revelations as divine; how often this has happened, the Papistic legends, the lives of the fathers, and daily experience testify.

V. II. The person receiving the command: Joseph, of the Davidic lineage originating: of this are hinted 1. Faith, and 2. Promptness. He did not doubt or drowse for long, but assenting to the angelic command, he hastened his pious flight; which is clear 1. From the assumption: 2. From the time of the assumption, which was carried out on the same night that he received the command.

VI. III. The person escaping by flight: That child is a newborn; that sweet Immanuel. That Lord flees, from whose sight (a) the earth flees: at whose threats (b) the waters and (c) the sea are in tumult. Scripture names the child (d) Christ, so that we may recognize him of whom it was said: A CHILD is born to us. However, the tender and divine child is not given to flight alone, but a foster-father and a virgin mother are joined to him: which mother is not called a wife, because (e) with the birth completed, suspicion was also dispelled.

VII. Human reason asks here: Why did God wish his Son to flee from those enemies whom he could have put to flight in countless ways? To which it is answered: 1. That in this act the mystery of divine dispensation and the humble ministry of Christ must be considered. 2. The manner of God's helping, who, where an ordinary means of salvation remains, does not seize upon an extraordinary one. 3. The empire or kingdom of Christ, which he had shown by his holy flight not to be of this world. These things concerning the persons.

VIII. The second class of circumstances contains the circumstances of 1. The time when the flight was undertaken. 2. The place where it was carried out. 3. The causes for which the flight was seized upon.

IX. The time of Christ's flight is either of its beginning or of its duration. And that of the beginning is either remote or near. Although the remote time is not expressly named in Scripture, it is nevertheless gathered not obscurely from some circumstances. (a) Epiphanius thinks the flight should be relegated to the second year from the birth of Christ, whom (b) Tostatus, Bishop of Avila, and (c) Piscator of Herborn follow. But those seem to us to think more correctly who believe that a few weeks intervened between the birth and the flight of Christ. For 1. it is certain that when Christ was born, the Magi arrived immediately after Christ was born, Matt. 2:1. 2. It is certain that when they had departed, the Angel appeared, v. 13. From where, therefore, will they compile a two-year period?

X. Nor, however, do we maintain that the Angel appeared on the same night after the departure of the Magi, but the history of the purification performed according to the law must entirely be inserted, Luke 2:22, 39, upon the completion of which the Angel of the Lord appeared and commanded the flight.

XI. The near time is called Night. There are those who think that many days intervened between the Angel's command and Joseph's obedience: Anselm, Euthymius, (d) Tostatus, (e) Salmeron, (f) Piscator of Herborn. But we, adhering to the text, more correctly maintain: that Joseph, on the same night that he received the divine command, took the child with his mother and fled into Egypt. 1. The express letter testifies to this. 2. The present danger urged it. For just as before the arrival of the Magi the citizens of Jerusalem were completely ignorant of Christ's birth; so before the day of purification, nothing certain was known about Christ, in particular, who had only just become known from the confession of Simeon and Anna the Prophetess, Luke 2. v. 27. seq., even to Herod himself, who gathered from that, that he had been deluded by the Magi, whence he intended the slaughter of the child. There was need, therefore, for Joseph to flee that same night, if he intended to escape the fury of Herod. Those who seem to embrace this opinion of ours are (a) Maldonatus, (b) Barradius, and others.

XII. The indefinite time of duration is expressed by these words, ἴσθι ἐκεῖ ἕως ἂν εἴπω σοί. and v. 15. καὶ ἦν ἕως τῆς τελευτῆς Ἡρώδε: these latter words indeed determine the former, yet they do not indicate a certain time. Those who labor to force an infinite time into a definite one are not of one opinion. There are those who define it as seven years, like the author of the Scholastic History; and those who follow him: There are those who posit three years, like (c) Nicephorus: The truth seems to determine one year, and if anything exceeds a year. For, in the year that Herod the Ascalonite died, in that year Joseph with his family was recalled from Egypt; as is evident from the Angel's promise: But Herod died in A.M. 3949, around Passover. Therefore. But Christ had fled into Egypt in A.M. 3948, as noted by the most famous Chronologist, Seth Calvisius, p. 463 of his Isagoge.

XIII. From what was said in th. 11, the circumstance of Place can be gathered. In the place, one must consider 1. the starting point. 2. the point through which. 3. the destination.

XIV. In defining the starting point, authors vary much. Some establish Nazareth, like Theophylact and Anselm in this place, as also (a) Piscator of Herborn: others Bethlehem, like (b) Epiphanius, (c) B. Hunnius, (d) Flaccius: others Jerusalem, (e) Magdeburg Centuries: others an indeterminate intermediate place between Jerusalem and Nazareth, like Palbartus in Pomerium. We do not defend the first opinion, the remaining which three we think can be reconciled from what was said in th. 10 & 11. For they do not err, who think that Joseph spent the night after the act of purification either in Jerusalem, or in Bethlehem, or in some nearby intermediate place, and received the angelic command.

XV. The limit through which is established by most that desert through which the children of Israel entered Palestine. Ludolph of Saxony reports (f) that Christ was seized in the desert by that thief who was suspended on his right at the time of the passion. But this narrative seems more like a fable than history, and not a little contrary to the angelic promise concerning a safe arrival in Egypt.

XVI. The limit to which is Egypt, and it is noted in v. 13, where one must observe the place, both general (Egypt) expressed in the text, and special (a) called Hermopolis or Heliopolis by authors. A question arises here: Did Christ perform miracles in Egypt? (b) Sozomen, Nicephorus, and from them (c) Barradius, and (d) Baronius affirm it. We think those miracles are figments of idle men, which conflict with the statement of the Evangelist John c. 2. v. 11. 2. With purer (e) antiquity: and with sounder adversaries, for whom (f) Maldonatus responds, who counts those miracles among Mohammedan fables.

XVII. There follows the circumstance of the causes: which are either principal, and noted in the text, or less principal, and devised by pious doctors.

XVIII. The principal causes of Christ's flight are two. 1. Herod's malicious intent: μέλλει Ἡρώδης ζητεῖν τὸ παιδίον, τῦ ἀπολέσαι αὐτό. GOD, who is all-knowing, had seen and foreseen Herod's malicious mind and the action which he was meditating, which was tyrannical; therefore he warns Joseph to withdraw the child from this growing evil without delay. It is asked here: Does GOD know future contingent evils? The Photinians deny and utterly deny this, as can be seen in the Theological lectures of Socinus c. 8. 9. 10. 11. from page 24 up to 40. We oppose 1. The present example concerning the infanticide, which certainly was future with respect to men, and evil with respect to GOD and men, indeed most evil, because it was highly contrary to divine precept and love of neighbor. 2. The sayings which proclaim that GOD searches and knows the hearts, thoughts, and reins of men Ps. 7. v. 10. Ps. 94. v. 11. 1. Paral. 28. v. 9. and indeed from afar, Ps. 139. v. 2. that is, when they are not yet in act, v. 4. but who is so absurd as to call all thoughts of men good: or so impious, that he would openly contradict Scripture, which in Gen. 6. v. 5. & 8. v. 21. pronounces all thoughts evil. 3. Specifically the passage, Isa. 41. v. 22. where by way of antithesis JEHOVA is said to foretell הַבָּאוֹת which are things to come. 4. To which pertain all those things, which partly Christ himself, partly his Apostles have foretold concerning the miserable state of the Church of our time, to which (alas!) the event responds too certainly.

XIX. It is further asked: Is it permitted for Christians, and specifically for teachers of the Church, to flee impending dangers? We affirm that it is permitted, if flight does not hinder or wound the glory of GOD, the safety of one's neighbor, and one's own conscience. But how or in what way this is or is not done, that is to be judged from the danger itself and other circumstances. Our affirmation is confirmed by the counsel of Christ, Matt. 10. v. 23. and the example in Matt. 2. v. 14. John 8. v. 59. Let them do, therefore, let the servants of Christ, the ministers of his word and Sacrament, do what he commanded or permitted, indeed what he himself did (see (a) Augustine, For he left us this example, that the servant should not think it unworthy to flee, when the Lord flees, says (b) Chrysologus. I pass over the law of nature, which bids men to withdraw themselves from dangers, even if they are not uncertain of divine help: for as long as ordinary means remain, extraordinary ones are not to be expected: For you shall not tempt the Lord your GOD. I pass over other examples both of the Apostles, Paul Acts 9. v. 30. Peter Acts 12. v. 17. and of the doctors of the Church, (c) Polycarp, (d) Athanasius, (e) Chrysostom, who all cleared themselves by the example of Christ.

XX. The second principal cause is the Prophetic prediction: therefore he fled and was recalled from Egypt, that what had been said through Prophecy might be fulfilled: Out of Egypt I have called my son.

XXI. Two things can be asked here. 1. Do predictions of things bring about necessity? The Calvinist Stoics affirm this. (f) Beza says: that GOD knows nothing will happen, which he has not decreed will happen. (g) Hyperius says: that with respect to GOD all things happen by absolute necessity: and Bucanus: What men or Angels do, they do necessarily, since GOD has decreed by his providence that this should happen. We deny this simply. We do indeed concede that GOD foresees not only the 'that' of all things, but also the 'why' and the 'how'; yet it is not to be concluded from this that GOD is the cause of the 'why'. Which elsewhere is explained more broadly. Briefly we say thus: Actions are threefold: some divine; others human; others diabolical. The former are predicted because God is certainly going to perform them; thus the resurrection of the dead was predicted: the latter and these are foretold because God, for certain reasons, foresees that they will happen; thus the betrayal of Judas, etc., was predicted. And yet in no kind of action is the prediction the cause. Beautifully (a) Jerome: It is not because God knows future things that it is necessary for us to do what He foreknew, but because He knows what we are going to do by our own will, because He is God.

XXII. Question 2. How is this prophetic prediction said to be fulfilled in the leading of Christ out of Egypt, when it seems to deal properly with the leading out of the Israelites? Answer: Scripture is said to be fulfilled in four ways, as the most famous Chemnitz notes in chapter 12 of the Harmony of the Gospels: 1. πρώτως (primarily), when the event corresponds to the prediction. 2. ἀναλόγως (analogously), when through a similarity of circumstances one prediction is accommodated to several things and acts. 3. γενικῶς (generally), when Scripture utters an oracle which can be applied to several things. 4. τυπικῶς (typically), when something is accommodated to another through the nature of a type. Junius and (b) Piscator of Herborn maintain that this prediction was fulfilled in the first way: but the fourth pleases most Orthodox [theologians], who say that Matthew refers to the Head and Bridegroom of the Church what Hosea had said about the body and the bride, because of the closest conjunction of the Head and the mystical body, and because of the type which the Israelite people bore in Egypt.

XXIII. The less principal causes of the flight into Egypt, and those devised by pious doctors, are: 1. that He might demonstrate Himself to be a man in all things like us. 2. that He might teach us to flee the fury of tyrants. 3. that He might reveal the manner of His kingdom not to be worldly. 4. that He might consecrate our flights.

XXIV. And these things are to be meditated upon by you in the flight of Christ, O fugitive soul, so that you may not despair: these are to be considered, so that you may learn to flee willingly and piously. For because the Savior flees, He flees for your sake, so that by His flight He might repair what you lost by your flight; so that by His flight He might prepare that by which you, while fleeing, are to be saved. You fled from Paradise into the desert of the world through impious disobedience: Behold! Christ flees into Egypt through prompt obedience; so that by this of His, He might correct that of yours. You must flee in this erroneous world, and the sweet fatherland must be deserted. Be present in spirit, and your Head flees, therefore

And you will flee, member. He left his fatherland, and remained in a profane land, so that he might sanctify the fatherland for you, however much: he remained there until the divine nod: And you remain in exile; until he shall say to you. It shall be, that you may hear the most joyful news: They are dead, who were seeking your soul.
