In the end and effects, because John also baptized for the remission of sins. And unless one and the same baptism is established, absurdities would follow. 1. That Christ was baptized with a different and diverse baptism from ours, and consequently that he did not consecrate or sanctify our baptism. 2. That the Apostles baptized by John received a different baptism from ours: for some, if not all, were disciples of John before they were called by Christ, such as Andrew, Peter, Philip, John 1, v. 40. But if this is so, how will that of the Apostle stand, Ephesians 4:4, One Lord, one faith, one baptism?

XVIII. From this it is clearly evident that the Canon of the Council of Trent is false and erroneous, which holds as follows: if anyone shall say that the baptism of John had the same power as the baptism of Christ, let him be anathema. Likewise the false consequences of the Jesuits: That sins were not remitted through the baptism of John, and, that after the baptism of John, the baptism of Christ had necessarily to be received.

XIX. It is clear from the preceding Chapter that the Baptist had attempted to hinder the purpose of Christ either by words or even by laying on of hands, yet with an example of singular modesty, but when Christ insisted, and asserted that the reason for the office of both demanded this, John acquiesced and consented without further hesitation. Therefore both descend into the Jordan and there Christ, for the sake of his admirable humility, was dipped in baptism by John, namely the Lord by a servant, the Holy One in Israel by a sinner, the Creator by a creature, and indeed by the water of the Jordan flowing past, and not by distilled, artificial, medicated water, nor prepared by certain prayers, consecrations, and exorcisms, which it is agreed is customary for the Papists. To one asking whether the baptism of Christ was performed by the immersion of Christ's body into water, or by the pouring of water over the body, and that either threefold or only once? he replies from that well-known saying of Theodoret, that I am not so confident as to dare to affirm anything which Scripture we do not know the manner.

XX. It is, however, worthy of note that Matthew and Mark say that Jesus, having been baptized, immediately ascended from the water, in order, namely, to show alacrity and a most ready will in beginning and completing the work committed to him by the Father, as if he were saying from Psalm 40:8, 'Lo, I come,' etc. Others bring forward such meditations concerning these words: that John, during the baptism of other men, preached in a fairly long discourse about this salutary washing, about repentance and faith in the Messiah who was soon to come, and that he inculcated upon those dipped in baptism, before they ascended from the water, with a truly heroic spirit, that they should bring forth fruits worthy of repentance. But because the reason for the baptism of the God-man is different from that of mere men, therefore John omitted such a thing in the baptism of Christ, whence it happened that, having received baptism, he ascended immediately.

XXI. After his ascent on the bank of the Jordan, Christ composed himself for prayer, as Luke attests. Although the formal words of the prayer are not expressed, there is no doubt that, having fallen upon his knees, he gave most devout thanks to God the Father that the time for the redemption of the human race had now arrived, and at the same time besought Him that the course of the ministry now about to be begun might be happily completed and with the salvation of many men.

XXII. The heavenly Father not only heard the most ardent prayers of Christ, but also deigned to confirm the beginning of his ministry with three illustrious miracles, of which the first is the opening or cleaving of the heavens, not indeed done physically in the manner of a chasm, nor allegorically, such as God promised in Malachi 3:10 when He bestows favorable weather and the fertility of the earth, nor as Peter saw heaven opened in a trance, but in a manner clearly singular, extraordinary, and miraculous, yet real and visible to bodily eyes, so that the bystanders might be taught that this Teacher was sent from heaven, who, with sin expiated and peace made between God and men through the ministry of the Gospel, would unlock the gates of heaven for those who believe. To this may be referred the type of Jacob's ladder, which Christ himself applied to himself, John 1, last verse.

XXIII. II. The second miracle is the visible appearance of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, which, descending from heaven, not only settled upon Christ but also remained upon him, not because Christ always carried about with him the form of that dove, but because all his words and deeds testified that Christ, according to his human nature, had most fully received the Holy Spirit, whose power never deserted him, whether in his sermons, his miracles, or his other actions. Although the Holy Spirit, in the infinity of his essence, is invisibly present everywhere and fills the orb of the earth, yet here he willed to show the invisible presence of his essence and power by the visible symbol of a dove. Whence we rightly say that the Holy Spirit himself descended when that form of a dove descended, inasmuch as it was the instrument or medium of this manifest revelation of the Holy Spirit.

XXIV. It must be known, however, that this descent of the Holy Spirit was: 1. The fulfillment of the divine oracle made to John (John 1:33), by which he was to be made certain that this Jesus was the Son of God and the true Messiah, out of that innumerable multitude of men flocking to his baptism. 2. An undoubted document that Christ was anointed not with bodily oil, but with the Holy Spirit and power, not indeed as if the Holy Spirit, descending in the form of a dove, then first anointed him, but rather to declare him as the anointed one, that is, the Messiah, by which it might be publicly made known to John and others that this was he who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and that this was that man of whom John had testified that he would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire.

XXV. A question occurs here: Whether the dove in which the Holy Spirit appeared was a true dove, or merely an image of one? Resp. It can be ignored piously and without any loss of salvation; nevertheless, because God, as Scripture testifies, is not accustomed to play with men by empty phantasms, nor does it seem likely that in this revelation God blinded the eyes of John and those standing around with a cataract, and Luke expressly calls it σωματικὸν εἶδος (bodily form), it is therefore highly probable that it was something corporeal. Meanwhile, although it cannot be affirmed with certainty that such a dove was like ours, yet we do not hesitate to assert with Dr. Hunnius, by the force of the alleged reasons, that it was something corporeal.

XXVI. The third miracle is the voice of the eternal Father sounding from the opened heaven, and according to Mark and Luke, directed to CHRIST, Thou art my son, etc. according to Matthew, but to John and those standing by, 'This is my son,' etc. The Evangelists vary the expression, yet the meaning remains the same, says Augustine.

XXVII. Chemnitz, and with him Dr. Winckelmann, says that the cause of the diverse narration is this most simple one: that the voice of the Father is said to have occurred twice, first to Christ, then to those standing by, so that He might be commended to them to be heard. Moreover, that voice is taken primarily from Ps. 2:7 and Isaiah 42, which seems to insinuate this: 'You are my son, not adoptive, not putative, but only-begotten and natural, whom I have begotten from eternity, and therefore most dear to me; in you I am well pleased,' as if He were saying, 'Not only do I acquiesce in you, embrace you with benevolence, and am well-affected toward you, but also in you and because of you I am of a placated mind toward the whole human race,' by which voice the heavenly Father declared that, because of the Son, He had now laid aside all indignation against us, and because of the same Son, He embraces believers with paternal benevolence.

XXVIII. But the voice of the Father might have seemed abrupt, for in Matthew 17, in the history of the transfiguration, these words are added: 'Hear him'; and there is no doubt that these also pertain to the present business of inauguration. Therefore, Christ was, as it were, solemnly ordained and called to the ministry by this voice of the Father; for it was not fitting that Christ the Messiah should seize that office by His own authority. And since He was clearly unknown as to His person, and yet had long since been deputed to this office, He had to be, as it were, ordained, presented, and commended from heaven by the Father to those standing by in this His baptism, as the beginning of His ministry, so that they might hear Him, who was publicly announced and declared to be the Messiah. And this was that admirable manifestation of the Trinity, from which, as Epiphanius testifies, many arguments can be drawn against Sabellius; among others, he also wrote thus: 'If you do not believe that in the divine essence, which is One, there are three distinct persons, accompany John to the Jordan, and you will see, etc.'

XXIX. You might ask why Christ, who is ἀναμάρτητος (sinless), wished to be baptized with that baptism which was instituted for sinners? A question ἀξιοθαύμαστος (worthy of wonder), to which Christ Himself responds, saying to John, 'It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.' Setting aside various interpretations for this time, we maintain that Christ means this: namely, that He comes and requests baptism from John, not as if He Himself in this washing needed it, but that it ought to be done in such a way that both John, by administering baptism, and He Himself, by receiving the same, might satisfy the duty in every respect, especially since His ministry pertains to that righteousness by which believers are to be sanctified before God unto eternal life, to fulfill not some part, but all things which pertain to it. perfect author of our salvation, not only by acquiring it through death, but also as a true and perpetual priest by applying it through certain means and instruments which He Himself sanctified, so that we may know that God wills to be effective through these until the consummation of the age.

XXX. Many more specific causes of the baptism of Christ are recounted elsewhere, among which these are not the least: I. That by His baptism He might sanctify and consecrate our baptism into a saving instrument and washing of regeneration, Tit. 3:5. II. That He might wash away our sins, and infuse into the baptismal water all that which He acquired by His merit, so that it might be applied to all who are baptized, and as it were appropriated. III. That by His example He might more deeply commend to us the dignity of baptism, and at the same time demonstrate its necessity against those who, superciliously despising baptism, say, or at least think to themselves, 'What would a little water profit me for salvation?' Which it is evident the Pharisees did, from Luke 7:30.

From those things which have now been treated, many and notable doctrines flourish, of which we shall note two: I. That we should worthily esteem and magnify our baptism. For although in the dispensation of our baptism the heaven is not visibly opened, nor can the whole Trinity be seen with bodily eyes, as it is evident happened in the baptism of Christ: yet it must be known that in our baptism we should not look only at the action of the minister, but rather it must be certainly established that the whole Trinity is most present at that baptismal act, although not visibly, for there we put on Christ, Gal. 3:27, who pours out His Holy Spirit upon us copiously, Tit. 3:6; there also sounds the voice of the good pleasure of the heavenly Father, who adopts us as sons to Himself, which voice is perceptible to faith alone.

II. That we should not approach the Ecclesiastical ministry unless legitimately called, because Christ did not wish to occupy it before He had been called forth by the voice of the heavenly Father to undertake the ministry. No one therefore, unless someone has been deemed worthy of this grace by God, let him not presume with rash daring to insert himself into it, or to extort a calling by evil arts, deceits, bribes, and other illegitimate means; but everyone ought to await a legitimate calling, and then in all the labors of his calling he will enjoy tranquility of conscience, will invoke God with confidence, will be of great courage in any dangers whatsoever, and will complete his entire course and ministry, received from the Lord Jesus, with joy. Acts 20, v. 24.

Latin:

XVII. Conveniunt enim 1.Causâ efficiente seu primo autore,qvi Deus: 2. Communi à Deo accepto mandato. 3. Materia seu elemento, qvæ aqva. 4. Formula baptizandi. 5. Fine & effectis, qvia Johannes qvoq; baptisavit in remissionem peccatorum. Et nisi unus idemqve statuatur baptismus, absurda seqverentur. 1. Christum alio & diverso baptismate esse baptizatum à nostro, adeog; nostrum baptismum non consecrasse nec sanctificasse. 2. Apostolos à Johanne baptisatos diversum à nostro accepisse baptisma: qvidá enim si nō omnes, anteqvam à Christo vocati essent discipuli Johannis fuerunt, ut pote Andræas, Petrus, Philippus Joh. 1, v. 40. Qvod si ita est, qvomodo stabit illud Apostoli Ephes. 4, 4. Unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma?

XVIII. Hinc liqvidò constat, falsum & erroneum esse Canonem Concilii Tridentini, qvi sic habet: si quis dixerit, baptismum Johannis habuisse eandem vim cum batismo Christi, anathema sit. Falsa item Jesuitarum consectaria: Per Babtismum Johannis non fuisse remissa peccata, Et, post baptismum Johannis necessariò percipiendum fuisse baptisma Christi.

XIX. Perspicuum est ex præcedente Cap, Baptistam conatum fuisse Christi propositum impedire vel verbis vel etiam injectâ manu, singulari tamen modestiæ exemplo, sed cùm Christus instaret, & utriusq; officii rationem hoc exigere asseveraret, acqvievit & annuit Johannes absq; ulteriori tergiversatione. Descendunt itaq; ambo in Jordanem & ibi Christus pro admirandâ sua humilitate à Johanne baptismo tinctus est, nempe Dominus à servo, Sanctus in Israël à peccatore. Creator à creaturâ, & qvidem aqvâ Jordanis præter fluente, non autem distillatitiâ, factitiâ, medicatâ, nec certis preculis, consecrationibus & exorcismus præparatâ, id quod Pontificiis solenne esse constat. Quærenti, num baptisatio Christi facta sit immersione corporis Christi in aquam, an aquæ super corpus effusione, eáq́, trinâ vel unâ duntaxat? ei resp. ex vulgato illo Theodoreti, me non adeò confitentem esse, ut audeam aliqvod affirmare, qvod Scriptura silentio præterit. Rem scimus, modum nescimus.

XX. Notatu autem dignum est, qvod Matthæus & Marcus dicunt, Jesum baptizatum confestim ex aqva ascendisse, ut nempe alacritatem & voluntatem promtissimam ostenderet in inchoando perficiendoq́; opere à patre sibi commisso, quasi dicat ex Psalmo 40, 8. Ecce venio &c. Alii circâ verba ista tales afferunt meditationes, Johannem in baptizatione aliorum hominum sermone benè longo prædicasse de hoc salutari lavacro, de pœnitentia & fide in Messiam brevi venturum, & baptismo tinctis, priusqvam ex aqva ascenderent, heroico planè spiritu inculcâsse, ut fructus pœnitentia dignos facerent. Verùm qvia baptismi ϑεανθρώπη alia fiat ratio qvàm ψιλω̃ν α̉νθρώπων, idcircò Johannem tale qvid in baptismo Christi omisisse, unde factum, qvòd accepto baptismo statim ascenderit.

XXI. Post ascensum in ripa Jordanis Christus ad orationem se composuit, attestante Luca. Licet autem verba formalia orationis non sint expressa; tamen nullum est dubium, qvin in genua sua provolutus, Deo Patri gratias egerit devotissimas, qvod jam adduxisset tempus redemptionis generis humani, eundemq́; simul obsecrârit, ut ministerii cursus jamjam inchoandus feliciter & cum multorum hominum salute consummetur.

XXII. Preces Christi ardentissimas Pater cœlestis non solùm exaudivit, sed etiam tribus illustribus miraculis ingressum ministerii confirmare dignatus est, qvorum I. Cœli apertio vel diffissio, non qvidem facta physicè in morem chasmatis, nec allegoricè, qvalem Deus promisit Malach. 3, 10. qvando commodam aëris tempestatem & terræ fœcunditatem largitur, nec ut Petrus in ἐκστάσει cœlum apertum vidit, sed modo planè singulari, extraordinario & miraculoso, reali interim ac corporeis oculis patente, ut edocerentur circumstantes, hunc Doctorem esse cœlitùs missum, qvi expiato peccato & pace inter Deum & homines factâ per ministerium Evangelii credentibus cœli portas sit reseraturus. Huc referatur typus scalæ Jacobæ, qvem Christus ipse ad se allegavit, Joh. 1. v. ult.

XXIII. II. Alterum miraculum est visibilis apparitio Spiritus sancti in forma columbæ, qvi cælitùs se demittens non solùm insedit Christo, sed etiam mansit super eum, non qvòd Christus columbæ istius speciem semper circumtulerit secum, sed qvia omnia ejus dicta & facta testarentur Christum juxta humanam Naturam Spiritum sanctum plenissimè accepisse, cujus virtus nunqvam tum in concionibus tum miraculis, aliisq; actionibus eum destitueret. Licet autem Spiritus sanctus essentiæ suæ in finitate invisibiliter ubiq; præsens sit, & orbem terrarum impleat: hîc tamen invisibilem essentiæ & virtutis suæ præsentiam visibili columbæ symbolo ostendere voluit. Unde rectè dicimus, descendisse ipsum Spiritum sanctum, cùm species illa columbæ descendit, qvippe qvæ hujus patefactionis manifestæ Spiritus sancti erat organum seu medium.

XXIV. Sciendum verò, qvòd hîc descensus Spiritus S. fuerit. 1. Complementum oraculi divini ad Johannem facti. Joh. 1, 33. qvo certior reddi debuit, hunc Jesum esse DEI filium, verumq; Messiam ex innumerâ ista hominum ad baptismum suum accurentium multitudine. 2. Indubitatum documentum, Christum esse unctum non oleo corporali, sed Spiritus S. & virtute, non qvidem ac si Spiritus S. columbæ formâ descendens eum tunc primum unxerit, sed potiùs ut unctum, id est, Messiam declararet, qvo publicè innotesceret Johanni & aliis, hunc esse conceptum à Spiritus S. & hunc esse virum illum, de qvo Johannes testificatus fuerit, qvòd Spiritus S. & igne baptizaturus esset.

XXV. Occurrit hic qvæstio: An Columba, in qva Spiritus sanctus apparuit, fuerit vera Columba, an verò illius simulacrum duntuxat? Resp. piè & absq; omni salutis jactura hoc posse ignorari, attamen qvia DEUS, Scriptura teste, non soleat ludere homines inanib⁹ phantasmatis nec verò videatur simile, hac in patefactione DEUM Johannis & circumstantium oculos glaucomate perstrinxisse, & Lucas expressè σωματικὸν εἶδος appellitet, ideò corporeum qviddam fuisse perqvàm probabile est. Interim licet certò non possit affirmari, qvòd talis qva fuerit columba, qvales nostræ; tamen corporeum qviddam fuisse vi allegatarum rationum cum D. Hunnio asserere non dubitamus.

XXVI. Tertium miraculum est Vox æterni Patris aperto de cælo sonans, & juxta Marcum & Lucam directa ad CHRISTUM, Tu es Filius &c. juxta Matthæum autem ad Johannem & circumstantes, Hic est filius meus &c. Variant locutionem Evangelistæ, salvâ tamen sententiâ, ait Augustin.

XXVII. Diversæ narrationis caussam Chemnitius & cum eo D Winckelmannus, hanc esse dicit simplicissimam, quòd vox Patris bis dicatur facta, primò ad Christum, deinde ad astantes, ut illis commendaretur audiendus. Desumpta est autem vox ista potissimùm ex Ps. 2, 7. & Isai 42. quæ hoc insinuare videtur: Tu es filius meus, non adoptivus, non putativus, sed unigenitus & naturalis, qvem ab æterno genui, adeóq; mihi carissimus, in te mihi complacitum est, quasi dicat, non solùm in te acqviesco, de benevolentiâ complector, & erga te benè affectus sum, sed etiam in te ac propter te sum animo placcato erga universum genus humanum, quâ voce Pater cœlestis declaravit, se propter filium omnem in nos indignationem jam deposuisse, & propter eundem credentes paternâ benevolentiâ complecti.

XXVIII. Verùm abrupta videri poterat vox Patris, nam Matth. 17. in transfigurationis historia adduntur hæc verba, Hunc audite; quæ qvin ad præsens qvoqve in augurationis negotium pertineant, nullum est dubium. Christus itaque hac voce Patris ad ministerium quasi solenniter ordinatus & evocatus fuit: nec enim erat concedens, ut Christus Messias illud propriâ autoritate invaderet. Et qvoniam qvoad personam planè ignotus erat, & verò ad hoc munus jam dudum deputatus, ideo in hoc suo baptismo utpote ministerii exordio à Patre cœlitùs quasi ordinandus, præsentandus & commendandus fuit circumstantibus, ut ipsum, qvippe Messiam publicè renunciatum ac declaratum audirent. Et hæc fuit admiranda illa Trinitatis patefactio, ex qva, Epiphanio teste, contra Sabellium multa depromi possunt argumenta; inter alia etiam sic scripsit: Si non credis in divina essentia, quæ Unica est, esse tres distinctas personas, comitare Johannem ad Jordanem, & videbis &c.

XXIX. Dicas cur Christus ἀναμάρτητος voluerit baptizari eo baptismo, qvi pro peccatoribus institutus est? Qvæstio ἀξιοθαύμαστος, ad qvam Christus ipse respondet, dicens ad Johannem, πρέπον ἐςὶν ἡμῖν πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην. Missis autem hæc vice variis interpretationibus, Christum hoc velle autumamus, se nimirum venire & petere baptismum à Johanne, non ac si ipse hoc lavacro indigeret, sed sic oportere fieri, ut uterqve cum Johannes baptismum administrando, tum ipse eundem suspiciendo undiqvaqve officio satis faciat, præsertim tum ministerium suum pertineat illius justitiæ, qvâ credentes gratias coram Deo ad vitam æternam sanctificandi sunt, non partem aliqvam, sed omnia, qvæ ad illam pertinent, implere. Debuit qvippe Christus esse perfectus autor nostræ salutis, non solùm eam per mortem acqvirendo, sed etiam tanqvam verus & perpetuus sacerdos eam applicando per certa media & organa, qvæ ipse sanctificavit, ut sciamus, Deum velle per ista esse efficacem usq; ad consummationem seculi.

XXX. Specialiores causæ baptismi Christi aliàs recensentur plurimæ, ex qvibus hæ non sunt postremæ: I. Ut baptismo suo baptismum nostrum sanctificaret & consecraret in salutare organum & lavacrum regenerationis, Tit. 3, 5. II. Ut peccata nostra ablueret, & in aqvam baptismalem omne id, qvod per meritum acqvisivit, immitteret, ut omnibus, qvi baptisantur, illud applicetur, & qvasi approprietur. III. Ut suo exemplo baptismi dignitatem nobis altiùs commendaret, simulq; necessitatem ejus demonstraret contra eos, qvi baptismum superciliose contemnentes dicunt, vel certè secum cogitant, qvid mihi paucula aqva ad salutem prodesset? Id qvod Pharisæos factitâsse constat ex Luca 7, 30.

Ex iis, qvæ jam pertractata sunt, multæ eæq; insignes doctrinæ efflorescunt, ex qvibus duas notabimus: I. Ut baptismum nostrum dignè æstimemus & magnificiamus. Licet enim in dispensatione nostri baptismi cælum non aperiatur visibiliter, nec tota Trinitas corporeis oculis conspici qveat, uti in baptismo Christi factum esse constat: scientum tamen in nostro baptismo non ad actionem ministri duntaxat respiciendum esse, sed certò potiùs statuendum, isti baptismali actui præsentissimè adesse totam Trinitatem, licet non verisibiliter, ibi enim Christum induimus, Gal. 3, 7. qvi Spiritus S. super nos effundit, copiosè Tit. 3, 6. ibi etiam sonat vox beneplaciti Patris cœlestis, qvi nos sibi in filios adoptat, qvæ vox soli fidei perceptibilis est.

II. Ut ad ministerium Ecclesiasticum non nisi legitimè vocati accedamus, qvia Christus illud occupare noluit, priusqvam voce Patris cœlestis factâ ad capessendum ministerium fuisset evocatus. Nemo igitur nisi quem Deus hac gratiâ dignatus fuerit, temerario ausu eidem se ingenere, aut malis artibus, dolis, largitionibus, aliisq́ve mediis illegitimis vocationem extorqvere prosumat, sed qvisq; legitimam vocationem expectare debet, & tunc in omnibus vocationis suæ laboribus gaudebit tranqvillitate conscientiæ, fiduciâ Deum invocabit, in qvibuslibet periculis erit ingenti animo, totumq; suum cursum ac ministerium à Domino Jesu acceptum cum gaudio consummabit. Act. 20. v. 24.


## 32 Thirty-second Disputation, On the Fasting and Temptation of Christ

He whom the heavenly Father had announced as King of kings and Lord of lords, immediately after the announcement was made, is left without crowds, and living with the beasts, he suffers hunger, and is received by Satan with vexations and mockeries. Pondering these things in your mind, you are struck with fear, and you dread that harder and more dangerous things threaten you. For if the author of all things, and he who fills all living things with abundance and satiety, is pressed by hunger for forty whole days, must we not succumb to starvation? If the impudent enemy takes up arms against God, what will he not dare against miserable creatures? If the most insane Satan wanted him who stands inflexible and immovable to fall, and him who had condemned to be condemned and to worship, what will he presume against us? What will he plot against us? Will he not act with all his might to lead us away from God, to seduce us, and to precipitate us into eternal destruction? Collect your mind; Christ is led of his own accord, nay, he is led by his own command (for his will is a command), and he undergoes all things for our sake: He hungered, so that he might recover what was lost by the first-formed; he was tempted, so that we might carry away the eternal crown of victory. For we could not be crowned unless he had conquered; he could not have conquered unless he had struggled; he could not have struggled unless he had had an enemy and tempter. Therefore, this is not so much to be dreaded as it is to be cherished and remembered with a grateful mind. That this very thing may be done, we gird ourselves for the contemplation of both the fasting and the temptation of Christ, conveniently expediting the business in three chapters, the first of which will consider Christ's fast. The second will contemplate the temptation. The last will append a practical meditation in a few words.

Thesis I.

In examining the fast of the Savior, following the son of the Evangelists, we shall direct our pen to three parts: the first will express the προηγούμενον of the fast: the second the fast itself: the last the ἑπόμενον of the fast.

II. The antecedent of the fast is the ἐπαγωγὴ or withdrawal into the desert. By this withdrawal, however, he was led away from the crowd of men, so that the supreme teacher of the Church and legate of GOD might come forth, as if sent more from heaven than taken from some town and the common herd of men.

III. At the beginning, regarding the ἐπαγωγὴν, it is asked: Is a rapture to be understood by it, by which the Savior was in reality and locally carried up into heaven, in which he learned his theology? Regarding this matter, such is the judgment of Smalzius: It is clearly probable that that happened at that time (he speaks of a certain local ascension and descension of Christ) when the Lord Jesus had already been baptized and indeed endowed with the Holy Spirit, but had not yet begun to perform his office, when, namely, he was preserved for 40 days and nights without food in the desert, not otherwise than Moses. And a little later: We are most persuaded that it is so, and we rejoice greatly that this mystery has been revealed to us through the sacred scriptures. But this assertion of Smalzius is not only not probable, but even impious, and diametrically opposed to the sacred scriptures. For the Holy Spirit, as is clear from the Gospel history, 1. drove Christ not into heaven, but into the desert. 2. not so that he might learn the Gospel, but so that he might be tempted by Satan. Matt. 4, 1. 3. Not so that he might enjoy the pleasant sight of GOD, but of Satan, and he was with the beasts, and the angels ministered to him. Mark 1, 13. 4. When the temptation was finished, he did not ascend into heaven, but Luke chap. 4, 14, connecting the following to the previous, says: And Jesus returned, namely from the desert, in the power of the Spirit into Galilee.

IV. Next, regarding the ἐπαγωγὴν in particular, we must weigh 1. Its efficient cause, or author, who is called the Spirit by the Evangelist Matthew, c. 4. v. 1. What kind of Spirit it was, Luke expresses when he says: Full of the Holy Spirit, he returned from the Jordan. It is signified that this whole deed was done by divine providence, and not by chance; nor rashly, but that it was governed by the counsel of the Spirit. Not as if he had hitherto lacked the guidance of the Spiri t: but because already from the appearance of the Spirit himself, by his more manifest impulse, he began to be driven to more sublime things.

V. II. The place, which is ἔρημος, i.e., a desert. However, what kind of desert this was is not agreed upon by all. So that I may stir up strife with no one on this point, I consider the opinion of the blessed Chemnitz and the illustrious Lord President, my teacher and revered patron, to be not inconsistent with the truth, understanding it to be a great desert for these reasons. 1. The remaining deserts are described by some addition, such as the desert of Judea, Ziph, Maon, etc. But the great desert is without addition. 2. In the remaining deserts there are certain habitations of men: but in this desert Christ lived his life with wild beasts for forty days.

VI. It is asked: Did Christ teach the life of hermits by his own example? From Christ's sojourn in the desert, the Papists seek a defense for the anchoritic austerity and bodily mortification of hermits. But did such a short time really make him a hermit, he who otherwise associated with the frequent crowd in such a way that the Jews called him a glutton and a drunkard in contrast to John the Baptist? Matt. 11, v. 19? Did our Redeemer go to the desert as a hermit either by private vow, or in imitation of others, or by the prescription of a rule? Matthew thinks otherwise, teaching: that Christ came into the desert by the impulse of the divine Spirit. Furthermore, if any kind of sojourn in the desert makes a hermit, it follows that just as Christ was a hermit for forty days, so the 4,000 men who were there for three days must have been hermits, especially since they were fasting and almost wasting away with thinness. Mark 8.

VII. III. The end, which is expressed by these words of Matthew: πειρασθῆναι ὑπὸ τῆ διαβόλε. The word πειράζειν signifies to explore, to make a trial, or to take an experiment of someone. There are two species of temptation: the one of probation, the other of seduction. The temptation of probation, by which God explores the faith and obedience of men so that it may become conspicuous, just as it is read that he tempted Abraham Gen. 22, v. 1, Moses Exod. 15, 25, the Israelites Exod. 20, v. 20, Deut. 8, v. 2, Tobias Tob. 12, v. 13, and many others. The temptation of seduction is a solicitation to apostasy, or impiety, and crimes, proceeding either from Satan himself, or from the world, or from one's own flesh, or from the ministers of evil spirits, wicked men. So that it may become known by what species of temptation the Savior was tempted, the author of the temptation, Satan, is expressed in explicit words.

VIII. Having considered the temptations, we approach the fast, which the Evangelists testify was completed during that whole time in which He stayed in the desert, not in the discrimination of foods, but by total abstinence from all human food, which also was not available in the desert place. Therefore, He was miraculously sustained by divine power without food, so that He did not feel hunger. And Matthew expressly makes mention of the nights: so that it might not be thought that such a fast was like that of the Jews, who fasted during the day and took food in the evening and night.

IX. On this occasion it is asked. I. Whether Popish fasts are to be approved? We are so far from approving such fasts that we rather judge that they should be rejected and eliminated from true Churches. The urgent reasons are the following: I. Because such fasts are hypocritical, ridiculous, Simoniacal, tyrannical, blasphemously superstitious against the merit of Christ, and a doctrine of demons. II. Concerning this choice of foods, there exists in the whole Holy Scripture of the New Testament no command or example, therefore it is deservedly disapproved as mere ἐθελοθρησκεία. Matt. 23, v. 9; c. 15, v. 5. III. In the New Testament, those Levitical distinctions of foods, which are in some way reintroduced by our adversaries, are abolished, contrary to the express command of the divine word. Acts 10, v. 15; Matt. 15, v. 17; 1 Cor. 8, 8; Rom. 14, 17. IV. By this choice of foods imposed upon the Church as if it were necessary, Christian liberty is attacked, which must nevertheless be asserted. 1 Tim. 4. from v. 1 up to 5. Rom. 14, v. 3. Col. 2, v. 16, v. 20, 21, 23. 1 Cor. 10, v. 25.

X. It is asked II. What is to be thought specifically about the Lenten fast? The Papists, out of a certain κακοζηλία, foist the Lenten fast upon the Church without divine authority, reasoning thus: Christ fasted for forty days. Therefore, it will also be necessary for us not to eat meat for forty days. But 1. it is mere folly to institute the Lenten fast in imitation of Christ. For there is no greater reason today why we should follow this example of Christ than there was formerly for the holy Prophets and other Fathers under the Law to imitate the fast of Moses. And yet we know that this came into no one's mind. Only Elijah, who was the minister for the restoration of the Law, did GOD preserve without food on the mountain for forty days for a nearly similar reason. 1 Kings 19, v. 8. II. It has nothing in common with the fast of Christ. They stuff their bellies so much at lunch every day that they easily pass the time of dinner without food. What is this like the fast of the Son of GOD?

III. The Savior and Moses did not complete a fast every year, but each only once in their whole life. IV. The Lenten fast is insulting 1. to GOD, because it obscures His singular miracle, which He performed when He exempted His Son from the necessity of eating. Do they not, in a sane audacity, emulate GOD, who strive for the same thing by their own virtue? 2. to Christ, because by stripping Him of His badge, they clothe themselves in His spoils. For by His fast, Christ expiated our gluttony and similar sins. Is not Christ deprived of His glory when merit is attributed to the Papistic fast? 3. To the Gospel. GOD set an end to this fast of Christ, so that He might seal the Gospel. Do those who transfer it to another use not diminish the dignity of the Gospel by just that much?

XI. Hunger is the consequence of fasting. Luke and Matthew testify that He Himself fasted for forty days, and when they were completed, then He hungered.

XII. It is asked: Did Christ truly hunger? The madness of the Manichaeans, in order to undermine the true humanity of Christ, denies that He was subject to our infirmities, and clamors that He suffered, was crucified, and died κατὰ δόκησιν καὶ φαντασίαν (by appearance and phantasy). However, although the human nature of Christ, because it is ἀναμάρτητος (sinless) and personally united with the λόγῳ (Word), was not subject to passions and infirmities, much less to death by the condition of nature; meanwhile, however, because the human race could not be redeemed from death and eternal damnation by CHRIST except through the most bitter passions, infirmities, and finally death itself: therefore, by assuming the human nature, the λόγῳ (Word) also assumed those infirmities which drew their origin from sin: but He assumed them not insofar as they have regard for any guilt, but insofar as they possess the condition of any punishment, and only those which the work of redemption required to be assumed by Him.

Latin:

Qvem Pater cœlestis regum Regem, & dominantium Dominum renunciaverat, post renunciationem factam statim turbis destitus, ac cum bestiis agens patitur inediam, atq; vexationibus & ludibriis à Satana excipitur. Hæc apud animum reputans percelleris, & durius periculosiusq; tibi imminere pertimescis. Si namq; omnium rerum autor, ac viventia cuncta copia & satietate explens, fame totos qvadraginta dies premitur, an non esurie nobis occumbendum? Si hostis impudens arma sumit in Deum, qvid non audebit in creaturas miseras? si insanissimus Satan voluit, ut is, qvi stat inflexibilis & imobilis, caderet; ut damnatu is, qvi damnaverat, adoraret, qvid sibi contra nos præsumet? qvid cótra nos molietur? nonne nos à Deo abducere, seducere, & in æternum exitium præcipitare totis aget viribus? Recollige animum, sponte suâ Christus ducitur, imò ipso jubente ducitur, (ejus enim velle jubere est) atq; omnia nostri causâ subit: Esurivit, ut saltem per protoplastos amissam recuperaret; tentatus, nos æternam victoriæ coronam reportaremus. Non enim possemus coronari, nisi hic vicisset; non potuisset vincere, nisi certasset; non potuisset certare, nisi inimicum & tentatorem habuisset. Ergo hoc non tam horrendum, qvàm gratâ potiùs mente colendum, recolendum. Qvod ipsum ut fiat, ad contemplationem tum jejunii, tum tentationis Christi nos accingimus, negotium commodè expedientes, tribus capitibus. Qvorum primùm considerabit Christi jejunium. Alterum contemplabitur tentationem. Ultimum paucis meditationem practicam, subjunget.

Thesis I.

IN expendendo Jejunii Salvatoris filium Evangelistarum secuti ad tria membra calamum dirigemus: Primum exprimet jejunii προηγούμενον: alterum ipse jejunium: ultimum jejunii ἑπόμενον.

II. Antecedens jejunii est ἐπαγωγὴ sive Subductio in desertum. Subductione autem hac ab hominum freqventia abductus, ut prodiret summus Ecclesiæ doctor & DEI legatus, tanqvam magis è cœlo missus, qvàm assumtus ex oppido aliqvo, & communi hominum grege.

III. Initio circa ἐπαγωγὴν qværitur: An per eandem intelligendus raptus, qvo Salvator reipsâ & localiter in cœlum evectus, in qvo Theologiam suam didicerit? De hac re Smalzii tale habetur judicium: Planè verisimile est, illud tunc temporis factum esse (loqvitur de locali qvâdam ascensione & descensione Christi) cùm Dominum Jesus jam baptisatus, & Spiritu sancto qvidem donatus esset, munus autem suum nondum obire cœpisset, cùm scil. 40. dies & noctes, absqve cibo in deserto, non secus ac Moses conservatus fuit. Et paulò pòst: Nobis id ita se habere persuasissimum, & hoc mysterium nobis per sacras literas revelatum esse plurimùm gaudemus. Verùm assertio hæc Smalzii non modò non verosimilis, verùm etiam impia, & sacris literis è diametro opposita. Nam Spiritus sanctus, ut ex historia Evangelica liqvet 1. Christum expulit non in cælum, sed desertum. 2. non ut addisceret Evangelium, sed ut tentaretur à Satana. Matth. 4, 1. 3. Non ut frueretur jucundo DEI aspectu, sed Satanæ, & erat cum bestiis, & angeli ministrabant ei. Marc. 1, 13. 4. Finita tentatione non ascendit in cœlum, sed Lucas cap. 4, 14. prioribus seqventia annectens ait: Et regressus Jesus, ex deserto scil. in virtute Spiritus sancti in Galilæam.

IV. Deinde circa ἐπαγωγὴν in specie perpendenda 1. Ejus causa efficiens, sive autor, qvi ab Evangelista Matthæo appellatur Spiritus, c. 4. v. 1. Qvalis fuerit Spiritus, Lucas exprimit, cum inqvit: Spiritu sancto plenus regressus à Jordane. Significatur totum hoc factum fuisse providentiâ divinâ, & non fortuitò; neq; temerè, sed consilio Spiritus fuisse gubernatum. Non qvasi hactenus caruerit ductu Spiritus: sed quòd jam ab apparitione ipsius Spiritus, manifestiore ipsius impulsu, & ad sublimiora agi cœperit.

V. II. Locus, qui ἔρημος sc. desertum. Qvale autem hoc fuerit defertum inter omnes non convenit. Ut nemini hac in parte litem moveam, veritati non absonam censeo opinionem B. Chemnitii, & Cl. Dn. Præsidis, præceptoris & patroni colendi, intelligentium desertum magnum ob has retiones. 1. Reliqva deserta per additionem aliqva describuntur, ut desertum Judææ, Ziph, Maon &c. Desertum verò magnum sine additione. 2. in reliqvis desertis qvædam sunt hominum habitationes: sed in hoc deserto Christus cum feris per qvadraginta dies vitam egit.

VI. Qværitur: An Eremitarum vitam suo exemplo docuerit Christus? Ex commoratione Christi in deserto Anachoreticæ Eremitarum austeritati & carnificinæ corporis Papistæ patrocinium qværunt. Itané verò Eremitam effecit tantillum temporis, qui aliàs cum freqventi populo ita versabatur, ut ipsum præ Johanne Baptista Judæi Epulonem & Heluonem vocarent. Matth. 11. v. 19? An vel ex voto privato, vel ad imitationem aliorum, vel ex præscripto regulæ desertum adiit Redemtor noster, ut Eremita? Aliter sentit Matthæus docens: Spiritus divini impulsu Christum in desertum vinisse. Præterea si qvaliscunq; commoratio in deserto facit Eremitam, conseqvens, ut Christus Eremita qvadraginta dierum fuit, ita 4000. viros triduanos Eremitas fuisse oportet, præsertim jejunos; & macie propemodum contabescentes. Marc. 8.

VII. III. Finis, qvi exprimitur his verbis Matthæi: πειρασθῆναι ὑπὸ τῆ διαβόλε Vocabulum πειράζειν significat explorare, periculum facere, vel experimentum sumere de aliqvo. Tentationis species duæ: Altera probationis, altera seductionis. Tentatio probationis, qvâ Deus hominum fidem & obedientiam explorat, ut conspicua fiat, qvemadmodum Abrahamum Gen. 22. v. 1. Mosen Exod. 15, 25. Israëlitas Exod. 20, v. 20. Deut. 8. v. 2. Tobiam Tob. 12. v. 13. aliosq́; plures tentasse legitur. Tentatio se ductionis est sollicitatio ad Apostafiam, vel impietatem, & scelera, profecta sive à Satana ipso, sive à mundo, sive à carne propria, sive à ministris cacodæmonum improbis hominibus. Ut innotescat, qvâ tentationis specie Salvator tentatus, disertis verbis exprimitur tentationis autor Satanas.

VIII. Expensis πειρασμών accessum facimus ad jejunium, quod testantur Evangelistæ peractum toto illo tempore, quo in deserto commoratus, non in discrimine ciborum, sed totali abstinentiâ ab universo cibo humano, qui etiam loco deserto non suppetebat. Miraculosè ergò divinâ virtute sine cibo sustentatus fuit, ut famem non sentiret. Et Matthæus diserte mentionem facit noctium: ne existimaretur tale fuisse jejunium, sicut Judæi, per diem jejunabant in vesperâ & nocte cibum sumebant.

IX. Hac occasione quæritur. I. An jejunia Papistica approbanda? Tantum abest, ut talia jejunia approbemus, ut potiùs eadem ex viris Ecclesiis rejicienda, & eliminanda censeamus. Rationes urgentes sunt sequentes, I. Quia talia jejunia sunt hypocritica, ridicula, Simoniaca, tyrannica, blasphemè superstitiosa contra meritum Christi, & doctrina dæmoniorum. II. De hoc ciborum delectu in tota sacra Scriptura N. Testamenti, nullum extat vel mandatum, vel exemplum, ideò ut mera ἐθελοθρησκεία meritò improbatur. Matth. 23. v. 9. c. 15. v. 5. III. In N. Testamento sublata discrimina ciborum illa Levitica, quæ ab adversariis aliqvo modo rursus introducuntur, contra expressum verbi divini mandatum. Act. 10. v. 15. Matth. 15. v. 17. 1. Cor. 8, 8. Rom. 14, 17. IV. Hoc ciborem delectu Ecclesiæ, ac si necessarius esset, imposito, Christiana libertas impugnatur, quæ tamen asserenda 1. Tim. 4. à v. 1. usq; ad 5. Rom. 14. v. 3. Cor. 2. v. 16. v. 20. 21. 23. 1. Cor. 10. v. 25.

X. Quæritur II. Quid in specie de jejunio quadragesimali sentiendum? Pontificii ex κακοζηλίᾳ quadam jejunium quadragesimale Ecclesiæ obtrudunt, sine divina autoritate, sic ratiocinantes: Christus quadraginta diebus jejunavit. Ergò etiam nos oportebit per quadraginta dies carnibus non vesci. Sed 1. mera stultitia est, jejunium quadragesimæ ad Christi imitationem instituere. Neq; enim major hodie ratio est, cur hoc Christi exemplum sequamur, quàm fuit olim sanctis Prophetis, & alijs Patribus sub Lege, imitari Mosis jejunium. Atqui scimus nemini hoc in mentem venisse. Eliam solum, qui instaurandæ Legis minister, simili fere de causa sine cibo in monte quadraginta dies DEUS conservavit. 1. Reg. 18. v. 8. II. Nihil affine cum jejunio Christi. Qvotidie sic farciunt ventrem in prandio, ut cœnæ tempus facilè absq; cibo transignant. Quid simile cum jejunio Filii DEI?

III. Salvator & Moses non qvotannis jejunio defuncti sunt, sed uterqve semel tantùm tota vita. IV. Jejunium Qvadragesimæ contumeliosum est 1. in DEUM, qvòd singulare ejus miraculum obscurat, qvod edidit, cùm filiùm suum exemit à necessitate edendi. Annon in sanâ audaciâ æmulantur DEUM, qvi idem suâ virtute affectant? 2. in Christum, qvi suum illi insigne detrahentes, ejus spoliis se vestiunt. Jejunio enim suo Christus nostram ingluviem, similiaq; peccata expiavit, Annon dum meritum jejunio Papistico tribuitur, Christus suâ gloriâ privatur. 3. In Evangelium. Huic jejunio Christi finem DEUS statuit, ut Evangelium obsignaret. Qvi in alium usum transferunt, annon tantundem imminuunt ex Evangelii dignitate?

XI. Conseqvens jejunii esuries est. Ipsum jejunasse qvadraginta diebus, & consummatis illis, deinde apetisse, testantur Lucas & Matthæus.

XII. Qværitur: An Christus verè esuriverit? Futor Manichæorum, ut subruat veram Christi humanitatem, obnoxium fuisse eundem nostris infirmitatibus pernegat, & ipsum κατὰ δόκησιν καὶ φαντασίαν passum, crucifixum, & mortuum tumultuatur. Ut ut autem humana Christi natura, qvia ἀναμάρτητος, & cum λόγῳ personaliter unita passionibus & infirmitatibus; nedum morti ex naturæ conditione fuerit obnoxia: interim tamen, qvia genus humanum, CHRISTUM à morte & æternâ damnatione, non nisi per acerbissimas passiones, infirmitates, & deniq; mortem ipsam redimi poterat: ideò λόγῳ assumendo naturam humanam assumsit etiam infirmitates istas, qvæ ex peccato originem traxerunt: sed assumsit eas non qvatenus culpæ alicujus respectum, sed qvatenus pœnæ alicujus conditionem fortiuntur, & eas tantùm, qvas ab eo assumi opus redemtionis reqwirebat.


### XIII. With the brevity with which it could be done, the fast of Christ having…

XIII. With the brevity with which it could be done, the fast of Christ having been dispatched, we move our foot forward to the temptation of Christ, the treatment of which we shall institute partly γενικῶς (generally), partly εἰδικῶς (specifically).

…XIV. In general, two things are to be unfolded. The first is: Why did Christ submit to temptations, and wrestle with the Devil as if in a hand-to-hand struggle? We posit the following causes for this matter. 1. The Epistle to the Hebrews, Ch. 2, V. 17, Ch. 4, V. 15, explains it in the sweetest words. In that He suffered, when He was tempted, He is able to who is tempted to help. Likewise, we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses: but one who has been tempted in all things according to the likeness, without sin. II. To show that there is an ἄσπονδον (implacable) war between Himself and the Devil, and that He therefore came to crush the head of the Serpent, Gen. 3. 15. and to destroy the works of the Devil, 1. John 3, 8. III. To teach that by the example of Himself as the head, all Christians also, as members, would have Satan as their most hostile enemy from the first time of their baptism. Syr. 2. v. 1. IV. To show with what weapons, and how, faith ought to oppose itself to temptations. V. So that in temptations we might have the hope of victory in Christ Jesus, who has been made our Leader against that strong armed one. For our nature, when it was still intact, engaged with this tempter and succumbed. But now human nature in that seed of the woman has again brought back victory from the temptations of Satan. VI. To prove by temptations that He is true man. VII. To show that he who has first been tested by various temptations performs the duty of the ministry of the Gospel rightly. Concerning which causes, see the Harmony of Chemnitz and the Sacred Meditations of the renowned President.

XV. The other is the manner: Whether, namely, Christ was tempted by Satan secretly through suggestion, or indeed manifestly through an assumed visible form? We assert that Christ was tempted in both ways. For Luke hints not obscurely that the temptation began immediately after He had come into the desert. Without doubt, therefore, he attacked Him with sharp darts, partly by soliciting Him inwardly to apostasy, partly by proposing terrifying objects in the desert. But when he did not succeed with this life, he attempts another, and finally the master of trickery proceeds into the arena, so that he may tempt more severely; he wants stones to be converted into bread by Christ, he shows the kingdoms of the world, and sought adoration, etc., all of which almost all theologians, agreeing on the visible approach of Satan, on his horrible mask, on a sounding voice formed in the air, on the handling of stones in his hand, explain.

XVI. Specifically, regarding the temptation, three distinct encounters of the Devil with Christ come into consideration.

XVII. The first encounter is of distrust. In order for this to be more correctly explained, three things must be weighed regarding it: 1. The approach of Satan: καὶ προσελθὼν αὐτῷ ὁ πειράζων (and the tempter came to him). Just as in the first temptation in paradise in a certain bodily form the Devil tempted her, and emerged the victor over the whole race: thus he also appears to Christ in some visible and bodily form, with the empty hope of obtaining victory.

XVIII. 2. The weapon with which the Devil attempts to strike Christ, which is contained in these words: εἰ ὑιὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ, εἰπὲ ἵνα οἱ λίθοι οὗτοι ἄρτοι γένωνται. The sense of these words, to use the words of the Blessed Hunnius, is as follows: Forty days ago a voice was heard from the upper air, which proclaimed you the Son of God. And you are indeed of the opinion that you suppose yourself to be that natural, only-begotten Son of God. But that that voice was nothing but an empty mockery is not difficult to gather from the fact that God, who provides for even the most contemptible little beasts, meanwhile manifestly neglects you, struggling with hunger and starvation. Furthermore, if you were the Son of God, you would be able by the power of your might to convert these stones into loaves. Make the attempt, therefore, if you like; I will present myself as a spectator, to see how beautifully, forsooth, you can make loaves out of those stones. But if that is impossible for you to perform, the thing itself refutes your persuasion as false.

XIX. 2. The parrying of the weapon. Christ blunts this fiery dart with the shield of Holy Scripture, saying from Deut. 8:3: Οὐκ ἐπὶ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ἄνθρωπος, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ παντὶ ῥήματι ἐκπορευομένῳ διὰ στόματος θεοῦ. Some falsely twist this testimony, as if it were said that souls are nourished not by visible bread, but by the word of God. That is indeed true in itself, but Moses looked to something else. For when no bread was at hand, he commemorates that manna was an extraordinary nourishment for the people, so that it might serve as a testimony for all time that the life of men is not enclosed in bread, but depends upon the nod and good pleasure of God. Therefore, 'word' is not taken for doctrine, but for the decree which God published regarding the maintaining of the order of nature and the cherishing of creatures. The response of Christ, therefore, as one relying strongly on the word, is: Even though I am hungry, God can nevertheless preserve me by His power, as He has done for so long a time until now, even without any food, so that there is no need for me to make loaves out of stones.

XX. The question is asked: Could Christ not have converted stones into loaves? Samosatenians, Arians, Photinians, and others of this ilk abuse the present passage to deny His eternal essential Deity, reasoning thus: Christ could not always perform a miracle. Therefore, He did not perform miracles by His own power, and therefore He was not true God. ry they commit a paralogism, treating a non-cause as a cause. For the cause of this intermission was not that He could not, but that He did not wish to gratify the tempter Satan, lest God be tempted. Furthermore, He was not withdrawn into the desert by this plan so that He might spend His time there performing miracles, but rather so that He might be tempted by the Devil according to the will of the Father. Therefore, so that He might feel that assault of Satan more keenly, He ought to have refrained at this time from the manifest usurpation and declaration of His majesty, and not to have received the insults of Satan by an extraordinary miraculous method, but by those customary weapons which the rest of the Saints also use, namely the word of God, as the sword of the divine Spirit.

XXI. The second encounter is one of preposterous confidence, in which we shall be occupied in considering three things. I. is the πραχθὲν (the act performed), which contains two things. 1. παράληψιν (the taking along). For the Devil takes Christ from the desert into the holy city Jerusalem, which is called holy κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of eminence), because it was the seat of divine worship, and because the temple of God was there, with the ark of the mercy seat. 2. ςάσις (the placing). He sets Him upon the pinnacle of the temple, that is, the highest peak of the temple.

XXII. The question is asked: Did the Devil truly and bodily lead Christ with him through the air on high to the pinnacle of the temple, or did he indeed present such illusions to the eyes and mind of Christ that He thought He was being led around and was in danger on the pinnacle of the temple, when in reality He was in the desert? We make Chemnitz's answer from his Harmony our own regarding the proposed question: Even if the emptying of the Son of God was great, I do not know, however, whether it is fitting to believe that the Devil could have so occupied the mind and soul of Christ with his illusions that He did not know where He was, and was thus deceived in His thoughts. He will not err, therefore, who retains the words of the Evangelists simply as they sound regarding the leading around. Matthew has the word παραλαμβάνει (takes along), Luke ἀνάγει (leads up). Both use the word ἵστημι (to set), which words seem to signify a local taking and stationing.

XXIII. The λεχθὲν (the thing said), in which two things are to be known. 1. The πρότασις (proposition) expressed in these words: εἰ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ, βάλε σεαυτὸν κάτω (if you are the Son of God, cast yourself down). As if he were saying: since you depend so much on the providence of the Father that, even when hungry in the greatest scarcity of things, you do not doubt that you can be sustained by Him even without bread, it is well: now cast yourself down, so that you may show even more that you depend on His providence, for no danger to you will come from there. 2. The confirmation (βεβαίωσις), which Satan proposes with these words: γέγραπται. ὅτι τοῖς ἀγγέλοις αὐτῶ ἐντελεῖται περὶ σῶ, καὶ ἐπὶ Χερῶν ἀρῶσί σε, μήποτε προσκόψης πρὸς λίθον τὸν πόδα σῶ. The sense of the words: And lest perhaps you fear that this will be joined with some danger: Behold for you a safe conduct promised by the testimony of Scripture. It is written, concerning all the sons of GOD, and especially concerning you, as the natural Son of GOD (if indeed that voice heard at the Jordan was true), He has commanded His angels concerning you, that they may lift you up in their hands, lest at any time you strike your foot against a stone.

XXIV. III. The Answer of the Savior, by which He confounds Satan, is contained in the following: πάλιν γέγραπται, Οὐκ ἐκπειράσεις κύριον τὸν θεὸν σῶ. By this response of His, He proposes this admonition: that the promises of GOD are to be understood in such a way, and applied in practice to our confidence, that we do not tempt GOD. Now, one is said to tempt GOD who seeks an experiment of the power, wisdom, goodness, and truth of GOD, not in the ordinary way, but out of presumption or without necessity.

XXV. The last encounter of the temptation is of apostasy. Since Luke treated this in the second place, the cause of the discrepancy is inquired into. It was not the purpose of the Evangelists to weave the thread of history in such a way that they always observed the order of time exactly, but only to collect the sum of events, so that they might propose in a mirror and table those things concerning Christ which are most useful to know. Therefore, it suffices to hold that Christ was tempted in three ways; but whether it was the third or the second struggle, there is no reason for us to labor anxiously.

XXVI. Three things serve for the knowledge of this last encounter: 1. The procatarctic cause, or the object of the temptation, which is the showing of all the kingdoms and the glory of the world, and it is proposed to us by the Evangelists thus: καὶ ἀναγαγὼν αὐτὸν ὁ διάβολος εἰς ὄρος ὑψηλὸν, ἔδειξεν αὐτῷ πάσας τὰς βασιλείας οἰκουμένης, ἐν τιγμῇ χρόνε.

XXVII. It is asked: How could the Devil have shown Christ all the kingdoms of the world and their glory on any mountain, and that in a moment of time? Setting aside the opinions of others, we accept those of B. Hunnius, who writes thus on the present passage: Someone will wonder how the Devil could have shown Christ all the kingdoms of this world, since there is no place on earth so high from which even one kingdom could be shown to him. But the manner is resolved from Luke, from whom it becomes clear that it was not the kingdoms themselves, but a certain phantom of men that was presented to the eyes of the Savior by Satan, and shown, because he represented the kingdoms of this world and their glory. XXVIII. II. The temptation itself, which is in these words: και λέγει αυτῷ, ταῦτά σοι δώσω, ἐὰν πεσὼν προσκυνήσῃς μοι. The hope of this temptation was that Christ might seek the inheritance, which GOD promised to the Son, from elsewhere than from GOD himself. Then, that enticed by the pomp of the world, he might subject himself to Satan, and adore the same. XXIX. III. The response of the Savior, by which he powerfully crushes the fiery and poisonous dart, and puts the enemy to flight, is such: ὕπαγε σατανᾶ. γέγραπται γὰρ κύριον τὸν θεὸν σᾶ προσκυνήσῃς καὶ ἀυτῷ μονῳ λατρεύσῃς. Just as if he were saying: Begone with your impudent demand, wicked and cursed Spirit; shall I, a slave of Gehenna, adore you, or grant you that worship which the divine law wishes to be asserted for the one and only GOD? Shall I receive from you the power of the kingdoms of the world? Far be that from me. Thus, in a few words, concerning the temptation of Christ.

XXX. It is evident from the premises that Christ abstained from all food and drink for forty whole days; what do you think you should do, O man? Fast from all sin, take no food of malice, take no feasts of pleasure, do not grow hot with any wine of luxury, fast from evil acts, abstain from evil words, do not touch the stolen bread of perverse doctrine, do not covet the deceptive foods of Philosophy, which will seduce you from the truth. It is also clear that the only-begotten Son of GOD was tempted by the Devil: therefore, let it be foreign to a Christian man that he should tempt GOD, by indiscriminately committing himself to some danger; by asking something from Him through unbelief; by demanding miracles without necessity; by setting or prescribing a limit to divine help; by investigating the foreknowledge of GOD through experiment; by trying to catch Christ in his speech. τῷ Θεῷ δόξα.

Latin:

XIII. Eâ, qvâ fieri potuit brevitate, expeditum jejunium Christi, pedem promovemus ad tentationem Christi, cujus tractationem partim γενικῶς, partim εἰδικῶς instituemus.

XIV. In genere evelvenda duo. Primum est: Cur Christus tentationes subjerit, & cum Diabolo confertâ quasi manu luctatus? Hujus rei causas ponimus seqventes. 1. Dulcissimis verbis exponit Epistola ad Hebr. C. 2. V. 17. C. 4. V. 15. In qvo passus est, cùm tentaretur, potens est ei, qui tentatur auxiliari. Item, non habemus Pontificem, qui non posset compati infirmitatibus nostris: sed tentatum per omnia secundũ similitudinem, absq; peccato. II. Ut ostenderet inter se & Diabolum esse bellum ἄσπονδον, seq; ideò venisse, ut caput Serpentis contereret, Gen. 3. 15. & opera Diaboli dissolveret, 1. Joh. 3, 8. III. Ut doceret ipsius ut capitis exemplo omnes etiam Christianos, ut membra, à primo baptismi tempore Satanam infensissimum hostem habituros. Syr. 2. v. 1. IV. Ut ostenderet, quibus armis, & quomodo fides sese tentationibus opponere debeat. V. Ut in tentationibus haberemus spem victoriæ in Christo Jesu, qui Dux noster contra fortem illum armatum factus. Natura enim nostra, cùm adhuc integra esset, cùm hoc tentatore congressa succubuit. Nunc verò natura humana in semine illo mulieris rursus victoriam ex Satanæ tentationibus retulit. VI. Ut tentationibus comprobaret, se verum esse hominem. VII. Ut ostenderet, illum ministerii Evangelii munus rectè obire, qui priùs variis tentationibus probatus sit. De quibus causis videatur harmon. Chemn. & Meditat. sacræ Cl. Præsidis.

XV. Alterum, est modus: An nimirum Christus occultè per suggestionem, an verò manifestè per assumtam visibilem formam à Satana tentatus? Utroq; modo tentatum Christum asserimus. Lucas enim haut obscurè innuit, tentationem incepisse statim, postquam venisset in desertum. Procul dubio ergo acutis ipsum telis petiit, partim ad Apostafiam intus sollicitando, partim objecta terrifica in deserto proponendo. Cùm verò hac non successit vitâ, aliam aggreditur, & demum in palæstram procedit milli artifex, ut graviùs tentet, à Christo vult lapides converti in panes, mundi regna ostendit, & adorationem petiit, &c. quæ omnia Theologi ferè omnes consentientes de visibili accessu Satanæ, de horribili ejus larva, de sonera voce in aëre formatâ, de gestione lapidum in manu, exponunt.

XVI. In specie circa tentationem tres distincti Diaboli congressus cum Christo in contemplationem veniunt.

XVII. Prim⁹ congressus est diffidentiæ. Is ut rectiùs enucleetur, perpendenda circa eundẽ tria: 1. Access⁹ Satanæ: χ' προσελθὼς ἀυτῶ ὁ πειράζων. Quemadmodũ in primâ tentatione in paradyso in corporali quâdã specie Diabolus Eam tentavit, & super totum genus victor evasit : ita visibili etiam, & corporali aliqvâ specie Christo apparet, spe inani victoriam conseqvendi.

XVIII. 2. Telum qvo Diabolus Christum ferire conatur, qvod in his verbis habetur : εἰ ὑιὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ, εἰπὲ ἵνα οἱ λίθοι οὗτοι ἄρτοι γένωνται. Verborum horum sensus, ut utar verbis B. Hunnii, talis : Ante dies qvadraginta audita est vox è superiore aëre, qvæ te Dei Filium proclamavit. Et tu qvidem es in illa opinione, ut te naturalem illum unigenitum Filium Dei esse autumes. Qvòd autem vox illa nil nisi inane ludibrium extiterit, hinc colligere difficile non est, qvòd Deus, qvi contemtissimas etiam bestiolas ait, te interim cum fame inædiaqve conflictantem manifestè negligit. Præterea si Filius Dei esses, & vi potentiæ tuæ valeres lapides istos in panes convertere. Fac E. periculum, si libet, ego me præbebo spectatorem, qvàm pulchrè scil. possis è lapidibus illis panes facere. Qvod si verò præstitu illud tibi impossibile, res ipsa tuam persvasionem uti falsam redarguit.

XIX. 2. Teli declinatio. Ignitum hoc telum clypeo sacræ Scripturæ Christus retundit, ex Deut. 8. v. 3. inqviens : Οὐκ ἐπὶ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ἄνθρωπος, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ παντὶ ῥήματι ἐκπορευομένῳ διὰ στόματος θεοῦ. Hoc testimonium falsò nonnulli detorqvent, quasi dictum esset, animas non ali pane visibili, sed Dei verbo. Est qvidem id in se verum, sed aliò respexit Moses. Nam cùm nullus ad manus esset panis, commemorat Man fuisse extraordinarium alimentum populo, ad documento testatum in omne tempus fieret, hominum vitam non esse inclusam in pane, sed pendere à nutu & beneplacito Dei. Itaq; verbum non pro doctrina capitur, sed pro decreto, qvod Deus publicavit, qvoad tuendam naturæ ordinem, & fovendas creaturas. Responsio ergò Christi, tanqvam fortiter verbo nitentis est : Etsi esuriam, Deus tamen sua potentiâ, ut hactenus tanto tépore fecit, servare me potest, etiam absq; omni cibo, ut non sit opus me ex lapidibus panes facere.

XX. Qværitur: An Christus non potuerit lapides in panes convertere? Samosateniani, Ariani, Photiniani & hujus farinæ alii abuntuntur præsenti loco, ad æternam essentialem Deitatem abnegendam, sic ratiocinantes : Christus non semper potuit miraculum edere. Ergò non edidit miraculâ piopriâ virtute, ideoq; nec verus Deus fuit. Verum paralogismum committunt, secundum non causam, ut causam. Nam causa hujus intermissionis erat, non quod non posset, sed quod noluerit gratificari tentatori Satanæ, ne Deus tentaretur. Deinde non erat in desertū in consilio hoc subductus, ut ibi exercendis miraculis vacaret, sed potiùs ut juxta voluntatem Patris à Diabolo tentaretur. Proinde ut impetum illum Satanæ persentisceret studentiùs manifestâ usurpatione & declaratione suæ majestatis hoc tempore se debuit abdicare, neq; extraordinariâ ratione miraculosâ, sed consuetis illis armis Satanæ insultus accipere, quibus etiam armis reliqui Sancti utuntur, nimirum verbo Dei, tanquam divini Spiritus gladio.

XXI. Alter congressus est confidentiæ præposteræ, in quo considerando circa tria versabimur. I. est πραχθὲν, quod duo continet. 1. παραληψιν. Assumit enim Diabolus Christum è deserto in sanctam civitatem Hierosolymam, quæ κατ' ἐξοχὴν sancta dicitur, quòd sedes esset divini cultus, & quòd ibi templum Dei, cùm arca propitiatorii. 2. ςάσις. Statuit ipsum super pinnaculum templi, id est, summum fastigium templi.

XXII. Quæritur: An revera & corporaliter Diabolus Christum per aërem in sublimi secum duxerit ad pinnaculum templi: an verò tales præstigias objecit oculis & animo Christi, ut putaret se circumduci, & in pinnaculo templi periclitari, cùm revera esset in deserto? Chemnitii ex Harmonia ad propositam quæstionem responsionem facimus nostram: Et si magna fuit Filii Dei exinanitio, nescio tamen, an conveniat semire, Diabolum præstigiis suis, ita potuisse occupare mentem & animum Christi, ut ne desciret, ubi esset, & ita in cogitationib9 falleretur. Non errabit. E. Opinor, qui verba Evangelistarum, simpliciter de circumductione, sicut sonant, retinebit. Matthæus verbum habet παραλαμβάνει, Lucas ανάγει. Uterq; utitur verbo ίςημι, quæ verba localem assumtionem & stationem significare videntur.

XXIII. λεχθὲν, in quo duo cognoscenda. 1. πρότασις expressa his verbis : εἰ ὐὸς εἶ ὗ θεδ, βάλε σεαυτὸν κάτω. Ac si diceret: quando quidem ita pendes à providentiâ Patris, ut ne esuriens quidem in summa rerum penuriâ dubites, te ab illo etiam sine pane sustentari posse, benè est: te ipsum jam deorsum præcipia, ut magis etiam ostendas, te ab ejus providentiâ pendere nihil enim inde tibi periculum futurum. 2. βεβαίωσις, quam proponit Satanas his verbis: γέγραπται. ὅτι τοῖς ἀγγέλοις αὐτῶ ἐντελεῖται περὶ σῶ, καὶ ἐπὶ Χερῶν ἀρῶσί σε, μήποτε προσκόψης πρὸς λίθον τὸν πόδα σῶ. Verborum sensus: Et ne fortè metuas, hoc cum periculo quodam fore conjunctum: En tibi salvum conductum Scripturae testimonio promissum. scriptum est, de omnibus filiis DEI, maximè de te, tanquam naturali Filio DEI (si modò vera illa vox apud Jordanem audita) mandavit angelis suis de te, ut tollant te manibus suis, ne quando impingas in lapidem pedem.

XXIV. III. Ἀπόκρισις Salvatoris, quâ Satanam confundit conprehensa sequentibus: πάλιν γέγραπται, Οὐκ ἐκπειράσεις κύριον τὸν θεὸν σῶ. Hac suâ responsione proponit hanc admonitionem: promissiones DEI ita esse intelligendas, & in usu ad fiduciam accommodandas, ne DEUM tentemus. Tentare autem DEUM dicitur, qui non ordinariò, sed ex praesumtione, vel citra necessitatem quaerit experimentum potentiae sapientiae, bonitatis, & veritatis DEI.

XXV. Ultimus tentationis congressus est ἀποστασίας. Hunc cum Lucas secundo loco pertractarit, inquiritur causa discrepantiae. Non fuit propositum Evangelistis historiae filum sic contexere, ut temporis rationem semper observarent exactè, sed rerum tantùm summam colligere, ut in speculo & tabula proponerent, quae de Christo maximè utilia sunt cognitu. Tenere ergò sufficiat, Christum tribus modis fuisse tentatum, quod autem vel tertium, vel secundum fuerit certamen, non est cur anxiè laboremus.

XXVI. Cognitioni ultimi hujus congressus tria inserviunt: 1. Causa procatarctica, sive tentationis objectum, quod est monstratio omnium regnorum, & mundi gloriae, atq; ab Evangelistis nobis ita proponitur: καὶ ἀναγαγὼν αὐτὸν ὁ διάβολος εἰς ὄρος ὑψηλὸν, ἔδειξεν αὐτῷ πάσας τὰς βασιλείας οἰκουμένης, ἐν τιγμῇ χρόνε.

XXVII. Quaeritur: Quomodo Diabolus Christo omnia regna mundi, & gloriam in mento quovis ostendere potuerit, idque in momento temporis? Missis reliquorum opinionibus acceptamus. B. Hunnii hac de re sic in locum praesentem scribentis: Mirabitur quispiam, quo pacto Diabolus Christo monstrare potuerit omnia regna mundi hujus, cum non sit ullus in orbe locus tam excelsus, è quo vel unum regnum ei monstrare potuerit. Sed modus solvitur ex Luca, ex qvo fit palàm, non ipsa regna, sed qvoddam hominum phantasma fuisse oculis Salvatoris objectum à Satana, & monstratum, qvòd mundi hujus regna gloriamq; repræsentarit. XXVIII. II. Ipsum tentamen, qvod his verbis: και λέγει αυτῷ, ταῦτά σοι δώσω, ἐὰν πεσὼν προσκυνήσῃς μοι. Spes hujus tentationis fuit, ut hæreditatem, qvam DEUS Filio promisit, Christus aliunde, qvam à DEO ipso peteret. Deinde ut illectus mundi pompâ se subjiceret Satanæ, ac eundem adoraret. XXIX. III. Responsio Salvatoris, qvâ ignitum & venenatum telum Potenter elidit, hostemq; in fugam ruit, estq; talis: ὕπαγε σατανᾶ. γέγραπται γὰρ κύριον τὸν θεὸν σᾶ προσκυνήσῃς καὶ ἀυτῷ μονῳ λατρεύσῃς. Perinde ac si diceret: Facesse cum impudenti tua postulatione improbe & maledicte Spiritus, egonè te gehennæ mancipium adorem, aut eum cultum tibi tribuam, qvem lex divina unico & soli DEO vult assertum? egone abs te regnorum mundi potestatem capiam? Id verò à me absit. Sic paucis de tentatione Christi.

XXX. Christum ex præmissis constat integros qvadraginta dies ab omni cibo & potu abstinuisse, qvid tibi, ô homo, faciendum reris? Jejuna ab omni peccato, nullum cibum sumas malitiæ, nullas capias epulas voluptatis, nullo vino luxuriæ concalescas, jejuna à malis actibus, abstine à malis sermonibus, noli contingere panes furtivos perversæ doctrinæ, non concupisces fallaces Philosophiæ cibos, qvi te à veritate seducent. Liqvet etiam à Diabolo Filium DEI unigenitum esse tentatum: Alienum ergo sit ab homine Christiano, ut is tentet DEUM, indiscertè periculo alicui se committendo; per incredulitatem aliqvod ab ipso petendo; miracula sine necessitate postulando; divino adjutorio terminum ponendo, vel præscribendo, DEI præscientiam per experimentum indagando, Christum sermone capiendo. τῷ Θεῷ δόξα.


## 33 Thirty-third Disputation, On the Years of the Ministry and the Whole Course of Christ

ON the Fast and the temptation of our Lord Jesus Christ which took place in the desert, we treated in the previous disputation; namely, that the Son of GOD, when he had scarcely entered upon his ministry, engaged in a huge duel: not with King Herod, who pursued him with deadly hatred in his infancy, so that he was forced to leave his country and flee into Egypt as an exile, Matt. 2, v. 14. Nor with the Pharisees and the leaders of the people, who always opposed him and contradicted his doctrine, as is declared throughout by the Evangelists, but with the Prince of this world, John 14, v. 29, with the Prince of the power of the air, Eph. 2, v. 2, with our adversary, 1 Pet. 5, v. 8, with the Devil, Matt. 4, v. 1, whom he finally conquered and cast out, John 12, v. 31. This victory obtained by JESUS CHRIST has brought forth for us the strongest hope in the greatest and most dangerous temptations: since the Leader, Heb. 12, v. 2, and our triumpher has been made against that strong armed man, Luke 11, v. 21. Rightly, therefore, Ambrose says: The victory of the Lord is the triumph of the servant. But since we have heard more than enough about these things in the preceding, order advises us to proceed to the following disputation: which treats of the years of the ministry and the whole course of Christ, which we shall declare in these five chapters, in the first of which we shall touch upon the nature of the Ministry. In the second we shall weigh the time of the years: in the third we shall state the impelling cause: in the fourth we shall join the end: in the fifth we shall cultivate the effect. O Christ, beginner and leader of the ministry, rule the hearts of your ministers with your holy Spirit.

Thesis I.

This first chapter demonstrates to us many controversies of the Papists concerning the nature of the ministry; of which we shall recount only two. 1. Whether the ministry of Christ was joined with political government and a certain papal monarchy? 2. Whether after the visible ministry of Christ, Peter was constituted head of the whole Church and prince in the place of Christ?

II. As regards this first question, without any doubt Christ governed his Church in this world: but that he began such a Monarchy as the Roman Pope, namely the Vicar of Christ, claims, we plainly reject. For Christ has not a worldly, but a heavenly kingdom, as he himself says in John 18:36: My kingdom is not of this world; if it were of this world, my servants would have fought. From which saying we can judge very well that there is a great difference between the kingdom of Christ and that of the Pope; whence we argue thus: The kingdom of Christ is spiritual, and not of this world. The kingdom of the Pope is not spiritual, but worldly, and of this world. Therefore the kingdom of the Pope is not the kingdom of Christ. The major premise is brought forward from the cited passage of John 18. The minor premise is proved again by this syllogism: Whoever claims for himself the right of donating and governing whole regions, he possesses a worldly kingdom. But the Pope claims such a right for himself. Therefore. Whence it almost follows that he can be called neither a disciple of Christ, much less his Vicar. For the disciples of Christ wish to be heard as humble, not proud, Rom. 12:16: Not thinking arrogantly of yourselves, but accommodating yourselves to the humble; do not be arrogant among yourselves. Ministers, not lords, Matt. 20:25, Mark 10:42, Luke 22:25: The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors. But you are not so. Spiritual, not worldly; John 15:19: And if you had been of the world, the world would love what is its own: but you were not of the world. For I chose you out of the world; therefore the world hates you. Here we see sufficiently how great a difference there is between the kingdom of Christ and the Pope. Therefore our conclusion is most firm: that Christ was not a monarch in the Papal manner; but that as far as heaven is distant from the lowest parts of the earth, so great a difference has intervened, and still intervenes, between the two.

III. Next, the Papists blather that the Apostle Peter, as the head of the whole Church and prince of all ministers, was appointed in the place of Christ by Christ himself, and they attempt to confirm this with three reasons: 1. from two passages of the Gospel, Matt. 16:18: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. And John 21:16, 17, 18: Peter, do you love me? Feed my lambs, feed my sheep. The Pontificians conclude from these sayings of Scripture: Therefore the primacy of the whole Church was committed to Peter; but when we look at the text itself, then the sense will appear far otherwise. For Christ, instituting an examination in the preceding verses, moved the question, that the disciples might tell him, whom they thought him to be? To this interrogation Peter answered in his own name and that of his brethren; Thou art the Christ the Son of the living GOD. Upon this rock Christ builds his Church, since no one can lay another foundation, besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 3. v. 10. Here, however, not the person, but the confession of Peter is that foundation upon which the Church leans. If the Church of Christ had been built upon the person of Peter, then certainly it would have stood poorly, when he denied Christ, and furthermore abjured him.

IV. In the other saying, John 21, Christ commanded Peter to feed the sheep and lambs, by the ministry of the Gospel; which itself, however, was not committed to Peter alone, but also to the remaining Apostles; nay, and to all sincere ministers of the Gospel. Since, therefore, to feed the flock of the Lord pertains not to Peter alone, but to all ministers of the Church; the Roman Pontiff cannot, from the fact that Christ commanded Peter to feed the sheep, prove that the prince of the Apostles, and consequently the Pontiff, as successor of the Apostle Peter, was constituted the supreme Monarch of the Church on this earth.

V. Secondly, the Papists name Peter the prince of the Apostles, because he had many privileges and prerogatives above others. Here theologians distinguish, and say that the Primacy is twofold; 1. Of order, when many are equal in office and power, yet one of them holds the first place, and precedes the others, so that in this way the order of place and session may be observed among them. In this sense the holy Fathers often testify that the Apostle Peter was the prince of the rest, and it can be easily conceded by us. 2. Of jurisdiction, when one not only holds the first place, but also has others subject to himself, who also depend upon him, acquiesce in his judgments, and undertake nothing without his will. That Peter neither had nor ever exercised such a primacy over the Apostles, but that all were endowed with equal honor and dignity, we piously believe, constantly teach, and can firmly demonstrate with many arguments. 1. Because Scripture passed over that in silence. 2. Because Peter was sent away in the same manner as the other Apostles, Acts 8. v. 14. 3. Because the Jews expostulated with him, Acts 11. v. 2. 4. Because they unanimously decided controversies, Acts 15. v. 5. 5. Because it was common to all the Apostles inspection, Galat. 1. v. 1. 6. Because Paul resisted him, in that he had been reproved, Galat. 2. v. 11. 7. Because Peter himself forbade lordship over the Apostles, 1. Pet. 5. v. 3. 8. Because they were equal in dignity, 2. Cor. 12. v. 11. 9. Because in the Apostle Paul far more excellent prerogatives shone forth than in Peter.

VI. Thirdly, they wish to prove the same by the most open testimonies of both Latins and Greeks. But since the whole Scripture cries out against it, why is the authority of these men put forward against God? Therefore it is firmly proved from these, that neither was the Apostle Peter the prince of the Apostles, nor can the Pope be named the successor of Peter.

VII. Now follows the second chapter, concerning the years of the ministry. It is declared throughout the Holy Scripture, namely when the ministry was begun by Christ, and when it was completed. When Christ was baptized, he was then nearly thirty years old, which Luke testifies in chapter 3. v. 23. Soon then after the action of Baptism, Christ began to teach and to perform miracles, as stands in Acts chapter 1. v. 21. and 22. During all the time, says the Apostle Peter, in which the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John unto that day that he was taken up from us. And Acts 10. v. 37. Beginning from Galilee after the baptism which John preached, how GOD anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all that were oppressed by the Devil.

VIII. But there is a great controversy, and indeed among some illustrious Theologians, concerning the certain time which intervened from the Baptism of Christ until the day of the ascension, and how that can be distributed into certain years.
