Chemnitz explained this at length in the prolegomena to his Harmony: it is not permitted for us to narrate so broadly: but those things which Chemnitz proposed must be run through briefly. First, he says, the common opinion even among the most ancient was that all those sayings and deeds, which are described in the Evangelical history from the Baptism of Christ until his passion, are to be comprehended within the space of only one year. Chemnitz indicates the assertors and reasons for this opinion, among whom not the least is Tatian the Apostate, formerly a disciple of Justin Martyr, who strove to defend this opinion sharply in his Harmony, so that he concluded all the acts of the public ministry of Christ within the course of one year, and those distinct feasts of the Passover in John 2. v. 13. and chapter 6. v. 4. [he reduced] to that one which is in Matthew 26. v. 2. is described, he joined. Tertullian, in his book against the Jews, also followed him, who openly declared that Christ suffered in the same year in which He had begun His public ministry, and he wished to prove this from Chronography, where he shows that Christ died in the fifteenth year of Tiberius. Augustine, in book 18 of The City of God, chapter 54, seems to agree with the same opinion. Clement of Alexandria also fosters the opinion of these men in book 10 of the Stromata, and confirms these with the saying of Isaiah 61:2. For the Alogians said that they would rather reject John the Evangelist than depart from this opinion concerning the single year of ministry, as Epiphanius testifies.

Latin:

DE Jejunio & Domini nostri Jesu Christi tentatione in deserto facta, in superiori egimus disputatione; qvod nimirum Filius DEI, cùm vix ministerium ingressus esset ingens adierit duellum: non cum regeHerode, qvi capitali odio ipsum in infantia ejus prosequebatur, ita ut patriam relinqvere, & in Ægyptum tanqvam exul fugere cogeretur, Matt. 2. v. 14. Neq; cum Pharisæis & populi primatibus, qvi semper ipsum opugnarunt & doctrinæ ejus contradixerunt, uti ab Evangelistis passim declaratur, sed cum Principe mundi, Joh. 14. v. 29. cum Principe potentiæ aëris, Ephes. 2. v. 2. cum nostro adversario, 1. Pet. 5. v. 8. cum Diabolo, Matth. 4. v. 1. qvem tandem vicit & foràs ejecit, Johnn. 12. v. 31. Hæc victoria à JESU CHRISTO obtenta, & nobis in maximis & periculosissimis tentationibus spem protulit fortissimam: cùm Dux Hebr. 12. v. 2. & triumphator noster factus sit contra fortem istum armatum, Luc. 11. v. 21. Rectè igitur Ambrosius Victoria Domini est triumphus servi. Cùm verò plus qvàm satis in præcedenti de his audiverimus, ad seqventem progredi disputationem ordo nos monet: qvæ de annis ministerii, totoq; Christi agit curriculo, qvod hisce qvinq; capitibus declarabimus, qvorum in primo Ministerii naturam attingemus. In secundo annorum tempus perpendemus: in tertio causam impellentem dicemus: in qvarto finem jungemus: in Qvinto effectum excolemus. Christe ministerii inceptor ductorq, ministrum Nostro tuo sancto Numine corda rege.

Thesis I.

Primum hoc caput, de naturą ministerii multas Papistarum controversias nobis demonstrat; qvarum duas tantùm recensebimus. 1. An Christi ministerium cum regimine Politico & qvadam Monarcha papali conjunctum fuerit? 2. An post visibile Christi ministerium Petrus caput totius Ecclesiæ & princeps loco Christi sit constitutus?

II. Primam hanc qvod attinet qvæstionem, sine ullo dubio Christus suam in hoc terrarum orbe gubernavit Ecclesiam: qvòd verò talem Monarchiam, qvalem venditat Romanus Papa, Christi scilicet Vicarius, incœperit, planè rejicimus. Christus enim non mundanum, sed cœleste habet regnum, ut ipse dicit Joh. 18. v. 36. Regnum meum non de hoc mundo; si de hoc mundo esset, ministri mei certassent. Ex qvo dicto judicare possumus optimè, magnam esse diversitatem inter Christi & Pontificis regnum; unde sic argumentamur: Regnum Christi est spirituale, & non de hoc mundo. Regnum Papæ non est spirituale, sed mundanum, & de hoc mundo. Ergò regnum Papæ non est regnum Christi. Major ex citato loco Joh. 18. prolata est. Minor rursus hoc syllogismo probatur: Qvicunq; jus donandi & gubernandi totas regiones sibi vendicat, is mundanum possidet regnum. Sed Papa tale jus sibi vendicat. Ergò. Unde penè seqvitur, qvòd nec Christi discipulus, multò minùs istius Vicarius nominari qveat. Nam discipuli Christi humiles, non superbi audire volunt, Rom. 12. v. 16. Non arroganter de vobis ipsis sentientes, sed humilibus vos ac commodantes; ne sitis arrogantes apud vos metipsos. Ministri, non domini Matth. 20. 25. Marc. 10. v. 42. Luc. 22. v. 25. Reges gentium dominantur iis, & qui potestatem habent super eas, benefici vocantur. Vos autem non sic. Spirituales, non mundani; Joh. 15. v. 19. Et si de mundo fuissetis, mundus qvod suum est, diligeret: sed non fuistis de mundo. Ego enim elegi vos ex mundo; propterea odit vos mundus. Hic satis videmus, qvàm magna inter Christi & Papæ regnum differentia sit. Firmissima ergò est conclusio nostra: Christum more Papali monarcham non fuisse; sed qvantum cœlum ab infimis terrarum partibus distat, tantùm inter utrumq; discrimen intercessisse, & adhuc intercedere.

III. Deinde Apostolum Petrum, tanqvam totius Ecclesiæ caput, & omnium ministrorum principem, loco Christi ab ipso Christo esse constitutum, Papiculæ blaterant, & tribus hoc rationibus confirmare conantur, 1. ex duobus locis Evangelii Matth. 16. v. 18. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo meam Ecclesiam. Et Joh. 21. v. 16. 17. 18. Petre diligis me, pasce agnos meos, pasce oves meas. Concludunt ex his Scripturæ dictis Pontificii: Ergo principatus totius Ecclesiæ Petro est comissus; sed qvondo ipsum textum intuemur, tunc sensus longè alius apparebit. Christus enim in præcedentibus examen instituens, qvæstionem movebat, sibi ut discipuli dicerent, qvemnam se esse putarent? Huic interrogationi Petrus suo & fratrum nomine respondit; Tu es Christus Filius DEI viventis. Super hanc petram ædificat Ecclesiam suam Christus, cùm aliud fundamentum nemo possit ponere, præter hoc, qvod positum est, quod est Jesus Christus, 1. Cor. 3. v. 10. Hîc autem non persona, sed confessio Petri est fundamentum illud, cui innititur Ecclesia. Si Christi Ecclesia supra presonam Petri ædificata esset, tunc certè malè stetisset, cùm ille Christum abnegaret, & insuper abjuraret.

IV. In altero dicto Joh. 21. Christus oves & agnos pascere Petrum jussit, ministerio Evangelii; qvod ipsum tamen non soli Petro commissum est, sed reliqvis etiam Apostolis; imò & omnibus sinceris Evangelii ministris. Cùm igitur pascere gregem Domini non soli Petro, sed omnibus Ecclesiæ ministris competat; non potest Pontifex Romanus ex eo, qvod Christus Petrum jussit pascere oves, probare, qvod princeps Apostolorum, & per conseqvens Pontifex, tanqvam successor Apostoli Petri, fuerit summus Monarcha Ecclesiæ in his terris constitutus.

V. Secundò, Petrum principem Apostolorum Pontificii nominant, qvia multa privilegia, & prærogativas habuit præ aliis. Hîc Theologi distinguunt, & Primatum esse duplicem dicunt; 1. Ordinis, qvando multi in officio & potestate pares sunt, unus tamen eorum primum tenet locum, & reliqvos precedit, ut ita inter istos loci & sessionis ordo servetur. Hoc sensu Apostolum Petrum reliquorum fuisse principem, sancti Patres sæpe testantur, & à nobis facilè concedi potest. 2. Juris dictionis, qvando unus non modo primum tenet locum, sed & alios sibi habet subjectos, qui etiam ab ipso dependent, ejus indiciis acqviescunt, & sine ipsius voluntate nihil suscipiunt. Talem primatum super Apostolos Petrum nec habuisse, nec unqvam exerciuisse, sed omnes pari honore & dignitate fuisse præditos, piè credimus, constanter docemus, & multis argumentis firmiter demonstrare possumus. 1. Qvia Scriptura silentio id præteriit. 2. Qvia Petrus eodem modo, ut alii Apostoli, ablegatus est, Act. 8. v. 14. 3. Qvia Judæi cum ipso expostularunt, Act. 11. v. 2. 4. Qvia unanimiter controversias deciderunt, Act. 15. v. 5. 5. Qvia omnibus Apostolis communis fuit inspectio, Galat. 1. v. 1. 6. Qvia Paulus ipsi restitit, eò, quòd reprehensus esset, Galat. 2. v. 11. 7. Qvia Petrus ipse dominium adversus Apostolos prohibuit, 1. Pet. 5. v. 3. 8. Qvia pares fuerunt dignitate, 2. Cor. 12. v. 11. 9. Qvia in Apostolo Paulo longè præstantiores emicuerunt prærogativæ, quàm in Petro.

VI. Tertiò, Idem apertissimis tam Latinorum, quàm Græcorum testimoniis probare volunt. Sed cùm reclamet tota Scriptura, quid istorum authoritas adversus Deum prætenditur? Firmiter ergò ex his probatum, nec Apostolum Petrum fuisse principem Apostolorum, nec Papam successorem Petri nominari posse.

VII. Seqvitur nunc caput secundum, de annis ministerii. Passim in sacra Scriptura declaratur, qvando nimirum ministerium à Christo inchoatum, & qvando absolutum. Baptizato Christo, tunc fermè triginta habuit annos, qvod Lucas testatur cap. 3. v. 23. Mox dein post Baptismatis actionem incepit Christus docere & miracula edere, ut in Actis cap. 1. v. 21. & 22. extat. Toto, inqvit Apostolus Petrus, tempore, in qvo ingressus & egressus inter nos est Dominus Jesus, incipiens à Baptismo Johannis usque ad illam diem, quo sumptus est à nobis. Et Act. 10. v. 37. Incipiens à Galilæa post Baptismum, quem prædicavit Johannes, ut Jesum Nazarenum unxerit DEUS Spiritu sancto & virtute, qui obambulavit benefaciendo & sanando omnes oppressos à Diabolo.

VIII. Sed magna, & qvidem inter nonnullos præclaros Theologos, est controversia, de certo tempore, qvod intervenit à Christi Baptismate usq; ad diem ascensionis, & qvomodo istud in certos distribui possit annos. Fusè Chemn. in proleg. Harm hoc explicuit: nobis non tam latè narrare licitum est: sed brevibus ea, quæ Chemn. proposuit, percurrenda sunt. Primùm, Vulgarem opinionem etiam apud vetustissimos fuisse, inqvit, omnia illa dicta & facta, quæ in Evangelica historia, à Baptismo Christi usque ad passionem ejus describuntur, unius tantùm anni spatio esse comprehendenda. Hujus opinionis assertores & rationes Chemn. indicat, inter qvos non ultimus est Tacianus Apostata, olim Justini Martyris discipulus, qvi acriter hanc opinionem defendere in Harm. sua studuit, ita ut omnia acta publici ministerii Christi, intra curriculum unius anni concluserit, & distincta ista festa Paschatos Joh. 2. v. 13. & cap. 6. v. 4. unico isti, qvod Matth. 26. v. 2. describitur, conjunxerit. Hunc deinde etiam secutus Tertullianus in lib. contra Judæos, qui Christum esse passum eodem anno, quo publicum inchoaverat ministerium, palàm protulit, & hoc ex Chronographia probare voluit, ubi ostendit Christum esse mortuum anno Tiberii decimo qvinto. Eidem sententiæ Augustinus in lib. 18. de civitate Dei, cap. 54. assentiri videtur. Horum etiam opinionem lib. 10. Stromatum Clemens Alex. fovet, hasq́; confirmat dicto Es. 61. v. 2. Alogiani enim dixerunt, se malle potius Johannem Evangelistam rejicere, quam ab hac sententia de unico anno ministerii, discedere, teste Epiphanio.


### IX. We, however, reject all those men and their followers, and we imitate that…

IX. We, however, reject all those men and their followers, and we imitate that order which John the Evangelist observed in his Gospel. He distinguished the time of Christ's ministry into three certain years, since he numbered several Passovers which fell within the time of Christ's ministry. The first, namely, which is described in John 2:13, after the miracle performed in Cana. The second, which is described in John 5:1, concerning which feast, however, there was and is a great dispute, both among the ancients and among the moderns. Chrysostom, Cyril, and Epiphanius do not wish this second feast (of which mention is made in John 5:1) to be the Passover, but Pentecost, to whom Chemnitz rightly opposed himself. We do not deny, he says in the preface to the Harmony, that individual years between one Passover and the next following had other, several feasts according to the Law: but because the times of each feast are certainly noted, Leviticus 23:15 and following, Deuteronomy 16:1. It will be easily gathered what should be thought. In the preceding chapter, verse 35, it is said that Christ came again from Judea into Galilee, before the following feast, of which the Evangelist makes mention in the following chapter. For it is expressly stated that Christ said to His disciples, 'There are yet four months, and then comes the harvest.' Now, in that region there were two harvests between Passover and Pentecost, namely, the barley and the wheat: which were begun after the Passover was finished, and were completed around Pentecost.

X. But since those two harvests were approaching, which can be proven from the fourth chapter; it necessarily follows that this was no other feast than the Passover: since the Israelites had been commanded by the Lord, Exodus 34:22, Leviticus 23:10, to bring a sheaf of the fruits and the firstfruits of the wheat harvest to the priest, who shall wave that sheaf of fruits before Jehovah. But this was done on the 16th day of the month Abib, which day is the second from the Passover. For on the fourteenth day of Abib the Jews celebrated the Passover, since on the same day they had gone out of Egypt, Exod. 13. v. 4. We therefore rightly conclude now that this feast cannot be Pentecost, which followed immediately in the first year of Christ's ministry: but it was the second Passover: which if it were joined to the first Passover, would constitute the whole year which Christ completed in his ministry. Many other things could be referred to here, but we refer the attentive reader to the Harm. Chemn., who has treated these matters at greater length.

XI. Now the third Passover follows, which is described in John 6. v. 4. This third solemn feast demonstrates the second year of Christ's ministry, and at the same time proves that Christ had already performed his office for two years: The fourth Passover is described in John 13. v. 1, in which Christ was affixed to the cross, and completes the third year. Chemnitius recounts that this last feast was omitted by Irenaeus. For in the third, in which Christ performed the miracle of the five loaves, Irenaeus thought that he himself was crucified. But it is evident that Irenaeus inconsiderately made one out of these two twin feasts of different years. For it is manifest that two feasts intervened between the Passover of John ch. 6. v. 4 and that Passover in which Christ was crucified: one of Tabernacles in ch. 7. v. 2 and another of the Dedication in ch. 10. v. 22. Thus four Passovers have been numbered by John the Evangelist, and not three, as Irenaeus thinks; and so Christ was in his ministry for three years, and began the fourth year, but did not complete it: whence Nicephorus says, he did not yet complete the whole four-year period. Luther and others wished to make this agree with the prophecy of Daniel ch. 9. v. 27. He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: but in the middle of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease. We pass over these things, however, and betake ourselves to other matters.

XII. Now follows the third chapter, which treats of the impelling cause. Christ undertook his ministry for four reasons: first, to satisfy the will of his Father: second, to fulfill prophecy: third, to propagate doctrine and remove errors: fourth, to make us certain of deliverance and redemption.

XIII. The will of the Father is made known from the Gospel, both as to what He has decreed in His eternal counsel concerning us, as far as it pertains to eternal salvation; and what He willed Christ to perform, namely, that he should teach, and preach the Gospel concerning the clemency and mercy of the heavenly Father toward the human race, to miserable mortals, so terrified by GOD, and oppressed by the mass of sins by the curse of the Law, and that he should raise them up on the last day; then what He requires of us, namely, that we repent, and believe in Christ. John 6. v. 38. 39. & 40. Matt. 3. v. 2. Mark 1. v. 15. Rightly therefore from theseling.

XIV. Furthermore, it was also necessary that Christ should enter upon his ministry, with respect to Prophecy. For thus the Prophet Isaiah prophesied concerning him, ch. 61, 1. The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon me, because Jehovah has anointed me to preach the gospel, he has sent me to bind up the broken-hearted: to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound. But since Christ was impelled by the Holy Spirit, he presided over the ministry, by which he might fulfill this prophecy spoken by Isaiah, since he himself came not to destroy the Law and the Prophets, but to fulfill them, Matt. 5. v. 17. Hence Christ says, that it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away, than for one apex of the Law to fall. Luke 16. 17.

XV. Thirdly, Christ undertook the ministry, in order to propagate doctrine, and to lead the people away from that error into which they had fallen: partly which they had begun concerning John the Baptist; partly which they had drawn from the false interpretation of doctrine put forth by the Scribes and Pharisees.

XVI. Fourthly, he willed to perform the ministry with respect to us. For just as he was born for the human race, died for our sins, and was raised for our justification: so also he undertook the ministry for our sake; so that we might be certain of our liberation and our redemption, since the son of man did not come to be ministered unto, but to minister himself, and to give his life as a redemption for many. Mark 10. v. 45. For Christ by ministering obtained salvation for us: wherefore Christ came to minister to us, that is, to repair again the lost salvation.

XVII. In this fourth chapter the end is to be declared to us, why Christ performed such a ministry. By this end three reasons are chiefly indicated, the first is the reason of instituting disciples. The second is the reason of working in ministers. The third is the reason of going before others with good examples.

XVIII. And first indeed, while he was in office, Christ spoke many things to his disciples, which they could not perceive with their mind, as Joh. 16. 18. They themselves confess. What is this, they say, that he says, we do not know what he is speaking about. Here we must diligently observe the weakness of the human mind, how blind it is in those most subtle mysteries of faith, about which it judges nothing certain, nor is human reason able to understand them. Whence 1 Cor. 2. v. 14. the natural man is said not to be capable of those things which are of the Spirit of GOD: for they are foolishness, nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. The disciples themselves lacked such perfect gifts, for which reason they had need of the instruction of Christ (who at that time was visibly conversing with them on earth), until the Holy Spirit should be sent to enlighten them.

XIX. Furthermore, Christ also presided over the ministry by reason of the manner of working in the ministers. Not only did those great works performed in this world (by which he was made manifest) seem sufficient to Christ: but also, after his glorious ascension, when he had bid farewell to this world, he wished to be made manifest by those miracles which he performed through his disciples. For the Apostles performed many miracles in their ministry, which they attributed in no way to their own virtues or human industry, but to divine goodness and power; by which they were rendered fit for explaining and teaching the Gospel, and for performing such great miracles, as stands in Mark 16. v. last. But in truth, this happened not only in the time of the Apostles; but it also happens daily to the ministers of the word in our time, that Christ is present with them, and works through the Holy Spirit, according to his promise in Matt. 28. v. 20. Behold I am with you, even to the end of the age.

XX. Thirdly, Christ entered upon the ministry by reason of going before others with good examples. Christ went before us with four examples in particular. First, he was candid and true in teaching, because he had the words of eternal life, John 6. v. 68. and he taught the truth, John 18. v. 37. We must also study this truth diligently, 1. Because it is commanded to us by GOD, Zech. 8. v. 18. Speak the truth. 2. Because by it we are especially like GOD, who is most truthful, nay, is truth itself, John 14. v. 6. I am the way and the truth and the life. 3. Because Christ went before us with his example in this, John 7. v. 7. therefore he testified of the world, that its works are evil. 4. Because others who are pious also invite us to the same by their example. 5. Because it is a testimony of true ingenuousness, which loves the light, and in no way fears it, John 3. v. 21.

He who devotes effort to the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, that they have been done according to GOD. Whence truth is a test for the ministers of human doctrines and opinions, as in all disciplines, so especially in religion, that they may be tested against the Canon of our Judge and Lawgiver GOD; lest anything be added or taken away. II. He was constant in confessing, because before the Jews He constantly confessed His doctrine, John 8. v. 51. In this also we ought to imitate Christ, when the confession of religion is demanded, it must necessarily be shown, whether they be friends or enemies who demand it. III. He was just in living. The same we shall embrace, lest we offer scandals to others, but strive to live piously and justly. IV. Finally, He was humble in ministering, John 13. v. 4. Upon this example we must studiously apply ourselves, that in the same way we may be imitators of Christ. Behold, for the creator of all things, to whom the whole world ought to have ministered, He ministered to us. O wonderful, pleasant, sweet thing! Why then are we ashamed to be humble? If Christ was not ashamed, whose imitators we ought to be. Although not in every single thing, yet let us strive most greatly to imitate His humility. For we do not wish to imitate Christ in such a way that we do not simultaneously wish to admire Him: For let us imitate Christ, as disciples their master, as servants their lord, as men their GOD, not perfectly, but according to our measure, as Nazianzen hints.

XXI. It remains for us finally to consider the effect of the ministry of Christ, which is contained in healing and performing miracles.

XXII. Christ is named in Scripture the true physician, who does not sit idle in His ministry, but cured the souls of men through the Gospel, and healed those wounds inflicted by the Devil in the fall of our first parents.

XXIII. This healing consists in the remission of sins, which is the effect of doctrine, as is to be seen in Matthew 9. v. 2: there He freed the paralytic not only from an external disease, but also from an internal disease, and restored to him complete health of both body and soul.

XXIV. Furthermore, He also confirmed His doctrine in His ministry with miracles, so that they might be as seals of doctrine and faith. For Christ worked miracles in His ministry for four reasons. 1. That He might demonstrate Himself to be the true Messiah sent by the Father into this world. 2. That He might prove that he is the true GOD, and of the same essence with GOD the Father and the Holy Spirit. 3. That he might prove that power had been given to him to remit sins. 4. That he might declare what bodily and spiritual benefits he himself bestows and gives to us. And thus we finish this disputation, and we ask Christ, the supreme Teacher, who entered upon his ministry and began to teach the topic of repentance, that he may give us new obedience, and to live according to his will. May the most kind Lord also grant that the greatest part of the ministers and preachers of the divine word may be such as build up and propagate his kingdom with great utility and fruit, by which the number of Christians may increase to the glory of his divinity and to the salvation of men. Amen.

Latin:

IX. Nos autem omnes istos istorumq́; asseclas rejicimus, ordinemq́; istum, quem Johannes Evangelista in suo observavit Evangelio, imitamur. Distinxit ille tempus ministerii Christi in tres certos annos, cùm aliqvot Paschata numerarit, quæ in tempus ministerii Christi inciderunt. Primum scilicet, quod describitur Joh. 2. v. 13. post miraculum in Cana editum. Alterum quod describitur Joh. 5. v. 1. de quo tamen festo magnum fuit & est certamen, tàm apud priscos, qvàm apud recentes. Chrysostomus, Cyrillus & Epiphanius hoc secundum festum (cujus sit mentio Joh. 5. v. 1.) non volunt esse Pascha, sed Pentecosten, quibus sese meritò opposuit Chemn. Nos non negamus, inquit in præfatione Harm. singulos annos inter unum Pascha & proximè seqvens, habuisse alia plura festa juxta Legem: sed quia cujuscunque festi tempora certò notata sunt, Levit. 23. v. 15. & seq. Deut. 16. v. 1. Facilè quid sentiendum sit colligi poterit. In præcedenti capite v. 35. dicitur, Christus rursum ex Judæa in Galilæam venisse, ante seqvens festum, cujus in seqvente Evangelista meminit capite. Expressè enim ponitur, quòd Christus discipulis suis dixerit, adhuc quatuor menses sunt, & messis veniet: Jam verò in ista regione duæ erant messes intra Pascha & Pentecosten, hordeacea scil. & triticea: quæ finito paschate inchoatæ, & circa Pentecosten absolutæ sunt.

X. Cùm autem istæ duæ messes instarent, quæ ex qvarto capite possunt probari; necessariò seqvitur, hoc non aliud fuisse festum qvàm Paschatis: cùm Israëlitæ à Domino erant jussi, Exod. 34. v. 22. Levit. 23. v. 10. Manipulum frugum afferre & primitias Messis triticeæ sacerdoti, qui agitabit manipulum istum frugum coram Jehovah. Hoc verò est factum die 16. mensis Abib, qui dies est à Paschate secundus. Nam decimoqvarto die Abib Judæi Pascha celebrarunt, cùm eodem die exiissent ex Ægypto, Exod. 13. v. 4. Rectè igitur jam concludimus, hoc festum non posse esse Pentecosten, quæ proximè primo, anno Christi ministerii secuta sit: sed secundum fuit Pascha: qvod si primo Paschati adjungeretur, totum constitueret annum, qvem Christus in ministerio absolvit. Multa alia possent huc referri, sed remittimus attentum lectorem ad Harm. Chemn. qvi de his egit prolixiùs.

XI. Nunc tertium sequitur Pascha, qvod describitur Joh. 6. v. 4. Hoc tertium solenne festum secundum ministerii Christi annum demonstrat, simul & probat Christum jam duos annos suo perfunctum esse officio: Qvartum Pascha Joh. 13. v. 1. describitur, in qvo Christus cruci affixus est, & tertium implet annum. Ultimum hoc festum ab Irenæo omissum esse recenset Chemnitius. Tertio n. in qvo Christus miraculum qvinq; panum edebat, Irenæus arbitratus est, ipsum esse crucifixum. Sed inconsideratè Irenæu ex geminis istis festis diversorum annorum unum effecisse, apertum est. Duo enim intra Pascha. Joh. cap. 6. v. 4. & inter illud Pascha, in qvo Christus crucifixus est, intercessisse festa: alterum Tabernaculorum cap. 7. v. 2. & alterum Encæniorum cap. 10. v. 22. manifestè apparet. Sic qvatuor Paschata à Johanne Evangelista numerata sunt, & non tria, ut Irenæus putat; & ita Christus triennium in ministerio fuit, & qvartum annum incepit, sed non complevit: unde Nicephorus inqvit, nondum implevit totum qvadriennium. Hoc convenire voluit Lutherus & alii cum Prophetia Danielis cap. 9. v. 27. Corroboravit quidem fœdus multis septimanavna: sed in medio septimanæ ipsius abolebit sacrificium & munus. Mittimus verò hæc, & ad alia nos conferimus.

XII. Seqvitur nunc tertium caput, qvod de causa agit impellente. Christus ministerium subivit qvatuor ob causas, primò, ut voluntati Patris sui satisfaceret: Secundò, ut Prophetiam impleret: Tertiò, ut doctrinam propageret, & errores adimeret: qvartò, ut nos deliberatione & redemptione certos faceret.

XIII. Voluntas Patris ex Evangelio innotescit, tum qvid de nobis, qvod ad salutem æternam attinet, in æterno consilio suo decreverit; tum qvid Christum præstare voluerit, nempè, ut doceret, & Evangelium de clementia & misericordia Patris cœlestis erga genus humanum, miseris mortalibus, ita DEI perterritis, & mole peccatorum a maledictione Legis oppressis prædicaret, illosq; in ultimo die suscitaret; tum quid a nobis reqvirat, nempe, ut resipiscamus, & credamus in Christum. Joh. 6. v. 38. 39. & 40. Matth. 3. v. 2. Mar. 1. v. 15. Recte ergo ex his concludi potest, qvod Christus volente DEO Patre ministerio functus est.

XIV. Deinde etiam opus erat, ut ministerium Christus ingrederetur, respectu Prophetiæ. Nam ita Propheta Esaias de illo vaticinatus est, c. 61, 1. Spiritus Domini Jehova super me, eo, qvod unxit Jehova me ad evangelizandum, misit me ad obligandum fractos animos: ad proclamandum captivis libertatem, & vinctis aperturam ergastuli. Cum autem a Spiritu sancto Christus impelleretur, ministerio præfuit, qvo vaticinium hoc ab Esaia dictum impleret, qvandoqvidem ipse non ad destruendam Legem & Prophetas, sed ad implendam venit Mat. 5. v. 17. Hinc Christus, facilius esse, inquit, cœlum & terram præterire, qvam Legis unum apicem excidere. Luc. 16. 17.

XV. Tertio, Christus ministerium suscepit, ut doctrinam propagaret, & populum ab illo errore, in qvem inciderat, abduceret: partim qvem de Johanne Baptista cœperat; partim qvem ex falsa doctrinæ interpretatione a Scribis & Pharisæis prolata, hauserat.

XVI. Qvarto, ministerio fungi voluit respectu nostri. Ut enim propter humanum genus natus, propter peccata nostra mortuus, & propter justitiam nostram resuscitatus est: sic qvoq; propter nos ministerium suscepit; qvo certi essemus de liberatione, nostraq; redemptione, qvandoqvidem filius hominis non venit, ut sibi ministraretur, sed ut ipse ministraret, ac daret animam suam redemptionem pro multis. Marci 10. v. 45. Christus enim ministrando nobis salutem adeptus est: qvare venit Christus ad ministrandum nobis, hoc est, ad salutem perditam iterum reparandam.

XVII. In qvarto hoc capite finis nobis est declarandus, cur Christus tali ministerio sit functus. Hoc fine tres præcipue indicantur rationes, prima est ratio instituendi discipulos. Secunda ratio operandi in ministris. Tertia ratio præeundi aliis bonis exemplis.

XVIII. Ac primum qvidem multa Christus cum in officio esset, discipulis suis est locutus, qvæ mente percipere non potuerunt, ut Joh. 16. 18. ipsi fatentur. Quid hoc est, ajunt, quod dicit, nescimus quid loquatur. Hic nobis diligenter humana mentis imbecilitas observanda est, quàm cœca ista sit in subtilissimis istis fidei mysteriis, de quibus nihil certi judicat, neq; ea intelligere humana valet ratio. Unde 1. Cor. 2. v. 14. Animalis homo dicitur, non esse capax eorum, quæ sunt Spiritus DEI: sunt enim stultitia, nec potest ea cognoscere, quia spiritualiter dijudicantur. Talibus perfectis donis etiam discipuli caruerunt, quapropter Christi (qui tum temporis visibiliter in terra cum istis versabatur) instructione opus habuerunt, donec Spiritus sanctus mitteretur ad illuminandos istos.

XIX. Deinde etiam ratione operandi in ministris Christus ministerio præerat. Non tantùm magna ista opera in hoc mundo edita (quibus clarescebat) sufficere Christo videbantur: sed etiam, post gloriosam ascensionem, cum huic valedixisset mundo, istis miraculis, quæ per discipulos suos operabatur, clarescere volebat. Nam multa Apostoli in ministerio ediderunt miracula, quæ minimè virtutibus suis propriis aut humanæ industriæ, sed divinæ bonitati & potentiæ attribuerunt; quâ idonei sunt redditi ad explicandum & docendum Evangelium, & ad edenda tanta miracula, uti in Marc. 16. v. ult. extat. Verùm enim verò hoc non solùm tempore Apostolorum accidit; sed etiam nostro tempore verbi ministris qvotidie id evenit, ut Christus illis adsit, & per Spiritum sanctum operetur, juxta suam promissionem Matth. 28. v. 20. Ecce ego vobiscum sum, usq; ad consummationem seculi.

XX. Tertiò, Christus ministerium ingrediebatur ratione præcundi aliis bonis exemplis. Qvatuor præcipuè exemplis nobis Christus præivit. Primò, candidus & verus fuit in docendo, quia vitæ æternæ verba habuit, Joh. 6. v. 68. & veritatem docuit. Joh. 18. v. 37. Huic veritati est & nobis studendum sedulò, 1. Qvia mandata est nobis à DEO Zach. 8. v. 18. Loquimini veritatem. 2. Qvia ea præcipuè sumus similes DEO, qui veracissimus, imò veritas ipsa est, Joh. 14. v. 6. Ego sum via & veritas & vita. 3. Qvia illius exemplo nobis Christus præivit, Joh. 7. v. 7. propterea testatus est de mundo, opera ejus mala esse. 4. Qvia ad eandem alii quoq; pii exemplo nos suo invitant. 5. Qvia Testimonium est veræ ingenuitatis, quæ lucem amat, ac neqvaqvam reformidat, Joh. 3. v. 21.

Qui dat operam veritati, venit ad lucem, ut manifesta fiant opera ipsius, quod secundum DEUM facta fuerint. Unde veritas ministris est examen doctrinarum & sententiarum humanarum, ut in omnibus disciplinis, ita in primis in religione, ut illæ probentur ad Canonem Judicis & Legislatoris nostri DEI; ne aliquid addatur & auferatur. II. Constans fuit in confitendo, quia coram Judæis suam doctrinam constanter confessus est, Joh. 8. v. 51. In hoc quoq; Christum nos imitari debemus, quando confessio religionis postulatur, necessariò est odenda, sive amici sint, sive hostes, qui eam postulant. III. Fuit justus in vivendo. Idem nos amplectemur, ne aliis scandala præbeamus, sed piè & justè vivere studeamus. IV. Deniq; humilis fuit in ministrando, Joh. 13. v. 4. Huic exemplo est nobis incumbendum studiosè, ut eodem modo Christi simus imitatores. Ecce enim omnium rerum creatorem, cui totus orbis administrare debuit, is nobis administravit. O rem mirabilem, suavem, dulcem! Quid ergò erubescimus humiles esse? si Christus non erubuit, cujus imitatores esse debemus. Licet non in singulis, tamen humilitatem ejus imitari maximè studeamus. Nam nos non volumus Christum ita imitari, ut non simul eum admirari velimus: Imitemur enim Christum, ut discipuli magistrum, ut servi dominum, ut homines DEUM, non perfectè, sed promodulo nostro, ut Nazianz. innuit.

XXI. Effectum ministerii Christi ultimò considerare nobis restat, qui sanando & miracula edendo continetur.

XXII. Christus in Scriptura verus nominatur medicus, qui non otiosus in ministerio sedet, sed hominum animas per Evangelium curavit, & istorum vulnera à Diabolo in lapsu nostrorum primorum parentum inflicta sanavit.

XXIII. Hæc sanatio consistit in remissione peccatorum, quæ effectus est doctrinæ, uti Matth. 9. v. 2. videndum: ibi paralyticum non solùm à morbo externo, sed etiam à morbo interno liberavit & integram sanitatem tàm corporis quàm animæ ipsi restituit.

XXIV. Deinde etiam doctrinam suam in ministerio confirmavit miraculis, ut tanquam sigilla essent doctrinæ & fidei. Nam quatuor ob causas Christus miracula in ministerio operatus est. 1. Ut demonstraret se esse verum Messiam à Patre in hunc mundum missum. 2. Ut probaret, se verum esse DEUM, ejusdemq; essentiæ cum DEO Patre & Spiritu sancto. 3. Ut comprobaret, sibi datam esse potestatem remittendi peccata. 4. Ut declararet, quæ beneficia corporalia & spiritualia nobis ipse largiatur & donet. Atq; sic finimus hanc disputationem, Christumq; summum Doctorem, qui ministerium ingressus est, & locum de pœnitentia docere incepit, rogamus, ut nobis novam det obedientiam, & juxta suam voluntatem vivere. Concedat qvoqve benignissimus Dominus, ut maxima pars ministrorum & verbi divini concionatorum sit, qui regnum suum magno usu & fructu ædificent ac propagent, quo numerus Christianorum accrescat ad numinis sui gloriam & ad hominum salutem. Amen.


## 34 Thirty-fourth Disputation, On the Doctrine of Christ

PREFACE.

Since the life and doctrine of Christ cohere with one another in a golden and most tight chain, the exposition of his doctrine deservedly follows the description of his life. But how variously do heretics turn their horns against this divine wisdom of his? The Pelagians thought that men before the Law given by Moses had been justified by the law of nature; after that time by the law of Moses; and finally by the new law, that is, of Christ. The Papists assert that Christ, besides precepts, also gave counsels of perfection. (Bellarm. Tom. 2. l. 2. de Mon. c. 7.) The Photinians follow these, in whose footsteps the Anabaptists also to some extent tread, who variously distinguish and describe the doctrine of Christ. Smalcius (in Cateches. Racov. c. 1. de offic. Prophet. p. 155.) says that it consists in the new covenant which Christ struck with us in the name of GOD, and he thinks that this concerns two things: 1. Concerning those things which pertain to GOD, 2. Concerning those things which pertain to men, where he posits faith; but he says that the former consists again: 1. in the perfection of moral precepts and the addition of new ones, 2. in perfect promises which were offered to no one in the O.T., such as eternal life and the gift of the H.S., as appears from Smalcius. (Catech. Racov. c. 5. de offic. Prophet. p. 232.) But how many errors are heaped together here? How many fallacies? They would require a most extensive treatment. But since the time limit for writing the theses for the preceding Respondents has... fixed, and to be observed by me, I shall provide the primary heads of the matters included in these three sections, intending to treat 1. of the doctrine of Christ, whether it is new? 2. Whether Christ perfected the moral Law? 3. What he added anew?

SECTION I.

I. But before all things it must be considered that the doctrine of Christ is not accepted here γενικῶς [generally], so as to include also the Law; for it will be treated in the second section; but εἰδικῶς [specifically], for the preaching concerning the gratuitous promise of the remission of sins, of righteousness, and of eternal life on account of Christ. And this is that doctrine which the Photinians dream did not pertain to the Fathers of the O.T., and therefore is new. Since this opinion is manifestly false, we shall confirm the negative with most certain foundations.

II. Firstly, because it sounded in paradise, Gen. 3, 15. Calvin dissents here without cause, who expounds the seed of the woman collectively concerning all men. For there are other passages besides this where this phrase is taken individually, Gen. 4, 25. Gen. 21, 13. But that this is the meaning of this passage is evident from the fact that no one under the sun could crush the head of the serpent, Ps. 49, 8, other than the Messiah alone, 1 John 3, 8. Col. 2, 15. He, however, is a singular person and existing individually.

III. Therefore the institution of the Papists is impious, who, against the truth of the Hebrew copies, understand the Blessed Mary by the Crusher of the serpent's head. For the verb of the masculine gender יְשׁוּפְךָ [he shall crush] is expressly added, and the relative suffix of the same gender to the verb תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ [you shall crush his], namely his heel; not to mention the version of Onkelos and the LXX Interpreters. Gesnerus (in c. 3. Gen. qvæst. 19.) Furthermore, by the head of the serpent is not understood a natural serpent, but that great Dragon, Apoc. 20, 2, because (1) he was able to speak to the woman. (3) to understand the words of the Lord cursing, which otherwise would have been in vain, and (4) he seduced Eve, 2 Cor. 11, 3. From which it appears that in this saying is found the most effective consolation against the furies of the Devil and death, which can be nothing other than the doctrine concerning Christ.

IV. Secondly, because it was known before the Law was promulgated (1) in clear letter, Gen. 12, 3. But what kind of blessing was that? Certainly not charitable, as pleases the Rabbis and Calvin. For who will prove that this custom of blessing in the name of Abraham prevailed in the whole world. Not priestly, nor patriarchal, on account of the universality of the thing and the speaker

GOD. Therefore it must needs be divine and purely gracious. Wherefore the cause of this universal blessing must be inquired into further. It could not reside in Abraham. For he was an idolater. Nothing else therefore remains but the promised Messiah, in whom all nations were to be blessed, Gal. 3, 14, 16. for which cause this promise is also repeated Gen. 22, 18. (2) The doctrine of Christ was also known from the sighs of Eve, Gen. 4, 1. of Lamech c. 5, 29. of Jacob Gen. 49, 18. (3) From types, Abel being killed Gen. 4, 8. Isaac being offered Gen. 22, 10. Joseph being sold Gen. 37, 28. cast into prison, chap. 39, 12. liberated, chap. 41, 14. (4) From the vision of Jacob's ladder, which is applied to Christ, John c. 1, 52.

V. Thirdly, after the Law was promulgated (1) from the clear letter Hab. 2, 4. For the instrumental cause of our justification is described there, namely faith; 2. the meritorious, the promised Messiah, whose merit applied by faith was also effective in the Old Testament; 3. the reward is promised, eternal life, all of which agree most exactly with the doctrine of Christ. (2) From the sighs of the Fathers, Ps. 14, 7. 2 Sam. 23, 15. (3) From types, both personal, Aaron Exod. 28, 29. Hebr. 9, 12. Samson, Jud. 15, 12. Matth. 27, v. 2. and real; the mercy seat, Exod. 25, 17. the scapegoat, Levit. 16, 2. the paschal lamb, Exod. 12, 6.

VI. Fourthly, Because the Fathers were justified and saved through it, Acts 4, 12. Nor does the exception of Socinus (de Servatore p. 91) hold, that this prophecy must be restricted to the time of the New Testament, because no mention is made of past time. For what else is contained under the word δεδομένον, than the inclusion of past time? 2. even if it could have been proven that the past is not read in the text, Socinus would still conclude nothing against us. For Scripture very often expresses universals and perpetual things in the present tense, to intimate their immutability, Rom. 2, 11. But that such is held in this saying is clear from Hebr. 13, 8. Apoc. 14, 6. and from the general rule of justifying, Rom. 4, 3. Hebr. 11, 4. Socinus objects (2) that the article ἡ is added to the noun σωτηρία, to indicate a new and unheard-of thing. But on what foundation? None. If you doubt, look at Acts 27, 34. Rom. 11, 11. and the truth will appear. And this opinion of ours concerning the justification of the Fathers is also confirmed by the saying Acts 10, 43. Acts 15, 11. Whence it is necessarily concluded that the doctrine of Christ is not new,

Nn 2

VII. Fifth, our negative is proved from the practice of Christ, who cited the writings of the O.T. To what end, if not to show that his doctrine was not born today or yesterday, and therefore that they should believe him? For he writes expressly (1) in John 5.46 that Moses wrote of him; and in Luke 24.25 he rebukes the disciples walking to the village of Emmaus because they had not believed those things which were written of him in Moses and the Prophets. He also seriously commands them to search the Scriptures, which at that time were none other than the O.T., and (2) adds the end, that they might obtain eternal life. Which counsel Paul followed in Acts 26.22 in teaching.

Latin:

PRÆLOQVIUM.

CUm aureâ arctissimaq; inter se cohæreant catenâ, vita & doctrina Christi, meritò vitæ descriptionem seqvitur doctrinæ ipsius expositio. Sed qvàm varii huic divinæ sapientiæ suæ cornua obvertunt Hæretici? Pelagiani existimarunt, homines antè Legem à Mose latam justficatos fuisse Lege naturæ; post illud tempus lege Mosis; tandem verò Lege nova, id est Christi. Pontificii asserunt, Christum præter præcepta etiam dedisse consilia perfectionis. (Bellarm. Tom. 2. l. 2. de Mon. c. 7.) Hos seqvuntur Photiniani, qvorum vestigia etiam aliqvatenus premunt Anabaptistæ, qvi doctrinam Christi variè distinguunt & describunt. Smalcius (in Cateches. Racov. c. 1. de offic. Prophet. p. 155.) dicit, eam consistere in novo fœdere, qvod Christus in nomine DEI nobiscum pepigit, istudq; versari putat circa duo, 1. Circa ea, quæ ad DEUM, 2. Circa ea, quæ ad homines, ubi ponit fidem; illa verò rursus dicit consistere. 1. in præceptorum moralium perfectione & novorum additione, 2. perfectis promissionib. quæ in V. T. nemini oblatæ fuerunt, qvales sunt vita æterna, & donum S. S. ut apparét ex Smalcio. (Catech. Racov. c. 5. de offic. Prophet. p. 232.) Verùm qvanti hic conglomerantur errores? qvot fallaciæ? Amplissimam reqvirerent tractationem. Qvoniam autem terminus conscribendarum thesium præcedentibus Dn. Respondentibus præfixus, & mihi observandus est, prima rerum capita tribus hisce sectionibus inclusa dabo, acturus 1. de doctrina Christi, an sit nova? 2. An Christus Legem moralem perfecerit? 3. Quid de novo addiderit?

SECTIO I.

I. Ante omnia verò considerandum est, doctrinam Christi hîc non accipi γενικῶς, ut etiã includat Legem; Agetur enim de ea in secunda sectione; Sed εἰδικῶς, pro concione de gratuita promissione remissionis peccatorum, justitiæ & vitæ æternæ propter Christum. Et hæc est illa doctrina, quam Photiniani ad Patres V. T. non pertinuisse, ideoq́; novam esse somniant. Quæ sententia cùm manifestè sit falsa, nos negativam certissimis fundamentis confirmabimus.

II. Primò, quia sonuit in paradiso, Gen. 3, 15. Præter causam hîc dissentit Calvinus, qui semen mulieris collectivè exponit de omnibus hominibus. Dantur enim & loca præter hunc alia, ubi hæc phrasis individualiter sumitur, Gen. 4, 25. Gen. 21, 13. Quod verò hæc significatio sit hujus loci, patet ex eo, quia nullus sub sole potuit conterere caput serpentis, Ps. 49, 8. quàm solus Messias, 1. Joh. 3, 8. Col. 2, 15. Is autem est persona singularis & individualiter existens.

III. Impium ergò est Pontificiorum institutum, qui contra Hebræorum exemplarium veritatem per capitis serpentini Contritorem intelligunt B. Mariam. Expressè enim additur verbum masculini generis יְשׁוּפְךָ ipse conteret, & affixum relativum ejusdem generis verbo תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ conteres ejus, scilicet calcaneum; ut non dicam de versione Onkelos & LXX. Interpretum. Gesnerus (in c. 3. Gen. qvæst. 19.) Per caput porrò serpentis non intelligitur Serpens naturalis, sed Draco ille magnus, Apoc. 20, 2. quia (1) loqvi potuit ad mulierem. (3) intelligere verba Domini maledicentis, quæ aliàs fuissent frustranea, & (4.) seduxit Evam, 2. Cor. 11, 3. Ex quibus apparet, in hoc dicto efficacissimam reperiri consolationem contra furores Diaboli & mortis, quæ nihil aliud, quàm doctrina de Christo esse potest.

IV. Secundò, quia nota fuit ante promulgatam Legem (1) in clara listera, Gen. 12, 3. Qvalis fuit verò illa benedictio? Non certè charitativa ut Rabinis & Calvino placet. Nam qvis probabit, hunc morem benedicendi in nomine Abrahami in toto terrarum orbe invaluisse. Non sacerdotalis, nec patriarchalis, ob rei universalitatem & loqventem

DEUM. Divina ergò & merè gratiosa sit necesse est. Qvapropter ulteriùs inqvirenda est causa benedictionis istius universalis. In Abrahamo residere non potuit. Fuit enim idololatra. Nihil ergò aliud superest, qvàm promissus Messias, in qvo benedicendæ fuerunt omnes gentes, Gal. 3, 14, 16. qva de causa & hæc promissio repetitur Gen. 22, 18. (2) Nota etiam fuit doctrina Christi ex suspiriis Evæ, Gen. 4, 1. Lamechi c. 5, 29. Jacobi Gen. 49, 18. (3) Ex typis, Abele interfecto Gen. 4, 8. Isaaco immolando Gen. 22, 10. Josepho vendito Gen. 37, 28. in carcerem projecto, cap. 39, 12. liberato, cap. 41, 14. (4) Ex visione scalæ Jacobææ, qvæ applicatur ad Christum, Joh. c. 1, 52.

V. Tertiò, post promulgatam Legem (1) ex clara litera Hab. 2, 4. Describitur enim ibi causa instrumentalis justificationis nostræ, nempe fides; 2. meritoria, promissus Messias, cujus meritum fide applicatum etiam efficax fuit in Veteri Testamento; 3. promittitur præmium, vita æterna, qvæ omnia exactissimè cum doctrina Christi conveniunt. (2) Ex suspiriis Patrum, Ps. 14, 7. 2. Sam. 23, 15. (3) Ex typis, tum personalibus, Aarone Exod. 28, 29. Hebr. 9, 12. Simsone, Jud. 15, 12. Matth. 27, v. 2. tum realibus; propitiatorio, Exod. 25, 17. hirco emissario, Levit. 16, 2. agno paschali, Exod. 12, 6.

VI. Quartò, Quia Patres per eam sunt justificati & salvati, Actor. 4, 12. Nec valet exceptio Socini (de Servatore p. 91.) hoc vaticinium esse restringendum ad tempus Novi Testamenti, qvòd nulla fiat mentio præteriti temporis. Nam qvid aliud continetur sub verbo δεδομένον, qvàm præteriti temporis inclusio? 2. licet evinci potuisset, præteritum non legi in textu, nihil tamen contra nos concluderet Socinus. Universales enim & res perpetuas in tempore præsente, ad innuendam earum immutabilitatem, sæpissimè effert scriptura Rom. 2, 11. In hoc dicto verò talem haberi, clarum est ex Hebr. 13. 8. Apoc. 14, 6. & ex generali justificandi regula, Rom. 4, 3. Hebr. 11, 4. Objicit (2) Socinus adjectum esse articulum ἡ nomini σωτηρία, ad indicandam rem novam & inauditam. Sed qvo cum fundamento? Nullo. Si dubitas, inspice, Actor. 27, 34. Rom. 11, 11. & apparebit veritas. Et hanc nostram de justificatione Patrum sententiam confirmat etiam dictum Act. 10, 43. Act. 15, 11. Unde necessariò concluditur, doctrinam Christi non esse novam,

Nn 2

VII. Quinto, probatur negativa nostra a praxi Christi, qui allegavit scripta V. T. In quem finem, nisi ut ostenderet, doctrinam suam non hodie aut heri natam, ideoque ipsi credant? Diserte enim (1) scribit Joh. 5. 46. quod Moses de ipso scripserit; Et Luc. 24. 25. discipulos in vicum Emaunticum ambulantes increpat, quod non credidissent iis, quæ in Mose & Prophetis de ipso scripta erant. Serio etiam ipsis præcipit, ut scrutentur Scripturas, quæ tunc temporis nullæ aliæ erant, quam V. T. & (2) addit finem, ut consequantur vitam æternam. Quod consilium sequutus est Paulus Act. 26. 22. in docendo.


### Section II. VIII. After the saving doctrine of Christ has been treated, in the second place…

SECTION II.

VIII. After the saving doctrine of Christ has been treated, in the second place it is asked, Did Christ perfect the moral Law? The Anabaptists, Photinians, and Papists defend the affirmative here, but we shall prove the negative with these reasons, of which (1) is taken from the designation of the Law in Ps. 19.8, where it is called perfect. Whence I proceed thus: The Law is called perfect, either according to a part, or according to the whole; If the former; no other part can be perfect than the moral Law, which, with the others abrogated, still endures: If the latter; the adversaries contradict themselves. (2) from the divine interdict, that we should not add or subtract anything, Deut. 4.2, c. 12.32, Prov. 30.6. (3) from the immutability of GOD, Mal. 3.6. (4) from the testimonies of the Fathers. Bede on c. 20 of Exodus: No number grows further than ten, and by this in the fullness of the number God established the fullness of the commandments. Whence Philo wishes the δεκάδα of the commandments to be called as it were δεχάδα, because it comprehends all kinds of numbers. But heretics oppose themselves to this opinion, and especially Smalcius from among the Photinians (Catech. Racov. c. 1. de offic. Proph. p. 156) and Ostorodus (in instit. c. 22 & seq.), moved especially by this assertion of Christ, Matt. 5.17: I came not to destroy the Law, but to fulfill it. We reply that Christ fulfilled the Law especially in four ways: 1. by right interpretation, 2. satisfaction, 3. by imputation, 4. by the beginning of renewal; the first of which, since it is properly of this place, we shall see through the individual commandments, whether anything has been added to them.

IX. Smalcius (in Cat. Rac. c. 1. de offic. Proph. p. 164, 165) thinks that to the first commandment was added, First, the form of prayer in Matt. 6.9, Luke 11.2. We reply that nothing new is held here. For various kinds of prayers are found in Da vid, as we see in the Psalms, and indeed sung before the whole Church, which is evident to the eye from the inscriptions of Psalm 4, Ps. 5, Ps. 31, etc. But if they think the novelty of this matter consists in the sequence of things and words, I say 1. that the same words are not retained in Matthew and Luke, which is discovered by comparison; 2. not the same things: for this clause is omitted in Luke, for thine is the kingdom etc. What? That even long ago in the time of Augustine (August. in Enchir. c. 115, 116.) the Latin version in Luke did not read, who art in heaven, and the whole third petition with the seventh, and the clause mentioned above. And although someone might say that, with the Greek source standing, he does not care about the discrepancy of the Latin version, yet since it cannot easily be believed that these were neglected in translating Luke, it is rightly gathered (Chemn. in Harm. c. 51, p. 785.) that this diversity teaches that the sequence of things and words is not to be urged too superstitiously. To say nothing of the perfection of the law, which does not consist in the form of praying. Luke 10, 27.

X. Examination concerning the worshipping of Christ John 5, 23. Phil. 2, 10. (Smak. in Catk. Rac. c. 1. de off. Proph. p. 170, 171.) R. That Christ was worshipped in the O. T. by reason of his divine essence (1) Deut. 6, 13. c. 10, 20. For it is not to be thought that Christ was outside the Father John 10, 30. for both are one, 1. John 5, 8. (2) by reason of his person, (1) Ps. 72, 11. 15. which is attributed to Christ on account of his eternal kingdom v. 7. his eternal birth v. 5. his universal dominion v. 8. his divine blessing v. 17. (2) Ps. 45, 12. Hebr. 1, 8. (3) Ps. 97, 7. Hebr. 1, 6. (4) The Israelite people worshipped him Ex. 4, 31. which is testified to be explained concerning Christ c. 3, 2. and is more clearly expounded c. 4, 5. c. 13, 21. 1. Cor. 10, 4. But it is especially to be held that the Photinians consider the adoration of Christ as an addition, about which, however, they do not all agree. 2. That Smalcius teaches that Christ is to be worshipped, and yet does nothing less. For Smalcius writes, (In Cat. Rac. p. 175, 176.) that he is worshipped as a secondary and mediate cause, through which the honor bestowed upon Christ tends to God 1. Cor. 8, 6. But R. that the phrase through whom is also attributed to the Father, Gal. 1, 1. (2) that the primary cause is also assigned to Christ Hebr. 12, 2. Acts 3, 15. Hebr. 5, 9.

XI. To the second commandment, which they most viciously distinguish from the first, Smalcius contends that it is added 1. That we should beware altogether of idols; 2. That we should not become participants of those things which are sacrificed to them, 1. John 5, 21. 1. Cor. 10, 14.

Reply to the former: it must be distinguished between cohabitation of necessity and of free will: if you consider the former; the answer is Lev. 19, 4. But if there is no collusion present, and necessity in a certain respect compels us, such as that of duty, we know what Elisha said to Naaman, 2 Kings 5, 19. If it is simple; we bring forward the examples of the Corinthian Church 1 Cor. 10, 27, the Ephesian [Church] Acts 19, 26, and the time of Arianism and Popery, where it is necessary that such association was certainly granted, since I do not see how they could have completely fled from idolatrous places.

XII. From which it appears, (1) that visiting idolatrous rites is not entirely forbidden, provided we keep ourselves within proper bounds; (2) the superstition of the Anabaptists is reproved, who do not wish to meet in the idolatrous temples of the Papacy, lest they be unequally yoked with unbelievers 2 Cor. 6, 14, (2) lest they tacitly approve of their idolatry, and (3) because it is written in Rev. 18, 4, 'Come out of her (Babylon), my people,' which arguments of theirs collapse by mere recitation.

XIII. To the second addition, I reply that a greater liberty is generally granted today in this regard than formerly in the Old Testament. For Paul, in the cited passage, does not forbid his hearers every use of things sacrificed to idols, v. 27, 28, but at least that which is done with scandal, v. 24, 28, 29; whence in 1 Cor. 8, 4 he says that an idol is nothing in the world, which, however, had a place in the Old Testament on account of the ceremonial laws, as is clear from Num. 25, 1, 2.

XIV. In the third Commandment, let there be a divorce of opinions. For some have persuaded themselves that the New Testament is more perfect than the Old, in that it abolishes all oaths; in whose number were the Manichaeans, Anabaptists, and Martyrs in the year of Christ 200, who rejected the oaths imposed upon them, whom many of the Fathers today, the Papists, have followed, judging that this concerns counsels of perfection. The Photinians, however, contend that in the New Testament, besides deceitful oaths, even rash ones, and indeed in a good cause, are forbidden, Matt. 5, 34 (Smalcius, C. Racov. c. 1, de off. Proph. p. 186, 187; Ostorod. in Instit. c. 25, p. 3, f. 163), and 2, that it is permitted only in the New Testament to swear in the name of Christ. I reply: 1, that the particle ὅλως is not a universal exclusive that forbids all oaths, as Ostorodius testifies (c. 25, p. 2, f. 163), but is to be restricted in this place to the subject matter. For in the same way Paul also says, 'All things are lawful for me' 1 Cor. 10, 23, when nevertheless sins must be excepted. But of what matter does Christ treat? Of those rash ones, who without necessity called God as a witness, when nevertheless they could have accomplished that by yes yes, no no v. 37, 2. Concerning swearing by creatures, which they judged to be free for themselves without fear of perjury v. 34, 35, 36. & Matth. 23. from v. 16. up to 22. Wherefore also another opinion runs.

XV. The Photinians indeed (Ostor. in Instit. c. 25. p. 3. s. 164.) in order to maintain that rash oaths are an addition of Christ, say here, because of the words of the law recited, that a manifest opposition is made between the doctrine of Moses and of Christ 2. that in the O. T. there is such a word which signifies falsely and mendaciously, but not swearing without cause, bringing forward for the sake of proof the passages Exod. 23, 1. Deut. 1, 20. where the word שָׁוְא is taken for a lie. Ostorodus Instit. c. 25. p. l. s. 162. Resp. (1) from v. 20. c. 5. Matth. (2) To the reason, sought from the particle שָׁוְא, I infer, that it is not permitted to argue from one example to another. For the clear letter testifies that this addition is none Os. 4, 15. Sir. 23, 7, 8. c. 27. v. 15. And since the word שָׁוְא Job 15, 31. Jer. 2, 30. signifies something vain and fruitless, I add Deut. 5, 11. Exod. 20, 7. Nor does the recitation of the words of the law help them (3); for it is alleged by Christ not nakedly, but with the false explanation of the Pharisees v. 43. (4) it is not said you have read, but you have heard, and indeed ἀρχαίοις, by whom also the chief princes are understood; whence Piscator translates, You have heard that by the ancients, which phrase is found 1. Corinth. 15, 6. But by the name of Christ 1. they also swore in the O. T. because they worshipped him, as we have given proof, 2. because he is true God, Rom. 9, 5.

XVI. They found nothing of perfection added to the fourth commandment, except that Smalcius, Catech. Racov. p. 189. says that the commandment concerning the sabbath is abolished, and therefore is enumerated among the commandments of the Decalogue, so that it may be denoted 1. the imperfection of the principal part of the law, 2. that a more perfect law, namely Christ's, was to be expected. But what do you think, Smalcius? is abolition the same to you as perfection, which you proclaim every commandment has obtained p. 162? 2. Prove that the sabbath, for the reason that it pertains to the moral Law, is abolished, and 3. that it is an indication of the perfection of the Law?

XVII. They also leave the fifth commandment untouched. But the addition to the sixth 1. is rash anger, Matth. 5, 22. (Ostor. c. 23. Inst. p. 3. s. 156. Smalcius in Cat. Rac. c. 1. de off. Pr. p. 195.) Resp. They cannot easily prove that this deals only with rash anger, since the word εἰκῆ, as Augustine testifies, was not found in the Greek Codex in former times. (2) If this is granted, what is that against us? For the same thing is read in the O.T. Lev. 19, 17. Prov. 27, 3. Eccles. 7, 10. But Ostorodus, desiring to obtain something, limits the sentence thus (c. 29. Instit. f. 145. & c. 27, 17. wherever in the O.T. it was commanded that we should not be angry with a brother, i.e., with anyone from the people, and indeed under such a penalty as is the fire of Gehenna. Resp. that brother is also taken in the O.T. most generally, for all men. Compare the passages Lev. 19. v. 18. & v. 33. 34. 2. that the fire of Gehenna is contained under the general curse, Deut. 27, 26.

XIII. 2. Addition, That we may not offend him with harsh words, Matth. 5, 22. Resp. not only harsh words, Jer. 18, 18. but also a grim countenance are reproved, Ps. 112, 10.

XIX. 3. Private vengeance, Matth. 5, 39. seq. Smalcius (Cat. Rac. c. 1. de off. Proph. p. 197.) Ostorodus (Inst. c. 27. p. 3. f. 175.) Resp. that these words are to be taken comparatively, namely in the comparison of a greater evil. 2. that not every private vengeance is excluded, even that undertaken in a case of necessity to protect life. For it is to be defended, not rashly poured out.

XX. 4. Public vengeance, Smalcius in the said place, Ostorod. Instit. c. 26. f. 164.) which they say consists in forensic accusation, 2. in the use of the sword. Resp. (1) political judgments are of the Lord himself, 2. Par. 19, 6. (2) they have the example of Christ, Joh. 18, 23. of Paul, Act. 23, 3. & 24, 10, c. 25, 8. how therefore Christ abrogated their use, I do not see. They object (1) the Photinians that these can be granted, if vengeance is absent, but they commit a manifest contradiction, since the compensation for damage unjustly brought, which we seek there, is nothing other than vengeance. Nor (2) does it have more foundation, that they say these forensic accusations are valid only towards strangers, but not towards brothers in Christ. For this saying 1. Cor. 6, 5, 6. seq. deals with light errors, v. 4, 2. with lawsuits, v. 6. with an impious magistrate. v. 1. before whom by this reasoning the Christian religion might be suspected.

XXI. (2) That the use of the sword is granted is clear (1) from the authority and divine concession of the same Rom. 13, 4. (2) from the terror struck into evil works, v. 3. (3) from vengeance, v. 4. 1. Petr. 2, 14. (4) from the removal of the impious. But Ostorodus's exception, (c. 28. Inst. p. 3. f. 186.) by the sword grave punishment, Matt. 10, 34. is cold. For the progression is made from the particular. 2, the contrary example is at hand, Matt. 26, 52. Apoc. 13, 10. All of which, since they are clear, demonstrate no addition.

XXII. On the seventh commandment: First, the lust for a woman, adds Smalcius, Ostorodius. I reply: the same is proven from the O.T. (1) from the divine prohibition, Exod. 20, 17. Sir. 9, 8. (2) from the Lord's rebuke, Ezech. 23, 16. (3) from the honest example of Job ch. 31, v. 9. in the dishonest, Gen. 39, 7.

XXIII. Secondly, concerning not putting away wives, except for adultery, and not marrying one who has been put away, Matt. 5, 32. ch. 19, v. 9. I reply: Christ, Matt. 19, 4. seq., opposes these also to the most ancient law, Gen. 2, 24. From which, however, it is not to be gathered that divine laws are opposed to one another. For the latter is not held as a commandment, but is only a concession, Matt. 19, 8. And although in Mark 10, 5. it seems to be called a commandment, yet it is rightly to be weighed what kind of thing that is, and what Moses commanded, namely, a bill of divorce, not the repudiation itself.

XXIV. Thirdly, concerning concubinage and polygamy, which Ostorodus adds, (Inst. ch. 24. p. 2. f. 159.) let verse 5 of Matt. 19 be considered. (2) the divine institution in the ark of Noah, Gen. 6, 19.

XXV. Fourthly, all whoredom, 1 Cor. 6, 15. impurity, Hebr. 12, 14. obscene speech, 1 Thess. 4, 3. jesting, Eph. 5, v. 4. Smal. (in Cat. Rac. p. 199.) Reply to 1 from Deut. 22, 20. s. Ezech. 16, 15. Jer. 5, 8. To 2. Deut. 23, 12, 13. To 3. & 4. Prov. 15, 2.

XXVI. On the Eighth Commandment: 1. Avarice, Heb. 13, 5. 1 Tim. 6, 11. (Smalcius in Cat. Rac. p. 203.) and Ostorodus (Inst. c. 31. p. 1. f. 230.) defines it as the desire to have more than is necessarily required for sustaining life. And he seeks the foundation of this opinion of his from Luke 12, 15, where he criticizes Luther’s version, which reads thus: Niemand lebt von dem / daß er viel Güter hat, saying that this one is better: Niemands leben bestehet in dem / daß er etwas übrigeshast. But Luther is wrongly criticized, since in the Greek text it is read περισσεύειν ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων: and furthermore, the definition is faulty which depicts avarice more from the accumulation than from the excessive and depraved appetite of a man toward wealth, concerning which, however, more is treated at length elsewhere. Moreover, the cited passages make nothing against us.

XXVII. 2. Luxury in food and drink, to which they also refer banquets, add also clothing, Luke 21, 34. Rom. 13, 13. Gal. 5, 21. (Smalcius in Catech.

Rac. p. 205. Ostorod. in Instit. c. 30. p. 3. f. 222, 223.) Resp. from Isa. 3, 16. Isa. 5, 22. Prov. 23, 20. Luke 14, 12. Deut. 21, 20. Ostorodus indeed objects (p. 1. f. 220.) that in the passages of Isaiah the luxury of clothing and food and drink is not there reproved, but that the Lord is at least reproaching the Israelites for His benefits; which is indeed true, but what is the cause of that reproach? Certainly nothing but luxury, which God had not granted to them.

XXIIX. Smalcius (in Catech. Rac. p. 205.) and Ostorodus (Instit. c. 30. p. 2. f. 221, 222.) write that the Ninth Commandment has attained its perfection in the inclusion of lies, not only those arising from a desire to deceive from the heart, but also reckless ones, 2. of all detractions, 3. of denunciations, 4. of calumnies, Eph. 4, 25. Rom. 1, 30. 1 Pet. 2, 1. Resp. These statements do not contradict us at all. For concerning lies, see Lev. 19, 11. Exod. 20, 16. Concerning detractions and calumnies, Ps. 15, 3. Concerning denunciations, Ps. 101, 5.

XXIX. They perfect the Tenth Commandment with these things; namely, that we should not set our mind upon desired things; even if we never think about bringing them to pass, but are content with the pleasure alone which they produce in the heart. (Smalcius in Cat. Rac. p. 206.) Resp. from Ps. 119, 133. וְאַל־תַּשְׁלֶט־בִּי כָל־אָוֶן where manifestly in אָוֶן (which Chemnitius, part 2, Loc. C. p. 108, wishes to derive from אָוָה, he coveted, he desired) concupiscence is noted as a root, which is certainly no less condemned than evil affections proceeding into effect. And why many words? Certainly the Apostle clearly says, I would not have known, unless the Law had said, Thou shalt not covet, Rom. 7, 7. Finally; even if they could prove that not everything is found according to the letter in the O.T. as it is in the N.T., yet let them distinguish, I pray, between the explanation of a thing and the addition of a new one, and the matter will be complete.

Latin:

SECTIO II.

VIII. Postquam de doctrina Christi salvifica actum est, secundo loco quæritur, An Christus Legem moralem perfecerit? Affirmativam hîc defendunt Anabaptistæ, Photiniani & Pontificii, sed nos negativam hisce probabimus rationibus, quarum (1) sumitur ab appellatione Legis Pf. 19. 8. ubi vocatur perfecta. Unde sic procedo: Lex vocatur perfecta, vel secundum partem, vel secundum totum; Si illud; nulla alia pars potest esse perfecta, quam Lex moralis, quæ reliquis abrogatis adhuc durat: Si hoc; sibiipsis contradicunt adversarii. (2) ab interdicto divino, ne aliquid addamus vel detrahamus, Deut. 4, 2. c. 12, 32. Prov. 30, 6. (3) ab immutabilitate DEI, Mal. 3, 6. (4) a testimoniis Patrum. Beda in c. 20. Exod. Nullus numerus crescit ampliùs, nisi usq; ad decem, ac per hoc in plenitudine numeri plenitudinem mandatorum Deus constituit. Unde Philo δεκάδα præceptorum dictam vult quasi δεχάδα, quod omnia numerorum genera comprehendat. Ast huic sententiæ sese opponunt Hæretici, & inprimis ex Photinianis Smalcius (Catech. Racov. c. 1. de offic. Proph. p. 156.) & Ostorodus (in instit. c. 22. & seq.) hac potissimum Christi moti assertione, Matth. 5, 17. Non veni Legem solvere, sed implere: Resp. Christum implevisse Legem potissimum quatuor modis, 1. per rectam interpretationem, 2. satisfactionem, 3. per imputationem, 4. per renovationis inchoationem; quorum prior, cum propriè sit hujus loci, per singula præcepta videbimus, num iis aliquid adjectum sit.

IX. Primo precepto additam putat Smalcius (in Cat. Rac. c. 1. de offic. Proph. p. 164. 165.) Primo, formam precandi Matth. 6, 9. Luc. 11, 2. Resp. hic nihil haberi novi. Varia enim precum genera reperiuntur apud Davidemus in Psalmis, & quidem toti Ecclesiæ præcantata, quod ex inscriptionibus Psalmi 4. Ps. 5. Ps. 31. &c. ad oculum patet. Si verò novitatem hujus rei consistere putant in rerum & verborum serie, dico 1. non eadem verba retineri apud Matthæum & Lucam, quod ex collatione deprehenditur; 2. non easdem res: Omittitur enim apud Lucam hæc clausula, quia tuum est regnum &c. Quid? quod jam olim Augustini tempore (August. in Enchir. c. 115. 116.) Latina versio apud Lucam non legerit, qui es in cœlis, tertiamq; petitionem totam cum septima, clausulaque suprà dicta. Etsi verò aliqvis diceret, se stante Græco fonte nihil curare discrepantiam versionis Latinæ, tamen cum non facilè credi possit, hæc in Luca vertendo fuisse neglecta, rectè colligitur (Chemn. in Harm. c. 51, p. 785.) diversitatem hanc docere, non nimis superstitiosè urgendam esse rerum ac verborum seriem. Ut nihil dicam de legis perfectione, quæ non consistit in forma precandi. Luc. 10, 27.

X. Scrutam. de adorando Christo Joh. 5, 23. Phil. 2, 10. (Smak. in Catk. Rac. c. 1. de off. Proph. p. 170, 171.) R. Adoratum fuisse Christum in V. T. ratione essentiæ divinæ (1) Deut. 6, 13. c. 10, 20. Non enim existimandum est, Christum fuisse extra patrem Joh.an. 10, 30. ambo enim unum sunt, 1. Joh. 5, 8. (2) ratione personæ, (1) Ps. 72. 11. 15. qui Christo tribuitur propter regnum æternum v. 7. æternam nativitatem v. 5. universale dominium v. 8. benedictionem divinam v. 17. (2) Ps. 45, 12. Hebr. 1, 8. (3) Ps. 97, 7. Hebr. 1, 6. (4) Populus Israëliticus adoravit eum Ex. 4, 31. quod de Christo explicandum esse testatur c. 3, 2. & clariùs exponitur c. 4, 5. c. 13, 21. 1. Cor. 10, 4. Imprimis verò tenendum est, Photinianos adorationem Christi pro additamento habere, de qva tamen ipsi non omnes consentiunt. 2. Smalcium docere Christum adorandum esse, & tamen nihil minùs facere. Nam Smalcius scribit, (In Cat. Rac. p. 175. 176.) eum adorari ut causam secundariam & mediam, per quod honor Christo collatus ad Deum tendit 1. Cor. 8, 6. Sed R. phrasin per quem etiam tribui Patri, Gal. 1, 1. (2) Christo etiam assignari causam primariam Hebr. 12, 2. Act. 3, 15. Hebr. 5, 9.

XI. Secundo præcepto, quod illi vitiosissimè distinguunt à primo, additum contendit Smalcius 1. Ut caveamus nos omnino ab idolis; 2. Ne participes fiamus eorum, quæ ipsis sunt immolata, 1. Joh. 5, 21. 1. Cor. 10, 14.

R. ad prius, distinguendum esse inter cohabitationem necessitatis & liberæ voluntatis: si prius attendis; responsum est Lev. 19, 4. si verò nulla adest collusio, & adigit nos necessitas secundum quid, qualis est officii, scimus, qvid Elisæus dixerit ad Naamanum 2. Reg. 5, 19. si simplex; proferimus exempla Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ 1. Cor. 10, 27. Ephesinæ Act. 19, 26. & tempus Arianismi, Papismi ubi certè ista conversatio concessa fuerit necesse est, cùm non videam, qvomodo loca idololatrica prorsus fugere potuerint.

XII. Ex qvibus apparet, (1) non omnino interdictum esse visitandi sacra idololatrica, si modò nos intra rectos continemus terminos (2) Anabaptistarum reprehenditur superstitio, qvi in templis idololatrici Papatûs convenire nolunt, ne trahant jugum cum infidelibus 2. Cor. 6, 14. (2) ne idololatriam ipsorum tacitè approbent, & (3) qvia scriptum est Apoc. 18. 4. Exite ex ea (Babylon) popule mi, qvæ ipsorum argumenta solâ recitatione corruunt.

XIII. Ad 2. additamentum resp. ferè majorem licentiam hodiè dari hac in parte, qvàm olim in V. T. Non enim Paulus dicto loco omnem idolothytorum usum suis auditoribus interdicit, v. 27, 28. sed eum saltem, qvi fit cum scandalo, v. 24, 28, 29. unde 1. Cor. 8, 4. dicit, idolum nihil esse in Mundo, qvod tamen V. T. propter leges ceremoniales locum habuisse, clarum est ex Num. 25, 1, 2.

XIV. In tertio Præcepto sententiarum sit divortium. Qvidam enim sibiipsi persuaserunt, N. T. Vetere perfectius esse, qvod omnia juramẽta tollat, in qvorum numero fuerunt Manichæi, Anabaptistæ & Martyres anno Christi 200. qvi juramenta ipsis imposita repudiarunt, qvos secuti sunt multi è Patribus hodie Pontificiis, censentes, hîc agi de côsiliis perfectionis. Photiniani verò contendunt in N. T. præter dolosa juramenta etiam temeraria, & quidem in causa bona prohibita esse, Matth. 5. 34. (Smalcius C. Racov. c. 1. de off. Proph. p. 186. 187.) Ostorod. in Instit. c. 25. p. 3. f. 163.) 2. concessum esse solum in N. T. jurare in nomine Christi. Resp. 1. particulam ὅλως non esse universalem exclusivam, qvæ omnia interdicat juramenta, teste Ostor. c. 25. p. 2. f. 163. sed restringendam esse hoc loco ad subjectam materiam. Nam eodem modo & Paulus dicit, omnia mihi licent 1. Cor. 10, 23. cum tamen peccata sint excipienda. De qva verò materia agit Christus? De juramentis temerariis, qvibus citra necessitatē testem in vocabant Dᴇᴜᴍ, cūm tamen efficere istud potuisfent per etiā etiam, non non v. 37, 2. De obtestatione per creaturas, qvam ipsis absq; metu perjurii liberam esse judicabant v. 34, 35, 36. & Matth. 23. à v. 16. usq; ad 22. Qvapropter & altera curruit sententia.

XV. Photiniani vero (Ostor. in Instit. c. 25. p. 3. s. 164.) ut juramenta temeraria pro additamentò Christi obtineant, dicunt híc, ob verba legis recitata, manifestam fieri oppositionem inter doctrinam Mosis & Christi 2. in V. T. haberi tale verbum qvod significat falsò & mendaciter, non antem sine causa jurare, probationis gratia adducentes loca Exod. 23, 1. Deut. 1, 20. ubi vocabulum שָׁוְא sumatur pro mendacio. Ostorodus Instit. c. 25. p. l. s. 162. Resp. (1) ex v. 20. c. 5. Matth. (2) Ad rationem, è particula שָׁוְא petitam, infero, non licitam esse argumentari ab uno exemplo ad alterum. Hanc additionem enim nullam esse clara testatur litera Os. 4, 15. Sir. 23, 7, 8. c. 27. v. 15. Et cùm Vocabulum שָׁוְא Job. 15, 31. Jer. 2, 30. significet vanum & frustraneum qviddam, addo Deut. 5, 11. Exod. 20, 7. Nec ipsos juvat (3) verborum legis recitatio; Allegatur enim à Christo non nudè, sed cum falsa Pharisæorum explicatione v. 43. (4) non dicitur legistis, sed audistis, & qvidem ἀρχαίοις, per qvos etiam intelliguntur præcipui principes; unde Piscator vertit, Jhr habt gehört/ dass von den Alten / qvalis phrasis reperitur 1. Corinth. 15, 6. Per nomen Christi vero 1. etiam jurarunt in V. T. qvia eum adorarunt, ut probatum dedimus, 2. qvia est verus Deus, Rom. 9, 5.

XVI. Præcepto qvarto nihil perfectionis invenerunt addiditum, nisi qvòd Smalcius Catech. Racov. p. 189. dicat, præceptum de sabbatho esse abolitum, ideoq́ve Præceptis Decalogi annumerari, ut denotetur 1. partis legis præcipuæ imperfectio, 2. perfectiorem legem videlicet Christi fuisse expectandam. Sed qvid sentis, Smalci? num tibi 1. abolitio idem est, qvòd perfectio, qvam unumqvodqve præceptum fortitum esse clamitas p. 162? 2. Probes sabbatum eâ ratione, qvâ pertinet ad Legem moralem, esse abolitum, & 3. esse indicium perfectionis Legis?

XVII. Qvintum præceptum etiam intactum relinquunt. Sexti verò additio 1. est ira temeraria, Matth. 5, 22. (Ostor. c. 23. Inst. p. 3. s. 156. Smalcius in Cat. Rac. c. 1. de off. Pr. p. 195.) Resp. Non possunt facile probare, hic solùm agi de ira temeraria, cùm vocabulum εἰκῆ, Augustino teste, in Græco Codice olim non inventum sit. (2) hoc concesso quid contra nos? Legitur enim idem in V. T. Lev. 19, 17. Prov. 27, 3. Eccles. 7, 10. Sed Ostorodus aliqvid obtinere cupiens, sic limitat sententiam ( c. 29. Instit. f. 145. & c. 27, 17. ubicunque in V. T. præceptum fuit, ne fratri, i. e. unicuique è populo irascamur, & quidem sub tanta pœna, qualis est ignis gehennæ. ' Resp. fratrem etiam in V. T. generalissime sumi, pro omnibus hominibus. Confer loca Levit. 19. v. 18. & v. 33. 34. 2. ignem gehennæ contineri sub generali maledictione, Deut. 27, 26.

XIII. 2. Additio, Ne verbis duris eum offendamus, Matth. 5, 22. Resp. non solùm verba aspera, Jer. 18, 18. sed & torvum vultum reprehendi, Pf. 112, 10.

XIX. 3. Vindicta privata, Matth. 5, 39. seq. Smalcius (Cat. Rac. c. 1. de off. Proph. p. 197.) Ostorodus (Inst. c. 27. p. 3. f. 175.) Resp. verba hæc accipienda esse comparatè, nimirùm in collatione majoris mali. 2. non omnem excludi etiam vindictam privatam, in casu necessitatis ad vitam tuendam susceptam. Defendenda enim ea est, non profundenda temerè.

XX. 4. Vindicta publica, Smalcius dicto loco, Ostorod. Instit. c. 26. f. 164.) quam consistere dicunt in accusatione forensi, 2. in gladii usurpatione. Resp. (1) judicia politica sunt ipsius Domini, 2. Par. 19, 6. (2) habent exemplum Christi, Joh. 18, 23. Pauli, Act. 23, 3. & 24, 10, c. 25, 8. quomodo ergò Christus usum eorum abrogaverit, non video. Excipiunt (1) Photiniani concedi ea posse, si absit ultio, sed manifestam committunt contradictionem, cùm nihil aliud sit recompensatio damni injustè illati, quam ibi petimus, quàm vindicta. Nec plus (2) fundamenti habet, quòd forenses has accusationes tantùm erga extraneos, non autem fratres in Christo valere dicunt. Dictum enim hoc 1. Cor. 6, 5, 6. seq. agit de erratis levibus, v. 4, 2. de litigiis, v. 6. de magistratu impio. v. 1. apud que hac ratione Christiana suspecta sit religio.

XXI. (2) Usum gladii concessum esse patet (1) ab autoritate & concessione ejusdem divina Rom. 13, 4. (2) à terrore malis operibus incutiendo, v. 3. (3) à vindicta, v. 4. 1. Petr. 2, 14. (4) à remotione impiorum. Ostorodi autem exceptio, (c. 28. Inst. p. 3. f. 186.) per gladium gravem pœnam intelligentis, Matth. 10, 34. frigida est. Progressio enim fit à particulari. 2, in promtu est contrarium exemplum, Matth. 26, 52. Apoc. 13, 10. Quæ omnia, cùm sint clara, nullam demonstrant additionẽ.

XXII. Septimo præcepto: Primò concupiscentiam mulieris, addit Smalcius, Ostorodius. Resp. idem evincitur ex V. T. (1) ab interdicto divino, Exod. 20, 17. Sir. 9, 8. (2) à reprehensione Domini, Ezech. 23, 16. (3) ab exemplo honesto Job. c. 31. v. 9. in honesto, Gen. 39, 7.

XXIII. Secundò, de non repudiandis uxoribus, nisi ob adulterium, & repudiatâ non ducendâ, Matth. 5, 32. c. 19. v. 9. Respondeo: Christus Mat. 19, 4. seq. hæc etiam opponit legi antiquissimæ, Gen. 2, 24. Ex quo tamen non colligendum est, leges divinas sibi invicem opponi. Posterius enim non habetur pro præcepto, sed tantùm est concessio, Matt. 19, 8. Et licet Marci 10, 5. videatur appellari præceptum, tamen rectè perpendum est, qvale sit illud, & qvidnam præceperit Moses videl. libellum repudii, non repudiationem ipsam.

XXIV. Tertiò, de Concubinatu & Polygamia, qvam Ostorodus addit, (Inst. c. 24. p. 2. f. 159.) consideretur versus 5. Matth. 19. (2) institutio divina in arca Noæ, Gen. 6, 19.

XXV. Quartò, omnem scortationem, 1. Cor. 6, 15. impuritatem, Hebr. 12, 14. obscœnos sermones, 1. Thess. 4, 3. jocos, Eph. 5, v. 4. Smal. (in Cat. Rac. p. 199.) Resp. ad 1. ex Deut. 22, 20. s. Ezech. 16, 15. Jer. 5, 8. Ad 2. Deut. 23, 12, 13. Ad 3. & 4. Prov. 15, 2.

XXVI. Octavo Præcepto: 1. Avaritiam, Hebr. 13, 5. 1. Tim. 6, 11. (Smalcius in Cat. Rac. p. 203.) eamq́; Ostorodus (Inst. c. 31. p. 1. f. 230.) definit per cupiditatem plus habendi, qvàm ad vitam sustentandam necessariò reqviritur.
