Et hujus suæ sententiæ fundamentum petit ex Luc. 12, 15. ubi carpit Lutheri versionem, qvæ sic sonat: Niemand lebt von dem / daß er viel Güter hat / dicens, meliorem esse hanc, Niemands leben bestehet in dem / daß er etwas übrigeshast. Verùm malè carpitur Lutherus, cùm in Græco textu legatur περισσεύειν ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων: Vitiosáq; præterea est definitio, qvæ avaritiam magis ex cumulo qvàm nimio pravoq́; hominis appetitu erga opes depingit, de qvibus tamẽ alibi prolixiùs agitur. Dicta autem allegata nihil contranos faciunt.

XXVII. 2. Luxuriam in cibo & potu, qvò referunt etiam convivia, adde & vestitum, Luc. 21, 34. Rom. 13, 13. Gal. 5, 21. (Smalcius in Catech.

Rac. p. 205. Ostorod. in Instit. c. 30. p. 3. f. 222, 223.) Resp. ex Esai. 3, 16. Esa. 5, 22. Prov. 23, 20. Luc. 14, 12. Deut. 21, 20. Excipit quidem Ostorodus p. 1. f. 220. ad loca Esaiæ vestium & cibi potusq́; luxuriam ibi non reprehendi, sed Dominum Israëlitin saltem sua exprobare beneficia; quod quidem verum est, ast quæ est causa istius exprobrationis? certè nil nisi luxuries, quam ipsis Deus non concesserat.

XXIIX. Nonum Præceptum perfectionem suam consecutum esse scribit Smalcius (in Catech. Rac. p. 205.) & Ostorodus (Instit. c. 30. p. 2. f. 221, 222.) in annexione mendaciorum, non solum ex animo fallendi cupido ortorum, sed etiam temerariorum, 2. omnium obtrectationum, 3. delationum, 4. calumniarum, Eph. 4, 25. Rom. 1. 30. 1. Petr. 2, 1. Resp. Hæc dicta nihil nobis contrariantur. De mendaciis enim vide Lev. 19, 11. Exod. 20, 16. De obtrectationibus & calumniis, Ps. 15, 3. De delationibus, Ps. 101, 5.

XXIX. Decimum præceptum perficiunt hisce; ne videlicet rebus expetitis animum adjiciamus; licet de iis perficiendis nunquam cogitemus, sed solâ, quam pariunt in corde, voluptate simus contenti. (Smalcius in Cat. Rac. p. 206.) Resp. ex Ps. 119, 133. וְאַל־תַּשְׁלֶט־בִּי כָל־אָוֶן ubi manifestè in אָוֶן (quod descendere vult Chemnitius parte 2. Loc. C. p. 108. à אָוָה concupivit, desideravit) notatur concupiscentia tanquam radix, quæ certè non minùs laudatur, quàm pravi affectus in effectum prodeuntes. Et quid multis? Certè Apostolus clarè dicit, non novissem, nisi Lex dixisset, non concupisces, Rom. 7, 7. Tandem; licet evincere possent, non omnia secundùm literam in V. T. quemadmodum in N. reperiri, tamen distinguant quæso inter rei explicationem, & novæ additionem, resq́; erit plena.


### Section III. XXX. After the treatment concerning the perfection of the commandments of Christ

SECTION III.

XXX. After the treatment concerning the perfection of the commandments of Christ; now it must deservedly be dealt with concerning the commandments added in particular. But according to the mind of Smalcius in Catech. Rac. p. 207. seq., there are two kinds of these. The former concern morals, but the latter concern ceremonies. Those again are threefold: (1) To deny oneself, which they wish to be nothing other than a bidding farewell to evil bodily and worldly pleasures, 1 John 2, 15, 16. the prohibition of which is nevertheless read in the last commandments of the Decalogue, and Amos 6, 3, 4. just as also concerning pride Lev. 26, 19. 2 Kings 18, 28. (2) To bear the cross of Christ; namely, that not only cheerfully let us not only endure all calamities, but even when necessity demands, let us undergo death for Christ; concerning which see John 15:20, 21; ch. 21:17, 18; Prov. 3:11. & 2. Weigh the example of Moses and Aaron, who approached Pharaoh with the greatest danger to their lives, for the sake of Jehovah and the people, Ex. 5:1; of Elijah, 1 Kings 18:15, 17; of Elisha, 2 Kings 6:31, (3.) To follow Christ: so that indeed there may be in us (1) trust in GOD, (2) love toward GOD and neighbor, Matt. 5:43, (3) humility Phil. 2:3, 4, such as is the washing of feet, John 13:4, (4) assiduity and universality in praying, 1 Tim. 2:2. Resp. Who is ignorant of the sayings concerning trust in GOD, Ps. 20:8; Jer. 17:7; (1) concerning humility, Isa. 66:2; (2) Zeph. 2:3; (3) concerning assiduous and general prayer, Ps. 119:62; and thus Abraham also prayed for the hostile Sodomites, Gen. 18:23; for Abimelech the Gentile, ch. 20:17; Moses for the idolaters, Exod. 32:11.

XXXI. Finally, love toward GOD is not excluded from the O.T., Luke 10:26; Matt. 22:37; nor is love toward men. For Ostorodius, ch. 27, p. 7, f. 171, taking these passages Lev. 19:17, Exod. 23:4 as referring only to an Israelite, errs greatly, which was demonstrated above in thesis 17. Furthermore, the manner of love is the same in both. For even in the O.T. men laid down their lives for one another, as the example of David delivering the Israelites, and of Moses desiring to be blotted out of the book of life for the sake of the Israelites, shows. Indeed, neither does the passage of Matthew alleged against us fight against us. For it is not found in the whole O.T., so that you may openly see that it is opposed to the traditions of the Pharisees. But what does Ostorodius answer to that? (Inst. ch. 2, p. 1, f. 175.) He says it is possible that these words, 'you shall hate your enemy,' were written somewhere in the Law, although today they are not found in it, just as also Matt. 2:23. 'He shall be called a Nazarene,' he says, does not exist today in the O.T. But, the impudence of the man, who (1) thinks that those things which could confirm his own most false opinion have perished! (2) Nor is it true what he brings forward concerning the saying of Matthew; for it is read in Zech. 6:12; Isa. 11:1; ch. 61:1.

XXXII. But the later new precepts, namely Baptism and the Lord's Supper, which concern ceremonies, we also say are good things of the N.T., but (1) Baptism was prefigured in the O.T. by the ark of Noah, Gen. 7:1; 1 Pet. 3:21; by the passage through the Red Sea, Exod. 14:29, 30; 1 Cor. 10:2; by circumcision, Col. 2:11; (2) promised, Ps. 29:20; Isa. 44:3. Concerning the Lord's Supper also the judgment is the same, for there are present (1) types: the Paschal lamb, Exod. 12:3; 1 Cor. 5:7; manna, Exod. 16:31; 1 Cor. 10:3; (2) promises, Ps. 23:1, 2, 5; Isa. 25:6. What therefore have you Heretics obtained that is new? Nothing.

Latin:

SECTIO III.

XXX. Post tractationem de præceptorum Christi perfectione; nunc meritò de præceptis in specie additis est agendum. Horum verò ex mente Smalcii in Catech. Rac. p. 207. seq. dantur duplicia. Priora versantur circa mores, posteriora autem circa ceremonias. Illa rursus sunt triplicia: (1) Seipsum abnegare, quod nihil aliud esse volunt, quàm malarum corporalium atq; mundanarum voluptatum valedictionem, 1. Joh. 2, 15, 16. cujus tamen interdictum legitur in ultimis Decalogi præceptis, & Amos 6, 3, 4. quemadmodum & de superbia Lev. 26, 19. 2. Reg. 18, 28. (2) Crucem Christi portare; ut videlicet non solùm hilari animo omnes perferamus calamitates, sed etiam exigente necessitate pro Christo mortem obeamus; de quo vide Joh. 15, 20, 21. c. 21, 17. 18. Prov. 3, 11. & 2. perpende exemplum Mosis & Aaronis, qui cum summo vitæ periculo accesserunt, in gratiam Jehovæ & populi, ad Pharaonem, Ex. 5, 1. Eliæ, 1. Reg. 18, 15, 17. Elisæi, 2. Reg. 6. 31, (3.) Christum sequi: ut nimirùm in nobis sit (1) fiducia in DEUM, (2) amor erga DEUM & proximum, Matth. 5, 43. (3) humilitas Phil. 2, 3. 4. qualis est pedum lotio, Joh. 13, 4. (4) assiduitas & universalitas in precando, 1. Tim. 2, 2. Resp. quem latent dicta de fiducia DEI, Ps. 20, 8. Jer. 17. 7. (1) de humilitate, Esa. 66, 2. (2) Soph. 2. v. 3. (3) de assidua & generali oratione, Ps. 119, 62. atq; ita Abraham etiam orabat pro inimicis Sodomitis, Gen. 18, 23. Abimelecho Ethnico, c. 20, 17. Moses pro idolatris, Exod. 32, 11.

XXXI. Tandem nec dilectio erga DEUM è V. T. excluditur, Luc. 10, 26. Matth. 22, 37; nec erga homines. Nam Ostorod. c. 27. p. 7. f. 171. hæc loca Levit. 19, 17. Exod. 23, 4. de solo Israëlita accipiens, valdè errat, quod suprà demonstratum est th. 17. Modus præterea dilectionis utrobiq; idem est. Nam & in V. T. homines pro se invicem posuerunt animas, ut Davidis liberantis Israëlitas, Mosis cupientis deleri è libro vitæ propter Israelitas, exemplum ostendit. Quin nec locus Matthæi allegatus contra nos pugnat. Non enim ille reperitur in toto V. T. ut apertè videas, eum oppositum esse Pharisæorum traditionibus. Sed quid ad illum Ostorodus respondet? (Inst. c. 2. p. 1. f. 175.) Possibile esse ait, hæc verba, odio persequaris inimicum tuum, scripta alicubi fuisse in Lege, licet hodiè in ea non reperirentur, quemadmodum etiam Matth. 2, 23. Christus Nazarenus vocabitur, dicit hodiè in V. T. non extare. Ast, impudentiam hominis, qui (1) ea, quæ ipsius falsissimam firmare possent sententiam, periisse censet! (2) Nec verum est, quod de dicto Matthæi profert; Legitur enim Zach. 6, 12: Esa. 11, 1. c. 61, 1.

XXXII. Posteriora verò præcepta nova, videl. Baptis mum & Cœnam Domini, quæ versantur circa ceremonias, & nos dicimus esse bona N. T. sed (1) Baptismum in V. præfiguratum per arcam Noæ Gen. 7, 1. 1. Petr. 3, 21 pertransitum per mare rubrum, Exod. 14, 29. 30. 1. Cor. 10, 2. per circumcisionem, Col. 2, 11. (2) promissum, Ps. 29, 20. Esa. 44, 3. De Cœna Domini quoq; idem est judicium, adsunt enim (1) typi: agnus Paschalis, Exod. 12. 3. 1. Cor. 5 v. 7. manna, Exod. 16, 31. 1. Cor. 10. 3. (2) promissiones, Ps. 23, 1, 2. 5. Esa. 25, 6. Quid ergò novi obtinuistis Hæretici? Nihil.


## 35 Thirty-fifth Disputation, On the Virtues and Miracles of Christ

Continuation.

Ambrose says no less truly than elegantly: It is a legitimate circumspection that we confess that, just as in the form of God nothing of the divine nature and fullness was lacking to Christ, so in that form of man nothing was lacking to him by which he might be judged an imperfect man. Leo in epist. 10. ad Flavian. c.3. Each nature retains its own property without defect. And just as the form of God does not take away the form of a servant, so the form of a servant does not diminish the form of God. For the only-begotten Son of God (inasmuch as he assumed a true and whole, yet holy, and from the filth of sins most free human nature, by the coming of the Holy Spirit, without any confusion of natures and properties into the unity of the ὑποστάσεως) was, because of Adam's fall, neither guilty, nor was there darkness in his mind, nor perversity in his will, nor aversion in his heart from the Law of God, to which he perfectly satisfied. Other men often require labor, exercise, and attention for an affection toward the good and an aversion from evils; but in Christ there is a certain natural conjunction to the good and alienation from iniquity, says Basil. It is evident, therefore, that natural things remained whole in Christ; to which perfection the twofold grace of God, of which one is called the grace of Union, the other Habitual, was added. Of the former we have spoken above; of the latter we shall now treat, as much as the narrowness of the theses will allow: 1. in general, whether it exists; 2. what it is; 3. in particular, concerning the virtues; 4. the gifts of the Holy Spirit; 5. the miracles, of which 6. a practical meditation will finally put an end. May God lead us into all truth!

Thesis I.

The Philosopher rightly says in l. 2. post. analy. c. 1. ζητῶμεν τέτταρα, τὸ ὅτι, διότι, εἰ ἔστι, τί ἐστιν. τὸ γὰρ ζητεῖν τί ἐστι, μὴ ἔχοντες ὅτι ἐστὶ, μηδὲν ζητεῖν ἐστὶ, text. 8. Not unmindful of this saying, we shall say whether and why such Habitual grace, of which we speak here, is given, which Thomas thinks must be brought forward for three reasons: 1. On account of the union of that soul with the Word of God.

II. For a receptive subject, the closer it is to the influencing cause, the more it participates in its influence. But that one, by the influx of grace is from God. And therefore it was most fitting that that soul, on account of the personal union, should receive the influx of divine grace. III. 2. On account of the nobility of that soul, whose operations it was fitting to reach more closely to God through knowledge and love, to which it is necessary that human nature be elevated through grace. IV to the human race, for Christ is the mediator of God and men, therefore it was fitting that he should have grace.

V. 4. That the humanity of Christ might have in itself a proper principle for eliciting works of a supernatural order, and might not elicit them by supernatural aid alone; because such a natural habit is simply for eliciting such works; but that the humanity might elicit them through a proper principle inherent in itself, and might operate by way of a principal cause through a form inherent in it. VI. But here one must accurately distinguish those things which are subjectively, formally, and habitually present in the human nature in Christ, from the properties of the divine nature, which we profess to have been really communicated to the nature assumed in the person of the Son of God, with which it is one ὑφιστάμενον. VII. 1. These depend upon the hypostatic union by the closest bond, which is between cause and effect: those are numbered among consequences rather, and κατ’ ἐξοχήν, than effects. 2. These precede in Christ; those follow, not indeed in order of time, but in order of nature and intellect. IIX. There are two main reasons for this assertion: 1. Because the habitual gifts of the soul of Christ were given no less by the Father and the Holy Spirit than by the Word, Ps. 45:8, John 3:34, Isa. 61:1, Luke 4:18, Acts 4:27. Nor yet is the human nature believed to be hypostatically united to those two persons. IX. 3. The union of the Word with the human nature was most perfect immediately from the very beginning of conception: however, it did not always have all habitual gifts perfectly, which will be made clear in the progress.

X. Γνόντες δὲ ὅτι ἐστὶ, τί ἐστι ζητῶμεν, i.e., After it is discovered to us that a thing is, that which follows next is to inquire, what it is? Arist. book 2, Posterior Analytics, text 1. Therefore, those gifts are qualities or habits, formally and subjectively inherent in the humanity itself or according to itself, by which it is informed and perfected, so that it may be a capable, suitable, and sufficiently disposed instrument, through which and with whose communion and cooperation the divine power of the Word may be able to exercise and perfect the operations of his divine majesty.

XI. For if the divinity, through the grace of indwelling (whence they are called θείας φύσεως κοινωνοὶ, 2 Pet. 1:4), spreads and diffuses the rays of its virtues into the Saints like a true light, and flows and pours out the streams of its good things into believers like a living fountain; it must be established that this happens much more fully and perfectly in that flesh in which the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells σωματικῶς.

XII. Whence these gifts have also obtained their name: for they are called Graces from the term from which, because they were given freely and proceeded from the grace of Union; but they are called Habitual from the term to which, because they are habits existing in the soul, through which Christ, as man, was able to do many things which otherwise he could not have performed by natural powers alone.

XIII. Moreover, those gifts (that we may examine the matter more closely) are divided by the Scholastics into habitual graces and gifts of the Spirit. They properly call those virtues by which a man is pleasing to GOD, such as faith, hope, and charity; they call the rest gifts, which perfect either the soul or the will.

XIV. Although very many confuse these, and call all supernatural goods pertaining to the soul sometimes habitual graces, sometimes gifts of the Spirit. For if you consider from whom they are, they are gifts of the Spirit, and all are also graces: if you consider what they are in the soul, they are infused habits of virtues. And thus if you join both, they are habitual graces, or habits infused by the Holy Spirit, and they are gratuitous.

XV. From which such a corollary arises: that all things must be attributed to the assumed nature of Christ which are necessarily required for its perfection.

XVI. Hence to the question: Whether there were cardinal virtues in Christ? Prudence, fortitude, temperance, justice; the answer is not difficult. Just as grace regards the essence of the soul, so virtue regards its power. And just as the powers of the soul are derived from its essence, so virtues are certain derivations of grace. But the more perfect any principle is, the more it impresses its effects. The grace of Christ, however, was most perfect. Therefore, from it proceeded virtues to perfect the individual powers of the soul, for all the acts of the soul. And thus Christ had all the virtues, Thom. p. 3, q. 7, art. 2.

XVII. We do not attribute faith, properly so called, to Christ. For since every habit receives its species from its object, and the object of faith is ἐλπι-

the substance of things hoped for, and the evidence of things not seen, Hebr. 11, 1. It is concluded that Christ, who sees God through his blessed knowledge by essence, could not have had faith, which pertains only to wayfarers, as such.

XVIII. Furthermore, two things in any habit deserve careful observation: 1. The matter about which any habit is concerned: 2. The formal object of the same. The reason for the one is different from that of the other. The former was not absent from Christ, who knew the most holy Trinity and all the mysteries of heavenly wisdom most excellently: The latter, insofar as that matter is formally abstracted from faith; for instance, insofar as the Trinity is something not evident, to that extent Christ's mind, seeing God by essence, was not concerned with this matter, that is, he did not see God through a glass and in a riddle, 1 Cor. 13, 2.

XIX. You ask: Is some perfection therefore taken away from Christ? I answer: Not at all; but the imperfection which the reason and nature of faith includes is removed from him. Is he who lacks spectacles, since he does not need them, more unhappy than he who, on account of the weakness of the so-called visual rays, has need of such an aid? I do not think so.

XX. The judgment regarding hope is almost the same. For as faith is of things which are not seen; so hope is of the same things which are not possessed, Rom. 8, 24. And indeed with respect to the primary object, which is God, the soul of Christ did not cease to enjoy him even in the very agony of death: With respect to the secondary: if indeed we understand by hope the expectation of any help promised by God: that is not foreign to Christ, whom nothing prevents from having hoped in this sense for liberation from evil, for resurrection, and for the glory of the body, Ps. 31, 1.

XXI. It is asked in this place: Whether that act of hope which we attribute to Christ proceeded from a habit? For otherwise it would follow that he himself was imperfect, as not being from a virtue, which conflicts with the perfection of Christ. But if it proceeded from some habit, it must necessarily have been the very virtue of hope itself. I answer: 1. An act is perfect even then, when it proceeds from a principle equally well or better disposed than if it were informed by a habit. For it is better for the soul to contemplate the glory of the body when it already possesses glory, than if, being destitute of such glory, it possessed the theological virtue of hope. For it is more certain that he who has the glory of the soul will also attain the glory of the body, than he who has the virtue of hope, and not yet the glory of the soul. What? That 2. one or another act is also accustomed to be produced sufficiently perfect by a bare power without a habit and other dispensation sometimes.

XXII. That which perfects the mind is knowledge or wisdom, which, besides that uncreated one by which God is, we establish as threefold: 1. Blessed, 2. Infused, 3. Acquired or Experimental.

XXIII. Those who acknowledge only the eternal [knowledge] in Christ, either take away the rational soul from him, or leave it imperfect, inasmuch as it is stripped of operation.

XXIV. For although the soul of Christ, through the grace of union, has attained uncreated blessedness in the person, it is not therefore to be despoiled of created blessedness in its own nature, for which knowledge and wisdom is required. For the act of one nature cannot be that of another. And since the λόγος assumed a nature λογικὴν, θελητικὴν καὶ ἐνεργητικὴν; it assumed indeed the δύναμιν of understanding, willing, and operating. For a mind that is ἄσοφος is not a mind, for if it is ἀνέργητος, it is also ἀκίνητος and ἀνύπαρκτος entirely.

XXV. Now blessed knowledge is that by which, as the rest of the blessed who have been translated to the glory of the heavenly life, he enjoys the vision of God, in which the highest glory and happiness of the blessed is placed; Or: By which he knows the Word and things in the Word.

XXVI. Which, however, leaves behind by a long interval the knowledge of all men, as many as ever were or are yet to be. For the more closely the soul of Christ is united to the λόγῳ, which is the fountain of all wisdom and knowledge, the more fully it receives that light of cognition than the other blessed. For the perfection of cognition is viewed not only on the part of the known, by reason of the medium, but also on the part of the knower, by reason of the power or habit.

XXVII. But what must be answered regarding the ignorance which Christ himself in Mark ch. 13 v. 32 professed? That very thing which Hilary [says in] book 10 de Trin.: The profession of the day not known is not an infirmity of ignorance, but a dispensation of silence. Or: through acquired and infused knowledge he could be ignorant of those things which he knew according to the blessed [knowledge].

XXIIX. Infused or implanted knowledge is that through which he knows things in their own proper nature through intelligible species proportional to the human mind.

XXVIII. Infused or innate knowledge is that by which he knows things in their own nature through intelligible species proportional to the human mind.

XXIX. This knowledge is not actual, but habitual, as it is appropriate to the receiving subject. For the nature of the human soul is so constituted that it understands sometimes in act, sometimes in potency, between which the habit is the medium: And because the medium is of the same genus as the extremes, it is rightly called habitual knowledge.

XXX. Acquired or experimental knowledge is that by which Christ knows all things possible to be known through the light of human reason. And although he did not have experience of individual things, yet he understood similar things from similar, contraries from contraries, effects from causes, and causes from effects.

XXXI. And we wish for that passage of Luke 2:40 to be referred here. Where it should be noted that there is a twofold progress of wisdom: 1. according to essence, insofar as the habit of knowledge itself is increased; 2. according to effect, insofar as someone, according to the same habit of knowledge, first demonstrates lesser things, afterwards greater things. In this way Christ is said to have progressed in knowledge.

XXXII. Therefore, in blessed knowledge, that progress which we have mentioned will have no place; because it is the effect of an agent of infinite power, which can produce the whole at once. But acquired knowledge, because it springs forth from the agent intellect, which operates successively; therefore, according to this, in his 12th year he produced greater motions than in infancy: in his 30th year, more illustrious ones than in his 31st. See Mr. Chemnitz, ch. 20, on the two natures, p. 126, a. b.

XXXIII. Thus far concerning those things which perfect the mind; there follows now that which perfects the will, Charity; which, just as it is the end of the commandment, the fulfillment of the law, and the bond of perfection, and never fails, 1 Tim. 1:5, Col. 3:14, Rom. 13:10, 1 Cor. 13:8, so it was most perfect and absolute in every respect in Christ. John 13:1, Rom. 5:6, 7. Those things which are held here and there concerning the quantity of these virtues in relation to the one of all, I pass over, knowingly and willingly, as they are more intricate than profitable. I pass now to

XXXIV. The gifts of the Holy Spirit, enumerated by Isaiah ch. 11:2, where 1. it is asked in general whether they were in Christ, 2. in particular concerning the gift of fear. To the first, Aquinas answers that every perfect thing according to the order of its nature needs to be helped by that which is of a higher nature. But since it is written of Christ, Isaiah 11, the Spirit rests upon him of the Lord; and Luke 4, 1. Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan; it is manifest from this that in Christ the gifts were most excellent.

XXXV. As regards what pertains to this, I answer: That there was in Christ the fear of God, not indeed in so far as it respects the evil of separation from God through guilt, nor in so far as it respects the evil of punishment for guilt, but in so far as it respects the divine preeminence itself, in that the soul of Christ was moved toward God by a certain affection of reverence, being led by the Holy Spirit.

XXXVI. Furthermore, since the flesh of Christ is not only an inanimate instrument of his divinity, but also subsistent and active, the madness and dementia of our adversaries is to be deplored, when they clamor, with Nestorius, that the flesh of Christ contributed no more to the performing of miracles than the flesh of the Apostles or the rod of Aaron.

XXXVII. For this is the difference between a conjoined and a separate instrument: that the former obtains the very powers of the principal agent (with which it is one subsistent entity) through real communication; but the latter perceives only the activities of the power, and with the principal agent (otherwise a form by assistance) constitutes only one thing by accident.

XXXIIX. There are added: 1. Sayings attributing the power of performing miracles to the assumed flesh: Acts 10, 38; John 5, 36. 2. Examples: Matthew 8, 3; Mark 9, 25; ch. 7, 34; John 9, 7; which are nothing other than the fruits of the exaltation of the man Christ, Mark ch. 16, v. 19, 20.

XXXIX. These miracles are certainly of such importance that even from these alone (whatever that spirit of giddiness may snarl) the divinity of Christ can be sufficiently evidently demonstrated and proven.

XL. Therefore we argue thus: Whoever has from himself the power and virtue of performing miracles, he is the true and eternal GOD, Ps. 77, 15. But Christ before the resurrection had that power of performing miracles; therefore he is the true and eternal GOD. I prove the major premise from the words of Ostorodt in Inst. ch. 10, p. 79, § 2. For he says thus: The words of Psalm 77 are not to be understood as if no one could perform miracles except the one God alone, but that all true miracles come from God, and He alone has the power from Himself to perform such things.

The same confirms the minor premise in ch. 19, p. 113, § 5. As for what concerns the apostles, who have done the same deeds as Christ, nay, as it appears, even greater than Christ: one should know that we do not simply say that Christ was in the divine form and equality for the reason that He did miracles, but that He had the power in Himself to do miracles: so that He was also able to communicate the same to others: which was not the case in the apostles, etc.

XL. Therefore our syllogism remains unshaken, even by the testimony of the adversary himself on page 79, who says thus (having undoubtedly forgotten himself): 'If now from the miracles of Christ his supposed divine nature were to be inferred, one would have to prove that Christ had the power from Himself to do such things, which we indeed know very well (note the inconsistency) that it cannot be proven.'

XLII. But, since the things said thus far are to be applied to pious use: let the perfection of the mighty works of Christ be a lamentation of our state. How great was the dignity of the human condition, how great the excellence of dignity beyond other creatures, how great the prerogative of divine gifts shone forth in the first-formed, when they were not yet infected by any plague of sins? They were in gratuitous gifts, assiduous contemplators of GOD, surrounded by innocence, inspired by charity, endowed with wisdom, supported by prudence, composed by temperance. Think therefore, O man, whence and through what you have come here! From paradise thrust into a valley of misery and tears, from obedient you have become disobedient, from temperate intemperate, from the image of GOD you have become the image of the Devil. O miserable change of affairs! Behold! Sin is that very deformity on account of which GOD detests you; sin is that iniquity on account of which the Devil embraces you: sin, I say, is that very infirmity on account of which the whole world is dissipated. Abstain therefore from evil, exercise yourself in good, persevere in both, and you will be a friend to GOD. For the further you are from sin, the closer you are to GOD.

XLIII. Let the performance of miracles be our consolation. Although you are pressed in this unclean world, have confidence, it is GOD who acts so that you are not suppressed. Just as in threshing the grains are pressed by the chaff; just as thorns come forth among flowers; and the rose, which is fragrant, grows with thorns, which prick: so it is necessary that you be pressed by adversity, and pricked by the stings of thorns, that it may offer a greater sweetness of fragrance to God; whom we ask from the heart thus: The evening has now come, stay with us, O Christ: And do not suffer your light to be extinguished! So be it, so be it!

Latin:

Continuatio.

NON minùs verè qvàm eleganter Ambrosius: Legitima, inqvit, circumspectio est, ut confiteamur, sicut in DEI forma nihil Christo defuit divinæ naturæ & plenitudinis: sic in illa forma hominis nihil ei defuisse qvò imperfectus homo judicaretur. Leo in epist. 10. ad Flavian. c.3. Tenet sine defectu proprietatem suam utraq; natura. Et sicut formam servi, DEI forma non adimit : Ita formam DEI, servi forma non minuit. Unigenitus enim filius DEI (qvippe, qvi veram, integramqve, sanctam tamen, & à peccatorum sordibus liberrimam humanam naturam, Spiritûs sancti superventu, absq; omni naturarũ & proprietatum confusione in ὑποστάσεως unitatem assumsit ) ob Adami lapsum neq; reus, neq; in mente ejus caligo, neq; in voluntate perversio, neq; in corde à Lege DEI, cui perfectè satisfecit, aversio fuit. Reliqvi homines labore & exercitatione, attentioneq; sæpè reqvirunt affectionem ad bonum, & averfionem à malis : Christo verò naturalis qvædam est conjunctio ad bonum, & abalienatio ab iniqvitate, ait Basilius. Naturalia igitur in Christo permansisse integra constat; cui perfectioni duplex DEI gratia, qvarum altera Unionis, altera Habitualis nuncupatur, accessit. De illa superiùs; de hac jam tantum, qvantum qvidem thesewn angustia patietur, acturi, 1. in genere; An sit; 2. quid sit, 3. in specie, de virtutibus, 4. Spiritûs sancti donis, 5. miraculis, dicemus, quibus 6. meditatio deniq; practica finem imponet. DEUS ducat nos in omnem veritatem!.

Thesis I.

REctè Philosophus l. 2. post. analy. c. 1. ζητῶμεν τέτταρα, τὸ ὅτι, διότι, εἰ ἔστι, τί ἐστιν. τὸ γὰρ ζητεῖν τί ἐστι, μὴ ἔχοντες ὅτι ἐστὶ, μηδὲν ζητεῖν ἐστὶ, text. 8. Nos hujus effati haud immemores, an & cur ejusmodi, qvâ de nobis hîc sermo est, Gratia habitualis detur; dicemus, qvam Thomas propter tria afferendam esse censet : 1. Propter animæ illius ad verbum DEI unionem.

II. Receptivum enim, qvantò propinqvius est causæ influenti, tantò magis de ipsius influentia participat. Iste autem gratiæ influxu est à Deo. Ideoqve maximè oportuit, ut anima illa, propter unionem personalem, divinæ influxum gratiæ reciperet. III. 2. Propter nobilitatem illius animæ, cujus operationes oportebat propinqviùs attingere ad Deum per cognitionem & amorem, ad qvem necesse est elevati naturam humanam per gratiam. IV. 3. Propter habitudinem ipsius Christi ad genus humanum, Christus enim mediator Dei & hominum est, ideò oportebat, ut haberet gratiam.

V. 4. Ut humanitas Christi haberet in se principium proprium eliciendi opera supernaturalis ordinis, & ea non eliceret solo auxilio supernaturali; qvia talis habitus naturalis sit simpliciter ad elicienda talia opera; sed ut humanitas ea eliceret, per proprium principium sibi inhærens naturale, & operaretur per modum causæ principalis per inhærentem sibi formam. VI. Accuratè autem hîc distingvenda sunt, quæ humanæ naturæ in Christo subjectivè formaliter & habitualiter insunt, a divinæ naturæ proprietatibus, quas assumtæ naturæ in persona Filii DEI, cum qua est unum ὑφισάμενον, realiter communicatas esse profitemur. VII. 1. Hæc ab unione ὑποϛατικῇ arctissimo nexu, qvi est inter causam & effectum, depédent: Illa inter consectaria potiùs, & ϰατεξομχὰς, qvàm effecta, numerantur. 2. Hæc in Christo præcedunt; Illa non temporis qvidem, sed naturæ & intellectûs ordine sequuntur. IIX. Cujus assertionis duæ potissimùm sunt rationes: 1. Qvia dona habitualia animæ Christi, non minùs à Patre & Spiritu sancto, qvàm λόγῳ data sunt, Pf. 45, 8. Joh. 3, 34. Esa. 61, 1. Luc. 4, v. 18. Act. 4, 27. Neq; tamé duabus illis personis humana natura ὑποϛατικῶς unita creditur. IX. 3. Unio ϰ̃ λόγꙋ cum humananatura personalis statim ab ipso conceptionis primordio fuit perfectissima: Dona autem habitualia non omnia semper perfectè habuit, id qvod in progressu patefiet.

X. Γνόντες δὲ ὅτι ἐϛὶ, τί ἐϛι ζητῶμεν, i. e. Postqvam esse rem nobis compertum est, illud proximè seqvitur, ut qværatur, qvid sit? Arist. l. 2. post Anal. r. t. 1. Sunt ergò dona illa, qvalitates seu habitus, ipsi humanitati formaliter & subjectivè in aut secundùm se inhærentes, qvibus informatur & perficitur, ut possit esse ὄργανον habile, idoneum ac sufficienter dispositum, per qvod & cum cujus communione ac cooperatione divina potentia ϰ̃ λόγꙋ divinæ majestatis suæ operationes exercere & perficere qveat.

XI. Si enim divinitas Sanctis per inhabitationis gratiam (unde θείας φύσεως κοινωνοὶ, 2. Petr. 1. v. 4. dicuntur) tanquam lumen verum virtutum suarum radios spargit & diffundit in Sanctos, & tanquam vivus fons bonorum suorum rivos influit & effundit in credentes; multò plenius & perfectiùs illa in ea carne fieri statuendum est, in qua tota plenitudo Deitatis σωματικῶς inhabitat.

XII. Unde & nomen sortita sunt isthæc dona: Gratiæ enim dicuntur à termino à quo, quia gratis data, & à gratia Unionis profecta sunt; Habituales verò à termino ad quem, quia habitus sunt in anima existentes, per quos Christus, quà homo, multa poterat, quæ alioquin solis naturalibus viribus præstare non potuisset.

XIII. Dividuntur autem illa dona (ut rem propiùs inspiciamus) à Scholasticis, in gratias habituales, & in dona Spiritus. Illas propriè vocant virtutes, quibus homo sit gratus DEO, uti est; fides, spes, caritas: dona vocant reliqua, quæ vel animam vel voluntatem perficiunt.

XIV. Quanquam permulti hæc confundunt, & omnia bona supernaturalia animum spectantia, modò gratias habituales, modò dona Spiritus vocitant. Si enim consideres, à quo sint, dona sunt Spiritus, omnia etiam gratiæ: si quid sint in anima, sunt habitus virtutum infusi. Et ita si utrumq; conjugas, fuerint gratiæ habituales, seu habitus infusi à Spiritu sancto, illiq; gratuiti.

XV. Ex quibus tale πόρισμα ebullit: Omnia assumtæ Christi naturæ tribuenda esse, quæ ad perfectionem eiusdem necessariò requiruntur.

XVI. Hinc ad quæstionem; Utrum in Christo fuerint virtutes cardinales? Prudentia, fortitudo, temperantia, justitia; responsio difficilis haud est. Sicut gratia respicit essentiam animæ, ita virtus respicit ejus potentiam. Et sicut potentiæ animæ derivantur ab ejus essentia: ita virtutes sunt quædam derivationes gratiæ. Quantò autem aliquod principium est perfectius, tantò magis imprimit suos effectus. Gratia Christi verò fuit perfectissima. Ergò ex ipsa processerunt virtutes ad perficiendum singulas animæ potentias, quo ad omnes animæ actus. Et ita Christus, habuit omnes virtutes, Thom. p. 3. q. 7. art. 2.

XVII. Fidem propriè dictam Christo non tribuimus. Nam cum omnis habitus ab objecto speciem accipiat, & fidei objectum sit ἐλπι-

ζομένων ὑπόςασις καὶ πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος ὀυ βλεπομένων, Hebr. 11, 1. efficitur, Christum, qui per scientiam beatam Deum videt per essentiam, fidem, quæ ad solos viatores, quâ tales, pertinet, habere non potuisse.

XIIX. Duo præterea in qvovis habitu observationem probè merentur: 1. Materia circa quam versatur aliqvis habitus: 2. Formale ejusdem objectum. Alia hujus, alia illius est ratio. Illa non abfuit à Christo, qui sacrosanctam Trinitatem, & omnis cœlestis sapientiæ mysteria optimè cognovit: Hoc prout materia illa fidei abstractum est formaliter; puta, qvatenus Trinitas est qviddam non evidens, eatenus Christi mens Deum per essentiam videns, circa hanc materiam non versabatur, id est, Deum non videbat per speculũ & ænigma 1. Cor. 13, 2.

XIX. Inqvis: Ergò aliqua Christo detrahitur perfectio? Resp. minimè verò: sed imperfectio, quam ratio & natura fidei includit, ab eo removetur. Qui conspicillis caret, cùm iis non egeat, estnè infelicior eo, qui ob radiorum, quos vocant, visivorum imbecillitatem, ejusmodi adminiculo opus habet? non puto.

XX. De spe idem ferè judicium. Nam ut Fides est rerum, quæ non videntur; ita spes est earundem, quæ non habentur, Rom. 8, 24. Et respectu quidem objecti primarii, quod est Deus, eô ne in ipso quidem mortis agone, animæ Christi frui desiit: Respectu secundarii: si nimitum per spem cujusvis auxilii à Deo promissi expectationem intelligimus: ea non est aliena è Christo, quem hôc sensu liberationem à malo, resurrectionem & corporis gloriam sperasse, nihil quicquam vetat, Ps. 31, 1.

XXI. Quæritur hoc in loco: An ille spei actus, quem tribuimus Christo, profectus fuerit ab habitu? Conseqveretur enim aliàs, ipsum fuisse imperfectum, utpote non ex virtute, id quod cum Christi perfectione pugnat. Si autem ab aliqvo habitu processit, ipsissimam spei virtutem fuisse necesse est. Resp. 1. Actum etiam tunc esse perfectum, quando procedit à principio æqvè benè meliusvè disposito, quàm si per habitum informetur. Nam ad gloriam corporis spectandam meliùs est anima deposita, cùm jam habet gloriam, quàm si hujusmodi gloriâ destituta, haberet virtutem spei Theologicam. Certius enim est eum, qui gloriam animæ habet, consecuturum etiam gloriam corporis, quam qui virtutem spei habet, & nondum gloriam animæ. Qvid? quod 2. unus vel alter actus etiam a potentia nuda sine habitu aliaq; dispensatione soleat aliqvando satis perfectus produci.

XXII. Quæ mentem perficit, est scientia vel sapientia, quam præter increatam illam, qua DEus est, triplicem statuimus, 1. Beatam, 2. Infusam, 3. Acquisitam vel Experimentalem.

XXIII. Qui solam æternam in Christo agnoscunt, aut animam rationalem ei adimunt, aut imperfectam, qvippe operatione exutam, relinqvunt.

XXIV. Quamvis enim anima Christi per unionis gratiam beatitudinem increatam consecuta sit in persona, non tamen propterea spolianda est beatitudine creata in sua natura, ad quam scientia & sapientia reqviritur. Actus enim unius naturæ non potest esse alterius. Et cùm λόγος assumsit naturam λογικὴν, θελητικὴν καὶ ἐνεργητικὴν; assumsit utiqve δύναμιν intelligendi, volendi, & operandi. Mens enim ἄσοφος non est mens, εἰ γὰρ ἀνέργητος, καὶ ἀκίνητος καὶ ἀνύπαρκτος πάντως.

XXV. Est autem scientia beata, quâ ut reliqvi beati ad cœlestis vitæ gloriam translati, DEI visione, in qua summa beatorum gloria & felicitas posita est, fruitur; Vel: Qua agnoscit verbum & res in verbo.

XXVI. Quæ tamen omnium, quotqvot unquam fuerunt; aut etiamnum futuri sunt, hominum scientiam longò post se intervallo relinqvit. Quo enim arctiùs unita est anima Christi τῷ λόγῳ, qui fons est omnis sapientiæ & scientiæ: hòc pleniùs recipit lumen illud cognitionis, quàm cæteri beati. Nam perfectio cognitionis non solùm ex parte cogniti, ratione medii, sed etiam ex parte cognoscentis, ratione potentiæ vel habitus spectatur.

XXVII. Quid autem ad ignorantiam, quam Christus ipse Marc. c. 13. v. 32. profectus est, respondendum? Id ipsum, quod Hilarius l. 10. de Trin. Professio nescitæ diei, non est ignorationis infirmitas, sed tacendi dispensatio. Vel: per acqvisitam scientiam & infusam potuit ignorare ea, quæ juxta beatam scivit.

XXIIX. Scientia infusa sive indita est, per quam cognoscit res in propria sua natura per species intelligibiles menti humanæ proportionales.

XXIIX. Scientia infusa sive indita est, per quam cognoscit res in propria sua natura per species intelligib. méti humanæ proportionales.

XXIX. Hæc scientia actualis non est, sed habitualis, qvippe subjecto recipienti congrua. Ita enim comparata est animæ humanæ natura, ut qvandoqve actu, qvandoq; potestate intelligat, inter qvæ est medius habitus: Et qvia medium ejusdem est generis cum extremis, rectè habitualis vocatur scientia.

XXX. Scientia acqvisita vel exprimentalis est, qvâ Christus cognoscit omnia per rationis humanæ lumen cognosci possibilia. Et qvamvis non singularum rerum experimentum ceperit, tamen ex similibus similia, ex contrariis contraria, ex causis effecta, ex effectis causas intellexit.

XXXI. Atq; huc illud Luc. 2, 40. relatum volumus. Ubi notetur, qvòd duplex sit profectus sapientiæ, 1. secundùm essentiam, qvatenus ipse scientiæ habitus augetur, 2. secundùm effectum, qvatenus aliqvis secundùm eundem scientiæ habitum primò minora, posteà majora demonstrat. Qvomodo Christus in scientia profecisse dicitur.

XXXII. In scientia igitur beata ille, qvem diximus, profectus locum nó habebit; qvia est infinitæ virtutis agentis effectus, qvi potest simul totum operari. Scientia verò acqvisita, qvia tantùm ab agente intellectu, qvi succesfivè operatur, repullulascit; ideò secundùm hanc anno 12. majores, qvàm in infantia: Anno 30. illustriores, qvàm anno 31. motus efficit. Vide Dn. Chemn. c. 20. de duab. nat. p. 126. a. b.

XXXIII. Hactenus de iis, qvæ mentem; seqvitur nunc, qvæ voluntatem perficit, Caritas; qvæ, sicuti est finis præcepti, legis complementum, & perfectionis vinculum, nec unqvam excidit, 1. Tim. 1, 5. Col. 3, 14. Rom. 13, 10. 1. Cor. 13, 8. Ita in Christo perfectissima & omnibus numeris absolutissima fuit. Joh. 13, 1. Rom. 5, 6, 7. Qvę de harum virtutum ad unam omnium qvantitate hinc inde habentur, sciens volens, qvippè intricata magis qvàm proficua, prætereo. Transeo jam ad

XXXIV. Dona Spiritus sancti, ab Esa. c. 11, 2. enumerata, ubi 1. qværitur in genere, utrum in Christo fuerint, 2. in specie de timoris dono. Ad primum respondet Aqvinas, qvòd omne perfectum secundùm ordiné naturæ suę indiget adjuvari ab eo, qvod est altioris naturę. Cùm autem de Christo scriptum sit, Esa. 11. reqviescit super eum Spiritus Domini; & Luc. 4, 1. Jesus plenus Spiritu sancto regressus est a Jordane, manifestum est inde, quod in Christo dona fuerint excellentissime.

XXXV. Secundum quod attinet, Resp. In Christo fuisse timorem Dei, non quidem, quatenus respicit malum separationis a Deo per culpam: nec, quatenus respicit malum punitionis pro culpa: sed, quatenus respicit ipsam divinam praeeminentiam, prout scilicet anima Christi quodam affectu reverentiae movebatur in Deum, a Spiritu sancto acta.

XXXVI. Porro, cùm caro Christi non modò sit ὄργανον ipsius divinitatis ἄψυχον, sed & ἐνυπόστατον κᾀ ἐνεργητικόν; deploranda est adversariorum nostrorum amentia & dementia, cum Nestorio carnem Christi ad edenda miracula non plus contulisse, quàm carnem Apostolorum aut virgam Aaronis, clamitantium.

XXXVII. Hoc enim inter instrumentum conjunctum & separatum interest, quòd illud ipsasmet principalis agentis (cum quo unum est ὑφιστάμενον) δυνάμεις, per realem communicationem obtinet: Hoc verò ipsas δυνάμεως ἐνεργείας percipit; & cum principali agente (alias forma per assistentiam) non nisi unum per accidens constituit.

XXXIIX. Accedunt 1. dicta virtutem efficiendi miracula assumtae carni attribuentia: Act. 10, 38. Joh. 5, 36. 2. Exempla Matth. 8, 3. Marc. 9, 25. c. 7, 34. Joh. 9, 7. quae nihil aliud sunt, quàm fructus exaltationis hominis Christi, Marc. cap. 16. v. 19, 20.

XXXIX. Quae miracula tanti certè sunt momenti, ut vel ex his solis (quicquid spiritus ille vertiginis ogganniat) divinitas Christi satis evidenter demonstrari possit ac evinci.

XL. Proinde sic argumentamur: Quicunque ex se potentiam & virtutem habet patrandi miracula, ille est verus ac aeternus DEUS Pf. 77, 15. Atqui Christus ante resurrectionem habuit istam miraculorum patrandorum virtutem: Ergò est verus & aeternus DEUS. Majorem ex Ostorodi verbis in Inst. c. 10, p. 79. §. 2. probo. Sic enim ait: Die Wort des Psalms 77. sind nicht also zuverstehen/ daß niemand könne Wunder thun/ denn nur der einige GOtt allein / sondern daß alle warhafftige Wunderwerck von GOtt herkommen / und Er allein Krafft von Ihm selber habe solche zu thun.

Minorem idem confirmat c. 19. p. 113. §. 5. Was aber die Apostel belanget/welche eben solche Thaten/wie Christus/ja/wie sichs ansehen läst/ noch grössere/denn Christus/gethan haben: Soll man wissen/daß wir nicht schlecht sagen/daß Christus in göttlicher Gestalt und Gleichheit darumb gewesen/weil Er Wunder gethan/sondern daß Er in ihm selber die Krafft gehabt/Wunder zu thun: also daß Er auch andern von derselben hat können mittheilen: welches in den Aposteln nicht gewesen/tc.

XL. Manet ergò Syllogismus noster inconcussus, vel ipsius adversarii testimonio pag. 79. sic (qui sui haud dubiè oblitus est) dicentis: So nun aus den Wunderwercken Christi/solte seine vermeinte Göttliche Natur colligirt werden/müste man beweisen/daß Christus von Ihm selber Krafft gehabt/solche zu thun/welches wir denn gar wohl wissen (attende inconstantiam) daß es nicht kan bewiesen werden.

XLII. Verùm, cùm hactenus dicta ad pium usum accommodanda sint: Virtutum Christi perfectio, sit status deploratio. Quanta dignitas humanæ conditionis, quanta excellentia dignitatis ultra ceteras creaturas, quanta donorum divinorum prærogativa in protoplastis, cùm nullâ adhuc peccatorum lue infecti essent, relucebat? Erant in gratuitis, contemplatores DEI assidui, innocentiâ stipati, caritate, afflati, sapientiâ dotati, prudentiâ fulciti, temperantiâ compositi. Cogita ergò ô homo, unde, & per quod huc veneris! Ex paradyso in miseriæ & lachrymarum vallem detrusus, ex obediente inobediens, ex temperante intemperans, ex imagine DEI imago Diaboli factus es. O miserabilem rerum permutationem! Ecce! peccatum illa ipsa est deformitas, propter quam te destatur DEUS; peccatum est illa iniquitas, propter quam te amplexatur Diabolus: peccatum, inquam, illa ipsa est infirmitas, propter quam dissipatur totus mundus. Abstine igitur à malo, exercita te in bono, persevera in utroque, & eris amicus DEO. Quò enim remotiùs à peccato, eò propinquiùs DEO.

XLIII. Miraculorum effectio sit nostra consolatio. Licet in hoc immundo mundo premaris, confide, DEUS est, qui facit, ut ne supprimaris. Sicut in tritura paleæ grana permuntur; sicuti spinæ inter flores prodeunt; & rosa, quæ redolet, crescit cum spinis, quæ pungunt: sic necesse est, ut adversitate premaris, & spinarum aculeis pungaris, ut majorem svavitatem odoris offerat Deo; qvem animitus ita rogamus: Vespera jam venit, nobiscum Christe maneto: Extingvi lucem nec patiare tuam! Fiat, fiat!


## 36 Thirty-sixth Disputation, On the Passion of Our Redeemer Jesus Christ

Continuation.

Although the second person of the most holy Trinity, the Son of GOD, from his very birth, undertook to carry out certain tasks or offices for the sake of acquiring our salvation: Nevertheless, it is evident from the undoubted oracles of Scripture that the history of the Passion in particular (which describes Christ's most bitter conflict with our enemies) is a compendious doctrine of this most holy merit. Since, therefore, almost all things that preceded this wondrous battle are understood from the previous disputations, it also follows as a duty that we should go forth to meet our Redeemer coming from Bozrah, and exulting in the greatness of his strength. This cannot be done otherwise than by a pious and most ardent consideration of the Lord's Passion, which we shall briefly weave together, comprised in these four chapters. In the first, we shall examine certain prophecies of the Old Testament in which the passion of Christ is treated: In the second, I shall look into the fulfillment of those prophecies according to the circumstances of the events: In the third, we shall resolve the more illustrious questions: In the fourth and final, we shall at last append a practical meditation. Do you, O JESUS CHRIST, only grant favor to our undertakings, so that all our words and thoughts may yield to the eternal glory of your passion and to our salvation!

Chapter I. On the prophecies of the Old Testament.

I. The passion of CHRIST (which is nothing other than the horrendous punishment of GOD, which Christ, for the sake of our sins, which out of ineffable love he had derived upon himself, by a wondrous tempering of divine justice and mercy, spontaneously sustained for the expiation of our sins and the propitiation of divine wrath, and the liberation of the whole human race) This passion of CHRIST, I say, the Prophets everywhere predicted in their θεοπνεύςοις books. For because the Lamb was slain from the foundation of the world, Apoc. 5. 8, and the obedience of CHRIST was an equally most effective comfort to the Patriarchs as it is to us, they speak of this saving merit in many prophecies and types.

II. Whence it is gathered that those predictions can be referred to two classes. 1. For there exist clear testimonies concerning the passion of Christ; 2. Certain histories of the Old Testament prefigured it.

III. The former prophecies are again twofold. For some touch generally upon the passion of the Son of God, such as that in the first Gospel concerning the bruising of the serpent, Gen. 3. v. 15, concerning the agonies of desertion, which are described Ps. 22. v. 2, 3, etc., concerning the waters of sorrows entering even unto the soul and the mire of the deep, Ps. 69. v. 2, 3, concerning the torrent in the way, Ps. 110. v. 7, etc.

IV. All the testimonies of the remaining Prophets can also be referred here, by which they depict the passion and death of our Savior so graphically that they seem to have lived at that very time when CHRIST was crucified. To this pertains c. 53 of Isaiah, where he discourses quite prolixly concerning the infirmities of CHRIST that were taken up, and c. 63, where he introduces our Redeemer ascending from Bozrah by an excellent dialogue. To which can be added the remaining testimonies from Dan. 9. v. 26, Zech. 13. v. 7, etc.

V. Furthermore, more specific ones describe certain sorrows separately and particularly. Thus the royal Prophet foresaw the snares of the traitor Judas, Ps. 41. v. 10, predicted the sale of CHRIST made for a vile price, Zech. 11. v. 13, who also complains of the flight and dispersion of the disciples, c. 13. v. 7, furthermore of the fury of the nations, Ps. 2. v. 1, of the scourging, Ps. 129. v. 4, of the insults and various reproaches, Ps. 22. v. 8, 9, etc., of the crucifixion, Ps. 22. v. 17, of the division of the garment, in the same Ps. v. 19, of the gall mixed with vinegar, Ps. 69. v. 23, of the agony of death, Ps. 22. v. 16, Is. 53. 8, of the piercing of the side, Zech. 12. v. 10, etc.

VI. Nor, however, do only clear predictions speak of the passion, but types or certain images also prefigured it, to which can be reckoned the offering of Isaac, Gen. 22, the sale of Joseph, Gen. 37. v. 28, the immolation of the paschal lamb, Exod. 12. v. 5, 6, 7, the sending forth of the goat bearing all iniquities, Lev. 16. v. 21, the exaltation of the bronze serpent, Num. 21, and the type of Jonah, which CHRIST transferred to himself, Matt. 12. v. 40. Other kinds of sacrifices and many histories, which occur here and there in the O.T., look to this.

Latin:

Continuatio.

QVamvis secunda sacrosanctæ Trinitatis persona, Filius DEI, ab ipsa statim nativitate, salutis nostræ acqvirendæ gratia munera sive officia aliqvot expedienda susceperit: Tamen Passionis præcipuè historiam, (qvæ acerrimum Christi cum hostibus nostris conflictum describit) compendiosam sanctissimi hujus meriti doctrinam esse, ex indubitatis scripturæ oraculis patescit. Qvum igitur omnia fermè, qvæ mirabilem hanc pugnam præcessêre, ex superioribus disputationibus intelligantur; ex debito etiam venit, ut Redemptori nostro de Bosra gradienti, & in magnitudine fortitudinis suę exultanti, obviam procedamus. Id qvod aliter fieri neqvit, qvâm piâ & ardentissimâ Passionis dominicæ consideratione, qvam qvatuor hisce capitibus comprehensam breviter pertexemus. In primo vaticinia qvædã Veteris Testamenti, in qvibus de Christi passione agitur, perlustrabimus: In secundo vaticiniorum illorum impletionem secundùm rerum gestarum circumstantias dispiciem: In tertio illustriores qvæstiones enodabimus: In qvarto & ultimo tandem & meditationem Practicam subjungemus. Tu modô, ô JESU CHRISTE, cœptis nostris annue, ut omnia dicta & cogitata nostra cedant in sempiternam passionis tuæ gloriam, & nostram salutem!

Caput I. de vaticiniis Veteris Testamenti.

I. Passionem CHRISTI (qvæ nihil aliud est, qvàm horrenda DEI pœna, qvam Christus propter peccata nostra, qvæ ex ineffabili dilectione in se derivârat, factô mirando temperamento justitiæ & misericordiæ divinæ, spontè sustinuit, ad peccatorum nostrorum expiationem, iræ divinæ placationem, & totius generis humani liberationem) Hanc, inqvam, CHRISTI passionem Prophetæ in libris suis θεοπνεύςοις ubiq; prædixerunt. Qvia enim Agnus occisus est ab origine mundi, Apocas. v. 8. & CHRISTI obedientia Patriarchis æqvè ac nobis efficacissimo solatio fuit, de salutifero hoc merito in multis vaticiniis & typis loqvuntur.

II. Unde colligitur, qvòd prædictiones illæ ad duas classes referri qvæant. 1. enim clara de passione Christi extant testimonia; 2. Historiæ qvædam Veteris Testamenti eam præfigurârunt.

III. Priora vaticinia rursus duplicia sunt. Qvædam enim generaliter Filii Dei passionem attingunt, qvale est illud in primo Evangelio de morsu serpentis, Gen. 3. v. 15. de angoribus desertionis, qvi describuntur Ps. 22. v. 2. 3. &c. de aqvis dolorum usq; ad animam intrantibus & limo profundi, Ps. 69. v. 2. 3. de torrente in via, Ps. 110. v. 7. &c.

IV. Referri huc possunt omnia reliqvorum etiam Prophetarum testimonia, qvibus passionem & mortem Salvatoris nostri adeò graphicè depingunt, ut eo ipso tempore, qvo CHRISTUS crucifixus est, vixisse videantur. Huc pertinet c. 53. Esaia, ubi de susceptis CHRISTI langvoribus prolixè satis disserit, & c. 63. ubi egregio dialogismo Redemptorem nostrum de Bosra ascendentem introducit. Qvibus reliqva addi possunt testimonia ex Dan 9. v. 26. Zach. 13. v. 7. &c.

V. Specialiora porrò dolores qvosdã seorsim & speciatim describũt. Sic Judæ proditoris insidias prævidit regius Propheta, Ps. 41. v. 10. venditionem CHRISTI vili precio factam prædixit Zach. 11. v. 13. qvi de fuga qvog; & dispersione discipulorũ conqveritur c. 13. v. 7. de furore porrò gentium, Ps. 2. v. 1. de flagellatione, Ps. 129. v. 4. de contumeliis & variis opprobriis, Ps. 22. v. 8. 9. &c. de crucifixione, Ps. 22. v. 17. de vestimenti divisione, eodem Ps. v. 19. de felle cum aceto mixto, Ps. 69. v. 23. de mortis agone, Ps. 22. v. 16. Es. 53. 8. de lateris transfixione Zach. 12. v. 10. &c. agitur.

VI. Neq; tamen prædictiones solùm perspicuæ de passione loqvũtur, sed typi etiam, vel imagines qvædam eam præfigurârunt, qvibus accenseri potest oblatio Isaaci, Gen. 22. Venditio Josephi, Gen. 37. v. 28. agni paschalis immolatio, Exod. 12. v. 5. 6. 7. hirci omnes iniqvitates portantis emissio, Lev. 16. v. 21. ænei serpentis exaltatio, Num. 21. & typ9 Jonæ, qvem CHRISTUS ad se transtulit, Matth 12. v. 40. Huc alia sacrificiorum genera, & plures historiæ spectant, qvę in V. T. passim occurrunt.


### Chapter II. On the fulfillment of prophecies

Chapter II. On the fulfillment of prophecies.

I. That all these prophecies were fulfilled with the most certain outcome will become clear from a more diligent narration of the circumstances, which we shall briefly subjoin. And first, indeed, we shall briefly run through the time of the passion, 2. The place, 3. The manner, 4. The causes.

II. Scripture determined the time 1. Generically, 2. Specifically. In general, indeed, where it made mention of the Paschal feast, Matt. 26, v. 2. For the true paschal lamb was to be slaughtered at this very time, which would fulfill the type of the Old Testament, concerning which it is read in Exod. 12, v. 5, 6; 1 Cor. 5, v. 7, 8.

III. Furthermore, in particular, almost all the moments of time or hours can be numbered. For at the very break of day Christ is captured by the Jews. Then at the 1st hour (the 6th for us) He is led to Pilate: at the 3rd hour (the 9th for us) He is condemned: at about the 6th (the 12th for us) He is crucified: at the 9th (perhaps the 5th for us) He expires with a great cry. All these moments of time serve for a more accurate consideration of the Lord's Passion.

IV. Then the place also can be described in various ways according to the diversity of the agonies. For 1. the place of the captivity is to be noted, where, however, even before the captivity He felt truly infernal agonies, so that by a certain stupendous miracle He sweated blood. This place Matt. 26, v. 36, etc., Mark 14, v. 32, call Gethsemane. For those who have traveled through Palestine (witness the most illustrious Gerhard in his Harmony of the Gospels, p. 46) report that Gethsemane was a village, or estate, situated at the roots of the Mount of Olives, and conspicuous for its gardens. See John ch. 18, v. 1, following.

V. For in a garden the first man sinned: in a garden CHRIST repaired salvation. Cf. August. serm. 71 de temp., Cyrill. lib. 11 in Joh. c. 31, Theophyl. in c. 18 Joh. The first man had also profaned gardens with sin; CHRIST therefore by His most perfect obedience sanctifies them again, consecrates them with most ardent prayers, and irrigates them with a shower of blood. As often, therefore, as we enter gardens, let us diligently strive that their pleasantness may not only charm our eyes, but that a pious remembrance of the Passion may also be excited in our soul.

VI. 2. The place of condemnation is to be observed, which occurred I. before Caiaphas, in the council of the Priests and Elders, Matt. 26, v. 57, Mark 14, v. 53, Luke 22, v. 54, John 18, v. 24. II. in the Roman Magistrate's praetorium, Matt. 27. v. 2. Mark 15. v. 1. Luke 23. v. 1. John 18. v. 28. III. In the assembly of the people Matt. 27. v. 22. Mark 15. v. 14. Luke 23. v. 21. John 19. v. 7.

VII. Finally, the place of death and punishment must be considered. For immediately, as soon as the condemnatory sentence was pronounced against CHRIST, he was led out by the soldiers from the city to the place of the most ignominious crucifixion. The Evangelists with one voice named this place Golgotha or the place of Calvary. Compare Matt. 27. v. 33. Mark 15. v. 22. Luke 23. v. 33. John 19. v. 17. Now Golgotha was a rocky hill, infamous for public executions, and near the city of Jerusalem.

VIII. This was the final destination of the leading out. For there are not wanting those among the ancients who write that the hill of Golgotha has its name from the skull of Adam buried in that same place. It is evident that this tradition has come down from the early fathers, from Cyprian, sermon on the Resurrection, a certain oration of Basil, Theophylact on chapter 27 of Matthew, and others.

IX. But we rightly leave this opinion, destitute of the authority of Scripture, in the middle, determining rather with other authors of proven faith that the hill of Calvary found its name from the skulls of the condemned and those affected by punishment. But that he willed CHRIST to be led to this area of the wicked, so that he might free us from the never-ending punishments of hell. And so on this hill, finally, between two thieves, the most just and most holy one, whom he had previously commended to the Father, peacefully gave up his spirit, Matt. 27. v. 50. Mark 15. v. 37. Luke 23. v. 46. John 19. v. 30.

X. From a more diligent consideration of Time and Place, the very Manner of the passion, or the whole series of events, is understood in great part, which others declare through distinct acts. To the first act they refer those things which happened in the garden, namely Christ's departure to the mount of olives, his anguish and sadness, his captivity, and the betrayal by Judas; to the second act can be referred those things which were done in the council of the priests before Caiaphas. Here belongs the false testimony of witnesses against Christ, the mockery of the soldiers, where he is covered, spat upon, etc., and Peter's denial, and his conversion.

XI. To the third act pertain those things which Christ suffered in the praetorium of Pilate; where a certain new accusation before Pilate occurs, the passing over of Christ, and the release of Barabbas, which is followed by another mockery of our Savior, by which he is exacerbated by scourging, the purple tunic in the wounds impression, the imposition of the crown of thorns, the ironic salutation and adoration. Finally, the passion of the Lord on the cross is reduced to the fourth act, with certain accompanying events; where the leading forth of Christ to the cross must be weighed, the crucifixion itself, the division of the garments, and the enumeration of the miracles, concerning the unusual darkening of the sun, the rending of the veil, the flowing forth of blood and water from the dead side of Christ, etc.

XII. But all these things are partly comprised in the preceding: yet some are of such great import that they cannot be described by any flood of genius or any abundance of words, but at every time they deserve the most diligent meditation, which we seriously commend to all Christians. Wherefore we shall also briefly subjoin the final circumstance, which the contemplation of causes provides.

XIII. The efficient causes of the passion, however, were many. First, the love and mercy of GOD the Father toward the human race, John 3:16, 1 John 4:9, Rom. 5:8. 2. The justice of GOD requiring a plenary and perfect satisfaction for sins. 3. The charity of the Son of GOD Himself, Gal. 2:20. 4. Sin, Isa. 53:4, 2 Cor. 5:21, 1 Pet. 2:24. To these and similar ones, the remaining efficient causes, such as the voluntary obedience of Christ, the malice and envy of the Jews, and the avarice of Judas, can easily be added.

XIV. The final cause of the passion and death of CHRIST can be viewed in various ways. First, the passion and death of Christ is a sacrifice for our sins, Dan. 9:24, Matt. 26:28, Rom. 4:25, Heb. 9:28. Second, liberation from the curse of the Law, Gal. 3:13, Rom. 8:3, from death and the power of the Devil, Heb. 2:14, from the eternal punishments of hell, Hosea 13:14. From which follow justification, regeneration, and eternal life.

Latin:

Caput II. de vaticiniorum impletione.

I. Omnia hæc vaticinia certissimo eventu impleta esse ex diligentiore circumstantiarum enarratione, quam paucis sujiciemus, elucebit. Et primò quidem tempus passionis, 2. Locum, 3. Modum, 4. Causas breviter precurremus.

II. Tempus scriptura 1. Genericè, 2. Specificè determinavit. In genere quidem, ubi Paschalis festi mentionem fecit Matth. 26, v. 2. Mactandus qvippe erat hôc ipso tempore verus agnus paschalis, qvi veteris Testamenti typum impleret, de qvo Exod. 12. v. 5, 6. 1. Cor. 5. v. 7. 8. legitur.

III. In specie porrò omnes penè temporis articuli vel horæ numerari possunt. Summô enim mane Christus à Judæis capitur. Deinde 1. horâ (nobis sextâ) ad Pilatum ducitur : 3. horâ (nobis 9.) damnatur : 6. fermè (nobis 12.) crucifigitur : 9. (nobis fortè 5.) magno cum clamore expirat. Omnes hi temporis articuli accuratiori Passionis Dominicæ considerationi inserviunt.

IV. Deinde Locus etiam pro angorum diversitate variè describi potest. 1. enim notandus est locus captivitatis, ubi tamen antè captivitatem qvoqve angores verè infernales persensit, ita ut stupendô qvodam miraculo sangvineum sudorem sudârit. Locum hunc Matt. 26. v. 36. &c. Marc. 14, v. 32. Gethsemane appellantant. Nam qvi Palæstinam perlustrârunt (teste Clariss. Gerhard. in harm. Evang. p. 46.) Gethsemane pagum, sive prædium, ad radices montis oliveti situm, & hortis conspicuum fuisse, referunt. Vide Joh. c. 18. v. 1. seq.

V. In horto enim primus homo peccavit : In horto CHRISTUS salutem reparavit. Conf. August. serm. 71. de temp. Cyrill. lib. 11. in Joh. c. 31. Theophyl. in c. 18. Joh. Hortos qvoq; primus homo peccato prophanaverat; CHRISTUS igitur perfectissimâ suâ obedientiâ eos iterum sanctificat, ardentissimis precibus consecrat, & sangvineô imbre irrigat. Qvotics igitur hortos ingredimur, sedulò annitamur, ne oculis tantùm blandiatur amœnitas, sed pia etiam passionis recordatio in animo excitetur.

VI. 2. Observandus est locus condemnationis, qvæ contigit I. coram Caipha, in Sacerdotum & Seniorum concilio, Matth. 26. v. 57. Mar. 14, v. 53. Luc. 22. v. 54. Joh. 18. v. 24. II. In Romani Magistratûs prætorio, Matth. 27. v. 2. Marc. 15. v. 1. Luc. 23. v. 1. Joh. 18. v. 28. III. In cœtu populi Matth. 27. v. 22. Marc. 15. v. 14. Luc. 23. v. 21. Joh. 19. v. 7.

VII. Tandem considerandus est locus mortis & supplicii. Statim enim, ut contemnatoria sententia contra CHRISTUM pronunciata fu it, à milittibus ex urbe eductus est ad locum ignominiosissimæ crucifixionis. Locum hunc Evangelistæ uno ore Golgatha vel Calvariæ locum nominârunt Confer. Matth. 27. v. 33. Marc. 15. v. 22. Luc. 23. v. 33. Joh. 19. v. 17. Erat autem Golgatha mons petrosus, publicis suppliciis infamis, & urbi Hierosolymæ vicinus.

VIII. Ultimus hic eductionis terminus fuit. Non enim desunt ex veteribus, qui montem Golgatha à Calvaria Adami ibidem sepulti, nomen habere scriptitant. Traditionem hanc à priscis patribus pervenisse, ex Cyprian. sermon. de Resurrect. Basilii quâdam orat. Theophyl. in c. 27. Matth. & aliis, constat.

IX. Verùm hanc sententiam scripturæ autoritate destitutam, meritò in medio relinquimus, statuentes potiùs cum aliis probatæ fidei autoribus, montem Calvariæ à craniis damnatorum, & supplicio affectorum, nomen invenisse. CHRISTUM autem ad hanc sceleratorum aream deduci voluisse, ut nos à nunquam desituris gehennæ suppliciis liberaret. In hoc itaque monte tandem inter duos latrones justissimus & sanctissimus, quem Patri priùs commendaverat, spiritum placidè emisit, Matth. 27. v. 50. Marc. 15. v 37. Luc. 23. v. 46. Joh. 19, v. 30.

X. Ex diligentiore Temporis & Loci consideratione ipse simul 'passionis Modus, seu tota rerum gestarum series, magna ex parte intelligitur, quam alii per act⁹ distinctos declarant. Ad primum actum referunt ea, quæ in horto contigerunt, Christi nimrum ad montem olivarum egressum, angorem & tristitiam, captivitatem, & Judæ traditionem; Adsecundum actum referri possunt, quæ in concilio sacerdotum coram Caipha gesta sunt. Hûc spectat falsa testium contra Chri stum depositio, militum illusio, ubi obtegetur, conspuitur, &c. & Petri abnegatio, ejusdemque conversio.

XI. Ad tertium actum ea pertinent, quæ Christus in prætorio Pilati passus est; ubi occurrit nova quædam coram Pilato accusatio, Christi præteritio, & Barrabæ dimissio, quam alia Salvatoris nostri illusio sequitur, quâ exacerbatur flagellatione, purpureæ tunicæ in vulnera impressione, spineæ coronæ impositione, ironicâ salutatione & adoratione. Ad qvartum deniq; actū reducitur passio Domini in cruce cum qvibusdam adjacentibus; ubi expendenda venit Christi ad crucem eductio, ipsa crucifixio, vestimentorum divisio, & miraculorum enumeratio, de inusitatâ Solis obscuritate, veli fissurâ, sangvinis & aqvæ ex demortuo Christi latere profluxu &c.

XII. Verùm hæc omnia partim in superioribus comprehenduntur: Qvædam verò tanti monumenti sunt, ut nullo ingenii flumine, nullâ verborum copiâ describi qveant, sed nullô non tempore diligentissimam meditationem mereantur, qvam omnibus Christianis seriò commendamus. Qvocirca ultimam etiam circumstantiam, qvam causarum contemplatio suppeditat, paucis subjiciemus.

XIII. Causæ autem efficientes passionis multæ fuerunt. Primò amor & misericordia DEI Patris erga genus humanum, Joh: 3, v. 16. 1. Joh: 4. v. 9. Rom. 5. v. 8. 2. Justitia DEI plenariam & perfectam pro peccatis satisfactionem reqvirens. 3. Ipsius Filii DEI charitas, Gal. 2, v. 20. 4. Peccatum Esa: 53. v. 4. 2. Cor. 5. v. 21. 1. Petr. 2. v. 24. His & similibus reliqvæ etiam causæ efficientes, qvales voluntaria Christi obedientia, Judæorum malitia & invidia, Judæ avaritia, facilè addi possunt.

XIV. Causa finalis passionis & mortis CHRISTI diversimodè spectari potest. Primò, passio & mors Christi est sacrificium pro peccatis nostris, Dan. 9. v. 24. Matth. 26. v. 28. Rom. 4. v. 25. Hebr. 9. v. 28. Secundò, liberatio à maledictione Legis, Gal. 3. v. 13. Rom. 8. v. 3. à morte & potestate Diaboli, Hebr. 2, v. 14. à pœnis inferni sempiternis, Osee 13. v. 14. Unde seqvuntur, Justificatio, regeneratio, & vita æterna.


### Chapter III. I. These things having been thus prefaced, we shall subjoin the more…

CHAPTER III.

I. These things having been thus prefaced, we shall subjoin the more illustrious questions. And first, indeed, it is accustomed to be asked concerning the person suffering: Whether, namely, the passion truly and really pertains to the whole person of Christ according to both natures and should be attributed to it? We embrace the affirmative, according to the undoubted rule of antiquity, which pronounces that actions and passions belong to the whole suppositum,

II. And therefore we believe and confess that all things which are said of this Son of man are also most truly said of the incarnate Son of GOD, on account of the identity of the person and the personal union. Especially since Scripture itself holds up the torch of truth before us, which, if we follow as we rightly should, we will easily avoid even the densest shadows of error.

III. For this [Scripture] testifies that the Prince of Life was killed, Acts 3:14; that the Church was acquired not just by a man, but (which is well to be noted) by the very blood of God, Acts 20:28; that the human race was reconciled to God through the death of His Son, Rom. 5:10; that God delivered up His own Son for us, Rom. 8:32; that the Jews crucified the Lord of Glory, 1 Cor. 2:8; that men are cleansed from sins by the blood of the Son of God, 1 John 1:7. What could be clearer, what more illustrious than these oracles of Scripture?

IV. Away, therefore, with the heretical voice of Nestorius: 'Do not boast, O Jew, for you did not crucify God, but a man.' Away with the Allœosis of Zwingli, and the Synecdoche of certain others, in explaining the sayings of Scripture, which are so clear and perspicuous that they prove quite evidently that in this difficult business of redemption, one nature alone is by no means to be understood or accepted for the whole person of Christ.

V. Therefore, that we may be best fortified against this error, it has pleased us to recount in this place the words of Dr. Luther from his greater confession concerning the Lord's Supper, in which he deals with the Allœosis of Zwingli: the words are as follows: 'This Zwingli calls ἀλλοίωσιν (allœosis), when something is said about the Divinity of Christ which is nevertheless proper to his humanity, and vice versa. For example, where it is said in Scripture: "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and so to enter into his glory?" where Zwingli trifles, saying that the word "Christ" in this place is taken for the human nature. Beware, I say, beware of this allœosis: for it is a certain mask of the Devil, which eventually fashions such a Christ that, according to its reasoning, I certainly would not wish to be a Christian. For this is what it intends: that Christ is nothing more, nor accomplishes anything more by his passion and life, than any other saint.' For if I allow myself to be persuaded to believe that only the human nature suffered for me, then truly Christ will be a Savior of no great value to me.' Thus far he.

VI. You object: That distinctive particles are nevertheless sometimes used by our own theologians, so that they confess that Christ suffered κατ’ ἄλλο (in another respect) in the flesh or according to the flesh. We answer that the matter is very different, and clearly foreign to the purpose. For not by those is the Zwinglian allœosis or synecdoche established, but only the distinction of natures is signified.

VII. And hence it is gathered that there is a twofold allœosis, the one orthodox and Lutheran, the other heterodox and Zwinglian. The former is dihoristikē; the latter is chōristikē; the former is distinctive, the latter exclusive. The former piously teaches and acknowledges two natures in one person united asynchytōs kai achōristōs; the latter utterly overturns that difficult mystery of redemption (as is gathered from the preceding words of Luther).

IIX. We conclude therefore (that we may at length proceed to other matters) that the eternal Son of the eternal God, God himself blessed forever, having been made a partaker of blood and flesh, similarly just as these children (sin excepted), Hebr. 2. v. 14. and true man, was the person suffering so many insults, so many bodily tortures, mental distresses, and finally the very most ignominious death of the cross.

IX. From the evidence and truth of this conclusion, the decision of a new controversy immediately arises, when the Photinians ask whether the passion of our Savior Jesus Christ satisfied for the sins of the human race? For if this proposition, God has suffered, can neither be rejected under that vain pretext of phraseōs agraphou, nor violently twisted into an entirely foreign sense, we deservedly subscribe to the affirmative opinion; otherwise the efficacy of divine power would utterly vanish, nay, the very redemption of the human race would be taken away, which scripture nevertheless emphatically urges, Rom. 3. v. 24. 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. 1. Cor. 6. v. 20. Eph. 1. v. 7. Col. 1. v. 14. 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. Hebr. 9. v. 12. 1. Petr. 1. v. 18, 19. 2. Petr. 2. v. 1. Apoc. 5. v. 9. etc.

X. Furthermore, scripture acknowledges Christ as our only Mediator, 1. Tim. 2. v. 5. Hebr. 8. v. 6. Just as, therefore, a mediator is between parties extremely at odds, in such a way that on account of that discord he sheds blood, undergoes death, and by the intervention of a certain price satisfies both parties: so that heavenly Mediator willed to be present between God, angered on account of sins, and us men, extremely at odds with the angered God, and with his own blood shed, Col. 1. v. 14. Hebr. 9. v. 12. he became obedient to the heavenly Father even unto death, even the death of the cross, Phil. 2. v. 8. and thus by a most sufficient satisfaction he fulfilled the office of Mediator.

XI. To this is added that he took our sins and infirmities upon him self, Isa. 53, v. 4, 5. Whence it follows again, that he offered himself for our sake, and thus made satisfaction to the eternal Father for us. And although the adversaries object here that Christ offered himself to GOD for our sins, not in the world, where he underwent death, but in the heavens, after his most glorious ascension: Nevertheless, Scripture is entirely ignorant of these and similar exceptions. With the same ease, therefore, that they are brought forward by the adversaries, they are rejected by us. See more on this controversy in the Anthropological disputation of the most Reverend and Illustrious Lord President, my revered Preceptor and Patron (disp. 25, on the state of restoration).

XII. From those things which have been brought forward thus far, a new question sprouts up: Namely, whether the satisfaction of CHRIST is universal? The Calvinists attempt to defend the negative, and contend that the merit of Christ is particular, and thus does not extend to all men indiscriminately, but only to those who are peculiarly preordained to it by the absolute decree of GOD, with all other individuals being excluded and rejected therefrom. Whence Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard: 'But did Christ take away the sins of the whole world, as you interpret it concerning individuals?' And certainly your statement seemed intolerable to us, that Christ died for the damned, etc.

XIII. We, in this controversy, again maintain the affirmative, constantly pronouncing that the most sacred merit of Christ is entirely universal, in whatever way and respect it may be considered. Therefore, that we may proceed in order, we assert that the λύτρον [ransom] paid by the Son of GOD comprehends: 1. The universality of all sins, as much original as actual; 2. The universality of both guilt and punishment; 3. The universality of all men whatsoever, not only of the elect, but also of the damned and the reprobate.

XIV. And first indeed, that Christ by his most sufficient satisfaction expiated all the sins of men, an eyewitness [ἀυτόπτης] testifies, and affirms it partly generally [γενικῶς], partly specifically [εἰδικῶς]: generally, concerning all sins in the universe, Tit. 2: CHRIST redeemed us ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας [from all iniquity], and 1 John 1: The blood of JESUS CHRIST the Son of GOD cleanses us from all sin. Specifically, concerning actual sins, we read in Heb. 9: The blood of Christ purges us from dead works, and 1 John 2: If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, JESUS CHRIST the righteous, who is the propitiation, etc.

XV. Next, concerning the universality of the punishment (for of the universality of the guilt we have treated thus far) the very well-known maxim of the Prophet (Isa. 53) is: The punishment was laid upon him. For if he made satisfaction for the guilt, why not also for the punishment? And with the guilt removed, the punishment also which is to be inflicted for the guilt is removed. Indeed, what kind of satisfaction for guilt would this finally be, without satisfaction for the punishment? Wherefore, there ought to be no doubt at all concerning this universality as well.

XVI. Finally, we shall prove the universality of the satisfaction of Christ, considered also with respect to all damned and reprobate men, from the indubitable testimonies of Scripture. But, because the question is primarily about the reprobate, let it suffice to have noted the following, such as: do not destroy with your food him for whom Christ died, Rom. 14:15. Likewise from 1 Cor. 8:11, where the Apostle writes: The brother who is weak will perish in your knowledge, for whom Christ died. And we read in Heb. 10:29: How much worse punishment do you think he will be deserving of, who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has regarded the blood of the Covenant as a profane thing, by which he had been sanctified.

XVII. You object, that many nevertheless suffer the most miserable shipwreck of eternal salvation? We answer that the reprobate are not damned because of the merit of Christ, which is most perfect and has expiated the sins of the whole world, as is clear from the above: but because of unbelief, by which, rashly rejecting that expiatory sacrifice of Christ, they bring swift destruction upon themselves, 2 Pet. 2:1. And to this point belongs that saying of Ambrose, Sermon 8 on Ps. 118: The Sun of righteousness has risen for all, has come for all, has suffered for all, and has risen for all. But if anyone does not believe in Christ, he defrauds himself of the general benefit, just as if someone were to exclude the rays of the Sun by closing the windows.
