And Augustine rightly says: The cup of immortality, which is made from our infirmity and divine power, indeed has it in itself to benefit all: but if it is not drunk, it does not profit.

XVIII. And, although our adversaries also bring forward Scripture itself for the overturning of the universality of the merit of Christ, yet if the matter is examined by the Lydian stone of truth, we discover that they argue for the most part from false explanations and hypotheses.

XIX. Wherefore, let these things suffice concerning the questions and controversies necessary to be known. For the remaining matters, which are wont to be disputed at sufficient length concerning this difficult subject, we deservedly reserve for other places and times.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

I. His ita prælibatis, qvæstiones illustriores subjiciemus. Et primò qvidem de persona patiente qværi solet: Utrum nimirum passio verè & realiter toti Christi personæ secundum utramqve naturam competat & tribuenda sit? Nos affirmativam amplectimur, juxta indubitatam antiqvitatis regulam, qvæ actiones & passiones totius suppositi esse pronunciat,

II. Ideoqve omnia, qvæ de Filio hôc hominis dicuntur, verissimè etiam de Filio DEI incarnato, propter personæ identitatem, & unionem personalem, dici credimus & confitemur. Præsertim qvumveritatis facem ipsa nobis scriptura præferat, quam meritò secuti, densissimas etiam errorum tenebras facilè declinabimus.

III. Hæc enim, Vitæ Principem interfectum esse, Actor. 3. v. 14. Ecclesiam non hominis tantùm, sed (quod probè notandum) proprio Dei sanguine acquisitam esse, Act. 20. v. 28. genus humanum Deo per mortem Filii ejus reconciliatum esse, Rom 5. v. 10. Deum propium Filium pro nobis tradidisse, Rom. 8. v. 32. Judæos Dominum Gloriæ crucifixisse, 1. Cor. 2. v. 8. homines sanguine Filii Dei, à peccatis mundari, 1. Joh. 1. v. 8. testatur, Quibus scripturæ oraculis ecquid clarius, ecquid illustrius?

IV. Facessat igitur Nestorii vox hæretica: Noli gloriari Judæe, Non enim Deum, sed hominem crucifixisti. Facessat Zvvinglii Allœosis, & Synecdoche qvorundam, in explicandis scripturæ dictis, quæ adeò clara & perspicua sunt, ut in arduo hoc redemptionis negotio pro integrâ Christi personâ alterutram duntaxat naturam nullo modô intelligendam vel acceptandam esse, satis evidenter evincant.

V. Proinde, ut quàm optimè adversus errorem hunc præmuniamur, placuit D. Lutheri verba hoc loco recensere è majori ipsius de Cœna Domini confessione, in quibus de Zvvinglii allœosi agit: verba autem sic habent: Hoc Zvvinglius vocat ἀλλοίωσιν, cùm aliqvid de Divinitate Christi dicitur, qvod tamen humanitatis propriu est, & contrà, V.G. ubi in scriptura dicitur: Nonnè hæc oportuit pati Christum, & ita intrare in gloriam suam? ubi nugatur Zvvinglius, quòd vocabulum Christus hôc locô pro humanâ naturâ sumatur, Cave tibi, cave, inqvam, tibi ab allœosi: Est enim larva qvædam Diaboli, quæ tandem talem Christum fingit, secundùm cujus rationes ego certè nolim esse Christianus. Hoc enim illa vult, quòd Christus nihil amplius sit, aut efficiat suâ passione & vitâ, quàm alius qvispiam sanctus. Si enim persuadere mihi patiar, ut credam, solam humanam naturam pro me passam esse, profectò Christus mihi non magni pretii Salvator erit. Hactenus ille.

VI. Obvertis: Particulas tamen distinctivas à nostris etiam Theologis nonnunqvam adhiberi, ita ut Christum κατ’ ἄλλο in carne vel secundùm carnem passum esse fateantur. Respondemus, rem esse diversissimam, planeq; à scopo alienam. Non n. per illas Zvvingliana allœosis aut συνεκδοχὴ stabilitur, sed naturarum duntaxat distinctio significatur.

VII. Atqve hinc colligitur, duplicem esse ἀλλοίωσιν, alteram orthodoxam & Lutheranam, alteram Heterodoxam & Zvvinglianam. Illa est διοριστικὴ; hæc χωριστικὴ; illa distinctiva, hæc exclusiva. Illa duas in una persona naturas ἀσυγχύτως καὶ ἀχωρίστως unitas piè docet atq; agnoscit; Hæc arduum illud redemtionis mysterium (sicut ex superioribus Lutheri verbis colligitur) penitus evertit.

IIX. Concludimus igitur(ut ad alia tandem progrediamur)qvòd æternus æterni Dei Filius, ipse Deus benedictus in secula, particeps factus sangvinis & carnis, similiter sicuti hi pueri (excepto peccato) Hebr.2. v. 14. & verus homo, fuerit persona patiens tot contumelias, tot cruciatus corporis, angustias mentis, ipsam deniq; mortem crucis ignominiosissimam.

IX. Ex conclusionis hujus evidentiâ & veritate novæ statim controversiæ decisio nascitur, qvando Photiniani qværunt, utrùm passio Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi pro peccatis generis humanis satisfecerit? Si enim propositio hæc, Deus est passus, aut vanô illô phraseως ἀγράφꙋ prætextu rejici, aut in alienum prorfus sensum violenter detorqveri neqvit, affirmativæ sententiæ meritò adstipulamur, aliàs divinæ virtutis efficacia penitus evanesceret, imò ipsa generis humani redemptio tolleretur, qvàm tamen emphaticè urget scriptura, Rom. 3. v. 24. 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. 1. Cor. 6. v. 20. Eph. 1. v. 7. Col. 1. v. 14. 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. Hebr. 9. v. 12. 1. Petr. 1. v. 18, 19. 2. Petr. 2. v. 1. Apoc. 5. v 9. &c.

X. Prætereà Christum Mediatorem nostrum unicum scriptura agnoscit, 1. Tim. 2. v. 5. Hebr. 8, v. 6. Qvemadmodùm igitur Mediator est inter partes extremè dissidentes, ita qvidem, ut propter dissidium illud sangvinem effundat, mortem subeat, & certi cujusdam pretii interventu utriqve parti satisfaciat : Ita cœlestis ille Mediator inter Deum ob peccata iratum, & nos homines à Deo irato extremè dissidentes, versari voluit, & propriô sangvine effusô, Col. 1. v. 14. Hebr. 9. v. 12. patri cœlesti obediens factus est usqve ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, Phil. 2. v. 8. adeoq; satisfactione sufficientissimâ Mediatoris officium explevit.

XI. Huc accedit, qvòd peccata & langvores nostros in se recepetit, Efa. 53, v. 4, 5. Unde iterum fequitur, quòd nostri caussâ sese obtulerit, adeoq; æterno Patri pro nobis fatisfecerit. Et quamvis hîc regerant adversarii, Christum sese obtulisse DEO pro peccatis nostris, non in mundo, ubi mortem subiit, sed in cœlis, post ascensionem gloriofissimam: Tamen has & consimiles exceptiones scriptura prorsus ignorat. Quâ igitur facilitate ab adversariis adferuntur, eâdem à nobis rejiciuntur. Plura de hac controversia vide in disp, Anthropolog. admodùm Reverendi & Clariss. Domini Præsid. Præceptoris & Patroni mei colendi (disp. 25. de stat. reparat)

XII. Ex iis, quæ hactenus allata sunt, nova repullulat quæstio: Utrum nimirum universalis sit CHRISTI satisfactio? Calviniani negativam defendere conantur, & meritum Christi particulare esse contendunt, atq; adeò non ad omnes promiscuè homines extendi, sed ad eos tantùm, qui absoluto DEI decreto ad id peculiariter præordinati, reliqvis omnibus & singulis indè exclusis & rejectis. Unde Beza in colloq. Mompel. Num verò Christus totius mundi peccata sustulit, ut vos de singulis interpretamini? Et certè nobis intolerabilis vox vestra visa est, Christum esse mortuum pro damnatis &c.

XIII. Nos in hâc controversiâ iterum affirmativam tuemur, constanter pronunciantes, meritum Christi sacratissimum omnino esse universale, quocunq; etiam modo & respectu consideretur. Quocirca, ut ordine procedamus, τὸ λύτρον à Filio DEI persolutum 1. Universalitatem omnium peccatorum, tàm originalis, quàm actualium; 2. Universalitatem, tàm culpæ, quàm pœnæ; 3. Universalitatem omnium omnino hominum, non electorum solùm, sed damnatorum etiam, & reproborum, comprehendere asserimus.

XIV. Et primò qvidem, quòd Christus satisfactione suâ sufficientissimâ omnia hominum peccata expiârit, testis ἀυτόπτης & partim γενικῶς, partim εἰδικῶς affirmat: γενικῶς, de omnibus in universum peccatis, Tit. 2. CHRISTUS redemit nos ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας, & 1. Joh. 1, Sangvis JESU CHRISTI Filii DEI emundat nos ab omni peccato. εἰδιxῶς, de actualibus peccatis, Hebr. 9. legimus: sangvis Christi purgat nos ab operibus mortuis, & 1. Joh. 2. Si qvis peccaverit, advocatum habemus apud Patrem, JESUM CHRISTUM, justū, qui est propitiatio &c.

XV. Deinde, de universalitate pœnæ (de culpæ enim universalitate hactenus egimus) gnome Prophetæ notissima est (Esa. 53.) Pœna ipsi imposita est. Nam si pro culpâ satisfecit, qvidni etiam pro pœna? Et sublatâ culpâ, pœna etiam pro culpa infligenda tollitur. Imò, qvæ hæc tandem esset satisfactio pro culpâ, absq; satisfactione pro pœna? Quocirca de hac etiam universalitate minimè dubitari debet.

XVI. Tandem universalitatem satisfactionis Christi, respectu omnium hominum damnatorum qvoqve & reproborum consideratam, ex indubitatis scripturæ testimoniis probabimus. At, qvia dè reprobis potissimùm qværitur, seqventia hæc annotasse sufficiat, ut: ne cibô illum perdas, pro qvo Christus mortuus est, Rom. 14. v. 15. Item ex 1. Cor. 8. v. 11. ubi Apostolus scribit: Peribit frater, qvi infirmus est, in tuâ scientiâ, propter qvem Christus fuit mortuus, Et Hebr. 10. v. 29. legimus: qvantò putatis, pejoribus afficietur suppliciis, qvi filium DEI conculcârit, & sangvinem Testamenti, ceu rem profanam, habuerit, per qvem fuerat sanctificatus.

XVII. Objicis, multos tamen miserrimum æternæ salutis facere naufragium? Respondemus, reprobos non propter Christi meritum damnari, qvod perfectissimum est, & totius mundi peccata expiavith, uti ex superioribus liqvet: sed propter incredulitatem, qvâ expiatorium illud Christi sacrificium temerè respuentes, celerem sibipfis interitum accersunt, 2. Pet. 2. v. 1. atq; huc pertinet illud Ambros. serm. 8. in Pf. 118. Sol justitiæ omnibus ortus est, omnibus venit, omnibus passus est, & omnibus resurrexit. Si qvis autem non credit in Christum, generali beneficiô ipse se fraudat, ut siqvis clausis fenestris radios Solis excludat. Et rectè Augustinus: Poculum immortalitatis, qvod confectum est de infirmitate nostra, & virtute divinâ, habet eqvidem in se, ut omnibus prosit: Sed si non bibitur, non proficit.

XIIX. Et, qvamvis adversarii ipsam etiam scripturam pro evrtendâ meriti CHRISTI universalitate, adducant, tamen si res ad Lydium veritatis lapidem examinatur, eos ex falsis plerumq; explicationibus & hypothesibus argumentari deprehendimus.

XIX. Quocirca hæc etiam de qvæstionibus & scitu necessariis controversiis sufficiant. Reliqva enim, qvæ de arduâ hac materia prolixè satis disputari solent, aliis locis & temporibus meritò reservamus.


### Chapter IV. I. I think that anyone can see how wide a field of…

CHAPTER IV.

I. I think that anyone can see how wide a field of doctrines opens, if we should wish to pursue whatever offers itself in this place and to dwell upon each individual point. Therefore, from the countless things that are available for practice, we shall choose only the better ones. And first indeed, if the history of the passion is considered with respect to GOD, it offers a mirror of eternal love toward the human race: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son. By the meditation of this immense love, sincerely loving him in return, let us sigh with Augustine: Lord Jesus, you loved me more than yourself, because you willed to die for me. Let it therefore be a shame not to love you in return, for so great a love of yours.

II. On the other hand, however, let each one also consider here how much sin displeased the divine Majesty. For sin inflicted so many wounds upon the most holy of saints; sin crucified him; sin delivered him to a most ignominious death. It is fitting to weigh this again with pious devotion, so that we may detest the depraved habit of sinning with the greatest zeal, as far as it can be done.

III. With respect to us, however, the passion of the Lord ought to be considered in such a way that, first, we apply the merit of Christ to ourselves by true faith. For if we shall exclaim: What have you committed, most loving child, that you were treated so? What is your crime? What is your fault? What is the cause of your death? What is the occasion of your condemnation? I am the wound of your pain, the guilt of your slaughter: I am the merit of your death; the wickedness of your vengeance: I am the bruise of your passion, the labor of your torment! Then let us insist upon the footsteps of CHRIST, 1 Pet. 2 v. 21, and let us take up our cross, Mark 8 v. 34, hoping that it will be that, if we suffer with him in the world, we shall reign there with all the elect, 2 Tim. 2 v. 11.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

I. Videre autem qvemlibet opinor, qvàm se latus doctrinarũ campus aperiat, fi, quæcunq; hôc locô se offerunt, perseqvi & in singulis immorari velimus. Itaq; ex innumeris, qvæ ad praxin suppetunt potiora tantùm eligemus. Et primò qvidem, si passionis historia respectu DEI consideratur, speculum æternæ erga genus humanum dilectionis præbet: Sic enim Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret. Hujus immensi amoris meditatione ipsum sincerè redamantes, cum August. suspiremus: Domine Jesu dilexisti me plus, qvam te, qvia mori voluisti pro me. Pudeat igitur non reamere te, pro tanto amore tuo.

II. E contrario autem, uniusqvisq; etiam hîc consideret, qvantùm divinæ Majestati peccatum displicuerit. Peccatum enim sanctorum sanctissimo tot vulnera inflixit; Peccatum eum crucifixit; Peccatum ignominiosissimæ illum morti tradidit. Hoc iterum piâ devotione expendere decet, ut pravam peccandi consvetudinem summô, qvoad fieri poterit, studiô detestemur.

III. Respectu nostri autem passio Domini ita considerari debet, ut primò nobis Christi meritum verâ fide applicemus. Si enim exclamabimus: Qvid commisisti, amantissime puer, ut adeò tractareris? Qvod scelus tuum? qvæ noxa tua? qvæ caussa mortis tuæ? qvæ damnationis tuæ occasio? Ego sum tui plaga doloris, tuæ culpa occisionis: Ego tuæ mortis meritum; tuæ vindictæ flagitium: Ego tuæ passionis livor, tui cruciatûs labor! Deinde vestigiis CHRISTI insistamus, 1. Petr. 2. v. 21. & crucem nostram tollamus, Marc. 8. v. 34. sperantes fore, ut, si in mundo compatiamur, illic cum omnibus electis regnemus, 2. Tim. 2. v. 11.


## 37 Thirty-seventh Disputation On the Heptalogue of Christ

Preface.

Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: For it is permitted to me, fixed in the contemplation of the crucifixion, to break forth with Isaiah into these words. For behold, the Lord of Hosts (Isa. 8) ascends the tree of the cross, that he may be usurped by the eyes of all: The King of Kings (1 Tim. 6, Apoc. 13) raises his voice like a trumpet, that his sound may be propagated into the whole world. Hear the Lord

The sun is darkened; the rock is rent; the earth is shaken; the veil is torn; the graves are opened; the dead are raised: and shall we alone remain sluggish? Far be it. Let us rather approach the chair of the cross, and with a devout mind hear the pronouncements of our heavenly teacher, not only because they are perpetual sacraments of his innocence, clemency, and other virtues: not only because they are most certain arguments of his fatherly love toward the Church; not only because they are truly most wholesome documents of εὐθανασίας: but also because they are the complements of all the actions of Christ, which we ought to imitate.

Thesis I.

Our Savior, now near to death, here brings forth seven apophthegms, more precious than all gold and gems. St. Bernard calls them seven leaves that are always green, which our vine put forth when it was lifted up upon the cross. The first of which is: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.

II. Here the true and only Priest and Pontiff of the New Testament prays for his enemies, for the most wicked and most cruel torturers, who, by wicked hands, fastening him to the cross, slew him, as the Lord Apostle says in Acts 2:23; he prays for the transgressors, which Isaiah had predicted concerning him many centuries before, chapter 53:12.

III. Polanus therefore errs, while he contends desperately that Christ did not intercede for the reprobate, but only for the elect. For the present text evidently shows the contrary, and the alleged prophecy of the Prophet implies the contrary.

IV. Christ adds the reason: For they know not what they do; not as if they were simply ignorant; for Christ himself denies such ignorance to the Jews in express words, John 15:22, 24. The sense of these words, therefore, is this: They indeed know my innocence, they know the false witnesses were suborned, they know it is a detestable vice to afflict and kill an innocent and well-deserving man with insults, injuries, and tortures: but that I am the Son of God, the promised Messiah, they do not know. For if they had known, they would by no means have crucified him; nor do they sufficiently deeply weigh the magnitude and atrocity of these crimes, and the punishments that will follow. Therefore, forgive them, most merciful Father, this blind zeal and fury.

V. Nor was this ardent prayer ineffectual, but valid, and it partly manifested itself soon, with the thief, the centurion, the soldiers, and others standing by the cross being converted, and partly at the feast of Pentecost, with three thousand being brought to a serious acknowledgment of their sins and a sincere conversion.

VI. The second word, which Christ said, having seen his Mother and the Disciple, sounds thus: Woman, behold thy son: Behold thy mother, John 19:26, 27. This pronouncement of our Savior is bipartite. In the first part, he commends John to his Mother as a son, as if he were saying, in the interpretation of Bernard: You are deprived of me, your Son, wherefore I deliver to you this one, beloved above all others, as a son, by whose presence you may be comforted in the meantime, while I am away. In the latter part, however, he commends Mary to John as a Mother.

VII. It is added in the Gospel history that John, with the greatest readiness of mind, took the blessed virgin into his own home from that hour, having no regard for the dangers. Proving in reality that his old observance and reverence toward the Lord still flourished in his heart; and that nothing had been diminished from it by the abominable punishment of the cross.

VIII. But he says to his Mother: Woman. Why this? Why does he not deign to call her by the sweetest name of mother, when she is consumed by sorrows? Perhaps, lest the maternal name should torture her pious heart; or, that he might remind her of the first promise concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head; or, that he might show that she, however much a Mother, in this business of the sacrifice which he is now expediting on the altar of the cross for the sins of the world, cooperates in nothing, nor has any prerogative above other mortals.

IX. Thus, therefore, even by the very appellation of woman, our Savior refutes the idolatrous and superstitious opinion of the Romanists, who assert that Mary is a helper in the work of the Son's Redemption.

X. Therefore, heavenly mercy prayed for his enemies; divine affection looked after his mother; now omnipotent philanthropy receives the converted thief. For thus with the third word he addresses the penitent thief: Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.

XI. As it seems to be able to be gathered from Matthew and Mark, this thief also at first cast insults at Christ, but a little later, weighing his innocence with a deeper investigation of the mind, he is suddenly converted. For behold, with warm sighs and words he commends himself to the mercy of the Savior:

Lord, I pray, remember me, when you come into your kingdom.

XII. Nor was this prayer fruitless. For there is promised to him not a distant, but a most present and immediate possession of the heavenly paradise. For the Lord of glory says: Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.

XIII. Paradise, however, here denotes not the garden of Eden, not the Papal limbo, but metaphorically the blessed seat of glory, of which that earthly paradise was once a type. Its rewards are so great that they cannot be measured, so many that they cannot be numbered, so abundant that they cannot be bounded, so precious that they cannot be valued.

XIV. Furthermore, the word 'with me' must be understood not only of the soul of the thief, to be joined to CHRIST, but also of the sufficiency and perfection of blessedness. For to be with CHRIST signifies the great sum of the highest good, the fullness of the highest joy, and all the riches of the heavens. For He is to be all in all to us, as the leader of the Apostles explains somewhere.

XV. He, therefore, who is not with Christ, cannot be anywhere but with the Devil. For there are two dwellings, one in eternal fire, the other in the eternal kingdom, Luke 16. Where, then, is the purgatory of the Romanists? It is certainly extinguished, as it were, in one stroke by this illustrious apophthegm of the Savior.

XVI. It is therefore more vain than Sicilian trifles what Bellarmine grumbles: that the thief expiated the punishments of purgatory by his patience and confession. For what! Was the thief therefore a martyr? Let us hear him himself: He did not have his hope of salvation and liberation from the punishments of his sins fixed on the dignity of his patience and confession, but solely on the memory of the gracious Christ hanging on the cross and expiating the sins of the world; he did not sell his death as a martyrdom, but as a punishment worthy of his crimes. For he says, 'We receive what is worthy of our deeds, but this man has done nothing wrong.' Lord, remember me, when you come into your kingdom.

XVII. By this very thing he also teaches us that no repentance is too late, provided it is true; and that the Lord does not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn and live, Ezekiel 33:11.

XIIX. Yet this example must not be abused for security. Hence Ecclesiastes ch. 5:5. He deceives himself and plays with his own death who thinks this: 'The indulgence of the final hour can help me'; but it should be rightly used against the atrocity of despair. For who would despair, if the thief was saved on the cross? Aug.

XIX. Having shown His omnipotence, the Savior now for the fourth time breaks forth into a lamentable cry of extreme kenosis, humility, and infirmity: My GOD, my GOD, why hast Thou forsaken me? The Savior felt not so much the supreme torments and pains of the body as the internal horrors of the soul of the wrath of GOD alienated from sinners, yet in such a way that He did not succumb, but in those very agonies trusted in GOD as His GOD.

XX. For He does not cry out simply, GOD, GOD, but My GOD, my GOD, why hast Thou forsaken me? Indicating not obscurely that, in that most grievous heat of temptations, He retained filial confidence in GOD His Father. Therefore, the true and genuine interpretation of this utterance comes to this.

XXI. Christ was then established at the extreme peak of temptations in the judgment of GOD, and thus He was dealing not with a placated Father, but with an angry judge, looking upon whom He wrestled with the temptation of desertion, and therefore, because He felt the pains of one forsaken, He also uttered the words of one forsaken.

XXII. But let it be far from us to maintain that GOD was forsaken by GOD, since Christ Himself openly professes in John 14 that He is in the Father, and the Father in Him. Let it likewise be far from us to assert that that most tight bond of personal union was disrupted and dissolved. For, as that golden and much-celebrated saying of Damascenus has it, the Logos never forsakes the flesh which He once assumed. The Logos emptied Himself, He did not withdraw protection from the flesh, He did not dissolve the union.

XXIII. If, therefore, we feel the temptations of desertion with Christ, and stick with the saints in the depths, let us pray to our GOD with a loud cry in the name of Christ our mediator, not doubting of being heard.

XXIV. This most grievous temptation having been overcome, He says: I thirst, John 19. 28. This single-word utterance of the Savior can be understood, first, in the literal sense, of natural thirst, from the lack of strength exhausted in the most harsh torments. For He had labored all night and day, had shed much blood, had not been refreshed with food and drink, had hung naked on the cross for over three hours in the heat of the sun and burning winds, thence His strength had dried up like a potsherd, and His tongue had cleaved to His jaws from thirst, Psalm 22, 16. For, as St. Cyril says somewhere, pains can do much to stir up thirst. For the innate heat exagitating, or, what is moist in the depth, they consume, and they burn the inward parts with painful fiery heats.

XXV. Partly in a mystical sense, concerning spiritual thirst, with which he anxiously thirsted for the human race at least. To which Bernard looks, while he discourses in this manner, no less sweetly than gravely: It is not sufficiently credible that the Lord spoke of bodily thirst, so that he might seek a carnal drink, who felt in an instant that he was about to die carnally: but rather we believe that he thirsted for the most ardent desire of our salvation. Lord, what is it that you thirst for? Did you not thirst for the salvation of our souls, the salvation of men, and our joy? Likewise; What do you thirst for, you who said, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and drink; you who are the fountain of life? I thirst, O man, for your salvation, your redemption.

XXVI. Therefore we truly establish both, that he was tormented by bodily thirst, and that, burning with most ardent love, he thirsted for the lost salvation of souls.

XXVII. These things therefore all being accomplished, he ends this λειτουργίαν with this Ἐπιτιχίῳ: It is finished. O truly joyful voice, and one never not to be revolved in the depths of our hearts! What, I ask, is finished? That which was to be finished is finished.

XXIIX. But let someone ask, in what way it accords with the truth that our Savior says everything is now finished, when he still had to die, and thus the last enemy, Death, 1 Cor. 15, was himself to be overcome through death and Resurrection?

XXIX. But it must be known that this apophthegm of Christ is to be referred to the execution of his most bitter passion. And although death was still to be undergone by Christ, yet, because the temptations of desertion, concerning which he had previously complained with a miserable voice, were now ceasing, and because likewise the Father, having dissipated the clouds of his anger and indignation, was again showing him a serene face, he certainly held the death now to be undergone as nothing, but rather, joyful, he offered himself to it. Therefore, with his whole soul he exclaims: it is finished.

XXX. O how many things the Savior embraces in this Ἐπιτιχίῳ! Adam's sin expiated, life repaired, prophecies fulfilled, the curse removed, the handwriting which was against us deleted, sin abolished, the expiatory sacrifice completed, and the approach to the heavens and the eternal joys of the heavens opened. In sum, all things are finished which, for the sake of liberating the human race, had to be done and suffered.

XXXI. Away, therefore, with the petty satisfactions of the Romanists. For if all things were transacted and completed by Christ on the cross, what need is there for the merits of our works? If all things were perfected by Christ in one offering, what are you doing, Romanists, with the sacrifice of the Mass, by which you proclaim that you offer Christ to the Father daily?

XXXII. Seventhly and lastly, towards evening the Savior cries out: Lord, into thy hands I commend my spirit. He borrowed these words from Psalm 31:6, and he proclaims them with a loud voice, now about to die.

XXXIII. Moreover, the Lord commends to the Father, in an anthropopathic manner, into His hands, not His Divinity, as Arius blasphemed, but His soul, which He had assumed as immortal, just as it is clear from various testimonies of Scripture that the word 'spirit' is taken for 'soul' (Acts 7:59, 1 Cor. 2:11, 2 Cor. 7:1, Heb. 12:23); and by thus commending His spirit to the Father, He brings it about that the souls of the just do not descend into hell, but rather to God. Euthymius on John. O sweet end of life, O inestimable charity, O ineffable security!

XXXIV. He cries out, however, with a strong voice, to show that He is by no means dying overcome by infirmity, but is laying down His soul of His own accord, which could have remained united to His body even then. But because it would not have been for the benefit of the human race in that way, He willingly delivers Himself to death, and with bowed head, He gives up His spirit.

XXXV. Thus, therefore, He now hangs dead upon the cross; and truly dead is He in whom, and from whom, the life and salvation of us all depends: but He is dead in such a way that no force snatched His soul from Him against His will; but He Himself, spontaneously and willingly, as if it were a deposit, restored it to the Father (John 10:18).

XXXVI. A truly excellent argument for the divine power in Christ shines forth from the fact that He gives up His spirit with a great cry. For it surpasses all the power of human strength that anyone, already dying, should speak with a loud and articulate voice, much less that he should cry out loudly, which the history testifies happened in Christ.

XXXVII. When, therefore, we too are placed on the threshold of death and must breathe out our soul, let us comfort ourselves with these words of Christ, being certainly persuaded that He has commended our own little soul, inserted into Himself through faith, into the hands of the Father, and having followed His example, we shall commend our soul from the body about to depart from its dwelling to the heavenly Father. Thus also Peter commands 1 Epist. ch. 4. 19. Thus David did Ps. 31, 6. Stephen Acts 7, 59. And let this suffice to have delineated, as briefly as could be done, the most holy Decalogue of our Savior, in a general way.

XXXVIII. Hear the Lord teaching on the altar of the cross, you proud and impenitent ones. The Word speaks, and will you harden your ears like an asp? He calls you to Himself, and will you kick against the goads? He intercedes for you, and will you despise such grace? For your sake the Lord of glory is subjected to the pains of hell: For your sake the eternal Son of GOD cries out that He is forsaken by God. Acknowledge, therefore, how great the gravity and atrocity of sin is before the divine tribunal, since it wrung that lamentable complaint from the author of life, the Son of GOD, GOD Himself blessed forever, that He should complain of being forsaken by God. He took upon Himself the misery of those whose nature He assumed, in which He shows how much they ought to weep who sin. Awake, therefore, awake, O hard and hardened sons of Adam, who are buried in the sleep of sins: Comply with the One teaching, lest you be forced to obey the one harming. He is indeed Mercy itself; but if you are unwilling to hear His voice, let Him be a consuming fire, Deut. 4. His wrath is kindled so that no one is able to resist Him, Job 19.

XXXIX. Approach also the chair of the cross, all you timid and grieving ones, and see how your heavenly Teacher awaits you, fixed to the cross, how He extends His arms for an embrace, how He lowers His head for a kiss, how He opens His mouth to teach and to call. O Man, says the Savior, see what I suffer for you. There is no pain like that with which I am tormented. I cry out to you, I who die for you. You are tormented by the burden of sins; console and raise yourself with my prayers and my blood. Are you deserted by all? Place your trust in my patronage. The gravity of sins tortures you; look at the thief, and weigh my clemency toward him. God Himself seems to be against you, and all things seem to be hostile; consider that your GOD is GOD. Your soul thirsts from sorrow, and you are given the vinegar of temptations to drink; refresh yourself with my blood shed for your sins. You see the imperfection of your wretched works; consider that all things have been perfected by me. You are occupied with the very horrors of death; do not doubt that I have broken through its gates, and commend your soul to me. Thus through labor you will pass into rest, through death into life, and you will triumph eternally. O blessed are we tos, if such a meditation on the words of Christ may arise in our mind day by day! O miserable and lost, if no concern for such great things touches us!

XL. O sweetest Lord JESUS CHRIST, may your last word on the cross be my last word in this light; and when I can speak no more, hear the final desire of my heart! O most loving Jesus, splendor of the Father's glory, Sun of justice, who for us were exalted on the altar of the cross, made sin for your enemies, solicitous for your own, propitious to the thief, thirsting for the salvation of all, you finished all things, and hence departed into eternal joys. Grant that the sacrosanct sighs of your cross may be for me a balm against spiritual starvation, sloth, despondency, melancholy, misfortune, and likewise lovelessness. O Lord Jesus, console the groaning, comfort the trembling, cherish the failing, receive the dying. O you who are our security, O you who are our health, O you who are our charity,

Jesus, author of clemency, hope of all joy, fountain of sweetness and grace, true delight of the heart; and delectation of the mind, consummation of love: O our boasting; the one salvation of the world: washed in your blood, I commend myself wholly to you. May these your holy hands defend me, Jesus Christ, in extreme perils, AMEN.

Latin:

Præloqvium.

AUdite cœli, & auribus percipe terra, quoniam Dominus locutus est: Licet enim mihi, in crucifixionis contemplatione defixo, cum Esaia in hæc verba prorumpere. Ecce namq; Dominus Exercituum (Esa. 8.) arborem crucis ascendit, ut omnium oculis usurpetur: Rex Regum (1. Tim. 6. Apoc. 13.) vocem tubæ instar exaltat, ut in universum terrarum orbem sonus ej⁹ propagetur. Audit Dominū

Sol, & obscuratur; petra, & divellitur; terra, & concutitur; velum, & discinditur; sepulchra, & aperiuntur; mortui, & suscitantur: & nos soli torpescemus? Absit. Accedamus potiùs ad crucis cathedram, cœlestisq; doctoris nostri pronunciata devotâ mente audiamus, non modò, quia innocentiæ, clementiæ, & aliarum ejus virtutum perpetua sunt Sacramenta: non modò, quia paterni erga Ecclesiam amoris certissima argumenta; non modò, quia verè εὐθανασίας saluberrima documenta:verùm etiam,quia omnium actionum Christi, quas imitari debemus, complementa.

Thesis I.

Profert hîc Sospitator noster, morti jam vicinus, septem apophthegmata, omni auro atq; gemmis preciofiora. D. Bernhardus appellat illa septem folia semper virentia, quæ vitis nostra, cùm in crucem elevata fuit, emisit. Quorum primum: Pater remitte illis, quia nesciunt, quid faciant.

II. Orat hîc verus & unicus Novi Testamenti Sacerdos & Pontifex pro hostibus suis, pro neqvissimis & truculentissimis tortoribus, qui per manus iniqvas cruci eum affigentes, interemerunt eum, uti D. Apostolus Act. 2, 23. ait; Orat pro transgressoribus, quod de ipso Esaias multis retrò seculis prædixerat cap. 53, 12.

III. Peccat ergò Polanus, dum efflictim contendit, Christum non pro reprobis, sed tantùm pro electis intercessisse. Contrarium enim præsens textus evidenter ostendit, contrarium allegatum Prophetæ vaticinium innuit.

IV. Addit Christus rationem: Nesciunt enim, quid fáciant; Non, ac si simpliciter nescivissent; Talem enim ignorantiam Judæis ipse Christus exertis denegat verbis, Joh. 15, 22, 24. Verborum ergò horum hic est sensus: Norunt quidem meam innocentiam, sciunt falsos subordinatos testes, sciunt detestandum vitium esse, insontem & benè meritum contumeliis, injuriis, cruciatibus afficere, & interficere: sed me DEI Filium, Messiam promissum esse, nesciunt. Nam si cognovissent, neqvaqvam crucifixissent; neq; satis profundè magnitudinem, & atrocitatem horum scelerum,insecuturarumq; pœnarum,perpendunt. Proinde remitte illis, Pater misericordissime, cæcum hunc zelum & furorem.

V. Neq; irrita, sed valida fuit ardens hæc precatio, & partim mox se exeruit, conversis latrone, centurione, militibus, ac aliis cruci astantibus, partim in festo Pentecostēs, tribus millibus ad seriam peccatorum agnitionem & sinceram conversionem perductis.

VI. Secundum verbum, quod Christus, visis Matre & Discipulo, dixit, ita sonat: Mulier ecce filius tuus: Ecce mater tua, Joh. 19, 26, 27. Bipartitum est hoc Salvatoris nostri pronunciatum. In priori parte Matri commendat Johannem, ut filium, quasi dicat, interprete Bernhardo: Tu me Filio privaris, unde tibi præ cunctis dilectum in filium hunc trado, cujus præsentiâ interim, dum absum, te soletis. In posteriori autem parte Mariam, ut Matrem, Johanni commendat.

VII. Additur in Evangelica historia, Johannem beatam virginem ex isthachorâ, nullâ periculorū habitâ ratione, summâ animi promtitudine ad se recepisse. Reipsâ comprobans, veterem erga Dominum observantiam & reverentiam in corde suo adhuc vigere; nec per abominandum crucis supplicium quicquam ex ea diminutū esse.

VIII. Dicit autem Matri: Mulier. Quid hoc? cur non dulcissimo matris nomine dignatur eam doloribus confectam? Fortè, ne materna pium cruciaret viscera nomen; aut, ut eam primæ promissionis, de semine mulieris contrituro caput serpentis, admoneret; vel, ut ostenderet, eam, qvantumvis Matrem, in hoc sacrificii negotio, quod pro peccatis mundi in ara crucis jam expediat, nihil cooperari, nec ullam præ cæteris mortalibus prærogativam habere.

IX. Sic ergò vel ipsâ appellatione mulieris, idolatatricam & superstitiosam Romanensium, Mariam in opere Redemptionis Filii adjutricem asserentium, sententiam Servator noster refellit.

X. Oravit igitur pro hostib⁹ cœlestis clementia; prospexit matri divina φιλοστοργία; nunc latronem conversum suscipit omnipotens φιλανθρωπία. Ita enim verbô tertiô allôqvitur latronem pœnitentem: Amen, dico tibi, hodiè mecum eris in paradysô.

XI. Utí ex Matthæo & Marco colligi posse videtur, & hic latro primitùs in Christum conjecit convitia, sed paulò pòst altiori mentis indagine innocentiam ej⁹ perpendens, subitò convertitur. Ecce enim calidis susupiriis & verbis se misericordiæ Salvatoris commendat:

Domine, rogans, memento mei, cum veneris in regnum tuum.

XII. Neq; sterilis fuit hæc precatio. Promittitur enim illi non longinqua, sed præsentissima & hodierna paradysi cœlestis possessio. Ait enim Dominus gloriæ: Amen, dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in paradiso.

XIII. Paradysus autem hîc non hortum Eden, non lymbum Pontificium, sed metaphoricè beatam gloriæ sedem, cujus olim paradysus ille terrestris typus fuit, denotat. Cujus præmia tàm magna, ut non possint mensurari, tàm multa, ut non possint numerari, tàm copiosa, ut non possint terminari, tàm preciosa, ut non possint æstimari.

XIV. Cæterùm, vocabulum Mecum non tantùm de anima latronis, CHRISTO conjungenda, sed & de sufficientia & perfectione beatitudinis intelligi debet. Esse enim cum CHRISTO, magnam boni summi summam, summi gaudii plenitudinem, omnesq; cælorum divitias significat. Est enim nobis futurus omnia in omnibus, uti Apostolorum corryphæus alicubi edisserit.

XV. Qvi ergò non est cum Christo, non potest esse, nisi cum Diabolo. Duæ enim habitationes sunt, una in igne æterno, altera in regno æterno, Luc. 16. Ubi ergò Romanensium purgatorium? Extinctum certè unô quasi impetu illustri hôc Salvatoris apophtegmate.

XVI. Gerris proinde vanius est Siculis, qvod Bellarminus oggrunnit; Latronem expiasse pœnas purgatorii suâ patientiâ & confessione. Ecqvid enim! An latro igitur fuit martyr? Audiamus ipsum: Nó spem salutis & liberationis à peccatorum suorum pœnis in patientiæ & confessionis suæ dignitate, sed in solâ gratiosi Christi in cruce pendentis & peccata mundi expiantis memoria defixam habuit; non pro matyrio, sed pro pœna sceleribus dignâ, mortem suam venditavit. Nam digna factis inqviens, recipimus, hic verò nihil mali gessit. Domine, memento mei, cùm veneris in regnum tuum.

XVII. Qvô ipsô etiam nos docet, nullam pœnitentiam esse seram, modò sit vera; Nec velle Dominum mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur & vivat, Ezech. 35. 11.

XIIX. Non tamen hôc exemplo abutendum ad securitatem. Hinc Eccl. c. 5, 5. Ipse se seducit & de morte sua ludit, qvi hoc cogitat: Potest mihi extremi temporis indulgentia subvenire; Sed rectè utendum adversus desperationis atrocitatem. Ecqvis enim desperet, si in cruce latro salvatus est? Aug.

XIX. Ostensâ suâ omnipotentiâ,Salvator jam qvartò in extremæ κενώσεως, humilitatis, & infirmitatis qverelam, lamentabili prorumpit voce: DEUS mi, DEUS mi, cur de feruisti me? Senfit Servator non tàm summos corporis cruciatûs & dolores, qvàm internos animæ horrores iræ DEI abalienati à peccatoribus, ita tamen ut non succumberet, sed illis ipsis angoribus in DEO tanqvam DEO suo,confideret.

XX. Non enim simpliciter clamat, DEUS, DEUS, sed DEUS mi, DEUS mi, cur deseruisti me? Haud obscurè indicans, se in illo gravissimo tentationum æstu, fiduciam filialem in DEO Patre suo retinere. Vera proinde & genuina pronunciati hujus interpretatio huc redit.

XXI. Erat Christus tum in extrema ἀκμῇ tentationum constitutus in judicio DEI, adeoq; agebat non cum Patre placcato, sed cum judice irato, qvé intuens luctabatur cum tentatione desertionis,ac proinde, qvia sentiebat dolores derelicti, proferebat etiã verba derelicti.

XXII. Absit autem statuamus, DEUM à DEO desertum fuisse, siqvidem Christus ipse apertè profitetur Joh. 14. se esse in Patre, & Patrem in ipso. Absit itidem afferamus, arctissimum illud unionis personalis vinculum fuisse disruptum & dissolutum. Nam, ut habet illud aureum Damasceni πολυθρύλλητον, λόγος carnem, qvam semel assumsit, nunqvam deserit. Exinanivit se λόγος, non subtraxit carni protectionem, non solvit unionem.

XXIII. Qvod si ergò cum Christo tentationes desertionis sentiamus, & cum sanctis in profundis hæreanius, cum clamore valido in nomine Christi mediatoris nostri pręcemur DEUM nostrum, de exauditione non dubitantes.

XXIV. Tentatione hâc gravissimâ superatâ, ait: Sitio, Joh. 19. 28. Potest hoc Salvatoris μονόφονον pronunciatum intelligi, primò, sensu literali, de siti naturali, ex defectu virium in asperrimis cruciatibus exhaustarum. Totâ enim nocte ac die laboraverat, plurimum sangvinis effuderat, cibo ac potu non erat refectus, ad Solis ardorem & urentes ventos ultrà tres horas in cruce nudus pependerat,inde virtus ejus instar testæ exaruerat, & lingva faucibus præ siti adhæserat, Psal. 22, 16. Multum enim, uti D. Cyrillus alicubi ait, possunt dolores ad commovendam sitim. Innatum enim calorem exagitantes, vel, qvod in profunditate humidum est, consumunt, & igneis ardoribus dolendis viscera urunt.

XXV. Partim sensu mystico, de siti spirituali, qvâ saltem generis humani anxiè sitiit. Qvò respicit Bernardus, dum non minùs svaviter, qvàm graviter, in hunc modum differit: Non satis credibile esti Dominum de siti corporali dixisse, ut potum peteret carnalem, qui in instanti sentiebat, se carnaliter moriturum: sed potiùs desiderium ardentissimum salutis nostræ ipsam sitivisse credimus. Domine qvid est, qvod sitis? Nonne sitiebas salutem nostrarum animarum, salutem hominum, & gaudium nostrum? item; Qvid sitis tu, qvi dixisti, si qvis sitiat, veniat ad me, & bibat; qui es fons vitæ? Sitio ô homo, tuam salutem, tuam redemtionem.

XXVI. Utrumq; ergò verè statuimus, & qvòd corporali siti cruciatus fuerit, & qvòd ardentissimo flagrans amore, deperditam animarum salutem sitierit.

XXVII. His igitur omnibus peractis, λειτουργίαν hôc finit Ἐπιτιχίῳ: Consummatum est. O verò lætam vocem, & nunqvam non imis volvendam pectoribus! Qvid qvæso consummatum est? Consummatum est, qvod consummandum erat.

XXIIX. At qværat qvis, qvô pactô veritati consonet, qvòd jam omne consummatú dicat Sospitator noster, cùm adhuc illi fuerit moriendum, adeóq; hostis ultima Mors, 1. Cor. 15. ipse per mortem & Resurrectionem superanda?

XXIX. Verùm sciendum est, hoc Christi apophthegma ad acerbissimę passionis executionem referendum. Et qvamvis adhuc mors obeunda Christo, tamen, qvia jam cessabant tentationes desertionis, de qvibus antea voce miserabili qverulatus, qvia itidé Pater, dissipatis irę & indignationis suę nebulis, faciem illi iterum ostendebat serenā, pro nihilo utiq; habebat mortem jam obeundā, sed potiùs lætabundus illi se offerbat. Totô proinde exclamat animô: consumatum est.

XXX. O qvàm multa hoc Ἐπιτυχίῳ Salvator complectitur! Adami peccatum expiatum, vita reparata, vaticinia impleta, maledictio sublata, deletum cheirographum, qvod adversum nos erat, peccatum abolitum, sacrificium expiatorium peractum, aditusq; ad cælos cælorumq; æterna gaudia reclusus. Summatim, consummata sunt omnia, qvæ pro genere humano liberando, facienda & patienda fuerunt.

XXXI. Facessant proinde Romanensium satisfactiunculæ. Si enim à Christo in cruce transacta & peracta omnia, qvid opus est nostris operum meritis? Si à Christo unâ oblatione consummata sunt omnia, qvid agitis Romanenses cum sacrificio Missæ, qvô vos Christum qvotidie Patri offerre clamitatis?

XXXII. Septimò & postremò circa vesperam exclamat Servator; Domine, in manus tuas commendo Spiritum meum. Mutuatus est hæc verba ex Psal. 31, 6. eaq; voce magnâ jam moriturus proclamat.

XXXIII. Commendat autem Dominus Patri ἀνθρωποπαδῶς in manus suas, non Divinitatem, uti Arrius blaspemabat, sed animam suam, qvam assumserat immortalem, qvemadmodum vocabulum spiritus pro anima accipi, patet ex diversis scripturæ testimoniis, Act. 7, 59. 1. Cor. 2, 11. & 2. Cor. 7, 1. Hebr. 12, 23: & ita commendans Patri spiritum efficit, ut justorum animæ non descendant in infernum, sed potius ad Deum. Euthym. in Joh. O dulcis vitæ terminus, ô inæstimabilis charitas, ô ineffabilis securitas!

XXXIV. Clamat verò voce validâ, ut ostendat, se neqvaqvam infirmitate victum mori, sed ultrò animam ponere, qvæ adhuc unita corpori manere potuisset. Verùm, qvia sic humano generi non consultum fuisset, morti se volens tradit, & inclinato capite spiritum emittit.

XXXV. Sic ergò jam in cruce pendet mortuus; & reverâ qvidem mortuus ille, in qvo, & ex qvô vita ac salus dependet omnium nostrum: Sed ita mortuus, ut nulla vis ipsi invito animam eripuerit; sed ipse eam spontè ac volens, tanqvam depositum qvoddam, Patri restituerit, Joh. 10, 18.

XXXVI. Præclarum verò prorsus divinæ virtutis in Christo argumentum ex eo elucet, qvòd cum clamore magno emittit spiritum. Omnem enim virium humanarum potentiam superat, ut qvis jam moriens, altâ & articulatâ voce loqvatur, nedum, ut altum clamet, id qvod in Christo evenisse historia testatur.

XXXVII. Qvando igitur & nos in limine mortis constituti, animam efflare debemus, solemur nos hîs Christi verbis, certò persuasi, qvòd & nostram animulam, per fidem sibi insertam, in manus Patris commendârit, & exemplum ipsius secuti, animam nostram è corporis domicilio egressuram, Patri cœlesti commendemus. Sic & jubet Petrus 1. Epist. c. 4. 19. Sic fecit David Ps. 31, 6. Stephanus Act. 7, 59. Et hæc brevitate, qvâ fieri potuit, maximâ, de sacrosancto Servatoris nostri Heptalogo, ὡς ἐν γενείᾳ, delineasse sufficiat.

XXXVIII. Audite Dominum in ara crucis docentem, vos tumidi & impœnitentes. Λόγ@ loquitur, & vos aures aspidis instar obdurabitis? Ad se vocat, & vos recalcitrabitis? Pro vobis intercedit, & tantam gratiam contemnetis? Vestri causâ doloribus inferni subjicitur gloriæ Dominus: Vestri causâ derelinqvi se à Deo clamat æternus DEI Filius. Agnoscite ergò, qvanta sit peccati gravitas & atrocitas coram tribunali divino, qvippe qvæ lamentabilem illam qverelam autori vitę, DEI Filio, ipsi DEO in secula benedicto, expressit, ut se à Deo derelictum conqvereretur. Qvorum suscepit naturam eorundé plagat miseriam, in qvô ostendit qvantum ipsi flere debeãt, qvi peccant. Expergiscimi ergò, expergiscimini, ô duri & indurati Filii Adæ, qvi somno peccatorum sepulti istis: Obseqvimmini docenti, ne cogamini obedire nocenti. Est qvidem ipsa Misericordia; si verò vocem ejus audire nolueritis, sit ignis consumens, Deut. 4. ita exardescit ira ejus, ut nemo ipsi valeat resistere, Job. 19.

XXXIX. Accedite etiam crucis cathedram omnes timidi & dolentes, & videte, ut cruci affixus vos expectet, ut brachia ad amplexũ extendat, ut caput ad osculũ demittat, ut os ad docendum & vocandum aperiat cœlestis Doctor vester. O Homo, inqvit Salvator, vide qvæ pro te patior. Non est dolor, sicut qvô ego crucior. Ad te clamo, qvi pro te morior. Peccatorum sarcina torqveris, precibus meis & sangvine meô te solare & erige. Desertus es ab omnibus? in meo patrocinio fiduciam pone. Gravitas peccatorum te excarnificat, latronem aspice, & meam erga ipsum clementiam perpende. Deus ipse tibi adversari, atq; omnia inimica esse videntur, DEUM tuum DEUM esse cogita. Sitit anima tua præ mœrore, & acetô tentationum potaris; sangvine meô pro tuis peccatis effuso te refice. Imperfectionem misellorum tuorum operum vides, à me omnia consummata esse cogita. In ipsis mortis horroribus versaris, me portas ejus perfregisse ne dubita, mihiq; animam tuam commenda. Sic per laborem in reqviẽ, per mortem in vitam transibis, & æternùm triumphabis. O nos beatos, si talis indies verborum Christi animo nostro surgat meditatio! O miseros & perditos, si nulla nos tantaru rerum tangat sollicitudo!

XL. O dulcissime Domine JESU CHRISTE, ultimum verbum tuum in cruce sit ultimum verbum meum in hac luce; & cùm ampliùs fari non possum, exaudi finale cordis mei desiderium! O amantissime Jesu, splendor paternæ gloriæ, Sol justitiæ, qui pro nobis in ara crucis exaltatus, pro inimicis peccatus es, pro tuis sollicitus, latroni propitius, pro salute omnium sitiendus consumasti omnia, & hinc emigrasti in æterna gaudia, Præsta, ut sacrosancta crucis tuæ suspiria mihi sint opobalsamum adversus spiritualem inediam, acedian, athymian, melanchian, dystychan juxtim & aphilian. O Domine JEsu consolare gementem, conforta trementem, fove deficientem, suscipe expirantem. O tu, qui nostra securitas, ô tu, qui nostra sanitas, ô tu, qui nostra charitas,

Jesu auctor clementiæ, Totíus spes lætitiæ, Dulcoris fons & gratiæ, Veræ cordis delitiæ; Et mentis delectatio, Amoris consummatio: O nostra gloriatio; Una mundi salvatio: In cruore tuo lotum, Me commendo tibi totum. Tuæ sanctæ manus istæ, Me defendant Jesu Christe, Extremis in periculis, AMEN.


### St. Bernard, in his book on the Formula of an Honest Life

St. Bernard, in his book on the Formula of an Honest Life:

Let Jesus be always in your heart, and let the image of the Crucified never depart from your mind. Let this be your food and drink, your sweetness and consolation, your honey and your desire, your reading and your meditation, your prayer and your contemplation. Your life and death and resurrection. Always think of him, etc.

THE SAME.

May the memory of the Crucified crucify every vice in us.

May I myself be mindful of GOD: may you, O Crucified, be mine! AMEN.

Latin:

D. Bernhardus lib. de Formula honestæ vitæ:

Sit Jesus tibi semper in corde, & nunquam imago Crucifixi ab animo tuo recedat. Hæc tibi sit cibus, & potus, dulcedo & consolatio tua, meltuum & desiderium tuum, lectio tua, & meditatio tua, oratio & contemplatio tua. Vita & mors & resurrectio tua. Semper illum cogita, &c.

IDEM.

Memoria Crucifixi crucifigat in nobis omne vitium.

Sim memor ipse DEI: sis crucifixe mei! AMEN.


## 38 Thirty-eighth Disputation, On the Death of Christ

The life of Christ has hitherto stood before us as a rule of living: his death follows, which is our redemption. Since, therefore, in the preceding sections we have lived with our life, let us now also die with him who endured death for us, and by meditating upon the same, we maintain our purpose, and that in the following 4 chapters of this work. In the first of which, the truth of the death of Christ must be proven; in the second, the end and effects are to be considered; in the third, the signs accompanying the death of the Lord are to be weighed; the fourth is to be concluded with practical meditation.

CHAPTER I.

I. Thesis. As the life of CHRIST suffered various insults from satanic instruments, so too did his death. Manichaeus, as witnessed by Augustine (book 15 against the Manichaeans, vol. 6 of his works, p. 109), denied that the Lord truly died, and with Marcion, converted the whole life of CHRIST into a phantastic image; hence he taught that CHRIST dies, suffers, and is crucified daily in onions, leeks, and other things of that kind, as witnessed by the same (book on faith against the Manichaeans, vol. 6 of his works, ch. 7, p. 210). Porphyry, that satanic offspring, pronounced that Christ was justly killed by the Jews (in his book on Philosophical Theology, as noted by Augustine, book 19 on the City of God, vol. 3 of his works, p. 236). Pelagius dared to defend impudently that the death of the Lord was in vain (Augustine, Epistle 95, vol. 2 of his works, p. 145). To whom are the corruptions of modern heretics hidden? Who, while they do not find hiding places for errors and blasphemies in the life of CHRIST, attempt to rise up against the death of the Lord. But with an unhappy attempt and clearly ill-fated success; for the bald and Nestorian offspring clings to the idolatrous Papal one; the viperous Photinian one clings to the fontal synagogue of the Rabbis, which how true it is, will be revealed in the following.

II. We make our beginning from the truth of the Lord's death; for unless this was truly accomplished, we still remain in our sins. We shall confirm the same, however, with the following irrefutable foundations: 1. It is taken from the perfect definition of death, which is the real separation of the body from the soul, or the real tearing away of the soul from the body, with the former departing locally from the latter.

This is exactly applied to the death of Christ, as is evident from the unanimous consent of the Evangelists: Matt. ch. 28, v. 50, ἀφῆκε τὸ πνεῦμα. Mark 15, v. 37, ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἀφεὶς φωνὴν μεγάλην, ἐξέπνευσε. Luke 23, v. 46, καὶ ταῦτα εἰπὼν ἐξέπνευσεν. John 19, v. 30, καὶ κλίνας τὴν κεφαλὴν, παρέδωκε τὸ πνεῦμα. Hence this irrefutable corollary results: Whoever truly sends forth their spirit, or soul, in such a way that its local separation from the body occurs, there also the subject in which such a separation occurs truly dies. :: III. 2. The consent of other witnesses provides this for us. 1. The Centurion confesses it: truly he was, etc., and with him the whole crowd of soldiers standing by. In whose testimony we note, in passing: 1. The innocence of the dying one, against the impious deed of the Jews; 2. His person, against the sacrilegious sect of the Photinians. The latter is noted in Luke 23, v. 47, ὄντως ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὗτος δίκαιος ἦν. The former in Matt. 27, v. 54, ἀληθῶς Θεοῦ υἱὸς ἦν οὗτος. 2. The women also standing by; for behold, those whom the appointed disciples had abandoned; these weak women followed him, and they proclaim the truth of his death and of his entire passion. 3. The soldier piercing the side of the Lord with a spear, and this 1. so that he might know from this whether he was clearly dead; or 2. if he were alive, that he might nevertheless be killed in this way, namely by the heart being touched; whence the Evangelist adds: when they saw that he was dead, they did not break his bones. 4. Nicodemus; for he, while he takes up the body of the Lord and desires to bury it, testifies that he is dead, since burial is appropriate only for the dead. Therefore our conclusion stands firm: that the body of Christ was truly dead for three days; by which we overturn all the calumnies of the bald-headed race of associates, by which, through some lie or other, they falsely attribute to us as if we were overturning the truth of the Lord's death. See Mart. cont. Menz., Sadael. de V. hum. nat. p. m. 84, Ursi. Cat. p. 219. Note here again in passing the year of his death, since even those who are not of the lowest rank have erred here. Irenaeus, book 2 against Heresies, ch. 39 & 40, along with others, about whom Augustine, book 2 on Christian Doctrine, ch. 28, thought the year of Christ's death was nearly the fiftieth; others the thirtieth; Tertullian in his book against the Jews, Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the Stromata, Lactantius, book 4, ch. 10, and Augustine, book 18 of the City of God, p. 54 (though he is contradictory to himself, as is evident from book 2 on Christian Doctrine, ch. 28). 3. Others note the thirty-first; as Apollinaris (reported by Jerome in ch. 9 of Daniel), Cyril in ch. 9 of Isaiah, Bede in his book on the reckoning of time, ch. 45, note the thirty-fourth, to whose opinions we also submit our own calculation, intending to render an account in the conflict concerning the errors of others, and to prove our own opinion, the basis for which foundation is this reason: that John arranges the entire ministry of Christ through four Passovers, namely from the time of his baptism, which was his thirtieth year.

IV. Regarding this first chapter, however, almost countless questions present themselves, the principal of which we shall examine very briefly. It is asked, therefore: 1. How death could apply to Christ, since death is the penalty for sin (Gen. 2:17; Rom. 5:12 & 17; ch. 6:23; 1 Cor. 15:21; Eph. 6:6; 1 Tim. 5:6; Ezek. 18:4; Jas. 1:15), whereas Christ 1. is immune from all sin, in whose mouth no deceit was found (Isa. 53:9), conceived by the Holy Spirit (Matt. 1:20), and 2. is the Prince of Life, holding authority over death? Answer: Death is the wages of sin (Rom. 6:23), by which all would have been compelled to perish if that wage had not been removed through death. Since no one among sinners could provide this, except for Him who was both without sin and able to make satisfaction for all, the Son of God took upon Himself the penalty that was to be paid by others; and for that reason, it was simply necessary that He die in order to make satisfaction for us. Whence to 1. I say: although Christ was immune from sin both through the integrity of the nature assumed, undefiled by any sin, and through the grace of the union with the τῷ λόγῳ, He nevertheless willed to undergo death voluntarily, because He assumed our mortal flesh for this purpose: that He might be able to die not for Himself, but for us, by diverting onto Himself the penalty which He Himself had not deserved. To 2. Answer: Augustine, against Felicianus. Christ is the Prince of Life having authority over death, as God, through His divine nature, but not only so, but also through His human nature, namely because of the grace of the union, yet in such a way that He destroys in that nature the one to whom the whole of nature was subject on account of sin. Add that the Lord of Life remained even in the midst of death; whence, in turn, Augustine elegantly says: 'Death dies more in Christ than Christ in death' (in Expl. Ps. 50, vol. 8, op. p. m. 256.) It is concluded, therefore, that it was necessary for Christ to die: 1. on account of the Father's will; 2. on account of the necessity of liberation; 3. on account of the fulfillment of the prophecies (1 Cor. 15:3; Gen. 3:15; Ps. 16:10; Acts 2:30; ch. 13:36; Dan. 9:26; Isa. 53:8).

V. 2. Was Christ truly a man in death? Hugh of Saint Victor, book 2, De Sacramentis, part 1, penultimate chapter; Lombard, book 3, Sentences, dist. 22; L. A. p. m. 607, affirm it. 1. Hugh proceeds thus: that the being of a man consists in the soul, in such a way that the soul is the whole subject, using the body only accidentally; whence, although in death the bond of body and soul has ceased, nevertheless the soul of CHRIST has remained whole in reality, and thus CHRIST is man. 2. Lombard. that the Divinity took up man, but never laid aside what was assumed; 3. that the conjunction of body and soul constitutes man; and which, although they were separated from one another in death, have nevertheless remained whole in the λόγῳ; that, if he had ceased to be man, he would have simultaneously ceased to be mediator, since he is mediator according to both natures; 5. that he is a priest forever; but a priest must necessarily be man. We, with Thomas, hold the negative (art. 4. sum. Theol. part. 3. quæst. 5.) and we deny that Christ was a true man in death, 1. because he truly died, 2. lacking soul and life; whence our subsumption is as follows: Every one who is truly dead, lacking life, and in whom the actual combination of essential parts constituting the whole suppositum ceases, he is in reality not man. R. e. that it collapses of itself 1. since a part cannot be the whole suppositum, although it may be the more principal one, whence the being of the whole as it were depends. To 2. the union is to be considered not only by reason of the whole assumed, but also of the parts. What he once assumed, he never lays aside; but the Word assumed flesh and soul, which he will never lay aside. Whence, although a natural dissolution of body and soul intervenes, he nevertheless retains what was assumed in the λόγῳ in the parts, and thus in the parts the whole, although in parts naturally distinct from one another. Hence what was assumed is considered 1. as it consists in itself by the perfect cohesion and coupling of the parts: 2. as the individual parts of the whole are coupled, not to one another, but to another, namely a third. In this way, therefore, he never laid aside what was assumed in the λόγῳ. To 3. Essential parts constitute the whole, namely if they are united to one another immediately, but not to another; whence, since there is a double union in Christ, they also must necessarily be distinguished. For there is 1. that of body and soul; in this, if a whole suppositum is to be made, namely man, it is necessary that these parts be coupled to one another immediately in act. 2. personal union, in which flesh and soul are coupled to the λόγῳ, not so that they constitute one natural suppositum, but a Personal one, which is God-man. To 4. Although the body was dead by natural death, it was not for that reason divided from the λόγῳ; for it remained even in death, what was assumed by the λόγῳ, in the λόγῳ. Therefore the office of mediator is perfect. Add that the instance is not valid, as will be shown in more detail in the conflict. To 5. He speaks of this not so much concerning the act of administration as the right of succession, that is, not as if Christ were always to be a priest in act, but because no one is ever to succeed him in this priesthood. Add that he did not cease to be a priest in death according to his human nature, insofar as he was perfectly united to the λόγῳ. From what has been said, therefore, it is clear: 1. The person of the Son of God never laid aside what was assumed. Here the harsh expression of the Coimbricenses (l. 1. Phys. Art. c. 2. quæst. 2. Art. 4.) is to be noted, that the union of the Word and humanity had been dissolved. Theol. c. 18. p. m. 394.) asserting that the humanity remained in the λόγῳ, namely, because the parts of his person remained united to the λόγῳ; for if that were true, Christ would be man and not man in death; not man, because he was dead; man, insofar as his parts were united to the divinity, which Lombard wishes. 3. The whole suppositum necessarily requires all its parts, nor can it subsist if any of the essential ones are absent; which is against Hugo. 4. For the being of a thing, an act must necessarily be posited, and mere potentiality does not suffice. Therefore, those scholastics seem to be lifting bricks who, while they strive to reconcile Thomas and Lombard, and (as Bonaventure l. 3. sent. dist. 221.) say that Christ was either aptitudinally man, or materially (as Alexander of Hales), or improperly (as Biel lib. 3. dist. 22.), entangle themselves in mere contradictions, and by the very fact that they assert Christ remained man in death, they make a non-man out of a man. For the conclusion of this question, we also wish to add this: that by this assertion of ours, in which we say that the dead Christ was not a true man, we in no way support the impious assertion of Pagninus and Beza, who call the body of Christ a corpse; since 1. for the designation of a corpse, putrefaction is necessarily required, which, how alien it is from the Lord's body, Paul testifies in Acts 2: v. 31, from Psalm 16. 2. It is not the death of a mere man, but of the Son of God himself; concerning which matter the Scholastics rightly say: Christ did not assume the ignominies of a dead body, because by them he could have merited nothing for us.

VI. 3. Whether the personal union was dissolved in death? That seems to be able to be elicited from certain statements. For 1. John 10: v. 18, Christ says: I have the power of laying down my soul; which power certainly does not belong to humanity; therefore, it must be attributed to the Divinity, which was able to lay down its soul, and by this laying down, dissolved the Union between itself and the human soul. 2. Matt. 27. the Lord cries out: Why hast thou forsaken me, my God? If, therefore, he was forsaken by God, the man Christ was not united to Him. 3. The very real death of Christ's body seems to argue the same; for, if the body could not die unless the soul departed, much less could it have died with the divinity present, since it vivifies much more than the soul. R. The doubts of this question contain nothing solid, since it is established from the aforementioned that the truth of this Union remained even in death, and in the unviolated corruption, on account of which Christ was called the Lord of life even in death. For as Thomas rightly says, Just as nothing takes away grace except sin, so much less does anything dissolve the union itself, except sin. Wherefore, although the soul departed locally from the body, it nevertheless remained perpetually in the hypostasis of the Son of God, as Damascene says, lib. 3 de Orthod. fid. c. 27. To 1. therefore, since all power is given to the flesh, and therefore this also; whence the flesh properly lays down the soul. To 2. concerning the delay of divine help, it is to be understood not of the tearing apart of the two natures in Christ; for if this tearing apart of the natures had happened on account of the complaint, it would follow that it did not happen finally in death, but while still in life, when Christ was crying out. Others respond to this argument differently, that this complaint of Christ is to be referred to the prayer performed in the garden, by which he asked that this cup might be taken from him, which he was nevertheless compelled to drink, and thus was not heard by the Father; but the former response pleases us more. To 3. Life, insofar as it is referred to the body, depends on the soul, which formally informs it; whence, when this ceases, that also ceases; but the divinity vivifies the body of Christ only effectively, and that not by necessity, but by will; whence, even if the flesh of Christ is vivifying even in death, John 6, it is not however formally, but insofar as it is the body of the Son of God, no less in death than in life. In place of a colophon in this question, note the impiety of Perkins, writing in Tom. 1. op. p. 256, in Expl. Symb., that the second death was also in Christ, which he defines by the separation of body and soul from God.

VII. Finally, it is asked, whether the eternal divinity of Christ is rightly denied because of his death? The Photinians think so, whose discourse let us hear

briefly. Thus the Racovian Catechism on the knowledge of Christ, ch. 1, p. 55. Show me how that is contrary to right reason? Firstly thus: that two essences, which are contrary to one another in their properties, can in no way be united in one person, such as these are: mortal and immortal, having a beginning and being without beginning, being mutable and immutable. Oster. in inst. Ger. 41. c. 6. If the Son of God truly died, as He indeed died, and is now a Son of God, then it is surely manifest that the same, when He died, could not at the same time have lived. But note that the heretics play most basely, 1. by a μεταβάσει εἰς ἄλλο γένος; for those things which are to be accepted concerning merely physical bodies, they accommodate to the person of CHRIST consisting of two natures; 2. by most wickedly examining such great mysteries by the balance of foolish reason; 3. by maliciously confusing diverse respects. Therefore, oppose these immovable foundations to them. 1. That opposite attributes cannot subsist in merely physical bodies, e.g., mortal and immortal; but they can subsist most excellently in the body of CHRIST supernaturally and deified; 2. That those contrary attributes are not attributed to Christ in one and the same respect, but according to the discretion and distinction of the natures; 3. That such great mysteries cannot be understood by the scrutiny of reason, since it is blind and does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. The narrowness of the pages forbids giving more on these matters.

Latin:

EXtitit nobis hactenus vita Christi vivendi regula: sequitur mors, quæ nostræ est redemptio. Quia ergò in præcedentibus viximus cum vita nostra, moriamur jam quoq; cum ipso, qui pro nobis mortem sustinuit, eandemqve meditando, nostrum continemus institutum, idq; seqventibus hujus capitibus 4. In qvorum primô, mortis Christi veritas probanda venit; Secundô, finis & effecta consideranda; Tertiô signa mortem Domini comitantia perpendenda; Qvartum meditatione practicâ concludendum.

CAPUT I.

I. Thesis. Ut vita CHRISTI varios satanicorum organorum passa est insultus, sic non minùs mors. Manichæus, teste Aug. (lib. 15. contra Man. tom. 6. operum p. m. 109.) Dominum verè mortuum negavit, & cum Marcione, totam vitam CHRISTI in phantasticam imaginem convertit; hînc qvotidie CHRISTUM mori, pati, crucifigi, in cæpis, porris portaculis, & id genus aliis, docuit, teste eôdem (l. defide contra Man. 10. 6. op. c. 77. p. m. 210.) Porphyrius, satanica soboles, justè Christum à Judæis occisum, pronunciavit (in lib. de Theologia philosophica, monente Aug. l. 19. de Civ. D. t. 3. op. p. m. 236.) Pelagius, irritam fuisse mortem domini, defendere impudenter ausus est. (August. Epist. 95. t. 2. op. p. m. 145.) Qvem latent corruptelæ modernorum hæredicorũ? qvi dum in vita CHRISTI latibula errorum & blasphemiarum non inveniunt, contra mortem Domini insurgere tentant. Sed infelici conamine & infausto planè successu; hæret enim soboles calva & Nestoriana cum idololatrica Papali; hæret viperina Photiniana cum fontica Rabbinorum synagoga qvod qvàm verum, in seqventibus patebit.

II. A veritate Dominicæ mortis exordium facimus; hæc enim nisi peracta verè, adhuc hæremus in peccatis. Confirmabimus autem eandem irrefutabilibus seqventibus fundamentis: 1. Sumitur à perfecta mortis definitione, quæ est realis corporis ab anima separatio, seu realis divulsio animæ â corpore, decedente localiter illâ ab hoc.

Exactè hæc accommodatur morti Christi, ut ex Evangelistarum unanimi constat consensu Matth. c. 28. v. 50. ἀφῆκε τὸ πνεῦμα. Marc. 15. v. 37. ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἀφεὶς φωνὴν μεγάλην, ἐξέπνευσε. Luc. 23. v. 46. καὶ ταῦτα εἰπὼν ἐξέπνευσεν. Joh. 19. v. 30. καὶ κλίνας τὴν κεφαλὴν, παρέδωκε τὸ πνεῦμα. Hinc irrefutabile hoc resultat πόρισμα: Qvicunq; reverà emittit spiritum, seu animam, ita, ut localis ejus â corpore fiat separatio, ibi qvoq; revera subjectum id, in qvo talis fit separatio, moritur. :: III. 2. Suppeditat nobis testium alioru consensus. Fatetur id 1.Centurio: verè fuit &c.&cum eâ tota militum astantiũ caterva.In qvorum testimonio obiter, not. 1. morientis innocentiam, contra impium judæorum factum; 2. Personam, contra sacrilegam Photinianorum sectam. Posterius notatur Luc. 28. v. 47. ὄντως ὁ ἄνθρωπος υ̊τός δίκαιος ἦν. Prius Matth. 27. v. 54. ἀληθῶς Θεᾶ ὑιὸς ἦν υ̊τος. 2. astantes quoq; mulieres; Ecce enim quem reliquerant testes constituti discipuli; hunc secutæ infirmæ fæmellæ, mortis veritatem, & totius passionis prædicant acta. 3. miles perforans latus Domini lanceâ, idqve 1. an planè mortuus esset, hinc ut cognosceret; vel 2. Si viveret, hôc tamen modô, tactô scil. corde, enecaretur; Unde Evangelista subjicit: cùm mortuum viderent, non fregerunt ossa ejus. 4. Nicodemus; is enim dum corpus Domini tollit, idqve sepellire cupit, mortuum esse testatur, cùm sepultura solis competat mortuis. Nostra ergò firma stat conclusio; Corpus Christi reverà per triduum mortuum fuisse; Qvâ evertimus omnes Calvæ gentis sociorum calumnias,qvibus per mendacium, nescio qvod, affingunt nobis, ac si veritatem mortis dominicæ everteremus. Vide Mart. cont. Menz. Sadael. de V. hum. nat. p. m. 84. Ursi. Cat. p. 219. Nota hic iterum obiter annum etiam mortis, cùm hîc lapsi fuerint non ex infimis qvique. Iren. l. 2. cont. Hæres. c. 39. & 40. cum aliis, de quibus Aug. l. 2. de doctr. Chr. c. 28. annum mortis Christi putârunt fermè qvinqvagesimum; an alii trigesimum; Tertul. in lib. adv. Jud. Clem. Alex. l. 1. strom. Lact. l. 40. c. 10. & Aug. l. 18. de Civ. D. p 54. (sibi licet contrarius, ut patet ex l. 2. de doctr. Chr. c. 28.) 3. Alii trigesimum primum; ut Apollinaris (referente Hieron. in c. 9. Dan.) Cyrill. in c. 9. Esa. Beda in l. de rat. temp. c. 45. trigesimum qvartum notant, qvorum sententiæ nostrum etiam subjicimus calculum, reddituri in conflictu de erroribus aliorum rationem, nostramq; probaturi sententiam, cujus fundamenti locô hæc notetur ratio, quòd Johannes totum ministerium Christi disponat per qvatuor Paschata, à tempore baptismatis nempe, qvod fuit annus tricesimus.

IV. Circa hoc verò primum caput innumeræ fermè se offerunt qvæstiones, qvarum præcipuas perspiciemus paucissimis. Qværitur ergò 1. quomodo mors Christo convenerit, cùm mors sit peccati pœna Ge. 2, 17. Rom. 5, 12. & 17. c. 6. 23. 1. Cor. 15, 21. Eph. 6, 6. 1. Tim. 5, 6. Ezech. 18, 4. Jac. 1, 15. Christus verò 1. sit immunis ab omni peccato, in cujus ore non inventus est dolus, Esa. 53, 9. de spiritu sancto conceptus Matth. 1. v. 20. 2. Princeps vitæ, in mortem tenens imperium? R. Stipendium peccati mors est, Rom. 6, 23. qvâ perire coacti fuissent omnes, si stipendium id per mortem non fuisset sublatum. Id v. cùm præstare nullus posset ex peccatoribus, præter eum, qvi sine peccato & esset, & potens pro omnibus satisfacere posset, Filius DEI in se pœnam, qvæ aliis persolvenda erat, recepit; & ob id simpliciter, ut pro nobis satis faceret suâ morte, necessarium fuit. Unde ad 1. dico: licet Christus fuerit à peccato immunis tàm per naturæ assumtæ, integritatem, nullô peccato inqvinatam; qvàm per Unionis cum τῷ λόγῳ gratiam, mortem tamen spontè subire voluit, quia ob id mortalem nostram carnem assumsit, ut mori non propter se, sed propter nos posset, derivando nempe pœnam in se, qvam non meruerat ipse. Ad 2. R. Aug. cont. Felic. Princeps vitæ habens in mortem imperium, qvà Deus, per naturam divinam, sed non tantùm, verùm & per naturam humanam, nempe ob unionis gratiam, Christus est, ita tamen, ut destruat in natura eum, cui propter peccatum tota erat subjecta natura. Adde, quòd Dominus vitæ in media etiam morte manserit; unde vicissim eleganter August. Mors magis moritur in Christo, qvàm Christus in morte (in Expl. Psal. 50. tom. 8. op. p. m. 256.) Concluditur ergò, Christus ut moreretur, fuisse necessarium 1. ob patris voluntatem; 2. ob liberationis necessitatem; 3. ob vaticiniorum impletionem, 1. Cor. 15, 3. Gen. 3. v. 15. Psal. 16, 10. Act. 2. v. 30. c. 13. 36. Dan. 9. 26. Esa. 53, 8.

V. 2. An Christus in morte reverâ fuerit Homo? Hugode Sanct. Vic. l. 2. de Sacra: partit. 1. c. pen. Lomb. l. 3. sent. dist. 22. L. A. p. m. 607. affirmant. 1. Hugo sic procedit; quòd Hominis esse consistat in anima, ita, ut anima sit totum suppositum, utens tantùm corpore accidentaliter; unde, licet in morte cessârit corporis & animę nexus, manserit támen nihilominus reverâ CHRISTI anima integra, & ita CHRISTUS homo. 2. Lombard.qvòd Divinitas susceperit hominem, assumtum autem nunqvani deposuerit; 3. qvòd conjunctio corporis & animæ hominem constitvat; qvæq́;, licet â se invicem in morte fuerint separata, manserint tamén integra in λόγῳ; qvòd, si cessasset esse homo, cessasset simul esse mediator, cùm sit mediator secumdùm utramq́; naturam; 5. qvòd sit sacerdos in æternum; Sacerdos autem necessariò homo debeat esse. Nos cum Thoma negativam tenemus (art. 4. sum. Theol. part. 3. quæst. 5.) & Christum in morte verum hominem fuisse, negamus, 1. qvòd verè fuerit mortuus, 2. carens animâ & vitâ; unde subsumtio nostra talis: Omnis verè mortuus carens vitâ, & in qvo cessat partium essentialium, totum suppositum constituentium, actualis combinatio, is reverà non est homo. R. e. qvòd per se 1. corruat, cùm pars non possit esse suppositum totum, licet ea sit principalior, unde totius quasi esse dependeat. Ad 2. unionem considerari non tantùm ratione totius assumti, sed & partium. Qvod semel assumsit, nunqvam deponit; sed verbum assumsit carnem & animam, qvæ nunqvam deponet. Unde, licet naturalis interveniat corporis & animæ solutio, retinet nihilominus assumtum λόγῳ in partibus, & ita in partibus totum, licet in partibus â se invicem naturaliter distinctis. Hinc assumtum consideratur 1. ut inse constat perfectâ partium cohæsione & copulatione: 2. ut singulæ partes totius copulatæ, non sibi invicem, sed alteri, tertio nempe. Hôc ergò modô assumtum nunqvam deposuit λόγῳ. Ad 3. Partes essentiales constituere totum, nempe si invicem sibi uniantur immediatè, non verò alteri; unde, cùm sit duplex in Christo unio, eædem qvoq; necessariò sunt distingvendæ. Nam est 1. corporis & animæ; in hâc, si fieri debet suppositum totum, nempe homo, ut immediatè actu sibi invicicem copulentur hæ partes, necefse est. 2. unio personalis, in qvā caro & anima copulantur λόγῳ, non ut unum constituant suppositum naturale, sed Personale, qvod sit homo Deus. Ad 4. Corpus licet morte naturali fuerit mortuum, non tamen ob id â λόγῳ divisum; mansit enim etiam in morte, qvod assumtum â λόγῳ erat, in λόγῳ. Perfectum igitur est mediatoris officium. Adde, qvòd non valeat instantia, ut pluribus ostendetur in conflictu. Ad. 5. loquitur id non tàm de actu administrationis, quàm fuccessionis jure, hoc est, non, quasi Christus semper actu sacerdos sit futurus, sed quòd nunquam ei quispiam in hoc sacerdotio sit succefsurus. Adde, quòd nec in morte sacerdos esse secundùm humanam naturam desieriť, qvatenus nempe fuit unitus perfectè τῷ λόγῳ. Ex dictis ergò patet, 1. Personam filii Dei nunqvam assumtum deposuisse. Ubi notanda dura locutio Conimbricensium (l. 1. Phys. Art. c. 2. quæst. 2. Art. 4.) solutam fuisse Unionem verbi, & humanitatis. 2. Partes essentiales, in constitutione totius, sibi invicem copulari immediatè, necesse esse. Hoc iterum nota contra Lomb. & ad hujus partes deslectentem Polanum (l. 6. Synt. Theol. c. 18. p. m. 394.) statuentem, mansisse in λόγῳ humanitatem, nempe, quia partes ejus personæ τῷ λόγῳ manserunt unitæ; id enim, si verum, erit Christus in morte homo, & non homo; non homo, quia mortuus erat; homo prout partes ejus erant divinitati unitæ, qvod vult Lomb. 3. Totum suppositum necessariò omnes partes reqvirere, nec si ulla essentialium absit, posse subsistere; qvod est contra Hugon. 4. Ad esse rei necessariò ponendum esse actũ, & non sufficere solam potentiam. Lateres ergò levare videntur scholasticorum illi, qui, dum Thomam & Lombardum conciliare student, & (ut Bonaventura l. 3. sent. dist. 221.) vel Christum aptitudinaliter hominem fuisse, vel materialiter (ut Alexander de Ales) vel impropriè (ut Biel lib. 3. dist. 22.) dicunt, meris se contradictionibus implicant, & eô ipsô, qvô Christum hominem in morte mansisse statuunt, ex homine non hominem faciunt.
