Pro conclusione hujus qvæstionis, & hoc additum volumus, nos hôc nostrô assertô, qvô dicimus, Christum mortuum verum non fuisse hominem, minimè patrocinari impiæ assertioni Pagnini & Bezæ, corpus Christi cadaver appellantium; cùm 1. ad cadaveris appellationem necessariò reqviratur putredo, qvæ qvàm sit aliena â corpore dominico, testatur Paulus Actor. 2: v. 31. ex Psal. 16. 2. non puri hominis, sed ipsius filii Dei mors sit; qvâ de re rectè Scholastici: Non assumsit Christus opprobria corporis mortui, quia illis nil potuisset nobis mereri.

VI. 3. An in morte fuerit soluta unio personalis? Id videtur posse elici ex dictis qvibusdam. Nam 1. Joh. 10. v. 18. inquit Christus: Ego potestatem habeo deponendi animam; Qvæ certè potestas non competere videtur humanitati; Divinitati ergò, quæ animam deponere potuit, & hâc depositione Unionem inter se, & animam humanam, solvit, tribuenda. 2. Matth. 27. clamat Dominus: Cur dereliquisti me Deus meus? Si ergò relictus fuit â Deo, non fuit eidem unitus, homo Christus. 3. videtur idem arguere & ipsa corporis Christi mors realis; Nam, si non potuit corpus, nisi animâ discedente, mori, multò minùs potuisset divinitate præsente, cùm ipsa multò magis vivificet, quàm anima. R. Nihil solidi continent quæstionis hujus dubitationes, cùm constet ex supradictis hujus Unionis etiam in morte veritas, & in violata corruptio, ob quam Dominus vitæ etiam in morte appellatus est Christus. Ut enim rectè Thomas, Sicut gratiam non tollit, nisi peccatum, ita multò minùs ipsam unionem quicquam solvet, præter peccatum. Qvare, licet anima τοπικῶς â corpore discesserit, perpetuò tamen in ὑποστάσει filii Dei mansit, ut ait Damasc. l. 3. de Orthod. fid. c. 27. Ad. 1. ergò, cùm omnis potestas fit data carni, ideoq; & hæc; unde caro propriè ponit animam. Ad 2. de dilatione auxilii divini, non de duarum in Christo naturarum divulsione id intelligendum esse; nam si propter querelam facta esset hæc naturarum divulsio, sequeretur, quòd non demum facta fuerit in morte, sed adhúc in vitâ, cùm Christus exclamâret. Aliter ad hoc argumentum respondent alii, querelam hanc Christi ad orationem in horto peractam, quâ petiit, ut auferetur de se calix iste, referendam esse, quẽ tamen bibere sit coactus, & sic non exauditus â patre; sed prior nobis placet responsio magis. Ad 3. vita quatenus refertur ad corpus, dependet ab anima, quæ id formaliter informat; unde cessante hâc, cessat & illa; divinitas verò vivificat corpus Christi effectivè tantùm, idque non ex necessitate, sed ex voluntate; Unde, etsi caro Christi sit etiam in morte vivifica Joh. 6. non tamen formaliter, sed prout est corpus Filii Dei, non minùs in morte, quàm in vita. Colophonis locô in hâc quæstione nota impietatem Perkinsii, scribentis Tom: 1. op. p. 256. in Expl. Symb. mortem secundam etiam in Christo fuisse, quam definit per separationem corporis & animæ â Deo.

VII. Postremò tandem quæritur, An rectè ex morte Christi æterna ejus negetur divinitas? Ita putant Photiniani quorum discursum audiam-

brevibus. Sic Catech. Racov. de cogn. Christi c. 1. p. 55. Zeige mir/ wie das/ der rechten Vernunfft zu wider ist? Erstlich also/ das zwey Wesen/ die in den Eigenschafften eines dem andern zu wider ist/ keines weges in einer Person können vereiniget werden/ als da sind: sterblich/ und unsterblich/ einen Anfang haben/ und ohn Anfang seyn/ Wandelbar und unwandedelbar seyn/ Oster. in inst. Ger. 41. c. 6. Ist GOttes Sohn warhafftig gestorben/ wie Er denn gestorben ist/ und ist nun ein Sohn GOttes/ so ist je offenbar/ daß derselbe/ da Er gestorben/ nicht zugleich hat leben können. Sed nota, turpissimè ludere hæreticos, 1. μεταβάσει εἰς ἄλλο γένος; quæ enim de corporibus merè Physicis sunt accipienda, illi ad CHRISTI personam duabus constantem naturis acccommodant; 2. pessimè tanta mysteria ad stultæ rationis trutinam examinare; 3. diversos confundere respectus malitiosè. Hæc ergò immota ipsis fundamenta oppone. 1. attributa opposita in corporibus merè Physicis subsistere non posse, v. g. mortale & immortale; posse autem optimè in corpore CHRISTI ὑπερφυσικῶς & Deificato; 2. Attributa illa contraria non unô & eodem prorsus respectu tribui Christo, sed pro discretione & distinctione naturarum; 3. Scrutiniô rationis tanta intelligi mysteria non posse, cùm cæca sit, & quæ spiritus DEI sint, non percipiat. Plura dare de his, angustia pagellarum vetat.


### Chapter II. Thesis I. We join the end of the death of CHRIST with its effects

CHAPTER II.

Thesis I. We join the end of the death of CHRIST with its effects; for He did not die in vain, but that He might effect something for us by His death. We shall name here the fruits, of which 1. Is the plenary satisfaction for the sins of the whole world, by which reason the death of this Son of God is called a sacrifice performed for the world, and a propitiation for its sins. Compare Is. 53, v. 6. John 1, v. 29. 1 John 1, 7. Note here 1. that Christ truly died for sins, therefore not in vain; 2. not for His own, but for others', Dan. 9, v. 24. Rom. 4, 25. Whence He is said to have died ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν Rom. 5, v. 8. 2 Cor. 5, v. 21, 3. of all, and for all; of all, because His blood is a propitiation not only for our sins, but also for the sins of the whole world 1 John 2, 2. He is the Lamb of God taking away the sins of the whole world, John 1, as much of the pious as of the impious 2 Pet. 2, v. 1. Rom. 14, v. 15. 1 Cor. 15, 3. For all, as much original, Rom. 5, 15, as actual, Is. 53, v. 4. 4. how? by deriving them into Himself, Is. 43, 24, by paying for them, Rom. 4, v. last, by entirely taking them

away, Rom. 8. v. 3. Hence he is said to have been made our priest, while he offered himself for us once on the altar of the cross. II. 2. liberation from the curse of the law, and eternal death; Gal. 3. v. 13. he was made κατάρα, on account of the curse of the law, and destroyed death by his death, Hos. 13. v. 14. 1. Cor. 15, 55. Heb. 2. v. 14. the magnitude of which curse was so great in him, that on account of it he began λυπεῖσθαι, ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν, and his soul was περίλυπος unto death; also with such agony, that pores of blood dripped in drops, Luke 22, 44. Heb. 5. 7. and he himself struggled as if with death, Matt. 26. v. 37. so that he began to pray most intensely on account of it, Luke 22, 44. Thus therefore, as has been said, he fulfilled the law, having been made mediator between God and men, so that by the shedding of his blood, and the intervention of death, he might confirm the testament once established. Death therefore being destroyed, there is no condemnation in those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8. 4. We die, but we do not die, because through death, by the power of the death of Christ, we pass to life. III. 3. The bestowing of eternal life. For death is swallowed up in victory, since the King of life died for you, that you might live eternally. Use these things said, candid Reader, against the manifold and pestiferous errors, 1. of the Zwinglians; 2. of the Papists; 3. of the Photinians. IV. 1. Of the Zwinglians s1. the absolute decree; For as long as this remains, the efficacy of the death of Christ is evacuated. We therefore oppose to this this constant thesis of ours: We were chosen before the foundations of the world were laid ἐν Χριστῷ, Eph. 1. 4. by which we overturn everything which Calvin objected to us lib. 1. Inst. c. 21. sect. 11. Rennech. in aurea salut. cat. p. m. 126. Zanchius l. 1. de nat. Dei tom. 1. op. p. m. 408. Kecc. Buc. Trelca. & others: 2. the cursed particularity, which converts the whole ἀπολύτρωσιν of the Son of God into a very small particle. For he died for all; Whence let this thesis of ours be the one opposed to them: Ὑπὲρ παντὸς γεύσηται θανάτου, Heb. 2. 9. nor will they save themselves by the abuse of the scholastic distinction between efficiency and sufficiency, as Paraeus contends in Ireni. c. 26. p. gr. 142. & others, when they define sufficiency as mere power only, with all act excluded, with Tossanus thus openly explaining himself. See what Paraeus writes in Coment. super Apoc. c. 5. v. 11. p. m. 219. in which he has Musculus as his adversary expressly in loc. sub. tit. de redempt. p. m. 326. the death of Christ therefore remains καθολικώτατος, and most universal. 3. malediction, or alteration, by which they transform the death of the eternal Son of GOD into the death of a mere man. Hence they dream that dying for the life of the world is something proper to a nature; thus most wickedly confounding the 1st and 2nd general rules of the Communication of Idioms, and as it were despoiling the death of Christ of all efficacy. Whence this thesis of ours stands contrary to them: The death of Jesus Christ is the death of the Son of God himself; for God alone can free us from evils, Ps. 130:8, especially from sin, the curse of the law, and eternal death. Wherefore, to die for the life of the world is not an ἰδίωμα [idiom] of a nature, but an ἀποτέλεσμα [result] of the whole person, yet in such a way that each nature acts according to what is proper to it, with the communication of the other. Therefore, to die is not of the humanity alone, but the Divinity also approaches this, though in itself it is ἀθάνατος [immortal]. V. 2. the inconstancy of the Papists, by which 1. some of them affirm that Christ satisfied only for original sins; others, that he indeed satisfied for all, yet in the meantime so that we also should add something of our own for actual sins committed. Against which impious assertion [stands] this thesis: By grace we are saved through the death of the Son of God. 2. They assert the idolatrous sacrifice of the Mass; against which know that Christ offered himself once, and without the shedding of blood (which ceases in the Mass), Heb. 9:22, there is no remission of sins. Observe here the absurdities of Perkins in his explanation of the Creed, p. 662, vol. 1 of his works, by which he says that the altar, on which the sacrifice of Christ was made, was the Divinity, with the end that he might transform that [sacrifice] only into that of a mere man. VI. 3. The rashness of the Photinians, 1. by which they assert that God could have saved men in another way, and even willed to, than through the death of the Son, as Socinus writes, Prael. ch. 14, 15, 16. Smalcius against D. Frantz in the place on the office of Christ, against Smiglecius, p. 142. Against whom note briefly the following foundations: 1. That God chose and willed that one medium; for we were chosen before the foundations of the world were laid, but in Christ JESUS; 2. that without death the law could not be satisfied, since its curse requires that; 3. that God does not will to save a transgressor without justice, Prov. 22:17; 4. that the law had necessarily to be fulfilled. 2. The impious blasphemy by which they assert 1. that the death of Christ does not pertain to the remission of sins, nor did Christ satisfy for us, but rather left some example for the rest. Against which note: as through man came death and sin, so through Christ alone comes life and liberation, Rom. 5:18. 2. That man can fulfill the divine law, and satisfy it by himself; against which assertion scripture manifestly testifies that there is none who does good, not even one, Eph. 2, 1. Ps. 14, 3. 2. Cor. 3, 5. Rom. 7, 3. that Christ merited many things for himself by his own death (in which error, along with the Anhaltines in Apol. Elect. Theol. opposita in defen. arg. 38. p. 43 for me, they have the Papists as ὁμοψήφες [like-minded]), namely universal dominion, exaltation, a name above every name. Against them, for the conclusion of this chapter, note 1. that scripture testifies that those things which were given to Christ were given not by merit, but freely; Phil. 2. 2. that the Lord had this glory long before his death; for he manifested it often, John 1, 2. & c. 3. That he entered into the exaltation, not because of the passion, but after the passion, which was nevertheless granted to him by grace, in full possession. Let them therefore learn to distinguish between order and cause.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

Thes. I. Finem mortis CHRISTI cum effectis conjungimus; mortuus enim est non frustra, sed nobis ut aliqvid suâ morte efficeret. Nominabimus hîc fructus, qvorum 1. Est plenaria pro peccatis totius mundi satisfactio, quâ ratione mors dicitur hæc filii Dei sacrificium præstitum pro mundo, & propitiatio pro ejusdem peccatis. Confer. Es. 53. v. 6. Joh. 1. v. 29. 1. Joh. 1. 7. Nota hîc 1. quòd Christus verè mortuus sit pro peccatis, non ergò frustra; 2. non propriis, sed alienis, Dan. 9. v. 24. Rom. 4. 25. Unde ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν mortuus dicitur Rom. 5. v. 8. 2. Cor. 5. v. 21, 3. omnium, & omnibus; omnium, quia sangvis ejus est propitiatio non tantùm pro nostris, sed etiam totius mundi peccatis 1. Joh. 2, 2. est agnus Dei tollens peccata totius mundi, Joh. 1. tàm piorum, quàm impiorum 2. Petr. 2. v. 1. Rom. 14. v. 15. 1. Cor. 15, 3. Omnibus, tam originalibus, Rom. 5, 15. quàm actualibus, Esa. 53. v. 4. 4. qvomodo? in se derivando, Esa. 43, 24. pro iis luendo, Rom. 4. v. ult planè auferen-

do, Rom. 8. v. 3. Hinc factus dicitur sacerdos noster, dum se obtulit pro nobis semel in ara crucis. II. 2. à maledictione legis, & eterna morte, liberatio; Gal. 3. v. 13. factus est κατάρα, propter legis maledictionem, destruxitq́; suâ morte mortem, Ose. 13. v. 14. 1. Cor. 15, 55. Hebr. 2. v. 14. cujus maledictionis tãta fuit in ipso magnitudo, ut ob eam ceperit λυπεῖσθαι, ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν, & περίλυπος anima ejus fuerit ad mortem; tantâ etiam agoniâ, ut pori sangvinis stillarent guttis, Luc. 22, 44. Hebr 5. 7. ipseq́ve luctaretur quasi cum morte, Matth. 26. v. 37. ut intensissimè orare ob id inceperit, Luc. 22, 44. Sic ergò, ut dictum, legem implevit, factus mediator inter Deum & homines, ut sangvinis sui effusione, & interventu mortis, confirmaret testamentum semel constitutum. Morte ergò destructâ, nulla est condemnatio in his, qvi sunt in Christo Jesu, Rom. 8. 4. Morimur, sed non morimur, qvia per mortem, vi mortis Christi, transimus ad vitam. III. 3. Vitæ æternæ collatio. Mors enim absorpta in victoriam est, cùm pro te mortuus sit Rex vitæ, tu ut viveres æternùm. Dictis his utere, candide Lector, contra multifarios & pestiferos errores, 1. Zvinglianorum; 2. Pontificiorum; 3. Photinianorum. IV. 1. Cvinglianorum s1. absolutum decretum; Hoc enim, qvamdiu manet, evacuatur mortis Christi efficacia. Opponimus ergò huic constantem hanc nostram thesin: Electi sumus ante jacta mundi fundamenta ἐν Χριστῷ, Ephes. 1. 4. qvâ evertimus omnia, qvæ nobis objecit Calvinus lib. 1. Inst. c. 21. sect. 11. Rennech. in aurea salut. cat. p. m. 126. Zanchius l. 1. de nat. Dei tom. 1. op. p. m. 408. Kecc. Buc. Trelca. & alii: 2. maledictam particularitatem, qvæ totam filii Dei ἀπολύτρωσιν in minimam convertit particulam. Mortuus enim est pro omnibus; Unde thesis ipsis opposita hæc nostra esto: Ὑπὲρ παντὸς γεύσηται θανάτου, Hebr. 2. 9. nec salvabunt se abusu distinctionis scholasticæ, inter efficientiam & sufficientiam, ut contendit Paræus in Ireni. c. 26. p. gr. 142. & alii, cùm sufficientiam pernudam tantùm potentiam omni excluso actu definiant, sic fe apertè explicante Tossano. Vide, qvæ scribit Paræus in Coment. super Apoc. c. 5. v. 11. p. m. 219. in qvibus adversarium sibi ex professo habet Musæulum in loc. sub. tit. de redempt. p. m. 326. manet ergò mors Christi καθολικώτατος, & maximè universalis. 3. maledictam ἀλλοίωσιν, quâ mortem æterni DEI Filii, in mortem ψιλῆ ἀνθρώπη, trànsformant. Hinc mori pro mundi vita, naturæ proprium aliqvod somniant; Sic pessimè prædicationes 1. & 2. gen. Comm. Idiomatum confundentes, mortemqve Christi omni efficaciâ qvasi spoliantes. Unde hæc ipsis nostra stat thesis contraria, Mors Jesu Chrissti est mors ipsius Filii Dei; Solus enim Deus nos à malis liberare potest, Psal. 130, 8. præcipue à peccato, legis maledictione, & æternâ morte. Qvocirca, mori pro mundi vita, non ἰδίωμα naturæ, sed ἀποτέλεσμα est totius personæ, ita tamen, ut qvælibet natura agat, qvod proprium est, cum communicatione alterius. Non ergò mori solius est humanitatis, sed huc etiam accedit Divinitas, per se qvidem ἀθάνατος. V. 2. Pontificiorum inconstantiam, quâ 1. affirmant qvidam eorum, Christum tantùm pro originalibus satisfecisse peccatis; qvidam, satisfecisse qvidem pro omnibus, interim tamen ut & nos pro actualibus commissis aliqvid de nostro adderemus. Contra qvod impium assertum hæc thesis: Gratiâ salvati sumus per mortem filii Dei. 2. Idololatricum asserunt Missæ sacrificium; contra qvod scito, semel se Christum obtulisse, & sine sangvinis effusione (qvæ cessat in Missa) Hebr. 9, 22. non fieri remissionem peccatorum. Animadverte hîc Perkins. ineptias in expl. Symb. p. 662. tom. 1. op. qvibus altare, in qvo factum sit Christi sacrificium, fuisse dicit Divinitatem, cum ob finem, ut illud tantùm in nudi hominis transformet. VI. 3. Photinianorum, 1. temeritatem, quâ asseverant, potuisse Deum aliô modô homines salvare, & velle etiam, quàm per mortem Filii, ut scribit Socin. præl. c. 14, 15, 16. Smalc. contra D. Fran. in loc. de Chri. offic. contra Smi. p. p. 142. Contra qvos nota brevibus seqventia fundamenta: 1, Unum illud medium Deum elegisse, & voluisse; electi enim sumus ante jacta fundamenta mundi, sed in Christo JESU; 2. sine morte non potuisse satisfieri legi, cùm id reqvirat ejus maledictio; 3. nolle Deum sine justitia salvare prævaricatorem, Prov. 22. v. 17. 4. legem necessariò fuisse implendam. 2. impiam blasphemiam, quâ asserunt 1. mortem Christi ad peccatorum remissionem non pertinere, nec pro nobis Christum satisfecisse, sed potiùs exemplum aliqvod reliqvisse. Contra qvod nota: ut per hominem mors & peccatum, ita per solum Christum vita & liberatio, Rom. 5, 18. 2. hominem posse implere legem divinam, & per se satisfacere ei; contra qvod assertum manifestè testatur scripturâ, quòd non sit, qvid faciat bonum, & ne unus qvidem, Eph. 2, 1. Ps. 14, 3. 2. Cor. 3, 5. Rom. 7, 3. sibi Christum suâ morte multa meruisse (in qvo errore cum Anhaldinis in Apol. Elect. Theol. opposita in defen. arg. 38. p. mihi 43. Pontificios habent ὁμοψήφες) nempe universale dominium, exaltationem, nomen supra omne nomen. Contra qvos, pro conclusione hujus capitis, nòta 1. quòd eas qvæ Christo data sunt, non ex merito, sed gratis data esse testetur scriptura; Phil. 2. 2. gloriam hanc habuisse dominum longè ante mortem; manifestavit enim eam sæpius, Joh. 1, 2. & c. 3. Exaltationem non propter passionem, sed post passionem, sibi ex gratia tamen donatam, plenariâ usurpatione ingressum esse. Discant ergò distingvere ordinem & causam.


### Chapter III. Thesis I. The miracles remain, the 1st of which is the eclipse of the sun,…

CHAPTER III.

Thesis I. The miracles remain, the 1st of which is the eclipse of the sun, concerning which Origen writes, whom Perkins follows, that it was seen only in Judea: But manifest Greek truth contradicts them: ἐπὶ πᾶσαν καὶ ὅλην τὴν γῆν [over all and the whole earth]. Tertullian also contradicts it in Apol. c. 21. Eusebius in Chron. p. 69 for me, Orosius l. 7, 7. indeed Suidas himself, as D. Seln. testifies, part. pæd. 2. Christ. The question is asked here, whether this eclipse was natural? We deny it, intending to render reasons in the conflict, the foundation of which note, that namely a natural one occurs at the time of the new moon, but this one occurred at the full moon, which is called παρασέληνον [beside the moon].

II. 2. The rending of the veil. The Greek word sounds καταπέτασμα [curtain], in Hebrew פָּרֹכֶת [parokhet], concerning which Exod. 26. v. 32, 33. which rending indicates 1. The unity of the Church; for as from the holy of holies and the temple, one place was made by this rending; so from two peoples one Church was made. 2. The opening of heaven; the veil stood in the way, so that access to the holy of holies was not open to everyone; the veil being rent, behold now we can enter heaven, Hebr. 1. c. 9. 12. c. 10, 8. 3. The abolition of the Ceremonial Law. It is rent from the top to the bottom, as a sign that the burnt offerings were now to cease, through whose blood the high priest had entered the holy of holies; and this legal worship was offered to him who entered, not through the blood of calves into the holy of holies, but through his own, restoring eternal peace to us.

III. 3. The earthquake, concerning which Eusebius narrates that it was also observed by the Gentiles, and that it overturned many houses in Bithynia.

IV. 4. The splitting of the rocks. The rocks are split, and behold the hearts of men are hardened: the stones sympathize with the creator, and man is touched by no compassion.

V. 5. The opening of the tombs. Men could not endure Christ, but behold, the tombs open themselves, that they may give place to Christ: men cast the living from them, behold, the earth offers itself, that it may receive the dead.

VI. 6. The resurrection of the dead. Observe from this the efficacy of the death of Christ; for the Lord of life had scarcely died, when his death was already working effectively; for the dead rise, and indeed with their bodies, so that not only souls, but not even bodies should remain in death.

VII. 7. The opening of the side of the Son of God, finally provides us with the greatest miracle; concerning which the Evangelist asserts with affirmation that he saw it with his own eyes, so that we might not doubt because of its magnitude, nor, having heard of it, conclude that it was a matter of little importance. Note here 1. The occasion by which it came to pass that the side of Christ was opened. This was the feigned piety of the Jews, by which they approached Pilate, asking that they might have the opportunity of breaking the legs of those crucified and burying them, so that the sight of them might not be abominable to those observing the Sabbath. The scoundrels, religious regarding the Sabbath, while meanwhile treating the Lord of the Sabbath most contumeliously: 2. The deed itself, of which the Evangelist says: when they had already seen that Christ was dead, they left his bones unbroken, but one of the soldiers pierced his side. Regarding this matter, Augustine says excellently: He dies in time, so that the breaking may be prevented; the breaking is prevented, so that the fulfillment of the scriptures may take place. Therefore, let no one think that this happened by chance. Regarding this, it is asked, Why were the bones of Christ not broken? R. Briefly from the text itself, that the scripture might be fulfilled, which is twofold, namely Exodus 12:47 and Zechariah 12:10. The former is typical, the latter prophetic. The typical refers to the Paschal lamb of the Old Testament, whose bones the Lord had forbidden to be broken. The Paschal lamb of the New Testament is Christ, John 1, taking away the sins of the world, with whose blood the doorposts of our hearts are smeared; they are saved from eternal destruction. Incidentally, the fantastic Calvinistic ἀρτοκλασία (breaking of bread) is exposed in this place, which, as the Evangelist testifies, has nothing in common with the breaking of the body of Christ; you shall not break a bone of him. The event confirmed the certainty of the prophetic [scripture]. It is asked 2. Who that person was who opened the side of the Lord. The Gospel of Nicodemus says he was called Longinus. Scholastics, adding more to the trifles of this man, said he was blind, and that by chance he received his sight through the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, in a peaceful fiction and a pleasant fantasy. We, while Scripture is silent, suspend our judgment also in this matter, since it is a thing by no means necessary to be known. 3. Consequent; Behold, for when the side was opened, blood and water flowed out copiously. Columbus thinks that the pericardium was touched, being filled with water; which error Perkins follows. inferio causa. salv. & dam. p. 20. tom. 1. op. c. 18. & in exp. Symb. p. m. 669. And therefore they think it was done naturally. But 1. this exposition is established against all Orthodox; 2. Anatomists; 3. it overturns the clear letter, which asserts that water did not drip from the side drop by drop, but that the same flowed out copiously. We, even if we are ignorant of the end, being destitute in this place of a clear letter, nevertheless say in an orthodox manner, 1. that it was a singular miracle; Whence also the Evangelist asserts with such asseveration that he saw with his own eyes, so that we might not doubt concerning the miracle which he narrated. 2. that by the distinct liquid the Sacraments of the New Testament were both signified; for the holy scripture also hands this down, namely that the same are to be performed through water and blood in the New Testament, See Hebr. 9. 14. c. 10, 29. c. 12. v. 24. 1. Petr. 1, 19. Zach. 9; 11.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

Thes. I. Restant miracula, qvorum 1. est solis Eclipsis, de qvâ scribit Orig. qvem seqvitur Perkins. quòd visa tantùm fuerit in Judæa: Sed contradicit ipsis manifesta veritas Græca: ἐπὶ πᾶσαν καὶ ὅλην τὴν γῆν. Contradicit qvoq; Tertul. in Apoll. c. 21. Euseb. in Chron. p. m. 69. Orof. l. 7, 7. imò ipse Suidas, ut testatur D. Seln. part. pæd. 2. Christ. Qværitur hîc, an Eclipsis hæc fuerit naturalis? nos negamus, reddituri rationes inconslictu, qvarum fundamentum hoc nota, quod scil. naturalis fiat tempore novilunii, hæc verò facta sit in plenilunio, qvod παρασέληνον dicitur.

II. 2. Veli scissimo. Vox Græca sonat καταπέτασμα, Hebreis פָּרֹכֶת de qvo Exod. 26. v. 32, 33. qvæ ruptio indicat 1. Unitatem Ecclesiæ; ut enim ex sancto sanctorum, & templo, unus factus hâc ruptione locꝰ; ita ex duobus populis una facta est Ecclesia 2. cœli apertionem; obstat velum, qvò minus cuivis ad sanctum sanctorum pateret aditus; ruptô velô, ecce jam cœlum intrare possumus, Hebr. 1. c. 9. 12. c. 10, 8. 3. Legis Ceremonialis sublationem. Rumpitur à supremo ad imum, insignum, jam cessatura holocausta, per qvorum sangvinem introierat sumus Pontifex sanctum sanctorum; atqve hunc cultum legalem oblatum eum, qvi intravit, non per sangvinem vitulorum, in sanctum sanctorum, sed per proprium, nobis æternam reparans pacem.

III. 3. Terræ motus, de qvo Euseb. narrat, â gentibus qvoqve fuisse eum observatum, & in Bythinia multas domûs evertisse.

IV. 4. Petrarum fissio. Finduntur petræ, & ecce obdurantur hominũ corda: compatiuntur creatori saxa, & nullâ commiseratione tangitur homo.

V. 5. Monumentorum apertio. Non poterant Christum pati homines, ecce verò, pandunt se monumenta, ut Christo dent locum : Vivum homines abjiciebant à se, ecce offert se terra, ut capiat mortuum.

VI. 6. Mortuorum resurrectio. Perspice hinc efficaciam mortis Christi; vix enim obierat vitæ Dominus, cùm efficaciter operaretur jam mors ejus; mortui enim surgunt, & corporibus quidem, ut non tantùm animæ, sed nec corpora in morte maneant.

VII. 7. Lateris filii Dei apertio, tandem miraculum nobis suppeditat maximum; quâ de re affeverando affirmat Evangelista, oculis se propriis illud vidisse, ne ob magnitudinem dubitaremus, nec eô auditô, rem parvi momenti fuisse, statueremus. Nota hic 1. Occasionem, quâ factum fuerit, ut aperiretur latus Christi. Erat hæc Judæorum simulata pietas, quâ Pilatum adierunt, rogantes, ipsis ut copia, crura frangendi crucifixorum, eosque sepeliendi, fieret, ne sci. aspicientibus abominabilis esset intuitus eorum sabbatho. Viri nebulones, religiosi in sabathum, contumeliosissimè interim tractantes sabbathi dominum : 2. Factum ipsum, de quo ait Evangelista : cùm jam vidissent Christum mortuum, ossa infracta reliquerunt, sed militum quidam, latus ejus perfodit. Hac dere præclarè Aug. Maturè moritur, ut impediatur fractio; impeditur fractio, ut fiat scripturarum completio. Nemo ergò fortè fortuna factum hoc accidisse putet. Circa hoc quæritur, Cur Christo ossa fracta non fuerint? R. brevibus ex ipso textu, ut impleretur scriptura, quæ duplex, Exodi nempe 12. v. 47. & Zach. 12. v. 19. prior est Typica, posterior Prophetica. Typica ad agnum Paschalem Vet. Test. respicit, cujus frangi ossa Dominus prohibuerat. Agnus Paschalis Nov. Test. Christus est, Joh. 1. tollens peccata mundi, cujus sanguine obliniti postes cordium nostrûm; servantur ab interitu æternô. Obiter detegitur hôc locô Phantastica ἀρτοκλασία Calvinistica, quæ, quid commune habeat cum fractione corporis Christi, testatur Evangelista; non frangetis ei os. Propheticæ certitudinem comprobavit eventus. Quæritur 2. Qvisnam ille, qui domini latus aperuit, fuerit. Evangelium Nicodemi Longinum dictum fuisse ait. Scholastici hujus nugis superaddentes plures, cæcum dixerunt, & fortè fortuna peraspersionem sangvinis Christi visum recepisse, placidô figmentô, & jucundâ phantasiâ confinxêrunt. Nos, tacente scripturâ, nostrum etiam in hâc parte, re nempe minimè scitu necessariâ, suspendimus judicium. 3. Conseqvens; Ecce enim, apertô latere, sangvis & unda copiosè profluit. Columbus ῶεικαρδιον fuisse tactum putat, aqvâ repletum; qvem errorem seqvitur Perkins. inferio causa. salv. & dam. p. 20. tom. 1. op. c. 18. & in exp. Symb. p. m. 669. Ideoqv́e naturaliter id factum putant. Sed 1. contra omnes instituta est hæc exposisitio Orthodoxos; 2. Anatomicos; 3. claram evertit literam, afferentem, non guttatim aqva stillâsse latus, sed eandem copiosè effluxisse. Nos, etsi finem ignoramus, destituti nempe hôc in loco literâ clarâ, orthodoxè tamen dicimus, 1. fuisse miraculum singulare; Unde etiam tantâ asseveratione asserit Evangelista, oculis se propriis vidisse, ne de eo, qvod narravit miraculo, debitarem9. 2. liqvore distinctô fuisse significata Novi Test. Sacramenta utraq; ; nam & hoc tradit sacra scriptura, nempe eadem per aqvam & sangvinem in Nov. Test. esse peragenda, Vide Hebr. 9. 14. c. 10, 29. c. 12. v. 24. 1. Petr. 1, 19. Zach. 9; 11.


### Chapter IV. Let this, O man, be your meditation on the death of CHRIST

CHAPTER IV.

Let this, O man, be your meditation on the death of CHRIST: for the death of Christ is your death, for He died for you; but also life, that you might live. How then would He not live now, for whom Life dies? How will the guilty one fear, whom justice absolves? Let your death, therefore, O pious CHRIST, be to me life in death, and life at the end of death!

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Hæc, tua, mors CHRISTI, ô homo, sit meditatio: mors enim Christi tua mors est, pro te enim mortuus est; sed & vita, ut tu viveres. Qvô pactô ergò jam non viveret, pro qvo moritur vita? Qvô modô timebit reus, qvem absolvit justitia? Sit ergò mors tua, ô pie CHRISTE, mihi in morte vita, & fine morte vita!


## 39 Thirty-ninth Disputation, On the Burial of Christ

Continuation.

The history of the saving Passion of Christ is divided into five acts, for the sake of consulting the memory: the first contemplates the deeds in the garden, occupied chiefly about Christ's going forth into the garden across the torrent Cedron, the occasion of the betrayal, the company of Judas, the manner of acting, the consternation of the soldiers, the safe conduct of the disciples, the fervor of Peter, the bonds of Christ: The second [contemplates] the deeds in the house of Caiaphas, considering the abduction of Christ to the High Priest, the denial of Peter, the inquiry concerning the doctrine of Christ i-on, with notable contumely, and a just defense of innocence: The third [part] considers the events before the judge in the praetorium, weighing the abduction of Christ to the secular judge, the scourging of Christ, the crowning with thorns, the interrogation of the judge, the response of Christ to the questions, and his silence: The fourth [part] considers the events at the place of execution, explaining the leading away of Christ to execution, the crucifixion, the title of the cross, the division of the garments, the final words of the suffering Christ, the opening of his side; The last [part] considers the events after death concerning the burial. With the four prior acts having been dispatched thus far in the preceding disputations, carried here by the breath of the heavenly breeze, we shall undertake to examine the burial in the present, συν θεῷ τῷ κειμένῳ, thematically.

Thesis I.

The first thing that must be weighed concerning the burial of Christ is, Was Christ buried? This question (ζήτημα) is examined for the confirmation of Christ's death; since it is not the living, but the dead, who are accustomed to be buried: And unless Christ had been entombed, it could have been objected to the preaching of the resurrection that the disciples had taken him down from the cross and were lying about the resurrection, or that he had been taken down from the cross half-alive and had been healed again.

II. That Christ was indeed buried, we elicit from three foundations: 1. From the open shadows drawn from types. Of the types, the most excellent type is Jonah, swallowed by the whale, and soon vomited out again on the third day, (a) and applied by Christ to himself, saying thus: As Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights. (b) There are many secondary ones: Joseph cast into prison, (c) and liberated from there again; (d) Samson shut up in the town of Gaza, and escaping from there, having broken through the gates of the town (e) etc.

III. 2. From the open oracles taken from the Prophets. The prophecies issued concerning the burial of Christ are two that are very clear: The former exists in the sixteenth Psalm, v. 10. Calvin interprets the Psalm threateningly, as if the Prophet here denounces the future vengeance of God upon the people, and by this saying shadows forth his own liberation; But 1. Against the Apostolic allegation, and the recitation of the words to the number, and the application made to Christ in Acts 2. v. 25. 2. Against the history of David, with which these words, if they are taken concerning David, conflict. For the sepulcher of Da vid convinces us that it stinks within, and that decay has consumed both flesh and bones of the Prophet, and that nothing remains except dust. See B. Hunn. in Calv. Judai. Later Esa. 53. v. 9. In which, by explaining it rightly and according to the analogy of faith, interpreters wear themselves out in various ways. Some hold the impious and the rich as synonyms. Some think an antimetabole is used by the prophet. Calvin, according to his custom of fashioning and refashioning, transforms the proper meaning of the sepulchre into a metaphorical one. But the truth is in the open, if only the sources are looked into more deeply, and the Evangelical fulfillment of this prophetic prediction is compared with one another. If you do this, you will discover that the true and genuine sense of the prophetic Aphorism is this: Christ will be honored with a burial by a rich man, understand Joseph of Arimathea (עָשִׁיר), after he has sustained death, (בְּמֹתָיו) and his sepulchre will be entrusted to be guarded by impious Jewish soldiers (רְשָׁעִים).

IV. 3. From the harmonic testimony of the four Evangelists, who with one voice unanimously testified to the burial of Christ. Nor does anything depart from the Truth in the fact that the first three assign the business of managing the burial to Joseph of Arimathea alone; but John adds Nicodemus to him. The reason for this matter is that Joseph alone undertook this business from the beginning, and obtained the power to bury the body from Pilate; but Nicodemus, approaching afterwards, lent a hand. Therefore, to the three earlier Evangelists, in a brief narrative, it seemed sufficient to attribute the office of burying to Joseph alone.

V. II. Concerning the burial of Christ, its cause must be known, which is twofold: either primary or administrative.

VI. The primary cause is God; who not only implanted the custom of burial in the minds of men, according to that saying: you are dust, and to dust you shall return, (a) commanded that duties be shown to the deceased, (b) which itself was both performed by the saints (c) and by the deprivation of burial he declares his divine wrath, (d) But he also specifically ordained that Christ be buried. In confirmation of the matter, we allege that saying of Paul, namely that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and was buried according to the Scriptures, etc., 1. Corinth. 15. v. 3.

VII. Two perform the administrative task. It must be seen by what praises each is commended by the Evangelists. The first of them is described 1. by his country, because he was born in Arimathea. What kind of city this was, is not agreed upon among the learned. We follow the opinion of St. Jerome, who maintains that this city is the one which is called רמתים by the Hebrews, and Arimatha by the LXX Interpreters, and is the native place of Samuel, and is distant twenty thousand paces from the City of Jerusalem. 2. by his fortune, because he was rich. And he is deservedly commended for his riches, not only for the possession of them, but also for their use, which was notably conspicuous in that he contributed them with a generous hand and in full measure to honor the burial of the LORD. 3. by his name, because he was called Joseph. The name reminds us of a type (a) Just as the body of the Patriarch Jacob, after he had gathered his feet upon the bed and breathed his last, was honorably committed to the earth by his son Joseph, having first been embalmed with spices: So, after the heavenly Jacob, the supplanter of the infernal serpent, had fallen asleep in a peaceful death on the bed of the cross, one of his spiritual sons, Joseph of Arimathea, treated his body, anointed with ointments and spices, with an honorable burial. 4. by his state of life, because he was a councilor, and indeed a Jerusalemite, namely one of the Elders of the people, or Senators co-opted into the Sanhedrin, as is evident from what follows, that he did not consent to the counsel and deed of his colleagues, who were conspiring for the death of Christ 5. by his piety, which shines forth, partly because he had shown himself a disciple of JESUS, having acted as his hearer and follower, although for a time, preceding this history, a secret one; partly, because he had been waiting for the kingdom of God, i.e., the Messiah and the liberation to be provided through him, and likewise the spiritual and heavenly kingdom to be initiated through him. 6. by his integrity, (a good and just man). Faith and religious piety are expressed in the preceding member; this explains his external conduct toward men, namely that he was beneficent, inflicting injury on no one, but a strenuous cultivator of justice, and kind toward all. 7. by the work performed regarding the burying of CHRIST. That he entered boldly to Pilate and asked for the body of Christ is recorded in the letters of the Evangelists. But the other 1. by the dignity of his office and likewise his piety, because he was a Pharisee, and a Prince of the Jews, who, fearing the hatred of his colleagues, did not had come to Christ by night, and among other parts of the sermon, had heard the type of the bronze serpent explained, as one may see from the third chapter of John. 2. from the zeal concerning Christ's burial. He is said to have brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, to nearly a hundred pounds, so that he might embalm the body of Christ with those aromatic ointments.

VIII. It is asked, whether in the business of religion, a matter indifferent, one should dissemble or confess one's opinion when demanded? Some play thus in the business of religion, pronouncing it free to cherish one thing in the heart and testify another in letters, and calling upon the examples of Nicodemus and Joseph, who were endowed with firm faith, for their defense. But men nourishing such hypocrisy, fortified by neither firm nor infirm faith, cannot protect themselves with the mentioned examples. For although they were secret disciples of Christ, they are not to be thought to have hypocritically dissembled the truth; rather, the contrary shines forth in John 7:51. Therefore, it is one thing to be a secret disciple of Christ, who strives seriously for the progress of faith and does not consent to known errors: it is another to hypocritically dissemble the truth when demanded. Those who do this deny Christ by the very act, which to impute to Joseph and Nicodemus, who were most devoted to the pursuit of piety, is most alien to us.

IX. 2. It is asked, how pious senators and magistrates ought to conduct themselves in judgments, and especially in more serious deliberations, if they are overcome by a multitude of votes, and see innocents condemned by unjust sentences? Admonished by the example of Joseph, senators and consuls ought to take care that they do not in any way consent to any unjust crime against their conscience, especially where snares are laid for the blood of the innocent and faithful; if they cannot prevent what is evil, they can at least do this, they can at least do this, that they do not approve it with their own vote.

X. III. Concerning the burial, the act of burial must be understood, which it is clear from the Evangelists was such: Power having been granted to them to take down the body of Christ from the wood, they transferred it from the public place into a nearby garden (for they did not wish to wash and anoint it under the cross in the sight of all), then they washed away the entire blood with which it was stained, they anointed the washed body with aromatics reduced to the form of an ointment, afterwards they wrapped the body in a clean linen cloth, and wrapped the head in a sudarium.

XI. It is asked, whether the body of Christ was immune from putrefaction? Far be it, that the body of Christ was embalmed so that it might be preserved from decay. David thought otherwise, having prophesied thus concerning Christ: Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption; by this very thing exalting the flesh of Christ above the common lot of the human race. Although, therefore, the soul truly departed from the body, the body nevertheless rested so securely that it did not fear even the bite of a single moth or worm, nor could the surrounding heat disturb the mixture of the four elemental qualities in the body, corrupt it, or induce putrefaction or corruption; and this 1. on account of the union with the λόγῳ; for it could not happen that the personal union should remain intact, and meanwhile the body be corrupted or putrefy. For what the λόγος has once assumed, He neither abandons nor exchanges for another. 2. On account of the abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit Himself, as a balsam and oil of gladness, bestowed upon the flesh of Christ without any measure. For just as balsam preserves bodies for a long time in the sepulchre, so the balsam of the Spirit, poured out in infinite ways, preserves the flesh of Christ without corruption unto infinity, and that above His fellows. 3. On account of the holiness of the flesh of Christ. For that our bodies putrefy happens in order to eradicate the root of sin, which, since it did not inhere in the flesh of Christ, did not require putrefaction either.

XII. 2. It is asked, If the body of Christ was immune from putrefaction, what then impelled Joseph to anoint the body of Christ? Some weakness of faith seems to underlie it, in that they desired to preserve Him from decay with aromatic ointments, [even though He was] to rise on the third day. But because they performed this duty by divine instinct, without a doubt, you would more correctly say that the prophecies concerning Christ who was to rise again had not escaped their knowledge, since the resurrection did not escape even the enemies, nor did they wish to argue against the same burial rites as being false, but rather, as the situation required, they did this to declare piety toward their teacher, which demanded that the honor and duty of burial be rendered to the dead by the disciples, committing the manner of fulfilling those prophecies to God in true humility of faith.

XIII. 2. It is asked, How ought we to conduct ourselves regarding the dead? Let us follow in the footsteps of Joseph and Nicodemus, and let us hold dear the dutiful service commended to us toward the deceased Christ; so that, just as they did, we also may honestly bury the bodies of the piously deceased, since they are the handiwork of divine hands, members of the mystical body of Christ, and dwellings of the Holy Spirit, warned by the serious divine command in Eccl. 7:37, do not withhold thanks from the dead.

XLV. 4. The question is asked, whether prayers should be poured out for the dead? We do not listen to nor dwell upon the fabulous inventions of the monastic brain, sprouting like old wives' tales from the curious foundation of purgatory; we are eager to hear a command drawn from the divine oracles, to see an example. But since they are unable to bring forward even a single saying or example from canonical Scripture, although they exert all the powers of their mind and intellect in searching, we bid farewell to the heterodox opinion concerning prayer for the dead, and we detest it as being diametrically opposed to Scripture.

XV. IV. What pertains to our subject is the time, both of the funeral being taken care of and of the delivery to burial; and of the rest taken in the sepulcher.

XVI. The Evangelists express the time of the funeral being taken care of as having been the day of preparation, the day immediately preceding the Sabbath, ὀψίας γενομένης, with the sun verging toward the setting.

XVII. The time of rest in the sepulcher is established as three days. On that very day on which the Savior died, the funeral was taken care of and he was delivered to burial. During the whole of the following day, which was the Sabbath, he lay in the sepulcher. For just as God, having finished the work of creation on the sixth day, rested on the seventh day (a): So the Son of God, having finished the work of redemption on the cross on the sixth day of the week, rested on the seventh day in the sepulcher. At the beginning of the following day, for twelve hours or thereabouts, he rested in the sepulcher, and on that very day he rose again.

XIIX. V. What is to be considered is the place, which the Evangelists describe: 1. As having been near Mount Golgotha, and thus outside the city walls. Following the custom of the Jews, we consider it more convenient for cemeteries to be outside rather than inside the city, other circumstances permitting, both to prevent contagion, and to signify that through death we enter from the fellowship of this life into another city, (b) and to guard against the superstitions of vigils, anniversaries, and sprinklings with holy water, etc., which are practiced around the sepulchers of the dead in the Papacy. On this matter, see the renowned theologian, Mr. Dr. Gerhard

XIX. 2. That it was in a garden. We are reminded of the sin committed by our first parents in the garden of paradise. 2. Of the passion begun and finished in the garden, through which sin was expiated and death overcome. 3. Of our frugality, that all flesh is grass, its days as the flower of the field. (c) 4. Of our resurrection, that our bones shall one day sprout like grass (d)

XX. 3. That it was a new tomb; And 1. For the certainty of the resurrection, lest if anyone else had been buried there, another might be believed to have risen. 2. For its remarkable purity. For just as his birth was purer than every birth, so his burial also had to have remarkable purity. 3. For reverence, because that body was a temple of the divinity, and therefore it was not fitting to be joined to corruptible bodies. 4. Because it was to be raised quickly, whereas others are to rise to immortality only on the last day: and therefore it was by no means to be joined to other dead.

XXI. 4. That it was the tomb of Joseph the just. He had died among thieves on the cross, but he willed to be buried in the tomb of a just man, because having died for sins, he was not to die again, but to distribute justice and life to those who believe. Rom. 4, 25.

XXII. 5. That it was another's tomb. When he lived his life, he had nowhere to lay his head, (a) therefore, even when called from life, he did not wish to have his own sepulcher. Why also should he have his own sepulcher, who was to remain in the sepulcher for only three days? Why should he have his own sepulcher, who willed to be killed and buried for the sake of others.

XXIII. 6. That it was hewn out of solid rock, so that the wicked Jews could not lie under any pretext that the disciples, penetrating to the tomb through some subterranean trench, had stealthily taken away the body of Christ from it.

XXIV. 7. That a huge stone had been rolled to the door of the tomb, so that no one might rage against the dead man, or steal him away. Divine providence wished to remedy all vain suspicions in this way also, and to pave the way for the glorious resurrection of Christ.

XXV. VI. It is a concomitant of the burial; which expresses the companions of the funeral, of whom Matthew (b) says thus: There were Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, sitting opposite the tomb. Mark (c): Mary Magdalene and Mary of Joseph were watching where he was laid. Luke (d): The women who had come with him from Galilee followed, and saw the tomb, and how his body was laid.

XXVI. VII. The purpose of the burial. The Lord willed to be buried, 1. that the prophecies of the Prophets might be fulfilled; 2. that together with Himself He might bury our sins in the sepulchre, and hide them forever from the sight of God; 3. that He might sanctify our κοιμητήρια [cemeteries], and imbue them with the life-giving fragrance of His death, and thus shake off the horror of the sepulchre, and bring the hope of resurrection; 4. That He might prefigure that mystical Sabbath of sanctification, in which our sins are to be buried by assiduous exercises of repentance, and we are to rest from the operation of impiety, (e) 5. That He might make the faith of His death greater and firmer.

XXVII. The last thing is the consequence of the burial, which is the approach of the chief Priests and Pharisees to Pilate, the petition concerning guarding the body of Christ for three days; the obtaining of the petition. Thus Matthew reports: (f) On the next day, which is after the preparation, the chief Priests and Pharisees gathered to Pilate, saying: Sir, we remember that that deceiver said while he was still alive: After three days I will rise again, command therefore that the sepulchre be guarded, &c. Matthew depicts with vivid colors an evil conscience, which attempts to strengthen by any means the evil cause it fosters, and fashions every reason suitable for promoting its design.

Glory to Christ the God-man.

Latin:

Continuatio.

Historia salvificæ Christi Passionis, in qvinqve, memoriæ consulendi gratia, dispescitur actus: primus gesta in horto contemplatur, occupatus potissimùm circa Christi egressum in hortum trans torrentem Cedron, occasionem prodendi, comitatum Judæ, formam agendi, consternationem militum, salvum conductum discipulorum, Petri fervorem, Christi vincula: Alter gesta in domo Caiphæ, considerans abductionem Christi ad Pontificem, Petri abnegationem, de Christi doctrinâ inqvisitionem, cum insigni contumelia, justâq; innocentiæ defensione: Tertius gesta coram judice in prætorio, perpendens abductionem Christi ad secularem judicem, Christi flagellationem, spineam coronationem, interrogationem judicis, Christi ad quæsita responsionem, & silentium: Qvartus gesta in loco supplicii, explicans Christi ad supplicium deductionem, crucifixionem, crucis titulum, vestimentorum partitionem, Verba Christi patientis postrema, lateris apertionem; Postremus gesta post mortem circa sepulturam. Qvatuor prioribus actibus in præcedentibus hactenus expeditis disputationibus, cælestis auræ flatu huc delati, sepulturam in præsenti, συν θεῷ τῷ κειμένῳ, θεματικῶς examinandam suscipiemus.

Thesis I.

PRimum, qvod circa sepulturam Christi perpendendum, est, An Christus sit sepultus? Expenditur hoc ζήτημα ob mortis Christi confirmationem; siqvidem non vivi, sed mortui sepeliri consveverunt: Et nisi Christus contumulatus, prædicationi resurrectionis opponi potuisset, discipulos ex cruce ipsum sustulisse, & mentiri resurrectionem, vel semivivum è cruce sublatum, iterum sanâsse.

II. Sepultum verò esse Christum, tribus elicimus fundamentis: 1. Ex apertis typorum depromtum adumbraculis. Ex typis excellentissimus maximè typus est Jonas, â Balæna absorptus, & tertiô mox die iterum eructatus, (a) atqve â Christo ad se accommodatus, sic inqviente: Sicut fuit Jonas in ventre ceti tribus diebus, & tribus noctibus, sie erit filius hominis in corde terræ tribus diebus, ac tribus noctibus. (b) Secundarii complures: Josephus in carcerem conjectus, (c) & inde rursus liberatus; (d) Simson oppido Gaza inclusus, atqve istinc, portis oppidi perruptis, elapsus (e) &c.

III. 2. Ex apertis Prophetarum desumtum oraculis. Vaticinia, de sepultura Christi edita, sunt duo admodùm clara: Prius extat in Psalmo decimo sexto v. 10. Interpretatur Psalmum Calvinus comminatorie, qvasi Propheta hîc denunciet futuram Dei vindictam populo, & dictô hôc sui liberationem adumbret; Verùm 1. Contra allegationem Apostolicam, & verborum ad numerum recitationem, ad Christumq; applicationem factam Act. 2. v. 25. 2. Contra historiam Davidis, cum qva verba hæc, Si de Davide sumantur, pugnant. Sepulchrum enim Davidis intus fætere, & cariem absumsisse tam carnem, tum ossa Prophetæ, nec quicquam restare, nisi pulverem, historia de David nos convincit. Vid. B. Hunn. in Calv. Judai. Posterius Esa. 53. v. 9. In quo dextrè & κατ' ἀναλογίαν πίστεως explicando, variè se macerant interpretes. Quidam impios & divitem pro synonymis habent. Quidā ἀντιμεταβολὴν a propheta usurpari autumant. Calvinus pro sua fingendi ac refingendi consvetudine, sepulchri significationem propriam in metaphoricam transformat. Sed veritas in aprico, si modò fontes penitiùs introspiciātur, cumq́; vaticinio hôc propheticô ejusdem complementum Evangelicum ἀλλήλοις conferatur. Hoc, si feceris, deprehendes, verum ac genuinum Aphorismi prophetici sensum esse hunc: Christus à divite, intellige Josephum Arimathæum (עָשִׁיר) honorificâ sepulturâ afficietur, postquàm mortem sustinuit, (בְּמֹתָיו) ejusq́; sepulchrum ab impiis Judæis militibus impiis (רְשָׁעִים) custodiendum commendabitur.

IV. 3. Ex harmonico quatuor Evangelistarum testimonio, qui uno ore unanimiter sepulturam Christi testati. Nec aliqvid Veritati decedit in eo, quòd tres priores negotium in curandâ sepulturâ soli Josepho Arimathæensi deferunt; Johañnes verò ipsi adjungat Nicodemum. Rei hujus causa, quòd Josephus solus â principio hoc negotium susceperit, & corporis sepeliendi potestatem â Pilato impetraverit; Nicodemus verò postmodùm accedens manus admovit. Ideò tribus Evangelistis prioribus, in brevi narratione visum fuit sufficiens, uni Josepho sepeliendi officium tribuere.

V. II. Circa Christi sepulturam cognoscenda ejus causa, qvæ duplex: vel primaria, vel administra.

VI. Primaria causa Deus est; qvi non modò sepulturæ morem hominum animis indidit, juxta illud: terra es, in terram reverteris, (a) officia defunctis exhiberi mandavit, (b) qvod ipsum & â sanctis præstitum (c) & privatione sepulturæ divinam suam iram declarat, (d) Sed etiam in specie Christum sepeliri ordinavit. In rei fidem allegamus illud Pauli, Christum nimirùm pro peccatis mortuum esse secundùm Scripturas, & sepultum secundùm Scripturas &c, 1. Corinth. 15. v. 3.

VII. Caussam administram obeunt duo. Singuli, quibus elogiis ab Evangelistis commendentur, videndum. Alter eorum describitur 1. à patria, quòd oriundus ab Arimathæa. Qualis hæc fuerit urbs, inter eruditos non convenit. Nos sequimur D. Hieronymi sententiam, autumantis, hanc urbem esse eam, quæ ab Hebræis רמתים, à LXX. Interpretibus Arimatha vocatur, patriaque est Samuelis, atque viginti millibus passuum ab Urbe Hierosolyma distat. 2. à fortunis, quòd dives. Et meritô propter divitias commendatur, non tantùm propter earundem κτῆσιν, sed etiam propter χρῆσιν, inde insigniter conspicuam, quòd eas ad sepulturam DOMINI cohonestandam, largâ manu, & πίονι μέτρῳ contulit. 3. ab appellatione, quòd dictus Josephus. Nomen admonet nos typi (a) Quemadmodum Patriarchæ Jacobi, postquam pedibus super lectum collectis, animam exspirâsset, â Josepho filio, corpus de mortuum, aromate priùs conditum, honorificè terræ demandatur: Sic, postquàm cœlestis Jacob, infernalis serpentis supplantator, in lectulo crucis placidâ morte obdormivisset, unus ex spiritualibus ipsius filiis, Josephus Arimatæensis, corpus ejus ungventis & aromatibus pollinctum, honestâ sepulturâ affecit. 4. à vitæ statu, quòd fuerit βουλευτής, & quidem Hierosolymitanus, unus scilicet ex Senioribus populi, sive Senatoribus in Synedrium cooptatis, ut conspicuum ex subsequentibus, quòd non consenserit consilio & facto collegarum suorum, in Christi necem conspirantium 5. à pietate, quæ elucescat, partim quòd discipulum se præbuerat JESU, auditorem & sectatorem ejus egerat, licet quoad tempus, hanc historiam antegressum, occultum; partim, quòd expectaverat regnum Dei, h. e. Messiam ac liberationem per ipsum præstandam, itemque spirituale & cœleste regnum per ipsum inchoandum. 6. ab honestate, (ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς καὶ δίκαιος) Fides & religiosa pietas expressa membro præcedente; hoc exponit externam ejus erga homines conversationem, quòd nimirùm fuerit beneficus, nemini injuriam inferens, sed strenuus justitiæ cultor, & benignus ergà omnes. 7. ab operâ navatâ circa sepeliendum CHRISTUM. Audacter eundem ingressum esse ad Pilatum, & postulâsse corpus Christi, literis proditum ab Evangelistis. Alter verò 1. ab officii dignitate pariter & pietate, quòd Pharisæus, ac Princeps Judæorum, qui veritus collegarum suorum odia, noctu ad Christum venerat, & inter cætera concionis membra, typum serpentis ænei expositum audierat, ut videre ex tertiô capite Johannis. 2. â studio circa Christi sepulturam. Attulisse dicitur mixturam myrrhæ & alöes,ad libras ferè centum, ut aromaticis istis ungventis corpus Christi condiret.

IIX. Quæritur, An in religionis negotio,res indifferens, sententiam suam exigenti dissimulare aut confiteri? Ludunt sic nonnulli in religionis negotio, liberum pronunciantes, aliud corde fovere,aliud literis testari, atqve in patrocinium vocantes exempla Nicodemi,& Josephi, in firmâ fide præditorum. Verùm homines,talem hypocrisin alentes, neqve firmâ,neq; infirmâ mūniti fide, nec commemoratis exemplis se tueri qveunt. Licet enim occulti Christi discipuli, non tamen veritatem hypocriticè dissimulâsse putandi; qvin contrarium elucescat Joh. 7. v. 51. Aliud itaq; , esse occultum Christi discipulum,qvi seriò ad profectum fidei contendit, & in agnitos errores non consentit: Aliud,postulatam veritatem hypocriticè dissimulare.Qvi hoc faciunt, abnegant ipsô factô Christum, qvod imputare Josepho & Nicodemo,pietatis studio detitissimis, â nobis sit alienissimum.

IX. 2. Quæritur, Quomodo pii senatores & magistratus in judiciis, & gravioribus præsertim consolationibus, se gerere debeant, si votorum multitudine superentur, & videant, injustis sententiis damnari innocentes? Exemplô admoniti Josephi, cavere sibi debent senatores & consules,ne contra conscientiam in facinus aliqvod injustum, præsertim ubi innoxiorum & fidelium sangvini insidiæ struuntur, ullô modô consentiant; si prohibere,qvod malum est,non possunt, hoc tamen possunt, hoc tamen possunt,ut suâ sententiâ non approbent.

X. III. Circa sepulturum cognoscendus est sepulturæ actus, qvem ex Evangelistis liqvet fuisse talem: Potestate iis factâ corpus Christi ex ligno deponendi, transtulerunt illud ex loco publico in hortum vicinium (neqve enim sub cruce in conspectu omnium illud abluere & ungere voluerunt)deinde sangvinem, qvô cruentatum erat, totū abluerunt,corpus ablutum aromatibus,ad ungventi formā redactis unxerunt, postea corpus sindoni mundæ implicârunt,caputq́ve sudario involverunt.

XI. Quæritur, An corpus Christi à putrefactione immune? Absit,propterea corpus Christi esse pollinctum, ut à putredine præservaretur. Aliter sensit David, sic de Christo vaticinatus: Non derelinqves animam meam in inferno, nec dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionẽ; hôc ipsô carnem Christi supra communem generis humani sortem extollens. Licet itaqve verè anima de corpore exivit, corpus tamen tam tutò qvievit, ut ne qvidem unius blattæ, vel tineæ morsûs reformidârit, aut ne qvidem calor circumstans mixturam qvatuor elementarium qvalitatum in corpore turbare, corrumpere, putrefactionem sive corruptionem inducere potuerit; Idq́; 1. propter unionem cum λόγῳ; Fieri enim non potuit, ut personalis unio maneret salva, & interim corrumperetur, vel putresceret corpus. Nam qvod λόγος semel assumsit, neq́; deserit, neq; cum alio commutat. 2. Propter effusionem largam ipsius Spiritus Sancti, tanqvam balsami & olei lætitiæ, contributi in carnem Christi, sine omni mensura. Sicut enim balsamum servat corpora diuturna in sepulchro: ita balsamum Sp. infinitis modis effusum, conservat carnem Christi sine corruptione in infinitum, idq́; præ consortibus suis. 3. Propter sanctitatem carnis Christi. Nam qvod corpora nostra putrescunt, sit ad extirpandam peccati radicem, qvæ cùm non inhæserit carni Christi, non eguit qvoq; putrefactione.

XII. 2. Qværitur, Si corpus Christi à putrefactione immune, quid igitur Josephum ad corpus Christi unguendum impulerit? Videtur aliqva fidei infirmitas subesse, qvòd aromaticis unguentis à putredine præservare cupiant, tertiô die resurrecturum. Sed qvia divinô procul dubiô instinctu, munus hoc obierunt, rectiùs dixeris, vaticinia de Christo resurrecturo, eorum cognitionem non effugisse, cùm resurrectio ne hostes latebat, nec falsitatis eadem sepulturæ officia arguere voluisse, sed pro re natâ fecisse hoc ad pietatem declarandam in præceptorem, qvæ exigebat, ut mortuo sepulturæ honor & officium deferatur à discipulis, modum vaticinia illa complendi in verâ fidei humilitate Deo committentes.

XIII. 2, Qværitur, Qvomodo nos circa demortuos gerere oporteat? Vestigiis insistamus Josephi & Nicodemi, atqve officiosam erga Christum defunctum operam nobis commendatam habeamus; ut, qvemadmodùm hi, sic & nos corpora piè defunctorum honestè funeremus, cùm sint manuum divinarum opificia, mystici corporis Christi membra, ac Spiritus Sancti domicilia, admoniti seriô mandatô divinô Eccl. 7. v. 37. mortuo non prohibeas gratiam.

XLV. 4. Qværitur, An pro defunctis preces fundendæ? Fabulosa cerebri monachalis commenta, è curioso purgatorii fundamento aniliter pullulantia, non audimus, nec moramur; gestimus audire ex divinis oraculis depromptum mandatum, videre exemplum. Verùm cùm ne unicum Scripturæ canonicæ dictum, atq; exemplum, licet in inqvirendo omnes animi ingeniiq; vires intendant, proferre valeant, valere jubemus cacodoxam opinionem de oratione pro defunctis, eandemq; tanqvam scripturæ è diametro oppositam, detestamur.

XV. IV. Qvod ad institutum nostrum facit, est tempus, tùm curati funeris, atqve sepulturæ traditi; tùm factæ qvietis in sepulchro.

XVI. Tempus curati funeris Evangelistæ exprimunt, fuisse diem parasceves, diem proximè præcedentem Sabbathum, ὀψίας γενομένης, Sole vergente ad occasum.

XVII. Tempus quietis in sepulchro constitutum triduum. Eo ipso die, qvâ mortuus Salvator, curatum funus, & sepulturæ traditum. Seqvente totô, qvi Sabbathum, in sepulchro jacuit. Sicut enim Deus, absolutô creationis opere die sexto, qvievit die septimo (a): Ita Filius Dei, peracto opere redemptionis in cruce die sextô hebdomatis, qvievit die septimo in sepulchro. Ineuntente die seqvente, duodecim horis aut circiter, qvievit in sepulchro, & eô ipsô die resurrexit.

XIIX. V. Qvod considerandum, Locus est, qvem describunt Evangelistæ, 1. Fuisse monti Golgatha vicinum, & sic extra urbis mœnia. Judæorum morem secuti, cœmeteria extra, qvàm intra urbem, aliis circumstantiis permittentibus, esse convenientius ducimus, tùm ad prohibendum contagium, tùm ad significandum, per mortem ex consortio hujus vitæ, in aliam nos ingredi civitatem, (b) tùm ad præcavendas superstitiones vigiliarum, anniversariorum, aspersionum per aqvam lustralem &c. qvæ circa sepulchra defunctorum inPapatu exercentur. Hâc de re videatur Cl Theol. Dn. D. Gerhardus

XIX. 2. Fuisse in horto. Admonemur peccati à protoplastis in horto paradisiaco perpetrati. 2. Passionis in horto cœptæ ac finitæ, per qvam peccatum expiatum, mors devicta. 3. Frugalitatis nostræ, quòd omnis caro foenum, dies ejus tanquam flos agri. (c) 4. Resurrectionis nostræ, quòd germinatura ossa nostra aliqvando sicut gramen (d)

XX. 3. Fuisse monumentum novum; Et 1. Ob certitudinem resurrectionis, ne si quis alius ibi fuisset sepultus, alius crederetur resurrexisse. 2. Ob insignem ejus puritatem. Quemadmodùm enim ejus nativitas omni nativitate purior erat, ita debuit etiam sepultura insignem habere puritatem. 3. Ob reverentiam, quia corpus illud divinitatis templum erat, ac proptereà non decebat corporibus corruptibilibus adjungi. 4. Quia celeriter erat suscitandum, cùm cætera extremo tantum die ad immortalitatem sint resurrectura: Ideoque cæteris mortuis minimè conjungendum.

XXI. 4. Fuisse monumentum Josephi justi. Inter latrones in cruce mortuus erat, sed in monumento justi sepeliri voluit, quia pro peccatis mortuus, non erat ulteriùs moriturus, sed justitiam & vitam credentibus distributurus. Rom. 4, 25.

XXII. 5. Fuisse monumentum alienum. Cùm vitam ageret, non habebat, ubi caput reclinaret, (a) ergò nec, ex vitâ evocatus, proprium habere voluit sepulchrum. Eccur etiam proprium haberet sepulchrum, qui triduum duntaxat in sepulchro commoraturus erat? cur proprium haberet sepulchrum, qui propter alios necari, ac sepeliri voluit.

XXIII. 6. Fuisse ex solidâ rupe excisum, ne improbi Judæi quâvis specie mentiri possent, discipulos, per subterraneam qvandam fossam ad sepulchrum penetrantes, corpus Christi ex eo furtim abstulisse.

XXIV. 7. Fuisse ad ostium monumenti advolutum ingens saxum, ne quis in mortuum sæviret, aut illud suffuraretur. Mederi & hoc pacto divina providentia omnibus vanis suspicionibus voluit, ac gloriosæ Christi resurrectioni viam sternere.

XXV. VI. Est Sepulturæ concomitans; quod exprimit comites funeris, de quibus ita Matthæus (b): Erant ibi Maria Magdalena, & altera Maria, sedentes contra sepulchrum. Marcus (c): Maria Magdalena & Maria Joseph adspiciebant, ubi poneretur. Lucas (d): Subsecutæ mulieres, quæ cum eo venerant de Galilæa, viderunt monumentum, & quemadmodùm positum erat corpus ejus.

XXVI. VII. Sepulturæ finis. Sepeliri voluit Dominus, 1. ut vaticinia Prophetarum implerentur; 2. ut unà secum in sepulchro peccata nostra sepeliret, & in æternum â conspectu Dei absconderet; 3. ut nostra κοιμητήρια sanctificaret, & vivifico mortis suæ odore perfunderet, ac ita sepulchri horrorem excuteret, & resurrectionis spem afferret; 4. Ut figuraret mysticum illud sanctificationis Sabbathum, quô peccata nostra assiduis pœnitentiæ exercitiis sepelienda, nobisq́; ab operatione impietatis quiescendum, (e) 5. Ut majorem ac firmiorem faceret fidem mortis suæ.

XXVII. Postremum est sepulturæ consequens, quod est accessus principum Sacerdotum, & Pharisæorum, ad Pilatum, petitio de custodiendo corpore Christi ad triduum; petiti impetratio. Sic refert Matthæus: (f) Alterâ die, quæ est post parasceven, convenerunt principes Sacerdotum, & Pharisæi ad Pilatum, dicentes: Domine, recordati sumus, quòd seductor ille dixit adhuc vivens: Post tres dies resurgam, jube ergò custodiri sepulchrum, &c. Vivis coloribus depingit Matthæus malam conscientiam, quæ causam, quam fovet malam, quoqvô modô firmare tentat, & nullas non rationes, instituto suo provehendo accommodas, effingit.

Christo Theanthropo gloria.


## 40 Fortieth Disputation, On the Descent of Christ into Hell

Hitherto we have considered the acts of Christ which occurred on earth; it follows that we contemplate the one which concerns hell. Therefore, just as we accompanied our Leader into the sepulchre, that we might be buried with Him from our sins: so we shall accompany Him descending into hell, that we may triumph with Him over hell; and we shall treat this article of the descent in such a way that we may be neither too curious outside of Scripture, nor too negligent in Scripture, following the path of Christian modesty.

I. That Christ descended into hell, although this is not found ῥητῶς [expressly] in Scripture, is confessed by 1. the Apostolic Creed, 2. the Athanasian, 3. the Confession of Augsburg, 4. the Formula of Concord, 5. the the consensus of the moderns. But what is to be understood by this phrase, there are diverse opinions of diverse people. First of all, the terms must be known beforehand. The Hebrew Scheol signifies 1. The place of the damned, Num. 16, 33. 2. The common receptacle of souls after death, as Keber is for bodies, as Luther teaches in Comment. Gen. c. 42, whom Paraeus unfairly criticizes in Comment. Gen. c. 42, since one must distinguish 1. between a receptacle for dwelling and for passing through, 2. between a common name and diverse things signified by the same name, so that there is one scheol for the pious, another for the impious. 3. Infernal pains, Ps. 116, 3. 4. Humiliation through afflictions, 1. Sam. 2, 6. 5. The grave, Job 14, 13. Which signification, however, seems not so much necessary as arbitrary. That Scheol primarily and properly denotes the grave, we by no means grant to Beza c. 2. Act. & Bucan. loc. 25. q. 2. The word ᾅδης in the N.T. signifies hell; it is also found used for infernal pains, Acts 2, 27; but never for the grave, contrary to Polanus, l. 6. syntag. c. 21; never for the state of blessed souls after death. To descend into hell in the O.T. signifies 1. to pass from this life, Gen. 37, 35; 2. to be placed in the place of the damned, Num. 16, 33; in the N.T. it is not expressly found.

II. Now we must see what descending into hell signifies when it is attributed to Christ; and we must look both to the symbols, in which this phrase is expressly found, and to Scripture. Setting aside the ancients, whose opinions others may consult, such as D. Crætherus in his tract on the descent, 1. The Photinians, as Smalcius in his refutation of the theses of D. Franz, p. 71, explain the descent to hell as the state of Christ after death, common to Him with all the dead. 2. Among the Papists, Durandus in 2. d. 22. q. 3., cited by Bellarmine, l. 4. de Christi anima c. 15, posits the descent not according to substance, but through effects; the rest commonly maintain a real presence. Bellarmine, ibid. The Calvinists vary strangely. For the sake of teaching, we proceed thus: Some explain the descent concerning Christ in His life, and indeed either concerning His acts (rightly understanding the term 1. of His whole humiliation, as Sohn, tom. 2. oper., 2. of the pains of hell in the garden and agony, Calvin, l. 2. inst. c. 16. s. 10, Polanus, l. 6. Syntagm. c. 12) or concerning the fruit of His acts, our liberation from hell and the devil, Bullinger, c. 2. Act. Others concerning Christ after His life; and these refer the descent either to the parts of His human nature, namely 1. to the body, so that to descend is to be buried, Beza, c. 2. Act., 2. to the soul, and explain the descent 1. concerning his migration into Abraham's bosom, Martyr class. 3. loc. 5. 16. n. 8. p. 379. 2. concerning the common state which all separated souls experience, Martyr. in expos. arti. p. 222. 3. concerning the arrival of the soul to the captives, announcing the joy of redemption, Cingl. explan. artic. 57. or to the whole man, and they explain the descent 1. through death, Bucer. on John 2. through τὸ being gathered to the dead, Id 3. through the manifestation made to the Fathers in a vision, Oecolam. comm. in Zach. 4. through the extreme degree of humiliation, by which he lay in the sepulchre for three days, as if overcome by death, Bucan. l. 25. q. 8. 5. through a real arrival into hell, Bucan. q. 6. Zanch. Adjet. 4. Among the Lutherans, Brentius in the Catechism explains the descent 1. concerning the liberation of the pious from hell through the death of Christ; 2. concerning the profound humiliation by which Christ was so buried that he seemed to have perished entirely; which opinion Bellarmine calumniously proposes, l. 4. de Christi anima c. 7. But the Formula of Concord, from the writings of Luther, recalls the orthodox to a unanimous consensus of public confession, whose opinion is to be explained more distinctly.

III. We assert, therefore, that in the Holy Scriptures there is held to be a twofold descent of Christ to hell, metaphorical, and proper and real. The former is defined by the torments and pains which CHRIST sustained for our sake. 1. Its seat is Isa. 53, Ps. 22, the history of the passion. 2. The subject which is Christ; by which, the human nature, namely the soul, Matt. 26, 38, the body, Luke 22, 44. 3. The time, both of his whole life, and in particular the time of the passion. 4. The place in particular is the garden and Golgotha. 5. The object is the pains of death and hell, Psalm 18, 5, the divine wrath, Psalm 88, 17, the bloody sweat, Luke 22, 44, the wounds, Isa. 53. 6. The mode consists in the desertion by God, Psalm 22, 1, the wondrous emptying, Phil. 2, 8 (yet without separation of the Deity), likewise the ineffable temptation, in which there was a natural flight from death, but without sin, Matt. 26, 39. 7. The end is the liberation of the human race from hell and death, Heb. 2, 14, which fruit if anyone wishes to call the descent to hell in its own way, we do not object. 8. This descent was completed when Christ, after he cried out, it is finished, John 19, 30, gave up his soul, having commended it to the Father. 9. It pertains, therefore, to the state of humiliation. Luther treats of this in Comment. Gen. tom. 6. Latin. Witteberg. But the real and properly so-called descent is that by which CHRIST, coming into hell, made himself present to the damned. And we understand this one alone in the Apostles' Creed. For we count the article of the descent as distinct from the rest 1. from the analogy of the others, 2. the nature of a compendium, which does not admit idle tautology, 3. the propriety of exegesis, which forbids the clear to be explained by the obscure: 2 we understand it literally 1. from analogy, 2. the nature of the symbol, 3. the order of the articles. The opinions of others strike against these members: that one, indeed, which is about the burial, also does violence to the meaning of the word adus, which cannot be taken for the sepulcher. Luther treats of this descent in the Torgau confession of the year 1533, vol. 6 of the Jena edition, and in the sermon for Easter Saturday in the domestic postil, and in the Formula of Concord, art. 9. The question here is 1. Whether this article of the Creed is contemporary with the rest, or inserted somewhat later? Calvin suspects the latter happened, Inst. book 2, ch. 16, sec. 8. See also Polanus, book 6, syntagm. ch. 21. Forster in Lex. p. 1782. he thinks, from the Constantinopolitan Creed the words, 'he was buried,' and from the Athanasian, 'he descended to the adu,' signifying one thing; as if two different things had been joined later. Erasmus refers its origin to Thomas Aquinas. But its antiquity is evident from those cited by Hutter, p. m. in F. C. art. 9, and Dr. Gerhard in the harmony of the resurrection, etc. Q. 2. Since the antiquity of the Apostles distinguished the Creed, which of the Apostles claims this article of the descent for himself? According to Augustine, sermon 115, St. Thomas; according to Mirandula, Philip; not before Dr. Cramer. Q. 3. Why did the Nicene omit this article? Dr. Gesner gives the reason, disp. 14, in F. C. Hutter, loc. cit., because it had not then come into controversy. Q. 4. Is the authority of the Creed alone sufficient to establish this article? Resp. Yes, as Dr. Cramer notes. Duns opines, as Mayron reports, 4 sentent., denying it, for it is supported by Scripture. For us, the creed does not constitute an article of faith, but confesses one established from Scripture.

IV. From what has been said, it is clear what must be answered to the question: Whether the descent of Christ into hell is an article of faith. A metaphorical descent is an article of faith, but not a distinct one, inasmuch as it is comprehended under the article of the passion; a real one is distinct from the others, and therefore is placed distinctly in the Creed. But if it is further asked whether this real descent is a fundamental article, we willingly admit that the reason for it is not exactly the same as with other fundamental articles. Now, for its understanding, there come to be considered

Latin:

HActenus Christi actûs, qui in terris evenêre, consideravimus; conseqvens est, ut eum, qui infernum respicit, contemplemur. Proinde, qvemadmodum Ducem nostrum in sepulcrum, ut nos peccatis sepelieremur, comitati sumus: Sic ad inferos descendentem, ut cum ipso de inferno triumphemus, comittabimur; & hunc descensûs articulum, ita, ut nec extra scripturam curiosiores, nec in scripturâ negligentiores simus, modestiæ Christianæ filium secuti, tractabimus.

I. Descendisse Christum ad inferos, ex scripturâ, licet ῥητῶς hoc in eâ non inveniatur, confitetur 1. Symbolum Apostolicum, 2. Athanasium, 3. A Confessio, 4. Form. Conc. 5. Doctorum vetustiorum & recentiorum consensus. Quid verò per hanc phrasin intelligendum, diversorum diversæ sunt sententiæ. Primùm omnium termini sunt præcognoscendi. Hebræum Scheol significat 1. Locum damnatorum, Num. 16, 33. 2. receptaculum commune animarum post mortem, ut Keber corporum, docente Luthero Comment. Gen. c. 42. quem iniquè perstringit Paræus Comment. Gen. c. 42. cùm distinguendum sit 1. inter receptaculum commorandi & transeundi, 2. inter nomen commune, & res diversas eôdem nomine significatas, ut sit aliud scheol piorum, aliud impiorum. 3. dolores infernales, Ps. 116, 3. 4. humiliationem per afflictiones, 1. Sam. 2. 6. 5. sepulcrum Job. 14, 13. Quæ tamen significatio non tam necessaria quàm arbitraria esse videtur. Scheol primò ac propriè sepulcrum denotare, Beza c. 2. Act. & Bucan. loc. 25. q. 2. minimè largiamur. Vox ᾅδης in N. T. infernum significat, pro doloribus infernalibus posita etiam invenitur, Act. 2, 27. pro sepulchro verò nunquam, contra Polan. l. 6. syntag. c. 21. nunquam pro animarum beatarum statu post mortem. Descendere in infernum in V.T. significat 1. transire ex hac vita, Gen. 37, 35. 2. collocari in locum damnatorum, Num. 16, 33. in N. T. expressè non habetur.

II. Nunc videndum, quid in infernum descendere, cùm Christo attribuitur, significet; & respiciendum tum ad symbola, in quibus expressè hæc phrasis habetur, tum ad Scripturam. Missis veteribus, de quorum sententiis alii possunt videri, ut D. Crætherus in tract. de desc. 1. Photiniani, ut Smalc. in refut. thes. D. Franz. p. 71. descensum ad inferos, de statu Christi post mortem ipsi cum omnibus mortuis communi, explicant. 2. Inter Pontificios Durandus in 2. d. 22. q. 3. apud Bellarm. l. 4. de Christi anima c. 15. descensum statuit non secundùm substantiam, sed per effectus; Reliqui communiter realem præsentiam tuentur. Bell. d. l. 3. Calviniani mirè variant. Nos docendi causâ sic procedimus: Alii descensum explicant de Christo in vitâ, & quidem vel de actibus (dextrè terminum intelligendo 1. de tota humiliatione, ut Sohn. tom. 2. oper. 2. de inferni doloribus in horto & agone, Calvin. l. 2. inst. c. 16. s. 10. Polan. l. 6. Syntagm. c. 12.) vel de actuum fructu, liberatione nostrâ ab inferno & diabolo, Bulling. c. 2. Act. Alii de Christo post vitam; & hi vel ad partes humanæ naturæ descensum referunt, nempe 1. ad corpus, ut descendere sit sepeliri, Bez. c. 2.
