Act. 2. ad animam, & descensum explicant 1. de migratione ejus in sinum Abrahæ, Martyr class. 3. loc. 5. 16. n. 8. p. 379. 2. de statu communi, qvem omnes animæ separatæ experiuntur, Martyr. in expos. arti. p. 222. 3. de adventu animæ ad captivos, annunciantis gaudium redemtionis, Cingl. explan. artic. 57. vel ad totum hominem, & descensum explicant 1. per mortem, Bucer. super Joh. 2. per τὸ mortuis aggregari, Id 3. per manifestationem Patribus in visione factam, Oecolam. comm. in Zach. 4. per extremum humiliationis gradum, qvô in sepulchro per triduum, tanqvam à morte devictus, jacuit, Bucan. l. 25. q. 8. 5. per realem in infernum adventum, Bucan. q. 6. Zanch. Adjet. 4. Inter Lutheranos Brentius in Catec. descensum explicat 1. de liberatione piorum ab inferno per mortem Christi; 2. de profunda humiliatione, qvâ Christus ita sepultus est, ut prorsus interisse videretur; qvam sententiam calumniosè proponit Bell. l. 4. de Christi anima c. 7. Verùm Form. Con. ex Lutheri scriptis, ad uanimem publicæ confessionis consensum revocat orthodoxos, qvorum sententia distinctiùs exponenda.

III. Asserimus ergò, in sacris literis duplicem haberi Christi ad inferos descensum, metaphoricum, & proprium ac realem. Ille definitur per cruciatus & dolores, qvos nostri causâ CHRISTUS sustinuit. Ejus 1. sedes est Esa. 53. Ps. 22. historia passionis. 2. Subjectum qvod, est Christus; quo, humana natura, utpote anima, Matth. 26, 38. corpus, Luc. 22, 44. 3. Tempus, tum totius vitæ, tum in specie tempus passionis. 4. Locus in specie est hortus & Golgatha 5. Objectum sunt dolores mortis ac inferni, Psal. 18, 5. ira divina, Psal. 88, 17. sudor sangvineus, Luc. 22, 44. vulnera, Esa. 53. 6. Modus consistit in Dei desertione, Psal. 22, 1. mirandâ exanitione, Phil. 2, 8. (sine tamen Deitatis separatione) tentatione item ineffabili, in qva naturalis fuit mortis fuga, sed sine vitio, Matth. 26, 39. 7. Finis est liberatio generis humani ab inferno & morte, Hebr. 2, 14. qvem fructum descensum ad inferos suô modô nominare si qvis velit, non refragamur. 8. Peractus est hic descensus, qvando Christus, postqvam clamavit, consummatum est, Johan. 19. 30. commendatam Patri animam emisit. 9. Pertinet ergò ad exinanitionis statum. De hoc agit Luther. in Comment. Gen. tom. 6. Latin. Witteberg. Realis verò & propriè dictus descensus est, qvô, CHRISTUS in infernum veniens, præsentem se damnatis monstravit. Et hunc solum in Symbol. Apostol. intelligimus. Nam 1. articulum descensus a reliquis distinctum numeramus 1. ex analogia reliquorum, 2. natura compendii, quod otiosam tautalogiam non admittit, 3. Proprietate exegeteos, quae clarum per obscurum explicari prohibet: 2 literariter eundem intelligimus 1. ex analogia, 2. natura symboli, 3. ordine articulorum. In haec membra aliorum sententiae impingunt: ea vero, quae est de sepultura, etiam significationi vocis adus vim infert, quae pro sepulchro sumi nequit. De hoc descensu agit Lutherus in con. Torgensi anni 1533. tom. 6. Jen. & in Conc. Sabbath. Pasch. postill. domest. & F. C. art. 9. Quaeritur hic 1. Antic Symboli articulus reliquis sit coaevus, an aliquanto post insertus? Posterius suspicatur factum Calvin. l. 2. inst. c. 16. l. 8. Vide & Pola. l. 6. syntagm. c. 21. Forsterus in Lex. p. 1782. putat, ex Symbolo Constantinop. verba, sepultus est, & ex Athanasiano, descendit eis adu, unum significantia; tanquam duo diversa postea fuisse conjuncta. Erasmus ejus originem ad Thomam Aquinate refert. Verum canities ejus patet ex allegatis ab Huttero p. m. in F. C. art. 9. & D. Gerhardo in harm. resurrect. &c. Q. 2. Cum ratione Apostolorum vetustas Symbolum distinxerit, quis Apostolorum sibi hunc descensus articulum vendicet? Secundum August. serm. 115. S. Thomas, secundum Mirandulam Philippus, not ante D. Cram. Q. 3. Cur Nicenum hunc articulum omiserit? Rationem dat D. Gesn. disp. 14. in F. C. Hutter. d. l. quia tum in controversiam non venerit. Q. 4. An Sola Symboli autoritas ad hunc articulum constituendum sufficiat? Resp. Ita, ut notat D. Cram. Duns opinatur, referente Mayron 4. sentent, negans, scriptura enim esse fulcitum. Nobis symbolum non constituit articulum fidei, sed ex scriptura constitutum confitetur.

IV. Ex dictis patet, quid ad Q. An descensus Christi ad inferos sit articulus fidei, respondendum sit. Metaphoricus descensus est fidei articulus, sed non distinctus, ut pote sub passionis articulo comprehensus; Realis est distinctus ab aliis, & idcirco distincte in Symbolo ponitur. Quod si ulterius quaeratur, an hic realis descensus sit fundamentalis articulus, sane non eandem prorsus illius, cum aliis articulis fundamentalibus, esse rationem, libenter fatemur. Nunc pro ejus cognitione consideranda veniunt


### V. 1. Seat. The ancients explained the type of Jonah concerning the descent, Matt. 12:40

V. 1. Seat. The ancients explained the type of Jonah concerning the descent, Matt. 12:40. 12, 40. item Heb. 2, 14. Ps. 22, 16. & other places. Bell. c. 12. Ps. 107, 9. Eccl. 24. Acts 2. Our own people [interpret] Hos. 13, 4. 1 Cor. 15. Eph. 4, 9. & some [interpret] Ps. 16, 9. Ps. 68, 19. Col. 2, 15. 1 Pet. 3, 19. as laying the foundations. We, with all respect to the judgment of others, understand Hos. 13 as referring to the fruit of the merit of Christ in general, which nevertheless can be referred to the descent as an ἐπινίκιον [song of victory]; Ps. 16 as referring to the metaphorical descent; Ps. 68 as referring to the ascension; Col. 2 as referring to the effect of the obedience of Christ, which nevertheless itself can also be referred to a special act of descent; but we establish the proper seat of this article at Eph. 4, 9. & 1 Pet. 3, 19. Q. 1. Is there absolutely no testimony for a real descent in the O.T.? A. In general, it has testimony concerning the fruit of the merit of Christ and his victory, which is sufficient; but it was not necessary that a special act of triumph be described. 2. May we also have a few testimonies from the N.T.? A. D. Gram. p. 117. because the descent is an act of another life, both by reason of the term to which, and by reason of the mode. 3. Why did the Evangelists omit it? A. Because they had neither been eyewitnesses of it, nor had they received the truth from the report of witnesses. D. Gerhard in harm. Let us now weigh the testimonies. 1. The passage Eph. 4, 9. Enjedin in expl. l. p. 300. understands it of the Father, regarding the profanation of the name and the glory that followed (by a manifest distortion of the text), or of the Son, regarding the humiliation, and properly, the burial and death. Calvin [understands it] of the incarnation in the womb, Polan. l. 6. syntag. c. 13. from Ps. 139, 15. of the humiliation, Buca l. 25. So also some of our own people. We understand it simply of a real descent to hell, attending to 1. the description of hell, which is called the lower part, 1. from the common opinion of men, as Theophil. says. 2. by reason of the glory of God, not of location; whence the placement into hell is expressed by the descent, Ps. 55, 16. 2. the opposition of ascension and descent; 3. the opposition of the highest place, which is heaven, and the lowest, which is hell, Luke 10, 15. 4. The unity of the subject, which is the incarnate Λόγος. 2. The passage 1 Pet. 3, 19. Aug. ep. 99. to Evod. [explains it] of Christ, [preaching] through his Deity to the disobedient in the time of Noah, whose souls were in the mortal body as in a prison; Smal. in refu. Franc. p. 25. explains it of Christ preaching to the Jewish nation, which had crucified him, and wishes those words, in the days of Noah, to be taken elliptically, as if it were 'as in the days of'. Eniedin p. 418. locor. with the same ellipsis posited, understands the Gentiles, who had been unbelieving for a long time, and aliens from the commonwealth of Israel. Calvi. l. 2, inst. c. 16. s. 9. takes it of the sense of the death of Christ reaching both to the blessed and the damned. Beza in notes p. 576. & Polan. l. 6. syntag. c. 21. of Christ To those who were then disobedient, Christ preaching through Noah, are now tormented in hell. Thus some of our own. See D. Winckel in his Commentary. Others [speak] of the seat of the blessed, who, though once at first unpersuadable, departed nevertheless by a late repentance, which is called φυλακὴ, the word being taken in a good sense, or with respect to the degrees of glory. D. Gesn. & Hutter. in the same place. Others [speak] of a real descent to the underworld. Which opinion we also embrace, attending to 1. The subject, which is the incarnate λόγος; 2. the time, after the ζωοποίησιν, with the human nature restored, which had ceased during the three days of death, since it is said ἀντιφατικῶς that he was a dead man, and that he was a true man; 3. the place, which is φυλακὴ, which word is commonly taken in a bad sense, Apoc. 20, 7. Matth. 25, 36, 4. The inhabitants of the place, who 1. are called Spirits, which word is inconveniently understood of men here; 2. unpersuadable, of whose late repentance, which is mentioned, it is spoken uncertainly; 3. it is added: τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ, where under it can be understood ἦσι, who are. 5. The preaching, which word is μέσον, and κηρύξειν signifies to cite, to challenge, to proclaim. Here we understand not so much a verbal announcement as a real manifestation. If you refer here to exc. 4, 6. εὐαγγελίζεσθαι, distinguish 1. between that which is absolutely the Gospel, and that which is to someone; 2. between per se, and per accidens. It seems to stand in the way that c. 4, 6. these, to whom it was evangelized, are said to live to God. But 1. it is not necessary that this passage be understood with ours as being about the same subject. 2. there only the end of the preaching of the Gospel is proposed, which is, that men, with the flesh mortified, may live to God in the spirit.

VI. 2. The subject which, is the whole Christ, about whom there is no controversy. Concerning the subject by which it is asked, whether Christ descended by his soul alone, or indeed also by his body. The Scholastics Lomb. l. 3. sent. dist. 22. (whom, however, distinguishing between the whole Christ, and the whole of Christ, Gesn. in the same place explains in a good sense) & Thom. p. 3. q. 52. art. 3. say that Christ descended according to his soul only, and therefore the whole Christ, not the whole of Christ. Thus the Fathers, whose manner of speaking Gesn. likewise explains. Thus the Papists simply place the body of Christ in the sepulcher, while the soul is meanwhile in the underworld. The Formula of Concord confesses that the whole Christ descended by soul and body. It is asked, for example, when the soul and body can be said to be present in a double respect, whether the body by its own idiom be in the sepulchre, the soul in its own idiom in paradise, both parts through personal union in hell; whether the body locally in the sepulchre, the soul definitively in hell, and in the same both parts personally; or finally whether the man Christ through the presence also of the natural union of soul and body, and thus do we gather from the Petrine passage, because Christ went away, ζωοποιηθεὶς.

VII. 3. The time, which 1. of the act concerning which it is asked, whether Christ at the very moment of death, when he gave up the spirit, descended, which Tho. p. 3. q. 52. art. 4. seems to wish; or immediately after burial; or a little before the resurrection, while the body was still lying in the sepulchre; or finally after the ζωοποίησιν, yet before the ἀνάστασιν at the moment of resurrection, which we conclude from the Petrine passage; 2. of the duration, concerning which Q. how long Christ was in hell? Certain Fathers gather from the type of Jonah that he remained in hell throughout the three days of death, and Tho. d. l. believes the soul was in hell for as long as the body was in the sepulchre. We do not measure this act of glorification by time, and where Scripture is silent, we consider it a gain to be silent.

VIII. 4. The place to which. The Papists in general define it as a subterranean place. Bellarm. c. 10. l. 4. on the soul of Christ. Specifically, Thom. p. 3. q. 52, art. 2. wishes that the soul of Christ by its substance entered only the limbo of the Fathers; Bellar. c. 16. [wishes it entered] all parts of hell. This is a fight about non-entities. We know that hell is a certain Where, [but] where it is, we do not know, and we understand that through the lower parts of the earth, and through the φυλακὴν in the places alleged above.

IX. 5. The mode. The descent of Christ was 1. real, as was the ascension, whence πορευθεὶς; 2. illocal, and therefore supernatural; 3. glorious and triumphal. We cannot explain the mode otherwise, nor yet do we detest, with certain Calvinists, the image of the descending Christ accustomed to be proposed to the common people. See Luther in Conc. Torg. We pass over the disputation of Mirandula concerning the mode of the presence of the soul in hell through operation, which presupposes that only the soul was in hell.

X. 6. The end, where it is asked to what end Christ descended, and therefore, what he did in hell? Concerning the Christolytes raving that Christ, having left his humanity in hell, ascended, Damasc. l. de hæres.; concerning the Marcionites dreaming that Christ, having left the pious in hell, led the impious with him, Iren. l. 1. c. 29. Concerning the Liberators, imagining that both the devils and the impious, having been converted, flew out with Christ, Danaeus makes mention: Let Cramer be seen in his tract on the descent. According to the Papists, Christ to the Fathers in limbo he conferred 1. essential blessedness, 2. liberation from prison, Bell. c. 16. 2. In purgatory he gave hope of life Thom. art. 2. yet he liberated no one from it, art. 8. 2. in the place of the damned he confounded them concerning their unbelief, art. 2. yet he liberated no one, art. 6. just as he did not liberate children from limbo, art. 7. Bell. d. l. To which we oppose 1. the immediate opposition of salvation and damnation, 2. the happy condition of the pious after death, Matt. 22, 30. Heb. 11, 35. Luke 9, Wis. 3, 3. the description of one hell, from which there is no redemption. Luth. in Ps. 16. tom. 2. Lat. Jen. says that he believes Christ felt pains in hell, until he is better informed. Aepinus, and Flacius in Clave, expressly defend that Christ descended in order to suffer. On the contrary we weigh 1. Christ crying out, it is finished; 2. commending his soul to the Father; 3. calling the thief to himself into paradise; 4. paying a sufficient ransom for sins by his death. We distinguish the ends of such teaching for the sake of the cause: Christ descended 1. with respect to himself, that he might fill all things, Eph. 4, 10. the knees of those in the underworld shall bow, Phil. 2, 10. that he might go as a conqueror from the lowest to the highest; 2. of the pious, that they might learn the love of Christ, the sufficiency of Christ's acts, the firmness of consolation; 3. of the Devils, that he might demonstrate to them that he is the powerful Lord who laid down his soul, and took it up again; 4. of the Damned, that he might show the promised Messiah, for their just punishment, in which way we accept the Petrine κηρύσσειν, and can explain δειγματίζειν Col. 2.

XI. 7. The fruits are gathered from the enumeration of the ends, concerning which we piously believe the ἐπινίκιον was sung in Hos. 13: 14, and 1 Cor. 15, 54. in which place it is asked whether Paul alleges the testimony of Hosea, and indeed alone. See Luth. in addit. Com. Os. Q. here whether the descent is a meritorious or satisfactory act? A. Aepinus & Flac. because it is a part of ignominy and humiliation, and has the same effect as passion and death. We, comparing the descent not with the passion, but with the resurrection, say that it was done for our justification, Rom. 4, 24. and we separate it from passive and active obedience, in which satisfaction consists. Furthermore, two special fruits of the descent are still reckoned by some: 1. the preaching of Christ made to the souls of the pious 1 Pet. 3. But we explained this passage above concerning the descent itself; 2. The resurrection of the holy dead, Matt. 27, 52. the cause of which, however, to it seems to be referred to the very death of Christ, although it may not be absurdly referred also to the descent of Christ.

XII. 8. Accidents. Here it is asked concerning the state of Christ in hell, whether being in hell was a punishment for him? Thomas seems to wish this, art. 1, and Cajetan in c. 2 of Acts calls it a punishment, because the soul of Christ was in a place not suitable to it, hell, and he refers this among the sorrows of death. Bellarmine, c. 16, says it should rather be said that Christ was in a place of punishment, without punishment. And rightly so. The opinion of Cajetan flows from the opinion concerning the soul alone descending, which we removed above. From the same opinion flows the question, whether it was a sorrow and punishment for the soul of Christ to be separated from the body? Cajetan affirms it, and Bellarmine in the said place concedes that it was some evil. We, with Gesner, concede indeed that there was a desire for union in the soul of Christ during the three days of death, but without punishment and sorrow, otherwise the souls of the pious would be in a state of punishment and sorrow before the resurrection, so that that desire implies not sorrow, but only a lesser degree of glory. Furthermore, to what state should the descent be referred? Flacius refers it to the emptying in his Clavis. Others posit an intermediate state, so that it may respect partly the state of humiliation, partly of exaltation, because through the descent Christ had not yet shown himself alive to men. Because, however, the states of Christ are distinguished not according to manifestation, but according to infirmity and glory, omitting the intermediate state, we refer it simply to the state of exaltation, as an act of one glorified and triumphant (not simply, because Christ suffered nothing in it, which reason would also adjudge burial to the state of exaltation). Whence this article, joined to the resurrection, is attributed to Thomas, and in the A. C. is separated from the acts of the emptying.

XIII. From these at last (for the narrowness of the pages prohibits us from instituting the special examination of those who dissent, which remained), we gather this definition of the descent of Christ to hell: The descent to hell is an act of the state of the exaltation of Christ, by which, in perfect humanity and divinity, after his vivification, having entered hell, he demonstrated himself with immense glory as a victor triumphing over his enemies, to the just judgment of the damned, so that the pious might acknowledge his love and receive firm consolation.

Latin:

V. 1. Sedes. Veteres de descensu explicarunt typum Jonae, Matth. 12, 40. 12, 40. item Hebr. 2, 14. Ps. 22, 16. & alia loca. Bell. c. 12. Ps. 107, 9. Eccl. 24. Ac. 2. Nostrates Os. 13, 4. 1. Cor. 15. Eph. 4, 9. & nonnulli Ps. 16, 9. Ps. 68, 19. Col. 2, 15. 1. Petr. 3, 19. fundamenta ponunt. Nos salvô aliorum judiciô, Os. 13. de fructu meriti Christi in genere, qvod tamen ad descensum uti ἐπινίκιον referri possit; Ps. 16. de descensu metapharico; Ps. 68. de ascensione; Col. 2. de effectu obedientiæ Christi, qvod tamen & ipsum ad specialem descensus actum referri possit, intelligentes, sedem articuli hujus propriam statuimus Eph. 4, 9. & 1. Petr. 3, 19. Q. 1. An prorsus nultum descensus realis in V. T. testimonium? R. In genere habere testim. de fructu meriti Christi & ejus victoriâ, qvod sufficit; specialem v. triumphi actum describi non erat necesse. 2. Curtâ pauca etiam N. T. habeamus testimonia? R. D. Gram. p. 117. qvia descensus est actus alterius vitæ, tum ratione termini ad qvem; tum ratione modi 3. Cur Evangelistæ omiserint? R. qvia ejus nec αὐτόπται fuerant, nec veritatem ex testium relatione acceperant. D. Gerhard. in harm. Jam perpendamus testimonia. 1. Locum Ephes. 4, 9. Enjedin. in expl. l. p. 300. intelligit de Patre, qvoad nominis profanationem & secutam gloriam (manifestâ textûs distractione,) vel de filio, qvoad humiliationem, & propriè, sepulturam ac mortem. Calviniam de incarnatione in utero, Polan. l. 6. syntag. c. 13. ex Ps. 139, 15. de humiliatione, Buca l. 25. Ita & nostratium aliqvi. Nos simpliciter de reali descensu ad infernum intelligimus, attendentes 1. inferni descriptionem, qvi inferior pars dicitur 1. ex communi hominum opinione, ut ait Theophil. 2. ratione gloriæ Dei, non sitûs; Unde collocatio in infernum per descensum exprimitur Ps. 55, 16. 2. oppositionem adscensionis & descensionis; 3. oppositionem loci supremi, qvi cælum, & infimi, qvi infernus, Luc. 10, 15. 4. Unitatem subjecti, qvod Λόγος incarnatus. 2. Locum 1. Petr. 3. 19. Aug. ep. 99. ad Evod. de Christo, Deitate per Noachum immorigeris prædicate, qvorum animæ erant in corpore mortali tanqvam carcere; Smal. in refu. Franc. p. 25. de Christo, genti Judaicæ, qvæ ipsum crucifixerat, prædicante explicat, vultq; ellipticè illa verba, temporibus Noæ, exponenda, per sicut temporibus. Eniedin p. 418. locor. positâ eâdem ellipsi, intelligit gentes, qvæ longô tempore incredulæ fuerant, & alienæ à rep. Israelis. Calvi. l. 2, inst. c. 16. s. 9. accipit de sensu mortis Christi tam ad beatos, qvàm damnatos perveniente. Beza in notis p. 576. & Polan. l. 6. syntag. c. 21. de Christo Christo per Noachum prædicantibus iis, qui tum fuerunt immorigeri, nunc inferno cruciantur. Ita quidam ex nostris. Vide D. Winckel. in Comment. Alii de sede beatorum, qui olim primùm inpersvasibiles, serâ tamen tandem pœnitentiâ discesserint, quæ dicatur φυλακὴ, voce in bonam partem sumtâ, vel respectu graduum gloriæ. D. Gesn. & Hutter. d. l. Alii de reali ad inferos descensu. Qvam sententiam & nos amplectimur, attendentes 1. Subjectum, qvod λόγος incarnatus; 2. tempus, post ζωοποίησιν, retintegratâ humanâ naturâ, qvæ triduo mortis desierat, qvippe mortuum esse hominem, & verum esse hominem, ἀντιφατικῶς dicuntur; 3. locum, qui φυλακὴ, qvæ yox communiter malam in partem sumitur, Apoc. 20, 7. Matth. 25, 36, 4. loci incolas, qui 1. dicuntur Spiritus, qvæ vox incommodè de hominibus hîc accipitur; 2. impersvasibiles, de quorum serâ pœnitentiâ, qvod dicitur, incertò dicitur, 3. additur: τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ, ubi sub intelligi potest ἦσι, qvi sunt. 5. Prædicationem, qvod vocabulum μέσον est, & κηρύξειν significat citare, provocare, edicere. Hîc non tam verbalem annunciationem, qvàm realem ostensionem intelligimus. Si referas huc exc. 4, 6. εὐαγγελίζεσθαι, distingve 1. inter id, qvod absolutè est Evangelium, & qvod alicui; 2. inter per se, & per accidens. Obstare videtur, qvod c. 4, 6. hi, qvibus Evangelizatum est, Deo vivere dicuntur. Sed 1. ut hic locus cum nostro de eodem subjecto intelligatur, necesse non est. 2. ibi solùm finis prædicationis Evangelii proponitur, qui est, ut homines carne mortificatâ spiritu Deo vivant.

VI. 2. Subjectum quod, est totus Christus, de qvo nulla controversia. De subjecto qvo qværitur, an solâ animâ, an verò etiam corpore Christus descenderit. Scholastici Lomb. l. 3. sent. dist. 22. (qvem tamen distingventem inter totum Christum, & totum Christi, in bonum sensum explicat Gesn. d. l.) & Thom. p. 3. q. 52. art. 3. Secundùm animam tantùm dicunt Christum descendisse, adeoq́ve totum Christum, non totum Christi. Ita Patres, qvorum locutionem itidem Gesn. explicat. Ita Pontificii simpliciter corpus Christi in sepulcro, animam intereà in inferno collocant. Form. Conc totum animâ & corpore descendisse Christum confitetur. Qværitur v. cùm duplici respectu anima & corpus præsens dici possint, an corpus suô idiomate fusit in sepulchro, anima suô idiomate in paradiso, utraq; pars per unionem personalem in inferno; an corpus localiter in sepulcro, anima definitivè in inferno, & in eadem utraq; pars personaliter; an deniq; homo Christus per præsentiam etiam naturalis unionis animæ & corporis, & sic nos colligim? ex loco Petrino, qvia Christus abiit, ζωοποιηθεὶς.

VII. 3. Tempus, qvod 1. actûs de qvô qværitur, an Christus in ipso mortis momento, qvando spiritum emisit, descenderit, qvod Tho. p. 3. q. 52. art. 4. velle videtur; an post sepulturam statim; an paulò ante resurrection nem, jacente adhuc corpore in sepulcro; an deniq; post ζωοποίησιν, ante tamen ἀνάστασιν in momento resurrectionis, qvod nos ex loco Petrino concludimus; 2. moræ, de qvo Q. quamdiu Christus in inferno fuerit? Patres qvidam per triduum mortis in inferno mansisse, ex typo Jonæ colligunt, & Tho. d. l. tamdiu credit in inferno animam fuisse, qvamdiu corpus in sepulcro. Nos hunc glorificationis actum tempore non metimur, & tacente scripturâ, silere, lucri æstimamus.

VIII. 4. Locus ad quem. Pontificii in genere locum subterraneum definiunt. Bellarm. c. 10. l. 4. de Christi anima. In specie substantiâ suâ animam Christi tantùm limbum Patrum fuisse ingressam vult Thom. p. 3. q. 52, art. 2. omnes inferni partes Bellar. c. 16. Pugna hæc est de non entibus. Nos infernum scimus certum esse Ubi, ubi sit, nescimus, idqve per inferiores terræ partes, & per φυλακὴν in locis supra allegatis intelligimus.

IX. 5. Modus. Descensus Christi fuit 1. realis, ut & ascensio, Unde πορευθεὶς; 2. illocalis, proinde & supernaturalis; 3. gloriosus, ac triumphalis. Aliter modum explicare non possumus, nec tamen imaginem Christi descendentis plebi proponi solitam, cum Calvinianis qvibusdam detestamur. Vid. Luther. in Conc. Torg. Mirandulæ disputationem, de modo præsentialitatis animæ in inferno per operationem, missam facim?, qvæ solam animã in inferno fuisse præsupponit.

X. 6. Finis, ubi qværitur quem in finem Christus descenderit, adeoq́, qvid in inferno fecerit? De Christolytis delirantibus, Christum, relictâ humanitate in inferno, ascendisse, Damasc. l. de hæres. de Marcionitis somniantibus, Christum, relictis piis in inferno, impios secum duxisse, Iren. l. 1. c. 29. De Liberatoribus, fingentibus, & Diabolos, & impios conversos, cum Christo evolâsse, Danæus mentionem facit: Videatur Cramerus in tract. de descens. Secundùm Pontificios Christus Patrib9 in limbo contulit 1. effentialem beatitudinem, 2. liberationem a carcere, Bell. c. 16. 2. In purgatorio spem vitae dedit Thom. art. 2. nullum tamen eo liberavit, art. 8. 2. in loco damnatorum eos de incredulitate confutavit, art. 2. nullos tamen liberavit, art. 6. uti nec pueros ex lymbo, art. 7. Bell. d. l. Qvibus opponimus 1. immediatam salutis & damnationis oppofitionem, 2. felicem piorum post mortem conditionem, Matth. 22, 30. Ebr. 11, 35. Luc. 9, Sap. 3, 3. unius inferni descriptionem, ex qvo nulla redemptio. Luth. in Pf. 16. tom. 2. Lat. Jen. dicit, se credere, Christum in inferno dolores sensisse, donec melius informetur. Aepinus, & Flacius in Clave, expresse defendunt, Christū descensisse, ut pateretur. Contra perpendimus 1. Christum clamantem, consummatum est; 2. animam Patri commendantem; 3. latronem ad se in paradisum vocantem; 4. morte sufficiens λύτρον pro peccatis persolventem. Nos fines ita docendi causà distinguimus: Descendit Christus 1. respectu sui, ut impleret omnia, Eph. 4, 10. inferorum genua flectentur, Phil. 2, 10. ab imis ad summa triumphator iret; 2. piorum, ut Christi amorem, actuum Christi sufficientiam, consolationis firmitatem discerent; 3. Diabolorum, ut iis se potentem Dominum animam posuisse, & refumsisse, demonstraret; 4. Damnatorum, ut promissum Messiam, ad justum eorum supplicium, ostenderet, qvo modo accipimus κηρύσσειν Petrinum, & δειγματίζειν Col. 2. explicare possumus.

XI. 7. Fructûs è finium enumeratione colliguntur, de qvibus ἐπινίκιον Ose. 13: 14. cantatum piè credimus, & 1. Cor. 15, 54. qvo in loco an Paulus, Oseae testimonium, & qvidem solum, alleget, qvaeritur. Videatur Luth. in addit. Com. Of. Q. hic an descensus sit actus meritorius sive satisfactorius? A. Aepinus & Flac. qvia sit pars ignominiae & humiliationis, & eundem habeat effectum cum passione & morte. Nos non cum passione, sed cum resurrectione conferentes descensum, eum propter justificationem nostram factum esse dicimus, Rom. 4, 24. eundemqve ab obedientiâ passivâ & activâ, inqvibus satisfactio consistit, separamus. Porrò, duo adhuc speciales descensus fructus accensentur ab aliqvibus: 1. praedicatio Christi piorum animabus facta 11. Petr. 3. Sed hunc locum supra de ipso descensu explicavimus; 2. Resurrectio mortuorum sanctorum, Matth. 27, 52. cujus tamen causa ad ipsam mortem Christi referenda videtur, licet non absurdè etiam ad Christi descensum referatur.

XII. 8. Accidentia. Ubiqværitur de statu Christi in inferno, an in inferno esse ipsi pœna fuerit? Videtur hoc velle Thom. art. 1. & Cajetan. in c. 2. Act. pœnam nominat, quòd anima Christi fuit in loco sibi non convenienti, inferno, hocq; inter dolores mortis refert. Bell. c. 16. dicendum potiùs ait, Christum fuisse in loco pœnæ, sine pœna. Et rectè. Sententia Cajetani fluit ex sententiâ de solâ animâ descendente, quâ supra removimus. Ex eâdem sententiâ fluit qvæstio, an animæ Christi fuerit dolor ac pœna, esse separatum à corpore? Aff. Cajetan. & concedit Bellar. d. l. fuisse aliqvod malum. Nos cum Gesn. desiderium quidem unionis in animâ Christi per triduum mortis fuisse concedimus, sed sine pœnâ & dolore, aliàs piorum animæ essent in statu pœnæ ac doloris antè resurrectionem, ut ita illud desiderium non dolorem, sed solùm minorem gloriæ gradum importet. Porrò, Ad quem statum descensus sit referendus? Flacius ad exinanitionem refert in Clave. Alii intermediurn ponunt statum, ut partim humiliationis, partim exaltationis statum respiciat, qvia per descensum nondum se vivum hominib? Christus exhibuerit. Qvia tamen status Christi non secundùm manifestationem, sed secundùm infirmitatem & gloriam distingvuntur, omisso statu intermedio, simpliciter ad exaltationis statum referimus, ut pote actum glorificati & triumphantis (non simpliciter, qvia nihil in eo Christus passus est, qvæ ratio etiam sepulturam exaltationis statui adjudicaret) Unde hic articulus resurrectioni junctus, Thomæ tribuitur, & in A. C. ab actibus exinanitionis separatur.

XIII. Ex his tandem (nam, quod restabat, speciale dissentientium examen, instituere pagellarū angustiâ prohibemur) hanc descensus Christi ad inferos colligimus definitionem: Descensus ad inferos est actus statûs exaltationis Christi, qvô perfectâ humanitate ac divinitate, post vivificationem, infernum ingressus, immensâ cum gloriâ se victorem de hostibus suis triumphantem, damnatis ad justum eorum judicium, demonstravit, ut pii ipsius amorem agnoscerent, & firmam consolationem acciperent.


## 41 Forty-first Disputation. On the Glorious Resurrection of Christ

That the article concerning the Resurrection of Christ is the foundation of the remaining articles of faith, which standing, our Christianity stands, and falling, it falls, Paul clearly indicates in 1 Cor. 15:14, 17, saying: If Christ has not risen, our preaching is vain, and our faith is also vain. Deservedly, therefore, must this article be defended and fortified against the φλυαρίας (babblings) of heretics, so that its truth may be manifest to all, and they may be certain of it. To which end we also subjoin the διάσκεψιν (examination) of this article to the preceding one concerning the descent into hell, with which it coheres in an indissoluble bond (because that contains the entry into glory, and this contains the progress in it), and we present it, enclosed in three chapters, to be debated. 1. will be concerning the truth of the resurrection, 2. concerning the quality of the resurrection, 3. concerning the abundance of its fruits.

Thesis 1. Augustine rightly affirms that even Pagans and Jews believe that Christ died, but that the same one rose from the dead is the proper faith of Christians. For the death of Christ pertains to all men indiscriminately; but his resurrection is, as it were, the effective application to Christians of his death and of the righteousness obtained through it. Paul himself inculcates this distinction of benefits in Rom. 4:25. Therefore, so that this faith may remain safe and sound against any insults of the Devil, we confirm the truth of the Resurrection of Christ with the following arguments.

II. Argument 1 is taken from the clarity of the prophecies, of which many occur in Scripture; in particular, those are illustrious: 1. Ps. 16:10, 'You will not abandon my soul in the grave, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption.' There is much debate among interpreters concerning this prophecy. We, not without reason, remain with the letter, and we refer it to the glorious resurrection of Christ; especially since we have infallible interpreters: 1. Peter in Acts 2:27 & 31, who, moved by the heavenly authority of this prophecy, concludes against human reason that the resurrection of Christ ought not to seem incredible, because David had already predicted it long ago by the instinct of the Holy Spirit; therefore, it was impossible for Christ to be held by death, v. 24. 2. Paul in Acts 13:35, who himself also demonstrates to the Jews of Antioch the truth of the resurrection of Christ by producing this prophecy, in which corruption is denied of the body of Christ, and from it concludes that it was necessary for it to be raised from death. But lest anyone, with the Jews, might object that the Psalmist is speaking of himself, therefore both interpreters add that these words must be understood of him whose body was affected by no injury of rot or corruption, which cannot be affirmed of David. Whence we conclude: Whoever did not remain in the sepulchre, nor saw corruption, he has risen: But Christ did not remain in the sepulchre, nor saw corruption: Therefore Christ has risen. II. Hos. 13. v. 14. I will redeem them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death: I will be thy death, O death; I will be thy sting, O grave. That in this prophecy the redemption of the Church is promised, and that extermination is denounced by Christ to death and hell in a triumphal song, is certain, which also Paul, this prophecy 1. Cor. 15. v. 55. alleging [it] to explain the manifold fruits of the resurrection of Christ from the dead, confirms it, while he converts this threat, already fulfilled in his own time, in v. 57 into a sarcasm, which the faithful, raised by the benefit of the resurrection of Christ, are to sing against death and hell. Hence we argue: Whoever has freed us from death, mortified death, destroyed the sepulchre and hell, he did not remain in death, the sepulchre, and hell, but has risen; But Christ, according to the prophecy, performed that: Therefore he also has risen. Let others be compared with these, as Gen. 3. v. 15. Ps. 110. v. 7. Isa. 53. v. 10. Dan. 9. v. 24. Mic. 2. v. 13.

III. Arg. 2. is taken from the testimony of the angels, the disciples, and the guards. Since angels are spirits of truth, it is a crime to deny faith to their testimony. For Christ wished to confirm the truth of his resurrection by the testimony of angels for this reason, that faith might be so much the more confirmed by them. Since, therefore, these witnesses affirm that Christ has risen, Mark 16. v. 6. Luke 24. v. 4, 5, 6, who will call it into doubt? Thus we owe no less faith to the testimony of the disciples, who, although the resurrection could not be persuaded to them unless they saw him raised with their own eyes, John 20. v. 25, and recognized him from the eating of fish, Luke 24. v. 42, nevertheless afterwards confirmed it both by their teaching, and by their life, nay even by their blood. The testimony of the guards of the sepulchre also confirms not a little the truth of the resurrection of Christ, who, terrified by an unusual earthquake and the sight of an angel, approach the city, and to the chief priests they announce all things which had happened, Matt. 28. v. 11. Thus those to whom the custody of the sepulchre had been committed, that they might hinder the resurrection, become, not without the singular providence of God, infallible heralds and witnesses of the resurrection. Nor does the deceit of the chief priests and elders effect anything, while they corrupt the soldiers with a quantity of money and teach them to lie boldly, v. 13, but the truth is confirmed more and more by the lie. For if the guards were sleeping, whence do they dare to affirm that the body of Christ was stolen away by the disciples? If one watching saw this, what negligence of duty was this, that he did not rouse the others, so that they might have driven off the thieves? If all saw it, do they lie splendidly in that they slept? Therefore this πείσμα stands unmoved: He, whom angels, disciples, and guards, nay even enemies, declare to have risen, truly has risen.

IV. Arg. 3. is taken from the manifold appearance of Christ. For Christ himself wished to prove the resurrection, while he exhibited himself to be seen alive several times, not only on the very day of the resurrection, but also during the 40 following days in which he conversed here on earth, the Evangelists testifying to that in many places; Luke in Acts c. 1. v. 12. and Paul 1 Cor. 15. v. 5. etc. Whence it is again firmly concluded that He, who truly died and was buried, yet offered himself afterwards to be seen and handled, was in very deed raised from the dead.

V. Arg. 4. is taken from the demonstration of the absurdities following from the denial of Christ's resurrection. The first of these is the denial of the authority of the Apostolic mission. It is certain that the authority of the Apostolic preaching is divine, because they preach by the command of Christ (a) and the operation of the Holy Spirit (b), and therefore there ought to be no less certainty of the faith of one believing the same. But if Christ did not rise, there is no certainty of faith; because the preaching of the Apostles, by which the contrary is asserted, would be vain; our faith, by which the same is believed, would be vain; the Apostles would be accused of false testimony, who preached that very thing, as the Apostle asserts 1 Cor. 15. v. 14, 15. Therefore, in order that the divine authority of the Apostolic mission may remain, it must be believed that Christ has risen. 2. The extenuation of the merit of Christ. Christ bore the sins of the whole world and their punishments by dying, (c) and by rising again demonstrated that he had overcome all things and conquered death (d). But if Christ did not rise, we are still in our sins, nor has Christ been made Lord of death, but rather overcome by death, he himself also perished. Which, because it is absurd, it is not permitted to deny that Christ was raised from the dead. 3. The condemnation of many martyrs. Experience is witness that many pious men underwent dangers for Christ and the confession of the Christian faith, endured any tortures, nay even death, and fell asleep in the faith of Christ dead and resurrected. But if Christ did not rise again, alas! with what insanity, with what miserable error were these poor men fascinated, that they underwent death for this faith, not faith, and perished eternally? Yet because no one can affirm this without absurdity, it remains infallibly true that Christ truly rose again from the dead. VI. The truth of Christ's resurrection having thus been proven, we assert with Paul that our resurrection can be apodictically proven from this 1. Cor. 15. v. 20. seq. for a double reason, 1. because the resurrection of Christ is the cause of our resurrection, 2. because Christ is said to have been made ἀπαρχὴ or the firstfruits of those who sleep. Therefore, there is a certain hope concerning the resurrection of our own bodies also from the sleep of death, since life and resurrection, just as death from Adam, draw their origin from Christ alone (e). But whether the resurrection of the dead can also be demonstrated from the principles of human reason is asked by some? A. We affirm that a solid ἀπόδειξιν of it can be constructed only from divinely revealed principles; yet we do not deny the illustration of this dogma by human reasons, especially since we have Scripture as a guide. (f)

VII. As regards the quality of the resurrection of Christ, certain things must be considered concerning it; 1. The time of the resurrection. Christ rose on the third day, just as he had promised Matth. 16. v. 21. c. 17. v. 23. Mark 10. v. 34. Luke 18. v. 33. which time he understood through the mystical destruction of the temple, John 2. v. 19. He did not wish to be detained in the sepulchre beyond the third day, lest the faith of the disciples be endangered, or lest anyone might rightly suspect that his body had experienced corruption, and that he had raised a different body from the sepulchre. Nor, however, ought he to have risen from the dead immediately on the first day; so that he might remove the suspicion of a feigned death, and illustrate the glory of an unusual resurrection. Thus neither on the second, so that he might sanctify the Sabbath, and honorably bury the Jewish synagogue; But he willed to rise on the third day, 1. according to the prophecy of Hosea 6. v. 2. He will revive us after two days: on the third day he will raise us up (viz. in his own person). To this prophecy Paul looked in 1 Cor. 15:4, while he affirms that Christ was raised on the third day according to the scriptures: 2. According to the figure, and a threefold one at that: of Isaac, Gen. 22:4, of Joseph, Gen. 41:1, of Jonah, Jon. 2:1, which figure Christ himself applies to himself, Matt. 12:39.

Latin:

Articulum de Resurrectione Christi, esse fundamentum reliquorum articulorum fidei, quo stante, stet, cadente, cadat noster Christianismus, clarè inhuit Paulus 1. Cor. 15. v. 14. 17. quiens: Si Christus non resurrexit, inanis est predicatio nostra, inanis etiam fides nostra. Meritò ergo hic articulus contra φλυαρίας hæreticorum defendendus & muniendus, ut omnibus pateat ejus veritas, ac de hoc certi esse possint. Quo fine & nos διάσκεψιν hujus articuli præcedenti de descensu ad inferos, cum quo indissolubili nexu cohæret, (quia ille ingressum in gloriam, hic progressum in illâ continet) subjungimus, & tribus capitibus inclusam, ventilandam exhibemus. 1. erit de resurrectionis veritate, 2. de resurrectionis qvalitate, 3. Fructuum ubertate.

Thes. 1. Christum mortuum etiam Paganos & Judæos credere, eundem verò à mortuis resurrexisse, fidem propriam Christianorum esse, rectè Augustinus affirmat. Nam mors Christi ad omnes, indiscretè pertinet homines; at ejus resurrectio est quasi mortis, & per eam partæ justitiæ ad Christianos efficax applicatio. Quam beneficiorum distinctionem inculcat ipse Paulus Rom. 5. v. 25. Hæc itaque fides ut sarta tecta contra quovis Diaboli insultûs maneat, Resurrectionis Christi veritatem, seqventibus confirmamus argumentis.

II. Arg. 1. sumitur à vaticiniorum claritate, quorum in scriptura benè multa occurrunt; imprimis v. illustria sunt illa: 1. Ps. 16. v. 10. Non derelinqves animam meam in sepulchro, nec permittes, ut sanctus tuus videat corruptionem. De hoc vaticinio multum ab interpretibus disceptatur. Nos non sine ratione in literâ manemus, idqve ad gloriosam Christi resurrectionem referimus; præsertim cùm infallibiles habeamus interpretes, 1. Petrum Act. 2. v. 27. & 31. qui motus hujus vaticinii autoritate cælesti, contra rationem humanam concludit, Christi resurrectionem incredibilem videri non debere, quia jam olim David eam Sp. S. instinctu prædixerat; Impossibile itaque fuisse, Christum à morte retineri v. 24. 2. Paulum Actor. 13. v. 35. qui & ipse Judæis Antiochenis veritatem resurrectionis Christi demonstratus, hoc producit vaticinium, in qvo de Christi corpore negatur corruptio, ac ex eo concludit, necesse fuisse illud ex morte excitari. Ne autem qvis cum Judæis excipere posset, Psalmistam loqvi de seipso, ideò uterqve interpres subjungit, de eo verba hæc intelligenda esse, cujus corpus nullâ putredinis aut corruptionis injuriâ affectum fuit, qvod de Davide affirmari neqvit. Unde concludimus: Qvicunq; in sepulchro non mansit, nec corruptionem vidit, is resurrexit: Atqvi Christus in sepulchro non mansit, nec corruptionem vidit: Ergò Christus resurrexit. II. Ose. 13. v. 14. Epotestate inferorum redimam eos; à morte redimam eos: ero mors tua, ô mors; ero morsus tuus, inferne. Hôc in Vaticinio Ecclesiæ redemtionem promitti, & morti ac inferno exterminium triumphali cantico à Christo denũciari, certum est, qvod & Paulus, hoc vaticinium 1. Cor. 15. v. 55. ad multiplices resurrectionis Christi ex mortuis fructus explicandos, allegans, confirmat, dum cominationem hanc suô jam tempore adimpletam v. 57. in sarcasmum convertit, qvem fideles, beneficio resurrectionis Christi resuscitati, morti ac inferno sint occenturi. Hinc argumentamur: Qvicunq; nos à morte liberavit, mortem mortificavit, sepulchrum & infernum destruxit, is in morte, sepulchro, & inferno non mansit, sed resurrexit; Atqvi Christus juxta vaticinium id præstitit: Ergò etiam resurrexit. His conferantur & alia, ut Gen. 3. v. 15. Ps. 110. v. 7. Esa. 53. v. 10. Dan. 9. v. 24. Mich. 2. v. 13.

III. Arg. 2. sumitur ab Angelorum, discipulorum, custodum testificatione. Cùm Angeli sint spiritus veritatis, nefas est, istorum testimonio fidem denegare. Nam ideò Christus voluit resurrectionis suæ veritatem angelorum testimoniô confirmare, qvò fides istis tantò esset cõfirmatior. Dum igitur hi testes Christum resurrexisse affirmant, Mar. 16. v. 6. Luc. 24. v. 4, 5, 6. qvis eam in dubium vocabit? Sic non minorem fidem testificationi discipulorum debemus, qvi, licet illis resurrectio persvaderi non potuit, nisi propriis oculis eum suscitatum viderent, Johan. 20. v. 25. & ex esu piscium cognoscerent, Luc. 24. vers. 42. tamen posteà eam & doctrinâ, & vitâ, imò sangvine confirmârunt. Non parùm qvoqve confirmat resurrectionis Christi veritatem custodum sepulchri testimonium, qvi terræmotu insolito, & angeli conspectu terrefeacti, urbem aggrediuntur, & principibus Sacerdotum annunciant, omnia quæ acciderant, Matth. 28. v. 11. Sic illi, quibus sepulchri custodia commissa erat, ut resurrectionem impedirent, non sine singulari Dei providentiâ fiunt infallibiles res surrectionis præcones ac testes. Nec quicquam dolus Pontificum & seniorum efficit, dum milites pecuniæ copiâ corrumpunt, eosque audacter mentiri docent, v. 13. sed magis magisque veritas mendacio confirmatur. Si enim custodes dormierunt, unde affirmare audent, corpus Christi â discipulis furtim ablatum esse? Si unus vigilans hoc vidit, quæ officii negligentia hæc fuit, ut reliquos non excitârit, quò fures pellere potuissent? Si omnes viderunt, splendide mentiuntur, quòd dormierint? Stat itaq; immotum πείσμα hoc: ille, quem Angeli, discipuli, & custodes, imò inimici resurrexisse perhibent, verè resurrexit.

IV. Arg. 3. sumitur à multiplici Christi apparitione. Voluit enim Christus ipse resurrectionem probare, dum se non tantùm ipso resurrectionis die, verùm etiam 40. diebus sequentibus, quibus hîc in terris conversatus est, vivum aliqvoties conspiciendum exhibuit attestantibus illud Evangelistis multis in locis; Luca in actis c. 1. v. 12. & Paulo 1. Cor. 15. v. 5. &c. Unde iterum firmiter concluditur, Illum, qui verè mortuus ac sepultus, se tamen post videndum, contrectandum præbuit, reverâ à mortuis resuscitatum esse.

V. Ar. 4. sumitur ab absurdorum è negatâ Christi resurrectione sequentium, demonstratione. Horum 1. est, autoritatis Apostolicæ legationis negatio. Certum est, Apostolicæ prædicationis autoritatem divinam esse, quia Christi mandato (a) & Sp. S. operatione (b) prædicant, ideoque fidei, eidem credentis, non minor certitudo esse debet. Si verò Christus non resurrexit, fidei nulla certitudo; quia vana esset prædicatio Apostolorum, quâ contrarium asseritur; vana nostra fides, quâ idê creditur; falsi testimonii Apostoli arguerentur, qui id ipsum prædicârunt, asserente Apostolo 1. Cor. 15. v. 14, 15. Quò ergò Apostolicæ legationis divina maneat autoritas, Christum resurrexisse credendum erit. 2. meriti Christi extenuatio. Christus peccata totius mundi, eorumque pœnas moriendo tulit, (c) & resurgendo se omnia superâsse, mortem vicisse, demonstravit (d) Ast si Christus non resurrexit, adhuc in peccatis sumus, nec Christus mortis dominus factus, sed potiùs à morte victus, ipse quóque periit. Quod, quia absurdum, negare non licet, Christum à mortuis suscitatum esse. 3. Multorum Martyrum damnatio. Multos piorum hominum, pro Christo & fidei Christianæ confessione, pericula subiisse, qvoslibet cruciatûs, imò mortem sustulisse, ac in fide Christi mortui & resuscitati obdormivisse, experientia testis est. Si autem Christus non resurrexit, eheu! qvâ insaniâ, qvô miserabili errore fascinati fuerunt miselli isti homines, ut mortem pro hâc fide non fide subierint, & in æternùm perierint? Hoc tamen quia sine absurditate nemo affirmare possit, adhuc infallibiliter verum manet, Christum verè à morte resurrexisse. VI. Probatâ itaq; Christi resurrectionis veritate, nostram resurrectionem hinc apodicticè probari posse, cum Paulo asserimus 1. Cor. 15. v. 20. seq. duplici ratione, 1. quia resurrectio Christi est causa resurrectionis nostræ, 2. quia Christus dicitur factus ἀπαρχὴ seu primitiæ dormientium. Spes itaq; certa est, de subsecutura etiam nostrorum è somno mortis resuscitatione; cùm à Christo solo vita & resurrectio, qvemadmodùm ab Adamo mors, originem trahat (e). An verò mortuorum resurrectio etiam ex rationis humanæ principiis demonstrari possit, à qvibusdam qværitur? R. Solidam ejus ἀπόδειξιν non nisi ex principiis divinitus patefactis extrui posse affirmamus; non tamen hujus dogmatis illustrationem rationibus humanis denegamus, præsertim cùm scripturam habeamus præviam. (f)

VII. Quod qualitatem resurrectionis Christi attinet, circa eam qvædam consideranda veniût; 1. Tempus resurrectionis. Resurrexit Christus tertiô die, prout promiserat Matth. 16. v. 21. c. 17. v. 23. Marc. 10. v. 34. Luc. 18. v. 33. qvodq́; tempus per mysticam templi destructionem intelligebat, Joh. 2. v. 19. Ultra tertium diem in sepulchro detineri noluit, ne fides discipulorum periclitaretur, néve jure qvis suspicaretur, corpus ejus sensisse corruptionem, & ipsum aliud corpus è sepulchro suscitâsse. Nec tamen primô statim die à mortuis resurgere debuit; ut simulatæ mortis suspicionem amoveret, & insolitæ resurrectionis gloriam illustrâret. Ita neq; secundô, qvò sabbathú sanctificaret, & synagogam Judaicam honestè sepeliret; Sed tertiô die, resurgere voluit, 1. juxta Prophetiam Ose. 6. v. 2. Vivificabit nos post biduum: die autem tertiô suscitabit nos (sc. in suâ persona). Ad hanc Prophetiam respexit Paulus 1. Cor. 15. v. 4. dum Christum tertiô die suscitatum secundùm scripturas affirmat: 2. Juxta figuram, eamq; triplicem: Isaaci, Gen. 22. v. 4. Josephi, Gen. 41. v. 1. Jonæ, Jon. 2. v. 1. quam figuram Christus ipse sibi applicat, Matth. 12. v. 39.


### VIII. 1. The efficient cause of the resurrection

VIII. 1. The efficient cause of the resurrection. The Holy Scripture attributes the resurrection of the Son both to the whole Trinity, and to God the Father, and to the Son individually: yet without any contradiction. For the virtue and power by which Christ was raised from the dead is considered 1. Essentially, and thus it is common to all three persons of the Holy Trinity, because the works of the Trinity ad extra are common and undivided: thus it is attributed to God, Acts 13:30, 1 Cor. 15:4, Col. 2:12. 2. Personally, and specifically it is attributed to God the Father, and to the Son: to the Father, Rom. 4:24. Heb. 13:20, and that 1. by reason of the principle, because the Son has all his power from the Father through eternal generation: thus therefore the principle of the resurrection of the Son also redounds to the Father: 2. by reason of the counsel, because the Son was delivered to death by the counsel and will of the Father, John 3:16, on this condition, that he should not see corruption, but should rise again on the third day: 3. by reason of the effect; because the Father subjected all enemies under his feet, as David prophesies, Ps. 110:1. It is attributed to Christ, and primarily according to his divinity, because he raised himself by the proper power of his deity, Rom. 1:4. (Because the Photinians deny this, Ostor. in disp. Ger. cont. Tradel. part 2, c. 10, p. 176; Smalcius de divin. Christi, c. 13, p. 84; In Catech, c. 11, de off. Christi p. 312.) we prove it 1. from the identity of power and operation with the Father: for whatever things the Father does, he himself also does likewise (g) 2. from the power of raising others: for he himself raises whom he will, (h) why therefore could he not also have raised himself, especially since he is the author of life (i) and has life in himself (k) 3. from the authority of laying down and taking up his life, which Christ attributes to himself, John 2:19, John 10:18. Then also according to his humanity, in such a way that it effectively concurred in the resurrection, and raised itself. Which assertion, since it is a thorn in the eyes of the Calvinists, (Pala. lib. 6. Syntag. c. 43; Buca. in L. C. loc. 62. q. 4, etc.) we prove it 1. From the communication of idioms resulting from the personal union with the Λόγῳ. For the humanity is not vivifying in itself and by itself, but because God united it to himself, which union was not dissolved by death either as regards the soul or the flesh, as Thomas also learnedly discusses, part 3, q. 53, art. 4. 2. From the testimony of Scripture itself proof, which attributes the resuscitation of the Son of God entirely to the Most High alone. John 2:19. John 10:18.

IX. 3. The matter or subject of the resurrection. We do not make this both natures of Christ, as Sohnius does, since changeability does not fall upon the divine nature, and thus neither does resurrection; nor properly the soul of Christ, since it is immortal, and therefore could neither die nor rise again; but the body of Christ, since it fell only according to the body, therefore it had to and could rise again only according to this. However, a phantastic body did not rise; otherwise the resurrection would be phantastic: but it was a true and numerically identical body, not as to qualities, but substance; for He who conferred glory upon the body did not take away its nature, which Christ not only asserted in words, but impressed upon all the senses of the disciples. Its form proves the truth and identity of the body of CHRIST, which, because it is determined and numerically the same, requires determined and numerically the same matter. But is it asked whether He retained the flesh, bones, blood, and internal members which He had before after the resurrection? The Photinians deny it (Socinus, De statu primi hominis, c. 8, p. 236; Ostorod, in Inst. c. 41, § 1). But 1. against the assertion of Christ, by which He affirms that He has flesh and bones, and opposes His body to a spirit or specter; 2. the perfection of the body. The body rose again, and that a human one, because this is what fell: now, however, flesh, blood, bone, and other things of this kind belong to the nature of a human body. Therefore these are not to be denied of the body of CHRIST: for although it is spiritual, it is nevertheless not a spirit. 3. the true resurrection. Resurrection is not the creation of a new body, but the recalling of a dead one to life. But the dead body of CHRIST was not without flesh, bones, blood, and other members: therefore without these it could not rise again. It is concluded from these things that we too are to receive our bodies numerically the same, as to substance and integral members; both because the members ought to be assimilated to the head; and because the resurrection of CHRIST was the example of our resurrection.

X. He adorns this body of Christ through the resurrection with certain new qualities: for it was made immortal, glorious, agile, subtle, i.e., spiritual. That the body of CHRIST was immortal after the resurrection, while in these lands it was, the Photinians deny, (Socin. de stat. prim. hom. c. 2. p. 273. Ostor. in Inst. c. 41. p. 393.) But for us this is an axiom of immovable truth: Whoever dies no more (l) but by his death destroyed him who had the power of death (m) and triumphed over death (n) is not mortal day be conformed to his glorious body. He repressed the rays of this brightness, however, while he showed himself alive to his disciples, on account of the weakness of their eyes, which could not bear them. The history described by Luke c. 24. v. 31. demonstrates agility and invisibility, where he is said to have vanished from the sight of two disciples at the inn of Emmaus, which pertains to nothing but a spiritual body endowed with agility. Its subtlety is proven by the penetration of the sepulcher, and his entry to the disciples through closed doors. This glory of the body, however, differs in its whole kind from that which he obtains from sitting at the right hand of God: for the former he has in common with the elect, but the latter not so.

XI. 4. The form or mode of the resurrection. Where two acts are to be considered: I. The union of body and soul. For, the soul willed to be reunited to the body in turn, on account of the power of acting upon the body, and the dependence upon the body. Therefore the body resumed the soul, which it had dismissed, and the soul the body, which it had laid down, and it vivifies that, so that it is now no longer without sense, without motion, without life, as before, dead thus, but it senses, is moved, and lives. But whether, this union having been made, Christ also received back into his veins the blood shed on the altar of the cross, is asked by some? Most of the followers of Calvin deny it, and say that it had long since putrefied, not without absurdity: for it follows from this 1: that our redemption was made with corruptible blood, contrary to the clear assertion of Peter 1. Epist. 1. v. 18. 2. that a deposition of a substantial part of the assumed nature was made, contrary to the rule of antiquity: What he once assumed, he never laid down. 3. that Christ saw corruption, contrary to Prophetic scripture; (o) and Apostolic (p). II. The exit from the sepulcher, which we believe with antiquity was made not by the yielding of the sepulchral stone, but rather by the penetration of the sepulcher. For he who as a mortal could enter life through the closed womb of a virgin, certainly as an immortal could come forth alive through a closed sepulcher. Although the Calvinists splendidly deny this (Joh. Crocius in convers. Prut. part. 1. considerat. prob. 9. p. 461.) it is nevertheless more true to us, because it increases the majesty and glory of Christ more, and appears more consistent with Scripture, which affirms that the earthquake, in which Christ rose, preceded the rolling away of the stone, and affirms that the end of the rolling away, not Christ's resurrection, but his manifestation (q) and affirms that Christ demonstrated himself to be the Son of God through the resurrection, (r)

XII. 5. The ends of the resurrection. Of these, 1. The fulfillment of prophecies. For the resurrection of Christ was predicted in the Scriptures, which must be fulfilled, on account of the immutable decree of God. Therefore Christ had to rise again so that the truth of his prophecies might be established. 2. The demonstration of the sufficiency of his merit. For if Christ had remained in death, it would have been an argument for the insufficiency of his merit. For where there is death, there is sin, because the former is the punishment of the latter. 3. The completion of the office of Mediator. Christ is our perpetual Mediator; therefore he ought not to have remained in death. For it was not sufficient to merit benefits by death, but it was also necessary that they be conferred through the resurrection. But how could he confer them if he had not risen?

XIII. There remains the abundance of fruits, or the effects of the resurrection, of which Scripture indeed enumerates many. Because of the narrowness of the page, we are permitted to see only two. The former concerns Christ, and is the manifestation of his glory. Through the resurrection of CHRIST his Deity is demonstrated, because he is the only-begotten and natural Son of God, begotten from the essence of the Father from eternity, and therefore true God, because he raised his own flesh by his own power, which is the property of God alone. Through the resurrection is also demonstrated the divine majesty communicated to his flesh through the union, which he had as the Son of Man at the very moment of conception, according to which the flesh itself also worked the resurrection, as proved in thesis 8. The latter concerns men, and is the resuscitation of bodies. This is twofold, 1. spiritual, consisting in the regeneration of the soul: for Christ died for all, that we ourselves might live (s) he raised us from sins, that we might walk in newness of life (t) 2. corporal, which is unto life or eternal blessedness. For the resurrection of CHRIST is the key to our resurrection, as Tertullian says. The question is raised here, Does this fruit pertain to all men indiscriminately? We answer briefly: Christ as Judge, by his omnipotent power and efficacy, will indeed resurrect all men from the dead on the last day, on account of the infallible decree, Heb. 9. v. 27. expressed: Truly, as redeemer, by virtue of merit & resurrection, he will only resurrect the faithful, whose resurrection, and not indeed that of the impious, depends as a fruit from Christ's resurrection, which we prove by the following reasons: 1. we take from the necessity of the resurrection, which is by virtue of the merit of Christ, with the adjunct, which is life & eternal salvation, as is evident from the context of the whole 15th chapter of 1 Cor. Who, however, dares to affirm that the impious will resurrect to life and eternal blessedness? 2. from the perpetual connection of the head with the members only. The resurrection of Christ relates to the resurrection of those rising by the virtue & merit of Christ's resurrection, as head to members: Therefore, those who are not members of the mystical body of Christ will not rise by virtue of the head's resurrection; because the head is essentially connected only to the members. 3. from the effect of Christ's resurrection. Christ is called ἀπαρχὴ of those rising, in that he sanctifies those depending thence by his resurrection: By what reason, however, will the resurrection of the impious be sanctified by the resurrection of Christ, since it is not conformed to the resurrection of Christ, nor are they Christ's? It remains, therefore, true that only the faithful rise by virtue & merit of the resurrection of Christ.

XIV. Thus far, therefore, you have heard that Christ has risen from the dead, O man, I pray you consider what you must now do. Rise also you quickly spiritually, so that you may be worthy to rise bodily: Rise quickly from sins to repentance, so that you may be worthy to rise from the sepulcher to glory: hasten the former without delay; await the latter faithfully and patiently. Christ is the head, you are a member; he has risen, you also will rise. Therefore let the infernal Lion rage, let enemies torture, let Tyrants kill: your Redeemer has revived, he will also vivify you, and the mortal bodies of all the faithful. Therefore come Lord, and do not delay; I come quickly, Amen. Even so come Lord Jesus!

Latin:

IIX. 1. Causa efficiens resuscitationis. Tribuit sacra scriptura resuscitationem filii, & toti Trinitati, & Deo Patri, & Filio singulatim: absq; omni tamen ἀντιλογίᾳ. Nam virtus & potentia, quâ Christus à mortuis suscitatus est, consideratur 1. Essentialiter, & ita omnibus tribus S. S. Trinitatis personis communis est, eò, quòd opera Trinitatis ad extra sint communia & indivisa: ita Deo tribuitur Act. 13. v. 30. 2. Cor. 15, v. 4. Col. 2. v. 12. 2. Personaliter, & in specie tribuitur Deo Patri, & Filio: Patri, Rom. 4. v. 24. Hebr. 13. v. 20. idq́; 1. ratione principii, quia filius omnẽ suam potestatem habet à Patre per æternam generationem: Sic ergò etiam principium resurrectionis filii ad Patrem redundat: 2. ratione consilii, quia filius consilio & voluntate Patris in mortem est traditus, Joh. 3. v. 16. hâc conditione, ut corruptionem non videret, sed tertio die resurgeret: 3. ratione effecti; quia omnes hostes pedibus ipsius pater subjecit, ut vaticinatur David, Psal. 110. v. 1. Christo tribuitur, & primum secundùm divinitatem, quòd propriâ suâ deitatis virtute seipsum resuscitaverit, Rom. 1. v. 4. (Hoc quia Photiniani negant, Ostor. in disp. Ger. cont. Tradel. part. 2. c. 10. p. 176. Smalcius de divin. Christi, c. 13. p. 84. In Catech, c. 11. de off. Christi p. 312.) id probamus 1. à potentiæ & operationis cum patre identitate: eadem enim, quæcunqve pater facit, & ipse similiter operatur (g) 2. ab alios suscitandi potestate: ipse enim, qvos vult, suscitat, (h) cur ergò non etiam seipsum resuscitare potuisset, præsertim cùm sit autor vitæ (i) & vitam in seipso habeat (k) 3. à propriâ ponendi & resumendi vitam autoritate, quam sibi ipse tribuit, Christus Joh. 2. v. 19. Joh. 10. v. 18. Deinde etiam secundùm humanitatem, ita, ut ea ad resuscitationẽ nem efficaciter concurrerit, & seipsam excitârit. Quæ assertio cùm sudes sit in Calvinianorum oculis, (Pala. lib. 6. Syntag. c. 43. Buca. in L. C. loc. 62. q. 4. &c.) nos eam probamus 1. Ab idiomatum ex unione personali cum Λόγῳ resultante communicatione. Non enim in se & per se humanitas vivifica est, sed quia Deus sibi eam univit, quæ unio nec quoad animam, nec quoad carnem, per mortem soluta fuit, ut eruditè disserit etiam Thom. part. 3. q. 53. art. 4. 2. Ab ipsius scripturæ approbatione, quæ resuscitationem filii Dei, toti tribuit ὑψίζῳ μόνῳ Joh. 2. v. 19. Joh. 10. v. 18.

IX. 3. Materia seu subjectum resurrectionis. Hoc non facimus utramque Christi naturam, uti Sohnius, cùm in naturam divinam non cadat mutabilitas, & sic nequè resurrectio; Nec propriè animam Christi, quippe quæ immortalis, ac propterea nec mori, nec resurgere potuit; Sed corpus Christi, quoniam secundùm corpus tantùm cecidit, secundùm hoc ergò tantùm resurgere debuit & potuit. Non autem surrexit corpus phantasticum; aliàs resurrectio esset phantastica: Sed fuit verum & numero idem corpus, non quoad qualitates, sed substantiam; qui enim gloriam corpori contulit, naturam non abstulit, quàm Christus non modò verbis asseruit, sed omnibus dispulorum sensibus ingessit. Comprobat veritatem & identitatem corporis CHRISTI, ejus forma, quæ, quia determinata & eadem numero, determinatam & eandem numero materiam appetit. Num verò & carnem, ossa, sangvinem, & membra interiora, quæ prius habuit, post resurrectionem retinuerit, quæritur? Negant Photiniani (Socinus de statu primi homin. c. 8. p. 236. Ostorod. in Inst. c. 41. §. 1.) Verùm 1. contra Christi assertionem; quâ se carnem & ossa habere affirmat, suumque corpus spiritui seu spectro opponit; 2. corporis perfectionem. Corpus resurrexit, idque humanum, quia hoc cecidit: jam verò ad naturam corporis humani pertinet caro, sangvis, os, & alia hujusmodi. Ergò hæc de CHRISTI corpore neganda non sunt: licet enim spirituale sit, spiritus tamen non est. 3. veram resurrectionem. Resurrectio non est novi corporis creatio, sed demortui in vitam revocatio. Demortuum autem CHRISTI corpus absque carne, ossibus, sangvine, & aliis membris non fuit: sine his itaque nec resurgere potuit. Concluditur ex his, quòd & nos nostra corpora eadem numero, quoad substantiam & membra integrantia, simus recepturi; tum, quia capiti assimilari debeant membra; tum, quia resurrectio CHRISTI fuit exemplum resurrectionis nostræ.

X. Hoc corpus Christi per resurrectionem novis quibusdam qualitatibus exornat: factum n. est immortale, clarum, agile, subtile f. Spirituale. Immortale corpus CHRISTI fuisse post resurrectionem, dum in his terris erat, Photiniani inficiantur, (Socin. de stat. prim. hom. c. 2. p. 273. Ostor. in Inst. c. 41. p. 393.) At nobis immotæ veritatis est axioma hoc : Qvicunqve non ampliùs moritur (l) sed per suam mortem destruxit eum, qui habebat mortis imperium (m) & de morte triumphavit (n) mortalis is non sine blasphemia dicitur. Clarum ipsius corpus fuisse Paulus asserit Phil. 3. v. 21. ubi nostra corpora qvondam conformia futura ipsius corpori glorioso ait. Hujus autem claritatis radios repressit, dum se discipulis suis redivivum exhibuit, ob oculorum eorum imbecillitatem, qui hos ferre non poterant. Agilitatem & invisibilitatem demonstrat historia à Luc. c. 24. v. 31. descripta, ubi è conspectu duorum discipulorum in hospitio Emauntico evanuisse dicitur, qvod non nisi corpori spirituali & agilitate prædito competit. Subtilitatem ejus probat sepulchri penetratio, & per januas clausas ad discipulos ingressus. Hæc tamen corporis gloria, toto genere ab ea differt, qvam ex sessione ad dextram Dei obtinet : illam n. communem habet cum electis, hanc v. non item.

XI. 4. Forma seu modus resurrectionis. Ubi duo actus considerandi : I. Corporis & animæ unio. Nam, voluit anima corpori vicissim reuniri, ob potentiam agendi in corpus, & dependentiam à corpore. Resumsit itaque corpus animam, qvam dimiserat, & anima corpus, qvod deposuerat, illudqve vivificat, ut jam non sine sensu, sine motu, sine vita, ut anteà, mortuum sic, sed sentiat, moveatur, & vivat. An v. factâ hâc unione, Christus qvoqve sangvinem effusum in ara crucis, intra venas receperit, à nonnullis qværitur ? Negant pleriqve sodalium Calvini, eumqve dudum putrefactum non sine absurditate ajunt : seqvitur enim hinc 1: corruptibili sangvine factam esse nostram redemtionem, contrà claram assertionem Petr. 1. Epist. 1. v. 18. 2. factam partis substantialis naturæ assumtæ depositionem, contra antiqvitatis regulam : Qvod semel assumsit, nunqvam deposuit. 3. Christum vidisse corruptionem, contra scripturam Propheticam ; (o) &l Apostolicam (p). II. E sepulchro egressio, qvam non per cessionem lapidis sepulchralis, sed potiùs sepulchri penetrationem factam esse, cum antiqvitate credimus. Qüenim mortalis clausô virginis uterô vitam ingredi potuit, utiqve immortalis clausô sepulchro redivivus prodire potuit. Licet splendide hanc negent Calviniani (Joh. Crocius in convers. Prut. part. 1. considerat. prob. 9. p. 461.) nobis tamen ca verior, quia majestatem & gloriam Christi magis auget, & cum scriptura convenientior apparet, quæ motum terræ, in quo Christus resurrexit, devolutionem lapidis præcessisse affirmat, finem devolutionis, non Christi resurrectionem, sed ejus patefactionem, annotat (q) & Christum per resurrectionem se filium Dei demonstrâsse, affirmat, (r)

XII. 5. Fines resurrectionis. Horum 1. Vaticiniorum impletio. Prædicta enim est Christi resurrectio in scripturis, quam impleri oportet, ob immutabile Dei decretum. Resurgere itaque debuit Christus ut vaticiniorum sua constet veritas. 2. Sufficientiæ meriti demonstratio. Nam si Christus mansisset in morte, de insufficientia meriti argumentum fuisset. Ubi enim mors, ibi peccatum, quia illa hujus pœna. 3. Mediatoris officii peractio. Christus perpetuus noster Mediator est; in morte ergò manere non debuit. Non enim suffiieiebat, morte beneficia mereri, sed ea etiam per resurrectionem conferri oportebat, Quomodo autem conferre potuit, si non resurrexisset?

XIII. Restat fructuum ubertas, seu effecta resurrectionis, quorum benè multa scriptura numerat. Nobis ob chartæ angustiam, bina tantùm videre licet. Prior Christum respicit, & est, gloriæ ipsius manifestatio. Per resurrectionem CHRISTI demonstratur ipsius Deitas, quòd nim. sit unigenitus & naturalis Dei filius, ex essentia patris ab æterno genitus, ideoq; verus Deus, quia carnem suam virtute propriâ resuscitavit, quod solius Dei proprium est. Per resurrectionem demonstratur item carnis ipsius per unionem communicata divina majestas, quam ut filius hominis in ipso conceptionis momento habuit, secundùm quam etiam ipsa caro resurrectionem operata est, ut th. 8. probatum. Posterior homines respicit, & est corporum resuscitatio. Hæc duplex, 1. spiritualis, in regeneratione animæ consistens: Christus enim pro omnibus fuit mortuus, ut nos ipsi vivamus (s) resuscitavit nos à peccatis, ut in novitate vitæ ambulemus (t) 2. corporalis, quæ est ad vitam seu beatitatem æternam. Est enim CHRISTI resurrectio clavis nostræ resurrectionis, ut Tertullianus ait. Movetur hîc quæstio, An hic fructus ad omnes indiscretè pertineat homines? Respondemus breviter: Christus ut Judex, omnipotente suâ virtute & efficacia, omnes quidem homines a mortuis in extremo die resuscitabit, ob infallabile decretum, Hebr. 9. v. 27. expressum: Verum, ut redemptor, vi meriti & resurrectionis, tantum suscitabit fideles, quorum resurrectio, non vero impiorum, ut fructus ex Christi resurrectione dependet, quod sequentibus probamus rationibus: 1. sumimus a necessario resurrectionis, quae sit vi meriti Christi, adjuncto, quod est vita & salus aeterna, prout constat e totius 1. Cor. 15. capitis contextu. Quis autem impios ad vitam & aeternam beatitudinem resurrecturos affirmare audet? 2. a perpetuo capitis cum membris tantum connexu. Christi resurrectio, se habet ad resurrectionem resurgeutium vi & meriti resurrectionis Christi, ut capitis ad membra: Qui ergo membra corporis mystici Christi non sunt, illi vi resurrectionis capitis non resurgent; quia caput essentialiter tantum membris connectitur. 3. a resurrectionis Christi effectu. Christus dicitur ἀπαρχὴ resurgentium, eo, quod sua resurrectione inde dependentem sanctificet: Qua autem ratione resurrectio impiorum, resurrectione Christi sanctificabitur, cum resurrectioni Christi conformis non sit, nec illi Christi sint? Manet itaque verum, tantum fideles vi & merito resurrectionis Christi resurgere.

XIV. Hactenus ergo Christum a mortuis resurrexisse audisti, o homo, quid jam tibi faciendum sit, cogites quaeso. Surge & tu cito spiritualiter, quo dignus sis resurgere corporaliter: Surge cito a peccatis ad poenitentiam, quo dignus sis surgere e sepulchro ad gloriam: cum illa sine mora propera; hanc fideliter & patienter exspecta. Christus caput, tu membrum es; surrexit illud, resurges & tu. Saeviat itaque Leo infernalis, torqueant inimici, occidant Tyranni: revixit Redemtor tuus, vivificabit etiam te, omniumq; fidelium corpora mortalia. Ergo veni Domine, & noli tardare; venio cito, Amen. Etiam veni Domine Jesu!


## 42 Disputation XLII. On the glorification of the body of Christ, and his diverse appearance

Thesis I.

Recently we recalled the saving resurrection of Jesus Christ to the file of our inquiry, and we polished it according to the plan of our undertaking; now the order demands that we also discuss something concerning its adjuncts. Which, that it may turn out happily,

— O God, reach out to us your right hand, helpful with your mercy!

II. Therefore, if we wish to estimate the matter correctly, two adjuncts of the resurrection of Christ come primarily to be considered, namely, 1. The true glorification of the body of Christ; and 2. His diverse appearing.

III. Moreover, the glorification of the body of Christ is that condition of it by which, after the satisfaction for the sins of the whole human race had been completed here on earth, it was endowed with the new qualities proper to glorified bodies.

IV. Where it is to be noted before all else that the gift of glorification concerns the human nature of Christ, yet not established outside of, but in the τῷ λόγῳ ὑποστάσει; nevertheless in such a way that it is meanwhile truly attributed to the whole Christ, though not to the whole of Christ, and indeed for this reason, because 1. the human nature does not subsist by itself, but in the ὑποστάσει τῷ λόγῳ, and thus makes both the whole and one Christ together with the λόγῳ: 2. because the properties of one nature are frequently attributed to the whole person, as is otherwise most well-known from the first kind of communication of idioms.

V. Sohnius in this place (a) makes a twofold glorification of Christ, divine and human, and attributes the latter to the human, the former to the divine nature of Christ, and by this reasoning joins the whole Christ and the whole of Christ, so that he does not fear to assert that glorification truly belongs both to the whole Christ and to the whole of Christ. Which opinion, as it is new in true theology, so it exists as alien to the Christian faith.

VI. For, although we may concede that this glorification can be attributed to the whole Christ, nevertheless we cannot but deny it to the whole of Christ, for the reason that the subject of such glorification is not the Deity, not the whole person of Christ according to both natures, as the antagonist plays, but the human nature of Christ; which, besides other things, is testified by,

VII. α. The emphasis and weight of this predication is that Christ is glorified. For it is certain that this belongs to Christ, not by reason of his divine nature, which is devoid of all change, (b) and from eternity to eternity is most perfect in itself, but by reason of his human nature, which is both mutable, and can be raised to a better state, and transferred from a lower degree of glory to a higher.

VIII. β. The inversion of passion and glorification, which belongs to Christ with respect to the same nature; and this exists as a certain (c) ἀνταποδοσις (recompense) of that.

IX. But when we properly ascribe glorification to the human nature of Christ, or as we otherwise speak, to his body itself, we do not understand, as some do, a body that is absolutely spiritual and celestial, but one that is truly physical in its ὐσίαν (essence), and indeed that very same body in which he first appeared on this earth, walked about in it, performed miracles, sustained passion and death, and indeed in which he himself also rose again after death was overcome. This can be confirmed by many most firm and clearly invincible arguments. For the sake of brevity, we shall propose only one or two.

X. Let this therefore be the first: If our bodies will be glorified in the same number, it is necessary that Christ's body, as such, was also glorified, if indeed those will be (d) conformed to this. But our bodies will be glorified in the same number. Therefore. The minor premise, although it is placed beyond the hazard of doubt among all good men, is nevertheless proven out of an abundance of caution.

XI. α. From 1 Cor. 15:53. 'This corruptible must put on incorruption.' Where the Apostle certainly points with his finger to our same essence, as Tertullian speaks. For he could not have spoken more expressly, unless he were holding his own skin in his hands.

XII. β. From Job 19:26. 'I shall again be surrounded by my skin, and in my flesh I shall see my God.' By which words, indeed, the numerical unity of our bodies is most clearly shown.

XIII. Let the second be: If Christ will never lay aside what he once assumed, it follows that he retained in his glorification the same body that he had in his passion: since the laying aside and the retention mutually exclude each other, so that where the one dominates, the other is cast out; and vice versa. But Christ will never lay aside what he once assumed. Therefore. The minor premise is most strongly confirmed,

XIV. α. From the very words of Christ, (e) see my hands and my feet, handle me, and see: By which words he shows that after his glorification he did not divest himself of his true and natural body, but in reality retained it.
