Nor is it to be thought that these things were done by the Lord with the disciples by some peculiar dispensation, in such a way that he would sometimes show his body as spiritual, as if it were physical, when he dealt with the Apostles so that they might recognize him; but that at other times he would assume the plenary condition of his spiritual body, when he vanished, when he entered to the Apostles with the doors shut, and when he suddenly withdrew himself from the eyes of others: for indeed, when he became invisible, he was not destitute of flesh or hands, but the eyes of men were held so that they would not (f) recognize him. Therefore, to argue from the impediment of the eyes to a diversity of body, the consequence is invalid.

XV. β. From his conversation with the disciples for 40 days, as well as his visible ascension into heaven. For Christ willed to observe, or rather to perform, all these things in such a way as to prove manifestly that he still retains the human body assumed in the womb of his mother, and carries it with him into heaven.

XVI. γ. From other sayings of Scripture, by which Christ after his glorification, as also after his ascension into heaven, is proclaimed as true man, as Matt. 16:27; 24:30; 25:31. Luke 21:27. The Son of man is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels. Matt. 26:64. From now on you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of the power of God, and coming in the clouds: as also Luke 21:36. Watch at all times, praying that you may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that are to come, and to stand before the Son of man.

XVII. 3. Let it be: If the body of CHRIST had been of one substance before his glorification, and had been made of another after it, then one thing would have struggled, and another would have been crowned. But the latter is ἄτοπον [absurd], because that which struggled must be crowned, and that which was weak must be glorified. Therefore the former is also.

XVIII. From these arguments, therefore, it is most manifestly evident that before and after the glorification of Christ's body, its numerical unity remained safe and intact. In order that this very thing may be more fully illustrated, we shall add the solution of that objection which is wont to be brought forward by some to the contrary. This, however, is as follows:

XIX. Wherever the proper πάθη [affections/properties] are removed, there also the subject of those πάθη is removed; and therefore, where there are new πάθη, there is also a new sub ject: But in the glorification of the body of Christ, his πάθη φυσικὰ (natural affections) were absent, and in their place (which will shine forth later from the endowments causing the glorification itself) succeeded πάθη πνευματικὰ (spiritual affections). Therefore, the physical body was also absent, and another was present, namely, a spiritual one. XX. But we respond to the Major premise, and indeed 1. that when accidents are removed, the subject itself is not immediately removed: since the consequence from the variation of qualities to the change of the subject is not valid. For one and the same substance can receive different accidents in itself, as e.g. water now cold, now heat; and yet its quiddity is in no way varied. Thus also the body of Christ in glorification put off physical infirmities, and, as will be shown in its place, assumed new qualities, and yet without either its corruption or essential change. Whence Tertullian rightly wrote concerning the resurrection of the flesh: God did not take away the substance to which He attributed an angelic quality. 2. that those πάθη (affections) are not affections of the body of Christ, as such, but as it is infirm for our sake. Therefore, with these removed, the infirmity is indeed removed, but not the body, insofar as it is a body. For in this respect they are not its own.

XXI. We acknowledge, however, that Christ was finally glorified as to His body only after He had rendered satisfaction for the sins of the whole human race by suffering and dying in these lands.

XXI. For this order was required by a. the majesty of God: since according to this it was fitting for Him to offer sacrifice in these lands before He entered into His glory, i.e., was glorified, Luke 24:26. For to enter into glory is, among other things, nothing else than to receive glorification shining forth fully in the body.

XXIII. β. The necessity itself, which strictly demanded that He should satisfy before He began to reign glorified; that He should suffer before He obtained heavenly glory.

XXIV. γ. His own will, which freely ordained that He should depart from here before He fully assumed glorification.

XXV. We by no means ascribe this glorification to the body of CHRIST as a reward for labor; since, if it were a reward, He certainly would never have had it as a reward before the completion of His labor, when nevertheless that transfiguration, which is reported to have happened on the mountain in Matthew 17, demonstrates to the eye that He had it in a certain way. For it was nothing other than a showing forth of that glorification.

XXVI. Moreover, those qualities with which the body of CHRIST was adorned immediately at the very moment of the resurrection completed that glorification.

XXVII. These, however, are of two kinds: for some pertain to the body, but others to the soul.

XXVIII. Those which pertain to the body are such endowments by which it was rendered glorious, so that it is and remains such for eternity.

XXIX. There are, moreover, primarily four of them: 1. is immortality, or impassibility, i.e., liberation from all kinds of sufferings; to which mortality or suffering is opposed.

XXX. 2. It is Glory or Brightness, by which the body of CHRIST was then made immune from all impurity, deformity, and defect, and on the other hand was most perfectly filled with ineffable light and splendor. Ignominy is opposed to it.

Latin:

Thesis. I.

PRoximè salutiferam Jesu CHRISTI resurrectionem sub disquisitionis limam revocavimus, eamque pro instituti nostri ratione expolivimus; nunc ordo postulat ut de ejus adjunctis etiam aliqvid differamus. Id qvod, ut feliciter eveniat,

— Deus ô mi porrige nobis Auxiliatricem clementi Numine dextram!

II. Itaq; si rem rectè, æstimare velimus, duo resurrectionis CHRISTI adjuncta præcipuè veniunt consideranda, nempe, 1. Vera corporis Christi glorificatio; & 2. diversa ejus apparitio.

III. Est autem glorificatio corporis Christi talis ejus conditio, quâ illud, peractâ hisce in terris satisfactione pro totius generis humani peccatis, novis qualitatibus corporum glorificatorum propriis fuit dotatum.

IV. Ubi ante omnia notandum, glorificationis donum concernere humanam Christi naturâ, non tamen extra, sed in τῷ λόγῳ ὑποστάσει constitutam; attamen ita, ut id intereà toti Christo, licet non toti Christi, verè attribuatur, & qvidem ideò, quia 1. humana natura non per se, sed in ὑποστάσει τῷ λόγῳ, subsistit, sicq; & totũ & unum Christum unà cum λόγῳ efficit: 2. quia unius naturæ propria freqventer toti personæ attribuuntur, ut aliàs ex primo communicationis Idiomatum genere est qvàm notissimum.

V. Sohnius hôc in loco (a) duplicem facit Christi glorificationem, divinam, & humanam, hancqve humanæ, illam v. divinæ Christi naturæ attribuit, atq; hâc ratione totum Christum, & totum Christi, conjungit, ita, ut & toti CHRISTO & toti Christi verè competere glorificationem, asserere nil vereatur. Qvæ sententiâ, ut in verâ Theologiâ nova, ita â fide Christiana existit aliena.

VI. Nam, licet concedamus, hanc glorificationem toti Christo posse attribui, tamen non aliter possumus, qvin eam toti Christi denegemus, ideò, quia subjectum ejusmodi glorificationis non est Deitas, non tota persona Christi secundùm utramqve naturam, ut Antagonista ludit, sed humana Christi natura; id qvod præter alia testantur,

VII. α. Emphasis & pondus hujus prædicationis, Christus est glorificatus. Nam hanc competere Christo, certum est, non ratione naturæ divinæ, quæ omnis mutationis expers, (b) & ab æterno in æternum in se perfectissima est, sed humanæ, quæ & mutabilis est, & in meliorem statum evehi, & ab inferiore gradu gloriæ in superiorem transferri potest.

VIII. β. Αντιστροφη passionis & glorificationis, quæ Christo ejusdem naturæ respectu competit; hæcque illius (c) ἀνταποδοσις quædam existit.

IX. Quando autem humanæ Christi naturæ, seu ut alias loquimur, ipsius corpori glorificationem propriè adscribimus, non intelligimus cum quibusdam corpus absolutè spirituale & cœlicum, sed reverà quoad ὐσίαν Physicum, & quidem illud ipsum, quô primùm in his terris apparuit, in eis obambulavit, miracula edidit, passionem & mortem sustinuit, imò quô ipsô etiam suparatâ morte resurrexit. Id quod multis firmissimis planeque invictis argumentis potest confirmari. Brevitatis causâ tantummodò unum atque alterum proponemus.

X. Hoc ergo 1. esto: Si corpora nostra eadem numerô glorificabuntur, & Christi corpus, quâ tale, fuisse glorificatum, necesse est, si quidem illa huic erunt (d) conformia. Atqui nostra corpora eadé numero glorificabuntur. Ergo. Minor, quamvis apud omnes bonos extra dubitationis aleam est posita, tamen ex abundanti probatur.

XI. α. Ex 1. Cor. 15, 53. Oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem. Ubi certè Apostolus eandem nostram essentiam, ut Tertullianus loquitur, digitô demonstrat. Magis enim expressè loqui non poterat, nisi cutem suam manibus teneret.

XII. β. Ex Job. 19, 26. Rursus circumdabor pelle meâ, & in carne meâ videbo Deum meum. Qvibus sanè verbis nostrorum corporum unitas numerica clarissimè ostenditur.

XIII. 2. esto: Si Christus, quod semel assumsit, nunquam deponet, sequitur, illum idem retinuisse corpus in glorificatione, quod habuit in passione: siquidem depositio & retentio se invicem tollunt, ita, ut ubi illa dominetur, hæc ejiciatur; & contra. Atqui, quod Christus semel assumsit, nunquam deponet. Ergo. Minor fortissimè confirmatur,

XIV. α. Ex ipsius Christi verbis, (e) videte manus meas, & pedes meos, contrectate me, & videte: Quibus verbis ostendit, se post glorificationem verum & naturale corpus non exuisse, sed reverà illud retinuisse. Nec æstimandum, peculiari quâdam dispensatione hæc à Domino cum discipulis fuisse gesta, ita, ut quandoq; corpus suum spirituale, tanquàm physicum ostenderet, qvando sid egit cum Apostolis, ut eum agnoverint: qvandoq; verò plenariam corporis sui spiritualis conditionem usurparet, qvando evanuit, ad Apostolos clausis januis ingressus fuit, aliorumq; ab oculis repentè se subduxit: Siquidem, qvando invisibilis factus fuit, non carne aut manibus destituebatur, sed oculi hominum, ne ipsum (f) agnoscerent, tenebantur, Argumentari itaq; ab impedimento oculorum ad diversitatem corporis, non valet conseqventia.

XV. β. Ex ejusdem per 40. dies cum discipulis conversatione, nec non visibili in cœlum adscensione. Hæc enim omnia CHRISTUS ita observare, veriùs peragere, voluit, ut manifestè probaret, se corpus humanum, in utero matris assumtum, adhuc retinere, & secum in cœlum subvehere.

XVI. γ. Ex aliis scripturæ dictis, quibus Christus post glorificationem, ut & in cœlum adscensionem, verus homo prædicatur, ut Mat. 16, 27; 24, 30; 25, 31. Luc. 21, 27. Filius hominis venturus est in gloriâ Patris sui cum Angelis suis. Matth. 26, 64. à modò videbitis filium hominis sedentem à dextris virtutis Dei, & venientem in nubibus: ut & Luc. 21, 36. Vigilate omni tempore, orantes, ut digni habeamini fugere ista omnia, qvæ futura sunt, & stare ante filium hominis.

XVII. 3. esto: Si corpus CHRISTI ante glorificationem aliâ fuisset substantiâ, & post eam etiã aliâ esset facta, tum aliud certasset, & aliud coronatum fuisset. Atqvi posterius est ἄτοπον, qvia illud coronandũ, qvod certavit, illud glorificandum, qvod infirmum fuit. Ergò & pri9.

XVIII. Ex hisce igitur argumentis manifestissimè patet, ante & post corporis Christi glorificationem, numericam ejus unitatem salvam & integram mansisse. Qvod ipsum, ut pleniùs illustretur, addemus solutionem illius objectionis, qvæ in contrarium à quibusdam afferti solet. Hæc autem talis est:

XIX. Ubicunqve tolluntur propria πάθη, ibi qvoqve tollitur subjectum istorum παθῶν; ideoq; ubi nova πάθη, ibi novum qvoq; subjectum: Sed in glorificatione corporis Christi abfuerunt ejus πάθη φυσικὰ, eorumq́; in locum (qvod postmodùm ex dotibus ipsam glorificationem causantibus elucebit) successerunt πάθη πνευματικὰ. Ergò etiam abfuit corpus physicum, & adfuit aliud, nempe spirituale. XX. Sed nos respondemus ad Majorem, & qvidem 1. qvòd sublatis accidentibus non statim tollatur ipsum subjectum: siqvidem, à variatione qvalitatum ad immutationem subjecti nó valet conseqventia. Potest enim una eademq́; substantia diversa in se recipere accidentia, ut e.g. Aqva modò frigus, modò calorem; & tamen ej⁹ qvidditas nullatenus variatur. Sic etiam corpus Christi in glorificatione exuit infirmitates physicas, &, ut suô locô ostendetur, assumsit qvalitates novas, & tamen sine sui vel corruptione, vel essentiali mutatione.Unde rectè scripsit Tertullianus de resurrect.carn.Non substantiam Deus abstulit, cui qvalitatem Angelicam attribuit. 2. qvòd πάθη ista non sint affectiones corporis Christi, qvà tale, sed qvà nostri causâ infirmum est. Iis igitur sublatis, tollitur qvidem infirmitas, non v. corpus,qvaten⁹ est corpus.Hoc enim respectu propria ejus non sunt.

XXI. Agnoscimus autem Christum tum demum qvoad corpus suum fuisse glorificatum, postqvàm in his terris patiendo & moriendo pro totius generis humani peccatis satisfactionem præstitit.

XXI. Nam istum ordinem reqvirebat a. Dei majestas: siqvidem juxta hanc oportuit eum priùs offerre in his terris sacrificium, qvàm suam in gloriam ingrederetur, h.e. glorificaretur, Luc. 24, 26. Est n. in gloriam ingredi, inter alia qvoqve nihil aliud, qvàm glorificationem in corpore plenariè fulgentem accipere.

XXIII. β. Ipsa necessitas, qvæ strictè postulabat, ut priùs satifaceret, qvàm glorificatus regnare inciperet; priùs pateretur, qvàm gloriâ cœlesti potiretur.

XXIV. γ. Propria ejus voluntas, qvæ liberè ita dispensabat, ut priùs ab hinc migraret, qvàm plenariè glorificationem assumeret.

XXV. Minimè autem hanc glorificationem corpori CHRISTI, ut laboris mercedem, adscribimus; si qvidem, si illa esset merces, certè eam tanqvàm mercedem ante sui laboris absolutionem nunqvam habuisset, cùm tamen qvoddammodò habuisse, transfiguratio illa, qvæ Matth. 17. in monte perhibetur facta, ad oculum demonstrat. Fuit enim nihil aliud,qvàm istius glorificationis ostensio.

XXVI. Absolverunt autem istam glorificationem qualitates illæ, qvibus corpus CHRISTI, statim in ipso resurrectionis momento, fuit adornatum.

XXVII. Hæ verò sunt duorum generum: quædam enim spectant ad corpus, qvædam verò ad animam.

XXVIII. Qvæ ad corpus spectant, sunt ejusmodi dotes qvibus illud gloriosum fuit redditum, ita, ut in æternum tale sit & maneat.

XXIX. Sunt autem illarum imprimis qvatuor: 1. est immortalitas, seu impassibilitas, h. e. liberatio ab omnibus passionum generibus; cui opponitur mortalitas vel passio.

XXX. 2. Est Gloria seu Claritas, qvâ corpus CHRISTI ab omni impuritate, deformitate, & defectu tunc immune factum, contra v. luce & splendore ineffabili perfectissimè repletum fuit. Ei opponitur ignominia.


### XXVI. Indeed, we maintain that the body of CHRIST, being holy and conceived by…

XXVI. Indeed, we maintain that the body of CHRIST, being holy and conceived by the Holy Spirit himself, was not properly and in itself subject to all these evils, and therefore there was no need for it to lay them aside in such a manner in the state of its glorification. Meanwhile, however, since He emptied Himself and took upon Himself all our infirmities, and thus was made subject to such defects, we cannot but attribute to Him a real laying aside of them and an assumption of perfect glory: although we are not ignorant that it was always glorious by the power and virtue of the personal Union.

XXXII. 3. is Power or Agility, by reason of which the body of CHRIST can move itself in a moment, and can be instantly wherever His spirit wills. Infirmity is opposed to this.

XXXIII. 4. is Subtlety or spiritual operation, to which the animal [operation] is opposed; of which the latter depended only naturally upon His soul: but the former consists even now solely in the most present governance of the Holy Spirit and of the λόγος Himself.

XXXIV. And this was certainly that quality by the virtue of which Christ was able to penetrate with His body through the sepulchral stone not yet rolled away, to stand suddenly in the midst of the disciples with the doors closed, and to become ἄφαντος; as has been demonstrated elsewhere.

XXXV. But the qualities which pertain to the soul are such endowmen ts, with which it was adorned to the highest perfection that can possibly fall to it as a created nature, whether we consider the intellect or the will.

XXXVI. As far as the intellect is concerned, Christ now knows most perfectly with his human mind all the secrets of all mysteries, whether they be past, present, or future, as if they were objects before his own eyes and senses.

XXXVII. But whether he knows and thinks of these, and whatever else might be said, by distinct and successive acts of thinking, or by ideas or intelligible species, it is not for us to pry into more deeply: Let it suffice for us if we know the fact, even if we do not grasp its manner exactly.

XXXIIX. As concerns the will, this too, by the gift of glorification, now wills most simply all things that are in harmony with the divine essence and will, and absolutely turns away from all things that are less in agreement with it: For indeed, to say it in a word, all these virtues—whether they be the four cardinal ones: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice; or those three theological ones: faith, hope, and charity; or those seven which others call the gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord—all these virtues, I say, he wills in the most perfect manner possible; nay, of such a kind that it is held to be even greater and more perfect than the most perfect will of the angels.

XXXIX. When, however, we assert that the body of CHRIST, together with his soul, is adorned with these as well as many other gifts, not only finite (in that they inhere in him subjectively), but also common with the elect in the other life (though differences of degree are preserved), we do not mean to detract in any way from the infinite glory and uncreated majesty which the flesh of CHRIST obtains from the personal union and the session at the right hand of God. For we consider that insofar as certain gifts are conferred upon it by the nature of glorification, not, however, by the grace of union. This is to be diligently observed against the Calvinists. And thus far concerning the first adjunct of the resurrection of CHRIST, namely, the glorification of his body.

XL. The second adjunct is his diverse appearance, which is a condition of CHRIST glorified in his body, by which he presented himself to be seen by the disciples and others, spoke with them, traveled, conversed, and ate and drank, and exhibited other testimonies of his true resurrection.

XLI. There is otherwise a twofold appearance of Christ; spiritual and corporal.

XLII. The spiritual is a representation of his grace, and is accustomed to occur, 1. in baptism, when he adopts us as brothers and co-heirs of eternal life.

XLIII. 2. In the Supper, when he renders us certain and indubitable of the adoption already made through the intervention of a most excellent pledge.

XLIV. 3. In daily repentance, when he accepts us again into grace, we who, having forgotten this adoption through failure, were again mindful of the same through contrition.

XLV. 4. In eternal life, when he will illuminate us, the elect, with his glory, and will bless us to the highest degree with eternal joys.

XLVI. But this spiritual appearance is not treated in this place.

XLVII. The corporal is the manifestation of the entire substance of Christ's body itself, which is twofold; for it either 1, has already been done long ago, or 2, is still expected to be in the future.

XLVIII. This, which is still future, will only be completed when Christ will appear in a visible manner on that critical day, about to pronounce judgment upon the good and the bad. Concerning which, however, it will be spoken elsewhere.

XLIX. That which was done long ago was then accomplished when Christ, having overcome death and assumed glorification, appeared to the Apostles and others in the same flesh: And concerning this appearance only are we concerned in this place.

L. To a plenary consideration of it, however, pertains primarily the order itself, which must be exactly observed in it: for if this is not observed, the whole will be obscure. This, indeed, according to the harmony of the Evangelical history, shall be established as follows:

LI. Indeed 1. Christ appeared to Mary Magdalene at the sepulcher, Mark 16:9 and John 20:11. Some doubt whether this appearance should be placed in the first position, since that which describes the manifestation of Christ made to the disciples at Emmaus precedes it, according to the opinion of those people. But it is most clearly evident from Mark, whom we follow in this place as a guide, that Christ, having been raised from the dead and at the same time glorified, πρῶτον, in the first place, appeared to Mary Magdalene.

LII. Papal writers contend that Christ, on the very day of his resurrection, nay, at the very hour, first of all appeared to the Blessed Virgin Mary, his mother, to whom this singular joy and glory was especially due, and who, on account of her incomparable love, had grieved more than all others over the passion of her son. But this is only an opinion, which Holy Scripture calls into doubt not only by silence, but even by contrary affirmation, when it asserts that Christ appeared first to Magdalene.

LIII. 2. He appeared to the women going to the sepulchre and returning from it, Matt. 28, 9. Mark indeed omits this appearance, as well as the following third one, and mentions in the second place that Christ appeared to the disciples going to Emmaus; nevertheless, it is understood from the other Evangelists that between the one which occurred to Mary Magdalene and the one which occurred to the disciples going to Emmaus, there must be interposed that which happened to the women returning from the sepulchre; nay, not only this, but also that which happened to Simon Peter. For the harmony of the Evangelists clearly teaches that those two appearances preceded that appearance of Christ which occurred to the disciples going to Emmaus.

LIV. Calvin thinks that this appearance of Christ made to these women, which Matthew describes, is the same as the appearance made to Mary Magdalene, which John describes: he asserts, therefore, that by synecdoche what was proper to one is extended by Matthew to all. But this opinion does not at all agree with the description of the Evangelists. For Mark mentions as something singular that Christ showed himself to be seen first of all to Mary Magdalene: nay, the very diversity of the circumstances, which a diligent inspection of the Gospel harmonies demonstrates to the eye, sufficiently confirms the diversity of these appearances.

LV. 3. He appeared to Simon Peter, which the disciples, hearing the news about the appearance of Christ made to those going to Emmaus, acknowledge, Luke 24, 34, and the Apostle Paul himself testifies, 1 Cor. 15, 5. Mark, as we have just perceived, omitted this appearance along with the preceding one, but because of the testimonies of those disciples, as well as of Paul himself, we judge that it must altogether be inserted between the manifestation made to the women returning from the sepulchre and that which occurred to those going to Emmaus, for the sake of the convenience of order.

LVI. Let the occasion, however, be noted in this place on which Christ appeared to Peter. Luke 24, 12 mentions that Peter ran alone to the sepulchre;

John 20:3. He contends that he ran out to that place with another disciple; so that by this reasoning it may be understood that Christ appeared either to Peter alone going to the sepulcher, or to the same person returning alone from the sepulcher, to which he had run with his companion, and having entered another way.

LVII. 4. He appeared to two going into Emmaus, Luke 24:15. Osiander in his Harmony, as also others, distinguish this appearance from that which happened to the disciples going into the country, which Mark describes in ch. 16:12, for a double reason: 1. because Mark expressly says those two went into the country to the village of Emmaus: 2. because Mark says the remaining disciples did not believe the report of those to whom Christ had appeared: Luke, however, asserts the plain contrary, namely, that having heard the report about Christ's manifestation, they joyfully proclaimed: The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon.

LIIX. But the Lord Doctor Gerhard in his Harmony, with Lyranus, rightly maintains that one and the same history is described by Mark and Luke: since all the circumstances agree, as he who looks into the text will easily notice.

LIX. Nor do the reasons which the authors of the contrary opinion use stand in the way. For in the first, that Mark says they went into the country, but Luke into the village of Emmaus, there is clearly no difficulty. For we distinguish between the middle of the way and its end or terminus: Luke wished to express the latter, but Mark the former; which the texts themselves demonstrate to the eye. But a greater difficulty seems to lie in the second, that Mark says the remaining disciples did not believe the report of those two; but Luke seems to assert the plain contrary. But the reconciliation of these is easy. For either each of the Evangelists attributes by synecdoche to the whole community what some of them did; or one of them considers faith not yet freed from all doubt, while the other considers their faith struggling against doubt. And by this reasoning, both to have believed and not to have believed can be said without any inconsistency.

LX. 5. He appeared to the disciples all together, except Thomas, gathered on the evening of the Passover, Mark 16:14. John 20:19 appends this appearance to that which happened to Mary Magdalene, but the order of history in Mark and Luke shows that it is to be placed only after that which occurred to those going to Emmaus.

LXI. Among other things, however, let it be noted here that the previous four appearances were only particular; but this fifth one, as well as all the following ones, besides that which we shall hear in its place happened to James, were general, which happened to the disciples either all, or to most of them, partly because they were to be freed from their unbelief and confirmed in the faith of this article, partly because they were to be witnesses of the Lord's resurrection, Luke 24, 28. Acts 1,

LXII. 6. He appeared again to the disciples John 20, 24. especially to Thomas, who had been absent in the preceding appearance, but now was present. John connects this appearance immediately with the preceding one, when he says in ch. 20, 26, that it took place on the eighth day after the former, which connection we also rightly observe in this place.

LXIII. 7. He appeared to seven disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, John 21, 1. For Christ wished to confirm his resurrection from the dead not only in Judea, namely in Jerusalem and its immediate vicinity, but also in Galilee, by various appearances, among which this very one is the first.

LXIV. This appearance, however, immediately follows that which was made to all the disciples together with Thomas; which the connective particle, μετὰ ταῦτα, manifestly shows. For this clearly shows the time when that happened; which, however, is not the next, or immediately joined with the time of the former, as Augustine thinks; but either following next, or not far distant, as the circumstances themselves prove.

LXV. 8. He appeared before a great multitude of disciples, on a certain mountain in Galilee; which appearance Matthew ch. 28, 16 and Paul 1 Cor. 15, 6 describe. This appearance happened a little before the return of the Apostles from Galilee into Judea, namely eight days before Christ's ascension, as the Lord Dr. Gerhard not improbably gathers from the circumstances in his Harmony, which see.

LXVI. Some, however, think that in this place Matthew and Paul, whom we joined above, by no means describe one and the same appearance of Christ: since Matthew makes express mention only of the eleven Apostles, but Paul of more than five hundred brethren. But the order of the appearances, which Paul recounts in the said place, manifestly shows that the appearance made before more than five hundred brethren is entirely the same as that which Matthew describes. And although Matthew makes mention only of the eleven disciples does not make, yet he by no means denies that others were also present; nay rather, when he says in verse 17, chapter 28, that some doubted, he shows that besides the Apostles others were also present, since the apostles had long since been confirmed in the truth of Christ's resurrection by so many of his appearances, that no room for doubt was left at all.

LXVII. 9. He appeared separately to James, who was called the brother of Christ, because he was born of the Virgin Mary's sister, Christ's maternal aunt. This appearance, although it is described by none of the Evangelists, Paul nevertheless makes express mention of it, and attaches it immediately to the one just explained in 1 Cor. 15. 7.

LXVIII. But let us not think as if this appearance, since all the Evangelists are silent about it, had been invented by Paul. For far be it from us to think such a thing of so great an Apostle: but let us firmly believe that it truly happened to James, especially since the credibility of this Apostle, a most select instrument of God, is by no means to be disparaged, and since not all things that happened were written down by the Evangelists and digested into books.

LXIX. 10. He appeared to all the Apostles as they were reclining at table, Mark 16. 14. And this is that appearance which took place on the very day of the resurrection, and it can deservedly be called the happy conclusion of all the appearances.

LXX. Aretius in his Theological Problems, Loc. 13, dares to attach to this appearance yet another, which, namely, was made to the disciples for the last time on the Mount of Olives in Acts 1, 12. But, since the whole text of that passage most manifestly shows that it agrees entirely with this tenth one of ours in all circumstances, we deservedly consider them one and the same.

LXXI. From these appearances of CHRIST just given, their number, if anyone desires it, can be gathered with little effort, so that there is no need to institute some superfluous repetition of it.

LXXII. Meanwhile, however, let this be observed in this place, that we have not recorded these appearances so that we might believe that Christ appeared only so many times, since he conversed with the disciples more often throughout 40 days; but those are brought forward from the whole history as the most certain arguments of the matter, which the Apostles handed down to memory, so that both they themselves, and all Christians, by looking at them in the battle against the devil, might establish that Christ, raised from the dead, is the true God; in the battle against the world, might understand his most present help; in the battle against their own flesh, might believe in a most certain victory; finally, in the battle against death, indeed in death itself, might certainly expect the resurrection of the whole flesh.

LXXIII. Which things all, that we, who also piously glory in the title of Christians, may certainly establish, understand, believe, and expect, — O God, stretch forth to us your helping right hand with your merciful divinity!

Latin:

XXVI. Eqvidem statuimus, CHRISTI corpus, utpote sanctum, & ab ipso Spiritu sancto conceptum, hisce malis omnibus propriè & per se non fuisse obnoxium, ideoq́; nec opus fuisse, ut illa tali modô in statu glorificationis suæ deponeret. Interim tamen, qvoniam se exinanivit, omnesq́; nostras infirmitates in se recepit, sicq́; ejusmodi defectibus factum fuit obnoxium, non aliter possumus, qvin ei realem eorum depositionem, perfectæq́; gloriæ assumtionem attribuamus: quamvis non ignoremus, illud vi & virtute Unionis personalis semper fuisse gloriosum.

XXXII. 3. est Potentia vel Agilitas, ob quam corpus CHRISTI se in momento movere, & ubicunqve ejus spiritus vult, protinus esse potest. Huic opponitur infirmitas.

XXXIII. 4. est Subtilitas seu spiritualis operatio, cui opponitur animalis; qvarum hæc tantùm ab ejus anima naturaliter dependebat: illa v. jam nunc in præsentissimâ Spiritus sancti ipsiusq́ve λόγε gubernatione unicè consistit.

XXXIV. Atqve hæc certè fuit qvalitas illa, cujus virtute Christus suo corpore per lapidem sepulchralem nondum revolutum penetrare, clausis foribus subitò in medio discipulorum stare, & ἄφαντος fieri potuit; ut alibi demonstratum est.

XXXV. Qvæ v. qualitates ad animam spectant, sunt ejusmodi dotes, quibus eousq; ad summam, quæ modò in eam tanquam naturam creatam cadere potest, perfectionem fuit ornata, sive spectemus intellectum, sive voluntatem.

XXXVI. Quod ad intellectum attinet, Christus jam humanâ suâ mente omnia omnium mysteriorum arcana, sive sint præterita, sive præsentia, sive futura, ac si oculis & sensibus ipsius essent objecta, perfectissimè novit.

XXXVII. Num autem hæc, & quæcunq; alia dici possint, sciat & cogitet, distinctis & successivis cogitandi actibus, sive ideis seu intelligibilibus speciebus, nostrum non est altiùs rimari: Sufficiat nobis, si rem novimus, licet ejus modum non exactè teneamus.

XXXIIX. Quod voluntatem concernit, & hæcce ex glorificationis dote jam omnia, quæ cum divinâ essentiâ & voluntate congruunt, simplicissimè vult, omniaqve, quæ cum illa minùs conveniunt, absolutè aversatur: Qvippè hæc, ut verbô dicam, omnes virtutes, sive sint illæ cardinales qvatuor, prudentia, fortitudo, temperantia, & justitia; sive tres illæ Theologicæ, fides, spes, & charitas; sive illæ septem, qvas aliàs vocant dona Spiritûs sancti, sapientia, intellectus, consilium, fortitudo, scientia, pietas, & timor Domini, omnes inqvã istas virtutes modô vult quam perfectissimô; imò ejusmodi, qvi etiam perfectissimâ Angelorum voluntate major & perfectior habetur.

XXXIX. Qvando autem CHRISTI corpus unà cum ejus anima hisce, ut & aliis multis dotibus, non tantùm (qvod illi subjectivè inhæreant) finitis, verùm etiam cum electis in altera vita (servatis tamen graduum differentiis) communibus exornatum esse asserimus, nihil qvicqvam intereà infinitæ gloriæ, atqve increatæ majestati, qvam caro CHRISTI ex unione personali, & sessione ad dextram Dei obtinet, derogatum volumus. Consideramus enim illud, qvatenus ei qvædam dona ex natura glorificationis, non v. ex gratia unionis conferuntur. Qvod diligenter contra Calvinianos observandum. Atq; huç usqve de primo resurrectionis CHRISTI adjuncto, nempe de ipsius corporis glorificatione.

XL. Alterum adjunctum est diversa ejusdem apparitio, quæ est conditio CHRISTI qvoad corpus glorificati, quâ se discipulis, ut & aliis, visendum præbuit, cum eis locutus est, iter fecit, conversatus est, edit, est, edit, & bibit, aliaq́ve veræ resurrectionis testimonia exhibuit.

XLI. Est alias apparitio Christi duplex; Spiritualis, & corporalis.

XLII. Spiritualis est repræsentatio ejus gratiæ, soletq́; fieri, 1. in baptismo, qvando nos in fratres & cohæredes vitæ æternæ adoptat.

XLIII. 2. In Cœnâ, qvando nos de facta adoptione præstantiffimi pignoris interventu certos indubitatosq́; reddit.

XLIV. 3. In qvotidiana pœnitentia, qvando nos qvi per defectionem hujus adoptionis obliti, rursus v. per contritionem ejusdem reeordati eramus, iterum in gratiam acceptat.

XLV. 4. In vita æterna, qvando nos electos gloriâ suâ collustrabit, æternisq́; lætitiis ad summum usq; beabit.

XLVI. Verùm de hâc spirituali apparitione hôc in locô non agitur.

XLVII. Corporalis est integræ ipsius corporis Christi substantiæ manifestatio, qvæ duplex; vel enim 1, jamdudum facta est, vel 2, adhuc futura expectatur.

XLVIII. Hæc, qvæ adhuc futura, tum demum perficietur, qvando Christus visibili modô in die illô critico apparebit, judex bonis & malis sententiam dicturus. De qvâ tamen alibi dicetur.

XLIX. Illa qvæ jam dudum facta, tunc fuit peracta, qvando Christus superatâ morte, assumptaq́; glorificatione, Apostolis & aliis in eâdem carne apparuit: Et de hâc apparitione tantùm hôc locô sumus solliciti.

L. Ad plenariam autem ejus considerationem spectat imprimis ipse ordo, qvi in illa exactè debet observari: hôc enim non observato, illa tota erit obscura. Is a. juxta historiæ Evangelicæ harmoniam talis constituetur:

LI. Eqvidem 1. apparuit Christus Mariæ Magdalenæ apud sepulchrum, Mar. 16, 9. & Joh. 20, 11. Dubitant nonnulli, num hæc apparitio primô locô sit ponenda, cùm eam illa, qvæ describit mani festatio nem Christi discipulis in Emaus factam, secundùm istorum opinionem præcedat. Sed manifestissimè patet ex Marco, qvem nos hoc in loco ut manudoctorem seqvimur, Christum à mortuis resuscitatum, simulq́; glorificatum, πρῶτον, primô locô, apparuisse Mariæ Magdalenæ.

LII. Pontificii scriptores contendunt, Christum in ipsa resurrectionis die, imò horâ, primò omniū apparuisse B. Virgini Mariæ, matri suę, cui potissimùm hæc singularis lætitia & gloria debita fuerit, qvæqve præ incomparabili amore plus cæteris omnibus de filii sui passione doluerit. Verùm hæc tantùm est opinio, qvam scriptura sacra nõ tantùm silentio, verùm etiam contrariâ affirmatione, in dubium vocat, qvando Christum Magdalenæ primùm apparuisse asserit.

LIII. 2. Apparuit mulieribus alterâ vice ad sepulchrum abeuntibus, & ab eo reversis, Matth. 28, 9. Marcus qvidem hanc apparitionẽ, ut & seqventem tertiam, omittit, & secundô locô discipulis in Emaus pergentibus Christum apparuisse commemorat; attamen ex aliis Evangelistis intelligitur, qvòd inter eam, qvæ facta est Mariæ Magdalenæ, & inter eam, qvæ facta est discipulis in Emaus abeuntibus, interponenda sit ea, qvæ evenit mulieribus à sepulchro reversis; imò non tantùm hæc, verùm etiam illa, qvæ facta est Simoni Petro. Siqvidem harmonia Evangelistarum manifestè docet, istas duas apparitiones præcessisse illam apparitionem Christi, qvæ discipulis in Emaus euntibus contigit.

LIV. Calvinus putat, hanc apparitionem Christi, his mulieribus factam, qvam Matthæus describit, esse eandem cum apparitione factâ Mariæ Magdalenæ, qvam describit Johannes: asserit igitur, per synecdochen ad omnes à Matthæo extendi, qvod unius fuit proprium. Sed hæc sententia minimè consentit cum descriptione Evangelistarum. Marcus n. veluti singulare qvid commemorat, qvòd Christus primò omnium Mariæ Magdalenæ se visendum præbuerit: Imò harum apparitionum diversitatem ipsissima circumstantiarum diversitas, qvã harmoniæ Evangelicæ diligens inspectio ad oculum demonstrat, satis confirmat.

LV. 3. Apparuit Simoni Petro, qvod discipuli, audientes nuncium de apparitione Christi euntibus in Emaus factâ, fatentur, Luc. 24, 34. ipseq; Apostolus Paulus testatur 1. Cor. 15, 5. Hanc apparitionẽ cum pręcedente Marcus, ut modò percepimus, prætermisit, sed ob illorũ discipulorũ, ut & ipsius Pauli testimonia hanc omninò inter manifestationẽ mulieribus à sepulchro reversis factã, & inter eam qvæ eununtib. in Emaus contigit, ob ordinis convenientiã inferendã esse, judicam 9.

LVI. Notetur autem hôc in locô occasio, qvâ Christus Petro apparuit. Luc. 24, 12. Petrum solum ad sepulchrum cucurrisse meminit;

Johannes v. c. 20, 3. cum cum alio discipulo ad illud excurruisse contendit; ut hâc ratione vel Petro soli ad sepulchrum abeunti, vel eidem à sepulchro, ad qvod cum socio suo excurrerat, soli reverso, aliamq́; viam ingresso, Christus apparuisse intelligatur.

LVII. 4. Apparuit duobus in Emaus abeuntibus Luc. 24, 15. Osiander in Harm. ut & alii hanc apparitionem distingvunt ab eâ, qvæ contigit discipulis in agrum abeuntibus, qvam describit Marc. c. 16, 12. duplicem ob rationem, 1. qvia Marcus expressè dicit, duos illos rus abiisse in castellum Emaus: 2. qvia Marcus dicit, reliqvos discipulos non credidisse nuncio eorũ, qvib⁹ Christus apparuerat: Lucas v. contrariũ planè asserit, qvòd nimirum, audito nuncio de Christi manifestatione, lætabundi proclamârint: Surrexit Dominus verè, & Simoni apparuit.

LIIX. Verùm Dn. D. Gerhardus in Harmonia suâ cum Lyrano rectè statuir, unam eandemq́; historiam à Marco & Luca describi: Siqvidem omnes circumstantiæ concordant, ut is, qvi textum introspiciet, facilè animadvertet.

LIX. Nec obstant rationes, qvibus contrariæ sententiæ autores utuntur. Nam in prima, qvòd Marcus dicit, illos rus, Lucas v. in castellũ Emaus, abijsse, planè nulla est difficultas. Distingvim⁹ enim inter viæ medium, & inter ejus finem seu terminum: hunc Lucas; illud verò Marcus, exprimere voluerunt; qvod ipsi textûs ad oculum demonstrant. Sed major difficultas in secundâ subesse videtur, qvod Marcus dicit, reliqvos discipulos non credidisse nuncio istorum duorum; Lucas v. planè contrarium asserere videtur. - Verùm horũ conciliatio est facilis. Nam vel uterq; Evangelistarum per synecdochen toti com̃unitati attribuit, qvod qvidam ex eâ fecerunt; vel alter eorum fidem nondum ab omni dubitatione liberam, alter v. fidem ipsorum dubitationi reluctantem considerat. Atq; hâc ratione & credidisse, & non credidisse, sine omni inconvenientia dici possunt.

LX. 5. Apparuit discipulis unà omnibus, exceptô Thomâ, congregatis in vespera Paschatos, Marc. 16, 14. Johannes 20, 19. hanc apparitionem subjungit illi, qvæ Mariæ Magd. contigit, sed ordo historiæ apud Marcum & Lucam ostendit, eam illi demum esse subjiciendam, qvæ facta est euntibus in Emaus.

LXI. Inter alia a. hic notetur, superiores qvatuor apparitiones tantùm fuisse particulares; hanc verò qvintam, ut & seqventes omnes, præter eam, quam Jacobo contigisse suô locô audiemus,æsse generales, quæ discipulis vel omnibus, vel eorum pluribus contigerunt, partim, quia ab incredulitate suâ liberandi, & in fide hujus articuli confirmandi erant, partim, quia debuerunt esse testes resurrectionis Dominicæ, Luc. 24, 28. Act. 1, 8. & c. 10, 41.

LXII. 6. Apparuit iterum discipulis Joh. 20, 24. imprimis v. Thomæ, qui in præcedente apparitione absens fuerat, jam a. præsens aderat. Johannes hanc apparitionem immediatè cum præcedente connectit, quando c. 20, 26. dicit, eam die octavo post priorem esse factam, quam connexionem nos etiam meritô hôc loco observamus.

LXIII. 7. Apparuit septem discipulis ad mare Tyberiadis, Joh. 21. 1. Nam Christus suam ex mortuis resurrectionem non tantùm in Judæa, videlicet Hierosolymis, & invicinia proxima, verùm etiam in Galilæa, variis apparitionibus, inter quas hæc ipsa prima, confirmare voluit.

LXIV. Hæc a. apparitio immediatè sequitur illam, quæ facta est omnibus unà cum Thoma discipulis; id quod connexiva particula, μετὰ ταῦτα, manifestè ostendit. Hæc n. tempus, quô illa contigerit, perspicuè ostendit; quod tamen non proximum, aut immediatè cum illius tempore, ut Augustinus existimat, conjunctum est; sed vel proximè seqvens, vel non longè distans, ut ipsæ circumstantiæ evincunt.

LXV. 8. Apparuit coram magna discipulorum freqventia, in qvodam monte Galilææ; quam apparitionem Matthæus c. 28, 16. & Paulus 1. Cor. 15, 6. describunt. Hæc apparitio paulò ante reditum Apostolorum ex Galilæâ in Judæam, octiduo scilicet ante Christi ascensionem, contigit, ut ex circumstantiis non improbabiliter colligit Dn. D. Gerhardus in Harmonia sua, quam vide.

LXVI. Existimant a. qvidam, hôc in loco Matthæum & Paulum, qvos nos supra conjunximus, neqvaquam unam eandemq; Christi apparitionem describere: cùm Matthæus tantùm undecim Apostolorum, Paulus v. plus quàm qvingentorum fratrum, expressam faciant mentionem. Sed ordo apparitionum, qvas Paulus dicto loco recenset, manifestè ostendit, apparitionem coram plus quám qvingentis fratribus factam, omninò esse eandem cum eâ, quam Matthæus describit. Et licet Matthæus undecim tantùm discipulorum mentionem faciat, tamen alios etiam adfuisse minimè negat; quin imò, cùm dicit vers. 17. c. 28. quosdam dubitâsse, ostendit, præter Apostolos etiam alios coràm fuisse, cùm apostoli de resurrectionis Christi veritate tot ejus apparitionibus jam dudum fuerint confirmati, ut nullus planè dubitationi locus ampliùs fuerit relictus.

LXVII. 9. Apparuit seorsim Jacobo, qui dictus fuit frater Christi, quod ex virginis Mariæ sorore, Christi matertera, natus esset. Hæc apparitio, licèt à nullo Evangelistarum describatur, Paulus tamen expressam ejus facit mentionem, eamq́; modò explicatæ statim subnectit 1. Cor. 15. 7.

LXVIII. Non autem putemus, ac si hæc apparitio, cùm omnes Evangelistæ de eâ taceant, à Paulo fuisset ficta. Absit enim, de tanto Apostolo tale qvid cogitemus: sed eam reverà Jacobo contigisse firmiter credamus, præsertim, cùm huic Apostolo, selectissimo Dei organo, fides haud qvaqvam sit deroganda, cumq́; non omnia ab Evangelistis conscripta, & in libros digesta sint, qvæ contigerunt.

LXIX. 10. Apparuit omnibus Apostolis discumbentibus, Mar. 16. 14. Atq; hæc est apparitio illa, qvæ ipso discensionis die facta est, omniumq́; apparitionum felix clausula meritò dici potest.

LXX. Aretius in suis Problem. Theolog. Loc. 13. huic apparitioni aliam adhuc, qvæ nimirum Act. 1, 12. in monte olveti ultimò discipulis sit facta, subnectere audet. Verùm, qvoniam eam cum hâc nostrâ decimâ qvoad omnes circumstantias planè convenire, tot9 textus illius loci manifestissimè ostendit, nos illas pro unâ eademq́; meritò habemus.

LXXI. Ex hisce autem modò datis CHRISTI apparitionibus facili negotio earum numerus, si qvis eam desiderat, potest colligi, ita ut non opus sit, qvandam ejus supervacaneam repetionem instituere.

LXXII. Interim tamen istud hôc locô observetur, nos hasce apparitiones non ideò consignâsse, ut crederem9, toties tantùm Christu apparuisse, cùm per 40. dies sæpiùs cum discipulis sit conversatus; sed illa ex tota historia tanqvam rei certissima argumenta proferuntur, qvæ Apostoli memoriæ prodiderunt, ut & ipsi, & omnes Christiani, eorum intuitu in pugnâ contra diabolum, Christum à mortuis resuscitatum, verum Deum statuerent; in pugnâ contra mundum, præsentissimum ejus auxilium intelligerent; in pugna contra propriam carnem, certissimam victoriam crederent; in pugna tandem contra mortem, qvippe in ipsissimâ morte, totius carnis resurrectionem certò expectarent.

LXXIII. Qvæ omnia, ut nos, qui etiam Christianorum titulò piè gloriamur, certò statuamus, intelligamus, credamus, expectemus, —— Deus ô mi porrige nobis Auxiliatricem clementi Numine dextram!


## 43 Disputation XLIII. On the conversation of Christ during the 40 Days, and the Instruction of the Disciples

In previous disputations it has been proven that CHRIST, the Savior of the world, having broken the bonds of death, not only rose again gloriously, but also appeared graciously to the weak and wavering, so that he might show himself alive to those whose dying faith charity commanded him to revive. Now it must be inquired what the revived Messiah said or did during the 40 days which, according to Scripture, intervened between his glorious resurrection and his majestic ascension. It will not be permitted here to gather together all the words and deeds of CHRIST performed after the resurrection and to treat them at great length, both because of the scarcity of pages and because some things seem more suitable for the pulpit than the lecture chair; but we shall treat only the principal ones, which provide material for disputation, an epitome of which is exhibited to us by St. Matthew ch. 28, v. 17 and following, and Mark ch. 16, v. 15 and following. Luke Acts 1, v. and following, which we shall: 1, briefly review; 2, raise the controversial questions within them; 3, adapt to Christian practice.

Thesis I.

The things which our glorious Immanuel, Christ, said and did in the presence of his disciples and the faithful during the space of 40 days after his resurrection, are either General or Special.

II. The general points are: I. That Christ showed himself alive not only to his disciples, the future heralds of his resurrection, but also to many others, witnesses of the same, 1 Cor. 15:6, Acts 1:3, and exposed the true resurrection of his true body to sight and touch: partly, that he might counter the folly of Marcion, (a) the fury of Manes, (b) and the sharpness of Mennon Simonis (c) who denied the true humanity of CHRIST; partly, that he might correct and confirm the doubting and suspicious faithful, Luke 24:39. II. It is that he held discourses with the disciples and the rest concerning the kingdom of GOD.

III. Luke, chapter 24, verses 27, 45, 46, teaches us who those discourses were and what kind they were. Namely, he did not hand down new dogmas not to be written but to be propagated by word of mouth, but he explained the scriptures concerning the passion, death, resurrection, and ascension of the Messiah to the heavens, and most solidly vindicated them from the corruptions and carnal dreams of the Pharisees concerning the temporal kingdom of the Messiah.

IV. Therefore the Jesuits are foolish, who seek patronage in these words of CHRIST for their traditions, for instance the carrying about of the body of CHRIST, pilgrimages, and in sum everything which the Papal Church can neither teach nor prove by testimonies of scripture, which Bellarmine does (d), saying: "Those things which the Lord promised he would say, John 16, he undoubtedly said after his resurrection, etc." R. I. What is the consequence, Bellarmine? Christ spoke to his disciples about the kingdom of God, therefore he commanded them traditions: this is similar to: The Roman Pontiff consults with the Jesuits about the propagation of the Roman Church, therefore he teaches the Gospel. II. Luke, chapter 24, verse 44, expressly testifies that Christ took from Moses and the Prophets and explained those things which he had previously said to the disciples more often. Whence I argue: Those things which Christ did not reveal to his disciples before his passion, and which are not contained in Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, those Christ neither explained nor commended to his disciples after his resurrection: But Christ did not reveal traditions to his disciples before his passion, as Bellarmine admits, who refers the doctrine of them to the 40 days, nor are they contained in Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms; therefore. III. Those traditions which were only invented after the ascension of Christ, and which fight against the doctrine of Christ, cannot be sold as traditions of CHRIST: Traditions, falsely so called Apostolic, are such. Therefore. The major premise is true, unless we wish to say that something exists before it exists; or that Christ is in contradiction to himself. The minor premise is proven by the blessed Chemnitz, (e) the most illustrious Lord Preceptor Gerhard, (f) and the Reverend Lord Preceptor Meisner. (g) As regards the saying of John 16:12 alleged by Bellarmine, let the Jesuit compare it with John 15:15, John 16:13, and 1 John 1:3-4, and he will see that Christ is speaking not of the tradition of new dogmas, but of the confirmation of things handed down through the Holy Spirit, John 16:13.

V. It does not suffice for the Jesuit to extort his traditions from this passage, but he continues, in his generosity, to elicit his seven Sacraments from the same; for thus he says in the aforementioned book: 'The Lord without doubt handed down the Sacraments in those days.' R. 1. We ask the Cardinal in a friendly manner to show a single iota upon which the institution of the Sacraments rests: for we dissolve his 'without doubt handed down' with 'without doubt did not hand down.' 2. Was not Baptism instituted in Luke 3:3-4, and the Holy Supper in Matthew 26:26 before those days; and cannot marriage and penance count the years of the world? Confirmation, ordination, and extreme unction were finally called sacraments properly so-called in the time of the Antichrist and were thus instituted by men, which the blessed Chemnitz, (h) Lord Gerhard, (i) and Lord Meisner (k) prove and refute the contrary arguments.

VI. Whence it is easy to judge what must be determined concerning those feigned and so-called Sacraments of the Papists. For since God alone is the institutor of the Sacraments, because the power of a Sacrament is from God alone, as their own prophet Thomas says somewhere, and as can be proven by the induction of all the Sacraments, it follows that those actions are in part not properly called Sacraments, but rather human figments.

VII. The special things which CHRIST said and did contain the instruction of the Apostles, by which He sent them out to all nations, and Christ's discourse concerning the power given to Him, which was placed before the instruction, and they are described in Matthew 28:16 et seqq. and Mark 16:15 et seqq.

VIII. Of the instruction, one must consider 1. The time, 2. The place, 3. The subject, 4. The summary.

IX. The time of the instruction is not expressly noted by the Evangelists, yet without doubt it was the time immediately preceding the ascension, which is manifest from the connection of the text.

X. The place where that instruction was carried out was the mountain of Galilee, and it is thought by most to have been Mount Tabor, which Josephus (l) calls Mount Itaburi cum, famous as much on account of its height and pleasantness as on account of the transfiguration of CHRIST, Matt. 17. v. 1, 2.

XI. The subject to which the instruction pertained were the eleven disciples, Matt. 28. v. 16, who nevertheless had not ascended the mountain of Galilee alone, but had joined many companions to themselves, so that they might behold the revived Christ: of whom some, having lapsed through human infirmity and being fascinated by the dominion of reason, doubted the true resurrection of CHRIST; but some, acknowledging Christ as the Messiah, religiously adored him, which not only the Greek phrase, but also the Syriac סגדין לֵהּ John 4. v. 22. and elsewhere, denoting religious adoration, prove.

XII. It is asked here, whether Christ according to both natures (and thus, as man, yet in personal union) can and ought to be religiously adored? We hold the affirmative: 1. Because this worship is promised to the son of man, Dan. 7. v. 14, where it is said of the son of man: וְיִפְלְחוּן לֵהּ and all languages shall serve him, which Chaldean phrase denotes nothing other than religious adoration, as Paul explains in Rom. 14. v. 11. Diligently compare the saying in John 5. v. 27, where that genuflection is referred to the son, Phil. 2. v. 9, 10. n. which meaning the word סְגַד obtains in 2 Kings 10. v. 10. Add Psalm 72. v. 11. and other prophecies. 2. That worship is commanded, John 14. v. 13, ch. 16. v. 23. 3. It was exhibited to CHRIST, who did not resist, by the disciples, Matt. 28. v. 16, by Thomas, John 20. v. 28, by the triumphant Church, Rev. 5. v. 12, 13. etc.

XIII. Therefore, the Calvinizing Jesuists and the Jesuitizing Calvinists are impious (I except Beza, who in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, Antithesis on the Person of Christ 20, attributes adoration to the flesh) who deny the worship of religious adoration to Christ as man, and invent some inferior worship for the flesh of Christ. Martin Calvinist. (m) Bellarmine (n) Where we especially marvel at the madness of the Jesuits, who deny the worship of λατρεία to the flesh of Christ, and yet attribute it to the fictitious transubstantiated bread, according to the Council of Trent, ch. 5, on the veneration of the Eucharist, Canon 6, nay, even to the mother of Christ herself, and to other saints, which we shall demonstrate to anyone asking in conflict.

XIV. Before Christ proposes the sum of the instruction, he prefixes as a document and foundation a discourse concerning the omnipotence truly and merely divine communicated to him: saying, ἐδόθη μοι πᾶσα ἐξουσία ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς: For when the ruler of the world was about to send unarmed soldiers into the profane and insane world, so that they might subjugate it to the faith, He wished to instruct his disciples concerning his omnipotence, lest they should flee out of weakness from those over whom they ought to be superior by divine command and power.

XV. Wherefore, we do not hesitate to assert that by πᾶσαν ἐξουσίαν (all authority) here is denoted παντοδυναμίαν (omnipotence), which Christ tacitly opposes to the power of the world: and we prove this 1. from the word πᾶσα (all): for to whom all power is granted, to him no power is denied: 2. from the periphrasis of that power: for it is called ἐξουσία ἐν ὀυρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς (authority in heaven and on earth): now this periphrasis is a description of infinite divine power, Gen. 24. v. 7. 1. Chron. 29. v. 11. Ps. 135. v. 3. Matth. 11. v. 25.

XVI. Nor is there any reason why the Calvinists should seek a hiding place here in the distinction between ἐξουσία (authority) and δύναμις (power), Piscat. in Observ. in h. l. For just as we do not deny that difference in certain subjects (as when I say: the Calvinists have the power [δύναμιν] to destroy images, they do not have the authority [ἐξουσίαν]: the Roman Pontiff has the power [δύναμιν] to harass Lutheran churches, they do not have the authority [ἐξουσίαν]), so we utterly deny that in God power [δύναμιν] and authority [ἐξουσίαν] are distinguished or separated, unless I should wish to posit an impotent God, that is, to deny God.

XVII. And we assert with Scripture that this divine omnipotence was given to Christ according to his human nature, against the Calvinists who deny it, Pisc. l. d. Bez. p. 1. Resp. ad Act. Coll. M. p. 133. to whom a response was given above in disp. 18. See on this matter the most illustrious Mr. Menz. in Martinio Elen. disp. 2. th. 95. seqq. and in Antimartin. p. 496.

XIIX. Upon this foundation, concerning communicated omnipotence, Christ built the very instruction and sending forth of the disciples: whence that sending forth is connected in the text by the particle ὖν (therefore) with the preceding.

XIX. This instruction contains 1. A mandate concerning the universal propagation of the Gospel, 2. A precept concerning the baptism of the faithful, 3. A threefold promise: Of which 1. concerning the ordinary fruit of faith, namely eternal salvation, and 3. concerning the gracious presence of Christ the God-man, pertains to all the faithful; 2. concerning the special and extraordinary effect of faith, namely miracles, pertains to at least some Christians.

XX. That Christ here commanded the universal calling of all men, there is no doubt, since Christ expressly orders the disciples to go out through the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature (namely, a rational one, for the Gospel is not to be preached, as was done by Brother Francis the ass) or to all nations: for after the partition wall of the middle was removed, Eph. 2. v. 14. the sheep were to be gathered into one fold.

XXI. Nor does it follow from this, however, that the Gentiles of the O.T. were in no way called to the kingdom of the Messiah, since they were not called in such a way. For from the denial of the mode of a thing, to the denial of the thing itself, the inference is weak. We indeed concede that the ministry of the divine word did not flourish among them (for they were unwilling to bear it) Ps. 147. v. 19, 20. yet not every means of arriving at the Church was lacking to them, which the Rev. Mr. Dr. Franz learnedly demonstrates (o)

XXII. But since the disciples of CHRIST, moved not by their own impulse but by the command of CHRIST, undertook the duties of teaching, it will not be irrelevant to ask, Can anyone today teach publicly without a calling and command? The Photinians say so: Theophilus Nicolaides (p) and Johannes Volkelius (q). We, for the sake of brevity, oppose the statement in Rom. 10. v. 15. Heb. 5. v. 4. He who desires more, let him consult Mr. Gerhard, vol. 6, loc. 5, sections following.

XXIII. The administration of baptism immediately follows the announcement and reception of the Gospel: Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

XXIV. This is not the first institution of Holy Baptism, which is evident from q. 5. th. But it is the solemn promulgation and declaration of a Baptism already long since instituted and administered, John 1. v. 25; that the Baptism hitherto administered in Judea pertains not to a certain people and time, but to all peoples whatsoever, devoted to the doctrine of CHRIST, for all times.

XXV. Because of the Photinians, the impious destroyers of all articles of faith, it must be asked in this place, Does Christ here speak of water Baptism? Hieronymus à Moscoro (r) and others deny it, who understand nothing else by baptism than doctrine. R. 1. It is incumbent upon the Photinians to prove that baptism ever signifies doctrine in Scripture, for this we deny; 2. And, even if it were most strongly proven, what would that signification have to do with the present passage, in which doctrine and baptism are expressly distinguished? For adults were first to be instructed in the doctrine of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and afterwards to be baptized. Hence, therefore, if the word, βαπτίζοντες, has the same signification as the word, μαθητεύσατε, according to the Photinians, it follows that it was possible for those to become disciples of Christ who were not instructed in his doctrine, which is absurd. 3. Paul in 1 Cor. 1:17 expressly testifies that there is a distinction between doctrine and baptism, when he denies that he was sent to baptize (primarily: for he undoubtedly baptized, not contrary to Christ's command, v. 15, 16), but to evangelize. But what kind of Apostolic and logical opposition would this be, if the word (evangelize) had the same sense as the word (baptize)? This, indeed: I was not sent to baptize, but to baptize, that is, not to teach, but to teach: absurd! irrational! We conclude, therefore, that baptism, both here and in many other places, denotes the baptism of water.

XXIV. It is further asked by the Photinians, is baptism necessary today? Do the Photinians not have the same mind on this question? Hieron. Moscorov. (r) admits that he accepts the necessity of baptism: Theoph. Nicolaid (s) considers baptism to be indifferent: But Johan. Sommeri (t), entirely denying the necessity of baptism, says that baptism does not pertain to us at all, nor is it used by us with sounder judgment than if someone were to wish to imitate and restore Noah's ark, Gen. 8, the yoke of Jeremiah, 28, or the arrows of King Joash, 2 Kings 13, without a certain command and mandate of GOD. R. That through which a Sacrament 1. We are regenerated, Tit. 3:5, 2. We put on Christ, Gal. 3:27, and 3. We are received into the covenant of God, that is necessary. By the sacrament of Baptism this is done, according to the cited passages, therefore.

XXV. From the decision of this question flows the refutation of that pernicious error, which the Calvinists err with the Photinians, that baptism does not confer regeneration: Zwingli in Confess. An. 30, art. 7, Calvin, book 4, inst. c. 15, Moscorovius, book of the same, p. 107. The passages cited in thesis 24 suffice for us, since the adversaries can put forward neither a passage of Scripture nor any reason. For it is clearly weak, what Moscorovius urges in the book of the same, that God nowhere endowed an external thing with the power to produce spiritual effects. For we do not maintain that that power of regenerating inheres in the water, but we join to the water the grace and operations of the Holy Spirit, who acts through the water as if through an instrument. Now, indeed, it is known that an instrument does not act by its own power, but by the power and influence of the principal agent, and thus produces an effect which it does not subjectively contain in itself.

XXVI. From what has been said, it is not difficult to respond to the Photinians, who deny infant baptism, Catech. Racov. p. 125, Moscorov. book of the same, c. 7, p. 117 ff. For he is firmly proven by the saying of the Messiah. John 3:5. Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God, from which such an argument can be connected: Whoever must enter into the kingdom of heaven, it is necessary that they be born again of water and the Spirit: Infants must enter into the kingdom of heaven. Therefore. Nor is there anything in the fact that they object: Nowhere in Scripture has infant baptism been commanded: We urge the command of Christ: Baptize all nations, and we say that something is contained in Scripture in a threefold way: 1. As to the letter and the sense: You shall not worship strange gods, Ex. 20, v. 5. II. As to the letter, and not as to the sense: pluck out your eye, and cast it from you, Matt. 5, v. 29. III. As to the sense, but not as to the letter: as, women are human beings: many things are to be baptized: We assert that infant baptism was commanded in this last way, firstly. Nor, 2, does it have any strength, what they object, that infants lack the use of reason, nor do they understand the action: For this heavenly regeneration does not depend on reason, but on the power of the Holy Spirit. What consequence is there, therefore? We are ignorant of how baptized infants are regenerated; therefore, they are not regenerated: None. For from our ignorance to the denial of a thing, the argument is not valid: otherwise I would conclude: We are ignorant of how the infants of the Old Testament were received into the covenant through the circumcision of the foreskin: we are ignorant of how infants יֹנְקֵי שָׁדַיִם sucking the breasts of their mothers, praise God: we are ignorant of how God is going to raise our bodies, therefore that has not been done, is, or will be. All absurd!

XXVII. To the command concerning the preaching of the Gospel and the administration of Baptism, the Messiah adds a threefold promise.

XXIIX. I. It is concerning the end of faith, proposed to all believers and those who persevere, and that is the salvation of souls, 1 Pet. 1, v. 9. He who shall have believed, etc.

XXIX. II. It is concerning the power of performing miracles: but signs, etc. Signs, as appears from the enumeration, were miracles which the Apostles and some others performed by the power and command of Christ. That power was not universal, but personal and temporal, i.e., limited to a certain time and persons. But that which the Evangelists attribute to all believers, that is to be understood not effectively but participatively. See Irenaeus, book 2, ch. 57, p. 160.

XXX. The end of miracles was either principal or less principal: The less principal was the utility of men, see August. book 1, on the utility of believing, ch. 16, beginning. c. 16. The principal confirmation of the doctrine, then at that time renewed and manifested.

XXXI. The doctrine having now been confirmed, miracles have long since ceased.

XXXII. It is therefore unjust that the Papists demand miracles from us, when we have a doctrine that is not new, but one confirmed by these very miracles: to whom we object that saying of Augustine, lib. 22. de civit. Dei c. 8: whoever still seeks prodigies in order to believe is himself a great prodigy, who does not believe while the world believes. It is folly that they invent miracles; for by that very act they betray their doctrine as being new and in need of miracles.

XXXIII. III. There is a promise concerning the gracious presence of Christ with the disciples, and with the whole Christian Church, concerning which we treated above in Disp. 20.

XXXIV. We, therefore, concluding, give thanks to our most benign Immanuel, that He deigned to illuminate us, sitting in the shadows of death, by the preaching of His word, and to call us graciously to the kingdom of grace through the ministry of the disciples. Grant, I beseech Thee, most benign JESUS, that we may long enjoy that light of Thy word. Dissipate the furies of the enemies who strive to extinguish the light of the Gospel: for Thou alone canst do this, because Thou art omnipotent. Speak, therefore, to them in Thy wrath, that the crowd of enemies may be put to shame. Let it be.

Latin:

SUperioribus Disputationibus evictum, CHRISTUM Mundi servatorem, mortis ruptis vinculis, non tantùm gloriosè resurrexisse, sed etiam infirmis titulantibus gratiosè apparuisse, ut vivum se ostenderet illis, qvorum fidem emorientem resuscitare jubebat charitas. Nunc inqvirendum est, quidnam Messias redivivus per dies 40. qui, juxta scripturam, inter resurrectionem ejus gloriosam, & ascensionem Majestaticam intercesserunt, dixit fecerit vé? Non licebit hic omnia CHRISTI dicta & facta, post resurrectionem peracta, in unum conglobare, & operosiùs pertractare, cùm ob pagellarum angustiam, tùm, qvòd nonnulla suggesto qvàm cathedræ videntur aptiora; sed præcipua tantùm, qvæ disputandi materiam præbent, qvorum epitomen nobis exhibent, D. Matthæus c. 28. v. 17. & seqq. Marcus c. 16. v. 15. seqq. Lucas Act. 1. v. seqq. qvæq́; 1. breviter recensebimus; 2, qvæstiones in illis controversas movebimus; 3. ad πράξιν Christianam accommodabimus.

Θέσις I.

QVæ Christus gloriosus noster Immanuel, post resurrectionem suam 40. dierum spatiô, coram discipulis & fidelibus dixit & fecit, illa vel sunt Generalia, vel Specialia.

II. Generalia sunt I. Quòd Christus non tantùm suis discipulis, resurrectionis futuris præconibus, sed etiam multis aliis, ejusdem testibus, 1. Cor. 15. v. 6. seipsum vivum exhibuit Actor. 1. v. 3. & veram veri sui corporis resurrectionem visu & tactui exposuit: partim, ut stultitiæ Marcionis; (a) furori Manetis, (b) & acumini Menn. Simonis (c) veram CHRISTI Hum. negantium, occurreret; partim, ut fideles dubitantes & suspicantes Luc. 24. v. 39. corrigeret & confirmaret. II. est, quòd sermones fecit ad discipulos, & reliqvos, de regno DEI.

III. Qvi & qvales sermones illi fuerint, docet nos Lucas c. 24. v. 27. 45, 46. Nimirum non tradidit nova dogmata non scribenda, sed oretenus propaganda, sed explicavit scripturas de passione, morte, resurrectione & ascensione Messiæ ad cælos, easq; â corruptelis & carnalibus somniis Pharisæorum de regno Messiæ temporali, vindicavit solidissimè.

IV. Ineptiunt ergò Jesuitæ, qvi suis traditionibus, puta Corporis CHRISTI circumgestationi, peregrinationibus, & in summa omnibus, quæ Pontificia Ecclesia scripturæ testimoniis neq; docere potest, neq; probare, in his verbis CHRISTI qværunt patrocinium, qvod facit Bellarminus (d) Illa, inqviens, quæ promittebat Dominus se dicturum, Joh. 16. dixit haut dubiè post resurrectionem suam &c. R. I. Quæ, Bellarmine, conseqventia? Christus locutus est discipulis suis de regno Dei E. illis mandavit traditiones: similis est huic: Pontifex R. cum Jesuitis consultat de Rom. Eccl. propagatione E. docet Evangel. II. Lucas c. 24. v. 44. expressè testatur, quòd Christus ex Mose & Prophetis ea reptierit & explicârit, quæ priùs discipulis sæpiùs dixerat. Unde argumentor: Quæ Christus discipulis suis ante passionem suam non revelavit, quæq; in Mose, Prophetis, & Psalmis non continentur, illa Christus discipulis suis post resurrectionem nec explicavit nec commendavit: Sed traditiones Christus discipulis suis ante passionem non revelavit, fatente Bellarm. qvi illarum doctrinam ad 40. dies refert, nec in Mose, Prophetis & Psalmis continentur E. III. Quæ traditiones post ascensionem Christi demum sunt inventæ, & pugnant cum doctrina Christi, illæ pro traditionib. CHRISTI venditari neqveunt: Trationes, falsò ita dictę Apostolicæ, sunt tales. E. Major est vera, nisi velimus dicere aliquid esse anteq, est; aut Christum sibi contradixisse. Minorem probant B. Chemnit. (e) Clariss. Dn. Præcept. Gerhardus (f) & Rev. Dn. Præceptor Meisnerus (g) Quod ad dictum Joh. 16. v. 12. à Bell. allegatum attinet, cum illo conferat Jesuita Joh. 15. v. 15. Joh. 16. v. 13. 1. Joh. 1. v. 3, 4. & videbit, facere Christum verba non de novorum dogmatum traditione, sed de traditorum confirmatione per Spiritum S. Joh. 16. v. 13.

V. Non sufficit Jesuitæ, ex hoc loco suas traditiones extorquere, sed idem pergit, pro sua liberalitate, ex eodem septem sua Sacramenta elicere; Sic enim dicit l. d. Dominus fine dubio tradidit Sacramenta in illis diebus. R. 1. Petimus à Cardinali amicè, ut unicum jota monstret, cui innitatur Sacramentor. institutio: Nam ejus (sine dubio tradidit) per (sine dubio non tradidit) solvimus. 2. Annon Baptismus Luc. 3. v. 3, 4. Sacra cœna Matth. 26. v. 26. ante illos dies fuit instituta; matrimonium, & pœnitentia mundi numerare possunt annos? Confirmatio, ordo, & extrema unctio, Antichristi demum tempore, sacramenta propriè ita dicta, vocabantur & ita ab hominibus instituebantur, quod probant, & contraria argumenta refutant, B. Chemn. (h) Dn. Gerhardus (i) Dn. Meisnerus (k).

VI. Unde promptum est judicare, quid statuendum de fictis & dictis Sacramentis illis Pontificiorum. Cùm enim Solus Deus sit Sacramentorum institutor, quia virtus Sacramenti est ex Solo Deo, ut proprius illorum propheta Thomas alicubi dicit, & inductione omnium Sacramentor. probari potest, sequitur, illas actiones partim non esse propriè dicta Sacramenta, sed potiùs humana figmenta.

VII. Specialia, quæ CHRISTUS dixit & fecit, continent instructionem Apostolorum, quâ illas ad gentes ablegavit universas, & concionem Christi de potestate sibi data, instructioni præmissam, & describuntur Matt. 24. v. 16. seqq. Marc. 16. v. 15. seqq.

VIII. Instructionis consideranda sunt 1. Tempus, 2. Locus, 3. Subjectũ, 4. Summa.

IX. Tempus instructionis expresse ab Evangelistis non notatur, fine dubio tamen fuit tempus ascensionem immediate antecedens, quod ex connexione textûs est manifestum.

X. Locus, ubi illa instructio est peracta, fuit mons Gallilæa, & à plerisque putatur fuisse mons Tabor, quem Josephus (l) montem vocat Itaburicùm ob altitudinem & amœnitatem, tùm ab CHRISTI transfigurationem Matth. 17. v. 1, 2. celeberrimus.

XI. Subjectum, ad qvod instructio pertinebat, fuerunt discipuli undecim, Matth. 28. v. 16. qvi tamen non soli in montem Galilææ ascenderant, sed plures sibi junxerant comites, ut Christum redivivum conspicerent: è qvibus nonnulli infirmitate humanâ lapsi, & rationis dominio fascinati, de verâ CHRISTI dubitabant resurrectione; qvidam verò Christum pro Messiâ agnoscentes, religiosè illum adorârunt, qvod non tantùm phrasis græca, sed & Syriaca סגדין לֵהּ Joh. 4. v. 22. & alibi religiosam notantes adorationem, evincunt.

XII. Qværitur hìc, An Christus secundùm utramq; naturam (& sic, ut homo, in unione tamen personali) religiosè adorari & possit & debeat? Nos affirmativam tenemus: 1. Qvia hic cultus filio hominis est promissus Dan. 7. v. 14. ubi de filio hominis dicitur: וְיִפְלְחוּן לֵהּ & omnes lingvæ ei servient, qvæ phrasis Chaldaica nihil aliud, qvàm religiosam adorationem notat, explicante Paulo Rom. 14. v. 11. Diligenter confer dictum Joh. 5. v. 27. ubi illa genuflexio ad filium refertur, Phil. 2. v. 9, 10. n. qvam significationem vox סְגַד obtinet 2. Reg. 10. v. 10. Adde Psal. 72. v. 11. & alia vaticinia 2. Cultus ille est mandatus, Joh. 14. v. 13. c. 16. v. 23. 3. CHRISTO non repugnanti exhibitus à discipulis, Matth. 28. v. 16. à Thoma Joh. 20. v. 28. ab Ecclesia triumphante Apoc. 5. v. 12, 13. &c.

XIII. Impii igitur sunt Calviniant Jesuizantes, & Jesuitæ Calvinizantes (excipio Bezam, qvi in Colloq. Montisbel. Antith. de Persona Christi 20. carni adorationem tribuit) qvi Christo homini adorationis religiosæ cultum denegant, & aliqvem inferiorem Hum. Christi cultum affingunt. Martin Calvinist. (m) Bellarminus (n) Ubi inprimis miramur Jesuitarum vesaniam, qvi λατρείας cultum carni Christi negant, & tamen ficto pani transsubstantiato tribuunt, juxta Concilium Trident. c. 5. de venerat. Eucharift. Can. 6. imò ipsi matri Christi, & sanctis aliis, qvod cuivis petenti in conflictu demonstrabimus.

XIV. Summam instructionis anteqvam proponat Christus, concionem de communicatâ sibi omnipotentiâ verè & merè divinâ, documenti & fundamenti loco præmittit: ἐδόθη μοι inqviens, πᾶσα ἐξουσία ἐν ὀρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς: Cùm enim dominator orbis in orbem profanú & insanum erat emissurus milites inermes, ut illum fidei subjugarent, voluit de omnipotentiâ suâ discipulos edocere, ne ex infirmitate fugerent illos, quibus superiores esse debebant mandato & Potentiâ divinâ.

XV. Qvare, non dubitamus asserere, per πᾶσαν ἐξουσίαν hîc notari παντοδυναμίαν, qvam Christus mundi potentiæ tacitè opponit: idq́; probamus 1. ex voce πᾶσα: cui enim omnis potestas est concessa, illi qvædam potestas non est negata: 2. περιφράσει illius potestatis: dicitur enim ἐξουσία ἐν ὀυρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς: hæc autem περίφρασις est descriptio infinitæ potentiæ divinæ, Gen. 24. v. 7. 1. Chron. 29. v. 11. Ps. 135. v. 3. Matth. 11. v. 25.

XVI. Nec est, qvod hîc latibulum qværant Calviniani in distinctione ἐξουσίας & δυνάμεως, Piscat. in Observ. in h. l. Ut enim non negamus, illam differentiam in certis subjectis (ut cum dico: Calviniani habent δύναμιν destruendi imagines, ἐξουσίαν non habent: Pontifex R. habet δύναμιν vexandi Ecclesias Lutheranas, ἐξουσίαν non habent) ita in Deo δύναμιν & ἐξουσίαν distingvi, vel separari, pernegamus, nisi velim Deum statuere impotentem, h. est, Deum negare.

XVII. Et hanc divinam omnipotentiam cum scriptura asserimus Christo datam secundùm humanam naturam, negantibus id Calvinianis Pisc. l. d. Bez. p. 1. Resp. ad Act. Coll. M. p. 133. qvibus responsum supra disp. 18. vide hac de re Clariss. Dn. Menz. in Martinio Elen. disp. 2. th. 95. seqq. & in Antimartin. p. 496.

XIIX. Huic fundamento, de communicatâ omnipotentia, Christus superstruxit ipsam instructionem & emissionem discipulorum: unde illa emissio in textu per particulam ὖν cum præcedentib9 connectitur.

XIX. Instructio hæc continet 1. Mandatum de universali Evangelii propagatione, 2. Præceptum de fidelium baptizatione, 3. Triplex promissum: Qvorum 1. de fidei fructu ordinario, salute scilicet æternâ, & 3. de gratiosâ Christi θεανθρώπου præsentiâ, ad omnes pertinet fideles; 2. de speciali & extraordinario fidei effectu miraculorum, ad qvosdam saltem Christianos.

XX. Universalem omnium hominum vocationem Christum hîc præcepisse, nullum est dubium, cùm Christus expressè jubeat discipulis, ut exeant per mundum universum, & Evangelium prædicent omni creaturæ (scilicet rationali, Evangelium enim piscibus & avibus &c. nonest prædicandum, ut à Fratre asini Francisco factum) sive omnibus gentibus: post maceriem enim medii parietis sublatam Eph. 2. v. 14. oves in unum ovile erant congregandæ.

XXI. Neque tamen hinc sequitur, Ethnicos V. T. nullo modo ad regnum Messiæ fuisse vocatos, cùm non tali modo fuerint vocati. Nam à negatione modi rei, ad rei negationem, infirma est collectio. Concedimus equidem, non viguisse inter illos verbi divini ministerium (illud enim perferre nolebant) Ps. 147. v. 19, 20. non tamen defuit illis omne ad Ecclesiam perveniendi medium, id quod eruditè demonstrat Rev. Dn. D. Franz (o)

XXII. Cùm verò discipuli CHRISTI non proprio motu, sed CHRISTI mandato permoti, docendi partes susceperint, non abs re erit, quærere, An quis hodie publicè docere possit absque vocatione & mandato? Ita ajunt Photiniani: Theophilus Nicolaides (p) & Johannes Volkelius (q). Nos brevitatis studio opponimus dictum Rom. 10. v. 15. Hebr. 5. v. 14. Plura qui cupit, adeat Dn. Gerhard. tom. 6. loc. 5. ss. seqq.
