XXIII. Evangelii anunciationem & receptionem immediatè excipit baptismi administratio: Baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti.

XXIV. Non hæc est prima S. Baptismi institutio, quod patet ex q. 5. th. Sed Baptismi jam dudum instituti & administrati Joh. 1. v. 25. solemnis promulgatio & declaratio; quòd Baptismus hactenus in Judæa administratus, non ad certum populum, & tempus, sed ad omnes omnino populos, doctrinæ CHRISTI addictos, omnibus temporibus pertineat.

XXV. Propter Photinianos, impios omnium articulor. fidei destructores, h. l. quærendum, An Christus hic verbafaciat de aqua Baptismo? Negat id Hieronym. à Moscoro. (r). & alii, qui per baptismum nihil aliud intelligunt, quàm doctrinam. R. 1. Photinianis probandum incumbit, aliqvando in scriptura baptismum significare doctrinam, hoc enim nos negamus; 2. Et, si vel maximè probaretur, quid illa significatio ad præsentem locum, in qvo expressè doctrina & baptismus distingvuntur? priùs enim instituendi erant homines adulti in doctrina Patris, filii & Spir. S. posteà baptizandi. Hinc igitur si vox, βαπτίζοντες, habet eandem significationem, qvam vox, μαθητεύσατε, juxta Photinianos, seqvitur, discipulos Christi fieri potuisse, qui in ejus doctrina non fuerunt instituti, qvod absurdum 3. Paulus 1. Cor. 1. v. 17. expressè testatur, distinctionem esse inter doctrinam, & Baptismum, qvando se negat ad baptisandum (primariò: baptizavit enim procul dubiò non contra Christi mandatum v. 15, 16.) esse missum, sed ad evangelizandum. Qvæ autem hæc esset oppositio Apostolica & Logica, si vox (evangelizo) haberet eundem sensum, qvam habet vox (baptizo)? Hæc nimirum: Ego non ad baptizandu, sed ad baptizandum sum missus, id est, non ad docendum, sed ad docendum: ἄτοπον! ἄλογον! Concludimus e. Baptismum, & hîc, & in aliis locis plurib. aqvæ denotare Baptism:

XXIV. A. Photinianis ulteriùs qværitur, an baptismus hodiè necessarius? Non eadem Photinianis de hâc qvæst. mens? Hieron. Moscorov. (r) fatetur, se admittere baptismi necessitatem: Theoph. Nicolaid (s) baptismum prove indifferenti habet: Sed Johan. Sommeri (t) baptismi necessitatem prorsus negans, dicit, Baptismum ad nos nihil pertinet, nec saniori à nobis judicio usurpatur, quàm si quis arcam Nohe, Gen: 8. jugum Jeremiæ, 28. aut regis Joas sagittas 2. Reg. 13. sine certo DEI jussu & mandato velit imitari & redintegrare. R. Per qvod Sacramentum I. Regeneramur, Tit. 3. v. 5. II. Christum induimus Gal. 3. v. 27. & III. in fœdus Dei recipimur, illud est necessarium. Per Baptismi sacramentum hoc fit, juxta dicta allegata, E.

XXV. Ex hujus qvæstionis decisione fluit refutatio pernitiosi illius erroris, qvem Calviniani cum Photinianis errant, Baptismum non conferre regenerationem: Cinglius in Confess. An. 30. art. 7. Calvinus lib. 4. inst. c. 15. Moscorovius l. d. p. 107. Nobis sufficiunt dicta allegata th. 24. cùm neq; dictum scripturæ, neq; rationem aliqvam adversarii possint reponere. Planè enim infirmum est, qvod Moscorovius l. d. urget, Deum nuspiam rei externæ eam vim indidisse, ut effectus produceret spirituales. Non enim statuimus, vim illam regenerandi in aqvâ hærere, sed aqvæ conjungimus gratiam & operationes Spiritus S. qui per aquam tanqve per instrumentum agit. Jam verò notum est, instrumentum non agere suâ virtute, sed vi & influentiâ principalis agentis, & ita affectum producere, qvem subjective in se non continet.

XXVI. Ex dictis non difficilè est, respondere Photinianis, pædobaptismum negantibus, Catech. Racov. p. 125. Moscorov. l. d. c. 7. pag. 117. seqq. Firmiter enim ille probatur ex dicto Messiæ. Joh. 3, 5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei, ex qvo tale necti potest argumentum : Qvicunq; debent ingredi in regnum cœlorum, illos ex aqva & spiritu renasci ancur necesse est : Infantes debent ingredi in regnum cœlor. E. Neq; est, qvod illi excipiant : Nullibi in scriptura pædobaptismum fuisse præceptum : Nos urgemus mandatum Christi : Baptizate omnes gentes, & dicimˣ, tripliciter aliqvid in Scripturâ contineri, 1. qvoad literam & sensum : Non adorabis Deos alienos Ex. 20. v. 5. II. qvoad literam, & non qvoad sensum : erue oculum, & projice abs te, Matth. 5. v. 29. III. qvoad sensum, sed non qvoad literam : ut ; mulieres sunt homines : multæ res sunt Baptizandæ : Hôc postremô modô pædobaptismum fuisse præceptum, asserimus nos primò. Neqve 2. qvicqvam roboris habet, qvod excipiunt, infantes carere rationis usu, nec actionem intelligere : Non enim hæc cælestis regeneratio à ratione pendet, sed à virtute Spiritus S. Qvæ igitur conseqventia ? Nos ignoramus, qvomodo infantes Baptizati regenerentur ; E. non regenerantur : Nulla. A nostrâ enim ignoratione, ad rei negationem, non valet argumentum : aliàs concluderem : Ignoramus, qvomodo infantes V. T. per præputii circumcisionem fuerint in fœdus recepti : ignoramˣ, qvomodo infantes יֹנְקֵי שָׁדַיִם fugentes ubera matrum, Deum laudent: ignoramus, qvomodo Deus sit suscitaturus nostra corpora, E. illud non factum, sit, aut fiet. Omnia absurda !

XXVII. Mandato de Evangelii prædicatione, & Baptismi administratione, Messias triplex subjungit promissum.

XXIIX. I. Est de fine fidei, omnibus credentibus, & perseverantibus, propositus, isq; est salus animarum 1. Petr. 1. v. 9. Qvi crediderit &c.

XXIX. II. Est de virtute edendi miracula : signa verò &c. Signa, ut apparet ex enumeratione, fuerunt miracula, qvæ Apostoli & nonnulli alii virtute & mandato Christi ediderunt. Fuit illa potestas non - universalis, sed personalis & temporalis i. e. certô tempore & personis limitata. Qvòd autem Evangelistæ omnibus credentibus attribuunt, id non effectivè sed participativè est intelligendum. vide Irenæum l. 2. c. 57. p. 160.

XXX. Finis miraculorum fuit vel principalis, vel minùs principalis : Minùs principalis, utilitas hominum, vide August. lib. 1. de utilit. cred. c. 16 princ. 16. principalis, confirmatio doctrinæ, tum temporis renovatæ & manifestatæ.

XXXI. Confirmatâ jam doctrinâ, dudum cessârunt miracula.

XXXII. Iniquum igitur est, quòd Pontificii à nobis miracula petunt, cùm tamen non novam, sed his ipsis miraculis confirmatam, habeamus doctrinam: quibus objicimus illud August. lib. 22. de civit. Dei c. 8. quisquis adhuc prodigia, ut credat, inquirit, magnum ipse est prodigium, qui mundô credente, non credit. Stultitia est, quòd miracula fingunt; eô ipsô enim doctrinam suam, ut novam, & miraculis indigentem, produnt.

XXXIII. III. Promissum est de gratiosâ Christi præsentia cum discipulis, & totâ Ecclesia Christianâ, de quâ supra Disp. 20. actum.

XXXIV. Nos igitur concludentes, gratias agimus Immanueli nostro benignissimo, quòd nos in tenebris mortis sedentes, verbi sui prædicatione illuminare, & discipulorum ministerio ad regnum gratiæ gratiosè vocare fuit dignatus. Concede quæso, JESU benignissime, ut illo verbi tui lumine diu frui possimus. Dissipa furores hostium, qui lucem Evangelii extinguere satagunt: Tu enim solus, qui hoc potes, quia omnipotens. Loquere igitur ad illos in furore tuo, ut hostium caterva pude fiat. Fiat.


## 44 Disputation Forty-Four. On the Ascension of Christ into Heaven

ΠΡΟΟΙΜΙΟΝ.

It is not without reason that D. Bernard very beautifully calls the Ascension of CHRIST into heaven the happy conclusion of His entire journey, because not only was that most blessed journey concluded with this sublime closing, but also an end is imposed upon the whole Evangelical history, which limit of the history of CHRIST D. Apostle Peter establishes. For just as a golden circle is concluded with a radiant gem; in the same manner, the more than golden circle of the journey of CHRIST is terminated by the ascension, as if by a sparkling gem. Do you wish to see the circle of the journey? Behold.

Christ himself shows: I came forth from the Father and have come into the world; again I leave the world, and go to the Father. Christ, in order to redeem the human race, made five miraculous leaps. The ancients said there were only three: the first from heaven into the Virgin's womb, which he made for us and for our salvation, as the Nicene Creed speaks; the second, when he descended to hell; the third, when he ascended into heaven. The more recent ones, both from the aforementioned chapter and from other places of Scripture, count five; which St. Gregory recounts in these words: Do you wish to know his leaps? He came from heaven into the virgin's womb, from the womb he came into the manger, from the manger he came to the cross, from the cross he came into the sepulcher, from the sepulcher he returned to heaven, etc. The end of all things, therefore, was the ascension into heaven, which was the completion of the entire divine dispensation. This, however, is briefly described by the Evangelists, but more broadly, more abundantly, and expressly by Luke in the Acts. Therefore, we wished to bring here what pertains to it from the said book, and to join it to the description of the Evangelists. But so that I may not appear to act unlearnedly and without method, I will treat two parts: 1. It will be about the truth of the Ascension of Christ into Heaven, 2. About its Utility.

Thesis I.

Before we approach the subject, it is pleasing to unfold the equivocation of the word "to ascend," which is polysemous in Holy Scripture, and is sometimes spoken of God anthropopathically (Gen. 17:22), and sometimes is understood properly concerning a change of place and a migration from a lower to a higher position.

II. In the place concerning the person of CHRIST, the ascension into heaven differs very greatly from the departure to the Father: for the former signifies an entry into the glory of the Father after the work of redemption was completed on earth; the latter, however, by no means signifies merely a progress from one place to another. Therefore, the word "ascend" is taken in its proper signification: to which the word "descend" corresponds diametrically, in the rite of the final judgment, according to that passage Acts 1:11. Conf. 1 Thess. 4:16, Matt. 25:31.

III. Therefore, concerning the ascension of CHRIST into the heavens, we affirm that it is not either an ἀφανισμὸς, that is, a sudden disappearance or vanishing of the body, such as is described in Luke 24:31, where CHRIST our Savior, sitting at the table, in a moment becomes invisible before the disciples at Emmaus:

ἄφαντος: or mere invisibility, just as he had already several times before made himself unseen by divine power.

IV. For the Evangelical history clearly testifies to something different, the letter of which is far plainer than that which can be easily evaded. Therefore, the Sacramentarians strive to inflict a notable injury upon our Churches.

V. Nor is it a certain metamorphosis, such as is depicted in Matthew 17, much less the dissolution of the body of Christ into the four elements, which was once the madness of the Apellitae, about whom St. Augustine writes: or the affixing of the body of Christ to the stars, and especially the solar body, which was once the insanity of the Manichaeans and Hermians (who were also called Seleucians). See the same place. VI. Nor a certain rapture, as the more recent Photinians have imagined, that Christ ascended into heaven twice, 1. before his death, which they wished to demonstrate from the rapture of Paul into the third heaven, arguing from the lesser to the greater. But 1. they act without any foundation of Scripture, with full sails; 2. Indeed, the cause brought forward by the Adversaries for this fictitious ascension refutes the figment itself.

VII. Nor was it a phantom, or an empty spectacle arranged by playful illusions, because Luke testifies that it was done while all the Apostles were watching, who expressly expresses him departing, πορευόμενον (which expression denotes motion from place to place), until a cloud received him. They are said to be looking, ἀτενίζοντες εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, i.e., that they had contemplated heaven with intent, fixed, and unmoved eyes, into which they saw Christ taken up. For that is what ἀτενίζειν is to the Greeks, to gaze with fixed and unmoved eyes, in the manner of lovers. Let the Calvinists therefore cease to slander in their usual manner.

VIII. But it is a true, visible, and real translation of the body of Christ from place to place, namely from a lower place to a higher one, and a local migration (τοπικὴ μετάστασις) of the assumed nature, as I shall subsequently prove clearly to the eyes (ὀφθαλμοφανερῶς).

IX. Moreover, it cannot be done better than that we should do in this place what we are otherwise accustomed to hold strictly to regarding the literal sense (τὸ ῥητὸν) in all articles of faith, especially in their historical description. This can be proved from several illustrious foundations of Scripture, both of the Old and New Testament.

X. I. From the Old Testament in two ways: 1. From predictions and prophecies. From the oracles of the Prophets, the sayings of the Psalms are most clear: Psalm. This Psalm, by the consensus of the most learned Hebrews, is understood of the Messiah, inviting all nations to exultation of soul, on account of Christ the conqueror, commemorating his ascent into the heavens, conspicuous for the brightness of eminent glory, august splendor, and most ample majesty, by which he sits upon his holy throne. Ps. 68:19: which passage cannot be understood otherwise than of which the Lord Apostle Paul preaches in the Ephesian Church concerning CHRIST, of which there are three: 1. The ascent εἰς ὕψος, by which phrase the true and historical ascent of CHRIST is described: 2. The Triumph, namely over spiritual enemies: 3. The fruit of the ascension, namely the munificent communication of gifts toward the pious, awaiting his second coming. Which, since they are so clear, it is a wonder that Calvin dares to write that these words are twisted by Paul to CHRIST. Far more correctly Fr. Junius writes that the Apostle teaches entirely the same thing which the prophet once intended, and that the matter itself speaks, and that this is the genuine sense to which Paul looked. These are his words, which he pursues more fully there. St. Jerome teaches in Ps. 103:19 that a prophecy concerning the Ascension of CHRIST is contained. And St. Augustine also explains this passage in the same way.

XI. 2. Of the Prophets: Dan. 7:13, 14. Where it was shown to the Prophet in dreams how Christ, the work of redemption having been completed, came into heaven and was placed at the right hand of the Father, his enemies having been conquered, Zech. 14:4, who expressed the place nearly five hundred years before, namely the Mount of Olives.

XII. 2. From a Type. The High Priest of the Old Testament bore a type of this thing, who entered once a year with the blood of expiation; which type is explained by the Apostle. Lord Dr. Gerhard enumerates more.

XIII. II. From the New Testament, the testimonies are partly historical, partly didactic, which are to be considered concerning this article of doctrine. Of the former order are Mark 16:19, Luke 24:51, Acts 1:9. Of the latter kind are, 1. Of CHRIST, John 6:62, John 16:28, 20:17, etc. 2. Of the Apostles, such as Peter in Acts 3:21 and Paul in Eph. 4:10, concerning which more fully and expressly later.

XIV. III. From the emphasis of all the words, which have great force for establishing the truth of this article and contain it in themselves. 1. For Mark, chapter 16:19, says ἀνελήφθη, that is, he was taken up. Moreover, the terminus from which and to which of this ἀνάληψις is described, Acts 1:11.

& 23. Concerning the latter of which St. Paul, ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ 1 Tim. 3:16. Whence the Ancients call it ἀνάληψιν. There are those who take it for ἄνω ἐλθεῖν; which we easily admit, but not concerning ἀνὰ, if anyone should wish to take it for repetition. 2. Luke 24:51. διέστη ἀπ' αὐτῶν he was separated, or, he withdrew from them, as in Acts 27:28: which is understood of any change of place or departure of Christ, because he immediately subjoins the word ἀναφέρεσθαι, i.e. ἀναφέρειν, that is, to be carried upward, as in Matthew 17:1, Mark 9:2. The LXX for עָלָה which they translate by χωρίζειν, διαχωρίζειν. He was not, however, lifted up, but a cloud received him, Acts 1:9, not because he became invisible in himself, but because he proceeded higher and further, and now that which the Prophet Daniel 7:13 saw is fulfilled. Add that he wished the Apostles to be spectators of all things and eyewitnesses, so that their testimony might be all the more certain. Whence that saying: One eyewitness is worth more than ten earwitnesses. See Dn. D. Gerhard in Harm. Evang. p. 526.

XV. From what has been said thus far, the truth of the event becomes clear, namely that the ascension is true and real, and that the reception from a lower place into a higher one is true; which having been demonstrated, we turn directly to the causes.

XVI. Here the efficient cause of Christ’s ascension immediately presents itself, which is the omnipotent power of God, from which the Son and the Holy Spirit are by no means excluded. For it is taken either essentially or personally: in the former way it is the common work of the three persons, because it is ad extra and indivisible; in the latter way it is also specifically attributed to God the Father and the Son, to the Father Acts 2:33, 5:30, 31, Eph. 1:20, to the Son John 3:13, John 20:17, Eph. 4:10, 16.

XVII. Hence in Micah 2:13 He is called פֹּרֵץ, surely for our sake. For just as He was incarnate not for Himself, but for us; was made subject to the law not for Himself, but for us; suffered, was crucified, and died not for Himself, but for us; and rose from the dead not for Himself, but for us: so also He ascended into heaven not for Himself, but for us, and since He is the firstfruits of our race, when He ascended into heaven, He established, offered, and commended us in Himself before the Father.

Latin:

ΠΡΟΟΙΜΙΟΝ.

NON abs re D. Bernhardus pulchrè admodùm Ascensionem CHRISTI in cœlum felicem totiùs itinerarii ipsius clausulam nominat, quia non tantùm sublimi hâc clausulâ conclusum est beatissimum illud iter, sed etiam toti Evangelicæ historiæ finis imponitur, quem terminum historiæ CHRISTI constituit D. Apostolus Petrus. Ut enim circulus aureus radiante concluditur gemmâ; eundem in modum itineris CHRISTI circulus plusquàm aureus, ascensione, veluti corruscante gemmâ terminatur. Vis circulum itineris cernere? En

Christus ipse monstrat: Exivi a Patre & veni in mundum; iterum relinqvo mundum, & vado ad Patrem. Christus, ut genus humanum redimeret, qvinqve mirabiles fecit saltus. Veteres dixerunt, tres tantum fuisse, primum de cœlo in Virginis alvum, qvem fecit propter nos & nostram salutem, ut Symbolum Nicænum loqvitur; Secundum, qvando descendit ad infernum; Tertium, qvando ascendit in cœlum. Recentiores tum ex prædicto capite, tum ex aliis Scripturæ locis, qvinqve numerant; qvos D. Gregorius his verbis recenset: Vultis saltus ejus cognoscere? De cœlo venit in uterum virginis, de utero venit in præsepe, de præsepio venit in crucem, de cruce venit in sepulchrum, de sepulchro rediit in cœlum &c. Omnium igitur finis fuit ascensio in cœlum, qvæ totius dispensationis divinæ complementum fuit. Hæc autem Evangelistis breviter describitur, latius, uberius, & ex professo a Luca an Actis. Ideo, qvę ad eam pertinent, ex dicto libro huc referre, & Evangelistarum descriptioni conjungere voluimus. Ne vero ἀπαιδεύτως καὶ ἀμεθόδως agere videar, duo membra tractabo: 1. Erit de veritate Ascensionis Christi in Cœlum, 2. De Utilitate.

Thesis I.

ANteqvam ad propositum accedamus, lubet æqvivocationem vocis τοῦ ascendere evolvere, qvæ πολύσημος est in S. Literis, & interdum ἀνθρωποπαθῶς de Deo dicitur Gen. 17, 22. interdum proprie de loci mutatione, & ab inferiore ad superiorem migratione intelligitur.

II. In loco de persona CHRISTI, ascensus in cœlum, longissime differt ab abitu ad Patrem: ille enim ingressum in gloriam Patris post redemtionis opus in terris peractum; hic vero neqvaqvam tantum progressum de loco uno in alterum significat. Proinde verbum ascendere in propria significatione accipitur: cui e diametro respondet verbum descendere, in ritu ad extremum judicium, juxta illud Act. 1, 11. Conf. 1. Theff. 4, 16. Matth. 25, 31.

III. De ascensione ergo CHRISTI in cœlos affirmamus, qvod non sit vel ἀφανισμὸς id est, disparitio aut evanescentia corporis subita, qvalis describitur Luc. 24, 31. ubi CHRISTUS Salvator noster, mensæ assidens, in momento coram discipulis Emaunticis fit ἄφαντος:

ἄφαντος: vel nuda ἀορασία, sicut jam olim aliqvoties divinâ virtute semetipsum inconspicuum fecerat.

IV. Diversum enim planè historia testatur Evangelica, cujus longè planior est litera, quàm quæ facilè eludi qveat. Insignem igitur injuriam Ecclesiis nostris affricare student Sacramentarii.

V. Neq; μεταμόρφωσις qvædam est, qualis depingitur Matth. 17. multò minùs dissolutio corpis Christi in quatuor elementa, quæ olim Appellitarum furor, de qvibus D. Augustinus: vel affixio corporis Christi ad sidera, & maximè corpus solare, qvę olim erat Manichæorum & Hermianorum (qvi & Seleuciani dicti sunt) insania, Vide ibidem. VI. Nèq; raptus qvidam, ut Photiniani recentiores finxerunt, Christum bis ascendisse in cælum, 1. ante mortem suam, qvem ex raptu Pauli in tertium cœlum demonstrare voluerunt, argumentando à minori ad majus. Sed 1. absq; fundamento Scripturæ passis plenisq; velis agunt; 2. Imò causa fictitii hujus ascensus ab Adversariis allata, figmentum ipsum refutat.

VII. Neq; phantasma fuit, vel inane per ludicras præstigias concinnatum spectaculum, qvia videntibus cunctis Apostolis factum testatur Lucas, qvi proficiscentem, πορευόμενον (qvæ locutio motu de loco ad locum notat) disertè exprimit, donec nubes ipsum susceperit. Intuentes dicuntur ἀτενίζοντες τ' ὂὐρανὸν i. e. intentis, defixis, & ammotis cælum contemplati fuisse oculis, in qvod Christum viderint sublatum. Id enim Græcis est ἀτενίζειν, fixis & immotis obtueri oculis, amantium more. Desinant proinde Calviniani more solito calumniari.

VIII. Verùm, est vera, visibilis, & realis translatio corporis Christi de loco in locum, nempe ex loco inferiori ad superiorem, & τοπικὴ μετάστασις naturæ assumtę, ut deinceps ὀφθαλμοφανερῶς probabo.

IX. Meliùs autem fieri neqvit, quàm, uti aliàs τὸ ῥητὸν in omnibus fidei articulis, præsertim in historicâ eorum descriptione, arctè tenere solemus, hoc in loco faciamus. Probari id potest ex fundamentis aliqvot illustribus Scripturæ, tum V. tum N. Testamenti.

X. I. Ex V. T. duobus modis: 1. A prædictionibus & vaticiniis. Ex Prophetarum oraculis maximè perspicua sunt dicta 1. Psalmorum: Psal. Hic Psalmus, consensu Doctissimorum Hebræorum, intelligitur de Messia, invitans omnes gentes ad exultationem animi, ob Christum triumphatorem, commemorans ejus in cœlos subvectionem, eminentis gloriæ, augusti decoris, & majestatis amplissimæ claritate conspicuam, quâ consideat in S. S. solio suo. Psal. 68, 19: qui locus non aliter, quàm de Messia, intelligi potest. Nam eadem de Propheta David prædixit, quæ D. Apostolus Paulus in Ecclesiâ Ephesinâ de CHRISTO prædicat, quorum tria sunt, 1. Ascensus εἰς ὕψος, quâ phrasi verus & historicus CHRISTI ascensus describitur: Triumphus, de hostibus spiritualibus nimirum: 3. Fructus ascensionis, nempe munifica donorum communicatio erga pios, expectantes alterum adventum ejus. Quæ, cùm adeò clara sint, mirum est, quòd Calvinus scribere audet, verba hæc â Paulo detorqveri ad CHRISTUM. Longè rectiùs Fr. Junius, omninò idipsum docere Apostolum, scribit, quod olim propheta voluit, & rem ipsam loqvi, sensum esse genuinum, ad qvem respexit Paulus. Hæc ille, quæ ibi fusiùs perseqvitur. D. Hieronymus docet in Psal. 103, 19. haberi vaticinium de Ascensione CHRISTI. Et hunc quoq; locum ita explicat D. Augustinus.

XI. 2. Prophetarum: Dan. 7, 13, 14. Ubi Prophetæ in somniis ostensum fuit, qvomodo Christus, peractô redemptionis opere, in cœlum venerit, & ad dextram Patris sit collocatus, devictis hostibus, Zach. 14, 4. qvi locum qvingentis fermè annis expressit, nimirùm montem Oliveti.

XII. 2. A Typo. Hujus rei typum gessit Summus Sacerdos. V. T. qvi cum sangvine expiationis die semel ingressus est; qvi typus explicatur ab Apostolo. Plures recenset Dn. D. Gerhardus.

XIII. II. Ex Nov. Test. testimonia partim sunt historica, partim didactica, quæ de hôc doctrinæ articulô sunt consideranda. Prioris ordinis sunt Marc. 16, 19. Luc. 24, 51. Actor. 1, 9. Posterioris generis sunt, 1. CHRISTI Johan. 6, 62. Joh. 16, 28. 20, 17. &c. 2. Apostolorum, ut Petri Actor. 3, 21. & Pauli Ephes. 4, 10. deqvibus posteà fusiùs, & ex professô.

XIV. III. Ex emphasi omnium verborum, quæ ad adstruendam hujus articuli veritatem, magnam vim habent & in se continent. 1. Marcus enim cap. 16, 19. ἀνελήφθη, id est, sursum receptus est. Describitur autem terminus â qvô, & ad qvem, hujus ἀναλήψεως, Act. 1, 11.

& 23. de qvô posteriore D. Paulus, ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ 1. Tim. 3, 16. Unde Veteres ἀνάληψιν vocant. Sunt, qvi accipiunt pro ἄνω ἐλθεῖν; qvod facilè admittimus non verò de ἀνὰ, si pro iteratione qvis sumere velit. 2. Lucas 24, 51. διέστη ἀπ' αὐτῶν disjunctus est vel, recessit ab eis, ut Act. 27, 28: qvod de qvâvis loci mutatione aut abitu Christi accipitur, qvia subjungit statim verbum ἀναφέρεσθαι, i. d. ἀναφέρειν, id est, sursum ferri, ut Matth. 17, 1. Marc. 9, 2. LXX. pro עָלָה qvod per χωρίζειν, διαχωρίζειν vertūt. 3. Act. 1, 9 ἐπήρθη, qvæ vox motûs ex loco in locū certissima nota est. LXX. hâc voce utuntur pro נָשָׂא Jon. 1, 15. נָסַע Job. 4, 12. 18. הָיָה Gen. 7, 17. רוּם Neh. 9, 5. גָּבַהּ Exod. 7, 20. Ps. 74, 5. qvæ significationes omnes huc qvadrant. Non autem elevatus est, sed νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν ἀυτὸν, Act. 1, 9. non qvod in sese ἄφαντος factus sit, sed qvia altiùs & longiùs profectus est, & jam completur, qvod Propheta Dan. 7, 13. vidit. Adde, qvòd Apostolos omnium spectatores & ἀυτόπτους esse voluit, ut tanto certius eorum esset testimonium. Unde illud: Pluris est oculatus testis unus, qvàm auriti decem. Vide Dn. D. Gerhard. in Harm. Evang. p. 526.

XV. Ex hactenus dictis elucescit rei gestæ veritas, veram nimirum & realem esse ascensionem, veramq; receptionem ex inferiori loco in superiorem, qvâ demonstratâ, rectà convertimus ad causas.

XVI. Ubi statim sese offert Efficiens ascensionis Christi causa, qvæ est omnipotens Dei virtus, à qva minimè excluduntur Filius, & Spiritus S. Vel enim essentialiter sumitur, vel personaliter: priori modô est commune trium personarum opus, qvia ad extra est, & indivisum: posteriori modô & in specie tribuitur Deo Patri, & Filio, Patri Act. 2, 33. 5, 30, 31. Eph. 1, 20. Filio Joh. 3, 13. Joh. 20, 17. Eph. 4, 10. 16.

XVII. Hinc Mich. 2, 13. פֹּרֵץ dicitur, nostrâ nimirum causâ. Ut enim non sibi, sed nobis incarnatus; non sibi, sed nobis legi subjectus; non sibi, sed nobis passus, crucifixus, mortuus; non sibi, sed nobis resurrexit ex mortuis: ita etiam non sibi, sed Nobis ascendit in cœlum, & qvum sit primitiæ generis nostri, qvando in cœlum ascendit, nos coram Patre in se constituit, obtulit, & commendavit.


### XVIII. Therefore, not by another’s, but by His own virtue and power, as much…

XVIII. Therefore, not by another’s, but by His own virtue and power, as much that which He possesses according to the flesh (which the Calvinists strenuously deny) from the Union truly received divine [power], just as with that which is proper to divinity, He raised His body to the heavens. See Thomas also Part 3, q. 57, a. 3. XIX. And hence the specific difference of Christ's ascension becomes clear, of which no similar example can be given in the nature of things: 1. Others raised to heaven made a complete departure from this world, as Enoch and Elijah: but Christ promised His presence on earth. 2. Others are said to be received by heaven: Christ is written to have occupied heaven itself, Acts 3:21. 3. Others are assumed into heaven and remain: but Christ is said to have been made superior to the heavens themselves; and to have penetrated the heavens themselves; indeed to have ascended ὑπεράνω πάντων (above all things). 4. Christ alone ascended into heaven in such a way that He sits at the right hand of the divine Majesty, which happens to none of the angels or saints for all eternity. XX. The cloud, which lowered itself to the summit of the mountain, received Christ and withdrew Him from the sight of the Apostles, not like the chariot of Elijah, so that it might be a support for Christ ascending, by way of a vehicle, because it merely hid Him, or as the Syrian Interpreter translates, He was hidden. XXI. Therefore that cloud was 1. A symbol of the glory and majesty, which appears from there, most illustrious, by which He was exalted; 2. A likeness of the presence of Christ after the ascension into the heavens; 3. An admonition, lest we measure the mystery with the measuring rod of reason, but rather consider that the veil of the cloud was interposed. XXII. In the O.T. similarly the glory of the God of Israel appeared over the tabernacle χειροποίητον (made by hands) in a cloud, Num. 9:15. Rightly therefore Bede: Everywhere the creature provides obedience to its creator: The stars indicate Him being born, they cover Him suffering: the clouds receive Him ascending, they will accompany Him returning to judgment. XXII. The matter, or subject, which ascends, is properly the human nature, because according to the divine nature He could not ascend. XXIV. And although the human nature does not ascend alone, but the person, who is God and man, whose it is to act and work (for they are of the supposita), ascends; yet the divine nature does not ascend by itself, because according to Thomas, Part 3, q. 57, a. 2, there is nothing higher and more sublime than the Deity, to which He could ascend, since it is immovable and non-local, but God is to be believed to have ascended according to His humanity. XXV. And so Holy Scripture speaks Ps. 8:6, Dan. 7:9, 10, Acts 2:3, 6,

Hence Gregory, Book 2 against Maximus, Homily 29: That nature, to which it was said, 'You are earth, and into earth you shall go,' today was going into heaven.

XXVI. Furthermore, while we have said that Christ ascended according to his human nature, we have not removed its reality, as the Photinians miserably believe. For it alone was not changed, because the same body remained, but it was not endowed with the same qualities. 1. After the ascension, he is not only called the son of man, but is also described with more words. Acts 1. 13.

XXVII. Augustine, in his book On Faith and the Creed, ch. 6, reports that there were heathens and heretics to whom the Christian religion was hateful for this reason above all, that it taught openly from Scripture that a terrestrial body could be in heaven. But what else does Ostorodus do in his Institutions, ch. 14, and the Socinians, while they most ineptly deny that a spiritual body can have flesh and blood?

XXVIII. For the Lord Apostle, 1 Cor. 15, joins two things in this expression: 1. Body, 2. Spiritual, namely substance and quality. For in the Pauline passage, the body is truly both spiritual and animal, which is manifest from the scope and context of the Apostle. 2. By the name of body, when the discourse is about man, the whole structure of all the parts of the human body is understood. 3. Christ himself says, 'You will see the son of man coming in the clouds of heaven,' Matt. 26. 64. But a spiritual body cannot be seen, by the testimony of Christ, Luke 24. 39. It is plain from this that the discourse is about an animal body. See Dr. Menzer in Exeg. A. C. p. 750.

XXIX. The object of the ascension, where he ascended to, is heaven. Where indeed by the appellation of heaven is not denoted 1. The air, which is also called heaven itself in Holy Scripture, Gen. 1, 26; 2, 19; Lev. 26, 19; Matt. 6, 26; Luke 8, 5. For if, says Augustine, these heavens were believed to be the place of God, birds would deservedly be better, since their life is nearer to God. Nor that heaven of the stars, Gen. 15, 15. For Scripture says that he ascended above all heavens, penetrated the heavens, and was made higher than the heavens.

XXX. 3. Nor a certain Empyrean heaven, which is a pure figment of the Scholastic-Calvinist brain (concerning which Thomas, p. 1, q. 68, c. 4). For it is an imaginary being, approaching most closely to the likeness of a carnal dream about a Talmudic and Mahometan heaven, presumed by the Calvinists, and sought from the puddles of the Scholastics (See what

Geiler von Kaysersberg noted from Rosetus & Bernardinus.) Entirely contrary to the Word of God, and long since overturned by our Theologians. XXXI. 4. Nor is it merely that glorious and blessed seat and dwelling-place of God, into which the souls of the Blessed, with the holy Angels, Moses, Elias, Enoch, and the Saints who have risen, are assumed. Which, although, as to what it is, the eye has not seen, etc. Isa. 64:4, 2 Cor. 2:9, we nevertheless believe it to be, because Scripture expressly teaches this, and that it is the proper seat for blessed souls. From this we relegate Numa, Socrates, Hercules, and the remaining dregs of infidel men, whom Erasmus and Zwingli perversely place therein. XXXII. It remains therefore that by heaven, into which Christ is said to have ascended, must be understood 6. The infinite kingdom and throne of God, which He occupies by His omnipresence and infinite power, from which all consideration of locality and physical circumscription must depart. XXXIII. For 1. The Savior Himself inculcates this in John 20:17, while by that phrase, 'I ascend to my Father,' He wishes to indicate that He, having now conquered death and the devil, is about to enter into His glory, etc. The ascension of CHRIST to the heavens is therefore equivalent to this ascension to the Father, whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain, who fills heaven and earth, not indeed by spaces of places, but solely by blessedness, glory, and the majesty of eternal and infinite power, as St. Augustine explains in Book 1 of the Sermon on the Mount. XXXIV. 2. St. Peter explains the same thing in Acts 2:33, while he interprets the ascension of CHRIST through His session. And although they are distinct articles, they nevertheless have a great affinity with one another, the terminus of the ascension, and the placement at the right hand of the Father, which is not obscurely hinted at in 1 Peter 3 and is piously taught in the Augsburg Confession, Article 3. XXXV. There, therefore, is this heaven, where the right hand of God is, which is not a place, nor can it be included in any place. Considering which, Calvin, on chapter 3 of Acts and on chapter 5 of Matthew, himself, driven by the force of truth, affirmed. XXXVI. Bellarmine contradicts this assertion of ours in Book 2 of the Incarnation, chapter 12, when he says that that heaven is corporeal, because 1. heaven and earth are opposed in Scripture as being of the same nature; 2. It is called the seat of GOD. But I say to 1. That from the hypothesis presupposed, let him posit what must first be proven. 2. In those passages which are cited, heaven is expressly named the throne of GOD. Will it then be corporeal? Ἄτοπον ἐξ ἀθεόλογον. 3. From the pronouncement of the philosopher, lib. 1. de cœlo, c. 9: Outside of heaven there is neither place nor time. To 2. it is childish to draw such conclusions from phrases of that sort. Much more correctly Augustine, l. 2. de ser. Dom. in monte: God is not contained by the space of places. And lib. de Cognit. Veræ: God himself is his own place; let everything that is besides God become vile, who protects us in the place of this life; may he himself be our place after life.

XXXVII. 2. The Calvinists wish to prove from many passages that Christ, by his ascension, came to a created place, Martinius p. 526 in Cath. fidei, both because Scripture itself calls it so, and from other similar instances.

XXXIIX. To this I oppose 1. The Rule of Procopius on ch. 3 of Isaiah: Ἀνθρώποις ὦσιν, ἀνθρωπίνως ἡ γραφὴ διαλέγεται. 2. I say that by the word for place, a corporeal surrounding is not always denoted, Isa. 26, 21; Hos. 5, 5. Scripture says that He ascended ὑπεράνω πάντων οὐρανῶν, Eph. 4, 10. Therefore, He did not remain among created things. Where it is to be noted, as the Greeks have observed, that when this word ὑπεράνω is placed absolutely, it signifies being in heaven, but when a genitive is added, it is to be far above and over, as in Eph. 1, 21. 4. Created heavens are at some time to perish, Ps. 102, 27. Christ, however, will remain in His heaven forever. 5. I oppose to them Fr. Junius, Part 2, Ope. Theol., p. 600: He ascended not only into heaven, but also above all heavens; and therefore the heavens are below Him, and the earth is inferior to both.

XXXIX. How much more modestly, therefore, did Justin write in Dial. cum Tryph. p. 279, than they: ὁ ἄῥῥητος πατὴρ καὶ κύριος τῶν πάντων οὔτε ποὶ ἀφί- κται, οὔτε περιπατεῖ, οὔτε καθεύδει, οὔτε ἀνίσταται, ἀλλὰ ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ ὅπη πότε μένει.

XL. The form, or manner of the ascension, is considered not only in that visible elevation of the body of Christ to the regions above, by which a true translation and visible one was concluded by the clouds and this visible heaven, but further Christ ascended, that He might sit at the right hand of the Father.

XLI. There are, therefore, two acts of the ascension: one visible, the other invisible. The former is called common, because angels, and also Enoch and Elijah, are said to have ascended into heaven: but the latter is proper, the right hand of God, at which He sat down; a thing which pertains to no man, nay, not even to any of the angels. Hebr. 1, 13.

XLII. Its terminus a quo is the Mount of Olives; the space through which, the air: the terminus ad quem, the clouds.

XLIII. The invisible act, however, is the triumph of CHRIST in the clouds of heaven, held up to the seat of the divine Majesty. Its terminus ad quem is the final terminus of the ascension, namely, the heaven ὑψηλότερον, which for that reason is not a place, because a terminus ad quem is not always a place.

XLIV. The Calvinists dissent, and strive to strike us with that saying in Acts 3:21. For Calvin, Beza, and many others refer it to ambiguous expressions (the Greeks call them ἐπαμφοτερίζοντα).

XLV. But 1. The rule of faith stands in the way, because the Holy Spirit is not λοξίας, nor does Holy Scripture play with amphibologies and ambiguities; 2. Logical συνάφεια, because they transpose the subject into the place of the predicate, when nevertheless the article ἀναφορικός distinguishes the subject from the predicate; 3. Grammatical συνέχεια, because τό δέχεσθαι is of the middle voice, denoting the past, because it is ἄοριστος; it is also never used passively, but always ἐνεργητικῶς. The sense therefore is this: it behooves heaven to have received Christ, namely at the time divinely appointed, after the resurrection from the dead. See more in the works of the renowned Lord Dr. Menzer in Anti Mart. p. 49, and Lord Dr. Meisner in Phil. Sob. part 1, p. 411, 412.

XLVI. By the word heaven, in the Pauline passage, to be caught up into the third heaven, 2 Cor. 12:2, is not understood the highest or extreme heaven, as the Sacramentarians always interpret it, if only they see that name dealing with the heavenly state, but the dwelling and throne of GOD.

XLVII. For here one ought not to number the heavens by reason of place, but the third heaven is called κατ̓ ἐξοχὴν that most excellent heaven, which Paul in v. 4 calls paradise, that is, the state or heavenly place of the blessed, in which God offers Himself to be seen by His elect, with ineffable joy and perpetual glory. But if anyone wishes to attend precisely to the number, we oppose to him that saying of Hilary: Let not the rashness of human nature presume anything for itself concerning the number of the heavens. See the renowned Lord Dr. Meisner in P. S. part 1, p. 81.

XLIIX. Furthermore, neither should that be passed over which Nahum in Consp. 467, Pierius against Lord Dr. Menzer, etc., and the remaining Calvinists gather from the ascension of Christ: Christ ascended into heaven from this earth, and is to remain in it until the final judgment. Therefore, He is far distant from the earth from the Church militant.

XLIX. But there is no force in this, because there are various modes of presence. For it does not follow: CHRIST is not present naturally, visibly, and in the ordinary way, therefore He cannot present Himself in the Church in any other mode whatsoever. CHRIST is removed at least by τοπικῇ & φυσικῇ παρουσίᾳ. 2. But the fact that CHRIST is not visibly present on earth in the ordinary way can detract nothing from the special οἰκονομίας of grace. For we have examples of the apparition of the same Christ, both He who ascended and He who put an end to His visible conversation. Thus He appeared to Stephen, Acts 7:56. Thus He showed Himself to be seen by Lord Paul on the road to Damascus, Acts 9:17. And there were many such visions of Him, Acts 26:16. One of this kind was offered at Corinth, Acts 18:9, and at Jerusalem, Acts 23:11, concerning which he says, 1 Cor. 9:1, Have I not seen J. CHRIST, and from which he confirms the certainty of the resurrection of Christ, 1 Cor. 15:3. He, now about to ascend into heaven, promises his presence on earth, Matt. 28:20. 4. He does not simply ascend, but ὑπεράνω πάντων ὐρανῶν, that he might fill all things, Eph. 4:10, not γυμνῇ τῇ θεότητι, but & σαρκωθεῖς, as Oecumenius speaks. 5. Therefore we invert the κατά βίαιον: Nay, because he was made higher than all the heavens, Heb. 7:26, so that it was necessary for heaven to receive him, Acts 3:21, i.e., to reign, 1 Cor. 15:25, therefore he can also be with his body wherever he wills to be, without injury to the truth of his body, even if the manner in which that can be done does not square with physical rules and properties. For all things are possible to God, who does with his body whatever he wills, and yet it remains a body, says Augustine.

L. I would now betake myself to the remaining matters, if the narrowness of the pages did not stand in the way:

LI. This meditation on the Ascension of Christ 1. Is useful πρὸς παράκλησιν (for consolation). For by it the business of our redemption and of His mission was consummated. For on account of sin we were slaves of Satan, and because of that heaven was closed. But by this departure of His, Christ unlocked heaven and showed the true way of ascending. Christ ascended into heaven in body; He wishes us also to ascend in heart. Let us ascend with Christ in heart, so that, when the day of His promise arrives, we may follow also in body. Augustine, serm. 175. de Temp. St. Paul exhorts us to this in Col. 3, 1. Heaven is our fatherland. Let us therefore seek the heavenly and future city. 2. πρὸς νυθεσίαν (for admonition). We must strive for holiness, because Christ, the θεάνθρωπος (God-man), victor over death and Satan, is present in all our actions Therefore, O man, consider three things in all your actions: 1. God, 2. Your neighbor, 3. Yourself. Let us live εὐσεβῶς or piously toward God, δικαίως or justly toward our neighbor, and σωφρόνως or soberly toward ourselves. If we do this, we shall enjoy both the presence of Christ and the service of the angels. To Christ our Victor and Triumpher, for his glorious ascension, be praise, honor, and eternal blessing, Amen.

Latin:

XIIX. Non ergò alienâ, sed propriâ virtute & potentiâ, tàm eâ, qvam secundùm carnem (qvod Calviniani strenuè negant) ex Unioste verè divinam accepit, quàm eâ, quæ divinitatis est propria, corpus suum ad cœlos evexit. Vide Thomam etiam Part. 3. q. 57. a. 3. XIX. Atqve hinc patescit differentia specifica ascensionis Christi, cujus simile exemplum nullum in Naturâ rerum dari potest: 1. Alii in cœlum elati, discessum prorsus fecerunt ex hôc mundo, ut Enoch & Elias: Christ⁹ verò præsentiam suam in terris promisit. 2. Alii cœlo recipi dicuntur: Christus cœlum ipsum occupasse scribitur, Act. 3, 21. 3. Alii in cœlum assumuntur, & manent: Christus verò Cœlis ipsis superior factus dicitur; cœlosq́; ipsos penetrasse; imò ὑπεράνω πάντων ascendisse. 4. Ascendit Christus solus ita in cœlum, ut sedeat ad dextram Majestatis divinæ, qvòd nulli vel angelorum vel sanctorum in omnem æternitatem obtingit. XX. Nubes, qvæ se ad montis verticem demisit, Christum suscepit, & subduxit è conspectu Apostolorum, non veluti currus Eliæ, ut esset adminiculum Christo ascendenti, per modum vehiculi, qvia tantùm abscondit ipsum, seu ut Syrus Interpres vertit, Occultatus est. XXI. Fuit ergò nubes ista 1. Symbolum gloriæ & majestatis, qvæ inde apparet, maximè illustre, qvâ exaltatus; 2. Simulacrum præsentiæ Christi post ascensionem in cœlos; 3. Admonitio, ne rationis decempedâ mysterium metiamur, sed potiùs cogitemus, velamen nubis interpositum esse. XXII. In V. T. similiter gloria Dei Israëlis super tabernaculum χειροποίητον in nube apparebat, Num. 9, 15. Rectè igitur Beda: Ubiqve creatura creatori suo præstat obseqvium: Astra indicant nascentem, patientem obnubunt: nubes recipiunt ascendentem, redeundem ad judicium comitabuntur. XXII. Materia, sive subjectum, qvod ascendit, est propriè humana natura, qvia secundùm divinam naturam non potuit ascendere. XXIV. Et licet humana natura sola non ascendat, sed persona, qvæ Deus & homo, cujus est agere & operari, (sunt enim suppositorum) ascendat; tamen divina natura per se non ascendit, qvia juxta Thomam, Part. 3. q. 57. a. 2. Deitate nihil altius & sublimius, qvô possit ascendere, qvandoqvidem illa est immobilis & illocalis, sed Deus secundùm humanitatem ascendisse credendus est. XXV. Et ita S. Scriptura loqvitur Psal. 8, 6. Dan. 7, 9, 10. Act. 2, 3. 6,

Hinc Gregorius Lib. 2. cont. Maxim. Hom. 29. Illa natura, cui dictum est, Terra es, & in terram ibis, hodie in cœlum ibat.

XXVI. Porrò, dum Christum secundùm humanam naturam diximus ascendisse, non sustulimus ejus veritatem, ut Photiniani miserè sentiunt. Nam sola non fuit mutata, quia mansit idem corpus, sed non iisdem qualitatibus præditum. 1. Post ascensionem non tantùm filius hominis vocatur, sed etiam pluribus describitur verbis. Apost. 1. 13.

XXVII. Augustinus Lib. de fide & Symb. c. 6. refert, fuisse Ethnicos, & hæreticos, quibus religio Christiana hoc potissimùm nomine invisa erat, quòd ex scriptura palam docuerit, corpus terrenum esse posse in cœlo. Quid autem aliud facit Ostorodus Instit. c. 14. & sociennes, dum ineptissimè negant, corpus spirituale, posse, habere carnem & sanguinem.

XXVIII. Nam D. Apostolus 1. Cor. 15. in hac locutione duo conjungit, 1. Corpus, 2. spirituale, nempe substantiam & qualitatem. Nam verè corpus in loco Paulino est & spirituale & animale, id quod ex scopo & contextu Apostoli manifestum est. 2. Corporis nomine, cùm de homine sermo est, toto compages omnium humani corporis partium intelligitur. 3. Christus ipse dicit, filium hominis videbitis, venientem in nubibus cœli, Matth. 26. 64. Corpus autem spirituale videri nequit, teste Christo, Luc. 24. 39. Planum hinc est, sermonem esse de corpore animali. Videatur Dn. D. Menzerus in Exeg. A. C. p. 750.

XXIX. Objectum ascensionis, quò ascendit, est cœlum. Ubi sanè cœli appellatione non notatur 1. Aër, qui & ipsum cœlum in S. Literis nominatur, Gen. 1, 26. 2, 19. Lev. 26, 19. Matth. 6, 26. Luc. 8, 5. Si enim his colis, ait Augustinus, locus Dei esse crederetur, meliores meritò forent aves, quippe quorum vita Deo est vicinor. Neq; illud cœlum stellarum, Gen. 15, 15. Scriptura enim dicit, ascendisse supra omnes cœlos, penetrâsse cœlos, & factum esse sublimiorem cœlis.

XXX. 3. Neq; cœlum quoddam Empyreum, quod purum putum cerebri Scholastico-Calvinistici, (de quo Thomas p. 1. q. 68. c. 4.) phantasma est. Etenim Ens est imaginárium, ad similitudinem carnalis somnii de Cœlo Thalmudico & Mahometico accedens quàm proximè, à Calvinistis præsumtum, ex Scholasticorum lacunis petitum (Vide, qua Keiser-

spergim. ex Roseto & Bernardino annotavit.) Verbo Dei prorsus contrarium, & à nostris Theologis jam dudum eversum. XXXI. 4. Neq; etiam est tantùm sedes & domicilium illud Dei gloriosum ac beatum, in qvod animæ Beatorum, cum S. Angelis, Moses, Elias, Enochs & S. qui resurrexerunt, assumuntur. Qvod, etsi, qvale sit, Oculus non vidit, &c. Esa. 64, 4. 2. Cor. 2, 9. credimus tamen esse, qvia hoc expressè Script. docet, & propriam sedem esse B. animis. Ex hôc relegamus Numam, Socratem, Herculem, & reliqvam hominum infidelium colluviem, qvos perverversè Eras. & Zvv. in eô collocant. XXXII. Relinqvitur ergò qvòd per cælum, in qvod Christus ascendisse dicitur, intelligendum sit 6. Infinitum Dei regnum & thronus, qvem suâ omnipræsentiâ & infinitô imperiô occupat, â qvô omnis respectus localitatis & circumscriptionis Physicæ facessere debet. XXXIII. Nam 1. Ipse Salvator hoc inculcat Joh. 20, 17. dum phrasi illâ, Ascendo ad Patrem meum, indicare vult, se, victâ jam morte & diabolô, in gloriam suam ingressurum esse &c. Æqvipollet igitur ascensio CHRISTI ad cælos huic Ascensioni ad patrem, qvem cæli cælorum capere non possunt, qvi cælum & terram implet, non qvidem locorum spaciis, sed solâ beatitudine, gloriâ ac majestate potentiæ æternâ & infinitâ, ut explicat D. Augustinus Lib. 1. de Serm. Dom. in monte. XXXIV. 2. Idipsum D. Petrus explicat Actor. 2, 33. dum ascensionem CHRISTI per sessionem interpretatur. Et licet sint distincti articuli, magnam tamen cognationem invicem habent, terminus ascensionis, & collocatio ad dextram patris, qvod haud obscurè innuitur 1. Petr. 3. & in Augustana Confessione Art. 3. piè traditur. XXXV. Ibi igitur cælum hoc, ubi textra Dei, qvæ non est locus, nec ullô locô includi potest. Qvod perpendens Calvin. super cap. 3. Actor. & super c. 5. Matth. ipse, vi veritatis adactus, affirmavit. XXXVI. Huic nostræ assertioni contrariatur Bellarminus lib. 2. de Incarnat. cap. 12. dum ait, Cælum illud esse corporeum, quia 1. cælum & terra in Scriptura opponuntur, tanquam ejusdem naturæ; 2. Ea dicitur sedes DEI. Verùm dico ad 1. Qvod ex hypothesi præsupponat, quæ priùs probanda. 2. In illis locis, quæ adducuntur, cœlum disertè nominatur thronus DEI. Anne erit corporeus? Ἄτοπον ἐξ ἀθεόλογον 3. Ex pronunciato philosophi lib. 1. de cœlo. c. 9. Extra cœlum neque locus neq; tempus est. Ad 2. pueriliter ex phrasibus ejusmodi colligere illos. Longè rectiùs Augustinus l. 2. de ser. Dom. in monte: Non spatiô locorum continetur Deus. Et lib. de Cognit. Veræ veræ: Deus ipse sibi locus est; vilescat totum, quicquid præter Deum est, qui nos tuetur in locô vitæ hujus; ipse post vitam sit locus noster.

XXXVII. 2. Calviniani ex multis locis probare volunt, Christum per ascensionem venisse ad locum creatum, Martinius p. 526. in Cath. fidei tum, quia Scriptura ipsa ita vocat, tum ex consimilibus aliis.

XXXIIX. Cui oppono 1. Regulam Procopii in c. 3. Esa. Ἀνθρώποις ὦσιν, ἀνθρωπίνως ἡ γραφὴ διαλέγεται. 2. dico, quòd vocabulo loci non semper corporale ambiens notetur, Esa. 26, 21. Os. 5, 5. Scriptura dicit, Ascendisse ὑπεράνω πάντων οὐρανῶν Eph. 4, 10. Ergò in creatis non mansit. Ubi notandum, quod Græci observârunt, Quando vox hæc ὑπεράνω absolutè ponitur, significare eam in cœlo, quando verò Genitivus additur esse longè, super, & supra, ut Eph. 1, 21. 4. Cœli creati aliquando perituri sunt, Ps. 102, 27. Christus autem in cœlo suo manebit in perpetuum. 5. Fr. Junium Part. 2. Ope. Theol. p. 600. illis oppono: Non solùm in cœlum, sed etiam supra omnes cœlos ascendit; ac proinde cœli sunt infra ipsum, terra utrisq; inferior.

XXXIX. Quantò modestiùs ergò scripsit Justinus in Dial. cum Tryph. p. 279. quàm illi: ὁ ἄῥῥητος πατὴρ καὶ κύριος τῶν πάντων οὔτε ποὶ ἀφίκται, οὔτε περιπατεῖ, οὔτε καθεύδει, οὔτε ἀνίσταται, ἀλλὰ ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ ὅπη πότε μένει.

XL. Forma, seu modus ascensionis, spectatur non tantùm in visibili illâ corporis Christi ad superos elevatione, quâ vera translatio & visibilis nubibus, & cœlô istô spectabili clausa fuit, sed ulteriùs Christę ascendit, ut sedeat ad dextram Patris.

XLI. Duo igitur actûs sunt ascensionis: Visibilis unus; invisibilis alter. Isse communis dicitur, quia angeli etiam, Enoch & Elias in cœlum ascendere dicuntur: hic verò proprius, Dextra Dei, ad quam consedit; id quod nulli hominum, imò nec ulli angelorum competit. Hebr. 1, 13.

XLII. Illius terminus â qvo, est mons Oliveti; spatium per qvod, aër: terminus ad qvem, nubes.

XLIII. Actus verô invisibilis est triumphus CHRISTI in nubibus cœli, usq; ad sedem Majestatis divinæ habitus. Hujus terminus ad qvem, est ultimus terminus ascensionis, nempe, cœlum ὑψηλότερον, qvod propterea nõ est locus, qvia termin⁹ ad qvẽ, non est semper loc⁹.

XLIV. Calviniani dissentiunt, & dicto illo Act. 3, 21, nos ferire satagunt. Calvinus enim, Beza, & multi alii, ad ambiguas locutiones (Græci vocant ἐπαμφοτερίζοντα) referunt.

XLV. Verùm obstat 1. Regula fidei, qvia non est λοξίας Spiritus S. neq; ludit S. Scriptura amphiboliis & ambiguitatibus; 2. Logica συνάφεια, qvia transponunt subjectum in locum prædicati, qvum tamen articulus ἀναφορικός distingvat subjectum à prædicato; 3. Grammatica συνέχεια, qvia τό δέχεσθαι est Mediæ vocis, notans præteritum, quia est ἄοριστος; Nunqvam etiam passivè, sed semper ἐνεργητικῶς usurpatur. Sensus igitur hic est: Christum oportet cœlum suscepisse, nempe statutô divinitus tempore, post resurrectionẽ â mortuis. Plura vide apud Cla. Dn. D. Menzerum in Anti Mart. p. 49. & Dn. D. Meisnerum in Phil. Sob. part. 1. p. 411. 412.

XLVI. Vocabulô cœli, in loco Paulino, raptum esse in tertium cœlum, 2. Cor. 12, 2. non intelligitur supremum seu extremum cœli, uti Sacramentarii semper, si modò nomen illud de statu cœlesti agere vident, interpretantur, sed domicilium & thronum DEI.

XLVII. Nam hîc cœlos numerare ratione loci non oportet, sed tertium cœlum vocatur κατ̓ ἐξοχὴν præstantissimum illud cœlum, qvod Paulus v. 4. vacat paradisum, id est, statum seu locum cœlestẽ beatorum, in qvo Deus electis suis se conspiciendum præbet, ineffabili cum gaudio, perpetuáqve cum gloria. Qvod si qvis numerum præcisè attendere vult, opponimus ei illud Hilarii: De numero cœlorum nil sibi præsumat humanæ naturæ temeritas. Vide Cl. Dn. D. Meisn. in P. S. part. 1. p. 81.

XLIIX. Porrò, nec illud prætereundum, qvod ex ascensione Christi colligit Nahum in Consp. 467. Pierius contra Dn. D. Menzerum &c. & reliqvi Calviniani: Christus ascendit in cœlum ex hâc terrâ, & in eâ mansurus est usq; ad extremum judicium. Ergò longè ab Ecclesia militante abest à terra.

XLIX. Verùm, nulla inest vis, quia varii sunt modi præsentiæ. Non enim sequitur: CHRISTUS naturaliter, visibiliter, & ordinariè nõ est præsens, Ergò nullô prorsus aliô modô sese in Ecclesiâ sistere potest. τοπικῇ & φυσικῇ saltem παρουσίᾳ sublatus est CHRISTUS. 2. Quòd autem CHRISTUS ordinariâ ratione in terris visibiliter non adest, id speciali οἰκονομίας gratiæ nihil detrahere potest. Apparitionis n. Christi ejusdem, & qui ascendit, & qui visibili conversationi finem imposuit, exempla habemus. Sic Stephano apparuit, Act. 7, 56. Sic D. Paulo videndum se præbuit in via Damascenâ, Act. 9, 17. Et plures ejusmodi visiones illi fuère, Act. 26, 16. Hujusmodi Corinthi oblata Act. 18, 9. & Jerosolymis, Act. 23, 11. de quib. ait. 1. Cor. 9, 1. Nonne vidi J. CHRISTUM, & ex quibus certitudinem resurrectionis Christi confirmat, 1. Cor. 15, 3. Ille jam ascensurus in cœlum suam præsentiam in terris pollicetur Matth. 28, 20. 4. Non simpliciter ascendit, sed ὑπεράνω πάντων ὐρανῶν, ut impleret omnia, Eph. 4, 10. non γυμνῇ τῇ θεότητι, sed & σαρκωθεῖς, ut Oecumenius loquitur. 5. κατά βίαιον ergò invertimus: Imò, quia omnibus cœlis factus est sublimior, Hebr. 7, 26. ita, ut oportuerit ipsum cœlum accipere, Act. 3, 12. i. e. regnare. 1. Cor. 15. 25. ideò etiam corpore suô esse potest, ubicunq; vult esse, sine læsione veritatis sui corporis, etiamsi modus, qvô id fieri possit, ad regulas & proprietates physicas non qvadret. Omnia enim possibilia sunt Deo, qui de corpore suo facit, quidquid vult, & tamen manet corpus, ait Augustinus.

L. Ad reliqva jam me conferrem, si pagellarum angustia non obstaret:

LI. Hæc meditatio Ascensionis Christi 1. Prodest πρὸς παράκλησιν. Illâ enim redemtionis nostræ & legationis suæ negocium consummatum. Nam propter peccatum mancipia Satanæ eramus, & ob id cœlum clausum. At hôc abitu suô Christus cœlum reseravit, & veram ascendendi viam monstravit. Ascendit Christus in cœlum corpore, nos qvoq; vult ascendere corde. Ascendamus cum Christo corde, ut, cùm dies ejus promissionis advenerit, sequamur & corpore. Augustinus serm. 175. de Temp. Ad hanc hortatur D. Paulus Col. 3, 1. Cœlum nostra patria est. Cælestem ergò & futuram inquiramus civitatem. 2. πρὸς νυθεσίαν. Sanctitati studendum nobis, quia Christus θεάνθρωπος, victor mortis & Satanæ, in cunctis actionibus præsens est. Tria ergò ô homo in cunctis actib. respicias: 1. Deum, 2. Proximum, 3. Teipsum. Erga Deum, εὐσεβῶς vel piè, erga proximum δικαίως, vel justè, erga nos ipsos σωφρόνως, vel sobriè vivamus. Hoc si egerimus, & præsentia Christi, & angelorum servitio fruemur. Christo Victori & Triumphatori nostro, pro ascensu suo glorioso, sit laus, honor & sempiterna benedictio, Amen.


## 45 Forty-fifth Disputation. On the Session of Christ at the Right Hand of the Father

The voice, 'Christ has ascended into Heaven,' is not to be feared. For the fear that might arise from the ascension is taken away by the majestic session of the Savior at the right hand of the Father. Therefore, whoever cannot see this Majesty in heaven, let him believe it to be at the right hand of the Almighty; whoever imagines heaven to be a certain place, let him begin to believe that this is not a place but infinite glory. But after enough and more has been done in the preceding sections regarding the ascension of Christ, it must now be examined with what fruit that glorious event is attended. For the ascension and the session are connected by an indissoluble bond, whence in the Apostles' Creed, if we believe Augustine, Bartholomew wished to connect these two. Indeed, Scripture itself asserts not only that Christ was taken up, but also that he sits at the right hand of God. Mark 16:19, Colossians 3:1, 1 Peter 3:21-22, Hebrews 12:2 affirm it. Hence it is that this σχέσις (relation) is said to designate the effect of Christ's ascension and the θεοπρεπεστάτην (most God-befitting) illustration of his majesty and glory. Concerning this, may Christ grant a good outcome, we are now about to inquire, not indeed according to ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν (private interpretation), but under the guidance of the most holy Spirit in the sacrosanct Word; that is, we shall see: 1. What the word 'right hand' signifies; 2. What it is to sit at the right hand of the Father; 3. According to which nature Christ is to be said to sit. Finally, with a brief exposition of the final cause, we shall include the practical use of this article.

Thesis I.

Most rightly did Nazianzen once say: πολλὰ ἀνθρωποπαθῶς λέγονται, ἀλλὰ θεοπρεπῶς νοῦνται (many things are spoken in human terms, but are understood in a God-befitting manner). If this rule deserves remarkable observation in any article, it deserves it most especially in this one. For many here think that the word 'right hand' denotes something Carnal, contrary to what the Fathers intended at various times; nay, contrary to what the Holy Spirit Himself intended, as we shall see in the progress [of this work]. II. For, to say nothing here of the crudity of the Anthropomorphites, or the sedentary [notion] of the Nestorians, who imagined two καϑέδρας [thrones], one in which the Father sits, another in which the Son sits: we marvel only at the Papists and Calvinists, that they do not fear to discourse so spiritedly about this right hand from the scrutiny of reason ἄτερ γραφῶν [without the Scriptures], outside of which, however, no one has ever been able to know perfectly what that is, whose right hand it is. III. For from them, to bring forward only Gregory of Valencia, it is evident how beautifully he himself agrees with the Zwinglians in the present business, to whom it is the more credible that the other Esauites give their vote, because they do not fear, with the modern Nestorian Calvinists, ὁμοϑυμαδὸν [with one accord] and with a clearly reckless daring, to annihilate the Majesty of Christ. In a word, he does not blush to make the right hand of the Father a seat and a certain place, so as to spite the Ubiquitists (thus he calls our people by calumny), in which opinion it is most manifest that the Calvinists also stand. IV. Martyr settles the matter similarly: he says that the Father can have a stature of great height, and a little son sitting [there], where nevertheless the Father's right hand is more widely extended than the little son's body is dilated. From which, there is no need for anxious divination as to what he wishes to infer in the present business, for anyone gathers that a certain seat is determined for that most glorious CHRIST, within the spaces of which he is enclosed, yet is nevertheless to be said to occupy the right hand of the Father. V. Zwingli certainly, when about to explain this right hand, always inclines to interpret it as a place, remitting nothing of the crudity of the Calvinist genius: whence his disciples point to it as the third heaven, where CHRIST is detained, into which he ascended, in which he will move about freely, and by the counsel of the Father, is to remain until the final judgment. Whether the passages by which they strive to prove their opinion, Acts 3:21, Mark 16:19, Ephesians 1:20, 1 Peter 3:22, Hebrews 1:3 & 7:26 & 8:1, Colossians 3:1, can be a patronage to them, we shall see in the investigation itself. VI. Following the Scripture, we have learned to think far otherwise of this right hand of the Father, whence [we hold] it not to be a certain place, but a divine and infinite Majesty and power, which is made clear from the various appellations and titles with which it is adorned and described by the Holy Spirit.…

VII. For, to bring forward only a few from many: Exod. 15:6, it is called the right hand magnified in strength; Ps. 77:11, the right hand of the Most High; Ps. 89:14, an arm with power; Isa. 48:13, the right hand measuring the heavens; Ps. 139:10, everywhere present; Isa. 48:13, creating all things; Matt. 25:31, the throne of the final judgment; ch. 19:28, the throne of Majesty; Luke 22:69, the right hand of the power of God; Heb. 1:8, a throne for ever and ever; Dan. 7:14, a throne of eternal power, etc.

IIX. These and similar passages are diametrically opposed to the speculations and trifles of the adversaries, and, unless they wish to contradict the Holy Spirit to His face, they will be forced to abandon their position and lay aside those crasser Anthropomorphic thoughts: For thus we conclude: Whatever right hand in Scripture is marked with the aforementioned titles, it is most rightly believed to denote not a place, but divine and infinite Majesty. But the former is true concerning the right hand at which CHRIST sits. Therefore, the latter also.

IX. What? That the adversaries themselves, in the question of what sits at the right hand of GOD, while they foist the whole person in place of the human nature, cannot escape, through this description of the right hand, this absurdity, by which it would follow that the divine nature is locatable, since it is claimed by them to sit with the human nature at the Father's right hand, which location of divinity is a mere dream, nay, pure blasphemy. But if they wish to avoid this ἄτοπον [absurdity], it is necessary that they either bring forward a better definition of the right hand from Scripture, or abandon their worse one.

X. It is not beside the point, moreover, for us to oppose Polanus here, and to show how the Holy Spirit limits this right hand to heaven, the higher regions, height, etc., just as in Eph. 1:20, Col. 3:1, Heb. 1:3, ch. 8:1, certain differences of place seem to be hinted at, for thus in part also will thesis 5 be satisfied.

…XI. We say, therefore, that these and similar passages help the adversaries little, since they ineptly conclude from them: Christ is in heaven, therefore He is only in heaven. For in a similar way one might conclude from the Lord's Prayer: Our Father is in heaven, therefore He is only in heaven: which consequence even if they should solve for us, they claim that their own sophistries, taken from those less correctly understood passages, have been solved.

XII. They therefore commit the gross fallacy of Ignoratio Elenchi. For Christ is not said to sit at the right hand of the Father in heaven for the reason that he obtains a determined place there, and is circumscribed by the same, but because he sits on the throne of God, which is said to be placed in heaven; 1 Kings 8:36, Psalm 2:4, Psalm 103:19, etc. Whose Majesty is nevertheless said to fill the whole earth, Isaiah 6:3, as Mr. Schröd. in Throno regali p. 60, refutes this objection of the adversaries at length.

XIII. This same right hand can be explained and defined from its works: our opinion can also be confirmed from the Fathers: but it is better to approach the most illustrious Mr. President, part 2: Phil. sobr. c. 1, s. 1, p. 17, 18, etc. One thing is still notable, which both the Papists and some Calvinists, driven by the force of truth, are compelled to confess, that it is better if the right hand of God is described through glory, power, and divine Majesty; whence even some more recent followers of Calvin cannot deny that Majesty.

XIV. Furthermore, Christ is said to sit at this right hand; what is denoted by this phrase must now be explained. To sit is properly said of the position of a human body, and thus it is opposed to standing or lying down: but metaphorically it is either to rest and remain, Luke 24:49, or to command and rule, 1 Kings 1:30, Isaiah 16:5.

XV. In this place it does not denote that actual situation which Christ used in sitting, Matthew 5:2, Luke 5:5, John 12:14; indeed, Tilenus himself, in the cited place, rejects it: nor does it denote that idle rest; for this, because Christ is the head of the Church, is most alien to him, in which he powerfully administers all things.

XVI. For although it is rightly said that he rests, Isaiah 53:10 and ch. 11:10, that rest does not denote every cessation, but only that which is opposed to the labors which befell Christ in the state of humiliation, undertaken for the sake of our sins, Isaiah 43:24.

XVII. Most correctly, therefore, it is said that to sit at the right hand of God is to be σύνθρονον and συνάιτιον with God, in which, with which, and through which, God gloriously and omnipotently executes all the virtues and actions of his infinite Majesty, indicated by the little word 'right hand', and that in this way, he may in Christ, with him, and through him, gloriously fill all things, govern all things, rule over all things, search all things, and struggle against the enemies and the gates of hell. Phil. Nicol. de omnipræsent. p. 466.

XVIII. Many and notable testimonies of Scripture confirm the truth of this description. For in Dan. 7, v. 13, 14, it is said that power, glory, and a kingdom were given to the son of man by the Ancient of Days, and indeed in such a way that this power must be called eternal. In Eph. 1, v. 20, 21, it is said that he is in the heavens above every power, might, dominion, and authority. One may compare Ps. 110, v. 1; Luke ch. 1, v. 32, 33; Matt. 25; Acts 2:36; 1 Cor. 15, v. 25; Heb. 1, v. 3, v. 8, 9, 13; Rev. 7, 16, 17.

XIX. Anyone of sound mind easily grasps how great a majesty all these things express. Whence it is evident that Bellarmine thinks less correctly, who calls the sitting at the right hand merely the blessedness of the elect: and he approves the φλυαρίας of Nebriensis, to whom it is less honorable to be at the right than at the left: he asserts that this sitting can happen to anyone, even to him who clings to the smallest corner of the world. For the first is against Scripture: the second is partly unproven, and partly too crude in this speculation of heavenly sitting: the third, however, is plainly blasphemous and futile. For if he understands it as pious, it is cuckoo-talk; if as wicked, it is diabolical, as if the most worthless impious man could be united to the λόγῳ, and become a participant equal with the Father in ἐξουσίας, which any candidly pious person would judge to be horrible to hear, let alone to say. For what, will the glory of him who has been established above everything that is named, in this age and the future, have as a companion some darker person lurking in the smallest corner of the world? Why does he not place his Francis, or if he desires to be grateful, his Ignatius Loyola (already fiery with eternal flames) at that right hand, if he esteems the matter so lightly, or if he thinks it can be earned, why does he tacitly accuse of impiety or insufficiency those who have not long since acquired that honor.

Latin:

NON metuenda vox est, Ascendit Christus in Cælum. Timor enim, qui esse potest ex ascensione, eripitur Majestatica Salvatoris ad dexteram Patris sessione. Qvisqvis ergò hanc Majestatem in cælo videre neqvit, credat esse in omnipotentis dexterâ: qvi cælum locum qvendam sibi imaginatur; hanc non locum sed infinitam gloriam credere incipiat. Postqvàm autem de ascensione Christi satis superq; in superioribus actum est, qvô fructu illa inclyta sit, nunc dispiciendum erit. Cohærent enim indissolubili nexu ascensio, & sessio, unde in symbolo Apostolorum, si Augustino credimus, Bartholomæus hæc duo connectere voluit. Imò ipsa scriptura Christum non modò assumptum asserit, sed considere etiam â dexteris Dei. Marc. 16. v. 19. Col. 3, 1. 1. Petr. 3, 21, 22. Hebr. 12, 2. affirmat. Hinc est, qvòd hæc σχέσις ex effectum ascensionis Christi, ac Majestatis & gloriæ ejus illustrationem θεοπρεπεστάτην, designare dicatur. De hâc jam, qvod Christus benè vertat, in præsentiarum disqvisituri sumus, non qvidem juxta ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν, sed ad ductum sanctissimi in sacrosancto verbo, Spiritûs; id est, videbimus, 1. qvid dexteræ vox significet; 2. Qvid sit, ad dexteram Patris sedere; 3. Juxta qvam naturam Christus sedere dicendus sit. Tandem succinctâ finalis causæ expositione, usum hujus articuli practicum involvemus.

Thesis I.

REctissimè Nazianzenus qvondam dixit: πολλὰ ἀνθρωποπαθῶς λέγονται, ἀλλὰ θεοπρεπῶς νοῦνται. Hæc regula si ullo in articulô, hôc maximè observationem insignem meretur. Multi enim hîc dexteræ vocem Carnale qvid denotare arbitrantur, contrà qvàm Patres voluerunt singulis temporibus; imò contra, qvàm ipse Spiritus sanctus, ut in progressu videbimus. II. Ut enim hîc nihil dicamus de Antropomorphitarum crassitie, Nestorianorum sellulariâ, qvi duas καϑέδρας finxere, unam, in qvâ Pater, alteram, in qva Filius sedeat: Pontificios tantùm & Galvinianos miramur, qvod ἄτερ γραφῶν tam animosè de dexterâ hâc ex rationis scrutinio disserere non vereantur, extra qvas tamen, qvid sit ille, cujus est dextera, perfectè nemo scire unqvam potuit. III. Ex illis enim, ut unicum tantùm de Valentia Gregorium adducamus, constat, qvàm bellè ipse cum Zvvinglianis in præsenti negocio conveniat, cui cæteros Esavitas suffragari eò magis credibile est, qvòd cum modernis Nestorianis Calvinistis ὁμοϑυμαδὸν, ausu planè temerariô, Majestatem Christi annihilare non metuant. Unô verbô, ut Ubqvitisitis ægrè faciat (sic nostros per calumniam vocat) dexteram patris sedem & locum certum facere, non erubescit, qvâ in sententia Calvinianos qvoqve esse, manifestissimum est. IV. Matyr simili rem expedit: Patrem proceræ staturæ, filiolum sectum confidentem habere posse, inqvit, ubi nihilominùs latiùs sit extensa patris dextera, qvàm filioli corpus dilatetur. Ex qvô, qvid in negocio præsenti inferre velit, anxiâ divinatione opus non est, qvivis enim colligit, determinari illô CHRISTO gloriosissimo certam sedem, cujus spaciis ille inclusus, dexteram Patris occupare nihilominùs dicendus sit. V. Zvvinglius certè, explicaturus dexteram hanc, eò semper inclinat, ut eam locum interpretando, nihil de Calvinismi genii crassitie remittat: unde ejus discipuli eam tertium cœlum, ubi CHRISTUS detineatur, in qvod ascendit, in qvo liberè versabitur, & de consilio patris, ad extremum judicium mansurus est, indigitant. Loca, qvibus sententiam suam probare nituntur, Actor. 3. vers 21. Marc. 16, 19. Ephes. 1, 20. 1. Petr. 3, 22. Hebr. 1, 3. & 7, 26. & 8. 1. Coloss. 3. v. 1. an ipsis patrocinio esse possint, in ipsâ disqvisitione videbimus. VI. Nos scripturam secuti, aliter longè de dextera hac Patris sentire didicimus, unde eam non certum locum, sed divinam ac infinitam Majestatem atque potentiam esse, asserimus, id quod ex variis appellationibus & titulis, quibus ornatur, & à Spiritu sancto describitur, liquidum redditur.

VII. Nam, ut ex plurimis pauca tantùm adducamus Exod. 15. v. 6. vocatur dextera magnificata in fortitudine; Psal. 77. 11. dextera excelsi; Psalm. 89. v. 14. brachium cum potentia; Esa. 48, 13. dextera mensurans cælos; Psal. 139, v. 10. ubique præsens, Esa. 48, 23. omnia creans; Matth. 25, 31. Thronus judicii extremi; c. 19. v. 28. Thronus Majestatis; Luc. 22, 69. dextera virtutis Dei; Hebr. 1, 8. Thronus in seculum seculi; Dan. 7, 14. Thronus potestatis æternæ, &c.

IIX. Hæc sanè & similia loca, è diametro speculationibus & nugis adversariorum sunt opposita, &, nisi ipsi Spiri Sanct. in os contradicere velint, locum suum relinquere, & crassiores illas Antropomorphiticas cogitationes deponere cogentur: Sic enim concludim? Qvæcunque dextera in scriptura jam dictis titulis insignita est, illa non locum, sed divinam ac infinitam Majestatem denotare, rectissimè creditur. At prius est verū de dextera, ad quam CHRISTUS sedet. E. & posteri?

IX. Qvid? quòd ipsi adversarii, in quæstione, quid sedeat ad dexteram DEI, dum pro humana natura, totam personam obtrudunt, non effugere possint, per hanc dexteræ descriptionem, hanc absurditatem, quâ seqveretur, divinam naturam locabilem esse, qvippe quæ cum humanæ ad Patris dexteram sedere, ab ipsis perhibetur, quæ tamen locatio divinitatis est merum somnium, imò puta pura blasphemia. Si verò hoc ἄτοπον evitare volunt, necessum est, ut vel ex scripturâ meliorem dexteræ definitionem adferant, vel suam deteriorem relinqvant.

X. Non præter rem v. est, nos hîc contraire Polano, & ostendere, qvomodo Spiritus sanctus hanc dexteram ad cælum, superiora, altitudinem &c. limitet, prout Eph. 1, 20. Col. 3, 1. Hebr. 1, 3. c. 8, 1. qvædam loci differentiæ innui videntur, sic enim ex parte qvoq; th. 5. satisfiet.

XI. Dicimus ergò, hæc & similia loca adversarios parùm juvare, qvippe ineptè inde colligunt: Christus est in cælo, E. est tantùm in cælo. Simili enim modô ex oratione Dominica qvis concludat: Pater noster est in cælis, E. est tantùm in cælis: quam Conseqventiam si nobis solverint, proprias strophast, ex locis illis minùs rectè intellectis desumptas, solutas esse autument.

XII. Committunt itaq; crasssam fallaciam Ignorationis Elenchi. Non enim ideò dicitur Christus sedere ad dexteram patris in cœlo, ut ibi locum determinatú nanciscatur, & per eundem circumscribatur, sed, quia sedet in throno Dei, qui collocatus esse dicitur in cœlo; 1. Reg. 8. v. 36. Psal. 2, 4. Pf. 103, v. 19. &c. Cujus nihilominùs Majestas omnem adimplere terram Esai. 6. v. 3. dicitur, ut Dn. Schröd. in Throno regali p. 60. hanc objectionem adversariorum plurib. diluit.

XIII. Potest eadem hæc dextera explicari & definiri ex operibus ejus: confirmari etiam nostra sententia ex Patribus: verùm præstat Clariss. Dn. Præsidii adire part. 2: Phil. sobr. c. 1. s. 1. p. 17. 18. &c. Unum notabile est adhuc, quod & Pontificii, & Calviniani nonnulli, veritatis vi adacti, confiteri coguntur, præstare, si dextera Dei per gloriam, potentiam, & Majestatem divinam describatur; Unde etiam recentiores Calvini sectatores nonnulli eam Majestatem non diffiteri possunt.

XIV. Porrò ad dexteram hanc Christus sedere dicitur, quâ phrasi, quid notetur, jam explicandum est. Sedere propriè dicitur de situ corporis humani, & sic stationi vel cubationi opponitur: Metalepticè autem est, vel quiescere & morari, Luc. 24, 49. vel imperare & regere, 1. Reg. 1. v. 30. Esa. 16, 5.

XV. Hôc in locô non notat situationum illam actualem, quâ sessione Christus Matth. 5, 2. Luc. 5, 5. Johan. 12, 14. usus est, imò ipse Tilenus, l. c. eam rejicit: Neq; etiam quietem notat otiosam illam; Hæc enim quia Christus caput Ecclesiæ, ab ipso alienissima est, in quâ omnia potenter administrat.

XVI. Quamvis enim quiescere rectè dicatur Esa. 53, 10. & c. 11, 10. quies tamen illa non notat cessationem omnem, sed tantùm eam, quæ opponitur laboribus, qui Christo in statu exiananitionis, peccatorum nostrorum causâ Esai 43, 24. susceptis, obvenerunt.

XVII. Rectissimè ergò dicitur, quòd sedere ad dexteram Dei, sit esse Deo σύνθρονον & συνάιτιον, in quâ, cum quâ, & per quam, Deus universas & omnes infinitæ suæ Majestatis virtutes & actiones, voculâ dexteræ subindicatas, gloriosè & omnipotenter exeqvitur, idqve hoc modo, ut in Christo, cum illo, & per illum, gloriose repleat omnia, gubernet omnia, dominetur omnibus, scrutetur omnia, lucteturqve adversus hostes & portas inferorum. Phil. Nicol. de omnipræsent. p. 466.

XVIII. Veritatem hujus descriptionis multa & insignia testimonia Scripturæ comprobant. Nam Dan. 7. v. 13, 14. dicitur, qvod ab antiqvo dierum data sit filio hominis potestas, gloria ac regnum, & ita qvidem, ut hæc potestas æterna dicenda sit. Eph. 1. v. 20, 21. dicitur, qvod sit in cœlis supra omnem potestatem, potentiam, dominium ac imperium. Conferri possunt Psal. 110. v. 1. Luc. c. 1. v. 32, 33. Matt. 25. Acter. 2. 36. 1. Corinth. 15. vers. 25. Ebrer. 1. v. 3. vers. 8. 9. 13. Apoc. 7, 16, 17.

XIX. Qvantam hæc omnia Majestatem exprimant, qvivis sanioris mentis facilè asseqvitur. Unde minùs rectè Bellarminum sentire constat, qvi ad dexteram sessionem tantùm beatitudinem electorum vocat: probatqve Nebriensis φλυαρίας, cui minùs honorificum, à dextris, qvàm à sinistris esse: asserit, hanc sessionem posse cuivis contingere, etiam ei, qvi in minimo Mundi angulo hæret. Primum enim est contra Scripturam: Alterum non probatum partim, partim verò crassum nimis, in speculatione hâc cœlestis sessionis: Tertium autem planè blasphemum & futile. Si enim intelligit piam, coccysmus est; si improbam, diabolicum, quasi neqvam impiissimus unitus posset esse λόγῳ, particeps fieri æqvalis cum patre ἐξουσίας, qvòd, qvàm horrendum auditu, nedum dictu sit, judicet qvivis candidè pius. Qvid enim, an gloria ejus, qvi constitutus est supra omne, qvod nominatur, in hoc & futuro seculo, socium habebit tenebriorem qvendam in minimo angulo mundi latitantem? Cur non Franciscum suum, vel si gratus esse cupit, suum Ignatium (jam igneum flammis æternis) Lojolam in illam dexteram collocat, si rem tam levem æstimat, aut si mereri posse censet, cur tacitè impietatis arguit aut insufficientiæ, qvi non dudum honorem istum acqvisiverint.


### XX. But that we may come to that which seems most to have difficulty here, it…

XX. But that we may come to that which seems most to have difficulty here, it must be examined according to which nature Christ sits at the right hand of the almighty Father.

XXI. We shall explain and confirm our thesis; afterwards we shall add what our adversaries maintain. We therefore maintain, and firmly believe, that this session at the right hand of the Father pertains to the person of Christ, but by reason of the assumed human nature, or according to the human nature, not indeed of itself, but by reason of the union, apart from which it is not even to be said to subsist.
