XXII. For it is falsely imputed to our Churches by our adversaries that we attribute the session to the human nature viewed in itself; for we desire as much as possible that this fiction, as being Nestorian and Eutychian, be foreign to us; indeed, we detest those who teach in this manner.

XXIII. But, lest anyone should here look for a knot in a bulrush, we think it must be explained how we assert that the session pertains to the person of Christ. For, if anyone wishes to interpret it not as glory, but as the acquisition of glory, the session does not pertain to the person of Christ by reason of the ὑποστάσεως τῶ λόγω, or by reason of the ὑποστάσει in itself and of itself; but to Christ by reason of the assumed flesh, whose condition it was that it could be raised and exalted to a better state. But if, on the other hand, one considers it as glory already acquired, the session pertains to Christ as he is man, yet not by the condition of his nature, but by the grace of the union.

XXIV. But that the proof of our assertion may be the more evident, we shall prove: I. That the divine nature was not exalted by this session, nor placed at the right hand of God: But II. That it pertains to the human nature. We show the former in this manner: According to which nature Christ had no need of anything; 2. is immutable; 3. is most high; 4. is always equal to the Father; 5. rules over all things from the beginning with the Father and the Holy Spirit; 6. would have exalted himself; 7. has the same blessedness with the Father, that [nature] could not or ought not to be exalted and placed at the right hand: But the former is true of the divine nature: Therefore, the latter is also true.

XXV. We believe the consequence of the major premise abounds in its own light. For those attributes are so constituted that they suggest to us the highest Majesty, to which nothing can be added, and which, on account of its immutability, argues for the same vigor in its possessor. The minor premise is proved by the following sayings and reasons:

XXVI. For that Christ, according to his divinity, did not stand in need of anything, it is clear from chapter 16, verse 15 of John, where he says: Whatever the Father has, is mine: Hence we conclude, with the hypothesis presupposed, that the Father has all things: The Father is in need of nothing, therefore neither is the Son, therefore neither is the session.

XXVII. But if they say that the Father does not have a session, it fights for us; therefore the Son also does not have it: therefore, as the most perfect one, he no longer had need of it. For what God is said not to have, confirms his Majesty rather than proves a need.

XXIIX. That Christ, according to his divinity, is immutable, appears from Psalm 102, verses 26, 27; Hebrews 1, verse 10; James 1:17: hence the Immutable cannot be exalted: for here that which was serving is said to rule, that which was humble, to be raised up: which indeed prove a huge change: But the divine nature is immutable, by the force of the cited passages. Therefore.

XXIX. The third is clear from Luke 1, verse 76, Psalm 89, verse 19, Daniel 5, verse 1: the fourth is proved from Hebrews 1, verse 3, Philippians 2:7: the fifth is deduced from Colossians 1:16, 17, John 5:17, 19, and following: The sixth is clear from this, because the exaltation, of which we speak here, is an external work, from which the divine nature of Christ cannot be excluded; yet this, if it is said by the adversaries to be exalted, would be less than itself, because it receives the exaltation, and greater than itself, because it perfects and performs the exaltation, which is certainly absurd.

XXX. The seventh member of the minor premise does not need proof; yet we add it for good measure: If Christ, according to his divine nature, does not have the same blessedness as the Father, according to it he would be less than the Father; But he is not less than the Father according to his divinity: Therefore he has the same blessedness with him. If this is so, since the Father has not needed exaltation, it must be said that the Son has not needed it either.

XXXI. More arguments could be produced, if the nature of the thesis allowed it; however, we proceed to the other member of the thesis, the proof of which aims at the same goal, that is, we will demonstrate that the human nature was exalted, and that this session at the right hand of the Father belongs to it, which is made manifest by the following reasons:

XXXII. 1. According to which nature Christ is less than the Father, according to the same he goes to the Father:

And yet, according to his human nature he is less than the Father. The connection of the major premise is proven by the Evangelist John, ch. 14, v. 28; the minor premise needs no proof, whence its truth is also established for the conclusion. For we know of no one who doubts whether that 'going' ought to be explained by his session and exaltation.

XXXIII. 2. The Holy Spirit himself confirms our thesis as if with a pointing finger, when in the description of this Majesty he makes mention not only of the person, but of the human nature itself in abstract terms, as is evident from 1 Cor. 15, v. 25, 26; Ps. 110, v. 1; Heb. 2, 8; Ps. 8, v. 8; John 5, v. 27.

XXXIV, 3. According to the nature by which Christ will sit on the throne of the power of God in the final judgment, according to that same nature he sits at the right hand of God: And yet that belongs to the human nature, therefore this does too. The connection of the major premise is sufficiently firm from the necessary coherence of the consequent and the antecedent. The minor premise is Christ's, Matt. 26, 64.

XXXV. 4. The very time of this exaltation supports us, where no sane person dares to deny that rule of Athanasius, which antiquity used most successfully against the Arians, while it commands that what Christ received in time must be attributed to his humanity: ὅσα ἂν λέγῃ ἡ γραφὴ, ὅτι ἔλαβεν ὁ ὑιὸς καὶ ἐδοξάσθη ὁ ὑιὸς, διὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα αὐτοῦ λέγει, οὐ διὰ τὴν θεότητα.

XXXVI. Thus, what else does the connection of the articles in the Creed mean, other than to show that the nature which traversed all places, both middle, lowest, and highest, sits at the right hand of God the Almighty Father? All of which could be confirmed at length by notable testimonies of the Fathers, were the matter not so manifest that anyone who wishes to think otherwise must be stubborn and contradicting the truth.

XXXVII. For Augustine most rightly infers that the name was given to Christ only as man, according to whom he was made obedient even to the death of the cross, which name, namely, the Son of God himself, God born of God, already possessed as an equal. And Cyril: To whom humility is appropriate, of these it is also said that they are exalted: but the human nature is a humble thing, therefore it is understood to be exalted as well.

XXXIIX. And it is strange that the Calvinists wish to call themselves associates of the Augsburg Confession, and wish to appear not to have deserted it, to which men in this business they contradict so boldly. For she wishes this session to be estimated as the end of the ascension, and from this she deduces with excellent consequence that as this pertains to the flesh, so also that pertains to the same.

XXXIX. But they are so doubtful in this part that they often disagree among themselves with conflicting opinions, although they all conspire in this, that because of the stiffness of their necks they are unwilling to allow human nature that which divinity has bestowed. With what fruit they resist Christ himself in this daring act, let them see; for if he is to return in the clouds, then at last they will feel to their own ruin whom they have pierced.

XL. Some imagine a double session, one which pertains to human nature, an inferior one, and another which pertains to the divine, a superior and more excellent one. To whom I respond with the words of my master, Meisner: If the session of which Scripture speaks comes about only by grace and in time, by what reasoning can it finally be applied to the λόγον? Is the λόγος also emptied, and is there a double right hand of God, or a twin throne of God? Away with these absurdities, which have no foundation in Scripture, etc.

XLI. Some concede that the person is exalted through the session at the Father's right hand, as if the person were some third thing and not the natures themselves. Hence others, intending to act more cautiously, refer the session primarily to the divinity, to whom we wish our arguments to be opposed; for the right hand of GOD cannot be placed at the right hand of GOD, but only that nature which was anointed, and which did not count it robbery to be equal to GOD. Whence Augustine: Who is it that sits at the right hand of the Father? The man Christ: for insofar as he is GOD, he is always with the Father and from the Father: and when he proceeded to us, he did not depart from the Father.

XLII. Whence it happened that the Seleucians, Hermians, and Proclianites were condemned by the Fathers because they denied that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father. Modern adversaries would have held this same opinion if they had not revoked this dogma of theirs in these times.

XLIII. But some are accustomed to doubt here how long Christ ought to sit at this right hand, since in 1 Cor. 15:24 it is said that Christ will hand over the kingdom. But Holy Scripture sufficiently declares the duration of this kingdom, namely that it will remain forever, as is clear from 2 Sam. 7:13, Ps. 89:37-38, Ezek. 37:25, Dan. 7:14, Luke 1:32-33, Eph. 1:20-21, Heb. 10:12-13.

XLIV. To the passage cited, it is answered that 'to deliver up the kingdom' can be understood here either that Christ is about to restore it to a better state, or that it ought no longer to be an empire as in the militant Church, but in the triumphant; where, just as a king's son, if he has conquered a province and enemies, can offer the kingdom to his father, while he himself nevertheless remains its Lord and King; so also Christ can be said to deliver the kingdom to the Father, while He Himself is nevertheless established in majesty.

XLVI. Moreover, this session of our CHRIST has notable uses and fruits: For see, that crucified King has led captivity captive, having power in heaven and on earth. Therefore the ancient Dragon will do no harm, nor death, nor hell; for He who sits at the right hand has conquered these enemies of ours, so that we need no longer fear them, but we shall rule over them, and we rejoice with the triumphant CHRIST.

XLVII. Since therefore no enemies stand in the way, who does not see that there is free access for us to the Father, which our mediator has prepared for us, without whom the eternal GOD was an enemy to us; He is now for us, who therefore is against us? The tumults of the enemies therefore ceasing, and their forces being broken, with GOD rendered a friend and reconciled to us, who would not congratulate himself that he can still furthermore be united to GOD Himself, that he has been rendered worthy, in whom the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit wishes to have His dwelling. All these things are to be referred in thanks to CHRIST, and to the slain Lamb, who is worthy to receive honor, power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and glory, and blessing.

Latin:

XX. Sed ut deveniamus ad id, qvod maximè videtur hîc difficultatem habere, dispiciendum est, secundùm qvam naturam Christus sedeat ad dexteram Patris omnipotentis.

XXI. Nos nostram thesin explicabimus & confirmabimus; post quid Adversarii statuant, adjiciemus. Statuimus ergò, & firmiter credimus, quòd sessio hæc ad dexteram Patris competat personæ Christi, sed ratione humanæ naturæ assumtæ, vel secundùm humanam naturam, non quidem per se, sed ratione unionis, extra quam ne subsistere quidem dicenda est.

XXII. Falsò n. nostris Ecclesiis ab adversariis affingitur, quòd sessionem humanæ naturæ in seipsâ spectatæ tribuamus, hoc enim commentum, ut Nestorianum & Eutychianum, alienum â nobis esse, quàm maximè cupimus, imò hunc in modum docentes, detestamur.

XXIII. Sed, ne quis hîc nodum in scirpo quærat, explicandum esse arbitramur, quomodo asseramus sessionem competere Christi personæ. Nam, si quis eam non gloriam, sed gloriæ acquisitionem interpretari velit, non competit personæ Christi sessio, ratione ὑποστάσεως τῶ λόγω, seu ὑποσάσει in se, & sui ratione; sed Christo, ratione assumtæ carnis, cujus hæc conditio erat, ut evehi & exaltari in meliorem statum posset. Si verò, ut gloriam jam acquisitam, attendat, competit sessio Christo, quà homo est, verùm non ex naturæ conditione, sed unionis gratiâ.

XXIV. Ut autem probatio assertionis nostræ eò sit evidentior, probabimus I. Divinam naturam non esse hâc sessione exaltatam, nec collocatam ad dexteram Dei: Sed II. Eam humanæ competere naturæ. Illud hunc in modum ostendimus: Secundùm quam naturam Christus nullô opus habuit; 2. immutabilis est; 3. altissimus; 4. Patri semper æqualis; 5. omnibus ab initio cum Patre & Spir. Sanct. dominatur; 6. seipsum exaltâsset; 7. cum Patre habet eandem beatitatem, illa exaltari & ad dexteram collocari non potuit aut debuit: At prius est verum de divinâ naturâ: E. & posterius.

XXV. Majoris consequentiam suâ luce abundare credimus. Ista enim attributa ita sunt comparata, ut summam nobis insinuent Majestatem, cui addi nihil possit, quæque propter suam immutabilitatem, eundem in possessore vigorem arguunt. Minor probatur ex sequentibus dictis & rationibus:

XXVI. Christum enim secundùm divinitatem non indiguisse aliqvô, constat ex cap. 16. v. 15. Johannis, ubi dicit : Qvæcunqve Pater habet, mea sunt: Hinc concludimus, præsuppositâ ὑποθέσει, qvòd pater habeat omnia: Pater nullius indigens est, E. neqve Filius, E neq; sessionis.

XXVII. Qvòd si dicant, Patrem non habere sessionem, pro nobis militat; E. etiam Filius non habet: E. illâ, tanqvam perfectissimus, jam non opus habebat. Qvæ enim Deus non habere dicitur, ipsius Majestatem potiùs confirmant, qvàm indigentiam comprobant.

XXIIX. Christum secundùm divinitatem, immutabilem esse, ex Psal. 102. v. 26, 27. Hebr. 1, v. 10. Jac. 1, 17. apparet : hinc Immutabile non potest exaltari: hîc enim id, qvod serviebat, dominari dicitur, qvod humile, extolli: qvæ sanè ingentem mutationem evincunt: Atqvi divina natura est immutabilis, vi dictorum allegatorum. E.

XXIX. Tertium ex Luc. 1. v. 76. Psal. 89. v. 19. Dan. 5. v. 1. constat: qvartum ex Hebr. 1. v. 3. Phil. 2: 7. probatur: qvintum ex Col. 1, 16. 17. Joh. 5, 17, 19. & seqq. deducitur: Sextum inde liqvet, qvia exaltatio, de qvâ hîc loqvimur, est opus ad extra, à qvo non potest excludi divina Christi natura; hæc tamen, si ab adversariis dicitur exaltata, esset se ipsâ minor, qvia exaltationem excipit, & se ipsâ major, qvia exaltationem perficit, & peragit, qvod certè est inconveniens.

XXX. Septimum minoris membrum opus probatione non habet; ex abundanti tamen illam addimus: Si Christus, secundùm divinam naturam, non habet eandem beatitudinem cum Patre, juxta eam esset minor Patre; Atqvi non est minor Patre juxta divinitatem: E.eandem cum ipso habet beatitudinem. Si hoc, cùm Pater non indiguerit exaltatione, neq; eâ Filium indiguisse, dici debet.

XXXI. Plura possent argumenta produci, si pateretur thesium ratio; accedimus tamen ad alterum thesews membrum, cujus probatio ad eundem scopum collimat, hoc est, demonstrabimus, humanam naturam esse exaltatam, & illi sessionem hanc ad dexteram Patris competere, qvod seqventibus rationibus sit manifestum:

XXXII. 1. Secundùm qvam naturam Christus est minor Patre, secundùm eandem vadit adPatrem:

Atqvi, secundùm humanam naturam est minor Patre, E. Majoris connexio est ab Evangelista Johanne c. 14. v. 28. comprobata; Minor probatione nullâ indiget, unde Conclusioni qvoq; sua veritas constat. Neminem n. scimus, qvi dubitet, an illud vadere, explicari per sessionem & exaltationem debeat.

XXXIII. 2. Thesin nostram qvasi intentô digitô ipse Spiritus sanctus confirmat, qvando in descriptione hujus Majestatis non personæ modò, sed ipsius humanæ naturæ abstractis vocabulis meminit, qvemadmodùm ex 1. Cor. 15. v. 25, 26. Ps. 110. v. 1. Heb. 2, 8. Psalt 8. v. 8. Joh. 5. v. 27. patet.

XXXIV, 3. Secundùm qvam naturam Christus in ultimo judicio sedebit in throno virtutis Dei, secundùm eam sedet ad dexteram Dei: Atqvi illud competit humanæ naturæ E, & hoc. Majoris connexio est satis firma ex cohærentia conseqventis & antecedentis necessaria. Minor est Christi, Matth. 26, 64.

XXXV. 4. Ipsum tempus exaltationis hujus nobis suffragatur, ubi nemo sanus negare audet, Athanasii illam regulam, qvâ felicissimê antiquitas contra Arrianos usa est, dum, qvæ Christus in tempore accepit, humanitati attribuenda esse jubet: ὅσα ἂν λέγῃ ἡ γραφὴ, ὅτι ἔλαβεν ὁ ὑιὸς καὶ ἐδοξάσθη ὁ ὑιὸς, διὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα αὐτῦ λέγει, ᾡ διὰ τὴν θεότητα.

XXXVI. Sic, qvid aliud sibi vult connexio articulorum in symbolo, qvàm qvòd ostendat, eam naturam sedere ad Patris Omnipotentis dexteram, qvæ omnia loca, tàm media, qvàm infima & supréma peragravit? Qvæ omnia insignibus Patrum testimoniis prolixê possent confirmari, nisi res ita in propatulo esset, ut, qvi secus sentire velit, oporteat eum esse pertinacem, & veritati contradicentem.

XXXVII. Rectissimè n. Augustinus infert, nomen Christo tantùm donatum esse ut homini, secundùm qvem filius factus est obediens usq; ad mortem crucis, qvod scil. nomen jam habebat ipse Dei filius, Deus de Deo natus æqvalis. Et Cyrillus: Cui humilitas congruit, his exaltari qvoq; dicitur: Humana verò natura res humilis est, ipsa ergò exaltari qvoq; intelligitur.

XXXIIX. Et mirum est, Calvinianos sese confessionis Augustanæ socios nuncupare velle, eámq; non de seruisse videri cupere, cui tamen in hoc negocio tam audacter contradicunt. Illa n. sessionem hanc, ut finem ascensionis, vult æstimari, qvarum ut hæc carni, ita qvoq; illam, eidem competere, optimâ Conseqventiâ deducit.

XXXIX. Verùm, hâc in parte ita dubii sunt, ut discrepantibus sententiis sæpè à se invicem discordent, qvamvis in hâc omnes conspirent, nolle humanæ naturæ ipsos id, qvod divinitas largita est, ob duritiem cervicis suæ, permittere. Qvô fructu v. hôc ausu ipsi Christo resistant, viderint, si rediturus est in nubibus, tum n. demum, qvem pupugerint, suô damnô sentient.

XL. Qvidam sessionem fingunt duplicem, unam, qvæ humanæ competit naturæ, inferiorem, alteram, qvæ divinæ, superiorem & excellentiorem. Qvibus, verbis Dn. mei præceptoris Meisn. respondeo: Si sessio, de qvâ scriptura loqvitur, ex gratia, & in tempore tantùm obvenit, qvâ tandem ratione ad λόγον applicari poterit? Num & λόγος exinanitus, & duplex Dei dextera, vel geminus Dei thronus est? Apage has ineptias, qvæ nullum in scriptura fundamentum habent, &c.

XLI. Qvidam per sessionem ad patris dexteram, personam exaltatam esse concedunt, qvasi verò persona esset tertium qvoddam, & non ipsæ naturæ. Hinc cautiùs alii acturi, sessioem ad divinitatem potissimùm referunt, qvibus argumenta nostra opposita esse volumus; dextera n. DEI in dextera DEI collocari non potest, sed illa natura tantùm, qvæ uncta est, & qvæ non arbitrata rapinam, æqvalem esse DEO. Unde August. Qvis est, qvi sedet ad dexteram Patris? homo Christus: nam in qvantum DEUS, semper cum Patre & ex Patre: & qvando ad nos processit, â Patre non recessit.

XLII. Unde factum est, ut Seleuciani, Hermiani, Proclianitæ, damnati sint â Patribus, qvòd Christum sedere ad dexteram Patris negaverint. Qvam sententiam moderni qvoq; tulissent adversarii, si istis temporibus hoc suum dogma non revocâssent.

XLIII. Dubitare a. hîc nonnulli solent, qvamdiu Christus sedere debeat ad dexteram hanc, cùm. 1. Cor. 15, 24. dicatur, traditurum Christum regnum. Verùm sacra scriptura satis declarat diuturnitatem hujus regni, qvòd scilicet in æternum usq; permansurum sit, ut ex 2. Sam. 7, 13. Psal. 89. v. 37, 38. Ezech. 37. v. 25. Dan. 7. v. 14. Luc. 1, 32, 33. Eph. 1, 20, 21. Heb. 10, 12, 13. liqvet,

XLIV. Ad locum allatum respondetur, quòd tradere regnum hîc accipi possit, vel, quòd Christus illud in meliorem statum sit redacturus, vel, quòd non ampliùs debeat esse imperium tanquam in militante Ecclesiâ, verùm triumphante; ubi, quemadmodùm regius filius, si devicit provinciam & hostes, patri offerre regnum potest, ipso nihilominus illius Domino & Rege manente; ita & Christus tradere Patri regnum, ipsô nihilominus in majestate constitutô, dici potest.

XLVI. Insignes autem usus & fructus habet hæc sessio CHRISTI nostri: Vide enim, crucifixus ille Rex est, captivam duceris captivitatem, habens potestatem in cælo & in terra. Nihilergò Draco antiquus nocebit, nihil mors, nihil infernus; qui enim sedet ad dexteram, hos nostros devicit hostes, ut illas timere ampliùs non debeamus, sed dominabimur illis, & jubilamus cum triumphante CHRISTO.

XLVII. Cùm igitur nulli obstent hostes, qui non videt, liberum nobis esse ad Patrem aditum, quem midiator noster nobis paravit, sine quô inimicus erat nobis æternus DEUS; Ille jam pro nobis, quis ergò contra nos? Cessantibus ergò tumultibus hostium, fractisq́ve viribus eorum, amicô redditô reconciliatoq́ve nobiscum Deô, quis non gratuletur sibi, quòd adhuc insuper uniri possit ipsi DEO, quòd dignus redditus sit, in quo mansionem suam Pater cum Filio & Spiritu sancto habere velit. Hæc omnia CHRISTO in gratiis referenda sunt, agnoq́ve occiso, qui est dignus accipere honorem, virtutem, & divitias, & sapientiam, & fortitudinem, & gloriam, & benedictionem.


## 46 Forty-sixth Disputation. On the State of Christ's Humiliation, and Exaltation

Continuation.

Most rightly does the blessed Augustine say: 'Not only are the words of the Word instructions for us, but the deeds of the Word are also examples for us.' Indeed, the life of Christ can teach us everything. The Savior himself gives assurance of this fact, (a) and the Apostles confirm it with their own reckoning, Paul (b) and Peter (c). All of which add a spur to us, that we may inquire more and more into the life of our Savior. Since this has been done thus far in several disquisitions, it is now our pleasure, by way of a conclusion, to make a compendium of all those things which exist concerning the entire course of Christ's whole life, and to include them collectively under the two states hitherto accepted for use in the schools of theologians, the former of which is called the STATE OF HUMILIATION or IGNOMINY, the latter the STATE OF EXALTATION or GLORY, foreshadowed in the Old Testament through Moses (d), Joseph (e), and Zechariah (f), as Tertullian attests (g). We shall imitate the rhetoricians, who briefly include in a conclusion or summary what they have said diffusely and sporadically in their oration; indeed, we shall imitate the Apostle himself, who with wondrous skill presents those two states included in the noble and classic aphorism of Phil. 2:6 ff., by which, as the proper and primary seat of these states, leading and shining the way, we establish three parts of our disquisition: 1. It will contain the state of Humiliation; 2. The state of Exaltation; 3. It will append the practice. Be present, O CHRIST, from on high, who, having been exalted, received gifts for men; endow us with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that your name may be exalted by us on this occasion.

I. In order to proceed distinctly in this part, to which we have destined the foreshadowing of the State of Christ's Humiliation, we shall briefly see: 1. The subject of the Humiliation; 2. The Humiliation itself.

II. The SUBJECT, in the Apostolic style, is Jesus Christ, the Word not to be incarnated, but Incarnate; yet not according to the divine nature, nor according to both, but only according to the human nature, according to which he exists IN THE FORM OF GOD.

III. We cannot, therefore, agree with the Calvinists, who either concerning the Word considered before the incarnation, and insofar as He is simply GOD, explain this emptying—see Beza (a), Junius and Tremellius (b), Sadeel (c), and the Anonymous author against the Royal Throne of Schroder (d)—or blather that CHRIST according to both natures is as much emptied as exalted; Sohnius (e) and Martinius against Menzer.

IV. For Photinianism is introduced in this way with full sails, while Christ according to the divine nature is sometimes rendered lesser than His Father through that emptying, see D. Gravv. In a thorough refutation of Petri Freye en/ p. 46. and following. Next, manifest violence is inflicted upon the Apostolic text by such Calvinistic distortions, which will become manifest to one inspecting it with a more accurate pupil, and B. Hunnius proved this with Achilles-like arguments in Commentary on the Epistle to the Philippians p. 67 for me and following. Hutter in L. C. p. 288. Luc. Osiander in notes on the Bible Ph. 2. p. 555 for me. compare, Heb. 2. v. 9. Ps. 8. v. 6. and what D. Chemn. has in vol. 1. loc. Com. p. 172 for me. Gesn. on Psalm 8

V. Nor is there any reason for the adversaries to fortify themselves with the authority of the Fathers, to whom it is agreed they attributed the humiliation of the divine nature; for we distinguish between the inclination of compassion and the evacuation or Emptying, of which the latter is as far removed from the former as God is from the change Ps. 102. v. 28, which the Emptying implies.

VI. Being certain about the subject, we approach the Emptying itself, which is evident to consist of two things from the Apostolic statement; 1. In the evacuation of Divine Glory; 2. In the most humble subjection in the form of a servant.

VII. Κένωσις or the evacuation of divine majesty is that by which Christ, who in the first moment of the Incarnation, according to the assumed humanity, had been truly and really anointed with the entire fullness of divine majesty (Ps. 45. v. 8. Is. 11. v. 2. Acts 10. v. 38.) did not consider it robbery to be ἶσα Θεῷ (equally to GOD) but, so that He might complete the work of redemption, for which He had come into the world, He voluntarily emptied Himself of that communicated Majesty, not indeed ἐκτικῶς (by possession), but ἐνεργητικῶς (by operation); not regarding the κτῆσιν (possession), but the χρῆσιν (use), not in act, as they say, primarily, but secondarily; just as the venerable antiquity is accustomed to declare it by the example of the sun covered by a cloud, and the moderns by that of a minor King.

IIX. Hence it appears that the opinion of Zanchius is absurd (a) which Beza approves (b) and Tossanus (c) which feigns that the Emptying of Christ gives the reason by which the ὁ Λόγος [Word], having deposited in the Father's hand all the authority which He had before the Incarnation, exercised Himself through the incarnation, in such a way, indeed, that the power deposited according to His Deity had to be restored to Him after the resurrection, and therefore He could not have communicated that power, inasmuch as it was deposited, with the human nature in the state of Humiliation.

IX. For why would Christ say that He ALWAYS works with the Father, John 5:17? Why would He have sometimes caused the rays of communicated Majesty to shine forth in the state of Humiliation, John 2:11? Why would the ὁ λόγος [Word] have produced miracles δι᾽ ἀρχῆς διὰ σαρκὸς [by the beginning through the flesh] (this is Athanasius's formula), μετὰ σαρκὸς [with the flesh]? See Chemnitz, book on the two natures in CHRIST, ch. 33, p. 540 of the edition.

X. The other member which constitutes the Humiliation can be called ταπείνωσις [humiliation], or the most humble subjection into the form of a servant, where two things come to be considered: 1. THE ASSUMPTION OF THE SERVILE FORM; 2. THE HUMBLE SUBJECTION UNTO DEATH.

XI. That assumed servile form is not the human nature itself, for He laid that aside in the state of Glory, but retained this; rather, as Isaiah ch. 53 interprets, it is the clearly servile status and condition of human nature, and as the Epistle to the Hebrews ch. 2:17 & 5:2 explains, it is the voluntary assumption of the defects and affections of our infirmity, sin excepted; to which point it pertains that in Psalm 8:5, Christ is said not to be חסר [lacking], but ותחסרהו [and you have made him lack].

XII. This servile form and condition shines forth immediately in Christ's ENTRY into this life, more in His PROGRESS, and most of all in His DEPARTURE.

XIII. For He could have been made man without conception and gestation in the womb of a Virgin, just as the first Adam was; and nevertheless He sustains a birth (to use the language of the Ephesian Synod) from a Virgin: to say nothing of a lowly and vile birth, such as hardly the poorest person experiences.

XIV. In the PROGRESS OF LIFE, that servile condition and the assumption of infirmities (natural ones, however, not personal) manifested itself more. He grew in wisdom and age, Isa. 7:16, Luke 2:14, in whom were hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Col. 2:3. He who is the bread of life, John 6:33, hungered, Matt. 4:2. He who is the fountain of living water, Jer. 2:13, thirsted, Matt. 11:19. He who is the strength of all, Ps. 18:2, felt weariness, John 4:6. He to whom all power in heaven and on earth was given, Matt. 28:18, has nowhere to lay His head, Matt. 8:28. He who was the master of all, yet ministers to the ministers, John 13. He who is the Lord of all, serves Matth. 20. v. 28. in brief: Majesty took on humility, virtue took on infirmity, and eternity took on mortality.

XV. And finally, in the DEPARTURE FROM LIFE, he was so far from being a servant that he was rather the lowest of men, Isa. 53. v. 3. A worm, and no man, Ps. 22. v. 7.

XVI. Let the Papists now see with what face they can imagine Christ to be harsher and more rigid than the saints, on the grounds that the latter experienced the same calamities in their flesh as we do, but he did not. See B. Chemnitz, part 3, Exam. Conc. Trid., p. 249. Let the followers of Flacius also deliberate with themselves how they wish to defend that the human nature of Christ is of a different species than ours.

XVII. It may be asked here: Because the emptying of Christ was so great that he did not refuse to undergo even the state of a servant, can he rightly be called our FELLOW-SERVANT? Danaeus is pleased to say so, in order that he may the better batter the adoration of the flesh of Christ, but without Scripture; if he provides even a jot of it for this matter, we will yield the palm. Because we hear that Christ was made a servant for us, we think that by that very fact he is exempted from the order of fellow-servants.

XVIII. Furthermore, the humble subjection and obedience unto the death of the cross was rendered by Christ to the Father: 1. In ACTING, while he subjected himself to the law, Gal. 4. v. 4. He is circumcised, he is offered, Luke 2. And that not for himself, as Piscator and his fellow-triflers babble, but for us, Rom. 5. v. 19.

XIX. Then in SUFFERING, not simply death, but even the death of the cross: to which we refer the whole act of the passion, in which Christ is depicted in vivid colors as a man of sorrows, Isa. 53. v. 3, whose antecedents, means, and consequences, if anyone weighs with a more accurate balance, he will discover an ineffable emptying, which it is not permitted to pursue further in such a light of the matter and the narrowness of this place. Let the supplement to this state be a noble question: Was the human nature of Christ, even in the state of emptying, omnipresent and everywhere with the Word, just as it now most presently governs all things in the state of exaltation?

R. The Word always and everywhere had the flesh most present to himself through the hypostatic union, but not to the creatures, which others express by distinguishing between the intimate presence, which he had to the flesh in this they concede the state, and the outermost, which they finally attribute to the state of Exaltation.

XX. The State of Exaltation follows the State of Humiliation, in the delineating of which we shall use the same thread of method as hitherto: 1. therefore, we shall attempt to smear onto this paper a few small things concerning the subject of Exaltation, 2. concerning the Exaltation itself.

XXI. The subject of Exaltation is CHRIST JESUS, with respect however not to the divine, but to the human nature, which we support with the following reasons: (1) Because humiliation respects the human nature, therefore also Exaltation, which mutually respect each other. (2) Because the Deity is at the highest pinnacle of Exaltation, Psalm 83:19, Dan. 5:21. And therefore is capable of or in need of no exaltation, Sir. 42:22. (3) Because this Exaltation is a χάρισμα to the Apostle: but God, who has all things from eternity κατὰ φύσιν, receives nothing in time κατὰ χάριν. (4) Because, if Exaltation happens to the divine nature, it would follow that it had been done by a higher being, which is ἄτοπον.

XXII. Therefore, they stray from the line of truth who understand this Exaltation as concerning the Person, with the natures excluded, Gryn. Psalm 110, or according to the Deity, Orthodox. Consens. Epist. Apol. p. 3, Theod. Beza. consp. ad demonstr. Hoffman. p. 77 & 89, or according to the divine and human nature together, Keker. Syst. Theolog. lib. 3, cap. 5, p. 365: Nor are those to be tolerated who refer this Exaltation only to the office of mediation; they are to be drawn into the circle of truth, which intervenes between Mediation and Exaltation. See Hütt. in L. C. p. 191, Mamphras. in Erot. in Art. visit. p. 262. And these things concerning the subject of Exaltation.

XXIII. THE EXALTATION ITSELF is the casting off of the servile form, and the plenary usurpation of Majesty (not finite, as the Calvinists dream, but infinite), communicated in the first moment of the Incarnation, Psalm 8:6, Psalm 110:7, Acts 2:35, Luke 24:16, Eph. 1:20, Heb. 2:6.

XXIV. Exaltation is distinguished into Inchoate and Complete: To the INCHOATE we refer the Descent of CHRIST into Hell, the Resurrection, and the Glorification of the Body: To the COMPLETE, the Ascension, and that solemn Inauguration or the Enthronement of CHRIST for the perfect and full usurpation of the heavenly Empire, the government of heaven and earth, and especially of the Church; to which will be added on the Day of Decree the Judgment of the living and the dead, John 5, v. 27.

XXV. With this Exaltation, and the gift of a name above every name, the truth of human nature can stand perfectly well. Because this cannot be explained in this narrow circle to which we have confined ourselves, we refer the reader to Chemnitz, book on the two natures of CHRIST, ch. 32, p. 555.

XXVI. We set aside, however, from this the error of the Photinians, who contend that the greatest part of divine glory simply accrued to Christ only after the Passion. See Ostorodt in Instit. Germ. ch. 13, Enjedin in Explic. Phil. confer. th. 9.

XXVII. Nor do we listen to those who, with the Loyalists and some of the Calvinists, maintain that Christ properly earned for HIMSELF this glory, by which, having cast off the form of a servant, He was crowned: For the Savior Himself taught us otherwise, John 8, v. 50. And the sacred page asserts this here and there, while it declares that Christ suffered, died, etc., for US.

XXVIII. May this consideration of the states of Christ render you, O MAN, HUMBLE IN LIFE, so that the same disposition may be in you which was in Christ Jesus, that you may not raise your crest, nor prefer yourself to others through empty glory, but think HUMBLY of YOURSELF: For see, I pray, your Lord, how He humbles Himself: O blessed are you, therefore, if you have assiduously occupied your eyes with the face of your humbled Christ, not indeed expressed on the napkin of Veronica with the Papists, but placed before your eyes in the sacred codex with the Christians, Gal. 3, v. 1, the face of a worm, and not a man. For thus all pride will be banished from your heart, and at length, sometime, like Him, you will be exalted, and you will sit, although not on the Throne of the Father, yet on the Throne of CHRIST, Apoc. 3, v. 21.

XXIX. CIRCUMSPECT IN DOCTRINE, so that you may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine, nor give credence to the Jews, who, because of the double state already explained, dream that the Messiah has not yet come, Mr. Dr. Franzius, disp. 3, on the Aug. Conf. th. 9, or, if they concede that He has come, they nevertheless make a double one for the double state, the one humble, the other glorious, Galatinus, on the Arcane Catholic Truth, book 4, ch. 2. Nor kick against the pricks with the Calvinists, for whom the Exaltation of the flesh of Christ is as a hardened stake in the eyes, which they attack from there with all their might, not knowing how much a man is to be valued, Is. 2. v. 2.

XXX. COURAGEOUS ON THE CROSS. For behold your IMMANUEL COMES John 16. v. 28. HE SAW Lam. 3. v. 5. HE CONQUERED Rev. 5. v. 5. so that you, O faithful Soul, who have COME into this abyss of miseries, and are forced to SEE hard things Ps. 60. v. 5., may not succumb, but may at length CONQUER 1 Cor. 15. v. 27. and through many tribulations go into the kingdom of Heaven Acts 14. v. 21. for not otherwise has He himself appointed a kingdom for you Luke 22. v. 29. Be therefore faithful even to the end, fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience, and at length you will obtain the victory, and you will be crowned with an unfading crown by Him.

TO WHOM ALONE BE GLORY.

Latin:

Continuatio.

REctissimè B. Augustinus, Non solùm, inquit, Verbi verba nobis sunt documenta, sed etiam Verbi facta nobis sunt exempla: Nimirùm, Omnia nos Christi vita docere potest. Cui rei ipse Servator fidem facit, (a) & suô confirmant calculô Apostoli, Paulus (b) & Petrus (c) Quæ omnia calcar nobis addunt, ut magis magisq́ve in vitam Servatoris nostri inquiramus. Qvod, cùm hactenus aliqvot disqvisitionibus factum sit, placet nunc Coronidis locô compendium facere omnium illorū, qvæ de toto totius vitæ Christi curriculo extant, illaq́ve statibus duobus, hactenus in Theologorum scholis usu receptis, συλλήβδην includere, qvorum prior STATUS EXINANITIONIS seu IGNOMINIÆ, alter STATUS EXALTATIONIS seu GLORIÆ dicitur, in V. T. adumbratis per Moysen (d) Josephum (e) Zachariam (f) attestante Tertullianô (g) Rhetores imitaturi, qvi, qvæ fusè & sparsim in oratione suâ dixerant, Conclusioni, seu Breviario breviter includunt; imò ipsum Apostolum, qvi mirô artificiô duos illos status, Aphorismo nobili & classico Phil. 2. v. 6. & seqq. inclusos exhibet, qvô, tanqvam statuum horum sede propriâ & primariâ, præeunte & prælucente, disqvisitionis nostræ tria constituimus membra: 1 Continebit statum Exinanitionis; 2. Statum Exaltationis; 3. Praxin subjunget. Adesto verò CHRISTE ex alto, qvi exaltatus dona pro hominibus accepisti, dona nos donis Spiritus S. qvò nomen tuum hâc vice à nobis exaltetur.

I. Distinctè in hoc membro, cui Statûs Exinanitionis CHRISTI adumbrationem destinavimus, ut procedamus, 1. Exinanitionis subjectum, 2. Exinanitionem ipsam paucis videbimus.

II. SUBJECTUM, stylô Apostolicô, Jesus Christus est, Λόγος non incarnandus, sed Incarnatus; nec tamen juxta divinam, neq́; utramq́;, sed solàm humanam naturam, juxta qvam IN FORMA DEI existit.

III. Non possumus ergò facere cum Calvinianis, qvi vel de Λόγῳ ante incarnationem considerato, & qua simpliciter DEUS est, Exinanitionem hanc explicant, vide Bezam (a) Junium & Tremellium (b) Sadielem (c) Anonymum contra Thronum Regalem Schroderi (d) vel CHRISTUM secundum utramque naturam tam Exinanitum, quam exaltatum blaterant; Sohnius (e) Martinius contra Menzerum.

IV. Introducitur enim hoc modo plenis velis Photinianismus, dum Christus secundum divinam naturam per exinanitionem illam aliquando Patre suo minor redditur, vide D. Gravv. In grundlicher Widerlegunge Petri Freye en/ p. 46. & seqq. Deinde textui Apostolico manifesta vis per hujusmodi detortiones Calvinisticas infertur, id quod accuratiori pupilla eum inspicienti manifestum fiet, & argumentis evicit Achilleis B. Hunnius Coment: in Epist. Philip. p. mihi 67. & seqq. Hutter. in L. C. p. 288. Luc. Osiander. in not. bib. Ph. 2. p. m. 555. confer, Hebr. 2. v. 9. Ps. 8. v. 6. & quæ habet D. Chemn. tom. 1. loc. Com. p. m. 172. Gesn. super Psal. 8

V. Nec est, ut Patrum autoritate se muniant adversarii, quos humiliationem divinæ naturæ tribuisse constat; distinguimus enim inter miserationis inclinationem; & evacuationem seu Exinanitionem, quarum hæc tantum distat ab illa, quantum Deus a mutatione Pf. 102. v. 28. quam importat Exinanitio.

VI. De subjecto certi, Exinanitionem ipsam aggredimur, quam in duobus ex dicto Apostolico consistere patescit; 1. In Gloriæ Divinæ Evacuatione; 2. Humillima in forma servi subjectione.

VII. Κένωσις seu divinæ majestatis evacuatio est, qua Christus, qui in primo Incarnationis momento, secundum assumptam humanitatem, universa divinæ majestatis plenitudine vere & realiter inunctus fuerat (Ps. 45. v. 8. Es. 11. v. 2. Act. 10. v. 38.) non rapinam duxit, esse ἶσα Θεῷ (æqualiter DEO) sed, quo opus redemptionis, propter quod in mundum venerat, perficeret, sponte se communicata illa Majestate evacuavit, non quidem ἐκτικῶς, sed ἐνεργητικῶς; non quoad κτῆσιν, sed χρῆσιν, non actu, ut loquuntur, primo, sed secundo; prout veneranda antiquitas exemplo solis nubi obducti, & neoterici Regis minorennis id declarare solent.

IIX. Absurdam hinc apparet Zanchii esse sententiam (a) quam approbat Beza (b) & Tossanus (c) quæ Exinanitionis Christi eam fingit rationem, quâ ὁ Λόγος omni ἐξουσίᾳ, quam ante Incarnationem habuit, in Patris manu depositâ, per incarnationem se exeruit, ita quidem, ut ei secundùm Deitatem deposita potestas post resurrectionem reddenda fuerit, ideoq́; nec potestatem illam, quippe depositam cum humana natura in statu Exinanitionis communicare potuerit.

IX. Quorsum enim Christus se cum patre SEMPER operari diceret, Joh. 5. v. 17.? Quorsum radios communicatæ Majestatis in statu Exinanitionis nonnunquam exoruisset, Joh. 2. v. 11.? Quorsum ὁ λόγος miracula δι᾽ ἀρχῆς διὰ σαρκὸς, (Athanasii est formula) μετὰ σαρκὸς edidisset? Vide Chemnitium lib. de duabus nat. in CHRISTO c. 33. p. m. 540.

X. Alterum, quod Exinanitionem constituit membrum, ταπείνωσις potest vocari, seu humillima in formam servi subjectio, ubiduo consideranda veniunt; 1. SERVILIS FORMÆ ASSUMTIO; 2. HUMILIS AD MORTEM SUBJECTIO.

XI. Assumta illa servilis forma, non est ipsa humana natura, illam enim in statu Gloriæ deposuit, hanc retinuit, sed, interprete Esa. c. 53. naturæ humanæ servilis planè status & conditio, explicante Epist. ad Hebr. c. 2. v. 17. & 5. v. 2. Defectûs & Affectûs nostræ infirmitatis, exceptô tamen peccato, spontanea susceptio: quorsum spectat, quod Psal. 8. v. 5. Christus non חסר sed ותחסרהו dicitur.

XII. Elucescit servilis hæc forma & conditio statim in Christi in hanc vitã INGRESSU, magis in PROGRESSU, maximè verò in EGRESSU.

XIII. Poterat enim homo fieri sine in utero Virginis conceptione & gestatione, prout Adamus primus: & nihilominùs nativitatem sustinet (ut usurpem os Ephesinæ Synodi) ex Virgine: ut nihil dicam de nativitate exili & vili, qualem vix pauperrimus experitur.

XIV. In VITÆ PROGRESSU servilis Illa conditio & infirmitatum, (naturalium tamen, non personalium) susceptio magis se exeruit. Sapientiâ & ætate crevit Esa. 7. v. 16. Luc. 2. v. 14. in qvo absconditi erant omnes Thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ, Col. 2. v. 3. Qui panis vitæ Joh. 6. v. 33. esurivit, Matth. 4. v. 2. Qui fons aqvæ vitæ, Jer. 2. v. 13. sitivit, Matth. 11. v. 19. Qui omninm robur, Psal. 18. v. 2. lassitudinem sensit Joh. 4. v. 6. Cui data omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra Matth. 28. v. 18. non habet, qvo caput reclinet Matth. 8. v. 28. Qui magister erat omnium, ministris tamen ministrat Joh. 13. Qui dominus omnium, servit Matth. 20. v. 28. breviter: suscepta est a Majestate humilitas, a virtute infirmitas, ab æternitate mortalitas.

XV. Et demum in VITÆ EGRESSU tantum abest, ut servus, ut potius virorum novissimus, Efa: 53. v. 3. Vermis, & non homo Pf 22. v. 7. fuerit.

XVI. Videant nunc Papicolæ, quâ fronte Christum sanctis duriorem & rigidiorem fingere possint, propterea, quòd hi easdem nobiscum calamitates in carne sua experti fuerint, ille verò non, item. Vide B. Chemnit. part. 3. Ex. C. T. p. m. 249. Deliberent etiam secum Flacii asseclæ, quomodo naturam Christi humanam, alterius esse speciei, ac nostra est, defendere velint.

XVII. Quæri hîc potest, An, quia tanta Christi facta est Exinanitio, ut etiam servitutis subire non detrectârit, noster rectè dici possit CONSERVUS? R. Danæo sic placet, quò eò meliùs adorationem carnis Christi possit arietare, verùm ἄτερ γραφῆς, cujus si apicem pro hac re dederit, dabimus herbam. Servum, quia Christum pro nobis factum audivimus, eo ipso â conservorum ordine illum exemptum esse putamus.

XVIII. Humilis porrò ad mortem usq; crucis subjectio & obedientia â Christo Patri præstita est, 1. In AGENDO, dum se legi subjecit, Gal. 4. v. 4. Circumciditur, Offertur, Luc. 2. Idŕ; non pro se, ut Piscator cum suis fociennis nugatur, sed pro nobis, Rom. 5. v. 19.

XIX. Deinde in PATIENDO, non simpliciter mortem, sed mortem etiam crucis : quò referimus totum passionis actum, in quo vivis coloribus Christus vir dolorum Esa. 53. v. 3. depingitur, cujus Antecedentia, Media, & Consequentia, si quis accuratiori trutinâ pensiculabit, ineffabilem deprehendet Exinanitionem, quam ulteriús perseqvi in tanta rei luce, loci verò hujus angustiâ non licet. Auctarium hujus status, sit Quæstio nobilis: An Christi humana natura in statu etiam Exinanitionis cum Λόγῳ omnipræsens & ubiq; fuerit, ficuti nunc in statu exaltionis præsentissimè omnia gubernat?

R. ὁ Λόγος semper & ubiqve sibi ipsi per unionem hypostaticam habebat præsentissimam carnem non autem creaturis, id quod alii efferunt distinguendo inter præsentiam intimam, quam carni in hoc statu concedunt, & extimam, quam statui Exaltationis demum tribuunt.

XX. Statum Exinanitionis seqvitur Status Exaltationis, in: qvô delineando, eôdem, qvô hactenus, methodi filo utemur: 1. ergò de Exaltationis subjecto, 2. de Exaltatione ipsâ paucula qvædam chartæ huic illinere conabimur.

XXI. Subjectum Exaltationis est CHRISTUS JESUS, respectu tamen non divinæ, sed humanæ naturæ, qvod nostram assertum, seqq. vallamus rationibus: (1) Qvia humiliatio respicit humanam naturam, E. & Exaltatio, qvæ se mutuò respiciunt (2) Qvia Deitas est in summo Exaltationis fastigiô, Psalm. 83. vers. 19. Dan. 5. v. 21. Ideóqve nullius exaltationis capax vel indigens Sir. 42. v. 22. (3) Qvia Exaltatio hæc Apostolo χάρισμα est: Deus verò, qvi omnia ab æterno habet κατὰ φύσιν, nihil in tempore accipit κατὰ χάριν (4) Qvia, si divinæ naturæ Exaltatio contingit, à sublimiore id factum fuisse seqvetur, qvod ἄτοπον.

XXII. A veritatis ergò aberrant linea, qvi Exaltationem hanc de Persona, exclusis naturis, Gryn. Psalm. 110. vel secundùm Deitatem, Orthodox. Consens. Epist. Apol. pag. 3. Theod. Beza. consp. ad demonstr. Hoffman. pag. 77. & 89. vel secundùm divinam & humanam naturam simul, Keker. Syst. Theolog. lib. 3. cap. 5. p. 365. intelligunt: Nec ferendi illi, qvi ad mediationis officium Exaltationem hanc tantùm referunt; in veritatis trahendi circum discrepantiâ, qvæ Mediationi & Exaltationi intercedit. Vide Hütt. in L. C. pag. 191. Mamphras. in Erot. in Art. visit. p. 262. Et hæc de Exaltationis subjecto.

XXIII. EXALTATIO IPSA, est forma servilis abjectio, & plenaria Majestatis, (Non Finitæ, ut Calviniani somniant, sed infinitæ) in primo Incarnationis momento communicatæ, usurpatio, Psal. 8. vers. 6. Psalm. 110. v. 7. Actor. 2. v. 35. Luc. 24. v. 16. Ephes. 1. vers. 20. Hebr. 2. v. 6.

XXIV. Distingvitur Exaltatio in Inchoatam & completam: Ad INCHOATAM referimus Descensum CHRISTI ad Inferos, Resurrectionem, & Corporis Glorificationem: Ad COMPLETAM Ascensionem, & solennem illam Inaugurationem, seu Inthronisationem CHRISTI ad perfectam & plenam cœlestis Imperii usurpationem, cœli terræq́; & imprimis Ecclesiæ gubernationem; cui accedet in Die Decretorio Judicium vivorum & mortuorum Joh. 5. v. 27.

XXV. Cum hac Exaltatione, & nominis supra omne nomen donatione, veritas humanæ naturæ optimè stare potest. Quod, cùm in angusto hôc, cui nos indidimus, circulo explicari non possit, ablegamus Lectorem ad Chemnit. lib. de duab. natur. CHRISTI. c. 32. p. 555.

XXVI. Sequestramus verò hinc errorem Photinianorum, qui Christo maximam divinæ gloriæ partem primùm post Passionem simpliciter cessisse contendunt. Vide Ostorodum in Instit. Germ. c. 13. Enjedin. in Explic. Phil. confer. th. 9.

XXVII. Nec audimus illos, quando cum Lojolitis & Calvinianorum nonnullis Christum gloriam hanc, quâ, abjectâ servi formâ, coronatus est, propriè SIBI meruisse statuunt: Aliter enim nos docuit Servator ipse Joh. 8. v. 50. Et hinc inde sacra pagina, dum Christum pro NOBIS passum, mortuum &c. asserit.

XXIIX. Reddat te, O HOMO, statuum hæc Christi consideratio, in VITA HUMILEM, ut idem sit affectus in te, qui fuit in Christo Jesu, ne cristas erigas, per inanem gloriam aliis te præferas, sed HUMILITER de TE sentias: Vide enim sis, Dominum tuum, quomodo se humilet: O TE ergò beatum, si faciem humiliati tui Christi assiduè oculis usurpaveris, non quidem in linteolo expressam Veronicæ cum Papicolis, sed in codice sacro ob oculos tibi positam Gal. 3. v. 1. cum Christicolis, faciem vermis, & non viri. Sic enim omnis superbia ex corde tuo exulabit, & tandem aliqvando, ut ille, exaltaberis, & sedebis, licet non in Throno Patris, tamen in Throno CHRISTI, Apoc. 3: v. 21.

XXIX. IN DOCTRINA CIRCUMSPECTUM, ne circumferaris quôvis vento doctrinæ, neqve Judæis fidem tribuas, qui propter duplicem jam enucleatum statum, Messiam nondum venisse somniant, Dn. D. Franzius disp. 3. in Aug. Conf. th. 9. vel, si venisse concedant, duplicem tamen pro duplici statu faciunt, alterum humilem, alterum gloriosum, Galat. de Arc. Cathol. Verit. l. 4. c. 2. Nec cum Calvinianis contra stimulum calcitres, quibus Exaltatio carnis Christi sudes præusta in oculis, qvam exinde totis lacertis impugnant, nescientes, qvanti homo æstimandus sit, Es. 2. v. 2.

XXX. IN CRUCE ANIMOSUM. Ecce enim IMMANUEL tuus VENIT Joh. 16. v. 28. VIDIT Thren. 3. v. 5. VICIT Apoc. 5. v. 5. ne tu, O fidelis Anima, qvæ in hoc Miseriarum Barathrum VENISTI, & dura VIDERE Psal. 60. v. 5. cogeris, succumbas, sed tandem VINCAS 1. Cor. 15. v. 27. & per multas tribulationes eas in regnum Cælorum Actor. 14. v. 21. non aliter enim tibi ipse disposuit regnum Luc. 22. v. 29, Esto ergò fidelis usq; ad finem, milita bonam militiam, retinens fidem & bonam conscientiam, & tandem victoriam obtinebis, coronâq; immarcessibili coronaberis ab eo.

CUI SOLI GLORIA.


## 47 Forty-seventh Disputation. On the Office of Christ in General, and Prophetic in Particular

Preface.

Just as he who desires to perceive and taste the beauty and sweetness of a pomegranate does not consider it enough for himself to have merely looked at or touched it, but judges that it must be cut open, the beautiful and harmonious order of the grains considered, and the sweetness tasted: so in no dissimilar way have we also hitherto looked upon the most precious pomegranate of the heavenly paradise, namely the wonderfully singular and singularly wonderful majesty and beauty of divine Christology, not with one or another glance, but we have dissected it, and in the first and second section of Christology, with a curious investigation of the mind, we have most abundantly fed our hungry souls with truth. Since therefore we have hitherto, with the help of the thrice-holy Deity, in the preceding inquiries, grain by grain and most inquisitively elucidated the individual things which are necessary for every pious and sensible person to know concerning the Person and life of our Redeemer, come, let us proceed to the elucidation of the third and last section, no less august and sublime, to learn the most holy office of our Mediator. Moreover, since by the testimony of the most wise Seneca, very much does the discourse profit, which creeps into the mind little by little, on this occasion, both by the command of pleasing brevity and the warning of convenient distinction, we are about to prove our diligence concerning the office of our God-man, both generally and specifically concerning the Prophetic office, with the highest Light and Divinity kindly shining upon us.

Thesis I.

That most honey-tongued Doctor of Orthodoxy, Augustine, asserted most excellently and most learnedly: Divinity without humanity is not a mediator; humanity without divinity is not a mediator: but between divinity alone and humanity alone, the mediator is human divinity and divine humanity.

II. For these two natures are bound together by so tight a knot, and so chained by an adamantine bond, that neither can exist or operate separately without the other.

III. Hence, the venerable antiquity wisely and piously called the divine action of Christ a humanized action, and his human action a deified one, and called the ἀποτέλεσμα itself θεαντρικὸν, which is neither merely divine nor merely human. And no less excellently than truly, the Blessed Damascene says: In the θεαντρικῇ action of Christ, although there are two actions really distinct, they nevertheless concur unitedly toward a common ἀποτέλεσμα, and have communion with one another.

IV. Because, as the Chalcedonian Canon holds, in the office each nature does what is proper to itself, with the communication of the other. For the Deity alone could not die, nor could humanity alone overcome death. Therefore, in order that death might be an equivalent price, the Son of God himself willed to die for us in the flesh he assumed.

V. The foundations of this orthodox opinion are most solidly constructed by those oracles of the Scriptures, from which it has been adamantly built up by the orthodox ancients, which, O Christ, are so clear that they deserve to be thought of as the very rays of the sun (as Theodoret speaks).

VI. Some of which show that the ἀποτέλεσμα of Mediation is to be ascribed to the whole Christ, or the whole person, as Galatians 3:13: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law; Ephesians 5:2: Christ gave himself for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor.

VII. But some demonstrate that the work of Redemption pertains also to the divine nature, as Acts 20:28: God purchased the Church; Romans 5:10: We were reconciled to God through the death of his Son; 1 John 1:7: The blood of Jesus Christ the Son of GOD cleanses us from all sin: 1 John 3. In this the Son of GOD appeared, that he might destroy the works of the Devil.

VIII. Finally, certain things confirm that the human nature of Christ is also not to be excluded from the works of Mediation, as, Gen. 3:15. The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent: Luke 9:56. The Son of man came to save souls: 1 Tim. 2:5. One Mediator of GOD and men, the Man Jesus Christ.

IX. When, therefore, the pious Ancients deny that Christ, as GOD, is Mediator, they are speaking of GOD alone, who is a consuming fire, Deut. 4:4, not of GOD or the incarnate λόγῳ. They do not exclude the divine nature from the office of Redemption, but they deny that it alone is the mediatorial cause.

X. Let there therefore depart from the minds and ears of Christians the impious opinion of Danaeus, by which he does not shudder to imagine that the human nature of CHRIST did no more in performing miracles than the rod of Moses did in the miracles performed before Pharaoh; likewise, that that voice of Christ raising Lazarus, and saying, Lazarus, come forth, was merely a bare sound, which contributed nothing to the life of Lazarus.

XI. Orthodoxy, rightly abhorring these blasphemies, believes and confesses that in the works of Mediation the human nature not only contributes its own natural operation, but at the same time effectively concurs, by the power of communicated virtue, both to those miracles and to the accomplishment of other ἀποτελέσματα.

XII. Let the Sacramentarian explain to me, I beseech you, whether to bruise the head of the serpent, to bless all nations, to remit sins, to save souls, to vivify, to reconcile the world to GOD, to restore eternal righteousness, etc., are human or divine operations? He will hardly deny that they are divine.

XIII. Now, however, Scripture assigns these actions, one and all, to the Seed of the woman Gen. 3, to Abraham c. 12, 18, 22, to the Son of Man Matt. 9, Luke 9, to the Branch of David Jer. 23 & 33, to the flesh of Christ John 6, and finally to the body of the flesh of Christ Col. 1, in express words.

XIV. Who, therefore, would be of such corrupt judgment as not to understand that the human nature of Christ concurs ἐνεργητικῶς to the accomplishment of these actions, not only according to its own virtues, but also according to that divine virtue which it received from the closest bond of union, both by reason of merit and in respect of efficacy. Therefore, the weak and futile affirmative of the Sacramentarian Spirit achieves nothing.

XV. Let the insane and profane error of the Loyola-followers also be banished from pious minds, by which, along with Francesco Stancaro and Lombard (who sowed the first seeds of this unhappy darnel), they contend that Christ is Mediator only according to his human nature.

XVI. Cardinal Bellarmine indeed attempts to cloak this impious delirium with some small distinction between the principle 'which' and 'by which': The principle 'which' was operating the works of the Mediator, he says, was not God alone, nor man alone, but both together, that is, the incarnate Word, or God made man: but the principle 'by which' those works were done by the Mediator was the human nature, not the divine.

XVII. But in truth: 1. he ignorantly opposes things that should not be opposed, namely, person and nature; 2. he futilely confuses things that should be distinguished, namely, natural properties with the office of the Savior; nor 3. does he attend to the end for which the λόγος assumed human flesh.

XVIII. This primary companion of the Jesuits surely urges above all that Pauline passage: 'One Mediator, the Man Christ Jesus,' and from there he contends to prove that Christ is Mediator only according to his human nature, and not according to his divine: Why, I ask, he says, did he add 'Man,' unless to express the nature according to which Christ is Mediator.

XIX. But with futile, vain, and clearly invalid attempts. For he gathers more than the antecedent admits. For the Apostle does not say that the Humanity, but that the Man is the Mediator. Moreover, the word 'Man' does not denote a ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον [mere man], or only the human nature of Christ, but the Man Christ Jesus, who is also true God.

XX. Hence Leo the First, Bishop of the Roman Church, discoursing more inquisitively upon this matter, said excellently: It does not matter from which substance Christ is named, since, with the unity of the Person remaining inseparably, he is the same, both entirely the Son of Man on account of the flesh, and entirely the Son of God on account of the one Deity with the Father.

XXI. Furthermore, if, wherever a person is denominated from a nature, that nature is to be understood exclusively: by a like reasoning it would also be concluded that Christ our Mediator is only according to his Deity exclusively in those places in which mention of the divine nature alone is expressed, 1 John 3:8, 1 John 4:9. Which, since it is altogether absurd, it follows that the instance of the Romanist leaders is feeble, discordant, and utterly incongruous. We are compelled to relegate other sophistries of the adversaries of the same color and odor to the course of the Exercise itself.

XXII. Let the detestable and execrable blasphemy of the Sacramentarian spirit also be warded off from the boundaries of the Church and banished even to hell, by which, without shame or any sense, without any foundation in the Scriptures, and against their most illustrious testimonies, it does not shudder to deny with an impious and abominable pen and mouth that CHRIST is the Mediator of all men.

XXIII. Although, however, the God-breathed Scripture asserts in words clearer than the sun that He is the Mediator of GOD and men, who gave Himself as a ransom for all, likewise, that He is the propitiation for the sins not only of us, but of the whole world, that He tasted death for all, that He bore the sins of the world, that He came into the world, that He might save that which was lost, not that He might judge the world, but that He might save the same.

XXIV. By what reason, therefore, by the Immortal GOD, will Sacramentarian sophistry be able to restrict the amplitude and universality of the merit of Christ, which regards all men entirely, to the small number of the Elect? O Satanic audacity, O execrable impudence!

XXV. What is it to accuse God the Father of perjury, God the Son of lying, to dictate to the Holy Spirit, to maliciously pervert the truth of Holy Scripture, to diabolically overturn its certainty, to tear up the foundation of all consolations, and to open the doors of despair to anxious consciences, if this is not it? But let us dismiss the abominable blasphemies of the Sacramentarian spirit, and commit them to divine judgment.

XXVI. Thus far, under the guidance of truth and simplicity, we have weighed the office of our mediator in general: it remains solely for this time that we suggest a few things concerning the Prophetic office of our Savior in particular.

XXVII. And, that we may begin from the line, as it is said, the prophetic office of Christ is that by which He informs us concerning the will of the Father and the way to eternal salvation.

XXIIX. For from His fullness we have all received grace for grace, because the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen GOD, the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known. Hence our heavenly Prophet himself says: The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon me, because he has anointed me to preach good tidings to the meek, he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, etc.

XXIX. In respect of this office he is called the supreme Prophet, Luke 7, 16. Counselor, Isa. 9, 6. Master, Matt. 23, 10. Shepherd, John 10, 11. Bishop of souls, 1 Pet. 2, 25. Teacher of the nations, Isa. 55, 4. Apostle of peace, Eph. 2, 17. of our confession, Heb. 3, 1. Evangelist, Isa. 61, 1. Lawgiver, [Isa.] 33, 22. light of the nations, Luke 2, 32.

XXX. For he revealed and announced to the world the true doctrine concerning eternal salvation, which immediately dispelled the thick darkness of ignorance of divine things, freed the human race from the kingdom of darkness, and informed them of the will of the heavenly Father and of obtaining immortality.

XXXI. Moreover, the Leader and perfecter of our faith has executed and still executes this most holy office today: 1. Immediately, both before the incarnation, from the beginning of the Church in paradise, revealing the will of GOD to the first-formed, instituting the ministry of the word and the Sacraments of the O.T. and predicting future events, and after it on earth, while he himself taught them to observe all things which he commanded, Matt. 28, 20, and which concern the kingdom of God, Acts 1, 3.

XXXII. 2. Mediately, by announcing the Gospel through his ministers, and by administering the Sacraments, the instruments of heavenly grace. For after he ascended on high, he gave gifts to men: and he gave some indeed as Apostles, and others as Prophets, and others as Evangelists, and others as Pastors and Teachers, as the Apostle of the nations speaks in his Ephesian [epistle]. And our Mediator himself addresses his disciples with these words: He who hears you, hears me.

XXXIII. Moreover, our Savior performed this most holy office, not only according to his humanity, but also by his Deity.

XXXIV. For although in the time of the O.T. the eternal λόγος was not yet covered in flesh, because the decree of the incarnation, to be in the last times, had been made from eternity, this pledge of the Son of GOD concerning the whole business of Redemption was as effective as if all things had already been accomplished from eternity.

XXXV. For Jesus Christ is yesterday, and today, the same forever, Heb. 13, 8. The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, namely by reason of the eternal decree

and of the promise made, and of the sacrifices, which were types, as well as of the vigor and efficacy of the Lord's passion, from which the pious Fathers from the foundation of the world were saved through faith.

XXXVI. But our Prophet, with respect to this office, did not have need to learn the will of GOD like other men, as Smalcius with his followers maliciously contends; since he is in the bosom of the Father, and therefore knows the whole will of GOD, which he has also revealed to us, John 1:18.

XXXVII. Indeed, from childhood as a true man he was full of wisdom, Luke 2. For the fullness of the Deity, that is, GOD himself, with all his divine power, wisdom, and glory, dwelt in him bodily, Col. 2:9 [16], and according to his human nature he was anointed from his mother's womb with the Spirit of Wisdom.

XXXIIX. Of the same dregs and flour is that pronouncement of Smalcius, by which he dreams that Christ's doctrine did not pertain to the Fathers of the O.T., and therefore is entirely new. For what? Shall we judge that to be new which was promulgated in Paradise, or that it did not pertain to the Fathers of the O.T. which was holily promised to the Fathers by Jehovah himself?

XXXIX. What, I ask, could have been added to the Law of God, as Moses taught it, when it was so perfect in all respects that Jehovah himself most severely prohibited anything from being added to it, Deut. 4:2, ch. 12:32.

XL. Far be it therefore that we should maintain that Christ either rendered it more perfect or added to it, when he publicly protested that he had added nothing to the law, nor had he perfected it, while he sends those who seek righteousness from the Law back to the Law of Moses, teaching them that they will live if they do those things which are written in the Law of Moses, Matt. 19:17, Luke 10:28.

XLI. If therefore the Mosaic Law has the efficacy of giving life, if only it be perfectly fulfilled, it follows that it is complete, and that nothing can be added to its perfection.

XLII. Let Smalcius therefore look to it, with his dregs, by what engines he strives to tear down and weaken this truth. For the foundations by which he attempts to shake our opinion are not iron, but earthen; not valid, but vain; not solid, but foolish; which, because of the narrowness of this page, we reserve for the conflict itself. And let this suffice to have delineated, as in a general way, the prophetic office of Christ as the occasion required.

XLIII. May the meditation of these things excite 1. the recognition of our ignorance. For GOD indeed created man in an excellent state, fashioned him in his own image, adorned his intellect with wisdom, crowned his will with justice, but he did not persist on this throne of majesty; rather, he lost every ornament, every honor. Adam fell, and in him we all fell. Hence so many and such great destructions have flowed forth into the human race. All wisdom perished, all knowledge vanished. The eyes of our mind are so covered with thick clouds of ignorance that we are dim-sighted in a faint light of things, blind in a moderate one, blinder in a greater one, and insane in the greatest, nor do we perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God; indeed, reason itself is so blinded that we perversely establish good as evil and evil as good. O change far unequal, and not to be sufficiently lamented by the length of any age! To one considering these things, the hair rightly stands on end, the mind shudders, the cheek weeps, the right hand stiffens. Acknowledge, O sons of Adam, your condition, thrice and four times unhappy: Ponder the fountain from whence so many destructions gush forth; never cease to run through in your thought the atrocity of sin causing these things. For this, this is what separated you from God, deprived you of the fellowship of angels, drove you from Paradise, infatuated your mind, blinded your reason, and associated you with the damned spirits, with whom you would have had to perish eternally, had not the eternal Son of God, moved by our misery, descended from heaven and snatched you from such great evils.

XLIV. Let the goodness of our Mediator excite the celebration of divine grace. For behold, O Man, how your misery drew the eternal λόγον from heaven, how the blindness of your mind inflamed the Son of God to the tireless performance of the prophetic office! Who, among all nations and places, would not judge that he should be proclaimed in the letters and languages of all, if the sun were to illuminate, calm, and recreate everything with the rays of its brightness in the middle of the night's storm? Behold, with the whole orb of the earth covered in thick clouds and mists of ignorance, the light of the nations rises, the light of the world springs up, the Sun of righteousness diffuses its rays; to those dangerously wandering in darkness and miseries, the day-spring from on high illuminates with the rays of his doctrine, calling them back into the royal path of blessedness; the heavenly lawgiver brings to life those dead in sins, inculcating repentance; the eternal Evangelist cheers the sorrowful, announcing the grace and peace of God. O therefore, truly joyful message! O lovable chief shepherd of souls! O admirable Prophet! Who here would not exclaim with Jacob: I am less, I am less, O Lord, than all thy mercies. Praise him therefore, O pious creatures, for he is good, and sing psalms to his name, for it is pleasant. Praise GOD the Father, who sent us this Prophet, promised many centuries ago: Praise GOD the Son, who visited, renewed, illuminated, and instructed us through the bowels of his mercy: Praise GOD the Holy Spirit, who still confirms and seals the instruction of our Prophet in our hearts: Praise the glorious Divinity from this time forth, and even for evermore.

XLV. Let the faithfulness of our 3rd Doctor excite attentive listening to the word. It is not the laws of Numa Pompilius here, not the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, not the Axioms of Aristotle, or the pronouncements of any other Man, but the word of the eternal Son of God himself, in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden, which is preached by the Ministers of the Church. For he who hears this, hears the Son of God himself. Therefore, let us meditate on the word of GOD with a devout mind, and prefer it to all the riches of the world with the Royal Psalmist. For it is a most useful treasure, a most precious pearl, a most excellent gem, a most preeminent κειμήλιον [treasure]. The word of GOD illuminates the mind, inflames the will with the love of heavenly things, feeds, heals, sanctifies, and vivifies the soul, and like a statue of Mercury, shows the way of eternal tranquility to pilgrims and militant Christians. O excellent thing, and worthy of the most ardent industry and the greatest exertion! O happy are they who in all adversities take refuge in this sacred anchor! O blessed are they who from their tenderest years have learned to prefer this word to all the riches of the world! Let your voice therefore sound, let it sound, O most happy Prophet, day and night in our ears. Speak Lord, for your servants are listening. Instruct us, most faithful Bishop, that we may keep your law, and observe it with our whole heart, so that we may be built up to the eternal glory of ineffable blessedness with all the Elect. Hear, O God of Israel, you who fashioned the ear and promised a hearing to those who pray devoutly, Amen!

Latin:

Præloqvium.

QVemadmodùm ille, qvi mali punici venustatem & svavitatem pervidere & gustare gestit, non satis sibi esse ducit, illud saltem aspexisse aut attigisse, sed dissecandum, granulorum pulchellum ac concinnum ordinem considerandũ, ac dulcedinem degustandam sibi omninò arbitratur: Ita non absimili ratione nos qvoqve hactenus cælestis paradisi preciosissimum pomum punicum, divinæ nimirùm Christologias mirabiliter singularem & singulariter mirabilem majestatem & venustatem non unô atqve alterô intuitu aspeximus, sed dispescuimus, singulatim, curiosâ mentis indagine, primâ & secundâ Christologias sectione, nostros famelicos veritatis animos affluentissimè pavimus. Cùm igitur hactenus, Trisagio adjuvante Numine, in prægressis disqvisitionibus singula, qvæ de Redemtoris nostri Persona & vitâ cuivis pio & cordato scitu sunt necessaria, granatim & inqvisitissimè enucleaverimus, agite, ad tertiæ & ultimæ sectionis non minùs augustæ & sublimis enucleationem accedamus, Sacrosanctum Mediatoris nostri officium cognituri. Cæterùm, cùm Sapientissimi Senecæ testimonio, plurimùm proficit sermo, qvi minutatim irrepit animo, hâc vice, & brevitatis gratæ jussu, & commodæ distinctionis monitu, de officio θεανθρώπε nostri cùm generatim, tùm de Prophetico speciatim, summô Lumine ac Numine benignè affulgente, nostram probaturi sumus industriā.

Thesis I.

PRæclarè omnino & pereruditè asseruit mellitissimus ille Orthodoxias Doctor Augustinus: Divinitas sine humanitate non est mediatrix; Humanitas sine Divinitate non est mediatrix: sed inter divinitatem solam & humanitatem solam mediatrix est humana divinitas & divina humanitas.

II. Etenim duæ hæ naturæ tam arctô se inter sunt ligatæ nodô, penitusq́; adamantinjô ita catenatæ vinculô, ut neutra sine altera seorsim vel sit, vel operetur.

III. Hinc scitè & piè veneranda antiqvitas, divinam Christi actionem dicebat actionem humanatam, humanam verò deificatam, & ἀποτέλεσμα ipsum vocabat θεαντρικὸν, qvod neq; nudè divinū, neq; nudè humanam sit. Et non miuùs egregiè qvàm verè Beatus Damascenus: In actione Christi θεαντρικῇ, etsi duæ actiones sunt realiter distinctæ, ad commune tamen ἀποτέλεσμα unitæ concurrunt, & communionem invicem habent.

IV. Qvia, ut habet Canon Chalcedonensis, In officio utraque natura agit, quod sibi proprium est, cum communicatione alterius. Sola enim Deitas mori non poterat, nec sola humanitas mortem vincere. Ut igitur mors posset esse precium æqvivalens, ipse DEI filius in assumtâ carne mori pro nobis voluit.

V. Fundamenta orthodoxæ hujus sententiæ solidissimè adstruunt illa Scripturarum oracula, ex qvib⁹ ea ἀδαμαντίνως ab orthodoxis veteribus est extructa, qvæ, me Christe, tam clara sunt, ut ipsi⁹ solis radiis (qvemadmodum D. Theodoretas loqvitur) Scripta putari mereantur.

VI. Qvorum qvædam ostendunt, toti Christo, sive toti personæ, ἀποτέλεσμα Mediationis adscribendum esse, ut Gal. 3, 13. Christus nos redemit à maledictione legis: Eph. 5, 2. Christus dedit seipsum pro nobis hostiam & oblationem Dei in odorem svavitatis.

VII. Qvædam verò demonstrant, opus Redemptionis ad divinam etiam naturam pertinere, ut Act. 20, 28. Deus acqvifivit Ecclesiā. Rom. 5, 10. Reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filii ejus: 1. Joh. 1, 17. Sángvis Jesu Christi filii DEI emundat nos ab omni peccato: 1. Joh. 3. In hoc apparuit Filius DEI, ut dissolveret opera Diaboli.

IIX. Quædam deniq; confirmant, Christi humanam etiam naturam ab operibus Mediationis non esse secludendam, ut, Gen. 3, 15. Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis: Luc. 9, 56. Filius hominis venit salvare animas: 1. Tim. 2, 5. Unus Mediator DEI & hominum, Homo Jesus Christus.

IX. Qvando ergò pii Veteres negant, Christum, ut DEUM, esse Mediatorem, loqvuntur de solo DEO, qvi est ignis consumens, Deut. 4, 4, non de DEO sive λόγῳ incarnato. Non excludunt à Redemtionis officiô divinam naturā, sed illam solam causam mediatricē inficiantur.

X. Facessat proinde â Christianorum animis & auribus impia Danaei sententia, qvâ fingere non exhorrescit, naturam CHRISTI humanā in patrandis miraculis non plus fecisse, qvàm fecerit virga Mosis in miraculis coram Pharaone editis; Item, vocem illam Christi excitantis Lasarum, & dicentis, Lasare, veni foras, fuisse duntaxat nudum sonitum, qvi ad vitam Lasari nihil contulerit.

XI. A qvibus blasphemiis meritò abhorrens Orthodoxia, credit, & confitetur, in operibus Mediationis humanam naturąm non duntaxat naturalem suam operationem conferre, sed simul efficaciter, vi communicatæ virtutis, tùm ad illa miracula, tùm alia ἀποτελέσματα perficienda concurrere.

XII. Edisserat mihi, obsecro, Sacramentarius, num conterere caput serpentis, benedicere omnibus gentibus, peccata remittere, animas salvare, vivificare, mundum DEO reconciliara, æternā justitiam reparare, &c. sint humanæ an divinę operationes? divinas esse vix negabit.

XIII. Jam verò Scriptura istas actiones ad unam omnes Semini mulieris Gen. 3. Abrahæ c. 12, 18, 22. Filio Hominis Matth. 9. Luc. 9. Germini Davidis Jer. 23, & 33. carni Christi Joh. 6. corpori deniqve carnis Christi Col. 1. expressis assignat verbis.

XIV. Ecqvis igitur adeò corrupti foret judicii, qvi non intelligat, humanam Christi naturam non duntaxat secundùm proprias virtutes, sed etiam secundûm divinam illam virtutem, qvam ex arctissimo unionis vinculo accepit, ad actiones istas tum ratione meriti, tum respectu efficaciæ perficiendas ἐνεργητικῶς concurrere. Nihil ergò obtinet Sacramentarii Spiritûs debilis & futilis affirmativa.

XV. Facesfat etiam â piis mentibus Lojolitarum vesanus & profanus error, qvâ cum Francisco Stancaro, & Lombardo, (qvi infelicis hujus lolii semina prima sparsit) Christum secundùm humanam naturam tantùm Mediatorem esse contendunt.

XVI. Palliare qvidem conatur Cardinalis Bellarminus impium hoc delirium aliqvâ distinctiuncula inter principium qvod & qvo: Principum, qvod operabatur opera Mediatoris, inqvit, non fuit Deus solùm, nec homo solùm, sed utrumq; simul, hoc est, verbum incarnatum, sive Deus humanatus: Principum autem, qvo illa opera à Mediatore fiebant, fuit natura humana, non divina.

XVII. Verumenimverò 1. opponit inscitè, qvæ non sunt opponenda, personam videlicet, & naturam; 2. confundit futiliter distingvenda, proprietates nimirùm naturales, cum Soteris officio; nec 3. attendit finem, propter quem λόγος humanam carnem assumsit.

XIIX. Urget sanè socius iste Jesuitarum primarius cumprimis istud Paulinum: Unus Mediator Homo Christus Jesus, & exinde probare contendit, Christum tantùm secundùm humanam naturam, & non secundùm divinam esse Mediatorem: Cur qvæso, ait, addidit, Homo, nisi ad exprimendam naturam, secundùm qvam Christus Mediator est.

XIX. Verùm irritis, vanidis, & invalidis planè conatibus. Plus enim colligit, qvàm antecedens admittit. Apostolus qvippe non dicit, Humanitatem, sed Hominem esse Mediatorem. Vox autem Hominis non notat ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον, vel tantùm humanam Christi naturam, sed Hominem Christum Jesum, qvi etiam verus Deus est.

XX. Hinc Leo primus Ecclesiæ Romanæ Episcopus, inqvisitiùs super hâc re edifferens, egregiè dixit: Non interest, ex qva Christus substantia nominetur, cùm inseparabiliter, manente unitate Personæ, idem sit & totus Hominis Filius propter carnem, & totus Dei Filius propter unam cum Patre Deitatem.

XXI. Præterea, si, ubicunq; â natura denominatur persona, natura illa intelligenda est exclusivè: parili qvoqve ratione & Christum Mediatorem nostrum esse tantùm secundum Deitatem exclusivè concludetur iis in locis, qvibus divinæ naturæ solius mentio exprimitur, 1. Joh. 3, 8, 1. Joh. 4, 9. Qvod, cùm absurdum omninò sit, seqvitur, elumbem, absonam, & penitus incongruam esse Romanensium Coryphæi instantiam. Alias ejusdem coloris & odoris adversantium argutias ad ipsum Exercitationis cursum cogimur rejicere.

XXII.
