Arceatur etiam ab Ecclesiæ pomeriis, & ad orcum usq; amandetur detestabilis & excreanda spiritus Sacramentarii blasphemia, quâ sine fronte & mente omni, sine Scripturarum fundamento omni, contra illustrissima earundem testimonia, stylo & ore supra modum impio & abominando negare non exhorrescit, CHRISTUM omnium Hominum Mediatorem esse.

XXIII. Cùm tamen verbis vel Sole clarioribus θεόπνευστος Scriptura asserat, eum esse Mediatorem DEI & Hominum, qui dederit semetipsum ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus, item, propitiationem pro peccatis non nostris tantùm, sed totius mundi, pro omnibus mortem gustasse, peccata mundi tulisse, in Mundum, ut salvaret quod perierat, non ut judicet Mundum, sed ut servet eundem, venisse.

XXIV. Quâ ergò, per DEUM Immortalem, ratione amplitudinem & universalitatem meriti Christi omnes omninò homines respicientem, ad pauculum Electorum numerum restringere Sacramentaria poterit Sophistria? O audaciam Satanicam, ô execrandam impudentiam!

XXV. Quid est DEUM Patrem perjurii, Deum filium mendacii arguere, Spiritui Sancto dicam scribere, S. Scripturæ veritatem malitiosè pervertere, ejusdem certitudinem diabolicè evertere, fundamentum omnium consolationum convellere, anxiisq; conscientiis fores desperationis aperire, si hoc non est? Sed mittamus spiritûs Sacramentarii abominandas blasphemias, judicioq; divino committamus.

XXVI. Hactenus ductu veritatis & simplicitatis mediatoris nostri officium in genere pensitavimus: Unicè hâc vice est in residuo, ut de officio Servatoris nostri Prophetico in specie paucula insinuamus.

XXVII. Et, ut à linea, quod dicitur, incipiamus, Officium Christi propheticum est, quô nos de voluntate Patris, & viâ ad æternam salutem informat.

XXIIX. Ex plenitudine enim ipsius omnes accepimus gratiam pro gratia, Qvia lex per Mosen data est, gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum exorta est. DEUM nemo vidit unqvam, Unigenitus Filius, qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit. Hinc ipse Propheta noster cœlestis ait : Spiritus Domini Jehovæ est super me, eò, quòd unxit me ad Evangelizandum mansuetis, misit me ad obligandum fractos animo, ad proclamandum captivis libertatem &c.

XXIX. Hujus officii respectu dicitur summus Propheta, Luc. 7, 16. Consiliarius, Esa. 9. 6. Magister, Matth. 23, 10. Pastor, Joh. 10, 11. Episcopus animarum, 1. Petr. 2, 25. Præceptor gentium, Esa. 55, 4. Apostolus pacis, Eph. 2, 17. nostræ confessionis, Hebr. 3, 1. Evangelista, Esa. 61, 1. Legifera c. 33. 22. lumen gentium, Luc. 2, 32.

XXX. Patefecit enim, & annunciavit mundo veram de salute æternâ doctrinam, quæ confestim crassas tenebras ignoranronis rerum divinaru dispulit, humanum genus à regno tenebrarum liberavit, de voluntate Patris cœlestis, & conseqvendâ immortalitate informavit.

XXXI. Executus est autem, hodieqve exeqvitur Dux & consummator fidei nostræ Sacrosanctum hoc munus 1. Immediatè, tum ante incarnationem, ab Exordio Ecclesiæ in paradiso, patefaciens Protoplastis voluntatem DEI, instituens ministerium verbi & Sacramentorum V.T. & prædicens res futuras, tùm post eam in terris, dum ipse docuit servare omnia, quæ mandavit Matth. 28, 20. & quæ regnum Dei concernunt Act. 1, 3.

XXXII. 2. Mediatè, Evangelium per ministros suos annunciando, & Sacramenta cœlestis gratiæ organa administrando. Postqvàm enim ascendit in altum, dona dedit hominibus: & dedit alios qvidem Apostolos, alios verò Prophetas, alios autem Evangelistas, & alios Pastores & Doctores, uti gentium Apostolus in Ephesinâ suâ loqvitur. Et ipse Mediator noster discipulos suos his alloqvitur verbis : Qvi vos audit, me audit.

XXXIII. Perfunctus est autem Servator noster munere hôc Sacrosanctô, non tantùm secundùm humanitatem, verùm etiam Deitate.

XXXIV. Qvantumvis enim V. T. tempore æternus λόγος nondum carne tectus erat, qvia tamen decretum incarnationis, temporibus novissimis futuræ, ab æterno erat factum, sponsio hæc filii DEI de toto Redemtionis negocio adeò efficax fuit, atq; si jam omnia ab æterno fuissent peracta.

XXXV. Est enim Jesus Christus heri, & hodiè, ipse in secula, Hebr. 13, 8. Agnus occisus ab origine mundi, videlicet ratione æterni decreti

& promissionis factæ, & sacrificiorum, quæ erant typi, nec non vigoris atq; efficaciæ passionis dominicæ, ex quâ pii Patres ab orbe condito per fidem fuêre salvati.

XXXVI. Non autem Propheta noster, hujus respectu officii, instar aliorum hominum, voluntatẽ DEI addiscere necesse habuit, ut Smalcius suis cũ affeclis malitiosè contendit; Siquidem in sinu Patris est, & proinde omnẽ DEI voluntatem novit, quam & nobis revelavit, Joh. 1, 18.

XXXVII. Imò à pueris ut verus homo plenus fuit sapientia, Luc. 2. Plenitudo n. Deitatis, hoc est, DEUS ipse, cű omni sua divina potentia, sapientia, atq; gloria in ipso habitavit corporaliter, Col. 2, 16. & secundú naturam suam humanã ab utero matris SpirituSapientiæ unctus fuit.

XXXIIX. Ejusdem fecis & farinæ istudSmalzii pronunciatum, quo Christi doctrinam ad Patres V. T. non pertinuisse, ideoq; planè novã esse somniat. Ecquid enim ? Anne novum fuisse, qvod in Paradyso promulgatum, anne ad Patres V. T. non pertinuisse, qvod Patribus à Jehova ipso sanctè promissum est, censebimus?

XXXIX. Ecqvid, qvæso, Legi Dei prout illam Moses docuit, addi potuisset, cùm adeò omnibus numeris absoluta fuerit, ut Jehova ipse aliqvid addi severissimè prohibuerit, Deut. 4, 2. c. 12, 32.

XL. Absit ergò statuamus, Christum vel perfectiorem eam reddidisse, vel adauxisse, cùm publicè protestatus fuerit, se legi nihil addidisse, neq; eam perfecisse, dum eos, qui ex Lege qværunt justitiam', ad Legem Mosis remittit, docens eos victuros, si fecerint ea, qvæ in Lege Mosis scripta sunt, Matth. 19, 17. Luc. 10, 28.

XLI. Si ergò LexMosaica habet efficaciam vivificandi, si modò perfectè impleatur, consequitur, eam integram esse, nec qvicqvam ad ejus perfectionem accedere posse.

XLII. Viderit ergò Smalcius cum suâ colluvie, qvibus machinis veritatem hanc convellere & labefactare annitatur. Fundamenta enim, qvibus nostram sententiam succutere conatur, non ferrea, sed terrea, non valida, sed vanida, nõ solida, sed stolida sunt, qvæ ob chartulæ angustiam ipsi reservamus conflictui. Et hæc pro re natâ de officio Christi Prophetico ὡς ἐν γενεικῷ delineâsse sufficiat.

XLIII. Excitet horum meditatio 1. nostræ ignorantiæ agnitionem. Creavit qvidem DEUS hominem in statu optimo, effinxit suam ad imaginem, condecoravit intellectum sapientiâ, coronavit voluntatem Justitia, sed in hoc majestatis throno non perstitit, verum omne ornamentum, decus omne perdidit. Cecidit Adam,& in illo cecidimus omnes. Hinc tot tantaq; exitia in genus hominum profluxerunt. Periit omnis Sapientia, evanuit omnis scientia. Mentis nostrae oculi adeo spissis ignorantiae nebulis sunt obducti, ut in tenui rerum luce caligemus, in mediocri caecutiamus, in majori caeci simus, in maxima insaniamus, nec ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei, percipiamus, quin ipsa ratio adeo excaecata, ut bonum malum, malum bonum, perverse statuamus. O commutationem longe imparem,& nullius aevi longinquitate satis deploranda! Merito haec consideranti Stat coma, mens horret, flet gena, dextrariget. Agnoscite g. o Filii Adae, conditionem vestram, terq; quaterq; infelicem: Perpendite fontem, unde tot exitia scaturiant; peccati atrocitatem haec causantem nunquam no cogitatione percurrite. Hoc, hoc enim vos a Deo separavit, angelorum consortio privavit, e Paradyso profligavit, mentem infatuavit, rationem excaecavit, damnatis spiritibus associavit, cum quibus aeternum vobis pereundum fuisset, nisi aeternus Dei filius, nostra commotus miseria, e caelo delapsus tantis e malis vos eripuisset.

XLIV. Excitet 2. Mediatoris nostri bonitas Gratiae divinae celebrationem. Ecce enim, o Homo, ut tua Miseria aeternum λόγον e caelo detraxerit, ut Mentis tuae caecitas Dei Filium ad Prophetici muneris indefessam functionem inflammavit! Quis non ubivis gentium & locorum, omnium literis & lingvis depraedicandum censeret, si sol media noctis tempestate claritatis suae radiis omnia collustraret, placaret, atq; recrearet? Ecce spissis ignorantiae nubib9 & nebulis universo terrarum orbe obducto, oritur lumen gentium, exurgit lux mundi, radios diffundit Sol justitiae, in tenebris & miseriis periculose deviantes radiis doctrinae suae illustrat oriens ex alto, in regiam beatitatis semitam revocando; in peccatis mortuos vivificat caelestis legifer, poenitentiam inculcando; maestos exhilarat aeternus Evangelista, gratiam & pacem Dei annunciando. O igitur nuncium vere laetabilem! O ἀρχιποιμένιων animarum amabilem! O Prophetam admirabilem! Quis hic cum Jacobo non exclamet: Minor, minor sum, Domine, cunctis miserationibus tuis. Laudate ergo ipsum, o pia pectura, quia bonus est, & psallite nomini ejus, quia suave est. Laudate DEUM Patrem, qui nobis Prophetam hunc, multis retrò seculis promissum, misit: Laudate DEUM Filium, qui nos per viscera misericordiæ suæ visitavit, renovavit, illuminavit, & informavit: Laudate DEUM Spiritum Sanctum, qui informationem Prophetæ nostri in cordibus nostris adhuc confirmat & obsignat: Laudate gloriosam Divinitatem ex hoc nunc, & usque in seculum.

XLV. Excitet 3. Doctoris nostri fidelitas attentam verbi ascultationem. Non hîc Numæ Pompilii leges, non Aphorissimi Hippocratis, non Axiomata Aristotelis, aut alius pronunciata Hominis, sed ipsius æterni Dei Filii, in quo omnes sapientiæ thesauri sunt absconditi, verbum est, quod a Ministris Ecclesiæ prædicatur. Hoc enim qui audit ipsum Dei Filium audit. Devotâ proinde mente verbum DEI meditemur, & omnibus mundi divitiis cum Psalte Regiô præferamus. Est enim thesaurus utilissimus, unio præciosissima, gemma præstantissima, κειμήλιον præcellentissimum. Verbum DEI mentem illuminat, voluntatem amore cœlestium inflammat, animum pascit, sanat, sanctificat, vivificat, viamq; sempiternæ tranquillitatis Mercurialis instar statuæ peregrinantibus & militantibus Christicolis demonstrat. O rem præclaram, & ardentissimâ industriâ, summâq; contentione dignissimam! O felices, qui in omnibus adversitatibus ad sacra hanc confugiunt ancoram! O beatos, qui à teneris unguiculis verbu hoc omnibus mundi præferre didicerunt divitiis! Sonet igitur, sonet vox tua, ô Propheta, felicissime, interdiu & noctu nostris in auribus. Loqvere Domine, quia adiunt servi tui. Instrue nos, Episcope fidissime, ut custodiamus legem tuam, & toto corde observemus, quò ad sempiternam ineffabilis beatitatis gloriam cum omnibus Electis ædificemur. Audi Deus Israel, qui aurem condidisti, exauditionemq; devotè orantibus promisisti, Amen!


## 48 Disputation Forty-eighth. Of the Sacerdotal Office of Christ

Thesis I.

The threefold office of Christ the God-man, Prophetic, Priestly, and Kingly, with a fuller explanation of that first one, next preceding disputation has presented to us a most approved matter. Therefore, the consideration of the second, namely the Sacerdotal office, will deservedly have to be substituted in a few words.

II. Moreover, this consists in the position and resolution of the definition of the Sacerdotal office of the Theanthropos; 2. In the use of the same; 3. and finally, the abuse.

III. The definition can conveniently be thus: The Sacerdotal office of Christ is that by which He fulfilled the divine law by the obedience of His most holy life, offered Himself voluntarily to God the Father on the altar of the cross once for all as a holy, perfect, and eternal sacrifice to expiate the sins of all men, applies the benefits obtained to believers through faith and the Sacraments, and intercedes incessantly for the same before His heavenly Father.

IV. In which definition deserve consideration: 1. Christ, as Priest or High Priest: 2. The Sacerdotal office itself, which regards 1. Satisfaction, 2. Intercession. Satisfaction comprises the fulfillment of the divine law, then the shedding of blood, and death itself. 3. The cause of that offering.

V. As regards the first, Christ Himself is called Priest, High Priest, Heb. 4:14, Mediator of the new Testament, Heb. 9:15, ch. 12:24. By which very thing the end and complement of the Priesthood of the Old Testament is shown before us. In the O.T., by reason of succession, though not by reason of present function, there were many High Priests or Priests: In the New, however, Christ alone, who grants that there is no one either with Him or after Him. Indeed, nor can anyone be. Wherefore He is proclaimed the one Mediator of God and men, 1 Tim. 2:5.

VI. The office of the High Priest in the O.T. was to guard the Law, to offer sacrifices, to intercede: Thus also our High Priest Christ had to fulfill the law. Indeed, that earth-shaking pronouncement of Deut. 27:26 made satisfaction necessary by reason of the law to be fulfilled: Cursed is he who does not continue in all things which are written in the book of the law, to do them. Gal. 3:10.

VII. Our first parents, by disobedience of their own kind, enormously and eminently, by deriving that first curse upon themselves, became impotent to keep the law also sanctioned by the Lord thereafter, together with their posterity. But because Christ had constituted Himself Mediator and Satisfier, He could not but satisfy the divine will of the Father by keeping that sanctioned law, by which we, liberated from the curse of this, might experience a benign God. Wherefore, the Apostle Paul writes in Gal. 4:4, 5, God sent forth His Son, made of a woman, made subject to the law, to redeem them that were under the law. See Rom. 8. v. 15. Gal. 3. v. 13. Christ did not redeem from the curse of the law, while he was made a curse for us. Thus Christ himself says Matth. 5. v. 17. I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill.

VIII. The perfect observance of the law was incumbent upon us who are powerless, Deut. 6. v. 5. Matth. 22. v. 37. 39. Therefore, Christ the intercessor also fulfilled it by keeping it most perfectly. Otherwise, the saints can keep the law in many things, but yet not perfectly, partly by reason of the act, partly by reason of the whole. Therefore, although someone may offend in one thing at least, he meanwhile remains guilty of the whole, Jac. 2. v. 10. Christ, by the course of his entire most holy life, satisfied not just in part, but in whole by keeping it exactly. Which thing the Pharisees themselves, hypocrites, when asked by Christ about the conviction of sin, willy-nilly tacitly had to admit, Joh. 8. v. 46. Wherefore he is called the end or perfection of the law, Rom. 10. v. 4.

IX. The transgression of the law, which indicated a harsh death for the offender, made satisfaction by reason of undergoing death necessary, Gen. 2. v. 16, 17. Now indeed all men die, but by that very fact neither is anyone able to reacquire eternal life for himself, much less for his brother, Psal. 49. v. 8, least of all for the whole human race. Indeed, because that is in place of a penalty, it cannot be meritorious or satisfactory. Furthermore, not only the penalty of temporal death, but especially of eternal death was intimated. Therefore, unless we were to undergo that eternal one, an ἀντίλυτρον was required. A created archangel, as a finite being created by God, could not perform that: since God, an infinite being, was offended, he was therefore not able to pay an equivalent price. Consequently, the Son of GOD, the λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο Joh. 1. v. 14, σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος μέτεσχε Hebr. 2. v. 14, that through death he might abolish him who had the power of death, i.e., the Devil.

X. Because, therefore, Christ is the God-man Mediator, he was able to pay an equivalent price. He sustained death, because he was not mere man, who was not able to perform that, nor mere God, who could not suffer and die; meanwhile, suffering or death was necessary, since without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins, Heb. 9. v. 22. Therefore the God-man performed it. Hence the blood of the Son of GOD is said to cleanse us from all sin; 1. Joh. 1. v. 8. Hebr. 9. v. 14. Col. 1. v. 14. 1. Petr. 1. v. 19. Apoc. 1. v. 5. Moreover, there is an equivalent reason for expiating the offense of the infinite GOD in the death of CHRIST, because God himself truly suffered in the flesh, 1. Pet. 3. v. 18. Act. 3. v. 15. 1. Cor. 2. v. 8. Hence it is said that God reconciled the world to himself, 2. Cor. 5. v. 19. by his blood

he acquired the Church for himself Then, although Christ, by reason of the duration of the act, which was of short time, did not undergo eternal death, which was impossible, yet by reason of the vigor and intensity, death can be equated to the eternal death of Christ. XI. Christ therefore offered a host or victim, not by offering a ram, or a goat, or a calf, or a bull, but himself, wherefore he is called our Passover, He offered himself, however, on the altar of the cross, and indeed once, The High Priest of the Old Testament did not enter into the holy of holies through his own blood, but through the blood of goats and calves, and indeed annually at a single repeated time: but Christ the High Priest and Mediator of the New Testament offered himself, he entered into the holy places through his own blood, and indeed once, because it was appointed for man to die once, XII.

There follows the 3rd cause. The High Priest of the Old Testament offered blood not his own, but another's, of goats and calves, for himself, and for the ignorance of the people, because he himself was also conceived and born in sins, CHRIST, the High Priest and Mediator of the New Testament, offered himself to God the Father not through another's, but his own blood, not for himself, because he was not a mere man, nor a man conceived and born in sins, but Holy, Justice itself, pious, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, whence he exists as a holy host; But for the expiation of the sins of all men, of the whole world, hence he is called the Lamb of God, taking away the sins of the world, whence he exists as a perfect host, eternal redemption whence he is an eternal host.

Latin:

Thesis. I.

TRiplex Christi Θεανθρώπꙋ officium, Propheticum, Sacerdotale, & Regium, cum uberiore istius primi explicatione, proximèpraecedens disputatio nobis exhibuit probatissimum. Meritò itaque consideratio secundi, Sacerdotalis nimirum, paucis substituenda erit.

II. Constat autem isthaec in positione & resolutione definitionis officii Θεανθρώπου Sacertotalis; 2. In ejusdem usu; 3. deniq́; abusu.

III. Definitio commodè ita esse potest: Officium Christi Sacerdotale est, quô divinam legem sanctissimae vitae suae obedientiâ adimplevit, seipsum hostiam sanctam, perfectam, & aeternam semel pro omnibus omnium hominum peccatis expiandis Deo Patri in ara crucis spontè obtulit, parta beneficia credentibus per fidem & Sacramenta applicat, pro iisdem apud Patrem suum coelestem indefinenter intercedens.

IV. In qua definitione considerationem merentur, 1. Christus, ut Sacerdos seu Pontifex: 2. Officium ipsum Sacerdotale, quod respicit 1. Satisfactionem, 2. Intercessionem. Satisfactio comprehendit divinae legis impletionem, tum sanguinis profusionem, ipsam mortem. 3. causa istius oblationis.

V. Primum quod attinet, dicitur ipse Christus Sacerdos, Pontifex magnus, Hebr. 4, 14. Mediator novi Testamenti, Hebr. 9. v. 15. c. 12, 24. Quo ipso finis & complementum Sacerdotii Vet. Test. coram ostenditur. In V. T. ratione successionis, licet non ratione praesentis functionis, plurimi fuerunt Magni Pontifices seu Sacerdotes: In Novo autem solus Christus, qui vel secum, vel post se neminem esse concedit. Imò nec quis esse potest. Quare Unus Mediator DEI & hominum praedicatur, 1. Tim. 2. v. 5.

VI. Sacerdotis Magni in V. T. officium erat, Legem custodire, Sacrificia offerre, Intercedere: Ita & noster Pontifex Christus legem implere debuit. Satisfactionem siquidem ratione legis implendae necessariam effecit pronunciatum illud terrisonum Deut. 27, v. 26. Maledictus, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in libro legis, ut faciat ea. Gal. 3. v. 10.

VII. Primi nostri Parentes, inobedientiâ sui generis, enormiter & eminenter tali, primum maledictum in se derivando, legê post quoq; à Domino sancitam servandi impotentes unà cum posteris facti sunt. Quia verò CHRISTUS Mediatorem ac Satisfactorem se constituerat, non poterat non satisfacere voluntati divinae Patris, servando istam sancitam legem, quô & ab isthujus maledictione liberati Deum benignum experiremur. Quare, scribit Apost. Paulus Gal. 4. v. 4, 5. emisit Deus filium suum, factum ex muliere, factum legi obnoxiũ, ut eos, qui legi erant obnoxii, redimeret. Vid. Rom. 8. v. 15. Gal. 3. v. 13. Christus non redemit ab execratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio. Sic Christus ipse inquit Matth. 5. v. 17. Non veni solvere legem, sed adimplere.

IIX. Perfecta observatio legis nobis impotentib9 incumbebat Deut. 6. v. 5. Matth. 22. v. 37. 39. Igitur & perfectissimè Christus intercessor eam servando implevit. Aliàs sancti in multis legem servare possunt, sed tamen non perfectè, partim ratione actus, partim ratione totius. Idcircò, licet aliqvis in uno saltem delinqvat, reus interim manet totius, Jac. 2. v. 10. Christus totius sanctissimæ vitæ curriculo non in tantum, sed in totum exactè servando satisfecit. Id qvod ipsi Pharisæi, hypocritæ, à Christo de peccati arguitione qvæsiti, nolentes volentes tacitè non diffiteri habebant Joh. 8. v. 46. Qvapropter dicitur finis seu perfectio legis Rom. 10. v. 4.

IX. Satisfactionem ratione mortis subeundæ necessariam effecit transgressio legis, delinqventi mortem asperam indicentis, Gen. 2. v. 16, 17. Jam qvidem omnes homines moriuntur, verùm eo ipso nec qvilibet sibiipsi vitam æternam reacqvirere valet, multò minus fratri suo, Psal. 49. v. 8. minimè omnium toti generi humano. Imò, qvia id sit pœnæ loco, meritorium aut satisfactorinm esse neqvit. Insuper non tantùm pœna mortis temporalis, sed maximè æternæ intimabatur. Igitur ni æternam isthanc subiremus, ἀντίλυτρον reqvirebatur. Archangelus creatus, ut ens finitum à Deo creatum, id præstare non poterat: Siqvidem Deus, ens infinitum, læsus erat, precium igitur æqvivalens persolvere non erat potens. Filius proinde DEI λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο Joh. 1. v. 14. σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος μέτεσχε Hebr. 2. v. 14. ut per mortem aboleret eum, qvi mortis habebat imperium, h. e. Diabolum.

X. Qvia itaq; Christus Θεάνθρωπος Mediator est, precium æqvivalens persolvere potuit. Mortem, qvia non nudus homo sustinuit, qvi id præstare non valebat, neq; nudus Deus, qvi pati moriq; non poterat, passio seu mors interim erat neceffaria, qvippe absq; sangvinis effusione non sit remissio peccatorum Heb. 9. v. 22. Idcircò θεάνθρωπος id præstitit. Hinc sangvis Filii DEI nos mundare dicitur ab omni peccato; 1. Joh. 1. v. 8. Hebr. 9. v. 14 Col. 1. v. 14. 1. Petr. 1. v. 19. Apoc. 1. v. 5. Est autem æqvivalens ratio expiandi infiniti DEI offensionem in CHRISTI morte, qvia ipse Deus reverà in carne passus est, 1. Pet. 3. v. 18. Act. 3. v. 15. 1. Cor. 2. v. 8. hinc dicitur Deus sibi reconciliâsse mundum, 2. Cor. 5. v. 19. Suo sangvine sibi acquisivisse Ecclesiam, Deinde, licet Christus ratione durationis actus, qui pauci temporis fuit, aeternam mortem non subierit, quod impossibile erat, ratione tamen vigoris et intensionis aeternae morti Christi mors equiparari potest. XI.

Obtulit igitur Christus hostiam seu victimam, non offerendo arietem, aut hircum, aut vitulum, aut taurum, sed seipsum, circò dicitur Pascha nostrum, Obtulit autem se in ara crucis, et quidem semel, Pontifex V. T. non per proprium sanguinem, sed per sanguinem hircorum ac vitulorum in sanctum sanctorum ingrediebatur, et quidem quotannis reiterata vice unica: Christus autem Pontifex Mag. Mediator N. T. seipsum obtulit, per proprium sanguinem ingressus est in sancta, et quidem semel, quia homini semel mori statutum erat, *XII.

Sequitur 3.* causa. Pontifex V. T. sanguinem non proprium, sed alienum, hircorum ac vitulorum, pro seipso, et pro populi ignorantia offerebat, quia et ipse erat in peccatis conceptus et natus, CHRISTUS, Pontifex et Mediator N. T. se Deo Patri obtulit non per alienum, sed proprium sanguinem, non pro se, quia non nudus homo, nec homo in peccatis conceptus et natus, sed Sanctus, Ipsa justitia, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus a peccatoribus, unde existit hostia sancta; Sed pro omnium hominum, pro totius mundi, peccatis expiandis, hinc vocatur agnus Dei, tollens peccata mundi, unde existit hostia perfecta, αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν unde est hostia aeterna.


### Wherefore he is called a Priest forever, XIII

Wherefore he is called a Priest forever, XIII.

From this results the fruit:

1. Liberation from the curse of the law; 2. Reconciliation of us with God; 3. Liberation from death and the power of Satan; 4. Cleansing from sins; 5. Acquisition of life and justice.

XIV. But it is no less of such a priestly office of Christ to apply these benefits. Which he also sufficiently performs, when he sends the Holy Spirit, who is the author of faith, by which the merit of Christ and the salutary benefits are applied, sealed, and confirmed, through the word and the Sacraments, which are the means by which the Holy Spirit wills to be efficacious.

For faith is from hearing the divine word Thus also the Sacraments are, by reason of those using them, either those that produce conviction, such as Baptism legitimately administered to infants, or those that confirm, such as Baptism and the Lord's Supper in adults using them legitimately and worthily. Concerning which more must be said elsewhere.

XV. Finally follows intercession, by which Christ the Priest intercedes for us before the Father through his merit and satisfaction. As the sacrificing priest in the O.T. was commanded to intercede for himself and the people: so also our Great High Priest, the Mediator of the N.T., Christ, intercedes for us before the Father willingly and kindly. The intercession of Christ for men is otherwise specified in Scripture as twofold: 1. General, in which way he prayed for all, even for the ungodly and transgressors, according to the words of Isa. 53, v. 12, Luke 23, v. 34; 2. Special, by which he prays only for the obedient, the teachable, and the pious, John ch. 17, v. 11. Such intercession is primarily attended to in this place. It can otherwise comprise certain sub-specified acts, or intercession for spiritual illumination, for its increase, for sealing and confirmation; for the non-imputation of committed debt, or insofar as it is greater, or lesser, etc. Wherefore he is called our Advocate, Rom. 8, v. 34, 1 John 2, v. 1, 2.

XVI. As regards the use of the other, secondly, it can consist: 1. In due thanksgiving, by acknowledging the mercy, kindness, and charity of God the Father and his only-begotten Son, Christ, in that the latter willed to be himself the λύτρον in our place and to pay it, and the former most willingly willed to acknowledge it as most sufficient. 2. In seriously detesting and not committing sins, by which the λύτρον is repudiated. 3. In using it against temptation and insults of any kind, whether of our common enemy the Devil, of death, and of sin; or against the denial of the truth of redemption: against diffidence concerning its sufficiency: against doubt concerning its universality and singularity.

XVII. Finally, it is pleasing to subjoin the abuse, thirdly, which pertains: 1. To the Photinians, who deny that Christ truly offered himself as a holy victim to the Father on the altar of the cross to expiate our sins, and who also profess that Christ by his death only left us an example, and that it is fitting and necessary that we also, necessity so requiring, attest the doctrine of faith by death, against the express words of Scripture. Rom. 4, v. 25, Rom. 5, v. 8, 9, 1 Pet. 2, v. 21, 24, 1 Cor. 15, v. 3, Rom. 5, v. 6, ch. 4, v. last, 1 John 2, v. 2, ch. 4, v. 10, Isa. 53, v. 3, 4, 5, 6, 2 Cor. 5, v. 21, Gal. 3, v. 13, etc.

2. To the Papists, 1. denying that Christ is Mediator according to both natures. See Bellarmine, book 4, on Christ, ch. 1, against the assertion proved above, and the rule of the Church: The names of the office belong to CHRIST according to both natures. 2. To those who, by their flagellations, masses, and good works, render the merit of CHRIST insufficient, against the stated passages of Isaiah 63:3, Revelation 19:15, 1 John 1:8. 3. To those contending that CHRIST earned something for himself by this passion and death. See Bellarmine, book 5, on CHRIST the Mediator, ch. 9, against Scripture, which asserts that the λόγον was incarnate for our sake, Isaiah 9:6, and against the clear 53rd chapter of Isaiah, in which verse 5, the cause and fruit of the passion and death of Christ is ascribed solely to us. Regarding the passage Philippians 2:9, see Pareus, Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, ch. 8, dub. 9, Frankfurt edition, 1608, col. 794, letter A. The Apostle teaches not the meritorious cause of glory, but the order and way to glory. 4. To those who offer Christ daily in the sacrifice of the Mass, albeit bloodlessly, against Scripture, especially since the New Testament does not allow for such a prefiguration or others: 5. To those who invoke the holy Fathers, and especially the Blessed Mary, as intercessors, against the stated passages of Isaiah 63:15, Deuteronomy 6:13, Matthew 4:11, Revelation 19:10, 1 Timothy 2:5, 1 John 2:2.

3. To the Calvinists, some of whom openly confess that CHRIST died only for the elect, not at the same time for the damned, not even according to the will or counsel of GOD, as may be read in Beza, in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, Tübingen edition, 1594, page 514, saying in the Antitheses: Certainly your statement has seemed intolerable to us, that CHRIST died for the damned. Likewise in the Response to the acts of the Colloquy, part 2, p. 221: I say again, and I profess before the whole Church of GOD, that it is false, blasphemous, and impious to say that CHRIST, whether regarding the effect or not, suffered, was crucified, died, and made satisfaction for the sins of the damned and those adjudged to eternal judgment, no less than for the sins of Peter, Paul, and all the Saints.

Some, by framing their language differently, as if agreeing with us, say that Christ died for all, namely as regards sufficiency. But not as regards efficacy. Which distinction the Scholastics used (see the Rev. and Illustrious Mr. President, disp. 13, q. 1, S. Anthrop.), understanding by the sufficiency of merit the act of redemption itself and the acquisition of salvation, but by efficacy the application of merit and the bestowal of the acquired salvation, so that the sense is that Christ indeed redeemed all men and each one by that very act, according to the counsel of God the Father, and restored life: because most persist in impenitence, it happens that not all perceive the efficacy of the merit and are saved, but only the elect. Thus, therefore, they refer the cause of the inefficacy to the incredulity of men, not to some absolute decree or good pleasure of GOD. The Calvinists, however, by the sufficiency of merit, wish to denote not the act of redemption itself, but only the potentiality, writing that CHRIST indeed could have satisfied for the sins of the whole world, but did not satisfy in the act itself, because it so pleased GOD the Father from eternity.

Beza openly sets forth this explanation in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, Tubingen edition, 1594, p. 548, at the end, where he says: I confess that the death of CHRIST could have sufficed for the sins even of the damned, if GOD had wished to benefit them.

Bucan gives his vote to this, Loc. 23, q. 20, Geneva edition, 1617, p. 226. Likewise Loc. 36, q. 23, p. 396: If you look at the power of the blood of CHRIST, it suffices for the redemption of all: but if you look at the eternal purpose and counsel of GOD, and the will of the Mediator, He died for the elect alone. Likewise Keckermann, lib. 3, system. Theol. c. 4, con. 1, who says thus: Just as the Prophetic office, so also the Priestly pertains to the elect alone, for Christ wished to satisfy only for the sins of these.

Therefore these men, distinguishing between sufficiency and efficacy, change not their mind but their tooth, not their spirit but their pen, agreeing openly with the rest in foundation and sense.

Pareus seems to depart from his associates regarding this question, while in Explicat: Catech. Ursin. Heidelberg edition, 1612, q. 20, num. 3, p. 258, he says thus: He (Christ) died for all, by the merit and sufficiency of the λύτρου, for believers only by application and efficacy. Likewise Comment, in Epist. ad Hebr. c. 9, v. 28, Heidelberg edition, 1613, col. 466, lit. D, πολλῶν of many: Is it not of all? He is said to have died for all. That He gave Himself for all, regards the effect of the offering of Christ, which, although it is proposed to all, does not however reach all, because many by their own infidelity reject the offering of Christ, and render it void for themselves. Hence it happens (it is added immediately) that the sins of not all, but of many, that is, only of believers, are taken away by the offering of Christ: In that sense it is also said in Rom. 5, v. 19, that many are justified by the obedience of Christ. If Pareus speaks from the heart, intending an explanation concerning the Scholastic distinction placed before, does he either openly repudiate the absolute decree of the damned, or is he inconsistent with himself?

Scripture, meanwhile, abundantly proves that Christ died for all the sins of all men. Inasmuch as, to touch upon at least a few, 1. Isa. 53. v. 6. from which we gather thus: Whoever have wandered like sheep, the iniquities of those the θεάνθρωπος, the Son of God, Christ, bore, having been laid upon Him by the Father. And yet not only the elect, but also the damned, and thus all men, have wandered like sheep. Therefore, Christ bore the iniquities not only of the elect, but also of the damned, and thus of all men, which were laid upon Him by the Father. That Calvinists say the Prophet speaks only of his own hearers cannot be borne by the evidence of the text. Furthermore, even if it were granted, it would not immediately follow that all and singular were reborn, or rather, were elect.

2. From Rom. 5. v. 18. 19. As far as condemnation extends, so far does the justification of life extend. And yet condemnation extends to all men who are not elect. Therefore, so does the justification of life. The consequence of the major premise is evident in v. 18 itself, and is plain from the comparison of v. 18 with v. 19, indeed the whole chapter. 3. From Matthew 18. v. 11. Luke 19. v. 10. Whatever had perished, Christ came to save that. And yet not only the elect, but all men had perished. Therefore, Christ came to save all men. 4. From 1 John 2. v. 2. Whoever is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world, he redeems not only some, as the elect, but all men by His death. And yet Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world. Therefore, He redeemed not only some elect, but all men by His death. Note in this saying: 1. the distribution, 2. the expression 'whole world'. Nowhere in Holy Scripture does the word 'world' denote only the elect, much less 'the whole world'. See 2. Corinthians 5. v. 14, 15. Colossians 1. v. 20. 1. Timothy 2. v. 6. ch. 4. v. 10. Titus 2. v. 16. Specifically, the satisfaction of Christ for the damned is proved 1. from Hebrews 6. v. 4, 5. & 6. where some who are damned are declared to have been once enlightened and partakers of the Holy Spirit, which could not have happened if Christ had not died for them. For application and collation always presuppose acquisition. The word 'recrucify' also deserves special observation. How could they recrucify Christ if His crucifixion had pertained to them in no way? 2. From chapter 10. v. 26, 27. etc. we gather thus: Sinners against the Holy Spirit trample underfoot the Son of God and the blood of the covenant by which they were sanctified. Sinners against the Holy Spirit are damned. Therefore, some who are damned were sanctified by the blood of the covenant. And, indeed, unless the Calvinists concede that He died for the most wicked sinners They find it necessary to deny the sin against the Holy Spirit entirely. See the Rev. & Most Illustrious Mr. President, disp. 13, q. 1, S. Antrop. on the statement of 2 Pet. 2, v. 1. 3. John 15, v. 1 & 2, CHRIST says: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman, every branch in Me not bearing fruit, he will take it away. By this statement it is clearly hinted that some can be damned who were true and genuine branches, who were grafted into Christ. As to what they infer concerning Pharaoh and others actually damned before the passion of Christ, that the death and satisfaction of CHRIST did not profit them, I respond: Although it cannot profit them to the extent that they are already subject to damnation, since there is no redemption from hell, meanwhile in life they ought not to have neglected the time of grace, in which they could have believed in Christ. Therefore, if Christ had not willed to die for them, then they could not have believed even in their own time, and thus could not be damned on account of unbelief, but would be excusable. For the judicial sentence holds thus: He who does not believe is judged, John 3, v. 18. Otherwise it would follow that neither Abraham and others saved before the satisfaction of CHRIST were saved on account of the merit of Christ, when nevertheless Christ is the only foundation of salvation, 1 Cor. 3, v. 11, Acts 4, v. 12, 15, v. 11, Rom. 4, v. 9, 17, etc. Setting aside some scrupulous and less fruitful questions raised on this matter, it is pleasing to conclude with this epiphonema: CHRIST JESUS, who out of immense mercy and kindness didst willingly desire to offer Thyself in our place and for our sake, a most holy, most perfect, and eternal sacrifice and victim, on the altar of the cross to GOD the Father, bring it about, we beseech Thee, most kindly, that we also, for this ineffable grace, may in turn unceasingly sacrifice to Thee our own offerings, namely praises and thanksgivings, in holiness and righteousness, which Thou wilt most clemently grant to us, who are by nature utterly powerless, through the grace of Thy Holy Spirit, lest by trampling upon Thy blood, shed for the expiation of our sins, we be found ungrateful and experience Thee as an accuser instead of an intercessor, and as a judge instead of a Mediator, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit livest and reignest for ever and ever, Amen.

Latin:

Quamobrem vocatur Sacerdos in aeternum, XIII.

Fructus exinde resultat 1. Liberatio a maledictione legis; 2. Reconciliatio nostri cum Deo; 3. Liberatio a morte et potestate Satanae; 4. Emundatio a peccatis; 5. Acquisitio vitae et justitiae.

XIV. Non minus autem de tali officio Christi sacerdotali est isthaec beneficia applicare. Id quod et sufficienter praestat, dum mittit Spiritum S. qui est auctor fidei, qua Christi meritum et salutaria beneficia applicantur, obsignantur, confirmantur, per verbum et Sacramenta, quae sunt media, quibus Spiritus S. vult esse efficax.

Nam fides est ex auditu verbi divini Sic et Sacramenta sunt ratione utentium vel conferentia fidem, ut Baptismus legitimè administratus infantibus, vel confirmantia, ut Baptism9 & Cœna Domini in legitime digneq́; usurpantibus adultis. De quibus alibi pluribus dicendum est.

XV. Sequitur tandem intercessio, quâ Christus Sacerdos pro nobis interpellat apud Patrem per meritum & satisfactionem suam. Ut Sacerdos sacrificans in V. T. pro se & populo intercedere jussus erat: Sic & Pontifex noster Magnus, Mediator N. T. Christus pro nobis apud Patrem sponte & benignè intercedit. Intercessio aliàs Christi pro hominibus duplex specificatur in Scriptura, 1. Generalis, quô pactô pro omnibus, etiam pro impiis & transgressoribus, juxta dicta Esa. 53. v. 12. Luc. 23, v. 34. oravit; 2. Specialis, quâ tantùm pro obedientibus, docilibus, & piis orat Joh. c. 17. v. 11. Qualis intercessio hôc locô potissimùm attenditur. Potest aliàs subspecificatos actûs aliqvos comprehendere, vel intercessionem pro illuminatione spirituali, pro ejus augmento, pro obsignatione & confirmatione; pro non imputatione indebiti commissi, vel qvatantenus majoris, vel minoris &c. Qvapropter vocatur Advocatus noster, Rom. 8. v. 34. 1. Joh. 2. v. 1, 2.

XVI. Usum alterius secundò qvod spectat, consistere potest 1. In debitâ gratitudine, Dei Patris, ejusq́; Filii unigeniti, Christi, agnoscendo misericordiam, benignitatem, charitatemq́;, Qvòd HIC nostri loco λύτρον esse ipsemet, & solvere, ILLE lubentissimè acceptando sufficientissimum agnoscere voluit. 2. In seriò detestando & non committendo peccata, qvibus λύτρον repudiatur. 3. In usurpando contra cujuscunq; generis tentationem & insultûs, vel hostis nostri communis Diaboli, mortis, & peccati; vel contra negationem de veritate redemptionis: contra diffidentiam de sufficientia: contra dubitationẽ de universalitate & singularitate.

XVII. Abusum deniq; tertiò subjungere lubet, qvi competit 1. Photinianis, Christum reverà pro peccatis nostris expiandis se victimam sanctam in ara crucis obtulisse Patri negantibus, nec non profitentibus, Christum suâ morte credentib9 nobis tantùm exemplum reliqvisse, etiam morte, necessitate ita reqvirente, doctrinam fidei contestari convenire ac debere, Contra expressa Scripturæ dicta. Rom. 4. v. 25. Rom. 5. v. 8, 9. 1. Petr. 2. v. 21, 24. 1. Cor. 15. v. 3. Rom. 5. v. 6. c. 4. v. ult. 1. Joh. 2. v. 2. 6. 4. v. 10. Esa. 53. v. 3, 4, 5, 6. 2. Cor. 5. v. 21. Gal. 3. v. 13. &c.

2. Pontificiis, 1. negantibus, Christum esse Mediatorem secundùm utramq; naturam. Vide Bellarminum lib. 4. de Christo c. 1. contra assertionem supra probatam, & Ecclesiæ regulam: Nomina officii competunt CHRISTO secundùm utramq; naturam. 2. Suis flagellationibus, missis, bonis operibus, CHRISTI meritum insufficiens reddentibus, contra dicta Esa. 63. v. 3. Apocal. 19. v. 15. 1. Johan. 1. v. 8. 3. Contendentibus, CHRISTUM sibi aliqvid istâ passione & morte promeruisse. Vid. Bellarmin. lib. 5. de CHRISTO Mediatore c. 9. contra Scripturam, λόγον propter nos incarnatum esse, Esa. 9. v. 6. asserentem, contra clarum Esa. 53. cap. in qvo v. 5. Causa & fructus passionis & mortis Christi unicè nobis adscribitur. Dictum Phil. 2. v. 9. quod attinet. R. Par. Comment. in Epist. ad Rom. c. 8. dub. 9. Edit. Francof. 1608. col. 794. lit. A. Apostolus non causam meritoriam gloriæ, sed ordinem & viam ad gloriam docet. 4. Sacrificio Missæ Christum qvotidiè offerentibus, licet incruentè, contra Scripturam, præsertim cùm N. T. præfigurationem talem & alias non patiatur: S. Sanctos Patres, & imprimis S. Mariam, intercessores invocantibus, contra dicta Esa. 63. v. 15. Deut. 6. v. 13. Matth. 4. v. 11. Apoc. 19. v. 10. 1. Tim. 2. v. 5. 1. Joh. 2. v. 2.

3. Calvinianis, qvorum qvidam apertè fatentur, CHRISTUM tantum pro electis, non insimul pro damnatis, ne quidem quoad voluntatem aut consilium DEI, mortuum esse, ut legere est apud Bezam, in Colloq. Mompelg. Edit. Tubing. 1594. pag. 514. inqvient. in Anthithes. Certè nobis intolerabilis vox vestra visa est, CHRISTUM esse mortuum pro damnatis. Item in Resp. ad acta Colloq. part. 2. p. 221. Iterum dico, & coram tota Ecclesia DEI profiteor, falsum, blasphemum, impium esse, dicere, CHRISTUM, sive quoad effectum, non minus pro damnandorum, & æterno judicio adjudicandorum peccatis passum, crucifixum, mortuum esse, & satisfecisse, qxàm pro peccatis Petri, Pauli, & omnium Sanctorum.

Qvidam linguam aliter informando, nobiscú qvasi consentientes, dicunt, Christum pro omnibus esse mortuum, scilicet qvoad sufficientiam. Sed non qvoad efficaciam. Qvam distinctionē usurpârunt Scholastici, (vide Rev. & Clar. Dn. Præs. disp. 13. q. 1. S. Anthrop.) per meriti sufficientiam ipsam redemptionis actum & salutis acqvisitionē, per efficentiā verò applicationē meriti & collationem salutis acqvisitæ, intelligentes, ut sensus sit, Christum qvidem homines universos & singulos actu ipsô, juxta consilium Dei Patris, redemisse, & vitam reparâsse: Qvia verò pleriq; in impoenitentia perseverant, hinc fieri, ut efficaciam meriti non omnes persentiscant, & salventur, sed tantùm electi. Sic ergò causam inefficaciæ referunt in hominum incredulitatem, non in absolutum qvoddam DEI decretum aut beneplacitum. Calviniani autem per sufficientiam meriti non ipsum redemptionis actum, sed potentiam tantùm notatam volunt, scribentes, CHRISTUM qvidem potuisse satisfacere pro peccatis totius mundi, sed non satisfecisse ipso actu, qvia DEO Patri ab æterno ita placuerit.

Qvam explicationem apertè ponit Beza in Colloqvio Mompelg. edit. Tubing. 1594. p. 548. in fin. iu qviens: Fateor, mortem CHRISTI potuisse sufficere pro peccatis etiam damnatorum, si DEUS voluisset illis prodesse.

Cui suffragium dat Bncan. Loc. 23. q. 20. Edit. Gen. 1617. p. 226. Item Loc. 36. q. 23. p. 396. Si vim sanguinis CHRISTI respicias, ad redemptionem omnium sufficit: Si verò propositum consiliumq́, DEI æternum, voluntatemq́, Mediatoris intuearis, pro solis electis mortuus est. Item Kecher. lib. 3. system. Theol. c. 4. con. 1. qvi ita ait: Ut officium Propheticum, ita etiam Sacerdotale pertinet ad solos electos, Nam pro horum peccatis tantùm Christus satisfacere voluit.

Mutant itaq; isthi, inter sufficientiam & efficientiam distinguentes, non mentem, sed dentem, non animum, sed calamum, cum reliqvis apertè fatentibus in fnndamento & sensu convenientes.

Pareus videtur à sociis discessum facere, qvoad hoc qvæsitum, dum in Explicat: Catech. Ursin. edit. Heidelb. 1612. q. 20. num. 3. p. 258. ita inqvit: Est mortuus (Christus) pro omnibus, meritô & sufficientiâ λύτρου, pro solis credentibus applicatione & efficaciâ. Item Comment, in Epist. ad Hebr. c. 9. v. 28. edit. Heidelb. 1613. col. 466. lit. D. πολλῶν multorum: An non omnium? Dicitur mortuus pro omnibus. Dedisse se pro omnibus, Effectum spectat oblationis Christi, qvi, licet omnibus propositus sit, non omnibus tamen obtingit, quia multi infidelitate suâ oblationem Christi respuant, sibiq́, irritam reddunt. Hinc sit (subnectitur statim) ut non omnium, sed multorum, hoc est, tantùm credentium peccata Christi oblatione tollantur: Eô sensu etiam dicitur Rom. 5. v. 19. Christi obedientiâ justificari multos. Qvod, si ex animo loqvatur Pareus, intendens explicationem circa distinctionem Scholastic. ante positam, vel coram repudiat decretum absolutum damnatorum, vel sibi non constat?

Scriptura interim, Christum pro omnibus omnium hominum peccatis mortuum esse, abundè comprobat. Utpote, ut saltem pauca attingamus, 1. Esa. 53. v. 6. ex quo ita colligimns: Qvicunq; ut oves errârunt, istorum iniquitates θεάνθρωπος, filius DEI, Christus, sibi à Patre impositas portavit. Atqvi non solùm electi, sed etiam damnati, & ita omnes homines, ut oves errârunt. Ergò non solûm electorum, sed etiam damnatorum, & ita omnium hominum iniquitates Christus à Patre sibi impositas portavit. Qvod Calvin. Prophetam de suis tantùm auditoribus loqvi, dicunt, non potest textûs evidentia ferre. Deinde, si maximè concederetur, non tamen statim seqveretur, omnes & singulos renatos, imô potius electos, fuisse.

2. Ex Rom. 5. v. 18. 19. Qvousq; se extendit condemnatio, eo usq; se extendit justificatio vitæ. Atqvi condemnatio se extendit ad omnes, qvi non sunt electi, homines. E. & justificatio vitæ. Majoris conseq. constat in ipso v. 18. tum plana est ex collatione v. 18. cum v. 19. imò totô cap. 3. Ex Matthæi 18. v. 11. Luc. 19, v. 10. Qvodcunq; perierat, ad illud servandum Christus venit. Atqvi non tantùm electi, sed omnes homines perierant. E. ad omnes homines servandos Christus venit. 4. Ex 1. Johan. 2. v. 2. Qvicunq; pro totius mundi peccatis propitiatio est, iste non aliqvos tantùm, ut electos, sed omnes homines suâ morte redemit. Atqvi Christus pro totius mundi peccatis propitiatio est. E. non aliqvos tantùm electos, sed omnes homines suâ morte redemit. Not. in hoc dict. 1. distributio, 2. expressio totius mundi. Nuspiam in Scripturâ S. vocabulum mundus, solos electos denotat, multò minùs totus mundus. Vid. 2. Corinth. 5. v. 14, 15. Coloss. 1. v. 20. 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. c. 4. v. 10. Tit. 2. v. 16. In specie, Satisfactio Christi pro damnatis probatur 1. ex Hebr. 6. v. 4, 5. & 6. ubi nonnulli, qvi damnantur, aliqvando illuminati & participes Spiritus S., prædicantur, qvod fieri non potuisset, si Christus pro iis non esset mortuus. Nam applicatio & collatio semper præsupponit acqvisitionem. Peculiarem etiam observationem meretur vocabulum recrucifigunt. Qvomodo recrucifigere possent Christum, si crucifixio hujus nihil eos attinuisset. 2. Ex cap. 10. v. 26, 27. &c. ita colligimus: Peccatores in Spiritum S. conculcant Filium DEI, & sanguinem fæderis, per, qvem fuerunt sanctificati. Peccatores in Spiritum S. damnantur. Ergò qvidam, qvi damnantur, sanguine fæderis fuerunt sanctificati. Et, sanè, nisi Calviniani concesserint, pro scelestissimis peccatoribus esse mortuum Peccatum in Spiritum S.penitus negare necesse habent. Vide Rev. & Clariss. Dn.Præs. disp.13.q.1. S. Antrop.de dicto 2.Petr.2.v.1. 3. Joh.15.v.1.& 2. inquit CHRISTUS: Ego sum vitis vera,& Pater meus agricola,omnem palmitem in Me non ferentem fructum,tollet eum. Qvô dictô luculenter innuitur, posse aliqvos damnari, qvi fuerunt veri & genuini palmites,qvi Christo insiti.Qvod inferunt dePharaone,& aliis anteChristi passionem actu damnatis, illis mortem & satisfactionem CHRISTI non prodesse,Resp. Licet eatenus,qvatenus jam ipsi damnationi subjecti sunt, eis prodesse neqveat, siqvidem ex inferno nulla redemtio, interim in vita tempus gratiæ, qvo in Christum credere potuissent, negligere non debuissent. Proinde,si Christus pro iis mori noluisset, tum etiam nec suo tempore credere, atq; sic propter incredulitatem damnari non potuissent,sed excusabiles forent. Nam sententia judicialis sic habet: Qvi non credit,judicatus est,Joh.3.v.18.Sic aliàs seqveretur,nec Abrahamum & alios salvatos ante CHRISTI satisfactionem, propter Christi meritum salvari,cùm tamen Christus unicum fundamentum salutis sit 1.Cor 3. v.11. Act.4. v.12. 6.15.v.11. Rom.4.v.9,17,&c. Sepositis nonnullis scrupulosis, minusq́; frugiferis qvæstionibus hâc de materiâ motis,isthôc Epiphonemate concludere placet: CHRISTE JESU, qvi nostri locô & gratiâ teipsum, hostiam & victinam Sanctissimam, perfectissimam, & æternam, in ara crucis DEO Patri offerre,ex immensa misericordia & benignitate ultrò voluisti, effice,qvæsumus,perbenignè, qvò & nos pro ineffabili isthâc gratiâ tibi vicissim nostras hostias,laudes scilicet,& gratiarum actiones, in sanctitate & justitia,qvam per Spiritus tui Sancti gratiam nobis à natura penitùs impotentib⁹ clementissimè concedes, indefinentur immolemus, ne sangvinem tuum, pro peccatis nostris expiandis effusum, nostris peccatis conculcando,ingrati reperti, ex intercessore accusatorem,ex Mediatore judicem te experiamur, qvi cum Patre & Spiritu S. vivis & regnas in seculorum secula, Amen.


## 49 Forty-ninth Disputation. On the Regal Office of Christ

With God. Preface.

Just as Ahasuerus, a king otherwise most powerful, chose for himself a bride, Esther, from a certain lower family, and loved her above all women, Esth. 2:17. So the King of kings and Lord of lords, Christ Jesus, out of mere mercy betrothed us wretched little men to himself, Hos. 2:19; whom he not only loves as a most beautiful bridegroom, but also protects, governs, and defends with a certain spiritual scepter and rule. Deservedly, therefore, the prophet Zechariah, announcing joy, addresses the Church in these words, Zech. 9:9: Rejoice, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation. Let us not only rejoice, but let us also eagerly gaze upon the adornment and splendor of our Bridegroom and King. For the most wise Solomon wisely says of that heavenly Solomon, Cant. 3:11: Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals. Wherefore it will also be our part to go forth to meet this King, and to acknowledge, gaze upon, and receive him. How this can and ought to be done will appear more clearly from the doctrine concerning the kingly office of Christ, which we shall describe in this present disputation. But lest we seem to act without method, 1. we shall demonstrate from the Holy Scriptures that our Savior Jesus Christ is King; 2. we shall proceed to the doctrine concerning the Kingdom of CHRIST; 3. we shall treat the more illustrious questions that are wont to be raised concerning this article; and 4. finally, we shall briefly subjoin a practical meditation. Do thou, O God-Man King, only favor our undertakings, so that all our words and thoughts may yield to the glory of thy name and kingdom, and to our edification!

Thesis I.

The office of Christ the King is (that we may begin from the definition) that by which he gathers his citizens through the ministry of the Word until the end of the world, and, having adorned them with excellent gifts, defends them bravely against the enemies in whose midst they rule, and finally crowns them with eternal glory and honor. See Hassenreff. in Loc. Theol. p. 353. Or, that we may comprehend many things in few, the kingly office of CHRIST is that by which he himself governs all things, in heaven and on earth, and especially the Church. Gerhard, vol. 1, Locor. Theol. p. 282.

II. The truth, therefore, of these and similar definitions, so that it may become more manifest, the royal dignity of Christ must be proven immediately at the very threshold from the Holy Scripture. Where first certain passages taken from the O. T., 2. We shall diligently note some titles by which the Savior is ennobled in the N. T.

III. Therefore, as regards the testimony of the Old Testament, we produce here Ps. 2 v. 6, where the Lord speaks thus: I have set my King upon my holy hill of Sion, which King is a little later said to be the son TODAY, i.e., begotten from eternity. That this entire Psalm treats in its proper and literal sense of our Redeemer, not only all the circumstances of the text, but also the Apostolic interpretation in the N. T. evidently and irrefragably convinces. The same Messiah is declared King more broadly and abundantly in Ps. 8.

IV. To this pertains Ps. 45 v. 2 & 7. I speak my works to the KING, thy throne O God is for ever and ever, the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of thy kingdom. To this, Ps. 72 can be referred throughout its entire context. And Is. 9 v. 7 it is read: The government is upon his shoulder, Prince of peace, his empire shall be multiplied, and of peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom he shall sit, to confirm it, and to strengthen it in judgment, etc. Jer. 23 v. 6. Behold the days come, saith the Lord, and I will raise unto David a righteous branch, and a King shall reign, and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.

V. Ezech. 34 v. 23 & 24. I will set up one shepherd over my sheep, and he shall feed them, my servant David, he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. And I the Lord will be their God, and my servant David a Prince in the midst of them. Dan. 2 v. 44. In the days of those kingdoms shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed, and his kingdom shall not be delivered to another people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.

VI. But especially Zechariah c. 9 v. 9 consoles the Church with such a message: Behold thy King cometh unto thee just and a Savior, he is poor and riding upon a colt the foal of an ass, etc., which words are to be understood of Christ, which may clearly shine forth from the collation of Matt. c. 21 v. 5 with the Prophetic text. Thus Hos. 3 v. 5 Christ is called King David, either because he was born from the lineage of David, or because David typically represented the coming Messiah by the magnitude of his bravely and strenuously performed deeds and especially by his royal government of the Israelites. And Mic. 5 v. 2 he is called מוֹשֵׁל a ruler in Israel.

VII. From the New Testament there is no reason why we should curiously search the sacred oracles for this sense, since they are known to almost everyone, such as that which the Magi asked in Jerusalem, Matt. 2, v. 2, where the King of the Jews was born, whose star they had seen in the East, and had come to worship him: That which is held in 1 Cor. 1, v. 25: He must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet: That which John saw written of Christ's name in Rev. 19, v. 16 in these words: King of Kings and Lord of lords; and that which is said in Luke 1, v. 33, He shall reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end.

IIX. Therefore, we constantly assert that our Savior is not only a King, but also more excellent than all kings, a fact which the cited testimonies of Scripture, from which the singular properties of this King simultaneously blossom forth, most evidently testify. Although, however, for the sake of brevity, many properties must be omitted, nevertheless we shall note the principal ones.

IX. For 1. from the preceding praises of Scripture we gather that our King is eternal, whose power shall never cease, Dan. 7, v. 4, whose kingdom shall have no end, Luke 1, v. 33. Therefore, no one shall take his crown: for it is fixed to his head, and cannot be taken away. 2. We see from this that Christ is an ecumenical King, who rules from sea even unto sea, Ps. 72, v. 8, to whom all power has been given in heaven and on earth, Matt. 28, v. 19, and a name above every name, Phil. 2, v. 10, of whom all the prophets testify, Acts 10, v. 43. Whence he is called King over all things, both in this age and in the future, Eph. 1, v. 21, 22, and the head of all principality and power, Col. 2, v. 10. The most illustrious and excellent Lord President, my honorable preceptor and promoter, noted more properties and prerogatives of this King in his Meditations on the Gospels, p. 339, 340, etc.

X. And thus we have demonstrated from the Scriptures so far that JESUS of Nazareth, the son of Mary, is King. Since, however, a king is named from his kingdom, it will be the next step for us to set forth in a few words what kind of kingdom this King has. But at the beginning we warn that because the kingdom of Christ is conducted differently with respect to the whole human race, differently with respect to the Church, differently with respect to this life, and differently with respect to the other, therefore this term is of the number of those which are called ἀφ’ ἑνὸς πρὸς ἕν, and thus it must be declared differently according to the diversity of the mode and form of administration in this kingdom.

XI. The kingdom of Christ is therefore considered either in this life, or in the other. In this life, it is in turn established as twofold, namely, of power and of grace. The kingdom of power is the general empire over all things, namely, the government of heaven and earth, the subjection of all creatures, the dominion in the midst of enemies, who are restrained and repressed by Christ as a most powerful King. Cf. Matt. 28:18; Ps. 8:7-8; Heb. 2:8; Ps. 110:2; Matt. 22:44; Acts 2:35; 1 Cor. 15:25, etc.

XII. The kingdom of grace is the special operation of mercy in the Church, namely, the mission, illumination, and confirmation of Apostles, Evangelists, Pastors, and Teachers; the gathering of the Church by the preaching of the Gospel and the administration of the Sacraments; the regeneration, sanctification, and vivification of believers; the application of His merit; the protection and preservation of the pious in calamities; and their deliverance; and finally, the outpouring of various gifts, concerning which benefits of the kingdom of grace, see Mr. Dr. Gerhard, vol. 1, L. p. 782, 783.

XIII. And although the Church, where this kingdom of Christ flourishes, still militates on earth, yet it is for the most part distinguished by the illustrious name of the kingdom of heaven. Hence, mention of the kingdom of heaven occurs so often throughout the parables that exist in the Gospel history, as can be seen in Matt. 20:1, 22:2, and especially in ch. 13, where this illustrious appellation is repeated more frequently. The reasons for this more distinguished title are recounted by Camer. Part 1, on the kingdom of Christ, ch. 2, q. 3.

XIV. For 1. it is governed and administered in a manner clearly heavenly by God, and indeed is preserved even in the midst of persecutions, so that it has absolutely no conformity with worldly kingdoms. 2. Because the subjects of this kingdom, namely true Christians, despise earthly things and sigh for heavenly things, where the King of glory sits at the right hand of the Father, Col. 3:1-2, where our citizenship (πολίτευμα) is, Phil. 3:20. 3. Because (by metalepsis) in this kingdom of heaven that true kingdom of eternal inheritance is acquired. See other reasons in Bede on the Gospel of Matt. 22, concerning the wedding garment.

XV. From which it is simultaneously understood that the kingdom of Christ can also be considered with respect to the other life. But it will especially be there the kingdom of justice and glory, which will be seen in the resurrection of the dead and the universal judgment of all men, indeed of the reprobate to damnation or eternal ignominy, but of the elect to the promised blessedness, where there is joy without sorrow, rest without labor, dignity without trembling, riches without loss, health without languor, and finally life without death, as pious antiquity speaks.

XVI. From all these things we now firmly conclude that the Messiah is King and has a kingdom. This dignity Christ Jesus did not allow to be snatched away from himself, so much so that even before Pilate, when he stood on the razor's edge, he confessed himself to be King, Matt. 27. v. 11, 12; this confession is designated by the Apostle in 1 Tim. 6. v. 13 as a good one. Wherefore it is necessary that we also constantly defend it, so that at long last we may pass from the kingdom of grace to the kingdom of glory, where we shall see our King face to face without end, together with all the elect.

Latin:

Σὺν Θεῷ. Præloqvium.

QUemadmodum Ahasverus, Rex aliàs potentissimus, ex inferiori qvâdam familiâ sponsam Estheram sibi elegit, eamq́; præ omnibus mulieribus adamavit, Esth. 2. v. 17. Sic Rex Regum & Dominus dominantium, Christus Jesus, nos miseros homunciones ex merâ misericordiâ sibi desponsavit, Os. 2. v. 19; qvos adbuc non tantùm Sponsi instar pulcherrimi diligit, sed etiam spirituali qvôdam sceptro & regimine protegit, gubernat, defendit. Meritò igitur gaudium annuncians Propheta Zach. 9. v. 9. Ecclesiam his verbis alloquitur: Exulta filia Sion, jubila filia Jerusalem: Ecce, Rex tuus venit tibi justus & Salvator. Neq; exultemus tantùm, sed avidè etiam ornatum splendoremq́; Sponsi & Regis nostri intueamur. Sapienter enim Salomon sapientissimus Cant. 3. v. 11. de Salomone illo cœlesti, Egredimini, inqvit, & videte, filiæ Sion, Regem Salomon in diademate, qvô coronavit illum mater sua in die desponsationis illius. Qvocirca nostrarum ctiam partium erit, ut Regi huic obviam procedamus, eumq́; agnoscamus, intueamur, excipiamus. Id qvomodo fieri possit ac debeat, ex doctrinâ de officio Christi regio patebit illustrius, qvod in præsenti hâc disputatione describemus. Ne autem ἀμεθόδως agere videamur, 1. qvidem ex sacris literis Salvatorem nostrum Jesum Christum Regem esse demonstrabimus; 2. Ad doctrinam de Regno CHRISTI progrediemur; Qvæstiones illustriores, qvæ de hôc articulô moveri solent, pertractabimus; & 4. tandem meditationem practicam breviter subjiciemus. Tu modò Rex Homo-Dive cœptis nostris annue, ut omnia dicta & cogitata nostra cedant in nominis ac regni tui gloriam, & nostri ædificationem!

Thesis I.

OFficium Christi Regis est (ut à definitione ordiamur,) qvô cives suos verbi ministeriô usqve ad finem mundi colligit, eosq́ve præclaris donis ornatos, contra hostes, in qvorum medio dominantur, fortiter defendit, ac tandem æternâ gloriâ & honore coronat. Vid. Hassenreff. in Loc. Theol. p. 353. Vel, ut multa paucis comprehendamus, Officium CHRISTI regium illud est, qvô ipse gubernat omnia, in cœlo & in terrâ, & imprimis Ecclesiam. Gerhard. tom. 1. Locor. Theol. p. 282.

II. Harum igitur & consimilium definitionum veritas, ut eò manifestior evadat, regia Christi dignitas in ipso statim limine ex sacro codice probanda erit. Ubi primò loca quædam ex V. T. desumta, 2. Titulos nonnullos, quibus Salvator in N. T. nobilitatur, diligenter annotabimus.

III. Veteris itaque Testamenti suffragium qvod attinet, producimus hîc Ps. 2. v. 6. ubi Dominus ita loqvitur: Ego constitui Regem meum super Sion montem sanctum meum, qvi Rex paulò post dicitur esse filius HODIE, i.e. ab æterno genitus. Qvem Psalmum integrum in sensu proprio & litarali de Redemtore nostro agere, non solùm omnes textus circumstantiæ, sed Apostolica etiam interpretatio in N. T. evidenter & irrefragabiliter convincit. Idem Messias Ps. 8. Rex latiùs atq; uberiùs declaratur.

IV. Huc pertinet Ps. 45. v. 2. & 7. Dico ego opera mea REGI, sedes tua Deus in seculum seculi, virga directionis, virga regni tui. Huc Ps. 72. per totum contextum referri potest. Et Es. 9. v. 7. legitur: Factus est principatus ejus super humerum ejus, Princeps pacis, multiplicabitur ejus imperium, & pacis non erit finis, super solium David, & super regnum ejus sedebit, ut confirmet illud, & corroberet in judicio, &c. Jer. 23. v. 6. Ecce dies veniant, dicit Dominus, & suscitabo Davidi germen justum, & regnabit Rex, & sapiens erit, & faciet judicium & justitiam in terra.

V. Ezech. 34. v. 23. & 24. Ego suscitabo super oves meas pastorem unum, & pascet eas, servum meum David, ipse pascet eas, & erit in pastorem. Ego autem Dominus ero in eis in Deum, & servus meus David Princeps in medio eorum. Dan. 2. v. 44. In diebus regnorum illorum suscitabit Deus cæli regnum, qvod in æternum non dissipabitur, & regnum ej9 populo alteri non tradetur, comminuet autem & consumet universa regna horum, & ipsum stabit in æternum.

VI. Præcipuè verò Zacharias c. 9. v. 9. Ecclesiarn tali consolatur nuncio: Ecce Rex tuus venit tibi justus & Salvator, ipse pauper & ascendens super pullum filiæ asinæ &c. qvæ verba de Christo intelligenda sunt, qvod ex collatione Matth. c. 21. v. 5. cum textu Prophetico perspicuè elucescat. Sic Os. 3. v. 5. Christus Rex David appellatur, vel qvia ex Davidis prosapiâ oriundus fuit, vel qvia David rerum fortiter ac strenuè gestarum magnitudine & regiâ imprimis Israëlitarnm gubernatione venturum Messiam typicè repræsentavit. Et Mich 5. v. 2. מוֹשֵׁל dominator in Israël nuncupatur.

VII. Ex N. Testamento non est, cur in hunc sensum curiosè conqviramus oracula sacra, qvum cuilibet fermè notissima sint, ut, qvòd Magi qværunt Hierosolymis Matth. 2. v. 2. ubi sit natus Rex Judæorum, cujus stellam viderint in Oriente, & venerint adorare eum: Qvòd. 1. Cor. 1. v. 25. habetur: Oportet ipsum regnare donec ponat omnes inimicos sub pedib. ejus: Qvòd Apoc. 19. v. 16. Johannes vidit scriptum Christi nomen his verbis: Rex Regum & Dominus dominantium; & qvòd Luc. 1. v. 33. dicitur, Regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum, & regni ejus non erit finis.

IIX. Proinde Salvatorem nostrum non Regem tantùm, sed Regibus etiam omnibus excellentiorem esse, constanter asserimus, id qvod adducta Scripturæ testimonia, ex qvibus singulares simul Regis hujus proprietates efflorescunt, evidentissimè testantur. Qvamvis autem brevitatis studio plures proprietates omittendæ sint: Tamen præcipuas annotabimus.

IX. Nam 1. ex præcedentibus Scripturæ elogiis Regem nostrum æternum esse colligimus, cujus potestas nunqvam desitura sit, Dan. 7. v. 4. cujus regnum non habeat finem, Luc. 1. v. 33. Nemo ergò coronam ejus tollet: Infixa enim est capiti, atq; auferri neqvit. 2. Videmus hinc, Christum Regem esse œcumenicum, qvi dominetur à mari usq; ad mare, Pf. 72. v. 8. cui data sit omnis potestas in cœlo & terra, Matth. 28. v. 19. & nomen super omne nomen, Phil. 2. v. 10. de qvo omnes Prophetæ testentur, Actor. 10. v. 43. Undi Rex super omnia dicitur, tàm in hoc, qvàm in futuro seculo, Eph. 1. v, 21. 22. & caput omnis principatûs & potestatis, Col: 2. v. 10. Plures Regis hujus proprietates & prærogativas notavit Clariss. & Excell. Dn. Præs. Precept. ac Promot. meus honorandus in meditat. Evang. p. 339. 340. &c.

X. Atq; ita JESUM Nazarenum Mariæ filium Regem esse, ex Scripturis hactenus demonstravimus. Qvum autem Rex à Regno denominetur, proximum erit, ut, qvale regnum Rex iste habeat, paucis subjiciamus. Principiò autem hoc monemus, qvia regnum Christi aliter respectu totius generis humani, aliter respectu Ecclesiæ, aliter respectu hujus, aliter respectu alterius vitæ geritur, ideò hunc terminum ex eorum numero esse, qvæ dicuntur ἀφ’ ἑνὸς πρὸς ἕν, atq; ita pro diversitate modi ac formæ administrationis in hoc regno aliter atqve aliter esse declarandum.

XI. Consideratur ergò regnum Christi vel in hâc vitâ, vel in alterâ. In hâc vitâ vicissim geminum constituitur, potentiæ nimirum, & gratiæ. Regnum potentiæ est generale imperium super omnia, nempè gubernatio cœli & terræ, subjectio omnium creaturarum, dominium in medio inimicorum, qui à Christo tanqvam Rege potentissimo coërcentur ac reprimuntur. Conf. Matth. 28. v. 18. Ps. 8. v. 7. 8. Hebr. 2. v. 8. Ps. 110. v. 2. Matth. 22. v. 44. Act. 2. v. 35. 1. Cor. 15. v. 25. &c.

XII. Gratiæ regnum est specialis operatio misericordiæ in Ecclesiâ, scilicet missio, illuminatio, confirmatio Apostolorum, Evangelistarum, Pastorum, & Doctorum, collectio Ecclesiæ prædicatione Evangelii & dispensatione Sacramentorum, regeneratio, sanctificatio, vivificatio credentium, applicatio sui meriti, protectio & conservatio piorum in calamitatibus, & liberatio, variorum deniq; donorum effusio, de qvibus regni gratiæ beneficiis Vid. Dn. D. Gerhardus tom. 1. L. p. 782. 783.

XIII. Et qvamvis Ecclesia, ubi regnum hoc Christi viget, adhuc in terris militet: Tamen illustri plerumq; regni cœlorum nomine insignitur. Hinc enim toties in parabolis, qvæ in historiâ Evangelicâ extant, passim occurrit mentio regni cœlorum, uti videre est Matth. 20. v. 1. 22. v. 2. præcipuè verò c. 13. ubi illustris hæc appellatio sæpiùs iteratur. Rationes insignioris hujus tituli recenset Camer. 1. Part. de reg. Christi c. 2. q. 3.

XIV. Nam 1. à Deo cœlesti planè modô regitur & administratur, imò in mediis etiam conservatur persecutionibus, ita, ut nihil omnino conformitatis cum regnis mundanis habeat. 2. Qvia subditi hujus regni, veri nimirum Christiani, terrena contemnunt, & superna suspirant, ubi Rex gloriæ sedet ad dexteram Patris, Col. 3. v. 1. 2. ubi πολίτευμα nostrum, Phil. 3. v. 20. 3. Qvia (per metalepsin) in hoc regno cœlorum acqviritur verum illud regnum æternæ hæreditatis. Alias rationes Vid. apud Bed. super Evang. Matth. 22. de veste nupt.

XV. Ex qvibus simul intelligitur, qvòd regnum Christi respectu alterius etiam vitæ considerari qveat. Præcipuè autem ibi erit regnum Justitiæ & gloriæ, qvod conspicietur in mortuorum resuscitatione ac universali judicio omnium hominum, & reproborum qvidem ad damnationem sive ignominiam æternam, electorum verò ad promissam beatitudinem, ubi gaudium sine mœrore, reqvies sine labore, dignitas sine tremore, opes sine amissione, sanitas sine langvore, vita deniq; sine morte, ut pia antiqvitas loqvitur.

XVI. Ex his omnibus jam firmiter concludimus, Messiam Regem esse, & regnum habere. Qvam dignitatem sibi qvoq; Christus Jesus præripinon est passus, adeò, ut etiam coram Pilato, cùm staret in acie novaculæ, se Regem esse confessus sit, Matth. 27. v. 11. 12. confessio hæc ab Apostolo 1. Tim. 6. v. 13. bona indigitatur. Qvocirca nos qvoqve constanter eam tueamur necesse est, ut tandem aliqvando ex regno gratiæ ad regnum gloriæ, ubi Regem nostrum sine fine à facie ad faciem videbimus, cum omnibus electis transeamus.


### XVII. This foundation having therefore been laid, we make an approach to more…

XVII. This foundation having therefore been laid, we make an approach to more illustrious questions. First, however, it is asked concerning the King himself, whether indeed the office of reigning truly and really belongs to him and should be attributed to him according to both natures? Where it must be noted altogether that Christ does not reign only according to his divine nature, but also according to his human nature, which has been placed at the right hand of the Father, and thus, sitting at the right hand of the Father, he reigns at the same time as GOD.

XVIII. But what it is to reign as GOD shines forth more clearly than the midday sun from many testimonies of Scripture. Especially from Ps. 24. v. 1: The earth is the Lord's and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it. Num. 11. v. 23: Is the Lord's hand shortened? Job 11. v. 7, 8: Can you find out the deep things of GOD? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty? It is higher than heaven—what can you do? Deeper than Sheol—what can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea, etc. Ps. 115. v. 3: Our Lord is in the heavens; he does whatever he pleases.

XIX. From these very things Christ and the Apostles borrow their own: Matt. 28: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Now, according to the divine nature, following the undoubted rule of Antiquity, nothing could be given to him; how, therefore, shall we exclude his humanity? To this pertains that passage in Phil. 2. v. 9: Therefore GOD has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of GOD the Father. 1 Pet. 3. v. 22: who is at the right hand of GOD, swallowing up death, so that we might be made heirs of eternal life heirs, having departed into heaven, with Angels, and powers, and mighty works subjected to him.

XX. Just as therefore of old in him, according to the pronouncement of the Apostle, at Col. 1. v. 16, 17. all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers. All things, I say, were created in him and through him, and he is before all, and all things consist in him: so now the whole Christ rules over the Angels once created by him, commands the devils, governs the stars of the heavens; he has the seas, rivers, and all things born from the earth subjected to his feet, the oxen and all the sheep, the beasts of the field, the birds of the air, and the fish of the sea, just as the Psalmist graphically describes this most universal dominion of Christ the θεανθρώπꙋ.

XXI. This dignity arises, however, 1. from that most intimate and ineffable union, by which the λόγος not only admitted, but assumed into the κοινωνίαν of this power and kingdom (which, as λόγος, he had and exercised from eternity) his own flesh, so that now that assumed flesh has been made a participant of that same kingdom, and of the same power, which was the power of the ꙋ λόγꙋ from eternity, and is, and will be his for all eternity. 2. It arises from the session of Christ at the right hand of GOD, concerning which a special disputation was recently instituted. Those who have been accustomed to rise up with a clearly reckless impulse against the majesty truly and really communicated to the flesh of Christ ought indeed to have evaluated these things a little more deeply and accurately. But it is not permitted to treat of these things at greater length at present.

XXII. Therefore, in place of a clearer decision, we append this two-membered conclusion from Orthodox Theologians: 1. That Christ at this present time, according to both natures, by his divine majesty and omnipotence (which the kingdom of grace as well as the kingdom of glory necessarily presupposes) not only rules in the Church, and over the Church, which acknowledges and worships him, but also most powerfully governs all, every, and individual creatures. 2. We assert that this infinite power of reigning belongs to Christ and is to be attributed to him in a different respect. For, insofar as he is God, he has it from eternity with God the Father and the Holy Spirit: Insofar as he is man, he received it by the grace of union, which, as is evident from the preceding, requires this especially, that Christ according to both natures truly present, should administer his kingdom. For if he were to administer it while absent, he would not be anointed with the infinite fullness of divine majesty.

XXIII. Furthermore, a question is usually raised here concerning the earthly and worldly kingdom, whether it is rightly attributed to the Messiah by the Jews? For they once trifled, and still trifle today, that the Messiah would establish such an empire on earth, in which, in this visible theater of the world, having been bravely subdued by force and arms and purged of the infidel dregs, the Jews alone, and those addicted to their religion, would rule in perpetual peace and happiness under Christ, and would abound in an affluence of all earthly things.

XXIV. That this dream of an earthly kingdom of Christ is most dangerous and most pernicious, the example of the Apostles themselves clearly shows, who, once imbued with this κακοδοξία in the school of the Pharisees, could with difficulty root out the seeds of that old error, but often repeated from Acts 1:7: Lord, wilt thou at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? Hence also in Matt. 18:1, a controversy was stirred up by the disciples, who would be the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?

XXV. We, therefore, on the contrary, establish not a worldly or earthly, but a spiritual kingdom of Christ, and we strengthen this opinion of ours first indeed by open testimonies of Scripture, then by the firmest and most solid consequences. As far as the testimonies are concerned, we first derive them from the Old Testament, which predicted the affections of this kingdom as if diametrically opposed to the world.

XXVI. Such is that in Zech. 9:9, where the prophet speaks of the poverty of the future Messiah, and thus most sufficiently refutes this worldly pomp and external splendor of the kingdom of the Jews. 2. That that secular glory and passion, or external contempt, are utterly opposed to each other, is so much in confession that it can almost be felt with the hands. Now, however, it is not the former, but rather the latter that is everywhere announced in the Prophetic books concerning the coming Messiah. See Isa. 53:4, 5, 6; Dan. 9:26. Therefore. 3. Furthermore, if this opinion were true, would not the kingdom of the Messiah have to be circumscribed by the limits of Jewish dominion alone? But now Scripture extends the dominion of the Messiah most widely from sea to sea and even to the ends of the earth. Ps. 72:8. Therefore.

XXVII. Then, the same is clearly gathered from the New Testament, if we listen to CHRIST himself. He indeed, about to be declared an earthly King, went away into a mountain; and with singular zeal declined this external dignity, John 6:15. This he proved more clearly before Pilate, where he says expressly, my kingdom is not of this world, if it were of this world were my kingdom, my ministers would certainly fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from hence; Joh. 18. v. 36. By which words, for establishing the spiritual rule of Christ, nothing could be said more clearly, nothing more illustriously, so that it is deservedly, with the very author of truth as interpreter, most plainly distinguished from worldly governments, Luc. 22. v. 25.

XXIIX. Moreover, this opinion concerning the spiritual kingdom can be strengthened by manifest reasons and consequences.
