For 1. who is ignorant that there is no proportion at all between a political kingdom and a divine and incorruptible person? Now we presuppose from Scripture that the Messiah is not a mere man, but θεάνθρωπον [God-man]. 2. The reason is sought from the annexed eternity. For every earthly empire is worldly, and will perish with the world. Now we acknowledge from the testimonies alleged above that the kingdom of Christ is eternal. You object from 1. Cor. 15. v. 24. The Son, however, will be subjected to God the Father, and will deliver his kingdom to him: Therefore he will not be an eternal King: We answer 1. that this text speaks only of the kingdom of grace; 2. Nor is it to be understood simply concerning this, except as regards the external form and administration. For there the preaching of the word will cease, the administration of the Sacraments will cease. But the kingdom of grace itself will pass into the kingdom of glory, where God will begin to be all in all in the blessed citizens of Christ.

XXIX. In what manner the Son of God himself will also be subjected to the Father, not indeed by laying aside the majesty truly and really communicated to the assumed flesh, but by abandoning only the external administration, by which he gathers the Church to himself in the world, to which he will put an end in the other life, and thus will as it were resign this government to the heavenly Father. Nor can the Hebrew words, Olam and Leolam, detract anything from the absolute eternity of the kingdom of Christ. For it is a fig-leaf and utterly feeble collection: These words sometimes denote a limited duration: Therefore in those places also, where they are used concerning King Christ and his eternal kingdom, they are to be taken limitedly, for a period of longer time. Therefore see the genuine explanation of these little words in Mr. D. Bald. in ref. Cat. Rac. page 138. Gerhard. tom. 1. L. C. s. de æterno Dei Fil. p. 462. 463. Hutt. in Loc. Theol. p. 868. Carmer. part. 1. de regno Christi c. 3. q. 4. p. 52.

XXX. More reasons could be accumulated here for the spiritual kingdom of Christ. But, since the truth of this opinion is partly from most evident and written by the ray of the Sun in the oracles of the Prophets, and is partly declared more abundantly by clear reasons by Mr. D. Cramer in the aforementioned place, we did not wish to do what has already been done here. We proceed, therefore, to other matters. For since we have hitherto denied worldly splendor to Christ, another question immediately arises, namely, whether these things are to be taken so absolutely and simply, or whether Christ is truly to return visibly to earth, and is to reign for at least a thousand years with the saints in various delights of the world? The latter, the Chiliasts or Millenarians, formerly attempted to defend.

XXXI. For these men, when they perceived that a twofold resurrection of men was to be asserted from Apoc. 20, v. 5, seq., said that Christ would return in visible form, that he would divide kingdoms, empires, and all provinces among his followers and disciples, having conquered worldly Kings, and would thus enjoy earthly delights with them for a thousand years, for which reason they were also named Chiliasts, for Χίλιοι signifies a thousand; concerning which error let Augustine be read, lib. 20 de civ. Dei c. 7. Lactantius also persists in the same, lib. 7 inst. c. 24, on the renewal of the world: His words are these: The Son of the highest and greatest God will come to judge the living and the dead, as the Sibyl testifies and says, etc. But he, when he has destroyed injustice and performed the greatest judgment, and has restored to life the just who have been from the beginning, will dwell among men for a thousand years, and will rule them with a most just empire. Thus far Lactantius. Tertullian also championed this dogma in his Apology, and others, as Jerome reports in c. 36 of Ezekiel, and Eusebius in lib. 3 of his history, last chapter.

XXXIII. But truly, whatever the aforementioned Millenarians may bring forward concerning the time of a thousand years, we determine that this error, since it savors of purely carnal thoughts and most manifestly clashes with the analogy of faith, is unworthy of refutation and deserves to be exploded. Nor will the passage of the Apocalypse open a window to this erroneous dogma, provided it be compared with other testimonies of the divine word. For Scripture hints at a double death: one of the soul, which is nothing other than the removal of divine grace through sins; the other of the body, which is the separation of the soul from the body.

XXXIV. To this twofold death corresponds a twofold resurrection: one of the soul, by which we migrate from the state of sin into the state of grace, Rom. 6, v. 4, Eph. 5, v. 14. The other is of the body, which on the last day with the soul again is to be united, either to life, or to everlasting shame, Dan. 12. Which things, according to the norm of Scripture and the analogy of faith, being presupposed, what the pronouncement of Revelation ch. 20, v. 5, 6, suggests, will easily be evident. It promises, namely, blessedness and holiness to all who have a part in the first resurrection, that is, who, grieving seriously over sins committed, constantly apprehend the most precious merit of Jesus CHRIST, the most blessed and most holy Redeemer: In these the second, that is, the eternal death, has no power. Augustine supports this assertion, l. 20 de Civ. Dei c. 7, saying: There are two resurrections, one the first, which is now of souls, which does not permit one to come into the second death: the other the second, which is not now, but is to be at the end of the age: and it is not of souls, but of bodies, which through the final judgment will send some into the second death, others into that Life, which has no death. With these things duly considered, Chiliasm expires completely.

XXXIV. Finally, we could here run out into a wider field of controversies, such as: 1. Whether a monarchical government of the Church ought to be established under one visible head and judge, as the Papists dream in vain? 2. Whether this royal majesty is the most powerful cause for which Christ is named in the Scriptures our Savior, God, the Son of God? which opinion the spirit of the Photinians strives to interpolate not without significant blasphemy. 3. Concerning the amplitude of the kingdom of grace, whether, namely, it extends itself throughout the whole world, where the affirmative could be openly demonstrated from the Apostle at Col. 1, v. 6 and 23. These, I say, and other controversies would have to be examined more fully. But, since questions of this kind for the most part cohere with distinct articles of faith, we shall reserve them either for their own places and times, or for the conflict itself, and we shall append a practical meditation very briefly.

XXXV. This consideration concerning the royal office of CHRIST is profitable, 1. πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, that we may acknowledge, weigh, and venerate the majesty of Christ. For immediately the pious mind is accustomed to ask from Psalm 2, who this Zionite King is by reason of his person, namely, the eternal Son of God, according to the open pronouncement of the heavenly Father: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee. Nor, however, ought the thought to stop here, but because the same Zionite King is commanded to ask for the nations as an inheritance, which, however, in so far as he is God, he possesses from eternity, there is included here also the human We understand the nature of Christ, enriched with that infinite glory and majesty. And in this way let us behold, admire, and venerate our King. 2. Since the kingdom of Christ is spiritual, anyone easily understands that the glory of the subjects is not of the present age, but still lies hidden in secret, etc.

XXXVI. Furthermore, this doctrine is useful πρὸς παράκλησιν (for consolation), whenever the Christian mind, overwhelmed by the densest darkness of persecutions, or indeed seeing everything in the Church, as a kingdom of grace, turned upside down, does not feel the efficacy of Christ reigning: which, however, as it is illuminated by the rays of divine consolation shining forth from the kingdom of glory, can easily dissipate even these little clouds of doubt. For is not Christ, the King of kings, most powerful? Come therefore to this King, you who are burdened, Matt. 11. v. 28.

XXXVII. Thirdly, πρὸς νηστείαν (for fasting), that 1. we may strive for holiness. For just as our King is the holiest of all saints: so let us also be a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, 1 Pet. 2. v. 9. 2. That we may yearn to seek the things above, Col. 3. v. 1, and at no time fail to aspire to the true πολίτευμα (citizenship) Phil. 3. v. 20, or the kingdom prepared for us from the foundation of the world, Matt. 25. v. 34, where, like heavenly and spiritual kings, Apoc. 1. v. 6, we shall carry off the crown of righteousness, 2 Tim. 4. v. 8, and of life, Apoc. 2. v. 10, promised to all the elect, and we shall see the King of glory himself without end, love him without weariness, and finally praise him without exhaustion, Amen.

Latin:

XVII. Hoc igitur jactô fundamentô, ad illustriores qvæstiones accesfum facimus. Primò autem de Rege ipso qværitur, Utrum nimirum regnandi officium secundùm utramq; naturam ipsi verè & realiter competat ac tribuendum sit? Ubi omninò notandum venit, qvòd Christus non regnet tantum modò secundùm divinam, sed etiam secundùm humanam naturam, qvæ collocata estad dexteram Patris, adeoq; sedens ad dexteram Patris, simul regnat, ut DEUS.

XVIII. Quid autem sit, regnare ut DEUS, ex multis Scripturæ testimoniis Sole meridianô clariùs elucet. Præsertim ex Pf. 24. v. 1. Domini est terra & plenitudo ejus, orbis terrarum, & universi, qvi habitant in eo. Num. 11. v. 23. Numqvid manus Domini invalida est, Job. 11. v. 7, 8. Forsitan vestigia DEI comprehendes, & usq; ad perfectum Omnipotentem reperies? Excelsior cœlô est, & qvid facies: Profundior infernô, & unde cognosces? Longior terrâ mensura ejus, & latior mari &c. Pf. 115. v. 3. Dominus noster in cœlo omnia, qvæcunq; voluit, fecit.

XIX. Ex his ipsis Christus & Apostoli sua illa mutuantur: Matth. 28. Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra. Jam secundùm divinam naturam, juxta indubitatam Antiqvitatis regulam, illi dari nihil potuit, qvomodo itaq; humanitatem excludemus? Huc pertinet illud ad Phil. 2. v. 9. Propter qvod DEUS exaltavit illum, & donavit illi nomen, qvod est super omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, cœlestium, terrestrium, inferorum, & omnis lingva confiteatur. qvia Dominus Jesus Christus in gloria est DEI Patris. 1. Pet. 3. v. 22. qvi est in dextera DEI, deglutiens mortem, ut vitæ æternæ hæredes efficeremur, profectus in cœlum, subjectis sibi Angelis, & potestatibus, & virtutibus.

XX. Sicut ergò olim in ipso, juxta pronunciatum Apostoli, ad Col. 1. v. 16, 17. condita sunt universa in cœlo & in terrâ, visibilia, & invisibilia, sive throni, sive dominationes, sive principatus, sive potestates. omnia, inquam, in ipso & per ipsum creata sunt, & ipse est ante omnes, & omnia in ipso constant : ita nunc totus Christus Angelis olim â se conditis dominatur, imperat diabolis, regit sidera cœlorum; maria, flumina, omnes ex terris nascentes res pedibus suis subjectas habet, boves & oves universas, pecora campi, volucres cœli, & pisces maris, sicut universalissimum hoc Christi θεανθρώπꙋ dominium Psaltes graphicè describit.

XXI. Oritur autem hæc dignitas 1. ex arctissimâ & ineffabili illâ unione, quâ λόγος non tantùm admisit, sed adsumsit in κοινωνίαν potentiæ ac regni hujus (quod, ut λόγος, ab æterno habuit & exercuit) carnem suam, ita, ut jam caro illa adsumpta particeps facta sit ejusdē istius regni, ejusdemq; potentiæ, quæ fuit ꙋ λόγꙋ potentia ab æterno, & est, & erit ejusdem in omnem æternitatem. 2. Oritur ex sessione Christi ad dexteram DEI, de quâ nuperè peculiaris instituta fuit disputatio. Quæ sanè paulò profundiùs atq; accuratiùs æstimare debebant, qui adversùs majestatem carni Christi verè ac realiter communicatam temerariô planè impetu insurgere consueverunt. Sed de his impræsentiarum prolixiùs agere non licet.

XXII. Evidentioris itaq; decisionis loco ex Orthodoxis Theologis bimembrem hanc conclusionem annectimus: 1. Christum nunc temporis, secundùm utramq; naturam, divinâ suâ majestate atq; omnipotentiâ (quam regnum gratiæ æqvè ac regnum gloriæ necessariò præsupponit) non tantùm dominari in Ecclesiâ, & super Ecclesiam, quæ ipsum agnoscit, & colit, sed etiam potentissimè gubernare universas, cunctas, & singulas creaturas. 2. Infinitam hanc regnandi potestatem Christo diverso respectu verè ac realiter competere & tribuendam esse, asserimus. Nam, in quantum Deus est, ab æterno illam habet cum Deo Patre & Spiritu Sancto : In quantum homo est, accepit illam ex unionis gratiâ, quæ, uti ex præcedentibus constat, hoc præcipuè reqvirit, ut Christus secundùm utramq; naturam reverà præsens, regnum suum administret. Si enim absens administraret, non infinitâ divinæ majestatis plenitudine inunctus esset.

XXIII. Deinde hîc de regno terreno & mundano moveri solet quæstio, utrum illud rectè à Judæis Messiæ tribuatur? Olim enim nugati sunt, hodieq; nugantur, Messiam tale imperium in terrîs constituturum, qvò in hôc visibili mundi theatro, vi armisq; fortiter subactô & ab infideliâ colluvie repurgato, soli Judæi, & religioni eorum addicti, in pace & felicitate perpetuâ, sub Christo dominaturi sint, & abundaturi rerum omnium terrenarum affluentiâ.

XXIV. Periculosissimum autem & perniciosissimum hoc esse deregno Christi terrestri somnium, ipsorum etiam Apostolorum exemplum evidenter ostendit, qvi semel in Scholâ Pharisæorum hâc xακοδοξίά imbuti, difficulter senè veteris illius erroris semina extirpare potuerunt, sed ex Act. 1. v. 7. plerumq; ingeminârunt: Domine, restituesné hôc tempore regnum Israël? Hinc etiam Matth. 18. v. 1. mota est controversia à discipulis, qvisnam major esset in regno cœlorũ?

XXV. Nos igitur è contrario, non mundanum, aut terrenum, sed spirituale Christi regnum constituimus, atq; hanc sententiam nostram primò qvidem apertis Scripturæ testimoniis, deinde firmissimis ac solidissimis roboramus conseqventiis. Testimonia qvod attinet, initiò qvidem ex Veteri Testamento ea desumimus, qvæ mundo êdiametro qvasi oppositas regni hujus affectiones prædixerunt.

XXVI. Tale est illud Zach. 9. v. 9. ubi propheta de paupertate futuri Messiæ loqvitur, adeóq; mundanam hanc Judæorum pompam externumq; regni splendorem sufficientissimè refutat. 2. Gloriam illam secularem, & passionem, sive contemptum externum, sibi penitus adversari, adeò in confesso est, ut manibus fermè palpari qveat. Jam autem non prius, sed posterius potiùs de venturo Messiâ in libris Propheticis passim enunciatur. Vide Es. 53. v. 4, 5, 6. Dan. 9. v. 26. Ergò. 3. Prætereà, si vera esset hæc opinio, nonne Messiæ regnum Judaicæ tantùm ditionis terminis circumscribendum esset? Jam verò Scriptura Messiæ dominium à mari ad mare & fines usq; terrarum latissimè extendit. Pf. 72. v. 8. Ergò.

XXVII. Deinde, ex Novo Testamento idem perspicuè colligitur, si CHRISTUM ipsum audiamus. Ille sanè, Rex terrenus declarandus, in montem abiit; & singulari studiô externam hanc dignitatem detrectavit, Joh. 6. v. 15. Id qvod coram Pilato clariùs comprobavit, ubi disertè, regnum meum, inqvit, non est de hôc mundo, si ex hoc mundo esset regnum meum, ministri mei utiqve decertarent, ne traderer Judæis. Nunc autem regnum meum de hinc non est; Joh. 18. v. 36. Qvibus verbis, pro spirituali Christi regimine adstruendo, nihil dici potuit clarius, nihil illustrius, ita, ut meritò, vel ipsô veritatis autore interprete, â mundanis gubernationibus planissimê distingvatur, Luc. 22. v. 25.

XXIIX. Manifestis insuper rationibus & conseqventiis hæc de regno spirituali sententia roborari potest. Nam 1. inter regnum Politicum, & personam divinam planè & incorruptibilem, nullam omnino proportionem dari, ecqvis ignorat? Jam Messiam non nudum hominem, sed θεάνθρωπον esse, ex Scripturâ præsupponimus. 2. Ratio ab adjunctâ æternitate petitur. Omne enim terrenum imperium mundanum est, & cum mundo interibit. Jam Christi regnum æternum esse, ex suprà allegatis testimoniis agnoscimus. Obvertis ex 1. Cor. 15. v. 24. Filius tamen subjicietur Deo Patri, eiqve regnum suum tradet: Ergò non erit Rex æternus: Respondemus 1. textum hunc tantùm de regno gratiæ loqvi; 2. Neq; de hôc simpliciter intelligendum esse, nisi qvoad externam formam & administrationem. Cessabit enim ibi verbi prædicatio, cessabit Sacramentorum administratio. Ipsum autem regnum gratiæ in regnum gloriæ transibit, ubi Deus in beatis Christi civibus incipiet esse omnia in omnibus.

XXIX. Qvô pactô ipse etiam Dei Filius Patri subjicietur, non qvidem majestatem adsumtæ carni verè & realiter communicatam deponendo, sed externam tantummodò administrationem, qva in mundo Ecclesiam sibi colligit, deserendo, cui in alterâ vitâ finem imponet, atq; ita hanc gubernationem Patri cœlesti qvasi resignabit. Neq; vocabula Hebræa, Olam & Leolam, absolutæ regni Christi æternitati aliqvid derogare possunt. Ficulnea enim planeq́; elumbis collectio est: Vocabula hæc interdum limitatam denotant durationem: Ergò in iis etiam locis, ubi de Rege Christo, regnoq́; ejus æterno usurpantur, limitatè, pro longioris temporis periodo, accipienda sunt. Genuinam ergò harum vocularum explicationem Vide apud Dn. D. Bald. in ref. Cat. Rac. pag. 138. Gerhard. tom. 1. L. C. s. de æterno Dei Fil. p. 462. 463. Hutt. in Loc. Theol. p. 868. Carmer. part. 1. de regno Christi c. 3. q. 4. p. 52.

XXX. Plures hîc rationes pro regno Christi spitituali cumulari possent. Verùm, cùm opinionis hujus veritas partim ex evidentissimis & Solis radiô scriptis Prophetarum oraculis elucescat, partim à Dn. D. Cramero d. l. perspicuis rationibus uberiùs declaretur, actum hîc agere noluimus. Ad alia igitur progredimur. Qvia enim, mundanum hactenus splendorem Christo denegavimus, alia statim suboritur Qvæstio, Utrum nimirùm hæc ita absolutè & simpliciter accipienda sint, an verò Christus visibiliter in terras rediturus, & per mille saltem annos, cum sanctis in variis mundi deliciis regnaturus sit? Posterius Chiliastæ sive Millenarii olim defendere conati sunt.

XXXI. Hi enim, cùm geminam hominum resurrectionem ex Ap. 20. v. 5. seq. asserendam esse deprehenderent, Christum dixêre in formâ visibili rediturum, regna, imperia, provincias omnes, devictis Regibus mundanis, inter asseclas & discipulos suos divisurum, adeóqve terrenas cum illis delicias captaturum per mille annos, qvam ob causam Chiliastæ etiam nuncupati sunt, Χίλιοι enim mille significat, de qvo errore legatur August. lib. 20. de civ. Dei c. 7. In eodem hæret Lactantius lib. 7. inst. c. 24. de renovat. mundo: Verba ejus hæc sunt: Veniet summi & maximi Dei Filius, ut vivos & mortuos judicet, testante atq; dicente Sibylla &c. Verùm ille, cùm deleverit injustitiam, judiciumq; maximum fecerit, ac justos, qvi à principio fuerint, ad vitam restauraverit, mille annis inter homines versabitur, eosqve justissimo imperio reget. Hactenus Lactantius. Patrocinatus qvoq; est dogmati huic Tertul. Apoll. & Alii, referente Hieronym. in c. 36. Ezech. & Euseb. lib. 3. hist. cap. ult.

XXXIII. Verumenimverò, qvicqvid etiam de mille annorum tempore prædicti proferant Millenarii, nos errorem hunc, qvum planè carnales cogitationes sapiat, & in fidei analogiam manifestissimè impingat, indignũ refutatione, meritoq; explodendum esse, statuimus. Neqve locus Apocalypseos erroneo huic dogmati fenestram aperiet, modò cum aliis verbi divini testimoniis conferatur. Scriptura n. duplicem innuit mortem, alium animæ, qvæ nihil est aliud, qvàm gratiæ divinæ per peccata ablatio; aliam corporis, qvæ est animæ à corpore separatio.

XXXIV. Geminæ huic morti duplex respondet resurrectio, animæ altera, qvâ è statu peccati in statum gratiæ migramus, Rom. 6. v. 4. Eph. 5. v. 14. Altera corporis est, qvod in die novissimo cum anima rursus undri debet, vel ad vitam, vel ignominiam sempiternam, Dan. 12. Qvib9, juxta Scripturæ normam, & fidei analogiam, præsuppositis, qvid pronunciatum Apocalysews c. 20. v. 5, 6. svadet, facilè patebit. Beatitudinem nimirùm & sanctitatem pollicetur omnibus, qvi habent partem in primâ resurrectione, id est, qvi de peccatis admissis seriò dolentes, pretiosissimum Jesu CHRISTI, Redemptoris Beatissimi & Sanctissimi, constanter apprehendunt meritũ: In his secunda, id est, æterna mors, non habet potestatem. Suffragatur assertioni huic August. l. 20. de Civ. Dei c. 7. inqviens. Duæ sunt resurrectiones, una prima, qvæ nunc est animarum, qvæ venire non permittit in mortem secundam : alia secunda, qvæ nunc non est, sed in seculi fine futura est : nec animarum, sed corporum est, qvæ per ultimum judicium alios mittet in secundã mortem, alios in eam Vitam, qvæ non habet mortem. Qvibus probè consideratis, Chiliasmus penitus expirat.

XXXIV, Tandem in latiorem hîc controversiarum campum excurrere possemus, qvales sunt, 1. An Monarchicum Ecclesiæ regimen sub uno visibili capite ac judice constitui debeat, ut frustra somniant Pontificii? 2. An regia hæc majestas potissima causa sit, ob qvam Christus in Scripturis Salvator noster, Deus, Dei Filius nominetur? qvam opinionem Photinianorum spiritus non sine insigni blasphemia interpolare studet. 3. De amplitudine regni gratiæ, utrum nimirum per orbem terrarum universum sese extendat, ubi affirmativa ex Apostolo ad Col. 1. v. 6. & 23. apertè demonstrari posset. Hæ, inqvam, aliæqve controversiæ fusiùs examinandæ essent. Verùm, cùm ejusmodi qvæstiones magna ex parte cum distinctis fidei articulis cohæreant, vel suis locis ac temporibus, vel ipsi etiam conflictui eas reservabimus, & meditationem practicam brevissimè subnectemus.

XXXV. Prodest autem hæc de regio CHRISTI officio consideratio, 1. πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, ut majestatem Christi agnoscamus; expendamus, veneremúr. Statim enim mens pia ex Psal. 2. qværere solet, qvis hic Rex Sionius sit ratione personæ, nimirùm æternus Dei Filius, juxta apertum Patris cœlestis pronunciatum; Filius meus es tu, ego hodiè genui te. Neq; tamen hîc subsistere debet cogitatio, sed qvia idem Rex Sionius gentes in hæreditatem postulare jubetur, qvas tamen, qva tenus Deus, ab æterno possidet, subincludi hîc etiam humanam Christi naturam, infinitâ illâ gloriâ & majestate ditatam intelligim?. Atq; hâc ratione Regem nostrum intueamur, miremur, veneremur. 2. Cùm regnum Christi spirituale sit, quilibet facilè intelligit, quòd gloria subditorum non sit de præsenti seculo, sed adhuc in abscondito lateat &c.

XXXVI. Prodest insuper hæc doctrina πρὸς παράκλησιν, quoties mens Christiana densissimis persecutionum tenebris obruta, imò omnia in Ecclesia, tanquam regno gratiæ, susq; déqve ferri conspiciens, non sentit efficaciam Christi regnantis: Quæ tamen, ut divinæ consolationis radiis ex regno gloriæ effulgentibus illustratur, has etiam dubitationis nubeculas facilè dissipare potest. Nonne enim Rex regum Christus potentissimus est? Venite ergò ad Regem hunc, qvi onerati estis Matth. 11. v. 28.

XXXVII. Tertiò πρὸς νηστείαν, ut 1. sanctitati studeamus. Qvemadmodùm enim Rex noster sanctorum omnium sanctissimus est: Ita nos qvoqve genus electum simus, regale sacerdotium, genus sancta, 1. Petr. 2. v. 9. 2. Ut superna qværere gestiamus, Coloss. 3. v. 1. & ad verum πολίτευμα Philip. 3. v. 20. seu regnum à mundi exordio nobis paratum Matth. 25. v. 34. nullo non tempore adspiremus, ubi Regum cælestium & spiritualium instar Apoc. 1. v. 6. Coronam justitiæ 2. Tim. 4. v. 8. & vitæ Apoc. 2. v. 10. electis omnibus promissam, reportabimus, & ipsum Regem gloriæ sine fine videbimus, sine fastidio amabimus, sine defatigatione deniq; laudabimus, Amen.


### To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 50 Fiftieth and Last Disputation. A Synopsis of the Whole Article on the Person, Life and Office of Christ

The profession of Christianity demands from us a perfect and saving knowledge of Christ, which requires that the tongue of a Christian man know nothing but Christ: both because he is the sole scope of the entire Scripture of the Old and New Testaments; and because the knowledge of Christ is as much more excellent than the knowledge of this world as earthly and heavenly, perishable and eternal things differ. Wherefore, deservedly with Bernard, We establish this higher philosophy of ours to be the knowledge of Jesus and Him crucified. Since we have hitherto examined this knowledge at greater length, it is our pleasure now to repeat the same concisely at the end of this Christological college, and to institute a peaceful discussion concerning it; we shall consider: 1. The Person; 2. The Life; and 3. The Office of Christ.

OF THE PERSON.

TH. I. We deservedly make a beginning from the knowledge of the person, since no one who is ignorant of the person of Christ can appropriately think and determine concerning His office. We do not, however, consider this here by reason of the divine οὐσία, which knowledge is treated in the place concerning God; but by reason of the gracious ὑπόστασις, in respect of which He is σύνθετος, consisting of two natures and one simple ὑπόστασις. And this consideration belongs to this place, and is completed in three parts: 1. The explanation of the natures; 2. The narration of the union; and 3. The exposition of the consequences of the union.

II. The natures must first be explained in general: where we must look at 1. The use of the word nature: Nature is derived from being born, and primarily denotes the generation of those being born, but in a broader sense, it denotes the essence of any thing. For us at present, nature is nothing other than a certain complete substance constituted by its own οὐσία, having in itself the principle of all operations. 2. The number of the natures: In Christ we acknowledge two natures, both in themselves and distinct in their properties; divine and human: whence the θεάνθρωπος, God-Man, exists. 3. The necessary concurrence of both, which was formerly signified by types, indicated by the names of the Messiah, predicted by prophetic oracles, demonstrated by apostolic sayings, confirmed by reasons, and illustrated by similitudes. Which, although they do not agree in all things, nevertheless illustrate to some extent the wonderful concurrence of both natures.

III. Concerning the divine nature of the Λόγος in particular, there are to be noted 1. The heretics who have attacked it. Three classes of these are established: 1. The τῶν ἀνυποστάτων, who deny the existence of Christ before the incarnation; 2. The τῶν ἑτερουσίων, who imagine the nature of Christ not to be consubstantial with the Father; 3. The τῶν ἀνομοίων, who imagine the same essence with the Father, but not the same power and operation. 2. The titles which are attributed to Christ regarding His divinity; some of which are Biblical, as when He is called God, namely σχετικῶς, insofar as it denotes the divine essence limited by a certain character; the Son of GOD, produced from eternity from the simple essence of God the Father; λόγος, which here in a heavenly sense denotes the substantial Word: Certain Ecclesiastical [terms], such as: αὐτόθεος, with respect to temporal production; ὁμοούσιος, to express the same substance with the Father, [though] a distinct ὑπόστασις. 3. The truth of the Divinity. it as proven in the place concerning God. Nevertheless, in abundance, 4. we adduce passages confirming the divinity of Christ: 1. It exists in Gen. 48:15-16, in which is contained the blessing made to Jacob by the uncreated angel. 2. It is read in John 1:1, etc., in which the λόγος is described. 3. It is Christ's own, confirming his existence before Abraham, John 8:58. 4. [It is] Paul's, calling CHRIST absolutely God blessed over all things forever, Rom. 9:5. 4. The necessity of the Divinity, which is evident, 1. from the magnitude of the evil, from which no one could free us except God alone; 2. from the magnitude of the good, which could come to us from no one except also God alone.

IV. Concerning the human nature, which was assumed in time, there are likewise to be considered 1. Heretics, who attacked the humanity with great zeal, and they are 1. Phantasiasts, asserting that CHRIST did not assume a true body, but a phantom; 2. Heterousians, denying that the flesh of Christ is consubstantial with us; 3. Apsychoi, stripping Christ of a human soul; 4. Aphthartodocetae, calling into doubt the truth of his sorrows and passion; 5. Monothelites, denying that there is a human will distinct from the divine. 2. Titles, from which the truth of the human nature is most especially evident. Some of these are abstract, such as: flesh, denoting the whole human nature synecdochically; seed: some are concrete, such as: Man, Son, firstborn, etc. 3. The truth of the human nature, which is established 1. by identity of substance: For he assumed our nature, both as to the whole; whence he is called the seed of the woman, of Abraham, of David, and everywhere, the Son of man: and as to the parts, namely the soul, which Scripture, the end of the incarnation, and the truth of nature prove; and the organic body, which establishes the human nature, which requires determined matter, and the truth of satisfaction. 2. By the property of the nature, and these either of the whole nature, such as, to be created, finite, to live, etc., or of the parts; of the soul, such as, to will, to understand: of the body, such as, to have figure, quantity, circumscription. 3. By the infirmity of both soul and body: Some of these are personal and damnable, which Christ did not assume, because they would have hindered the redemption: certain miserable ones, which Christ assumed along with [us], because they were no impediment to his perfection, knowledge, and grace. But just as the humanity of Christ agrees with us regarding essence, properties, and infirmities; so also it differs, by reason of purity, conception, birth, and personality.

IV. The necessity of his nature is evident from his necessary suffering, the shedding of blood, death, and compassion.

V. These two natures are so personally united that there is one Christ, only one person. One must consider the foundation, parts, and nature of this union. The foundation of the union is the incarnation, concerning which must be noted: 1. The explanation of the word. For the word is ἄγραφος, yet most customary in the Church, and it denotes the act by which the λόγος took up human nature into the unity of his ὑπόστασις, and united it most closely to himself. 2. The proof of the incarnation. In the Old Testament it is predicted as future, Isa. 9:6, Jer. 23:5, Mic. 5:2; in the New Testament it is declared as having happened, John 1:14, Col. 2:9, 1 Tim. 3:16. 3. The determination of the subject. The incarnation is indeed said to be the work of the whole Trinity, truly efficiently and inchoatively: but it belongs to the Son alone, formally and terminatively, who became what he was not, and remained besides what he was. The reasons why it was necessary for the Son to be incarnate are very many and obvious among the orthodox Fathers. But when we say the Son was incarnate, we understand not only the person, but also the divine nature, limited by a certain character. 4. The determination of the time. The incarnation was accomplished in the middle age of the world, according to a reckoning not mathematical, but historical and common, by which everything that lies between the beginning and the end is called the middle. 5. The definition of the incarnation, which is as follows: The incarnation is a divine and supernatural action, by which the eternal Son of God assumed human nature, whole, holy, and formed from the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary, into the unity of his ὑπόστασις, without confusion, and thus became true man, so that he now subsists in two natures, divine and human, personally united.

VI. The parts of the incarnation are two: One, the formation of the flesh, which the angel describes in Luke 1:35. Of this must be examined: 1. The efficient cause, which is the Holy Spirit, to whom the conception is attributed not σπερματικῶς, but δημιουργικῶς, κατ' ἐξοχὴν. 2. The material [cause] in which, is the mother of the Lord, of whom below; Material, from which, which are the parts of man, soul and body, both produced in the womb of Mary; the former without matter, the latter from matter, which by reason of its being present was the σπερματικὴ mass, which the ordinary mode of generation requires; By reason of the virgin, fashioned in the womb of Mary; By reason of quality, most holy, and immune from all sin. 3. Formal, or the mode of production. We seriously maintain that the soul was produced ordinarily and mediately, through the traducian process: the body made ἐν τῷ νῦν and suddenly: the whole humanity conceived in an instant, immediately after the annunciation of the angel, and the assent of the Blessed Virgin, so that thus the soul might be united with the body simultaneously and suddenly. 4. Final, which is our salvation. For as all things are for our sake, so also the conception of Christ was brought about for us, and for our salvation.

VII. The second, the assumption of the flesh. Where it must be explained, 1. Whether it happened? Which the passage in Hebrews 2 proves, where it is predicated of Christ, as the subject, v. 9, that he was made a partaker of flesh and blood, as the children, v. 14, and that he assumed the seed of Abraham, v. 16. 2. Who assumed it? The Λόγος alone, of course, because he alone was incarnate. 3. What was assumed? Flesh, or the Seed of Abraham, or, as the Fathers call it, Human nature. 4. Into what was it assumed? Namely, into the unity of the person of the Son of God. 5. How, whether the body was assumed by means of the soul? Where it must be said, in the assumption of the body and soul there was no order, but they were assumed simultaneously and at once without distinction of time and order into the ὑπόστασιν of the Λόγος. 6. Finally, how long does the assumption last? Which the canon of the Orthodox Fathers explains: What the Λόγος once assumed, he will never lay aside.

IIX. The nature of the union must be examined. Where must be observed, 1. The explanation of the terms, as they are 1. Jesus, which signifies savior, and properly belongs to Christ alone. 2. Christ, which denotes anointed, and is said not of both, but only of the human nature. 3. Person, which is used in that meaning in him, in which it denotes three things: 1. Substance: 2. A simple ὑπόστασιν, consisting of one nature: 3. A composite ὑπόστασιν, subsisting in two natures. 4. Union, which signifies the coupling of several things, by which they become one. 2. The annotation of heretics. There are both ancient ones of them, such as: Ebionites, Cerinthians, Samosatenians, Apollinarians, Nestorians, Eutychians, Μονοφυσίται, ἀκέφαλοι, Μονοθελίται, Accidentarii, Scholastics; and more recent ones, such as: Calvinists, Jesuits, Neo photinians, Vorstians. 3. The position of the thesis of the true personal union. We confess that our Lord Jesus CHRIST, although He is GOD and man, is nevertheless not two, but only one CHRIST, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person. This thesis is confirmed by the sayings of Scripture, the Symbols of the Church, the votes of Councils, and the testimonies of the Fathers.

IX. Communication follows union, which is threefold: 1. ὑποστάσεως; where must be noted 1. The explanation of the term. For the term connotes every participation of one thing. 2. The assertion of personal communication. Calvinists deny this: we affirm it, and prove it by the unity of the ὑποστάσεως of Christ, by the very subsistence of the flesh, by the definition of communication, by the introduction of the absurd, etc. 2. Of the natures, which we assert to be true and real, with the F. C. art. 8. p. 606, and we confirm this by the authority of Scripture, the foundation of the analogy of faith, and Orthodox antiquity. This differs from the personal, 1. In order, by which the former precedes the latter; 2. In the relation of the natures, which in the former case behave more passively, in the latter more actively: For in the former we say that two natures are united: in the latter they are said to communicate with one another. From this arise the predications of the ἑτεροῦ of the natures, called personal, concerning which the Theologian passes judgment, asserts them to be rightly real, and says that in them nature is predicated of nature, as disparate things of disparate things, affirms that they are not to be called paronymous, nor to be reduced to these by way of ἀναλογίας, names them mystical by reason of the union, advises that one should abstain from abstractive ones, because it is safer, and thinks that Christ, as man, is less significantly and ambiguously called the natural Son of GOD. 3. Of the idioms, concerning this in general must be noted 1. The usage of the term. For we judge that the term, Communication of Idioms, although it is ἄγραφος, yet because it was introduced by the necessity of speaking, for firm reasons which we shall give to one requesting them, ought to be retained in the schools for explaining Theological controversies. 2. The explanation of the terms, abstract and concrete. To theologians, the abstract denotes one nature, considered distinctly in the union: but the concrete expresses only the person. 3. The meaning of the Communication of Idioms. For it signifies the mode by which properties are said of Christ through distinct formulas of Scripture. 4. The determination of the genera; of which we acknowledge 3, with the F. C. 5. The reason for the order, which varies for some: but the little dispute is easily composed by a distinction between the order of nature and of doctrine; we have observed the latter.

X. Now, in particular, we must see 1. The genus, which is called ἀλλοίωσις, ἀντίδοσις, ἐναλλαγή, and κοινωνία ὀνομάτων, ἐπίζευξις ὀνομάτων, οἰκείωσις. It is described as that in which the properties of the natures are predicated of the person. This happens in two ways: For either the properties of one or the other nature are predicated of the composite person, the divine on account of the divinity, the human on account of the humanity: or the properties of the assumed humanity are predicated of the uncomposite person λόγῳ. II. The genus is called κοινοποίησις, κοινωνία ἐνεργειῶν, περίφρασις. It is described as that in which a certain ἀποτέλεσμα is attributed to the person, in the producing of which each nature acts, with the communication of the other. The subject in this genus is the whole person, of whom the ἀποτέλεσμα is enunciated in some way reciprocally. The question is raised here, whether death for the life of the world is an ἀποτέλεσμα? This we affirm with the Orthodox.

XI. III. The genus is called the communication of majesty, ἀποθέωσις, θεοποίησις, μεταποίησις, etc., by which not an equalization of natures, but an exaltation of the flesh is expressed. It is described as that in which truly infinite and uncreated gifts, communicated to the flesh by the λόγος through personal union, are enunciated of the human nature. The subject is the human nature, which receives the gifts from the divine. The Calvinists deny that such a communication and exaltation has happened to the flesh: We, for the sake of confirming it, have produced arguments 1. general, from the indwelling of the fullness of the divinity, Coloss. 2. v. 9; from those things given to Christ in time; from the session at the right hand of God. 2. Special, for the demonstration of certain idioms, as for Omnipotence in general we urge the sayings in Matth. 28. v. 18, Ephes. 1. v. 20. In particular for the δυνάμει ζωοποιητικῇ, Joh. 6. v. 48, and c. 1. Johan. 1. v. 3, for the δυνάμει θαυματουργικῇ, Marc. 16. v. 19, 20. Actor. 2. v. 33, c. 10. v. 38, for the power of remitting sins, Matth. 9. v. 6, for the judicial power, Joh. 5. v. 27. For omniscience, Esa. 11. v. 1, Joh. 3. v. 34, Col. 2. v. 3. For gracious presence we bring forward the sayings, Matth. 28. v. 20, Marc. 16. v. 20, Joh. 6. v. 56, arguments from the nature of the head, from the institution of the Supper, from the rule of the Fathers, that the offices of the mediator are appropriate to both natures. For the universal presence of the whole Christ, which denotes present dominion over all creatures in heaven and earth, to be confirmed, we likewise produce the sayings Psal. 71. v. 8, Psal. 110. v. 2, Eph. 1. v. 20, 21, arguments agreeable to the analogy of faith, namely from the personal union, from the ὑποστάσεως τῇ λόγῳ com munication, from the exaltation of human nature to the right hand of God. Concerning the cult of religious adoration, John 5:22, 23; Phil. 2:9, etc.; Apoc. 5:13. Thus far the person of Christ.

Latin:

PErfectam & salutarem Christi cognitionem, à nobis exigit, Christianismi professio, quæ vult, ut hominis Christiani lingva nil aliud noscat nisi Christum: tùm, quia is unicus universæ scripturæ V. & N. T. scopus est; tùm quia Christi notitia tantò præstantior notitiâ hujus mundi, quantò distant res terrenæ & cælestes, caducæ & æternæ. Qvare, meritò cum Bernardo, hanc nostram sublimiorem Philosophiam statuimus, scire Jesum & hunc crucifixum. Qvam scientiam, qvia hactenus fusius lustravimus, jam eandem συντελικῶς sub finem collegii Christologici repetere, deq́; eâ placidam συζήτησιν instituere placet; consideraturi, Christi 1. Personam; 2. Vitam; & 3. Officium.

DE PERSONA.

TH. I. A personæ cognitione meritò initium facimus, cùm nemo, qvi personam Christi ignorat, de officio convenienter sentire & statuere possit. Hanc v. hîc non consideramus ratione ὐσίας divinæ, qvæ cognitio in loco de Deo pertractatur; sed ratione ὑποστάσεως gratiosæ, cujus respectu σύνθετος est, duabus constans naturis, & unâ simplici ὑποστάσει. Et hæc consideratio hujus est loci, ac absolvitur tribus partibus: 1. Naturarum explicatione; 2. Unionis enarratione, & 3. Conseqventium unionis expositione.

II. Naturæ primò in genere explicandæ sunt: ubi videndus 1. Vocis naturæ usus: Dicitur natura à nascendo, & primò nascentium generationem, latiori v. significatione, cujusq; rei essentiam denotat. Nobis in præsentia natura nihil aliud est, qvàm substantia qvædam completa per ὐσίαν suam constituta, habens in se principium omnium operationum. 2. Naturarum numerus: In Christo duas agnoscimus naturas, tùm in se, tùm suis proprietatibus distinctas; divinam & humanam: unde θεάνθρωπος, Homo-Deus existit. 3. Necessarius utriusqve concursus, qvi olim fuit typis significatus, Messiæ nominibus indicatus, Propheticis oraculis prædictus, Apostolicis dictis demonstratus, rationibus confirmatus, & similitudinibus illustratus. Qvæ, licet per omnia non conveniant, mirabilem tamen utriusq; naturæ concursum qvadantenus illustrant.

III. De Divina natura τοῦ Λόγου in specie notanda veniunt 1. Hæretici, qvi eam oppugnârunt. Horum 3. Constituuntur classes: 1. τῶν ἀνυποστάτων, Christi existentiam ante incarnationem negantium; 2. τῶν ἑτερουσίων, Christi naturam patri non consubstantialem fingentium; 3. τῶν ἀνομοίων, eandem cùm patre essentiam, sed non potentiam & operationem, fingentium. 2. Tituli, qvi Christo, qvoad divinitatem, tribuuntur; qvorum qvidam Biblici, ut, cùm dicitur Deus, sc. σχετικῶς, qvatenus essentiam divinam certô charactere limitatam denotat; Filius DEI, ab æterno ex fimplici essentia Dei patris productus; λόγⓓ, qvi hîc significatione cœlesti, λόγον substantialem notat: Qvidam Ecclesiastici, ut : ἀυτόθεⓓ, respectu productionis temporalis; ὁμούσιⓓ, ad eandem cum Patre substantiam, ὑποsasιⓓ distinctam, exprimendam. 3. Divinitatis veritas. Hanc fusiùs hîc non probamus,sed ut probatam in loco de Deo præsupponimus. Ex abundanti tamen 4. loca divinitatem Christi confirmantia, adducimus: 1. Extat Gen. 48. v. 15. 16. in qvo benedictio, Jacobo ab angelo increato facta, continetur. 2. legitur Joh. 1. v. 1. &c. in qvo λόγⓓ describitur. 3. Ipsius Christ us est, suam ante Abrahamum existentiam confirmantis, Joh. 8. v. 58. 4. Pauli, CHRISTUM absolutè Deum super omnia benedictum in secula, nuncupantis, Rom. 8: v. 5. 4. Divinitatis necessitas, qvæ patet, 1. è magnitudine mali, â qvo nos nemo, nisi solus Deus, liberare potuit; 2.è magnit. boni, qvod â nemine, nisi etiam solo Deo, nobis obvenire potuit.

IV. De natura humana, qvæ in tempore assumpta est, consideranda itidem sunt 1. Hæretici, qvi magno studio humanitatem allatrârunt, & sunt 1. φανταςικοὶ, CHRISTUM non verum corpus, sed φανταςικον assumsisse, asserentes; 2. ἑτερόυσιοι, carnam Christi nobis consubstantialem, negantes; 3. ἄψυχοι, Christo animam humanam detrahentes; 4. ἀφθαρδοκήται, dolorum & passionem veritatem in dubium vocantes; 5. μονοθελήται, distinctam voluntatem â divinâ humanam abnuentes. 2. Tituli, ex qvibus vel maximè humanæ naturæ veritas patescit. Horum qvidam abstracti, ut: σαρκὸς, synecdochicè totam humanam naturam denotans; semen: qvidam concreti, ut: Homo, Filius, primogenitus &c. 3. Naturæ humanæ veritas, qvæ astruitur 1. substantiæ identitate: Nam nostram assumsit naturam, & qvoad totum; unde semen mulieris, Abrahæ, Davidis, & passim, Filius hominis dicitur: & qvoad patres, nimirum animam, qvam probat Scriptura, incarnationis finis, naturæ veritas; & corpus organicum, qvod adstruit naturę humanæ, qvæ reqvirit determinatam materiam, & sanctisfactionis, veritas. 2. Naturæ proprietate, easque vel naturæ totius, ut, creatum, finitum esse, vivere &c. vel partium; animæ, ut, velle, intelligere: corporis, ut, figuram, qvantitatem, circumscriptionem habere 3. Infirmitate tàm animæ, qvàm corporis: Harum qvædam sunt personales & damnabiles, qvas Christus non assumsit, quia redemtioni obfuissent: qvædam miserabiles, qvas Christus coassumsit, quia perfectioni, scientiæ, & gratiæ ipsius non erant impedimento. Ut autem humanitas Christi, qvoad essentiam, proprietates, & infirmitates nobiscum convenit; sic qvoqve differt, ratione puritatis, conceptionis, nativitatis, & personalitatis.

IV. Naturæ necessitas, patet, è necessaria passione, sangvinis effusione, morte, & compassione.

V. Hæ duæ naturæ ita personaliter unitæ sunt, ut unus sit Christus, una tantùm persona. Hujus unionis videndum est, fundamentum, partes, & natura. Fundamentum unionis est incarnatio, circa qvam annotanda sunt 1. Vocis explicatio. Nam vox ἄγραφος est, in Ecclesia tamen usitatissima, & notat actum, qvô λόγος humanam naturam in ὑποστάσεως unitatem suscepit, sibiqve arctissimè univit. 2. Incarnationis probatio. In V. Testamento futura prædicitur, Esa. 9. v. 6. Jerem. 23. v. 5. Mich. 5. v. 2. in Nov. Test. facta declaratur, Joh. 1. v. 14. Coloß. 2. v. 9. 1. Tim. 3. v. 16. 3. Subjecti determinatio. Dicitur qvidem incarnatio opus totius Trinitatis, verùm efficienter & inchoativè: Solius verò Filii est, formaliter & terminativè, qvi factus, qvod non erat, & mansit præterea, qvod erat. Rationes, cur filium incarnari oportuerit, apud Patres orthodoxos obviæ sunt plurimæ. Filium autem cùm incarnatum dicimus, non tantùm personam, sed & naturam divinam, certò charactere limitatam, intelligimus. 4. Temporis potatio. Peracta est incarnatio in media mundi ætate, secundùm supputationem, non mathematicam, sed historicam & vulgarem, qvâ omne id dicitur medium, qvod inter Principium & finẽ interjacet. 5. Incarnationis definitio, qvæ talis: Incarnatio est divina & supernaturalis actio, qvâ æternus Dei Filius naturam humanam integrã, sanctam, & ex adumbratione Spiritus S. in utero virginis Mariæ formatam, in unitatem suæ ὑποστάσεως, sine confusione, assumsit, atq; ita verus homo factus est, ut jam in duabus naturis, divinâ & humana, personaliter unitis, subsistat.

VI. Partes incarnationis sunt duæ: Una, Carnis formatio, qvam describit angelus Luc. 1. vers. 35. Hujus dispicienda est, 1. Causa efficiens, qvæ est Spiritus Sanctus cui conceptio non σπερματικῶς, sed δημιουργικῶς, κατ' ἐξοχὴν, attribuitur. 2. Materialis in qva, quæ mater Domini, de qva infra; Materialis ex qua, quæ sunt partes hominis, anima & corpus, utraqve in utero Mariæ producta; illa sine materia, hæc ex materia, quæ ratione inesse fuit massa σπερματικὴ, quam ordinarius generationis modus reqvirit; Ratione virginis in utero Mariæ elaborata; Ratione qvalitatis sanctissima, & ab omni peccato immunis. 3. Formalis seu productionis modus. Animam ordinariè & mediatè, per traducem productam: corpus ἐν τῷ νῦν & subitò factum: totam humanitatem in instanti, statim post annunciationem angeli, & assensum B. Virginis, conceptam seriò statuimus, ut ita simul subitoque uniretur anima cum corpore. 4. Finalis, quæ nostra salus. Ut enim omnia nostri causa, sic qvoqve conceptio Christi propter nos, & nostram salutem facta est.

VII. Altera, Carnis assumtio. Ubi explicandum, 1. An facta sit? quod probat locus Hebr. 2. Ubi de Christo, tanquam subjecto, v. 9. prædicatur, quòd particeps factus sit carnis & sangvinis, ut pueri, v. 14. & quòd assumserit semen Abrahæ, v. 16. 2. Quis assumserit? Solus nimirum Λόγος, quia hic solus incarnatus. 3. Quid assumtum sit? Caro, seu Semen Abrahæ, vel, ut Patres vocant, Humana natura. 4. In quid assumtum sit? Nempe in Filii Dei personæ unitatem. 5. Quomodo, an corpus mediante anima assumtum sit? Ubi dicendum, in assumtione corporis & animæ nullum fuisse ordinem, sed simul & semel sine distinctione temporis & ordinis in ὑπόστασιν Λόγου assumta sunt. 6. Denique, quàm diu duret assumtio? Quod explicat canon Orthodoxorum Patrum: Quod Λόγος semel assumsit, nunquam deponet.

IIX. Naturæ unionis videnda est. Ubi observanda, 1. terminorum explicatio, ut sunt 1. Jesus, qui salvatorem significat, & soli Christo propriè convenit. 2. Christus, qui unctum notat, & non de utraqve, sed humana natura tantùm dicitur. 3. Persona, qui in eo usurpatur significatu, quô tria denotat: 1. Substantiam: 2. Simplicem ὑπόστασιν, unâ naturâ constantem: 3. ὑπόστασιν compositam, in duabus naturis subsistentem. 4. Unio, qui plurium rerum copulationem, quâ illæ unum fiunt, significat. 2. Hæreticorum annotatio. Sunt illorum & Veteres, ut: Ebionitæ, Carinthiani, Samosateniani, Apollinaristæ, Nestoriani, Eutychiani, Μονοφυσίται, ἀκέφαλοι, Μονοθελίται, Accidentarii, Scholastici; & Recentiores, ut: Calviniani, Jesuitæ, NeoPhotiniani, Vorstiani. 3. Theseos veræ unionis personalis positio. Confitemur, Dominum nostrum Jesum CHRISTUM, licet DEUS & homo sit, non duos tamen, sed unum tantùm CHRISTUM esse, non confusione substantiæ, sed unitate personæ. Hæc thesis firmatur Scripturæ dictis, Ecclesiæ Symbolis, Conciliorum suffragiis, & Patrum testimoniis.

IX. Unionem excipit communicatio, quæ triplex: 1. ὑποστάσεως; ubi notanda 1. Vocis explicatio. Vox enim omnem unius rei participationem connotat. 2. Communicationis personalis assertio. Hanc negant Calviniani: nos affirmamus, & probamus, ὑποστάσεως Christi unitate, ipsâ carnis subsistentiâ, communicationis definitione, absurdi inductione &c. 2. Naturarum, quam veram ac realem esse, cum F. C. art. 8. p. 606. asserimus, idq́; confirmamus, Scripturæ autoritate, analogiæ fidei fundamine, Orthodoxâ antiqvitate. Hæc à personali differt, 1. Ordine, qvô illa hanc antecedit; 2. naturarum habitudine, quæ illic se magis habent passivè, hîc magis activè: Nam illic dicimus, duas naturas uniri: hîc dicuntur invicem communicare. Oriuntur ex hâc naturarum ἑτεροῦ prædicationes, personales dictæ, de quibus judicium fert Theologus, eas rectè reales asserit, inq́ve iis naturam de natura, ùt disparata de disparatis, prædicari ait, paronymicas nec dicendas, nec per ἀναλογίας ad has reducendus, affirmat, ratione unionis mysticas denominat, ab abstractivis, qvia tutiùs, abstinendum svadet, & Christum, qvâ hominem, naturalem DEI filium, minùs significanter, & ambiguè dici existimat. 3. Idiomatum, De hâc in genere notanda 1. Vocis usurpatio. Vocem enim, Communicationis Idiomatum, licet ἄγραφος sit, loqvendi tamen necessitate introductam, ob firmas rationes, qvas petenti dabimus, ad controversias Theologicas explicandas, in scholis retinendam esse censemus. 2. Terminorum, abstracti & concreti, explicatio. Theologis abstractum notat alteram naturam, in unione distinctè consideratam: Concretum verò tantùm personam exprimit. 3. Communicationis Idiom. significatio. Significat enim modum, qvô propria, per distinctas Scripturæ formulas, de Christo dicuntur. 4. Generum determinatio; qvorum 3. cum F. C. agnoscimus 5. Ordinis ratio, quæ nonnullis variatur: sed facilè liticula componitur, distinctione inter ordinem naturæ & doctrinæ; hunc nos observavimus.

X. In specie jam videndum 1. Genus, quod dicitur ἀλλοίωσις, ἀντίδοσις, ἐναλλαγή, καὶ κοινωνία ὀνομάτων, ἐπίζευξις ὀνομάτων, οἰκείωσις. Describitur, quòd in illo de persona prædicentur naturarum propria. Hoc fit dupliciter: Nam vel de persona συνθέτῳ prædicantur alterutrius naturæ propria, divina propter divinitatem, humamana propter humanitatem: vel de persona λόγῳ ἀσυνθέτῳ prædicantur humanitatis assumtæ propria. II. Genus dicitur κοινοποίησις, κοινωνία ἐνεργειῶν, περίφρασις. Describitur, quòd in illo personæ attribuatur certum ἀποτέλεσμα, in qvo producendo utraqve natura agit, cum communicatione alterius. Subjectum in hoc genere est tota persona, de qvâ ἀποτέλεσμα enunciatur aliqvaliter reciprocè. Qværitur hic, an mors pro mundi vita ἀποτέλεσμα sit? Id quod cum Orthodoxis affirmamus.

XI. III. Genus, dicitur majestatis communicatio, ἀποθέωσις θεοποίησις, μεταποίησις &c. quibus non naturæ exæqvatio, sed carnis exaltatio exprimitur. Describitur, quòd in eo de humana natura verè infinita & increata dona τῷ λόγῳ per unionem personalem ipsi communicata, enunciantur. Subjectum est humana natura, qvæ dona â divina accipit. Carni talem communicationem & exaltationem obtigisse, negant Calviniani: Nos pro eâ confirmandâ produximus argumenta 1. generalia, ab inhabitatione universæ plenitudinis divinitatis, Coloss. 2. v. 9. à datis Christo in tempore; à sessione ad dextêram Dei. 2. Specialia, pro demonstratione certorum idiomatum, ut pro Omnipotentia in genere urgèmus dicta Matth. 28. v. 18. Ephes. 1. v. 20. In specie pro δυνάμει ζωοποιητικῇ, Joh. 6. v. 48. & c. 1. Johan. 1. v. 3. pro δυνάμει θαυματουργικῇ, Marc. 16. v. 19. 20. Actor. 2. v. 33. c. 10. v. 38. pro δυνάμει remittendi peccata, Matth. 9. v. 6. pro δυνάμει δικαστικῇ, Joh. 5. v. 27. Pro omniscientia, Esa. 11. v. 1. Joh. 3. v. 34. Col. 2. v. 3. Pro præsentia gratiosa afferimus dicta, Matth. 28. v. 20. Marc. 16. v. 20. Joh. 6. v. 56. argumenta, â natura capitis, ab institutione cœnæ, â regula Patrum, quòd officia mediatoris utriqve naturæ conveniant. Pro præsentia totius Christi universali, qvæ notat præsens dominium in omnes creaturas in cœlo & terra, confirmandâ, producimus itidem dicta Psal. 71. v. 8. Psal. 110. v. 2. Eph. 1. v. 20. 21. argumenta analogiæ fidei consentanea, nimirum ab unione personali, ab ὑποστάσεως τῇ λόγῳ communicatione, ab humanæ naturæ ad Dei dexteram evectione. Pro cultu religiosæ adorationis Joh. 5. v. 22. 23. Phil. 2. v. 9. & s. Apoc. 5. v. 13. Hactenus persona Christi.


### Of Life

OF LIFE.

XII. As regards life, we shall consider it in two states of the covenant; of which the one is called the Exinanition, the other the Exaltation: both shadowed forth in the Old Testament through Moses, Joseph, and Zechariah; explained in the New Testament, Phil. 2:6, etc. The subject of these states is Christ, the incarnate Logos: not according to both, nor the divine, but the human nature alone. Now, Exinanition is humble obedience and subjection in the form of a servant even unto the death of the cross, Philip. 2:5. In which definition two acts are expressed: 1. The κένωσις of divine glory, which does not signify a deprivation of the possession of majesty, but of its use, which theologians are accustomed to declare by the example of the sun covered by a cloud, or a king who is a minor: 2. The ταπείνωσις or most humble subjection in the form of a servant: Here it must be explained, what is the form of a servant? namely, not the human nature itself, but the servile state and condition of the human nature, the defects and affections of our infirmity, sin however excepted. Then, what is humble subjection? Namely, the obedience rendered by Christ to the Father in acting and suffering.

XIII. To this exinanition belongs the whole history of the Gospel from the nativity to the burial inclusively, which we shall briefly narrate. We premise his nativity, concerning which must be weighed: 1. The birth of Christ, which the genealogy described by Matthew and Luke sets forth, which indicates that Christ was sprung from the tribe of Judah, the family of David, and that in respect to both parents, as well the putative as the true. 2. The Mother of Christ, whose name is Mary, which denotes the bitterness of sorrows. Her person is explained by the consideration of: 1. Her state, that she was a Virgin, because of the prediction of Isaiah ch. 7:14, and remained so in and after birth, as is piously believed; espoused to Joseph, Matt. 1:18, for reasons concerning which consult the Fathers. 2. Her family, that she was sprung from the tribe of Judah, from the house of David, 2 Sam. 7:12. 3. Her titles, of which some are Biblical, κεχαριτωμένη, εὐλογημένη, not actively, but passively: Some are Ecclesiastical, as when she is called, holy Virgin, etc. 4. Her dignity, for which she is deservedly venerated and honored, but wrongly religiously adored. 3. Christ's birth itself, for the unfolding of which 1. Circumstance; time, which is noted in Luke 1, v. 5, chapter 2, verse 1. Place, which is called Bethlehem of Judea, Luke 2, v. 4. 2. Matter, namely the Person being born, who is God-man; God not without humanity, man not without deity: Mode, which is twofold: Interior, concerning which it is asked, Did Mary give birth with the womb closed, or opened? Resp. We acknowledge that CHRIST was born from the womb, because we read it; we are ignorant of the mode, because we do not read it: but we incline more to the affirmation of the former. Exterior, voluntary poverty. End, which redounds to us: for to us the angels announce great joy.

XIV. There follows the circumcision of Christ; where one must inquire into 1. The reason for the circumcision: for CHRIST, by reason of Himself, did not need circumcision; yet for our sake He willed to be circumcised. 2. The imposition of the name: For while He received the sacrament of circumcision in the flesh, the name, and that by a certain reason new, Iesus is added. Soon after the circumcision CHRIST is visited by the Magi, arising from the east, is adored, and is honored with gifts, as can be seen in Matthew ch. 2, v. 1. A little later He is presented to the Lord in the Jerusalem temple by His Mother and Joseph, according to the Law in Ex. 13, v. 2, and 15, and is received in the arms by Simeon, son of Jonathas, teacher of Gamaliel, a just man. Where at the same time Mary underwent the days of purification, and offered a pair of turtledoves, as the law so willed. To the presentation Matthew subjoins the tyrannical persecution of Herod, on account of which Christ was forced to flee. He also explains the circumstances of the flight, which are twofold, 1. Of the persons, of whom there are three; the Angel persuading the flight; Joseph receiving the command; the newly born Boy, escaping by flight. 2. Of the things, namely the Time of the flight: for it was accomplished with a few weeks having intervened between the birth and the flight, on the same night that Joseph received the command. Place: He flees, from Bethlehem, (as is probable) through that desert through which the sons of Israel entered Palestine, into Egypt, where He remained for a year, and if anything more passes.

XV. The Evangelist also makes mention of the education of Christ, in which must be observed 1. the leading to God, concerning which Luke treats in ch. 2, verse 41. 2. the instruction in honesty, the effect of which is expressed in verse 52. προέκοπτε σοφίᾳ &c. which words denote the progress of wisdom, both finite, which grew habitually, and infinite, which grew effectually. He adds the deeds performed, because in his 12th year he disputed in the temple v. 46, because he was obedient and subject to his parents. XVI. Finally, Christ, about to undertake his ministry, willed to be inaugurated into it through baptism. The circumstances of this to be noted are: 1. Time, which falls at the beginning of December or the end of November, which notation of time indicates the 30th year of Christ's age about to be completed shortly. Place, which is the Jordan at Bethabara. 2. Ministerial cause, which is that of John the Baptist. 3. Manner; for the Lord was dipped by a servant in the flowing water of the Jordan. Regarding the manner, because Scripture is silent, we do not know more. 4. Miracles following the baptism: the opening and spreading of the heavens; the visible appearance of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove; the Father's discourse to the Son. 5. The end of the baptism is the consecration of our baptism as a salutary instrument of renewal. XVII. Scarcely consecrated to his ministry, he suffers fasting and is received by the temptations of Satan. For after the baptism was completed, he was led away by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the Devil: therein he abstained from all food for 40 days, not without divine power. Finally, hungering, he underwent the temptations of the Devil, both hidden and manifest, which Matthew enumerates in chapter 4, verse 3, etc. The temptation having been overcome, he presided over his ministry for three years and a little more, by teaching, by remitting sins, and by confirming his doctrine with miracles, to which the flesh of Christ did not merely hold itself as an ὄργανον of divinity in Christ, but as ἐνυπόςατον καὶ ἐνεργητικόν. XIIX. Finally, his emptying is most especially seen in his passion, which is reduced to 4 acts, such that to the 1st are referred those things which happened in the garden; to the 2nd, those which were carried out in the council of the Priests before Caiaphas; to the 3rd, those which CHRIST suffered in the praetorium of Pilate; to the 4th, finally, the passion and those things to be noted concerning it are reduced. The subject of the passion is the whole person, according to both natures. The end is a sufficient satisfaction for the sins of all men in the universe, and liberation from the curse of the law, the devil, and hell. XIX. Death follows the passion, the truth of which is to be proven, which the definition of death proves, and the Centurion confirms, etc. While Christ is said to have died, we do not indeed deny that he ceased to be a man for a very brief time; nevertheless, we do not establish that the dissolution of the personal union occurred on that account, much less that the divinity of CHRIST we deny. 2. The consequences are to be noted, which are miracles, namely: the unnatural eclipse of the sun, the rending of the veil, the earthquake, the splitting of the rocks, the opening of the tombs, the resurrection of the dead, etc.

XX. The dead are accustomed to be buried, which also happened to Christ. 1. The author of the burial was Joseph, originating from Arimathea. 2. This was the act: for they washed the body, anointed it with spices, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, and bound the head with a napkin. 3. The time, both of the burial, which is determined by the Evangelist as the day of preparation; and of the rest, which is the three days; for in the sepulcher he did not see corruption. 4. The place was a garden near Mount Golgotha, and a new tomb. 5. The end is the fulfillment of the prophecies.

XXI. We have seen Christ humbling himself extremely: there follows the Exaltation, which is the solemn and plenary usurpation of the majesty communicated at the first moment of his birth. Its 5 degrees are: 1. The descent into hell, concerning which it must be known: 1. that it is an article of faith, the foundations of which are held to be illustrious in the scriptures; 2. that it is real, Eph. 4, verse 9, 1 Pet. 3, v. 19; 3. that the whole Christ descended; 4. that he descended after the ζωοπόιησιν, yet before the ἀνάστασιν, to the lower parts of the earth. 2. The Resurrection, the truth of which must be examined; the time, which is the third day; the cause, the whole Trinity; distinctly, the Father, the Son, and he as regards his divinity; the subject, the body of Christ, true, the same in number, and endowed with qualities; the form, which is the reunion of body and soul, the penetration of the sepulchral stone; the end, the fulfillment of the prophecies, the resurrection of the members of Christ. 3. The Ascension, which is the true elevation of the body, on the 40th day from the resurrection, upward from the Mount of Olives. Where is expressed: the term from which, the Mount of Olives; the manner, which is a visible elevation; the term to which, the heaven ὑψηλότερον, which is not a place, but the majesty and excellence of God; the fruit, by reason of Christ, enthronement into glory; by reason of us, the opening of heaven. 4. The sitting at the right hand of God, by which with equal power and equal majesty, he governs all things powerfully and presently in heaven and on earth with God the Father. For the right hand of God here denotes the power of God, his majesty. To sit is to reign forever. 5. The return for judgment. Many sayings of Scripture prove its truth; Matthew ch. 24, v. 30 indicates its quality; Luke Acts 1, v. 11 and Paul 2 Thess. 1, v. 7 determine the term from which. The time is hidden. Thus far the life.

Latin:

DE VITA.

XII. Vitam quod attinet, eam in duobus Statibus συνθήκην considerabimus; quorum alter Exinanitionis, alter Exaltationis dicitur: uterque in Vet. Testam. adumbratus per Moysen, Josephum, Zachariam: in Nov. Test. explicatus, Phil. 2. vers: 6. & s. Subjectum horum statuum est Christus, Λόγος incarnatus: non secundùm utramque, nec divinam, sed solam humanam naturam. Est autem Exinanitio humilis in formâ servili ad mortem usque crucis obedientia & subjectio, Philip. 2. v. 5. In qua definitione duo exprimuntur actus: 1. Gloriæ divinæ κένωσις, quæ non significat στέρησιν κτήσεως majestatis, sed χρήσεως, quam Theologi exemplô solis nube obducti, Regis minorennis, declarare soliti sunt: 2. ταπείνωσις seu Humillima in forma servi subjectio: Hic explicandum, quid sit forma servi? scilicet non ipsa humana natura, sed naturæ humanæ servilis status & conditio, defectus & affectus nostræ infirmitatis, peccatô tamen exceptô. Deinde, quid sit humilis subjectio? scilicet Patri â Christo præstita obedientia in agendo & patiendo.

XIII. Ad hanc exinanitionem pertinet tota historia Evangel. â nativitate ad sepulturam usque inclusivè, quam breviter enarrabimus. Præmittimus ejus nativitatem, circa quam expendenda sunt 1. Christi ortus, quem exponit Genealogia, â Matthæo & Luca descripta, quæ Christum ex tribu Juda, familiâ Davidis oriundum indicat, idque respectu utriusque parentis, tam putatitii, quàm veri. 2. Christi Mater, cujus nomen est Maria, quod notat dolorum acerbitatem. Persona ejus explicatur consideratione 1. statûs, quòd fuerit Virgo, ob prædictionem Esa. cap. 7. v. 14. & mansit in & post partum, ut piè creditur; desponsata Josepho, Matth. 1. v. 18. ob causas, de quibus Patres consule. 2. Familiæ, quòd orta fuerit de tribu Juda, è domo Davidis, 2. Sam. 7. v. 12. 3. Titulorum, quorum quidam Biblici, κεχαριτωμένη, εὐλογημένη, non activè, sed passivè: Quidam Ecclesiastici, ut cùm dicitur, Virgo sancta &c. 4. Dignitatis, ob quam meritò veneratur & honoratur, sed malè religiosè adoratur. 3. Christi nativitas ipsa, cujus evolendæ 1. Circumstantia; tempus, quod notatur Luc. 1. v. 5. cap. 2. verf. 1. Locus, qui vocatur Bethlehem Judæ, Luc. 2. v. 4. 2. Res, nim. Persona nascens, quæ est homo Deus; Deus non sine humanitate, homo non sine deitate: Modus, qui duplex: Interior, de quo quæritur, An Maria peperit utero clauso, an aperto? Resp. CHRISTUM ex utero natum esse agnoscimus, quia legimus; modum ignoramus, quia non legimus: sed magis tamen ad prioris affirmationem inclinamus. Exterior, spontanea paupertas. Finis, qui in nos redundat: nobis enim angeli annunciant gaudium magnum.

XIV. Succedit Christi circumcisio; ubi inqvirenda est 1. Circumcisionis ratio: CHRISTUS enim ratione sui circumcisione non indiguit; nostri tamen causâ circumcidi voluit. 2. Nominis impositio: Dum enim circumcisionis sacramentum in carne recepit, nomen, idq́; certâ ratione novum, Inoys accedit. Mox post circumcisionem CHRISTUS â Magis, ab oriente oriundis, visitatur, adoratur, & muneribus honoratur, ut videre est apud Matth. c. 2. v. 1. Paulò post Domino in templo Hierosolymitano â Matre & Josepho presentatur, juxta Legem Exc. 13. v. 2. & 15. â Simeone, filio Jonathæ, præceptore Gamalielis, viro justo, ulnis excipitur. Ubi unà Maria purificationis dies sustinuit, & par turturum, lege ita volente, obtulit. Præsentationi Matthæus subjungit tyrannicam Herodis persecutionem, ob quam Christus fugere coactus fuit. Explicat etiam fugæ circumstantias, quæ duplices, 1. Personarum, qvarum tres sunt; Angelus fugam svadens; Josephus mandatum accipiens; Puer recens natus, fugâ evadens. 2. Rerum, nimirum Tempus fugæ: est enim paucis inter nativitatem & fugam septimanis interjectis peracta, eâdem nocte, quâ Josephus mandatum accipit. Locus: Fugit, ex Bethlehem, (ut probabile est) per desertum illud, per quod filii Israel Palæstinam ingressi sunt, in Ægyptum, ubi per annum, & siquid excurrit, mansit.

XV. Mentionem qvoqve facit Evangelista educationis Christi, in quâ spectanda 1. ad Deum adductio, de quâ agit Lucas c. 2. verf. 41. 2. ad honestatem informatio, cujus effectus exprimitur verf. 52. προέκοπτε σοφίᾳ &c. quæ verba profectum notant sapientiæ tùm finitæ, quæ crevit habitualiter, tùm infinitæ, quæ crevit effectualiter. Addit res gestas, quòd anno 12. disputaverit in templo v. 46. quòd obediens fuerit, & subjectus parentibus. XVI. Tandem Christus aggressurus ministerium suum, per baptismum eidem inaugurari voluit. Hujus annotandæ 1. circumstantiæ: Tempus, quod incidit ad principium Decembris, vel finem Novembris, quæ notatio temporis Christi annum ætatis 30. brevi complendum, indicat. Locus, qui Jordanis in Bethabara. 2. Causa ministralis, quæ Johannis Baptistæ. 3. Modus; Tinctus enim est Dominus â servo, aqvâ Jordanis præterfluente. Plura de modô, quia Scriptura tacet, nos nescimus. 4. Miracula, baptismum insecuta: Cœli apertio & diffusio; visibilis Spiritûs Sancti in specie columbæ apparitio; Patris ad filium sermocinatio. 5. Finis baptismi est nostri baptismi in salutare organon renovationis consecratio. XVII. Vix ministerio consecratus, inediam patitur, & Sathanæ tentationibus excipitur. Nam peractô Baptismo, in desertum â spiritu subducitur, ut tentaretur à Diabolo: inibi ab omni abstinuit per 40. dies cibô, non sine divinâ virtute. Tandem esuriens, Diaboli subiit tentationes, & occultas, & manifestas, qvas enumerat Matth. cap. 4. vers. 3. &c. Superatâ tentatione, ministerio per triennium, & quod excurrit, præfuit, docendo, peccata remittendo, doctrinam miraculis confirmando, ad quæ caro Christi se non tantùm habuit ut ὄργανον divinitatis in Christo, sed ἐνυπόςατον καὶ ἐνεργητικόν. XIIX. Maximè deniqve exinanitio in passione ejus conspicitur, quæ ad 4. actus reducitur, ita, ut ad 1. referantur ea, quæ in horto contigerunt; ad 2. quæ in concilio Sacerdotum coram Caipha peracta sunt: ad 3. quæ CHRISTUS in prætorio Pilati passus est: ad 4. deniqve passio, & quæ circa eam notanda, reducitur. Subjectum passionis est tota persona, secundùm utramqve naturam. Finis est, pro peccatis omnium in universum hominum sufficiens satisfactio, à maledictione legis, diaboli, & inferni, liberatio. XIX. Passionem excipit mors, cujus 1. probanda veritas, quam probat mortis definitio, confirmat Centurio &c. Mortuus dum Christus dicitur, hominem eum esse desiisse ad tempus perbreve, non qvidem negamus; tamen propterea factam esse unionis personalis solutionem, non statuimus, multò minùs CHRISTO divinitatem denegamus. 2. notanda confequentia, quæ sunt miracula, nim. Solis ecclipsis non naturalis, Veli scissio, Terræ motus, Petrarum scissio, Monumentorum apertio, Mortuorum resurrectio,&c.

XX. Mortui sepeliri consuevêre, quod & Christo accidit. Sepulturæ 1. autor fuit Josephus, ab Arimathæa oriundus. 2. actus hic est: Corpus enim ablutum aromatibus unxerunt,sindoni mundæ implicârunt, & caput sudario involverunt. 3. Tempus, tùm sepulturæ, quod determinatur ab Evangelista, dies parasceves: tùm quietis, quod triduum; In sepulchro enim corruptionem non vidit. 4. Locus, fuit hortus monti Golgathæ vicinus, & monumentum novum. 5. Finis est vaticiniorum impletio.

XXI. Vidimus Christum extremè sese humiliantem: sequitur Exaltatio, quæ est solemnis & plenaria majestatis in primo nativitatis momento communicatæ usurpatio. Gradus ejus 5. sunt, 1. Decensus ad inferos, de qvo sciendum, 1. quòd sit articulus fidei, cujus fundamenta in sacris illustria habentur; 2. quòd sit realis, Ephes. 4. vers. 9. 1. Petr. 3. v. 19. 3. quòd totus Christus descenderit; 4. quòd post ζωοπόιησιν, ante tamen ἀνάστασιν descenderit, ad inferiores terræ partes. 2. Resurrectio, cujus dispicienda veritas; Tempus, qvod dies tertius; Causa, tota Trinitas; distinctim, Pater, Filius, isqve qvoad divinitatem; Subjectum, corpus Christi, verum, idem numero, & qvalltatibus ditatum; Forma, quæ corporis & animæ reunio, lapidis sepulchralis penetratio; Einis, vaticiniorum impletio, membrorum Christi resurrectio. 3. Ascensio, quæ est vera corporis, die 40. à resurrectione, è monte oliveti sursum versus elevatio. Ubi exprimitur, terminus â qvo mons oliveti; modus, qui est visibilis elevatio; terminus ad quem, cœlum ὑψηλότερον, qvod non est locus, sed Dei majestas & excellentia; Fructus ratione Christi, in gloriam inthronisatio; ratione nostri, cœli apertio. 4. Ad dexteram Dei sessio, quâ pari potentiâ & æqvali majestate, cum Deo patre omnia potenter & præsenter in cœlo & terra gubernat. Dextera enim Dei hîc notat potentiam Dei, majestatem. Sedere, est regnare in æternum. 5. Reditus ad judicium. Hujus veritatem probant plurima Scripturæ dicta; qualitatem Matthæus c. 24. v.30 indicat; Terminum â qvo determinat Lucas Actor. 1. v. 11. Paulus 2. Thess. 1. v. 7. Tempus absconditum est. Hûc usque vita.


### On the Office

ON THE OFFICE.

XXII. There now remains to be briefly subjoined the knowledge of the office, without which the mere knowledge of the person and life profits men nothing for salvation. It is considered 1. Generally. Where the efficient cause is to be noted, which is the whole Trinity, but κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν [pre-eminently] God the Father. The matter in which or subject, which is the whole Christ according to both natures: concerning which are all men, as Scripture proves. The final cause is the glory of God, the illustration of divine mercy and justice, likewise redemption, and our salvation.

XXIII. Then specifically, and 1. The Prophetic [office], by which he informs us of the will of the Father, and the way to eternal salvation. In respect of this office he is called the supreme Prophet, Counselor, Teacher, etc. There are two parts: 1. The external promulgation of doctrine, which contains the preaching of the Gospel, which is not new; the interpretation of the Law, not its augmentation, and the prediction of miracles. 2. The internal efficacy, by which the faithful are moved so that they may grasp with the mind and retain in the heart what is taught. He executed this office immediately, and mediately through ministers.

XXIV. 2. The Priestly [office], by which he was ordained to make satisfaction to God for men. In respect of this he is called the great High Priest, Mediator of the New Testament, Savior, etc. Concerning this office must be considered 1. The calling of the person, which divine testimony, the voluntary emptying of Christ, and the comparison of the person of Christ and Melchizedek prove. 2. The execution of the office, which is completed in three parts; 1. The perfect fulfillment of the Law, for which the righteousness of both the person and the work was required: Christ had both, not for himself only, but also for us: for himself insofar as he was man, for us, insofar as he was man for us. 2. Plenary satisfaction, which was accomplished on the altar of the cross, and is meritorious, universal, and alone sufficient. 3. Intercession, by which he applies to us the merits obtained.

XXV. 3. The Kingly [office], by which he himself, the God-man, governs all things in heaven and on earth, but especially the Church. By reason of this he is called King, Leader, Prince, etc. This office is considered in the mode of administration, and its limit. The administration is not done by external and corporal force, but by the power of the Spirit, i.e., by the Word and Sacraments; and it respects the present life and the future: By reason of the present life it is called the kingdom, 1. of power, which is the general dominion over all things, 2. of grace, which is the special operation of mercy and goodness in the Church. This he administers, laws by prescribing to subjects, by defending the same from enemies, by adorning them with rewards. In respect of the future life, it is called the kingdom of justice and glory, which will be seen in the resurrection of the dead, and the judgment both of the wicked to damnation, and of the pious to blessedness. The end of the kingdom with respect to the οἰκονομία will be, when the Son is about to deliver the kingdom to the Father, he will be subjected to Him, who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all, blessed for ever, Amen.

Latin:

DE OFFICIO.

XXII. Subjungenda jam restat breviter officii cognitio sine quâ nuda cognitio personæ & vitæ ad salutem hominib9 nihil prodest. Consideratur 1.Generatim. Ubi notanda Causa efficiens, quæ est tota Trinitas, sed κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν Deus Pater. Materia in quâ seu subjectum, quod totus Christus secundùm utramq; naturam: circa quam, sunt omnes homines, probante Scripturâ. Finalis est Dei gloria, misericordiæ & justitiæ divinæ illustratio, item redemptio, & nostra salus.

XXIII. Deinde speciatim, & 1. Propheticum, quo nos de voluntate Patris, & viâ ad salutem æternam informat. Hujus officii respectu dicitur summus Propheta, Consiliarius, Magister &c. Partes duæ sunt: 1. Externa doctrinæ promulgatio, quæ continet Evangelii prædicationem, quæ nova non est; Legis interpretationem, non auctionem, & miraculorum prædictionem. 2. Interna efficacia, quâ moventur fideles, ut capiant mente, & corde retineant, quæ docentur. Executus est hoc officium, immediatè, & mediatè per ministros.

XXIV. 2. Sacerdotale, quô ordinatus est ad satisfaciendum Deo, pro hominibus. Hujus respectu dicitur Pontifex magnus, Mediator Nov. Test. Salvator &c. Circa hoc officium consideranda veniunt 1. Personæ vocatio, quam probant divina testificatio, voluntaria Christi exinanitio, personæ Christi & Melchisedeci comparatio. 2. Officii executio, quæ tribus absolvitur partibus; 1. Legis perfectâ impletione, ad quam reqvirebatur justitia & personæ & operis: utramqve Christus habuit, non sibi tantùm, sed & nobis: sibi qvatenus homo, nobis, qvatenus homo pro nobis. 2. Plenariâ satisfactione, quæ peracta est in ara crucis, & est meritoria, universalis, & sola sufficiens. 3. Intercessione, quâ nobis parta merita applicat.

XXV. 3. Regium, quô ipse θεάνθρωπος, gubernat omnia in cœlo & terra, imprimis verò Ecclesiam. Hujus ratione dicitur Rex, Dux, Princeps &c. Consideratur hoc officium in administrationis modo, & illius termino. Administratio non fit vi externâ & corporali, sed virtute spiritûs h. e. verbô & Sacramentis; & respicit vitam præsentem, & futuram: Ratione præsentis vitæ dicitur regnum, 1. potentiæ, qvod est generale dominium super omnia, 2. gratiæ, qvod est specialis operatio misericordiæ, & bonitatis in Ecclesia. Hoc administrat, leges subditis præscribendo, eosdem ab hostibus defendendo, præmiis ornando. Ratione futuræ vitæ, dicitur regnum justitiæ & gloriæ, quod conspicietur in suscitatione mortuorum, & judicatione tùm impiorum ad damnationem, tùm piorum ad beatitudinem. Terminus regni respectu οἰκονομίας erit, cùm filius regnum Patri traditurus, ei subjicietur, qui ei omnia subjecit, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus, benedictus in secula, Amen.


### The End

THE END.

Latin:

FINIS.
